raw_record.support_text: Erlotinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor approved for non-small-cell lung cancer and pancreatic cancer, was reported to cause fulminant hepatic failure. The paper describes a patient with stage IV non-small-cell lung cancer who died of fulminant hepatic failure as a result of treatment with erlotinib.
raw_record.extra_details: A 67-year-old Caucasian female with stage IV non-small-cell lung cancer and an EGFR L858R mutation received erlotinib 150 mg/day orally as part of a phase II trial. After mild liver test elevation (ALT 80 U/L at 2 weeks), erlotinib was stopped and restarted at 100 mg/day; 10 days after restart she developed anorexia with painless jaundice and was hospitalized. Peak ALT 2210-2171 U/L, AST 1888 U/L, total bilirubin up to 28.7 mg/dL, INR up to 9.5. A liver biopsy was performed on 05-05-2006. The patient died on 05-13-2006 of fulminant hepatic failure attributed to erlotinib. Report notes erlotinib liver toxicity is usually mild to moderate and that two large NSCLC trials (731 and 1059 patients) reported no hepatotoxicity; overall trial experience did not report severe systemic toxicity before this case.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report three cases of severe hepatic impairment which was caused by erlotinib in patients with non-small cell lung cancer. They note that the majority of erlotinib hepatotoxicity presents as mild or moderate hepatic dysfunction and that severe hepatic impairment has been documented rarely.
raw_record.extra_details: Three cases of severe hepatic impairment attributed to erlotinib in patients with locally advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer after failure of at least one standard chemotherapy regimen; reported although severe hepatic impairment is rarely documented, with the majority of hepatotoxicity being mild or moderate. Most common adverse reactions are acneiform rash and diarrhea. Erlotinib is an oral quinazoline-based EGFR/HER1 tyrosine kinase inhibitor approved by the FDA in 2004.

raw_record.support_text: In case 1, both gefitinib and erlotinib were administered, and grade 3 hepatotoxicity occurred even though the therapeutic effects were evident. The case table records Hepatotoxicity (grade 3)/Case 1, attributing the injury to erlotinib along with gefitinib.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1, a 73-year-old EGFR mutation-positive (L858R) postoperative NSCLC patient, developed grade 3 hepatotoxicity during erlotinib therapy (given 2nd line after gefitinib) requiring treatment switch. In cases 2 and 3 erlotinib was not administered; the authors speculated erlotinib might not cause severe hepatotoxicity but presented no such negative data. Erlotinib is metabolized in the liver by CYP enzymes such as CYP3A4 with >80% of dose in feces; CYP2D6 polymorphisms are associated with gefitinib- and/or erlotinib-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A 77-year-old man with stage IIIB lung adenocarcinoma developed drug-related acute hepatitis complicated by renal deterioration (aspartate aminotransferase 1400 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 1299 U/L, creatinine 4.4 mg/dL) 12 days after starting erlotinib 100 mg/day. Viral causes and liver metastases were excluded, and Roussel-Uclaf causality assessment classified the erlotinib-related hepatitis as probable. Fatal lactic acidosis caused death 2 hours after admission. The authors report this as the second case of fatal erlotinib-induced liver toxicity in a lung cancer patient, noting the previous case died after about 11 days from fulminant hepatitis.

raw_record.extra_details: Dose 100 mg/day; onset of hepatitis 12 days after erlotinib initiation; AST 1400 U/L, ALT 1299 U/L, creatinine 4.4 mg/dL, urea nitrogen 55 mg/dL; RUCAM causality score classified as probable; viral hepatitis and liver metastases excluded; fatal lactic acidosis within 2 hours of admission; discussion attributes lactic acidosis to erlotinib-related hepatitis with initial liver failure plus metformin-induced lactate production and metformin accumulation from acute renal deterioration; authors note this is the second fatal erlotinib liver toxicity case in a lung cancer patient (prior case died ~11 days from fulminant hepatitis).

raw_record.support_text: A 77-year-old man with stage IIIB pulmonary adenocarcinoma received 100 mg daily erlotinib (an epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor) after chemo- and radiotherapy failed. Twelve days after starting erlotinib he developed acute drug-related hepatitis complicated by renal deterioration (aspartate aminotransferase 1400 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 1299 U/L, creatinine 4.4 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 55 mg/dL). Viral causes of hepatitis were excluded and CT ruled out hepatic metastasis; by the Roussel-Uclaf causality assessment the erlotinib-related hepatitis was classified as 'probable'. The English-language discussion further states that in this patient renal function suddenly worsened as a consequence of acute liver failure, causing metformin accumulation and ensuing fatal lactic acidosis, with the patient dying two hours after admission.

raw_record.support_text: The study concerns PM-DILI, i.e., drug-induced liver injury caused by phenylmethanesulfonamide (PM), distinguishing PM-DILI-susceptible individuals from PM-tolerant subjects using cytokine biomarkers. PM-DILI patients were sampled at injury stage and at recovery stage, confirming PM as a human hepatotoxic agent in this cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: Referred to as PM-DILI throughout. Six susceptibility-related cytokines (CCL2, CCL11, CXCL10, CX3CL1, TNF-α, VEGF) were candidate biomarkers distinguishing PM-DILI-susceptible from PM-tolerant subjects; four cytokines (CXCL1, EGF, IFN-γ, IL-10) differed between injury and recovery stages. Prediction models built from pilot and replication studies: single-cytokine TNF-α (OR 19.0) and CCL2/MCP-1 (OR 15.4); tri-cytokine '(TNF-α and CCL2) or VEGF' had OR 105.0 with 95.3% positive prediction rate.

raw_record.support_text: The authors attribute the liver injury to valsartan based on the chronological relationship between drug administration and the adverse effect, the absence of other potential causes of liver disease (other drugs, alcohol, prior chronic hepatopathy, hepatotropic viruses, bile duct obstruction), and the rapidly progressive improvement after drug withdrawal. They report that no other case of valsartan-associated hepatotoxicity was found in MEDLINE 1998-2001.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of acute hepatitis of probable drug origin in a patient on valsartan; valsartan was stopped on suspicion and evolution was favorable with progressive normalization of liver tests. Liver biopsy showed irregular inflammatory infiltrate with lymphocytes, eosinophils and polymorphonuclear cells, focal hepatocyte necrosis, feathery hepatocyte degeneration and some canalicular bile thrombus. At discharge (one month later) bilirubin was 4 mg/dl and transaminases had normalized; enzymatic normalization confirmed at two months. Case was reported to the Servicio Nacional de Farmacovigilancia. Etiologies excluded included hepatitis viral PCR, CMV, EBV and HSV serology, and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (normal biliary tract). No prior valsartan hepatotoxicity case found in the reviewed literature.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that to their knowledge 18 cases of angiotensin receptor blocker causing liver injury have been reported, of which three cases were due to valsartan use, listed in Table 3.
raw_record.extra_details: Three reported human cases of liver injury attributed to valsartan (doses 80 mg or not specified, latency 2 weeks-5 months; AST 360-1,292 IU/L, ALT 776-1,664 IU/L); one case had liver biopsy; no re-exposure reported. Overall in the 18-case series hepatocellular injury was most common with cholestatic and mixed patterns also observed; no causality score or liver failure/transplant/death reported for these prior cases.

raw_record.support_text: A 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes treated with gliclazide and valsartan 80 mg/day for 5 months developed progressive jaundice over 2 weeks with generalized pruritus. Liver tests showed AST 738 U/l, ALT 1664 U/l, GGT 352 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 385 U/l and total bilirubin 23.6 mg/dl (direct fraction); viral, autoimmune and metabolic studies were negative and a liver biopsy was reported as acute hepatitis of probable drug origin. Valsartan was withdrawn on the suspicion of drug-induced hepatitis, with progressive normalization of liver tests and complete enzymatic recovery two months after admission. The case was reported to the national pharmacovigilance service.
raw_record.extra_details: Valsartan 80 mg/day taken for 5 months for hypertension; biopsy showed acute hepatitis of probable drug nature with irregular lymphocytic, eosinophilic and polymorphonuclear infiltrate, focal hepatocyte necrosis, feathery degeneration and a canalicular bile thrombus; R-ratio-compatible markedly elevated transaminases with total bilirubin 23.6 mg/dl; dechallenge led to progressive normalization, bilirubin 4 mg/dl at hospital discharge (one month) and full enzyme normalization at two months. Case reported to the national pharmacovigilance service.

raw_record.support_text: In a multicenter, double-blind, parallel-group trial of donepezil (1, 3 or 5 mg/day) versus placebo in 161 patients with mild to moderately severe Alzheimer's disease, the paper explicitly states that donepezil was not associated with any hepatotoxicity, in contrast to acridine-based cholinesterase inhibitors. Donepezil had no clinically significant effect on vital signs, haematology or clinical biochemistry tests.
raw_record.extra_details: Clinical trial context: 161 patients (55-85 years), once-daily donepezil 1, 3 or 5 mg or placebo for 12 weeks, followed by 2-week single-blind placebo washout; 141 completed treatment. The negative hepatotoxicity conclusion contrasts donepezil with acridine-based cholinesterase inhibitors, which the paper presents as having an observed association with hepatotoxicity (not a named agent, so not extracted).

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes E2020 (donepezil) and notes it is a selective acetylcholinesterase inhibitor not associated with liver toxicity in man. It states that in a recently disclosed 24-week phase III clinical trial with E2020 at doses of 5 and 10 mg in patients with Alzheimer's disease, improvements in cognition and global function were seen, and importantly, hepatotoxicity was not observed with this agent.
raw_record.extra_details: 24-week phase III trial at 5 and 10 mg doses in Alzheimer's disease patients; hepatotoxicity not observed; E2020 also described in the abstract as not associated with liver toxicity in man.

raw_record.support_text: In this phase II dose-ranging study of donepezil in patients with Alzheimer's disease, the drug at 5 mg/day was reported to be well tolerated, with no evidence of hepatotoxicity observed.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II dose-ranging study of donepezil in Alzheimer's disease patients, 5 mg/day dose; tolerability conclusion stated as 'no evidence of hepatotoxicity'; the paper's explicit conclusion does not support a human DILI relationship.

raw_record.support_text: In an open-label extension study of 133 patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease receiving donepezil (up to 10 mg/day) for up to 98 weeks, donepezil was well tolerated with no evidence of hepatotoxicity reported in the safety analysis.
raw_record.extra_details: Open-label extension study of 133 Alzheimer's disease patients (mild to moderate) who completed a previous 14-week double-blind placebo-controlled trial; donepezil up to 10 mg/day; interim analysis at 98 weeks; safety monitored by physical examinations, laboratory tests and vital sign measurements.

raw_record.support_text: In a phase 2 clinical trial, 5 mg of donepezil hydrochloride improved cognitive and global function in patients with mild to moderately severe Alzheimer's disease, and these benefits were obtained without peripheral cholinergic adverse events, laboratory test abnormalities, or hepatotoxic effects. This is an explicit statement that no hepatotoxicity occurred with therapeutic donepezil use.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase 2 clinical trial in patients with mild to moderately severe Alzheimer's disease; 5 mg donepezil hydrochloride improved cognitive and global function without laboratory test abnormalities or hepatotoxic effects. Donepezil is the piperidine-based cholinesterase inhibitor Aricept (E2020), well absorbed with ~100% oral bioavailability, peak plasma concentrations 3-4 h, elimination half-life ~70 h.

raw_record.support_text: In a case of pulmonary tuberculosis, treatment with ethionamide 1 g daily alone was started, and the next day the patient developed nausea, anorexia and malaise which persisted. On 22.3.62 liver function tests showed bilirubin 1.5 mg/100 ml, thymol turbidity 9 units/ml, and alkaline phosphatase 22 K.A. units. Ethionamide was stopped and treatment changed to isoniazid and PAS; symptoms disappeared and liver function tests returned to normal. The discussion notes that in this patient rechallenge with ethionamide after recovery from jaundice produced nausea, anorexia and malaise and renewed disturbance of liver function tests.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients being treated for pulmonary tuberculosis; one patient (Case III) also received isoniazid concurrently. In Case II ethionamide was given alone and rechallenge reproduced symptoms and liver function disturbance.
raw_record.extra_details: Three cases were reported. In Case II ethionamide alone produced nausea, anorexia and malaise with abnormal liver function tests (bilirubin 1.5 mg/100 ml, thymol turbidity 9 units/ml, alkaline phosphatase 22 K.A. units) within days; symptoms and LFTs resolved after stopping. In Case III (also on isoniazid) jaundice was noted with abnormal LFTs (bilirubin 5.8 mg/100 ml, thymol turbidity 6 units/ml, alkaline phosphatase 22.8 K.A. units) and urine showing bile and excess urobilin/urobilinogen; jaundice resolved within a month and LFTs normalized within six weeks after stopping drugs. Discussion: no other cases of jaundice occurred in the hospital except in patients receiving ethionamide; rechallenge in Case II and in previously reported cases (Rist; Moulding and Goldstein) produced recurrence. Differential diagnoses (homologous serum hepatitis, infectious hepatitis) were considered and excluded; isoniazid and PAS were given later without ill effect.

raw_record.support_text: The study reports three cases of jaundice attributed to ethionamide among patients with newly diagnosed previously untreated pulmonary tuberculosis. Jaundice developed after 3, 4, and 5 months of ethionamide therapy (1 g daily, co-administered with streptomycin or isoniazid), preceded by nausea, anorexia and malaise, and recovery was prompt when ethionamide was withdrawn. In 62 patients completing six months' therapy the incidence of jaundice was approximately 5 per cent, and liver function tests were transiently disturbed in 5 further cases.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients had newly diagnosed previously untreated pulmonary tuberculosis; the three indexed cases received ethionamide with co-administered streptomycin or isoniazid (unresolved co-exposure).
raw_record.extra_details: Three cases of jaundice; onset after 3-5 months of therapy; jaundice preceded by nausea, anorexia and malaise; recovery after ethionamide withdrawal; ~5% jaundice incidence over six months in 62 patients; transient liver-function-test disturbance in 5 further cases. Hepatotoxicity from ethionamide was judged greater than expected from prior reports.

raw_record.support_text: A patient receiving streptomycin, isoniazid, and ethambutol developed painless jaundice with pale stools and dark urine, with elevated bilirubin (201 µmol/l), alkaline phosphatase (976 U/l), γ-glutamyltransferase, and aspartate transaminase (264 U/l); a liver biopsy showed cholestasis. Testing excluded viral and autoimmune causes. After jaundice was initially attributed to isoniazid, treatment was restarted with ethambutol alone, and within six days alkaline phosphatase rose from 767 to 1225 U/l and aspartate transaminase from 144 to 356 U/l, and on rechallenge with ethambutol plus streptomycin enzymes again rose. Subsequent treatment with isoniazid and streptomycin was uneventful, attributing the cholestatic jaundice to ethambutol.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic jaundice (pale stools, dark urine, bilirubin 201 µmol/l, ALP 976 U/l, γGT 616 U/l, AST 264 U/l); liver biopsy showed cholestasis. Causality supported by rechallenge: ALP rose 767→1225 U/l and AST 144→356 U/l on ethambutol 700 mg/day alone, and ALP 812→1128 U/l and AST 76→228 U/l on ethambutol+streptomycin rechallenge, with improvement on drug withdrawal. Initial treatment (from 17 Nov 1983) was ethambutol 750 mg (15 mg/kg) daily, isoniazid 300 mg daily, streptomycin 0.5 g IM twice weekly. Excluded HBV, HAV, CMV, smooth muscle and antimitochondrial antibodies, Paul Bunnell; normal liver ultrasound. Paper notes ethambutol hepatotoxicity is poorly documented; CSM has received one report of hepatitis and one of hepatic cirrhosis attributed to ethambutol with uncertain cause.

raw_record.support_text: Ethambutol, which previously had not been noted to produce hepatic injury of any type, was recently reported to induce an instance of cholestatic jaundice. The role of the drug was confirmed by readministration (Gulliford et al. 1986).
raw_record.extra_details: Single reported instance of cholestatic jaundice; causality confirmed by rechallenge (readministration) per Gulliford et al. 1986. Previously not known to produce hepatic injury of any type.

No significant increases in adverse effects were reported versus placebo, and there were no serious adverse events related to the treatment.

raw_record.extra_details: NCT03124108, 12-week, double-blind phase II trial comparing elafibranor 80 mg, elafibranor 120 mg, and placebo (45 patients). Reported that liver function tests showed no signs of hepatotoxicity; no serious adverse events related to treatment; most common adverse effects were mild-to-moderate digestive disorders such as nausea and diarrhea. Also states elafibranor did not induce or exacerbate pruritus.

raw_record.support_text: Human safety data on alpha-lipoic acid (ALA) are reported from more than 35 clinical studies (>1300 individuals, 600-2400 mg/day, up to 24 months). In the double-blind placebo-controlled ALADIN II study (24 months, 600 and 1200 mg/day), treatment-related adverse events were monitored across body systems and clinical chemistry parameters including SGOT, SGPT, gamma-GT, alkaline phosphatase and total bilirubin; the authors report no differences in safety parameters between treatment groups and placebo over the entire study, and general tolerability was very good (94% for 1200 mg/day group versus 100% placebo). No drug-related liver injury is reported.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Oral supplementation/administration in humans; therapeutic doses of 600-2400 mg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: >35 clinical studies with >1300 participants, doses typically 600-2400 mg/day, durations weeks to 24 months. ALADIN II double-blind placebo-controlled study monitored liver chemistries (SGOT, SGPT, gamma-GT, alkaline phosphatase, total bilirubin) and found no differences vs placebo; tolerability very good (94% for 1200 mg/day group vs 100% placebo). General safety assessment (oral LD50 >2000 mg/kg bw in rats; no mutagenicity/genotoxicity).

raw_record.support_text: Tienilic acid (ticrynofen), 2,3-dichloro-4-(2-thenoyl)phenoxy acetic acid, is a uricosuric diuretic whose association with severe liver damage was analyzed in 340 cases by Zimmerman et al. The high frequency of hepatotoxicity led to withdrawal of the drug in the United States and other countries. Homberg and colleagues reported as many as 67 cases, with death in the acute phase in 11; histology in 36 biopsies did not correspond with chronic active hepatitis, and anti-LKM2 antiorganelle response occurred in about 50% of cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Uricosuric diuretic; 340 cases analyzed by Zimmerman et al.; 67 cases reported by Homberg with 11 acute-phase deaths; histologic changes in 36 biopsies not consistent with chronic active hepatitis; delayed recovery in 14 cases responded to prednisolone and azathioprine; anti-LKM2 antiorganelle response in ~50% of cases; high hepatotoxicity frequency led to drug withdrawal in the US and other countries.

raw_record.support_text: A 49-year-old non-alcoholic, previously healthy man on tienilic acid 250 mg daily for mild hypertension developed jaundice 6 weeks later. He was admitted with transaminases 88 and 63 times the upper limits of normal, prothrombin time and factor V at 20% and 23% of normal, and high titres (500) of liver/kidney microsomal type 2 autoantibodies, considered specific for tienilic acid hepatotoxicity. Viral and HIV serology was negative. He rapidly worsened and would have died had liver transplantation 8 days later not been possible. The report is titled 'Fulminant hepatitis due to tienilic acid' and frames the transplant as secondary to tienilic-acid-induced fulminant hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 250 mg daily for mild hypertension (given in place of an amiloride/hydrochlorothiazide combination); latency to jaundice about 6 weeks; transaminases 88x and 63x upper limit of normal; prothrombin time and factor V 20% and 23% of normal; LKM type 2 autoantibodies titre 500 considered specific for tienilic acid hepatotoxicity; negative viral (A, B, C, cytomegalovirus, herpesvirus) and HIV serology; negative immunological tests otherwise; would have died without liver transplant performed 8 days after admission.

raw_record.support_text: Between 1973 and 1983 the authors detected 71 patients with anti-LKM2 antibody, of which 67 corresponded to acute hepatitis with a definite history of tienilic acid (ticrynafen) therapy. The four remaining cases had similar hepatitis but intake of the drug just before the hepatic injury could not be established.
raw_record.extra_details: 67 of 71 anti-LKM2-positive patients had acute hepatitis with a definite history of tienilic acid (ticrynafen) therapy; the remaining four had similar hepatitis but drug intake just before injury could not be established. Anti-LKM2 (also listed as cytochrome P450 2E1 in the entity list) is the associated antibody marker.

raw_record.support_text: Tienilic acid (TA), a uricosuric diuretic used to treat hypertension, was first marketed in Europe in 1976 and introduced in the US in 1979, then rapidly withdrawn from the US market in 1980 because of its hepatotoxic secondary effects. The incidence and clinical features of 340 reported cases supported an immune mechanism for TA-induced hepatitis, and a specific autoantibody (anti-LKM2, directed against a liver-kidney microsomal component) was detected only in patients with TA-induced hepatitis, serving as a specific marker.
raw_record.extra_details: Uricosuric diuretic used in hypertension; marketed in Europe 1976, US 1979, withdrawn from US market 1980 due to hepatotoxic effects; 340 reported cases of hepatitis supporting an immune (immunoallergic) mechanism; specific anti-LKM2 autoantibody against a liver-kidney microsomal (endoplasmic reticulum) component, a specific marker of TA-induced hepatitis; TA was devoid of direct hepatotoxic effect in laboratory animals.

raw_record.support_text: Ticrynafen (Tienilic acid), the third loop diuretic approved by the FDA in May 1979 for hypertension, received several hundreds of liver injury case reports in the months after approval. A retrospective analysis of 340 of these cases showed most presented with hepatocellular injury and jaundice; jaundice was present in 246 of 287 patients with sufficient information, and about 10% of jaundiced patients died. Ticrynafen was withdrawn from the US market in 1980.
raw_record.extra_details: Also known as Tienilic acid; approved by the FDA in May 1979 for hypertension; several hundred liver injury cases reported to the manufacturer; retrospective analysis of 340 cases; jaundice present in 246 of 287 patients with sufficient clinical information; ~10% of jaundiced patients died; withdrawn from the US market in 1980.

raw_record.support_text: Ticrynafen, a uricosuric diuretic agent which causes hepatocellular injury in man as an apparent idiosyncratic reaction, was studied. At concentrations equivalent to therapeutic blood levels, the drug reduced bile flow and sulfobromophthalein excretion in isolated perfused rat liver, effects enhanced by previous phenobarbital treatment, suggesting a cytochrome P-450 metabolite.
raw_record.extra_details: Uricosuric diuretic used for hypertension with hyperuricemia/gouty diathesis; withdrawn from US market a few months after introduction due to hepatic injury among recipients. Analysis of 336 cases of TR-associated hepatic injury: injury usually hepatocellular, often a syndrome resembling severe acute hepatitis with very high aminotransferase levels and mortality approaching 10%. Long delay between therapy initiation and injury onset cited as more consistent with metabolic idiosyncrasy than hypersensitivity. Animal findings (excluded from evidence basis): IPRL showed reduced bile flow and sulfobromophthalein excretion and aspartate aminotransferase release; effects enhanced by prior phenobarbital (100 mg/kg i.p. daily × 3 days) in rats, suggesting a cytochrome P-450 metabolite.

raw_record.support_text: Anti-liver/kidney microsome type 2 (anti-LKM2) antibodies have so far only been detected in patients suffering from tienilic acid-induced hepatitis. Of twenty serum samples containing anti-LKM2 antibodies from patients with hepatitis, 19 were from patients treated with tienilic acid either concomitantly or previously in France or the United States, with anti-LKM2 titers by immunofluorescence varying from 1:100 to 1:10,000.
raw_record.extra_details: Twenty serum samples containing anti-LKM2 antibodies were from patients suffering from hepatitis, 19 of whom were treated with tienilic acid either concomitantly or previously in France or the United States; anti-LKM2 titers by immunofluorescence ranged from 1:100 to 1:10,000 (patients CAI and JOR had titers of 1:2000 and 1:500). Five control sera from patients without hepatitis who were taking 250 mg tienilic acid per day for >1 year contained 5-15 µM tienilic acid and showed no hepatitis. Anti-LKM2 antibodies are immune markers associated with tienilic acid-induced hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Ticrynafen (tienilic acid), a loop diuretic approved by the US FDA on May 2, 1979 for hypertension, generated hundreds of reported liver injury cases after marketing. A retrospective analysis of 340 of these cases showed that most presented with hepatocellular injury and jaundice; jaundice was recorded in 246 of 287 patients with sufficient information, and about 10% of the jaundiced patients died. Ticrynafen was withdrawn from the US market in 1980.
raw_record.extra_details: Brand name ticrynafen; loop diuretic; approved by US FDA on May 2, 1979 for hypertension; hundreds of liver injury cases reported to manufacturer after marketing; retrospective analysis of 340 cases; hepatocellular injury with jaundice; jaundice in 246 of 287 patients with sufficient clinical information; about 10% of patients with jaundice died; withdrawn from the US market in 1980.

raw_record.support_text: In this cohort of 80 patients with chronic DILI/HILI, synthetic drugs were the causative agents in 27/80 (33.7%) cases. Clarithromycin was among the commonly implicated synthetic drugs (7 cases).
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated as a causative agent of chronic DILI/HILI in 7 of 80 cases. Cohort-level characteristics: RUCAM scores 6-8 (n=74) and >=9 (n=6); R value hepatocellular in 71.2%, mixed in 20.0%, cholestatic in 8.8%; DILI severity mild/moderate, no severe, fatal, or transplantation outcomes; histology showed inflammatory necrosis and fibrosis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that the patient developed acute liver failure 10 days after initiating clarithromycin therapy. Other causes of ALF including viral, ischemic, autoimmune, Wilson's disease and hemochromatosis were excluded, and echocardiography showed a normal ejection fraction. The initial rise in AST and ALT (to about 1,000 U/L each) preceded the hypotension from hemorrhagic shock by one day, so it could not be attributed to shock liver, although the sharp rise on day 3 (to >6,000 U/L) might have been partly due to hepatic ischemia from massive upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage. The patient had normal renal function throughout clarithromycin therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of ALF developing ~10 days after starting clarithromycin; AST and ALT rose to >=6,000 U/L with grade III hepatic encephalopathy and ammonia 96 umol/L; massive bleed with coagulopathy (PT >100 s, platelets 35,000/uL); postmortem liver (1980 gm, golden-brown) showed massive hepatocyte necrosis with sparing of periportal hepatocytes and diffuse sinusoidal congestion, no inflammation or fibrosis; autopsy negative for HSV-1/2 and CMV by immunohistochemistry. Liver biopsy and EGD postponed due to hemodynamic instability and coagulopathy. Patient died after cardiac arrest. The sharp day-3 rise in AST/ALT might have been partly due to hepatic ischemia from GI hemorrhage/coagulopathy. Concomitant medications (chronically administered, including prednisone) considered unlikely causes.

raw_record.support_text: Idiosyncratic drug-induced fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) is reported after clarithromycin use with exclusion of known causes of FHF. In this case the biopsy was consistent with drug-induced toxicity, other causes of FHF were absent, and the patient had no preceding liver dysfunction. Fever, eosinophilia, eosinophilic infiltration on biopsy, and a 1-week sensitization period support an immunologically mediated idiosyncratic reaction, and nonzonal panacinar necrosis is characteristic of an idiosyncratic phenomenon. The authors conclude the idiosyncratic drug reaction leading to FHF was associated with clarithromycin exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient developed FHF within 72 h; peak enzymes LDH 3529 U/L, ALP 1095 U/L, AST 2255 U/L, ALT 1974 U/L; total bilirubin rose to 33.4 mg/dl, unconjugated bilirubin 0.0 mg/dl, PT 21 s, activated PTT 51 s. Transjugular biopsy showed moderate cholestasis and microvesicular steatosis with increased eosinophilic infiltrate in portal tracts and hepatic lobules, ballooning degeneration and occasional hepatocyte dropout, no bile duct injury. Progressive encephalopathy, coagulopathy, hemodynamic instability, metabolic acidosis, and respiratory failure; terminal extubation on day 13. Same paper notes clarithromycin reported associated with cholestatic hepatitis in a patient treated for Mycobacterium chelonae lung infection, and that the manufacturer reports mild LFT elevations in <1% of patients. Acetaminophen-associated FHF was not supported (see separate record).

They note that while a presumption that clarithromycin hepatotoxicity is dose related is reasonable, an immune-toxicologic hypothesis cannot be excluded. The paper reports a fatal case of fulminant hepatitis in a young patient with documented past episodes of hypertransaminasemia who ingested the drug.

raw_record.extra_details: Fatal fulminant hepatitis case report; the drug is generally well tolerated and described as a very rare cause of fulminant liver failure, either alone or by inhibiting the metabolism of other drugs. Authors consider both a dose-related (intrinsic) presumption and an immune-toxicologic (idiosyncratic) hypothesis for the hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A 75-year-old male with type 2 diabetes developed liver injury 49 days after starting ipragliflozin (50 mg/day) to replace sulfonylurea: AST rose from 13 to 622 U/L, ALT from 9 to 266 U/L, ALP from 239 to 752 U/L, and γ-GTP from 19 to 176 U/L, with total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL. Hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, and EBV serologies were negative, while a lymphocyte transformation test for ipragliflozin was positive. CT showed mild fatty liver. After discontinuing ipragliflozin with liver supportive therapy, he was discharged 18 days later with AST and ALT reduced to 20 and 13 U/L. The authors describe this as a case of ipragliflozin-induced liver injury, emphasizing the need to monitor liver function during SGLT2 inhibitor therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single case in a 75-year-old Japanese male with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and mild fatty liver (NAFLD background); sulfonylurea therapy had been replaced by ipragliflozin.
raw_record.extra_details: Ipragliflozin (SGLT2 inhibitor) 50 mg/day; liver injury developed 49 days after start. Peak AST 622 U/L, ALT 266 U/L, ALP 752 U/L, γ-GTP 176 U/L; total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL (no jaundice), ZTT 3.5 U, TTT 0.4 U. Negative IgM hepatitis A antibody, hepatitis B antigen, hepatitis C virus antibody, IgM CMV antibody, and IgM EB VCA antibody; positive lymphocyte transformation test for ipragliflozin. Abdominal CT showed mild fatty liver with no nodular lesions. Patient was admitted for liver supportive therapy and discharged 18 days later with AST 20 U/L and ALT 13 U/L after discontinuation. Report recommends monitoring liver function during SGLT2 inhibitor therapy.

raw_record.support_text: Paroxetine was attributed to 10 DILI cases, predominantly hepatocellular (70%). Three cases (33%) met nR-based Hy's law criteria with no reported fatalities/liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: 10 of 843 registry DILI cases; Hep 70%/Chol 10%/Mix 20%; female 80%, lymphopenia 20%, eosinophilia 33%; 3 (33%) fulfilled nR-based Hy's law, no fatalities/transplantation; hepatocellular subset had highest mean ALT.

raw_record.support_text: Liver needle biopsy showed bile canalicular dilation and proliferation, moderately expanded portal tracts infiltrated by lymphocytes and plasma cells, and bile canalicular obstruction, intracytoplasmic bile retention and confluent necrotic foci; these findings were considered to be due to drug-induced liver injury. Paroxetine was the drug stopped, after which all hepatic and cholestatic enzymes and bilirubin gradually decreased to normal within 14 weeks, with no other detectable cause for the findings.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of paroxetine-associated drug-induced liver injury in a hospitalized patient. Combined hepatocellular and cholestatic features: histology showed bile canalicular dilation/proliferation, portal lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltration, bile canalicular obstruction, intracytoplasmic bile retention and confluent necrotic foci; marker eosinophilia was present. Dechallenge (stop of paroxetine only, other medications continued) led to normalization of hepatic and cholestatic enzymes and bilirubin within 14 weeks. Abdominal ultrasound, CT, endoscopy and ERCP ruled out biliary/pancreatic abnormalities; no viral damage seen. Discussion notes six prior paroxetine hepatotoxicity case reports, four of which were hepatocellular and mixed-type (hepatocellular and cholestatic) damage.

raw_record.support_text: Paroxetine is described as a rare cause of reversible hepatotoxicity; in this study paroxetine caused reactive hepatitis in one patient. Histologic features include portal mononuclear infiltrate with mild interface activity, cholestasis, Kupffer cell hyperplasia, and hepatocellular injury ranging from rare small necroinflammatory foci to confluent necrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Reversible hepatotoxicity is a rare complication. Histologic morphology ranges from reactive hepatitis to panacinar hepatitis; in this study caused reactive hepatitis in one patient.

raw_record.support_text: An 84-year-old woman developed severe acute hepatitis 3 days after starting paroxetine 10 mg/day for chronic mild depression, with markedly elevated transaminases (AST 2208 IU/L, ALT 2110 IU/L), hyperbilirubinemia, prolonged INR (2.13), hyperammonemia and stage I hepatic encephalopathy. Viral, autoimmune and metabolic liver disease were excluded, and use of the Naranjo probability scale suggested that paroxetine was the probable cause of hepatitis (total score 7). The injury resolved after discontinuation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single reported case in an 84-year-old woman with chronic atrial fibrillation, arterial hypertension, brain atherosclerosis and prior transient ischemic attacks, taking concurrent verapamil, ticlopidine, spironolactone and nimodipine; a role for drug-drug interaction was considered unlikely by the authors.
raw_record.extra_details: Paroxetine is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor; hepatotoxicity is reported as very rare with only a few prior severe cases, all with favorable prognosis after discontinuation. Injury appeared 3 days after first dose at 10 mg/day. ALT rose to 2110 IU/L, AST to 2208 IU/L with normal alkaline phosphatase, mild GGT increase, total bilirubin 2.5 mg/dL, INR 2.13, ammonia 335 mg/dL, hepatic encephalopathy stage I. Naranjo score 7. Patient advised to avoid future paroxetine and other SSRIs. Paroxetine is metabolized by CYP2D6; the authors note the mechanism is idiosyncratic.

raw_record.support_text: Among 16 chronic DILI patients with liver biopsy, seven had cirrhosis; the drugs related to liver cirrhosis in these cases included bentazepam.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic DILI case progressing to cirrhosis in a DILI cohort.

raw_record.support_text: Cases of chronic hepatocellular-type idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity are tabulated. Bentazepam was attributed as the sole culprit drug in two cases: case 2 (hepatocellular damage, persistent at 10 months, antinuclear antibody titer 1/80) and case 4 (chronic hepatitis with portal inflammatory infiltrate, piecemeal necrosis, bile duct proliferation, and portal-to-portal fibrosis showing regenerative nodules; recovery at 26 months). Another bentazepam case (case 11) in the cholestatic/mixed table showed mixed-pattern injury persistent at 16 months with anti-smooth muscle antibody 1/160. These cases were classified definite or probable by causality assessment.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic idiosyncratic DILI registry. Case 2: F/51, raised enzymes, 152 d therapy, 28 d onset, persistent (10 mo). Case 4: F/60, jaundice, 277 d therapy, 150 d onset, chronic hepatitis histology, recovery (26 mo). Case 11: F/47, raised enzymes, mixed pattern, persistent (16 mo), anti-smooth muscle antibodies 1/160.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that a causal relation between the use of bentazepam and hepatic injury can confidently be established because alternative explanations were ruled out and withdrawal was followed by rapid clinical improvement and return of laboratory findings to normal. Bentazepam is a benzodiazepine marketed in Spain since 1981 for anxiety disorders; rechallenge was not attempted for ethical reasons.
raw_record.extra_details: 65-year-old man with prior peptic ulcer, chronic constipation, and transient ischaemic attacks; previously stopped triflusal due to gastrointestinal bleeding and took only oral lactulose during bentazepam therapy. Bentazepam given at the manufacturer's recommended dose of 25 mg three times daily for severe anxiety; symptoms (abdominal discomfort, progressive asthenia, anorexia, weight loss) appeared ~4 months after start, with no improvement after dose reduction to 25 mg/day, and the drug was stopped at 13 months. At presentation AST 152 U/L, ALT 142 U/L, total bilirubin 18.6 µmol/L (direct 6.8), γ-GT 109 U/L, with normal alkaline phosphatase, plus leukopenia (3.5 × 10⁹/L) and thrombocytopenia (130 × 10⁹/L). Liver biopsy showed expanded portal areas with dense lymphocytic/monocytic infiltrate disrupting the limiting plate, lymphoid aggregates, marked portal-to-portal fibrosis with transition to cirrhosis in some areas, and marked parenchymal collapse. Viral (Hep A/B/C, CMV, EBV) and autoimmune serologies were negative. After stopping the drug, symptoms improved dramatically; by the eleventh week AST fell to 66 U/L, ALT to 53 U/L, and γ-GT to 85 U/L, and counts normalized by 4 months. Authors attributed the injury to an idiosyncratic metabolic mechanism (no rash, fever, eosinophilia, or granulomatous infiltrate; long latency), and noted benzodiazepines generally have very low hepatotoxic potential.

raw_record.support_text: The case report describes a patient who developed a hepatocellular pattern of injury with aminotransferase elevations about 10 times the upper normal limit and minimal bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase elevation, after other causes (viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, alcoholic hepatitis, acetaminophen toxicity, Wilson disease, malignancy, and sepsis) were excluded. After fimasartan was discontinued, liver enzymes normalized within 3 weeks; accidental readministration of fimasartan reproduced the hepatotoxicity with a quicker enzyme rise, and enzymes again normalized after stopping the drug. The paper notes no other hepatotoxicity cases were seen among 2506 patients prescribed fimasartan for >3 months and 1636 for >10 months, indicating the reaction is rare, and it may appear late (even after 10 months) and occur in patients without prior problems on other ARBs.

raw_record.support_text: Fenclozic acid (Myalex), an NSAID, was withdrawn from late stage clinical development in patients as a result of hepatotoxicity. In a clinical trial in 12 patients receiving 400 mg/day, two subjects experienced a severe adverse drug reaction and a further four subjects showed elevated liver enzymes; DILI was also observed in two subjects at other trial centres who became jaundiced. Onset on 400 mg/day was between 17 and 35 days after the first dose, with elevated circulating alkaline phosphatase, serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase, and serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase; the biochemical changes in the jaundiced subjects were interpreted as indicative of cholestasis rather than parenchymal cell damage. All patients recovered within a few days of cessation of the drug. In preclinical species fenclozic acid was not a hepatotoxin, but when administered to humans it resulted in dose-dependent DILI, and this human-specific DILI led to its withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: Fenclozic acid ([2-(4-chlorophenyl)-1,3-thiazol-4-yl]acetic acid), brand name Myalex, was a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug withdrawn from clinical development due to human hepatotoxicity. Clinical trial in 12 patients at 400 mg/day: two subjects had a severe adverse drug reaction and four subjects showed elevated liver enzymes; two subjects at other trial centres became jaundiced with DILI. Onset 17-35 days after first dose; elevated alkaline phosphatase, SGOT, and SGPT; jaundiced subjects' biochemical changes interpreted as cholestasis rather than parenchymal cell damage. All patients recovered within a few days of drug cessation. Authors describe the human DILI as dose-dependent. Preclinical species (rat, mouse) did not show hepatotoxicity; repeated oral dosing of mice at 50 or 100 mg/kg/day for 7 days did not induce DILI, though acute hepatic necrosis after a single 10 mg/kg oral dose was observed in a mouse autoradiography study.

raw_record.support_text: The hepatotoxicity observed in humans could not be replicated in any of the animal species tested, making the drug a classic example of an apparently human-specific hepatotoxicant. The pattern of liver injury exhibited a clear dose-response relationship and was evident in numerous patients during clinical trials; in one trial, 2 of 12 patients who received fenclozic acid at 400 mg/day became jaundiced after 4 weeks. Therefore, the pattern of liver injury cannot be considered idiosyncratic.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose-dependent, non-idiosyncratic human-specific hepatotoxicity; in one clinical trial 2 of 12 patients receiving 400 mg/day became jaundiced after 4 weeks; the injury pattern exhibited a clear dose-response relationship and was evident in numerous patients during clinical trials.

FDA spontaneous report data are inappropriate for calculating relative incidences.

raw_record.support_text: N-methylformamide was first evaluated in a clinical trial in 1956, and treatment was discontinued due to hepatic injury. The authors state that animal studies predicted hepatic damage would complicate clinical trials, that toxicology studies confirmed hepatic toxicity as the limiting organ toxicity, and that studies at several institutions confirmed reversible hepatic toxicity. This establishes N-MF as a cause of human hepatic injury when used therapeutically as an investigational anticancer drug.
raw_record.extra_details: N-MF (N-methylformamide) is a polar solvent with antineoplastic activity undergoing phase 1/2 evaluation as an anticancer drug. In a 1956 clinical trial, treatment was discontinued due to hepatic injury. Reversible hepatic toxicity was confirmed at several institutions; hepatic injury is the limiting organ toxicity. The compound did not appear myelosuppressive or neurotoxic, and was not reported to be hepatotoxic in the toxicology setting beyond this.

raw_record.support_text: An early clinical trial of N-methylformamide (NMF) in man showed hepatotoxicity, which was described as an unacceptable side effect, and as a result interest in further chemotherapeutic studies of NMF was lost. NMF later regained attention due to its lack of myelotoxicity. A subsequent report (paragraph 5) notes that the most frequent side effects in man are anorexia, nausea and hepatotoxicity, based on two recent phase I clinical trials.
raw_record.extra_details: N-methylformamide (NMF) is an antineoplastic agent; early clinical trial in man demonstrated hepatotoxicity that was an unacceptable side effect, leading to loss of interest in further chemotherapy studies. NMF lacks myelotoxicity. In man the most frequent side effects are anorexia, nausea and hepatotoxicity, reported from two recent phase I clinical trials. Confusingly, a separate entity in the input entity list maps the 'NMF' surface form to N-methyl-D-aspartate; the paper text unambiguously refers to N-methylformamide.

raw_record.extra_details: Drug discontinued 6 days prior to admission after nausea, vomiting, and malaise. Liver biopsy showed 80-90% hepatic necrosis, mild portal infiltrate with moderate-to-severe eosinophilia, and few plasma cells; damage predominantly hepatocellular with minimal ductal involvement. Strong temporal relation: symptoms of hepatocellular failure developed within 6 weeks of initiating disulfiram. No acetaminophen use and negative viral/autoimmune serologies except ANA 1:160. Progression to grade III hepatic encephalopathy, coagulopathy (INR 3.8), factor V decreased to 20%; underwent successful OLT on hospital day 5; normal liver function 84 weeks post-transplant.

The patient was discharged with a diagnosis of disulfiram hepatitis and remained well.

The paper also cites Raneck and Andreasen's 6 cases of possible disulfiram hepatotoxicity, of which 5 were circumstantial and 1 showed abnormal liver chemistries on rechallenge.

raw_record.support_text: In this series of 82 patients with suspected disulfiram adverse liver reactions, four patients died during the initial hospitalisation and four underwent successful liver transplantation. Deceased or transplanted patients had higher serum bilirubin, AST, AST/ALT ratio and INR values than those who recovered, with no difference in age, sex, or duration of treatment. The study frames these as drug-induced liver injury cases attributed to disulfiram.
raw_record.extra_details: 82 patients with disulfiram suspected adverse liver reactions (1979-2004 reports); median ALT 46xULN and bilirubin 6.0xULN across the cohort. 49 patients fulfilled Hy's rule (ALT>=3xULN + bilirubin>=2xULN), with a 16% (8/49) mortality/transplantation rate. 4 patients died, 4 underwent liver transplantation. Liver biopsy in one patient who used alcohol showed eosinophilic infiltration and no evidence of alcohol-induced injury. In a multivariate analysis, bilirubin (P=0.0005, OR 1.214, CI 1.088-1.355) was the only independent predictor of death or liver transplantation. Median treatment duration 42 days (IQR 35-60). Two patients had documented alcohol use during treatment.

raw_record.support_text: This case report reemphasizes that disulfiram can be hepatotoxic and may trigger severe acute hepatitis in a small number of patients. Clinical evidence of hepatitis occurs some time after initiation of disulfiram therapy and may take several weeks to recover following discontinuation of the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity figure is supported by a case report; autoantibodies to cytochrome P450 1A2 (CYP1A2) were expressed in a case of disulfiram-induced hepatitis, but remained high even after recovery, arguing against direct involvement of these autoantibodies in liver cell injury. Histological changes on liver biopsy are reported as quite diagnostic. Latency occurs some time after therapy initiation and recovery may take several weeks after discontinuation. Paper cautions that many patients fail to mention past alcoholism and disulfiram treatment.

raw_record.support_text: Disulfiram induced toxic hepatitis in a 44-year-old alcoholic after 10 days of therapy at a total dose of 3.75 g. His bilirubin peaked at 6.9 mg/100 ml and SGOT was 2040 units, with only slightly elevated alkaline phosphatase, no eosinophilia, and resolution on drug removal; reinstitution caused recurrence within 10 days. A liver biopsy showed only mild cytoplasmic degeneration of hepatocytes, increased binucleated cells consistent with regeneration, and a minimal focal histiocytic reaction. Separately, six cases of disulfiram-induced hepatitis were reported from Denmark, five of whom died in hepatic coma with no evidence of viral hepatitis, and rechallenge confirmed hepatitis due to disulfiram in the remaining case.
raw_record.extra_details: Patients were chronic alcoholics treated for alcoholism (the indication for which disulfiram is used, so not a departure from therapeutic use). Index case: 44-year-old, 10 days therapy, total dose 3.75 g, bilirubin 6.9 mg/100 ml, SGOT 2040 units, slightly elevated serum alkaline phosphatase, no eosinophilia, associated urticaria, recurrence of hepatitis within 10 days on rechallenge; liver biopsy showed mild cytoplasmic hepatocyte degeneration, increased binucleated cells (regeneration), and minimal focal histiocytic reaction. Six Danish cases of disulfiram-induced hepatitis: five died in hepatic coma without evidence of viral hepatitis; the remaining case was confirmed by rechallenge. Authors suggested a positive patch test could establish an allergic mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: A 44-year-old man with a history of alcoholism, after three months of sobriety, began disulfiram therapy (0.5 gm daily for five days then 0.25 gm daily). Ten days into therapy he rapidly developed fatigue, malaise, and jaundice without fever. Disulfiram, chlordiazepoxide hydrochloride, and methylphenidate hydrochloride (the latter two taken for months) were stopped; bilirubin peaked at 6.9 mg/100 ml and SGOT at 2,040 units with only slight serum alkaline phosphatase elevation, and hepatitis resolved in six weeks. After rechallenge with disulfiram 0.25 gm daily, the same biochemical and clinical sequelae recurred in ten days (with urticaria and no other medication), again improving after drug discontinuation, supporting disulfiram as the cause of the hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case report. Two episodes reproducible on rechallenge. Standard dosage 0.5 gm daily for five days then 0.25 gm daily; rechallenge at 0.25 gm daily reproduced sequelae within ten days. Peak bilirubin 6.9 mg/100 ml and SGOT 2,040 units with only slight alkaline phosphatase elevation; no fever or eosinophilia on the first episode, urticaria present on rechallenge. Rapid resolution of hepatitis after withdrawal; liver tests normal in six weeks. HAA negative on two occasions. Patient had a prior episode of hepatitis after halothane anesthesia in 1968. First episode occurred with co-medications chlordiazepoxide and methylphenidate; rechallenge episode occurred without other medication, supporting disulfiram attribution.

raw_record.support_text: Among 62 patients with acute liver failure (ALF), the etiology was considered viral in 26; in 5 other patients ALF was considered due to toxic hepatitis caused by the administration of ketoconazole, α-methyl dopa, halothane, pyroxicam, and disulfiram, respectively. Thus disulfiram was attributed as the cause of toxic hepatitis leading to ALF in one patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Attribution made in a single ALF patient within a 62-patient acute liver failure series; drug administration identified as the cause of toxic hepatitis leading to acute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that idiosyncratic disulfiram-induced toxic hepatitis, although rare, is a potentially fatal adverse drug reaction that may be mediated by a hypersensitivity mechanism or direct hepatotoxicity, and that disulfiram should be discontinued if hepatotoxicity is suspected. Their patient was transplanted for fulminant hepatic failure secondary to an idiosyncratic reaction to disulfiram.
raw_record.extra_details: Presentation generally within 4-8 wk of disulfiram initiation with fatigue, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, jaundice, fever, rash, and pruritus. Histology showed both hepatocellular and canalicular changes with fibrosis, focal or periportal necrosis, and Lafora-like bodies (ref 7). Clinical recovery usually occurs within 2 wk after drug cessation; deaths due to hepatic coma have been reported. The reported patient was transplanted (orthotopic liver transplantation) for fulminant hepatic failure secondary to the idiosyncratic reaction; diagnosis potentially mediated by hypersensitivity mechanism or direct hepatotoxicity. Case was in an alcoholic patient who was transplanted despite a short abstinence period; the mechanism noted is uncertain.

Five patients had evidence of hepatitis, four of whom had symptoms so severe they required hospitalisation, and liver biopsy in four cases showed acute hepatitis. raw_record.support_text: A 49-year-old woman undergoing aftercare for chronic alcoholism (liver function tests normal at baseline) was started on disulfiram 250 mg daily; she took no medication except vitamin B1. Jaundice appeared 13 days after treatment onset, and acute liver failure was diagnosed on day 18 after a total disulfiram dose of 4.5 g (Quick value <10%, bilirubin 460 µmol/l, GPT 5099 U/l, GOT 4142 U/l) together with early renal failure (creatinine 300 µmol/l). Viral infection, autoimmune hepatitis and metabolic liver disease were excluded, and toxicology tests were negative. The patient died 25 days after starting disulfiram in hepatic coma from fulminant hepatitis with hepatorenal syndrome; biopsy and autopsy showed acute hepatic dystrophy without cirrhosis. The temporal relationship, exclusion of other causes, and histology compatible with chemical-toxic hepatitis indicated a disulfiram-induced fulminant hepatitis. The authors state that disulfiram hepatotoxicity is a very rare idiosyncratic reaction that is often fatal.

Paper also notes the first 1974 report of disulfiram-induced hypersensitivity hepatitis and roughly 30 published cases of severe or fulminant disulfiram hepatitis worldwide, and recommends immediate discontinuation on liver-enzyme rise or jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes disulfiram-induced hepatitis reported in humans: Keeffe and Smith first reported a case in 1974, Ranek and Andreason reported six additional cases in 1977 of whom five died, and Kristensen reported toxic liver damage in a nonalcoholic female treated with disulfiram for nickel dermatitis who developed liver-enzyme elevation upon rechallenge. Incidence of disulfiram-induced fatal hepatitis is reportedly 1 in 30,000 treated patients per year, and an analysis of reports to the Danish committee on adverse drug reactions implicated disulfiram in 5 of 52 (10%) drug-related fatalities.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Primary illustrative case is a pediatric (adolescent) patient; general use context is therapeutic aversion therapy in adults with chronic alcoholism. One reported case involved a nonalcoholic female treated for nickel dermatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Onset of hepatotoxicity occurs within 4-6 weeks (range 2-24 weeks) of starting treatment. Symptoms include fatigue, headache, fever, pruritus, rash, myalgia, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, jaundice, light stools, dark urine, and hepatomegaly; symptoms usually resolve within 2 weeks of stopping, and liver function may need up to 12 weeks to normalize. Biopsy may show predominantly hepatocellular degeneration with focal or extensive hepatocellular necrosis and portal/periportal eosinophilic infiltration. Disulfiram-induced liver failure requiring liver transplantation first reported in 1989 (Vanjak et al), with 3 total transplant cases reported; the paper's case is the first reported pediatric OLT for disulfiram-induced fulminant hepatic failure. Most reports suggest an idiosyncratic hypersensitivity reaction as the primary mechanism; an alternative proposed mechanism is carbon disulfide-induced hepatic injury from covalent binding of electrophilic reactive metabolites.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a 35-year-old man with alcohol misuse history who received a subcutaneous implant of the oral drug disulfiram (Esperal) in his left buttock three months before presenting with severe acute liver failure. After surgical excision of the implant and supportive treatment, hepatic synthesis and detoxification normalized with uneventful recovery, supporting disulfiram as the cause. The learning points explicitly state that idiosyncratic drug induced hepatitis attributable to disulfiram is a rare but well described cause of acute liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Unusual route: subcutaneous implant (Esperal) of the oral drug rather than standard oral dosing; patient had ongoing alcohol misuse with binge three days before admission; liver transplantation was considered but declined due to alcohol misuse under German transplant legislation.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of a 35-year-old man presenting with fatigue, vomiting, jaundice and drowsiness. Laboratories showed massive increases in AST (60,620 U/l), ALT (16,726 U/l), LDH (38,180 U/l), GLDH (12,211 U/l), total bilirubin (179 µmol/l), lactate (5.2 mmol/l), severe coagulopathy (INR 8.29; factor V 12%; thrombocytopenia 16,000/µl) precluding biopsy. Progressive encephalopathy, fluid-refractory hypotension, anuric renal failure requiring haemodiafiltration. Common causes (viral hepatitis A-C, Wilson's disease, autoimmune liver disease, comprehensive drug screen) excluded. Implant placed three months prior; dechallenge by immediate implant excision with recovery and normalization of hepatic synthesis/detoxification after six ICU days, discharged without neurological sequelae. Alias: Esperal.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of a 29-year-old patient who developed drug-induced liver injury (DILI) that progressed to vanishing bile duct syndrome (VBDS) after administration of the NSAID pelubiprofen. VBDS is characterized by ductopenia and cholestasis, triggered in this case by an adverse drug reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: 29-year-old female patient; no history of other drugs or herbal medication and was a social drinker. Patient then had more than 10 episodes of vomiting and nausea and was admitted to the emergency department; DILI progressed to VBDS, requiring liver transplantation. The authors state no prior case of VBDS related to pelubiprofen has been reported.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that ampicillin, one of the most commonly used antibiotics, can cause recurrent cholestatic hepatitis, and recommend considering this adverse effect during diagnostic evaluation of patients with hepatic lesions. A case summary describes a 23-year-old patient hospitalized for recurrent, limited cholestasis symptoms; on three occasions ampicillin use led to cholestasis symptoms, with clinical and biochemical recovery on discontinuation of the antibiotic, negative workup otherwise, and no recurrence one year after stopping ampicillin, with the causal relationship deemed probable on the Naranjo scale. The discussion notes that ampicillin-related hepatotoxicity is very rare and usually causes hepatocellular injury, and that this appears to be the only reported case of cholestatic toxicity secondary to ampicillin.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of a 23-year-old patient; recurrent cholestasis symptoms on three separate ampicillin exposures, with clinical and biochemical recovery on drug withdrawal and no recurrence one year later; causality assessed as probable on the Naranjo scale. Atazanavir is a competitive inhibitor of uridine diphosphate-glucuronosyl transferase 1A1 and can lead to elevations in unconjugated bilirubin in a significant number of patients; elevated total bilirubin was the most common laboratory abnormality, but these elevations were asymptomatic, reversible, and not associated with hepatotoxicity.

Liver enzyme abnormalities (ALT/SGPT, AST/SGOT Grades 3-4) were minimal (0-3%).

raw_record.support_text: A 65-year-old woman prescribed pregabalin (Lyrica) 125 mg/day for neuropathic pain following tuberculous meningitis sequelae presented with malaise, anorexia and mucocutaneous jaundice after one month of treatment. Labs showed AST 302 U/l, ALT 665 U/l, GGT 307 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 181 U/l and total bilirubin 3.8 mg/dl; viral, autoimmune, iron, ceruloplasmin, alpha-1-antitrypsin and alphafetoprotein workups were normal, and ultrasound showed normal hepatic parenchyma with no biliary dilation. After pregabalin was withdrawn the patient improved rapidly and liver biochemistry normalized within 8 weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: 65-year-old woman; pregabalin 125 mg/day for one month for neuropathic pain after tuberculous meningitis; presented with malaise, anorexia and jaundice; AST 302 U/l, ALT 665 U/l, GGT 307 U/l, ALP 181 U/l, total bilirubin 3.8 mg/dl; competing causes excluded (hepatotropic viruses, autoantibodies, iron/ceruloplasmin/alpha-1-antitrypsin/alphafetoprotein normal; biliary tract not dilated); rapid clinical recovery and normalization of liver biochemistry within <8 weeks after drug withdrawal; reported to hospital pharmacy and pharmacovigilance center. Causality classified as 'probable' adverse reaction to pregabalin by the CIOMS scale. Authors state this is the first reported case of jaundice associated with pregabalin; a prior letter (Crespo et al) reported increased intrahepatic cholestasis attributed to pregabalin, and the product label lists infrequent (>1/100 and <1/1,000) AST/ALT elevation.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes it is possible that pregabalin induced the liver injury in this patient, obtained a 'probable' classification using the causality assessment from the International consensus criteria, and reported the acute liver injury as being of hepatocellular type. Pregabalin was given as 75 mg twice daily for herpes zoster starting 12 days before admission, following unsuccessful tramadol and acetaminophen.
raw_record.extra_details: 61-year-old male with 1-2 weeks history of sickness, nausea, vomiting, and itching. Peak labs: aspartate aminotransferase 50x ULN, alanine aminotransferase 35x ULN, bilirubin 354 µmol/l, peak INR 4.2 (normalized by discharge, INR 1.2 and bilirubin 75 mmol/l at 6-week follow-up; all liver tests normal at 6 months). Concomitant jaundice noted as carrying ~10% risk of death or liver transplantation. Nausea began ~8 days into pregabalin. Hepatitis and autoantibody serologies negative; no hepatic vein thrombosis on CT. Hepatocellular type per International consensus criteria; 'probable' causality classification. Prior treatment with tramadol and acetaminophen (unrelated to injury onset). Pregabalin is not subject to hepatic metabolism.

Post-hoc analysis of NCT02227797 phase I dose-finding study (University of Minnesota, 2015-2017); 58 of 65 participants with evaluable PK and genotype data. Study hypothesis addresses CYP51A1 genetic polymorphism effects on VCZ hepatotoxicity risk; in vitro azole-binding Kd to fungal CYP51A vs human CYP51A1 = 10 nM vs 2,290 nM. Background: hepatotoxicity is among the most common adverse effects of azole antifungals (>5%), especially when trough concentrations exceed 5 mg/L.

raw_record.support_text: In this study, no hepatotoxicity or nephrotoxicity reactions associated with the use of intravenous voriconazole were detected in either of the two dosing regimens (BID or TID). The eight reported adverse reactions related to intravenous voriconazole are characterized in Table 3, with the main adverse reaction being photophobia (6/8), two of them with elevated peak concentrations (>10 µg/mL).
raw_record.extra_details: Intravenous voriconazole, both BID and TID dosing regimens in pediatric immunocompromised patients with suspected aspergillosis. Adverse reactions observed included photophobia, visual alteration, and hallucinations; no hepatotoxicity or nephrotoxicity was reported.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that hepatotoxicity and visual symptoms are common adverse effects of voriconazole therapy, and retrospectively evaluated 401 patients undergoing voriconazole therapy to assess the effect of treatment modification based on therapeutic drug monitoring on these adverse effects.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective cohort of 401 patients on voriconazole therapy with target trough concentration (Cmin) 1-5 microg/mL. Hepatotoxicity occurred in 6.0% of patients after a median of 10 days; initial Cmin was not significantly associated with hepatotoxicity, but hepatotoxicity was significantly correlated with Cmin at onset of adverse effects, with a Cmin cut-off of 3.5 microg/mL. Voriconazole was discontinued after hepatotoxicity in 62.5% of affected patients; with dose adjustment, treatment was completed in 8/9 patients with hepatotoxicity. A significant preventive effect of treatment modification on hepatotoxicity was demonstrated.

raw_record.support_text: Based on RUCAM, a total of 18 patients (12.9%) were diagnosed as probable or highly probable to have DILI due to voriconazole, with a mean RUCAM score of 7.78 (±1.2). By R value type, five patients (3.8%) were hepatocellular injury, five (3.8%) cholestasis type, and eight (5.7%) mixed type. By CTCAE grading, 27.8% (5/18) were grade 1, 38.9% (7/18) grade 2, 33.3% (6/18) grade 3, and no patients with grade 4.
raw_record.extra_details: Of 140 voriconazole-treated patients (mostly elderly, hospitalized, with various comorbidities and CYP2C19 genotypes), 24.3% (34/140) had at least one AE; hepatotoxicity was the most common AE [12.9%; median steady-state voriconazole Ctrough 6.57 mg/l (IQR 4.28–8.22 mg/l)]. DILI causality assessed with RUCAM (mean score 7.78 ±1.2). R value types: hepatocellular (5), cholestatic (5), mixed (8). CTCAE grades: 5 grade 1, 7 grade 2, 6 grade 3, none grade 4. 66.7% experienced hepatic toxicity within 7 days of first dose, 94.4% within 15 days. Steady-state Ctrough was significantly higher in the hepatotoxicity group (6.57 vs 4.17 mg/l; p=0.021) and in the CTCAE grade ≥2 group (8.20 vs 4.17 mg/l; p=0.016). ROC analysis: steady-state Ctrough >3.61 mg/l associated with increased hepatotoxic events, AUC 0.645 (95% CI 0.534–0.757, p=0.047).

raw_record.support_text: This cohort study of voriconazole-treated patients found that voriconazole-related liver injury was associated with serum trough concentration; in the present study the critical trough concentration above which liver injury likely occurred was 4.375 mg/L, consistent with published meta-analyses and prior reports showing increased liver injury incidence at troughs above 3.0-6.0 mg/L.
raw_record.extra_details: Risk of voriconazole liver injury increased with higher serum trough concentrations (this study critical value 4.375 mg/L; prior reported critical values 3.5, 4.0, 4.2, 5.5, 6.0 mg/L). Voriconazole-related liver injury was associated with hypoproteinemia (24.78% of 1372 patients); protein binding 58%. Adding voriconazole early after lung transplantation increased liver injury risk (OR 4.37, 95% CI 1.53-12.43, p=0.006). Transplant status was negatively related to liver injury, attributed to closer monitoring. Japan multicenter TDM study (n=401) showed liver injury unrelated to initial trough (AUC 0.562, OR 1.67, p=0.292) but related to trough at time of adverse reaction (AUC 0.725, critical value 3.5 mg/L, OR 5.20, p<0.001). No association found with bacterial infection, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, or chronic renal failure. CYP2C19 and UGT1A4 gene polymorphism correlations unclear. Patients with severe infections showing systemic inflammation (n=64) were excluded.

raw_record.support_text: In a pharmacokinetic study of 55 patients receiving voriconazole (VRC) for invasive fungal infections, hepatic toxicity (cholestatic hepatopathy) grade 3 was reported as an adverse event 'probably associated with VRC therapy' in 7 patients (13%). Only grade 1 hepatic cytolysis was observed, so no separate analysis of the association between VRC exposure and cytolytic toxicity was performed.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestasis was graded by ALKP and/or gamma-GT elevations: grade 1 >3x ULN, grade 2 >5x ULN, grade 3 >20x ULN (NCI grades). 7 of 55 patients (13%) had grade 3 cholestatic hepatopathy. Only grade 1 hepatic cytolysis occurred (no quantitative cytolytic exposure analysis). In the PK model, CL decreased by 52% in patients with grade 3 cholestasis, and elimination half-life doubled (average t1/2z 12 h). Omeprazole inhibited VRC CL by 20% (not significant). 505 VRC plasma concentrations on 197 occasions (median 8/patient). Patients included hematological malignancy/neutropenia (64%), solid organ transplantation, chronic liver disease, and hepatosplenic candidiasis.

raw_record.support_text: Voriconazole, the newest of the azoles, also has been reported to cause hepatotoxicity, likely through an idiosyncratic mechanism, as supratherapeutic drug levels have not been associated with increased DILI. In an observational series from Kings College Hospital, of 29 patients with severe liver dysfunction treated with voriconazole, 69% had liver injury, 35% had elevated aminotransferases, 15% cholestasis, and 45% mixed.
raw_record.extra_details: Observational series from Kings College Hospital: of 29 patients with severe liver dysfunction treated with voriconazole, 69% had liver injury, 35% elevated aminotransferases, 15% cholestasis, and 45% mixed. Supratherapeutic drug levels were not associated with increased DILI, consistent with an idiosyncratic mechanism. Caution advised in patients with severe liver dysfunction.

raw_record.support_text: A 44-year-old man with pulmonary aspergillosis developed severe hepatotoxicity after six weeks of voriconazole (200 mg twice daily, initially intravenous then oral), with ALT 899 U/L, AST 821 U/L, ALP 256 U/L and γ-GGT 451 U/L; ALT and AST were more than five times the upper limit of normal. The patient had taken no other medications (including herbal products or supplements) recently, so voriconazole was discontinued due to consideration of voriconazole-induced hepatotoxicity, and five days later liver enzymes slightly declined; he was re-admitted with hepatic insufficiency.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Normal CYP2C19 metabolizer genotype with a low (not high) voriconazole trough concentration; history of old tuberculosis and chronic gastritis.

raw_record.support_text: The 10-year-old boy was started on intravenous voriconazole (7 mg/kg twice daily), which was tolerated with stable liver functions during 42 days of IV therapy. When switched to oral voriconazole, his liver enzymes began to rise (anicteric hepatitis with normal bilirubin). After stopping oral voriconazole for 2 days, liver enzymes returned to normal; restarting low-dose voriconazole again caused liver enzymes to remain elevated, and a second trial at very low oral dose reproduced the same pattern of hepatitis with normal bilirubin.

raw_record.extra_details: Antifungal treatment for gastrointestinal basidiobolomycosis. On dechallenge (stopping oral voriconazole for 2 days) enzymes normalized; rechallenge with low-dose and very low oral voriconazole reproduced elevated liver enzymes/anicteric hepatitis with normal bilirubin. Table 1 enzyme values cited but not reproduced in text.

raw_record.support_text: A 61-year-old woman with sarcoidosis and severe pulmonary hypertension was admitted for COVID pneumonia and developed Aspergillus fungemia, for which voriconazole was initiated. Two weeks into the voriconazole course, an acute liver injury was diagnosed that was stated to be most probably related to voriconazole. Despite discontinuation of the drug, her condition deteriorated and ultimately resulted in mortality.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had multiple concurrent medications (riociguat continued, treprostinil briefly initiated, prednisone) and severe comorbidities (stage IV sarcoidosis, severe pulmonary hypertension, COVID-19 pneumonia); voriconazole required discontinuation of macitentan due to a category X interaction before initiation.
raw_record.extra_details: Voriconazole 300 mg BID started on day 39 of admission; acute liver injury developed about two weeks into treatment (approximately day 22 of voriconazole). Serial labs showed rising ALT (up to >3,600), AST (up to 1,364), and INR (up to 6.28); onset of abdominal fullness and fluctuating mental status. Voriconazole was discontinued on day 22 of therapy and supportive management including N-acetylcysteine was given, but the patient died. Diagnosis considers voriconazole the reason for acute hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: Among 25 patients with hematological malignancies and invasive aspergillosis receiving voriconazole, abnormal liver function tests occurred in 48% (12/25). Voriconazole-related serious adverse events (SAEs) included hepatotoxicities in 5 patients, with patterns of abnormal liver function tests being cholestatic (n=3), hepatic (n=1), or mixed (n=1). One patient (patient 7) required discontinuation of voriconazole because of severe hepatotoxicity deemed to be probably related, but finally died from hepatic failure 11 days after discontinuation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients had hematological malignancies and invasive aspergillosis; many had neutropenia, and some had undergone allogeneic HSCT, some with GVHD.
raw_record.extra_details: Abnormal liver function tests in 48% (12/25); voriconazole-related SAEs in 8/25 including hepatotoxicity in 5. Patterns of abnormal LFTs: cholestatic (n=3), hepatic (n=1), mixed (n=1). Two patients discontinued voriconazole due to SAEs; patient 7 had severe hepatotoxicity deemed probably related and died from hepatic failure 11 days after discontinuation. Median duration of IV voriconazole therapy 8 days (IQR 7-14); loading dose 12.0 mg/kg/day, maintenance 7.7 mg/kg/day. A trough plasma concentration of >=5.83 mg/l was the only independent risk factor independently associated with an SAE (adjusted OR 7.745, 95% CI 1.064-93.570; p=0.043). Trough concentrations did not depend on CYP2C19 genotype (EM/HEM/PM).

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 140 patients with mild-to-moderate hepatic dysfunction (Child-Pugh A or B) receiving voriconazole for suspected invasive aspergillosis, acute liver injury (ALI) occurred in 44 patients (31.4%). Drug causality was assessed with the RUCAM scale, and all 44 patients scored above six points, indicating a high probability of drug-related hepatotoxicity. High trough voriconazole plasma concentration (OR 1.59, 95% CI 1.29-2.02, p=0.013) and voriconazole treatment duration (OR 1.06, 95% CI 1.03-1.10, p=0.005) were identified as independent risk factors for hepatotoxicity in multivariate regression.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with mild-to-moderate hepatic dysfunction (Child-Pugh A or B); underlying hematologic malignancy (leukemia), immunosuppression, and hypoproteinemia were common; therapy for invasive aspergillosis/lung fungal infection.
raw_record.extra_details: ALI in 44/140 patients (31.4%); RUCAM scores above 6 (high probability of drug-related hepatotoxicity). Independent risk factors: trough voriconazole plasma concentration (OR 1.59, 95% CI 1.29-2.02, p=0.013) and voriconazole treatment duration (OR 1.06, 95% CI 1.03-1.10, p=0.005). Median trough concentration 5.07 mg/L in ALI group vs 2.70 mg/L control; median treatment duration 21 vs 9 days. Optimal cutoffs for ALI: trough VPC 3.81 mg/L (AUC 0.81) and treatment duration 10 days (AUC 0.74). All-cause mortality higher in ALI group (29.5% vs 10.4%, p=0.005) but fatalities mostly attributed to underlying hematologic malignancy. Tigecycline combination use not significantly associated (29.5% vs 18.8%, p=0.153). Possible mechanisms discussed: CYP450-dependent metabolism with hepatic impairment, reduced bile excretion retaining drug/metabolites including voriconazole N-oxide, and reduced glutathione reserves. Recommendations for therapeutic drug monitoring and dose adjustment.
