raw_record.support_text: Voriconazole-induced hepatotoxicity is described as a relatively rare but serious clinicopathologic entity. The paper reports a patient with alcoholic cirrhosis who developed hepatic encephalopathy due to voriconazole administered for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis and who showed marked improvement in mental status with dose adjustment of the drug. Histopathologic examination of the explanted liver revealed numerous rhomboid-shaped crystals deemed secondary to liver injury after voriconazole-induced hepatotoxicity. Voriconazole was considered the likely cause of the hepatic encephalopathy; the drug was discontinued, mental status gradually improved, and therapy was restarted at a reduced dose that was tolerated without further supratherapeutic levels.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pre-existing alcoholic cirrhosis (advanced decompensated liver disease, MELD 37-41); supratherapeutic plasma voriconazole trough (13 μg/mL) despite standard therapeutic dosing.
raw_record.extra_details: 51-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and prior Crohn's disease; voriconazole (Vfend) dosed 400 mg twice daily for 1 day then 150 mg twice daily, later reduced to 175 mg/day after rechallenge. Presented with progressive jaundice, ascites, splenomegaly; labs at second admission serum ammonia 194 μmol/L, ALT 35 U/L, ALP 94 U/L, total bilirubin 21.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 20.8 mg/dL, INR 2.1. Developed hepatic encephalopathy (confusion and stupor) about 10 days after discharge; improved after discontinuation and tolerated lower dose. Native liver biopsy at deceased donor liver transplant showed severe hepatocellular degeneration associated with cholestasis and marked hepatic cholangial/ductular proliferation with cirrhosis, suggestive of acute/subacute liver injury, plus intracellular and extracellular deep amber-yellow rhomboid crystals staining golden yellow under polarized light (voriconazole drug crystals). Alcoholic cirrhosis and decompensated liver failure required liver transplant; death not attributed directly to voriconazole.

raw_record.support_text: In an observational study of adults with severe liver dysfunction treated with at least 4 doses of voriconazole, 69% of patients showed changes in liver function tests during therapy: elevated transaminases in 35%, cholestasis in 15%, or a combination of both in 45%. There was a correlation between an initial loading dose greater than 300 mg (4.5 mg/kg) and the risk of hepatotoxicity (p < 0.001).

raw_record.support_text: Lapatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 and epidermal growth factor receptor, used in advanced or metastatic breast cancer. In a study seeking genomic markers for DILI susceptibility, a significant association of HLA-DQA1*02:01 with lapatinib-related DILI was found in exploratory (35 cases, OR=2.6, P=0.03) and validation (24 cases, OR=9.0, P=0.00008) studies.
raw_record.extra_details: Lapatinib-related DILI discussed in the context of genomic susceptibility markers. HLA-DQA1*02:01 association: exploratory 35 cases/283 controls OR=2.6 (P=0.03), validation 24 cases/155 controls OR=9.0 (P=0.00008); PPV 0.17, NPV 0.97; allele frequency 0.13 Whites, 0.10 Chinese, 0.09 African-Americans, 0.008 Japanese; indication advanced or metastatic breast cancer.

raw_record.support_text: Lapatinib (Tykerb/Tyverb, GlaxoSmithKline), a HER2 and EGFR inhibitor approved for advanced or metastatic HER2-positive breast cancer, has been associated with liver injury and a low incidence of National Cancer Institute CTCAE grade 3 isolated alanine aminotransferase (ALT) elevation (3%) and potentially life-threatening concurrent ALT elevation with hyperbilirubinemia (Hy's Law, 0.6%). Previous investigations found the Class II allele HLA-DRB1*07:01 (and DQA1*02:01 in linkage disequilibrium) is associated with lapatinib-induced liver injury and Hy's Law cases, and this association was prospectively validated in a large, well-controlled, randomized clinical trial.
raw_record.extra_details: Low incidence (~3%) NCI CTCAE grade 3 isolated ALT elevation and ~0.6% potentially life-threatening concurrent ALT elevation with hyperbilirubinemia (Hy's Law) in treated breast cancer patients. HLA-DRB1*07:01 (with DQA1*02:01) associated with lapatinib-induced liver injury and Hy's Law; high negative predictive value but moderate positive predictive value limits it as a prospective predictive biomarker. Association prospectively validated in the EGF105485 (TEACH, NCT00374322) randomized Phase III trial of lapatinib vs placebo for 12 months in HER2-positive early breast cancer; GWAS and whole-genome sequencing identified no additional associations beyond HLA-DRB1*07:01. Approved for use in combination with other targeted chemotherapy agents.

raw_record.support_text: The study evaluated predictors of time to lapatinib-induced hepatotoxicity in a retrospective cohort. Lapatinib was the treatment under study, and hepatotoxicity was defined as an outcome attributable to lapatinib. Concomitant use of H2 blockers significantly increased the hazard of time to lapatinib-induced hepatotoxicity (adjusted HR 1.855, 95% CI 1.190–2.892), and use of CYP3A4 inducers significantly increased the incidence of lapatinib-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All participants were female patients with metastatic breast cancer, so sex differences could not be assessed; retrospective single-center design.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective cohort study of lapatinib-treated patients. H2 blocker use was an independent predictor of time to hepatotoxicity (unadjusted and adjusted HR 1.855, 95% CI 1.190–2.892 in Model I; HR 1.842, 95% CI 1.181–2.872 in Model II), while PPI use appeared protective (unadjusted HR 0.602, 95% CI 0.394–0.919; age, height, and BSA were not significant predictors). CYP3A4 inducers significantly increased the incidence of hepatotoxicity, attributed mechanistically to increased reactive-metabolite formation. CYP3A4 inhibitors were not a significant factor. Concomitant H2 blockers and CYP3A4 inducers were concluded to be important factors increasing hepatotoxicity incidence.

raw_record.support_text: Hy's law cases were identified during treatment of cancer patients with the HER2/EGFR dual tyrosine kinase inhibitor lapatinib (Tykerb/Tyverb) in a previous study, and liver chemistry data of 20 oncology patients with HLA markers meeting the Hy's law threshold were examined. The authors note that, based on pharmacogenetic investigations of lapatinib-associated hepatotoxicity and previously reported work implicating HLA-mediated mechanisms in drug-induced liver injury, carriage of specific HLA alleles (HLA-DQA*02:01/DRB1*07:01) is considered a strong and possibly diagnostic indicator of DILI caused by specific drugs; a breast cancer patient carrying at least one copy of these alleles is more susceptible to lapatinib-associated liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Breast cancer oncology patients treated with lapatinib; susceptibility conditioned on carriage of at least one copy of the HLA-DQA*02:01/DRB1*07:01 alleles; patient population with pre-existing metastatic disease and heavy prior treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Lapatinib is a HER2/EGFR dual tyrosine kinase inhibitor (brands Tykerb/Tyverb). 20 oncology patients with HLA markers meeting the Hy's law threshold were examined in a targeted safety study. HLA-mediated mechanism implicated; lapatinib studies were not included in the aggregated GSK oncology data sets used to derive the new mDISH thresholds.

Among three patients who received lapatinib at 900 mg/m²/dose BID, grade 3 toxicity (1 diarrhea, 2 liver dysfunction) developed, and 2 of the 3 were removed from therapy; the 900 mg/m²/dose BID dose was deemed too toxic and the study was amended to lower the starting dose to 700 mg/m²/dose BID.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatic abnormalities are estimated to occur in less than 1% of patients taking imipramine. Jaundice has been documented in several cases, usually with a cholestatic biochemical picture, and liver biopsies in four cases showed features consistent with phenothiazine-type cholestatic changes. A rechallenge with imipramine in the Weaver et al. (1977) report produced prompt but transient elevation of SGOT, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin. The present case is described as the longest reported period of jaundice after imipramine, lasting more than 12 months, with initial biopsies showing marked cholestasis and absent bile ducts progressing to portal fibrosis and early-cirrhosis morphology.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic abnormalities in <1% of patients; typical presentation with a prodrome of fever, myalgias, nausea and anorexia lasting several days before bilirubinuria, jaundice and/or pruritus; clinical symptoms developed 2-3 weeks after initiation; resolution within several days to weeks of discontinuing therapy. Reported case had jaundice for >12 months; initial biopsies showed marked cholestasis with loss of visible bile ducts that later reappeared, with progression to portal fibrosis and early-cirrhosis morphology (still alive at 134 months). Weaver et al. (1977) rechallenge produced prompt but transient SGOT, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin elevations. An 80-yr-old woman given both imipramine and desipramine developed severe exfoliative dermatitis, severe LFT abnormalities, and died of presumed sepsis 8 weeks later (co-attribution, competing cause).

raw_record.support_text: In all seven children described, the most likely cause of the liver damage was halothane; other causes of postoperative hepatitis, including viral and bacterial infection, hypoxia, hypotension, and other drug toxicities, were absent. All cases had a history of previous halothane anaesthesia, and halothane-related antibodies were detected in six of the seven children. One of the seven children (case 6) died; at necropsy the liver showed confluent necrosis with extensive cell loss and reticulin collapse.

raw_record.extra_details: Seven paediatric cases of halothane hepatitis (case series) referenced from the National Halothane Study and retrospective data. Adults: mortality 56% among 86 adults with severe hepatitis after halothane anaesthesia, similar in seropositive (~75% with halothane-related antibodies) and seronegative patients. Retrospective incidence in children was 2/165 400 halothane anaesthetics in one study and 1/200 311 in another. Laboratory findings included markedly elevated bilirubin (up to 861 µmol/l) and aspartate transaminase (>1500–5080 IU/l). Halothane antibody present in 6/7 children; in seronegative cases antibody may be bound to antigen/immune complexes. One child (case 6) died; another boy placed on the liver-grafting list started on methylprednisolone died on postoperative day 18 with a shrunken 480 g liver showing confluent necrosis and reticulin collapse. Adult National Halothane Study: unexplained severe massive liver cell necrosis incidence 1 per 35 000 anaesthetics, rising to 1 in 3500 after multiple exposures. Possible cross-sensitisation with enflurane is discussed but the halothane antibody did not react with the enflurane-related antigen.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports three patients in whom hepatitis developed in relation to halothane anesthesia. The authors conclude that the evidence supports the diagnosis of a halothane-induced sensitization reaction with hepatitis, based on the characteristic temporal relation between halothane exposure and fever/jaundice, onset with chills and high fever, significant eosinophilia, antecedent atopy and drug-hypersensitivity reactions, occurrence of the hepatitis after a second halothane exposure in two of the three cases, and histologic features consistent with drug-induced hepatitis. Biopsies showed severe hepatitis with bridging necrosis, and all three patients recovered fully.

raw_record.extra_details: Serial SGOT (normal 15–35 IU/ml) and serum bilirubin (normal 0.1–1.4 mg/dl) values were recorded after halothane exposure for each patient (e.g., Patient 1 SGOT 1600 IU/ml at 2 days, bilirubin 2.66 mg/dl at 7 days; Patient 2 SGOT 2480 IU/ml at 6 days, bilirubin 13.50 mg/dl at 13 days). Histology showed severe hepatitis with bridging necrosis and, in one case, granulomata and giant cells; Patient 3 had eosinophilia rising to 11%. The authors noted absence of epidemiologic or serologic evidence of type B hepatitis and excluded postoperative cholestasis or centrilobular necrosis attributable to shock/multiple transfusions. All patients recovered fully.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 11 patients with halothane hepatitis seen at two hospitals during the last four years, prompted in part by the authors' experience that at least some of the cases could have been avoided. It notes reported mortality of 67 to 96%, which is probably biased by inclusion of more severe cases, but maintains that halothane hepatitis must be regarded as a very dangerous condition, even though its occurrence is still disputed by some anaesthetists.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 patients (Cases 1-11) at two hospitals over four years; seven referred from other hospitals to a liver disease unit and four treated at a regional general hospital, with presumably higher mortality in the referred group due to more severe cases. Reported mortality 67-96% (likely biased toward severe cases). Occurrence of halothane hepatitis is disputed by some anaesthetists, and at least some of the cases could have been avoided. Halothane administered as an anaesthetic agent.

raw_record.support_text: Sera from three patients with halothane hepatitis reacted with halothane-induced neoantigens in rat liver microsomes by immunoblotting: patient 1 recognized 100 kDa and 76 kDa neoantigens, patient 2 the 100, 76, 59 and 54 kDa neoantigens, and patient 3 the 57 kDa neoantigen. These neoantigens were shown to carry the trifluoroacetyl (TFA) hapten derived from halothane metabolism, establishing the immune response to halothane-modified liver proteins in humans.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis is an immune-mediated form of DILI. Antibodies in the sera of halothane hepatitis patients recognize TFA-modified neoantigens (100, 76, 59, 54, 57 kDa) that are formed when the reactive CF3COX metabolite of halothane covalently binds liver microsomal proteins. The 59 kDa-TFA neoantigen was identified as a microsomal carboxylesterase glycoprotein (EC 3.1.1.1); antibodies reacted only negligibly with the native unmodified protein. TFA-lysine only partially inhibits antibody binding, indicating epitopes comprise the TFA hapten plus portions of the carrier protein. Similar TFA-labeled proteins were detected in the liver of a halothane-treated patient (100, 76, 59, 54 and 57 kDa forms), supporting relevance of the rat neoantigens to human halothane hepatitis. TFA labeling occurs via direct reaction of CF3COX with proteins; sodium trifluoroacetate, ethyl trifluoroacetate, and trifluoroethanol administered to rats produced no detectable protein labeling.

raw_record.support_text: Antimitochondrial antibodies were detected by the fluorescent antibody technique in seven of nine sera from patients with jaundice after halothane anesthesia, indicating drug-induced jaundice following halothane exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Exposure was via halothane anesthesia. Antimitochondrial antibodies detected in 7 of 9 jaundiced patients with the indirect fluorescent antibody technique; interpreted as helping differentiate drug-induced jaundice from viral hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 14 jaundiced patients divided by cause of jaundice, Group II consisted of seven patients with presumably previously normal livers and acute onset hepatitis of different causes, including halothane-induced hepatitis in three patients; diagnoses were based on patient history, clinical characteristics, and liver biopsy or autopsy findings.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients with halothane-induced acute hepatitis were included as one cause among seven patients in a jaundice cohort (Group II, hepatocellular jaundice) studied for plasma amino acid patterns; diagnosis was based on history, clinical characteristics, and liver biopsy or autopsy findings.

raw_record.support_text: Halothane-associated DILI (hepatic necrosis) case reports were analyzed for liver-injury pattern, eosinophilia, hepatic necrosis, inflammatory reaction, and death/liver transplantation outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: 49 individual case reports; median age 49 y; 36 female/13 male; median treatment duration not stated; HC 100%, Cs/mixed 0%; peripheral eosinophilia present in 47% (17/49 reported); hepatic eosinophilia present in 33% (18/49 reported); hepatic necrosis 89%; inflammatory reaction 70%; death or liver transplant 53%; liver biopsy reported in 45/49 cases.

raw_record.support_text: The paper studies halothane hepatitis in human patients, characterizing a 63-kDa liver microsomal protein that is covalently modified by the trifluoroacetyl halide metabolite of halothane and serves as a neoantigen. Only 1 of 40 patients diagnosed with halothane hepatitis had serum antibodies that reacted with the TFA-63-kDa protein at a level significantly higher than antibodies from a variety of control patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Study identifies a 63-kDa rat liver microsomal protein covalently modified by the trifluoroacetyl halide metabolite of halothane, proposed as a neoantigen relevant to halothane hepatitis. Immune response was assessed by ELISA of serum antibodies from halothane hepatitis patients against the native and TFA-63-kDa protein; only 1 of 40 diagnosed halothane hepatitis patients showed antibody reactivity significantly above controls.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports halothane-induced hepatitis in human patients, detected via anti-TFA antibodies. Of six patients examined, three were negative for hepatitis A and B virus, partially confirming unexplained hepatitis following halothane anesthesia, though non-A, non-B viral hepatitis could not be excluded. The specificity of the antibody response for patients developing halothane-induced hepatitis was confirmed by the absence of antibody in individuals exposed to halothane without developing liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Six patients examined for anti-TFA (trifluoroacetyl) antibodies; 3 of 6 were negative for hepatitis A and B viruses; non-A, non-B viral hepatitis could not be excluded in any patient. Antibody was absent in halothane-exposed individuals who did not develop liver disease. Mechanism discussion proposes halothane is metabolized in hepatocytes to reactive species that alter protein antigenicity.

raw_record.support_text: Sera from 10 patients with halothane hepatitis stained TFA-labeled proteins in hepatocytes from a rat exposed to halothane, whereas sera from nine patients with multiple halothane exposures but no evidence of toxicity did not stain the same halothane-exposed rat liver. This identifies halothane as causing an immune-mediated hepatotoxicity directed against trifluoroacetylated hepatic proteins (halothane hepatitis).
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism is an immune response against hepatic proteins altered by the trifluoroacetyl (TFA) metabolite acting as immunogens. Evidence: sera from 10 patients with halothane hepatitis immunostained TFA-labeled proteins in halothane-exposed rat hepatocytes, while sera from 9 patients with multiple halothane exposure without toxicity did not.

raw_record.support_text: The results indicate that neoantigens of 100, 76 and 57 kD, recognized by antibodies from patients with halothane hepatitis, are expressed in livers of humans anesthetized with halothane. Livers from two patients exposed to halothane expressed the neoantigens, whereas normal human liver and livers from patients exposed to other anesthetics did not. The discussion states that halothane is metabolized by cytochrome P-450 to reactive metabolites, and that expression of the neoantigens, in susceptible individuals, evokes the antibody response underlying halothane hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis is an immune-mediated injury in susceptible individuals; patients with halothane hepatitis develop antibodies to halothane-induced liver neoantigens (100, 76, and 57 kD) that are also found in livers of halothane-exposed rats and rabbits. Halothane is metabolized in the liver by cytochrome P-450 via oxidative and reductive pathways to reactive metabolites; neoantigen expression occurs by covalent binding of the oxidative metabolite TFA-halide to microsomal proteins, with antibodies binding epitopes combining the TFA hapten plus protein structural features. Human neoantigens were not detected in liver samples from three halothane hepatitis patients (biopsies taken at 6, 23 and 26 days after exposure, following liver damage), attributed to antigen loss from hepatocyte destruction or protein turnover. Control sera (normal blood donor, patient with multiple halothane exposures without liver damage, acetaminophen-overdose liver failure patient) did not recognize the neoantigens.

raw_record.support_text: All 38 Japanese patients had been diagnosed from clinical and biological evidence as having halothane hepatitis, with onset of jaundice or abnormal liver function within less than 3 weeks of anesthesia; none abused alcohol or took other known hepatotoxic drugs at illness onset. Five cases were fulminant hepatitis; two who received large fresh blood transfusions for fulminant hepatic failure developed secondary chronic active hepatitis and liver cirrhosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis developed within <3 weeks of halothane anesthesia in all 38 cases. Jaundice group (24 cases) had female:male ratio 2:1 (4:1 among fulminant cases), pyrexia (>38°C) in all jaundice patients, eosinophilia (>=6%) in 64–68%, and 42% had prior halothane anesthesia; 5 cases of fulminant hepatitis were included. Two patients had secondary chronic active hepatitis and liver cirrhosis attributed to large fresh-blood transfusion for fulminant hepatic failure. HLA-Bw44 was increased in non-jaundice patients (RR 6.86, P<0.001) and HLA-Bw52 and DR2 in jaundice patients; Aw24-Bw52-DR2 haplotype frequency was high in jaundice patients (Hf=0.2362). All patients recuperated with complete recovery of liver function except the two with transfusion-related complications.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports patients afflicted with halothane hepatitis, some of whom died from complications of fulminant hepatic failure. Patients 3 and 5 exhibited normal levels of cross-reactive proteins yet both died from complications of fulminant hepatic failure and exhibited very large elevations in plasma AST indicating massive hepatic necrosis. Seven patients with halothane hepatitis were analyzed for expression of 52-kDa and 64-kDa cross-reactive proteins, while patient 6, who did not develop encephalopathy and survived, exhibited very low amounts of these proteins.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven patients with halothane hepatitis were studied (patients 1-7). Patients 3 and 5 died from complications of fulminant hepatic failure with very large elevations in plasma AST indicating massive hepatic necrosis. Patient 6 survived without encephalopathy. Liver samples were collected at least 17 days after halothane exposure for six patients and 6 days for the remaining patient. This record reflects the halothane-induced hepatitis attribution in a human case series; the paper's main focus is on the immunochemical characterization of cross-reactive 52-kDa and 64-kDa proteins and epoxide hydrolase, which are not themselves the injuring agents.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 'Our patient with halothane hepatitis,' who received total body washouts and awoke completely with normal cerebral function, but whose hepatic reserve was insufficient; massive liver necrosis was seen at autopsy when she eventually died. This attributes the patient's hepatitis and fatal massive hepatic necrosis to the inhalational anesthetic halothane in the context of a case managed with total body washout for hepatic coma.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient received total body washout for hepatic coma, awoke with normal cerebral function, but hepatic reserve was insufficient; massive liver necrosis was confirmed at autopsy. Mentioned in the context of a series/washout case discussing treatment of halothane hepatitis and Reye's syndrome.

raw_record.support_text: The diagnosis of halothane hepatitis is primarily clinical, with fever, chills, anorexia, nausea, myalgia, mild abdominal pain, and jaundice occurring in combinations. Jaundice occurs in 10-28 days following a single exposure to halothane and earlier (3-17 days) in cases of multiple exposures. The paper frames halothane as an established cause of this postoperative hepatitis, with an anesthetic's recurrent well-documented hepatitis relapsing on a controlled halothane challenge and resolving with avoidance.
raw_record.extra_details: Two postoperative cases (multiple exposures in case 1, single exposure in case 2); other causes of jaundice excluded (sepsis, surgical trauma, ileus, other drug toxicities, hypoxemia/hypotension, hepatitis A/B, CMV, EBV). Case 2 had a more gradual onset of cholestatic hepatitis. Fever is typically the first sign after a fever-free interval; about 21% of adults have no fever. Histology may show multifocal spotty centrilobular necrosis with eosinophilic infiltrate but is often absent or indistinguishable from viral hepatitis; a spectrum of severity occurs from massive hepatic necrosis to milder injury. Halothane hepatitis can be complicated by fulminant hepatic failure with encephalopathy; positive halothane antibodies found in 75% of patients with fulminant hepatic failure, 70% without encephalopathy; eosinophilia in a minority. A controlled halothane challenge in an affected anesthesiologist reproduced hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper identifies halothane as a drug implicated in inducing liver injury, being the causative agent in 5 of 53 patients with drug-related liver disease. Halothane produced both cytotoxic and cholestatic damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane was the causative agent in 5 of 53 patients; produced both cytotoxic and cholestatic damage.

raw_record.support_text: Among 15 patients listed for a highly urgent orthotopic liver transplantation (OLT) due to acute liver failure at the center, 25% of cases were classified as medication induced, with halothane and propyothiouracyl (an apparent misspelling of propylthiouracil) named as the causal agents. These drug-induced cases resulted in listing for urgent transplantation, along with the other acute liver failure etiologies reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed as one cause of medication-induced acute liver failure among 15 patients at a single transplantation center; the medication-induced category accounted for 25% of the acute liver failure patients (combined with propylthiouracil). Of the 15 ALF patients overall, 6 were transplanted with 100% survival, 6 died awaiting OLT, and 4 recovered spontaneously.

raw_record.support_text: Case 1: a 36-year-old woman developed fever, jaundice, and markedly elevated transaminases beginning ~36 hours after a second halothane exposure (umbilical herniorrhaphy, following herniorrhaphy under methoxyflurane). A liver biopsy 21 days after jaundice onset showed swollen centrolobular cells with cell-membrane breakdown, focal centrolobular necrosis marked by pigmented macrophages, and moderate cholestasis, consistent with drug-induced cholestatic jaundice with early hepatic necrosis. She recovered.
raw_record.extra_details: Biopsy disclosed swollen centrolobular cells forming foamy cord syncytium, rare acidophilic body, focal resolved centrolobular necrosis with pigmented macrophages, moderate cholestasis, no eosinophils. Described as similar to drug cholestatic jaundice but with greater cell swelling than most cholestatic agents; the earliest stage of liver-cell injury in the series.

raw_record.support_text: A national surveillance program of fulminant hepatic failure found that of the first 150 cases reported in October 1968, 36 were associated with halothane, ranking halothane second only to viral hepatitis as the prime cause of fulminant hepatic failure. Thirty-one of the 36 patients died, and 75% (27/36) had received halothane more than once. Hepatitis occurred much more frequently after halothane than after cyclopropane or ether.
raw_record.extra_details: Halogenated hydrocarbon anesthetic. Injury manifested as fulminant hepatic failure with marked hepatic necrosis clinically characterized by deepening jaundice, hepatic coma, fluid retention, clotting disturbances, and death. 36 of the first 150 fulminant hepatic failure cases reported to the 1967 national surveillance program (~42 institutions) were associated with halothane, ranking second to viral hepatitis; 31/36 died; 27/36 had multiple halothane exposures. Reported rechallenge: an anesthetist with prior jaundice after halothane use developed a sustained shaking chill, severe muscle cramps, then typical hepatitis after 5 minutes of 1-2% halothane in oxygen in a controlled study (Klatskin). Since 1963 reports there has been debate as to whether halothane is a true hepatotoxin or a sensitizing agent; a hypersensitivity reaction is suspected because manifestations could not be reproduced in laboratory animals, with some patients showing eosinophilia, drug rashes, and antimitochondrial antibodies. Halothane-associated hepatitis was clinically/pathologically indistinguishable from fulminant viral hepatitis. Hepatitis occurred more frequently after halothane than after cyclopropane or ether.

raw_record.support_text: Serum antibodies from a group of 40 halothane hepatitis patients reacted to a significantly greater extent with both the purified trifluoroacetylated (TFA-) 80-kDa protein (p < 0.001) and the native 80-kDa protein (p < 0.001) than did sera from 32 control patients in an ELISA. Three of the 40 halothane hepatitis patients, but none of the controls, had antibodies reacting appreciably more with the TFA-80-kDa protein than with the native protein. This indicates that halothane hepatitis patients develop an immune response to liver proteins in which the covalently bound trifluoroacetyl group from the reactive trifluoroacetyl halide metabolite of halothane is a key epitope.
raw_record.extra_details: Study concerns the immunopathogenesis of halothane hepatitis: halothane is metabolized to a reactive trifluoroacetyl halide that covalently trifluoroacetylates liver microsomal proteins (e.g., an 80-kDa protein and previously reported 63-kDa target). Serum antibodies from 40 halothane hepatitis patients reacted significantly more with purified TFA-80-kDa and native 80-kDa proteins by ELISA than did sera from 32 control patients (p < 0.001 for both); 3/40 patients but no controls reacted appreciably more with the TFA-80-kDa over the native protein (absorbances 1.019 vs 0.331, 0.755 vs 0.229, 0.613 vs 0.137). An immunochemically related protein was detected in human liver microsomes. Supporting data from halothane-treated rats are included.

raw_record.support_text: Halothane is listed at range 18 among the drugs most implicated in DILI with established diagnosis using RUCAM in 15 cases. Toxic liver injury due to the volatile anesthetic Halothane is frequently associated with the appearance of serum anti-CYP 2E1 antibodies, and clinical studies verified that 25/56 (45%) patients diagnosed with Halothane hepatitis have autoantibodies that react with human CYP 2E1.
raw_record.extra_details: Volatile anesthetic; ranked 18 among drugs most implicated in DILI; established diagnosis using RUCAM in 15 cases; serum anti-CYP 2E1 antibodies in 25/56 (45%) patients with Halothane hepatitis; CYP 2E1 is the predominant oxidative-metabolism isoform (CYP 2A6 contributory; in vitro reductive pathway via CYP 2A6 and 3A4); trifluoroacetylated CYP 2E1 may bypass immunologic tolerance.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses 'halothane hepatitis' as a recognized clinical entity, reporting antimitochondrial antibodies in 10 of 15 patients with halothane hepatitis, and frames it as a differential diagnostic consideration versus viral hepatitis. It also describes patients with jaundice after exposure to halothane, and notes that failure to demonstrate Australia antigen in their sera militates against a viral-hepatitis cause.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis featured jaundice after halothane exposure in a series including 15 patients; differential diagnosis against viral hepatitis. Antimitochondrial antibodies found in 10 of 15 patients. Lymphocyte stimulation in response to halothane was detected and correlations noted; sensitization was temporary and not detectable before jaundice appearance. Australia antigen was absent from sera. The paper leaves open whether the sensitizing agent is unmodified halothane, a metabolite, or a protein-halothane complex.

raw_record.support_text: In the Fulminant Hepatic Failure Surveillance Study analysis of the first 150 cases from 73 centers, 35 of the patients developed massive liver necrosis less than three weeks after halothane anesthesia, and 27 (77 per cent) of these had multiple exposures to halothane. The paper describes halothane-associated fulminant hepatic failure as a small but clinically important risk, noting that this complication was present in nearly one quarter of the reported cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant Hepatic Failure Surveillance Study; 150 cases collected from 73 centers; 35 patients developed massive liver necrosis less than 3 weeks after halothane anesthesia; 27 (77%) had multiple exposures to halothane; risk judged small but complication present in nearly one quarter of reported cases. Paragraph 57 notes postoperative 'unexplained' fever after halothane exposure is an important warning sign to investigate before further exposure, and advises avoiding multiple exposure when possible.

raw_record.support_text: In a lymphocyte-stimulation study, diagnoses of drug-induced hepatitis were made following halothane anesthesia in nine patients (and methoxyflurane in one). Halothane-induced stimulation of lymphocytes, measured by ³H-thymidine incorporation into DNA, was observed in ten of 15 such patients, while controls (three halothane-exposed patients without jaundice, nine patients with hepatic disease, six healthy persons) showed none. The authors conclude this supports the hypothesis that sensitization to halothane may be involved in the pathogenesis of hepatic damage following halothane.
raw_record.extra_details: Nine of 15 patients with diagnoses of drug-induced hepatitis had hepatitis following halothane anesthesia. Halothane-induced lymphocyte stimulation (serologically measured by incorporation of ³H-thymidine into DNA) was seen in ten of 15 such patients versus none of the controls (three halothane-exposed patients who did not develop jaundice, nine with hepatic disease, six healthy persons), supporting a sensitization mechanism in hepatic damage following halothane anesthesia.

raw_record.support_text: Halothane-induced hepatitis occurred with an infrequent and low-titered specific (LKM) antibody: anti-LKM1 was present in 25% of cases at low titer, and two of the six cases tested were positive.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane-induced hepatitis associated with infrequent, low-titer anti-LKM1 antibody (present in 25% of cases); 2 of 6 cases tested were positive.

raw_record.support_text: Of the 32 patients with hepatic encephalopathy investigated, 20 had fulminant hepatic failure, including three with halothane-associated hepatitis. All were stuporose or in coma with grade III or grade IV encephalopathy.
raw_record.extra_details: Three of the 20 patients with fulminant hepatic failure had halothane-associated hepatitis progressing to fulminant hepatic failure; all patients were stuporose or in coma with grade III-IV encephalopathy.

raw_record.support_text: The paper investigates halothane hepatitis, a drug-induced liver injury that occurs in patients exposed to the anesthetic halothane. Sera from halothane hepatitis patients recognized TFA-protein adducts and the E2 subunit of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH), suggesting molecular mimicry between TFA-protein adducts and constitutively expressed self-proteins as part of the immune etiology of halothane hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis, a drug-induced hepatitis caused by the volatile anesthetic halothane, is treated as an established clinical entity. The study focuses on the immunochemical etiology: sera from several halothane hepatitis patients (patients 1-7) contained antibodies against hepatic TFA-protein adducts that cross-reacted with the E2 subunit of PDH and a 52 kDa protein, consistent with molecular mimicry. In 5 of 7 patients, abnormally low immunodetectable amounts of the 52 and 64 kDa proteins were present in liver biopsies; aberrant expression was suggested as a susceptibility factor. OSHA-adjacent mechanistic details: antibody recognition inhibited by N-ε-TFA-L-lysine and lipoic acid. Patients 9-11 died of post-operative cardiac failure after anesthesia with drugs other than halothane (not halothane-attributed injury). Occupational/environmental exposure to HCFCs plus later clinical exposure to halothane, enflurane, or isoflurane was raised as a possible cross-sensitization risk but no DILI claim is made for enflurane or isoflurane.

raw_record.support_text: Among 14 patients with fulminant hepatitis, the etiologies included drug-induced hepatitis in 4 cases, attributed to acetaminophen (2 cases), isoniazid (1 case), and halothane (1 case).
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as cause of drug-induced fulminant hepatitis in 1 of 14 patients in the study cohort; the study assessed plasma CEA levels in patients with maximum hepatic dysfunction.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports on patients with halothane-related hepatitis: lymphocyte transformation testing was uniformly negative in 29 such patients, and the test was judged not useful in diagnosing this condition as opposed to viral hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: 29 patients with halothane-related hepatitis; lymphocyte transformation testing was uniformly negative in all 29 and was not found useful for diagnosis versus viral hepatitis. Halothane is an inhalational anaesthetic; phenotype is hepatitis (acute fulminant-type context).

raw_record.support_text: Analysis of 94 reports to the Swedish Adverse Drug Reaction Committee of patients with liver injury after surgery and halothane anaesthesia (including 13 fatal cases) revealed no other factors responsible for the liver injury than the halothane administration. Eighty-two percent of the total material and 12 of 13 fatal cases had multiple exposures, and the liver injury appeared more severe after repeated exposures, with higher maximum serum bilirubin and SGOT values after an increasing number of halothane exposures.
raw_record.extra_details: 94 ADR reports evaluated in three steps by the Swedish Adverse Drug Reaction Committee (medical officer, working party, full committee) with complete medical records; 13 fatal cases; 82% of the total and 12/13 fatal cases had multiple halothane exposures; injury more severe after repeated exposures with higher maximum serum bilirubin and SGOT values; reports from 1966-1972 (Böttiger et al. 1973) plus 1973 cases.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes halothane hepatic necrosis as a human liver-injury entity with age-related morbidity and mortality similar to viral hepatitis. In the authors' small series of five patients with halothane hepatic necrosis, there was one death, in an adolescent female. Related text notes that unexplained postoperative fever is one of the most constant features indicating liver damage from halothane, and that jaundice is typically delayed unless there have been multiple exposures to halothane anesthesia.
raw_record.extra_details: Series of five patients with halothane hepatic necrosis; one death in an adolescent female. Unexplained postoperative fever is a constant feature indicating liver damage; jaundice typically delayed unless multiple halothane anesthesia exposures. Age-related morbidity and mortality similar to viral hepatitis. Presented under the heading 'Halothane Hepatitis'.

raw_record.support_text: Immunochemical studies showed that sera from the majority of halothane hepatitis patients contain IgG antibodies that react with halothane-carrier conjugates expressed in the livers of animals or humans treated with halothane. These antibodies are thought to play a role in the pathogenesis of this drug reaction because they mediate antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity killing of hepatocytes from halothane-treated rabbits in vitro and are not detectable in sera from normal individuals, from halothane-exposed patients without liver damage, or from patients with viral or intrinsic-compound hepatitis such as acetaminophen.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis is an immunologically mediated drug reaction. Sera from the majority of halothane hepatitis patients contain IgG antibodies (isotype IgG) reacting with halothane-carrier conjugates; the antibodies mediate ADCC killing of halothane-treated rabbit hepatocytes in vitro and are absent in normal individuals, halothane-exposed patients without liver damage, and patients with viral or acetaminophen hepatitis. The neoantigens (100, 76, 59, 57, 54 kd) were localized to the microsomal fraction and identified as trifluoroacetyl (TFA)-carrier proteins; of 68 sera tested, 41 (60%) contained antibodies to halothane-induced neoantigens. Findings are drawn from patients and from immunochemical studies of halothane-treated rabbit and rat liver microsomes.

raw_record.support_text: In patients with the presumed diagnosis of halothane hepatitis, antibody sensitization to halothane-altered rabbit liver membranes was detected in 8 out of 12 patients using indirect immunofluorescence, antibody cell-mediated cytotoxicity, and confirmed by ELISA; such circulating antibodies were not found in patients with halothane exposure but no liver damage or with other liver diseases. Sensitization was also demonstrated by testing lymphocytes in vitro. The paper further describes halothane metabolism (oxidative route) being required for expression of drug-related antigens on liver cell membranes, with at least three polypeptide antigens localised to the microsomal subfraction.
raw_record.extra_details: Antibody to halothane-altered (rabbit) liver membranes detected in 8/12 patients with presumed halothane hepatitis by indirect immunofluorescence, antibody cell-mediated cytotoxicity, and ELISA; not detected in halothane-exposed patients without liver damage or in other liver diseases. Sensitization also demonstrated by in vitro lymphocyte testing, with some sero-negative cases' lymphocytes secreting halothane antibody into supernatant. Oxidative halothane metabolism after enzyme induction required for antigen expression on liver cell membranes; immunoblotting revealed at least three polypeptide antigens in the microsomal subfraction of liver homogenates. Studies in animals and humans suggested all exposed individuals generate the antigen, with the defect in susceptible patients lying in the immune response rather than antigen generation.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses patients with halothane hepatitis and contrasts their autoantibody patterns with those in patients with hepatic reactions caused by drugs other than halothane, describing cases of hepatitis caused by tienilic acid and dihydralazine. In halothane hepatitis, sera contain autoantibodies against multiple human hepatic microsomal proteins, with marked inter-individual variation in response intensity and in the number and nature of the microsomal proteins recognized; formation of TFA-modified protein antigens is proposed to cause immune dysregulation in exposed patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis studied in human patients; sera contain autoantibodies to multiple TFA-modified hepatic microsomal proteins with marked inter-individual variation in intensity and in the number/nature of proteins recognized; the most intense responses were seen in three patients with hepatitis; immune-mediated reaction proposed via covalent binding of TFA-groups and immune dysregulation; autoantibodies also seen in some halothane-treated patients without hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: A single case of drug-induced hepatitis was attributed to halothane, occurring three days after exposure, among 940 patients who received the drug in hospital.
raw_record.extra_details: One case of drug-induced hepatitis attributed to halothane, three days after exposure; 940 patients were exposed in hospital. BCDSP monitoring cohort.

raw_record.support_text: Halothane hepatitis is described as a well-recognized entity: acute liver failure after halothane anesthesia is characterized by extensive liver necrosis and carries a mortality rate of about 80%, with death due primarily to bleeding, infection, and renal failure. Encephalopathy may be a nonlethal complication. In three patients with halothane hepatitis, bleeding was controlled with fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate, and platelets; infection was controlled with isolation and avoidance of steroids; and acute renal failure was managed with hemodialysis; these patients survived 18, 9, and 1 month after discharge.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis following anesthesia; acute liver failure with extensive liver necrosis, ~80% mortality; death due primarily to bleeding, infection, and renal failure; encephalopathy may be a nonlethal complication. In three affected patients, management used fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate, platelets, isolation precautions without steroids, and hemodialysis; survivals post-discharge were 18, 9, and 1 month.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe humans with halothane-induced liver injury: one patient recovered from severe hepatic failure after four halothane exposures and later bled from esophageal varices with liver fibrosis on biopsy; three patients in Boston developed postoperative cholestatic jaundice after multiple halothane exposures, with biopsy in one showing hepatocellular disease; and serum from seven patients with halothane-associated hepatitis tested negative for Australia antigen. The clinical and pathological diagnoses were 'massive hepatic necrosis, probably due to halothane', and halothane hepatitis was regarded as not dose-related but with occasional fatal sequelae.
raw_record.extra_details: Injury followed multiple/repeated anesthetic exposures (e.g., four exposures in one patient) and was described as not dose-related; presentations included postoperative cholestatic jaundice, hepatocellular disease on biopsy, hepatitis, hepatic fibrosis with esophageal variceal bleeding after recovery, and massive hepatic necrosis; occasional fatal sequelae were noted; serum of 7 halothane-hepatitis patients was negative for Australia antigen; halothane hepatitis to be suspected when unexplained postoperative fever or jaundice occurs.

raw_record.support_text: The three patients treated had acute hepatic necrosis induced by the anaesthetic agent halothane, and one made a complete recovery. These patients were treated by human-human cross-circulation as whole liver support for liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Anaesthetic agent. Three patients treated by human-human cross-circulation for acute hepatic necrosis; one made a complete recovery.

raw_record.support_text: Between October 1 1986 and October 1 1988, 55 serum samples from patients with a putative clinical diagnosis of halothane-associated hepatitis were sent to the Liver Unit at King's College Hospital for testing. In each case there was a history of a hepatitic illness developing after a halothane anaesthetic in the absence of peroperative surgical or anaesthetic complications, and all samples were negative for HBsAg and hepatitis A IgM.
raw_record.extra_details: Sera from 40 patients with halothane-associated hepatitis were included in the final analysis (55 received; excluded were 5 with illness developing >28 days after exposure, 9 sampled >=3 months after onset, 4 after an enflurane/isoflurane anaesthetic, and 3 with hepatitis after repeated occupational exposure). Serologic exclusions ruled out hepatitis B, hepatitis A, cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus. Study context: evaluation of the anti-TFA-albumin ELISA in these sera.

raw_record.support_text: A 55-year-old woman who underwent cholecystectomy under halothane anesthesia in 1967 developed postoperative vomiting, dark urine, jaundice and a tender enlarged liver, with marked eosinophilia and elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase and SGOT; liver biopsy was interpreted as subacute hepatitis and the diagnosis was halothane-induced hepatitis. She recovered and a later cataract extraction under halothane-free anesthesia was uneventful.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane given in 1967 for cholecystectomy; symptoms began by postoperative day 13 (indigestion, chills, vomiting), dark urine day 18, jaundice day 22. raw_record.support_text: Serum samples from 56 patients with halothane hepatitis were analyzed by immunoblotting, and 34 were found to contain antibodies to trifluoroacetyl (TFA)-labeled liver-protein antigens; of the 22 immunoblot-negative sera, 8 contained antibodies to halothane-induced antigens detectable by ELISA. raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis denotes halothane-induced hepatitis in humans. The paper studies the immunochemistry of trifluoroacetyl (TFA)-protein antigens generated when halothane is metabolized to TFA-chloride by cytochromes P-450, and detects antibodies to these halothane-induced antigens in sera from patients with halothane hepatitis (34/56 positive by immunoblotting; 8 of the 22 immunoblot-negative sera positive by ELISA). raw_record.support_text: For patients with a poor intrinsic prognosis such as halothane hepatitis or drug idiosyncrasy, liver transplantation should be considered early. raw_record.support_text: Eight cases of hepatitis occurring after halothane anesthesia were thoroughly evaluated by clinical and laboratory investigations, and despite detailed investigations no other cause could be detected to account for the hepatitis. Hepatitis developed after the first exposure to halothane in three instances, after the second exposure in four, and after three exposures in one patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 8 patients (ages 36-72; 7 female, 1 male). Three cases followed first halothane exposure, four the second, one the third. Latency to jaundice/hepatitis was earlier after repeat exposure (2nd-4th day) than after initial exposure (4th-10th day). Two prior exposures were followed by unexplained jaundice in two patients. Prodromal symptoms (nausea, anorexia, epigastric/RUQ discomfort) and remittent fever (100-105 F, often with shaking chill) preceded jaundice in most patients. Lab findings: SGOT 118-1,550, SGPT 75-1,600, total bilirubin 2.4-30 mg, slight to moderate alkaline phosphatase elevation, prothrombin time 14-29 sec; leucocytosis in two and eosinophilia in two cases; blood/urine/throat cultures and Australian antigen negative; transfusion reaction tests negative. Two patients died (one previous exposure each; bilirubin >15 mg, prothrombin 19 and 29 sec; autopsy revealed massive hepatic necrosis; neither was treated with corticosteroids). Corticosteroids (Prednisone) used in four surviving patients.

raw_record.support_text: In patients with halothane-associated hepatitis, five (63%) of the eight cases studied had detectable anti-LSP antibodies, with titres, with one exception, low (<1:50). Immunopathology proposed to be similar to that in virus infection, with antibodies to a neoantigen on hepatocytes of halothane-anaesthetised rabbits, formed via metabolic degradation of halothane through an oxidative pathway, and a dual T-cell/lymphocyte cytotoxic response against halothane-altered and LSP determinants.

raw_record.support_text: The pathological liver specimens from the two postoperative cases shared many of the findings typical of severe halothane hepatitis, explicitly attributing the patients' liver injury to halothane exposure during their operative course.
raw_record.extra_details: Postmortem findings in two cases: Case 1 liver 1,510 g with generalized centrilobular necrosis, collapse of stroma, prominent bridging, disruption of sinusoidal pattern, marked cholestasis and canalicular plugging, enlarged portal tracts with round cell infiltrate and ductular proliferation; Case 2 liver 820 g with reticulin collagen around sclerotic central veins, absence of viable hepatocytes in centrilobular zone, focal bile stasis, lymphocyte-infiltrated triads and bile duct proliferation. Case 1 died on the sixteenth postoperative day after a course of acute renal failure (creatinine rising to 10.7 mg/100 ml), SGOT rising to 4200, LDH to 6250, and total bilirubin to 7.8 mg/100 ml; kidneys showed cortical tubular necrosis and calcium oxalate crystals. raw_record.support_text: In a series of 25 patients with acute liver failure, the aetiology was viral hepatitis in all but one patient. raw_record.support_text: The study analyzed 20 cases of halothane hepatitis notified in institutional pharmacovigilance between 2012-2016, involving 18 women and 2 men aged 35-65 years. Free radicals produced by liver metabolism of halothane can modify cellular proteins and introduce neo-antigens to the immune system; sensitization to these neo-antigens induces a more severe response after multiple exposures, with most type 2 hepatitis cases occurring after repeated contact.
raw_record.extra_details: 20 halothane hepatitis cases notified in institutional pharmacovigilance 2012-2016; 18 women and 2 men aged 35-65 years; cholestatic pattern in 12 cases and cytolytic in 8; 3 fulminant cases resulted in death. Mechanism: halothane metabolism in the liver produces free radicals that modify cellular proteins and create neo-antigens; immune sensitization to neo-antigens causes more severe response after repeated exposure, and most type 2 hepatitis cases occur after repeated contact. Paper notes newer halogenated anesthetics (enflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane) are less metabolized in the liver and cause few cases of sensitization.

raw_record.support_text: Among 62 patients with acute liver failure (ALF), the etiology was considered viral in 26; in 5 other patients ALF was considered due to toxic hepatitis caused by the administration of ketoconazole, α-methyl dopa, halothane, pyroxicam, and disulfiram, respectively. raw_record.support_text: The study used an ELISA to detect P450 2E1 autoantibodies in sera from halothane hepatitis patients and other groups. raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis is an immune-mediated hepatotoxicity in humans. Of 55 halothane hepatitis patients, 25 (45%) had anti-P450 2E1 autoantibodies that reacted with conformational epitopes of native P450 2E1 and inhibited chlorzoxazone 6-hydroxylation (P450 2E1) activity in human liver microsomes and in TN5 cells expressing human P450 2E1; sera from anesthesiology personnel subclinically exposed to anesthetic gases (11/36, 31%) also reacted but less strongly. Halothane formed TFA-P450 2E1 adducts with purified reconstituted human P450 2E1 in an NADPH-dependent manner. The autoantibodies reacted more with P450 2E1 than with P450 3A4.

raw_record.support_text: Acute hepatic necrosis, whether due to fulminant hepatitis or drug toxicity, carries an appalling mortality. In the latest account from the Fulminant Hepatic Surveillance Study (Trey et al., 1970) the mortality of the 284 patients who went into coma was 82%, with a figure of 96% for those with a halothane-induced hepatic necrosis. The text explicitly attributes hepatic necrosis to halothane using an induced-injury construction.
raw_record.extra_details: From the Fulminant Hepatic Failure Surveillance Study (Trey et al., 1970); among the 284 patients who went into coma the overall mortality was 82%, and it was 96% among those with halothane-induced hepatic necrosis. The 96% figure applies to halothane-induced hepatic necrosis cases who had progressed to coma.

raw_record.support_text: In a UK follow-up study of 44 patients with drug-induced hepatotoxicity, halothane was among the specific drugs implicated as a cause of hepatic injury; patients with abnormal hepatic evaluation at a median 5-year follow-up had previously taken halothane.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported among 44 patients with drug-induced hepatotoxicity followed for a median of 5 years (range 1-19); 8 patients had persistent hepatic enzyme elevation and 5 had persistently abnormal scans/ultrasound without enzyme elevation. raw_record.support_text: The authors report data to strengthen the association of halothane with hepatocellular injury and describe features relevant to clinical and pathologic recognition of the hepatic injury. Although hepatic dysfunction is uncommon after exposure to halothane, halothane is presented as a cause of hepatocellular injury/hepatitis in humans.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane-exposed patients developed hepatitis characterized by fever developing after the fourth postoperative day, persisting into the second week, recurring after an afebrile period, quickly followed by jaundice, and often absolute peripheral eosinophilia. After a single exposure, jaundice is rare within the first week but appears earlier after reexposure. Histology (electron microscopy) showed smaller autophagic vacuoles, sinusoidal blebs, loss of outer mitochondrial membrane segments with infolded inner membranes, and shattered/curled cristae in hepatocytes and ductular cells. Circulating antimitochondrial antibodies at 1:10 serum dilution were detected in six patients studied at the authors' institution.

raw_record.support_text: The study cohort comprised patients with fulminant hepatic failure, including six patients with halothane-associated hepatitis. The patient with the highest halothane-group immune-complex levels had pneumonia.

raw_record.support_text: Among the 77 FHF patients representing the natural history of fulminant hepatic failure, halothane hepatitis was the underlying diagnosis in 8 patients. Halothane (anesthetic) is identified as an agent causing hepatitis that progressed to fulminant hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: Among patients with acute hepatitis, drug hepatitis was attributed to halothane in 1 patient with uncomplicated hepatitis, 1 survivor of fulminant hepatitis, and 6 patients who died of fulminant hepatitis, identifying halothane as a cause of drug-induced hepatitis, including fatal fulminant courses.

raw_record.support_text: In the study of 36 patients with fulminant hepatic failure, liver failure was attributed to halothane associated hepatitis in three patients. raw_record.extra_details: Halothane associated hepatitis was the attributed cause of fulminant hepatic failure in 3 of the 36 patients.

raw_record.support_text: Using the ELISA, halothane-related antibodies were detected in sera from 16/24 patients with halothane-associated liver failure, at titres from 1:100 to 1:25,600. raw_record.extra_details: Halothane (1,1,1-trifluoro-2-bromo-2-chloroethane) anaesthesia may rarely cause massive liver cell necrosis (halothane-associated liver failure). Antibodies against halothane-induced hepatocyte-surface antigens were detected in 16/24 such patients (titres 1:100-1:25,600); immune mechanisms are implicated in pathogenesis. Antibodies were absent in 26 normal blood donors, 5 healthy anaesthetists, 12 repeatedly-exposed patients with normal liver function, and 32 patients with other liver diseases. Detection method developed is an ELISA after serum absorption with normal rabbit liver microsomal fraction.

raw_record.support_text: In-vitro sensitization (inhibition or stimulation of leukocyte migration) in response to a liver homogenate obtained from rabbits pre-treated with halothane was found in eight of 12 patients with halothane-associated hepatitis in 1975. After this first report on involvement of an immune-mediated mechanism in halothane hepatitis, it is established today that antibodies against trifluoroacetylated proteins are responsible for the development of this rare but sometimes deleterious sequel of anaesthesia.
raw_record.extra_details: Immune-mediated halothane hepatitis; antibodies against trifluoroacetylated proteins responsible; reported clinical features include fever (~88%, onset 4-7 days), jaundice (~100%, onset 4-11 days up to 4 weeks), eosinophilia 8-32%, serum auto-antibodies 25-44%; diagnostic ELISA using purified trifluoroacetylated liver microsomal proteins reported sensitivity 79%.

raw_record.support_text: Clinical data are presented on 12 patients with presum ed halothane-associated hepatitis, each having had one or more previous halothane anaesthetics, with intervals between anaesthesia and jaundice of 3-14 days. raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 12 patients with presumed halothane-associated hepatitis; 7 of 12 died (patients 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12), rest survived. Each patient had 1-2 previous halothane anaesthetics, 6 days to 7 years before the index exposure; interval between anaesthesia and jaundice 3-14 days. Postoperative pyrexia and autoantibodies (LKM 1/80-1/120, SMA 1/20) variable. Leucocyte-migration test: with liver homogenate from halothane-exposed rabbits as antigen, migration index (sensitisation) was abnormal in 8 of 12 patients while normal for healthy controls (median 1.06, range 0.77-1.21), other liver diseases (1.0), and halothane-no-hepatitis (1.0); halothane-hepatitis group migration index 0.98 (0.81-1.19). raw_record.support_text: In the cohort of 33 patients with acute hepatic encephalopathy due to toxic or viral hepatitis, 16 had toxic hepatitis, of which 8 patients were attributed to halothane, 3 to disulfiram, 1 to sulfamethoxazole with trimethoprim, 1 to paracetamol, 2 to pregnancy, and 1 to vincristine plus X-ray therapy. raw_record.extra_details: 8 of 16 toxic-hepatitis patients in a study of acute hepatic encephalopathy (grades I-IV); patients with toxic hepatitis were considered a physiochemical etiologic group.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes halothane-induced liver disease (halothane hepatitis) as a cardinal feature of halothane anesthesia. It reports a 7-fold greater incidence of halothane hepatitis in the National Halothane Study among patients with multiple exposures than single exposures, with approximately 85% of cases occurring after multiple exposures, and shorter latency and greater severity/fatality in multiple-exposure cases. The paper also cites mortality rates from halothane jaundice of approximately 15 to over 50% and notes that survivors generally have an excellent outcome.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis is presented as a distinct clinical entity whose histology may resemble viral hepatitis; distinguishing features include massive zonal (centrilobular) necrosis, granulomata, fatty infiltration, early periportal cholestasis, pseudoductular proliferation, and polymorphonuclear and eosinophilic infiltration. Between-exposure association: incidence was 7 times greater with multiple than single exposures in the National Halothane Study; approximately 85% of cases (mean 84% across series totaling 393 cases, e.g., Moult and Sherlock 92%, Klion 71%, Bottiger 82%, Walton 95%, Inman and Mushin 82%, Peters 80%) follow multiple exposures. Multiple-exposure cases had shorter latency (single exposure interval 11.7 days) and more severe and more fatal injury; closely spaced exposures (e.g., 69% of Moult and Sherlock cases with >1 exposure in 4 weeks; 80% of cases with two exposures within 28 days) favored hepatitis. Mortality from halothane jaundice ranges ~15 to >50%; rare chronic liver disease with recurrent hepatitis reported from repeated exposures. Peters et al. described necrotic, resorptive, and regenerative histologic stages.

raw_record.support_text: Serum from 11 patients with halothane-associated fulminant hepatic failure, when incubated with hepatocytes from a halothane-pretreated rabbit, produced IgG-class immunoglobulins depositing in a linear membrane pattern; after absorption with normal hepatocytes, seven of the 11 samples showed a granular pattern specific to halothane-pretreated hepatocytes (not seen with ether-pretreated hepatocytes). Control serum from people without liver disease and from anesthetists or repeatedly halothane-exposed patients did not show this.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of 11 patients with halothane-associated fulminant hepatic failure. Serum contained IgG antibodies reacting with the liver-cell membrane of halothane-pretreated rabbit hepatocytes (linear pattern with unabsorbed serum; granular pattern after absorption with normal hepatocytes in 7/11). Nine of 11 absorbed serum samples induced lymphocyte cytotoxicity against halothane-treated hepatocytes, but not against normal hepatocytes. Similar antibodies/cytotoxicity absent in anesthetists and patients repeatedly exposed to halothane, and in controls without liver disease. Antibodies were detected more often in serum collected after recovery than during the acute phase (all four samples at 8-24 weeks positive; 5/10 within first three weeks positive). This supports an immune-mediated humoral mechanism for halothane-induced fulminant hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: Specifically sensitized lymphocytes were demonstrated in a 27-year-old male patient with halothane-induced hepatitis. A strong proliferative response (stimulation index 8) was induced by serum collected from a healthy donor 60 min after halothane anaesthesia; sera taken before, 30 or 120 min after anaesthesia did not stimulate the patient's lymphocytes. The test was done in quintuplicate 10 days after halothane exposure.

Halothane is also listed among substances known to have sensitizing potency that frequently give positive LTT results in patients with suspected drug-induced hepatic injuries (p:6).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that shortly after halothane was commercialized it was implicated in postoperative hepatitis, and that there now exist sufficient arguments to affirm the existence of halothane hepatotoxicity in humans and animals. The human evidence is twofold: retrospective studies of the circumstances of postoperative hepatitis and prospective studies measuring biologic parameters after halothane administration.

Reported hepatitis predominantly followed multiple halothane administrations (82-95% of cases) spaced less than 28 days (55-75% of hepatitis after multiple exposures), based on three series of 130, 170, and 76 attributed cases. HBsAg was the only viral marker systematically searched in one series and was found in only 1 of 76 patients.

raw_record.support_text: The study reported markedly elevated cholesterol ester hydrolase (CEH) activity in livers of patients with hepatitis, with levels markedly elevated in 2 patients with toxic and halothane-related hepatitis as well as those with viral hepatitis, though the number of such cases was small.

The elevated CEH activity was linked to hepatocyte necrosis and returned to normal on resolution of hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Among 29 patients with acute and subacute hepatic failure, one patient had acute hepatic failure due to recurrent halothane exposure; this patient recovered and left hospital alive without requiring liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: In a clinical study the incidence of halothane-induced liver injury (halothane hepatitis) was compared between phenobarbital-treated and untreated patients. The incidence was significantly higher in phenobarbital-treated patients than in untreated controls (7/100 vs. 1/179, p < 0.01), and remained higher when restricted to patients not previously exposed to halothane anesthesia (4/71 vs. 1/168, p < 0.05). raw_record.support_text: In three cases, halothane-induced acute hepatitis was severe and accompanied by bridging necrosis and hepatic functional abnormalities persisting for 6 weeks to 3 months; the lesions healed within 10 to 14 months except for minimal residual portal fibrosis and fatty infiltration. In none of these surviving patients did the lesion progress to chronic aggressive hepatitis.

A hypersensitivity reaction was considered the likely mechanism; corticosteroids were used in two patients with apparent benefit while the third recovered without them.

raw_record.support_text: The paper uses halothane, a volatile anesthetic agent, as a model for studying the molecular pathogenesis and genetic basis of drug-induced human disease, and its associated clinical syndrome, halothane hepatitis. Isolated reports of unexplained hepatitis following halothane exposure led to the retrospective National Halothane Study, which confirmed an association between human halothane exposure and the occurrence of otherwise unexplained hepatitis. The paper also states that biotransformation of halothane appears to be a prerequisite for halothane hepatotoxicity to occur.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis is framed within the broader category of idiosyncratic drug reactions that are host-dependent, dose-independent, unpredictable, occur at low overall incidence (< ~1:10 000 to ~1:100 000), and can be severe (prolonged immunosuppressive therapy, liver transplantation, or death). The National Halothane Study was the retrospective study confirming the human association. Approximately 20% of the administered dose is metabolized via oxidative and reductive pathways; oxidative biotransformation is catalyzed (perhaps not exclusively) by cytochrome P4502E1. The trifluoroacyl chloride intermediate reacts with cellular nucleophiles to form trifluoroacetylated proteins and phospholipids, with N6-trifluoroacetyl-L-lysine (CF3CO-Lys) identified as the major liver protein adduct.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of liver cell DNA synthesis and mitoses in acute liver failure, the control group included two patients with drug hepatitis attributed to halothane (patient no. 12) and disulfiram (patient no. 14), respectively. raw_record.support_text: Twenty-nine patients became jaundiced after three exposures to halothane anaesthesia; their ages ranged from 19 to 77 years (mean 55.7±16.0) and 17 (59%) died. In cases with three halothane exposures, the interval between the third exposure and onset of jaundice ranged from 1 to 25 days (mean 4.6 days). Fourteen additional patients exposed two times to halothane also developed jaundice, and among 16 patients with four to six halothane exposures, 10 (63%) were reported to have died from liver failure. The paper attributes these episodes of jaundice and deaths from liver failure to halothane anaesthesia exposure.

Interval between first and third exposure ranged from 14 days to five years (75% within 28 days); interval between third exposure and onset of jaundice 1-25 days, mean 4.6 days. Some patients were induced with propanidid (case 77) or methohexitone (case 97), which were not themselves attributed as causes. raw_record.support_text: Halothane was one of the major culprit drugs causing hepatotoxicity in the Homberg series of 157 drug-induced hepatitis cases, with 6 cases; the paper also discusses halothane hepatitis as an immune-mediated reaction, noting antibody to halothane-altered cells was present in patients with halothane hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: 6 cases in the Homberg drug-induced hepatitis series; halothane hepatitis hypothesized to involve halothane or a metabolite expressed on liver cell surface coupled to protein providing immunogen and target for antibody-mediated attack, consistent with rapid onset.

raw_record.support_text: Serum antibodies from a group of halothane hepatitis patients reacted significantly more (ELISA) with the TFA 57-kD protein (p = 0.001) and the native 57-kD protein (p = 0.005) than did sera from control patients; 4 of 40 halothane hepatitis patients, but none of the controls, showed appreciably greater reactivity with the TFA-labeled (trifluoroacetylated) form.
