raw_record.support_text: Five incidents of toxic hepatosis following halothane anesthesia occurred within the last two years. Two patients died in hepatic failure and three died of other causes but had microscopic evidence of liver damage including focal necrosis. The hepatic failure was explained by postulating a special 'affinity' of halothane to the liver or on the basis of specific sensitivity of a given individual. Histological evaluation by liver biopsy was usually possible, and the morphological appearance, when correlated with the patient's history, was described as typical (Klinge, O.: Toxic Hepatosis Associated with Halothane Anesthesia, Klin. Wschr. 43: 1042, 1965).
raw_record.extra_details: Five cases of toxic hepatosis following halothane anesthesia: two patients died in hepatic failure, three died of other causes with microscopic liver damage including focal necrosis. Differential diagnosis of liver damage of other origin discussed; liver biopsy evaluation usually possible. Source cited: Klinge, O., Toxic Hepatosis Associated with Halothane Anesthesia, Klin. Wschr. 43:1042 (Oct.) 1965.

raw_record.support_text: The paper cites halothane as an example of a previously unsuspected drug reaction: a six-year study of 850,000 patients who underwent anesthesia yielded inconclusive evidence of halothane liver toxicity, but such toxicity was subsequently demonstrated by casual observations by two anesthesiologists. This is used to illustrate the value of spontaneous reporting and individual clinical observations over intensive monitoring for detecting drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Cited an inconclusive six-year study of 850,000 anesthesia patients for halothane liver toxicity; toxicity was subsequently demonstrated by casual observations by two anesthesiologists. Used in the paper as evidence that intensive monitoring programs cannot wholly substitute for spontaneous reporting.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 73 patients with drug-induced hepatitis, mitochondrial antibody was present in the serum of 3 patients: 1 of 17 with reactions to halothane, 1 of 15 with reactions to chlorpromazine, and 1 of 4 with reactions to sulfonamides. In all of these cases serum tests for Australia antigen were negative.
raw_record.extra_details: Drug-induced hepatitis diagnosed in a series of 73 patients; 17 had reactions to halothane. The single halothane case with mitochondrial antibody had a titer of 1:500 in the third week of illness and was not retested (paragraph 59); serum Australia antigen tests were negative.

raw_record.support_text: The paper opens by stating that hepatic necrosis is a rare complication of halothane anesthesia, with an incidence of 1 in 7000 exposed persons and a 20 to 50 per cent mortality rate. Patients with halothane hepatitis were then studied with an in vitro susceptibility test, establishing halothane as a cause of human drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence stated as 1 in 7000 halothane-exposed persons; mortality 20-50%. Risk factors cited: obese women over age 40, multiple halothane anesthetics within 28 days, and prior reactions such as unexplained postoperative fever. Familial susceptibility suggested by case reports in pairs of closely related women and by strain differences in rats. Proposed mechanism: reductive metabolism under conditions favoring this pathway forms unstable electrophilic intermediates that bind covalently to tissue macromolecules, culminating in cell death. Reaction described as rare and dose-independent. The study enrolled 11 patients with halothane hepatitis whose lymphocytes showed increased cytotoxicity to a phenytoin-metabolite system compared with controls.

raw_record.support_text: Five patients with established halothane-induced hepatitis were investigated, including two previously reported, all tested between seven and 21 days after the development of jaundice. All were Australia antigen negative and showed the biochemical profile of hepatocellular jaundice, with no other cause for the jaundice found. Liver biopsy on one patient showed areas of focal cellular necrosis with some centrilobular cholestasis.
raw_record.extra_details: Five patients with established halothane-induced hepatitis (case series). All developed jaundice after multiple halothane anaesthetic exposures; one case (WC) had a previous episode of postoperative jaundice after halothane four years earlier ascribed to halothane, and subsequently received several non-halothane anaesthetics without complications. All were Australia antigen negative with hepatocellular jaundice; liver biopsy in one patient (ER) showed focal cellular necrosis with some centrilobular cholestasis. Clinically, all recovered within two months. The paper suggests a delayed hypersensitivity (type IV) mechanism, citing production of macrophage migration inhibition factor by patient lymphocytes incubated with halothane (halothane-MIF test).

raw_record.support_text: Halothane is listed among monoamine oxidase inhibitors, iproniazide, zoxazolamine, and cinchophen as drugs incriminated in the hepatocellular form of drug-induced hepatitis, in which lesions are characterized by diffuse hepatocellular necrosis and inflammation indistinguishable from viral hepatitis, necrosis is frequently massive, and the death rate often reaches 50%. Separately, the paper argues halothane is not a classic intrinsic hepatotoxin but causes hepatitis via a drug sensitization reaction affecting as few as one in 10,000 individuals.
raw_record.extra_details: 41 patients with halothane-induced hepatitis (table reproduced from Toxicity of Anesthetics, 1968); latent period to fever single exposure 6.5 days (1-12) and multiple exposures 3.0 days (1-10); latent period to jaundice single 10.7 days (4-17) and multiple 6.4 days (2-12); fever 93%, leukocytosis (>10,000) 50% (9/18), eosinophilia 6%-25% in 42% (8/19); described as a drug sensitization, not intrinsic hepatotoxic, reaction, not dose related, affecting as few as one in 10,000; high death rate and recurrence of hepatitis after reexposure.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 57-year-old man who underwent two operations (femoral hernia repair followed by ligation of a saphenous varix three days later), with anesthesia maintained by halothane during both procedures. Six days after the second operation he developed spiking fevers up to 105°F, jaundice, and markedly deranged liver chemistries, which returned to normal or near-normal forty-five days after the second operation. A liver biopsy on day 21 showed fatty metamorphosis, liver-cell necrosis, and round-cell infiltration of the portal tracts. The authors add this as a case of hepatitis apparently due to halothane, having reasonably excluded hypoxia, hypotension, pre-existing liver disease, and exposure to other toxins as causes.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case added to those reported by Lindenbaum and Leifer and by Bunker and Blumenfeld. Patient exposed to halothane anesthesia during two procedures (femoral hernia repair and, three days later, ligation of a saphenous varix). Onset six days after the second operation with spiking fevers to 105°F, jaundice, and markedly deranged liver chemistries; values normal or near-normal by forty-five days after the second operation. Day-21 liver biopsy showed fatty metamorphosis, liver-cell necrosis, and round-cell infiltration of portal tracts. Hypoxia, hypotension, pre-existing liver disease, and other toxin exposure were reasonably excluded.

raw_record.support_text: Halothane (1,1,1-trifluoro-2,2-chlorobromoethane), a universally accepted nonflammable anesthetic agent, has been incriminated as a cause of a hepatitis-like reaction. The paper notes the need to distinguish between the liver's response to infectious diseases, hepatotoxins, and drugs that produce sensitization reactions, framing halothane hepatitis in the sensitization (allergic/idiosyncratic) category. Historical features of 41 cases of hepatitis following halothane anesthesia are tabulated, including 23 deaths, and the presented patient died with hepatic and renal failure after massive hepatic necrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane is described as incriminated as a cause of a hepatitis-like reaction (allergic/sensitization category distinct from infectious and hepatotoxin responses). Presented case: postoperative jaundice with SGOT rising to 9,750 units/100 cc, total bilirubin to 7.8 mg/100 cc, alkaline phosphatase to 440 units/100 cc, LDH to 3,800 units/100 cc, prothrombin time 29.9 sec; serum negative for serum hepatitis antigen; required exchange plasmapheresis and supportive care; died two months after initial operation with hepatic and renal failure; autopsy showed massive hepatic necrosis with severe central lobular necrosis. Table of 41 cases of hepatitis following halothane anesthesia: 71% women, 68% multiple exposures, 56% mortality (23/41), 15% prior drug allergy, febrile reactions in 8/28 multiple exposures, recurrence 100% in 7 reexposed patients, interval between exposures 2 days to 1 year and between attacks 1 month to 4.5 years.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports analyses of antibodies in 12 patients diagnosed with halothane hepatitis (HH), using several ELISA formats including a TFA-RSA ELISA, halothane-treated rabbit microsomal protein ELISA, and a TFA-lysine blocking ELISA. The patients are referred to as 'suspected HH patients' and 'presumptive HH', and halothane hepatitis is treated as an established immune-mediated diagnosis in this context.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis is framed as an immune-mediated injury: 'a basic premise of halothane hepatitis research is that, although the initial immune response is hapten-specific, this response broadens to a generalized autoimmune response to self proteins, especially to microsomal proteins.' Sera from 12 patients with suspected halothane hepatitis were tested by TFA-RSA ELISA, halothane-treated-microsome ELISA (with/without pre-absorption), and TFA-lysine blocking ELISA; one serum (patient No. 2) also tested positive for anti-hepatitis C virus, and it is noted the patient may have been misdiagnosed or had a concurrent hepatitis C infection.

raw_record.support_text: In the King's College Hospital 1993-94 acute liver failure cohort, halothane is listed among idiosyncratic drug reactions as a cause of ALF. Paragraph 33 notes the prognosis for drug-induced ALF, including that of halothane, is poor once grade 3-4 encephalopathy appears and prothrombin time is prolonged more than 50 s over control.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among idiosyncratic drug reactions causing ALF in the 1993-94 cohort; drug-induced ALF (including halothane) carries a poor prognosis with grade 3-4 encephalopathy and prothrombin time >50 s prolonged over control.

raw_record.support_text: The discussion states that considerable controversy has surrounded hepatic injury associated with halothane, but that the passage of time and accumulation of cases has led to near consensus regarding the reality of the clinical syndrome. The study analyzed a large number of cases with both biopsy and autopsy material, documenting spotty, submassive, and massive hepatic necrosis, with 13 fatal cases showing massive necrosis with nearly all hepatocytes destroyed.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane anesthesia, with severity of liver injury related to repeated exposures within a 3-month interval. Necrosis included spotty (biopsy, n=12), submassive (biopsy n=16, autopsy n=30, biopsy n=8), and massive (autopsy, n=13 fatal cases). Inflammatory infiltrates predominantly lymphocytic with variable neutrophils, plasma cells, and eosinophils; cholangiolar proliferation, cholestasis, and endophlebitis of terminal hepatic venules in some cases; early fibrosis and postnecrotic cirrhosis in some cases. Authors note sharply outlined centrilobular necrosis as more characteristic of halothane injury than classical viral hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Among the 203 patients with postoperative jaundice after halothane anaesthesia, the overall death rate was 23%. In patients with UHFH (unexplained hepatitis following halothane), the death rate due to hepatic failure was 17%, higher among men (22%) than women (15%); obesity and a short latent period between anaesthesia exposure and onset of jaundice were poor prognostic signs.
raw_record.extra_details: 203 patients with postoperative jaundice after halothane exposure; overall death rate 23%; hepatic failure death rate 17% in the UHFH group (men 22%, women 15%); obesity and short latency between anaesthesia and jaundice were poor prognostic signs. Immunological findings: HBsAg in only one UHFH patient; in the UHFH group incidences of liver-kidney microsomal (LKM), thyroid autoantibodies and autoimmune complement fixation were significantly higher than in the identifiable group after halothane; LKM antibody in 19 (25%) of UHFH patients with titres up to 1/160; SMA detected in 25% (UHFH) and 21% (identifiable) of patients; AMA in only two patients, neither classified as UHFH.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reviews the historical evidence that repeated halothane anesthesia is linked to liver damage, noting that although the very existence of halothane hepatitis was debated in the early 1970s, later studies seemed to confirm that severe hepatic dysfunction did follow halothane anesthesia, albeit rarely, with an incidence between one in 6000 and one in 20,000. Multiple halothane exposures were associated with decreasing latency before manifestation and increasing severity of liver dysfunction.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of severe hepatic dysfunction after halothane anesthesia estimated between 1 in 6000 and 1 in 20,000. Multiple halothane exposures associated with decreasing latency to manifestation and increasing severity. In a nationwide UK review (Walton et al., 1976), 204 postoperative jaundice cases were reviewed blindly by a panel of hepatologists, with 76 classified as unexplained fulminant hepatic failure (UHFH); 95% followed multiple halothane anesthesia and 55% reexposure within 4 weeks; increased incidence in the obese and middle-aged women; thyroid autoantibodies present in a high proportion, supporting an immune hypothesis. In prospective studies, repeat halothane was associated with higher AST (urologic patients vs trichloroethylene) and significantly elevated ALT in 4 of 18 patients (vs 0 of 21 controls) during cervical carcinoma anesthesia, with a hepatitic picture on liver biopsy in two; later similar prospective studies did not reproduce these findings. Note: causality certainty is graded here from the paper's concluding characterization of halothane hepatitis as a recognized entity, despite historical debate.

raw_record.support_text: Halothane, introduced into anesthesia practice in 1956, has been the most studied of the hepatotoxic inhalation anesthetics. More than 1,500 case reports of postanesthetic liver complications have accumulated, and the syndrome has become known as halothane hepatitis. Patients develop jaundice (~11 days after a single exposure, ~6 days after multiple exposures) and the injury is often severe, with a 50% mortality; approximately 20% of anesthetized patients show mildly elevated liver enzymes. The incidence of severe liver injury is 1:30,000-100,000 anesthetized patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis; more than 1,500 case reports; most complications occur after multiple anesthesias, though injury can occur after a single exposure; onset 7 days after one exposure vs 3 days after more than three exposures; jaundice around 11 days after single exposure or ~6 days after multiple exposures; 50% mortality; survivors require ~3 months for recovery; incidence of severe injury 1:30,000-100,000 anesthetized patients; ~20% of anesthetized patients show mildly elevated liver enzymes; delayed onset and shortened interval after repeat exposures suggest a memory component; proposed mechanisms include cytochrome P-450 activation to an active/reactive metabolite and an autoimmune response producing severe hepatic necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: The editorial discusses halothane hepatitis as a form of human drug-induced liver injury occurring after halothane anesthesia, encompassing both severe or fulminant cases and more frequent mild, often asymptomatic cases. It notes that features of hypersensitivity are present in no more than approximately 25 per cent of cases and occur equally in severe and mild halothane-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases include fulminant hepatic failure after halothane anesthesia (11 patients, 14 serum samples); centrilobular necrosis seen in many cases is characteristic of true hepatotoxicity; the paper concludes that 'idiosyncrasy' is a more appropriate designation than 'hypersensitivity', accommodating both idiosyncratic allergic reactions and metabolic idiosyncrasy with enhanced toxic-metabolite production; halothane is also described as toxic to cultured hepatocyte membranes and hepatotoxic in several animal models.

raw_record.support_text: In a group of 34 patients with fulminant hepatic failure (27 died, 7 survived after repeated transfusions), the probable causes of fulminant hepatic failure included virus hepatitis (15 patients), halothane anesthesia (14 patients), Reye's syndrome (4 patients), and multiple hepatic abscesses (1 patient). Serum samples were taken during deep hepatic coma before exchange transfusion.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane anesthesia was listed among probable causes of fulminant hepatic failure in 14 of 34 patients; other probable causes were virus hepatitis (15), Reye's syndrome (4), and multiple hepatic abscesses (1). Attribution is explicitly 'probable' and competing causes are present.

raw_record.support_text: Among the 48 DILI cases requiring liver biopsy, halothane anesthetic agent was reported as one of the most common causes of DILI (Table 2: halothane anesthesia 5/48, 10.4%).
raw_record.extra_details: 5/48 (10.4%) of DILI cases in this liver biopsy series; anesthetic agent setting.

raw_record.support_text: Liver microsomal proteins or purified proteins were probed by NaDodSO4/PAGE and immunoblotting with sera from four patients with halothane hepatitis. The sera reacted with a 59-kDa-TFA carboxylesterase neoantigen (and additional TFA neoantigenic fractions of 100, 76, and 54 kDa), and a neoantigen recognized by these patients' antibodies was identified as 59-kDa-TFA carboxylesterase, indicating that halothane produces this drug-induced immunogen in humans with halothane hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: The paper focuses on identifying the drug-induced immunogen/neoantigen (59-kDa-TFA carboxylesterase) in halothane hepatitis. Sera from four halothane hepatitis patients reacted with the 59-kDa-TFA neoantigen and additionally with liver microsomal TFA neoantigen fractions of 100, 76, and 54 kDa in individual patients. Antibodies in most patients were directed against new epitopes formed by covalent attachment of the TFA moiety (derived from the reactive TFA halide metabolite of halothane) to carrier proteins rather than to the TFA hapten itself. The mechanism is described as an allergic/immune-mediated drug hypersensitivity reaction. Rat studies showed no labeling by sodium trifluoroacetate, ethyl trifluoroacetate, or trifluoroethanol, supporting direct TFA halide labeling of microsomal proteins.

raw_record.support_text: The paper lists halothane among drugs that induce immunoallergic drug-induced hepatitis in humans, and states that anti-LKM1 antibodies present in the sera of several patients recovering from severe hepatitis after halothane treatment interacted specifically with hepatocytes from halothane-treated rabbits.
raw_record.extra_details: Described as inducing immunoallergic (immunoallergic) drug-induced hepatitis in humans; several patients recovered from severe hepatitis after halothane treatment. Anti-LKM1 antibodies from these patients were characterized; their interaction with hepatocytes from halothane-treated rabbits is a supporting animal finding.

raw_record.support_text: In Case 7, a 41-year-old woman developed jaundice and deep coma with progressive liver failure after halothane anesthesia used for a radium implantation and, three weeks later, for a total hysterectomy. The authors conclude that the clinical course and pathologic findings — a 1,580 gm pale yellow-tan, extremely firm liver with diffuse, primarily central necrosis and no evidence of regeneration — were consistent with toxic hepatitis caused by halothane anesthesia administered during the two surgical procedures. The patient ultimately died from infectious complications of hysterectomy in a debilitated state.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane general anesthesia given for two surgical procedures (cervical radium implantation followed three weeks later by total hysterectomy). Patient obese, deeply jaundiced (bilirubin 28 mg/100 cc, direct 19.2 mg/100 cc), SGOT 1,280 units, prothrombin time 26 s (control 12 s), serum ammonia 226 µg/100 cc, progressed to deep coma. Exchange transfusions transiently reversed coma on four occasions (12 units infused, 11 removed each time). Course complicated by ascites, peritonitis, candidemia (C. albicans), Klebsiella urine infection, and emergence of chronic liver disease. Death followed left-sided seizure, hemiplegia, and intracranial hemorrhage from a probable ruptured mycotic aneurysm. Postmortem liver 1,580 gm, pale yellow-tan, extremely firm, with diffuse primarily central necrosis, viable hepatocytes but no regeneration.

raw_record.support_text: Among the 55 postoperative patients in this study, initial hospitalization was due to various conditions, including halothane-induced hepatitis in one patient. The paper thus explicitly attributes an episode of hepatitis to halothane exposure in that individual.
raw_record.extra_details: One patient among 55 postoperative patients had a prior hospitalization for halothane-induced hepatitis; no latency, dose, histology, or severity details are given in the provided text.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents a table describing 'Unexplained jaundice following halothane anaesthesia in 701 patients collated from reports' (adapted from Cousins, Plummer and Hall, 1984). The reported features include that 63% were females, 62% were obese, 74% had multiple exposures, the mortality rate was 54%, and days to onset of clinical jaundice were 8.3 days after single exposures and 5.7 days after multiple exposures. This constitutes human case-series evidence attributing clinically apparent liver injury (unexplained jaundice) to halothane used as an anaesthetic.
raw_record.extra_details: 701 patients collated from reports; 63% female, 62% obesity, 74% multiple exposures, mortality rate 54%; days to onset of clinical jaundice 8.3 days (single exposures) and 5.7 days (multiple exposures); adapted from Cousins, Plummer and Hall (1984). Presented in the context that halothane undergoes reductive biotransformation producing radical intermediates, unlike the oxidative biotransformation of other volatile anaesthetics.

raw_record.support_text: The paper analyses halothane hepatitis in humans, using sera from four patients with halothane hepatitis that contained antibodies to the 100, 76 and 57 kDa TFA-antigens. These sera reacted with antigens of very similar apparent molecular masses expressed in livers from two patients who had received halothane anaesthesia, but not in normal human liver or livers from patients given other anaesthetics, indicating humans exposed to halothane express TFA-liver protein antigens analogous to those in halothane-treated animals and recognized by antibodies from patients who developed halothane hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: The paper frames halothane hepatitis as an extremely rare, idiosyncratic immune-mediated liver injury in patients anaesthetized with halothane. Mechanism: oxidative metabolism of halothane to trifluoroacetyl (TFA) halide generates TFA-labelled liver protein antigens (major species ~100, 76 and 57 kDa); patient antibodies recognize these TFA-protein antigens. Antigen expression detected in livers of two halothane-exposed cardiac-surgery patients (who died of post-operative cardiac failure, not hepatitis) but not in normal liver or livers from patients given other anaesthetics. Antigen expression is believed to occur in all humans exposed to halothane, with only very few developing clinical hepatitis. Supporting data: antigen generation abolished by piperidine removal of covalently bound TFA groups and only partially inhibited by the TFA-lysine hapten; antigen expression decreased by deuterated halothane (CF3CDClBr), confirming oxidative-metabolism requirement; reproducible in halothane-treated rabbits and rats.

raw_record.support_text: Halothane is given as an example of a drug with very well documented hepatotoxicity, with numerous case reports and case series and positive rechallenge, and was commonly reported to be associated with hepatotoxicity in early DILI research.
raw_record.extra_details: Inhalational anesthetic; rechallenge reproduced DILI; listed in Table 1 with more than 100 reported cases of drug-induced liver injury (LiverTox).

raw_record.support_text: The paper introduces a rare but severe form of hepatitis caused by the inhalation anesthetic halothane, and describes that a high proportion of patients with this toxicity had specific lymphocytes and antibodies in their blood directed against halothane-altered liver neoantigens. Examples include a leukocyte cell migration test suggesting that 8 of 12 patients with unexplained fulminant hepatic failure after halothane had specific T-cell lymphocytes, a direct lymphocyte cytotoxicity assay positive in three of four patients, and circulating IgG antibodies detected by indirect immunofluorescence (7 of 11 patients) or ELISA (16 of 24 patients).
raw_record.extra_details: Rare but severe form of hepatitis caused by this inhalation anesthetic (CF3CHClBr), still widely used in adults in the UK and Europe and an agent of choice for children. Immune-mediated mechanism: patients had specific lymphocytes and antibodies against halothane-altered liver neoantigens; leukocyte cell migration (T-cell) test positive in 8/12 patients with unexplained fulminant hepatic failure after halothane; direct lymphocyte cytotoxicity assay positive in 3/4; indirect immunofluorescence 7/11; ELISA 16/24.

raw_record.support_text: Patients diagnosed with halothane-associated massive liver cell necrosis (halothane hepatitis) produce serum antibodies that recognize trifluoroacetylated liver microsomal proteins; in an ELISA study two of six such patients had serum antibodies reactive with TFA-RSA, and the reactive trifluoroacetyl chloride metabolite (CF3C(O)Cl) formed from oxidative halothane metabolism covalently binds lysine residues of microsomal proteins. Separate ELISA findings (paragraph 10) show sera from 10 halothane hepatitis patients reacted with purified rat liver TFA-proteins. The injury is thus attributed to halothane in humans, with the trifluoroacetyl chloride adduct as the proposed immunologic mechanism rather than an independently causal entity.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane-associated massive liver cell necrosis in patients; the reactive metabolite trifluoroacetyl chloride (CF3C(O)Cl), formed from oxidative halothane metabolism by cytochromes P-450, covalently binds lysine residues of liver microsomal proteins. In an ELISA study 2 of 6 patients diagnosed with halothane-associated massive liver cell necrosis had serum antibodies reactive with trifluoroacetylated RSA; removal of the TFA moiety with 1 M piperidine abolished patient antibody recognition. In a separate ELISA, sera of 10 halothane hepatitis patients reacted with several purified rat liver TFA-proteins (TFA-100 kDa 9/10, 80 kDa 5/10, 63 kDa 1/10, 59 kDa 2/10, 58 kDa 5/10, 57 kDa 2/10). Anti-TFA antibodies localized trifluoro-acetylation to the perivenous region of the liver lobule; low-level TFA-proteins also formed in extrahepatic tissues (testes, kidney, heart, lung, respiratory/olfactory nasal epithelium) and in liver Kupffer cells, proposed to have a role in the patients' immune response.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that halothane exposure occasionally results in severe hepatic necrosis, and that the rarity of unexplained hepatitis following halothane (UHFH) and the lack of correlation with dose or duration of exposure suggest an idiosyncratic response in affected individuals. All 17 patients in the study were diagnosed from clinical and biochemical evidence as having 'halothane hepatitis', with features of acute hepatocellular damage on biopsy.
raw_record.extra_details: 17 patients with unexplained hepatitis following halothane anaesthesia (UHFH), all Caucasian, with clinical and biochemical diagnosis of halothane hepatitis; liver biopsies showed features of acute hepatocellular damage and, in one case, submassive necrosis. None had epidemiological evidence of viral hepatitis (all HBsAg-negative; 7 Vermont patients hepatitis A antibody-negative), none abused alcohol, and none took other known hepatotoxic drugs at illness onset. HLA A and B locus typing found no statistically significant association (deviations for A1, A11, BW22 not significant after correction), so HLA typing has no predictive value; an abnormal immune response to a halothane metabolite bound to liver cell membrane was proposed as a possible mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: Halothane (anesthetic, used for phlebectomy/cholecystectomy) was listed among drugs with proved liver drug-injury, with a combined lesion with chronic active hepatitis plus sub-massive necrosis and granuloma as a peculiarity. Severe injury with collapse and bridging hepatic necrosis occurred twice after halothane anesthesia.
raw_record.extra_details: Indication: anesthesia for phlebectomy/cholecystectomy; peculiarities: granuloma, sub-massive necrosis, chronic active hepatitis; two cases with collapse and bridging hepatic necrosis developing cholestasis 5-7 days after surgery; piece-meal necrosis and micro-granuloma on biopsy.

raw_record.support_text: Sera from 10 patients with unexplained hepatitis following multiple halothane anesthesia were used; halothane hepatitis was defined clinically as severe, otherwise unexplained, histologically confirmed hepatitis occurring within 4 weeks after halothane exposure in patients with normal preoperative liver function. These patients developed autoantibodies specifically targeting CYP2E1.
raw_record.extra_details: Ten patients with halothane hepatitis (severe, histologically confirmed hepatitis within 4 weeks after halothane anesthesia in patients with normal preoperative liver function, negative for hepatitis viral markers and no exposure to other hepatotoxic drugs or alcohol); injury associated with anti-CYP2E1 autoantibodies targeting conformational epitopes on the G-helix and the J'/K'' helices of CYP2E1.

raw_record.support_text: In a previous study, 67% of a group of 24 halothane hepatitis patients had specific serum reactivity against trifluoroacetylated liver microsomal proteins from halothane-treated rats, and this increased to 79% with purified TFA-labeled proteins. A significant number of halothane hepatitis patients did not react to the trifluoroacetylated neoantigens, which led to the discovery that halothane hepatitis was often associated with serum antibodies directed against native proteins such as protein disulfide isomerase, P58, ERp72, and CYP2E1.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis studied across a group of 24 patients; serum antibodies detected against trifluoroacetylated microsomal proteins (67-79%) and against native proteins (protein disulfide isomerase, P58, ERp72, CYP2E1). CYP2E1 autoantibodies reported in 45-70% of halothane hepatitis patients' sera, thought to be induced by immunogenic TFA-CYP2E1 adducts. Cytochrome 2A6 can oxidatively metabolize halothane to form TFA adducts including TFA-CYP2A6. A prior report described a patient who died after a 28-yr interval between halothane exposures.

raw_record.support_text: In a single patient ('this lady'), the author states that although it is not possible to prove this, the responsibility of fluothane for the jaundice seems convincing. The patient received no other agent even suspected of hepatotoxicity; intra-abdominal operation near the liver and antibiotics were also considered but were excluded because the patient was hospitalized for suture of her ulnar nerve and antibiotics were not given within seven weeks before jaundice onset.
raw_record.extra_details: Fluothane is halothane anesthesia given in a surgical setting. Single case report attributing jaundice (icterus) to fluothane; the author notes proof was not possible but responsibility for the jaundice seemed convincing. Competing causes (intra-abdominal operation near the liver, antibiotics) were considered and excluded because the operation was on the ulnar nerve and antibiotics were not administered within 7 weeks before jaundice onset.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports immunochemical assays to detect antibodies in the sera of patients with a clinical diagnosis of halothane hepatitis. In an immunoblotting procedure using microsomal proteins from halothane-treated rabbits or rats, 42 of 68 (62%) patients with a clinical diagnosis of halothane hepatitis tested positive for halothane-induced antibodies, confirming halothane as the cause of human liver injury (hepatitis) in these patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Patients carry a clinical diagnosis of halothane hepatitis. Antibody detection via immunoblotting (42/68, 62% positive), and via ELISA using halothane-treated rabbit microsomes (16/24, 67%; 28/39, 72%) or TFA hapten as TFA-rabbit serum albumin (2/6, 33% to 5/6, 83%). The hepatotoxic reactive metabolite is trifluoroacetyl (TFA) generated from halothane, forming liver microsomal neoantigens; antibodies also cross-react with neoantigens from the structurally related acyl halide metabolite of enflurane, suggesting potential cross-sensitization after enflurane exposure.

raw_record.support_text: Among 81 patients with fulminant hepatitis, 11 (14%) were classified as fulminant drug-induced hepatitis. The cause was attributed to halothane in 2 cases. The mean age of patients with fulminant drug-induced hepatitis was significantly higher than those with fulminant hepatitis type B (p<0.001) and fulminant hepatitis of unknown etiology (p<0.05).
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed cause of fulminant drug-induced hepatitis in 2 of 11 drug-induced cases in a Japanese cohort (1980-1999). Drug group survival rate 36%.

raw_record.support_text: Of 2609 patients with postoperative S-ALT elevation and hepatitis, four were determined to have halothane hepatitis, as the authors concluded there was no explanation for the hepatitis other than halothane after detailed investigation. A fifth patient with a differential diagnosis of pulmonary embolism was excluded from the hepatitis group. Two of the four had jaundice; all recovered fully.
raw_record.extra_details: 4 cases among 2609 surgical patients; clinical picture typical of acute hepatitis with tiredness, nausea, vomiting and pyrexia of undetermined origin beginning on postoperative days 1-4 (temperature 39-39.5 C); 2 of 4 had jaundice; all four were women aged 55-69, overweight (73-105 kg), and allergic to various substances; 3 had previous halothane anesthesia more than 5 years earlier, and 2 had reacted with fever after the first exposure; patient 4 had severe hepatitis (prothrombin time <40%) with hepatic coma grade 1, treated with steroids, and a protracted course; the other 3 had milder hepatitis with rapid restitution; all recovered fully. Liver biopsy in patient 2 showed acute hepatitis. Hepatitis A and B serology negative, no blood transfusion within 6 months, stable medication, no alcohol abuse, no intraoperative hypotension or hypoxia.

raw_record.support_text: In the etiology distribution of acute liver failure in this cohort, diagnoses of Amanita phalloides ingestion, Wilson's disease, hepatitis A, ischemic hepatitis (shock liver), and halothane reaction accounted for 3 (3%) cases attributed to halothane reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: 3 cases (3%) of the ALF cohort attributed to halothane reaction; grouped with Amanita phalloides ingestion, Wilson's disease, hepatitis A, and ischemic hepatitis in the etiology breakdown.

raw_record.support_text: A 29 year old woman was transferred with fulminant hepatic failure secondary to halothane anaesthesia. raw_record.support_text: Six women were diagnosed with halothane-induced hepatitis based on criteria of no pre-existing liver disease, hepatitis onset within two weeks of halothane exposure, and no alternative explanations. All had jaundice and high transaminase levels, all were female, and most were obese; the interval between anesthesia and hepatitis was two days in the one previously exposed patient and six to ten days in the others. Three patients died with autopsy findings consistent with post-halothane hepatitis, and no other causes such as prior hepatotoxin exposure, shock, or hepatitis B infection were found.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All affected patients were women, markedly obese or at upper limits of normal weight, and from closely related families of common ethnic origin; only the patient with prior halothane exposure had a short (two-day) latency.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane anesthesia exposure; all six cases satisfied the diagnostic criteria for hepatitis induced by halothane. Clinical features included jaundice, high transaminase levels, fever rising to 40°C (104°F) in five of six, peripheral eosinophil counts above 500/mm3 in three, and two-to-ten day interval from anesthesia to hepatitis. Three patients died; autopsy findings were consistent with post-halothane hepatitis, and alternative causes (prior hepatotoxin exposure, shock, hepatitis B virus) were excluded. Survivors remained healthy with no recurrence. Anti-HBs testing was performed on three surviving patients; a four-to-five-generation survey of 154 blood relatives revealed no additional cases of postoperative hepatic injury.

In challenged patients, jaundice was a feature of all but one initial episode but of only half of the second episodes, and features thought to indicate a hypersensitivity reaction (myalgia, arthralgia, skin rash, nasal congestion, cough, allergic history) were noted in only one-third or less of both groups.

Initial-episode features: jaundice in 9 of 10, hepatic enlargement 3, hepatic tenderness 3, myalgia 2, skin rash 1, nasal congestion 1, cough 1, allergic history 3; second episodes: jaundice 5, hepatic enlargement 2, hepatic tenderness 3, myalgia 2, nasal congestion 1, cough 1, allergic history 3. Onset of illness ranged from several hours to 1 year after halothane exposure; single anesthetic exposures had onset of several hours to 10 days. raw_record.support_text: The editorial states that Klatskin and Kimberg's case report provides important evidence that halothane is a cause of liver injury: an anesthetist with recurrent episodes of hepatitis typically temporally related to working and thus anesthetic exposure had a flare-up precipitated by a carefully performed provocative exposure to halothane, and remained well for at least 12 months after returning to work without likely halothane exposure. Together with at least eight published cases of recurrent jaundice after separate halothane exposures and two similar patients known to the authors, the editorial concludes 'It seems highly probable that halothane was responsible for the recurrent episodes of liver damage in all these patients,' and notes the Fulminant Hepatic Necrosis Surveillance Study indicates halothane is an important cause of fulminant hepatic necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Liver damage recognized more frequently after re-exposure to halothane; index case was an occupationally exposed anesthetist; combined with retrospective evidence that massive hepatic necrosis is no more frequent after halothane than after other anesthetics.
raw_record.extra_details: Injury attributed to a hypersensitivity reaction rather than direct hepatotoxicity: no hepatic lesions in laboratory animals, injury in only a small proportion of exposed subjects, not dose-related, variable latent period, variable morphology with hepatitis-like lesions a common form, often with fever, eosinophilia, arthralgia, and skin rash. Retrospective studies of 856,000 patients plus an additional 300,000 patients were cited as major evidence against a cause-and-effect relationship with postoperative liver damage, with massive hepatic necrosis no more frequent after halothane than other agents, yet the editorial resolves in favor of a causal role. At least 8 published cases of recurrent jaundice after separate exposures and 2 personal cases; index anesthetist remained well for at least 12 months after avoiding exposure; less severe forms of liver damage occur and, as in the reported patient, may progress to cirrhosis; overall incidence remains unknown.

raw_record.support_text: Of 203 patients with postoperative jaundice submitted to a panel of hepatologists, 76 were classified as having unexplained hepatitis following halothane anaesthesia (UHFH) after excluding those with identifiable causes. Hepatitis followed multiple exposure to halothane in 95% of cases, with repeated exposure within four weeks in 55%; 13 patients died in acute hepatic failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Most cases followed repeated halothane exposure (95% multiple exposure; repeat exposure within four weeks in 55% of cases).
raw_record.extra_details: Nationwide survey of postoperative jaundice in the British Isles (November 1970 over three years) with hepatologist panel classification blinded to anaesthetic agent. 76 UHFH cases; 13 died in acute hepatic failure. 29 patients obese, 52 aged 41-70, 53 women. Rapid onset of jaundice, male sex, and obesity were poor prognostic signs; eosinophilia was the only impressive hypersensitivity stigma. UHFH group had higher incidence of liver kidney microsomal (LKM) and thyroid antibodies and autoimmune complement fixation than patients with identifiable jaundice causes. In 3 of 5 re-exposed patients jaundice did not recur. Paper notes that rapidly repeated exposure 'may cause hepatitis' but complication is probably rare, and comparative risks of halothane vs nonhalothane anaesthesia could not be determined.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that halothane use carries a small risk of liver damage and that the occurrence of hepatic necrosis could be largely prevented, since it only occasionally occurs after a single anaesthetic. Twenty-seven of the 35 patients of Trey and colleagues, 30 of the 42 patients of Klion and colleagues, and all of the authors' own patients had two or more anaesthetics with halothane before developing massive hepatic necrosis, and almost all showed prior features (jaundice, fever, or both) after earlier anaesthetics that could have alerted to halothane hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Most cases occurred after two or more halothane anaesthetics; hepatic necrosis only occasionally follows a single anaesthetic.
raw_record.extra_details: As a general anaesthetic, halothane is described as the most widely used and its desirable properties outweigh the small risk of liver damage. Cases from Trey (27/35) and Klion (30/42), plus the authors' own patients, developed massive hepatic necrosis after repeated exposure; nearly all had earlier jaundice and/or fever indicating possible halothane hepatotoxicity. The authors also conclude that halothane hepatitis is a definite entity whose frequency is higher than currently accepted and that unexplained postoperative fever lasting longer than five days should deter further halothane use.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes two distinct forms of liver damage associated with halothane anaesthesia. The milder form is characterised by elevation of serum aminotransferases, usually below three times the upper limit of normal, and occurs after about 20% of anaesthetics. The severer, much less frequent form is associated with fulminant hepatic failure and a high mortality, occurring more often after multiple exposures to halothane.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Occurs at anaesthetic (therapeutic) exposure; the severe form is much more frequent after repeated halothane anaesthetics, and cases may be preceded by earlier milder reactions to previous halothane anaesthetics.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe form associated with fulminant hepatic failure and high mortality; analysis of published reports of halothane hepatitis describing 10 or more patients shows high female:male ratio (1.6:1), previous halothane exposure in 78%, peripheral eosinophilia 21%, auto-antibodies 29%; Inman and Mushin reported 82% of cases had been exposed on at least one previous occasion and 80% within 28 days; shorter interval between exposures is associated with shorter period between last anaesthetic and onset of jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report strong circumstantial evidence implicating halothane as the cause of acute hepatocellular jaundice in 6 patients. In all 6 cases, otherwise unexplained fever and/or bilirubinuria developed within 7 days after halothane anesthesia, and further exposure after a short interval resulted in acute hepatocellular jaundice; similar episodes have been ascribed to a hepatic injury resulting from hypersensitivity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with carcinoma of the cervix undergoing repeated (up to 4) halothane anesthetics for radium insertions at approximately weekly intervals; two of six patients (cases 5 and 6) died in hepatic coma.
raw_record.extra_details: Six patients (aged 46-68) each received 2-4 halothane anesthetics; acute hepatocellular jaundice developing within 7 days of anesthesia with re-exposure after a short interval; death in hepatic coma in 2 cases (maximal serum bilirubin 12.6 and 38.0 mg/100 ml, SGOT 975 Karmen units); autopsy in case 6 showed submassive/massive hepatocellular necrosis with centrilobular cholestasis and fat-filled vacuoles in surviving cells; injury ascribed to hypersensitivity. Multiple other drug exposures (tetracycline, nitrofurantoin, penicillin, streptomycin, chlorpromazine, aspirin, chloramphenicol, prochlorperazine, sulphafurazole, thiethylperazine) were recorded but halothane was identified as the cause.

raw_record.support_text: In a randomized controlled trial, 39 patients receiving repeated general anaesthetics for radium treatment for carcinoma of the uterine cervix were allocated to anaesthetics with or without halothane, and SGPT was monitored before each anaesthetic. Four of 18 patients in the halothane group had SGPT levels above 100 IU/l before the third radium treatment, whereas no patient in the 21-patient control group did (one-tailed test, P < 0.025). One halothane patient reached a maximum SGPT of 1800 IU/l and another 900 IU/l; neither had symptomatic illness or altered other liver function tests, but liver biopsies showed changes characteristic of hepatitis. Seven halothane patients showed an SGPT rise greater than 20 IU/l versus one control (P < 0.02).

raw_record.extra_details: Randomized controlled trial in 39 patients. 4/18 halothane patients had SGPT >100 IU/l before the third radium treatment vs 0/21 controls (P<0.025). raw_record.support_text: Case 5 is a 4-year-old boy who had a mole removed under general anesthesia with halothane. One week later he developed fever, vomiting, diarrhea, and increasing fatigue, and appeared pale; an emergency visit showed markedly elevated transaminases (AST 10,388; ALT 5,233), thrombocytopenia (platelets 58,000), coagulopathy (PT 23.2, PTT 38.6), and elevated total bilirubin (2.6, direct 1.6). He was admitted with acute liver failure, and a liver biopsy was consistent with halothane toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (4-year-old boy); exposure via general anesthesia with halothane during mole removal
raw_record.extra_details: Latency about one week after anesthesia. Admission AST 10,388 and ALT 5,233; platelets 58,000; PT 23.2; PTT 38.6; total bilirubin 2.6 with direct fraction 1.6. Liver biopsy consistent with halothane toxicity. Liver functions recovered with supportive treatment; stage 0 hepatic encephalopathy; did not require liver transplantation. Brain 1H MRS showed a mildly increased alpha 1H peak (3.75 ppm) in this patient.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses patients with halothane hepatitis (halothane-induced human DILI) who develop circulating antibodies to TFA neoantigens after halothane exposure. Using immunoblotting with liver microsomal proteins from halothane-treated rabbits or rats as test antigen, 42 of 68 (62%) patients with halothane hepatitis tested positive for halothane-induced antibodies. The paper notes prior halothane exposure would identify patients at increased risk of a hypersensitive reaction on further halothane exposure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Re-exposure to halothane after prior sensitization carries increased risk of a hypersensitive reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis patients produce antibodies to trifluoroacetyl (TFA) neoantigens. On immunoblotting, 42/68 (62%) were positive; ELISA results varied with antigen (TFA-RSA: 2/6, 16/24, 5/6, 12/40; halothane-treated rabbit microsomes: 16/24 (67%) and 28/39 (72%)). Neoantigen targets include ER proteins ERp99 (grp94/endoplasmin), calregulin, and 57/59/80/58 kd TFA proteins. Antibodies also cross-react with liver microsomal neoantigens produced by enflurane, suggesting potential cross-sensitization, though this remains speculative rather than a confirmed enflurane DILI claim.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a 50-year-old woman who developed fever and jaundice with biochemical evidence of severe hepatitis 1 day after her third halogenated anesthetic (halothane), which evolved from acute hepatitis with bridging and piecemeal necrosis to quiescent cirrhosis over 10 months. The authors state that a causal association between halothane anesthesia and acute hepatitis with jaundice is accepted, and report the case as a further example of halothane hepatitis evolving to cirrhosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Repeated halothane exposure: three successive anesthetics within a 4-week period (first and third halothane, second enflurane), with an additional halothane anesthetic 3 years earlier; patient had a prior history of 'liver disease' investigation for right upper quadrant pain (gallstones ruled out).
raw_record.extra_details: 50-year-old woman with cancer of the cervix; fever and jaundice appeared 1 day after the third halothane anesthetic (cesium implant, March 5, 1979), the previous anesthetics being curettage with halothane (Feb 8) and cone biopsy with enflurane (Feb 23). Liver biopsy 10 days after jaundice onset showed acute hepatitis with bridging necrosis and piecemeal necrosis; a second biopsy after 10 months showed quiescent cirrhosis with residual piecemeal necrosis. Initial labs: serum aspartate transaminase 516 mmol/l (0-48), alkaline phosphatase 278 mmol/l (0-90), bilirubin 356 mmol/l (0-90); positive smooth muscle autoantibody (IgM, 1:320) and thyroid microsomal antibody (1:1,600); negative hepatitis B surface antigen and anti-hepatitis A antibody; no eosinophilia; abstinence from alcohol, no transfusions, no hepatitis contact. Clinical features included jaundice, spider nevi, smooth hepatomegaly (4 cm), and ascites that resolved after 6 weeks; full clinical recovery from hepatitis. Pathogenesis noted as undefined, with both direct toxicity and hypersensitivity implicated.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that halothane causes two types of hepatotoxicity in humans: a milder form (minor serum transaminase increases, ~20% of patients, attributed to cytotoxic effects of halothane metabolites) and the severe halothane hepatitis (1 in 10,000) that can lead to massive hepatic necrosis and death, possibly via an immune response to halothane-modified (trifluoroacetylated) liver proteins. Among 20 patients with clinically defined halothane hepatitis (otherwise unexplained hepatitis within 28 days of halothane anaesthesia), 13 had liver failure and 12 died; 17 (85%) had autoantibodies to human liver microsomal carboxylesterase (CES1), which the authors report as a target antigen localized to the centrilobular region, consistent with the pattern of halothane hepatitis damage.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Severe idiosyncratic form typically followed repeated prior halothane anaesthesia (median 2 exposures, interval from 7 days to 10 years); mild intrinsic-like form in ~20% of patients.

raw_record.support_text: Halothane had been widely used as an anesthetic and causes two forms of liver damage: a mild increase in serum aminotransferase seen in up to 20% of patients, probably from direct toxicity by drug metabolites, and a more severe form characterized by massive hepatocyte necrosis and acute liver failure. Susceptibility to the severe form was enhanced in adults, females, and obese persons, and increased with frequency of exposure. Severe halothane hepatitis was uncommon after first exposure (1 in 35,000 patients) but its incidence rose to 1 in 3700 after the second exposure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Susceptibility to the severe form was enhanced in adults, females, and obese persons, and increased with the frequency of prior exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Two forms described: mild aminotransferase elevation (up to 20% of patients, attributed to direct metabolite toxicity) and a severe immune-mediated form with massive hepatocyte necrosis and acute liver failure. Incidence of severe halothane hepatitis was 1/35,000 after first exposure and 1/3700 after second exposure. Mechanism: halothane is oxidatively metabolized by CYP2E1 with release of bromide to form trifluoroacetyl chloride, which covalently binds to proteins as trifluoroacetylated (TFA) adducts presented on hepatocyte membranes; anti-P450 2E1 autoantibodies detected by ELISA in 14 of 20 sera from patients with halothane hepatitis.

raw_record.extra_details: 4 of 18 halothane-allocated patients developed SGPT >100 IU/L versus none of 21 controls. Two of these 4 patients had liver biopsies showing liver damage with histological changes characteristic of hepatitis (patients 1 and 17). Highest SGPT values were 1350 and 1800 IU/L. Comparison of log fractional SGPT increases between first and third measurement gave mean 0.71 ± 0.31 for halothane vs 0.03 ± 0.10 for controls (one-tailed P=0.013); four patients with SGPT >100 IU/L were all in the halothane group (one-tailed P<0.025). No patient became clinically jaundiced, and no bilirubin exceeded 1 mg/100 ml.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that cholic acid (CA) was chosen over chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) because of better tolerance and less hepatotoxicity, noting CA had been used without side effects since 1994 at Cincinnati Children's Hospital for inborn errors of bile acid metabolism and studied at doses up to 20 mg/kg per day in adults. In their study, no major adverse events were attributed to CA, although a few patients complained of diarrhea. They conclude that CA is not hepatotoxic and is overall well tolerated.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Assessment based on a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study in patients with lipodystrophies; CA was administered at 15 mg/kg per day (maximum 1500 mg/day).
raw_record.extra_details: No major adverse events were attributed to CA, apart from a few complaints of diarrhea. CA had previously been used without side effects since 1994 for inborn errors of bile acid metabolism and studied at doses up to 20 mg/kg per day in adults for gallstones, mild hypertriglyceridemia, bile acid kinetics, and cholesterol absorption. The study did not confirm the previously reported serum TG-lowering effect of CA. The paper also notes CDCA is a more potent FXR agonist than CA but was avoided due to better tolerance and less hepatotoxicity of CA.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that cholic acid (CA) is now recognized as the bile acid of choice for 3β-HSD and Δ⁴-3-oxo-R deficiencies because it is not hepatotoxic and is effective therapy, and concludes that prolonged oral CA therapy is safe. This is supported by prospective follow-up of 15 children with primary bile acid synthesis defects (initial mean dose 13 mg/kg, 6 mg/kg at last evaluation, median treatment follow-up 12.4 years) in which serum liver biochemistries and sonography normalized and post-treatment liver biopsies showed marked improvement, with CA tolerated well.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Treatment in children (median age at start 3.9 years, range 0.3-13.1) with primary bile acid synthesis defects (3β-hydroxy-Δ⁵-C₂₇-steroid oxidoreductase [3β-HSD] or Δ⁴-3-oxosteroid 5β-reductase [Δ⁴-3-oxo-R] deficiency).
raw_record.extra_details: 15 patients (13 with 3β-HSD, 2 twin sisters with Δ⁴-3-oxo-R deficiency) from 10 families, followed prospectively from 1993 to 2007 at Bicêtre Hospital. Liver biopsies after at least 5 years of CA therapy in 14 patients showed marked improvement, especially in 3β-HSD deficiency. Atypical urinary metabolites reduced 500-fold (3β-HSD) and 30-fold (Δ⁴-3-oxo-R). Two women had normal pregnancies during treatment. Study aimed to assess long-term effectiveness and safety of oral cholic acid; the paper explicitly asserts CA is not hepatotoxic (vs. chenodeoxycholic acid also used for bile acid replacement).

raw_record.support_text: Safety data from carfilzomib trials show that this drug causes minimal hepatotoxicity. In an integrated safety analysis on 526 patients treated with single-agent carfilzomib, grade 3 or more hepatic adverse events occurred in 6.3% of patients, mainly as liver enzyme elevations. Reports of acute hepatic failure (0.6%), hepatic encephalopathy (0.2%), and veno-occlusive liver disease (0.2%) were also present in the safety summary, some fatal.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Multiple myeloma patients on single-agent carfilzomib treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Integrated safety analysis of 526 patients on single-agent carfilzomib; grade 3 or more hepatic AEs in 6.3% of patients mainly as liver enzyme elevations; acute hepatic failure 0.6%, hepatic encephalopathy 0.2%, veno-occlusive liver disease 0.2%, some fatal. Portal/veno-occlusive liver disease represents vascular-type liver injury among the reported phenotypes.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a 43-year-old woman who developed severe liver injury ~6 weeks after self-administering an artemisinin herbal supplement (125 mg orally two or three times daily for general health maintenance) that reportedly contained no other active ingredients. The temporal relationship to artemisinin intake and lack of other potential etiologies suggested HDS-induced liver injury secondary to artemisinin; the Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) score was 7, suggesting a 'probable' association. The liver-injury pattern at presentation was hepatocellular (R ratio >10), evolving into a prolonged cholestatic phase, with liver biopsy showing cholestatic hepatitis (marked cholestasis with mild portal and lobular inflammation), and the patient improved after discontinuation with normal liver tests one year later; rechallenge was not performed.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Self-administered herbal supplement taken without medical supervision; monotherapy with reportedly no other active ingredients; no competing etiologies identified.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 125 mg orally two or three times daily for ~6 weeks for general health maintenance. Presentation: 1-week history of arthralgia and jaundice; total bilirubin 15.4 mg/dL, ALT 675 U/L, AST 175 U/L, ALP 208 U/L, INR 1.1. Liver biopsy showed cholestatic hepatitis with marked cholestasis and mild portal and lobular inflammation. RUCAM score 7 (probable). Pattern at onset hepatocellular (R ratio at onset >10) evolving into prolonged cholestatic phase. Improvement and normal liver tests 1 year after discontinuation; rechallenge not performed.

raw_record.support_text: A 58-year-old previously healthy man who took sildenafil 50 mg 1 month before symptom onset was diagnosed, on the basis of criteria for drug-induced liver disorders and the Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale, with probable sildenafil-induced cholestatic hepatotoxicity. He used no other medications, and his laboratory values improved without treatment, returning to normal 4 months after onset.
raw_record.extra_details: Presenting with jaundice, pruritus, and malaise. Labs: AST 42 IU/l, ALT 64 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 476 IU/l, total bilirubin 8.5 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 6.3 mg/dl, albumin 3.6 g/dl, eosinophils 2.8%. Liver biopsy showed marked intrahepatic cholestasis with bile stasis in canaliculi around the peripheral area and minimal portal necroinflammation. Viral hepatitis, autoimmune, and obstructive etiologies excluded. Symptom onset about 1 month after a single 50 mg dose; recovered without treatment by 4 months.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a well-documented case of acute mixed hepatitis attributed to sildenafil (Viagra) in a 56-year-old man with no notable medical history who took sildenafil 25 mg on 5 and 7 May 2003 for erectile dysfunction. Causality was rated probable (score 8) by the Danan et al. liver injury assessment scale, based on onset within 30 days, >50% decrease in total bilirubin within 180 days after stopping sildenafil, and no clinical, biological, morphological, or histological evidence of another cause of acute liver injury. The ALAT/alkaline phosphatase ratio was 3.2; liver biopsy showed resolving cholestatic hepatitis and the authors noted many eosinophils suggesting a possible immuno-allergic hepatotoxicity mechanism. The patient recovered with normal liver biology by 10 July.
raw_record.extra_details: 56-year-old man, no other medications taken, alcohol <10 g/day. Sildenafil (Viagra) 25 mg taken on May 5 and 7, 2003. Icterus from June 3, 2003; jaundice, liver tests peaked with ALAT 8xN, ASAT 3.5xN, GGT 12-13xN, alkaline phosphatase 2-2.5xN, total bilirubin 6.5-8xN (conjugated predominance), prothrombin 100%. Danan causality score 8 (probable). Liver biopsy: resolving cholestatic hepatitis, discrete lobular cholestasis, rare apoptotic bodies, non-congestive centrilobular sinusoidal dilation with Kupffer cell hyperplasia, portal cholangitis with lymphocytes and eosinophils. Possible immuno-allergic mechanism. No rechallenge. Prior literature case (Maroy) of cytolytic hepatitis with likely ischemic origin in a coronary patient excluded from attribution here. Drug metabolized by CYP3A4/CYP2C9.

raw_record.support_text: The letter reports a case of acute liver toxicity induced by sildenafil citrate (Viagra). While therapeutic dosages (25–100 mg/day) are usually well tolerated, the authors describe a case of acute liver toxicity attributed to sildenafil.
raw_record.extra_details: A 49-year-old man with diabetes (treated with glibenclamide) and no liver disease risk factors took Viagra 50 mg/day for erectile dysfunction; routine blood tests were normal when sildenafil was started. Four weeks later he developed right hypochondriac pain without fever, jaundice, or encephalopathy, with palpable hepatomegaly and an increase in serum aminotransferases (AST 7.4x normal, ALT 1.2x) while GGT, ALP, and total bilirubin remained normal. Prothrombin time, hematocrit, leukocyte and eosinophil counts were normal; tests for hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis B core antibody, IgM and total anti-hepatitis A, anti-hepatitis C, and IgM anti-cytomegalovirus were negative, and anti-mitochondrial, anti-nuclear and anti-smooth muscle antibodies were absent. Liver tests normalized after drug withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a patient with a hepatotoxic reaction presenting with general malaise, severe jaundice, and pruritus, which turned out to be caused by the at-first unrevealed use of sildenafil. The injury appears hepatocanalicular, characterized by a hepatocellular liver test pattern combined with extensive cholestasis on liver biopsy. They caution that use of sildenafil may not be readily disclosed by the patient or his doctor.
raw_record.extra_details: Rarely noted complication of sildenafil (phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor for erectile dysfunction). Case: 59-year-old previously healthy man admitted with jaundice, pruritus, anorexia, nausea, fatigue, and weight loss since 7 weeks; tender liver palpable two to three fingers below right costal margin. Liver biopsy showed extensive cholestasis; injury described as hepatocanalicular. Laboratory values: total bilirubin 89 µmol/l (normal <17), ALT 1665 U/l (<30), AST 1077 U/l (<30), APh 173 U/l (30-100), GGT 102 U/l (<40) about 6 weeks before admission; at admission bilirubin 307, AST 47, ALT 59, APh 210. Patient denied other substances except about one alcoholic drink per week; was prescribed ursodeoxycholic acid 300 mg three times daily for pruritus a few days prior.

raw_record.support_text: A 58-year-old female with beta thalassemia major was admitted with fever, fatigue, abnormal liver function test results (aspartate aminotransferase 167 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 250 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 102 U/L, total bilirubin 3.79 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.37 mg/dL) and hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis after 25 days of treatment with oral deferasirox 1500 mg/day for chronic iron overload. Despite extended examination no obvious cause of the fever, hepatitis, or hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis was found, and the diagnosis was compatible with tubular dysfunction, drug-induced hepatitis, and hypersensitivity reaction due to deferasirox. Use of the Naranjo probability scale revealed that the adverse reaction was probable; all pathological findings were fully reversible.

raw_record.support_text: Based on the course of laboratory parameters over time, normal ultrasound findings, and the absence of other hepatotoxic agents, the authors conclude that the patient developed hepatic/cholestatic hepatitis as a result of temozolomide (TMZ) treatment. Although histological confirmation was declined, the hepatitis was detected early (normal bilirubin at detection), TMZ was discontinued early, and the patient survived the toxicity, in contrast to the fatal liver failure case reported by the German Drug Commission.
raw_record.extra_details: TMZ is an alkylating cytostatic drug, orally administered, converted to active metabolite MTIC; undergoes renal elimination; frequently reported hepatic side effects include elevation of AST, ALT and GGT. Only a few cases of severe liver damage due to TMZ have been reported; most were associated with hepatitis virus reactivation or interaction with other hepatotoxic drugs, while Goldbecker and Dixit described individual cases of hepatotoxicity caused by TMZ alone. In the reported patient, serum bilirubin and liver enzymes normalized during follow-up but GGT remained elevated; jaundice resolved and no neurological symptoms developed over 3 months; patient had glioblastoma and was lost to further follow-up after the third month. The German Drug Commission (2011) reported a fatal case of liver failure concurrent with leukocytopenia in which bilirubin reached 11 mg/dl and rose more than twofold, ending in death from hepatic encephalopathy and liver failure. Literature cases: bilirubin 11 mg/dl, MTIC, Goldbecker case, German Drug Commission case, TMZ monotherapy.

raw_record.support_text: The patient presented with icteric sclera, generalized jaundice, mild right upper quadrant tenderness and a palpable liver edge; LFTs on arrival showed AST 1,400, ALT 2,253 and TB 9.9. The RUCAM/CIOMS causality scale, a validated tool for assessing causality in suspected DILI, gave a score of 9, suggestive of a highly probable adverse drug reaction. The patient was only taking rosuvastatin and admitted no other drugs, supplements, or herbal products.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of rosuvastatin-associated DILI. RUCAM score 9 (highly probable). LFTs on presentation: AST 1,400, ALT 2,253, TB 9.9, normal CBC and electrolytes; later AST 942, ALT 1,312, ALP 167, TB 17.2. Liver biopsy showed acute severe hepatitis with portal and lobular mixed inflammatory infiltrate (neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils) with interface activity and bile duct damage, interpreted as a likely immune-mediated drug reaction. Workup for chronic liver disease, autoimmune antibodies (ASMA, ANA, anti-LKM), hepatotropic viruses, HSV/CMV/EBV, and copper/iron/trichrome stains was unrevealing. Treated with IV N-acetylcysteine for 5 days and Ursodiol without enzyme improvement; evaluated for possible liver transplantation; patient remained stable without hepatic encephalopathy. Abdominal ultrasound showed nonspecific hepatitis findings and CT showed mild periportal edema. Patient denied alcohol and other co-medications.

raw_record.support_text: In this prospective U.S. drug-induced liver injury study, statin-associated liver injury showed prolonged latency in some cases, with 5 of 22 patients having taken the agent for a year or more before onset of acute injury. Prolonged latency was seen with most types of statins, including atorvastatin, simvastatin, fluvastatin, and rosuvastatin, presenting with both hepatocellular and cholestatic patterns of liver injury; other causes of liver disease were systematically excluded and liver test elevations resolved with statin discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: From the Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network prospective study: statins initially implicated in 61 cases, with careful adjudication finding 22 (36%) convincing (>50% likelihood). All major statins were implicated at rates similar to their relative U.S. use. Prolonged latency up to >1 year seen in 5 of 22 patients; both hepatocellular and cholestatic biochemical patterns occurred; some cases had autoimmune hepatitis-like features with ANA/SMA positivity, and 2 of 6 autoimmune cases developed self-sustained autoimmune hepatitis requiring long-term immunosuppression. Histology included cholestatic hepatitis, confluent necrosis, and steatosis (often pre-existing fatty liver). One fatal case of acute-on-chronic liver failure occurred in the statin series. Study systematically excluded other liver disease causes and liver tests resolved on drug discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: In the hepatic toxicity section, hepatic transaminase elevations greater than three times ULN on consecutive visits were infrequently observed in rosuvastatin-treated patients and were not associated with clinical evidence of hepatic dysfunction or failure, occurring at a rate similar to other marketed statins. Two reported cases of jaundice had no relationship to rosuvastatin that could be determined; both patients had elevated liver function tests but no evidence of hepatotoxicity, and jaundice resolved after discontinuing therapy. The paper explicitly concludes no hepatotoxicity relationship for rosuvastatin in these findings.
raw_record.extra_details: Data from 12,569 patients receiving 5-80 mg daily in 27 controlled clinical trials within the rosuvastatin development program, and from 10,200 patients in the New Drug Application. Transaminase elevations >3x ULN occurred at 0-0.4% across 5-40 mg doses (Table 3) and were mostly transient, resolving or improving with continued therapy or brief interruption. Two jaundice cases were reported with no relationship to rosuvastatin determined and no evidence of hepatotoxicity. Routine liver function monitoring before and 12 weeks after initiation and dose increases is recommended as for all statins.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN prospective study of 899 idiosyncratic DILI cases, rosuvastatin was implicated in 0.8% of the definitive, highly likely, or probable total DILI cases and showed a long latency period profile of DILI (>60 days postexposure).
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated in 0.8% of adjudicated (definitive, highly likely, or probable) DILI cases in the DILIN prospective study of 899 idiosyncratic DILI cases; long latency profile (>60 days postexposure).

raw_record.support_text: In a randomized 6-week trial in patients with hypercholesterolemia, clinically relevant increases in hepatic transaminases or creatine kinase, indicative of hepatotoxicity or myotoxicity, were not observed with rosuvastatin. A single ALT >3 times the upper limit of normal occurred in 1 patient in the rosuvastatin 20-mg group and was considered related to trial treatment, but no persistent hepatic transaminase increases or clinically meaningful hepatotoxicity were observed.
raw_record.extra_details: Doses 5-80 mg over 6 weeks in hypercholesterolemia patients; one isolated ALT >3x ULN at 20-mg group considered treatment-related; no persistent transaminase or CK increases.

raw_record.support_text: In clinical trials of rosuvastatin, adverse events occurred at similar rates in the rosuvastatin and placebo groups. No clinically significant increases in liver function tests or creatinine kinase levels were reported, and no hepatotoxicity or myotoxicity was seen. The text explicitly states that no hepatotoxicity was observed with rosuvastatin in these trials.
raw_record.extra_details: Findings reported from clinical trial data comparing rosuvastatin with placebo; no clinically significant increases in liver function tests were reported, and no hepatotoxicity was seen. Author notes that additional clinical studies and postmarketing analyses will be important to confirm the safety profile of pitavastatin and rosuvastatin.

raw_record.support_text: In the US DILIN prospective study, only 22 of 1188 suspected DILI cases were accepted after adjudication as true statin-induced DILI, with mostly mild-moderate self-limited injury and a likely idiosyncratic class effect. Rosuvastatin accounted for 4 of these 22 adjudicated cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Adjudicated rosuvastatin DILI cases: US DILIN n=4; Swedish 1988-2010 n=2. DILIN aggregate (all statins): hepatocellular 12/22, cholestatic 9/22, 4 severe, 1 fatal; latency 34 days to >10 years.

raw_record.support_text: Four case reports in the table attribute liver injury to rosuvastatin. These include a 54 M on 2.5 mg for 8 months (peak ALT 709 U/L, ALP 2,055, IgG 1,857; liver biopsy), a 47 M on 5 mg for 4 months (peak ALT 201 U/L, ANA+ and ASMA+), a 47 M on 5 mg for 1.5 months with jaundice and pruritus (peak ALT 2,260 U/L; liver biopsy), and a 64 M on 10 mg for 4 months (peak ALT 775 U/L, jaundice and abdominal pain). All show a predominantly aminotransferase (hepatocellular) pattern with clinical hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Four reported cases at daily doses of 2.5-10 mg; latency from 1.5 to 8 months; presenting symptoms included generalized weakness, abdominal pain, jaundice, pruritus, fatigue, anorexia, malaise; peak ALT 201-2,260 U/L; bilirubin 3.53 mg/dL in one case; ANA/ASMA positive and elevated IgG (1,857) in some cases suggesting autoimmune features; liver biopsy performed in two cases (Kawasaki 54 M and Shah 2019).

They noted that previous reports on acute severe liver dysfunction induced by febuxostat are scarce and recommended monitoring liver function test parameters to avoid progression of febuxostat-induced liver damage, especially in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and those undergoing HD.

raw_record.extra_details: Case report of acute severe liver dysfunction (acute liver injury) attributed to febuxostat in an HD patient. Febuxostat was administered as an alternative to allopurinol for hyperuricemia; the patient had previously been on oral allopurinol. The drug-induced lymphocyte stimulation test (DLST) was negative for both febuxostat (92% SI) and allopurinol (101% SI). The case also involved severe hyperkalemia with severe liver dysfunction, and no HLA-B*58:01 (patient profile HLA-A*24:02, HLA-B*52:01, HLA-DRB1*15:02); no study has reported an association between these HLA alleles and DILI, so the HLA association with the febuxostat reaction remains unclear. Authors recommend frequent liver function monitoring and possibly lower than usual febuxostat doses in CKD/HD patients.

raw_record.support_text: A liver biopsy showed striking canalicular cholestasis with bile plugs in dilated canaliculi and occasional portal tracts with a prominent lymphocytic infiltrate and mild piecemeal necrosis. On withdrawal of oxycodone his liver function tests improved: one day after stopping oxycodone his bilirubin was 138 μmol/L (<20), ALP 188 u/L (40–110), GGT 34 u/L (<50), ALT 59 u/L (<45), and AST 53 u/L (<40). This case links oxycodone to a cholestatic liver injury supported by dechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of cholestatic liver injury attributed to oxycodone. Liver biopsy showed canalicular cholestasis with bile plugs in dilated canaliculi and a prominent lymphocytic infiltrate with mild piecemeal necrosis in occasional portal tracts. On dechallenge liver tests improved: bilirubin 138 μmol/L (<20), ALP 188 u/L (40–110), GGT 34 u/L (<50), ALT 59 u/L (<45), AST 53 u/L (<40). CT cholangiogram indicated pathology at the hepatocellular level rather than ductal obstruction. A co-existing gallbladder full of calculi was present but ductal obstruction was excluded. Competing causes (serum copper/caeruloplasmin, α-fetoprotein, α-1 antitrypsin, iron studies, ANA, ANCA, anti-LKM1, AMA, ASMA) were unremarkable.
