raw_record.support_text: The authors state that although salicylates have little direct toxic effect on the liver in large therapeutic doses, there are increasing reports of children and adults with rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and rheumatic fever who developed hepatotoxicity while on high-dose aspirin therapy. In Case 2, a four-year-old girl with rheumatic fever treated with aspirin (100 mg/kg/day) developed nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain on day 12 with salicylate 26.8 mg/dl and SGOT (AST) 1325 iu/l; after a two-day discontinuation and re-institution at a reduced dose (80 mg/kg/day), AST fell to 109 iu/l and liver function returned to normal. The paper concludes the hepatotoxicity is dose-related and reversible and not a hypersensitivity reaction.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose aspirin therapy; risk appears restricted to patients with connective tissue disorders (rheumatic fever, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus).
raw_record.extra_details: Case 2: 4-year-old girl, aspirin 100 mg/kg/day; symptoms of nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain on day 12 of therapy; serum salicylate 26.8 mg/dl and SGOT (AST) 1325 iu/l (79.34 nkat); Hepatitis B antigen and mononucleosis spot tests negative; aspirin discontinued two days, then reinstituted at 80 mg/kg/day; after 10 days salicylate was 18 mg/dl and SGOT (AST) 109 iu/l (6.53 nkat); liver function tests normal at three-month follow-up. Mechanism concluded dose-related (hepatotoxicity appears when salicylate concentrations exceed ~25 mg/dl) and reversible on dose reduction, not a hypersensitivity reaction; saturated formation of salicyluric acid and salicyl phenolic glucuronide at therapeutic doses increases minor metabolites, possibly hepatotoxic in uniquely sensitive connective-tissue-disorder patients. Typical features across reports: anorexia, malaise, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain; SGOT/SGPT elevation; hyperbilirubinaemia unusual; alkaline phosphatase normal or slightly increased; biopsy shows preserved lobular architecture, widened sinusoidal spaces, focal hepatocyte necrosis, degeneration and ballooning with anisocytosis and mitotic figures.

raw_record.support_text: In the present case report, acute liver failure (ALF) was induced by an overdose of acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) taken in a suicide attempt; the resulting serum salicylate concentration was 1,180 µg/mL. The authors note that ASA-induced hepatic injury is a well-known dose-related phenomenon tied to the intrinsic hepatotoxicity of salicylate, whereas ASA-induced ALF is rare. The patient developed ALF with hepatic coma and received emergency living donor liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose of ASA in a suicide attempt by an adult without an antecedent viral infection; patient presented with ALF with hepatic coma.
raw_record.extra_details: Serum salicylate concentration 1,180 µg/mL (toxic range considered 350–700 µg/mL; severe poisoning ≥700 µg/mL). Histopathology showed swelling and microvesicular steatosis consistent with Reye's syndrome, but presence of cholestasis and periportal neutrophil infiltration contraindicated Reye's; loss of hepatocytes and cholestasis were also noted. Patient received emergency LDLT; ALF score at transplantation was 4.

raw_record.support_text: A 20-year-old woman ingested 66 g of acetylsalicylic acid (ASA, aspirin) in a suicide attempt. Nine days after ingestion she developed hepatic encephalopathy and was diagnosed with acute liver failure with hepatic coma, accompanied by acute pancreatitis and acute renal failure, attributed to the ASA overdose. She was treated with emergency living donor liver transplantation using a left lobe graft and subsequently recovered. ASA-induced hepatic injury is described as a well-known adverse effect, with ALF from ASA overdose being rare.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/supratherapeutic exposure (66 g ASA, ~200 tablets) in a suicide attempt; concurrent acute pancreatitis and acute renal failure; outcome required living donor liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Blood salicylate 1180 µg/mL on admission; hepatic atrophy and diffuse low-density hepatic parenchymal areas on CT, diffuse atrophy with steatosis on MRI; progressive liver test deterioration with elevated PT-INR (MELD 28 then 42); treated with gastric lavage, activated charcoal, bicarbonate, steroid pulse, plasma exchange, and continuous hemodiafiltration without improvement; acute hepatic coma with encephalopathy on day 9; successful LDLT and discharge. ASA also known as aspirin.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report that salicylates (aspirin) therapy in patients with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis caused hepatic dysfunction and, in three of their patients, hepatic encephalopathy that resolved when aspirin was discontinued. Evidence of acute hepatic failure included severely impaired mental function with striking transaminase elevations, prolonged prothrombin time, elevated blood ammonia, and an EEG consistent with metabolic encephalopathy. All three patients were subsequently rechallenged with aspirin and developed recurrent hepatotoxicity, and hepatotoxicity to aspirin was obtained even in the absence of encephalopathy.

raw_record.extra_details: Three patients developed hepatotoxicity with hepatic encephalopathy and signs of acute hepatic failure while on aspirin for JRA; all three recovered when aspirin was discontinued and each had recurrent hepatotoxicity upon rechallenge. In Patient 2, liver biopsy one week after onset showed ballooned hepatocytes with regeneration, focal pseudoacinar formation around dilated canaliculi, and Kupffer cell hypertrophy. Mentation recovered and liver tests normalized (e.g., SGOT) after stopping aspirin. The paper notes prior reports of hepatic dysfunction in up to 60% of JRA/SLE patients treated with salicylates, generally considered benign with mildly elevated liver enzymes.

raw_record.support_text: A 92-year-old woman developed jaundice with dark urine and itching 16 days after starting memantine (5 mg/d for the first 8 days, then 10 mg/d for the next 8 days). Laboratory tests showed increased AST, ALT, gamma-glutamyltransferase, total and direct bilirubin, and ALP. Memantine was discontinued, symptoms resolved by 7 days, and liver enzymes normalized after 20 days. Based on biochemical, clinical, and instrumental parameters, criteria of drug-induced liver disorders, and the Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale, the authors diagnosed probable cholestatic hepatitis induced by memantine. The conclusion states that memantine is a probable cause of drug-induced hepatitis with cholestasis, with alternative causes (mechanical obstruction, viral hepatitis, primary biliary cirrhosis) excluded.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Very elderly patient (92-year-old woman) with mixed moderate dementia and behavior disorders and comorbid hypertension and heart failure; patient was taking concurrent digoxin (0.125 mg/d), lisinopril (5 mg/d), tiapride (50 mg/d), alprazolam (0.25 mg/d), and promazine (10 mg/d), which were continued during the event.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose: memantine 5 mg/d for first 8 days, escalated to 10 mg/d for next 8 days; jaundice, dark urine, and itching onset on day 16. Lab values at day 1: AST 74 U/L (normal 5-30), ALT 132 U/L (5-56), gamma-GT 155 U/L (4-20), total bilirubin 4.3 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.5 mg/dL, ALP 912 U/L (38-126). Diagnosis of probable cholestatic hepatitis by Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale and criteria of drug-induced liver disorders. Dechallenge: signs/symptoms disappeared 7 days after memantine withdrawal; liver enzymes normalized after 20 days. Negative HAV, HBV, HCV, antimitochondrial antibodies, and direct Coombs test; ultrasonography excluded mechanical obstruction. Mechanism not identified; authors discuss memantine lysosomal accumulation/phospholipidosis and effects on canalicular transport proteins as possible mechanisms.

raw_record.support_text: The authors reason that fulminant hepatic failure in the two HIV-infected patients can be ascribed to didanosine (ddI): both received ddI for 13 weeks, neither had prior liver disease, no superimposed infection including hepatitis viruses was found, and although both received concomitant therapy, those drugs were judged not responsible (zidovudine hepatotoxicity is rare with macrovesicular rather than microvesicular steatosis; ketoconazole had been given continuously for 22 months). They compare their two cases with the previously reported case (Lai et al., 1991), all showing fulminant hepatitis after 13-15 weeks of ddI with similar symptoms and prior normal liver function.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: HIV-infected patients (CDC stage IV) receiving concomitant therapy (zidovudine, aerosolized pentamidine, ketoconazole); authors argued these co-medications were not responsible for the hepatic impairment.
raw_record.extra_details: Two own cases plus one previously reported case (Lai et al., 1991), all fatal. ddI doses 7.5, 11, and 12 mg/kg/day; duration from ddI start to first symptoms 13-15 weeks. Inaugural symptoms: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dyspnoea. Normal liver function before the episode; transaminases did not exceed 5-10x normal. Admissions showed moderate cytolysis, anionic cholestasis, and lactic acidosis; histology on post-mortem biopsy showed extensive diffuse microvesicular steatosis with mild centrolobular cholestasis and no necrosis or fibrosis. Death from major hepatic failure with cardiovascular shock. ddI and ketoconazole withdrawn on day 1; thiamin had no effect. Included for comparison: zidovudine-related fatty liver (macrovesicular) and one previous ketoconazole vesicular steatosis case were considered unlikely causes.

raw_record.extra_details: First case of non-cirrhotic portal hypertension (NCPH) in an HIV-infected adolescent described in Brazil. HIV viral load undetectable for 12 years. Indicators included gradual CD4+ T cell decrease, prolonged thrombocytopenia, elevated alkaline phosphatase, splenomegaly, and severe liver fibrosis by transient elastography. Authors recommend investigating NCPH in HIV patients on long-term ddI or with portal hypertension indicators.

raw_record.support_text: Takeda's fasiglifam (TAK-875), the most advanced FFA1 agonist candidate at the time, had its phase III clinical trials discontinued in December 2013 due to reports of idiosyncratic liver toxicity observed within an extended population of patients. The paper states the hepatotoxicity is almost unanimously linked to the highly lipophilic character of the molecule rather than its action at the receptor.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase III clinical trials by Takeda were discontinued in December 2013 due to reports of idiosyncratic liver toxicity in an extended patient population. Hepatotoxicity is attributed to the highly lipophilic character of the molecule rather than its action at the receptor (FFA1 is primarily expressed in pancreas and brain). Development failure led to a decrease in FFA1 agonist research.

raw_record.support_text: The Kaplan–Meier analysis shows an increased incidence in the fasiglifam arms for time-to-first-occurrence of ALT > 3 × ULN compared with placebo and active comparators (log-rank test, p < 0.0001). Most events in fasiglifam treatment arms occurred in the first 6 months, and although the 50 mg dose showed higher event rates than the 25 mg dose, the log-rank test comparing 50 versus 25 mg was not significant at the 5% level.
raw_record.extra_details: Randomized trial of fasiglifam 25 and 50 mg vs placebo and active comparators (sitagliptin 100 mg, glimepiride) in type 2 diabetes. ALT >3 × ULN: 2.8% fasiglifam (134/4819 for 25/50 mg) vs 0.5% placebo and 0.8% active comparator; ALT >5 × ULN 1.2%, ALT >10 × ULN 0.5%, ALT >3 ×ULN + TBIL>2 × ULN 0.1%, AST >3 × ULN 1.6%. Liver Safety Evaluation Committee (LSEC) adjudication for fasiglifam: 1 highly likely, 35 probable, 11 possible, 5 unlikely, 5 excluded. Primary injury pattern by R value was hepatocellular (fasiglifam 2.2% vs placebo 0.3%). Hospitalization for liver injury in fasiglifam arms: 12 (0.2%); no liver-related deaths or transplants. Serious liver injury (no deaths or transplants) defined as ALT >8 × ULN, ALT >3 × ULN + TBIL >2 × ULN, hospitalization, or death/transplant.

raw_record.support_text: Fasiglifam (TAK-875), an oral FFAR1 (GPR40) agonist for glucose lowering in type 2 diabetes, had its development discontinued because of the rare DILI incidence detected in a phase 3 study. The investigators recruited 43 patients with TAK-875 DILI and 129 matched treated controls from the clinical trials for a GWAS; ALT was elevated after treatment and total bilirubin was also increased, consistent with experimental models showing inhibition of bile acid transporters by TAK-875. No genome-wide significant association signal was found.
raw_record.extra_details: Development discontinued due to rare DILI incidence in a phase 3 study; DILI cases and controls recruited from the clinical trials for a GWAS (43 cases, 129 matched controls). ALT and total bilirubin both increased, consistent with inhibition of bile acid transporters (cholestatic/mixed pattern). GWAS (with 1000 Genomes Phase 3 imputation, 13,477,278 autosomal variants) yielded no genome-wide significant signals; TAK-875 DILI shared genetic aetiology with the cholestatic/mixed (CM)-DILI iDILIC-DILIN GWAS more than with all-DILI or hepatocellular-DILI; a CM-PRS exactly distinguished TAK-875 DILI cases from controls with AUROC 0.61 (95% CI 0.51-0.71). Indication/class: glucose-lowering FFAR1 agonist in type 2 diabetes.

The LSEC consensus causality assessment was that a causal role for fasiglifam was highly likely (75-95% likelihood).

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a rare case of repeated drug-induced liver injury caused by phenprobamate, a widely used muscle relaxant, describing it as a strong probability due to repeated toxicity. A 28-year-old male with jaundice (skin, eye, urine icterus) developed DILI after 2 weeks of phenprobamate use for muscle relaxation with no other medication, herbal use, or addiction; he had been hospitalized a year earlier with a similar 'probable' phenprobamate toxicity that fully resolved on withdrawal, and he self-restarted the drug 2 weeks prior. After ruling out viral, autoimmune, biliary, and genetic causes, the offending drug was stopped and liver tests significantly normalized within one month.
raw_record.extra_details: Repeated/rechallenge injury: patient had a prior hospitalization one year earlier with a 'probable' phenprobamate DILI that fully recovered after withdrawal, then self-restarted the drug and developed a second episode. Phenprobamate was used for muscle relaxation (muscle relaxant in sports medicine) for 2 weeks; no comorbidities, preexisting liver disease, ethanol/smoking, other treatments, or herbal use. Other causes excluded (hepatitis A-E, CMV, EBV, HSV, VZV, biliary obstruction, autoimmune markers ANA/ASMA/anti-LKM/AMA and IgG/IgG4, Wilson disease, hemochromatosis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency). Liver tests significantly normalized within one month of withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: Two patients with acarbose-induced hepatotoxicity are presented; only three prior cases of hepatotoxicity related to acarbose treatment were reported. The clinical course of patient 2 showed acute hepatocellular injury while patient 1 showed chronic hepatocellular injury by international consensus criteria; both lacked hypersensitivity features (fever, rash, eosinophilia) and had a relatively long latency, suggesting a metabolic idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity caused by acarbose or its metabolites, mainly 4-methylpyrogallol derivatives. The paper concludes that hepatotoxicity, although a very rare adverse event of acarbose therapy, can be severe.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients described; patient 2 showed acute hepatocellular injury and patient 1 chronic hepatocellular injury per international consensus criteria. Hypersensitivity features (fever, rash, eosinophilia) absent; relatively long latency between drug intake and symptom onset. Resolution after stopping drug and absence of alternative explanations led authors to strongly suggest acarbose as the cause. Mechanism attributed to metabolic idiosyncrasy, possibly involving acarbose metabolites, mainly 4-methylpyrogallol derivatives. Only three prior acarbose hepatotoxicity cases reported (five total), all in Spanish patients (three from South Spain), suggesting possible genetic variation in acarbose metabolism.

raw_record.support_text: The authors attribute the hepatic abnormalities in both patients to acarbose, stating that the temporal relation between institution of acarbose therapy and onset of hepatic abnormalities, the resolution after stopping the drug, and the absence of alternative explanations strongly suggest the implication of acarbose. They further describe the mechanism as a metabolic idiosyncrasy, caused by the original compound or its metabolites, mainly 4-methylpyrogallol derivatives, given the long latency and absence of hypersensitivity features.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases in NIDDM patients treated with acarbose 50 mg three times daily. Case 1 (45-year-old man): mild transaminase elevation (AST 62, ALT 127 U/l rising to 153) with normal bilirubin/ALP/GGT, onset about 18 months after start, classified as chronic hepatocellular injury by international consensus criteria; enzymes normalized 4 months after withdrawal. Case 2 (54-year-old woman): fatigue, dark urine, jaundice after 5 months of treatment, AST 2436, ALT 2556 U/l, total bilirubin 4.67 mg/dl (direct 3.19), GGT 601, ALP 174 U/l, classified as acute hepatocellular injury; normalized within 5 months of stopping. Viral hepatitis (A, B, C by PCR, CMV, EBV) and autoimmune serologies, iron and copper studies, and abdominal ultrasonography were unremarkable in both. Features of hypersensitivity (fever, rash, eosinophilia) were absent, and only three prior cases of acarbose-related hepatotoxicity were reported.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a new case of acute liver toxicity in a diabetic patient treated with acarbose (50 mg t.i.d. per os) that fulfills the criteria of a 'probable' adverse event related to the use of acarbose, i.e., a temporal relationship, a favorable course after stopping the drug, and absence of other known causes of liver disease. They conclude that acute liver damage induced by acarbose should be suspected when abnormal liver tests develop after starting acarbose.
raw_record.extra_details: 57-year-old woman with noninsulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM); acarbose 50 mg t.i.d. per os for 2 months. On admission: scleral jaundice, right-upper-quadrant pain, nausea, dark urine, light stools, slightly tender hepatomegaly. Peak ALT 1580 IU/L, AST 1090 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 220 IU/L, GGT 497 IU/L, bilirubin 3.8 mg/dl, ferritin 1290 ng/ml. Serologies for HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM, anti-HCV, anti-HAV IgM, anti-EBV, anti-CMV IgM negative; autoantibodies negative; iron/copper, ceruloplasmin, alpha-1-antitrypsin normal. No liver biopsy, no rechallenge. Clinical course spontaneously favorable; all biochemical abnormalities subsided within 5 weeks; patient well 8 months later on glipizide.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a new case of acute liver toxicity in a diabetic patient that fulfills criteria of a 'probable' adverse event related to the use of acarbose. Acarbose is an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor that is minimally absorbed in the gut, rarely inducing moderate aminotransferase elevations in treated patients, with more severe liver damage being very unusual. The case fulfills the three criteria of temporal relationship, favorable course after stopping the drug, and absence of other known causes of liver disease, so acute liver damage induced by acarbose should be suspected when liver-test abnormalities develop after starting acarbose.
raw_record.extra_details: 57-year-old woman with noninsulin-dependent diabetes mellitus treated with acarbose 50 mg t.i.d. per os for 2 months; developed right upper quadrant pain, nausea, dark urine, lightening of stool color, and scleral jaundice 1 week before admission. Elevated ALT (1,580 IU/L), AST (1,090), GGT (497), alkaline phosphatase (220), bilirubin 3.8 mg/dl, and ferritin (1,290 ng/ml); viral and autoimmune serologies negative; abdominal ultrasonography normal. Spontaneous recovery within 5 weeks; liver biopsy not performed and no rechallenge. Causality rated 'probable' based on temporal relationship, favorable course after drug stopping, and absence of other known liver disease causes. Patient remained well on glipizide 8 months after the episode.

raw_record.support_text: A 65-year-old woman with non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, on long-term glibenclamide, had acarbose (100 mg three times daily) added to her treatment in mid-1993. Two months later she developed jaundice, malaise, and anorexia, with elevated liver enzymes (AST 638 U/L, ALT 690 U/L, total bilirubin 9.9 mg/dL with direct bilirubin 7.84 mg/dL, GGT 156 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 221 U/L). Viral hepatitis and autoantibodies were ruled out, and ultrasonography showed a normal liver, so the authors attribute the hepatic injury to acarbose and describe it in the title as 'Hepatic Injury Caused by Acarbose.' After acarbose was stopped, bilirubin fell to 1.8 mg/dL and AST/ALT decreased within 4 weeks, with laboratory results normal within 9 months.
raw_record.extra_details: 65-year-old woman with NIDDM; concurrent glibenclamide background therapy (indicated 7 years prior). Acarbose 100 mg three times daily; latency ~2 months. Symptoms: malaise, anorexia, jaundice. Labs: AST 638 U/L, ALT 690 U/L, total bilirubin 9.9 mg/dL (direct 7.84 mg/dL), GGT 156 U/L, ALP 221 U/L. Viral hepatitis and antinuclear/anti-smooth-muscle antibodies excluded; ultrasonography showed normal liver and no dilated bile ducts. Dechallenge: 4 weeks after stopping acarbose, bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL, AST 159 U/L, ALT 155 U/L; normalized within 9 months. Outpatient management (patient refused hospitalization). Acarbose is a competitive α-glucosidase inhibitor that delays carbohydrate absorption and decreases postprandial glucose.

raw_record.support_text: Case 2 describes a 54-year-old woman prescribed acarbose (50 mg three times daily) for NIDDM who developed fatigue, dark urine, and jaundice with markedly elevated transaminases (AST 2436 U/l, ALT 2556 U/l, total bilirubin 4.67 mg/dl with direct bilirubin 3.19 mg/dl), after which viral and autoimmune causes were excluded and liver tests normalized within 5 months of stopping acarbose. The temporal relation between acarbose therapy and symptom onset, resolution after discontinuation, and absence of alternative explanations strongly suggest the implication of acarbose as the cause of the liver injury, classified as acute hepatocellular injury per international consensus criteria.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients reported (patient 1 with chronic hepatocellular injury; patient 2 with acute hepatocellular injury). Case 2: 50 mg three times daily; onset of fatigue/dark urine 5 months after starting; jaundice on exam; AST 2436 U/l, ALT 2556 U/l, total bilirubin 4.67 mg/dl (direct 3.19 mg/dl), GGT 601 U/l, ALP 174 U/l; viral hepatitis A/B/C (PCR), CMV, EBV excluded; no autoantibodies; normal liver/gallbladder on ultrasound; normal liver tests within 5 months of stopping. Mechanism attributed to metabolic idiosyncrasy rather than hypersensitivity (no fever, rash, or eosinophilia; long latency), possibly involving the parent compound or 4-methylpyrogallol metabolites; authors note all five reported acarbose hepatotoxicity cases (three prior plus these two) were Spanish, three in South Spain, suggesting genetic variation in acarbose metabolism; hepatotoxicity described as a very rare but potentially severe adverse event of acarbose.

raw_record.support_text: In the paper's conclusion regarding acarbose therapy, the authors note that the three previously reported cases of acarbose-associated hepatotoxicity and the two patients presented here were all Spanish, and suggest genetic variations in acarbose metabolism could account for the hepatotoxicity. They conclude that hepatotoxicity, although a very rare adverse event of acarbose therapy, can be severe, and that clinicians should be aware of this possibility when prescribing the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Five cases total considered (three previously reported plus two presented in this paper), all Spanish; most detected in South Spain, suggesting genetic variation in acarbose metabolism could account for hepatotoxicity. Hepatotoxicity is stated to be a very rare adverse event of acarbose therapy that can be severe.

raw_record.support_text: A 40-year-old woman with schizophrenia (on fluphenazine decanoate) and NIDDM (on glibenclamide) developed vomiting, abdominal pain, and jaundice about 2 months after acarbose (100 mg every 8 h) was added. AST was 1938 IU/L, ALT 2350 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 325 IU/L, and total bilirubin 188 µmol/L with mildly decreased prothrombin time; viral, iron/copper, and autoantibody tests were negative. Acarbose was stopped while fluphenazine and glibenclamide were maintained, and ALT fell to 69 IU/L after 2.5 months and normalized by 10 months. On acarbose rechallenge (50 mg thrice daily) the enzymes rose again within a week (peak ALT 87 IU/L) and returned to normal after discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: The authors judged the temporal relation between acarbose initiation and injury onset plus the dechallenge and positive rechallenge response as highly suggestive of acarbose-induced acute hepatotoxicity, probably of idiosyncratic type, potentially severe but unpredictable; monitoring of aminotransferases during acarbose treatment was recommended. Patient had concurrent NIDDM and treated schizophrenia; glibenclamide and fluphenazine were continued throughout and were not implicated. Positive rechallenge: AST 37 IU/L and ALT 87 IU/L within a month of restarting acarbose, normalizing after withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of acute liver toxicity due to acarbose in a diabetic patient. They conclude the acute liver damage was probably related to acarbose, fulfilling the three criteria of temporal relationship, favorable course after stopping the drug, and absence of other known causes of liver disease, and state that acute liver damage induced by acarbose should be suspected when liver test abnormalities develop after starting acarbose.
raw_record.extra_details: 57-year-old woman with noninsulin-dependent diabetes mellitus treated with acarbose 50 mg t.i.d. per os for 2 months before onset; symptoms included right upper quadrant pain, nausea, dark urine, lightened stool color, and scleral jaundice with slightly tender hepatomegaly. Peak enzymes on admission: ALT 1,580 IU/L, AST 1,090 IU/L, GGT 497 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 220 IU/L, bilirubin 3.8 mg/dl, ferritin 1,290 ng/ml; viral and autoimmune serologies negative. Spontaneous recovery with all abnormalities subsiding within 5 weeks; no liver biopsy and no rechallenge; patient remained well on glipizide 8 months later. Concomitant medication ciclobutirol (laxative); cisapride started after acarbose was stopped.

raw_record.support_text: A 65-year-old woman with non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, on glibenclamide, had acarbose (100 mg three times daily) added in mid-1993. Two months later she presented with malaise, anorexia, and jaundice; AST was 638 U/L, ALT 690 U/L, total bilirubin 9.9 mg/dL (direct 7.84), γ-glutamyltransferase 156 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 221 U/L. Viral hepatitis and autoimmune antibodies were excluded, and ultrasonography was normal. After acarbose was stopped, bilirubin decreased to 1.8 mg/dL within 4 weeks and laboratory values normalized within 9 months. The authors conclude that acarbose caused the hepatic injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Added to pre-existing glibenclamide therapy for non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus; a co-medication, though causality was attributed to acarbose. Dose 100 mg three times daily; latency ~2 months; symptoms included malaise, anorexia, and jaundice; baseline transaminases AST 638 U/L, ALT 690 U/L, total bilirubin 9.9 mg/dL (direct 7.84), GGT 156 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 221 U/L. Viral hepatitis and antinuclear/anti-smooth-muscle antibodies excluded; ultrasonography normal; no liver biopsy performed. Injury classified as 'hepatocellular' per international consensus criteria; mechanism unknown, compatible with metabolic idiosyncrasy given long latency and absent hypersensitivity; dechallenge led to resolution (bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL at 4 weeks, laboratory values normal within 9 months). Managed as outpatient.

raw_record.support_text: A 40-year-old woman with NIDDM developed jaundice, hepatomegaly, and abdominal tenderness plus markedly elevated transaminases (AST 1938 IU/L, ALT 2350 IU/L) and bilirubin 188 µmol/L two months after acarbose (100 mg every 8 h) was added to her glibenclamide and fluphenazine treatment. After acarbose was discontinued her enzymes normalized, and reinstitution of acarbose (50 mg thrice daily) caused enzymes to rise again within a week, normalizing after withdrawal; the temporal relation and dechallenge/rechallenge effects are described as highly suggestive of acarbose-induced acute hepatotoxicity, probably of idiosyncratic type.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 40-year-old woman; onset ~2 months after starting acarbose 100 mg every 8 h for NIDDM. Peak AST 1938 IU/L, ALT 2350 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 325 IU/L, total bilirubin 188 µmol/L (conjugated 171 µmol/L), mild prothrombin decrease, hepatomegaly on ultrasonography. Serologies for viral and non-viral infectious hepatitis, iron/copper studies, and autoantibodies normal/negative. Dechallenge: AST fell to 50 IU/L and ALT to 69 IU/L at 2.5 months, normal by 10 months. Positive rechallenge: acarbose 50 mg thrice daily led to rising AST 37 IU/L and ALT 87 IU/L after a week peaking at 1 month, normalizing 1-4 months after withdrawal. Concurrent co-medications glibenclamide (10 mg/day) and fluphenazine decanoate (25 mg IM monthly) were maintained throughout; patient was a mild wine drinker. Authors suggest monitoring serum aminotransferases during acarbose treatment.

raw_record.support_text: Three patients developed liver injury attributed to acarbose: following cessation of acarbose, transaminase activities returned to normal; a 53-year-old woman with NIDDM developed symptomless hepatomegaly after 4 months of acarbose (300 mg daily) with AST 591 IU/L, ALT 1189 IU/L, and total bilirubin 24 µmol/L, and 1 month after cessation AST fell to 56 IU/L and ALT to 123 IU/L. Serology for hepatitis B and C viruses, PCR for hepatitis C and G viruses, antibodies against hepatitis A, cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus, and antinuclear/antismooth-muscle/antimitochondrial antibodies were all negative, with normal iron and copper studies. The paper characterizes acarbose-induced liver injury as low in incidence, unpredictable, and idiosyncratic rather than intrinsic, and likely toxic-metabolic dependent rather than hypersensitivity-related due to lack of skin rash, fever, or arthralgia, long onset latency, and absence of granulomas and eosinophils on biopsy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients had non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM) as the treated indication.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients (a series); dosages and latency: one 53-year-old woman received 300 mg acarbose daily for 4 months before onset. Lab values for that case: AST 591 IU/L, ALT 1189 IU/L, total bilirubin 24 µmol/L; 1 month after cessation AST 56 IU/L, ALT 123 IU/L. Dechallenge led to normalization/improvement of transaminases in all patients. Liver biopsies in the latter two patients (2 weeks and 1 month after hepatomegaly onset) showed mild lymphocytic infiltration in lobules and portal tracts, ceroid-containing macrophages, Councilman bodies, liver-cell regeneration, and mild partial portal fibrosis, without lysosomal glycogen accumulation. Alternative causes excluded (viral, autoimmune, iron/copper, ultrasound). Authors recommend regular serum aminotransferase monitoring during acarbose treatment.

raw_record.support_text: Acarbose-related liver injury has been reported in humans. Early trials reported increases in transaminases or rarely jaundice in 3.8% of acarbose users versus 1.1% on placebo. The first case report was a 65-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes taking acarbose 300 mg/day for 2 months, presenting with malaise and anorexia and a hepatocellular damage laboratory pattern, with spontaneous recovery after discontinuation. Subsequent case series indicated that acarbose-related liver toxicity reports mostly came from Japan and Spain, had an average latency of 2–6 months after therapy initiation, frequently recurred after rechallenge, and were predominantly hepatocellular injuries.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus on therapeutic acarbose; general treatment population, not restricted to renal impairment. Post-marketing reports predominantly from Japan and Spain.
raw_record.extra_details: Index case: 65-year-old woman, type 2 DM, acarbose 300 mg/day for 2 months, malaise and anorexia, hepatocellular damage pattern, spontaneous recovery after discontinuation. Early trials: transaminase elevations or rarely jaundice in 3.8% of users vs 1.1% placebo. Case series: average latency 2–6 months, frequent recurrence after rechallenge. Indication: type 2 diabetes mellitus (alpha-glucosidase inhibitor). Putative mechanisms (unproven): CYP2E1 induction, increased reactive oxygen species production, and influence of sex hormones; acarbose hepatotoxicity likely not via metabolites given low and unpredictable incidence.

raw_record.support_text: The rs2302387 (ABCB4 L59L) and rs4148115 (ABCB11) polymorphisms are associated with mithramycin-induced acute transaminitis in two independent studies in adult patients with thoracic malignancies and in pediatric patients with Ewing sarcoma; mithramycin toxicity is predicted to be most severe in patients harboring variant genotypes conferring low expression of ABCB4 and ABCB11. The paper concludes that mithramycin induces cholestasis in individuals harboring genetic profiles susceptible to bile acid accumulation (ABCB4 and/or ABCB11 gene variants), and a dose-escalation clinical trial (NCT01624090) is assessing mithramycin therapy in patients with wild-type alleles.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Susceptibility appears restricted to individuals harboring ABCB4 and/or ABCB11 variant genotypes conferring low bile transporter expression (bile acid accumulation); study populations were adult patients with thoracic malignancies and pediatric patients with Ewing sarcoma.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed human injuries include mithramycin-induced acute transaminitis, hepatotoxicity/LFT elevations, and cholestasis. Two independent clinical studies (adult thoracic malignancies; pediatric Ewing sarcoma) reported the association of rs2302387 and rs4148115 with transaminitis. Mechanism: inhibition of FXR gene expression and ligand-induced FXR activation, deregulation of bile transport, and intracellular bile acid accumulation; not a direct ABCB11 inhibitor and unlike CDCA/CsA did not decrease bile synthesis; CYP8B1 and RALBP SNPs were additionally associated with mithramycin-induced hepatotoxicity in the ongoing dose-escalation trial NCT01624090.

raw_record.support_text: In their Phase I study of mithramycin (PA-144, NSC 24559), the authors report that the toxic reactions at the dosage schedules employed were severe, including protracted vomiting, hepatotoxicity, and marked thrombocytopenia associated with bleeding and occasionally death.
raw_record.extra_details: Aliases: mithramycin, PA-144, NSC 24559. Phase I study: 46 patients received 78 courses at 25-90 gamma/kg/day for five days; 9 courses by slow infusion in 5% dextrose, 69 courses by rapid IV injection. Drug was reported effective in embryonal cell carcinoma of the testis. Toxicity included protracted vomiting, hepatotoxicity, marked thrombocytopenia with bleeding and occasionally death. KOFMAN et al. noted decreased toxicity at 25 gamma/kg by slow infusion. BROWN and KENNEDY observed 25% mortality from drug toxicity at 50 gamma/kg/day x 5, but this mortality was attributed to overall drug toxicity, not specifically hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The phase I/II clinical study of mithramycin monotherapy in Ewing sarcoma (NCT01610570) was ceased due to hepatotoxicity. Approximately 75% of treated patients had dose-limited hepatotoxicity with acute injury starting within days of administration, noted at 25 µg/kg/dose and requiring dose de-escalation; notable transaminitis appeared within 72 h of treatment, reaching levels up to 500x the upper limit of normal, with resolution often taking 1-3 weeks. The hepatic injury was transient, rarely symptomatic, and did not require intervention, but significantly hampered the clinical utility of mithramycin. Investigations suggested the hepatotoxicity was related to inhibition of farnesoid-X receptor signaling and germline variants in bile acid flow/disposition genes (e.g., ABCB4, ABCB11).
raw_record.extra_details: Mithramycin (plicamycin) is an antineoplastic antibiotic; commercial production was discontinued in 2000 partly due to a narrow therapeutic window and severe toxicity. Hepatotoxicity was dose-limited in the Ewing sarcoma phase I/II monotherapy trial (NCT01610570), occurring at 25 µg/kg/dose and requiring dose de-escalation, with no efficacy demonstrated. ~75% of treated patients affected; acute injury within days; transaminitis up to 500x ULN within 72 h; resolution in 1-3 weeks; injury transient, rarely symptomatic, no intervention needed. Proposed mechanism: inhibition of farnesoid-X receptor signaling and germline variants in bile acid flow/disposition genes (ABCB4, ABCB11).

raw_record.support_text: Twelve patients with various malignancies (six MPM, two esophageal cancers, two lung cancers, two synovial sarcomas) were treated with mithramycin over twenty cycles. Nine patients experienced transient, asymptomatic dose-limiting transaminitis at 25 mcg/kg per infusion, and percutaneous biopsies revealed apoptotic hepatocellular death; three patients had no hepatotoxicity and tolerated dose escalation to 30 mcg/kg per infusion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with malignancies (malignant pleural mesothelioma, esophageal, lung cancers, synovial sarcomas); therapeutic intravenous infusion dosing; dose-limiting transaminitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Twelve patients treated, 20 cycles, all evaluable. Nine patients (75%) experienced transient, asymptomatic dose-limiting transaminitis at 25 mcg/kg per infusion; three patients (two MPM, one esophageal) had no hepatotoxicity and tolerated 30 mcg/kg per infusion. Eight patients experienced clinically significant (≥grade 3) transaminase elevations approximately 24 h after the third infusion. Mithramycin caused a >13-fold increase in geometric mean ALT (21 U/l [12–36] vs 363 U/l [138–895]) and AST (20 U/l [13–29] vs 269 U/l [116–622]), indicative of hepatocellular damage and/or injury. Biopsies showed apoptotic hepatocellular death. Peak and steady-state mithramycin plasma levels were 20 nM and 8 nM, respectively, below the 50–100 nM needed for tumor regression in preclinical models. No objective responses in seven evaluable patients. Pharmacokinetic parameters were not associated with transaminase elevations (P≥0.20).

raw_record.support_text: In a case report, a patient developed significant hyperbilirubinemia within four weeks of starting carbimazole and continued to rise for one more week after stopping the drug before normalizing over two months; aminotransferases were mildly elevated at two-to-three times normal. Liver biopsy revealed cholestatic hepatitis with paucity of bile ducts, and the patient showed a good response to drug withdrawal, supporting carbimazole-induced cholestasis.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis with paucity of bile ducts on biopsy; hyperbilirubinemia appeared within 4 weeks of starting carbimazole, rose one more week post-discontinuation, normalized over 2 months; aminotransferases mildly elevated to 2-3x normal; recovered after drug withdrawal; steroids did not affect the liver disease course; patient received radioiodine. Discussion notes carbimazole hepatotoxicity is dose-independent and thought to be an allergic reaction.

raw_record.support_text: A 37-year-old woman with Graves' disease was treated with carbimazole 30 mg/day; within 15 days she developed potentially life-threatening adverse effects including agranulocytosis and severe mixed hepatotoxicity with severe cholestatic jaundice. Her symptoms and laboratory abnormalities resolved after carbimazole was withdrawn, and the hepatotoxicity is explicitly attributed to carbimazole treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 37-year-old woman with Graves' disease receiving carbimazole 30 mg/day; severe mixed hepatotoxicity with severe cholestatic jaundice developed within 15 days of starting therapy and resolved on drug withdrawal. Causality rated as 'probable' on the Naranjo probability scale. Agranulocytosis (confirmed by bone marrow biopsy) was treated with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, and thyroid ablation with iodine-131 was subsequently performed. The discussion characterizes hepatotoxicity as a rare adverse effect that is usually dose- and age-related, and the conclusions note that severe liver failure may occur in patients receiving this drug.

raw_record.support_text: In a patient hospitalized with limb weakness and severe hypokalemia who was diagnosed with autoimmune hyperthyroidism and started on carbimazole 20 mg BID, carbimazole-induced hepatotoxicity was suspected on a subsequent admission for jaundice and pruritus and the drug was discontinued. Bilirubin rose significantly to 560 μmol/L and exceeded 650 μmol/L despite discontinuation, a liver biopsy confirmed cholestatic liver disease, and the paper concludes this case highlights severe and prolonged carbimazole-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient with autoimmune (TSH receptor antibody positive) hyperthyroidism treated with carbimazole 20 mg BID and atenolol 25 mg daily; jaundice and pruritus as presenting symptoms; bilirubin rose to 560 μmol/L then exceeded 650 μmol/L despite drug discontinuation and remained high for 2-3 weeks after stopping; liver biopsy confirmed cholestatic liver disease; treated with cholestyramine 4 g TID for pruritus and corticosteroids for immune modulation; severe and prolonged hepatotoxicity; injury is idiosyncratic and not dose-dependent.

raw_record.support_text: A 45-year-old female with severe hyperthyroidism was treated with Carbimazole 30 mg/day. Within six weeks of starting therapy, she developed potentially life-threatening acute cholestatic hepatitis and agranulocytosis as adverse effects to carbimazole; her symptoms and laboratory abnormalities resolved after the offending drug was withdrawn. The report describes carbimazole-induced acute cholestatic hepatitis together with agranulocytosis as an extremely rare idiosyncratic side effect of carbimazole treatment that is considered dose- and age-related.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 30 mg/day for hyperthyroidism; onset within six weeks of therapy; acute cholestatic hepatitis with concurrent agranulocytosis (presented with bluish skin discoloration, right hypochondriac pain, high-grade fever, deep jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, semi-conscious state, Glasgow coma scale 11/15); symptoms and laboratory abnormalities resolved after drug withdrawal. Authors describe the cholestatic hepatitis plus agranulocytosis combination as extremely rare, idiosyncratic, and dose- and age-related.

raw_record.support_text: A MEDLINE search identified 30 previously published cases of hepatotoxicity related to treatment with methimazole or carbimazole in which the nature of the hepatic injury was described; 19 of these were also cholestatic.
raw_record.extra_details: Aggregate account of 30 previously published hepatotoxicity cases related to methimazole or carbimazole treatment in which hepatic injury nature was described, 19 being cholestatic. Paper concludes that older patient age and higher drug dose are risk factors for cholestatic injury (Endocr Pract. 2002;8:222-224).

raw_record.support_text: A 38-year-old male developed jaundice and severe hyperbilirubinemia beginning about 1 year after starting carbimazole (40 mg with levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily as block-and-replace) for Graves' disease. He had no prior history of liver disease and had taken no other prescribed, over-the-counter, or illicit substances. Carbimazole was stopped; liver biopsy showed a mixed cholestatic-hepatitic injury (cholestatic more prominent), and it was considered most likely to represent a drug-related liver injury. Liver function slowly improved and the jaundice resolved completely.

raw_record.support_text: A 33-year-old female with Graves' disease developed acute pancreatitis associated with mild cholestatic hepatitis and erythema nodosum one month into carbimazole therapy (45 mg daily), when she was already euthyroid. Carbimazole was interrupted and pancreatic and liver function normalized two weeks later. Rechallenge with a single dose of carbimazole led to a new episode of acute pancreatitis and cholestatic hepatitis one day later. The authors state that carbimazole should be added to the list of drugs capable of inducing these reactions and emphasize discontinuing the drug when pancreatic dysfunction appears.
raw_record.extra_details: Mild cholestatic hepatitis; rechallenge with a single dose of carbimazole reproduced pancreatitis and cholestatic hepatitis within one day. Liver tests showed slight AST/ALT rises with greater alkaline phosphatase (632 U/L, normal 80-270) and gamma-glutamyl-transferase (915 U/L, normal 0-50) increases and normal bilirubin; liver enlarged 3 cm. Liver function normalized two weeks after drug interruption. Concurrent acute pancreatitis and erythema nodosum were also attributed to carbimazole. Shortened interval between drug intake and symptom onset with repeated exposure and the hypersensitivity reactions point to an immune-mediated mechanism. Paper also notes (citing reference [1]) that severe, sometimes fatal hepatitis can rarely occur with carbimazole therapy, though less commonly than with methimazole.

raw_record.support_text: A previously healthy 30-year-old woman with thyrotoxicosis treated with carbimazole 60 mg daily presented with one week of scleral and urine discoloration and pruritus. Investigations showed hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 208 µmol/L, conjugated 124 µmol/L) and elevated liver enzymes (ALT 224 U/L, AST 163 U/L, ALP 347 U/L). A probable diagnosis of carbimazole-induced cholestatic hepatitis was made; the drug was discontinued, other causes of hepatitis and cholestasis were excluded, and LFTs normalized within four weeks. The authors conclude that carbimazole-induced hepatitis, although rare, should be considered in jaundiced thyrotoxic patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had Graves' disease/thyrotoxicosis and was concurrently taking propranolol; carbimazole was discontinued and she was treated with steroids and switched to propylthiouracil. Dechallenge with drug withdrawal was followed by recovery.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose carbimazole 60 mg daily; onset of symptoms (icterus, pruritus) approximately one month after starting treatment. Admission labs: total bilirubin 208 µmol/L, conjugated 124 µmol/L, ALT 224 U/L, AST 163 U/L, ALP 347 U/L; bilirubin peaked by day 6 (445 µmol/L) before declining; LFTs normalized within 4 weeks and remained normal at 6 months. Described as carbimazole-induced hepatitis with severe cholestasis. Other causes of hepatitis and cholestasis excluded. Radioiodine or surgery considered but not arranged; substitution of carbimazole with propylthiouracil reported without increased hepatotoxicity as the liver-injury mechanism is said to differ between the two thionamides.

DILIsym modeling predicted hepatotoxicity at ≥175 mg BID driven predominantly by bile acid accumulation with a lesser contribution from mitochondrial electron transport inhibition and no contribution from oxidative stress.

raw_record.support_text: Upon readmission (February 1979) after a cumulative indomethacin dose of about 10000 mg, the patient developed nausea, edema and disturbed liver function (total bilirubin 1.9 mg/dl, GOT 1008 mU/ml, GPT 567 mU/ml, ALP 193 mU/ml, LDH 295 mU/ml). Indomethacin was discontinued. Peritoneoscopy and histology showed a rough liver surface with multiple scars, many destroyed lobules, irregular fibrosis and inflammatory cell infiltration, and the patient was diagnosed with drug-induced hepatitis with submassive necrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report. Cumulative dose approximately 10000 mg; injury diagnosed as drug-induced hepatitis with submassive necrosis. Laboratory findings at diagnosis: total bilirubin 1.9 mg/dl, GOT 1008 mU/ml, GPT 567 mU/ml, ALP 193 mU/ml, LDH 295 mU/ml, KICG 0.047, BSP retention 40.2% at 45 min. Hepatitis B surface antigen/antibody not detected. Histology: destroyed lobules, irregular fibrosis, inflammatory cell infiltration. Dechallenge (indomethacin discontinuation) followed by gradual improvement of BSP retention (24.7% on April 17, 10% on June 17).

raw_record.support_text: The authors believed the causative aetiology of the hepatotoxicity in their patient was α-methyldopa after excluding other causes of hepatitis such as infection and autoimmune hepatitis. The low titre of ANA and elevated IgG were considered a non-specific association of idiosyncratic immunologically mediated hepatic injury from α-methyldopa. The paper states α-methyldopa-induced hepatotoxicity is rare, that the drug can cause severe hepatitis, and that ceasing the medication usually results in rapid improvement.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report attributing hepatotoxicity to methyldopa after excluding infection and autoimmune hepatitis; low-titre ANA and elevated IgG regarded as non-specific markers of idiosyncratic immunologically mediated injury. Authors note α-methyldopa-induced hepatotoxicity is rare, cannot be predicted, and that routine liver function test monitoring during treatment can help manage potential hepatitis; most cases improve rapidly once the drug is stopped. Hydralazine was ruled out as the cause in this instance because it was discontinued in the early postpartum period.

raw_record.support_text: This follow-up of six patients with alpha-methyldopa-induced chronic type of injury demonstrated depletion of liver fat and collagen content after drug withdrawal. Characteristic histologic findings included various forms of hepatitis, marked fatty infiltration, and collagen deposition, and the paper states that alpha-methyldopa has been shown to induce liver damage after short- and long-term exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Six patients (1-6) with alpha-methyldopa-induced liver damage on follow-up. At symptom onset, nonfatty tissue 44.0%-85.5% of liver, increasing to 76.5%-98.5% at follow-up; severe fatty accumulation in three, moderate in two, none in one. Fibrous trabeculae >1.9% of liver tissue in first biopsy in four patients. Patient 4 showed chronic aggressive hepatitis-like reaction with 41% necrotic tissue and second biopsy showed cirrhosis with 16% connective tissue. Liver tests: all six had elevated ASAT and ALAT; patients 4 and 6 had elevated alkaline phosphatase; patient 4 had high bilirubin (335 U/l) and low albumin. Thrombotest <100% in four patients; albumin below normal in two. Authors note no correlation between fat and fibrosis and propose multiple immunologic, metabolic, cytotoxic, and genetic mechanisms may contribute to liver cell injury. Drug forms reactive metabolites during hepatic biotransformation; chronic fatty accumulation regarded as sign of chronic damage.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports the clinical and biochemical picture of alpha-methyldopa-induced hepatic injury in 36 patients, which occurred in two phases: acutely after beginning treatment (group A, cases 1–14, mean 3.4 ± 0.4 months) and after several years of alpha-methyldopa treatment (group B, cases 15–36, mean 36.5 ± 2.9 months). One patient (case 8) died with hepatic coma and belonged to group A.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective study of 36 patients with alpha-methyldopa-induced liver damage; two phases: group A (cases 1-14) acute onset (mean latency 3.4 ± 0.4 months, bilirubin elevated, ALAT/ASAT high) and group B (cases 15-36) chronic course (mean latency 36.5 ± 2.9 months, initially mild epigastric pain, dyspepsia, nausea, colic); total drug consumed before onset was about 10 times higher in group B; one fatal case with hepatic coma (case 8). Histology showed hepatitis with or without necrosis and chronic active hepatitis (CAH), with fatty liver accumulation ranging 20-40% of the biopsy typical in prolonged onset; 5/7 group A patients had acute hepatitis (71%) and 2/7 a CAH-type reaction (29%), versus 10/16 (63%) and 6/16 (37%) in group B. Occurrence of injury in four members of one family (cases 5, 6, 12, 13) noted. One death with hepatic coma.

raw_record.support_text: This case series describes six patients with liver injury after exposure to alpha-methyldopa, ranging from 24 to 96 months before symptom onset. The disease developed chronically with gradually increasing epigastric pain, dyspepsia, nausea, and weakness; patient 4 was jaundiced. Withdrawal of the drug resulted in improvement of symptoms. Histology showed reactive hepatitis in five patients, one case of chronic aggressive hepatitis-like changes with massive necrosis, and cirrhosis in patient 4.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic therapeutic exposure (onset after 24-96 months of use); chronic, gradual development of symptoms.
raw_record.extra_details: Six patients. Symptoms: mild epigastric pain, dyspepsia, nausea, weakness for several months; patient 4 jaundiced. Withdrawal improved symptoms. Liver histology: reactive hepatitis in five patients; one patient had chronic aggressive hepatitis-like changes with massive necrosis; patient 4 developed cirrhosis, and cirrhosis appears in patient 4 (fibrosis content 16%). Five patients showed slight Kupffer cell proliferation at follow-up. Morphometry quantified fatty infiltration and fibrosis percentages in individual patients (e.g., severe fatty infiltration 30.5%, mild 2.5%).

raw_record.support_text: Histologic alterations in 31 patients with hepatic injury after alpha-methyldopa exposure were investigated: 7 developed liver injury within 6 months and 24 after several years (mean 5 years). Short-term-exposed patients had acute and severe hepatitis, four with icterus, and two died of hepatic coma; long-term-exposed patients had fatty accumulation and increased fibrous trabeculae. The authors conclude that alpha-methyldopa may induce hepatocellular injury after both short- and long-term exposure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Some patients received concurrent therapy with digoxin, nitroglycerine, furosemide, glibenclamide, and occasional analgesics, kept unchanged during the study; none were alcohol abusers.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 31 patients (20 women, 11 men) with alpha-methyldopa-induced liver injury; diagnosis based on case history, biochemistry, serology, histology, and follow-up after drug withdrawal. Seven patients developed injury within 6 months (short-term) and 24 after several years (mean 5 years, long-term). Short-term group: marked parenchymatous degeneration, focal/confluent/massive necrosis and inflammation, acute and severe hepatitis, 4 with icterus, 2 died of hepatic coma. Long-term group: fatty accumulation and increased fibrous trabeculae, initially mild dyspepsia, nausea, colics. Histology findings included reactive hepatitis, chronic active/persistent hepatitis-like reactions, and massive necrosis (up to 47%). Liver function differences in serum albumin, bilirubin, and transferases; no change in alkaline phosphatase or Thrombotest. Patients 28D and 31D died.

raw_record.support_text: The table 'Incidence of Cyclophosphamide Toxicity in 66 Patients' lists adverse effects of cyclophosphamide, including liver toxicity occurring in 1 of 66 patients, among other toxicities such as alopecia (8 patients) and thrombocytopenia (5 patients).
raw_record.extra_details: Liver toxicity was reported in 1 of 66 patients with lymphosarcoma/reticulum cell sarcoma treated with cyclophosphamide in this series. Cyclophosphamide was given orally (adult doses 1.5 to 4 Gm/month) and intravenously. Other adverse effects reported: alopecia (8), thrombocytopenia <100,000/mm3 (5), severe nausea and vomiting (3), fatal toxicity (2), ileal perforation (1), skin rash (1), sterile cystitis (1).

raw_record.support_text: The author reports a patient with hepatic necrosis in whom the only recognized hepatotoxic agent received was halothane, given on one occasion, and states it appears highly unlikely that the hepatic necrosis was caused by halothane. No blood transfusion had been given, there was no contact with infectious hepatitis, and the liver histology did not support hepatitis. By exclusion, the author concludes that this was probably a cyclophosphamide-induced hepatic necrosis, a complication not previously attributed to this drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case report; diagnosis reached by exclusion after ruling out halothane (received once), blood transfusion, and infectious hepatitis exposure; histology did not support hepatitis. Described as a complication not previously attributed to the drug.

raw_record.support_text: A single case of drug-induced hepatitis was attributed to cyclophosphamide after three days of use, among 559 patients who received the drug in hospital.
raw_record.extra_details: One case of drug-induced hepatitis attributed to cyclophosphamide after three days of use; 559 patients were exposed in hospital. BCDSP monitoring cohort.

raw_record.support_text: The case report exemplifies the role of cyclophosphamide (CPA) as the drug responsible for severe sub-acute and chronic hepatitis in a patient, and suggests the natural history of the disease, based on an immune mechanism, is not rapidly interrupted by drug withdrawal. The responsibility of CPA was established because prior transaminase activity was normal and there was no chronic liver disease, the clinical liver injury (fatigue and dark urine) occurred two months after starting CPA, no new or hepatotoxic drugs were given during the same period, and other causes of severe chronic hepatitis were excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency of liver injury ~2 months after starting cyclophosphamide; onset with fatigue and dark urine. Normal immunoglobulin levels and absence of anti-nuclear, anti-smooth muscle and anti-LKM1 auto-antibodies argued against classic autoimmune hepatitis. Withdrawal was not followed by prompt improvement (transaminases did not improve significantly and jaundice worsened after two weeks); second liver biopsy ~5 months later still showed histological activity, though decreased. There was apparent benefit from corticosteroids, but early withdrawal due to onset of diabetes caused secondary bilirubin elevation and slight transaminase increase, reversed by reintroduction of low-dose prednisone and budesonide. Early onset cirrhosis was demonstrated three months after drug introduction on biopsy. Non-causal/co-medication details: patient was on CPA as a new treatment; no other new drugs or suspected hepatotoxins during the period.

raw_record.support_text: Cyclophosphamide is described as known to be toxic to hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cells, with several clinical reports of hepatotoxicity after cyclophosphamide use. In the authors' previous report, 7 of 17 patients who received cyclophosphamide at 200 mg/kg developed SOS (five mild, two moderate) with maximum bilirubin levels of 4.2–21 mg/dl; maximum weight gain ranged from 3.5 to 29%. A recent study showed a correlation between exposure to cyclophosphamide metabolites and development of SOS.

raw_record.extra_details: Known to be toxic to hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cells (mechanism); in a prior report 7/17 patients (five mild, two moderate) developed SOS with maximum bilirubin 4.2–21 mg/dl and weight gain 3.5–29%; a recent study correlated cyclophosphamide-metabolite exposure (4-hydroxycyclophosphamide interpatient variability) with SOS development. Also frequently associated with hemorrhagic cystitis, interstitial pneumonitis, and hypoxia (non-hepatic).

raw_record.support_text: In a phase II study of amifostine given as protection before high-dose cyclophosphamide (HDCY, 7 g/m²) for PBPC mobilization in 29 non-Hodgkin's lymphoma patients compared with a historical group, amifostine reduced the intensity of cardiac, pulmonary and hepatic toxicity and significantly reduced the frequency and severity of mucositis. The hepatic toxicity is thus attributed to HDCY and mitigated by amifostine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose cyclophosphamide (7 g/m²) given for PBPC mobilization and tumor reduction in non-Hodgkin's lymphoma patients, with amifostine cytoprotection administered prior to it.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II study: 29 NHL patients (22 aggressive, 7 indolent) received 58 amifostine infusions before HDCY; comparison was a historical group of 33 aggressive-NHL patients treated with VACOP-B followed by HDCY. Amifostine reduced the intensity of hepatic (as well as cardiac and pulmonary) toxicity; no deaths in the protected group versus 2/33 in the historical group (from cardiac or pulmonary toxicity). Amifostine did not prevent the aplastic phase after HDCY.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of a 68-year-old Chinese female with breast cancer, suggesting that CYP2B6*7 and ALDH3A1*2 variants may contribute to her severe and prolonged hepatotoxicity induced by cyclophosphamide after two cycles of chemotherapy with epirubicin and cyclophosphamide.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient received two cycles of combination chemotherapy with epirubicin and cyclophosphamide for breast cancer; the patient carried CYP2B6*7 (A785G/G516T/C1459T) and ALDH3A1*2 variant alleles, indicating a genetic-susceptibility context.
raw_record.extra_details: 68-year-old Han Chinese woman with breast cancer; reported as the first carrier of the rare CYP2B6*7 allele in the Han Chinese population. Hepatotoxicity was severe and prolonged after two cycles of therapy. Proposed mechanism: CYP2B6*7 may increase 4-OHCP (4-hydroxycyclophosphamide) formation predisposing to toxicity, and ALDH3A1*2 may reduce detoxification of activated cyclophosphamide metabolites; POR*28 genotype relationship to cyclophosphamide bioactivation was considered unclear.

raw_record.support_text: Patients with naproxen-induced liver injury (NAP-DILI) were studied. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells from these patients were assessed with lymphocyte transformation test and IFN-γ ELIspot, and T-cell clones were generated and tested for drug specificity. T-cells were exposed to NAP, its oxidative metabolite 6-O-desmethyl NAP (DM-NAP), its acyl glucuronide (NAP-AG), or synthesized NAP-AG human-serum albumin adducts. The whole study confirms an immune-mediated basis for naproxen-induced idiosyncratic liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Idiosyncratic NSAID-induced DILI attributed to naproxen at therapeutic exposure. Immune-mediated: CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells expressing a range of Vβ receptors proliferated and secreted IFN-γ and IL-22 when exposed to the oxidative metabolite 6-O-desmethyl naproxen (DM-NAP), but not when exposed to NAP itself, NAP-AG, or NAP-AG albumin adducts. CD4+ TCC activation was HLA-DQ-restricted and APC-dependent; no cross-reactivity with structurally related drugs. Authors found no evidence that carboxylate bioactivation (acyl glucuronide formation) is the pathogenic mechanism for naproxen-associated DILI.

raw_record.support_text: In approximately 50,000 liver transplant cases reported to the United Network for Organ Sharing from 1990 to 2002, 270 were associated with ALF secondary to DILI (0.5%); one case was related to naproxen.
raw_record.extra_details: One liver-transplant case associated with ALF secondary to DILI in the UNOS registry (1990-2002).

raw_record.support_text: In compiled study data, only 1 case of hospitalization associated with naproxen was reported among 37,671 patients (incidence 3 per 100,000), and only 1 patient died due to naproxen-induced liver toxicity among 51,942 patients consuming NSAIDs (death rate 2 per 100,000).
raw_record.extra_details: One hospitalization among 37,671 patients (3 per 100,000) and 1 death explicitly attributed as naproxen-induced liver toxicity among 51,942 NSAID users (2 per 100,000). No latency, dose, histology, or R ratio reported.

raw_record.support_text: One month after starting naproxen the patient developed jaundice which resolved after stopping the drug. With no evidence of viral hepatitis A (HBs antigen negative), no alcohol consumption, and liver biopsy findings of a resolving acute hepatitis-type lesion with eosinophilic infiltration and steatosis, the authors diagnosed drug-induced hepatitis; rechallenge was not performed given the severity. The absence of direct hepatotoxicity was supported by a report of a 25 g accidental naproxen ingestion without liver abnormalities.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report; jaundice appeared one month (fixed sensitization period of 1-6 weeks across 3 reported cases) after starting naproxen and resolved within about 2-3 weeks of withdrawal, with hepatomegaly resolving first and mild residual jaundice clearing 10 days later. Biopsy showed a resolving acute hepatitis-type lesion with PAS-positive pigment in Kupffer cells/portal phagocytes (prior liver cell death), mild steatosis, portal tract oedema with mononuclear and some eosinophilic infiltration. Elevated serum aspartate transferase (17 u) at discharge and alkaline phosphatase 7.0 Bodansky units. Viral hepatitis A and HBsAg excluded; alcohol excluded. Authors supported a hypersensitivity response (sudden onset of fever, eosinophils in infiltrate, rarity, fixed sensitization period) over direct hepatotoxicity, citing a 25 g accidental ingestion without liver abnormality and naproxen pharmacokinetics. Rechallenge not performed.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a 30-year-old woman who developed jaundice and intractable pruritus shortly after taking naproxen. Her liver biochemical profile revealed a mixed cholestasis and hepatitis pattern, and consecutive liver biopsies showed focal lobular inflammation, hepatocyte drop-out, and progressive loss of the small interlobular bile ducts (ductopenia). A biopsy two years after onset showed partial recovery of some bile ducts, and the biochemical profile returned to near normal only after 10 years.
raw_record.extra_details: Individual case of a 30-year-old woman with jaundice and intractable pruritus shortly after naproxen use. Mixed cholestasis and hepatitis pattern; histology showed focal lobular inflammation, hepatocyte drop-out, and ductopenia (progressive loss of small interlobular bile ducts). Partial bile-duct recovery seen at 2 years; biochemical profile returned to near normal only after 10 years; recovery sustained after 17-year follow-up. Authors note naproxen-associated liver toxicity is a rare entity and should be considered in any patient presenting with cholestasis shortly after its use; liver injury most commonly shows a mixed pattern and may take years to resolve.

raw_record.support_text: In the TARGET trial, nine cases of serious liver abnormalities were judged to be probable drug-induced hepatitis, of which one (0.02%) was associated with the use of naproxen; raised transaminase levels reversed after the drug was stopped.
raw_record.extra_details: One of nine adjudicated cases of probable drug-induced hepatitis in the TARGET trial (0.02%); raised transaminase levels reversed after drug discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: Table 1 lists one patient (case 6) with DILI attributed to naproxen taken therapeutically: a 65-year-old man on 1000 mg/day for pain who developed jaundice with a mixed injury pattern (TB 4.5xULN, ALT 9.7xULN, ALP 3.4xULN), classified Moderate severity and CIOMS 'Highly probable'. The study is framed as NSAIDs-induced idiosyncratic liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case (65/M, pain), 1000 mg/day for 44 days, onset 48 days, co-meds tetrazepam, ranitidine, heparin, bisoprolol, metamizole, jaundice, mixed pattern, TB 4.5xULN, ALT 9.7xULN, ALP 3.4xULN, Moderate hospitalized, lost to follow-up, CIOMS 'Highly probable'.

raw_record.support_text: In the TARGET clinical trial, clinical hepatitis was rare regardless of drug used, with one case of clinical hepatitis adjudicated to naproxen (0.02%).
raw_record.extra_details: TARGET trial (chronic osteoarthritis therapy); one case of clinical hepatitis adjudicated to naproxen (0.02%).

raw_record.support_text: A 67-year-old non-alcoholic woman without prior liver disease took naproxen 500 mg daily by mouth starting 21 April 1986 for hip pain; on 3 May she became jaundiced and was admitted on 9 May with acute icteric hepatitis (total bilirubin 78 µmol/l, ALT 450 IU/l, AST 330 IU/l, ALP 280 IU/l, GGT 349 IU/l, eosinophils 3.8×10⁹/l). Liver biopsy showed fibrosis, portal inflammatory infiltrate, and moderate hepatocellular necrosis; hepatitis B surface antigen was absent, and anti-hepatitis A IgM was absent. The drug was discontinued and clinical symptoms disappeared and liver function tests improved within days. In the comment the authors state the propionic-acid-derived drugs were the cause of the hepatic injury, citing institution of treatment before symptoms, quick improvement after discontinuation, and the fact that several cases of hepatitis induced by naproxen have been reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral dose 500 mg daily; jaundice developed ~12 days after starting naproxen (complained of nausea, abdominal pain, malaise on 30 April). Serum bilirubin 78 µmol/l, ALT 450 IU/l, AST 330 IU/l, ALP 280 IU/l, GGT 349 IU/l, eosinophils 3.8×10⁹/l. Histology: fibrosis, portal tract inflammatory infiltrate, moderate hepatocellular necrosis. Hepatitis A/B and autoimmune serologies negative; ultrasound and ERCP normal. Dechallenge: symptoms disappeared and liver tests improved within days. Authors note hepatitis induced by naproxen is rarely associated with hypersensitivity, in contrast to ibuprofen hepatitis. Patient had an episode of unexplained jaundice six years earlier.

raw_record.support_text: Naproxen has an EBGM_NW of 0.56, below baseline, signifying that statistically it is unlikely to be associated with liver injury (classified as a false negative), yet it was recognized to be implicated as a cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in the US, Sweden, and Spain, with 12 cases (N=784) found in the Swedish registry (Suzuki et al., 2010). Clinical manifestations of naproxen-related liver injury are rare (1-3 per 100,000 users) and usually result only in serum enzyme elevations, and intrinsic toxicological mechanisms combined with critical risk factors can result in idiosyncratic reactions.
raw_record.extra_details: NSAID for pain, fever, and arthritic pain; EBGM_NW 0.56 below baseline (classified false negative FN, statistically unlikely association); recognized cause of ALF in US, Sweden, Spain with 12 cases (N=784) in Swedish registry (Suzuki et al., 2010); clinical injury rare (1-3 per 100,000 users) usually only serum enzyme elevations; intrinsic toxicological mechanisms (off-target interactions, mitochondrial disruption, immune-mediated toxicity, interference with hepatobiliary transport) combined with critical risk factors result in idiosyncratic reactions.

raw_record.support_text: Conditioning regimens containing busulfan are described as well known to induce hepatotoxicity in human HPCT recipients, ranging from elevated liver enzyme levels to hepatitis and hepatic veno-occlusive disease (HVOD). In paediatric patients most autologous and allogeneic recipients had regimen-related grade 1–2 elevations of AST/ALT, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase, or bilirubin with none of grade 4. In adult patients 15% of serious adverse events involved hepatotoxicity, and HVOD occurred in 8.2% of 61 adult allogeneic recipients (fatal in two patients) and in 2.5% of 42 autologous recipients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Administered as intravenous conditioning therapy prior to haematopoietic progenitor cell transplantation, co-administered with single-dose melphalan 140 mg/m2 or cyclophosphamide 50 mg/kg/day for 4 days; patients had underlying disease requiring transplant.
raw_record.extra_details: In paediatric patients (n=55, aged 0.3–17.2 y) most regimen-related elevations of AST/ALT, GGT or bilirubin were grade 1–2, none grade 4. In adults, 15% of serious adverse events involved hepatotoxicity; HVOD in 8.2% of 61 adult allogeneic HPCT recipients (fatal in two) and 2.5% of 42 adult autologous recipients; serious bilirubin elevations in three patients and AST elevations in one patient, two of these among those with HVOD. In a separate report, HVOD occurred in 4 of 31 autologous and 3 of 36 allogeneic paediatric recipients receiving bodyweight-based IV busulfan, all mild-to-moderate and resolving with symptomatic treatment within 18 days.

raw_record.support_text: Ten patients with stage 4 disease were given oral busulfan (BU) at 20 mg/kg with dose adjustments to maintain a steady-state concentration of 1,350 ng/ml. One of these patients developed grade 4 hepatic toxicity and died of veno-occlusive disease (VOD) on day 68, his BU Css being 1,305/1,397 ng/ml. This attributes fatal hepatic veno-occlusive disease to the high-dose busulfan-based conditioning regimen.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose myeloablative conditioning prior to autologous transplant for stage 4 (metastatic) breast cancer; busulfan co-administered with cyclophosphamide (and paclitaxel plus ciprofloxacin in the treatment cohort), an unresolved co-conditioning exposure; all patients had advanced (stage 4) disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral BU 20 mg/kg with dose adjustment to a target BU steady-state concentration (Css) of 1,350 ng/ml; affected patient had BU Css around 1,305-1,397 ng/ml; developed grade 4 hepatic toxicity and died of veno-occlusive disease (VOD) on day 68 post-transplant; a second patient in this group had grade 3-4 toxicity with pulmonary IPS. A historical comparison arm (BU/CY without paclitaxel and ciprofloxacin) also had a patient die of VOD on day 51 and another with grade 3 hepatic toxicity who died of RSV pneumonia on day 59; overall 4 of 25 (16%) in that arm had grade 3-4 regimen-related toxicity, 4 of 25 died of treatment-related mortality.

raw_record.support_text: Regarding hepatic complications following busulfan (BU) administration in ADA SCID patients undergoing reduced-intensity conditioning for gene therapy, the paper states no clinically significant hepatotoxicity occurred, such as hyperbilirubinemia or sinusoidal obstruction syndrome. Transient ALT (27.5% of subjects) and AST (57.5%) elevations above age-based norms were observed in the 1-2 months after BU treatment, and 5 subjects (12.8%) had Grade II ALT elevation; however, these laboratory abnormalities self-resolved, did not require intervention, and were not significantly correlated with previous BU AUC values.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with adenosine deaminase severe combined immunodeficiency (ADA SCID) undergoing reduced-intensity conditioning (busulfan) for gene therapy; population is pediatric (infants).
raw_record.extra_details: No clinically significant liver injury (hyperbilirubinemia or sinusoidal obstruction syndrome) occurred. Transient ALT elevations above age-based norms in 11 subjects (27.5%) and AST elevations in 23 subjects (57.5%) in the 1-2 months after treatment, with peak ALT and AST at mean 35 days post-infusion; Grade II ALT elevation in 5 subjects (12.8%), mostly in the BSA cohort (44.4% of BSA cohort vs 5% of ABW and 0% of TDM cohort). These laboratory findings were not correlated with prior BU AUC and all self-resolved without intervention.

raw_record.support_text: The paper categorizes hepatotoxic agents by mechanism as intrinsic toxicity or host idiosyncrasy, and applies this to its patient: 'Our patient had clinical features of hypersensitivity reactions, such as fever and eosinophilia... Thus, the adverse reactions to saridon are considered to be an idiosyncratic type of reaction.' The paper frames the patient's drug-induced hepatitis and hepatic granulomas as an adverse reaction to saridon.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of drug-induced hepatitis with hepatic granulomas attributed to saridon. The reaction was classified as idiosyncratic because the patient had hypersensitivity features including fever and eosinophilia, and granuloma is considered a hallmark of delayed hypersensitivity reactions. The exact time to onset of liver injury was not known; the paper notes most patients with drug-induced hepatitis and hepatic granulomas develop symptoms 10 days to 4 months after starting the causative drug, though longer latent periods occur.
