raw_record.support_text: A 75-year-old male with recurrent retroperitoneal undifferentiated/unclassified soft tissue sarcoma was started on oral pazopanib 800 mg/day. Two weeks later he showed signs of liver dysfunction (elevated serum liver enzyme levels) and pazopanib was stopped; after 1 week he was restarted at 400 mg/day and 6 days later presented with fever, malaise, fatigue, and appetite loss together with severe liver dysfunction (elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin). He was admitted, pazopanib was stopped, and liver biopsy confirmed drug-induced hepatitis; after treatment with hepatoprotectors and prednisolone he recovered from drug-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of severe pazopanib-associated liver dysfunction in a 75-year-old male with recurrent retroperitoneal undifferentiated/unclassified soft tissue sarcoma. Initial dose 800 mg/day produced liver enzyme elevation within 2 weeks (treatment stopped); rechallenge at reduced dose 400 mg/day led 6 days later to fever, malaise, fatigue, appetite loss, and severe liver dysfunction with elevated transaminases and bilirubin. Liver biopsy confirmed drug-induced hepatitis. Treated with hepatoprotectors and prednisolone; recovered and discharged. Tumor showed complete response but regrew 4 months after cessation. Pazopanib is an orally bioavailable VEGFR-1/2/3, c-kit, and PDGFR-alpha/beta tyrosine kinase inhibitor.

raw_record.support_text: Based on the updated RUCAM, pazopanib may be considered a probable cause of DILI in the first case report. RUCAM was applied retrospectively; the subscale for cholestatic or mixed injury was used because R ratio (ALT/ALP) was 3, indicating mixed liver injury, and the total score was 8, giving a causality grading of probable.
raw_record.extra_details: First case report in the present series; retrospective updated RUCAM application; R ratio (ALT/ALP) of 3 classified mixed liver injury; total RUCAM score 8 = probable.

raw_record.support_text: The case report states that the patient also had liver dysfunction as a result of pazopanib therapy, noting this liver dysfunction may reduce warfarin's hepatic metabolic capacity and coagulation factor production, contributing to elevated PT-INR. The authors later refer to 'recommended monitoring for pazopanib hepatotoxicity'.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case of a patient receiving pazopanib and warfarin who developed liver dysfunction and an abnormally elevated PT-INR; pazopanib plasma concentrations were abnormally high. Authors recommend therapeutic drug monitoring of pazopanib in addition to monitoring for pazopanib hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A 46-year-old woman with angiosarcoma on pazopanib (recently increased from 400 to 600 mg daily) presented with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and jaundice, with AST 719 U/L, ALT 910 U/L, and total bilirubin 10.1 mg/dL (direct 7.8 mg/dL); ultrasound showed no biliary pathology. Pazopanib was believed to be the causative agent and was stopped, after which symptoms and hepatic function returned to baseline. The authors note that pazopanib has potentially fatal hepatotoxicity among its side effects.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report. Patient with stage II angiosarcoma undergoing chemotherapy; pazopanib dose increased from 400 to 600 mg daily shortly before symptom onset (temporal association). Labs: AST 719 U/L, ALT 910 U/L, total bilirubin 10.1 mg/dL (direct 7.8 mg/dL); jaundice; nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain. Abdominal ultrasound showed no biliary pathology. Clinical and laboratory improvement on drug cessation (dechallenge); patient discharged stable and asymptomatic. Pazopanib is a selective tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for renal cell carcinoma and soft tissue sarcoma; its GI side effects range from diarrhea, nausea, vomiting to potentially fatal intestinal perforation and hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In patients with advanced renal cell carcinoma receiving first-line pazopanib (n = 44), 34 % developed liver toxicity (elevated bilirubin or liver transaminase levels), reaching maximum toxicity at a median of 60 days after starting therapy; resolution occurred within a median of 3-21 days after stopping in all but one patient, and liver dysfunction recurred in 27 % after restarting. In an analysis of pazopanib monotherapy clinical trial patients, 18 % of renal cell carcinoma patients (n = 586) had ALT elevations >=3x ULN and 5 % >=8x ULN, with 87 % occurring within 18 weeks; among 1,830 pazopanib study patients there were two adjudicated cases of pazopanib-related liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Pazopanib is a VEGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor used at 800 mg orally once daily for advanced renal cell carcinoma. Liver toxicity with elevated bilirubin or transaminases in 34 % of 44 first-line patients; ALT >=3x ULN in 18 % and >=8x ULN in 5 % of 586 RCC patients, mostly within 18 weeks; recovery in 91 % (30 % while continuing therapy); 65 % of 31 rechallenged patients had no ALT recurrence; two adjudicated pazopanib-related liver failure cases among 1,830 patients. In the COMPARZ trial pazopanib showed higher incidences of ALT and bilirubin elevations than sunitinib (95 % CI for relative risk excluding unity).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states explicitly that pazopanib is known to cause liver toxicity and that a relationship between pazopanib exposure and alanine transaminase (ALT) elevations has been described in clinical trials. The study investigated this exposure-liver toxicity relationship in real-world patients and evaluated management of pazopanib-induced liver toxicity in routine care.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective observational cohort study (Pazopanib Exposure and Liver Toxicity). Liver toxicity observed in 25 of 133 patients (19%); pazopanib exposure was comparable in patients with vs without liver toxicity (27.7 mg/L vs 28.1 mg/L). The study did not demonstrate a clear relationship between pazopanib exposure and occurrence of pazopanib-induced liver toxicity. Seven patients permanently discontinued pazopanib after liver toxicity; of the remaining 18, continuation/restart was successful in 16, with half continuing at the same dose as prior to liver toxicity. Liver toxicity definition centered on ALT elevations.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity is described as an expected event for pazopanib, manifested by increases in serum transaminases (ALT and AST) and bilirubin. In clinical trials in renal cell carcinoma and soft tissue sarcoma, approximately 18% of patients experienced ALT >3×ULN, 5% ALT >8×ULN, and 2% had concurrent ALT >3×ULN and bilirubin >2×ULN in the absence of alkaline phosphatase >3×ULN. Hepatotoxicity was also reported as a dose-limiting toxicity in this pazopanib plus paclitaxel study.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity is an expected/known event of pazopanib. Majority (92.5%) of transaminase elevations occurred within the first 18 weeks of treatment. In RCC and STS clinical trials ~18% had ALT>3×ULN, 5% had ALT>8×ULN, 2% had concurrent ALT>3×ULN and bilirubin>2×ULN without ALP>3×ULN (Hy's Law-like pattern). In the present pazopanib+paclitaxel study 4 patients had grade 3 or 4 transaminase elevations, and hepatotoxicity was a DLT. Pharmacogenetic exploration of HFE, UGT1A1, CYP3A4, CYP2C8, ABCB1, ABCG2, OATP1B1 markers. Pazopanib is a weak inhibitor of CYP3A4/CYP2C8.

raw_record.support_text: Pazopanib is described as having well-known liver toxicity. In the phase III PALETTE study, a grade >=2 elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALAT) occurred in 10% of pazopanib-treated patients (placebo 3%) and aspartate aminotransferase (ASAT) in 8% (placebo 2%), with no increase in total bilirubin. In the renal-cell carcinoma study, CTCAE grade >=3 ALAT elevation was found in 12% (placebo 1%), ASAT 7% (<1%) and total bilirubin 3% (1%), and two patients were assessed as having died due to abnormal hepatic function. The paper recommends caution prescribing pazopanib in patients with abnormal liver enzymes and bilirubin and temporary discontinuation at grade >=3 elevations.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence data from the PALETTE soft tissue sarcoma trial (grade >=2 ALAT 10% vs 3% placebo, ASAT 8% vs 2%; no total bilirubin increase) and an RCC study (grade >=3 ALAT 12% vs 1%, ASAT 7% vs <1%, total bilirubin 3% vs 1%; two deaths attributed to abnormal hepatic function). Recommendation to temporarily discontinue at grade >=3 elevations and stop permanently if abnormalities recur after restart.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that liver injury is a major adverse event of pazopanib. It cites the PALETTE study, where grade 3 or more increased liver enzymes occurred in 17% of patients, and reports that in the present study 2 patients experienced severely increased liver enzymes, both successfully managed by adequate treatment withdrawal or dose reduction. The accompanying adverse events table lists AST and ALT increases up to grade 4 during pazopanib therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Pazopanib administered as first- and second-line treatment for solitary fibrous tumor (SFT). Liver injury cited as a major adverse event; in the PALETTE study grade >=3 increased liver enzymes occurred in 17% of patients. Adverse events table documents AST increase (up to grade 3: 22.2%) and ALT increase (up to grade 4: 11.1%) among treated patients.

raw_record.support_text: A 75-year-old male with metastatic renal cell carcinoma presented with new-onset nausea, decreased appetite, and jaundice, with abnormal liver profile testing (ALT 484 U/L, AST 277 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 562 U/L, total bilirubin 7.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 6.2 mg/dL). He had started pazopanib six weeks prior; liver enzymes and synthetic function tests had been normal during this treatment. He denied significant acetaminophen use or herbal supplements. ANA, anti-smooth muscle antibody, anti-LKM-1, anti-mitochondrial antibody, ceruloplasmin, ferritin/iron profile, and viral hepatitis (A, B, C) testing were unrevealing. Liver biopsy showed a moderate portal-tract inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes with admixed eosinophils and neutrophils) and cholestasis without cirrhosis. The patient was diagnosed with pazopanib-induced hepatotoxicity and offered supportive care; he did not develop signs or symptoms of acute liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient with metastatic renal cell carcinoma (indication), with metastasis to ribs, thoracic vertebrae, and pancreas.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity noted 6 weeks after starting pazopanib. Cholestatic hepatitis on biopsy with portal and lobular mixed lymphocytic and neutrophilic inflammation and mild steatosis. Labs evolution: ALT rose to 484 U/L (from 25) and improved to 183 U/L; total bilirubin rose from 7.9 to 16.1 mg/dL; INR 1.02-1.25. No acute liver failure. Discussion notes clinical-trial incidence of hepatotoxicity as high as 53%; differential consideration of Stauffer's syndrome (paraneoplastic cholestasis).

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 34 patients with metastatic RCC treated with pazopanib, 4 patients (12%) were admitted to hospital because of liver toxicity and 3 patients (9%) were treated with prednisolone (median dose 50 mg, range 25–100 mg). One patient with grade 4 increased bilirubin had a liver biopsy demonstrating cholestatic hepatitis, responded to prednisolone 100 mg daily, had pazopanib interrupted for 215 days until normal liver tests occurred, and resumed pazopanib at ultra-low doses. The discussion frames liver toxicity as a significant adverse effect affecting patients treated with pazopanib, most often resulting in drug interruption and permanent discontinuation, and describes this as pazopanib-induced liver toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC); UGT1A1 (TA6/TA6 vs TA7 allele) genotyping informing dosing and rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: 34 patients evaluated; 4 (12%) admitted to hospital for liver toxicity; 3 (9%) treated with prednisolone (median 50 mg, range 25–100 mg); one patient with grade 4 increased bilirubin had a biopsy showing cholestatic hepatitis, responded to prednisolone 100 mg daily, pazopanib interrupted for 215 days until normal liver tests, then resumed at 200 mg every third day for 3 months and 200 mg every second day for 8 months. Of 9 patients with elevated liver enzymes and wild-type TA6/TA6 genotype, progressive disease was seen in 7 (78%). Discussion notes some outcome improvement may reflect very low dosing rather than the UGT1A1 polymorphism.

raw_record.support_text: In pazopanib-treated patients with solid tumors, a key liver safety signal was concurrent elevation of ALT (>3 × ULN) and total bilirubin (>2 × ULN) without biliary obstruction, reflecting extensive hepatocyte damage. The authors characterized 26 such patients and performed detailed causality assessments per DILIN criteria (definite, highly likely, probable, possible, unlikely), adjudicating four cases that met criteria for Hy's Law, of which two carried HLA-B*57:01. Across the combined datasets, ALT >3 × ULN and >5 × ULN events occurred in 20% and 11% of pazopanib-treated patients, respectively, and HLA-B*57:01 carriage was associated with higher risk of ALT elevation ({OR, 2.0 for >3 × ULN and OR, 2.1 for >5 × ULN}).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with solid tumors (n=2,190 combined) treated with pazopanib at various doses either as monotherapy or in combination with other agents; baseline liver-metastasis and baseline ALT considered as covariates.
raw_record.extra_details: ALT elevation was the hepatotoxicity phenotype; 26 cases had ALT >3 × ULN plus total bilirubin >2 × ULN, adjudicated by DILIN causality criteria (definite/highly likely/probable/possible/unlikely); four cases met Hy's Law criteria; two Hy's Law cases were HLA-B*57:01 carriers; ALT >3 × ULN in 20% and >5 × ULN in 11% of pazopanib-treated patients; HLA-B*57:01 associated with ALT elevation (OR 2.0, 95% CI 1.3-3.1 for ALT>3xULN; OR 2.1, 95% CI 1.3-3.6 for ALT>5xULN; HR 2.5 for time to >3xULN; HR 3.4 for time to >5xULN); no patients carried both Gilbert UGT1A1 and HLA-B*57:01 risk genotypes; no additional HLA genotype associations; HLA carriage frequency ~6%.

raw_record.support_text: Among 46 benznidazole-treated Chagas disease patients, 12 (26%) had adverse reactions, all of which included skin toxicity. Three patients also showed liver toxicity, with a slight elevation of transaminases in two cases; in one patient severe hepatotoxicity occurred after 30 days of treatment, with the histological finding of drug-induced liver injury (DILI), which resolved successfully with high-dose steroid therapy. Therapy was discontinued in 8 patients (17%) due to severe side effects.
raw_record.extra_details: Adverse reactions occurred in 12/46 treated patients (26%); liver toxicity in 3 patients, with slight transaminase elevation in 2; one patient developed severe hepatotoxicity after 30 days of benznidazole 5 mg/kg (max 300 mg/day) with histological drug-induced liver injury (DILI) that resolved with high-dose steroid therapy; DILI case has been described elsewhere. Treatment was combined with B-complex vitamins and cetirizine; 8 patients (17%) discontinued due to severe side effects. Population treated for chronic Chagas disease.

raw_record.support_text: An asymptomatic 52-year-old woman who received phenytoin sodium for 11 years was found to have elevated serum aminotransferases; assays for hepatitis A, B, and C were negative and a liver biopsy showed chronic persistent hepatitis. The authors report this as documentation of phenytoin-induced chronic persistent hepatitis, proven by histology and with its etiology confirmed by drug withdrawal and by rechallenge with phenytoin.
raw_record.extra_details: 52-year-old woman; phenytoin sodium for 11 years; asymptomatic with elevated serum aminotransferases; negative serology for hepatitis A, B, and C; liver biopsy showed chronic persistent hepatitis; etiology confirmed by drug withdrawal and rechallenge with phenytoin (phenytoin therapy alone). Phenytoin had previously been associated with acute hepatotoxicity, with chronic liver enzyme abnormalities attributed to enzyme induction and no prior reports of chronic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of phenytoin hypersensitivity syndrome, a rare reaction characterized mainly by fever, skin eruptions, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and hepatotoxicity. It developed in a 27-year-old patient with surgically corrected tetralogy of Fallot who received phenytoin for one month for exercise-induced sustained ventricular tachycardia; phenytoin was discontinued and the patient was treated with methylprednisolone then oral prednisone, with clinical improvement. The syndrome generally appears within six weeks of starting phenytoin and is fatal in up to 40% of patients who develop hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported 300 mg/day for one month; reaction appeared about four weeks after starting treatment (syndrome generally within six weeks). Patient had surgically corrected tetralogy of Fallot and was treated for exercise-induced sustained ventricular tachycardia, receiving no other medication at the time. Presented with fever, pustular rash on trunk/extremities, lymphadenopathy, elevated liver enzymes, hypotension, and increased liver mass; treated with methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisone, recovering and discharged. Syndrome is a rare, potentially fatal hypersensitivity reaction more common in blacks, occurring early in therapy; rechallenge with even milligrams of phenytoin is dangerous, and fatalities up to 40% occur among those who develop hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Phenytoin was the second-leading cause of DILI, implicated in 6.7% of the 313 human cases. Together the anti-epileptic drugs accounted for 11.2% of cases. Phenytoin was also implicated in chronic liver injury with mild liver test abnormalities in two patients.
raw_record.extra_details: 6.7% of 313 DILI cases. Chronic liver injury with mild liver test abnormalities in two patients. Anti-epileptic drugs as a class accounted for 11.2% of cases.

raw_record.support_text: Jinjuvadia and colleagues used ICD-9 codes to identify DILI cases in a University of Michigan database, attributing DILI cases secondary to Dilantin (phenytoin) among the four drugs of special interest (Augmentin, Dilantin, valproic acid, isoniazid), which together accounted for 51 of 119 DILI cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Phenytoin (Dilantin, Mylan Pharmaceuticals) is one of four drugs (with Augmentin, valproic acid, isoniazid) to which 51 of 119 DILI cases were attributed in an ICD-9 coded hospital database study (1994-2000).

raw_record.support_text: Phenytoin was listed among the other agents causing idiosyncratic drug-induced acute liver failure (≥2 cases).
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as a cause of idiosyncratic drug-induced acute liver failure with at least 2 cases in this series. These patients typically presented subacutely with low aminotransferases, high bilirubin, and more frequent ascites.

raw_record.support_text: Of the 20 patients with acute hepatic disease attributed to diphenylhydantoin (DPH) therapy, 14 recovered a few weeks after DPH was discontinued and six died; only two of the six deaths were the direct result of the hepatic drug reaction, with the others dying from unrelated causes while improving. Long-term follow-up of ten patients showed eight recovered without recurrence and two had sequelae (persistent hepatomegaly and abnormal liver function tests, one with some scarring on a second biopsy).
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 20 patients with acute hepatic disease while on diphenylhydantoin (DPH) for seizure control, with various underlying illnesses (grand mal epilepsy, brain tumor, preeclampsia, cerebral thrombosis, etc.). Latent period from starting therapy to symptom onset typically 1-16 weeks (one case at 2 years). Morphologic injury types: mononucleosis-like injury (4 cases), viral hepatitis-like injury (4, one severe cholestasis), hepatocellular degeneration/necrosis in 13 patients (12 acute, 1 chronic), submassive necrosis (1), massive necrosis (1), granulomas with/without cellular injury, chronic persistent hepatitis, ground-glass cells, reticuloendothelial cell malignancy. Features consistent with DPH hypersensitivity: rash, fever, eosinophilia (up to 48-50%), atypical lymphocytes; two patients had lymph node biopsies with atypical lymphoid hyperplasia consistent with DPH hypersensitivity. Demographics ages 20-76, both sexes, various races. Laboratory values included SGOT up to 3,510 and bilirubin up to 24 mg/dl with elevated alkaline phosphatase. Two patients (Patients 10 and 11, massive/submassive hepatocyte necrosis) died in hepatic failure directly from the drug reaction; other deaths were from pneumonia, sepsis, metastatic brain tumor, renal failure, pulmonary embolism, and cerebrovascular accident. Dechallenge with DPH discontinuation led to recovery in 14 patients. HBsAg-negative and monospot/heterophile-negative serology in tested patients.

raw_record.support_text: Two patients died of hepatic failure; both had massive hepatic necrosis induced by phenytoin and chlorpropamide respectively. The remaining 51 patients recovered clinically and biochemically after a mean interval of 63 days.
raw_record.extra_details: One of two fatal cases in the study; massive hepatic necrosis with death from hepatic failure. Also listed in the morphological table under massive/submassive necrosis and under hepatocanalicular cholestatic injury, indicating varied reactions.

raw_record.support_text: Phenytoin was among the drugs implicated as a cause of hepatic injury in a follow-up study of 44 patients with drug-induced hepatotoxicity; patients with abnormal hepatic evaluation at follow-up had previously taken phenytoin.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported in the 44-patient drug-induced hepatotoxicity cohort followed a median of 5 years; continuation of the implicated drug >6 months after an abnormal index biopsy was most associated with abnormal follow-up.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that phenytoin hepatotoxicity is well documented, although the incidence has been estimated to be less than one percent, and proposes hypersensitivity and toxic metabolite formation as the two most commonly cited mechanisms.
raw_record.extra_details: Review of 30 phenytoin hepatotoxicity case reports: AST elevated in 90% (peak 4395 mU/ml), ALT in 70% (peak 2048 Sigma Frankel units/ml), ALP in 86% (>2800 IU/L), bilirubin in 73% (peak 37.5 mg/dL), PT elevated in 37% and on admission in 64% of cases; time to peak LFT ranged from 1 day to 6 weeks, normalization 2 weeks to >1 year. Six fatal cases reported since 1965 (~12% mortality, 6/50); Danish Board of Adverse Drug Reactions 1968-1978 reported 7 phenytoin cases, 1 fatal (14.3% death rate). Fatal-case autopsies showed massive/diffuse hepatic necrosis, hepatocellular necrosis, and hepatocellular with cholestatic damage; hepatic failure/coma preceded some deaths. Common associated features included eosinophilia (22/24), leukocytosis, lymphocytosis, atypical lymphocytes, and skin rashes (maculopapular up to toxic epidermal necrolysis).

raw_record.support_text: The paper documents 45 reported cases of phenytoin hepatitis, including the present patient, with confirmation of hepatitis by demonstration of hepatic necrosis at necropsy or by transaminase elevation greater than 150 U with a compatible clinical course. Many cases had liver biopsy confirmation and exclusion of other likely causes. This is presented as an established human DILI relationship for phenytoin.
raw_record.extra_details: 45 documented cases of phenytoin hepatitis. Onset of reaction 7-56 days after initiation (mean 28 days), with two exceptions (one psychiatric patient ~18 months, and one case with cholestatic jaundice onset 40 years after initiation that cleared on withdrawal and recurred on rechallenge). Systemic hypersensitive features included morbiliform rash (90%), exfoliative rash (44%), eosinophilia (56%), jaundice (88%), leukocytosis (70%), lymphadenopathy (70%). Severe hepatitis (19 patients) defined as death from hepatic failure, total bilirubin >10, SGOT/SGPT >1000, or both SGOT/SGPT >500 and total bilirubin >5; 8 died from hepatic failure. Mortality in severe cases 40%; overall mortality 18%. Sex distribution nearly equal (20 male/25 female); race predilection for blacks (24/45). In the present patient, rechallenge with 1 g IV after recovery from a moderate episode produced massive hepatic necrosis; prior rechallenges used smaller oral doses with absent or limited hepatic necrosis. Mean time from onset to drug discontinuation was 6 days in mild and 14 days in severe hepatitis, suggesting early withdrawal decreases mortality.

raw_record.support_text: The DILIN Retrospective Study is creating a registry of patients who sustained severe and potentially irreversible liver injury due to isoniazid, phenytoin, valproic acid, and combination amoxycillin/clavulanic acid at any time since 1994. These drugs were chosen because they have characteristic signatures in clinical presentation.
raw_record.extra_details: Included in the DILIN Retrospective Study registry of patients with severe and potentially irreversible drug-induced liver injury since 1994; drug was selected due to its characteristic clinical-presentation signature.

raw_record.support_text: The authors investigated liver biopsy specimens from patients with hepatotoxicity due to five drugs, including phenytoin, among six patients with drug-induced hepatitis; phenytoin is reported as the cause of the hepatotoxicity in its case(s). The abstract notes peroxisomal proliferation (number increased 1.5 to 4.2 times and smaller organelles) and surface density exceeding the upper control value in phenytoin hepatitis livers.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as one of five drugs causing drug-induced hepatitis in six patients. Peroxisomal changes attributed in this case included proliferation with smaller organelle size and surface density exceeding the upper control value.

raw_record.support_text: In the authors' series of 313 cases of DILI, 76.6% of patients with drug-induced ALF were attributed to ATT; other patients who presented with ALF included users of phenytoin (n = 5), who were thus reported as a non-ATT cause of drug-induced acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented as one of the causes of drug-induced acute liver failure in the authors' DILI series, distinct from the predominant ATT-associated cases; n = 5.

raw_record.support_text: In the UNOS liver transplant cohort of drug-induced acute liver failure recipients, phenytoin was implicated in 10 of 137 (7.3%) non-acetaminophen cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Tied with valproate at 10 of 137 non-APAP cases (7.3%). Diagnosis at transplant was acute hepatic necrosis from an implicated drug.

raw_record.support_text: One of the 24 FHF patients had hepatitis caused by hypersensitivity to the prescribed medication phenytoin, resulting in fulminant hepatic failure. The paper explicitly attributes this patient's FHF to phenytoin hypersensitivity.
raw_record.extra_details: 1 patient; hepatitis due to hypersensitivity to prescribed phenytoin, progressing to fulminant hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: The DILIN Retrospective Study establishes a nationwide registry of patients who had suffered in the past severe idiosyncratic liver injury associated with the administration of phenytoin. Paragraph 59 lists phenytoin as one of the implicated medications for DILI cases enrolled into the retrospective protocol (5 cases).
raw_record.extra_details: 5 DILI cases enrolled in the DILIN retrospective protocol.

raw_record.support_text: Phenytoin was a recognized cause of liver injury in the DILIN cohort; there were significantly more severe/fatal liver injury events due to phenytoin in African-Americans than in Caucasians (86 vs. 14%, P=0.008), although overall severity and outcome comparisons were reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Associated with immune-allergic type of injury commonly presenting a mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic pattern; African-Americans represented 50% of phenytoin DILI cases, and experienced a significantly higher rate of severe/fatal liver injury (86% vs 14%, P=0.008).

raw_record.support_text: The initial diagnosis in this case report was a drug reaction secondary to diphenylhydantoin (phenytoin), which was therefore discontinued. The patient's liver injury was evidenced by centrilobular necrosis on biopsy (with patchy leukocyte infiltration), elevated serum bilirubin (1.55 mg/100 ml, mostly conjugated) and SGOT of 180 units, and he recovered after treatment with prednisone.
raw_record.extra_details: The paper records diphenylhydantoin (phenytoin) under its synonym 'diphenylhydantoin'. Case presented as a severe toxic/drug reaction; liver histology showed centrilobular necrosis with patchy leukocyte infiltration (H&E), and follow-up biopsy after 9 days of steroid therapy showed near-complete regeneration with residual scarring. Labs: serum bilirubin 1.55 mg/100 ml (1.10 conjugated, 0.45 unconjugated), SGOT 180 units, alkaline phosphatase 2.95 Bessie-Lowry units, prothrombin time 15 sec (control 13 sec), total protein 6.5 G/100 ml with albumin 2.9 G. Diphenylhydantoin was discontinued and the reaction was treated symptomatically with acetylsalicylic acid; prednisone (30 mg/day increased to 60 mg/day) was started on hospital day 3; patient became afebrile and asymptomatic by hospital day 5. Acetylsalicylic acid and prednisone were given to treat the reaction and are not attributed as the cause.

raw_record.support_text: In two larger case compilations of phenytoin-induced liver failure, 10 of 44 patients and 2 of 20 patients died of liver failure. In the survivors, liver function normalized within a few days of discontinuing phenytoin. Over 90% of those affected were adults.
raw_record.extra_details: Case compilations of phenytoin-induced liver failure: 10 of 44 patients and 2 of 20 patients died of liver failure; survivors recovered normal liver function within days of drug discontinuation; over 90% of affected patients were adults.

raw_record.support_text: Anticonvulsants were the most common offending drugs (21 of 27 definite DRESS/DIHS cases; 77.7%). Phenytoin was the most common individual drug (12 cases; 44.4%), followed by carbamazepine (8 cases; 29.6%). Other drugs such as allopurinol, dapsone, and nevirapine were also identified. Hepatitis was the most common visceral involvement, present in 23 patients (85.1%), with ALT (mean ± SD) 569 ± 911.5 U/L and AST 474 ± 743.0 U/L.
raw_record.extra_details: Phenytoin identified as culprit drug in 12 of 27 definite RegiSCAR-scored DRESS/DIHS cases (44.4%); most common indications were epilepsy and prophylaxis after neurological surgery or cranioencephalic trauma; hepatitis with elevated ALT/AST was the most common visceral involvement (23/27 patients, 85.1%) in this cohort.

raw_record.support_text: The case is a 50-year-old female with a seizure disorder well controlled on phenytoin since 2011 who developed mild-to-moderate liver enzyme elevations during therapy that normalized once phenytoin was discontinued.
raw_record.extra_details: Ultrasound of the liver in January 2016 showed changes of fatty infiltration (steatosis) and fibrosis; prolonged liver enzyme elevation resulted in phenytoin-induced hepatic fibrosis; reported as the first such case in the literature; this case differs from most phenytoin-induced hepatic injury cases in lacking immune-allergic features.

raw_record.support_text: One phenytoin (PHT) patient in this randomized trial of primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures had anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and abnormal liver function tests, which were attributed to drug-induced hepatitis. When PHT was discontinued the symptoms disappeared and laboratory values returned to normal; no other patient required withdrawal of medication. Transient liver enzyme elevations occurred on one or more occasions in both the VPA and PHT groups, more frequently in the PHT group, but were described as generally mild.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case in a 21-patient phenytoin arm of a randomized seizure trial. Presentation included anorexia, nausea, vomiting and abnormal liver function tests; full resolution of symptoms and normalization of laboratory values on drug discontinuation (dechallenge). Mild transient liver enzyme elevations (elevated SGPT in 6 and SGOT in 8 of 21 PHT patients) also occurred in the PHT group but were not characterized as DILI and did not require withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: The ILIAD reliability study enrolled its first 40 patients including five cases of phenytoin hepatotoxicity. The paper describes these as cases of drug-induced liver injury used to test RUCAM causality score reliability.
raw_record.extra_details: 5 of 40 DILI cases in the ILIAD study cohort; patients with a diagnosis of phenytoin hepatotoxicity. Cohort-wide median time to onset was 42.5 days, 73% hospitalized, 15% overall required liver transplantation (not drug-specific).

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 306 patients receiving phenytoin (27 adverse reactions attributable to phenytoin, 8.8%), one patient manifested phenytoin-induced hepatitis without a rash four weeks after the first dose.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient developed phenytoin-induced hepatitis without an erythematous rash, occurring four weeks after the first dose. Study overall: 30 of 306 patients had an adverse reaction; 27 (8.8%) were attributable to phenytoin, including one liver reaction. Indication was treatment of seizures and, in most other patients, prophylaxis after head trauma; phenytoin was the only antiepileptic drug administered.

raw_record.support_text: In a population-based Icelandic study of drug-induced liver injury, the most commonly implicated agents included phenytoin (4% of 51 cases). Cases were adjudicated by RUCAM with 94% classified as highly probable (n=18) or probable (n=30).
raw_record.extra_details: ~2/51 (4%) of DILI cases attributed (phenytoin listed as a commonly implicated agent with 4%); causality per RUCAM (94% of all cohort cases highly probable or probable). All cohort cases recovered with median time to resolution of liver tests 67 days.

raw_record.support_text: Phenytoin was one of the antiepileptic drugs (with carbamazepine, lamotrigine, valproic acid and levetiracetam) identified as culprit drugs that induced drug-induced liver injury in the context of DRESS in the present cohort (antiepileptic group n=15). The category showed hepatocellular (43%), cholestatic (36%), and mixed (21%) injury with mild (27%), moderate (67%), and severe (6.7%) severity and no liver-related deaths.
raw_record.extra_details: DILI co-occurred with DRESS; aggregated antiepileptic category n=15; duration 40 d, latency 33 d; eosinophilia 93%; ALT 11x ULN; Hy's law 23%. Also reported by Huang et al. 2021 (cited) as a DILI-DRESS culprit (20%).

raw_record.support_text: Of the neuropsychiatric drugs, phenytoin use (eight cases) was frequent among causes of drug-induced liver injury acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Eight cases; rash occurred in four phenytoin cases, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome was caused by phenytoin in one subject.

raw_record.support_text: Phenytoin was among the top 10 drugs involved in LA DILI Registry cases, with n = 4 cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Among the top 10 drugs in the LA DILI Registry, n=4 cases.

raw_record.support_text: Phenytoin-associated DILI case reports were analyzed for liver-injury pattern, eosinophilia, hepatic necrosis, inflammatory reaction, and death/liver transplantation outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: 100 individual case reports; median age 28 y; 53 female/47 male; median treatment duration 4 weeks; HC 36%, Cs/mixed 64%; highest incidence of peripheral and hepatic eosinophilia of the studied drugs (peripheral present in 77%, 81/100 reported; hepatic present in 72%, 43/100 reported); hepatic necrosis 31%; inflammatory reaction 89%; death or liver transplant 13%; liver biopsy reported in 50/100 cases.

raw_record.support_text: The anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome is characterized by fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, and later internal target organ disease including hepatitis. For each anticonvulsant, liver involvement ranged from mild elevations in transaminases to fulminant hepatic necrosis. Among 53 patients there were 89 exposures to anticonvulsants and 81 adverse reactions (35/36 exposed to phenytoin, 22/27 to phenobarbital, 25/27 to carbamazepine), and no drug appeared more toxic than another.
raw_record.extra_details: Anticonvulsant hypersensitivity reaction with clinical features including fever, skin rash, lymphadenopathy, nephritis, and hematologic abnormalities. Liver involvement ranged from mild transaminase elevations to fulminant hepatic necrosis. 35/36 phenytoin-exposed patients had an adverse reaction.

raw_record.support_text: Phenytoin is listed among the main 10 drugs leading the Latin American DILI Registry with n = 4 cases, with RUCAM-based causality assessment.
raw_record.extra_details: 4 cases in the Latin American DILI Registry; RUCAM-based causality assessment used.

raw_record.support_text: The DILIN retrospective study is a nationwide registry that includes patients who experienced liver injury within the past 10 years after consuming one of 8 drugs: phenytoin, isoniazid, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid, valproic acid, nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, minocycline, and quinolone antibiotics. The goals include establishing a database of patients with severe DILI due to any of these medications. The paper also notes the idiosyncratic nature and low incidence of DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among 8 drugs included in the DILIN retrospective registry for patients with severe DILI due to these medications.

raw_record.support_text: A 73-year-old African-American woman with Alzheimer's disease was prescribed phenytoin 100 mg three times daily after two seizures. Four weeks after starting the drug she was hospitalized with high fever, confusion, altered mental status, and a diffuse maculopapular pruritic rash. Laboratory values showed elevated aspartate aminotransferase (peak 96 IU/L), alanine aminotransferase (peak 77 IU/L), alkaline phosphatase (peak 521 IU/L), and eosinophilia, consistent with an anticonvulsant hypersensitivity reaction with hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS) in a 73-year-old woman; onset ~4 weeks after starting phenytoin 100 mg 3 times/day. AHS features included fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatitis, and laboratory abnormalities with eosinophilia (eosinophils up to 19%). Selected laboratory values: AST up to 96 IU/L, ALT up to 77 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase up to 521 IU/L, total bilirubin <1 mg/dl, phenytoin level 11.7 µg/ml on admission. Phenytoin was discontinued on hospital day 3 as the rash persisted and elevated eosinophils indicated an allergic drug reaction.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a life-threatening case of phenytoin hypersensitivity syndrome, a rare reaction primarily characterized by fever, skin eruptions, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and hepatotoxicity. The reaction developed in a 27-year-old black man treated with phenytoin for one month for exercise-induced sustained ventricular tachycardia; phenytoin was discontinued and he was treated with corticosteroids, with improvement five days after admission. The authors note the reaction usually develops within six weeks of starting phenytoin therapy and may be fatal in up to 40 percent of patients who develop hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 27-year-old man with surgically corrected tetralogy of Fallot treated for exercise-induced sustained ventricular tachycardia; taking no other medications.
raw_record.extra_details: Phenytoin 300 mg/d for one month; reaction developed approximately four weeks after starting therapy; last dose taken about 36 hours before admission; life-threatening presentation with elevated liver function tests, scleral icterus, hepatosplenomegaly; treated with discontinuation of phenytoin plus intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g/d for three days, then 90 mg/d for three days, converted to oral prednisone; paper states reaction may be fatal in up to 40% of patients who develop hepatotoxicity and usually develops within six weeks of starting phenytoin.

raw_record.support_text: The patient developed characteristic features of the anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS) with multisystem organ dysfunction, including liver and kidney dysfunction, after treatment with phenytoin. The diagnosis of AHS was essentially established by the characteristic clinical picture together with skin biopsy findings, eosinophilia, absence of a septic focus, negative culture and serology results, and response to corticosteroid therapy, excluding infection and connective tissue disease as causes.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Case of anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS) with multisystem organ dysfunction, including liver and renal dysfunction; single adult patient.
raw_record.extra_details: AHS case report. Liver tests initially: AST 532 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase 392 IU/L, total bilirubin 3.3 mg/dl (56 µmol/L), alkaline phosphatase 321 IU/L; by third hospital day AST rose to 2710 IU/L and total bilirubin to 5.0 mg/dl (85 µmol/L). Myoglobinuria, creatine kinase 4522 IU/L (100% MM); platelet count fell to 18 x 10^3/mm³. Serology negative for hepatitis A, B, C, HIV, CMV, EBV; negative blood/urine/skin lesion cultures. Skin biopsy showed mild perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with upper dermal edema consistent with a drug reaction. Liver and renal function improved after discontinuing antibiotics/inotropes and starting high-dose methylprednisolone (40 mg IV every 4 h); patient discharged 4 weeks after admission without reported liver transplantation or death.

raw_record.support_text: Cholestatic jaundice developed in a 64-year-old woman who had received phenytoin sodium for more than 40 years. Discontinuation of phenytoin resolved the hepatic abnormalities, which recurred on rechallenge, strongly suggesting a causal relation. Re-discontinuation gave complete resolution; a liver biopsy taken during therapy showed cholestasis compatible with biliary obstruction, although no obstruction was ever demonstrated. The biochemical and histologic findings were interpreted as an unusual response to phenytoin therapy.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of 32 subjects with anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS) manifesting after starting anticonvulsant therapy, the implicated drugs were phenobarbitone (2 cases), phenytoin (22 cases) and carbamazepine (8 cases), used either prophylactically after craniotomy or for epilepsy. Evaluation showed hepatitis in 18 of the 32 subjects (56.3%) as part of the systemic findings. Treatment consisted of stopping the causative drug, and no new lesions occurred after valproic acid was substituted for continued therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hypersensitivity syndrome cases; 19 of 22 phenytoin cases were craniotomy patients with concurrent anaesthetics, systemic antibiotics and analgesics (unresolved co-exposures), the remainder were epilepsy patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Phenytoin was the culprit in 22 of 32 AHS cases (19 post-craniotomy prophylactic, 3 epilepsy). Hepatitis occurred in 18 of 32 total cases (56.3%) as part of AHS, which also included fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, leucocytosis and lymphocytosis; latency from start of therapy to eruption was 2-4 weeks (mean about 3 weeks). Stopping the causative drug produced clinical response (approximately 13 days).

raw_record.support_text: A figure summarizes 23 cases of phenytoin-induced hepatotoxicity plus the present case. Most patients developed hepatotoxicity within 6 weeks of first phenytoin exposure, predominantly within 1 to 3 weeks, with no apparent relation to dosage or blood level.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients were predominantly adolescents or young adults with equal sex distribution; Black persons outnumbered whites by nearly 2:1.
raw_record.extra_details: Based on 23 reviewed cases plus one present case. Onset typically within 1-3 weeks of first exposure, >80% within 6 weeks, sometimes delayed days after drug discontinuation; no dose- or blood-level dependence. Features included rash (all cases; desquamative in 66%, pruritic in 60%), fever (>90%, up to 40.9 C), clinical jaundice (55%), lymphadenopathy (75%), hepatomegaly (65%), splenomegaly (35%), hemorrhagic tendencies (40%), leukocytosis (two-thirds, up to 35,600/mm3), eosinophilia (70%), atypical lymphocytes (~40%). Pathogenesis interpreted as hypersensitivity reaction (eosinophilia, rash, lymphadenopathy, fever, exfoliative dermatitis); a direct toxic effect was excluded by lack of dose-level relation. Separate finding: Jacobsen and associates reported slight increases in serum alkaline phosphatase and ALT with few uni- or paucicellular necroses in asymptomatic chronic phenytoin patients, with no permanent liver damage.

raw_record.support_text: Clinical trials of ibufenac are reported to indicate the drug is hepatotoxic, with a reported incidence of jaundice of about 1 in 80 patients. The type of jaundice was not defined, but liver biopsy in one case preserved normal architecture with no evidence of bile stasis; the jaundice was mild and liver function returned rapidly to normal after withdrawal of ibufenac.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported incidence of jaundice about 1 in 80 patients; jaundice type not defined; liver biopsy in one case showed preservation of normal architecture with no evidence of bile stasis; jaundice was mild and liver function rapidly returned to normal after withdrawal. After normal dosage (2.4 g) the circulating concentration is about 0.1 mM, at which in vitro conjugation inhibition is considered possible. Rats given 100-250 mg/kg orally for 27 weeks showed no liver damage, while 625-1,000 mg/kg caused liver cell damage.

raw_record.support_text: The authors concluded that observations of disturbances in liver function during treatment with Ibufenac indicated that the drug was hepatotoxic. Raised S.G.O.T. titres occurred in fourteen of 36 patients investigated (transient in four), a concurrent elevation of lactic dehydrogenase in one patient was shown to be a hepatic isoenzyme, and two patients developed jaundice with extremely high S.G.O.T. and S.G.P.T. levels; three additional reports of jaundice among approximately 400 patients receiving Ibufenac in rheumatic clinics in Great Britain were also received.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases were rheumatoid arthritis patients on long-term Ibufenac therapy (e.g., Case 2, a 45-year-old secretary, took 285 g Ibufenac over 101 days, escalating from 2 g to 3 g daily; S.G.O.T. rose from 22 to a peak of 1160 units and S.G.P.T. to 1250 units, serum bilirubin peaked at 4.9 mg with jaundice, and liver tests returned to ~normal within a few weeks after withdrawal). Jaundice cleared within ~18 days; both jaundiced patients ran a mild course. Hepatotoxicity was judged to impose a serious limitation on long-term use in rheumatoid arthritis.

raw_record.support_text: In a second trial of Ibufenac in 45 patients treated for 1 to 16 months for rheumatoid arthritis, the only clinically important adverse effect was hepatic dysfunction, observed in 14 of the 36 patients investigated for this, with jaundice occurring in 2 of those 14. The authors state that the frequency of the hepatic toxicity observed in this series imposes considerable limitations on the use of Ibufenac and contraindicates prolonged and unrestricted treatment with the product.
raw_record.extra_details: Ibufenac = 4-isobutylphenylacetic acid, compared to calcium aspirin in the controlled first-week trial; second trial of 45 rheumatoid arthritis patients treated for 1 to 16 months. Hepatic dysfunction in 14 of 36 patients investigated (2 of whom had jaundice). Authors conclude the frequency of hepatic toxicity imposes considerable limitations on and contraindicates prolonged unrestricted use. Also reported: dyspepsia frequency reduced vs prior treatment, minimal occult fecal blood loss, frank hyperuricemia in 13 and slight hyperuricemia in 9 of 43 patients.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 157 cases of drug-induced hepatitis, a heterogenous group of drugs consisting of ajmaline, aminopterine, isaxonine, isoniazid, perhexiline, phenylbutazone and troleandromycine was identified as causing drug-induced hepatitis in which antiorganelle antibodies were absent or rare.

raw_record.support_text: In 9 of 19 patients treated long term with perhexiline (dosage adjusted on the basis of clinical response, mean maximal daily dose 200 ± 24 mg/day), the drug was stopped after 1 to 22 months because of toxic adverse effects, which included biochemical or clinical hepatotoxicity in 4 patients. Liver biopsy in one patient (no. 2) confirmed the presence of hepatitic changes, and hepatotoxicity was among the adverse effects at plasma perhexiline concentrations of 720 to 2680 ng/ml.
raw_record.extra_details: Perhexiline is a prophylactic anti-anginal agent used for chronic angina (dosage 50-400 mg/day, ~8.8 ± 1.7 months). Hepatotoxicity occurred in 4 of 9 patients whose therapy was stopped for toxic adverse effects; biopsy in 1 patient showed hepatitic changes. Toxic adverse effects were associated with plasma perhexiline concentrations of 720-2680 ng/ml (mean 1281 ± 251 ng/ml); no adverse effects developed at concentrations below 700 ng/ml. Two patients died of worsening severe left ventricular failure (not hepatotoxicity) after 4 weeks of therapy. Perhexiline dose was being adjusted on the basis of clinical response, not plasma concentration.

raw_record.support_text: A 28-year-old man treated with finasteride 1 mg/day for 2 months for androgenetic alopecia presented with jaundice and acute liver dysfunction (AST 2581 IU/L, ALT 5416 IU/L, gamma-GTP 177 IU/L, total bilirubin 5.0 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL, LDH 1055 IU/L). Viral and autoimmune hepatitis were excluded, and a lymphocytes stimulus test (LST) against finasteride was positive. Finasteride-induced acute hepatitis was diagnosed; after discontinuing finasteride and steroid pulse therapy (methylprednisolone sodium succinate 500 mg/day for 3 days) his condition improved and returned to normal 20 days after admission.
raw_record.extra_details: The authors deduce the hepatic cell damage occurs by an allergic reaction mechanism. Finasteride, a steroid type II 5alpha-reductase inhibitor, given at 1 mg/day for 2 months for androgenetic alopecia; reported as the first AGA case of finasteride-induced acute hepatitis. Patient had serious general fatigue and poor appetite leading to drug discontinuation 3 days prior. No viral or autoimmune hepatitis, no liver swelling or ascites; APTT 38.0%. LST against finasteride positive. Recovered to normal status 20 days after admission following steroid pulse therapy.
