raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac was the most common offending agent in this study, responsible for DILI in 31 (41.3%) patients. Diclofenac injury was hepatocellular in 54.8% of cases and equally cholestatic or mixed in the remaining cases, with a mean time interval between intake and symptoms of 11.2 ± 5.3 days.
raw_record.extra_details: 31 cases (41.3%); hepatocellular 17 (54.8%), cholestatic 7 (22.6%), mixed 7 (22.6%); acute 10, chronic 21; time interval 11.2 ± 5.3 days; 4 of the 7 deceased cases had diclofenac-induced injury (all with chronic liver disease); liver biopsies showed focal necrosis with lymphocytes and plasma cells in 5 cases, cholestatic hepatitis in 1, and autoimmune with abundant eosinophilia in 1; RUCAM causality assessment applied.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that hepatotoxicity has been reported in several patients given diclofenac, with one death attributed directly to drug therapy, and that four of these patients were later restarted on other NSAIDs (including naproxen and piroxicam) without adverse effects.
raw_record.extra_details: Several patients affected in reported cases; one death was attributed directly to diclofenac therapy. Four affected patients were subsequently restarted on other NSAIDs (naproxen, piroxicam) without adverse effects, which is not presented as a general negative for those agents.

raw_record.support_text: From the Spanish DILI database study of chronic injury following acute idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury, 2 patients with chronic hepatocellular injury developed chronic hepatitis, 1 due to diclofenac and another due to bentazepam.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic hepatocellular injury case that developed chronic hepatitis after an acute idiosyncratic DILI episode; case included only if it received a definite or probable CIOMS causal assessment score. One of 2 chronic-hepatitis cases in the chronic hepatocellular group.

raw_record.support_text: The study included 16 patients with liver injury initially suspected of idiosyncratic DILI (iDILI), diagnosed by clinical causality assessment including RUCAM. Subgroup DicloDILI comprised patients suffering from iDILI due to Diclofenac. All DicloDILI patients had a causality likelihood of at least "highly likely" for iDILI due to Diclofenac, and the MH cell test was positive for Diclofenac only in DicloDILI patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Four patients were diagnosed with iDILI due to Diclofenac (DicloDILI) based on clinical causality assessment including RUCAM, all with causality likelihood of at least 'highly likely'. MH cell test was positive for Diclofenac only in DicloDILI patients, while co-medications tested negative. Among DicloDILI patients, DicloDILI2 had the lowest ITGB3-positive cell level and the worst outcome, requiring liver transplantation; DicloDILI3 recovered within a few weeks after cessation of Diclofenac administration. Diclofenac is a suspected inducer of idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN Prospective Study cohort, DILI due to analgesics was usually hepatocellular in nature; for example, all 12 cases of diclofenac DILI were hepatocellular.
raw_record.extra_details: 12 attributed DILI cases in the DILIN cohort, all hepatocellular; among analgesic DILI cases in the cohort there was only one death and no liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: In the U.S. Drug Induced Liver Injury Network prospective registry, 30 of 1221 adjudicated cases were attributed to eight different NSAIDs, with a mean latency of 67 days, most showing a hepatocellular pattern of injury. Diclofenac was the most frequently implicated NSAID (16/30 cases) characterized by hepatocellular injury; 17 cases resulted in hospitalization or prolongation of hospitalization and one patient died from complications of Stevens–Johnson syndrome attributed to diclofenac. The Network studies idiosyncratic drug hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: DICLIN prospective registry of 1221 adjudicated cases; 30 total cases attributed to eight NSAIDs, of which diclofenac accounted for 16/30 (most frequent). Mean age 52 y, 24/30 (80%) women, 21/30 (70%) Caucasian; mean latency 67 days. Presenting features: nausea 73%, jaundice 67%, dark urine 67%; peak AST 898 U/L, ALT 1060 U/L, total bilirubin 12.2 mg/dl, ALP 326 U/L; hepatocellular pattern most common (70%); autoantibodies detected in 33% of cases. Seventeen cases resulted in hospitalization or prolongation; one death from complications of Stevens-Johnson syndrome attributed to diclofenac.

raw_record.support_text: In this study of 26 cases of drug-induced acute intrahepatic cholestasis (AIC), the causative drugs of four prolonged cases were identified as tiopronin, chlorpromazine and diclofenac. Two of these patients either died or underwent liver transplantation. The prolonged cases showed marked liver cell injury and cholestasis, with disappearance of interlobular bile ducts in the portal triads (vanishing bile ducts).
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as a causative drug of prolonged drug-induced acute intrahepatic cholestasis. Prolonged cases showed marked liver cell injury and cholestasis, vanishing interlobular bile ducts, and significantly higher maximal total bilirubin (35.2±13.8 mg/dL) with markedly longer bilirubin half-life (78.8±69.6 days) vs non-prolonged cases (16.8±8.1 mg/dL, 22.1±12.7 days). Canalicular MRP2 staining was weakened with pericanalicular vesicular redistribution. Two of the four prolonged patients died or underwent liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN prospective registry, diclofenac accounted for 13 of 899 adjudicated DILI cases, one of the top 10 individual agents.
raw_record.extra_details: 13 adjudicated DILI cases in the DILIN registry.

raw_record.support_text: This case-control study evaluates genetic susceptibility to diclofenac-induced liver injury. The 24 diclofenac hepatotoxicity cases were compared with hospital (n=46) and community (n=100) controls, examining genotypes for ABCC2, UGT2B7, and CYP2C8. Combined analyses showed that homozygous UGT2B7*2 plus heterozygous ABCC2 C-24T was present in 7 (29%) of the 24 diclofenac hepatotoxicity patients versus 3 (6%) of hospital controls (OR, 5.9, 95% CI, 1.4–25.5) and 10 (10%) of community controls (OR, 3.7, 95% CI, 1.2–11.1); UGT2B7*2 homozygosity with CYP2C8 Wt/*4 gave ORs of 12.4 and 29.2 for diclofenac liver-injury development.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of 24 diclofenac hepatotoxicity cases versus hospital (n=46) and community (n=100) controls. Genetic associations: ABCC2 C-24T T-allele possession OR 5.02 (95% CI 1.71–14.7) vs hospital controls and 6.25 (95% CI 2.38–16.7) vs community controls; borderline association for ABCC2 G-1023A vs hospital controls only; no association for G1249A or T3563A. Combined genotypes: UGT2B7*2 homozygosity with ABCC2 C-24T heterozygosity in 7/24 cases (OR 5.9 vs hospital, 3.7 vs community); UGT2B7*2 homozygosity with CYP2C8 Wt/*4 in 5/24 cases (OR 12.4 vs hospital, 29.2 vs community). No significant genotype differences between severe and milder disease subgroups.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that diclofenac-associated hepatitis has been considered rare, with up to 15% of patients possibly having mild increases in serum transaminases. In short-term trials only 19 of 1227 patients had transaminase elevations more than three times normal, in only two of whom (0.16%) the medication was a probable cause; in long-term trials three of 1173 patients developed hepatitis, with no fatalities and reversal on drug discontinuation. In the English and French literature, including the authors' patients, there are 26 cases of significant liver disease (four fatal) in which diclofenac was implicated.
raw_record.extra_details: Diclofenac-associated hepatitis: in short-term trials 19/1227 patients had transaminase elevations >3x normal (0.16% probable drug causality); long-term trials 3/1173 developed hepatitis with no fatalities, all reversible on discontinuation. 26 cases of significant liver disease (four fatal) reported in English and French literature including these patients. Case 3 showed jaundice and AST rise on initial exposure and again on rechallenge (bilirubin 263 µmol/L, AST 1970 IU/L initially; AST 1280 IU/L on rechallenge), biopsy showing chronic active hepatitis/panlobular hepatitis with piecemeal and spotty lobular necrosis, mild fibrosis, occasional eosinophils; enzymes normalized after drug discontinuation. Case 2 considered possible diclofenac-induced hepatotoxicity but enzymes remained normal after discontinuing the drug/prednisone.

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac was the most incriminated drug in the DILI group (16 patients, 40%). Of 28 hepatocellular patients, 14 (50%) were caused by diclofenac, and of 4 mixed-injury patients, 2 (50%) were caused by diclofenac. Diclofenac accounted for 66.6% (4 patients) of the mortality cases. Exposure duration was 10.5 ±1.5 days with 13.5 ±1.4 days to symptom onset.
raw_record.extra_details: 16 of 40 DILI patients (40%); hepatocellular injury in 14 cases, mixed injury in 2; duration 10.5±1.5 days, time to symptoms 13.5±1.4 days; accounted for 66.6% (4 patients) of the 6 mortality cases (p=0.28). RUCAM-based DILI classification.

raw_record.support_text: Five cases of hepatitis associated with diclofenac, the most commonly prescribed non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug in the United Kingdom, were reported from one unit over a 12-month period. All were on diclofenac at presentation, four of the five having started the drug within the previous three months; the presentation was that of an acute hepatitis, three with jaundice, and liver function tests were grossly abnormal in all cases, with no viral markers, no foreign travel/blood transfusion, and normal liver ultrasound.
raw_record.extra_details: Five cases in one unit over 12 months; average age 63 (four women, one man); three with jaundice; four of five had started the drug within the previous three months. Liver biopsy in four cases showed acute hepatitis with cell damage and inflammation predominating. Four patients improved rapidly on stopping diclofenac and fully recovered within three months; one developed features suggestive of chronic active hepatitis that was steroid responsive. Previous single cases of diclofenac-associated hepatitis are cited, including three fatal ones, suggesting hepatitis may be commoner than supposed.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective review of out-patient hepatology clinic cases at Sahlgrenska University Hospital (1995–2005) with causality assessment by International Consensus Criteria, drug-induced liver injury cases constituted 6% of all out-patients and 3% of referrals and occurred more often in women. The authors conclude that antibiotics and diclofenac were the most common causes of drug-induced liver injury among out-patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Identified among out-patient hepatology referrals at an urban Swedish university hospital (1995–2005); DILI cases represented 6% of all out-patients and 3% of referrals, occurring more often in women. Causality was assessed using the International Consensus Criteria (highly probable, probable, possible, unlikely, excluded). Study excluded cases of acute liver injury with coagulopathy (INR >1.5) and those leading to liver transplantation. Antibiotics (broad class, not recorded as a single named agent) were also cited as the most common cause.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states diclofenac is a commonly used drug frequently reported to cause DILI, and that the Björnsson Iceland prospective population-based study implicated diclofenac as a common agent linked to DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: Frequently reported to cause DILI; DILI risk 11:100,000 (95% CI 4-24), comparable to ulipristal acetate; a prospective randomized trial found liver-related hospitalization potentially caused by diclofenac was 23 per 100,000 and Hy's law occurrence 12 per 100,000 patients; Likelihood score category A (well-known cause, >50 published cases); SMPC advises hepatic function monitoring with prolonged use.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports the clinical characteristics of DILI cases included in the main GWAS, stating that a variety of different causative drugs were represented. Among them, diclofenac was the most common with 67 cases, followed by nitrofurantoin with 64 cases.
raw_record.extra_details: DILI GWAS (862 European ancestry DILI cases); diclofenac was the most common causative drug with 67 cases.

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac, an NSAID still in use, has been associated with rare cases of immune-mediated toxicity. In one case, a 53-year-old female had to undergo liver transplantation due to hepatic failure caused by an inadvertent re-challenge to diclofenac ten months after she had first presented with jaundice and increased serum liver enzymes.
raw_record.extra_details: Case: 53-year-old female first presented with jaundice and increased serum liver enzymes, then ten months later suffered hepatic failure caused by an inadvertent re-challenge to diclofenac, requiring liver transplantation; hepatotoxicity associated with rare immune-mediated toxicity; separate non-hepatic immune-mediated haemolytic anaemia case not attributable to covalent red-cell binding but requiring the metabolite 4'-hydroxy-diclofenac acyl glucuronide.

raw_record.support_text: Serum antibodies directed against diclofenac protein adducts were measured in seven patients with diclofenac-associated hepatotoxicity, 20 subjects who took diclofenac without hepatotoxicity, and four healthy controls. Three of the hepatotoxicity patients presented with jaundice, two presented with hepatic failure (patients 25 and 27), and two presented with raised liver enzymes. All seven patients with drug-associated liver injury had serum antibodies recognizing diclofenac-induced protein antigens expressed in rat liver nuclear fractions, whereas such antibodies were not detected in healthy controls.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven patients with diclofenac hepatotoxicity were studied: three presented with jaundice, two with hepatic failure (patients 25 and 27), and two with raised liver enzymes. All 7 patients with drug-associated liver injury had serum antibodies to diclofenac-induced protein antigens (85 kDa, and 97 kDa in most), versus 12/20 diclofenac-treated subjects without hepatotoxicity and 0/4 healthy controls (P=.003). Recognition of putative human liver adducts (130, 216, 240 kDa) in the liver of a patient with diclofenac-induced hepatic failure was confirmed by competitive inhibition with free diclofenac, but not glycine. Background immunochemical work linking adduct formation to acyl glucuronide metabolites and supporting rat experiments are mechanistic/preclinical only.

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac is listed at position 5 in the RUCAM-based ranking of drugs causing DILI with verified causality (Table 10).
raw_record.extra_details: Ranked #5 in the RUCAM-based top-ranking of drugs causing DILI with verified causality (Teschke, 2018d).

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac is listed as the second most frequent drug, n = 13, among the main 10 drugs leading the Latin American DILI Registry with RUCAM-based causality assessment.
raw_record.extra_details: 13 cases in the Latin American DILI Registry; RUCAM-based causality assessment used.

raw_record.support_text: In 1164 first-time out-patients in a Swedish University hospital hepatology clinic (1995-2005), all suspected drug-induced liver injury (DILI) cases were causality assessed with the International Consensus Criteria. DILI with at least a possible causal relationship was found in 77 cases (6.6%). Antibiotics were the most common class causing DILI, followed by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, with diclofenac most often responsible for the drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Identified as the single nameable agent most often responsible for DILI in a cohort of 77 causality-assessed (International Consensus Criteria) DILI cases (6.6% of 1164 patients). Overall cohort: median age 58 years, 56% female; hepatocellular pattern 37 (48%), cholestatic 31 (40%), mixed 12%. Antibiotics were the most common class causing DILI, followed by NSAIDs. Hepatology out-patient clinic database analysis, Sweden, 1995-2005.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report five cases of biopsy proven hepatitis associated with the use of diclofenac, including one case with clinical, biochemical and histopathological features of chronic active hepatitis that required and responded to long-term corticosteroids. Lobular hepatitis was prominent, and severe cholestasis was present in only one case. In paragraph 3 they note that between 1983 and 1989, when over 8 million diclofenac prescriptions were issued in Australia, the Australian Adverse Drug Reaction Committee received 79 suspected diclofenac hepatotoxicity reports, of which 25 were considered 'probably' or 'certainly' linked to diclofenac, suggesting a crude incidence of 3 to 10 cases per million prescriptions.
raw_record.extra_details: Five cases of biopsy-proven hepatitis associated with diclofenac use; lobular hepatitis prominent, severe cholestasis in only one case. One case had features of chronic active hepatitis requiring and responding to long-term corticosteroids. Drug withdrawal resulted in rapid resolution of abnormal liver function tests except in the chronic active hepatitis patient, whose LFTs remained abnormal over 7 months and who responded clinically, biochemically and histopathologically to corticosteroids. Pharmacovigilance (1983-1989, Australia, >8 million diclofenac prescriptions): 79 suspected hepatotoxicity reports, 25 'probably' or 'certainly' linked, crude incidence 3-10 cases per million prescriptions; voluntary reporting likely under-estimates true incidence, especially 'transaminitis'.

raw_record.support_text: Table 1 lists two patients (cases 1 and 12) with DILI attributed to diclofenac taken therapeutically for pain. The first case was a 76-year-old woman on diclofenac 50 mg/day who developed jaundice with ASMA 1/80, hepatocellular-type injury (TB 2.9xULN, ALT 24xULN, ALP 2.6xULN), classified Moderate severity and CIOMS 'Highly probable'. The second was an 80-year-old woman on diclofenac 75 mg/day with jaundice, hepatocellular injury (TB 4.9xULN, ALT 38xULN, ALP 1.9xULN), Moderate severity and CIOMS 'Highly probable'. The study is framed as NSAIDs-induced idiosyncratic liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases. Case 1 (76/F, lumbar pain), 50 mg/day for 93 days, onset 30 days, co-meds levothyroxine and metamizole, jaundice, ASMA 1/80, TB 2.9xULN, ALT 24xULN, ALP 2.6xULN, Moderate severity, resolution at 221 days. Case 12 (80/F), 75 mg/day for 171 days, onset 171 days, co-meds telmisartan, allopurinol, glibenclamide, ebastine, troxerutin, jaundice, TB 4.9xULN, ALT 38xULN, ALP 1.9xULN, Moderate, hospitalized, resolution at 348 days. CIOMS 'Highly probable' for both. Indication: pain.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of 44 patients classified as having drug related hepatotoxicity by International Consensus Group criteria (with suggestive/compatible onset, suggestive dechallenge course, exclusion of alternatives incl. liver biopsy, and positive rechallenge where available), table 1 lists the responsible drugs. Diclofenac was implicated in four patients (cases 1, 6, 7, 8): one presented with liver failure on a histology of acute hepatitis, and three with raised enzymes on chronic hepatitis, with follow-up ranging 3.5-7.7 years.
raw_record.extra_details: Analgesic/NSAID class. Case 1: liver failure, acute hepatitis, follow-up 5.2 y; cases 6,7,8: raised enzymes, chronic hepatitis, follow-ups 4, 3.5, 7.7 y. Initial presentation most commonly jaundice (n=24) or abnormal liver blood tests (n=17); 3 patients presented with hepatic failure manifest as encephalopathy.

raw_record.support_text: Patients with diclofenac hepatotoxicity were identified from hospital records and adverse hepatotoxicity reports to the Committee on Safety of Medicines, and the causal relationship of liver injury to diclofenac was established using International Consensus Criteria, requiring suggestive or compatible timing, a suggestive post-cessation course, exclusion of alternative causes, and a positive rechallenge response. A reaction was classified as diclofenac hepatotoxicity when the first three criteria were met, or two of three with a positive rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Patients were Caucasian diclofenac-treated subjects. Adjudication used the International Consensus Criteria (Benichou, 1990): timing from intake/withdrawal to onset of the reaction (suggestive 5-90 days from initial intake or compatible), course after cessation (decrease in liver enzymes by 50% within 30 days), exclusion of alternative causes by detailed investigation, and positive rechallenge response. The study tested the hypothesis that susceptibility to diclofenac hepatotoxicity is genetically determined by CYP2C9 polymorphisms (NCBIGene:1559) impairing 4'-hydroxylation and increasing reactive metabolite production; patients were genotyped for CYP2C9 allelic variants and screened for novel CYP2C9 polymorphisms.

raw_record.support_text: The study group comprised 24 patients (18 female, six male; aged 24-70 years, median 54) with diclofenac-induced hepatotoxicity. Six presented with jaundice, three with hepatic failure and 15 with raised liver enzymes on routine monitoring; diagnoses included 13 acute cytolytic hepatitis, two acute cholestatic injury, eight chronic hepatitis (biopsy proven) and one subacute hepatic necrosis. Ten patients were taking other drugs concomitantly, including other CYP2C9 substrates.
raw_record.extra_details: 24 diclofenac-induced hepatotoxicity patients (18 female, six male; age 24-70 y, median 54). Presentations: six with jaundice, three with hepatic failure, 15 with raised liver enzymes on routine monitoring. Diagnoses: 13 acute cytolytic hepatitis, two acute cholestatic injury, eight chronic hepatitis (biopsy proven), one subacute hepatic necrosis. Ten patients took other drugs concomitantly, six of them other CYP2C9 substrates (sulphamethoxazole, indomethacin, ibuprofen) and another cimetidine (a general P450 inhibitor). Study also reported CYP2C9 genotyping and kinetic analysis of diclofenac 4'-hydroxylation in human liver microsomes (no difference in Km among CYP2C9*1/*2/*3; Vmax lower in CYP2C9*3 heterozygotes, P=0.057).

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac is noted as the only non-antibiotic among the top ten drugs in the DILIN registry and is one of the five drugs present among the ten most common DILI-causing drugs in at least two of three prospective studies (DILIN, Iceland, Spain).
raw_record.extra_details: NSAID; top-ten drug in DILIN, Icelandic, and Spanish registries; in the ten most frequently implicated drugs across three DILI registries; listed in Table 1 with >100 reported DILI cases (LiverTox); strongly associated with DILI in GPRD studies.

raw_record.support_text: Among reported cases, 26 met inclusion criteria where diclofenac was the sole suspected drug, the patient recovered after drug withdrawal, no other treatment or probable cause of hepatic dysfunction was found, and serial liver function tests were available including a recovery-phase value. Serology for hepatitis A and B was negative in 15 tested, and imaging ruled out biliary obstruction in 7 cases; one liver biopsy favored drug-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: 26 cases analyzed; average age 64 years (range 37-84), 70% female. Main features included jaundice (total bilirubin deviate ratio >2) in half, hepatomegaly (sometimes painful), anorexia, nausea; itch, malaise, or vomiting less common; 25% asymptomatic; mild thrombocytopenia in 2 reports; no extrahepatic hypersensitivity phenomena reported. Onset within first 6 months in 18/21 reports; median duration of exposure 76 days (range 6-417 days); median cumulative dose 8.7 g (1.4-63.5 g). Dominant biochemical feature was raised transaminases with lesser rises in alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyltransferase, and bilirubin; severity ranged to fortyfold transaminase elevations. Significant log dose vs log peak AST (r²=0.68, slope 0.91, p=0.0001) and ALT (r²=0.71, slope 1.04, p=0.001) relations. Transaminases fell exponentially after withdrawal with post-peak half-lives of 13.7 days (AST) and 13.2 days (ALT).

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac was the second-most frequent drug among the top 10 involved in LA DILI Registry cases, with n = 13 cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Second most frequent drug in the LA DILI Registry, n=13 cases.

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac-associated DILI case reports were analyzed for liver-injury pattern, eosinophilia, hepatic necrosis, inflammatory reaction, and death/liver transplantation outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: 60 individual case reports; median age 56 y; 49 female/11 male; median treatment duration 8 weeks; HC 58%, Cs/mixed 42%; peripheral eosinophilia present in 13% (55/60 reported); hepatic eosinophilia present in 37% (27/60 reported); hepatic necrosis 54%; inflammatory reaction 93%; death or liver transplant 18%; liver biopsy reported in 32/60 cases.

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac, the most frequently prescribed NSAID, causes minimal serum transaminase elevations in about 15% of patients; severe hepatic dysfunction is rare but 27 case reports of severe diclofenac-induced hepatitis have been described worldwide, including four fatalities. This report describes the second case of diclofenac-induced liver failure successfully treated by orthotopic liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Diclofenac produces a type II idiosyncratic liver injury; most cases are thought to occur by a metabolic mechanism, though hypersensitivity cases occur. In this case the mechanism was probably a hypersensitivity reaction, evidenced by short exposure duration, dramatic response to rechallenge, and eosinophils in the liver biopsy. Repeated hepatotoxicity on rechallenging with diclofenac has been described, while challenge with a different NSAID was not hepatotoxic, indicating an idiosyncratic rather than class effect. About 15% of patients show minimal transaminase elevations; 27 reported cases of severe hepatitis include 4 fatalities; this is only the second liver-failure case successfully treated by orthotopic liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: Aithal et al. investigated the relationship between CYP2C9 genotype and susceptibility to hepatotoxicity in 24 patients with diclofenac-induced hepatotoxicity, compared with 100 healthy controls for the CYP2C9*2 and *3 alleles, and found that the frequencies of these alleles were similar in patients and controls. This explicitly attributes a human hepatotoxic response to diclofenac.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 24 patients with diclofenac-induced hepatotoxicity vs 100 healthy controls; CYP2C9*2 and CYP2C9*3 allele frequencies did not differ between patients and controls, indicating no association between these CYP2C9 genotypes and diclofenac hepatotoxicity susceptibility.

raw_record.support_text: Helfgott et al. described the development of significant hepatitis in seven patients treated with diclofenac, with one associated death. Signs and symptoms of hepatotoxicity began several weeks after initiation of therapy and resolved 4 to 6 weeks after the therapy was stopped. The paper frames this under 'Hepatotoxicity' of the newer NSAIDs, noting no clear explanation and that most data come from postmarketing surveillance or case reports; in the United States the FDA requires monitoring serum transaminases and liver function tests within 8 weeks of starting diclofenac.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven patients developed significant hepatitis, with one associated death; onset several weeks after initiation of therapy and resolution 4-6 weeks after stopping. No clear explanation given and incidence not felt increased vs other NSAIDs. Data mostly from postmarketing surveillance and case reports. US FDA requires monitoring serum transaminases/liver function tests within 8 weeks of initiating therapy.

raw_record.support_text: In a Brazilian study of acute liver failure (ALF) across 12 transplant centers, drug-related ALF causes included NSAIDs (21%), with diclofenac reported in n=5 attributed cases of DILI leading to ALF.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as a cause of DILI-ALF in a cohort of patients undergoing liver transplantation for ALF; n=5 cases reported.

raw_record.support_text: Seventy-one patients with idiosyncratic drug-induced hepatitis were described and the causative drug for each patient was tabulated; diagnosis was considered definite or probable based on exclusion of other causes and a temporal relationship.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases 13-17. Histology: acute mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic hepatitis (cases 13,14), acute hepatocellular hepatitis (cases 15,16), none (case 17). Max bilirubin 5-55 µmol/l.

raw_record.support_text: In the Indian tertiary-care DILI cohort of 80 patients, diclofenac was listed among the other drugs implicated as a cause of DILI at 2% of cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed as a cause in 2% of 80 DILI cases (about 1-2 patients).

raw_record.support_text: In the DILI cohort, diclofenac was attributed as the causative agent in 3 of the 6 NSAID-associated cases. DILI was established as the final diagnosis, supported by RUCAM scoring.
raw_record.extra_details: Diclofenac was the attributed NSAID cause in 3 of 22 DILI cases in this cohort; median maximum RUCAM of the DILI group was 6 (3-10).

raw_record.support_text: A 68-year-old woman on diclofenac 100 mg/day developed low-grade fever, lassitude and pathological bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase and transaminase values within two weeks; findings resolved after drug withdrawal and recurred a week after rechallenge with fever, lassitude, a maculopapular rash, clinical jaundice and abnormal liver function (bilirubin 88.9 µmol/l, aspartate transaminase 90 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 274 IU/l, 42% eosinophils). The paper presents this as one of two patients with a liver hypersensitivity reaction following diclofenac treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients reported; acute hepatotoxicity shortly after initiation of diclofenac. Case 1 was a 68-year-old woman treated for diffuse joint pains/recurrent knee effusions; recurrence on rechallenge; eosinophilia (42% eosinophils), maculopapular rash, skin and bone-marrow findings; HBsAg, antismooth muscle and antimitochondrial antibodies absent; resolution after withdrawal. Hepatic side effects of diclofenac described as very rare. Diclofenac sodium (Voltaren) is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory and analgesic.

raw_record.support_text: A 52-year-old man taking diclofenac for painful pseudogout developed nausea, vomiting, dark urine, pale stools, and jaundice, with an enlarged liver; liver function tests were consistent with acute hepatitis (bilirubin 126 µmol/l, aspartate aminotransferase 1375 IU/l). Hepatitis B and A serology were negative and he took no other regular medication. Diclofenac was withdrawn and the jaundice resolved completely over seven days. Rechallenge with diclofenac five weeks later produced vomiting and jaundice again (bilirubin 201 µmol/l, aspartate aminotransferase 1150 IU/l); liver biopsy specimens showed moderately severe acute hepatitis with canalicular cholestasis, Kupffer-cell proliferation, and plasma cells and eosinophils in the inflammatory infiltrate. Diclofenac was stopped and symptoms and liver function test results normalized.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report with positive dechallenge-rechallenge; symptoms recurred on rechallenge. Liver biopsy showed moderately severe acute hepatitis with canalicular cholestasis, Kupffer-cell proliferation, plasma cells and eosinophils. Relevant laboratory values: bilirubin 126 µmol/l (7.4 mg/100 ml) initially and 201 µmol/l (11.8 mg/100 ml) on rechallenge; aspartate aminotransferase 1375 IU/l initially and 1150 IU/l on rechallenge. Enlarged liver (4 cm and later 2 cm below right costal margin). Viral hepatitis excluded (HBsAg, HAV IgM, EBV, CMV negative). Indication: painful pseudogout of right knee; no alcohol abuse or other regular medication. Jaundice resolved within days of withdrawal in both episodes, liver function normal within six weeks and at three months.

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac is attributed as the sole culprit in case 5 (F/56, jaundice, chronic hepatitis on biopsy with portal inflammatory infiltrate, piecemeal necrosis and moderate portal fibrosis disrupting lobular architecture, persistent at 6 months, antinuclear antibodies 1/40). The episode is ascribed to diclofenac as single drug. Case was classified definite or probable.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 5: jaundice, TB 11.9 mg/dL (peak), ALT 39.8xULN, 743 d therapy, 700 d onset, persistent (6 mo). Also appears as co-suspect with amoxicillin-clavulanate in case 21 (cholestatic, persistent 7 mo).

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac was the NSAID most often responsible for DILI, with 14 of 77 cases. The ascribed pattern distribution was seven hepatocellular, five cholestatic and two mixed, and six of the cases had jaundice (bilirubin ≥2 ULN).
raw_record.extra_details: 14 of 77 DILI cases; 7 female/7 male; pattern 7 hepatocellular/5 cholestatic/2 mixed; duration of treatment mean 24 (2-60) days; time to biochemical resolution mean 52 (10-150) days. Six jaundice cases detailed (bilirubin 2.1-16 ULN), some with very high AST/ALT.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that DILI cases related to drugs such as diclofenac, which was well represented in the cohort (66 cases), were recorded as causal agents of DILI. Diclofenac showed a smaller, non-significant increase in rs2476601 minor allele frequency compared with controls.
raw_record.extra_details: 66 cases in the cohort, identified as a causal agent of DILI; rs2476601 association not significant (OR 1.17, 95% CI 0.67–2.04, P = .59).

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac and other NSAIDs are known idiosyncratic hepatotoxins. The paper reports 13 cases of diclofenac hepatitis (including the present case), two with a fatal outcome, with jaundice in eleven patients, marked elevations in bilirubin, AST, ALT, and alkaline phosphatase, and normalization of enzymes within 4-13 weeks in most survivors. The authors conclude it seems most probable that these 13 patients had hepatitis as a result of diclofenac usage, with a reversible hepatitis related to diclofenac use in the presented patient and one survivor developing steroid-responsive chronic active hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: 13 diclofenac hepatitis cases (12 previously reported + present case), 2 fatal fulminant hepatitis; 10 women and 3 men, average age 63 years (range 46-79); 6 on diclofenac alone, others co-medicated; presentation usually within 3 months of starting diclofenac (range 1 week to 11 months). Eleven patients jaundiced with dark urine and pale stools; pruritus, nausea, vomiting relatively infrequent. At presentation bilirubin 1-22x, AST 2-45x, ALT 7-47x, alkaline phosphatase 1.6-4.6x upper limit of normal. Normalization in 4-13 weeks in 10 survivors; one survivor developed steroid-responsive chronic active hepatitis. One patient with fatal fulminant hepatitis while taking diclofenac and glafenine was excluded due to ambiguity of cause. The patient presented here had hepatocellular necrosis with ultrastructural changes (ER vesiculation, lamellated bodies, mitochondrial pleomorphism with paracrystalline inclusions) in zone 3, without microvesicular steatosis or cholestasis; improvement after diclofenac discontinuation. Diclofenac rechallenge on two occasions reproduced hepatitis in patients 1, 6, and 11.

raw_record.support_text: A study comparing 24 patients with diclofenac hepatotoxicity against controls (48 diclofenac-exposed, 112 unexposed) concluded that the UGT2B7*2 and ABCC2 -24CT variants contributed significantly to the risk of diclofenac-induced DILI, whereas CYP2C8 plays no important role.
raw_record.extra_details: Genetic-risk study of 24 diclofenac hepatotoxicity cases; UGT2B7*2 (increased enzyme function) and ABCC2 -24CT variants significantly increased diclofenac-induced DILI risk; proposed mechanism via UGT2B7-mediated formation of diclofenac acyl glucuronide forming covalent protein adducts; CYP2C8 and CYP2C9 variants not significantly associated.

raw_record.support_text: The paper notes that Aithal et al investigated cytokine gene polymorphisms in 24 patients with diclofenac-induced liver injury, 48 diclofenac-exposed controls, and up to 321 healthy controls, observing a higher frequency of IL-10 and IL-4 variants in diclofenac DILI patients compared with controls.
raw_record.extra_details: Diclofenac-induced liver injury studied in 24 patients vs 48 diclofenac-exposed and up to 321 healthy controls; higher frequency of IL-10 and IL-4 variants in cases. Genetic study of diclofenac DILI (Donaldson 2008) reported HLA DRB1*13 as protective.

raw_record.support_text: In a population-based Icelandic study of drug-induced liver injury, the most commonly implicated agents included diclofenac in 4 (8%) of 51 cases. Cases were adjudicated by RUCAM with 94% classified as highly probable (n=18) or probable (n=30).
raw_record.extra_details: 4/51 (8%) of DILI cases attributed; causality per RUCAM (94% of all cohort cases highly probable or probable). All cohort cases recovered with median time to resolution of liver tests 67 days.

raw_record.support_text: Of the 82 patients identified with AIH, 11 (13.4%) were considered to have drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis (DIAIH), with RUCAM scores probable for all 11 cases (6-8). The implicated drugs included diclofenac (n=1) among others. In the non-nitrofurantoin DIAIH group, the drugs (statins n=4 and diclofenac n=1) were discontinued by primary care physicians upon receipt of abnormal liver tests.
raw_record.extra_details: 1 of 11 DIAIH cases attributed to diclofenac, with RUCAM causality 'probable' (score 6-8) for all DIAIH cases. The drug was in the non-nitrofurantoin group (74.1% of that group discontinued by primary care physicians on abnormal liver tests).

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes susceptibility to diclofenac-induced hepatotoxicity in relation to genetic variants. Daly et al. investigated UGT2B7, CYP2C8, and ABCC2 polymorphisms in 24 patients who had suffered diclofenac-related iDILI compared with 48 intrahospital subjects taking diclofenac without liver injury and 112 healthy controls; the ABCC2 c.-24C>T variant in the 5'UTR was more common in the diclofenac-related iDILI patients, and the ABCC2 rs717620 variant was associated with an increased risk of hyperbilirubinemia and mortality in iDILI patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Diclofenac-related iDILI studied in a case-control genetic analysis (Daly et al.): 24 iDILI patients, 48 hospital controls taking diclofenac without liver injury, and 112 healthy controls. ABCC2 c.-24C>T was more common in cases (OR 5.0, p=0.005 vs hospital controls; OR 6.3, p=0.0002 vs healthy controls). Authors concluded ABCC2 allelic variants predispose to iDILI via formation and accumulation of reactive metabolites. In a separate study (Huang et al.), ABCC2 rs717620 T variant was associated with increased risk of hyperbilirubinemia and mortality in iDILI patients.

raw_record.support_text: A group of eight patients with drug-induced cholestasis caused by drugs other than tiopronin was analyzed (Table 3). Patient 7, F/51, received diclofenac for headache with a maximum bilirubin of 12 mg/dl and jaundice.
raw_record.extra_details: Drug-induced cholestasis with jaundice; F/51 given for headache; maximum total bilirubin 12 mg/dl.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports five patients treated with diclofenac who developed hepatitis, with four of five treated a few weeks or months before liver dysfunction ensued, four of five returning to normal on drug withdrawal, and one patient re-exposed to diclofenac whose liver function again became abnormal, supporting a direct association between diclofenac and hepatitis in these cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Five cases seen within 1 year in a single gastroenterology unit (Oxford region) despite no demographic factors such as increased diclofenac prescription rate or abnormal dosage. Four of five patients had liver dysfunction that returned to normal on drug withdrawal; one rechallenge was positive. Histopathology showed lobular and portal hepatitis with a predominantly hepatocellular cytotoxic pattern of cell damage; cholestasis was observed in case 2 only. One patient (case 2) did not fully recover and developed chronic active hepatitis (CAH), steroid responsive, a progression not previously reported; that patient also received dextropropoxyphene, which was deemed unlikely to contribute because its pathology is distinct. Until May 1988 the UK Committee on Safety of Medicines had received 39 reports of abnormal liver function tests and 33 reports of jaundice following diclofenac. Three cases of fulminant hepatitis have been reported (references 1-3), but most patients appear to recover after stopping diclofenac.

raw_record.support_text: A table of the top 48 drugs worldwide causing idiosyncratic DILI with verified causality assessed by RUCAM lists diclofenac with 46 RUCAM-based DILI cases, categorized as a CYP substrate (CYP+), referenced to Zanger (116). Separately (p29), peripheral blood monocytes from patients suspected to have diclofenac-induced DILI converted to hepatocyte-like cells increased ITGB3 when incubated with diclofenac, framed as a suspected cause.
raw_record.extra_details: 46 RUCAM-verified DILI cases; CYP substrate (CYP+); aryl glucuronides proposed as responsible reactive metabolites in diclofenac DILI, evidence not compelling (p32); biomarker (ITGB3) study on patients suspected of diclofenac-induced DILI (p29).

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports five cases of biopsy-proven hepatitis developing between six and 20 weeks after administration of diclofenac. All patients recovered without sequelae and resolution of symptoms occurred three to 12 weeks after drug cessation. The abstract notes that three of the five patients developed transient circulating autoantibodies, suggesting immune mechanisms may be important, and that the incidence of severe hepatic dysfunction related to diclofenac appears low, on the order of one case per 50-100,000 prescriptions.
raw_record.extra_details: Five biopsy-proven cases of diclofenac hepatotoxicity seen at one hospital over two years; latency 6-20 weeks after drug start. One patient had clinical, biochemical and histopathological features of chronic active hepatitis treated with corticosteroids; three of five had transient circulating autoantibodies suggesting immune-mediated injury. All recovered without sequelae; LFTs normalized 7-16 weeks after withdrawal, except the chronic active hepatitis patient who remained biochemically abnormal for 8 months. Case 1 (72-year-old male, diclofenac 75 mg daily) developed deep jaundice six weeks after start with severe portal and lobular cholestatic hepatitis on biopsy; hepatitis B, A, EBV, CMV serologies negative; biliary obstruction excluded by ultrasound and ERCP. Incidence of severe hepatic dysfunction estimated at about one case per 50-100,000 diclofenac prescriptions. Diclofenac was the most commonly prescribed NSAID in Australia by 1986 with over two million prescriptions annually.

raw_record.support_text: In one series of 180 patients with diclofenac-related hepatotoxicity, 33% were detected by routine laboratory analyses and 67% by symptoms (67% of these jaundiced); 79% were female and 71% were over 60 years of age. Hepatic injury was apparent by 1 month in 24%, by 3 months in 63%, and by 6 months in 85% of cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Series of 180 diclofenac-related hepatotoxicity cases; 33% detected by routine labs, 67% by symptoms (67% of these jaundiced); 79% female, 71% older than 60 years; injury apparent by 1 month in 24%, 3 months in 63%, 6 months in 85%. NSAID hepatotoxicity can present as acute hepatitis with jaundice, fever, nausea, greatly elevated transaminases, sometimes eosinophilia, or as chronic active hepatitis with serological and histological features. A rechallenge from an error in generic and non-generic diclofenac prescribing resulted in liver transplantation for one patient.

raw_record.support_text: A case of diclofenac-induced hepatitis in a 53-year-old Indian woman with recurrent jaundice is presented. The diagnosis was suspected from the liver biopsy appearance and confirmed by the temporal association with drug usage and cure on withdrawal of the drug. Diclofenac, a widely used NSAID, is described as having documented but rare hepatotoxicity ranging from asymptomatic hepatic enzyme elevation to symptomatic hepatic injury and even fulminant hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: 53-year-old Indian woman with recurrent jaundice; liver biopsy showed diffuse hepatocellular degeneration, extensive bridging necrosis, a dense mixed inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes, plasma cells, many eosinophils), acidophilic bodies, and mild hepatocytic cholestasis. Labs: total bilirubin 17.8 mg/dl, direct 12.8 mg/dl, SGOT 1448 IU/l, SGPT 862 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 622 U/l; prolonged prothrombin time (6 s over control) normalized after vitamin K; transient ANA positivity with negative repeat and LE-cell tests; HBsAg (ELISA) and anti-HCV (2nd-gen Abbott ELISA) negative; liver palpable 5 cm below costal margin. No peripheral eosinophilia or rash; patient not alcoholic. The agent was taken for joint pain. Case highlights awareness of this entity, first suspected on examination of the liver biopsy.

raw_record.support_text: Nimesulide and diclofenac lead the list of NSAIDs in the LATINDILI registry, diclofenac heads the NSAID list in the Spanish registry, and diclofenac-induced hepatotoxicity led the DILIN registry list with 12 patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Registry attribution: leads the NSAID list in LATINDILI and the Spanish registry, and caused diclofenac-induced hepatotoxicity in 12 patients in the DILIN registry. No biochemical pattern, phenotype, or severity specified for these registry cases.

raw_record.support_text: Four patients taking diclofenac were hospitalized with a liver-related diagnosis and ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, or bilirubin >2×ULN, adjudicated as possibly or probably related to study medication with RUCAM scores of 2, 5, 5, and 6. The crude proportion of liver-related hospitalizations due to diclofenac was 0.023% (rate=16, 95% CI 4–40 hospitalizations per 100,000 patient-years).

raw_record.support_text: This paper describes five cases of hepatitis with clinical features indicating a direct link with diclofenac. All patients presented with acute hepatitis (three jaundiced) after taking the NSAID diclofenac up to presentation, four having started within the previous 3 months, with no alternative causes identified. Liver function tests were grossly abnormal showing a hepatitic picture; liver biopsy in 4 cases showed acute hepatitis with inflammation and hepatocyte damage. Liver dysfunction returned to normal on drug withdrawal in four of five cases (full recovery by 3 months); one patient developed steroid-responsive chronic active hepatitis. The authors conclude that hepatotoxicity associated with diclofenac is documented and may be commoner than previously supposed.
raw_record.extra_details: Five cases in one gastroenterology unit over a 12-month period; three were jaundiced; four of five had started diclofenac within the previous 3 months. Liver biopsy in 4 cases showed acute hepatitis with inflammation and hepatocyte damage. Dechallenge: liver dysfunction returned to normal on drug withdrawal in four of five cases with full recovery by 3 months; one patient developed steroid-responsive chronic active hepatitis. Case 1 details: 70-yr-old woman, diclofenac 50 mg TDS for osteoarthrosis, jaundice with pale stools and dark urine 3 weeks after starting; bilirubin 178 umol/l, AST 1328 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 819 IU/l, gamma-GT 345 IU/l, INR 1.4; negative auto-antibody screen; normal LFTs within 3 months after stopping drug. Previously only sporadic single cases (including three fatal) had been described.

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes an 11-year-old girl who developed anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS), a potentially fatal multisystem disorder, after receiving oral phenobarbital for 10 days following a focal seizure. During the course, she developed jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, raised serum transaminases (AST 179 IU/dL, ALT 475 IU/dL), elevated bilirubin (total 6.5 mg/dL, direct 4 mg/dL), and reduced serum protein and albumin. Other etiologies (hepatitis A, hepatitis B, infectious mononucleosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and Kawasaki disease) were ruled out. Using Naranjo's causality method, the event was assessed to be probably caused by phenobarbital. The patient recovered, with normalization of hepatic and renal parameters, after withdrawal of phenobarbital and treatment with methylprednisolone.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (11-year-old girl); hepatic involvement occurred as part of anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: Phenobarbital given orally for 10 days after a focal seizure; fever on day 6, rash on day 9, drug withdrawn on day 13. On day 20 developed facial puffiness, jaundice, and tender hepatomegaly. Laboratory values: AST 179 IU/dL, ALT 475 IU/dL, total bilirubin 6.5 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 4 mg/dL, creatinine 2.12 mg/dL, serum protein 5.36 g/dL, albumin 2.29 g/dL. Serum phenobarbital 14.2 µg/mL (within therapeutic range) on day 12. Naranjo causality assessment scored the event as probably caused by phenobarbital. raw_record.support_text: After autopsy microscopic study and dismissing other causes of hepatic damage, a diagnosis of DILI was made. The patient had received sevoflurane, propofol and fentanyl as anesthetics for an arthroscopic lavage, and died within 3 days; the autopsy showed a necroinflammatory lesion with perivenular predominance affecting about 70% of the organ and hepatocellular necrosis with ceroid deposits, without bilirubin accumulation, and no evidence of viral, bacterial or fungal infection.

Histology: necroinflammatory lesion, perivenular predominance, affecting approximately 70% of liver parenchyma, hepatocellular necrosis with ceroid material deposit and without bilirubin accumulation; no viral, bacterial or fungal infection; blood and synovial fluid cultures negative. Patient deteriorated rapidly, lapsed into coma and died within 3 days despite CPR; no liver enzyme analyses were performed. Liver injury identifier is the DILI disease entity.

raw_record.support_text: A 16-year-old boy ingested an unknown quantity of potassium dichromate in a suicide attempt and developed vomiting, diffuse abdominal pain, and acute renal and liver failure in January 1996. Supportive treatment and dimercaprol did not prevent deterioration of renal and liver function within two days. On day 6 orthotopic cadaveric liver transplantation was performed; histopathological examination of the explanted liver showed diffuse hepatocellular necrosis. The patient recovered after transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adolescent (16-year-old boy); intentional suicide ingestion of an unknown quantity, i.e., overdose exposure; poison obtained from a school chemical laboratory.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver failure progressed over six days leading to orthotopic cadaveric liver transplantation. Histopathology of the explanted liver showed diffuse hepatocellular necrosis. Serum chromium levels decreased over time, suggesting chromium accumulation in the liver. Plasmapheresis and hemodialysis did not remove substantial chromium from circulation as documented by filtrate measurements. Dimercaprol (250 mg IV twice daily) was administered as chelation treatment. Patient recovered uneventfully and was discharged on postoperative day 14 with normal laboratory findings; normal liver and kidney function at two-year follow-up. Authors recommend delaying liver transplantation to allow the native liver to extract chromium.

raw_record.support_text: A 22-year-old physically healthy extreme-sportswoman with a history of an eating disorder ingested 20,000 mg of niacinamide (Niacinamid) on a single day, based on Internet research, to improve training performance and treat constipation. She developed clinically apparent abdominal pain and within 3 days acute liver failure (INR > 8.9, factor V < 5%, transaminases 12,000–14,000 U/L; negative hepatitis markers and liver immunology). She met King's College criteria, was listed for liver transplantation, and received a donor liver; the explant histology showed subtotal hepatocyte necrosis. The conclusion section attributes the acute toxic liver failure and transplantation need to the vitamin B3 (niacinamide) overdose.

Hepatitis markers and liver immunology negative. Met King's College criteria and was placed on the liver transplant list; underwent transplantation with graft from a 63-year-old donor, extubated 2 h postoperatively, discharged after 19 days. Explant histology showed subtotal hepatocyte necrosis. The conclusion notes that acute toxic liver failure with transplantation need from vitamin B3 overdose was already described for the sustained-release (retard) galenic form and is now shown for the pure form; good interdisciplinary management averted the lethal outcome.

raw_record.support_text: A 35-year-old schizophrenic man developed hepatic toxicity after a daily dose of 9 g nicotinamide, presenting with nausea and vomiting and increased serum transaminase and bilirubin concentrations. A liver biopsy showed increased portal fibrosis and cholestasis. After discontinuation of nicotinamide the symptoms disappeared rapidly and all liver function tests returned to normal in 3 weeks; a nicotinamide rechallenge produced reappearance of symptoms and increased transaminase concentrations in less than 2 weeks. The paper concludes this report illustrates that very large doses of nicotinamide can be hepatotoxic in susceptible people.

raw_record.support_text: The Homberg et al. series of 157 cases of drug-induced hepatitis identified the major culprit drugs causing hepatotoxicity as clometacin (29 cases), α-methyldopa (12 cases), troleandromycin (11 cases), ajmaline (8 cases), halothane (6 cases) and perhexiline (6 cases), with the drugs most often associated with autoimmune serologic reactions being clometacin (17/29), fenofibrate (4/4), papaverine (4/5) and tienilic acid (3/3).
raw_record.extra_details: Most common culprit in Homberg series of 157 drug-induced hepatitis cases (29 cases); 17/29 also had autoimmune serologic reactions characterized by antismooth muscle antibody (ASMA) and antinuclear antibody (ANA).

raw_record.support_text: In a second heterogenous group of drugs causing drug-induced hepatitis, including clometacin, fenofibrate, oxyphenisatin and papaverine, antismooth muscle, antinucleus and antimitochondria antibodies were found in isolation or in different combinations in 70% of cases; 30 cases of clometacin-induced hepatitis were traced from the presence of antismooth muscle antibodies.
raw_record.extra_details: 30 cases of clometacin-induced hepatitis traced in sera via antismooth muscle antibodies; associated with antismooth muscle, antinucleus and antimitochondria antibodies (group 2 with autoimmune-like features).

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 30 patients with clometacin-induced hepatitis (CIH), initial liver biopsies mostly showed acute hepatitis, with 17 cases (68%) being acute cytolytic hepatitis (centrolobular clarified and balloonized hepatocytes, two with multinucleated giant hepatocytes and two with moderate eosinophilic infiltration). Seven patients (28%) showed stigmas of chronic active hepatitis, and one case showed micronodular cirrhosis. A repeat biopsy after rechallenge with clometacin in one patient showed severe acute hepatitis with aggravation of hepatic lobule lesions. Mortality related to the first hepatitis was 13% (4/30), with three patients dying in the acute phase of hepatocellular insufficiency with hepatic encephalopathy.
raw_record.extra_details: 30-patient case series of clometacin-induced hepatitis with autoimmune features. Histology: 68% acute cytolytic hepatitis, 28% chronic active hepatitis, 1 case micronodular cirrhosis; rechallenge in one patient aggravated lesions. First-hepatitis mortality 13% (4/30): 3 died rapidly of hepatocellular insufficiency with hepatic encephalopathy, 1 in the 4th month after downhill progression. The 26 survivors clinically and biochemically recovered within ~2 months of drug withdrawal, with anti-tissue antibodies (anti-actin cable, anti-N, anti-M2) becoming undetectable 3-9 months after clometacin withdrawal. Autoimmune markers: anti-smooth muscle (anti-actin cable) antibody present in 70% (21/30); anti-actin cable positivity in 19; anti-N in 16 (14 in common with anti-SM); transient drug-induced anti-M2 in 2; anti-LKM absent. Mean serum gammaglobulin 23 g/l, >18 g/l in 73%.

raw_record.support_text: Seven clinical cases of clometacin-induced hepatitis are described; both clinical and biological features supported immunologically mediated hepatitis, and circulating anti-nuclear and/or anti-smooth muscle antibodies were demonstrated in four of the seven cases. The seven patient sera were obtained from two liver units, establishing clometacin as a cause of human hepatitis, and the paper then investigated its immunological mechanism in vitro using human hepatocyte/lymphoid-cell co-cultures.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven cases (mostly elderly females, ages 52-81; one male); daily clometacin dose 300-650 mg, therapy duration 2-50 months; AST (as fold increase over upper normal limit) and PT (% of normal, ranging ~20-87%) at presentation; anti-smooth muscle and/or anti-nuclear antibodies present in 4 cases; compound also referred to by chemical name 3-(4-chlorobenzoyl)-6-methoxy-2-methylindol-1-yl acetic acid (brand Duperan, mol. wt 357.8); studied at 6 x 10^-4 M in human hepatocyte cultures with patient sera to characterize the immunologically mediated mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatitis induced following treatment with clometacin, an arthritis medication, was described in 30 patients: 75% had hepatocellular injury and 25% had cholestatic injury. Hepatitis was reported as directly responsible for death in three patients. Of seven patients with clometacin DILI, four had HLA-B*08 antigens, and four had chronic active hepatitis with autoantibodies in three cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Arthritis medication; 30 patients with 75% hepatocellular and 25% cholestatic injury; hepatitis directly responsible for death in three patients; HLA-B*08 antigens in four of seven DILI patients; chronic active hepatitis with autoantibodies in three cases; postulated as a model for autoimmune drug-induced hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Of the 30 patients with clometacin hepatitis, all treated with clometacin for various rheumatic conditions, 29 were females aged 32-84 years. Daily dose was 150-750 mg (mean 396 mg) with regular intake in 66% of cases; onset of hepatitis followed drug intake by 10 to 2,190 days. The study retained 7 'definite' rechallenge-positive and 23 'probable' cases of clometacin-induced chronic active hepatitis (CIH) after excluding other causes and applying the imputability method of Dangoumau.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Case series of 29 females and 1 male treated for rheumatic conditions; indication and predominant sex noted descriptively, not a strict susceptibility restriction.
raw_record.extra_details: 30 patients with clometacin hepatitis; 7 'definite' rechallenge-positive and 23 'probable' cases; 26 'possible'/'doubtful' cases eliminated. Daily dose 150-750 mg (mean 396 mg), one patient (case 25) up to 2,000 mg/day; onset 10-2,190 days (median 230); prodromal symptoms (asthenia 64%, fever >38°C 36%, nausea/vomiting/anorexia 64%). Biologically mainly cytolytic hepatitis with mild cholestasis; bilirubin 20-509 µmol/l; ASAT 2-57xN, ALAT 3-100xN; prothrombin time <30% in 4 cases, all fatal of hepatic failure (cases 15, 19, 25, 29). Autoantibodies detected (anti-smooth muscle, anti-nucleus, anti-actin) in most sera; blood eosinophilia in 13%. Other causes (hepatitis A/B, CMV, HSV, EBV, alcoholism, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, Wilson's disease) excluded.

raw_record.support_text: From our 30 cases and several other reports it appears that clometacin-induced hepatitis (CIH) is idiosyncratic in nature: absence of dose dependence (dose was 4 times less than the pharmacological dose in 25% of patients), low incidence of toxicity under therapy (about 60 cases of hepatotoxicity reported per about 1 million people treated), and prompt recurrence following rechallenge, which also occurred in 7 of our patients. Some features of CIH resemble autoimmune chronic active hepatitis (lupoid hepatitis).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Marked female predominance (97%) in the series; autoimmune/lupoid-like features; rechallenge setting described separately.
raw_record.extra_details: 30 cases of clometacin-induced hepatitis (CIH). Low incidence: ~60 hepatotoxicity cases per ~1 million treated. Dose was 4 times below the pharmacological dose in 25% of patients. Rechallenge in 7 patients reproduced chills, fever, abdominal pain, diarrhoea and jaundice with transaminase elevations; incubation periods shortened with each exposure (1-120 days, median 22 days for the second episode; 1 day for the third). No death from rechallenge; transaminases normalized within days to 2 months. Hypergammaglobulinemia and anti-tissue antibodies (anti-SM of anti-actin type and anti-N) present.

raw_record.support_text: In an institutional case series, five cases of medically refractory severe cholestatic DILI were identified, defined by persistent serum bilirubin >20 mg/dL. Hepatotoxic medications included phentermine, methimazole, OxyElite, and two cases of the anabolic steroid methyl-1-etiocholenololepietiocholanolone. Cholestatic DILI was defined as ALP greater than two times the upper limit of normal secondary to a drug exposure known to cause intrahepatic cholestasis.
raw_record.extra_details: One case of severe cholestatic DILI (persistent bilirubin >20 mg/dL, ALP >2x ULN, >345 U/L) treated with 5 sessions of 8-hour MARS albumin dialysis; patient recovered with normalization of liver tests at outpatient follow-up. No hepatic encephalopathy or extrahepatic organ dysfunction; INR remained <2.

Cause of death in both cases was toxic nephropathy/circulatory failure, not liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: A 49-year-old male was treated with ketoprofen (200 mg/day) along with noramidopyrine and tiemonium for renal colic. On day two he developed fever, weakness, right hypochondrium pain, mild elevation of serum aminotransferases and significantly high alkaline phosphatases, with subsequent jaundice. Viral hepatitis and other causes of hepatopathy were excluded. Ketoprofen was withdrawn on day four, jaundice disappeared three days later, and biological abnormalities normalized within five weeks. The paper concludes this cholestatic hepatitis is probably due to treatment with ketoprofen.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute hepatitis due to ketoprofen, an NSAID; only one other similar case report found in the literature. 49-year-old male admitted March 1988 for renal colic with moderate renal insufficiency (creatinine 115 µmol/l). Ketoprofen 200 mg/day; fever (38.2°C) and weakness on day two. No hypereosinophilia; viral hepatitis serologies negative (A, B, non-A non-B); abdominal echography normal; liver histology not obtained. Jaundice resolved three days after drug withdrawal; laboratory values returned to normal within 5 weeks. No alcoholism, no anti-tissue antibody. Concomitant drugs noramidopyrine and tiemonium were not considered causative. Named cholestatic hepatitis phenotype recorded under other_specific_phenotype.

raw_record.support_text: This letter reports severe nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and steatohepatitis in a patient on ketoprofen, noting that NAFLD due to non-steroidal antiinflammatory drugs is rare. The case describes a 45-year-old white woman who developed fatigue, abdominal discomfort, and low-grade fever 5 days after starting ketoprofen (80 mg twice daily) for tension-type headache; she denied alcohol and other potentially hepatotoxic medications, and vira, autoimmune, and metal metabolism causes were excluded, with imaging showing massive fatty infiltration of the liver.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of severe NAFLD and steatohepatitis attributed to ketoprofen taken at 80 mg twice daily for tension-type headache. Onset of fatigue, abdominal discomfort, and low-grade fever 5 days after initiation on a stable dose; the patient developed mild cutaneous and scleral jaundice with increased bilirubin and enzyme levels. Liver function tests were normal 1 year earlier. Viral hepatitis (A, B, C, E, G; CMV; HSV; EBV) and autoimmune liver screens were negative, and iron, copper, ceruloplasmin, and alpha-1-antitrypsin were within normal limits. Abdominal sonography and CT showed massive fatty infiltration of the liver. No alcohol or other potentially hepatotoxic medications; the patient took atenolol and hydrochlorothiazide for goiter and hypertension.

raw_record.support_text: Anecdotal reports describe hepatitis caused by ketoprofen at doses of 75-200 mg daily, with hepatitis onset 2-10 days after starting the drug; one patient had cholestatic hepatitis with micro- and macrovesicular steatosis involving less than 20% of hepatocytes. In the present case, fatty liver infiltration combined with a mixed cholestatic and hepatocellular pattern of liver biochemistry was attributed to ketoprofen, with the authors proposing inhibition of mitochondrial function, fat and ROS accumulation, lipid peroxidation, hepatocyte apoptosis/necrosis, and injury to bile secretory components as effectors of ketoprofen hepatotoxicity.

Proposed mechanism: inhibition of mitochondrial function, fat and reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, lipid peroxidation, hepatocyte apoptosis and necrosis, and injury to bile secretory components. Natural history of drug-induced NAFLD usually benign but could progress to cirrhosis; lifetime cirrhosis risk not reliably predictable.

raw_record.support_text: BCNU (carmustine) at higher doses in humans is known to lead to long-term hepatic and pulmonary toxicity, in some cases causing death as a result of pulmonary fibrosis. In a recent phase II study, patients with recurrent glioblastoma and no prior chemotherapy received 80 mg/m² BCNU; two of 40 patients developed grade 4 pulmonary toxicity after four cycles, while hepatic toxicity grade 3 was observed in two patients at the third cycle and grade 2 in two patients at cycles 2 and 3, as measured by serum bilirubin. BCNU was discontinued in four patients because of grade 2 or 3 pulmonary and hepatic toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Higher-dose BCNU is known to cause long-term hepatic and pulmonary toxicity in humans, with possible death from pulmonary fibrosis. Phase II study in recurrent glioblastoma patients (no prior chemotherapy) at 80 mg/m²: 2 of 40 patients developed grade 4 pulmonary toxicity (by DLCO) after four cycles (8 weeks between cycles); hepatic toxicity grade 3 in two patients at the third cycle and grade 2 in two patients at cycles 2 and 3, measured by serum bilirubin; BCNU discontinued in four patients for pulmonary and hepatic toxicity grade 2-3; pulmonary toxicities were irreversible and possibly under-reported, with only 10 of 40 patients completing four or more cycles.

raw_record.support_text: Abnormal liver function studies developed in 29 of 93 (31.2%) evaluable patients treated with BCNU (carmustine). Ten patients (10.8%) had severe, delayed hepatotoxicity (median onset day +40, range +19 to +76) that was fatal in eight patients (8.6%). Clinically this was painless cholestatic jaundice with ascites and progressive hepatic insufficiency; two patients slowly improved. Pathology in eight of nine patients showed massive centrilobular hemorrhagic necrosis, while one melanoma patient with prior dacarbazine exposure had veno-occlusive disease at necropsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatotoxicity was significantly dose-related: 6/17 (35.3%; 95% CI 14.2-61.7%) patients at BCNU 1500-2850 mg/m2 vs 4/76 (5.3%; 95% CI 1.5-13.0%) at 600-1200 mg/m2 (P<0.01). At 1200 mg/m2 the incidence of severe was 6.1% and fatal hepatic necrosis 3.0%. CNS tumor diagnosis was also associated (9/44, 20.5% vs 1/49, 2.0%; P<0.01). A transient asymptomatic liver enzyme elevation pattern was seen in 19 patients. Fatal in 8/10 (8.6%); 2 recovered. Pathology: massive centrilobular hemorrhagic necrosis (8/9); veno-occlusive disease in one patient with prior dacarbazine exposure (co-suspect). No correlation with mannitol, anticonvulsants, or corticosteroids. BCNU hepatic toxicity grading scale defined (grades 0-4).

Jaundice (6%) and hepatic coma (4%) were listed as toxic reactions of BCNU therapy in the series.

On liver biopsy, centrilobular necrosis was apparent without sclerosis of the central vein. Over a 6-week period the liver function returned to normal and the ascites resolved.

raw_record.extra_details: One of 11 treated patients (C.P., astrocytoma grade IV). Discussion: when BCNU doses exceed 1200 mg/m², persistent liver-test elevations may indicate toxic centrilobular necrosis; the affected patient recovered from this hepatotoxic picture, and progressive hepatic failure may be minimized by limiting total BCNU dose to 1200 mg/m² given over a three-day period. raw_record.support_text: High-dose BCNU given before autologous bone marrow transplantation produced dose-dependent hepatotoxicity: no liver enzyme alterations up to 10 weeks at doses up to 1000 mg/m², one death from liver failure with centrilobular necrosis at 1200-1400 mg/m², and mildly elevated transaminases and alkaline phosphatase without hyperbilirubinemia at 800-1200 mg/m². raw_record.extra_details: Drug referred to as BCNU. Dana-Farber Center: no enzyme alterations up to 10 weeks at doses up to 1000 mg/m²; 1 death from liver failure 6 weeks after 1200-1400 mg/m² with centrilobular necrosis on histology; mildly elevated transaminases and alkaline phosphatase without hyperbilirubinemia in longer follow-up at 800-1200 mg/m². Another study: transient reversible changes in 19 patients below 1200 mg/m², fatal hepatotoxicity in 7/12 at 1500-2850 mg/m²; fatal liver disease became overt only after 2 months then progressed rapidly.

raw_record.support_text: Serial liver-function studies and, when available, liver biopsy, radioisotopic scanning, and histologic specimens were used to assess the frequency of liver toxicity due to BCNU in 45 patients with Hodgkin's disease. Only two patients (4 per cent) had liver-function abnormalities that were not explained by primary disease or prior chemotherapy; in only one of the two was the magnitude of the hepatic toxicity sufficient to be a contributing factor in the patient's death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with Hodgkin's disease receiving BCNU; liver-function abnormalities not explained by primary disease or prior chemotherapy.
raw_record.extra_details: In a study of 45 patients, serial liver-function tests (plus biopsy, radioisotopic scanning, and histology when available) were monitored because animal toxicity data indicated marked hepatic (and renal) toxicity. Liver-function abnormalities attributable to BCNU occurred in 2 patients (4%); in one, hepatic toxicity was severe enough to be a contributing factor in the patient's death. No renal toxicity due to BCNU was identified.

raw_record.support_text: In a 30-patient series treated with BCNU (carmustine) for malignant tumors, hepatitis was severe in four patients and fatal in two: one melanoma patient given BCNU 1,200 mg/m² developed liver necrosis one month after treatment and died two weeks later in hepatic coma, with autopsy showing central lobular necrosis consistent with a toxic drug insult to the liver; one glioma patient given BCNU 600 mg/m² twice died of portal hypertension with ascites and liver dysfunction two months after the second course; and a glioma patient and a hepatoma patient had severe but reversible hepatitis. Overall, 14 of 30 evaluable patients (46%) had abnormal liver function tests unexplained by their primary disease, with toxicity occurring at all dose levels and most pronounced in hepatocellular enzymes (SGOT/SGPT).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Severely ill patients with malignant tumors (glioma, melanoma, hepatoma, colorectal carcinoma) receiving concurrently dexamethasone (8-64 mg/day) and, in some, prophylactic nystatin/trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; two additional patients had liver-test abnormalities possibly related to underlying hepatoma or colorectal carcinoma.
raw_record.extra_details: BCNU (carmustine) at cumulative doses of 600-1,200 mg/m². Of 30 evaluable patients, 14 (46%) had one or more abnormal liver function tests (SGOT, LDH, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin) unexplained by primary disease; in 10 of these, elevations were minimal (<2-3x SGOT/alkaline phosphatase), self-limited and asymptomatic, occurring a median of 3 months after treatment (range 2-6 months). Four patients had severe hepatitis, fatal in two (one with hepatic necrosis/central lobular necrosis and hepatic coma, autopsy-consistent with toxic drug insult; one with fatal portal hypertension, ascites and liver dysfunction). Eleven patients were evaluable at 3-4 months and 8 (73%) had abnormal liver tests; alkaline phosphatase abnormalities occurred later and resolved more slowly; hyperbilirubinemia occurred only in the four severe-hepatitis patients.

raw_record.support_text: In two Phase 1 studies, AB-506 (an HBV capsid inhibitor) was given at 160 mg or 400 mg daily for 28 days to subjects with chronic HBV infection. Four subjects (all Asian) had Grade 4 alanine aminotransferase (ALT) elevations during HBV DNA decline, with three events leading to treatment discontinuation; in a follow-up study, 2 Asian healthy subjects had serious transaminitis events leading to treatment and study termination. No subjects had bilirubin elevations or signs of hepatic decompensation. The authors conclude that these findings suggest AB-506 hepatotoxicity contributed to the ALT elevations, and the AB-506 development program was terminated because of these findings.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings restricted to Asian subjects; observed in both subjects with chronic HBV infection and healthy subjects; transient severe ALT flares with treatment/study discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase 1 randomized double-blinded studies; AB-506 doses 160 mg or 400 mg daily for 28 days; Grade 4 ALT elevations in 4 CHB subjects (2 at each dose) plus 2 serious transaminitis events in Asian healthy subjects; no bilirubin elevations or hepatic decompensation; mean HBV-DNA declines 2.1 log10 IU/ml (160 mg) and 2.8 log10 IU/ml (400 mg); AB-506 development program terminated because of these hepatotoxicity findings.

raw_record.support_text: A 63-year-old man admitted for management of a frontal lobe abscess developed elevated liver enzymes within 48 hours of receiving meropenem, peaking at day 5 (ALT 1160 U/L, AST 787 U/L, ALP 297 U/L, GGT 252 U/L). Meropenem was ceased and liver function normalised; on rechallenge the patient again developed rapidly increasing liver enzymes with a mixed hepatocellular/cholestatic pattern. Other possible causes of liver injury were excluded after extensive investigation, and the report states the case demonstrates that meropenem can cause severe liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Meropenem administered IV 2 g every 8 hours for a frontal lobe abscess. Liver enzymes rose within 48 h and peaked on day 5 (ALT 1160, AST 787, ALP 658, GGT 575 U/L); bilirubin peaked at 39 µmol/L (24 µmol/L direct) on day 4. Injury was a mixed hepatocellular/cholestatic pattern. Dechallenge led to normalization; rechallenge produced a rapid rise in liver enzymes again. Other possible causes of liver injury were excluded. Patient was asymptomatic, non-jaundiced, and transferred to rehabilitation. Concurrent antimicrobials included vancomycin initially and then ceftriaxone plus metronidazole; causal attribution to meropenem was supported by the rechallenge.

raw_record.support_text: As indicine-N-oxide showed promising results as an anticancer agent in in vitro and in vivo assays, clinical trials were conducted for acute leukemia; however, due to severe hepatotoxicity, the compound was not further tested. One clinical trial investigated indicine-N-oxide in patients with progressive acute leukemia refractory to standard chemotherapeutics (10 patients: 6 ALL, 3 AML, 1 AMML; ages 4–67 years). A lyophilized form at 3.0 g/m2 was given intravenously for five consecutive days; two patients achieved complete remission and one partial remission. Most patients experienced side effects such as mild nausea, mild diarrhea, maculopapular rash, and jaundice, and the authors concluded that indicine-N-oxide has anticancer activity but needs modification to remove unwanted side effects.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients had progressive acute leukemia (ALL, AML, AMML) refractory to standard chemotherapeutics; ages 4–67 years.
raw_record.extra_details: Pyrrolizidine alkaloid from Heliotropium indicum. Lyophilized form given intravenously at 3.0 g/m2 for five consecutive days. Outcomes in the trial: 2 complete remissions, 1 partial remission. Reported side effects included mild nausea, mild diarrhea, maculopapular rash, and jaundice. The compound was not further tested owing to severe hepatotoxicity.
