raw_record.support_text: Indicine N-oxide was used to treat leukemia. In a dose-seeking study, 22 patients with refractory acute leukemia received indicine N-oxide daily for five consecutive days; five patients had severe hepatic toxicity, probably due to veno-occlusive disease induced by indicine N-oxide. In a separate Phase II study of 31 children with leukemia, hepatotoxicity was mild (grade 1 or 2) in 63% and moderate (grade 3) in 9% of patients, and three patients (9%) experienced severe hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with refractory acute leukemia (adults) and children with acute lymphoblastic, acute non-lymphoblastic leukemia, or CML blast crisis; therapeutic antileukemic use in oncology patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose-seeking study: 22 patients with refractory acute leukemia received indicine N-oxide daily for 5 consecutive days; severe hepatic toxicity in 5 patients, judged probably due to veno-occlusive disease induced by indicine N-oxide; among these, one ALL patient had a complete remission and one had a partial remission; two of 11 ANLL patients had complete remission; one of three CML blast-crisis patients had partial remission. Phase II study (Miser et al.): 31 children treated at 2000 mg/m2/day for 5 days (14 patients) and 2500 mg/m2/day for 5 days (17 patients); hepatotoxicity mild (grade 1-2) in 63%, moderate (grade 3) in 9%, severe in 9% (three patients); one ALL patient at each dose level achieved complete response (6 and 1 month), one CML patient partial response (4 months); no ANLL complete responses.

Hepatotoxicity was experienced by 13 patients: 11 developed asymptomatic elevations of transaminases, 1 developed hyperbilirubinemia, and 1 developed ascites. raw_record.support_text: The paper states that daptomycin has been found to cause DILI in a small number of cases, with DILI documented in 3% of participants in initial clinical trials without concordant GGT increases. It reports the present case (a patient treated with daptomycin for MRSA bacteremia who developed asymptomatic elevated transaminases with other etiologies ruled out and normalization of transaminases after drug discontinuation) and reviews six additional published case reports of daptomycin-induced hepatotoxicity on patients without pre-existing liver disease, in most of which transaminases returned to normal about one to two weeks after daptomycin was discontinued. Case details include peak ALT up to 8050 U/L, AST up to 6020 U/L, and elevated total bilirubin (e.g., 5.8 mg/dL) in some patients, with no acute liver failure reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Lipopeptide antimicrobial used for gram-positive infections including MRSA and VRE. Present case: asymptomatic elevated transaminases without hyperbilirubinemia, multiorgan failure, or CK elevation; other etiologies ruled out; transaminases normalized after discontinuation. Table of 7 cases (present + 6 reviewed): doses 4-10 mg/kg/day IV or 500 mg IV/day; days to onset 2-35; peak ALT 48-8050 U/L, AST 107-6020 U/L, AP 118-935 U/L, TB up to 5.8 mg/dL; some cases with AKI and myositis/CK>20,000 U/L; no acute liver failure reported. DILI was documented in 3% of participants in initial clinical trials without concordant GGT increases; higher doses (8 vs 6 mg/kg/day) associated with reversible skeletal muscle effects.

raw_record.support_text: Use of the Naranjo probability scale indicates a probable relationship between hepatotoxicity with acute renal failure and daptomycin treatment in the patient, since these adverse events occurred after administration and improved following discontinuation. The patient experienced significant elevations in AST, ALT, and serum creatinine without CK abnormalities, had no sepsis or pre-existing hepatic or renal disease to explain the reaction, and the abnormalities did not recur when his oral (non-daptomycin) drug therapy resumed upon discharge.
raw_record.extra_details: 35-year-old male with suspected osteomyelitis treated with daptomycin for about 5 weeks, presented to the emergency department with elevated serum creatinine and liver transaminases; no CK elevation and no rhabdomyolysis; hepatic and renal function improved after daptomycin discontinuation; causality assessed as probable by the Naranjo scale; no recurrence of the liver/renal abnormalities upon resuming prior oral medications (daptomycin not resumed); authors note hepatotoxicity with acute renal failure appears very uncommon and recommend periodic monitoring of liver function and creatinine.

raw_record.support_text: A 56-year-old woman developed abrupt onset of jaundice and clinical evidence of cholestasis two years after beginning treatment with terbinafine for a skin infection; she was referred for persistent elevation of serum alkaline phosphatase and pruritus. A subsequent liver biopsy showed intrahepatic cholestasis, ductopenia, portal fibrosis and reduction of interlobular bile ducts. She stopped taking terbinafine and her symptoms subsided, but alkaline phosphatase remained elevated (~500 U/L) and ductopenia persisted, with negative antimitochondrial antibody and other chronic-liver-disease testing.
raw_record.extra_details: 56-year-old white woman; terbinafine (Lamisil, Novartis) used as antifungal for common skin infection. Abrupt onset of jaundice and cholestasis; symptoms subsided on dechallenge. Persistent elevation of serum alkaline phosphatase >75% liver fraction (550 U/L initially, ~500 U/L over 10 months) and persistent pruritus, with normal liver function studies. Antimitochondrial antibody and autoimmune liver antibodies negative; endoscopic retrograde cholangiogram normal. Initial biopsy showed moderate intracellular and canalicular cholestasis and occasional portal area without interlobular bile duct; follow-up biopsy at 20 months showed discrete portal fibrosis, spotty cholangiodegeneration, and reduction of interlobular bile ducts without cholangitis, granulomata, steatosis, or necroinflammatory injury. Paper notes potential idiosyncratic drug reactions from terbinafine were first reported in 1994 (2 patients with mixed cholestatic-hepatocellular hepatitis, one with increased ALP for ≥3 months) and a similar prolonged cholestasis case in 1996 with recovery of liver-cell-damage parameters after 6 months.

raw_record.support_text: In the reported case, cholestasis was well documented as attributable to terbinafine, which had been prescribed for its usual indication (therapeutic antifungal use). The paper emphasizes the need for a high level of clinical suspicion for early diagnosis of drug-induced liver injury and presents this case to raise awareness of pharmacological hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of terbinafine-induced cholestatic hepatotoxicity prescribed for its usual indication. Usual toxicity pattern is cholestatic, typically prolonged (2-12 months), with possible progression to ductopenia. Latency (exposure-jaundice/icterus) ranges from 2 to 6 weeks; maximum bilirubin peak typically occurs 3-5 weeks after drug discontinuation. Resolution after withdrawal is usually the rule. No specific treatment exists, though ursodeoxycholic acid has been tried with success. Recent description of an association between HLA-A*33:01 and susceptibility to terbinafine cholestatic hepatotoxicity. Exact mechanisms not yet fully elucidated; some metabolites can bind hepatobiliary proteins and promote an immune reaction. Figure 1 shows chronological evolution of liver biochemistry abnormalities in relation to terbinafine use and withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: Drug-induced liver disease accounts for about 50% of acute or subacute liver failure in the United States. The authors report a case of terbinafine-induced severe liver failure requiring liver transplantation. A variety of antifungal medications are known to cause a range of liver injury from mild hepatocellular-cholestatic injury to acute/subacute liver failure, and terbinafine (Lamisil), a widely prescribed antifungal for onychomycosis, is one antifungal associated with such liver injuries.
raw_record.extra_details: 50-year-old African American male with onychomycosis treated with terbinafine for approximately 3 months. At the 3-month outpatient visit he was jaundiced with dark urine, acholic stools, weight loss, anorexia, myalgias, and pruritus; labs showed AST 95 IU/L, ALT 149 IU/L, total bilirubin 29 mg/dL, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL. After 33 days, at outside hospital admission: AST 228 IU/L, ALT 144 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 497 IU/L, albumin 2.2 mg/dL, bilirubin 68.6 mg/dL, BUN 114 mg/dL, creatinine 14.2 mg/dL. Negative serologies for hepatitis A/B/C, ANA, ASMA, AMA, HIV; undetectable serum acetaminophen; normal ceruloplasmin. His condition deteriorated, requiring hemodialysis and orthotropic liver transplantation. Explant pathology showed portal areas lacking corresponding bile ducts (cholestatic liver disease). The report notes terbinafine usually produces mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic injury that is reversible after discontinuation, with previous reports of prolonged cholestasis and disappearance of interlobular bile ducts. Brand: Lamisil (Novartis).

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that significance (P ≤ .05) for rs2476601 was seen for DILI cases due to several causal drugs including terbinafine (P = .01). Terbinafine is identified as one of the causal drugs of DILI in the adjudicated cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: Known to have HLA alleles as main genetic risk association for its DILI; 15 cases in rs2476601 analysis, OR 3.23 (95% CI 1.29–8.1), P = .01.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of terbinafine-induced cholestatic hepatitis in a 75-year-old woman treated with the antifungal terbinafine. Jaundice followed by pruritus appeared after four weeks of therapy, with mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic liver test abnormalities. After drug withdrawal, serum bilirubin returned to normal within three months, but anicteric cholestasis persisted for over six months, and a liver biopsy after six months showed centrilobular cholestasis, discrete portal fibrosis, and a reduction in the number of interlobular biliary ducts. The authors conclude that terbinafine should be added to the list of drugs that can cause reduction in interlobular bile ducts and be considered a potential hepatotoxin that may cause severe liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of terbinafine-induced cholestatic hepatitis with reduction in interlobular bile ducts (ductopenia). Reported in a 75-year-old woman; jaundice and pruritus developed after 4 weeks of therapy, mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic liver test abnormalities; serum bilirubin normalized within 3 months after withdrawal but anicteric cholestasis persisted >6 months; liver biopsy showed centrilobular cholestasis, discrete portal fibrosis, and reduced interlobular biliary ducts. The paper states this is the first reported case of terbinafine-induced cholestatic hepatitis with reduction in ILBD and cites two earlier reports of histologically documented cholangitis. Mechanism is unknown; no hypersensitivity stigmata described. The paper recommends terbinafine be considered a potential hepatotoxin and rapid drug withdrawal upon detection of liver test abnormalities.

raw_record.support_text: Fifteen well characterized patients with liver injury attributed to terbinafine who were enrolled into the ongoing DILIN Prospective registry study are presented. Most patients were symptomatic with pruritus and jaundice, 2 were hospitalized and 1 required eventual liver transplantation, and most had either a cholestatic or mixed liver injury pattern at onset with a generally favorable prognosis. One potential fatal case had a distinctly severe hepatocellular injury at onset and underwent liver transplantation within 3 weeks of presentation. During follow-up, 6 patients were treated with corticosteroids, and the majority (54%) had protocol-determined chronic liver injury, far above the overall DILIN cohort rate (18%).
raw_record.extra_details: 15 DILIN registry cases of terbinafine-attributed DILI; 2 hospitalized; 1 liver transplant (a potential fatal case with severe hepatocellular injury at onset, transplanted within 3 weeks); cholestatic or mixed pattern at onset; chronic liver injury in 54% of followed patients vs 18% overall DILIN; median BMI 24.2 vs 27 kg/m2 overall; 6 treated with corticosteroids; no patients with chronic injury had underlying chronic liver disease. HLA-A*33:01 present in 10 of 11 European ancestry cases. FDA removed the need for liver biochemistry monitoring with terbinafine in 2001 due to favorable post-marketing safety profile.

raw_record.support_text: A 56-year-old woman presented with jaundice, pruritus, anorexia and vomiting, with elevated liver enzymes (AST 676 U/L, ALT 425 U/L, ALP 384 U/L, GGT 406 U/L, total bilirubin 19.87 mg/dL). Her history included a recently completed 2-month course of terbinafine 250 mg/day for onychomycosis ending 6 weeks before admission, with no other drug intake, liver disease, alcohol, or parenteral drug abuse. Serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, and C and autoantibodies were negative. A liver biopsy obtained during the eighth week after terbinafine discontinuation revealed cholestatic hepatitis, and use of the Naranjo probability scale indicated a probable relationship between terbinafine and cholestatic hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case: 56-year-old woman, terbinafine 250 mg/day for ~2 months for onychomycosis, stopped 6 weeks before admission; jaundice and pruritus starting one week before admission. Peak serum bilirubin 60.2 mg/dL at ~8 weeks after discontinuation; liver biopsy showed cholestatic hepatitis. Naranjo probability scale indicated a probable relationship. UDCA (1000 mg/day) was given for elevated liver enzymes and intractable pruritus; liver tests normalized by 15 weeks after terbinafine cessation (AST 30, ALT 32 U/L, total bilirubin 1.17 mg/dL). Competing viral/autoimmune causes ruled out.

raw_record.support_text: A 55-year-old male on Terbinafine 250 mg once daily for onychomycosis for 1 month developed progressive jaundice and pruritus. LFTs showed a mixed cholestatic hepatitis picture (bilirubin 13.6 mg/dL, AST 119 U/L, ALT 216 U/L, GGT 205 U/L, ALP 202 U/L, R ratio 3) with negative viral serologies, autoimmune markers, and negative biliary obstruction workup. A liver biopsy showed extensive intraductal and canalicular cholestasis, minimal lobular inflammation, and portal tract expansion with mixed infiltrate and Kupffer cell hyperplasia, with no autoimmune hepatitis or granuloma. A diagnosis of Terbinafine-induced liver injury was made (RUCAM score 9, highly probable); he was given ursodeoxycholic acid for 3 months and recovered.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 250 mg once daily for onychomycosis; jaundice latency ~1 month after start. Bilirubin 13.6 mg/dL (direct 11.7), AST 119 U/L, ALT 216 U/L, GGT 205 U/L, ALP 202 U/L, R ratio 3 (mixed). RUCAM score 9 (highly probable). Biopsy showed maintained lobular architecture, extensive intraductal and canalicular cholestasis, minimal lobular inflammation, portal tract expansion with mixed infiltrate, Kupffer cell hyperplasia; no autoimmune hepatitis or granuloma. Treated with ursodeoxycholic acid 300 mg three times daily until LFT normalization (~3 months), with a prolonged recovery phase of 3 months after drug discontinuation. Discussion notes Terbinafine DILI incidence 0.5-3/100,000 exposed; reported phenotypes include acute hepatitis, cholestasis or mixed picture, acute liver failure, and vanishing bile duct syndrome; latency to jaundice generally 2-6 weeks, bilirubin peaks 3-5 weeks after discontinuation, normalization 2-12 months; rarely acute/subacute liver failure requiring liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: A case report describes a rarely documented but important adverse hepatic reaction caused by oral terbinafine in a woman in her thirties who presented with jaundice, malaise, itching, nausea, decreased appetite, weight loss, dark orange urine and intermittent epigastric pain, three weeks after completing a 3-week course of oral terbinafine for a fungal nail infection. Liver biopsy findings were consistent with chronic active hepatitis secondary to a drug reaction. The background notes that terbinafine may rarely cause cholestasis, and this case illustrates an unusual delayed presentation with jaundice following cessation of terbinafine.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral terbinafine taken in a 3-week course for a fungal nail infection (trichophytic onychomycosis/chronic cutaneous mycosis). Delayed presentation with jaundice approximately 3 weeks after finishing treatment. Symptoms included jaundice, malaise, pruritus, nausea, decreased appetite, weight loss, dark orange urine and intermittent epigastric pain. Liver biopsy consistent with chronic active hepatitis secondary to a drug reaction. The paper notes terbinafine may rarely cause cholestasis; delayed development of erythema nodosum secondary to terbinafine could not be excluded. Patient used paracetamol for pain; no alcohol use.

raw_record.support_text: The report describes a previously healthy 24-yr-old man prescribed terbinafine 250 mg daily for onychomycosis who, at the end of a 3.5-week course, developed progressive loss of appetite, jaundice, and severe pruritus. Serum bilirubin peaked at 30.9 mg/dl 3 weeks after discontinuing terbinafine, and a liver biopsy showed hepatocellular and canalicular cholestasis with a mild-to-moderate mixed portal cellular infiltrate, portal tracts lacking bile ducts, and necrotic bile duct changes with features of cholangitis. Liver tests normalized 100 days after stopping terbinafine, and the paper identifies this as terbinafine-induced icteric hepatitis, the fourth reported case.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report (fourth reported case of terbinafine-induced icteric hepatitis). Terbinafine 250 mg daily for onychomycosis; injury appeared at end of a 3.5-week course. Peak serum bilirubin 30.9 mg/dl (peaked 3 weeks after discontinuation). Initial tests: AST 296 IU/L, ALT 584 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 222 IU/L, GGT 318 IU/L, prothrombin time 11.1 s. Histology: hepatocellular and canalicular cholestasis, pseudoxanthoma/cholate-stasis foamy hepatocytes, mild-to-moderate mixed portal infiltrate with eosinophils, bile duct paucity in some portal tracts, necrotic bile ducts with mild neutrophil infiltration, ductular proliferation, hepatocyte pleomorphism/mitoses/apoptotic bodies; predominantly cholestatic picture with cholangitis. Symptoms improved ~6 weeks after discontinuation; liver tests normalized 100 days after stopping terbinafine. No acute viral hepatitis or biliary tract disease; no other medications or alcohol. Biochemically a mixed cholestatic-hepatocellular liver disease.

raw_record.support_text: A 41-year-old man developed severe hepatic dysfunction following a 3.5-week course of terbinafine (250 mg/day), with marked pruritus, jaundice, malaise, anorexia and loin pain. Serum bilirubin rose to a peak of 718 µmol/l with alkaline phosphatase 569 U/l, alanine aminotransferase 90 U/l, aspartate aminotransferase 63 U/l and a prolonged prothrombin time of 21 s unresponsive to vitamin K. Transjugular liver biopsy showed canalicular cholestasis consistent with a drug reaction; symptoms resolved 11 months after drug cessation and liver function tests normalized by 15 months. The paper describes this as the most severe cholestatic reaction reported to date, with recovery without liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Onychomycosis indication; terbinafine 250 mg once daily for about 1 month (case reported as a 3.5-week course). Transjugular liver biopsy showed canalicular cholestasis with eosinophils in one portal tract and sparsely in sinusoids, in keeping with a drug reaction. Symptoms: pruritus, jaundice, malaise, anorexia, loin pain; pruritus resolved 10 months after stopping terbinafine and LFTs normalized at 15 months; patient recovered without liver transplantation. raw_record.support_text: Oral terbinafine is reported to be associated with the rare development of symptomatic idiosyncratic hepatobiliary dysfunction (1:45,000–1:54,000), with onset about 4–6 weeks after starting therapy, and the authors describe three patients who developed this disorder while taking terbinafine 250 mg/day for about 3–4 weeks. The hepatitis produced has features of both hepatocellular necrosis (elevated hepatic enzyme concentrations) and cholestatic injury (elevated alkaline phosphatase and cholesterol), and the US product monograph recommends monitoring serum hepatic enzymes for terbinafine courses longer than 6 weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: Estimated incidence of symptomatic idiosyncratic hepatobiliary dysfunction with oral terbinafine of 1:45,000–1:54,000. Latency approximately 4–6 weeks between start of medication and liver injury. Three case reports: (Case 1) 54-year-old male, terbinafine 250 mg/day for 3 weeks, SGPT/ALT 407 IU/l (7.4x ULN), ALP 273 IU/l (2.2x ULN), bilirubin 143 µmol/l, ALT/ALP ratio 3.4; liver biopsy suggested drug-induced effect with hepatocyte degeneration; liver function returned to normal over 6 months after discontinuation. (Case 2) 42-year-old female, terbinafine 250 mg/day for 4 weeks, ALT 521 IU/l (17.4x ULN), ALP 214 IU/l (1.6x ULN), total bilirubin 5.3 mg/dl, ALT/ALP ratio 10.9. (Case 3) 74-year-old female (on stable prednisone, omeprazole, theophylline, albuterol), terbinafine 250 mg/day for 4 weeks, ALT 333 IU/l, AST 308 IU/l, ALP 157 IU/l, ratio 8.2; worsened liver tests after discontinuation. Viral hepatitis excluded and no prior liver disease or alcohol abuse in the cases.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of cholestatic hepatitis induced by the oral fungicidal drug terbinafine, characterized by a prolonged course and mild reduction in the number of interlobular bile ducts (ILBD). In the discussion they explicitly conclude terbinafine is the offending agent, noting its four-week latency to jaundice, normalization of bilirubin and aminotransferases within three months of cessation, and exclusion of other causes of liver disease, while concurrent medications (nicergoline, fenofibrate) taken for four years were considered unlikely to be responsible.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 75-year-old female patient treated for cutaneous candidiasis; concurrent nicergoline (5 mg daily) and fenofibrate (100 mg daily) were deemed unlikely offending agents because both had been taken for four years before terbinafine.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral terbinafine 250 mg/day for three weeks; onset of asthenia, anorexia, weight loss a few days after discontinuation, jaundice within ~4 weeks of start, followed by pruritus. Laboratory values ~2 weeks after discontinuation: total bilirubin 89 µmol/L (conjugated 70), ALT 277 IU/L, AST 242 IU/L, γGT 321 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 375 IU/L; normal eosinophil count and prothrombin time. Cholestyramine relieved pruritus; bilirubin normalized 10 weeks after stopping terbinafine, but anicteric cholestasis persisted, with γGT still elevated 17 months later. Percutaneous liver biopsy 6 months after withdrawal showed reduction of interlobular bile ducts (visible in 16 of 23, 70%, portal tracts; ILBD/portal tract ratio 0.7 vs 0.9-1.8 in normal liver), occasional lymphocytes between biliary cells, minimal portal/periportal fibrosis, mild mononuclear infiltration, mild centrilobular canalicular cholestasis and minimal hepatocyte necrosis; negative copper stains. The authors note terbinafine-induced hepatitis is considered uncommon (five prior self-limited cases; liver tests showed cholestatic and cytolytic features resolving within 2-6 months, with cholangitis and centrilobular cholestasis in two biopsied cases), and asymptomatic transaminase elevations occur at an estimated incidence of 1/120,000.

raw_record.support_text: All 15 patients with terbinafine hepatotoxicity enrolled as high causality cases in the Drug Induced Liver Injury Network were more than 40 years old (median 57 years), 53% female, with a median latency to onset of 38 days (range 24-114 days). At DILI onset 80% were jaundiced, median ALT was 448 U/L and alkaline phosphatase 333 U/L; one subject required liver transplantation for acute liver failure and several showed ongoing injury at 6 and 24 months. The conclusions state that terbinafine hepatotoxicity most commonly presents with a mixed or cholestatic liver injury profile with frequent residual chronic cholestatic injury, and confirmed a strong genetic association of HLA-A*33:01 with terbinafine DILI among Caucasians.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All 15 patients were older than 40 years (median 57); genetic susceptibility restricted to HLA-A*33:01 carriers in European ancestry participants (also one African American HLA-A*33:01 carrier and two East Asians with HLA-A*33:03).
raw_record.extra_details: Antifungal agent associated with rare instances of hepatotoxicity. Enrolled high-causality cases from the Drug Induced Liver Injury Network; median latency 38 days (range 24-114 days); 80% jaundiced at onset; median ALT 448 U/L and alkaline phosphatase 333 U/L. One subject required liver transplantation for acute liver failure; 7/13 (54%) remaining subjects had ongoing liver injury at 6 months and 4 had persistently abnormal liver biochemistries at month 24. Presenting profile most commonly mixed or cholestatic with frequent residual chronic cholestatic injury. High-resolution HLA genotyping confirmed 10/11 (91%) European ancestry participants carried the HLA-A*33:01, B*14:02, C*08:02 haplotype (carrier frequency 1.6% in European controls); one African American carried HLA-A*33:01 and two East Asian patients carried HLA-A*33:03. Molecular docking studies indicated terbinafine may interact with HLA-A*33:01 and A*33:03.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents the first reported case of terbinafine-associated cholestatic liver dysfunction in a hepatic allograft recipient. Terbinafine therapy is generally well tolerated, but the incidence of symptomatic acute liver injury is 2.5 cases per 100,000 person-months of therapy, and liver injury has been reported both in patients with preexisting liver disease and in apparently healthy patients; many case reports describe prolonged cholestatic dysfunction, and rare cases of fulminant hepatic failure necessitating transplantation have been reported.

raw_record.extra_details: Case of a 51-year-old man started on terbinafine (~4 weeks earlier) for onychomycosis who developed elevated liver enzymes (total bilirubin 55.4 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 392 U/L, AST 246 U/L, ALT 265 U/L). A second liver biopsy after terbinafine discontinuation showed marked centrilobular cholestasis and severe bile duct damage, along with portal inflammation, mild portal fibrosis, and hepatocellular iron accumulation. Symptoms included progressive jaundice, malaise, and nausea. Patient was managed supportively but died suddenly ~3 months after terbinafine was discontinued, with no autopsy performed; hepatic function was improving at the time.

The serum contained significantly increased IgG4 subclass autoantibodies to ERp58, CYP2E1, and TFA, more than two standard deviations above control values. Only co-medication was oral contraceptives; no co-suspect liver agent identified.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe desflurane-induced acute liver failure in a 53-year-old woman with achalasia, hypertension, type 2 diabetes and hyperlipidaemia who underwent a Heller myotomy. She received desflurane (1.2 MAC) anaesthesia, and 10 days later a repeat myotomy under desflurane (0.9 MAC) anaesthesia. She developed acute liver failure 96 hours after surgery (serum ALT 11,600 U/L, pH 7.06, INR 3.7) and died despite supportive management. Postmortem confirmed massive hepatic necrosis and significantly elevated trifluoroacetyl chloride-specific IgG4 antibodies, consistent with an inhalational anaesthetic agent being the cause of the necrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: 53-year-old woman with achalasia, hypertension, type 2 diabetes and hyperlipidaemia; desflurane at 1.2 MAC during first Heller myotomy and 0.9 MAC at repeat surgery 10 days later; serum ALT peaked at 943 U/L after first surgery (attributed to antibiotic toxicity); acute liver failure 96 h after second surgery (ALT 11,600 U/L, pH 7.06, INR 3.7) with death despite supportive management; postmortem showed massive hepatic necrosis and elevated trifluoroacetyl chloride-specific IgG4 antibodies (optical density 0.585; reference range <0.233). Desflurane is metabolised to inorganic fluoride and trifluoroacetyl chloride but, owing to its low blood:gas partition coefficient and resistance to degradation, is metabolised less than halothane, enflurane and isoflurane.

raw_record.support_text: A 37-year-old, obese woman who had prior exposure to halothane and other fluorinated inhalation anesthetics underwent desflurane anesthesia and developed severe hepatotoxicity. Several fluorinated inhalation anesthetics have been associated with hepatotoxicity; although desflurane is considered safest, the authors diagnosed desflurane-induced hepatitis in this patient who may have been sensitized by previous halothane exposure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient may have been sensitized by previous halothane exposure; obesity; other anesthetics/analgesics (etomidate, alcuronium, fentanyl, metamizole, piritramide, nitrous oxide, oxygen) also given during the desflurane anesthesia.
raw_record.extra_details: Twelve days postoperatively developed macular erythematous rash, then jaundice, dark urine, pruritus, malaise, nausea, epigastric pain. Labs: eosinophils 1280/µL, ALT 1776 U/L, AST 1258 U/L, GGT 48 U/L, ALP 185 U/L, total bilirubin 29.4 mg/dL, ammonia 61 µmol/L, PT 37%, PTT 50 s, antithrombin III 27%. Liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis with extensive centrilobular necrosis and mild lobular/portal inflammation. Anti-TFA IgG antibody titers rose (0.083 day 22 to 0.159 day 25, 0.108 day 27; 0.062/0.057/0.084 days 34/35/41; negative control 0.064, positive control 0.562), implicating trifluoroacetylated-protein hypersensitivity shared with halothane. Patient transferred to hepatology unit on postoperative day 30 for observation and potential liver transplantation; no encephalopathy at admission. Hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, infectious hepatitis, and autoimmune hepatitis excluded.

(2005), which enrolled 332 patients from a prior Phase III trial, continued 380 mg or 190 mg intramuscular monthly XR-NTX (naltrexone/Vivitrol) treatment with psychosocial support produced continued reduction in heavy drinking and, among placebo-treated patients switched to Vivitrol, a significant reduction in drinking, with no evidence of hepatotoxicity and no increased discontinuation due to adverse events.
raw_record.extra_details: Long-acting injectable intramuscular formulation (Vivitrol, Alkermes), 380 mg or 190 mg monthly for 12 months in an open-label extension study of 332 patients; explicit statement that no hepatotoxicity was observed, in addition to no increased discontinuation due to adverse events. The paper reports a physiological improvement from reduced alcohol intake (decrease in serum gamma-glutamyl transferase) rather than any liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: In a randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled study of extended-release naltrexone (XR-NTX) in opioid-dependent patients with a very high prevalence of chronic HCV infection, there was no evidence of drug-induced liver injury during treatment relative to placebo (Lucey et al., 2008). Liver enzyme (ALT, AST, GGT) elevations >3x ULN occurred in both arms without significant differences between XR-NTX and placebo, no patient had total bilirubin >2x ULN combined with ALT >3x ULN, elevations resolved toward baseline with continued treatment, and no jaundice, variceal hemorrhage, ascites, or encephalopathy was associated with the elevations.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Opioid-dependent patients with high prevalence of chronic HCV infection; XR-NTX given as extended-release intramuscular formulation.
raw_record.extra_details: Randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial. ALT >3x ULN at any postbaseline visit in 21/107 (19.6%) XR-NTX vs 11/85 (12.9%) placebo (p=.876); AST in 15/107 (14.0%) vs 9/85 (10.6%) (p=.713); GGT in 25/107 (23.4%) vs 18/85 (21.2%) (p=.811). No bilirubin >2x ULN with ALT >3x ULN in either arm. Peak ALT 578 IU/ml in a placebo patient and 402 IU/ml in an XR-NTX patient. Elevations improved and returned toward baseline in all patients with follow-up; no jaundice, variceal hemorrhage, ascites, or encephalopathy. Elevations >3x ULN occurred primarily, but not exclusively, in patients with chronic HCV. AST comparison in HIV-positive vs HIV-negative XR-NTX patients yielded p=.018, not significant after Bonferroni correction (requires p<.003).

raw_record.support_text: The current study monitored 74 alcoholic patients who received 25 mg of naltrexone (NTX) daily in the first week and then 50 mg daily for the remaining 12 weeks. After 12 weeks, hepatic enzyme alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels showed no elevation except in one subject, and the results strongly supported that NTX did not induce abnormalities in liver function tests or elevate liver enzymes; a statistically significant decrease in ALT and AST was observed. The paper concludes NTX is not hepatotoxic at the recommended daily dose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Alcoholic patients; ordinary recommended therapeutic dose (25-50 mg/day); open-label prospective monitoring rather than a randomized controlled design.
raw_record.extra_details: 74 patients; 25 mg/day week 1 then 50 mg/day for 12 weeks; no ALT/AST elevation except in one subject; statistically significant decrease in ALT and AST during the study; authors state NTX is not hepatotoxic at recommended daily dose and may benefit patients with elevated liver enzymes.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report eight cases of phenprocoumon-induced liver damage, three of which presented with (sub-)acute liver failure, two treated by orthotopic liver transplantation and one with a fatal outcome. Phenprocoumon-induced liver damage was diagnosed in 0.1% of patients presenting with liver disease at the First Department of Internal Medicine of the University of Mainz.
raw_record.extra_details: 8 reported cases; 3 with (sub-)acute liver failure, 2 treated by orthotopic liver transplantation, 1 fatal outcome; diagnosed in 0.1% of all patients presenting with liver disease at the University of Mainz; latency 6-64 months among (sub-)acute liver failure cases vs 3-11 months in others; histopathology ranged from severe hepatitis with massive hepatocellular bridging necrosis (cases 1-3) to only minor changes (case 4), with zone III accentuation in less severe cases; portal and periportal hepatitis in every case except case 4; marked bile-duct alterations with degenerative epithelial changes in cases 1 and 5; increase of eosinophilic granulocytes in most samples; primarily hepatitic (cytolytic) picture with rarely cholestatic features.

raw_record.support_text: The report concludes that a hepatitis-like syndrome may occur as a rare side effect of phenprocoumon therapy, and that substituting phenprocoumon by acenocoumarol may be feasible. The patient described suffered recurrent venous thromboembolic disease and had two episodes of phenprocoumon-induced hepatitis, with elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin that returned to near normal after cessation.
raw_record.extra_details: A 43-year-old female with recurrent venous thromboembolic disease had two episodes of phenprocoumon-induced hepatitis; liver enzymes and bilirubin nearly normalized after cessation of oral anticoagulation. A prolonged but temporary protein C deficiency was observed after the second episode (initially also low antithrombin III, free protein S, and FII), attributed by the authors to slowly restituting liver synthesis after hepatitis rather than vitamin K deficiency. No cross-reactivity to acenocoumarol was seen in this patient.

raw_record.support_text: A 58-year-old man presented with jaundice 6 months after aortic valve replacement. The final diagnosis of phenprocoumon (Marcoumar®)-induced hepatitis progressing to cirrhosis was based on recurrence of jaundice after re-exposure to the drug, improvement after withdrawal, and centrilobular necrosis with eosinophilic infiltration in the liver biopsy; antibodies to hepatitis C virus were absent.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of the coumarin anticoagulant phenprocoumon (Marcoumar®) used for prophylaxis of thromboembolic disorders. Diagnosis rested on positive rechallenge (recurrence of jaundice within 4 weeks after drug re-institution), improvement after withdrawal (heparin substitution), and liver biopsy showing recent centrilobular liver cell necrosis with eosinophilic infiltration; the injury progressed to cirrhosis. Competing causes excluded: HAV, HBV, HCV (anti-HCV absent), EBV, CMV, HSV, toxoplasmosis, HIV serologies negative; ceruloplasmin, α1-antitrypsin normal. Laboratory findings during relapse: bilirubin 138 µmol/l, ALAT 589 IU/l, ASAT 479 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 208 IU/l, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 566 IU/l, LDH 416 IU/l, serum bile acids 300 µmol/l, α-fetoprotein 700 µg/l; reduced ICG and antipyrine fractional clearances. Patient had changed from acenocoumarol (Sintrom®) to phenprocoumon 1 month after aortic valve surgery; recent blood-product exposure initially raised suspicion of non-A, non-B hepatitis. Liver functions were normal before surgery.

raw_record.support_text: In this cohort of 501 patients with liver disease, drug-induced liver injury (DILI) was most often caused by NSARs, amoxycillin, other antibiotics or phenprocoumon. Patients were diagnosed using stringent criteria, with 9.2% of unclear cases classified as cryptogenic.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among the agents most often causing drug-induced liver injury in a cohort of 501 patients with liver disease; DILI was most often caused by NSARs, amoxycillin, other antibiotics, or phenprocoumon. No specific phenotype, severity, or biochemical pattern is attributed to phenprocoumon in this passage.

raw_record.support_text: The cause of the painless jaundice was an acute, cholestatic hepatitis; the histology (severe acute hepatitis with confluent bridging necrosis and discreet eosinophilic infiltration) was compatible with drug-induced hepatitis. The diagnosis of phenprocoumon-induced hepatitis was supported by the negative viral hepatitis serology and the absence of other causes of hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: 78-year-old female, obese (153 cm, 81.5 kg), painless jaundice with marked skin and scleral icterus. Laboratory findings: bilirubin 11.5 mg/dl (direct 6.4), GOT 1332 U/l, GPT 714 U/l, gamma-GT 234 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 424 U/l, LDH 900 U/l, Quick <8%, mild eosinophilia (5%), elevated ANA 1:320. Histology: severe acute hepatitis with confluent bridging necrosis and discreet eosinophilic infiltrate, no alcoholic or obstructive findings. Negative viral serology (HAV/HBV/HCV, CMV, EBV). Incidental cholecystolithiasis (post-cholecystectomy anatomy) with no mechanical cholestasis on ultrasound, CT, and ERCP. Diagnosis supported by negative viral serology and absence of other causes.

raw_record.support_text: In Case Two, a 46-year-old woman developed hepatotoxicity 7 months after starting oral anticoagulant therapy with phenprocoumon; other causes of acute hepatitis were excluded and liver function had previously been normal. The clinical and laboratory findings were highly suspect to be related to phenprocoumon.
raw_record.extra_details: Case Two: hepatotoxicity 7 months after starting oral anticoagulant therapy with phenprocoumon (following thrombolysis of pulmonary embolism and thrombotic occlusion of the inferior vena cava, correlated with oral contraception). ALT 86 U/L and AST 184 U/L, GGT 87 U/L, AP 171 U/L, GLDH 15.2 U/L; total bilirubin, CHE, immunoglobulins, acute- and chronic-phase markers within normal range; viral (hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV, HSV, HIV), autoimmune and hematological causes excluded. No biopsy due to lack of consent. After stopping phenprocoumon and switching to LMWH (Fragmin), liver enzymes normalized within about 2 months; recovery consistent with drug attribution.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that all three individuals in the study suffered from phenprocoumon-induced liver failure, with cases of acute liver failure (ALF) that were highly urgent, two of which required liver transplantation. The authors note that because all three individuals suffered from phenprocoumon-induced liver failure, the aetiologies of liver failure that can be commented on are limited.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of ARFI elastography in acute liver failure (ALF). All three enrolled patients had phenprocoumon-induced liver failure and were assessed with shear-wave velocity (SWV) measurements; serial examinations in one case showed decreasing aminotransferases, bilirubin, and shear-wave velocities during follow-up. Two of the three patients underwent urgent liver transplantation. The paper cautions that high shear-wave velocity does not prove cirrhosis in the setting of acute liver injury with massive necrosis and inflammation.

raw_record.support_text: After withdrawal from phenprocoumon therapy and switching to low molecular weight heparin, liver tests gradually normalized; aminotransferase levels rapidly increased again when phenprocoumon was resumed. Phenprocoumon-associated necrotizing hepatitis was diagnosed by clinical course, liver histology (necrotizing hepatocellular injury in zone 3 of the acinus) and a positive lymphocyte transformation test, and liver enzymes normalized after restart of prednisolone. The authors conclude that, though severe hepatic adverse effects of phenprocoumon are rare, physicians should consider coumarin derivatives as a potential source of hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case in a 52-year-old female on anticoagulation after aortic valve replacement due to aortic stenosis. Latency about 7 months between start of anticoagulation and disease manifestation; serological tests for viral, autoimmune and metabolic hepatitis were negative; first lymphocyte transformation test with phenprocoumon was negative, a repeat test one week later was positive. Rechallenge on resuming phenprocoumon produced rapid rises in aminotransferases; dechallenge (switch to low molecular weight heparin) led to gradual normalization; prednisolone immunosuppression was restarted before recovery. The authors note severe hepatic adverse effects of phenprocoumon are rare.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of coumarin-induced acute liver failure (phenprocoumon-induced) in a patient that followed a fulminant course. The context describes anticoagulation after 'cumarininduziertem akutem Leberversagen' and the patient's post-coumarin-induced liver failure with subsequent liver transplantation, attributing the liver failure to coumarin/phenprocoumon therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Coumarin (phenprocoumon)-induced fulminant acute liver failure ('cumarininduziertem akutem Leberversagen' / 'phenprocoumoninduziertem Leberversagen') in a single patient, requiring liver transplantation. Case report of coumarin-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report three women with phenprocoumon-induced liver injury in which cholestasis was clinically predominant. Latency from the start of oral anticoagulation was 6, 18, and 6 months. No liver-replacement therapy was needed and no corticosteroids were given; the course was prolonged in each patient but all three clinically recovered. The text frames coumarin treatment as a possible etiology of acute liver failure even after prolonged administration without prior problems.
raw_record.extra_details: Three women (aged 62 in the described representative case) treated with oral phenprocoumon (Falithrom brand) as anticoagulation, in one case started ~18 months before admission after a TIA with no other medication; no corticosteroids given, course prolonged but all three recovered, no liver-replacement therapy and no fatal or transplantation outcome. Cholestasis with jaundice clinically predominant; latency 6, 18, and 6 months. The authors note cross-reactions between different coumarin preparations can occur.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes phenprocoumon-induced liver damage (phenprocoumoninduzierter Leberschaden), first described in 1963. According to a BfArM analysis based on spontaneous reports it constitutes ~2% of all phenprocoumon side effects and ~1% of all hepatopathies are phenprocoumon-induced. The clinical picture is extremely variable, ranging from simple hepatitis to (sub)acute liver failure with fatal outcome, as in the presented case. Hepatopathy typically occurs 3-9 months after starting phenprocoumon, with latencies up to 7 years reported; in the presented case the patient had taken Marcumar (phenprocoumon) for 6 years.
raw_record.extra_details: Sold as Marcumar; anticoagulation indication. Latency typically 3-9 months, up to 7 years; present patient used phenprocoumon for 6 years. Clinical spectrum from simple hepatitis to (sub)acute liver failure with death. BfArM spontaneous-report analysis: ~2% of phenprocoumon side effects and ~1% of hepatopathies attributed to phenprocoumon. Four cases of this complication occurred in the authors' patient population during 2006-2008, two fatal; a Mainz case series illustrates the broad clinical spectrum. An immunologic genesis is considered likely (borderline ANA titer, exacerbation upon re-exposure, 'drug-allergic' course); cross-sensitization with other coumarins noted. Steroid therapy attempted without influence on outcome. Histology showed portal inflammatory infiltrate, group necrosis with cholestasis, collapse zone with clearing, and focal fiber increase; the course evolved into rapidly developing liver cirrhosis with subacute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: Among a cohort of 70 patients with biopsy-confirmed hepatic sarcoidosis, one patient had been diagnosed with drug-induced liver injury (DILI) attributed to phenprocoumon, occurring 8 years before the sarcoidosis diagnosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported in a cohort of hepatic sarcoidosis patients; the DILI episode occurred 8 years before the diagnosis of sarcoidosis. No biochemical pattern, reaction type, or severity level is specified.

raw_record.support_text: Over the past 20 years the authors collected a series of 30 patients with drug-induced liver disease (DILD) in whom phenprocoumon was highly suggestive to be the causative agent. They show that 15 of them had sensitized lymphocytes toward this substance, indicating that at least in a subgroup of patients, immunological/allergic processes may play a role in the pathogenesis of the liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 30 patients with DILD in whom phenprocoumon was highly suggestive as the causative agent. Clinical/histological spectrum ranges from mild acute hepatitis to (sub)acute liver failure [1,3], with a few reports of cholestatic hepatitis [2,4]; proposed mechanism is immunologically mediated, supported by positive lymphocyte transformation test (LTT) in 15 of 30 patients, activation of CD4-positive memory T cells in three case reports, and eosinophilic infiltrates without blood eosinophilia or allergic signs (exanthema, fever). Patients: 51 of 204 suspected drug-induced allergic liver disorder cases had taken coumarin derivatives; 28 excluded, 30 analyzed. Median drug intake until DILD appearance was 6 months (26 patients); one patient had injury 24 h after first intake; four patients had taken the drug >5 years. In seven patients the drug had not yet been withdrawn at LTT. Indications: atrial fibrillation (60%), mitral valve replacement (16%), coronary heart disease (8%); two patients for thromboembolic events (one with pANCA/MPO vasculitis). Eighteen patients took other drugs besides phenprocoumon. Coumarin derivatives related DILD reported rarely worldwide.

raw_record.support_text: The report describes 2 patients with phenprocoumon-induced hepatic failure, which necessitated liver transplantation in 1 case. Once they recovered spontaneously or were transplanted, both showed recurrence of liver damage when oral anticoagulation with acenocoumarol was attempted. Therefore acenocoumarol may not be a safe therapeutic alternative for patients who survived severe phenprocoumon-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: 2 patients with fulminant hepatic failure attributed to phenprocoumon; 1 case necessitated liver transplantation, the other recovered with supportive care; hepatotoxicity described as rare but potentially life-threatening complication of phenprocoumon and warfarin anticoagulation. Both patients later showed recurrence of liver damage when switched to acenocoumarol.

raw_record.support_text: A Mainz working group reported that of 7,523 patients seen 1992-2002 in the clinic for liver diseases of various etiologies, 0.1% (8/7,523) had a phenprocoumon-induced liver disease. Between 1992 and 2002, 29 clinic patients needed orthotopic liver transplantation due to acute liver failure; in 2 of these cases phenprocoumon was regarded as the probable hepatotoxic agent.
raw_record.extra_details: 0.1% (8/7,523) of clinic patients had phenprocoumon-induced liver disease; 2 cases required orthotopic liver transplantation for acute liver failure with phenprocoumon judged the probable hepatotoxic agent. In a separate retrospective acute liver failure study (2002-2008, 134 Ruhr region patients), drug toxicity was the leading cause (36.9%, n=53) and phenprocoumon was the second most common toxic drug (n=9; 6.7%). Across 20 VKA hepatotoxicity publications (1980-2012, 31 patients), 26 patients had hepatotoxicity under phenprocoumon; more women affected, median age 60 years (range 30-90). VKA hepatotoxicity generally appears after a latency of several months with unspecific symptoms and painless jaundice; both transaminases and cholestasis parameters are elevated; cross-reactivity between coumarin derivatives is described.

raw_record.support_text: Within the Sebode et al. report discussed in the commentary, phenprocoumon was the most common cause of DILI in the large university medical center in Hamburg, with metamizole as the second most common cause after phenprocoumon.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as the most common cause of DILI ahead of metamizole in the Hamburg university medical center case series.

raw_record.support_text: The presented patient developed drug-induced liver failure attributed to phenprocoumon. A characteristic time relationship between drug exposure and onset of jaundice (4 months after beginning therapy; 2-8 months in previous reports) was present, and histopathology, time course, and exclusion of other etiologic factors argue for drug-induced liver failure due to phenprocoumon. Prior case reports showed milder hepatotoxicity that reversed after discontinuation and causality was proven by rechallenge, which was not possible in the present case for ethical reasons (donor liver not exposed).
raw_record.extra_details: Oral anticoagulant (coumarin type); jaundice appeared ~4 months after starting therapy (reported range 2-8 months in prior reports). Prior case reports mainly showed milder, reversible hepatotoxicity with causality proven by rechallenge; rechallenge not performed here for ethical reasons (donor liver not exposed). The patient's native liver was explanted (received a donor liver), prompting histopathologic evaluation of the explanted liver. Ischemic liver cell necrosis and Budd-Chiari syndrome (as a potential complication of factor-V-Leiden mutation) were excluded by color flow imaging and histopathology. Pathogenesis hypotheses discussed: accumulation of toxic epoxide metabolites and an autoimmune reaction; lack of substantial inflammatory infiltrate is seen as consistent with a hypothesized direct toxic/apoptotic effect of epoxides on hepatocytes.

raw_record.support_text: A 61-year-old woman was referred for painless jaundice with a hepatitis constellation and already impaired liver function. She had been treated with phenprocoumon for chronic atrial fibrillation for two years. Infectious, autoimmune, and metabolic causes were largely excluded, leading to the diagnosis of a drug-induced toxic hepatopathy. Histology showed liver cell necrosis with a mild inflammatory reaction. The course was complicated by a perforated duodenal ulcer requiring surgery, after which liver function worsened; the patient declined liver transplantation and improved only slowly with symptomatic treatment. The authors conclude that liver damage can occur even after long-term uneventful phenprocoumon use.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 61-year-old woman treated with phenprocoumon for chronic atrial fibrillation for 2 years. Presented with painless jaundice, hepatitis constellation, and impaired liver function; infectious, autoimmune, and metabolic causes largely excluded. Histology showed liver cell necrosis with mild inflammatory reaction. Course complicated by perforated duodenal ulcer requiring surgery with subsequent worsening of liver function; patient declined liver transplantation and was treated symptomatically with slow improvement. Authors conclude liver damage (Leberschädigung) can occur after long-term uneventful phenprocoumon use.

raw_record.support_text: The drug-induced liver disease (DILD) diagnosis for patients was based on International Consensus Meeting criteria: alanine aminotransferase >2 times ULN, conjugated bilirubin >2 times ULN, or a combined increase of ASAT, alkaline phosphatase and total bilirubin with one >2 times ULN; identification of phenprocoumon with a temporal relationship to elevated liver enzymes; and exclusion of other causes of liver or biliary-tract disease and excessive alcohol use.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Anticoagulated patients; liver biopsy performed in only 2 of 30 patients because of bleeding risk; six patients were accidentally reexposed and in one of these a transaminase increase was noted at first exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: 30 phenprocoumon-induced liver injury cases. Liver injury pattern classified per International Consensus Criteria as hepatocellular, cholestatic, or mixed. In the two biopsied patients, lobular hepatitis with bridging necrosis was described; no evidence of autoimmune hepatitis (no relevant autoantibodies, normal IgG). Liver enzymes and clinical symptoms normalized after withdrawal (dechallenge). raw_record.support_text: A retrospective analysis of patients treated for liver disease between 1992 and 2002 revealed eight cases of phenprocoumon-induced hepatotoxicity, including three cases of (sub-) acute liver failure that resulted in two orthotopic liver transplantations and one fatal outcome. Five patients with phenprocoumon-induced hepatitis recovered after anticoagulation was switched to another coumarin derivative or low molecular weight heparin. In all patients the liver injury was predominantly of a hepatitic type; massive confluent liver cell necroses were histologically present in the (sub-) acute liver failure cases, whereas patients without liver failure showed mild portal to moderate active lobular hepatitis.

raw_record.extra_details: Eight cases of phenprocoumon-induced hepatotoxicity: three progressed to (sub-)acute liver failure (two orthotopic liver transplantations, one fatal outcome); five cases of phenprocoumon-induced hepatitis recovered after switching anticoagulation. Histology: massive confluent liver cell necrosis in the liver-failure cases; mild portal to moderate active lobular hepatitis in the non-failure cases. A BfArM (German Federal Institute for Drugs and Medical Devices) retrospective analysis since 1990 reported 4390 possible phenprocoumon-related adverse reactions, 2% with hepatitis and 0.2% with liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: The authors attribute an acute pseudo-cholangitis hepatitis to tamsulosin in a 65-year-old man treated for benign prostatic hypertrophy, based on a suggestive 11-day latency after drug introduction, a >50% drop in ALAT within 2 days of stopping the drug with full normalization at 5 weeks, and the absence of any other cause of acute liver injury. Applying the consensus expert criteria, the causality (imputability) score was 8, corresponding to probable imputability. The presence of portal eosinophils suggested an immunoallergic mechanism, and histology showed punctate intralobular necrosis with predominantly centrolobular intracanalicular cholestasis.
raw_record.extra_details: A 65-year-old man treated for prostate adenoma with tamsulosine (Omix) 0.4 mg/day, having previously taken Serenoa repens (Permixon) for 2 months. Acute hepatitis with jaundice, fever and right upper quadrant pain presented after 11 days of tamsulosin. Labs: ALAT 9x ULN, ASAT 7x ULN, GGT 7x ULN, alkaline phosphatase normal, total bilirubin 127 micromol/L, conjugated 40 micromol/L, prothrombin 86%. Liver biopsy showed punctate intralobular necrosis with predominantly centrolobular intracanalicular cholestasis and portal inflammatory infiltrate with lymphocytes, plasma cells and eosinophils, without bile duct damage. Negative viral (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs, anti-HCV) and autoimmune serologies; no biliary obstruction on cholangio-MRI/ERCP; negative blood cultures. Dechallenge: ALAT 3x ULN 2 days after stopping, complete normalization at 5 weeks. Residual isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (30-40 micromol/L) attributed to Gilbert syndrome. Presentation described as pseudo-angiocholitis; paper notes no prior published case of clinical tamsulosin-induced hepatitis, though a study of 82 patients on tamsulosin for 2 weeks found one patient with ALAT/ASAT 2-3x ULN resolving in 2 months. The paper also notes rare cytolytic or cholestatic hepatitis cases reported with other alpha-1-blockers (alfuzosin, prazosin, terazosin).; note_competing_causes_excluded: Other causes were excluded (non-lithiasic, no hepatic ischemia, negative viral/autoimmune serologies); amoxicillin-clavulanic acid was started at admission only after tamsulosin was stopped.

raw_record.support_text: Osimertinib (80 mg/day) was started as sixth-line therapy in a 62-year-old woman with EGFR T790M-mutated NSCLC. On day 15 she developed general malaise; after reduction to 40 mg/day she was admitted with high fever and elevated serum AST (284 IU/L) and ALT (183 IU/L). No other cause was found, and fever and transaminase elevations improved immediately after discontinuation, leading to the diagnosis of drug-induced fever and hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case in a 62-year-old woman with relapsed stage IV NSCLC harboring EGFR L858R and acquired T790M, receiving osimertinib as sixth-line therapy. Initial dose 80 mg/day; reduced to 40 mg/day after day-15 general malaise; hepatotoxicity (AST 284 IU/L, ALT 183 IU/L) with high fever noted three days after the reduced dose, prompting emergency ward admission. No other cause identified; fever and transaminase elevations resolved after osimertinib discontinuation (dechallenge). Oral desensitization with milled osimertinib tablets mixed in lactose was performed over ~2 weeks (0.1 mg/day up to 40 mg/day on day 17) with no recurrence of hepatotoxicity or fever for the following 6 months on 40 mg/day. The paper notes osimertinib treatment is permanently stopped in 7–13% of patients due to drug-induced toxicities and that severe hepatotoxicity was the most common drug-induced side effect in clinical trials.

raw_record.support_text: A 66-year-old woman with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma started osimertinib 80 mg once daily. One month later she developed grade 2 hepatotoxicity (AST 106 U/L, ALT 63 U/L); after discontinuation her liver function improved to near normal within 10 days. Rechallenge at a reduced dose (40 mg) produced grade 2 deterioration within a week and, after a second discontinuation, worsened to grade 4 (AST 1302 U/L, ALT 551 U/L). The hepatotoxicity was considered osimertinib related because she had no history of liver disease, viral hepatitis, or habitual alcohol intake, and her liver metastases were improving on osimertinib. Osimertinib was later successfully readministered using a desensitization method.

Rechallenge at reduced 40 mg dose caused grade 2 deterioration within 1 week; after second discontinuation enzymes worsened to grade 4 (AST 1302 U/L, ALT 551 U/L). No viral hepatitis, liver disease, or alcohol intake; liver metastases were improving, supporting causality. Osimertinib withheld 5 weeks until enzymes normalized, then successfully restarted via a desensitization method; at 5 months after rechallenge brain metastases, pulmonary tumor, and pleural effusion had decreased.

raw_record.support_text: Repaglinide is a fast, short-acting meglitinide analog antidiabetic drug approved for type 2 diabetes. In rare cases elevated liver enzymes have been noted. The authors report a patient who developed cholestatic hepatitis while taking repaglinide.
raw_record.extra_details: First published report of cholestatic hepatitis related to repaglinide. A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes took repaglinide 1 mg/day, increased to 2 mg/day one month before presentation; presented with 2-week history of itching and jaundice and was admitted. Labs: AST 83 U/L (normal <37), ALT 183 U/L (normal <40), ALP 307 U/L (normal <136), GGT 303 U/L (normal <85), total bilirubin 12.2 mg/dl with direct bilirubin 9.4 mg/dl, serum creatinine 1.3 mg/dl. No toxic habits and denied other drugs/herbal remedies. Viral serology and autoantibody screening negative; MR cholangiography showed no pathology. Liver biopsy showed expanded portal areas with mild bile duct proliferation and moderate inflammatory infiltrate (mainly lymphocytes with some eosinophils) and hepatocyte ballooning. After repaglinide discontinuation laboratory findings normalized within a month. Causality strongly supported by temporal eligibility, exclusion of alternative causes, histologic features, and rapid improvement after drug withdrawal. Presence of some eosinophils in the inflammatory infiltrate suggests a possible immune mechanism.

Laboratory testing showed elevated aspartate aminotransferase (83 U/l), alanine aminotransferase (183 U/l), alkaline phosphatase (307 U/l), γ-glutamyl-transferase (303 U/l), and total bilirubin (12.2 mg/dl with direct 9.4 mg/dl); serology ruled out viral causes, autoantibody screening was negative, and imaging including MR cholangiography was normal. raw_record.extra_details: First published report of cholestatic hepatitis related to repaglinide. Latency approximately 2 months; 2-week history of pruritus and jaundice at presentation. Laboratory values: AST 83 U/l (normal <37), ALT 183 U/l (normal <40), ALP 307 U/l (normal <136), GGT 303 U/l (normal <85), total bilirubin 12.2 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 9.4 mg/dl; serum creatinine 1.3 mg/dl. Liver biopsy: expanded portal areas with mild bile duct proliferation, moderate inflammatory infiltrate (predominantly lymphocytes with some eosinophils), and hepatocyte ballooning. Viral serology negative, autoantibodies negative, MR cholangiography unremarkable. Rapid improvement and normalization within one month after drug withdrawal (positive dechallenge, no rechallenge). Authors note causal role strongly supported by temporal eligibility, exclusion of alternative causes, histology, and improvement after withdrawal; presence of eosinophils suggests a possible immune mechanism. Repaglinide is a meglitinide analog antidiabetic; its clearance depends on hepatic enzyme activity and hepatic blood flow, factors impaired in the elderly.

raw_record.support_text: Captopril, a competitive ACE inhibitor used for hypertension and heart failure, is associated with dermatologic, hematologic, and pulmonary adverse effects, but hepatotoxicity is extremely rare. The paper presents a patient with severe cholestatic jaundice induced by captopril. The patient was initially diagnosed and treated for cholangitis, but the authors conclude that patients treated with captopril who develop 'atypical cholangitis' should be suspected of captopril-associated liver damage; a review of the literature showed similar occurrences.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report and review of the literature (Arch Surg 1996;131:670-671). A 65-year-old woman with essential hypertension took captopril 25 mg three times daily for the past 2 months before onset. Presented with abdominal pain, fever, and jaundice of 2 days' duration; initially diagnosed and treated as cholangitis. On admission: bilirubin 56 umol/L (3.3 mg/dL), aspartate aminotransferase 465 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 515 U/L, gamma-glutamyltransferase 585 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 157 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 1330 U/L. The clinical picture was described as severe cholestatic jaundice mimicking 'atypical cholangitis'; hepatotoxicity considered extremely rare. Literature review showed similar occurrences in other patients.

raw_record.support_text: The paper attributes hepatocellular and cholestatic jaundice to captopril, stating it is usually predominantly cholestatic, resembling hepatocanalicular cholestasis due to chlorpromazine and penicillamine, while acute hepatocellular injury has also been observed. Hepatic reactions were reported after 2, 6, and 20 months of captopril treatment, and in one case rechallenge produced a relapse. An earlier paragraph notes 29 cases of liver dysfunction due to captopril had been reported to the UK Committee on Safety of Medicines, with 9 cases of hepatocellular jaundice (2 deaths), 8 cholestatic jaundice (1 fatal), and 3 patients with hepatorenal syndrome (all fatal), and 164 hepatic adverse reactions notified to the WHO database.
raw_record.extra_details: Doses varied from 12.5 mg to 150 mg/day. Latency: cholestasis began 5 weeks after start in case 1; hepatotoxicity reported after ~2, 6, and 20 months of treatment; rechallenge produced relapse in one case. CSM: 29 cases of liver dysfunction due to captopril - 9 hepatocellular jaundice with 2 deaths, 8 cholestatic jaundice (1 fatal), 3 hepatorenal syndrome (all died); estimated incidence 0.09 per 1000 captopril-treated patients (likely underestimate, ~10% reporting). WHO database (Uppsala, Jan 1989, worldwide excluding UK): 164 hepatic adverse reactions, 64 serious clinical liver disease. Hepatitis A, B, CMV, EBV serology negative in presented cases. Captopril used for hypertension and heart failure; hepatotoxicity described as rare; 40% transient eosinophilia in early weeks; AST 10-25% above ULN in 4 of 5 patients on captopril plus hydrochlorothiazide; vigilance advised in elderly especially when combined with diuretics.

raw_record.support_text: Captopril therapy was concluded to be the cause of cholestasis in this case, since all other possible causes for cholestasis were satisfactorily eliminated. The drug had been withdrawn shortly before admission; during 4 weeks of monitoring serum total bilirubin fell to 109 µmol/L while alkaline phosphatase remained elevated at 464 U/L. The patient later sustained a cardiac arrest and died of gangrenous bowel with superior mesenteric artery thrombosis, judged unrelated to Captopril therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of captopril-attributed cholestasis. Liver biopsy showed normal architecture with marked canalicular and hepatocellular cholestasis involving the majority of each lobule, most severe centrilobularly, with scattered lymphocytes, neutrophils and eosinophils in portal tracts and no granulomas. Autoantibodies to nuclei, mitochondria and smooth muscle absent; hepatitis A/B/C and EBV serology negative; normal biliary tree on ERCP and ultrasound. After drug withdrawal, serum total bilirubin fell to 109 µmol/L (alkaline phosphatase 464 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 297 U/L, aspartate transaminase 41 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transaminase 224 U/L, creatinine 0.38 mmol/L, urea 28 mmol/L). Patient died of gangrenous bowel with superior mesenteric artery thrombosis, unrelated to captopril; autopsy showed normal biliary tree. All other possible causes of cholestasis were eliminated.

raw_record.support_text: The described patient plus 20 other published cases of hepatic injury associated with captopril administration are reported. In all patients captopril dosages were within the recommended range, jaundice was present at admission with bilirubin levels between 4.0 and 34.2 mg/dL, and the liver injury pattern was cholestatic or mixed cholestatic and hepatocellular in all but one patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Aggregates the index case with 20 additional published captopril-associated hepatic injury cases; dosages within recommended range; lag period 1 week to 10 months; jaundice present at admission with bilirubin levels 68-585 mmol/L (4.0-34.2 mg/dL); cholestatic or mixed cholestatic/hepatocellular pattern in all but one patient. Cholestatic jaundice defined as ALP >3x ULN with AST/ALT <8x ULN; aminotransferases at least 2x ULN in all patients; ALP above 3x ULN in all but three.

raw_record.support_text: Following captopril withdrawal, the patient's jaundice almost disappeared and her biochemical pattern progressively returned to normal. The paper concludes that both the onset of symptoms and the evolution of the picture support a diagnosis of captopril hepatotoxicity, and notes that clinical and biochemical normalization usually follows drug withdrawal, although at least one captopril case has been described with death due to hepatic failure secondary to hepatic necrosis. Mechanism discussion (paragraph 21) indicates the present case was attributed to hypersensitivity to captopril because the patient, despite renal failure, received a low dose and underwent haemodialysis three times a week without captopril supplementation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had pre-existing renal failure, was receiving a low dose of captopril, and underwent haemodialysis three times a week without captopril supplementation.
raw_record.extra_details: Jaundice and elevated liver biochemistry appeared around the time of captopril treatment; within three days of withdrawal the jaundice almost disappeared and the biochemical pattern progressively returned to normal, supporting dechallenge. A previously described captopril case resulted in death due to hepatic failure secondary to hepatic necrosis. Mechanism speculated to be hypersensitivity (the authors' view for this case) or a direct toxic effect via kinase II inhibition increasing prostaglandins and leukotrienes; the low dose was argued to weigh against dose-related direct toxicity. No cross-reaction between captopril and ACE inhibitors lacking a proline has been reported (reference [10]).

raw_record.support_text: The discussion states that MTX commonly causes liver function impairment. It reports that although a few studies found no correlation between MTHFR C677T mutations and liver function impairment, a large number of studies indicate a strong association, including a meta-analysis of 14 studies (1714 children) showing the C677T mutant gene was significantly associated with hepatotoxicity, and several reports confirming a significantly higher risk of hepatic impairment in patients with mutant genotypes. In the present study, the authors found significant differences in the incidence of hepatic impairment among MTHFR C677T genotypes, with a significantly higher risk in CT+TT mutant carriers than in CC wild-type carriers, a conclusion also supported by stratified analysis in the low-risk group.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paediatric acute lymphoblastic leukaemia patients treated with high-dose MTX (HD-MTX); hepatic-impairment risk was significantly higher in MTHFR C677T CT+TT mutant carriers than in CC wild-type carriers in the study population and in the low-risk subgroup.
raw_record.extra_details: MTX use is limited by drug-related toxicities including bone marrow suppression, abnormal liver and kidney function, skin mucosal damage, and gastrointestinal reactions. Liver function impairment was assessed as a grade II or higher toxic reaction. Supporting literature: Zhu et al. meta-analysis of 14 studies (1714 children) found C677T mutant significantly associated with hepatotoxicity; El-Khodary et al. reported higher serum glutaminase levels in CT/TT carriers; the C677T mutation was suggested to cause a rapid increase in cysteine levels after MTX chemotherapy as a potential mechanism of liver function impairment.

raw_record.support_text: In a CCSG randomized study of childhood leukemia patients free of disease for 2.5–3 years, those continued on chemotherapy developed serious chronic toxicity. Among 7 children continued, a child on daily methotrexate for 255 days developed hepatosplenomegaly, elevated liver enzymes, bony osteoporosis, and severe scoliosis; a percutaneous liver biopsy demonstrated cirrhotic changes, and liver function tests returned to normal after methotrexate was discontinued. Two other patients had clinical evidence of liver disease with altered liver function and hepatosplenomegaly after 461 and 1211 days of methotrexate maintenance, both improving after discontinuation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric childhood leukemia patients on chronic maintenance therapy; one patient also received methotrexate plus four other drugs cyclically as an unresolved co-exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic methotrexate toxicity. CCSG randomized study (1966): 7 children continued treatment, 3 developed serious chronic toxicity. Daily methotrexate for 255 days led to hepatosplenomegaly, elevated liver enzymes, osteoporosis and scoliosis, with cirrhotic changes on biopsy; liver function normalized after discontinuation. Two further children on methotrexate maintenance for 461 and 1211 days had liver disease with altered liver function and hepatosplenomegaly, improving on discontinuation. Minnesota series: hepatic fibrosis in 12 children, usually asymptomatic despite abnormal BSP excretion and transiently elevated OCT/SGOT immediately after methotrexate. CCSG 903 maintenance methotrexate (30 mg/m² twice weekly p.o.): predominant clinical toxicity hepatic; of 216 patients on study >4 months, 80 had elevated liver enzymes (median time to definite elevation 167 days); liver biopsy showed significant cirrhosis in 5 and fibrosis in 9 (moderate fibrosis mean 389 days, cirrhosis mean 530 days on MTX); 9 of 11 with fibrosis/cirrhosis had prior acute methotrexate toxicity. Pathologic findings in MTX-induced liver disease (12 patients): portal fibrosis 10/12, enlarged/double-nucleated hepatic cells 9/12, portal inflammation 7/12, periportal fat 4/12, cholestasis 1/12, hepatic necrosis 1/12.

raw_record.support_text: The paper records HD-MTX-related toxicities following methotrexate treatment in pediatric non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) patients, including hematological suppression, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, oral mucositis, vomiting, and diarrhea, with adverse events graded by CTCAE 3.0. A total of 355 courses of high-dose methotrexate (HD-MTX) therapy were analyzed across 93 pediatric patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric NHL patients treated with high-dose methotrexate as part of chemotherapy.
raw_record.extra_details: 93 pediatric patients (median age 8.8 years; LBL, BL, ALCL, DLBCL); 355 courses of HD-MTX analyzed; adverse events graded by CTCAE 3.0 and dichotomized into grade 0/I/II versus III/IV; plasma MTX level >0.2 umol/L at 48 h seen in 63 (17.7%) courses. Hepatotoxicity recorded as one of the HD-MTX-related toxicities; no specific pattern, severity, dose, or latency for the hepatic injury is provided.

raw_record.support_text: In this study of children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), no significant association between the SLC19A1 polymorphisms rs2838958, rs1051266 and the rs56292801 polymorphism of miR-5189 and MTX-induced side effects (hepatotoxicity, mucositis and other adverse events) was found. Logistic regression showed a significant association between the CT genotype of the rs1131596 SLC19A1 polymorphism and a higher risk of developing severe hepatotoxicity, and the combination of the TT genotype of rs1131596 with the AA genotype of rs56292801 conferred a statistically significant risk of severe hepatotoxicity. A statistically significant correlation between patient age and liver toxicity was also reported, with most hepatotoxicity cases in children aged 5-10 years.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients with childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) treated with MTX-based therapy at a single center
raw_record.extra_details: Paper investigates pharmacogenetic predictors of MTX-induced hepatotoxicity. No significant association of rs2838958, rs1051266 (SLC19A1) or rs56292801 (miR-5189) with MTX-induced hepatotoxicity when considered individually; CT genotype of rs1131596 and the combination of TT(rs1131596)+AA(rs56292801) significantly linked to severe hepatotoxicity risk. Hepatotoxicity statistically correlated with age, most cases in children aged 5-10. Study limitation: relatively small, genetically homogeneous population from one geographic area.

raw_record.support_text: The stated aim of this work was to assess the therapeutic value of Black seed oil in protection against methotrexate induced hepatotoxicity in Egyptian children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Forty newly diagnosed ALL patients received MTX as part of their chemotherapy treatment protocol with delayed leucovorin rescue, and methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity is the attributed drug-related liver injury being protected against rather than being questioned.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (ages 4-13 years) with newly diagnosed acute lymphoblastic leukemia; methotrexate given as part of standard chemotherapy protocol with delayed leucovorin rescue after each MTX dose.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of 40 consecutive newly diagnosed ALL children (28 males, 12 females; mean age 9.17±3.81 years, range 4-13) randomly assigned to MTX + Black seed oil (Baraka soft gelatin capsule 450 mg, 80 mg/kg/day in three divided doses for one week after each MTX dose, n=20) versus MTX + placebo for one week (n=20), with 20 healthy age/sex-matched controls. Leucovorin rescue (Ca leucovorin) dosed at 10 mg/m2 every 6 hours beginning 48 hours after MTX infusion, adjusted per methotrexate levels. MTX-induced hepatotoxicity is the target condition Black seed oil is tested to protect against (protective agent, not itself extracted as a DILI cause).
