raw_record.support_text: In a pharmacogenetic cohort of children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) treated with methotrexate (MTX), gastrointestinal- and liver-associated adverse events (AE) were the two main reasons for MTX discontinuation. Liver-associated AE ('hepatotoxicity') was attributed to MTX and was analyzed against genetic markers: 11 SNPs were significantly associated with hepatotoxicity. Carriers of MTRR rs1801394 had about a 2.5-fold higher hazard rate to develop hepatotoxicity and to discontinue MTX because of AE, and wild-type MTHFD1 rs2236225 had a 1.64-fold higher hazard rate for hepatotoxicity compared with mutated patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA); folic acid supplementation reduced hepatic AEs.
raw_record.extra_details: MTX was withdrawn due to adverse events in 10/119 patients (8.4%) in the cohort. Gastrointestinal- and liver-associated AEs were the 2 main reasons for MTX discontinuation. 11 SNPs were significantly associated with MTX hepatotoxicity; MTRR rs1801394 carried ~2.5x higher hazard for hepatotoxicity and for AE-related MTX discontinuation; wild-type MTHFD1 rs2236225 gave 1.64x higher hazard for hepatotoxicity. Results were consistent with prior JIA and rheumatoid arthritis studies.

raw_record.support_text: High-dose methotrexate (HD-MTX) is used to treat malignant tumors in children and young adults, but systemic exposure to MTX often results in liver injury (drug-induced liver injury, DILI), which limits sustained administration. In a cohort of 374 patients receiving initial HD-MTX, moderate/severe DILI was the outcome modeled, with female gender, ABCB1 rs1128503 genotype, SLCO1B1 haplotypes, and MTX dosage identified as independent factors.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric/young-adult patients with malignant tumors (ALL, CNS tumors, NHL, osteosarcoma); high-dose MTX (above 20 mg/kg or 500 mg/m2) administration, which the authors explicitly note is a therapeutic dose.
raw_record.extra_details: HD-MTX is described as presenting a potentially lethal risk including DILI. Study of 374 patients with initial HD-MTX; moderate/severe DILI outcome. G allele of ABCB1 rs1128503, *1b/*1b and *1b/*15 haplotypes of SLCO1B1, female gender, and MTX dosage were independent factors for moderate/severe DILI. Predictive model ROC AUC = 0.805 including 24h MTX concentration. Patients with GA/AA genotype of ABCB1 rs1128503 had higher 24h MTX concentration than GG; SLCO1B1 *1b/*1b group had lower dose-adjusted concentration than *1a/*1a; IV plus triple intrathecal route gave higher C/D than IV alone. Mechanism/relevant genes: ABCB1 and SLCO1B1 (folic acid cycle transporters/enzymes).

raw_record.support_text: A 53-year-old woman being treated for B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia received a high-dose course of methotrexate (MTX) infused intravenously in less than 2 h instead of 24 h because the patient accidentally increased the infusion rate, constituting a high-dose MTX intoxication. In the aftermath, her alanine aminotransferase rose to 114 UI/L (~5x upper limit of normal) at h48 and her total bilirubin rose to 104 µmol/L by J4, alongside nausea/vomiting, oliguria, rising creatinine (up to 398 µmol/L), and pancytopenia; hemofiltration was started at J5. The paper frames this as an accidental high-dose MTX intoxication rather than explicitly labeling the hepatic abnormalities as hepatotoxicity or DILI.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Accidental overdose resulting from shortening of a 24 h intravenous infusion to less than 2 h (increase of infusion rate by the patient); single case in a 53-year-old woman with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia; co-administered tienam, amikacine, purinéthol, and folinic acid rescue.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of high-dose methotrexate intoxication. ALT 114 UI/L (~5x ULN) at h48, ~1.5x at J3, 24 UI at J4; total bilirubin 41 µmol/L at J3 and 104 µmol/L at J4 (ULN <17 µmol/L); methotrexate levels 99, 89, and 93 µmol/L at h48/J3/J4; creatinine rose from 65 to 398 µmol/L; oliguria; pancytopenia (platelets 42 G/L, hemoglobin 73 g/L, leukocytes 0.8 G/L); hemofiltration initiated at J5; folinic acid rescue increased to 50 then 200 mg/m²/6h. The paper describes the event as MTX intoxication with renal, marrow, mucocutaneous and digestive toxicity; it does not explicitly discuss the liver enzyme/bilirubin elevations as hepatotoxicity or DILI.

raw_record.support_text: The case report concludes that severe and life-threatening complications, including acute liver failure and acute kidney injury, can arise from high-dose methotrexate administration. Extracorporeal treatments such as CRRT and MARS, along with glucarpidase therapy, were used to manage methotrexate toxicity and facilitate recovery of renal and hepatic function. Earlier text discusses determining best extracorporeal therapies for methotrexate clearance and notes a falsely elevated immunoassay methotrexate level of 900 µmol/L at 48 h versus a specific HPLC-based measurement of 3.87 µmol/L.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose (overdose/supratherapeutic) methotrexate administration in the setting of renal insufficiency; hepatocellular insufficiency present in the patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Methotrexate intoxication led to acute liver failure and acute kidney injury. Immunoassay-based methotrexate measurement at 48 h gave a falsely elevated level of 900 µmol/L (due to cross-reactivity with metabolites, not measurable by immunoassay up to 48 h after glucarpidase use); specific HPLC measured 3.87 µmol/L. Management included glucarpidase, extracorporeal therapies (CRRT/CVVHDF and MARS), with rebound effect observed after cessation of CVVHDF. Patient recovered renal and hepatic function.

raw_record.support_text: This case series describes seven psoriasis patients with acute methotrexate toxicity resulting from overdosing of methotrexate. The acute cumulative dose of methotrexate ranged from 35 mg to 150 mg taken over 3–7 days and was responsible for acute toxicity, which included deranged liver function (hepatotoxicity). All cases presented with ulceration, bleeding and pain in skin lesions; five had oral mucosal ulceration and two had genital mucosal involvement. Five cases recovered and two expired after receiving injectable folinic acid.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure in psoriasis patients: acute cumulative methotrexate dose 35–150 mg taken over 3–7 days. Case 1 co-ingested paracetamol and diclofenac with methotrexate for joint pain; cases 5 and 6 were alcoholic, and both expired.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven cases (6 male, 1 female; ages 35–57 years). Deranged liver function tests included SGOT up to 510 U/L and SGPT up to 420 U/L (normal 0–37 and 0–40 U/L). Two cases died due to grossly deranged liver function tests, renal function tests and pancytopenia leading to septicaemia; the other five recovered. Serum methotrexate levels (available in cases 2,3,4,5,7) ranged 0.21–97 μmol/L. Acute methotrexate toxicity is attributed to inhibition of DNA synthesis in rapidly proliferating cells, with higher doses causing deranged liver function, lowered blood counts and skin/mucosal necrosis. All patients treated with intravenous folinic acid (leucovorin) 20 mg 6-hourly then 10 mg 6-hourly until counts normalized. No patients had pre-existing renal or hepatic disease.

raw_record.support_text: A 51-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate and prednisone presented with altered mental status, jaundice, and mucosal ulceration. She was admitted to the ICU for septic shock in the setting of severe pancytopenia, acute renal failure, and acute liver failure, presented as a case of methotrexate toxicity (acute liver failure attributed to methotrexate).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting: patient took methotrexate 15 mg daily instead of the prescribed 15 mg once weekly; competing factors include daily alcohol use in the setting of alcohol use disorder, septic shock, and concurrent prednisone use.
raw_record.extra_details: 51-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis; presented with altered mental status, jaundice (scleral icterus), and oral mucosal ulceration; admitted to ICU for septic shock with severe pancytopenia and acute renal failure in addition to acute liver failure. Paper notes methotrexate toxicity can occur at doses higher than 500 mg/m2 and that long-term methotrexate use can lead to hepatic toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Patient C, a 37-year-old male with acute exacerbation of dermatomyositis/polymyositis, was initially treated with high dose prednisone, methotrexate (MTX) 15 mg/wk im, and cyclosporine 4 mg/kg/day. MTX was suspended after a month's time because of hepatotoxicity, while cyclosporine was suspended after 2 weeks for renal failure and arterial hypertension and prednisone was tapered. Thus the hepatotoxicity that led to MTX discontinuation is attributed to methotrexate.
raw_record.extra_details: MTX dosing 15 mg/wk intramuscular; suspended after approximately one month due to hepatotoxicity in a 37-year-old male with dermatomyositis/polymyositis. Patient was also receiving prednisone and cyclosporine; cyclosporine was discontinued for renal failure/hypertension, not liver injury, leaving MTX as the attributed hepatotoxic agent.

raw_record.support_text: A 51-year-old woman with severe rheumatoid arthritis and insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, on weekly intramuscular methotrexate (increased from 7.5 mg to 15.0 mg), developed cirrhosis (Roenigk grade IV) on repeat liver biopsy when cumulative MTX reached 1,300 mg; MTX was then discontinued and she showed no deterioration in hepatic function over the following year. The paper frames this as MTX hepatotoxicity, and the patient had no other hepatotoxic medications (diabetes precluded prednisone, and azathioprine was refused).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had pre-existing liver abnormality (baseline liver biopsy Roenigk grade IIIA), poorly controlled insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, and severe rheumatoid arthritis; treated concurrently with salsalate; weekly intramuscular dosing.
raw_record.extra_details: 51-year-old woman with 16-year history of severe seropositive erosive nodular RA and 7-year history of poorly controlled IDDM; no alcohol abuse. Prior unsuccessful therapy with intramuscular gold and D-penicillamine; offered azathioprine but refused; no prednisone due to IDDM. MTX started at 7.5 mg intramuscularly weekly and increased to 15.0 mg; monthly liver enzymes and albumin remained normal although alkaline phosphatase and gamma glutamic acid were persistently elevated. Cirrhosis (Roenigk IV) confirmed on second biopsy at cumulative MTX dose 1,300 mg; MTX discontinued with no deterioration in hepatic function over the past year.

raw_record.support_text: Liver toxicity assessed in 21 patients with rheumatoid arthritis and four others receiving long-term low-dose weekly methotrexate revealed acute hepatitis in one patient and elevated transaminase levels in 12 (48 percent). Liver biopsy in 17 patients after a mean cumulative dose of 1,950 mg of methotrexate (range 915 to 3,125 mg) showed mild fibrosis in six and no cirrhosis. The authors conclude that hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis due to methotrexate may be less common in rheumatoid arthritis than has been reported in psoriasis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with rheumatoid arthritis receiving long-term low-dose weekly methotrexate (7.5-25 mg/week, oral or intramuscular); no cirrhosis was found; hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis judged possibly less common in rheumatoid arthritis than in psoriasis.
raw_record.extra_details: 21 patients originally enrolled, 15 continued for mean 42 months (mean cumulative dose 2,021 mg, range 915-3,705 mg). Liver biopsy in 17 patients after mean 1,950 mg (range 915-3,125 mg): mild fibrosis in 6, no cirrhosis. Acute hepatitis in 1 patient; elevated transaminases in 12 patients (48%). Transaminases monitored every 4-8 weeks during therapy.

raw_record.support_text: In a postal survey of U.K. consultant dermatologists documenting methotrexate prescribing and monitoring practice, 12% of respondents reported experience of patients developing irreversible liver damage (severity not defined) attributable to methotrexate therapy. Among 49 reported deaths in methotrexate-treated patients, two were due to liver failure in the absence of reported alcohol consumption.
raw_record.extra_details: Documented in a postal questionnaire sent to all 531 consultant members of the British Association of Dermatologists (January 2004; 71% response rate) describing methotrexate prescribing/monitoring practice. 12% of respondents reported patients developing irreversible liver damage (severity not defined). Of 49 deaths reported, 18 were due to myelosuppression, six to possible pulmonary fibrosis, two to liver failure in the absence of reported alcohol consumption, and four as a consequence of liver biopsy. Methotrexate described as potentially toxic; monitoring of liver function tests and aminoterminal peptide of type III procollagen commonly performed.

raw_record.support_text: Methotrexate, an antineoplastic and immunosuppressive agent used in therapy for leukemia, lymphoma and several solid tumors, can lead to acute elevations in serum liver enzymes and, in some cases, development of chronic liver injury, progressive fibrosis, cirrhosis and portal hypertension. In this study the damage caused was moderate, though some individuals displayed a clear cholestatic phenotype.
raw_record.extra_details: Antineoplastic and immunosuppressive agent used in leukemia, lymphoma and several solid tumors. Can lead to acute elevations in serum liver enzymes and, in some cases, chronic liver injury, progressive fibrosis, cirrhosis and portal hypertension. In this study the damage was moderate, with some individuals showing a clear cholestatic phenotype.

raw_record.support_text: DILI-inducing antineoplastics were methotrexate, nedaplatin, cisplatin, carboplatin, pemetrexed, gefitinib and imatinib; antineoplastics accounted for 13 patients (3.07%) of DILI cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Antineoplastic; antineoplastics accounted for 13 patients (3.07%) of DILI cases.

raw_record.support_text: In the cohort of 103 patients receiving 2 courses of high-dose methotrexate (HD-MTX), hepatic toxicity was the most frequent toxicity, occurring in 36 patients (35%), mainly as an increase in blood liver enzymes. Among these, 14 were grade I, 14 grade II, and 8 grade III, with no grade IV hepatic toxicities. Hepatic toxicity occurred mainly after the first cycle (32/36, 89%), and 4 patients had hepatic toxicity after both cycles, including 1 with grade III after both. All hepatic toxicities were reversible within less than 15 days.
raw_record.extra_details: High-dose methotrexate (HD-MTX) chemotherapy given over 2 courses totaling 195 cycles in 103 patients. Hepatic toxicity in 36/103 (35%) patients, mainly increased blood liver enzymes; 14 grade I, 14 grade II, 8 grade III, none grade IV. Mainly after cycle 1 (32/36, 89%); 4 patients affected after both cycles (1 grade III in both). All hepatic toxicities reversible within less than 15 days. Hepatic toxicity was the most frequent of all toxicities reported.

raw_record.support_text: In partitioned analysis of liver biopsy samples from MTX-exposed versus nonexposed individuals, functional pathway analysis identified upregulation in 35 of 42 fatty acid modification genes and elevations in genes associated with mitochondrial fatty acid elongation. Pathology reports indicated that at least 70% of biopsy samples displayed the fatty metamorphosis commonly associated with MTX hepatotoxicity, and gene expression related to triacylglycerol synthesis was upregulated.
raw_record.extra_details: 27 patients (18 psoriatic, 9 nonpsoriatic) with rheumatic diseases including psoriasis, lupus, RA, psoriatic arthritis, UDCTD/CREST, polymyositis, or Sjogren's syndrome; liver pathology ranged Roenigk Grade I (n=12), Grade II (n=14), Grade III (n=3). MTX exposure duration 2-17 years, cumulative dose 1.5-12.6 g; 29 MTX-exposed samples vs 10 controls. Upregulation of fatty acid modification genes (p=0.000079, FET), fatty acid elongation (p=0.0055), triacylglycerol synthesis (p=0.012); AGPAT3 and PPAP2B validated by qPCR. Histology showed striking steatosis (clear regions) at Grade II and III.

raw_record.support_text: Among 189 RA patients on methotrexate (MTX) at baseline, 51 underwent MTX dose de-escalation or discontinuation during follow-up; recorded reasons for MTX tapering/stopping included hepatotoxicity (n=10). Additionally, hepatotoxicity (n=20) was reported among the reasons for failure to use MTX at baseline in RA patients treated with adalimumab or etanercept. The paper thus documents hepatotoxicity as a reason for MTX non-use, dose reduction, or discontinuation in this human cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: MTX given parenterally (76.2%) or orally (23.8%) at median 10 mg/wk (IQR 7.5-12.5) in RA patients on TNF inhibitors (adalimumab or etanercept). Hepatotoxicity was a reason for baseline non-use of MTX (n=20) and for MTX dose de-escalation/discontinuation during follow-up (n=10); other reasons included intolerance, disease remission, poor compliance, alopecia, thrombocytopenia, surgery, and recurrent infections.

raw_record.support_text: Patients in this randomized RA treatment-strategy trial withdrew due to MTX-related adverse events including liver toxicity (n=6 in the intensive group vs n=1 in the conventional group). Hepatic adverse events were reported in 55% of intensive-group vs 35% of conventional-group patients (p=0.001). The paper explicitly attributes these liver-toxicity withdrawals to methotrexate (MTX-related AE).
raw_record.extra_details: In rheumatoid-arthritis patients on standard MTX therapy comparing intensive vs conventional treatment strategy. Withdrawal due to MTX-related liver toxicity occurred in 6/149 I-group and 1/140 C-group patients; hepatic adverse-event percentage was 55% (I) vs 35% (C), p=0.001. There was no association between strategy group and withdrawal due to MTX-related AEs (OR=1.985, 95% CI 0.82-4.80, p=0.128). AEs were mostly mild.

raw_record.support_text: In this case report of a 69-year-old man with a progenitor cell leukemia (acute lymphocytic leukemia), maintenance therapy was discontinued after 6 months secondary to methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Maintenance therapy for acute lymphocytic leukemia was discontinued after 6 months because of the hepatotoxicity. No biochemical, histologic, or latency details are provided in the abstract.

raw_record.support_text: A 69-year-old man with poorly differentiated acute lymphocytic leukemia received induction therapy in November 1998 achieving complete remission; consolidation therapy was discontinued after one cycle due to severe cytopenias, and maintenance therapy was discontinued after 6 months secondary to methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported in a single 69-year-old man with acute lymphocytic leukemia; maintenance therapy was discontinued after 6 months because of the methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity, without further characterization of the liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: Adverse effects reported only for the conservative-treatment group included reversible hepatotoxicity due to oral methotrexate in 1/16 (6%) participants (also mucositis due to oral methotrexate in 3/16 (19%) participants), cutaneous hypersensitivity to mechlorethamine, and cutaneous toxicity to methoxsalen and UVA. This is from the Kaye 1989 trial, reported within a Cochrane systematic review.
raw_record.extra_details: Reversible hepatotoxicity due to oral methotrexate occurred in 1/16 (6%) participants in the conservative-treatment arm of the Kaye 1989 trial, reported for treatment of mycosis fungoides (consistent with oral methotrexate use). Methotrexate-associated mucositis was reported separately in 3/16 (19%) participants.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that a considerable number of RA patients do not tolerate long-term treatment with methotrexate (MTX) due to toxicity to the liver, the lungs, the haemopoietic system and other organs. In the comparative trial, 'Liver and biliary system disorders' were reported in 11/13 MTX-treated patients (8 mild, 0 moderate, 3 severe; two cases were not rated for severity), whereas no such disorders were reported with CPH 82.
raw_record.extra_details: MTX given at 10 mg/week for rheumatoid arthritis. Trial adverse-event table reports 'Liver and biliary system disorders' in 11/13 MTX-treated patients (8 mild, 0 moderate, 3 severe); two cases were not rated for severity of the hepatic function disorder. The paper frames liver toxicity as a well-documented reason patients discontinue long-term MTX; folic acid supplementation may reduce side-effects.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective cohort of patients on low-dose MTX, 279 patients experienced hepatotoxicity, an incidence rate of 35.68%. Risk factors for hepatotoxicity associated with low-dose MTX were analyzed, and Random Forest was selected to predict the hepatotoxicity associated with low-dose MTX (AUC 0.97), framing MTX as the cause of the liver injury of interest.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective cohort of patients taking low-dose MTX; 279/782 (35.68%) experienced hepatotoxicity. Random Forest model (AUC 0.97) was selected to predict MTX-associated hepatotoxicity. Risk factors analyzed included BMI, age, number of drugs, number of comorbidities, antibiotics use, male gender, alcohol use, infectious liver disease, dyslipidemia, kidney disease history, folic acid dose, type 2 diabetes, first-time MTX use, other immunosuppressive agents, and Chinese patent medicines. Hepatotoxicity severity (e.g., liver-test thresholds defining the outcome) was not reported in the provided text.

raw_record.support_text: Methotrexate (MTX) is an effective systemic antipsoriatic agent but needs monitoring because it carries a risk of liver fibrosis; the text states that the concerns of MTX-related hepatotoxicity are real, with serial liver biopsies considered the gold standard for monitoring patients for liver fibrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective clinical audit of 65 patients with moderate to severe psoriasis on long-term MTX (1999-2003); 278.9 patient-MTX years, mean cumulative dose 2000 (SD 1838) mg, mean duration 4.3 (SD 3.9) years. Of 30 liver biopsies (graded by Roenigk classification, Tru-Cut needle, ultrasound-guided), 26 (86.6%) showed normal histology or mild to moderate steatosis, 3 had focal fibrosis, and 1 had early (stage 4) cirrhosis. Higher cumulative MTX dose correlated significantly with high mean (>4.2 µg/l) P3NP levels (p=0.002) and with maximum P3NP levels (p=0.03); median P3NP >5.8 µg/l correlated with histological severity. Mild-to-moderate steatosis was noted not to be specific for MTX toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Among 124 patients with features of idiosyncratic drug-induced acute liver failure (ALF) in this prospective nationwide DILI study from India, the principal drug classes causing ALF included methotrexate (N = 1; 0.8%).
raw_record.extra_details: 1 of 124 idiosyncratic drug-induced ALF cases (0.8%) was attributed to methotrexate in a prospective nationwide DILI cohort.

raw_record.support_text: Nine of the 68 primary-role DILI fatality cases died of chronic liver failure more than 26 weeks after DILI onset. Methotrexate, known to cause an insidious fibrosis, accounted for one of these chronic liver failure fatalities.
raw_record.extra_details: Methotrexate is described as known to cause insidious fibrosis leading to chronic liver failure; it accounted for one of 68 primary-role DILI fatalities in the DILIN cohort, with death occurring more than 26 weeks after DILI onset.

raw_record.support_text: A case report described diffuse accumulation of 99mTc-MDP in the liver of a patient with methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity; the authors postulated that inhibition of protein synthesis by methotrexate disrupted the cell membrane, allowing calcium influx and high-affinity MDP binding to calcium.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report (Flynn & Treves 1987) of methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity causing diffuse liver uptake of 99mTc-MDP; proposed mechanism of protein-synthesis inhibition leading to membrane disruption and calcium ingress.

raw_record.support_text: In case 30 (BM, 57-year-old male with carcinoma of the larynx), methotrexate therapy was associated with clinical toxicity recorded as 'Oral severe NV, hepatic,' and the authors noted 'Probable liver toxicity, biopsy-focal necrosis and mild acute inflammation.' The patient was alive with progressive disease 121 days after starting MTX.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 30: 57-year-old male with laryngeal carcinoma treated for head/neck cancer; MTX 96 mg (60 mg/sq m) weekly, total 264 mg over 14 days; clinical toxicity described as severe oral, nausea/vomiting and 'hepatic'; liver biopsy showed focal necrosis and mild acute inflammation; the episode was characterized by the authors as 'Probable liver toxicity' and was not fatal (patient alive, tumor progressing, 121 days after start of MTX).

raw_record.support_text: One case each of liver transplantation for suspected drug-induced liver injury was associated with apresoline, dextropropoxiphen and methotrexate with a probable causal relationship.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case among 17 transplant patients with a probable causal relationship.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses the mechanism by which MTX (methotrexate) causes hepatotoxicity and concludes the hepatic malfunction is probably due to a direct toxic action of the drug because most patients are affected and the reaction is dose dependent, arguing against genetic variations or hypersensitivity. Histologic findings approximate mild drug-induced hepatitis without cholestasis.
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism involves binding dihydrofolic reductase, blocking conversion of folic acid to folinic acid and nucleic acid/protein synthesis; direct toxic action assessed as dose dependent with most patients affected; 22 patients studied, only 4 transfused during the 6 months prior; bilirubinemia in only 2 patients and bile stasis in only 2; histology described as mild drug-induced hepatitis without cholestasis (anicteric hepatitis) per Popper, not induced by an immunologic reaction.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 80 DILI patients (42 men; median age 38) at a tertiary care hospital in India, causality was assessed with the Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM). DILI was caused by a single prescription medication in 30%, by complementary/alternative medicine in 12%, and by multiple prescription agents in 58% of cases. Most commonly implicated drugs were antitubercular drugs (42%), antiepileptic drugs (16%), antiretroviral drugs (12%), methotrexate (6%), and other drugs including atorvastatin, paracetamol, etoposide, diclofenac, interferon and thalidomide (2% each). 4% of patients died due to liver disease; 52% had jaundice.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as cause in 6% of 80 DILI cases (about 5 patients) in an Indian tertiary-care DILI cohort with RUCAM-based causality assessment; median duration of therapy for the cohort 31.5 days; hospital mortality 4% (not drug-specific).

raw_record.support_text: In this cohort of 65 patients with suspected DILI at an Indian tertiary care hospital, causality was assessed with RUCAM. DILI was caused by a single prescription medication in 28%, by complementary/alternative medicine in 9%, and by multiple prescription agents in 63% of cases. Among the drugs implicated, methotrexate accounted for 5% of cases and other specifically named drugs (paracetamol, etoposide, interferon, itraconazole and thalidomide) together accounted for 8%.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among the most commonly implicated drugs in a cohort of 65 DILI patients (methotrexate 5%); median duration of therapy 31 days (range 1-184 days); 34 patients had jaundice (52.3%); overall mortality 10.7% (7 patients) with 3 deaths (4.6%) attributed to liver disease, not specified per drug.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatic toxicity was attributed to MTX in a trial: one patient developed cirrhosis (with serum transaminase elevations and a low serum albumin level 10 months before the cirrhosis diagnosis), one had recurrent serum transaminase elevations and refused liver biopsy, so MTX was discontinued, and one had persistent serum transaminase elevations, a low serum albumin value, and moderate to severe hepatic necrosis on liver biopsy. The paper notes rigorous monitoring is needed to identify patients at risk for serious liver disease and that 6.5% of patients withdrew from the study due to adverse events attributed to MTX.
raw_record.extra_details: MTX given over a period of several years; three cases of hepatic toxicity reported, including one cirrhosis case (transaminase elevations 1-2x normal and low serum albumin 10 months prior), one case with recurrent transaminase elevations who refused biopsy and had MTX discontinued, and one with persistent transaminase elevations, low serum albumin, and moderate to severe hepatic necrosis on biopsy; 6.5% of patients withdrew due to adverse events attributed to MTX; commentary notes American College of Rheumatology guidelines could have led to earlier recognition of this toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A 69-year-old man with a history of progenitor cell acute lymphocytic leukemia received induction and consolidation therapy for his leukemia. Consolidation therapy was discontinued after one cycle due to severe cytopenias, and maintenance therapy was discontinued after 6 months secondary to methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity. The paper explicitly frames hepatotoxicity as induced by methotrexate in this single human patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity occurred during maintenance therapy for acute lymphocytic leukemia and led to discontinuation of maintenance therapy after 6 months. No dose, latency, or specific severity details are provided.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that three patients presented with several hepatic comorbidities and demonstrated deterioration of general clinical condition when treated with hepatotoxic therapies such as methotrexate and isoniazid, explicitly characterizing methotrexate as hepatotoxic.
raw_record.extra_details: Labeled as a hepatotoxic therapy in the case series; three patients with hepatic comorbidities treated with methotrexate and isoniazid showed deterioration of general clinical condition.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of 53 human DILI cases with liver biopsy, methotrexate was listed among the causative DILI drugs in the immunomodulator/immunosuppressor category, with a necroinflammatory (N) histological pattern. It was also among the drugs related to ANA positivity in one DILI case (p:39).
raw_record.extra_details: Histological pattern: necroinflammatory (N). One of 53 biopsy-confirmed DILI cases in the series.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective review of methotrexate treatment, elevation of liver enzymes occurred in 13 patients and was the most common adverse event; in 4 patients enzymes were chronically elevated during therapy. Liver biopsies in 3 of these patients showed grade II portal fibrosis in one patient who had received a high cumulative dose of methotrexate. In a separate prospective study of 21 patients, 7 had transient elevations of liver transaminases and 1 developed acute 'hypersensitivity' hepatitis, leading to discontinuation of methotrexate.
raw_record.extra_details: Low-dose weekly methotrexate used for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis in adults. One series of 87 patients reported 13 occurrences of elevated AST/ALT with drug discontinued in 3 (mean cumulative dose 1058 mg, range 90-3722 mg; mean weekly dose 7.85 mg); 1 case of hepatic fibrosis at a mean cumulative dose of 3875 mg. Liver biopsy in one patient showed grade II portal fibrosis. Acute 'hypersensitivity' hepatitis occurring in the first few weeks of treatment was reported in one prospective patient (Weinstein et al. 1985) and led to drug discontinuation; the authors state they did not personally encounter this problem. Elevated AST/ALT was the most common adverse event, generally manageable by dose adjustment.

raw_record.support_text: Among 92 patients treated with single-agent methotrexate for low-risk metastatic gestational trophoblastic tumors, methotrexate toxicity occurred in 36 patients (39.1%), and none of the toxic effects was life threatening. Mild neutropenia, hepatotoxicity, and rash were occasionally encountered. Per the toxicity table, hepatotoxicity occurred in 3 patients, and chemotherapy was changed because of toxic reaction in all 3 hepatotoxicity cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 3 of 92 patients with low-risk metastatic gestational trophoblastic tumors treated with single-agent methotrexate developed hepatotoxicity; toxicity was mild and not life threatening; chemotherapy was changed to actinomycin D because of the toxic reaction in all 3 hepatotoxicity cases.

raw_record.support_text: Among patients treated with methotrexate (MTX) for thyroid-related eye disease, several reported minor gastrointestinal upset but only 5% (1 patient) needed to discontinue the medication because of hepatic toxicity, which normalized after discontinuation; no major complications were noted. The paper also notes that elevated liver enzymes, fatigue, and nausea have been reported as the most common MTX side effects, usually occurring within 3 months of treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: 1 of 20 patients (5%) in the cohort discontinued MTX due to hepatic toxicity that normalized after discontinuation (positive dechallenge). MTX used for active thyroid-related eye disease (TRO). Elevated liver enzymes, fatigue, and nausea cited as the most common MTX side effects, typically appearing within 3 months of treatment.

raw_record.support_text: In a 69-year-old man treated for poorly differentiated acute lymphocytic leukemia, maintenance therapy was discontinued after 6 months secondary to methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity. The patient had previously been treated with induction and one cycle of consolidation therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Methotrexate hepatotoxicity occurred during maintenance therapy in an adult with acute lymphocytic leukemia and required discontinuation of maintenance therapy after 6 months. Mentioned only as an aside in a case report of Langerhans cell histiocytosis following acute lymphocytic leukemia.

raw_record.support_text: In this comparative clinical trial of low-risk gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, hepatotoxicity was reported as a common toxic effect of methotrexate treatment: it occurred in 31/59 patients in the 8-day methotrexate-folinic acid (MTX-FA) regimen and 9/48 patients in the weekly methotrexate regimen (50 mg/m² without dose escalation). Drug toxicity necessitated changing chemotherapy in 13.6% (8/59) of the MTX-FA group and 2.1% (1/48) of the MTX group.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity counts: 31/59 in the 8-day methotrexate-folinic acid regimen and 9/48 in the weekly methotrexate regimen (50 mg/m², no dose escalation) for low-risk GTN. Comparison of weekly vs 8-day MTX-FA regimens in a single-institution trial of 107 patients; weekly regimen reported less toxic and better tolerated. Hepatotoxicity drug-necessitated change in chemotherapy.

raw_record.support_text: A 28-year-old mestizo man with inflammatory arthritis and sicca symptoms was started on methotrexate, which achieved a good response, but one year later methotrexate was changed to leflunomide because of liver toxicity, attributing the drug-related liver injury to methotrexate in this patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Methotrexate was given with a good response and was switched to leflunomide after one year because of liver toxicity. The patient had positive anti-double-stranded DNA and anti-nucleosome antibodies and an inflammatory-arthritis/sicca presentation.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 154 DILI patients, methotrexate was one of six drugs with more than 5 cases analyzed specifically and showed 9 significant test differences.
raw_record.extra_details: Methotrexate DILI cases had very mild differences compared with normal test ranges; significant differences were expected versus the drugs with the most severe profiles (APAP highest ALT, flupirtine highest bilirubin).

raw_record.support_text: In 273 Caucasian RA patients treated with methotrexate (MTX), MTX-related hepatotoxicity and alopecia were more common in patients with the RFC-1 80AA genotype (OR 3.5, P=0.01; OR 2.4, P=0.04, respectively). The MTHFR 677T allele was associated with increased activity of aminotransferases (OR 3.4, P=0.02). Adverse effects leading to MTX withdrawal occurred in 17% of patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Study population: 273 Caucasian rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patients treated with MTX for at least 6 months or stopped because of adverse effects. MTX-related hepatotoxicity more frequent with the RFC-1 c.80G>A 80AA genotype (OR 3.5; P=0.01). MTHFR c.677C>T 677T allele associated with increased aminotransferase activity (OR 3.4; P=0.02). Adverse effects reported by 53% of patients and led to MTX withdrawal in 17%.

raw_record.support_text: Patients with leukemia or histiocytosis X in complete remission were studied by sequential liver function tests and percutaneous liver biopsies (light and electron microscopy) during methotrexate treatment. Hepatomegaly usually developed, yet fibrosis appeared even without hepatosplenomegaly or abnormal liver function. Initially hepatocellular changes were seen by light microscopy, progressing to portal inflammation and fibrosis with continued therapy. Ultrastructural changes included double-nucleated hepatic cells, mitochondrial swelling, and dilatation of the endoplasmic reticulum. The authors conclude that (1) liver biopsy is the only accurate way to follow the extent of liver damage, (2) discontinuation of therapy can result in a return toward normal structure, and (3) the pathologic changes are secondary to methotrexate therapy, not the basic disease process.
raw_record.extra_details: Sequential liver biopsies (light and electron microscopy) in patients with leukemia or histiocytosis X in complete remission during methotrexate treatment. Hepatomegaly developed in 8 of 11 patients at the time of methotrexate toxicity (absent before starting therapy); fibrosis was found in the absence of hepatosplenomegaly or abnormal liver function and persisted even after physical findings and liver function returned to normal. Histologic progression from hepatocellular changes to portal inflammation and fibrosis with continued therapy; ultrastructural changes included double-nucleated hepatic cells with minor nucleolar changes and decreased perichromatin, variable fat and glycogen content, mitochondrial swelling, dilatation of endoplasmic reticulum, and sinusoidal filament-collagen-basement membrane formation. Authors conclude liver biopsy is the only accurate way to follow extent of liver damage, discontinuation of therapy can result in return toward normal structure, and changes are secondary to methotrexate therapy rather than the underlying disease. Note: hepatic toxicity is insidious, an important consideration given methotrexate is pursued in nonmalignant conditions such as skin disorders and immunologic diseases.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of patients receiving MTX, hepatic toxicity was the most frequently observed toxicity, with grade 3-4 hepatic toxicity occurring in 25 patients (32%). No deaths due to toxicity occurred, while grade 3-4 hematological, mucosal, and renal toxicities were seen in 13 (17%), 4 (5.1%), and 2 (2.6%) patients respectively.
raw_record.extra_details: Grade 3-4 hepatic toxicity occurred in 25 of 78 patients (32%), the most frequent toxicity; 49 patients (64%) had at least one grade 1-4 toxicity; no deaths from toxicity. Median creatinine clearance at MTX administration was 89.1 mL/min/1.73m2; only one patient had CLcr < 60. The SLCO1B1 c.388A>G and c.521T>C polymorphisms were not significantly associated with grade 3-4 hepatic toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Dr. Mackenzie reported on about 90 patients treated for over five years with methotrexate who had repeated liver biopsies. No excess of tumors was detected, and at the doses used and manner of administration the liver changes were very mild—a small amount of fibrosis but not progressive liver disease, no cirrhosis, and no liver failure. A couple of patients had chronic active hepatitis, and a possible correlation between Sjögren's syndrome and hepatic lesions was noted.
raw_record.extra_details: Approximately 90 patients treated for more than five years with low-dose methotrexate who had repeated liver biopsies. Findings: very mild liver changes with a small amount of fibrosis but not progressive liver disease, no cirrhosis, and no liver failure; no excess of tumors; a couple of patients with chronic active hepatitis; possible correlation between Sjögren's syndrome and hepatic lesions. Dr. Zvaifler commented that patients who have trouble with low-dose methotrexate appear to be those with decreased renal function (adequate renal function should be ensured).

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity is considered the most serious effect limiting long-term use of low-dose MTX; hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis have been reported in psoriatic patients on prolonged MTX therapy, and serious hepatotoxicity has also been described in RA patients treated with MTX. In the authors' own RA cohort, nonserious hepatotoxicity with portal round cell infiltrates and mild portal fibrosis was found in 41 patients who underwent percutaneous liver biopsy after a cumulative MTX dose of 1550.5 ± 235.5 mg; side effects resolved without sequelae on discontinuation.

In the paper's own cohort, nonserious hepatotoxicity was found; 15 of ~136 patients (11%) discontinued therapy due to various side effects but resolved without sequelae.

raw_record.support_text: In a study comparing methotrexate with cyclosporine in 88 psoriasis patients, methotrexate was started orally at 15 mg/week (split into three 12-hourly portions, per Weinstein/Frost schedule) and increased to 22.5 mg after four weeks if no PASI25 response was achieved; no folic acid was given. After 16 weeks 60% of methotrexate-treated patients achieved PASI75, but methotrexate had to be discontinued in 12 of 43 patients due to hepatotoxicity. raw_record.support_text: In a post-hoc analysis of a randomized controlled trial in rheumatoid arthritis patients treated with methotrexate (MTX), hepatotoxicity leading to MTX withdrawal was associated with absence of folate supplementation and high body mass index. raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity was defined as ALT >3x ULN (table footnote). Severe hepatotoxicity occurred in 36/137 (26%) of the placebo group vs 11/274 (4%) of the folate group; with BMI 20-25 hepatotoxicity occurred in 16/190 (8%) and with BMI 30-35 in 10/51 (20%). Univariate OR for folate supplementation 0.12 (0.06-0.24), multivariate OR 0.10 (0.04-0.21); BMI multivariate OR 1.09 (1.01-1.17) per unit. MTX was withdrawn in 126 patients, 91 due to toxicity. raw_record.support_text: The paper states that an increase in liver enzymes is common in rheumatoid arthritis patients on methotrexate (MTX), though these elevations are often mild and do not require discontinuation of treatment. In the authors' cohort only two patients (0.3%) discontinued MTX for hepatotoxicity, one of whom continued treatment after a successful rechallenge. An analysis of 3808 RA patients treated an average of 55.8 months in 27 prospective studies found that 769 (20.2%) had at least one episode of raised liver enzyme and only 3.7% stopped MTX because of liver toxicity; another series (Khabbazi et al.) reported liver enzyme elevation in 108/809 (13.3%) patients, with only 0.5% requiring permanent MTX discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Relationship framed for MTX used at therapeutic doses for rheumatoid arthritis. Liver enzyme (ALT) elevation is common but usually mild and often does not require stopping therapy; discontinuation for hepatotoxicity was rare (0.3% in the present study; 3.7% across 27 prospective studies of 3808 RA patients with 20.2% having at least one raised liver enzyme episode). One of two patients in the present study who stopped for hepatotoxicity resumed MTX after a successful rechallenge. Other studies cited: Khabbazi et al. 809 patients (13.3% liver enzyme elevation; 0.5% permanent discontinuation), Bologna et al. 56/452 (12.4%) with elevated liver enzymes leading to 63 (13.9%) discontinuing for toxicity. No acute liver failure, transplantation, or death attributed to MTX liver injury in this article.

raw_record.support_text: In osteosarcoma patients receiving high-dose methotrexate (MTX) chemotherapy, MTX-induced hepatic toxicity was graded: 61 patients had grade 1-2 and 48 had grade 3-4 hepatic toxicity. Patients with severe (grade 3-4) hepatic toxicity had a remarkably higher incidence of the MTHFR rs1801133 TT genotype than those with mild toxicity (33.3% vs 14.8%, p=0.04), and the T allele added 1.98-fold risk (95% CI 1.15-3.41, p=0.01) for severe hepatic toxicity. MTX concentration at 72 h was also significantly related to the severity of hepatic toxicity (0.20 ± 0.26 vs 0.13 ± 0.05 μmol/L, p=0.03).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Children and adults (10-65 years) with osteosarcoma; high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy regimen given for therapeutic treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: 109 patients treated; hepatic toxicity graded by CTCAE (grade 1-2, n=61; grade 3-4, n=48). Severe hepatic toxicity (grade 3-4) more frequent in MTHFR rs1801133 (C677T) TT genotype carriers (33.3% vs 14.8%, p=0.04); T allele OR 1.98 (95% CI 1.15-3.41, p=0.01). MTX plasma level at 72 h higher in severe hepatic toxicity group (0.20 ± 0.26 vs 0.13 ± 0.05 μmol/L, p=0.03). No association of rs1801133 with hematological or renal toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A cohort of 109 Chinese osteosarcoma patients who sequentially received high-dose methotrexate (MTX) therapy was studied. The extent of MTX-induced toxicity, including hematological toxicity, hepatic toxicity, renal toxicity and mucositis, was scored from grade 1 to 4, with severe toxicity defined as a grade score of ≥3. Patients with severe hepatic toxicity had a remarkably higher incidence of the TT genotype of the MTHFR rs1801133 (C677T) variant than those with mild toxicity (33.3% vs. 14.8%, p = 0.04).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chinese osteosarcoma patients treated with high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy
raw_record.extra_details: 109 patients; MTX-induced hepatic toxicity graded 1-4 with severe defined as grade ≥3; severe hepatic toxicity associated with MTHFR rs1801133 (C677T) TT genotype (33.3% vs. 14.8%, p=0.04); MTHFR genotyping proposed to predict MTX-induced toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 100 patients with rheumatoid arthritis chronically treated with methotrexate (MTX, mean cumulative dose 3595 mg, mean 7.07 years), a statistically significant correlation was found between liver stiffness (LS) assessed by FibroScan and MTX cumulative dose (r²=0.64, p<0.0001) and duration of treatment (r²=0.36, p<0.0001), with only a weak correlation to ALT. Liver biopsy in 5 of 11 patients with LS >7.0 kPa showed mild or moderate perisinusoidal fibrosis (Kleiner score 1A and 1B) in two. The authors state that MTX-induced liver injury is dose-dependent, interpreted as direct toxic damage related to increased oxidative stress, and that significant liver fibrosis has been reported in patients with RA and psoriasis chronically treated with MTX (incidence up to 23%, and 8.2% in a psoriasis cohort with cumulative doses exceeding 1500 mg).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic long-term therapeutic use (mean 7.07 years, ~10 mg/week) for rheumatoid arthritis; study patients had no diabetes mellitus or metabolic syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver stiffness (LS) assessed by transient elastography (FibroScan), whole-population mean LS 4.93±1.87 kPa; correlation with cumulative MTX dose r²=0.64 (p<0.0001), treatment duration r²=0.36 (p<0.0001), weak ALT correlation r²=0.050 (p=0.0250), weak BMI and γGT correlations; mean LS significantly higher in patients with cumulative dose >4000 mg (n=22) vs <4000 mg (n=76) (p<0.0001); liver biopsy in 5 patients (cumulative dose 3510–13,000 mg, LS 7.1–11.6 kPa) showed Kleiner score 1A and 1B perisinusoidal fibrosis in 2 and lobular inflammation (Kleiner 1) in 4; fibrosis incidence reported earlier as up to 23% in RA/psoriasis and 8.2% in a psoriasis cohort with cumulative doses >1500 mg; sequential biopsy studies found no severe fibrosis or cirrhosis after ~4 years/2000 mg. Injury interpreted as direct toxic damage related to increased oxidative stress, dose-dependent.

raw_record.support_text: The main concern of long-term treatment with methotrexate is the development of hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis. Raised transaminases were found in 18 of 306 patients treated in trials for 16 weeks or more (prevalence 6%; 95% CI 4-9%), with the rise noted between 3 weeks and 6 months, usually transient. Of 20 patients having a liver biopsy after a mean cumulative dose of 2633 mg over a mean of 132 weeks, only one had fibrosis; it was concluded that surveillance biopsy is unnecessary in inflammatory bowel disease.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic long-term treatment in inflammatory bowel disease; risk of liver damage depends partly on the nature of the disease being treated.
raw_record.extra_details: Raised transaminases in 18 of 306 trial patients (6%, 95% CI 4-9%), rise between 3 weeks and 6 months, usually transient; abnormal LFTs may be absent despite hepatotoxicity. Liver biopsy: 1 of 20 patients had fibrosis after mean cumulative 2633 mg methotrexate over mean 132 weeks; authors concluded surveillance biopsy is unnecessary in IBD.

raw_record.support_text: The study evaluated transient elastography (TE) for detecting methotrexate (MTX)-induced liver fibrosis among Chinese psoriasis patients receiving MTX. The paper repeatedly frames MTX as the cause of liver injury and fibrosis (e.g., detecting 'MTX-induced liver injury, defined as Roenigk grade ≥3a'), confirming the robust performance of TE in detecting significant liver fibrosis in this cohort, and noting that TE-based LS measurements were associated with BMI, diabetes mellitus, and obesity but not correlated with the total cumulative dose of MTX.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic therapeutic MTX treatment for psoriasis in a Chinese (Hong Kong) patient population; patients with pre-existing metabolic risk factors (obesity, diabetes mellitus) showed higher fibrosis on TE; some patients met only TCD or only TE criteria for biopsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective observational diagnostic-performance study of 34 psoriasis patients receiving MTX. Significant liver fibrosis defined as Roenigk grade ≥3a on liver biopsy; TE LS cut-off 7.1 kPa gave 100% sensitivity and 68% specificity, PPV 26.7%, NPV 100%, AUROC 0.76 (95% CI=0.59-0.93). TE-based LS correlated with BMI (r=0.441, P=0.009), body weight, and waist circumference but not with total cumulative dose of MTX (r=0.202, P=0.25) or duration of use (r=0.004, P=0.98). Comparison with other cohorts (Rongngern: AUROC 0.78, PPV 50%/NPV 84% for Roenigk ≥3a; Khandpur: TE detected 4/19 Ishak ≥F1 fibrosis cases; Berends: 50% sensitivity/88% specificity).

raw_record.support_text: The paper attributes most of the severe histological liver changes seen in psoriatic patients treated with methotrexate to the treatment. Nearly half of methotrexate-treated patients had hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis (46%), with mild to moderately severe fatty change in all but two of those, a combination uncommon in the U.K. except in alcoholic liver disease; no patient had a history of alcoholism and features of alcoholic hepatitis were consistently absent. These changes are said to be similar to those previously attributed to methotrexate in psoriasis and other conditions.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic therapeutic treatment in patients with severe psoriasis.
raw_record.extra_details: In the methotrexate-treated group, 7 (19%) had cirrhosis and 10 (27%) had fibrosis; 46% had fibrosis or cirrhosis overall. Bromsulphthalein retention was inadequate as a diagnostic test: one patient who had discontinued methotrexate four months previously had normal bromsulphthalein retention (4%) but established cirrhosis on biopsy. Of 20 methotrexate-treated patients without cirrhosis or fibrosis, all but three showed more severe fatty change, nuclear vacuolation, and inflammation than the untreated group.

raw_record.extra_details: Three of seven biopsied patients had abnormal liver biopsies (fibrosis grade 2 or 3); six of seven abnormal-biopsy cases had fibrosis grade 3, with cirrhosis (or early/very early cirrhosis) in most, including at post-mortem 5 months after DHS in case 1. Cumulative methotrexate doses were 1.0 g (case 1), 0.5 g (case 6) and 3.4 g (case 7). Liver enzyme monitoring was unhelpful in detecting fibrosis; frequent false elevations occurred with normal biopsies and one grade-3 fibrosis/cirrhosis patient had entirely normal enzymes. Dynamic hepatic scintigraphy had 83.3% sensitivity and 81.5% specificity for detecting fibrosis of grade 2 or worse, with 98.5% predictive value of a normal scan.

raw_record.support_text: Methotrexate-induced pathological liver changes in IBD were described in two case series. In one, 11 patients treated for a median of 18 months (range 7-58) with a mean cumulative dose of 1225 mg (range 220-3400 mg) showed 5 cases of mild steatosis, one case each of granulomatous hepatitis with mild portal fibrosis, slight sinusoid dilation, and periportal fibrosis, and 3 normal biopsies. In another, 20 patients biopsied after a mean methotrexate duration of 131.7 weeks and mean cumulative dose of 2633 mg had normal or Roenigk grade I changes in 17 (85%) and grade II-IIIb changes in 3.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients receiving methotrexate therapeutically; histological changes assessed by liver biopsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Study 1: 11 IBD patients, median 18 months (7-58), mean cumulative dose 1225 mg (220-3400 mg); 5 mild steatosis, 1 granulomatous hepatitis with mild portal fibrosis, 1 slight sinusoid dilation, 1 periportal fibrosis, 3 normal. Study 2: 20 patients, mean duration 131.7 weeks (66-281), mean cumulative dose 2633 mg (1500-5410 mg); 17 normal or Roenigk grade I, 3 grade II-IIIb. Abnormal serum transaminase levels are not predictive of hepatic histological changes. Risk factors for liver injury: alcohol consumption, obesity, diabetes mellitus, >1500 mg dose, and frequent dosing intervals (in psoriatic patients).

raw_record.support_text: Methotrexate sodium is used as monotherapy in the long-term management of severe psoriasis, and liver fibrosis is described as its main disadvantage. The text notes that studies vary on the prevalence of methotrexate-induced liver injury in patients with psoriasis, and recommends evaluation of liver enzyme levels, procollagen III peptide (PIIINP) levels, and periodic liver biopsies during therapy. The conclusions further frame transient elastography and FibroTest as effective noninvasive tools for monitoring hepatotoxicity in patients receiving methotrexate for psoriasis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings in patients with psoriasis receiving long-term methotrexate; comorbidities such as obesity, alcohol intake, and diabetes mellitus may increase the risk of liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver fibrosis is cited as the main disadvantage of methotrexate; recommended monitoring includes serial liver enzymes, PIIINP, periodic liver biopsy, and (per 2009 AAD guidelines) biopsy consideration in low-risk patients with persistent abnormal LFTs or after cumulative methotrexate dose of 3.5-4.0 g. In the study cohort (77 patients), transient elastography was abnormal in 9/50 (18%; range 7.1-11.3 kPa) and FibroTest (METAVIR >F1) abnormal in 11/70 (16%); cumulative methotrexate dose (r=0.31) and duration of therapy (r=0.36) correlated with abnormal FibroTest results. All 5 biopsied patients showed steatosis, and 2 had hepatic fibrosis, 1 with a sinusoidal pattern attributed to steatohepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses MTX (methotrexate)-induced cirrhosis, noting that in patients with psoriasis the reported incidence of MTX-induced cirrhosis ranges from 0-26%, with reported cases of fatal MTX-related cirrhosis and of cirrhosis requiring transplantation. It further states that since 1989 cases of cirrhosis in the rheumatoid population on MTX have been reported, and that the prevalence of MTX-associated cirrhosis in rheumatoid arthritis remains to be determined.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings pertain to rheumatoid arthritis patients treated with methotrexate; in the authors' own cases identifiable risk factors for developing cirrhosis were elderly age at first MTX use, total MTX dose (>3900 mg), and alcohol ingestion (case 3).
raw_record.extra_details: Reported incidence of MTX-induced cirrhosis in psoriasis ranges from 0-26%; fatal cases of MTX-related cirrhosis and cirrhosis requiring transplantation have been reported. Walker et al. case-controlled retrospective study reported 24 cases of cirrhosis and severe liver disease with a 5-yr cumulative incidence of 1/1000 treated patients, identifying late age at first use of MTX and duration of therapy as independent predictors of cirrhosis. Hepatitis B and C were excluded in the patients. Fibrosis/cirrhosis is the clinical phenotype; histology lacked excess stainable iron or alpha-1-antitrypsin globules.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that the serious complications of methotrexate therapy, especially hepatic and pulmonary toxicity, warrant attention, and that hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis remain a major concern for regular prescribers of methotrexate. In a prospective ultrastructural study of 15 rheumatoid arthritis patients, an increase in hepatic sinusoidal collagen, the ultrastructural marker of fibrosis, was demonstrated in five of the 15 patients after 2 years of treatment, and noninvasive (radioisotopic) tests were found inferior to biopsy for detecting methotrexate-induced toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings reported in rheumatoid arthritis patients receiving therapeutic methotrexate; fibrosis detected ultrastructurally (increased sinusoidal collagen in 5 of 15 patients after 2 years).
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis described as a serious complication of methotrexate therapy; prospective ultrastructural study showed increased hepatic sinusoidal collagen in 5 of 15 RA patients after 2 years despite normal light microscopic findings; radioisotopic noninvasive tests were inferior to liver biopsy for detecting methotrexate-induced hepatic toxicity. ACR Subcommittee on Hepatic Toxicity and Methotrexate monitoring recommendations (p.19) advise baseline CBC, creatinine, liver function tests, hepatitis B/C serology, serial liver function tests every 4-8 weeks, and liver biopsies under specified conditions (elevated AST in 5 of 9 or 6 of 12 yearly readings, or fall in serum albumin).

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective study of Japanese patients with noninfectious scleritis treated with methotrexate (MTX), adverse effects of MTX including hepatotoxicity were observed in almost 50% of the patients at some point during follow-up; most effects were tolerable or improved with dose adjustment. Despite ocular remission, tapering or discontinuation of MTX was required for 2 patients owing to MTX adverse effects, indicating the importance of monitoring cumulative adverse effects of MTX.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings restricted to Japanese patients with noninfectious scleritis treated with MTX as corticosteroid-sparing immunosuppressive therapy; MTX was used in combination with ongoing monitoring as part of standard care.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity observed in almost 50% of patients at some point during follow-up; mostly tolerable or improved with dose adjustment. Two patients required tapering or discontinuation of MTX due to adverse effects, despite ocular remission. hepatotoxicity reported only as an adverse effect without detailed laboratory, histologic, or severity characterization.

raw_record.support_text: In 49 psoriatic patients receiving long-term low-dose methotrexate who underwent liver biopsy, 12 were found to have hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis consistent with methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity, and the study concludes that ultrasound and radionuclide scans cannot reliably replace liver biopsy in detecting significant methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity in these patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings restricted to psoriatic patients receiving long-term once-weekly low-dose oral methotrexate.
raw_record.extra_details: Cumulative methotrexate doses ranged from 0.5 g to 10 g (median 2.8 g) over 1-13 years (median 5.3 years); 49 patients studied (26 male, 23 female, age 22-69 years, median 46). Injury manifest as hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis (12 patients with fibrosis or cirrhosis). Ultrasound failed to detect any of the 12 patients with fibrosis/cirrhosis; radionuclide scans missed 1 of 3 cirrhosis and 5 of 9 fibrosis cases.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that high-dose methotrexate (HD-MTX, ≥1 g/m²) chemotherapy in osteosarcoma, although improving survival, 'can however lead to harmful toxicities including renal toxicity, myelosuppression and liver damage.' The study cohort consisted of 114 osteosarcoma patients treated with HD-MTX (12 g/m² per course, up to 12 courses, 4 h infusion) under the EURAMOS-1 protocol, and liver damage was assessed by measuring plasma alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase at 48 h after MTX infusion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose methotrexate chemotherapy (12 g/m² per course, up to 12 courses, 4 h infusion) for primary high-grade osteosarcoma in patients ≤45 years of age; administered in combination with doxorubicin and cisplatin, with or without ifosfamide/etoposide or interferon-α per EURAMOS-1 randomized treatment arm; given with leucovorin rescue, hydration, and urinary alkalinization.
raw_record.extra_details: HD-MTX defined as ≥1 g/m²; MTX plasma levels showed associations with alanine aminotransferase (liver damage marker) at 48 h after infusion; no specific liver-injury severity, biochemical pattern, or clinical phenotype beyond 'liver damage'/'MTX-induced liver toxicity' was stated; the study is a pharmacogenetic investigation of ADME gene variants (SULT1E1, CYP2B6, CYP4F8) on MTX pharmacokinetics and toxicities.

raw_record.support_text: This retrospective longitudinal study, coupled with genetic testing, provided a thorough examination of the hepatotoxic effects induced by HD-MTX, incorporating clinical and biochemical parameters, MTX concentrations at multiple time points, drug interactions, and MTX administration methods. The study established a nomogram predicting risk of moderate/severe DILI (grade≥2) and identified potential risk and protective genetic factors.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose MTX (HD-MTX) therapy in patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemia, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, or osteosarcoma; Han Chinese population; some patients received intravenous plus triple intrathecal injection route rather than intravenous injection alone.
raw_record.extra_details: DILI graded ≥2 (moderate/severe). Nomogram predicting risk of moderate/severe DILI included sex, MTX dose, C24h MTX concentration, ABCB1 rs1128503, and SLCO1B1 haplotypes; model AUROC 0.805 (95% CI 0.750-0.859), AUPRC 0.515. ABCB1 rs1128503 identified as a possible independent risk factor and SLCO1B1 haplotypes as protective factors for moderate/severe DILI. Higher dose-adjusted MTX concentration was more prevalent with the intravenous plus triple intrathecal route.

raw_record.support_text: High-dose MTX-induced toxicity was recorded and graded per CTCAE 3.0 in osteosarcoma patients. At least one episode of grade 3-4 liver toxicity was experienced by 26 of 37 patients (70.3%), defined as the presence of grade 3 or higher symptoms. This attributes clinically significant dose-related liver injury to high-dose methotrexate therapy in humans.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose MTX infusion as part of osteosarcoma therapy in a CTCAE-graded prospective cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: Grade 3-4 liver toxicity (CTCAE 3.0, defined as grade >=3) occurred in 26/37 patients (70.3%). Plasma MTX levels at 24, 48, and 72 h (median 4.7, 0.65, 0.3 µmol/L) were not significantly associated with severe liver toxicity; MTX levels at 48 h were associated with severe mucositis (P=0.007) and kidney toxicity (P=0.002), and at 72 h with severe mucositis (P=0.046) and kidney toxicity (P=0.002). No candidate SNP (SLC19A1 80G>A, MTHFR C677T/A1298C, ATIC C347G) correlated significantly with severe liver or kidney toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The study shows that large MTX doses in a short period (6 months or less) produce a modest but significant impairment in galactose elimination capacity, without changes in antipyrine clearance and routine liver function tests, consistent with a defect in liver cell function detectable only by quantitative, dynamic tests.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose, short-duration (≤6 months) MTX chemotherapy with total dose described as far beyond the safe limits; post-surgical oncology patients.
raw_record.extra_details: At end of treatment (150-266 days after initial assessment), galactose elimination capacity (GEC) was reduced by 17% versus baseline, generally still within the normal range but markedly reduced (>30%) in four of the patients; difference from baseline was significant (P=0.013, Wilcoxon signed-rank test). AP clearance (available in 8 patients) and antipyrine half-life (12.7±5.3 h before vs 12.2±3.0 h after) showed no significant change; no significant changes in routine liver function tests (albumin, cholesterol, prothrombin activity). Data interpreted as a defect in liver cell function detectable only by quantitative dynamic tests. Discussion asserts the relationship of MTX treatment to chronic progressive liver disease is well established and probably dependent on cumulative dose; repeated MTX-related toxic hepatitis (transient transaminase increases returning to normal in days) may progress to chronic liver disease characterized by fibrosis or cirrhosis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that methotrexate is known to be hepatotoxic when given in high dosage, and that in the doses generally used for treating psoriasis, liver damage has only recently been recognized as a serious problem. In their studied patients, hepatic fibrosis developed after as little as one year of methotrexate treatment, and after three years of treatment cirrhosis or some degree of hepatic fibrosis was present in about 50% of cases. They note that, unlike many other methotrexate side effects, hepatic fibrosis is potentially irreversible and may progress to cirrhosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term (chronic) methotrexate use for psoriasis; most patients received a 'continuous low dose' schedule at minimum effective doses; severity of liver damage correlated with duration of treatment and the paper excludes three patients with disputed cirrhosis aetiology.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic fibrosis developed after as little as one year; after three years cirrhosis or some degree of hepatic fibrosis was present in about 50% of cases. Of 14 patients treated for more than 30 months, six had cirrhosis and another five showed fibrosis, in some cases severe. Liver disease severity correlates with treatment duration. Liver function tests were of little predictive value though raised alkaline phosphatase suggested fibrosis/cirrhosis; hepatomegaly during treatment was associated with considerable fibrosis or cirrhosis; liver biopsy was the only reliable assessment. Preliminary data suggest intermittent dosage may be less hepatotoxic than continuous low dose. In a Shapiro et al. (1970) study of 20 psoriatic patients no significant differences in liver function or biopsy findings were found between methotrexate-treated and topical-treatment-only groups after only 3-30 months of treatment.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe the histopathologic changes of methotrexate (MTX)-induced hepatotoxicity as well recognized, reporting on the hepatotoxic effects of long-term (10-year) MTX therapy. In most of the patients' biopsy material the pathologic findings ranged from normal to mild changes, including portal fibrosis, steatosis, inflammation, cholestasis, and sinusoidal dilatation/congestion, and the study failed to show progression to severe fibrosis and cirrhosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term chronic therapeutic exposure (10 years of MTX therapy) rather than short-course or single-agent-acute use; findings describe histologic spectrum rather than an acute idiosyncratic event.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 21 patients (with 5 repeat biopsies) on long-term MTX therapy. Initial biopsies: mild portal fibrosis with infrequent short septa and minimal patchy sinusoidal centrilobular (zone 3) fibrosis in 5 samples; no loss of architecture, complete septa, or nodular regeneration. Other changes included cholestasis (1 sample), epithelioid cell granulomas with inflammation (2 samples), lipogranulomas (1 sample), and sinusoidal dilatation/congestion with mild focal sinusoidal fibrosis (3 samples). Repeat biopsies (grade IIIA initial samples): no increase in fibrosis and no cirrhosis in 4 patients; 1 downgraded to grade II. Repeat biopsies in patients 3 and 21 (12-44 months after first biopsies, while still on MTX) showed portal/periportal inflammation, focal limiting-plate disruption, mild piecemeal necrosis, and perilobular inflammation (grade IIIB); patient 21 had >50% fat accumulation and moderate lymphoplasmacytic portal inflammation with eosinophils and polymorphonuclear cells involving one duct. Study concludes no progression to severe fibrosis or cirrhosis over 10 years. Pathogeneses (mechanism of liver cell damage/fibrosis) stated as unknown.

raw_record.support_text: In a group of 37 patients treated with methotrexate, liver biopsies showed established or developing cirrhosis in 7 and varying degrees of hepatic fibrosis in another 10; among the remaining 20, non-specific reactive hepatitis was seen in 17 and 3 were normal. In a subgroup of 28 patients investigated regardless of whether liver disease was clinically suspected, 3 had cirrhosis, 9 had hepatic fibrosis, 14 had non-specific changes, and 2 were normal.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term, chronic treatment for psoriasis (indication-restricted patient population).
raw_record.extra_details: Among 37 methotrexate-treated psoriatic patients, 7 had cirrhosis (active micronodular cirrhosis with inflammation and piecemeal necrosis in 4 cases, one with features of severe chronic aggressive hepatitis, and one inactive mixed micronodular/macronodular cirrhosis after discontinuing methotrexate four months previously). 10 patients showed mainly portal fibrosis (short septa extending around lobules, some with moderately severe portal and intralobular fibrosis), with nuclear vacuolation a constant feature and fatty change in 9 cases. Non-specific changes (mononuclear infiltration, focal necroses, acidophil bodies, fatty change, nuclear vacuolation) were found in 17. Severity of liver damage correlated with duration of methotrexate treatment: mean 17.7 ± 3.4 months for normal/non-specific histology vs 32.9 ± 6.6 months for fibrosis (P<0.05) and 46.9 ± 4.9 months for cirrhosis (P<0.001 vs normal/non-specific group); analogous values for the 28 unselected Newcastle patients were 19.6 ± 4.1, 35.2 ± 7.0, and 48.7 ± 5.9 months respectively.

raw_record.support_text: This clinical study of 49 psoriatic patients treated with long-term, low-dose, once-weekly methotrexate (MTX) examined sequential liver biopsy findings. No significant correlation was found between biopsy findings and cumulative dose or duration of treatment, and none of the 49 patients developed cirrhosis. The authors conclude that long-term, low-dose, once-weekly MTX may be significantly less hepatotoxic than previously stated, implying MTX hepatic damage is cumulative-dose related per published recommendations but this was not confirmed in their patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term, low-dose, once-weekly administration for psoriasis; patients with high alcohol consumption generally not treated with MTX and ongoing patients advised to minimize alcohol intake.
raw_record.extra_details: 49 patients with sequential liver biopsies; no cirrhosis occurred during long-term treatment. Histologic findings included steatosis and fibrosis (e.g., one patient deteriorated from steatosis to fibrosis with elevated liver enzymes). Biopsy findings did not correlate with cumulative dose, duration, or mean weekly dose (not above 20 mg weekly). 11 patients had fibrosis on the first biopsy; none deteriorated, 5 improved with no fibrosis on the last biopsy. Four patients stopped MTX due to liver biopsy findings (fibrosis or patient unwilling to continue monitoring). Authors suggest fibrosis alone need not contraindicate continued MTX therapy.

raw_record.support_text: Methotrexate is reported to have hepatotoxicity as a rare side effect. Of patients with psoriasis receiving methotrexate daily, 3% to 5% developed cirrhosis after being given 1.5 g of the drug. In patients with rheumatoid arthritis who had received 1.5 g of methotrexate or 2 years of therapy, bridging fibrosis or cirrhosis (Roenick class IIIB or IV) was found in only 2 of 114 patients, one of whom was suspected of excess alcohol intake. The correlation of weekly pulse dosages of methotrexate with liver function tests is poor; enzyme elevations occur frequently but do not appear to reflect serious hepatic toxicity or the development of histologic fibrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Low-dose methotrexate for psoriasis or rheumatoid arthritis; weekly pulse dosing; findings pertain to patients with risk factors (alcoholism, diabetes, obesity) excluded from certain comparisons.
raw_record.extra_details: 3% to 5% of daily-dose psoriasis patients developed cirrhosis after cumulative 1.5 g of methotrexate; bridging fibrosis or cirrhosis (Roenick class IIIB or IV) in only 2 of 114 rheumatoid arthritis patients after 1.5 g or 2 years of therapy, one case with suspected excess alcohol intake; correlation of weekly pulse dosing with liver function tests is poor, and enzyme elevations may return to baseline despite continued therapy; suggested association with hypoalbuminemia needs confirmation.

raw_record.support_text: During low-dose methotrexate therapy, mild serum transaminase elevations frequently occur within 2 to 3 days of dosing and promptly return to normal, but these transient abnormalities do not predict hepatotoxicity. Liver enzymes are not necessarily elevated when cirrhosis or fibrosis develops; in one series 88 of 277 patients with biopsy-proven liver damage had no evidence of liver disease by history, physical examination, or serum transaminases, and liver biopsy was considered the only reliable means of monitoring for toxicity. A biopsy revealing portal fibrosis or cirrhosis mandates cessation of methotrexate, and a pretreatment biopsy is recommended in the setting of pre-existing liver disease.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Low-dose weekly methotrexate therapy (initiated at 7.5 mg/week, up to 15 mg/week) in rheumatoid arthritis patients; risk relates to cumulative dosing; pre-existing liver disease is a consideration for pretreatment biopsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Transient transaminase elevations occur 2-3 days after dosing and resolve; serum enzymes are not reliably elevated when fibrosis/cirrhosis develops. Liver biopsy is the only reliable monitoring tool; in one series 88 of 277 patients with biopsy-proven liver damage had no evidence by history, physical exam, or transaminases. Routine pretreatment biopsy deferred until cumulative dose of 1500 mg (per Groff and coworkers); subsequent biopsies every 1-2 years; biopsy showing portal fibrosis or cirrhosis mandates drug cessation.

raw_record.support_text: Methotrexate (MTX) is effective for treating psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis, but its potential hepatotoxicity remains a concern. The paper frames liver biopsy as the gold standard for detecting MTX-induced liver injury, and the study investigated transient elastography for detecting MTX-induced liver fibrosis in Chinese psoriasis patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Observed in Chinese adult psoriasis patients receiving MTX; significant fibrosis was correlated with obesity and diabetes and not with MTX cumulative dose or duration of use.
raw_record.extra_details: Of 228 patients screened, 34 met inclusion criteria; 9 (26.5%) had significant liver fibrosis (Roenigk grade ≥3a). Transient elastography had an area under the ROC curve of 0.76 (95% CI 0.59-0.93; P=0.021); a cut-off of 7.1 kPa gave 100% sensitivity and 68% specificity. Liver biopsy was performed when liver stiffness was ≥7.1 kPa or total cumulative dose of MTX was ≥3.5 g. Fibrosis correlated with BMI ≥30 kg/m², waist circumference ≥138 cm, and glycated haemoglobin ≥7.8%.
