raw_record.support_text: The study demonstrated a clear relationship between methotrexate (MTX) therapy and chemically and histologically defined liver damage. The rapidity of onset and severity of abnormal liver function tests correlated with the intensity of therapy, with more hepatotoxicity observed in the group showing hematologic and gastrointestinal chemotherapy side effects. LFT abnormalities following intermittent MTX resolved completely within one month after cessation, and continued moderate-dose MTX therapy was associated with normal or near-normal liver function without progressive hepatic damage, including in patients with eye disease.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: One patient with pre-existing liver disease developed a somewhat more severe functional abnormality; his liver function returned to normal after cessation of therapy and repeated biopsies showed no further deterioration. Therapy was given for otherwise healthy ocular disease or as part of leukemia chemotherapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity included abnormal SGOT/SGPT and BSP retention, with histologic findings of portal fibrosis, fatty metamorphosis, mild toxic degeneration of hepatic parenchymal cells, and slight bile stasis. LFT abnormalities correlated with intensity of therapy and resolved within one month after cessation of intermittent MTX. Five patients received maintenance MTX 10-25 mg/m² IV once weekly for 3 months to 1.5 years; liver function returned to normal in 4 of 5, while one had persistent abnormalities (SGOT 30-60, SGPT 60-130, BSP 7-11%). Four intensive-therapy patients died of infectious complications of leukemia 4-6 months post-study with hepatic disease not involved; all showed leukemic portal infiltration, one with moderate fatty metamorphosis, one with slight portal fibrosis and moderate fatty metamorphosis.

raw_record.support_text: A patient treated with MTX (methotrexate) at 40 mg/m² for 5 doses for a lung neoplasm and psoriasis developed oral toxicity and thrombocytopenia after the 5th dose, then jaundice (total bilirubin 9 mg%, direct 5.4, indirect 3.6 mg%; BSF 58%; SGOT, SGPT and alkaline phosphatase normal), a palpable liver, pulmonary edema, and hepatic coma, followed by death; at autopsy the liver showed complete disruption of lobular architecture with blood and bile stasis, edema and atrophy of hepatocytes. The accompanying comment states the clinical and biochemical picture of hepatic and renal toxicity had a clear anatomopathological correlate. In another patient (case 2) bilirubin rose from 0.45 to 3.61 mg% and he died 9 days after a single 40 mg/m² MTX dose with a hepatorenal insufficiency picture. In case 5, BSF rose from 9 to 19% after the 4th dose and to 35% after the 7th, with parallel alkaline phosphatase rises and mild bilirubin increase; the comment concludes that although the terminal picture was attributable to progression of cerebral metastases, it seems probable that the therapy produced progressive hepatic toxicity, and BSF increase argues against a bone origin of the alkaline phosphatase rise.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients had advanced lung neoplasms (some with bone/cerebral metastases) and received MTX as palliative systemic chemotherapy at 40 mg/m² per dose; one case received concurrent telecobaltotherapy; one patient had long-standing psoriasis. Case 5's terminal picture was partly confounded by progression of cerebral metastases.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 40 mg/m² intravenously, up to 7 doses; case 1 received 5 doses and died in hepatic coma (bilirubin 9 mg%, BSF 58%, transaminases and alkaline phosphatase normal, later palpable liver, pulmonary edema; autopsy: disrupted lobular architecture, blood and bile stasis, edema and hepatocyte atrophy, portal infiltrate); case 2 died 9 days after one dose with hepatorenal insufficiency (bilirubin rose 0.45 to 3.61 mg%, azotemia 20 to 115 mg%, uricemia 4.75 to 9.25 mg%); case 5 showed rising BSF 9 to 19 to 35% and alkaline phosphatase 1.80 to 3.24 to 7.70 U with mild bilirubin rise. A further case (case 3) treated with MTX plus telecobaltotherapy died with agranulocytosis and acute renal failure, without an attributed hepatic claim.

raw_record.support_text: Liver toxicity was studied by sequential examination, liver function tests, and percutaneous liver biopsies (light and electron microscopy) during methotrexate treatment in patients whose leukemia or histiocytosis X remained in complete remission. Fibrosis was found even without hepatosplenomegaly or abnormal liver function and persisted despite normalization of physical findings and liver function. Initially hepatocellular changes were seen by light microscopy, progressing to portal inflammation and fibrosis with continued therapy. The authors conclude that the pathologic changes are secondary to methotrexate therapy, not the basic disease process, and stress the insidious nature of this hepatic toxicity in nonmalignant uses of the drug.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with leukemia or histiocytosis X in complete remission receiving methotrexate therapy; finding specifically that fibrosis can develop absent hepatosplenomegaly or abnormal liver function.
raw_record.extra_details: 10 patients studied by sequential liver function tests and percutaneous biopsies (light and electron microscopy); hepatomegaly usually developed; fibrosis persisted despite normalization of physical findings and liver function; light microscopy initially showed hepatocellular changes progressing to portal inflammation and fibrosis; ultrastructural changes included double-nucleated hepatic cells with minor nucleolar changes and decreased perichromatin, varied cytoplasmic fat and glycogen, mitochondrial swelling, dilated endoplasmic reticulum, and sinusoidal slender filaments with collagen and basement membrane formation; authors state liver biopsy is the only accurate way to follow the extent of liver damage and discontinuation of therapy can result in return toward normal structure; toxicity also noted as concern for nonmalignant uses (skin disorders, immunologic diseases).

raw_record.support_text: In this cohort of 278 liver biopsies taken over 30 years, MTX-induced liver fibrosis (≥Roenigk grade 3a) was seen in 15% (19 patients) of the psoriasis population. Progression to a higher stage of liver injury mostly occurred at a cumulative dose range between 1500 and 6000 mg (about 2 years at 15 mg weekly), and progressive liver damage was infrequent above 6000 mg. Additionally, fibrosis/cirrhosis (Roenigk ≥ 3a) was detected in 41 biopsies from 24 patients at some point during MTX treatment, and histological findings led to discontinuation in only 6/41 biopsies.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with psoriasis receiving low-dose, long-term MTX; findings restricted to a cohort managed per international biopsy monitoring guidelines.
raw_record.extra_details: 278 liver biopsies over 30 years; MTX-induced liver fibrosis (Roenigk grade ≥3a) in 15% (19 patients); fibrosis/cirrhosis detected in 41 biopsies from 24 patients; progression occurred mainly at cumulative dose 1500-6000 mg (about 2 years at 15 mg weekly) and was infrequent above 6000 mg; histology led to MTX discontinuation in only 6/41 biopsies; 16 patients had repeat biopsy after significant earlier abnormalities (mean 14 months) with improvement in 10, no change in 5, and worsening in 1; treatment was described as relatively safe despite hepatotoxicity risk.

raw_record.support_text: The study used the Roenigk grading system to assess liver damage in liver biopsy specimens obtained from patients with rheumatic disease or psoriasis who had received methotrexate (MTX) therapy. Grade I was normal histology, Grade II included fibrous spurs and patchy fibrosis, Grade IIIA mild portal fibrosis with septa, Grade IIIB spotty necrosis or septal fibrosis with bridging, and Grade IV was cirrhosis defined by bridging with regenerating nodules. The graded histologic spectrum (fibrosis, bridging fibrosis, cirrhosis) reflects liver injury attributed to chronic MTX exposure in these patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with rheumatic disease (rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, psoriatic arthritis, polymyositis, Sjogren's syndrome, UDCTD/CREST) or psoriasis receiving chronic methotrexate therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver biopsy specimens graded by the Roenigk criteria; Grades range from I (normal, including mild lobular hepatitis, mild focal fatty metamorphosis, Kupffer cell hyperplasia) to IV (cirrhosis with bridging and regenerating nodules). Graded features include fibrous spurs in the portal area, fibrosis in the space of Disse, thickened liver cords, septal fibrosis, portal-to-portal or portal-to-central vein bridging, spotty hepatocellular necrosis, and steatohepatitis. In the study cohort (29 patients), MTX cumulative doses ranged from 1.5 to 12.6 g, therapy exposure from 2 to 17 years, and weekly doses from 7.5 to 25 mg/week; observed grades ranged from 1 to 3b.

raw_record.support_text: In the authors' experience, the risk of hepatotoxicity from methotrexate (MTX) is higher than earlier suggested. Three patients from a prospective study of 76 patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) followed with sequential liver biopsies developed cirrhosis, giving a point prevalence of cirrhosis of 2.63%; two additional patients of the 76 developed Roenigk Grade III B changes (moderate to severe fibrosis) requiring cessation of MTX. Over 14 years of clinic use, the 5-year cumulative incidence of cirrhosis was 9.4/1000 treated patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with rheumatoid arthritis treated with low-dose pulse methotrexate; coexposure to high-risk alcohol consumption in the Australian population considered a contributing risk factor.
raw_record.extra_details: 5-yr cumulative incidence of cirrhosis 9.4/1000 treated patients; point prevalence of cirrhosis 2.63% (3/76) in a prospective serial-biopsy cohort; Roenigk Grade III B (moderate to severe fibrosis) changes in 2 additional patients; cirrhosis developed after >4 yr of MTX (case 2 had non-specific lobular hepatitis after 3.3 yr); monitoring of AST/ALT every 4-6 weeks recommended; supports ACR guidelines for hepatotoxicity monitoring; American/ACR guidelines recommend liver biopsy for AST elevations in 5 of 9 determinations within 12 months.

raw_record.extra_details: 1991 meta-analyses of 636 RA patients: 24% progressed to some fibrosis and 2.7% to cirrhosis after MTX therapy. In a related comparison, 66 RA patients underwent 110 liver biopsies with only 15 meeting ACR-triggered biopsy; a single cirrhosis in an IDDM patient would have been missed, leading to a recommendation that IDDM patients be included in the risk group.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective cohort of 210 patients with rheumatoid arthritis treated with long-term, low-dose, pulse methotrexate (follow-up up to seven years), no cirrhosis was observed and only six persons had fibrotic changes, all graded as 'mild' hepatic fibrosis (grade III changes). The authors concluded that the observations suggest a low, but definite, hepatotoxic potential in patients with rheumatoid arthritis receiving long-term, low-dose, pulse methotrexate therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with rheumatoid arthritis; long-term low-dose pulse methotrexate therapy; hepatic fibrosis was mild (grade III changes) with no cirrhosis in this cohort. Proposed risk factors included age, alcohol ingestion, obesity, diabetes mellitus, and renal insufficiency.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective analysis of 210 methotrexate-treated rheumatoid arthritis patients, up to seven years of use; only six persons had fibrotic changes on liver biopsy, all 'mild' hepatic fibrosis; no cirrhosis. Mean age of patients with grade III changes was 59 years; five of six denied significant alcohol intake, all had normal renal function, five were obese, three had glucose intolerance/overt diabetes. Only one patient had LFTs greater than two times normal at grade III biopsy; three of six grade III patients never had elevated LFTs. Total dose/duration linked to eventual liver damage; three patients had received less than 1,200 mg at grade III biopsy. Five of six patients with grade III had methotrexate discontinued; one showed reversal to grade II on later biopsies while continuing therapy. Authors noted inadequate laboratory markers (LFTs, albumin) for hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In a letter on methotrexate hepatotoxicity in psoriasis, the authors (who first published a detailed account of methotrexate's hepatotoxic effects in live psoriasis patients) report on four of their original patients who had been treated with 2.5 mg methotrexate daily for 6-8 days with 3-7 days' rest for almost 10 years. Two show no liver fibrosis, one presented with a full picture of cirrhosis one year earlier, and the other has histological evidence of cirrhosis, illustrating that some patients develop cirrhosis while others escape fibrosis on frequent small-dosage methotrexate regimens.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with severe psoriasis on chronic low-dose oral methotrexate (2.5 mg daily for 6-8 days with 3-7 days' rest) for ~10 years; one patient also had an alcohol intake of 6 pints (3.5 L) of beer per week.
raw_record.extra_details: The authors contest the claim that hepatic fibrosis is an invariable consequence of prolonged low-dose oral methotrexate, noting that two reinvestigated patients showed no fibrosis whereas two others developed cirrhosis. A separate group of four patients with prior abnormal liver function tests switched to parenteral methotrexate after an initial oral low-dose regimen of over two years showed no fibrosis on current liver histology.

raw_record.support_text: In comparing first and last liver biopsies among 49 patients receiving long-term, low-dose, once weekly oral methotrexate for severe psoriasis, there was improvement in 12, no change in 28, and deterioration in nine, with none developing cirrhosis. Liver biopsy findings prompted discontinuation of methotrexate in four of the 49 patients. The authors conclude that the risk of development or progression of liver disease during continued low-dose weekly MTX treatment is modest and that routine liver biopsy requirements should be reconsidered.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with severe psoriasis on long-term, low-dose, once weekly oral methotrexate; serial liver biopsy cohort; continued MTX exposure between biopsies.
raw_record.extra_details: 182 liver biopsies performed over 10 years; 49 patients had two or more biopsies. Mean cumulative MTX dose at first biopsy 2743 mg (range 315-10,024) over 275 weeks (range 26-738); a further 2362 mg (range 390-7155) over 225 weeks (range 60-460) between first and last biopsies. Histologic groups: normal; steatosis alone; inflammation without fibrosis; fibrosis; cirrhosis. Deterioration in 9/49, no new cirrhosis; MTX discontinued in 4 patients due to biopsy findings. 124 biopsies performed in these patients (cost/morbidity consideration). The paper frames the study as prompted by concern over possible MTX hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Oral methotrexate (MTX) used for severe psoriasis has potential hepatotoxicity; in this prospective study of 25 MTX patients (mean cumulative dose 3.9 g, range 0.2–11.1 g), liver biopsy grading showed 21 patients with normal liver histology (grade I), three with steatosis (grade II), and one with mild fibrosis (grade IIIA), assessed as MTX-induced hepatic damage.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with severe psoriasis receiving oral MTX; prolonged/chronic treatment with cumulative dosing.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective cohort of 25 MTX psoriasis patients, mean cumulative MTX dose 3.9 g (range 0.2–11.1 g). Liver biopsy grading: 21 grade I (normal), 3 grade II steatosis, 1 grade IIIA mild fibrosis. Study compared dynamic hepatic scintigraphy (DHS) and serum PIIINP as screening tests against liver biopsy (gold standard); concluded DHS promising for early MTX-induced hepatic damage detection but not suitable to grade severity, and that regular liver biopsies remain mandatory for safe prolonged MTX use. Fibrosis and steatosis are attributed MTX-induced phenotypes.

raw_record.support_text: In this retrospective analysis of 181 patients treated with methotrexate (MTX) for acute lymphoblastic leukemia who developed toxicity, hepatotoxicity was the most common MTX-induced toxicity (56.8%). Among these, transient elevated hepatic enzymes were noted in 84%, cholestatic hepatitis in 4%, and mixed hepatitis in 11.5%. Toxicity was most common during the chemotherapy induction phase (67.6%) at a dose of 5 g/m2, with a median time to MTX toxicity of 10 days after administration.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia population (114 B-cell ALL, 6 T-cell ALL; mean age 17.4 years, 50% under 10 years) treated with combination chemotherapy protocols (EORTC 49%, HyperCVAD 32%, Saint Jude 15%); MTX given at 5 g/m2 during induction phase.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective single-center cohort (Farhat Hached University Hospital) 2008-2017, 181 patients, 55% male, patients selected for having developed toxicity while on MTX. Hepatotoxicity incidence 56.8%; transient elevated hepatic enzymes 84%, cholestatic hepatitis 4%, mixed hepatitis 11.5%. Median latency 10 days after MTX administration; toxicity most frequent at induction phase (67.6%). Other MTX toxicities: acute kidney injury 16%, cutaneous lesions 13.8% (mucositis most predominant), gastrointestinal disorders 6.9% (vomiting, diarrhea), hematologic disorders 4.4%, neurologic symptoms 2.2%. Conclusion notes MTX toxicity ranges from minor events to life-threatening reactions.

raw_record.support_text: Among the 38 DILI cases in the SR/IR group, the RUCAM causality grading for high-dose methotrexate (HD-MTX) was highly probable in 5 (13.2%) cases, probable in 31 (81.6%) cases, and possible in 2 (5.3%) cases. In the HR-1 and HR-2 DILI groups, high (probable + highly probable) causality grading was detected in 100% of HD-MTX cases. The paper concludes that HD-MTX is a main causative agent of DILI during consolidation therapy in childhood ALL.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric ALL consolidation therapy; high-dose methotrexate given as part of a combination chemotherapeutic regimen; pre-existing liver conditions identified as a shared risk factor across stratification groups.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective study of 117 Korean childhood ALL patients receiving interim maintenance HD-MTX therapy, transient liver toxicity, which may include reversible chemical hepatitis, was seen in 85% of the patients and in 60% of the cycles, with hyperbilirubinemia seen in 30% of patients. Almost all patients had elevations in SGOT and/or SGPT after HD-MTX, which were framed as transient and reversible, of minor clinical importance, not requiring dose adjustment and not leading to chronic liver disease.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric childhood ALL patients receiving high-dose (HD-MTX) interim maintenance methotrexate therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Transient liver toxicity (possibly reversible chemical hepatitis) in 85% of patients and 60% of cycles; hyperbilirubinemia in 30% of patients and 20% of cycles; SGOT/SGPT elevations in almost all patients but described as clinically insignificant and not leading to chronic liver disease. Associated MTX-related toxicities in the same study included nephrotoxicity (5% of patients), stroke-like syndrome, and peripheral neuropathy.

raw_record.support_text: Case report of a 14-year-old patient with osteosarcoma being treated with high-dose methotrexate. During the sixth high-dose methotrexate course, very high plasma methotrexate levels were measured together with renal insufficiency, hepatitis, mucitis, and moderate myelosuppression. The authors state that given the very high plasma methotrexate levels and the clinical (mucitis) and biological (hepatitis, renal insufficiency) picture, methotrexate may have been responsible for these complications, and the Naranjo adverse-event imputability algorithm concluded a probable relationship between the observed adverse events and methotrexate.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (14 years) with osteosarcoma treated with high-dose methotrexate; concurrent renal insufficiency; high-dose infusion regimen.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis occurred during the sixth high-dose methotrexate course associated with very high plasma methotrexate levels, mucitis, renal insufficiency, and moderate myelosuppression. Naranjo imputability algorithm concluded a probable relationship. Intensified alkaline diuresis and increased folinic acid doses were insufficient; carboxypeptidase G2 and aminophylline were given as second-line rescue. Clinical symptoms regressed and laboratory parameters normalized within 2 weeks. Plasma homocysteine, measured as a marker of methotrexate antifolate activity, was significantly elevated during the intoxication. Methotrexate courses were resumed and the patient recovered.

Adjuvant chemotherapy was then initiated according to the MAP protocol (which includes high-dose methotrexate, doxorubicin, and cisplatin), but because of the toxicity of high-dose methotrexate the patient suffered acute liver failure (hypertransaminasemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and coagulopathy), requiring treatment with cholestyramine and activated charcoal, so chemotherapy was changed to cisplatin with Adriamycin.

A liver biopsy was recommended after cumulative use of 1.5 g because liver damage does not correlate with liver enzyme increases.

raw_record.support_text: This cohort of 41 psoriasis patients receiving long-term methotrexate therapy was evaluated for methotrexate-induced liver injury using liver biopsy (Roenigk grade ≥3a) as the gold standard and transient elastography. Methotrexate is treated as the cause of the liver fibrosis/injury being monitored; TE values >7.0 kPa provided acceptable accuracy (AUROC=0.78, 95% CI 0.63-0.93) and a high NPV of 84% for excluding methotrexate-induced liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Psoriasis indication requiring long-term methotrexate therapy; non-obese Asian population; histopathologic assessment (Roenigk grading).
raw_record.extra_details: 41 patients evaluated by transient elastography and liver biopsy; histopathologic evidence of methotrexate-induced liver injury defined as Roenigk grades ≥3a. Total cumulative methotrexate dose and host factors (age, gender, metabolic syndrome and its components) were not significantly associated with TE values ≥7.1 kPa or Roenigk grades ≥3a. TE cut-off 7.1 kPa gave sensitivity 50%, specificity 83.9%, PPV 50%, NPV 83.9%, accuracy 75.6% in this study.

raw_record.support_text: The authors, who were the first to publish a detailed account of the hepatotoxic effects of methotrexate in psoriasis patients, respond to Dahl et al.'s suggestion that liver fibrosis is an invariable consequence of prolonged frequent small-dose oral methotrexate. They continue prescribing 2.5 mg methotrexate daily 6-8 days with 3-7 days' rest and report reinvestigation of four patients on this regimen for almost 10 years: two show no fibrosis (one with alcohol intake of 6 pints of beer per week), one presented with a full picture of cirrhosis one year ago, and one has histological evidence of cirrhosis. They state terms such as 'invariable' are not yet justified, but attribute hepatotoxicity (fibrosis/cirrhosis) to methotrexate.

raw_record.extra_details: Letter correspondence in response to Dahl et al. Authors were first to publish a detailed account of methotrexate hepatotoxicity in psoriasis patients. Described as still the best available drug for severe cases needing systemic therapy; authors emphasize ascertaining the safest schedule. Histology: two patients show no fibrosis, one presented with full picture of cirrhosis one year prior, one has histological evidence of cirrhosis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report, based on their studies on methotrexate and the liver including considerable follow-up data on MTX-treated patients with liver biopsies, that MTX-induced liver cirrhosis is in general nonaggressive. They note a patient with ascites whose serum PIIINP and laboratory values for alkaline phosphatases and serum transaminases decreased after discontinuation of MTX, and state that psoriatics on long-term MTX should still have a liver biopsy at least once their total cumulative dose exceeds 1.5 g.

raw_record.extra_details: Discussion concerns monitoring of MTX-induced liver toxicity. In the referenced study, of 24 patients without arthritis with biopsy-proven fibrosis, six to eight (25%-33%) had normal serum aminoterminal propeptide of type III procollagen (PIIINP) below the 95% specificity cut-off, showing normal PIIINP is not a reliable basis to avoid or delay routine liver biopsies. MTX-induced cirrhosis in general described as nonaggressive; patients with fibrosis and negative PIIINP had low-grade, mostly inactive fibrosis. One patient with ascites showed declining PIIINP, alkaline phosphatases, and serum transaminases after discontinuing MTX.

raw_record.support_text: The follow-up investigation of MTX-treated psoriasis patients confirms the earlier study suggesting that MTX-induced liver cirrhosis is not aggressive. When biopsies were evaluated blind, no progression was found in most later serial biopsies, and in 14 cases the cirrhosis diagnosis could not be confirmed in the latest liver biopsy. The paper describes these as patients with MTX-induced liver cirrhosis, attributing the cirrhosis/ fibrosis to methotrexate therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Psoriasis patients on chronic MTX; the paper identifies prior heavy alcohol intake, previous treatment with arsenics and vitamin A, male sex, and ongoing alcohol intake as contributing factors to the cirrhosis frequency; a lowering of the weekly dose together with advice to avoid alcohol was proposed to explain histologic improvement.
raw_record.extra_details: 29 patients with MTX-induced liver cirrhosis (20 male, 9 female); average cumulative MTX dose at first cirrhosis diagnosis 3,130 mg, higher than in the 1980 study; serial-biopsy cumulative cirrhosis index grading (grades 1-4) showed no progression in most cases and in 14 cases cirrhosis was not confirmed on latest biopsy; alcohol intake proven to increase tendency to fibrosis and cirrhosis in MTX-treated patients; patients 3, 4, 20, 21, 25 died without signs of liver failure. The 29 patients plus 4 without follow-up biopsies represent 7.4% of all MTX-treated patients. Data from other studies comparing daily oral, 25-mg weekly single, and 15-mg divided intermittent oral schedules for relative hepatotoxicity were noted as inconclusive. Serial liver biopsies stated as the only reliable means of evaluating MTX-induced morphological liver changes.

raw_record.support_text: Investigators examined 169 liver biopsy samples from 71 psoriasis patients who underwent liver biopsy as part of monitoring methotrexate treatment. Patients treated with methotrexate who had risk factors for liver disease (especially type 2 diabetes or excess weight) were at higher risk for developing severe liver fibrosis compared with patients without such risk factors, even when low cumulative methotrexate doses were given. The authors conclude methotrexate should be considered a higher risk drug in patients with type 2 diabetes (Grade B evidence).

raw_record.support_text: The study assessed 24 psoriasis patients who had a recent liver biopsy during methotrexate (MTX) use, evaluating Fibroscan and Fibrotest for detecting significant MTX-induced hepatic fibrosis, confirming that MTX use is associated with hepatic fibrosis in psoriasis patients.

raw_record.extra_details: MTX acts by inhibiting DNA synthesis and via anti-inflammatory effects on T-cell mediated immune responses. Long-term side effect includes liver fibrosis and cirrhosis due to MTX hepatotoxicity; dermatologic guidelines recommend liver biopsy at every 1500 mg cumulative dose. Study of 24 patients comparing Fibroscan (n=20, median 6.4 kPa, range 3.3-18.4 kPa) and Fibrotest against liver histology (Metavir score): Fibroscan correctly identified 88% without significant fibrosis (<F2, ≤7.1 kPa); Fibrotest identified 83% with significant fibrosis (≥F2, >0.31). Liver biopsy carries 0.01-0.1% mortality risk due to postprocedural pain and bleeding.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports MTX-related liver toxicity in psoriasis patients, with serial liver biopsies documenting perisinusoidal fibrosis, steatosis, regenerative activity, and regenerative nodules that progress with cumulative methotrexate dosage (Roenigk grades advancing from I to IV by 4 g cumulative MTX). The authors note that histological exams suggest stellate-cell proliferation mediates the toxic lesion caused by MTX, and that the incidence of cirrhosis in psoriatic patients treated with MTX is higher than in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Psoriasis patients undergoing chronic methotrexate therapy; the paper notes patients presented liver lesions prior to MTX use that may relate to psoriasis, and that cirrhosis incidence in psoriatic patients treated with MTX is higher than in rheumatoid arthritis patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Serial liver biopsies in 13 patients (case series); cumulative MTX doses of 1 g, 1.5 g, 2 g, 3 g and 4 g; histology showed perisinusoidal fibrosis, steatosis, swollen hepatocytes, regenerative activity/nodules, sinusoidal dilation, congestion and cellular hyperplasia; Roenigk fibrosis/cirrhosis grades progressed from I to IV with increasing cumulative dose; sinusoidal dilation/congestion were not directly related to MTX dose; proposed mechanism involves stellate-cell proliferation.

raw_record.extra_details: Autoimmune hepatitis attributed to MTX; patient improved on drug withdrawal; complete resolution within 4 months of discontinuation, no prior autoimmune disease, confirming diagnostic criteria of drug-induced autoimmunity. WHO-UMC Probable, Naranjo Score 7 (probable), RUCAM 5. Reported as the second case of autoimmune hepatitis associated with MTX; the first case (2011) occurred in a 57-year-old man after 11 years of MTX, confirmed by liver biopsy, with complete normalization of laboratory parameters 5 months after stopping the drug.

raw_record.support_text: Methotrexate is reported to cause hepatic toxicity in rheumatoid arthritis patients: three of eight patients with adverse events in Weinblatt et al.'s study had hepatic toxicity, one with biopsy-proven cirrhosis and repeated transaminase elevations. A separate Australian group reported three male RA patients who developed cirrhosis after methotrexate therapy, with risk factors including advanced age (average 69 years), total methotrexate dose above 3900 mg, and alcohol intake in one case, and estimated a 5-year cumulative cirrhosis incidence of 9.4 per 1000 treated patients. Another cirrhosis case was reported in a male RA patient heterozygous for alpha-1-antitrypsin (PiMZ) deficiency.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Rheumatoid arthritis indication; cirrhosis cases occurred in elderly patients (average age 69), after high cumulative methotrexate dose (>3900 mg), with alcohol intake in one case, and in one patient with heterozygous alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency (PiMZ phenotype); subjects with pre-existing risk factors or liver susceptibility.
raw_record.extra_details: Includes biopsy-proven cirrhosis, repeated transaminase elevations (marker of toxicity in ACR guidelines), 5-year cumulative cirrhosis incidence of 9.4 per 1000 treated patients; authors suggest screening methotrexate-treated patients with abnormal liver function tests for alpha-1-antitrypsin levels/phenotype. In a separate long-term prospective biopsy study (Kremer et al., 27 RA patients, mean 6.3 biopsies over 8.2 years, AST checked every 4-6 weeks, dose reduced by 2.5 mg/wk for abnormal AST), Roenigk score increased significantly with time but changes were not clinically relevant and other histologic/ultrastructural scores did not progress; this was deemed reassuring on methotrexate safety in a carefully monitored low-alcohol population.

raw_record.support_text: In the section on Hepatotoxicity, transaminase level elevations after methotrexate ingestion are described as very common but usually spontaneously reversible and not associated with permanent hepatic injury. The Lederle representative presented 148 liver biopsies from 111 rheumatoid arthritis patients: among 98 liver specimens obtained 28-40 months after starting methotrexate (cumulative dose 750-2,250 mg), 13 showed mild fibrosis and 2 showed moderate to severe fibrosis, whereas 16 patients receiving a total dose >2,250 mg had no fibrosis.

raw_record.extra_details: 148 liver biopsies from 111 RA patients from Lederle's cumulative files. Transaminase elevations after ingestion are very common, usually spontaneously reversible, and not associated with permanent hepatic injury; persistent transaminase elevations are considered an indication for liver biopsy. Among 98 specimens taken 28-40 months after starting therapy (cumulative dose 750-2,250 mg), 13 showed mild fibrosis and 2 moderate-to-severe fibrosis; no fibrosis in 16 patients with total dose >2,250 mg. 54% of mild-fibrosis patients and both moderate-to-severe-fibrosis patients had below-normal serum albumin during therapy vs 25% of no-fibrosis patients. Treatment: weekly oral low-dose pulse methotrexate, 7.5-15 mg, up to 12-18 weeks clinical trials, some patients on therapy up to 9 years.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective analysis of 103 selected patients receiving 2 cycles of systemic high-dose methotrexate (HD-MTX, 3 g/m2) as ambulatory CNS prophylaxis for aggressive lymphoma, adverse events included 8 (8%) grade III hepatotoxicity events, mostly cytolysis, which was the most frequent grade III adverse event; 8 patients discontinued after 1 cycle for toxicity, including 3 with grade II hepatotoxicity. The paper further states that although severe hepatic cytolysis from MTX is rare, a simple increase in liver enzymes is frequently observed and is usually transient and spontaneously reversible.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Selected patient cohort (age < 60, albumin > 34, PS 0-1, normal renal and hepatic function) receiving HD-MTX as ambulatory CNS prophylaxis for aggressive lymphoma after induction therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: HD-MTX at 3 g/m2, 2 planned cycles, ambulatory regimen, 2013-2016; among 103 patients, 92 (89%) completed 2 cycles; grade III hepatotoxicity (mostly cytolysis) in 8 (8%) events was the most frequent grade III AE; 3 grade II hepatotoxicity events contributed to discontinuation after 1 cycle; toxicity graded by NCI-CTCAE v4.0; MTX clearance not monitored; 84% grade I/II and 16% grade III/IV AEs overall. HD-MTX used across indications incl. osteosarcoma, ALL, CNS lymphoma.

raw_record.support_text: In a second operation on the same patient (in an orthopedic hospital, under N2O/O2/halothane anesthesia), the patient with suspected hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI) received a total of 175 g sorbitol and 50 g fructose IV in two-thirds electrolyte solutions intraoperatively and on postoperative days 1 and 2. A few hours after surgery, the Quick prothrombin time was 19%, serum transaminase activity was increased, and renal retention values rose. The patient was transferred to a medical intensive care unit on postoperative day 2; the discharge diagnosis was again 'transient postoperative liver failure of unclear cause.'
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient with hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI); perioperative IV parenteral nutrition setting; co-exposure to fructose infusions.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: a 49-year-old woman with HFI who had experienced a similar transient postoperative liver failure two years earlier during a first orthopedic operation where sorbitol (125/50/75/50 g) and fructose (25/25/50 g) were infused IV. In the second episode, liver and coagulation values normalized within a few days after stopping glucose-exchange substances (sorbitol/fructose) and substituting coagulation factors, and the patient was discharged with the diagnosis of transient postoperative liver failure; she was later referred for metabolic diagnostics of HFI after her sister refused elective surgery due to prior experience. Laboratory values at peak included SGOT 726 U/l, SGPT 984 U/l, total bilirubin 4.6 mg/dl, Quick 9%, with renal retention (urea up to 84 mg/dl, creatinine 1.9 mg/dl). Sorbitol is metabolized to fructose and exerts its toxicity in HFI by this pathway.

raw_record.support_text: In a case report, the authors describe a patient who developed cholestatic hepatitis after vaginal application of AVC cream, a sulfonamide-based product. They state the temporal relation between AVC cream application and onset of symptoms, plus a prior history of fever with earlier use, strongly supports the diagnosis of sulfanilamide-induced cholestatic hepatitis. Exclusion of extrahepatic biliary tract obstruction and absence of other histologic changes also supported this diagnosis, even though absorption of sulfanilamide by the vaginal mucosa is incomplete.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Unusual route/formulation: drug administered as a vaginal cream (AVC cream); systemic absorption by the vaginal mucosa is reported to be incomplete, with blood levels below 1.0 mg/100 ml.
raw_record.extra_details: Diagnosis of sulfanilamide-induced cholestatic hepatitis supported by temporal relation between AVC cream application and symptom onset, prior fever with earlier use, exclusion of extrahepatic biliary obstruction, and absence of other liver histology changes. The paper notes hepatic injury following vaginal sulfonamide application had not previously been recorded; a prior report concerned eosinophilic pneumonia after AVC cream application. The article concludes that hepatic injury may follow vaginal administration of a sulfonamide-based drug.

raw_record.support_text: Déticène (dacarbazine, DTIC), an alkylating agent used for over 15 years in palliative treatment of malignant melanoma, is generally considered low toxicity with minor side effects (nausea, vomiting, moderate marrow suppression, influenza-like syndrome). Since 1979, a rare but often fatal complication has been recognized: acute hepatic failure from extensive hepatic necrosis caused by acute occlusion of the hepatic veins, either at the suprahepatic level (Budd-Chiari syndrome) or at the intrahepatic level, classified as hepatic veno-occlusive disease (MVO). The mechanism of these events remains debated.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: a 53-year-old woman on sequential dacarbazine monotherapy for malignant melanoma of the right leg (tumor resected 4 months earlier; untreated moderate arterial hypertension in history) developed acute hypovolaemic shock a few hours after the second chemotherapy infusion, with absent peripheral pulses, right hypochondrial pain/guarding, and slight flank dullness. Right-heart catheterization hemodynamic studies confirmed hypovolaemic shock. Diagnosis of hepatic veno-occlusive disease (MVO) was established; after massive fluid resuscitation (4 L macromolecules over 2 hours) plus dopamine (10 µg·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹) and corticosteroid therapy, outcome was favorable. Liver injury was acute hepatic failure by extensive necrosis from acute hepatic vein occlusion (Budd-Chiari or MVO). Second course began 48 h prior. Paper notes such veno-occlusive complications are rare but often fatal.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses dacarbazine hepatotoxicity in humans, noting that serological signs of liver damage during previous dacarbazine treatment cycles have been described for some patients who developed Budd-Chiari syndrome (BCS) or veno-occlusive disease (VOD) after dacarbazine treatment (Ceci et al. 1988), and references case reports of patients suffering from severe/acute massive liver damage after dacarbazine treatment. The authors' own observations were made in animals, but they treat dacarbazine as an established cause of hepatic VOD/BCS and liver damage in treated patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Human reports describe Budd-Chiari syndrome (BCS) and veno-occlusive disease (VOD) after dacarbazine chemotherapy treatment. Case literature: serological signs of liver damage in patients who later developed BCS/VOD; 17 patients with severe liver damage after dacarbazine (prior liver tests did not indicate pre-existing damage); acute massive liver damage in some patients. The paper contests the proposed allergic (eosinophilia-mediated) etiology (10 patients with prior peripheral eosinophilia vs other reports of severe damage without eosinophilia and frequent eosinophilia without liver damage in dacarbazine patients), and its own data do not support a contribution of dacarbazine light-decay products to hepatotoxicity. Used as an antineoplastic agent.

raw_record.support_text: A 68-year-old patient treated adjuvantly with Dacarbazine for lymph node metastases of malignant melanoma developed severe shock on the fourth day of the second treatment cycle, with increasing hepatomegaly, a massive increase in transaminases, and a decreased Quick value. The patient died of cerebral hemorrhage five days after beginning the second Dacarbazine cycle; autopsy showed severe liver cell necroses and liver vein thromboses with no melanoma metastases, consistent with veno-occlusive liver disease following Dacarbazine therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of death due to veno-occlusive liver disease (VOD) following Dacarbazine treatment of malignant melanoma (adjuvant therapy, second course). First course showed no intolerance; shock appeared on day 4 of the second cycle. Findings included hepatomegaly, massive transaminase increase, decreased Quick value, and death from cerebral hemorrhage 5 days after start of second cycle. Autopsy showed severe liver cell necroses and liver vein thromboses. Authors discuss hepatotoxicity of Dacarbazine, mechanism of liver vein thrombosis, possible hemostasiologic changes, and sensitization to Dacarbazine and/or previous liver cell damage. Prior surgeries one month earlier: cholecystectomy and appendectomy for gallbladder empyema.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a new case of fatal hepatic toxicity due to dacarbazine (DTIC), a drug used for 20 years in melanoma treatment, noting only few published cases of this complication. In the presented 50-year-old woman on her second course of DTIC (250 mg/m² daily for 5 days), acute vascular hepatic toxicity from DTIC was suspected; post-mortem histology confirmed fulminant hepatitis with medio-lobular extensive necrosis and dilated hepatic veins, and the patient died 5 days later.
raw_record.extra_details: 50-year-old woman with malignant melanoma; second course of dacarbazine (DTIC) 250 mg/m² daily for 5 days; pre-course basal labs were normal except eosinophilia (1.4x10⁹/L). On day 2 of second course developed abdominal pain, nausea, fever, then shock and respiratory failure/anuria. Peak labs: ALT 2348 IU/l, AST 5160 IU/l, LDH 20430 IU/l, INR 3.95, serum protein 2.8 g/100 ml. Treated with high-dose dexamethasone (250 mg/6 hourly) and recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (100 mg) without benefit. Patient died 5 days later; post-mortem showed fulminant hepatitis with medio-lobular extensive necrosis, poor inflammatory infiltration, and dilated hepatic veins without thrombi or vessel-wall inflammatory infiltrate. Complications previously reported as Budd-Chiari syndrome, veno-occlusive disease, or small hepatic vessel thrombosis; allergic pathogenesis discussed given occurrence during second course and eosinophilia. Doppler sonography confirmed patent main hepatic and portal veins. Indication: melanoma treatment.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that this patient manifested a rapidly progressive form of veno-occlusive disease of the liver attributed to a toxic etiology, in this case due to DTIC. Competing causes were excluded at autopsy: a normal heart ruled out congestive heart failure, there was no evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation in other organs, and severe hepatic damage from shock alone would have been accompanied by marked renal and other organ abnormalities. The paper frames this as a case of DTIC-induced hepatic veno-occlusive disease with a fulminant course.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Treatment for melanoma as the indication; single-patient case with the authors uncertain whether the reaction reflects a distinctive DTIC effect or this particular patient's individual response to the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case: initial clinical picture of fever, epigastric pain, and hepatomegaly with nonspecific hepatic laboratory tests (variable elevations of SGOT, bilirubin, and alkaline phosphatase). Pathologic findings were a rapidly progressive veno-occlusive disease of the liver; the brief clinical course precluded the fibrosis reported in other cases. The same VOD-like clinical syndrome may occur with many different chemotherapeutic agents; 4 of 5 previously reported evaluable cases had such liver failure contribute to or cause death. DTIC is metabolized in the liver but there is no evidence that its metabolites cause the lesion. No other reported patient had onset of liver dysfunction after as brief a drug exposure as this patient.

raw_record.support_text: A 56-year-old woman with BRCA1-mutated ovarian cancer developed a severe acute hepatocellular liver injury (ALT 3,350 U/L, AST 2,993 U/L, ALP 215 U/L) with jaundice (total bilirubin up to 11.4 mg/dL) and elevated INR (up to 2.1) with concern for impending fulminant liver failure, 3.5 months after starting olaparib maintenance therapy. Liver biopsy revealed submassive necrosis with lobular collapse, portal/lobular inflammation, cholestasis, and acute cholangitis consistent with immune-mediated drug-induced liver injury (IM-DILI). Injury resolved after olaparib withdrawal and prednisone treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported case in the United States of acute and severe immune-mediated drug-induced liver injury from olaparib; only one prior case reported in Italy (responsive to prednisone). Liver tests were normal up to 1 month prior to hospitalization; onset ~3.5 months after initiation. Liver biochemical pattern was hepatocellular with an R score of 40. Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) score was 7, indicating a probable association. Biopsy showed submassive necrosis with lobular collapse, moderate-severe portal and lobular lymphocytic inflammation, cholestasis with focal hepatocyte rosettes, acute cholangitis with bile duct injury, ductular proliferation, and ceroid-laden histiocytes; no portal fibrosis. Treated with oral prednisone 60 mg/d starting hospital day 3; liver tests improved with eventual normalization and prednisone tapered over 4 weeks without recurrent injury. Patient was not rechallenged with another PARP inhibitor. Olaparib is a first-in-class oral PARP inhibitor.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of a 70-year-old female who experienced significant CTCAE Grade 4 hepatocellular injury after initiating first-line maintenance Olaparib for Stage 3C high grade serous ovarian cancer associated with a deleterious BRCA mutation. Her liver injury resolved upon discontinuation of Olaparib, promptly recurred upon rechallenge, and liver enzymes returned to baseline after discontinuing Olaparib again. Investigations for infectious, metabolic, and autoimmune etiologies were unremarkable. Olaparib is described throughout as causing drug-induced liver injury, supported by the positive rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: 70-year-old female; first-line maintenance Olaparib for Stage 3C high grade serous ovarian cancer with deleterious BRCA mutation; CTCAE Grade 4 hepatocellular injury; injury resolved on discontinuation and promptly recurred on rechallenge (first documented positive rechallenge for Olaparib-induced liver injury); abdominal ultrasound and computed tomography and assessments for infectious, metabolic, and autoimmune etiologies unremarkable; liver enzymes returned to baseline after second discontinuation. Patient subsequently tolerated Niraparib maintenance therapy, interpreted by the authors as no cross-reactive hepatotoxicity between PARP inhibitors. Only two prior case reports of Olaparib-induced liver injury necessitating discontinuation are cited.

raw_record.support_text: Liver function tests were recorded on all patients throughout the study, but no hepatotoxicity was detected. One female patient had a transient rise in S.G.O.T. and alkaline phosphatase during the 6th-9th month of benorylate treatment with no other adverse effects or change in serum bilirubin or thymol turbidity; her values returned to normal and remained so for about 7 months, and the authors did not attribute this to hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients had rheumatic disease; benorylate given as 40% suspension at up to 8 g/day over up to 2 years.
raw_record.extra_details: Fifty-two patients with rheumatic disease received benorylate for up to 2 years; liver function tests recorded at intervals throughout the study. The authors concluded no serious side effects attributable to benorylate were reported and that benorylate is satisfactory for long-term treatment of rheumatic disease. The one female patient's transient S.G.O.T. and alkaline phosphatase rise returned to normal spontaneously and was not labeled DILI/hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that a case report had the final diagnosis of 'Ondansetron (OSDN)-induced hepatotoxicity'. GPT-4's alternative prediction attributed the elevated liver enzymes to gestational hyperemesis and olanzapine, but the clinician noted the LLM missed that symptoms and labs resolved upon stopping the medicine, confirming the ondansetron-induced hepatotoxicity diagnosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report final diagnosis of ondansetron-induced hepatotoxicity. Marked elevation in liver enzymes (AST and ALT) escalated during treatment and normalized after stopping the medicine and post-delivery; GPT-4 incorrectly attributed the injury to gestational hyperemesis and olanzapine; olanzapine itself was not the attributed cause.

raw_record.support_text: The authors discuss a newborn who developed a transient cholestatic hepatitis possibly induced by carbamazepine taken by his epileptic mother (400 mg/day) during gestation and breastfeeding. Applying the Naranjo algorithm, the causal relationship between the cholestatic hepatitis and transplacental carbamazepine exposure was judged probable. The hepatic adverse effects of carbamazepine are known, and because the drug crosses the placental barrier and is excreted in breast milk, infants of epileptic mothers may develop hepatic dysfunction.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Exposure was via transplacental passage and breastfeeding; the affected individual is a newborn of an epileptic mother treated with carbamazepine 400 mg/day, not a directly treated adult patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report in French (RÉSUMÉ). Between the third and seventh week of life the infant developed marked increases in gamma-glutamyltransferase, conjugated bilirubin, and bile acids. Diagnostic work-up excluded biliary atresia and metabolic or infectious etiologies. The authors recommend updating the carbamazepine monograph to warn clinicians of this possibility. Transient course reported.

raw_record.support_text: A report from Sydney of eight patients with carbamazepine hepatitis highlighted carbamazepine as a cause of a febrile illness, often with jaundice and abnormal serum biochemistry. Three patients presented with features suggestive of cholangitis, and despite serum biochemistry being classifiable as cholestatic, hepatocellular, or mixed, the histological appearance was invariably granulomatous hepatitis. The paper concludes that carbamazepine causes a granulomatous hepatitis as an unpredictable hepatic drug reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Granulomatous hepatitis present in all eight reported cases; serum biochemistry patterns varied (cholestatic, hepatocellular, or mixed); three patients had features suggestive of cholangitis and one had surgery for suspected cholecystitis; fever and jaundice reported; swift and complete resolution on drug withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: A 43-year-old woman with MCTD developed trigeminal neuralgia and started carbamazepine (200 mg daily). Two weeks later she developed high fever, systemic rash, and severe liver dysfunction (AST 1,105 IU/L, ALT 766 IU/L), and was admitted because carbamazepine-associated hepatotoxicity was strongly suggested. The liver injury was attributed to carbamazepine on the basis of the temporal relationship following its initiation.
raw_record.extra_details: Carbamazepine 200 mg daily; injury appeared two weeks after initiation; severe liver dysfunction with AST 1,105 IU/L and ALT 766 IU/L accompanied by high fever and systemic rash in a patient with mixed connective tissue disease; hepatotoxicity was described as 'strongly suggested' as the reason for hospital admission.

raw_record.support_text: In an Acute Liver Failure Study Group (ALFSG) cohort, which categorized patients into DILI-ALF (drug-induced liver injury progressing to acute liver failure) versus APAP-ALF groups, carbamazepine was named among the causative drugs responsible for non-APAP hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among causative drugs for non-APAP hepatotoxicity in the ALFSG DILI-ALF cohort (this study subgroup N=39; larger study N=52).

raw_record.support_text: In the study one patient developed a cholestatic hepatitis and another a severe hyponatremia, and four cases showed an increase in gamma glutamyl transferase. The text explicitly states these are all known side-effects of carbamazepine and recommends periodic checks of liver enzymes, electrolytes, and a hemogram during carbamazepine treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: One patient developed cholestatic hepatitis during carbamazepine treatment in the study; four cases showed an increase in gamma glutamyl transferase. The paper states these are known side-effects of carbamazepine and recommends periodic liver enzyme checks. Elevated GGT was reported as a laboratory finding without characterization as clinically meaningful DILI.

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes a patient who developed a severe hypersensitivity reaction to carbamazepine, presenting as DRESS syndrome, which further complicated into hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) and vanishing bile duct syndrome (VBDS). The authors state this is, to their knowledge, the first reported case of carbamazepine-induced HLH and VBDS, attributing the bile duct injury (ductal/cholangiopathy-type liver injury) to carbamazepine.
raw_record.extra_details: Anti-epileptic drug (AED) causing DRESS syndrome, which complicated into HLH and vanishing bile duct syndrome. DRESS typically manifests 2-6 weeks after drug initiation. Liver biopsy showed areas of missing bile ducts; no CK19-positive small bile ducts were detected, only CK7-positive cholestatic liver cells; bilirubin fluctuated during treatment. HHV-6 immunofluorescence staining in liver tissue was negative. No eosinophilia was observed despite fever, dark urine, and rash on admission. DRESS-associated immune dysregulation (T-cell proliferation, cytokine storm including IFN-gamma, TNF-alpha, IL-2) and elevated IL-1, IL-2, IL-6 by carbamazepine are proposed mechanisms.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report that their patient satisfied all seven Japanese diagnostic criteria of DRESS (DIHS), including liver dysfunction (criterion 4) and HHV-6 reactivation, after taking a specific drug. At patch testing only carbamazepine showed a positive reaction while phenobarbital, sodium valproate, and zonisamide were negative. The authors accordingly attribute the DRESS episode with liver dysfunction to carbamazepine, and further cite Syn et al.'s similar case in which carbamazepine caused both DRESS and acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case of DRESS (DIHS) that met all seven Japanese diagnostic criteria (definitive), which include liver dysfunction, fever, abnormal blood findings, lymphadenopathy, and HHV-6 reactivation. Patch test was positive only for carbamazepine; phenobarbital, sodium valproate, and zonisamide were explicitly negative, and HHV-6/HHV-7/CMV were not reactivated at the time of patch testing. Switching therapy to phenobarbital did not cause DRESS. The authors cite Syn et al.'s similar carbamazepine case reporting both DRESS and acute liver failure. Anticonvulsant cross-reactivity and an arene-oxide/epoxide-hydrolase/cytochrome P450 detoxification hypothesis were discussed but considered inapplicable to this patient.

raw_record.support_text: Carbamazepine-associated DILI case reports were analyzed for liver-injury pattern, eosinophilia, hepatic necrosis, inflammatory reaction, and death/liver transplantation outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: 60 individual case reports; median age 45 y; 32 female/28 male; median treatment duration 5 weeks; HC 40%, Cs/mixed 60%; peripheral eosinophilia present in 27% (49/60 reported); hepatic eosinophilia present in 32% (38/60 reported); hepatic necrosis 37%; inflammatory reaction 100%; death or liver transplant 17%; liver biopsy reported in 38/60 cases.

raw_record.support_text: The anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome is characterized by fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, and later internal target organ disease including hepatitis. For each anticonvulsant, liver involvement ranged from mild elevations in transaminases to fulminant hepatic necrosis. Among 53 patients there were 89 exposures to anticonvulsants and 81 adverse reactions (25/27 exposed to carbamazepine).
raw_record.extra_details: Anticonvulsant hypersensitivity reaction with clinical features including fever, skin rash, lymphadenopathy, nephritis, and hematologic abnormalities. Liver involvement ranged from mild transaminase elevations to fulminant hepatic necrosis. 25/27 carbamazepine-exposed patients had an adverse reaction.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a patient demonstrating a variety of body systems affected in an idiosyncratic drug hypersensitivity reaction to carbamazepine. Although a 'definite' causal association of carbamazepine with the adverse events could not be established because rechallenge was not attempted, the case fulfilled criteria for a 'probable' adverse drug reaction using the Naranjo probability score.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report of idiosyncratic drug hypersensitivity to carbamazepine presenting with hepatotoxicity, erythema multiforme, lymphadenopathy, and eosinophilic leukocytosis. Liver function tests were elevated and then decreased over hospitalization; tests for Hepatitis A and B, cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus were negative. Hypersensitivity reactions to drugs typically occur after a sensitization period of 1-5 weeks and are often accompanied by fever, rash, eosinophilia and granulomatous infiltrate in the liver. Rechallenge was not attempted; probable causality per Naranjo score.

raw_record.support_text: Carbamazepine is listed among the main 10 drugs leading the Latin American DILI Registry with n = 5 cases, with RUCAM-based causality assessment.
raw_record.extra_details: 5 cases in the Latin American DILI Registry; RUCAM-based causality assessment used.

raw_record.support_text: Cases of granulomatous hepatitis following carbamazepine have been documented. In one group of three patients, all had been treated with carbamazepine for less than one month and presented with a febrile illness associated with mild elevations in liver function studies; liver biopsies revealed noncaseating granulomatous hepatitis, and two patients also exhibited acute cholangitis. The liver dysfunction disappeared with drug discontinuation, though alkaline phosphatase levels remained elevated for several months. A hypersensitivity reaction has been implicated as the cause.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients treated with carbamazepine for less than one month; febrile illness with mild liver function elevations; liver biopsy showed noncaseating granulomatous hepatitis; two patients also had acute cholangitis; liver dysfunction resolved after carbamazepine discontinuation; alkaline phosphatase remained elevated for several months; hypersensitivity reaction implicated as cause; granulomatous hepatitis can be associated with a cholangitic process confusable with biliary tract infection.

raw_record.support_text: The clinical picture in Case 1 (49-year-old woman, Ms. A) was thought to be consistent with a drug-induced hepatitis, most likely due to administration of carbamazepine. Her symptoms (nausea, vomiting, anorexia, jaundice) and laboratory elevations returned to normal after 6 weeks following drug stoppage.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1: 49-year-old woman treated with carbamazepine 1200 mg/day (serum level 105 µg/dl) during the fourth week of treatment developed nausea, vomiting, anorexia, scleral jaundice, and right upper abdominal tenderness; liver 10 cm midclavicular. Labs: serum bilirubin 5.7 mg/dl (peak 10 mg/dl), SGOT 319, SGPT 384, alkaline phosphatase 623 (peak 700) milliunits/ml, LDH 236; 2+ bilirubinuria; hepatitis B studies negative; ultrasound showed no biliary obstruction. Carbamazepine was stopped and symptoms resolved over 3 weeks with labs normal after 6 weeks. Injury was reported as a drug-induced hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Carbamazepine was among the top 10 drugs involved in LA DILI Registry cases, with n = 5 cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Among the top 10 drugs in the LA DILI Registry, n=5 cases.

raw_record.support_text: The antiepileptic drug carbamazepine was incriminated in 2 patients (25% of cholestatic cases) with a cholestatic injury pattern. Exposure duration was 60 days with 60 days to symptom onset.
raw_record.extra_details: 2 patients with cholestatic injury (25% of the 8 cholestatic cases); duration 60 days, time to symptoms 60 days. RUCAM-based DILI classification.

raw_record.support_text: Carbamazepine was attributed to 8 DILI cases, predominantly hepatocellular (62%). Two cases (29%) met nR-based Hy's law criteria and 1 true Hy's law case occurred; fatal cases were reported for carbamazepine.
raw_record.extra_details: 8 of 843 registry DILI cases; Hep 62%/Chol 12%/Mix 25%; female 75%, lymphopenia 40%, eosinophilia 50%; 2 (29%) fulfilled nR-based Hy's law, 1 true Hy's law with death/liver transplantation. Fatal cases reported.

raw_record.support_text: In this case report, the patient presented with clinical manifestations of DRESS syndrome including a severe form of cholestatic hepatitis (without eosinophilia). Because the patient had recently been started on carbamazepine, the authors concluded it is likely that carbamazepine was the causative agent of the liver injury. They also noted that, in view of cross-reactivity with phenytoin, prior phenytoin exposure might have sensitized the patient to carbamazepine.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case of DRESS syndrome (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms but without eosinophilia). Recent onset of carbamazepine. Cross-reactivity with phenytoin suggested as possible prior sensitization to carbamazepine. Authors recommend withdrawing the offending drug and avoiding structurally related aromatic anticonvulsants (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbitone).

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes two patients with carbamazepine-induced granulomatous liver injury. Both had moderately increased serum aminotransferases but little histologic evidence of hepatocellular necrosis, with intralobular inflammation limited to scattered small granulomas and more striking portal triad changes with granulomatous inflammation and focal acute inflammation particularly around small bile ducts. The paper concludes that carbamazepine should be added to the list of therapeutic agents causing granulomatous liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients with granulomatous liver injury (granulomatous hepatitis); moderately increased serum aminotransferases with little histologic hepatocellular necrosis; portal triad granulomatous inflammation and focal acute inflammation around small bile ducts; fever and night sweats present, eosinophilia absent; rapid and complete resolution of all symptoms and abnormalities. The occurrence of granulomas was suggested to reflect immunologic hypersensitivity. Carbamazepine is structurally related to imipramine, an occasional cause of cholestatic liver injury. Prior reported carbamazepine liver-injury cases: one with mixed cholestatic and hepatocellular injury in which deliberate rechallenge caused dramatic recurrence of symptoms (Ramsay); and one child with fulminant hepatic necrosis. raw_record.support_text: In this cohort of DILI-DRESS cases from two prospective Western DILI registries, the antiepileptic drugs carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin, valproic acid and levetiracetam were identified as culprit drugs that induced drug-induced liver injury in the context of DRESS (n=15 antiepileptic cases). The predominant injury pattern in the antiepileptic category was hepatocellular (43%), cholestatic (36%), and mixed (21%), with severity graded mild (27%), moderate (67%), and severe (6.7%), and no liver-related deaths or transplantations.

The report frames this as a case of toxic hepatitis caused by carbamazepine, aggravated by the drug's effect on hepatic cytochrome P-450 involved in haem metabolism.

Hepatic porphyria was excluded; porphyrin analysis compatible with variegate porphyria. No other drugs, no alcohol use. The introduction also notes carbamazepine hepatotoxicity can manifest as asymptomatic transaminase and GGT elevation, acute hepatitis, granulomatous hepatitis, or vanishing bile duct syndrome.

raw_record.support_text: A 16-year old patient with carbamazepine-induced hepatotoxicity, associated with hypersensitivity manifestations of fever, rash and eosinophilia, is described. Mononuclear leucocytes from the patient were more sensitive to oxidative metabolites of carbamazepine than control cells, and serum from the patient recognised a single 94 kDa protein band on human liver microsomes, which none of 25 control sera recognised. The paper presents this as a human case of carbamazepine hepatotoxicity with an immunoallergic/autoantibody basis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (16-year old); therapeutic anti-epileptic use for generalized epilepsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 400 mg/day; fever developed 4 weeks after start of therapy, generalized rash after 5 weeks, and jaundice after 6 weeks; associated with fever, rash and eosinophilia. In vitro mononuclear leucocyte susceptibility to carbamazepine oxidative metabolites generated by induced murine and human hepatic microsomes; patient serum, but none of 25 control sera, recognised a 94 kDa protein band on human liver microsomes via immunoblot. Proposed immunologic/immunoallergic mechanism, possibly with a deficiency in cellular detoxification (epoxide hydrolase) predisposing to idiosyncratic toxicity.

Combination of prednisolone and azathioprine markedly improved the liver dysfunction and the patient experienced complete recovery within one month.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 75-year-old man with ileal GIST with peritoneal dissemination. Regorafenib was given orally at 120 mg/day (October 2013), discontinued after 9 days due to fever, restarted on day 15 after recovery; elevated ALT (274 IU/l), AST (385 IU/l) and T-Bil (1.1 mg/dl) on day 28, therapy terminated; worsening on readmission at day 31 with further increase to T-Bil 5.2 mg/dl, AST 1,840 IU/l, ALT 2,534 IU/l at day 37. Negative hepatitis B/C, ANA and alpha-SMA; normal IgG. Liver biopsy showed interface hepatitis with plasma cell infiltration; responded to prednisolone plus azathioprine, complete recovery within one month with no relapse after withdrawal of immunosuppressants and tapering prednisolone to 5 mg/day. Diagnosis: drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis (DIAIH).

raw_record.support_text: In the previously published GRID study, severe liver dysfunction occurred in a 49-year-old Japanese man with metastatic GIST who discontinued regorafenib treatment due to acute hepatic failure that was considered drug related. The patient was hospitalized 9 days after beginning his second cycle with symptoms of hepatic failure, regorafenib was discontinued, and the patient died 2 weeks later. The current post-marketing surveillance study reported no deaths due to severe liver injury related to regorafenib.
raw_record.extra_details: Case from the GRID pivotal phase 3 clinical trial in GIST: 49-year-old Japanese man with metastatic GIST hospitalized 9 days after beginning his second cycle of regorafenib with symptoms of hepatic failure; regorafenib was discontinued and the patient died 2 weeks later. As a result, further enrollments were suspended and, per a Japanese regulatory approval requirement, weekly liver function testing is recommended during the first 2 months of regorafenib therapy. The current observational post-marketing surveillance study in Japanese GIST patients reported no deaths due to severe liver injury related to regorafenib, and liver/hepatic function abnormalities were fewer with dose reductions and drug holidays.

raw_record.support_text: In this human case series of chronic hypervitaminosis A, cirrhotic patients had consumed significantly more vitamin A than patients without cirrhosis (mean daily intake 135 ± 31.4 × 10³ IU/day vs. 65.7 ± 9.2 × 10³ IU/day; mean total cumulative intake 366 ± 94 × 10⁶ IU vs. 91 ± 40 × 10⁶ IU). A minimal continuous daily consumption of 25,000 IU/day over 6 years produced similar histological liver lesions to 100,000 IU/day over 2½ years, and discontinuous consumption of 300,000 IU/day over 10 years also resulted in cirrhosis, attributing chronic high-dose vitamin A intake as the cause of the cirrhosis.

raw_record.support_text: A 58-year-old man with psoriasis vulgaris, without prior liver disease, alcohol consumption, or cholelithiasis, was started on retinol 1 mg/kg/day in May 1984 and given for a 12-week period. At the end of the twelfth week he developed pruritus, dark urine, and acholic stool, with alkaline phosphatase up to 420 U/liter, gamma glutamyl transpeptidase up to 380 U/liter, and jaundice with bilirubin up to 400 µmol/liter (80% direct). The authors present this as the first case with clinical and pathologic evidence of acute cholestatic jaundice induced by retinol therapy, describing it as a biochemical and morphologic cholestatic hepatitis.

raw_record.extra_details: Retinol (referred to by the brand names Tigason in Europe and Tegison in the USA) is described chemically as an aromatic retinoid. Symptoms and signs: pruritus, dark urine, acholic stool, jaundice; alkaline phosphatase up to 420 U/l (normal 10-85), gamma glutamyl transpeptidase up to 380 U/l (normal 20-53), bilirubin up to 400 µmol/l (normal 2-17), 80% direct. Authors note prior reports of transient slight transaminase elevations in <10% of treated patients, histologic changes resembling viral hepatitis, and mild cholestasis in a few cases.

raw_record.support_text: Capecitabine (CAP), an antineoplastic agent used to treat colon cancer, is known to cause mild hepatotoxicity; however, the paper reports a previously unreported severe, late acute liver injury. A 63-year-old man receiving the fifth cycle of CAP monotherapy developed fatigue and jaundice with markedly elevated transaminases (AST 2,448 U/L; ALT 1,984 U/L). Discontinuation of CAP reversed the delayed CAP-induced acute hepatic injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral prodrug of 5-fluorouracil (pyrimidine analogue); conventional dose of 1,250 mg/m2 twice daily, delayed onset during the 10th day of the fifth treatment cycle. Markedly elevated transaminases (ALT 1,984 U/L, AST 2,448 U/L), total bilirubin 23.03 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 20.8 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 523 U/L. Recovery after CAP discontinuation (dechallenge); two-week follow-up showed declining transaminases and normal labs at six-month follow-up. Viral hepatitis (A, B, C, E, EBV, CMV, HSV) and autoimmune panels negative; no hepatic metastases on CT. Suggested mechanism is direct hepatotoxicity via hepatic microsomal metabolism producing toxic substances; CAP therapy is known to cause DILI usually with high bilirubin, and transaminases rarely rise >5x upper limit of normal.

raw_record.support_text: The case report describes a patient who experienced severe liver toxicity and clinical signs of severe hepatitis due to Capecitabine treatment, with no other adverse effects from Capecitabine. Other explanations were ruled out and the diagnosis of DILI was confirmed by liver biopsy, which showed idiosyncratic DILI with no hepatic steatosis; the patient had a mixed-pattern type B (dose-independent) DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient had severe increases in liver enzymes (ALT, AST, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase) and clinical symptoms of DILI; no DPYD mutation was found by gene sequencing; type B (dose-independent) reaction; toxicity could have led to a fatal outcome though the patient survived with no fatal outcome.

Patient 1 died; Patient 2 recovered after fluid replacement, urine alkalinization and continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). Mechanism attributed to dysfunction of cell membranes and mitochondria due to disorder of cellular ion transporters.

Histology shows cholestasis with dilated centrolobular bile canaliculi filled with bile pigment, minimal/no parenchymal necrosis, no inflammatory infiltrate. raw_record.support_text: In the authors' prospective trial, patients who all underwent liver resection then received 5-fluorouracil by hepatic arterial infusion (15 mg/kg weekly bolus). Only one patient (6% of 18 evaluable) developed 5-fluorouracil-induced hepatitis. The other hepatic arterial infusion-related toxicities were hepatic arterial thrombosis or arteritis in three patients (17%), and six patients (33%) required cessation or dose reduction because of systemic 5-fluorouracil toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Administered by hepatic arterial infusion as post-resection adjuvant chemotherapy; all patients underwent liver resection before receiving 5-fluorouracil.
raw_record.extra_details: Weekly bolus hepatic arterial infusion at 15 mg/kg (approx 600 mg/m2/wk); 5-fluorouracil-induced hepatitis occurred in 1 of 18 evaluable patients (6%). No severity (e.g., acute liver failure, grade) or biochemical pattern reported. Related toxicities in the same cohort were hepatic arterial thrombosis/arteritis (17%) and systemic 5-fluorouracil toxicity requiring cessation/dose reduction (33%), which are not DILI.

It also describes that bicyclol lowered the occurrence rate of DILI in breast cancer patients receiving a 5-fluorouracil plus cyclophosphamide plus epirubicin regimen (6.1% vs 24.5% without bicyclol).

raw_record.support_text: Because well-known causes of liver disease were excluded, the interval between the beginning of treatment with candesartan cilexetil and the onset of liver injury, the regression of liver abnormalities after withdrawal of the treatment, and the result of liver biopsy strongly suggested the diagnosis of candesartan cilexetil-induced hepatotoxicity. Liver histology showed marked portal inflammation, ductopenia with vacuolar degeneration of biliary cells, ductular cholestasis, and portal fibrosis with porto-portal septa.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case report from a Geriatric Medicine division. Onset of liver injury occurred within 1 week to 3 months of starting candesartan cilexetil; abnormalities regressed after drug withdrawal (dechallenge), and biopsy was compatible with drug-induced hepatotoxicity. Laboratory data peaked at admission (total bilirubin 27.2 mg/dL, conjugated 22.1 mg/dL, AST 1367 IU/L, ALT 918 IU/L, PT 52%) and normalized over 8 weeks. Histology: marked portal inflammation (lymphocytes, monocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils), ductopenia confirmed by cytokeratin 7 immunostaining, vacuolar degeneration of residual interlobular duct biliary cells, peripheral ductulogenesis, ductular cholestasis with marginal concretions, portal fibrosis and porto-portal septa, bilirubinostasis, and zonal micro- and macrovesicular steatosis. Other causes excluded: previous hepatic/biliary disease, alcohol abuse, viral hepatitis, biliary obstruction, autoimmune hepatitis/cholangitis, liver ischemia, Wilson's disease, bacterial infection.

In a 4-week ulcer healing trial by Farup and colleagues, zaltidine therapy in 135 patients resulted in an 8% incidence of marked transaminasemia (5 to 10 times normal) and severe biopsy-documented hepatocellular injury in one patient, suggesting possible intrinsic toxicity of the drug.
