raw_record.support_text: A case report described two Japanese patients who had initially received bosentan monotherapy and experienced liver toxicity. After dose reduction or discontinuation, liver function was normalized, and patients received retreatment with a combination of bosentan and UDCA, after which subsequent liver function tests showed no abnormalities.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of two Japanese patients on bosentan monotherapy who developed liver toxicity, with normalization of liver function after dose reduction or discontinuation (dechallenge response). Retreatment with a combination of bosentan and ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) produced no abnormal liver function tests, suggesting a compensatory/protective role for UDCA.

raw_record.support_text: Bosentan significantly inhibits the bile salt export pump, considered the cause of the observed severe toxicity. In clinical trials, 11% of bosentan patients had ALT >3xULN (RR 5.11, 95% CI 2.25-11.61), two patients had combination ALT and bilirubin elevation, and two patients developed liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Clinical trial: 658/280 patients; ALT/AST >3xULN 11.0/2.0 (RR 5.11, 95% CI 2.25-11.61); >5x 6.9; >8x 4.9; combination ALT and bilirubin elevation 2/0; liver failure 2/0; withdrawal due to liver toxicity not reported. Mechanism: inhibition of bile salt export pump considered the cause of the observed severe toxicity; nonclinical increase in ALT and hepatocyte degeneration in dogs at high dose.

raw_record.support_text: In the exploratory STRIDE-6 study, 12 patients discontinued bosentan because of acute hepatotoxicity (of whom 50% had been rechallenged with bosentan with recurrent increased hepatic transaminases), reflecting the known association of acute hepatotoxicity with ET receptor antagonists including bosentan. Additionally, in the STRIDE-2 study the incidence of elevated hepatic transaminases (>3x ULN) was 11% for the open-label bosentan group.
raw_record.extra_details: STRIDE-6: 12 of 13 bosentan safety discontinuations were for acute hepatotoxicity (1 for rash); 50% of these 12 were rechallenged with bosentan with recurrent increased hepatic transaminases. STRIDE-2: elevated hepatic transaminases >3x ULN occurred in 11% of open-label bosentan patients (reversed in all cases). Acute hepatotoxicity is a known class effect of ET receptor antagonists.

raw_record.support_text: Bosentan, approved in 2001 for pulmonary hypertension, had 2 unequivocal Hy's Law cases among roughly 600 total patients (only about 300 treated for more than 4 weeks) and an 11% rate of at least 3x transaminase elevation. The paper states that cases of significant hepatotoxicity have been seen in the United States, with no fatal hepatic injury or transplants to date, and suggests that monitoring (monthly transaminase checks, risk-management distribution) may mitigate risk.
raw_record.extra_details: Indication: pulmonary hypertension. Premarketing experience included 2 unequivocal Hy's Law cases and an 11% rate of >=3x ULN transaminase elevations (reported among ~600 patients, ~300 treated >4 weeks). Approved with a risk-management program: limited distribution (also a teratogen) and monthly transaminase monitoring. No fatal hepatic injury or liver transplants reported in the US to date.

raw_record.support_text: A 39-year-old male with systemic sclerodermia and pulmonary hypertension was switched to bosentan (62.5 mg b.i.d) on April 27th 2006. Liver function tests on May 4th 2006 showed transaminitis (AST 3.3xULN, ALT 16xULN) while ALP, G-GT, total serum bilirubin and PT were normal. Acute viral hepatitis was excluded, abdominal ultrasonography was normal, and bosentan was suspected and stopped while other drugs were continued; the patient improved quickly (ALT 1.6xULN on May 10th 2006). The diagnosis of bosentan-induced acute cytolytic hepatitis was retained with no other cause found, and the authors estimated the causal relationship as 'probable'.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report in a patient with systemic sclerodermia complicated by sclerodactyly, digital necrosis, Raynaud's syndrome, pulmonary fibrosis, and renal involvement, treated for pulmonary hypertension. Concomitant drugs (iloprost, dextropropoxyphene, paracetamol, prednisone, enalapril, diltiazem) were continued while bosentan was stopped, and the patient improved. Bosentan 62.5 mg b.i.d; transaminitis developed within days (AST 3.3xULN, ALT 16xULN); ALP, G-GT, bilirubin and PT normal; acute viral hepatitis excluded; no inflammatory/infectious syndrome, no cardiac dysfunction; normal liver and biliary tract on ultrasound. Bosentan not restarted (no rechallenge). Causal relationship estimated as 'probable' by the authors.

raw_record.support_text: Of the 13 patients who discontinued bosentan because of safety concerns, 12 were due to hepatotoxicity and 1 due to rash. Six of the 12 patients with hepatotoxicity had been re-challenged with bosentan with documented recurrence of acute hepatotoxicity before enrollment, and 8 of the 12 had discontinued bosentan within the first 3 months of therapy. Elevated hepatic transaminases (5 to 8 times ULN in some) resolved after bosentan discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: 12 of 13 patients who discontinued bosentan for safety concerns did so due to hepatotoxicity (1 due to rash); 6 of 12 had documented recurrence of acute hepatotoxicity upon rechallenge; 8 of 12 discontinued within the first 3 months of therapy; elevated transaminases reached 5-8 times ULN in some patients and resolved after drug discontinuation. Reported in a PAH clinical-trial safety subset recruiting patients switched from bosentan with prior hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Bosentan is described among drugs known to cause hepatic dysfunction in humans. It causes increases in serum ALT and AST in 10–11% of patients at levels at least 3 times the upper limit of normal and in 4% at levels greater than 8 times ULN (NDA, 2001). Fattinger et al. reported that bosentan-induced cholestatic liver injury developed within the first 4 weeks of treatment, with increased serum bile acid levels preceding increased ALT by 5–7 days.
raw_record.extra_details: ALT/AST ≥3x ULN in 10–11% and >8x ULN in 4% of patients (NDA 2001); cholestatic liver injury within first 4 weeks of treatment; increased serum bile acids preceded ALT elevation by 5–7 days; concomitant glyburide treatment increased incidence of liver injury to 29%.

raw_record.support_text: The paper develops a physiologically based kinetic model for the cholestatic drug bosentan and its metabolite RO 47-8634, predicting BSEP-mediated BA efflux inhibition upon repeated oral administration of 500 mg bosentan twice daily. It references the clinical trial of Fattinger et al. (2001), which reported the highest DILI incidence at this dosing regimen and in which 18% of healthy participants developed liver injury during the trial; both observed and simulated data showed a significant increase in systemic bile acid concentrations upon repeated bosentan administration.
raw_record.extra_details: Bosentan is characterized as a cholestatic drug. DILI incidence of 18% among healthy participants reported in the clinical trial of Fattinger et al. (2001) at a dosing regimen of 500 mg twice daily (oral). Proposed mechanism: bosentan and its metabolite RO 47-8634 inhibit BSEP-mediated bile acid efflux, increasing intrahepatic BA levels, as simulated with the PBK model. The metabolite RO 47-8634 is modeled only as a contributor via BSEP inhibition/aggravator and is not independently attributed as the causal liver-injuring entity in humans.

raw_record.support_text: In univariate logistic regression and Fisher's exact tests in the Caucasian PAH cohort, CYP2C9*2 was the only polymorphism significantly associated with occurrence of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) in patients treated with bosentan (odds ratio 95% CI = 2.29–∞; P = 0.003), while a SNP in SLCO1B1 (rs11045819) showed only a trend for association with bosentan-induced liver injury. This documents DILI events attributed to therapeutic bosentan exposure in PAH patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Analysis was restricted to the 56 Caucasian patients from a 92-patient, predominantly female (71%) PAH cohort; more than half (57.1%) were coadministered an OATP1B1 inhibitor (most commonly sildenafil).
raw_record.extra_details: Larger study cohort of 92 ethnically diverse PAH patients (61% Caucasian). CYP2C9*2 (rs1799853) was also significantly associated with increases in ALT (beta=2.16, P=0.024) and AST (beta=1.92, P=0.016) in multivariate regression adjusted for BMI; SLCO1B1 rs11045819 showed only a trend for DILI. Bosentan is metabolized to Ro 48-5033 (hydroxylation) and Ro 47-8634 (O-demethylation), further hydroxylated to Ro 64-1056; in vitro CYP2C9 formed only Ro 48-5033. The study investigated reduced-function SNPs in CYP2C9, CYP3A4, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, BSEP, and MRP2 as potential biomarkers for stratifying PAH treatment. In vitro microsome and recombinant-enzyme findings are supporting preclinical data.

raw_record.support_text: In a commentary on a comparative study of oral bosentan vs nebulised iloprost in 31 patients with portopulmonary hypertension (all Child-Pugh class A or B cirrhosis), the authors note both treatments had favourable safety profiles and that there was only one case of drug-induced liver injury, which occurred with bosentan and resolved with dose reduction. The commentary adds that bosentan causes derangement of liver enzymes in approximately 10% of patients, and that concerns have been raised about its use in patients with pre-existing hepatic dysfunction.

raw_record.support_text: In a 71-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis who had prior skin allergy to aspirin, penicillin, and cotrimoxazole, bosentan (62.5 mg twice daily, increased to 125 mg twice daily) was started for recurrent digital ulcers. About 6 weeks later she developed fever, generalized maculopapular exanthema, headache, and hepatitis with 20-fold increased ALT and marked eosinophilia (2500/ml). Bosentan was stopped and she improved within 4 days with normalization of eosinophils; hepatitis virus serologies and HHV-6 PCR were negative. The authors assume the case relates to DRESS (drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms), which they suggest is the third case of hypersensitivity related to bosentan.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis and a history of hypersensitive skin reactions to aspirin, penicillin, and cotrimoxazole (suggested sulfonamide-nonantibiotic cross-reactivity/overall allergic predisposition); single-patient case of DRESS with liver cytolysis.
raw_record.extra_details: Bosentan is an endothelin-1 receptor antagonist used for pulmonary arterial hypertension and digital ulcers in systemic sclerosis; it contains a -SO2NH2 sulfonamide moiety. Onset about 5-6 weeks after treatment start; fever 38°C, maculopapular exanthema, headache; ALT 20-fold elevated; eosinophil count 2500/ml; rapid clinical improvement and ALT improvement within 4 days of discontinuation plus normalization of eosinophils; RegiSCAR criteria for DRESS fulfilled; negative hepatitis virus serologies and HHV-6 PCR; ultrasound excluded biliary problems. Reported as the third case of hypersensitivity related to bosentan; DRESS death occurs in 10% of cases due to visceral complications such as fulminant hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Despite concerns over liver toxicity, bosentan was used successfully in portopulmonary hypertension (PoPH). In 11 patients with Child A cirrhosis and WHO functional class III-IV PoPH treated with bosentan for at least one year, bosentan was well tolerated and no drug-related liver injury was observed. In a separate retrospective noncomparative case series of 31 PoPH patients with Child A and B cirrhosis (18 treated with bosentan, 13 with inhaled iloprost), both treatments were safe in terms of liver function.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with portopulmonary hypertension (PoPH) with Child A/B cirrhosis; WHO functional class III-IV; bosentan given for at least one year in the 11-patient group; comparison cohort in the 31-patient series included inhaled iloprost.
raw_record.extra_details: In the 11-patient group (Child A cirrhosis) bosentan showed improved 6MWD and VO2max with reduced pulmonary vascular resistance at 1 year, with no drug-related liver injury observed. In the 31-patient series (18 bosentan, 13 inhaled iloprost; 3-year follow-up), bosentan showed better survival (p=0.029) and event-free survival (p=0.017) than inhaled iloprost and both treatments were safe in terms of liver function.

raw_record.support_text: A 78-year-old woman developed mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic liver injury three weeks after starting clopidogrel 75 mg/day and aspirin following percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stents. Liver profile improved after clopidogrel was discontinued, but on hospital day 5 clopidogrel was reintroduced and liver enzyme levels rose again; it was again discontinued with gradual improvement. An extensive work-up including hepatitis and rheumatologic screening, ultrasonography, MRI, and ERCP was normal. The Maria and Victorino scale for drug-induced hepatotoxicity indicated a probable relationship (score of 14) between clopidogrel and mixed hepatocellular injury and cholestatic jaundice.
raw_record.extra_details: Clopidogrel 75 mg/day co-administered with aspirin 325 mg/day after PCI with drug-eluting stents; injury appeared 3 weeks after starting therapy. Positive rechallenge: reintroduction on day 5 of hospitalization caused liver enzyme rise, re-discontinuation led to improvement within 3 days and marked improvement at 2-week follow-up. Maria and Victorino causality score 14 (probable). Mixed hepatocellular injury and cholestatic jaundice. Patient presented with abdominal pain, jaundice (1 week), and black stools. Competing causes (hepatitis, infectious mononucleosis, rheumatologic disease, biliary obstruction) excluded. Reported as the ninth case report of clopidogrel-induced mixed hepatocellular injury and cholestatic jaundice and the second confirmed with positive rechallenge.

raw_record.support_text: The patient was diagnosed with clopidogrel-induced severe hepatitis. After discontinuing clopidogrel, AST increased to 2,107 U/L, ALT to 1,567 U/L, and bilirubin to 37 mg/dL (predominately direct), and INR rose to 2.1 despite empiric vitamin K. A brief course of prednisone and ursodiol led to normalization of liver biochemistries.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: liver biopsy showed severe acute hepatitis with mixed inflammatory portal tract infiltrates (plasma cells, neutrophils, eosinophils), bile ductular reaction, patchy hepatocyte ballooning degeneration, and extensive periportal hepatocyte dropout without fibrosis. Peak ALT 1,567 U/L, AST 2,107 U/L, bilirubin 37 mg/dL (predominantly direct), INR 2.1 with coagulopathy and jaundice. Naranjo and RUCAM scores both 8, indicating probable drug-induced hepatitis. Patient treated with prednisone and ursodiol and recovered with normalization of liver biochemistries. Prior reported clopidogrel-induced hepatitis cases range from reversible injury and recovery to acute hepatic failure and death, with onset between 3 and 180 days and rechallenge-confirmed injury in some cases; clopidogrel liver injury has been reported as cholestatic, hepatocellular, or mixed.

raw_record.support_text: According to the International Consensus Meeting, the type of liver damage in this case was hepatocellular. Applying the CIOMS (Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences) score, the causality assessment of clopidogrel-induced liver injury was probable, based on no history of liver or biliary disease, negative diagnostic work-up excluding other causes of acute hepatitis, clopidogrel being the recently added drug, worsening of liver injury during drug administration, and resolution-linked evidence; the presence of thrombocytopenia (a known clopidogrel side effect) provided additional evidence of drug involvement.
raw_record.extra_details: A 63-year-old man with diabetes and ischaemic disease, on chronic human insulin, captopril, molsidomine, simvastatin and aspirin (>3 years without adverse reaction), started clopidogrel 75 mg daily for percutaneous coronary stenting. Nineteen days after starting clopidogrel he developed tea-coloured urine and jaundice; he was hospitalized on day 54 (clopidogrel and all other drugs stopped) and died on day 56 after grade IV encephalopathy, significant haemoptysis, and 2 days after hospitalization. Autopsy not performed. Liver biochemistries on day 54/day 56: total bilirubin 78/80 µmol/L, ALT 336/297 U/L, AST 303/208 U/L, GGT 160/156 U/L, ALP 186/185 U/L, prothrombin time 27%/28%. Thrombocytopenia 90×10³/mm³; negative viral/autoimmune serologies; normal liver and biliary tract on ultrasound; CIOMS causality score = probable.

raw_record.support_text: A 75-year-old woman developed hepatotoxicity days after starting clopidogrel (Plavix) for elective cerebral aneurysm coiling. Liver enzymes were elevated (AST 1362 IU/L, ALT 716 IU/L, ALP 160 IU/L) with elevated total and direct bilirubin, and the Maria and Victorino diagnostic scale of hepatotoxicity scored 10. Enzymes trended down after drug discontinuation, and a single 75 mg re-challenge produced a worsening pattern on day 2 that normalized by day 4, confirming the diagnosis of drug-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient's only new medication was clopidogrel, started 5 days prior; long-term co-medications included esomeprazole, levothyroxine, pregabalin, and risedronate.
raw_record.extra_details: Symptoms were nausea, vomiting and bloating. Maria and Victorino hepatotoxicity score 10. Positive drug re-challenge with a single 75 mg dose: worsening liver enzymes on day 2 followed by normalization by day 4. Patient improved and was discharged; complete normalization of liver enzymes at 2-week follow-up. Viral hepatitis, autoimmune antibody, blood culture, ultrasound, and HIDA scan work-ups were negative.

raw_record.support_text: In 92 paediatric patients with IBD receiving mercaptopurine (mean dosage 1.25 mg/kg/day), patients with wild-type TPMT and mercaptopurine-induced hepatotoxicity showed significantly (p < 0.05) higher concentrations of 6-MMP (>5700 pmol/8 × 10⁸ red cells) than patients without hepatotoxic events. The paper suggests high TPMT activity and subsequent accumulation of 6-MMP could play an important role in the pathogenesis of mercaptopurine-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paediatric patients with inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, indeterminate colitis); wild-type TPMT genotype; therapeutic dosing (mean 1.25 mg/kg/day).
raw_record.extra_details: Mercaptopurine-induced hepatotoxicity in patients with wild-type TPMT was associated with 6-MMP >5700 pmol/8 × 10⁸ red cells vs non-hepatotoxic patients (p<0.05); high TPMT activity and subsequent 6-MMP accumulation proposed as playing a role in the pathogenesis of hepatotoxicity. 6-MMP is a metabolite discussed mechanistically, not independently attributed as the causal entity.

raw_record.support_text: In children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia receiving maintenance therapy that included daily oral 6-mercaptopurine (6MP), a group of patients developed gastrointestinal symptoms and 6MP-induced hepatotoxicity with elevated aminotransferases and jaundice. Other potential causes (viral hepatitis, sepsis, leukemic infiltration of the liver, and other hepatotoxic drugs such as methotrexate) were ruled out as far as possible: when 6MP was held, the symptoms and signs of hepatitis resolved despite continuation of methotrexate, and rechallenge with 6MP resulted in similar adverse effects. The paper states that 6MP has been reported to be toxic to the liver as well as to the bone marrow and intestine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients (ages 3-17 years) with ALL on maintenance chemotherapy; received combination therapy including methotrexate, vincristine, and prednisone; small case series of 4 symptomatic children compared with asymptomatic children.
raw_record.extra_details: Symptomatic patients had AST 174-385 IU/L, ALT 204-558 IU/L, bilirubin up to 243 µmol/L (elevated direct bilirubin up to 213 µmol/L); doses 52-100 mg/m². Lower 6MP peak concentrations and AUC, longer time to peak in symptomatic patients suggested impaired absorption and/or hepatic accumulation. TPMT activity 10-27 units/ml pRBC consistent with homozygous wild-type genotype, ruling out low-TPMT-related hematologic toxicity as the mechanism. Possible proposed mechanisms include selective hepatic toxicity of methylated nucleotide (meMPN) metabolites or a hypersensitivity reaction developing after weeks to months of sensitization; rechallenge reproduced the adverse effects.

raw_record.support_text: Among 233 pediatric IBD patients treated with thiopurines (230 started on azathioprine, 3 on mercaptopurine), 50 patients (21.5%) developed thiopurine-induced adverse events leading to cessation of therapy. Under hepatobiliary disorders, hepatotoxicity occurred in 5 patients: one grade 1 (mild), two grade 2 (moderate), and two grade 3 (severe). The paper attributes this hepatotoxicity to thiopurine therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population with inflammatory bowel disease; mercaptopurine was also used as a switch agent after azathioprine in some patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Mercaptopurine was the first thiopurine in only 3 patients; thiopurine-induced hepatotoxicity is reported for the combined cohort (5 patients, 10% of 50 AE cases). Median time to onset 59 days [IQR 32–976]; CTC grades 1–3.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports adverse effects resulting from treatment with azathioprine and mercaptopurine, divided into dose-independent allergic-type reactions and dose- and metabolism-dependent nonallergic-type reactions. Citing a large 1985 study by Present et al. during treatment of IBD with mercaptopurine, it lists overall adverse-effect risk (15%), pancreatitis (3%), bone marrow depression (2%), infection (7%), hepatitis (0.3%), and miscellaneous allergic reactions (2%), thereby attributing hepatitis as an adverse effect of mercaptopurine therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis reported as an adverse effect in IBD treatment with mercaptopurine at a frequency of 0.3% (Present et al., 1985, large study). Other reported adverse-effect frequencies: overall risk 15%, pancreatitis 3%, bone marrow depression 2%, infection 7%, miscellaneous allergic reactions 2%. The paper also notes azathioprine is a pro-drug converted to mercaptopurine and that adverse effects are classified as dose-independent allergic-type or dose/metabolism-dependent nonallergic-type reactions, but does not assign hepatitis to either category.

raw_record.support_text: A single case of drug-induced hepatitis was attributed to mercaptopurine after nine days of use, among 52 patients who received the drug in hospital.
raw_record.extra_details: One case of drug-induced hepatitis attributed to mercaptopurine after nine days of use; 52 patients were exposed in hospital. BCDSP monitoring cohort.

raw_record.support_text: Over the initial ten-year period of the prospective DILIN cohort study, 1434 cases of drug-induced liver injury were enrolled and underwent causality assessment, of which 27 were attributed, at least in part, to a thiopurine, including 12 to 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP) and 15 to azathioprine. After excluding 5 cases in which liver injury was considered only possibly related to the thiopurine, 22 cases (10 attributed to 6-MP and 12 to Aza) fulfilled the predefined inclusion criteria and were analyzed.
raw_record.extra_details: 10 of 22 included DILIN cases were attributed to 6-mercaptopurine (10-year prospective DILIN cohort, total 1434 DILI cases). Combined 6-MP/Aza expert DILIN causality was definite in 2 (9%), very likely in 12 (54%), and probable in 8 (36%); RUCAM median 6.5 with 4 highly probable, 14 probable, and 4 possible. One 11-year-old boy received 6-MP for acute lymphocytic leukemia. Most patients were adults with autoimmune conditions, most commonly inflammatory bowel disease (55%). Presenting features included symptoms attributable to liver injury in all but one patient (jaundice 73%, nausea 64%, fatigue and abdominal pain 50%); viral serologies negative except one patient with stable pre-existing chronic hepatitis C; imaging showed no biliary obstruction.

raw_record.support_text: In the large experience of Present et al in 396 patients treated with 6-mercaptopurine over a mean follow-up of about 5 years, reported toxicity included pancreatitis (3.3%), bone marrow depression (2%), allergic reactions (2%), and drug hepatitis (0.3%). This attributes drug hepatitis, a form of drug-induced liver injury, as a toxicity of 6-mercaptopurine treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Drug hepatitis occurred in 0.3% of 396 patients treated with 6-mercaptopurine (Present et al series), mean follow-up of 5 years; other reported toxicities in the same series included pancreatitis 3.3%, bone marrow depression 2%, and allergic reactions 2%. The paper also notes a patient may benefit from switching from azathioprine to 6-mercaptopurine especially if intolerance is due to unspecific side effects like nausea or to hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Six of 29 (20.7%) patients discontinued mercaptopurine due to adverse events considered related to the study drug: four stopped due to nausea, one due to hepatotoxicity and one due to arthralgia. One patient discontinued mercaptopurine due to an adverse event (hospitalization for corticosteroid-induced myopathy) that was not considered related to the treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: One patient in a randomized trial (OPTIC) of mercaptopurine vs placebo in ulcerative colitis discontinued mercaptopurine due to hepatotoxicity that the investigators considered related to the study drug; leading to drug discontinuation. In the same trial, abnormal liver function tests (elevation of transaminases, alkaline phosphatase and/or gamma-glutamyltransferase, and hypoalbuminaemia) were reported as adverse events in 15 (9.1%) mercaptopurine-treated patients vs 4 (4.0%) in the placebo group, but these isolated liver-test changes were not characterized as DILI.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that hepatotoxicity (drug hepatitis) associated with 6-MP/AZA therapy is a dose-related adverse event that typically resolves on reduction or discontinuation of 6-MP/AZA, and that these dose-related events, hepatotoxicity in particular, correlate with high 6-MMPR (methylated metabolite) levels. Seven of the 10 study patients had experienced a dose-dependent hepatic event while receiving 6-MP, and all events resolved once 6-MP was discontinued, with no recurrence after conversion to 6-TG.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose-related drug hepatitis in IBD patients; hepatotoxicity correlates with elevated 6-MMPR (6-methylmercaptopurine ribonucleotide) methylated metabolite levels; 7 of 10 study patients had a dose-dependent hepatic event on 6-MP that resolved on discontinuation and did not recur after conversion to 6-TG. Historical figures cited: drug hepatitis ~0.3% of therapy, with overall estimated 6-MP/AZA toxicity ~15% (bone marrow depression ~2%). Methylated metabolite (6-MMPR) role in hepatic pathogenesis treated as mechanism, not as an independently causal entity.

raw_record.support_text: In the histopathologic study of human drug-induced liver injury, Group I (zonal injury) included eight cases, among which two were associated with the therapeutic administration of mercaptopurine. The lesion showed severe centrolobular fatty metamorphosis with intracytoplasmic coarse or medium-sized lipid globules, necrotic liver cells or loss of cytoplasmic basophilia and nuclear pyknosis, occasional PAS-positive pigmented macrophages in necrotic zones, and minimal portal inflammation with occasional bile ductule proliferation; cholestasis was noted in two of the group's cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Zonal injury (Group I) with severe centrolobular fatty metamorphosis characterized by intracytoplasmic coarse or medium-sized lipid globules; liver cells necrotic or showing loss of cytoplasmic basophilia and nuclear pyknosis; occasional pigmented macrophages containing PAS-positive material in necrotic zones; inflammation not conspicuous except for enlarged Kupffer cells; minimal portal inflammation and occasional proliferation of bile ductules; cholestasis was noted in two cases of the group. Two cases reported.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 173 IBD patients treated with azathioprine or 6-MP, 4.6% developed hepatotoxicity; mean MeMPR levels were significantly higher in these patients compared to those with no adverse effects. The paper groups 6-MP with azathioprine as thiopurine drugs where high-normal TPMT activity may confer an increased risk of liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Thiopurine drug (6-MP) used in inflammatory bowel disease, considered together with azathioprine. In the cited study of 173 patients, 4.6% developed hepatotoxicity with significantly higher mean MeMPR levels; MeMPR had poor sensitivity/specificity and should not replace liver blood test monitoring. High-normal TPMT activity may confer increased risk of liver damage via elevated methylated thiopurine metabolites.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective study of 30 IBD patients treated with 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP), hepatotoxicity was reported as a 6-MP-related adverse event, causing discontinuation in 1 of the patients. The figure caption for individual 6-MMPR concentration curves additionally identifies this patient as having drug-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient (1 of 30) discontinued 6-MP because of hepatotoxicity during an 8-week prospective study in IBD (Crohn's disease/ulcerative colitis) patients at a mean 6-MP dose of 0.71 mg/kg (CI95% 0.66-0.76). In this study 6-MMPR concentrations did not correlate with ALT, AST, bilirubins or the occurrence of hepatotoxicity, and TPMT genotype was not predictive of hepatotoxicity. Drug-related adverse-event discontinuations (6-MP related, n=10) comprised intolerance (2), leukopenia (4), hepatotoxicity (1), and pancreatitis (3).

raw_record.support_text: Among 60 long-latency DILI cases (>365 days) in the DILIN study, mercaptopurine (n=3) was among the most commonly implicated agents.
raw_record.extra_details: Long-latency DILI (>365 days); n=3 cases in the DILIN Prospective Study cohort.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity results in the withdrawal of thiopurine drugs, azathioprine (AZA) and mercaptopurine (MP), in up to 10% of patients with inflammatory bowel disease. The study enrolled unselected patients with acute thiopurine hepatotoxicity who were offered allopurinol co-therapy with low-dose AZA or MP, implying thiopurine therapy itself caused the hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity led to withdrawal of MP in up to 10% of inflammatory bowel disease patients; 11 unselected patients (3 Crohn's disease, 8 ulcerative colitis) with acute thiopurine hepatotoxicity were treated with allopurinol co-therapy plus low-dose AZA/MP; starting AZA/MP dose determined by TPMT activity (two patients intermediate TPMT) then reduced to 25% for allopurinol co-therapy; 9/11 (82%) remained in long-term remission (median 42 months) with normal liver tests.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports short- and long-term toxicity in 396 patients with ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease treated with 6-mercaptopurine (Present et al.). Adverse events included pancreatitis (3.3%), allergic reactions (2%), drug hepatitis (0.3%), infection (7.4%), neoplasm (3.1%) and bone marrow suppression (2%). Hepatitis is listed among non-allergic reactions that can occur months to years after therapy initiation and are dose-dependent, treated by temporary drug stoppage and dose lowering.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported drug hepatitis in 0.3% of 396 IBD (ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease) patients (Present et al.). Hepatitis is a non-allergic, dose-dependent reaction that can occur months to years after starting therapy and is managed by temporarily stopping or lowering the dose. Also described together with azathioprine as a hepatotoxicity concern that can occur in a fraction of patients; therapeutic doses titrated up to 1.5 mg/kg/day for 6-mercaptopurine.

raw_record.support_text: In a 49-year-old man with ulcerative colitis, 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP) was used for maintenance therapy while in clinical remission, but 6-MP was subsequently discontinued secondary to hepatotoxicity and pancytopenia. The hepatotoxicity is clinically attributed to 6-MP and warranted treatment discontinuation in this individual patient.
raw_record.extra_details: 6-MP was used for maintenance therapy in a patient with ulcerative colitis (diagnosed 1992); it was discontinued concurrently due to hepatotoxicity and pancytopenia, before escalation to infliximab therapy.

raw_record.support_text: In reviewing their extensive experience with 6-mercaptopurine in 396 patients with inflammatory bowel disease and approximately 1800 patient-years of follow-up, Present 1989 reported a higher incidence of adverse reactions, including a 0.3% incidence of drug-induced hepatitis, along with significant infection (7.4%), pancreatitis (3.3%), neoplasm (3.1%), bone marrow suppression (2.0%), and allergy (2.0%).
raw_record.extra_details: 0.3% incidence of drug-induced hepatitis among 396 patients with inflammatory bowel disease treated with 6-mercaptopurine over approximately 1800 patient-years of follow-up (Present 1989). Other reported adverse reaction rates: significant infection 7.4%, pancreatitis 3.3%, neoplasm 3.1%, bone marrow suppression 2.0%, allergy 2.0%.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 396 patients with inflammatory bowel disease (120 ulcerative colitis, 276 Crohn disease) treated with 6-mercaptopurine over 18 years and followed for a mean of 60.3 months, toxicity directly induced by 6-mercaptopurine included drug hepatitis in 1 patient (0.3%). These complications were reversible in all cases with no mortality.
raw_record.extra_details: Drug hepatitis reported as directly induced by 6-mercaptopurine in 1 of 396 patients (0.3%) with inflammatory bowel disease (120 ulcerative colitis, 276 Crohn disease); complication reversible with no mortality. Disease indication was steroid-dependent or intractable inflammatory bowel disease, fistulas, or need to avoid resection.

raw_record.support_text: The thiopurines 6-MP and AZA are useful for IBD but have significant hepatotoxicity. In a study of almost 3500 patients, AZA/6-MP-induced hepatotoxicity occurred in 3.4% of patients, with an overall incidence of about 1% per patient-year in IBD patients on 6-MP/AZA, with no difference between AZA and 6-MP. Most mild thiopurine-induced liver injury occurs in the first few months of therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings in IBD patients on thiopurine therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: AZA/6-MP-induced hepatotoxicity occurred in 3.4% of patients in a study of almost 3500 patients; overall hepatotoxicity incidence approximately 1% per patient-year. No difference in hepatotoxicity incidence between AZA and 6-MP. Most mild thiopurine-induced liver injury occurs in the first few months of therapy; transient enzyme elevations may resolve spontaneously without dose adjustment. Serious thiopurine hepatotoxicity grouped into three categories: hypersensitivity (arises 2-3 weeks after initiation, cholestatic profile with elevated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase), dose-dependent endothelial cell injury (manifesting at 3 months to 3 years as peliosis hepatis, nodular regenerative hyperplasia, veno-occlusive disease, sinusoidal dilatation and/or fibrosis), and idiosyncratic cholestatic reaction with severe jaundice that may not resolve after drug withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that Aza (azathioprine) and 6-MP (6-mercaptopurine) caused liver injury in humans, with frequent injury after dose escalation (59% of patients), indicating partial dose-relatedness and intrinsic hepatotoxicity at higher doses, while the authors conclude that Aza and 6-MP should be added to a growing list of agents with both idiosyncratic and intrinsic hepatotoxic potential.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Includes dose escalation within therapeutic use; prognosis generally favorable except in patients with pre-existing liver disease; concurrent corticosteroid use and underlying immune-mediated diseases are common in this population.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective DILI case-series study with well characterized patients and good follow-up; injury most often occurs within 3 months of exposure or dose escalation, often in women, with non-specific symptoms followed by jaundice; two patterns: transient mildly symptomatic aminotransferase elevation and cholestatic hepatitis with modest ALT and Alk P elevations and moderate-to-severe jaundice (cholestasis verified by biopsy, low serum Alk P); occurrence of sinusoidal obstruction syndrome and nodular regeneration supports intrinsic hepatotoxicity; a patient developed prominent hepatotoxicity from 6-MP after an episode of jaundice on Aza, consistent with documented cross-sensitivity to cholestatic injury between the two purine analogues.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report two cases of severe cholestasis associated with high levels of 6-mercaptopurine (6 MP) metabolites occurring after orthotopic liver transplantation. Applying the Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale, the temporal relationship of abnormal liver enzymes with high 6 MP metabolite levels, normalization of the liver biochemistry after drug withdrawal, absence of other offending agents, and other reported cases argue strongly in favor of 6 MP as the 'probable' cause of cholestasis. Histological features attributed to cholestatic 6 MP hepatotoxicity include severe intrahepatic cholestasis in a centrilobular location, centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis, and sinusoidal dilatation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Liver transplant recipients (post-orthotopic liver transplantation) receiving 6 MP as immunosuppression.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases of severe cholestasis with high 6 MP metabolite levels; liver biochemistry normalized over several weeks after 6 MP withdrawal. Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale classified 6 MP as 'probable' cause of cholestasis. Histology: severe intrahepatic cholestasis (centrilobular), centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis, sinusoidal dilatation. 6 MP hepatotoxicity may present with varied manifestations ranging from asymptomatic rise in serum aminotransferases, cholestasis associated with nausea and vomiting, to venoocclusive disease (VOD) with portal hypertension, hepatoportal sclerosis, peliosis hepatitis, and nodular regenerative hyperplasia. 6 MMP (6-methylmercaptopurine) metabolite levels correlate with hepatotoxicity, whereas 6 thioguanine levels do not.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report on 3 patients with IBD who underwent liver biopsies due to elevated aminotransferase levels suspected to be due to 6-MP. The biopsy samples exhibited centrilobular injury characterized by ceroid-laden macrophages, hepatocyte anisonucleosis, lipofuscin pigment, and centrilobular steatosis. Aminotransferase levels returned to normal or remained borderline elevated after the 6-MP dose was decreased (1 patient) or discontinued (2 patients).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis) receiving 6-MP therapeutically for IBD.
raw_record.extra_details: Three cases of 6-MP hepatotoxicity (2007-2011) from teaching case files. Case 1: 38-year-old man with ulcerative colitis on 6-MP monotherapy (50 mg/day escalated to 100 mg/day, then reduced to 75 then 50 mg/day), ALT 82 U/L, AST 42 U/L, AP 74 U/L; 6-TGN 312 pmol/8x10^8 RBC, 6-MMP ~2900 pmol/8x10^8 RBC; negative hepatitis serology, normal ceruloplasmin, negative anti-mitochondrial/anti-smooth muscle antibodies; ultrasonography suggested fatty liver; also on amoxicillin 250 mg/day. Histology showed centrilobular injury with ceroid-laden macrophages, hepatocyte anisonucleosis, lipofuscin pigment, and centrilobular steatosis; aminotransferases normalized or stayed borderline after dose decrease or discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: In Case 2, a 2-year-old male with Langerhans cell histiocytosis was started on second-line therapy with mercaptopurine and cladribine. After about 6 months of mercaptopurine he developed hyperbilirubinemia, hepatomegaly, and high alkaline phosphatase (1424 IU/L), so mercaptopurine was stopped considering drug-induced cholestasis. A liver biopsy to differentiate drug-induced cholestasis from hepatic histiocytosis was in favor of drug-induced hepatitis, and his liver enzymes continued to be mildly altered on follow-up, with imaging findings indistinguishable from sclerosing cholangitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (2-year-old male) patient treated for Langerhans cell histiocytosis; mercaptopurine given together with cladribine as second-line therapy; hepatic histiocytosis remained a competing differential for the cholangitis/fibrosis; liver enzymes did not fully normalize after stopping the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Drug-induced cholestasis was clinically considered and mercaptopurine was stopped (dechallenge); liver biopsy favored drug-induced hepatitis. Presented with hyperbilirubinemia, hepatomegaly, and alkaline phosphatase 1424 IU/L after about 6 months of mercaptopurine. Follow-up imaging (ultrasound) showed sclerosing cholangitis with periductal band-like echogenicities, coarse echotexture, lobulated margins, findings indistinguishable from sclerosing cholangitis; liver enzymes remained mildly altered on follow-up.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatitis was diagnosed when abnormal liver function studies developed that had not been present before 6-mercaptopurine initiation. Although hepatitis occurred in 11 patients, only 1 patient had hepatitis shown to be directly induced by 6-mercaptopurine: a 55-year-old man with intractable ulcerative colitis requiring continuous steroid therapy who became icteric about 6 months after starting 6-mercaptopurine. Liver biopsy showed cholestasis with inflammation suggestive of drug hepatitis; liver tests returned to normal on withdrawal, and jaundice recurred upon self-rechallenge and resolved again on stopping 6-mercaptopurine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single 55-year-old patient with ulcerative colitis requiring continuous steroid therapy; patient refused surgery and self-rechallenged; jaundice and cholestatic changes on biopsy with recurrence on rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Only 1 of 11 total hepatitis cases during 6-mercaptopurine therapy could be shown as directly drug-induced; the other 10 cases were attributed to infection. Icterus appeared ~6 weeks into the fourth month (about 6 months) of therapy. Liver biopsy showed cholestasis with inflammation suggestive of drug hepatitis; liver function tests normalized on withdrawal; jaundice recurred on rechallenge and resolved on stopping again. Overall 6-mercaptopurine toxicity directly induced in 30 patients (7.6%), all reversed on withdrawal with no deaths.

raw_record.support_text: 6-Mercaptopurine (6-MP), introduced in the 1950s as an antineoplastic agent for leukemias and lymphomas, is a thiopurine that has been implicated along with azathioprine in liver injury. Reports of liver injury, sometimes fatal, appeared shortly after introduction, and more than 100 cases of liver injury attributed to Aza and 6-MP have been reported. In large prospective and retrospective studies on drug-induced liver injury, Aza and 6-MP are frequently listed as common causes.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Veno-occlusive disease and nodular regenerative hyperplasia are reported with higher doses and long-term treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: 6-MP is an active thiopurine; Aza is its prodrug, and the two are blamed jointly. In many cases association was confirmed by prompt recurrence of injury upon readministration (rechallenge). Both are associated with transient, usually mild and self-limited serum enzyme elevations, and both are implicated in clinically apparent hepatotoxicity that can be severe, leading to prolonged intrahepatic cholestasis or acute liver failure, plus veno-occlusive disease and nodular regenerative hyperplasia at higher doses/long-term use. The current DILIN prospective cohort analysis enrolls thiopurine injury cases adjudicated as probable, very likely, or definite.

raw_record.support_text: Based on clinical history and histologic findings, lenalidomide-induced hepatotoxicity was suspected and the drug was discontinued. The patient had complete normalization of his liver function profile 16 days following discontinuation and follow-up MRI revealed complete regression of the hepatic lesions into simple regenerative nodules. The prompt resolution after lenalidomide discontinuation confirmed a lenalidomide-induced hepatotoxicity and liver nodules necrosis. The paper suggests the role of lenalidomide's antiangiogenic effect in hepatic regenerative macronodules infarction.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had pre-existing cirrhosis (micronodular liver) with multiple (more than 30) well-circumscribed hepatic nodules measuring up to 20 mm in the right lobe; initial suspicion of multifocal HCC was excluded by biopsy, which showed multiple infarcted regenerative nodules.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a single patient. Ultrasound and MRI showed multiple infarcted regenerative nodules with thick rim enhancement on arterial/portal phases and no washout. Histology showed localized hepatocyte proliferation with fibrotic bands and coagulation necrosis. Prompt improvement on dechallenge: complete normalization of liver function 16 days after lenalidomide discontinuation; complete regression of liver lesions on MRI at 3 months and 1 year. Authors note reported cases of lenalidomide-induced hepatotoxicity are rare and no prior report of liver necrosis; mechanism attributed to the antiangiogenic effect of lenalidomide.

raw_record.support_text: A 45-year-old woman with undifferentiated connective tissue disease developed cholestatic hepatitis after 4 weeks of quinacrine 100 mg/day. The Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) scale was 6, indicating a probable causal relationship between the offending drug and liver damage. Based on clinical history, laboratory investigations, and liver biopsy findings, the diagnosis of quinacrine-induced cholestatic hepatitis was made, and liver enzymes normalized over about 5 months after stopping the medication.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case, 45-year-old African American woman with undifferentiated connective tissue disease; quinacrine 100 mg/day for refractory disease; onset ~4 weeks after starting; symptoms fatigue, anorexia, nausea, diffuse abdominal pain, scleral icterus, dark tea-colored urine; peak labs AST 629 IU/l, ALT 913 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 914 IU/l, total bilirubin 11.0 mg/dl (later peaked at 22.9 mg/dl ~3 weeks after onset); hepatology service described a mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic pattern; liver biopsy showed canalicular cholestasis without periportal cholestatic ductular reaction plus patchy loss of pericentral hepatocytes and stellate sinusoidal fibrosis (prior central zone injury); labeled acute cholestatic hepatitis and quinacrine-induced cholestatic hepatitis; RUCAM score 6 (probable); all medications held except long-term prednisone; liver enzymes normalized over ~5 months; infectious and autoimmune hepatitis excluded; abdominal ultrasound unremarkable.

raw_record.support_text: The mechanism of injury in vemurafenib hepatotoxicity is unknown. In 63 patients with vemurafenib hepatotoxicity, a cholestatic or mixed pattern of liver injury was more common at presentation than a hepatocellular pattern (65% vs 35%). Most patients presented within 2 months of drug initiation, and the estimated reporting rate of vemurafenib hepatotoxicity was 5.13 (95% CI, 3.8-6.4) per 1000 patient-years of exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency to liver injury onset mostly within 2 months; estimated reporting rate 5.13 (95% CI 3.8-6.4) per 1000 patient-years; 63 patients with vemurafenib hepatotoxicity; cholestatic or mixed pattern (65%) vs hepatocellular (35%); treatment by dose reduction or discontinuation (17/63 continued at a decreased dose, 25 rechallenged, 20 able to complete therapy); mechanism unknown; associated histology (Figure 1) of granulomatous hepatitis with lymphocytic infiltration of bile ducts and canalicular cholestasis in zone 3; approved for melanoma with BRAF mutations; liver test elevation 30% with 11% grade 3-4; fatal hepatic failure reported: No.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses nafcillin-induced cholestasis and states that while nafcillin is known to affect bilirubin transport and cause conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, the case report and others suggest nafcillin can also cause a hypersensitivity-mediated liver injury. The described patient developed an allergic, eosinophilic, cholestatic pattern of liver injury. Supporting human data cited include 6/46 patients developing eosinophilia, 8.1% of 119 treated patients developing liver function abnormalities, and transaminitis in one of 32 patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity more associated with intrahepatic cholestasis, rarely with skin eruptions or fever; eosinophilia described. Case series (Lestico, Presti, Mazuryk, Nahata) reported cholestasis, eosinophilia, microvesicular/macrovesicular steatosis, prolonged cholestasis (>40-80 days), and response to prednisone in one case. One reported case (69/F) died; several required hemodialysis. Cholestasis lasted 3 months in current 71/F case.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a fatal case of nafcillin-induced hepatotoxicity confirmed by liver biopsy, with total bilirubin peaking to 21.8 mg/dl and an extensive negative evaluation for other causes of hepatic injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 53-year-old woman receiving nafcillin 12 g/day IV for MSSA bacteremia/osteomyelitis; jaundice with mild disorientation appeared on day 15 with total bilirubin 9.6 mg/dL, direct 7.3 mg/dL, ALP 388 IU/L, AST 67 IU/L, ALT 24 IU/L, GGTP 878 IU/L; peak total bilirubin 21.8 mg/dL. Dechallenge produced a mild transient drop in AST/ALT/ALP/GGTP. Extensive workup negative (coombs, ANCA MPO/PR3, RF, ASMA, ANA, HLA B27, complement, LKM, AFP, anti-TPO); ultrasound and MRCP excluded obstruction. Liver biopsy showed diffuse hepatocanalicular cholestasis with focal centrizonal bile infarct, periportal hepatocellular swelling and mild nodular hyperplasia-like changes; diagnosis of cholestatic jaundice secondary to nafcillin was made and ursodiol (10 mg/kg) started. No fulminant hepatic failure, coagulopathy, or encephalopathy at that time; GGTP and ALP remained >1500 IU/L on follow-up. Prior ertapenem had been discontinued before nafcillin. Patient had pre-existing renal insufficiency (creatinine 2 mg/dL, GFR 26 mL/min).

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of liver failure attributable to nafcillin use in a 68-year-old male treated for methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus osteomyelitis. After 4 weeks of antibiotic therapy he presented with painless jaundice, required drug discontinuation, and a liver biopsy showed findings consistent with drug-induced liver injury; liver function tests trended toward normal with cessation of nafcillin, and he was discharged with a diagnosis of nafcillin-induced acute liver injury. The abstract frames nafcillin-induced acute liver injury as a rare and potentially fatal complication known since the 1960s.
raw_record.extra_details: Intravenous nafcillin 2 g every 4 h, on therapy for 4 weeks at presentation; presenting labs bilirubin/direct bilirubin 9.4/8.2 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 311 IU/L, aspartate transaminase/alanine transaminase 109/127 IU/L; painless jaundice, dark urine, grey stools, 20-lb weight loss; imaging showed no hepatobiliary/pancreaticobiliary obstruction; serology negative for viral, autoimmune, Wilson disease, and hemochromatosis; liver biopsy consistent with DILI; positive dechallenge with LFTs peaking at day 7 of admission and trending normal after nafcillin cessation; recovered and discharged. Intro labels cholestatic hepatitis as a rare complication of nafcillin; first cohort study (Viehman et al., 224 patients on antibiotics >1 month) reported acute hepatic toxicity in 4% of nafcillin users, no significant difference vs oxacillin (3%).

raw_record.support_text: The paper tabulates five case reports of nafcillin-induced hepatotoxicity, noting nearly all listed cases had a cholestatic pattern of drug-induced liver injury. All cases used nafcillin 12 g/day (except case 5 where dose was not reported), with onsets from day 5 to week 6. Outcomes were complete resolution with supportive treatment in four cases, while one case (osteoarthritis, no eosinophilia) ended with the death of the patient secondary to fulminant liver failure. Liver biopsies in all listed cases showed necrosis, inflammatory cell infiltration, and fibrosis changes not specific for drug-induced hepatic injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Five case reports aggregated (Table 2): nafcillin 12 g/day for MSSA infections (bacteremia, osteomyelitis, cellulitis, septic arthritis); onset day 5 to week 6; all cholestatic pattern; peripheral eosinophilia in cases 1 (11.7%), 2 (20.7%), and 5 (20%); liver biopsy findings of necrosis, inflammatory cell infiltration and fibrosis; recovery within four to twelve weeks for idiosyncratic injury; one fatal case secondary to fulminant liver failure. Recovery in most cases with supportive treatment.

raw_record.support_text: A 53-year-old female patient developed toxic hepatitis due to levofloxacin after receiving a single 750 mg dose of levofloxacin tablets for a pulmonary infection 10 days earlier. She experienced itching, redness, and rash, followed on day 5 by abdominal pain, vomiting, and jaundice. She was deemed a liver transplant candidate but suffered cardiopulmonary arrest and died before transfer; multiple organ failure was secondary to the toxic hepatitis. The authors emphasize that hepatotoxicity and death due to levofloxacin are uncommon.

Presented at emergency department 10 days post-dose with confusion (GCS 12), acute hepatic failure with hepatic encephalopathy, hypoglycemia (53 mg/dL), and multiple organ failure. Toxic hepatitis resulted in fatal outcome: patient was a liver transplant candidate but had cardiopulmonary arrest and died before transfer to a transplant center. Hepatic necrosis described in the general context of drug-induced hepatotoxicity. No other co-suspect drug is reported.

raw_record.support_text: The final diagnosis for this 36-year-old male patient is Levofloxacin-induced hepatotoxicity. The patient presented with cellulitis and pain and was medicated with levofloxacin.

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes an unequivocal association between levofloxacin and acute fatal hepatitis. Other causes of hepatitis were excluded, no associated drugs could be incriminated, and histology was highly suggestive of a drug-induced immunoallergic hepatitis. Using a validated international scoring system, causality between levofloxacin and acute hepatitis was classified as 'probable'. The manufacturer notes transaminases may be abnormal during levofloxacin treatment, and in a clinical study comparing levofloxacin 500 mg twice daily with ceftriaxone for pneumonia, AST and ALT increased in 3.5% and 4.8% of 314 levofloxacin-treated patients. The rarity of the reaction suggests an immunoallergic reaction, supported by numerous eosinophils in the biopsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal acute hepatitis; histology showed regenerative hepatocytes in periportal area with cholestasis and numerous eosinophils, interpreted as drug-induced immunoallergic hepatitis. Causality scored 'probable' by a validated international scoring system. In a comparative pneumonia study, levofloxacin 500 mg twice daily was associated with AST and ALT elevations in 3.5% and 4.8% of 314 patients. Competing causes of hepatitis excluded; no co-drugs incriminated.

raw_record.support_text: A 36-year-old man with infected bronchiectasis was treated with IV levofloxacin 500 mg q24h. The drug was stopped on suspicion of levofloxacin hepatotoxicity, and liver enzymes and bilirubin progressively normalized over 3 weeks. The adverse reaction was reported to the national pharmacovigilance system (report 31.289).

Reported to national pharmacovigilance system (number 31.289). Only 7 cases of acute hepatitis due to levofloxacin have been published (Medline to April 2012). A Japanese study estimated 88 million levofloxacin prescriptions over 6 years with 87 hepatic adverse reactions probably secondary to the drug.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 30 patients, liver damage was attributed to cyclofenil. The long delay before signs of liver damage appeared, the lack of relation between maximum ALAT (alanine aminotransferase) level and dosage of cyclofenil, and the histologic picture made a direct toxic effect improbable.
raw_record.extra_details: 30 patients with liver reactions. 80% of reactions occurred one to four months after initiation of therapy; only four patients reacted within a month. The delay, lack of skin rash, lymphadenopathy, and prominent eosinophilia argued against a hypersensitivity reaction; injury was attributed to metabolic idiosyncrasy. Histology resembling viral hepatitis showed lymphohistiocytic portal inflammation, hepatocyte ballooning, hepatocellular necrosis, and lymphocytic/histiocytic infiltration; liver biopsies in six patients also showed slight cholestasis with bile plugs, one showed epithelioid granulomas, and increased hepatocellular lipofuscin was seen in five patients. Based on registered sales of ~3.3 million 100 mg tablets during 1971–80 and assumed treatment of two tablets daily for 90 days, the incidence of reported liver reactions in Sweden was estimated at 1.3%; a geographic difference in susceptibility was speculated. The injury was reported as not more serious than isoniazid-induced liver damage despite longer treatment before recognition.

raw_record.support_text: Aplaviroc (GSK873140, ONO-4128, AK-602), a small-molecule CCR5 antagonist licensed from Ono Pharmaceuticals, appeared well tolerated on short-term administration apart from mild/moderate gastrointestinal effects. However, chronic administration produced cases of severe liver toxicity, leading to early termination of Phase IIb studies in treatment-naive patients in September 2005. A further case of elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin in a treatment-experienced patient from the Phase III trial ended all development activities on aplaviroc. The authors note the absence of reported human hepatotoxicity with the other advanced CCR5 antagonists supports the idea that these findings are compound specific rather than due to CCR5 blockade.
raw_record.extra_details: CCR5 antagonist for HIV-1 therapy. Chronic administration produced severe liver toxicity, leading to early termination of Phase IIb studies in treatment-naive patients in September 2005; a further case of elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin in a treatment-experienced patient in the Phase III trial ended all development. In a Phase IIa study, 600 mg b.i.d. for 10 days gave mean viral load reduction of 1.66 log10 copies/ml; short-term administration showed only mild/moderate GI side effects (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain). No hepatotoxicity attributed to CCR5 blockade itself; absence of hepatotoxicity with other advanced CCR5 antagonists supports compound specificity.

raw_record.support_text: Among three CCR5 inhibitors with preliminary clinical trial data, aplaviroc had its development halted after the development of severe hepatotoxicity in one individual, which necessitated liver transplantation, and a 1% rate of grade 3/4 alanine aminotransferase elevation among other patients on therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: CCR5 inhibitor (chemokine receptor 5 antagonist) for HIV. Severe hepatotoxicity in one individual necessitated liver transplantation; a 1% rate of grade 3/4 alanine aminotransferase elevation was seen among other patients on therapy. Development of the drug was halted.

raw_record.support_text: Aplaviroc, a GlaxoSmithKline CCR5 antagonist compound, demonstrated antiviral activity with minimal toxicities in short-term monotherapy studies. In phase 2b trials, four out of roughly 300 patients developed severe hepatotoxicity that, on liver biopsy, was consistent with drug-induced hepatitis, leading to cessation of the trial. Similarly, one out of 26 patients in a phase 3 trial had alanine aminotransferase elevated to 24 times normal; no deaths occurred, the hepatitis resolved with aplaviroc discontinuation, the trial was stopped, and clinical development of aplaviroc was terminated.
raw_record.extra_details: CCR5 antagonist (GlaxoSmithKline). Phase 2b: 4 of ~300 patients developed severe hepatotoxicity with liver biopsy consistent with drug-induced hepatitis, leading to trial cessation. Phase 3: 1 of 26 patients showed ALT elevation to 24 times normal; no deaths, hepatitis resolved on aplaviroc discontinuation; trial stopped and clinical development terminated. Aplaviroc produced 1.0-1.6 log10 viral load reduction in 10-day monotherapy.

raw_record.support_text: Clinical development of the first CCR5 antagonist aplaviroc had to be terminated in October 2005 owing to severe hepatotoxicity, which raised concerns about possible class-specific hepatotoxic effects of this new ARV drug class.
raw_record.extra_details: First CCR5 antagonist; clinical development terminated in October 2005 owing to severe hepatotoxicity, prompting concern about class-specific hepatotoxic effects of CCR5 antagonists.

raw_record.support_text: The development of the CCR5 antagonist aplaviroc was stopped due to hepatotoxic adverse events associated with jaundice in four study participants. The mechanism for these possible hepatotoxic reactions remains unknown, though it was suggested CCR5 deficiency increases vulnerability to additional hepatotoxic agents.
raw_record.extra_details: HIV-1 CCR5 antagonist; development program stopped because of hepatotoxic adverse events with jaundice in four study participants (clinical trial setting); mechanism unknown; suggested CCR5 deficiency increases vulnerability to additional hepatotoxic agents via cytokine imbalance.

During phase IIb trials three subjects developed severe hepatotoxicity deemed secondary to drug-induced hepatitis. Additionally, 1 of the first 44 subjects enrolled in a phase III trial of aplaviroc developed severe hepatotoxicity, and the trials and development of aplaviroc were stopped.

Severe hepatotoxicity deemed secondary to drug-induced hepatitis occurred in 3 subjects in phase IIb trials and in 1 of the first 44 subjects enrolled in a phase III trial; trials and development of aplaviroc were stopped as a result.

In contrast, the original anti-HIV trials with Plerixafor were discontinued because of cardiac disturbances, not liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: The authors of this letter state: 'We do not deny glafenine-induced hepatotoxicity, but we estimate that its prevalence might be lower than that suggested by Stricker et al.' This affirms a positive human causal relationship between glafenine and liver injury while disputing the case count and prevalence in the cited 38-case analysis (in which 12 cases were graded 'probable', 15 'possible', and 11 'unclassifiable' or 'unlikely').
raw_record.extra_details: The authors contest the attribution in 7 of the 12 'probable' cases: in Cases 2, 4, 9 and 13 serology for autoimmune chronic active hepatitis was not done; Case 2 had unusually long latency intervals (transaminase peak 85 days after first administration and 80 days after stopping); Case 6 also took methyldopa, a recognized hepatotoxic drug taken for over a year; Cases 9 and 15 involved irregular drug intake complicating temporal assessment; Case 32 histology was considered more suggestive of non-A, non-B viral hepatitis. The authors emphasize the prevalence may be lower than reported rather than denying glafenine-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In the 51 patients with drug-induced hepatitis, each causative drug was identified per patient; glafenine was the causative drug in one patient (patient 41) with the poor metabolizer phenotype for dextromethorphan oxidation.
raw_record.extra_details: Causative drug of drug-induced hepatitis in one patient (patient 41) who was a CYP2D6 poor metabolizer for dextromethorphan; the paper notes the PM association in this single case may be fortuitous and requires further investigation.

raw_record.support_text: A 52-year-old man with stage IIIB kappa light chain multiple myeloma treated with bortezomib (1.3 mg/m2 on days 1, 4, 8, 11 every 3 weeks) developed severe liver enzyme elevations (AST 1,856 U/L, ALT 2,865 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 510 U/L, GGT 139 U/L) 3 days after his second bortezomib dose; bilirubin was normal and hepatitis B/C and CMV serology were negative. Liver biopsy showed severe lobular activity with confluent necrosis, and the increase was considered toxic hepatitis. After bortezomib was discontinued, liver enzymes normalized within 2 weeks, which suggested this drug was the cause of the severe hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report in a 52-year-old male with relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma who had previously progressed on high-dose dexamethasone. Onset occurred 3 days after the second bortezomib dose (1.3 mg/m2 days 1,4,8,11 every 3 weeks); peak AST 1,856 U/L and ALT 2,865 U/L with normal bilirubin; liver biopsy showed severe lobular activity and confluent necrosis. Hepatitis B/C and CMV serology negative; no prior liver disease or alcohol abuse. Enzymes recovered to near-normal within 2 weeks after bortezomib discontinuation; patient later tolerated a thalidomide-containing regimen. The paper cites a previously reported case with a similar pattern (enzyme peak 3 days after the second dose) and describes bortezomib as a selective reversible proteasome inhibitor. Authors conclude the drug 'strongly suggests... was the cause of the liver injury' and that acute drug-induced hepatitis should be considered.

raw_record.support_text: For troglitazone, early clinical trials indicated serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) elevations greater than three times the upper normal range in 1.9% of 2510 treated patients, and subsequent case reports demonstrated liver toxicity in humans treated with troglitazone. The authors hypothesize that toxic quinones derived from CYP3A4-dependent metabolism (troglitazone induces CYP3A4), possibly influenced by genetic differences in CYP3A4 induction or metabolic activation, could cause the rare cases of hypersensitivity-associated liver damage; they also note PPARγ is expressed at functionally significant levels in steatotic livers, so hepatotoxicity may stem from abnormal target gene expression in patients with fatty livers.
raw_record.extra_details: ALT >3x ULN in 1.9% of 2510 treated patients in early clinical trials; liver toxicity demonstrated in subsequent case reports; hypothesized mechanism: troglitazone induces CYP3A4 and potentially toxic quinones from CYP3A4-dependent metabolism may cause the rare hypersensitivity-associated liver damage; PPARγ not appreciably expressed in normal liver but expressed at functionally significant levels in steatotic livers, so hepatotoxicity may result from abnormal target gene expression in patients with fatty livers.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that the mechanism of troglitazone-induced liver damage is idiosyncratic rather than allergic and that the type of liver injury is hepatocellular rather than cholestatic in most cases. The described patient had no signs of allergic reaction and negative drug-induced lymphocyte stimulation tests, and her laboratory data and liver biopsy (hepatocyte necrosis around the central vein with mild lobular infiltration and portal inflammation/fibrosis, compatible with protracted acute hepatitis) revealed hepatocellular liver dysfunction that improved after troglitazone was withdrawn.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient was on troglitazone 400 mg/day at therapeutic dose for diabetes alongside gliclazide 80 mg/day, pravastatin 10 mg/day, aspirin 81 mg/day, and levothyroxin 100 µg/day. On admission: AST 223 U/l, ALT 422 U/l, ALP 397 U/l, GGT 204 U/l, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dl. Liver tests improved to AST 36 U/l and ALT 43 U/l four weeks after troglitazone discontinuation (dechallenge). Marginal transaminase elevation first noted in month 9; dysfunction developed during month 19 of use. DLST and 48-h skin patch tests were negative for troglitazone, pravastatin, aspirin, gliclazide, and levothyroxin. In combined North American clinical trials, liver dysfunction (ALT >3x ULN) occurred in 48 (1.9%) of 2,510 troglitazone-treated patients, with average onset at 147 days and peak between months 3-7; 20 of 48 continued the drug and all returned to baseline ALT. The paper notes troglitazone-induced liver dysfunction may progress irreversibly despite discontinuation, eventually leading to liver transplantation or death, and discusses the FDA recommendation to discontinue if ALT exceeds 3x ULN.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a 47-year-old man who developed acute subfulminant hepatotoxicity after consuming only four doses of troglitazone. He experienced vomiting and dehydration, and despite prompt discontinuation of troglitazone his symptoms progressed to jaundice and fatigue; he had no history of exposure to other hepatotoxins. Evaluation revealed transaminitis without underlying liver disease, and liver biopsy showed patchy cholestatic hepatitis with plasma cells and eosinophils, hepatocellular giant-cell transformation, and fat accumulation, consistent with severe drug-induced hepatitis; the patient was managed supportively and liver function returned to normal. Earlier reports (Gitlin, Neuschwander-Tetri and colleagues, 1998) described severe hepatotoxicity associated with troglitazone in patients who consumed it for at least 1 month and received supportive care or liver transplantation. The authors emphasize the unpredictable nature of troglitazone hepatotoxicity and its potentially life-threatening effects.
raw_record.extra_details: Current case: acute subfulminant hepatotoxicity after only four doses, with vomiting, dehydration, jaundice, fatigue, transaminitis, no other hepatotoxins, no underlying liver disease. Biopsy: patchy cholestatic hepatitis with plasma cells and eosinophils, hepatocellular giant-cell transformation, and fat accumulation; no chronic liver disease. Managed supportively with eventual normalization of liver function. Earlier 1998 reports (Gitlin and Neuschwander-Tetri, respectively) described severe troglitazone hepatotoxicity after at least 1 month of use treated with supportive care or liver transplantation. Authors highlight the unpredictable (idiosyncratic) nature and potentially life-threatening effects and call for vigilant monitoring of liver enzyme levels.

raw_record.support_text: At least 10 cases of hepatitis due to troglitazone, a thiazolidinedione used to treat diabetes mellitus, were reported in 2000, contributing to its removal from the marketplace. Most studies showed severe lesions with zone 3 necrosis, bridging and confluent necrosis, or submassive necrosis with reactive bile ductules; portal infiltrates were mononuclear or mixed lymphocytic-plasmacytic with eosinophils, and hepatocyte ballooning, apoptosis, and cholestasis were frequent; portal and lobular granulomas were present in one case.
raw_record.extra_details: Thiazolidinedione antidiabetic; at least 10 cases reported in 2000 leading to market withdrawal; severe lesions with zone 3, bridging, confluent or submassive necrosis with reactive bile ductule formation (neocholangioles); portal infiltrates mononuclear or mixed lymphocytic-plasmacytic with eosinophils; hepatocyte ballooning, apoptosis and cholestasis; one case with portal and lobular granulomas.

raw_record.support_text: In this patient, the time course of hepatic dysfunction and its improvement after withdrawal of troglitazone were completely consistent with drug-induced hepatotoxicity, and no viral or autoimmune cause was identified; the authors conclude the patient experienced troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity. A second-generation TZD added later was well tolerated, suggesting differences between first- and second-generation TZDs.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic dysfunction resolved after troglitazone withdrawal; no other viral or autoimmune cause identified; second-generation TZD (rosiglitazone or pioglitazone class) later tolerated, suggesting inter-generation differences. In clinical trials, troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity (defined as ALT greater than three times the upper limit of normal) was identified in 1.9% of 2,510 patients. Troglitazone induces and is metabolized by cytochrome P4503A4 and has a lipophilic α-tocopherol side chain.

raw_record.support_text: In an inception cohort of 7568 new troglitazone users, five hospitalized patients with acute liver injury were identified for which other explanations were not apparent: in four, hospitalization was the direct result of troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity, and in one the elevated serum transaminase and creatine kinase were diagnosed as troglitazone related. Ten of 19 liver-related hospitalizations were excluded as unrelated liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 7568 new troglitazone users (49.7% women, 82.6% age >=45 yr, median use 140 days, 4020 person-years). Five cases of acute hospitalized liver injury (elevated transaminases), four with jaundice (two cholestatic, two hepatocellular); one patient with hepatocellular injury developed hepatic encephalopathy with submassive hepatocellular necrosis on biopsy and died (reported to FDA); three recovered, one lost to follow-up (diagnosis of drug-induced jaundice). Ages 55-85 yr, therapy duration before onset 2 wk to 9 months; no prior known liver disease. Incidence rates per million person-years (95% CI): hospitalization 1244 (404, 2900), hospitalized jaundice 995 (271, 2546), ALF 240 (6.3, 1385). Excluded unrelated causes included hepatic malignancy, chronic hepatitis C, hemochromatosis with cirrhosis.

raw_record.support_text: In US clinical trials of troglitazone in 2510 patients, about 5% developed ALT elevations greater than 1.5-fold above normal and 48 patients (1.9%) had elevations more than threefold above normal; no deaths were reported in the trials. However, FDA reports since December 15, 1997 recorded liver transplantation and death in three of 500,000 US-treated patients and two deaths among 150,000 patients treated in Japan, and distribution of the medication in Britain was halted within one month on the basis of reports of hepatic dysfunction.
raw_record.extra_details: US trials (n=2510): ~5% ALT >1.5x normal, 1.9% (48 patients) >3x normal; of those, 65% had 3-10x, 25% 10-20x, 10% >20x ALT elevation; no trial deaths. FDA spontaneous reports since Dec 15, 1997: liver transplantation/death in 3 of 500,000 US-treated patients and 2 deaths of 150,000 Japan-treated patients. Britain halted distribution within one month due to reports of hepatic dysfunction. Mechanism argued to be metabolic idiosyncrasy rather than immunoallergic (rare fever, rash, arthralgia, lymphadenopathy; rarely positive autoantibodies; no hepatic granulomas; no dense panlobular lymphocytic infiltrate or interface hepatitis; no distinguishing biopsy histology; absent in viral hepatitis comparison). Prescribing information (July 1998) recommends ALT monitoring at start, monthly for 8 months, then every 2 months for the rest of the first year; continue/dose and discontinue thresholds for ALT >1.5x and >3x normal.
