raw_record.support_text: The paper states that the mechanism of troglitazone-induced liver damage is idiosyncratic rather than allergic and that the type of liver injury is hepatocellular rather than cholestatic in most cases, although hypersensitivity has been reported in one autopsy case of fulminant hepatitis. The presented patient showed no allergic signs and had a negative DLST, and laboratory data plus liver biopsy revealed hepatocellular liver dysfunction. Combined North American clinical trials of troglitazone detected liver dysfunction (ALT >3x ULN) in 48 of 2,510 patients (1.9%), with onset on average at 147 days and peak between months 3 and 7; postmarketing experience estimated significant hepatocellular injury (liver failure) at about 1 in 57,000, and the paper notes troglitazone-induced liver dysfunction may progress irreversibly despite discontinuation, eventually leading to liver transplantation or death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: null
raw_record.extra_details: North American clinical trials: liver dysfunction (serum ALT >3x ULN) in 48/2,510 patients (1.9%); mean latency to liver dysfunction 147 days, peak months 3–7; 20 of 48 patients continued troglitazone despite ALT elevation but returned to baseline. Postmarketing incidence of significant hepatocellular injury/liver failure ~1/57,000. Presented case: asymptomatic liver dysfunction after 19 months of troglitazone with ALT ~18x ULN without elevated bilirubin, marginal transaminase elevation first noted at month 9; patient had two prior episodes of drug allergy, negative DLST, and liver biopsy (3 weeks after discontinuation) showing fairly nonspecific hepatitis without true hepatocellular necrosis; liver function normalized promptly after drug discontinuation (Iwase et al.). FDA recommendation: test ALT weekly if 1.5–3x ULN and discontinue if >3x ULN. Injury may progress irreversibly to liver transplantation or death. Exact mechanism of troglitazone hepatotoxicity remains to be clarified.

raw_record.support_text: The paper illustrates troglitazone as a recognized causal DILI association emerging from multiple data streams: among 2,510 subjects treated in pre-approval controlled studies, 0.2% developed ALT rises >30× upper limit of normal and two subjects developed concomitant hyperbilirubinemia, which the paper describes as a harbinger for the post-marketing cases of serious DILI that later emerged. Among 585 study subjects in the NIH Diabetes Prevention Program treated with troglitazone, one developed fatal hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: In pre-approval controlled studies of 2,510 subjects, 0.2% developed ALT rises >30× ULN and two subjects developed concomitant hyperbilirubinemia; among 585 subjects in the NIH Diabetes Prevention Program, one developed fatal hepatotoxicity. These pre-approval signals were a harbinger for later post-marketing cases of serious DILI.

raw_record.support_text: In combined North American clinical trials, ALT elevations more than three times the upper limit of normal were seen in 48 of 2,510 patients (1.9%) treated with troglitazone versus 0.6% on placebo, and two patients were confirmed to have suffered serious hepatocellular injury from an idiosyncratic drug reaction. Troglitazone was associated with idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity, with some patients showing severe or fatal liver damage, leading to its withdrawal from the US and Japanese markets in March 2000. The recommended therapeutic dose was 200-600 mg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: ALT >3x ULN in 1.9% (48/2,510) troglitazone-treated patients vs 0.6% placebo; two patients confirmed to have serious hepatocellular injury from an idiosyncratic reaction; some patients showed severe or fatal liver damage; withdrawn from US and Japanese markets March 2000; recommended dose 200-600 mg/day; hepatotoxicity was not predicted in conventional animals or cynomolgus monkeys (300-1200 mg/kg/day for 52 weeks).

raw_record.support_text: In combined North American clinical trials, troglitazone was associated with liver dysfunction (serum ALT >3x ULN) in 48 (1.9%) of 2,510 patients, with an average onset interval of 147 days. The authors note that troglitazone-induced liver dysfunction may progress irreversibly despite drug discontinuation, eventually leading to liver transplantation or death, and state that the FDA recommended ALT monitoring to prevent severe troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity. Postmarketing experience gave an incidence of significant hepatocellular injury (liver failure) of about 1 in 57,000, while report rates of jaundice, hyperbilirubinemia, and more severe injury decreased after regular ALT monitoring was recommended; current labeling recommends ALT monitoring to decrease the risk of rare idiosyncratic liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: In the Iwase et al. case described, ALT was ~18x ULN without elevated bilirubin, liver-function tests normalized promptly after discontinuation, and liver biopsy (3 weeks after discontinuation) showed fairly nonspecific findings of hepatitis without true hepatocellular necrosis. Combined NA trials: 48/2510 (1.9%) with ALT >3x ULN, mean latency 147 days, peak between months 3 and 7; 20/48 continued drug yet all returned to baseline ALT. Postmarketing significant hepatocellular injury/liver failure incidence ~1 in 57,000. More than 1.6 million US patients treated, ~600,000 for >1 year, with no reported deaths from hepatic failure or liver transplant among patients treated >1 year. FDA recommended weekly ALT testing if ALT 1.5-3x ULN and immediate discontinuation for ALT >3x ULN; current troglitazone labeling recommends ALT monitoring at baseline, monthly for the first year, and quarterly thereafter.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone's major adverse effect is hepatotoxicity. Among 2500 patients prescribed troglitazone, 2.2% had more than a 3-fold elevation of serum aminotransferase levels, and two of these had reversible jaundice, developing within 1 to 4.5 months of starting the drug. Liver biopsies in these two cases showed hepatocyte necrosis, bridging necrosis, portal inflammation, and evidence of cholestasis, with recovery 3 months after discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: 2.2% of 2500 patients had >3-fold aminotransferase elevation; two cases of reversible jaundice within 1-4.5 months; biopsies showed hepatocyte necrosis, bridging necrosis, portal inflammation, and cholestasis; recovery 3 months after discontinuation. High incidence of liver failure leading to liver transplantation or death prompted removal from the market in Great Britain and the United States.

raw_record.support_text: Patients (n=7,658) receiving troglitazone provided 4,020 person-years; 5 were hospitalized with acute liver injury, an incidence of 1,244 per million person-years (95% CI 404–2,900), far greater than the expected 10–22/million. Case reports documented idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity after ≥1 month of treatment, and one patient developed acute subfulminant hepatotoxicity after only 4 doses with biopsy showing patchy cholestatic hepatitis, recovering after palliative treatment. Because of the high incidence of liver injury, troglitazone was withdrawn from the market.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 7,658 patients (4,020 person-years); 5 hospitalized with acute liver injury; incidence 1,244 per million person-years (95% CI 404–2,900) vs expected 10–22/million. Case reports of idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity after ≥1 month; one case of acute subfulminant hepatotoxicity after 4 doses whose biopsy showed patchy cholestatic hepatitis with plasma cells and eosinophils, hepatocellular giant cell transformation, and fat accumulation; patient recovered after palliative treatment. Withdrawn from market. Proposed mechanisms: reactive intermediates, apoptosis (potentially irreversible in acute liver failure), oxidative stress, mitochondrial damage, bile salt transporter inhibition, fibrosis. Injury described as idiosyncratic and not dose-related at clinically meaningful doses; low PPARγ affinity necessitates higher doses.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone was among the prominent drugs causing idiosyncratic drug-induced acute liver failure (≥4 cases) and has subsequently been withdrawn.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as a cause of idiosyncratic drug-induced acute liver failure with at least 4 cases in this series; the drug was subsequently withdrawn. These patients typically presented subacutely with low aminotransferases, high bilirubin, and more frequent ascites.

raw_record.support_text: The first glitazone, troglitazone, had to be withdrawn from the market in 2000 because of several cases of severe acute hepatitis and liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Troglitazone, a glitazone originally approved for type 2 diabetes, was withdrawn from the market in 2000 because of several cases of severe acute hepatitis and liver failure (citations 239, 240). The other glitazones (rosiglitazone, pioglitazone) do not appear to have the same degree of hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In the Diabetes Prevention Program, one death due to liver disease occurred in the troglitazone treatment group, contributing to the decision to withdraw troglitazone from the DPP. Also, elevations of liver enzymes (ALT or AST) to at least 10 times the upper limit of normal occurred in 7 of 585 (1.2%) troglitazone participants versus 1 (0.2%) in placebo and 0 in metformin, a statistically significant difference; no significant differences among drug arms were seen for elevations to at least 3.0 times ULN. The DPP discussion notes that troglitazone's potential for rare but potentially fatal hepatotoxicity was recognized only after tens of thousands of patients were treated.
raw_record.extra_details: Troglitazone arm of the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) was stopped 4 June 1998 following a liver-disease death in a troglitazone-treated participant and safety concerns; troglitazone was later withdrawn from the US market (~2 years later). LFT >=10 (ALT or AST) occurred in 7/585 (1.2%) troglitazone participants vs 1/582 (0.2%) placebo and 0/587 metformin (P<0.01, Fisher's exact); no significant difference among drug arms for LFT >=3. Mean troglitazone exposure ~0.9 years; paper describes the agent's 'rare but potentially fatal hepatotoxicity.' Liver enzymes not measured on the same schedule in the ILS group.

raw_record.support_text: In combined North American clinical trials of troglitazone, liver dysfunction (serum ALT >3x ULN) was detected in 48 (1.9%) of 2,510 patients, appearing on average 147 days after starting the drug with a peak between months 3-7. The paper states that troglitazone-induced liver dysfunction may progress irreversibly despite discontinuation, eventually leading to liver transplantation or death, and endorses the FDA recommendation for ALT monitoring to prevent severe troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity, labeled as rare idiosyncratic liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Combined North American trials: ALT >3x ULN in 48/2510 (1.9%); mean onset interval 147 days, peak at months 3-7; 20/48 continued troglitazone despite ALT elevation and all returned to baseline ALT. Presenting case had ALT ~18x ULN without bilirubin elevation at month 19 (marginal transaminase elevation first noted month 9); liver biopsy (3 weeks after discontinuation) showed nonspecific hepatitis without true hepatocellular necrosis; liver tests normalized after drug stop. Postmarketing incidence of significant hepatocellular injury (liver failure) ~1/57,000; ~50% of ALT elevations in pre-approval trials (25% >10x ULN) normalized while on drug. >1.6 million US patients treated, ~600,000 for >1 year with no reported death from hepatic failure or liver transplant in patients treated >1 year. FDA recommendation: weekly ALT if 1.5-3x ULN and immediate discontinuation if >3x ULN; current labeling advises ALT monitoring at baseline, monthly for first year, quarterly thereafter to reduce risk of rare idiosyncratic liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: A woman developed liver dysfunction during the 19th month of troglitazone treatment, with ALT elevation ~18 times the upper limit of normal without elevated bilirubin. Troglitazone was withdrawn and insulin was started; liver-function tests improved (AST 36 U/l, ALT 43 U/l) within 4 weeks of discontinuation. A liver biopsy 3 weeks after stopping showed hepatocyte necrosis around the central vein, mild intralobular infiltration, and portal inflammatory infiltrate and fibrosis, findings the authors describe as compatible with protracted acute hepatitis. Drug-induced lymphocyte stimulation tests and skin patch tests for troglitazone were negative.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of troglitazone-induced liver dysfunction; dechallenge with prompt improvement after discontinuation; ALT up to ~18x ULN without bilirubin elevation; developed during 19th month of treatment with marginal transaminase elevation first noted in the 9th month; biopsy showed hepatocyte necrosis around central vein, mild intralobular infiltration, portal inflammatory infiltrate and fibrosis compatible with protracted acute hepatitis; DLST negative for troglitazone and pravastatin; 48-h skin patch tests negative for troglitazone, pravastatin, aspirin, gliclazide, and levothyroxin; patient had no clinical signs of allergic reaction.

raw_record.support_text: Most reported cases of troglitazone hepatotoxicity were hepatocellular, with one mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic case, and all acute liver failure cases showed parenchymal collapse.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver biopsies in two patients revealed hepatocellular reactions consistent with idiosyncrasy. Acute liver failure cases all showed parenchymal collapse.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone was introduced in 1997 but was withdrawn in 2000 due to cases of idiosyncratic severe hepatotoxicity, including fatalities and the need for liver transplants. In the UK, troglitazone was available for only a few weeks in 1997 before being withdrawn by its distributor as reports of hepatotoxicity accumulated.
raw_record.extra_details: Withdrawn in 2000 due to idiosyncratic severe hepatotoxicity; reported cases included fatalities and need for liver transplants. In the UK the drug was available only for a few weeks in 1997 before withdrawal by its distributor as hepatotoxicity reports accumulated. Successor thiazolidinediones (rosiglitazone, pioglitazone) showed no evidence of similar hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, an oral hypoglycemic drug withdrawn from the market due to numerous post-marketing reports of acute liver failure, had ALT >3× ULN in 1.9% of subjects in pre-approval trials, with two cases of elevated bilirubin and ALT among approximately 2600 subjects. After approval, 1 case of ALF requiring liver transplantation occurred among 585 subjects in a post-marketing trial, and 3 possible cases of drug-induced acute liver failure occurred in a database of roughly 9000 people; the paper estimates life-threatening hepatotoxicity rate between 1:585 and 1:3000.
raw_record.extra_details: Withdrawn from market due to post-marketing reports of acute liver failure; ALT>3× ULN in 1.9% of ~2600 pre-approval subjects; two cases of elevated bilirubin and ALT; one ALF requiring liver transplantation among 585 subjects in a post-marketing trial; 3 possible cases of drug-induced ALF in a database of roughly 9000 people; retrospective analysis showed 1.7% ALT>5× ULN and 0.3% ALT>8× ULN; precise event rate cannot be calculated, estimated life-threatening hepatotoxicity rate between 1:585 and 1:3000.

raw_record.support_text: The paper cites a study characterizing 83 patients with liver failure following troglitazone therapy, of whom 63% were women, using this as an early example of female over-representation in drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of characteristics of 83 patients with liver failure following troglitazone therapy; 63% of the patients were women.

raw_record.support_text: Rezulin (troglitazone), a hypoglycemic agent launched in 1997, was recognized pre-approval to carry a hepatotoxic risk, prompting labeling precautions calling for close monitoring and frequent liver function tests. Lawsuits were later filed over failure to monitor and warn adequately about the product.
raw_record.extra_details: Marketed as Rezulin (Parke Davis); launched 1997; pre-approval recognition of hepatotoxic risk led to label precautions for close monitoring and frequent liver function tests. Case report (by one of the authors, J.T.O.D.) describes a woman with diabetes who developed Rezulin-associated cirrhosis and was placed on a liver transplant list; Rezulin therapy initiated 12-10-97 and discontinued 10-98; glyburide (Glynase) was changed to glimepiride (Amaryl) for uncontrolled blood glucose.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, the first glitazone approved by the US FDA, proved to be hepatotoxic and was withdrawn from the market after reports of several dozen deaths and cases of severe hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation. An observational retrospective inception cohort using US claims data confirmed that troglitazone use was associated with a marked increase in the risk of acute idiopathic liver injury and acute liver failure leading to hospitalisation. In controlled clinical trials, troglitazone was associated with a ~3-fold greater incidence of significant (>3x ULN) ALT elevations than placebo.
raw_record.extra_details: Withdrawn from market after reports of several dozen deaths and severe hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation. Retrospective inception cohort assembled from claims data of a large multistate US healthcare organisation showed marked increase in risk of acute idiopathic liver injury and acute liver failure leading to hospitalisation. In controlled trials, troglitazone showed a ~3-fold greater incidence of ALT elevations >3x ULN than placebo. In a troglitazone-insulin combination study, 3 patients on troglitazone 600mg had ALT >3x ULN during the 26-week treatment period; one patient discontinued permanently due to jaundice and hyperbilirubinaemia. Hepatotoxicity is not a glitazone class effect.

raw_record.support_text: A patient presented with elevated liver chemistries (ALT 653 U/L, AST 413 U/L, total bilirubin 1.5 mg/dl) that appeared 5 months after beginning troglitazone therapy, in the absence of other prescription medications, alcohol, viral hepatitis, or autoimmune markers. She was told to stop troglitazone. The paper collectively reports this as part of 'troglitazone hepatotoxicity' in two patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient continued taking troglitazone in error after initially instructed to stop; 4 weeks later aminotransferases further elevated with increased total bilirubin and prothrombin time and decreased albumin, and she appeared jaundiced/icteric. Urgent liver biopsy showed zone 3 necrosis with hemorrhage and hepatocyte dropout, occasional foci of bridging necrosis to triads, active cell injury (acidophilic bodies, cell swelling, lobular disarray), minimal macrovesicular steatosis, mild non-prominent cholestasis, enlarged Kupffer cells, diffuse mononuclear infiltrate, and early pericentral and bridging fibrosis on trichrome stain. Histology reflected severe hepatocellular injury; improvement (decreased aminotransferases and bilirubin, normal prothrombin time) occurred within 18 days after stopping troglitazone with oral vitamin K supplementation.

raw_record.support_text: A 59-year-old diabetic man presented with progressive liver dysfunction after 1 year of troglitazone therapy. His overall presentation was considered consistent with troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity; liver biopsy showed submassive necrosis, transaminase and bilirubin levels were markedly elevated, and viral serologic test results were negative.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient had taken troglitazone for 1 year with normal baseline liver enzymes; troglitazone and simvastatin were stopped upon presentation. ALT rose from 8350 to 21667 nkat/L and bilirubin increased from normal to 308 µmol/L (18 mg/dL). On evaluation, total bilirubin 444 µmol/L (26 mg/dL), alkaline phosphatase 7.36 µkat/L, ALT 10583 nkat/L, AST 5.26 µkat/L; prothrombin time normal; mild ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody positivity (1:80); negative viral serology; unremarkable ultrasound and CT. Liver biopsy showed submassive necrosis. Treated with prednisone 20 mg twice daily; at 5-month follow-up liver enzymes were normal. Concurrent medications included ramipril, diltiazem, furosemide, insulin, glyburide; alcohol intake insignificant.

raw_record.support_text: This case series of 11 patients illustrates the heterogeneous pattern of drug-induced liver injury associated with troglitazone. The 11 cases had clinical patterns that were either entirely consistent with troglitazone toxicity or highly inconsistent with progression of any identified or probably pre-existing liver condition. With regard to troglitazone, the clinical features of the series are consistent with and suggestive of an injury that is mainly mitochondrial.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 patients accrued as a clinical case series; patterns attributed wholly to troglitazone or highly inconsistent with progression of pre-existing liver disease. Patient 3 developed acute liver failure with submassive necrosis and death; patients 2 and 7 had obvious acute liver injury that progressed to cirrhosis; patients 6, 9, 10 and 11 had late-detected insidious cirrhosis often presenting as portal hypertension. Acute hepatocellular or mixed injury occurred within the typical delayed onset window, whereas cirrhosis/portal-hypertension cases were diagnosed 1.5 to 3 years from start of exposure (patients 5, 6, 9, 10, 11). Microvesicular steatosis was present in patients 6, 7 and 8, and frequently seen features included bile ductular proliferation, bile stasis/cholestasis, and varying degrees of necrosis, inflammation and fibrosis. Progression of injury after drug discontinuation was common. Injury is suggested to be mainly mitochondrial. Symptoms were often none, mild or non-specific.

raw_record.support_text: In combined North American clinical trials of troglitazone, 48 (1.9%) of 2510 treated patients had ALT over three times the upper limit of normal versus 3 (0.6%) of 475 placebo patients; 12 (0.6%) of 2510 had peak ALT over 10 times ULN versus none on placebo; only two patients developed jaundice and clinically overt hepatitis. The actual number of acute liver failure cases was nearly 100 among 2 million patients treated, i.e., about 1 in 20,000, as predicted from the trials.
raw_record.extra_details: Combined North American trials: ALT>3x ULN in 48/2510 (1.9%) vs 3/475 (0.6%) placebo; ALT>10x ULN in 12/2510 (0.6%) vs none. Two patients had jaundice and clinically overt hepatitis. Predicted ~1/2000 jaundice and ~1/20,000 ALF; nearly 100 ALF cases in 2 million treated patients (Graham 2003). Withdrawn; example of rapidly progressing hepatotoxicity resistant to monitoring.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, used to manage diabetes by decreasing insulin resistance, has a clear tendency to cause hepatic injury. In clinical trials, approximately 48 (2%) of at least 2500 treated patients developed aminotransferase elevations at least three times the upper limit of normal, versus about 3 (0.6%) of 475 placebo-treated patients, with elevations resolving even in patients who continued treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented as a case report (PMID 10795774) of a patient with jaundice presenting approximately four months after starting troglitazone; liver chemistry tests were normal at start of treatment and returned toward normal after discontinuation in many study subjects. Four prior case reports document severe hepatotoxicity (two improved on discontinuation, one required liver transplantation, one died); at least 21 deaths have been attributed to troglitazone in the US and Japan. In clinical trials, aminotransferase elevations were usually detected 3-7 months after starting treatment. The reported mechanism is idiosyncratic or immunologic, not dose related, unpredictable, and can be associated with eosinophilic infiltrates; biopsy in the present case showed a chronic hepatitis pattern with scattered eosinophils. The patient was also taking pravastatin and glucotrol, judged unlikely to have caused the injury (pravastatin can raise aminotransferases early in treatment; no case reports link glucotrol to hepatotoxicity although mild cholestasis is occasionally related), but an untoward pravastatin-troglitazone interaction could not be excluded. FDA/manufacturer now recommend monitoring liver chemistries before and periodically during troglitazone therapy and discontinuing if aminotransferases reach three times the upper limit of normal. Treatment indication: diabetes (insulin resistance).

raw_record.support_text: Soon after troglitazone was marketed, cases of acute liver failure (ALF) in treated patients were reported to the FDA, prompting Dear Health Care Professional letters and a 1999 FDA advisory committee review of 43 reported U.S. ALF cases; within two more years 94 cases of ALF had been reported. In a retrospective inception cohort of 9369 troglitazone users, the study estimated incidence of idiopathic ALF and hospitalized acute liver injury and identified five patients hospitalized with 'troglitazone-induced acute liver injury' (elevated transaminases/bilirubin), one of whom (an 85-year-old man) died; ALF diagnosis required hepatic encephalopathy, liver transplantation, or death in the setting of acute severe liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: FDA-reported ALF cases (43 by the March 1999 advisory committee, 94 two years later); four 'Dear Health Care Professional' letters issued. Study cohort of 9369 troglitazone users (1997-1998); five hospitalized patients with troglitazone-induced acute liver injury; troglitazone use duration 0.5-9 months; all five had other diabetes therapy (insulin, some metformin); elevated ALT (62-978 IU/L), AST, total bilirubin (3.1-15.6 mg/dl); one death (85-year-old). ALF endpoint required hepatic encephalopathy, liver transplantation, or death in setting of acute severe liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: For troglitazone, the incidence of ALT ≥3×ULN in controlled clinical trials was approximately 3 times greater than that of placebo, and 12 cases of a 10-fold elevation of ALT were reported. From data on troglitazone- and other drug-induced hepatocellular disease, about 10% of patients with ALT >10×ULN will develop jaundice, and about 10% of those with jaundice could die of hepatic insufficiency. The authors state that hepatotoxicity reported with troglitazone, which led to withdrawal of the compound from the market, is probably specifically related to properties of this molecule.
raw_record.extra_details: Withdrawn from the market because of hepatotoxicity. In controlled clinical trials ALT ≥3×ULN incidence was approximately 3 times placebo; 12 cases of ≥10×ULN ALT were reported. Of patients with troglitazone- or other drug-induced hepatocellular disease with ALT >10×ULN, ~10% develop jaundice, and ~10% of those jaundiced could die of hepatic insufficiency. Among the thiazolidinediones, only troglitazone induces CYP3A4; only troglitazone shows the excess ALT incidence, supporting non-class-effect hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In the ALF Study Group collection from 1998-2003, four cases each of troglitazone and bromfenac DILI (drug-induced liver injury) progressing to acute liver failure were identified in 1998-9.
raw_record.extra_details: Four cases of troglitazone DILI identified in 1998-9 within the ALF Study Group registry; patients had subacute evolution, higher bilirubin and lower spontaneous survival compared with acetaminophen ALF.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, the first drug for improving insulin resistance, was reported to cause severe hepatotoxicity in patients shortly after its introduction in Japan and the U.S. in March 1997. Following this, the Japanese government recommended monthly liver function assessment and the U.S. FDA recommended ALT monitoring. The authors report on a patient who developed liver dysfunction after 19 months of troglitazone treatment, highlighting uncertainty about how long liver-function tests should be continued to detect troglitazone-induced liver dysfunction.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatotoxicity reported in patients soon after market introduction in Japan and the U.S. (March 1997). Regulatory responses: the Japanese government recommended monthly liver-function assessment; the U.S. FDA recommended ALT measurement before therapy, monthly for the next 8 months, every 2 months for the remainder of the first year, and periodically thereafter. Case report: patient developed liver dysfunction after 19 months of troglitazone treatment; authors note the unknown duration of monitoring needed to detect troglitazone-induced liver dysfunction.

raw_record.support_text: The letter corrects the number of known cases: not 25 but 90 patients with liver failure occurred during troglitazone therapy, 70 with fatal outcome, of whom 10 patients underwent liver transplantation. Additionally, a healthy subject died of liver failure in the troglitazone group of a diabetes prevention study, prompting the U.S. authority to unblind 585 study participants for safety reasons so they had to stop troglitazone therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: 90 patients with liver failure, 70 fatal, 10 requiring liver transplantation during troglitazone therapy; one healthy person died of liver failure in the troglitazone arm of a diabetes prevention study, leading the FDA to unblind 585 participants for safety. The paper also criticizes FDA fast-track approval of troglitazone. Idiosyncratic liver failure is described as not preventable by liver-enzyme monitoring.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report two cases with severe troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity; neither patient had preexisting liver disease. Both were also receiving an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor for hypercholesterolemia, but had taken it for more than two years prior to onset and recovered from their liver disease while continuing that agent, so it was not implicated as the cause.
raw_record.extra_details: Two new cases plus four previously published cases (patients 3–6). Dose 200–400 mg/day of troglitazone for a type 2 diabetes indication; onset of elevated serum aminotransferases typically 4–6 months after start (mean 124.5 days; range 35–176 days). Histopathology in the five biopsied patients showed hepatocellular necrosis with bridging fibrosis, mild–moderate cholestasis, and a portal inflammatory infiltrate without interface hepatitis; steatosis and granulomas were absent. Peak ALT values 405–1230 units/liter; peak bilirubin 5.9–29.5 mg/dl. Patient 5 required liver transplantation (treated with 400 mg/day); fatal hepatotoxicity occurred in the oldest patient (85 years). Both new patients recovered over ~7 weeks after troglitazone was discontinued while other therapies were maintained. Neither subject had monitoring of liver function after starting troglitazone. Authors note earlier onset/more severe damage may relate to advancing age or higher dose, but require further validation.

raw_record.support_text: In early studies troglitazone was generally well tolerated; in 2,510 U.S. clinical-trial patients, reversible liver-enzyme increases above 3 times the upper limit of normal occurred in 1.9% of troglitazone-treated patients vs 0.6% of placebo-treated patients. However, larger-scale prescription has led to 43 known cases (as of 9/99) of severe liver damage associated with troglitazone, resulting in 28 deaths. The authors note it is unclear to what extent the liver damage resulted from the drug vs other factors and whether the hepatotoxicity was substance specific (PPAR-gamma mediated) vs idiosyncratic.
raw_record.extra_details: Early U.S. trial (2,510 patients) showed reversible liver-enzyme increases >3x ULN in 1.9% of troglitazone-treated vs 0.6% placebo; 20 patients discontinued for liver-function abnormalities. On larger-scale use, 43 known cases of severe liver damage (as of 9/99) with 28 deaths. Paper notes it is unclear to what extent damage resulted from the drug vs other factors and whether hepatotoxicity was substance-specific (PPAR-gamma mediated) vs idiosyncratic.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes an autopsy case of fatal subacute hepatic failure after administration of troglitazone in a 63-year-old woman. Liver dysfunction developed about five months after initial troglitazone treatment, and the patient died despite hepatic auxiliary treatments such as plasmapheresis. Autopsy revealed focal liver cell necrosis, cholestasis and steatosis with lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltration and lack of regenerative activity. The authors state the fatal subacute hepatic failure was 'due unequivocally to troglitazone' and proposed metabolite aberration with accumulation of hepatotoxic metabolite(s), categorized as idiosyncratic liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal subacute hepatic failure in a 63-year-old woman with a history of non-insulin-dependent diabetes and hypothyroidism and no prior liver disease, treated for NIDDM. Dose: troglitazone 200 mg twice a day (400 mg/day), increased to 600 mg/day, then reduced to 400 mg/day. Latency about 5 months before liver dysfunction; presented with jaundice and hepatic failure and died despite plasmapheresis, FFP, and methylprednisolone pulse. Autopsy showed focal liver cell necrosis, cholestasis, and steatosis with lymphocyte and neutrophil infiltration and lack of regenerative activity. Proposed mechanism is accumulation of hepatotoxic metabolite(s) as an idiosyncratic liver injury. Markers of viral hepatitis were negative; co-prescribed glibenclamide (2.5 mg/day) and thyroxine (0.05 mg/day). FDA and MHW in Japan had issued warnings about troglitazone-related liver function side effects.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone (n = 4) was one of only two hypoglycemic compounds causing drug-induced liver injury acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Four cases.

raw_record.support_text: The paper compares troglitazone's pathomechanism with the newer insulin sensitizers, stating that clinical study data show severe hepatic damage and a general trend to increases in transaminase levels for troglitazone, whereas these findings do not occur for the successor drugs such as rosiglitazone.
raw_record.extra_details: Described as a hepatotoxic idiosyncrasy caused by quinone formation from the alpha-tocopherol (vitamin E) moiety, catalyzed mainly by CYP 3A4; individual CYP3A4 expression level modulates susceptibility; troglitazone is an inducer of CYP 3A4 and appears able to boost its own toxicity. Clinical data show severe hepatic damage and a general trend to increased transaminase levels; clinical hepatotoxicity was the reason this drug was not regarded as safe.

raw_record.support_text: The case report states 'Our patient developed liver injury from troglitazone', which was administered for about 2.25 years (25 September 1997 to 9 January 2000) without elevated ALT or AST. In January 2000 she presented with mild jaundice (total serum bilirubin 42.5 µM, 2.5 mg/dl) and increased alkaline phosphatase (4.84 µkat/L, 290 IU/L), and other possible causes of liver injury were excluded by history, course, laboratory, imaging, and hepatic histopathology.
raw_record.extra_details: Biopsy showed hepatitis and cholangitis with a likely immune-mediated component (nonnecrotizing granulomas in portal triads and a distorted bile duct), treated with prednisone, azathioprine, and ursodiol. The paper also notes troglitazone proved to be a frequent and severe hepatotoxin, leading to its withdrawal from the US market in March 2000 and earlier voluntary withdrawal in the UK. Latency to recognition about 2.25 years with biochemically silent injury; patient recovered over the ensuing 8 months.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone appears to have caused fulminant hepatic failure in the presented case, since other causes of liver failure such as viral hepatitis, alcohol intake, autoimmune disorders, and Wilson's disease were all excluded. The paper frames the case as troglitazone-induced fulminant hepatitis and discusses the mechanism of troglitazone-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of drug-induced fulminant hepatic failure/hepatitis. Liver biopsies in two less severe cases (including one with jaundice) confirmed the hepatocellular nature of the injury, consistent with an idiosyncratic drug reaction. Autopsy in the fatal case showed extensive hepatic architectural derangement from massive parenchymal necrosis and collapse with ductular proliferation and cholestasis. The patient took the appropriate daily dose of 400 mg with well-controlled plasma glucose and no hypoglycemia, and the plasma troglitazone concentration 3 days after discontinuation was below the detection limit, indicating overdose was not the cause. Positive drug-induced lymphocyte stimulation test and eosinophilia suggested hypersensitivity as the underlying cause, though no skin rash or lymphadenopathy was present. Liver damage was progressive even after drug withdrawal, ultimately developing into liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: The Diabetes Prevention Programme (DPP), which showed lifestyle intervention and metformin reduced progression from impaired glucose tolerance to overt diabetes, originally included a troglitazone arm. This treatment arm of ~1000 people had to be discontinued after a fatal case of troglitazone-related hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal hepatotoxicity occurred in the DPP diabetes-prevention arm (impaired glucose tolerance/prediabetic population, ~1000 participants), which led to discontinuation of the troglitazone treatment arm of the trial.

condition_group: exposure=therapeutic_use+population=human+population_context=hepatitis_c

raw_record.support_text: Liver injury was observed in 2.00% of patients treated with troglitazone in this study, higher than the known incidence in Japan; prescription of the drug had been suspended in hospitals where troglitazone-induced liver injury was encountered early. Although complicating diseases such as chronic hepatitis C and fatty liver were considered possible causes, all patients had normal ALT before taking troglitazone, so troglitazone appeared to be responsible, and histology did not suggest viral hepatitis or other diseases.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver injury incidence 2.00% in this study, above the known incidence in Japan, with >5% frequency in two hospitals. All patients had normal ALT before starting troglitazone; chronic hepatitis C and fatty liver were assessed but not supported by histology. Concurrent medications were analyzed and none played a role in the liver injury. Reported death was nearly three times more frequent in Japan (0.0042%) than in North American/European Caucasian populations (0.0017%). CYP2C19 poor metabolizer frequency is higher in Japanese (18-23%) versus Caucasians (3-5%); CYP2C19 homozygote frequency was 50% in affected patients. Glibenclamide co-administration did not differ significantly between those with and without liver injury (P=0.33).

condition_group: exposure=therapeutic_use+population=human+population_context=metabolic_fatty_liver_disease

raw_record.support_text: The first thiazolidinedione, troglitazone, was studied in 10 patients who had NASH and was associated with improved aminotransferase levels, but the drug was withdrawn from clinical use because of severe idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Troglitazone was withdrawn from clinical use because of severe idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity. Studied as a NASH treatment in 10 patients; although steatohepatitis was unchanged in control subjects, four of seven treated subjects showed a 1-point improvement in necroinflammatory grade.

condition_group: exposure=therapeutic_use+population=human+population_context=type_2_diabetes

raw_record.support_text: During clinical trials, troglitazone (TRG) proved to be hepatotoxic in 1.9% of patients receiving therapy for Type II diabetes; hepatic failure and death were reported in a few cases, and as a consequence of safety concerns TRG was withdrawn from the US market in March 2000.
raw_record.extra_details: Therapy with troglitazone has been associated with severe hepatic injury in a small percentage of patients; hepatotoxic in 1.9% of patients during clinical trials; hepatic failure and death reported in a few cases; withdrawn from the US market in March 2000 due to safety concerns. Indication: Type II (non-insulin-dependent) diabetes mellitus; first thiazolidinedione antidiabetic agent.

raw_record.support_text: A 58-year-old man contracted severe hepatitis 2 months after troglitazone was started for type 2 diabetes; the liver damage progressed after drug withdrawal, became fulminant, and the patient died 8 weeks after onset. Autopsy showed massive hepatic necrosis and cholestasis with inflammatory cell infiltration. A positive drug-induced lymphocyte stimulation test for troglitazone indicated the liver damage was mediated by hypersensitivity to troglitazone.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency ~2 months after starting troglitazone; disease progressed after withdrawal; death occurred 8 weeks after onset of liver damage. Positive drug-induced lymphocyte stimulation test for troglitazone; hypersensitivity-mediated mechanism. Autopsy: massive hepatic necrosis and cholestasis with inflammatory cell infiltration. Reported as the first autopsy case of troglitazone-induced fulminant hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, a thiazolidinedione antidiabetic agent, was withdrawn from the market in 2000 due to its association with idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity. Two female patients (47- and 70-year-old) with type II diabetes mellitus stopped taking troglitazone (400 mg/day) after 23.5 and 16 weeks, respectively, due to increased serum ALT, and autoantibodies to aldolase B were detected in their sera.
raw_record.extra_details: Thiazolidinedione antidiabetic agent for type II diabetes; withdrawn from market in 2000. During clinical trials 1.9% of patients had ALT increases greater than 3 times the upper limit of normal; fulminant hepatic failure reported in some patients after long-term treatment (>4 weeks). In the present case series, two female patients (47 and 70 years old) ceased 400 mg/day after 23.5 and 16 weeks due to increased serum ALT; anti-aldolase B autoantibody titer remained high for several weeks after stopping. Aldolase B was identified as an autoantigen by 2D electrophoresis and amino acid sequencing; anti-aldolase B autoantibodies also elevated in chronic hepatitis (n=40) and liver cirrhosis (n=40) patients versus healthy subjects (n=80). Hepatotoxicity not reproduced in experimental animals. Troglitazone brands Noscal (Sankyo) and Rezulin (Parke-Davis).

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports hepatotoxicity due to troglitazone and describes two cases of severe liver injury related to troglitazone administration. Troglitazone (Rezulin), the first thiazolidinedione approved by the FDA for type II diabetes, had been prescribed to more than 1.1 million patients, and its hepatotoxicity led to drug withdrawal from some markets and recommendations for more stringent liver function test monitoring.
raw_record.extra_details: Two female patients (both 51 years old) with type II diabetes on troglitazone 200 mg daily for 20-23 weeks before presentation. Case 1: nausea, weakness, progressive jaundice; bilirubin 4.5 mg/dl, ALT 718 U/L, AST 707 U/L, prothrombin time 14 sec, albumin 3.3 g/dl; liver biopsy showed ballooning degeneration with foci of panacinar hepatocellular necrosis with extensive bridging necrosis and fibrosis, moderate canalicular cholestasis, moderate bile ductular proliferation, and mild portal mononuclear infiltrate without interface hepatitis or steatosis; improvement after drug discontinuation (bilirubin fell to 1.2 mg/dl, transaminases and PT normalized). Co-administered medications (verapamil, lansoprazole, simvastatin in case 1; quinapril, simvastatin, conjugated estrogens in case 2) were ongoing before troglitazone and maintained after discontinuation. Hepatitis A/B/C serologies and ANA negative; ERCP showed normal extrahepatic biliary tree.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone was withdrawn in 1999 after spontaneous reports of 94 cases of acute liver failure. In a cohort of 7568 new troglitazone users, the point estimates for hospitalization and acute liver failure were 1244 and 240 per million person-years of exposure, respectively, versus background rates of 10-22 per million person-years. In pre-approval controlled clinical trials in type 2 diabetes, troglitazone was associated with ALT elevations above three times the upper limit of normal in 1.9% versus 0.60% in placebo-treated patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Withdrawn in 1999 after spontaneous reports of 94 cases of acute liver failure; cohort of 7568 users gave hospitalization rate 1244 and acute liver failure 240 per million person-years vs background 10-22 per million. Pre-approval trials: ALT >3x ULN in 1.9% (vs 0.60% placebo, 0.60% ALT >10x ULN); jaundice in 0.5%; acute liver failure ~1 in 20,000 treated patients; broad post-approval use associated with acute liver failure, liver transplantation, and death at intolerable frequency. Used in type 2 diabetes mellitus (thiazolidinedione).

raw_record.support_text: Liver failure reported with troglitazone was usually acute, occurred unpredictably even after extended periods of use, and had a low rate of spontaneous recovery; progression to liver failure became irreversible within a 1-month interval or less for most patients. The incidence of troglitazone-induced liver failure remained elevated and the cumulative risk increased progressively with increasing duration of drug use. The analysis was based on a U.S. health care database cohort of 3 million people across 10 states, representative of national troglitazone usage in patients with type 2 diabetes.
raw_record.extra_details: Outcome was acute liver failure; transplantation or death were reported outcomes. Patients younger than 60 years and men were more likely to recover spontaneously; concomitant metformin use possibly reduced the risk of transplantation or death, though this could have been a chance finding given the large number of comparisons. Study cohort: U.S. type 2 diabetes patients from a health care database (3 million people, 10 states), representative of national usage.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report two patients who had severe hepatotoxicity associated with troglitazone (Rezulin) administration, a thiazolidinedione oral antihyperglycemic agent used for type 2 diabetes. Patient 1, a 44-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes, had taken troglitazone 200 mg daily for 4 weeks followed by 400 mg daily, presenting 20 weeks after starting with nausea, fever, and progressive jaundice; biopsy showed diffuse hepatocyte necrosis with bridging necrosis, regenerating hepatocytes, intracanalicular cholestasis, and early fibrosis, and she gradually improved over 3 months after discontinuation. Patient 2, a 65-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, started troglitazone 400 mg/d and presented 6 weeks later with nausea, anorexia, pruritus, and jaundice; histology revealed hepatocyte necrosis with bridging necrosis, fibrosis, and a portal infiltrate (plasma cells and eosinophils), with marked improvement after discontinuation. Both patients had negative serologies for hepatitis A, B, C, mononucleosis, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus.
raw_record.extra_details: Brand name Rezulin; thiazolidinedione oral antihyperglycemic agent for diabetes. Dose 200-400 mg daily; latency 20 weeks (patient 1) and 6 weeks (patient 2). Patient 1: jaundice, tender enlarged liver, prolonged cholestasis, albumin drop to 18 g/L, prothrombin time 14.8 s, ascites, concern for subacute hepatic necrosis; biopsy showed diffuse hepatocyte necrosis with bridging necrosis, regenerating hepatocytes, intracanalicular cholestasis, no steatosis, early fibrosis; gradual improvement over 3 months (bilirubin decreased to 171 µmol/L). Patient 2: bilirubin 342 µmol/L, alanine aminotransferase 19.42 µkat/L, cholesterol 12.9 µmol/L; ANA test and ERCP negative; biopsy showed hepatocyte necrosis with bridging necrosis, fibrosis, portal inflammatory infiltrate of plasma cells and eosinophils, minimal cholestasis; after 3 months bilirubin 78.66 µmol/L and ALT 5.48 µkat/L. Positive dechallenge (improvement after discontinuation, other medications maintained); negative workup for viral and autoimmune causes. Discussion notes hepatotoxicity is usually intrinsic or idiosyncratic.

raw_record.support_text: In this patient with type 2 diabetes, the time course of hepatic dysfunction and subsequent improvement after withdrawal of troglitazone were described as completely consistent with drug-induced hepatotoxicity. No viral or autoimmune causes for the hepatic dysfunction were identified, and the authors conclude that the patient experienced troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient on insulin whose hepatic dysfunction resolved and liver tests normalized within several months of stopping troglitazone. In clinical trials, troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity defined as ALT >3x ULN occurred in 1.9% of 2,510 patients. A second-generation TZD (rosiglitazone) was later tolerated. Troglitazone has a lipophilic alpha-tocopherol side chain, induces and is metabolized by CYP3A4, and is metabolized to a quinone derivative.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents a series of 11 patients with liver injury attributed to troglitazone therapy for type 2 diabetes. For example, Patient 1, a 65-year-old woman, developed mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic jaundice after 6 weeks of troglitazone 400 mg/day, with alternative causes methodically excluded, and liver biopsy showing bridging necrosis and fibrosis. Patient 4's first biopsy was explicitly labeled 'troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity' showing chronic active hepatitis with bridging fibrosis, progressing to cirrhosis in several patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 11 patients (personal patients treated by an author plus additional cases) on troglitazone for type 2 diabetes: mean age 61±9 years, mean time on drug 10.4±9.9 months, with clinically apparent liver injury sometimes arising within months after drug discontinuation. Histology spanning bridging necrosis/fibrosis, cirrhosis, micro- and macrovesicular steatosis, submassive hepatic necrosis, chronic active hepatitis, and portal hypertension complications. Patient 3 died while awaiting liver transplantation; Patients 5 and 6 died from complications of liver disease years after drug cessation; Patient 8 presented with acute liver failure, ascites and myositis and later developed cirrhosis/portal hypertension; Patient 1 showed mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic jaundice with ALT/AST elevations; troglitazone 400 mg/day in Patient 1. Eosinophils noted in some biopsies.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, the first drug for improving insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes, was reported to cause severe hepatotoxicity in patients in Japan and the U.S. The U.S. FDA and Japanese government issued liver-monitoring recommendations. The authors report a patient who developed liver dysfunction after 19 months of troglitazone treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and Graves' disease; concurrently treated with gliclazide, pravastatin, aspirin, and levothyroxin; troglitazone 400 mg/day added in combination with gliclazide.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency of 19 months from troglitazone start to abrupt transaminase rise (AST 308 U/l, ALT 470 U/l); earlier marginal elevations (AST 39, ALT 55) at 9 months. Withdrawal led to rapid improvement (AST 36, ALT 43 four weeks after discontinuation). Liver biopsy showed hepatocyte necrosis around the central vein with mild lobular infiltration and portal inflammatory infiltrate and fibrosis, compatible with protracted acute hepatitis. DLST and patch tests were negative for troglitazone and other drugs; no allergic clinical signs. The paper states the mechanism is idiosyncratic rather than allergic and the injury is hepatocellular in most cases; it also references a reported autopsy case of fulminant hepatitis with hypersensitivity to troglitazone.

raw_record.support_text: An autopsy case of fatal subacute hepatic failure after administration of troglitazone is described. The liver dysfunction developed about five months after a 63-year-old woman was initially treated with troglitazone, and she died despite hepatic auxiliary treatments such as plasmapheresis. Autopsy findings revealed focal liver cell necrosis, cholestasis, and steatosis with infiltration of lymphocytes and neutrophils and lack of regenerative activity. The authors state the hepatic failure was due unequivocally to troglitazone, and propose a mechanism of metabolite aberration with accumulation of hepatotoxic metabolite(s), categorized as idiosyncratic.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 63-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus and hypothyroidism, who also received glibenclamide (2.5 mg/day) and thyroxine (0.05 mg/day) as co-medications.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose history: troglitazone started at 200 mg twice daily on May 21, 1997, increased to 600 mg/day on June 16, then reduced to 400 mg/day after 2 weeks because treatment failed to improve her condition. Liver dysfunction developed about 5 months after initial treatment; malaise without fever or eruption began during that summer; on October 14, 1997 jaundice and liver dysfunction were found and all drugs were withdrawn. The patient developed hepatic failure and died despite plasmapheresis and other auxiliary treatments. Autopsy showed focal liver cell necrosis, cholestasis, steatosis, infiltration of lymphocytes and neutrophils, and lack of regenerative activity. Proposed mechanism: metabolite aberration due to accumulation of hepatotoxic metabolite(s), in an idiosyncratic category. FDA (US) and MHW (Japan) had issued warnings about troglitazone liver-function side effects, and reports of liver dysfunction after several months of continuous use were accumulating.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a case of fatal hepatitis associated with troglitazone. An 85-year-old man with type 2 diabetes developed severe hepatic dysfunction after troglitazone therapy (started 5 months prior, increased to 400 mg/day after 15 weeks); abdominal pain, malaise and jaundice developed and alanine aminotransferase reached 608 U/L. A diagnosis of troglitazone-induced hepatitis seemed likely, symptoms progressed to confusion, agitation, ascites and edema, and liver biopsy showed submassive hepatic necrosis; the patient died 8 weeks after presentation. The paper notes that in rare cases troglitazone use is associated with fatal hepatotoxicity and that news of six deaths and one liver transplantation led to withdrawal of the product from the British market.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that hospitalization rates for acute idiopathic liver injury among troglitazone-exposed patients were 55- to 124-fold greater than expected background rates (10-22 per million person-years), and that the incidence of idiopathic ALF among troglitazone-exposed patients was increased more than 240-fold. Additional evidence cited includes a 485-fold greater reporting of ALF with troglitazone than glipizide in the FDA adverse drug reaction database, three patients registered with the United Network for Organ Sharing for liver transplantation with troglitazone cited as the cause, whereas none were registered for sulfonylureas or metformin, and fatal/mortal ALF cases in postmarketing and randomized trial cohorts. The paper concludes that the high rate of ALF observed with troglitazone was not caused by type 2 diabetes itself.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, an antidiabetic drug, caused life-threatening idiosyncratic reactions in patients. Mild, reversible hepatotoxicity appeared in pre-marketing clinical trials in <2% of patients; after marketing in early 1997 several cases of severe, even fatal, liver failure emerged, forcing market withdrawal in 2000. Affected patients had elevated serum enzymes and bilirubin and signs of hepatocellular necrosis and cholestasis; livers showed necrosis and inflammatory infiltrates including neutrophils. Injury was idiosyncratic with no obvious dose relationship.

raw_record.extra_details: Mild reversible hepatotoxicity in <2% of pre-marketing trial patients; several cases of severe, even fatal, liver failure after market entry in 1997; withdrawn from the market in 2000; elevated serum enzymes and bilirubin; signs of hepatocellular necrosis and cholestasis; necrosis with inflammatory infiltrates including neutrophil accumulation; authors note it is not currently possible to predict which patients will develop liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 19 patients with lipoatrophic diabetes treated with troglitazone (continued beyond the study period), one patient (U1) developed fatigue and an eightfold increase in ALT concentration after 10 months of therapy. While the patient was on troglitazone, ALT was within normal range 3 weeks before the elevation was detected; GGT, bilirubin, and synthetic function remained normal; viral hepatitis A, B, and C serology and autoantibodies were negative. A liver biopsy performed 3 days after troglitazone discontinuation showed an eosinophilic infiltrate consistent with toxicity due to hypersensitivity to the drug. Troglitazone was stopped and aminotransferase concentrations returned to normal 3 months later.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single reported case in a patient with lipoatrophic diabetes receiving prolonged troglitazone treatment continued beyond a clinical study.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency about 10 months; ALT rose eightfold (prior transient ALT rise to 1134 nkat/L, normal <668 nkat/L, occurred 3 months before troglitazone started and normalized). Liver biopsy 3 days after discontinuation (6 days after peak ALT) showed chronic inflammatory infiltrate with many eosinophils and moderate piecemeal necrosis, small foci of lobular inflammation and hepatocellular apoptosis, preserved architecture, no steatosis, confluent necrosis, or fibrosis; electron microscopy showed no mitochondrial or peroxisomal abnormalities. Dechallenge led to slow improvement with ALT normalization 3 months after stopping; hypersensitivity/eosinophilic infiltrate attributed to the drug.

raw_record.support_text: A 6-year-old Tunisian child treated for epileptic absences with sodium valproate and ethosuximide developed drug hypersensitivity syndrome with hepatitis. Imputability of both drugs was deemed probable from chronological and clinical features; positive rechallenge with ethosuximide confirmed its toxicity, and sodium valproate was also held responsible because patch testing was positive and followed by a generalized eruption. The outcome was favourable after drug discontinuation and corticosteroid therapy.

Drug hypersensitivity syndrome included fever, morbiliform skin eruption with vesicular and target lesions, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia (2x10^9/l), lymphocytosis (8.95x10^9/l), monocytosis, leukocytosis, and abnormal liver function tests (AST 70 U/l, GGT 50 U/l, LDH 1020 U/l). Positive rechallenge with ethosuximide confirmed toxicity. HHV6 antibody titers rose from 40 to 120 within 15 days; favourable outcome after drug discontinuation and corticosteroid therapy. Reported as the first case of DHS with ethosuximide.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the first case of ramipril-induced liver injury proven by positive rechallenge, and (per the RUCAM assessment) the case was classified as 'highly probable' with a score of 12 of 15. The patient presented with jaundice and highly elevated ALT and ALP (mixed pattern), developing 10 months after starting ramipril, with normalization after rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: First ramipril DILI case proven by positive rechallenge; RUCAM score 12/15 ('highly probable'); time to onset 10 months; presented with jaundice and highly elevated ALT and ALP; outcome was normalization after dechallenge/rechallenge. Pattern expected to include cholestasis but hepatocellular damage also possible.

raw_record.support_text: This case report is described as the fifth known case of ramipril-induced hepatotoxicity. Following discontinuation of ramipril, the patient's alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin began declining promptly, though biochemical markers had not yet returned to baseline at one month post-discharge. The biopsy revealed bland cholestasis with no ductular changes.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of ramipril-induced hepatotoxicity, the fifth known case. Current case: bland cholestasis with no ductular changes on biopsy; onset 8 weeks after beginning ramipril (latency range 5 weeks to 10 months across cases); ALP and bilirubin declined after discontinuation but not returned to baseline at one month; prior cholestatic cases (biopsies showing cholestasis and bile duct necrosis) returned to near baseline at 6 and 14 months. Two other prior cases: one mixed pattern (markedly elevated ALT and ALP, minimal bilirubin increase, parenchymal inflammation on biopsy, unintended positive rechallenge confirming diagnosis) and one unclassifiable (mild liver enzyme increases, no biopsy). Symptomatic presentation varied from incidental blood-work findings to jaundice and severe pruritus. Cholestasis described as the most common liver injury pattern in ACEI-induced hepatotoxicity. First described cross reactivity between ramipril and methimazole in recurrent DILI.

raw_record.support_text: Chloroform, a halogenated hydrocarbon, causes CNS depression, cardiac arrhythmias, and hepatotoxicity. A 19-year-old man who ingested approximately 75 mL of chloroform in a suicide attempt developed liver function abnormalities with peak AST of 224 IU/L, ALT of 583 IU/L, and total bilirubin reaching 16.3 mg/dL, and was successfully treated with intravenously administered N-acetylcysteine and supportive care without permanent sequelae. Serum chloroform on admission was 91 μg/mL. Hepatocellular toxicity is thought to result from free radical-induced oxidative damage.

raw_record.extra_details: Ingested ~75 mL chloroform; admission serum chloroform 91 μg/mL (average fatal serum level in inhalational poisoning reported as 64 μg/mL). Liver test peaks: AST 224 IU/L, ALT 583 IU/L, total bilirubin 16.3 mg/dL, PT 21.3 s (INR 2.25); values normalized by hospital day 8. Mechanism described as free radical-induced oxidative damage; hepatocellular toxicity. Chloroform synonym trichloromethane.

raw_record.support_text: A 23-year-old man developed jaundice of the skin and sclerae by the sixth hospital day after intentionally inhaling an unknown quantity of laboratory-grade chloroform from a soaked towel while intoxicated with beer. A percutaneous liver biopsy on the 11th day, 10 days after chloroform exposure, showed resolving centrilobular necrosis with fatty droplets in mid-zonal surviving cells, dropout of hepatocytes, and dilated sinusoids lined by Kupffer cells. The jaundice rapidly resolved and the patient was discharged in good condition.

raw_record.support_text: Chloroform intoxication produces hepatic injury seen after two to five days, which is the result of liver cell necrosis; prothrombin time and transaminase values are markedly elevated while bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase tend to be minimally abnormal. Alcohol or barbiturates that induce hepatic microsomal enzymes increase chloroform-induced liver cell damage, whereas enzyme inhibitors such as disulfiram prevent hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Ingestion/poisoning context; in this report chloroform was voluntarily inhaled or ingested at 'chloroform parties', either accidentally or as a suicidal gesture.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 19-year-old boy who ingested chloroform; liver function tests showed SGOT rising to 8,080 IU, SGPT to 10,250 IU, and LDH to 9,280 IU by days 3-4, with total bilirubin up to 2.7 mg/100 ml and prolonged prothrombin time (patient 19.3 sec vs control 11.9 sec); values normalized by day 90. Hepatic injury is attributed to liver cell necrosis from toxic metabolites formed by hepatic enzymes rather than direct injury; alcohol/barbiturate enzyme induction worsens the injury and disulfiram prevents hepatotoxicity. Also associated with renal damage appearing within 24-48 hours.

raw_record.extra_details: Plasma chloroform levels declined rapidly by headspace GC; initial laboratory values on arrival showed AST 21 IU/L, ALT 40 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, PT 13.4 s, APTT 28.4 s; WBC 14,400 with 79% neutrophils. Acute exposure causes hepatic necrosis generally between day 2 and 5 peaking day 5-7; death may occur secondary to hepatic and renal failure. raw_record.support_text: The first two cases of jaundice and death following the administration of chloroform were reported by Heyfelder in 1848, marking the earliest recognition of hepatic dysfunction and damage as a complication of anaesthesia. Chloroform had been introduced as an inhalation anaesthetic, and human liver injury after therapeutic anaesthetic use was reported.
raw_record.extra_details: First two cases (Heyfelder, 1848) of jaundice and death after chloroform anaesthesia; within the first decade of the 1900s Bevan and Favill reported about 30 isolated case reports of 'the late poisonous effects of anesthetics' after chloroform and diethyl ether. The AMA Committee on Anesthesia recommended that 'the use of chloroform as the anesthetic for major operations is no longer justifiable,' citing delayed chloroform poisoning following 'in a by no means inconsiderable percentage of cases'; the paper notes the recommendation lacked an approximate numerical incidence value. Experimental laboratory work in dogs established central hepatic necrosis as the typical chloroform lesion, but the drug was not administered in an acceptable clinical manner.

raw_record.support_text: A case series of seven patients (ages 20-57) who received chloroform (CHC) as an anesthetic during open thoracic surgery is presented; post-mortem examination showed acute centrilobar necrosis of the liver in all seven. Two patients (cases 4 and 5) died, on the third and fourth postoperative days respectively, with shock/jaundice; case 6 developed toxic hepatitis with jaundice and recovered; case 7 had mild jaundice. The accompanying text emphasizes 'the dangers of chloroform administration under other than optimal conditions' and possible contraindications to chloroform during anesthesia for open thoracic procedures.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: General anesthesia delivered by inhalation (CHC) during open thoracic surgery; some cases complicated by hypotension and hemorrhage; one patient (case 5) had chronic alcoholism with Laennec's cirrhosis. The paper notes dangers of administration under other than optimal conditions and possible contraindication in open thoracic anesthesia, with deaths occurring on the third and fourth postoperative days.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven cases, ages 20-57. Acute centrilobar necrosis of the liver found at post-mortem in all cases; cases 4 and 5 died (third and fourth postoperative days) with shock, fever, fibrillation, and jaundice; case 6 had toxic hepatitis with jaundice and recovered; case 7 had mild jaundice. Laboratory results included bilirubin values up to 120 and cephalin flocculation up to 4 plus. Premedication was 0.3 mg scopolamine or atropine. Anesthesia durations and operative times are tabulated, with moderate hypotension reported in some cases.

raw_record.support_text: In Group I, 106 patients receiving chloroform anesthesia were studied with liver function tests (serum bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, prothrombin time, thymol turbidity, thymol flocculation, and cephalin flocculation) taken at delivery and on the third postpartum day. Although routine liver function tests were unsatisfactory for revealing liver damage from chloroform anesthesia, two patients showed clear liver damage: one developed clinical jaundice and a second had a subclinical significant elevation of serum bilirubin with 40% bromsulphalein retention after 45 minutes, while other tests remained normal. The paper frames these findings as toxic hepatitis from chloroform anesthesia.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Inhalation anesthetic given during delivery; patients with a history of previous liver disease, diabetes mellitus, and severe toxemia were excluded from receiving chloroform anesthesia.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of 106 patients in Group I before SGPT was available; one patient developed clinical jaundice and a second had subclinical significant serum bilirubin elevation with 40% bromsulphalein retention after 45 minutes. Cephalin flocculation and alkaline phosphatase were normal in both affected patients. Fifty-two percent of patients had abnormal serum alkaline phosphatase (4 to 10 mM units) prior to delivery and 25% on day 3; 25% had 3- and 4-plus cephalin flocculation before delivery, falling to 7% on day 3. Study conducted at a local charity hospital with the highest incidence of toxic hepatitis; most patients were Negroes. Group II controls (39 patients, local or no anesthesia) showed only occasional minor SGPT variations and no such liver damage, aside from one incidental infectious hepatitis case.
