raw_record.support_text: Ibuprofen was attributed to 25 DILI cases with hepatocellular (44%) and mixed (44%) patterns. Fatal cases were reported for ibuprofen among the most frequent causative drugs; 6 (25%) cases met the nR-based Hy's law criteria and 2 (33%) of these had death/liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: 25 of 843 registry DILI cases; Hep 44%/Chol 12%/Mix 44%; female 48%, lymphopenia 23%, eosinophilia 17%; 6 (25%) fulfilled nR-based Hy's law, 2 (33%) true Hy's law (death/liver transplantation).

raw_record.support_text: A 65-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of tea-colored urine, jaundice, and anorexia with impaired liver function after taking a single ibuprofen-sustained release capsule the day before onset due to headache. The authors made a diagnosis of liver failure due to taking ibuprofen-sustained release capsules. After 9 days of hepatoprotective and nutritional therapy the symptoms improved, liver function returned to near normal, and follow-up at 2 weeks showed normal liver function tests.
raw_record.extra_details: 65-year-old man; single ibuprofen-sustained release capsule taken the day before symptom onset for headache. Presenting features: 4-day history of tea-colored urine, oil avoidance, jaundiced skin, anorexia, impaired liver function. Diagnosis of liver failure attributed to ibuprofen; hepatotoxic drugs discontinued, then hepatoprotective agents, nutritional support, correction of acid-base and electrolyte abnormalities. Marked improvement after 9 days (no discomfort, subsided jaundice, clear urine, near-normal liver tests), discharged, normal liver function at 2-week follow-up. No formal causality instrument reported.

raw_record.support_text: Among 20 patients with acute liver failure, drug-induced liver injury was the attributed etiology in 5 (25.0%), including ibuprofen in 1 patient. The paper therefore attributes ALF/DILI to ibuprofen in this patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as the DILI etiology in 1 of 20 ALF ICU patients; clinical phenotype is acute liver failure in an ONSD study.

raw_record.support_text: The study characterized 26 ibuprofen DILI cases from the Spanish DILI Registry, noting that ibuprofen-induced liver injury usually develops within four weeks of treatment initiation and presents as hepatocellular type liver damage, though characteristics varied considerably between patients. The paper concludes the risk of developing ibuprofen-induced liver injury is low given the drug's extensive worldwide use but can have life-threatening consequences. Registry data showed hepatocellular injury in 15 (58%) and cholestatic/mixed in 11 (42%) cases, with 2 fatal and 1 liver transplantation outcome among the ibuprofen cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 26 ibuprofen DILI cases in the Spanish DILI Registry (N=26 ibuprofen vs 76 other NSAIDs vs 844 non-NSAIDs). Median time to onset 15 days (range 3-1767), median treatment duration 16 days (1-1826). Clinical presentation: jaundice 17 (65%), hospital admission 14 (58%), eosinophilia 6 (24%), lymphopenia 4 (17%), positive autoantibody titers 6 (27%). Prior to this, ibuprofen was considered to have very limited hepatotoxicity. Higher OTC doses marketed in Spain (200 and 400 mg) vs US (200 mg only) hypothesized to explain higher ibuprofen DILI frequency in Spain; threshold dose for idiosyncratic DILI and reactive-metabolite/oxidative-stress/JNK mechanism discussed. A multicenter Italy study reported higher adjusted risk of liver damage for ibuprofen than for diclofenac. Severity: mild 9 (35%), moderate 14 (54%), severe 0, fatal 2 / liver transplant 1 (12%). Hy's law criteria met in 11 (42%). 11 of 13 (85%) resolved within 1 year. No characteristic drug signature; diabetes mellitus trend more common in ibuprofen DILI patients (7, 27%); lower hypertension prevalence (2, 10%).

raw_record.support_text: The authors point out the inadvertent minimization of ibuprofen's toxicity, describing a patient who had the Stevens-Johnson syndrome plus toxic hepatitis due to ibuprofen, published in the New York State Journal of Medicine in 1978. At that time there had been 17 other reported cases of ibuprofen-induced hepatotoxicity, plus five cases of serious dermatologic problems (erythema multiforme bullosum including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis) reported to the manufacturer.
raw_record.extra_details: Toxic hepatitis reported in a patient who also had Stevens-Johnson syndrome due to ibuprofen. At the time there had been 17 other published cases of ibuprofen-induced hepatotoxicity (total 18 cases). Kantor's earlier review (December 1979) described ibuprofen hepatic toxicity as very rare; the letter is written to counter that minimization. Related serious dermatologic reports (erythema multiforme bullosum/Stevens-Johnson syndrome/epidermal necrolysis) had been filed with the manufacturer (Upjohn).

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 60 patients with acute hepatitis (19 drug-induced), drug-induced hepatitis was attributed to acetaminophen (three patients), ibuprofen (one patient), and ketoconazole (one patient). Ibuprofen is therefore reported as a cause of human drug-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as the cause of drug-induced hepatitis in 1 of 19 drug-induced acute hepatitis cases (5.2%) within a 60-patient acute hepatitis cohort; no details on dose, latency, outcomes, or overdose given.

raw_record.support_text: Ibuprofen was responsible for 4 (10%) of the cases in the 40-patient DILI cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as a causative DILI agent in 4 of 40 patients (10%).

raw_record.support_text: In the 7-day double-blind crossover trial of ibuprofen, aspirin, prednisolone and placebo, there was no uniform trend in serum transaminase levels (SGOT, SGPT) with any of the drugs or placebo. Although transaminases exceeded the upper limit of normal in 2 of 8 patients on ibuprofen, in one of these patients such increases also occurred after lactose, so no drug-related DILI was attributed.
raw_record.extra_details: 7-day double-blind crossover trial in 9 rheumatoid arthritis patients; serum SGOT/SGPT showed no uniform trend with ibuprofen versus placebo; ULN exceeded in 2 of 8 patients on ibuprofen, one of whom also had increases after lactose, so elevations were not attributed to the drug.

raw_record.support_text: DILI-inducing NSAIDs were APAP, celecoxib and ibuprofen; NSAIDs accounted for 17 patients (4.01%) of DILI cases.
raw_record.extra_details: NSAID; NSAIDs accounted for 17 patients (4.01%) of DILI cases.

raw_record.support_text: In this 40-year-old woman who had a history of taking ibuprofen, clinical diagnosis was an ibuprofen-induced liver injury resulting in persistent cholestasis and hyperlipidemia, supported by a RUCAM score of 6 (modest probability of DILI) with severe liver injury (stage III) and a pathology diagnosis of DILI at stage IV with features of bile duct injury and loss of bile duct structures consistent with vanishing bile duct syndrome (VBDS).
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM score 6 with R=0.32 (grade III/severe liver injury); pathology DILI stage IV; liver biopsy on day 28 showed biliary injury and absence of small terminal bile ducts around hepatic arteries in >50% of portal tracts with bile salt deposition; Ishak necroinflammatory activity score 5 and fibrosis score 2; second biopsy day 213 showed acute VBDS with some autoimmune-hepatitis features; persistent hyperbilirubinemia and hyperlipidemia with no significant improvement after 10-month follow-up; normal PT; viral serology and autoantibodies negative excluding hepatitis A/B/C/E, CMV, PBC, PSC; concurrent diabetes treated with acarbose and metformin; treated with ursodeoxycholic acid, polyene phosphatidylcholine, silibinin, glutathione.

raw_record.support_text: One patient in this study received a liver transplant as a result of ibuprofen-induced hepatotoxicity following therapeutic use. Clinically significant hepatotoxicity from ibuprofen is rare, although elevated transaminases have been reported with therapeutic doses. The paper also notes a reported case in which therapeutic doses of ibuprofen induced subacute liver failure requiring transplantation 10 weeks after onset of hepatotoxicity symptoms, with other causes excluded and a temporal relationship strongly favoring a drug-related etiology.
raw_record.extra_details: One patient in this study received a liver transplant following therapeutic ibuprofen use. Clinically significant hepatotoxicity is rare; elevated transaminases with therapeutic doses have been reported. A separate reported case of subacute liver failure required transplantation 10 weeks after onset of hepatotoxicity with therapeutic doses, other causes excluded and temporal relationship favoring drug-related etiology.

raw_record.support_text: In the TARGET clinical trial, clinical hepatitis was rare regardless of drug used, with two cases of clinical hepatitis adjudicated to ibuprofen (0.05%).
raw_record.extra_details: TARGET trial (chronic osteoarthritis therapy); two cases of clinical hepatitis adjudicated to ibuprofen (0.05%).

raw_record.support_text: Zoubek et al. examined ibuprofen-induced hepatotoxicity in 21 cases from the Spanish DILI Registry and five cases from the Latin American DILI Registry, in comparison with other NSAID- and non-NSAID-induced DILI cases. The authors reported that ibuprofen was the most frequent NSAID known to cause DILI in Spain and that 29% of NSAID DILI cases were attributed to ibuprofen; it was only the third-leading hepatotoxic drug in Latin America, behind nimesulide and diclofenac.
raw_record.extra_details: 21 ibuprofen-induced DILI cases in the Spanish DILI Registry and 5 in the Latin American DILI Registry; ibuprofen was the most frequent NSAID cause of DILI in Spain and third-leading hepatotoxic drug in Latin America; 29% of NSAID DILI cases were attributed to ibuprofen. Authors postulated the higher frequency in Spain versus the USA may relate to dose, since over-the-counter ibuprofen is available in both 200- and 400-mg formulations in Spain versus only 200-mg in the USA.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a patient who had Stevens-Johnson syndrome plus toxic hepatitis due to ibuprofen, noting that 17 other cases of ibuprofen-induced hepatotoxicity had been reported at that time, along with five cases of serious dermatologic problems (erythema multiforme bullosum variants including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis).
raw_record.extra_details: Toxic hepatitis reported due to ibuprofen; at the time of writing 17 other cases of ibuprofen-induced hepatotoxicity had been reported. The authors' own patient had the first reported case of combined Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic hepatitis due to ibuprofen. Reference is made to a further reported patient with lymphopenia and hepatotoxicity from ibuprofen.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report their patient as the first reported case of combined Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic hepatitis due to ibuprofen. They also cite a second published patient with lymphopenia and hepatotoxicity from ibuprofen, and conclude that hepatotoxicity and various cutaneous disorders caused by ibuprofen may not be as rare as comments in the Kantor article would suggest.
raw_record.extra_details: Letter to the editor: first reported case of combined Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic hepatitis due to ibuprofen; additionally references the Stempel and Miller pediatric case of lymphopenia and hepatic toxicity from ibuprofen. Authors argue hepatotoxicity and cutaneous disorders caused by ibuprofen may be less rare than suggested.

raw_record.support_text: In the Spanish registry, which has included more than 800 cases, ibuprofen heads the NSAID hepatotoxicity list.
raw_record.extra_details: Heads the NSAID list in the Spanish registry (>800 DILI cases); no biochemical pattern, phenotype, or severity reported.

raw_record.support_text: A drug lymphocyte stimulation test performed on a patient who presented with fever, skin rash, and brown urine after taking ibuprofen tested positive only for ibuprofen. A liver biopsy supported the diagnosis of drug-induced liver injury, and the patient's skin lesions were diagnosed as multiform exudative erythema, supporting a definitive diagnosis of allergic-type drug-induced liver disease caused by ibuprofen and complicated by systemic hypersensitivity.

raw_record.extra_details: Presented with fever (39°C), skin rash (multiform exudative erythema), and brown urine; admission labs: AST 1,492 U/L, ALT 1,860 U/L, ALP 323 U/L, total bilirubin 15.3 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 10.4 mg/dL, INR 1.76, elevated IgE 11,900 IU/mL; negative for hepatitis B, C, antinuclear antibodies and HHV-6; drug lymphocyte stimulation test positive only for ibuprofen; liver biopsy 14 days after discontinuation supported DILI; treated with IV methylprednisolone 1,000 mg daily for 3 days followed by tapered oral corticosteroid; rash resolved and liver tests normalized over 4 weeks.

raw_record.support_text: This is a case report of an adult female with severe jaundice after taking ibuprofen who developed persistent cholestasis, hyperlipidemia, and vanishing bile duct syndrome. The DILI from ibuprofen was identified by clinical features and liver biopsy, with a Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) score of 6 and pathological features of cholestasis with stage four drug-induced injury as well as loss of bile duct structures. Laboratory abnormalities improved after cessation of ibuprofen, and a second liver biopsy on day 213 confirmed vanishing bile duct syndrome.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single case in a 40s female, no prior liver disease; ibuprofen 300 mg bid by mouth 2-3 days per month for menalgia; concurrent oral acarbose and metformin for type II diabetes.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM score 6; liver biopsy showed cholestasis with stage four drug-induced injury and loss of bile duct structures; persistently high bilirubin with hyperlipidemia over about one month; second biopsy on day 213 confirmed VBDS; negative autoantibodies (AMA-M2, ASMA, RO-52, LKM, SLA, anti-glycoprotein-210); jaundice, fatigue, dark urine; no ascites or hepatomegaly; spleen palpable 3 cm below left costal margin; symptoms began ~30 days progressive jaundice after intermittent ibuprofen over six months. Background notes ibuprofen may produce unpredictable, idiosyncratic type B reactions (hypersensitivity reaction).

raw_record.support_text: Two young male patients developed severe cholestatic DILI following low-dose ibuprofen intake (400 mg), lacking conventional risk factors. raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Two young (32- and 29-year-old) male patients without conventional risk factors, one with prior Omicron (COVID-19) fever and one after jogging; both genetically predisposed through ABCB11/BSEP compound heterozygous mutations (p.V444A, p.A1028A, with p.A865V in Patient 1). raw_record.support_text: The paper reports the first known case of drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis secondary to letrozole. The diagnosis was based on the time lapse between drug exposure and onset of hepatitis, exclusion of non-drug-related causes, improvement after drug withdrawal, and letrozole being listed as a potential cause of drug-induced liver disease in the product label, achieving a Roussel-Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) score of 9.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM score 9; diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis confirmed by liver biopsy; asymptomatic acute liver derangement managed with steroids. The paper notes there were no published instances of clinically apparent liver injury with long-term letrozole therapy as of 2017 and no cases of severe jaundice, acute liver failure, chronic hepatitis, or vanishing bile duct syndrome attributed to letrozole, which are relevant negatives for these specific endpoints rather than a negative for DILI overall. Letrozole is metabolized by the cytochrome P450 system and strongly inhibits CYP 2A6 and, to a lesser extent, CYP 2C19; a toxic or immunogenic metabolite was proposed as a mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: For molnupiravir, the authors state that hepatotoxicity or hepatic adverse effects are not clearly understood and that it is too early to comment on molnupiravir-induced hepatotoxicity (drug-induced liver injury) because clinical data on its use are limited. Elevated serum aminotransferase levels were noticed in clinical trials but were uncommon, mild, and less frequent than with placebo, and episodes of clinically apparent liver injury were not reported in prelicensure studies of more than 900 patients given 800 mg twice daily for five days. The short duration of therapy and lack of major hepatic metabolism are given as plausible justifications for the lack of severe adverse events and hepatic injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral prodrug of the ribonucleoside analog N-hydroxycitidine (NHC); used for mild-to-moderate COVID-19 (EUA 23 Dec 2021); elevated serum aminotransferases uncommon, mild, and less frequent than placebo; no clinically apparent liver injury reported among >900 patients given 800 mg twice daily for 5 days; authors state it is too early to comment on molnupiravir-induced DILI due to limited data; short therapy duration and lack of major hepatic metabolism cited as justifications for lack of hepatic injury; contraindicated in COVID-19 patients with abnormal liver function profiles.

raw_record.support_text: In this phase I study, PHA-793887 was poorly tolerated, with two patients experiencing severe acute hepatic failure, one of them dying because of drug-related toxicity, leading to halting of further clinical development. The severe hepatotoxicity of PHA-793887 was considered not target-related because hepatotoxicity had not been documented for other CDK inhibitors in clinical use. In animals, liver effects were observed only at lethal doses with AUC ≥20 µM·h and Cmax ≥14 µM, whereas the mean AUC₀⁻∞ in patients at 44 and 66 mg/m² was 10.14 and 13.07 µMh with mean Cmax of 3.60 and 5.80 µM, indicating hepatotoxic exposure in humans was a fraction of that causing toxicity in animals.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase I dose-escalation study in patients with advanced solid tumors (dose levels 11, 22, 44, and 66 mg/m²). Two of 18 evaluable patients experienced severe acute hepatic failure; one died of drug-related toxicity. Further clinical development was halted. Toxicity judged not target-related (no other CDK inhibitor in clinical use showed hepatotoxicity); PHA-793887 is a pyrrolo[3,4-c]pyrazole structurally different from other CDK inhibitors. Preclinical liver effects only at lethal doses (AUC ≥20 µM·h, Cmax ≥14 µM); human mean AUC₀⁻∞ at 44 and 66 mg/m² was 10.14 and 13.07 µMh, mean Cmax 3.60 and 5.80 µM. DILI liver_injury_identifier corresponds to acute liver failure (UMLS:C0162557).

raw_record.support_text: In this phase I trial of PHA-793887, one patient treated at 66 mg/m² experienced a drug-related grade 4 hepatic failure with pancytopenia, and one patient treated at 44 mg/m² had a fatal hepatorenal failure. There was no dose relationship in the rate of clinical adverse events, but there was a clear dose relation with regard to their severity. Biochemical abnormalities related mainly to liver biochemistry tests, with evidence of a dose relation in the frequency and severity of AST, ALT and bilirubin elevations; all grade ≥3 liver biochemistry toxicity developed during cycle 1 within 2–4 days after initial drug administration and generally improved over 3–4 weeks.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Phase I dose-escalation study in patients with advanced solid tumors; an investigational agent.
raw_record.extra_details: One drug-related grade 4 hepatic failure with pancytopenia at 66 mg/m²/day and one fatal hepatorenal failure at 44 mg/m²/day; two patients died during study (one from fatal hepatorenal failure, one from disease progression). Grade ≥3 AST and ALT elevations occurred in 2 of 9 patients at 44 mg/m² and 1 of 3 at 66 mg/m²; bilirubin grade ≥3 in 1 of 9 at 44 mg/m² and 2 of 3 at 66 mg/m². All grade ≥3 liver biochemistry toxicity developed during cycle 1 within 2–4 days of first dose and improved over 3–4 weeks; affected patients were not re-treated. Kinetic parameters: terminal half-life 6–13 h, Vss 1.9–2.2 L/kg, clearance 0.14–0.48 L/h/kg.

A full workup ruled out other secondary causes and a liver biopsy confirmed DILI. The paper concludes that cephalosporins other than cefazolin should be recognized as potential causes of DILI.

Rise and fall of enzymes closely paralleled initiation and cessation of cefepime; competing causes ruled out; liver biopsy confirmed DILI. Female patient.

No MTD was reached; monotherapy dose escalation stopped at 380 mg due to gastrointestinal TEAEs.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxic jaundice occurred in 5% of 40 patients (about 2 patients) treated with albendazole for hydatid disease caused by E. granulosus. Twenty-one patients (53%) with 37 cysts (59%) showed evidence of healing; recurrence during observation occurred in 9.5% of patients with a positive response. The paper presents clinical phenotyping as hepatotoxic jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: A 25-year-old Hispanic woman was diagnosed with albendazole-induced granulomatous hepatitis after ruling out other possible causes, based on laboratory studies, liver biopsy, medical history, detailed drug history, and spontaneous improvement of her liver biochemical profile after medication withdrawal. The diagnosis was supported by the CIOMS-Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method, which showed a likely correlation between hepatocellular damage and drug toxicity as the etiology. The histologic pattern was granulomatous hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Granulomatous hepatitis (granulomatous inflammatory reaction with epithelioid macrophages and mononuclear cells) as the attributed phenotype in a 25-year-old Hispanic woman in Colombia. Diagnosis supported by CIOMS-Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method showing a likely correlation; other causes (infectious, autoimmune, sarcoidosis) ruled out; liver biochemical profile improved spontaneously after drug withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: Among 42 patients with alveolar echinococcosis treated between 2002 and 2016, liver transplantation was eventually required in two patients, one of whom required transplantation for albendazole hepatotoxicity that precluded continued treatment (the other for recurrent cholangitis). This explicitly attributes human hepatotoxicity to albendazole therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient being treated for alveolar echinococcosis; liver transplantation was required because albendazole hepatotoxicity precluded continued treatment. Overall series: 42 AE patients (2002-2016); two required liver transplantation (one for albendazole hepatotoxicity, one for recurrent cholangitis).

raw_record.support_text: To assess the correlation between albendazole and liver injury, the RUCAM scale was applied. The R ratio (ALT/ULN divided by ALP/ULN) was 48, meeting the hepatocellular pattern criterion (R ≥5). Scoring: drug taken 2 weeks before symptom onset (2 pts), improvement within 30 days of stopping the drug (2 pts), no risk factors (0), no co-administered drugs (0), no viral hepatitis, biliary obstruction, alcoholic or ischemic hepatitis (2 pts), and known hepatotoxic drug (2 pts). Including the response to re-exposure item (3 pts, attributing a liver injury 8 years earlier to albendazole), the total score was 11, indicating a definitive (definite) drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of albendazole-induced drug-induced liver injury (DILI). RUCAM score 11 (definitive), with R ratio 48 (hepatocellular). RUCAM items: drug taken 2 weeks before symptom onset, improvement within 30 days of stopping drug, no risk factors, no co-administered drugs, alternative causes (viral hepatitis, biliary obstruction, alcoholic/ischemic hepatitis) excluded. Re-exposure item (3 pts) reflects a prior liver injury 8 years earlier also attributed to albendazole. Other causes (viral hepatitis, biliary obstruction, alcoholic hepatitis) excluded; abdominal ultrasound showed normal liver, gallbladder, bile ducts, and pancreas. Patient treated with supportive therapy including fluids, discharged on hospital day 9 with improvement, and liver enzymes normalized on outpatient follow-up. Paper also notes amoxicillin/clavulanate and acetaminophen are the most common DILI causes, and herbal medicine (한약) accounts for 40.2% of DILI cases in Korea.

raw_record.support_text: The biochemical profile during the first hospitalization evidenced cholestasis; during the second admission after five months of anti-parasitic treatment the damage pattern shifted to hepatocellular with marked increases of aminotransferases that lessened progressively with albendazole withdrawal, normalizing at four months without additional intervention. Between both hospitalizations there was no therapeutic intervention different from the anti-parasitic prescription. The authors diagnosed albendazole-induced liver damage after establishing progressive clinical and para-clinical improvement following withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report (Columbia). Indication was hydatidosis (echinococcosis); albendazole given as routine anti-parasitic treatment. Initial cholestatic pattern progressed after five months to a hepatocellular pattern with marked aminotransferase elevation; values improved after albendazole withdrawal and normalized by four months; dechallenge-associated recovery without additional conduct. Competing cause (inflammatory reaction from parasite death) considered and deemed unlikely responsible for the hepatocellular damage since albendazole is effectively used without clinically significant hepatic effects in similar cases. Patient was asymptomatic with normal hepatic profile three months after discharge.

raw_record.support_text: A 72-year-old patient treated for alveolar echinococcosis with albendazole (400 mg twice daily) developed a drug-toxic hepatitis. Six weeks after starting albendazole, transaminases and alkaline phosphatase rose progressively, with GOT leading at 20x the upper limit of normal (GOT 693 U/l, GPT 338 U/l, AP 164 U/l) and clinical dizziness and upper abdominal pain. Other hepatitis causes (viral hepatitis, toxic damage from other drugs/substances, ischemia) were excluded, establishing the diagnosis of a medication-induced toxic hepatitis during albendazole therapy. The drug was paused and transaminases fell markedly within a week, with complete laboratory remission within 19 days.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of one 72-year-old patient treated for inoperable alveolar echinococcosis (WHO stage IIIb, probable case). Diagnosis framed as 'a.e.' (most likely) drug-toxic hepatitis under albendazole; other causes (viral hepatitis, other drugs, ischemia) excluded. No liver synthesis/clearing impairment and no blood count pathology at any time; complete laboratory remission 19 days after pausing albendazole. Therapy subsequently switched to mebendazole. Albendazole dosing 400 mg twice daily (4 h target level 1-3 µmol/l).

raw_record.support_text: Applying the RUCAM score for the albendazole-related group confirmed the high likelihood of liver disorder associated with medicine ingestion, with scores ranging from 10 to 13 points for all patients. In one patient, re-exposure occurred. Albendazole is listed as one of the three DILI groups (acetaminophen, albendazole, and others) in the study.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM scores ranged from 10 to 13 points for all patients, confirming a high likelihood of medicine-associated liver disorder; re-exposure occurred in one patient.

raw_record.support_text: A 38-year-old Middle Eastern female presented with fatigue, malaise, and jaundice after recent treatment with albendazole for two large hydatid liver cysts. She had significant progressive transaminase and bilirubin elevation despite stopping albendazole; a transjugular liver biopsy showed severe acute hepatitis with patchy necrosis, a distorted reticulin framework, and no plasma cell infiltration. She progressed to fulminant hepatic failure and received orthotopic liver transplantation 13 days into admission. RUCAM score was 6, indicating probable drug-induced hepatitis.

The diagnosis was based on the clinical record, drug consumption history, improvement of clinical and laboratory tests after discontinuation, and exclusion of other causes, and was supported by the CIOMS/RUCAM scale, which showed a 'likely' correlation between hepatocellular damage and drug toxicity.

Background context in the paper notes mild aminotransferase elevation in up to 15.6% of albendazole cases that resolves with temporary withdrawal without comorbidity, and only two prior published cases where transaminase elevation and symptoms obliged definite treatment suspension.

It recommends screening for adverse reactions such as liver-test alterations and leukopenia during prolonged treatment.

raw_record.extra_details: Reported as a frequent adverse effect of long-term albendazole treatment together with alopecia and neutropenia. Authors recommend screening for liver-test alterations and leukopenia every 2 weeks for the first 3 months, then monthly during the first year, then every 3 months. Albendazole is metabolized in the liver to the active metabolite albendazole sulfoxide, whose blood levels should be monitored especially in case of hepatocellular dysfunction and/or cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: A 7-year-old boy given albendazole 400 mg single tablets for routine deworming on 4 occasions over three years developed jaundice each time within 7 days of administration, totaling four episodes of hepatitis with no other cause. Each episode resolved spontaneously and liver enzymes were normal at follow-up and between episodes. RUCAM/CIOMS score of 12 was compatible with drug-induced hepatitis, and the NADRPS score of 8 was suggestive of probable drug-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (7-year-old boy); routine deworming indications; four separate single 400 mg oral doses.
raw_record.extra_details: Four episodes of hepatitis/jaundice, each developing within 7 days of a single 400 mg albendazole tablet; no alternative cause identified; spontaneous resolution with normalized liver enzymes between episodes; RUCAM/CIOMS score 12; NADRPS score 8 (probable drug-induced hepatotoxicity). Albendazole is an orally administered broad-spectrum antihelmintic; hepatitis reported after prolonged use for hydatid cyst/neurocysticercosis, with this being the first report of repeated episodes following single doses.

raw_record.support_text: Niperotidine is an H2 antagonist structurally related to ranitidine. Twenty-five cases of acute hepatitis (including one death from fulminant hepatitis) associated with niperotidine use were reported in Italy between March and August 1995, and the drug was withdrawn from the market. The methylenedioxy group of niperotidine (absent in ranitidine) is known to undergo metabolism to catechol and quinone metabolites.
raw_record.extra_details: H2 antagonist structurally related to ranitidine; 25 cases of acute hepatitis reported in Italy between March and August 1995, including one death from fulminant hepatitis; drug withdrawn from the market. Methylenedioxy group (absent in ranitidine) metabolizes to catechol and quinone metabolites, implicated in toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In this 26-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of pioglitazone monotherapy (7.5, 15, 30, or 45 mg once daily) in 408 patients with type 2 diabetes, the overall adverse event profile of pioglitazone was similar to placebo, and the authors state there was no evidence of drug-induced hepatotoxicity or drug-induced elevations of alanine aminotransferase levels in this study. The conclusion reiterates no evidence of drug-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Multicenter double-blind placebo-controlled clinical trial; 408 randomized patients with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c >= 7.0%, FPG >= 140 mg/dl, C-peptide > 1 ng/ml); pioglitazone 7.5, 15, 30, or 45 mg once daily for 26 weeks. Authors report no evidence of drug-induced hepatotoxicity or drug-induced elevations of alanine aminotransferase levels, and an adverse event profile similar to placebo.

raw_record.support_text: A 39-year-old black woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and heart failure presented with fatigue, dark brown urine, nausea, pruritus, and loss of appetite. Pioglitazone was promptly discontinued because her symptoms were consistent with hepatotoxicity, and pioglitazone was identified as a potential cause. Liver enzymes checked 13 days after initial presentation were abnormal (ALT 490 U/L, AST 360 U/L, ALP 851 U/L, total bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL), and 2.5 months after stopping pioglitazone the symptoms resolved and serum liver enzymes returned to normal. In the conclusions, the Naranjo adverse-effect assessment scale suggested a probable causal link between pioglitazone and hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo scale rated probable causality. Symptoms were fatigue, dark brown urine, nausea, pruritus, loss of appetite; liver tests at 13 days: ALT 490 U/L, AST 360 U/L, ALP 851 U/L, total bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.0 mg/dL, indirect bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL. Symptoms resolved and enzymes normalized 2.5 months after drug cessation. The paper notes the sequence of events and magnitude of enzyme elevation were not clear in this case. Authors recommend not re-using a thiazolidinedione in patients who previously had associated hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: This post-marketing surveillance study of pioglitazone (15 or 30 mg once daily) in over 8700 patients with type 2 diabetes reported improvements in glycaemic control and lipid profiles. The paper notes that these results are similar to evidence from randomized controlled trials, citing that 'These studies and others also reported improvement of serum lipid levels and no evidence of hepatotoxicity with pioglitazone.'

raw_record.support_text: The first of two cases of reversible pioglitazone-induced jaundice was a 49-year-old diabetic man who presented with scleral icterus and acholic stools 6 months after starting pioglitazone. Serum bilirubin was 5.7 mg/dL with AST approximately threefold elevated, ALT approximately eightfold elevated, and alkaline phosphatase 2.5 times normal. Ultrasound was normal and other causes of liver injury were excluded. Liver biopsy showed a mixed hepatocellular cholestatic injury pattern with cholestasis, portal inflammation, and bile duct injury. After pioglitazone was discontinued the bilirubin and AST declined, with liver enzymes normal by 48 weeks. The patient was also taking glyburide, metformin, lisinopril, and omeprazole, but jaundice did not occur until pioglitazone was added.

raw_record.support_text: A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, morbid obesity and other comorbidities, already on insulin glargine, glimepiride, metformin, simvastatin and sertraline, had pioglitazone 30 mg/day added 24 days before admission. She presented with markedly elevated AST (2,144 U/l) and ALT (2,760 U/l) with normal bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, albumin, ferritin and prothrombin; viral and autoimmune serologies were negative and no liver biopsy was performed. Using the Spanish Pharmacovigilance System algorithm, she was diagnosed with probable acute drug-induced liver disease and the case was reported to the Basque Country Pharmacovigilance Unit. After stopping all oral medication and treating with insulin, transaminases declined rapidly and normalized within 30 days.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes nifedipine-induced hepatitis as a rare type of drug-induced liver injury that presents in an idiosyncratic manner, acutely within days or subacutely within 4-8 weeks after medication start, with chronic/latent cases diagnosed up to 3 years later. Symptoms include jaundice, nausea, chills, rigors, diaphoresis, fatigue, and abdominal pain; laboratory investigations show profound elevations in AST, ALT, GGT, and conjugated bilirubin, with possible eosinophilia, and liver biopsy typically shows immune cell infiltration, cholestasis, and a steatohepatitis picture. Treatment is drug discontinuation with supportive care; all published instances were self-limiting without mortality due to fulminant liver failure but can take months to resolve.
raw_record.extra_details: Known but very rare clinically-apparent hepatitis that can take months to resolve; a case is presented in a 78-year-old Caucasian female with no prior liver or autoimmune disease. Latency: acute (within days) or subacute (4-8 weeks); chronic/latent cases up to 3 years after drug start. Symptoms: jaundice, nausea, chills, rigors, diaphoresis, fatigue, abdominal pain. Labs: profound elevations in AST, ALT, GGT, conjugated (and total) bilirubin; peripheral eosinophilia possible. Histology: immune-cell infiltration, cholestasis, steatohepatitis. Treatment: immediate drug discontinuation and supportive care; no randomized evidence for corticosteroids. All published cases self-limiting, no mortality from fulminant liver failure. Listed among idiosyncratic antihypertensive causes of DILI.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present the largest series of nimesulide-related hepatotoxicity published to date, comprising 57 patients, and state that their analysis highlights the potential of nimesulide to induce serious liver injury, including acute liver failure (ALF). The cohort was predominantly female (86%), with 61% women older than 60 years and 43% over 65; the series also included a pediatric case that developed severe hepatotoxicity and required liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: 57 patients with nimesulide-related hepatotoxicity; female predominance (86%), 61% women older than 60 years, 43% over 65 years; included a pediatric case requiring liver transplantation. One fatal case: 57-year-old woman treated for osteoarthritis with nimesulide 200 mg/day who developed jaundice 3 days after intake, fulminant hepatitis with severe coagulopathy (INR 3.9), and died of multiorgan failure while awaiting liver transplantation. Cholestatic/mixed pattern documented in 50% of patients with latency within 7 to 15 days; hepatocellular injury predominated (71%) in patients with latency over 15 days; most patients (79%) developed injury after 15 days from therapy initiation; jaundice in 84%, hospitalization in 58%. Literature data (Kwon et al. 2019) on 33 cases: 85% women, median age 57 years, age ≥55 years a risk factor.

raw_record.support_text: The paper documents a case of severe hepatotoxicity induced by nimesulide treatment in a previously healthy woman, and a retrospective study in which nimesulide treatment induced serious reactions in 19 patients, including severe hepatitis in 8 of those patients.

raw_record.support_text: In the nimesulide-DILI series, a hepatocellular pattern of liver injury was present in all acute liver failure (ALF) cases except one that was classified as mixed (case 12). Liver histology from six patients showed severe hepatocellular necrosis ranging from submassive injury with extensive centrilobular necrosis and collapsed areas to massive multiacinar necrosis. Twelve patients developed ALF, of whom five died from multiorgan failure (cases 12, 22, 31, 52, 56), three were transplanted (cases 23, 35, 39), and four recovered spontaneously. The prescribed dose was 200 mg/day in 10 cases (83%) indicated for pain.
raw_record.extra_details: Nimesulide-DILI cases; prescribed dose 200 mg/day in 10/12 cases indicated for pain; 12 of the series developed acute liver failure (ALF); 5 died of multiorgan failure (3 while waiting for transplant), 3 were transplanted, 4 recovered spontaneously after 45-150 days (median 60 days). Latency longer in ALF patients (60 vs 30 days, p=0.108); cumulative dose median 10,500 mg (ALF) vs 6,000 mg (non-ALF), p=0.133. Histology showed centrilobular and multiacinar severe hepatocellular necrosis. ALF patients had higher mean TBL, AST, and INR (all p<0.001); most showed AST>ALT and ALP <= 4x ULN; half had AST/ALT ratio >1.5 vs 6.7% without ALF (p=0.002). Nine patients (75%) took concomitant drugs; transient ibuprofen (case 45) and diclofenac (case 12) intake had incompatible temporal relationships (no intake within 18 and 16 days, respectively, of symptom onset), leaving nimesulide as the attributed cause.

raw_record.support_text: A 49-year-old woman presented at the emergency department with acute hepatic failure and a MELD score of 25.0, 2 weeks after taking nimesulide, with a probable diagnosis of toxic hepatitis. She was transferred to a liver transplant unit; after supportive care and acetylcysteine, a liver biopsy revealed micronodular cirrhosis associated with acute hepatitis with features suggestive of autoimmune hepatitis. She was then started on azathioprine 50 mg/day and prednisolone 30 mg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: Nimesulide 100 mg twice daily for 3 days for oral pain, taken 2 weeks before admission; presented with worsening jaundice, soft stools and dark urine, then new-onset jaundice one week later. MELD score 25.0. Led to transfer to a specialist liver transplant unit with probable toxic hepatitis; treated with supportive care and acetylcysteine. Liver biopsy showed micronodular cirrhosis with acute hepatitis showing features suggestive of autoimmune hepatitis (AIH). After azathioprine 50 mg/day and prednisolone 30 mg/day, a biopsy 28 months later showed almost full remission with only mild fibrosis and no significant inflammatory infiltrate. The paper notes nimesulide is referred to in published reports as hepatotoxic but its association with triggering AIH symptoms is rare; cirrhosis reversibility after 2 years is highlighted.

raw_record.support_text: Nimesulide leads the NSAID list in both the LATINDILI registry and the Spanish registry of drug-induced liver injury cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Leads the NSAID list in the LATINDILI registry and the Spanish registry (>800 cases); no biochemical pattern, phenotype, or severity reported in this passage.

raw_record.support_text: In a single-center series of 57 orthotopic liver transplantations for acute liver failure (1988-2005), five cases were diagnosed as NSAID-induced fulminant hepatitis based on exclusion of any other potentially hepatotoxic medication and other causes of liver failure. Three of these five cases were related to nimesulide at doses of 100-600 mg/day; all required liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: 3 of 5 cases of NSAID-induced acute liver failure; doses 100-600 mg/day; clinical hepatitis arose 2 days to 2 months after therapy initiation; all required orthotopic liver transplantation for acute liver failure with progressive encephalopathy and Factor V <20% of normal. Cited incidence of nimesulide-induced liver injury approx 0.1 per 100,000 treated patients but often severe course.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that in 2009 the authors' series included 43 well documented cases of nimesulide-induced liver damage associated with a wide clinical and histological spectrum of hepatotoxicity, the largest series of nimesulide hepatotoxicity ever reported. Main presenting symptoms were jaundice (70%), malaise (65%), and pruritus (50%); two thirds of patients started liver toxicity 15 to 90 days after drug intake, with only 11% having a latency shorter than 15 days, and normalization exceeded 90 days in 27% of cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Largest reported series of nimesulide hepatotoxicity (43 well documented cases). In the authors' institution, 5 of 30 cases (17%) had severe liver injury. Nine patients developed severe liver disease and fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) occurred in 6 cases, predominantly females older than 50 years (per Walker et al); 2 patients died before liver transplant due to multiorgan failure, and a 9-year-old girl successfully underwent orthotopic liver transplantation. ALT/aspartate transaminase: a wide range of variations; per Bjarnason, 33 case reports showed ALT elevation of at least 2-fold in 100% and 5-fold in 89% of patients. Liver damage spectrum included acute hepatitis, cholestasis, mixed forms, and massive and submassive hepatic necrosis: hepatocellular necrosis in 64%, cholestatic hepatitis in 27%, pure cholestasis in 9%. Symptoms: jaundice, malaise, pruritus; latency 15-90 days in two-thirds, only 11% shorter than 15 days; normalization exceeded 90 days in 27%; in cholestatic injury, alkaline phosphatase normalization can exceed 1 year. Proposed mechanism (unconfirmed): reactive metabolite formation and genetic variation in drug metabolism.

raw_record.support_text: In this reply, the authors defend their conclusion that nimesulide was the cause of the patient's hepatotoxicity based on convincing evidence. Nimesulide had been taken 1 week prior to the presentation of an acute hepatocellular damage ('acute hepatocellular' picture), which they describe as much more consistent with an idiosyncratic reaction to a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug; amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, taken at least 1 month before symptoms, was excluded as the cause because its hepatotoxicity is typically cholestatic and a delay beyond a month is exceptional.
raw_record.extra_details: Single attributed case; nimesulide taken 1 week before hepatitis presentation. Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid was a concurrent co-exposure but was excluded as the cause (its hepatotoxicity is characteristically cholestatic and delay beyond ~1 month is the exception). The original article (J Intern Med 2000; 247: 153-55) is titled 'Fatal hepatitis and renal failure during treatment with nimesulide', indicating a fatal outcome. The Israeli Ministry of Health allowed nimesulide reintroduction, attributed to the rarity and postulated idiosyncratic nature of the effect rather than doubt about the nimesulide-liver-disease association; authors recommend awareness, liver enzyme monitoring, and avoiding concomitant hepatotoxic medications.

raw_record.support_text: In the authors' six patients, nimesulide produced drug-induced hepatitis characterized by severe hepatocellular necrosis in 67% of cases (all women, three over 65 years of age), whereas a pure cholestatic pattern resembling ethinyl-estradiol or androgen-induced cholestasis was found in the two male cases. The nimesulide-induced liver injury is attributed to both idiosyncratic pathogenic mechanisms: immunoallergic hypersensitivity (two patients, 33%, had increased blood and tissue eosinophilia) and metabolic idiosyncrasy involving hepatotoxic metabolites such as 4-hydroxy-nimesulide.
raw_record.extra_details: Six patients; hepatocellular necrosis pattern in 67% of cases, all women, three above 65 years; pure cholestatic pattern in the two male cases (sex-dependent pattern distribution not previously reported for other NSAIDs); centrilobular lesion location; main metabolite 4-hydroxy-nimesulide; two patients had an underlying cholestatic disease diagnosed during the injury; blood and tissue eosinophilia in one hepatocellular and one cholestatic case suggesting immunoallergic mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: The letter refers to a well-documented case description of fatal acute liver injury secondary to the use of nimesulide (by Merlani et al.), stating that the causal relationship between liver injury and nimesulide in this case is likely and remains undisputed.
raw_record.extra_details: The case (Merlani et al.) is a fatal acute liver injury attributed to nimesulide. The letter is a methodological critique of the reported incidence calculation for hepatic adverse drug reactions (ADRs) among NSAIDs; it argues the odds-ratio method is flawed because NSAID-related adverse effects are dominated by gastrointestinal reactions and denominators vary, and that reporting rates are dynamic. As background, 195 hepatic adverse effects for nimesulide were reported to health authorities and Helsinn between 1985 and 2001 (123 serious, 72 non-serious) against roughly 304 million treated patients; nimesulide ranked fifth among NSAIDs worldwide in 2000, and after a temporary suspension in Israel in 1999 its licence was reinstated.

raw_record.support_text: Nimesulide, a selective COX-2 inhibitor / sulfonamide derivative, is described as newly causing drug-induced liver disease in the year 2000. It has been associated with several reports of fulminant hepatic failure including fatal hepatitis: Van Steenbergen et al. reported four women with centrilobular or panlobular necrosis and two men with bland intrahepatic cholestasis (jaundice in 5 of 6), all resolving after drug discontinuation; McCormick et al. described a woman with fulminant hepatic failure after resuming nimesulide for back pain who underwent emergency liver transplantation and died of primary graft nonfunction; Weiss et al. reported six patients with acute hepatitis that resolved on discontinuation, except one case where drug was continued and fatal hepatic necrosis ensued.
raw_record.extra_details: Selective COX-2 inhibitor for rheumatic disorders / back pain, not available in the US. Van Steenbergen cases: jaundice presenting in 5/6, liver enzymes returned to normal 6-17 months after discontinuation. McCormick case: AST 2014 IU/L, ALT 2857 IU/L, emergency liver transplantation for fulminant hepatitis, died of primary graft nonfunction; explant showed massive necrosis. Weiss cases: ALT elevated ~15x normal, fatigue/nausea/vomiting; recovery within 2-4 months on discontinuation; one case continued drug 2 weeks after symptomatic, died 6 weeks later in hepatorenal syndrome.

raw_record.support_text: Van Steenbergen et al. described six patients with nimesulide-induced acute hepatitis, showing either a hepatocellular necrosis pattern (4 patients) or pure cholestasis (2 patients). One patient died from pancreatic carcinoma five months after the diagnosis of toxic liver injury, while the remaining five patients had liver test results return to normal within six to 17 months of follow-up.
raw_record.extra_details: Six patients; 4 with hepatocellular necrosis pattern, 2 with pure cholestasis; 5 recovered (liver tests normal within 6-17 months); one death was from pancreatic carcinoma, not liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: Nimesulide was attributed to 9 DILI cases, predominantly hepatocellular (78%). Seven cases (78%) met nR-based Hy's law criteria and 1 (14%) led to death/liver transplantation; fatal cases were reported for nimesulide.
raw_record.extra_details: 9 of 843 registry DILI cases; Hep 78%/Chol 22%/Mix 0%; female 89%, lymphopenia 25%, eosinophilia 33%; 7 (78%) fulfilled nR-based Hy's law, 1 (14%) true Hy's law with death/liver transplantation; high mean TBL at recognition.

raw_record.support_text: A Naranjo probability scale score of 6 indicated a probable relationship between hepatotoxicity and nimesulide therapy in the reported patient. The authors note many prior reports of potential nimesulide hepatotoxicity and that an idiosyncratic reaction is likely involved, with possible mechanisms including hepatic bioactivation of nimesulide, nitroreductive activation of its aromatic nitro group, generation of reactive metabolites inducing oxidative stress and mitochondrial injury, mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening, ATP depletion, and release of apoptosis-inducing mediators. The conclusion states that nimesulide use, especially in women and the elderly, could pose a risk for hepatotoxicity and that prescribers should consider the possibility of nimesulide-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report with a Naranjo probability score of 6 (probable relationship). An idiosyncratic reaction is likely involved. Proposed mechanism: hepatic bioactivation of nimesulide via nitroreductive activation of its aromatic nitro group producing reactive metabolites that induce intracellular oxidative stress and mitochondrial injury; mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening leading to ATP depletion, osmotic swelling, and release of apoptosis-inducing mediators. Conclusion notes potential risk particularly in women and the elderly, and recommends early drug discontinuation if hepatitis is suspected.

raw_record.support_text: Nimesulide is listed among the main 10 drugs leading the Latin American DILI Registry with n = 11 cases, with RUCAM-based causality assessment.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 cases in the Latin American DILI Registry; RUCAM-based causality assessment used.

raw_record.support_text: In the NSAIDs group, 14 patients (70%) had liver damage attributable to nimesulide. Cases of fulminant and subacute hepatitis, sometimes fatal, have been documented, and two pathological patterns of nimesulide-induced DILI (hepatocellular necrosis and pure cholestasis) have been documented. The only 3 patients with hepatic failure, encephalopathy and ascites due to DILI belonged to the nimesulide group; one of them died while on the waiting list for liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Potent anti-inflammatory/analgesic/antipyretic, widely used clinically; documented fulminant and subacute hepatitis, sometimes fatal; two DILI patterns (hepatocellular necrosis and pure cholestasis) possibly related to patient gender; in this case series 50% were women with higher frequency of cytolytic and lower frequency of cholestatic patterns than males; majority of cases above age 40; highest mean aminotransferase values but shortest recovery time; the only 3 patients with hepatic failure, encephalopathy and ascites due to DILI belonged to this group, one dying on the waiting list for liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: This report describes a case of fatal hepatotoxicity secondary to the NSAID nimesulide. The patient, a 57-year-old woman treated for chronic lumbago for about 90 days, had acute liver dystrophy with pronounced hepatocellular necrosis and mild cholestasis at autopsy, markedly elevated transaminases and bilirubin, and died 21 days after transfer. Causality was scored 9 points ('highly probable') using a modified Van Steenbergen system, and the toxicity profile suggested an idiosyncratic reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Therapeutic use for chronic lumbago for ~90 days; NSAID, preferential COX-2 inhibitor. On admission ALT 2786 U/l, AST 2135 U/l, total bilirubin 490 umol/L, Quick 32% with progression; histology showed extensive confluent centrilobular liver cell necrosis and acute liver dystrophy with mild cholestasis. Patient died 21 days after transfer to intensive care; post-mortem showed profound jaundice, lung congestion and ischemic bowel damage. Modified Van Steenbergen causality score 9 points = 'highly probable'.

raw_record.support_text: Nimesulide-associated hepatitis was diagnosed, and the patient was treated with methylprednisolone. Liver function tests and aspartate and alanine aminotransferase levels improved rapidly and were within normal limits 3 weeks after admission; the patient was discharged asymptomatic. The paper reports this as the 12th case of nimesulide-associated liver injury published, with unclear frequency and mechanism, and notes nimesulide causes two characteristic histologic patterns: centrilobular hepatocellular necrosis and pure cholestasis resembling ethinyl estradiol- or androgen-induced cholestasis. This patient showed extensive centrilobular necrosis with a mixed eosinophil-rich infiltrate and a severe vasculitis of hepatic veins.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient admitted with nausea, vomiting, severe abdominal pain, hepatic encephalopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, pleural effusions, and icteric sclerae. Symptoms recurred 5 days after nimesulide was restarted and the patient was readmitted after 12 days of repeated intake (positive rechallenge). Laboratory findings showed the typical pattern of acute liver failure (AST 1006 U/l, ALT 1115 U/l, prothrombin time 39%, bilirubin 2.2 mg/dl) with marked eosinophilia (35%). Cavography/duplex sonography excluded large-vein thrombotic outflow block (Budd-Chiari) but showed drop-out of hepatic vein branches and decreased portal flow; biopsy showed centrilobular necrosis in zones 3 and 2, mixed eosinophil-rich inflammatory infiltrate, and severe vasculitis of hepatic vein branches. Viral, autoimmune, and metabolic causes excluded. Concurrent medication was oral contraceptives (cyproterone acetate 2 mg/day and ethinyl estradiol 0.035 mg/day for 5 months). Treated with methylprednisolone (100 mg/day, tapering to 4 mg) and diuretics; recovered within 3 weeks. Reported as the 12th published case of nimesulide-associated liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: Two of the patients with nimesulide-associated hepatotoxicity reported by Grinola et al. died from fulminant liver failure resulting from hepatocellular insufficiency; in one, the post-mortem hepatic lesion was massive hepatic necrosis with total loss of liver architecture. The other three patients had elevated liver enzymes and other indices of abnormal liver function that returned to normal 20-30 days after drug cessation, and these cases showed eosinophilia reflecting a drug-associated hypersensitivity reaction. The author notes further investigations are indicated to establish whether nimesulide formulations contribute to the hepatotoxicity associated with this drug in Uruguay.
raw_record.extra_details: Five patients with nimesulide-associated hepatotoxicity (Grinola et al., cases from Uruguay): 2 died from fulminant liver failure (hepatocellular insufficiency) with massive hepatic necrosis and total loss of liver architecture in one post-mortem; the other 3 had elevated liver enzymes that normalized 20-30 days after drug cessation, with eosinophilia indicating a hypersensitivity reaction.

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes severe hepatic damage and hemolysis occurring in a patient receiving nimesulide. Drug involvement is supported by a temporal relationship between drug intake and the clinical picture, careful exclusion of other causes of liver injury, and histologic features compatible with drug-induced liver toxicity. CIOMS scale assessment yielded a score of 6 points, within the 'probable' category, though the fulminant outcome prevented assessment of the effect of dechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of severe hepatic damage progressing to acute liver failure and fulminant liver failure with hepatic encephalopathy; patient received an orthotopic liver transplant on day 25 and was alive 20 months later with mild biochemical cholestasis. CIOMS causality score 6 points (probable). Prolonged drug exposure; accumulation of aberrant (reactive) metabolites (idiosyncratic metabolic mechanism) speculatively implicated. Co-occurring hemolytic anemia with negative Coombs test, no autoantibodies, and no response to steroids. Liver tests showed high bilirubin (up to 51.6 mg/dl), AST up to 240 U/l, ALT up to 110 U/l, AP up to 1099 U/l, GGT up to 565 U/l.

raw_record.support_text: A case series of patients with nimesulide-DILI is described: median nimesulide dose 200 mg/day (range 100-200 mg), mainly used for pain due to arthritis, osteoarthritis, or trauma. Median latency to injury was 40 days (range 3-238 days), with 83% of patients having a latency shorter than 90 days and eight patients (14%) developing injury after 6 months of treatment. Hepatocellular damage was the most frequent pattern (38 patients, 67%), followed by mixed (12 patients, 21%) and cholestatic (7 patients, 12%) injury. Common features included jaundice (81%), hospitalization (51%), and encephalopathy (21%).
raw_record.extra_details: Adjudicated case series of nimesulide-DILI (nimesulide-induced liver injury). Median dose 200 mg/day (range 100-200), 83% on 200 mg/day; indications pain from arthritis, osteoarthritis, or trauma. Median latency 40 days (range 3-238), 83% <90 days, 14% after 6 months. Patterns: hepatocellular 38/57 (67%), mixed 12/57 (21%), cholestatic 7/57 (12%). Symptoms: asthenia 37%, nausea 37%, vomiting 32%, pruritus 16%. Jaundice 81%, hospitalization 51%, encephalopathy 21%; admission independent of injury type (p=0.783). Biochemistry on admission: mean TBL 13 x ULN, AST 20 x ULN, ALT 18 x ULN, ALP 2 x ULN, mean INR 1.9. Peripheral eosinophilia 16%; no rash, immunoallergic manifestations, or autoimmune features. Cholestatic/mixed cases had more pruritus (p=0.004), less jaundice (p=0.031), higher ALP (p<0.001), lower ALT and AST (p<0.001, p=0.007) than hepatocellular cases.

raw_record.support_text: Table 1 lists three patients (cases 2, 3 and 10) with DILI attributed to nimesulide taken at 200 mg/day for osteoarthritis. Case 3 showed jaundice with hepatocellular injury and CIOMS 'Highly probable'. Case 10 showed eosinophilia with cholestatic injury (TB 1.2xULN, ALT 1.2xULN, ALP 5xULN), CIOMS 'Highly probable'. The study is framed as NSAIDs-induced idiosyncratic liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective analysis of 46 patients with drug-induced liver injury, 14 cases with liver damage were attributed to nimesulide (70% of the NSAID/anti-inflammatory group). These patients had a median ALT of 700 IU/l, 11 of 14 presented with jaundice, 3 developed severe hepatic failure with encephalopathy and/or ascites, one patient died while on the waiting list for liver transplant, and one developed autoimmune hepatitis with ANA positivity. Liver biopsies in 6 patients showed centrilobular or panlobular bridging necrosis with mild intrahepatic cholestasis. Most patients received a single dose of nimesulide.
raw_record.extra_details: 14 of 46 DILI cases attributed to nimesulide (70% of anti-inflammatory/NSAID group; all 6 NSAID-group liver biopsies were nimesulide-exposed). 7 men/7 women, mean age 58; 1 patient had pre-existing chronic HBV/HCV with persistently normal ALT. Jaundice prevalence 78.6% vs 34.4% (p=0.013); median ALT 700 IU/l (range 120-2400); 3/11 developed severe hepatic failure with encephalopathy and/or ascites (subacute hepatic failure); 8 cytolytic, 3 cholestatic, 3 mixed patterns; biopsies showed centrilobular or panlobular bridging necrosis with mild intrahepatic cholestasis; 1 patient died on liver transplant waiting list; 1 patient developed autoimmune hepatitis with ANA positivity; others recovered within follow-up; recovery time significantly shorter versus other patients (4 vs 8 weeks, p<0.001); most patients received a single dose of the medication.

Laboratory tests showed markedly elevated bilirubin (total 17.6, direct 13.5), GPT 1705, GOT 1397, alkaline phosphatase 512 and GGT 823; viral (A, B, C, HIV, CMV, Epstein-Barr), atypical-bacteria and autoantibody (AMA, ANA, SMA, anti-DNA, LKM-1) markers were all negative. The patient improved and was discharged after 3 weeks, framed as a clinical case of acute hepatitis caused by nimesulide.

raw_record.extra_details: NSAID and selective COX-2 inhibitor with a sulfonanilide group, metabolized in liver to 4-hydroxy-nimesulide; 0.1% eliminated unchanged in urine. Nimesulide hepatotoxicity risk was added to its product information in January 2000 after cases of hepatitis. In the Spanish Pharmacovigilance System (FEDRA) database there are 20 suspected hepatic adverse reactions with nimesulide; 84% were women with a mean age of 66.2 years, of which 8 had only liver enzyme abnormalities and the rest symptomatic hepatotoxicity. Reported manifestations are cholestasis and hepatocellular necrosis, which (if administration is not interrupted) can progress to acute liver failure, encephalopathy and even death. Mechanism described as idiosyncratic metabolic, dose-independent and host-dependent, through aberrant metabolic pathways producing toxic metabolites or converting hepatic antigens into neoantigens triggering an immunoallergic reaction (supported by peripheral and tissue eosinophilia) or by toxic accumulation after a long latent period. In the present case the patient recovered after 3 weeks with improving liver tests; laboratory and imaging findings are recorded.

raw_record.support_text: A 76-year-old man with a history of alcoholic liver disease and renal insufficiency mistakenly ingested Colchicum autumnale (autumn crocus) instead of wild garlic. After a 12-hour latency he developed nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, then somnolence, respiratory failure and cardiac deterioration. Laboratory tests revealed rhabdomyolysis, coagulopathy, and deterioration of renal and hepatic function. Toxicological analysis disclosed colchicine in urine (6 μg/l) and serum (9 μg/l) on day 2. The patient died on day 3 of asystolic cardiac arrest.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Accidental off-label ingestion of Colchicum autumnale plant mistaken for wild garlic (supratherapeutic colchicine exposure); pre-existing alcoholic liver disease and renal insufficiency; 76-year-old patient; pneumonia as complicating infection.
raw_record.extra_details: Colchicine is an antimitotic alkaloid that blocks mitosis by preventing DNA synthesis and tubulin polymerization. Poisoning follows a latent period of 4-12 h with a second intoxication stage (24-72 h) that includes hepatic injury together with heart failure, arrhythmias, renal failure, respiratory distress, coagulopathy, bone marrow depression and neuromuscular involvement. Toxicology confirmed colchicine 6 μg/l in urine and 9 μg/l in serum on day 2. The patient died on day 3 of asystolic cardiac arrest (cardiovascular collapse), not from liver failure; phase 3 features leukocytosis and alopecia.

raw_record.support_text: A 71-year-old woman ingested a plant she thought was wild garlic (Allium ursinum) but which was actually Colchicum autumnale (autumn crocus). Toxicology analysis confirmed colchicine in gastric lavage, blood (5 µg/l) and urine (30 µg/l). She developed arrhythmias, liver failure, pancreatitis, ileus, and bone marrow suppression with pancytopenia, plus alopecia in the third week; treatment was supportive and five months later she had no clinical or laboratory signs of poisoning.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Accidental oral overdose/poisoning from ingestion of Colchicum autumnale (autumn crocus) mistaken for wild garlic; 71-year-old woman; plant-source colchicine exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Colchicine binds tubulin and blocks mitosis (antimitotic), primarily affecting tissues with rapid cell turnover, producing gastroenterocolitis, bone marrow hypoplasia with pancytopenia, and alopecia; toxicity in tissues without rapid cell turnover caused arrhythmias, acute liver failure and pancreatitis. Blood colchicine 5 µg/l and urine 30 µg/l by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Managed with gastric lavage, oral activated charcoal and saline infusion; supportive care only. Patient recovered without clinical or laboratory signs five months later.

raw_record.extra_details: Colchicine is the antimitotic alkaloid in autumn crocus, also used medically for familial Mediterranean fever and gout. Prognostic rule cited: >100% survival below 0.5 mg/kg ingestion and 100% mortality above 0.8 mg/kg. Serial colchicine levels on days 1-3: serum 5, 3, 5 µg/l; urine 14, 30 µg/l (days 2-3). Peak hepatocellular enzymes on day 3. The patient recovered (normal lab values and electromyography at 5 months).

raw_record.support_text: A 61-year-old hemodialysis patient on colchicine for pericarditis (escalated from 0.5 mg to 1 mg once daily) developed diarrhea, confusion, and hypotension, followed by multiple-organ failure with leucopenia, acute liver failure, and rhabdomyolysis; he died 36 hours after ICU admission. The final diagnosis was colchicine poisoning, confirmed by characteristic mitotic arrests found at post-mortem examination of the esophagus, small bowel, and bone marrow.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic kidney disease/dialysis patient with kidney transplant and chronic allograft nephropathy; colchicine dose escalated from 0.5 mg to 1 mg o.d.; on cyclosporin, prednisolone, and rosuvastatin (possible drug-drug interactions).
raw_record.extra_details: Laboratory worsening: AST rose to 5330 IU/l, ALT to 1361 IU/l, LDH to 7260 IU/l, INR to 3.52 24 h after ICU admission. Colchicine poisoning staging described: initial GI symptoms (day 1), multiple-organ failure with bone-marrow suppression and myopathy (days 2–7), possible recovery. Mechanism: binds tubulin, disrupts microtubules. Diagnosis based on toxidrome; no correlation between plasma level and severity. Post-mortem mitotic arrests in esophagus, small bowel, bone marrow. Patient died 36 h after ICU admission from refractory shock.

raw_record.support_text: The survey reports that etifoxine can be associated with acute hepatitis showing a cytolytic or mixed biological pattern of liver injury, based on 18 previously reported cases plus 11 additional cases. Evidence supporting a causative role includes uniform liver damage (64% cytolytic hepatitis among acute liver injury cases), time to onset after starting etifoxine of ≤2 months in 92% of cases, lack of association with known hepatotoxicants in 68%, exclusion of non-drug causes of hepatitis in most patients, and favorable outcome after etifoxine discontinuation in all patients with available follow-up. The causal relationship was considered plausible in 64% of patients who developed acute liver injury; the mechanism is unknown, and the lack of clear clinical or biological signs of hypersensitivity supports an idiosyncratic rather than immune-allergic mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: Total of 29 acute hepatitis cases (18 previously reported in detail plus 11 additional). Time to onset ≤2 months in 92% of cases; 64% cytolytic pattern on acute liver injury; no known hepatotoxic co-medication in 68% of cases; other common causes (viral hepatitis, biliary tract abnormalities) excluded in most patients; favorable outcome after etifoxine discontinuation in all patients with available follow-up. Causal relationship judged plausible in 64% of acute liver injury patients. Mechanism unknown; classified as idiosyncratic (non-immune-allergic). Setting is ordinary therapeutic use of etifoxine as anxiolytic.

raw_record.support_text: A 31-year-old diabetic man taking oxymetholone 50 mg twice a day for two months for body building presented with fatigue, progressive jaundice, intense pruritus and pale stools. LFTs showed cholestasis with negative viral, autoimmune and tropical serology; the RUCAM score was +8 and the R factor was 0.3. Liver biopsy showed centrilobular hepatocanalicular bilirubinostasis with cholestatic rosettes and mild sinusoidal collagenisation, consistent with DILI. The patient developed subacute liver failure (SALF) with grade 1 hepatic encephalopathy and acute kidney injury but recovered with medical management and therapeutic plasma exchange without transplantation, with complete normalization of LFTs.
raw_record.extra_details: Body-building off-label use; 50 mg twice daily for 2 months; RUCAM score +8; R factor 0.3; peak total bilirubin 35.6 mg/dL (rising to 51 mg/dL); histology: bilirubinostasis, cholestatic rosettes, mild sinusoidal collagenisation, mild lobular lymphocytic inflammation; subacute liver failure with hepatic encephalopathy (serum ammonia 102 µmol/L) and acute kidney injury (creatinine 1.8 mg/dL); treated with 8+ sessions of therapeutic plasma exchange; complete recovery at 12-week follow-up, no transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: A 65-year-old man with myelofibrosis was started on Oxymetholone 100 mg daily. Jaundice and hepatic enlargement appeared within six weeks, with serum bilirubin 62 µmol/l, ALT 263 IU/l and alkaline phosphatase 402 IU/l. After Oxymetholone was withdrawn, liver size and liver function tests returned to normal, establishing hepatotoxicity attributed to Oxymetholone.
raw_record.extra_details: Case in a 65-year-old man with myelofibrosis and prior splenectomy. Dose 100 mg daily; jaundice and hepatic enlargement within six weeks; bilirubin 62 µmol/l (normal<17), ALT 263 IU/l (normal<23), alkaline phosphatase 402 IU/l (normal 30-100); full resolution after drug withdrawal (positive dechallenge). The paper also notes generically that hepatotoxicity is almost always associated with 17-alpha alkylated steroids such as Oxymetholone and that deteriorating liver function warrants dose reduction or withdrawal since continued therapy may result in hepatic coma and death.

Peliosis hepatis was the only significant histologic abnormality.

raw_record.support_text: A letter by Lucena et al. attributed 14 cases of hepatotoxicity up to 1998 to ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, enoxacin and ofloxacin. Quinolone-associated hepatotoxicity has been reported as hepatocellular damage, cholestatic damage, ductopenia, and acute liver failure and death, with biopsy findings of central-zone necrosis and mixed inflammatory infiltrates with abundant eosinophils.
raw_record.extra_details: One of four quinolones (with ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, ofloxacin) to which 14 hepatotoxicity cases up to 1998 were attributed (Lucena letter). raw_record.support_text: Enoxacin is a broad-spectrum quinolone antibiotic. The authors report a case of a patient with acute liver damage (clinically overt hepatitis) caused by enoxacin, noting that clinically overt hepatitis induced by enoxacin had not previously been described.
raw_record.extra_details: 27-year-old woman admitted with jaundice, itching, dark urine and pale stools starting 17 days prior; no history of chronic liver disease, allergy, alcohol abuse, transfusion or surgery. Took enoxacin 400 mg t.i.d. orally after a flu-like syndrome 9 days before admission; itching began after the second dose. The paper also describes two case histories of hepatic dysfunction developing during fusidic acid therapy.

Mechanism: interference with bile salt transport and secretion. A patient required dialysis for acute tubular necrosis attributed to severe hyperbilirubinaemia (up to 739 µmol/L) after fusidic acid therapy. Case 2 (oral fusidic acid 500 mg three times daily) died at home; no post-mortem, and death not directly attributed to the liver injury.

She presented with hepatitis-like features including jaundice, a widespread macular rash, liver function derangement, and significant coagulopathy, with a presumptive diagnosis of acute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: Ten probable cases of acute liver injury occurring 5-24 days after trimethoprim (TMP) treatment were identified among reports to the SADRAC from 1980 to 1989, with recovery within 2 months of stopping treatment. The distribution of biochemical patterns was comparable to that seen with the TMP/SMX combination, suggesting a contributing role for TMP in some reactions previously attributed to sulfamethoxazole. TMP-induced hepatitis was subsequently confirmed in a retrospective study of UK clinical records, finding 10 cases of liver disorders including four with cholestatic hepatitis, with the risk of idiosyncratic liver disease in patients exposed to TMP alone similar to that for TMP/SMX (3.8/100,000 users).
raw_record.extra_details: Ten probable acute liver injury cases occurred 5-24 days after TMP treatment (SADRAC reports, 1980-1989), with recovery within 2 months after discontinuation. A retrospective UK study confirmed TMP-induced hepatitis with 10 liver disorder cases including four with cholestatic hepatitis; risk of idiosyncratic liver disease in TMP-alone users was similar to TMP/SMX users (3.8 per 100,000 users). Distributions of biochemical patterns resembled the TMP/SMX combination, suggesting a contributing TMP role in reactions previously attributed to SMX.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity is described as a common adverse event during idelalisib combination therapy or monotherapy, characterized by ALT and AST elevations rarely accompanied by alkaline phosphatase or bilirubin elevation, suggestive of hepatocellular damage. The transaminase elevations are mostly noticeable in the first 8–12 weeks (median 5.3 weeks) with a plateau within week 20, often normalize after dose cessation or dose reduction, but in some cases an acute liver insufficiency based on an autoinflammatory reaction may be observed. The autoimmune nature was confirmed by lymphocytic infiltrate in liver biopsies, increased CCL-3 and CCL-4, and decreased peripheral blood regulatory T cells.
raw_record.extra_details: Transaminitis onset in first 8–12 weeks (median 5.3 weeks), plateau within week 20 in the relapse/refractory setting; activity normalizes following dose cessation or dose reduction; occasional acute liver insufficiency due to an autoinflammatory reaction. In treatment-naïve patients ALT/AST elevation seen more often; ALT/AST elevation noted in 79% of younger patients with CLL treated with idelalisib and ofatumumab (54% grade ≥3). Younger age and mutated IGHV identified as significant risk factors. Autoimmune nature confirmed by lymphocytic infiltrate on liver biopsy, increased proinflammatory cytokines CCL-3 and CCL-4, decreased peripheral regulatory T cells; transaminitis resolved after drug hold or steroids. HBV/HCV/CMV/HIV status assessment recommended before treatment initiation or in case of unexpected hepatotoxicity. In a separate co-exposure setting, the combination of idelalisib, lenalidomide and rituximab was poorly tolerated and led to premature termination of two clinical trials; Cheah et al. noted grade ≥3 transaminitis in six of seven patients with two deaths, one from acute liver failure.

raw_record.extra_details: Biopsy in 2 subjects with severe transaminitis showed increased perforin-positive (activated) CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell infiltrate and CD20+ periportal lymphocytes, suggesting an immune-mediated cause; steroids and/or mycophenolate mofetil treated the hepatotoxicity; median time from steroid initiation to reduction of transaminitis to grade ≤1 was 8 days (range 3-21). Rechallenge: 6 of 12 subjects developed recurrent transaminitis within 1-4 days of re-exposure; 4 of 5 rechallenged off steroids recurred (grade 2,1; grade 3,2; grade 4,1) vs 2 of 7 rechallenged on steroids. 16 subjects (67%) received steroids for transaminitis. Higher day-28 CCL-3 and CCL-4 were associated with hepatotoxicity; lower Treg percentages were associated with on-drug toxicity.
