raw_record.support_text: This case report describes a patient who developed severe acute hepatitis with progression to liver cirrhosis during treatment with acitretin (the main metabolite of etretinate). Histology 2 months after discontinuation showed severe inflammatory features with porto-portal bridging necrosis and eosinophilic infiltrates, and three follow-up biopsies showed progressive portal fibrosis and septa culminating in macro-nodular cirrhotic transformation over 9 months, while liver parameters normalized. The authors conclude that 'a severe hepatotoxic reaction with progression to liver cirrhosis may occur during treatment with this agent' and that acitretin should be added to the list of potentially hepatotoxic drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report (acitretin is the main metabolite of etretinate). Case presented with tender enlarged liver (4 cm from costal margin), spider naevi, and markedly elevated aminotransferases (ALT 790, AST 635 IU/l), elevation of GGT (81 IU/l) and alkaline phosphatase (166 IU/l), and later slight bilirubin elevation. Dechallenge with drug discontinuation led to clinical improvement and normalization of liver parameters. Serial liver biopsies over 9 months: severe acute hepatitis with porto-portal bridging necrosis and eosinophilic infiltrates and slight intrahepatocellular cholestasis at 2 months, progressing to portal fibrosis/septa and macro-micronodular cirrhotic transformation; no accumulation of fat-storing cells (in contrast to vitamin A intoxication). Negative serologies for hepatitis A/B, CMV, EBV, HSV, toxoplasmosis, brucellosis, syphilis; no autoantibodies. Authors recommend adding acitretin to the list of potentially hepatotoxic drugs.

raw_record.support_text: In a patient case report, after acitretin 25 mg twice daily was started, liver function tests rose 2 days later (ALT 237 U/L, ALP 440 U/L, bilirubin 41 µmol/L) from normal baseline. Acitretin was discontinued and ALT returned to normal within 5 days; ALP peaked at 679 U/L and remained elevated at 191 U/L 6 months later, consistent with acitretin-induced human liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of a patient treated for erythrodermic/pustular psoriasis. Dose 25 mg twice daily, latency 2 days after start; baseline liver functions normal (ALP 93 U/L, ALT 12 U/L, bilirubin 8 µmol/L). Post-exposure ALT 237 U/L, ALP 440 U/L rising to peak 679 U/L, bilirubin 41 µmol/L; ALT normalized over 5 days after dechallenge, ALP still 191 U/L at 6 months. Same patient developed bone marrow features consistent with drug-induced agranulocytosis and total scalp alopecia. Paper notes that hepatic toxicity is a well-recognized retinoid side-effect, with up to 30% of acitretin-treated patients developing raised aminotransferases, 10% ALP elevations (generally mild/transient), and genuine toxic hepatitis rare; hepatotoxicity attributed to retinoids possibly via apoptosis or direct toxic necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: Acitretin causes transient elevation of liver enzymes that is dose dependent and usually reverses to normal after dose reduction or discontinuation of therapy. Severe hepatotoxic reactions from retinoids are rare; in a dataset of 1877 patients receiving oral acitretin, only 0.26% showed overt chemical hepatitis, but severe hepatotoxic reactions are rare.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver enzyme elevation is dose dependent and usually reverses after dose reduction or drug discontinuation; severe hepatotoxic reactions are rare. In a dataset of 1877 patients on oral acitretin, only 0.26% showed overt chemical hepatitis (Katz, Waalen, & Leach, 1999).

His psoriasis worsened and acitretin was reintroduced at a lower dose, with no evidence of liver damage during 15 months of follow-up.

raw_record.support_text: Lorlatinib is primarily metabolized by CYP3A4 and UGT1A4. When lorlatinib was combined with a strong CYP3A4 inducer such as rifampin, severe hepatotoxicity occurred in 10 of 12 patients. Therefore, lorlatinib use is contraindicated with strong CYP3A4 inducers and should be avoided with moderate inducers such as efavirenz, nevirapine, and etravirine; if concomitant use is unavoidable, ALT, AST, and bilirubin should be monitored 48 hours after initiation and at least three times during the first week of therapy.

Overall mortality since the dexamethasone/cyclophosphamide regimen fell to 28%; historical 68% mortality prior to the regimen. Therapy included steroids (dexamethasone), cyclophosphamide, Fuller's earth, charcoal, lavage.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that even when paraquat (PQ) is ingested in a small amount it is extremely toxic and that immediately after ingestion the compound accumulates in different organs, with a spectrum of complications—including gastrointestinal injuries, respiratory failure, renal failure, hepatotoxicity, and lung fibrosis—evolving over time; the suggested mechanism of toxicity is production of reactive oxygen species causing cell damage. These complications are described in the context of a case report of a 15-year-old boy with PQ poisoning who required hemodialysis and ultimately survived.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intentional/suicidal ingestion (pesticide poisoning) in a 15-year-old boy; no antidote available; treatment included hemodialysis and methylprednisolone.
raw_record.extra_details: Lethal herbicide contributing to high mortality among pesticide-related deaths, common in low/middle income countries and agrarian Bangladesh; even small ingestions are toxic; mechanism attributed to reactive oxygen species-driven cell damage; companion complications include acute kidney injury, lung injury/fibrosis, and respiratory failure; this case report patient survived.

raw_record.support_text: A 45-year-old female presented after allegedly ingesting 10 mL of 20% paraquat (PQ) following a familial dispute, experiencing projectile vomiting, dizziness, and generalized body aches. On the second day after ingestion she became icteric and developed shortness of breath and a 'paraquat tongue'; liver function tests showed drastic elevations in bilirubin, AST, and ALT (Day 2: total bilirubin 18.4 mg/dL, AST 724 U/L, ALT 339 U/L), and the authors state the patient had 'now developed acute kidney injury and hepatitis.'
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose: deliberate ingestion of 10 mL of 20% paraquat following a familial dispute.
raw_record.extra_details: 45-year-old female; developed jaundice (scleral icterus), tongue ulcers ('paraquat tongue'), ARDS, and acute kidney injury. LFT values from ingestion: Day 0 total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, AST 55 U/L, ALT 61 U/L; Day 2 total bilirubin 18.4 mg/dL (direct 15.4), AST 724 U/L, ALT 339 U/L; Day 3 total bilirubin 25.8 mg/dL (direct 22.0), AST 531 U/L, ALT 396 U/L. Managed with gastric lavage, activated charcoal, IV methylprednisolone (125 mg then 40 mg thrice daily), antibiotics, antiemetics, and IV fluids in ICU; supplemental oxygen avoided.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of patients with paraquat poisoning, five of the six patients who survived more than 8 days after ingestion of paraquat showed intrahepatic cholestasis without bile duct injury, characterized by bile plugs in bile canaliculi and bile-filled Kupffer cells mainly in the centrolobular zone. Separate patients (Cases 5, 7, 8) showed necrotizing bile duct injury affecting bile ductules, interlobular, septal, and extrahepatic bile ducts, with intraductal and periductal neutrophil infiltration.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paraquat poisoning by ingestion (overdose context); findings based on autopsy/liver tissue examination of the affected patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Three cases (5, 7, 8) showed necrotizing injury of the bile ductules, small/medium interlobular, septal, and (in Case 8) extrahepatic bile ducts, with epithelial swelling, necrosis, inspissated bile, and neutrophil infiltration. Five of six patients who survived more than 8 days showed intrahepatic cholestasis without bile duct injury. In Case 8 electron microscopy showed bile canaliculi with dilatation, wall thickening, and microvilli degeneration, though the authors noted this finding was not reliable due to postmortem autolysis.

raw_record.support_text: A single patient with paraquat poisoning presented with an acute cholestatic hepatitis that was followed by persistent cholestasis lasting up to 4 years, which faded when treatment with ursodeoxycholic acid was given. Mild bile duct cell damage was still present 2 years after the acute paraquat poisoning, and paraquat was absorbed percutaneously through damaged skin after repeated exposure over 2 weeks.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Poisoning by paraquat absorbed percutaneously through damaged skin after repeated exposure over two weeks; not therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report: acute cholestatic hepatitis followed by persistent cholestasis for about 4 years that faded on ursodeoxycholic acid treatment; mild bile duct cell damage (cytoplasmic vacuolization, nuclear size variation) present on biopsy 2 years after poisoning; centrolobular bile plugs with sparse focal hepatocellular necrosis; high serum paraquat concentration in the acute phase; diagnosis of cholestatic hepatitis; patient received ursodeoxycholic acid 15 mg/kg daily.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective study of 36 pregnant patients exposed to paraquat (from the Ramathibodi Poison Center Toxic Exposure Surveillance System), all had oral exposure. Systemic effects mainly comprised acute kidney injury (AKI), found in 13 patients (36.1%), and the paper reports that AKI, hepatotoxicity, and maximum white blood cell count significantly differed between dead and surviving patients, indicating paraquat hepatotoxicity as a clinical feature in these human overdose cases.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnant patients (restricted population); oral ingestion of the herbicide (poisoning/overdose exposure).
raw_record.extra_details: 36 pregnant patients (mean age 22.7 years, mean gestational age 23.1 weeks), all with oral paraquat ingestion over a 5-year period. Hepatotoxicity, AKI, and maximum WBC count significantly differed between dead and surviving patients. Overall pregnant-patient mortality 25% and in-hospital offspring mortality 44.4%, all deaths in patients with systemic toxicity; median hospital stay 6 days; treatment included intravenous dexamethasone and cyclophosphamide. Paraquat = 1,1'-dimethyl-4,4'-bipyridylium dichloride; toxicity attributed to redox cycling generating reactive oxygen species.

raw_record.support_text: Among 20 patients with acute liver failure, drug-induced liver injury was the attributed etiology in 5 (25.0%), including pyrazinamide in 1 patient. The paper therefore attributes ALF/DILI to pyrazinamide in this patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as the DILI etiology in 1 of 20 ALF ICU patients; clinical phenotype is acute liver failure in an ONSD study.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective cohort of TB patients, 38 developed DILI due to anti-TB drugs, with pyrazinamide identified as the causative drug in 16 patients. Patients with pyrazinamide-induced liver injury showed no association with mitochondrial DNA variants.
raw_record.extra_details: In 38 TB patients who developed DILI during anti-TB therapy, pyrazinamide was the attributed causative drug in 16. DILI defined as ALT >=5x ULN, or ALT >=3x ULN with total bilirubin >=2x ULN. No association with mitochondrial DNA variants was found for pyrazinamide-induced liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: Challenge with antituberculosis drugs in 16 patients on a modified regimen showed PZA provoked liver injury in seven patients (and INH in six, combined INH+RMP in one). The authors state both PZA and INH have a well-established dose-related hepatotoxic potential, leading to clinically manifest liver damage in a small percentage of patients treated with presently recommended doses.
raw_record.extra_details: Challenge with PZA provoked liver injury in 7 of 16 patients on a modified antituberculosis regimen; described as a well-established dose-related hepatotoxicant causing clinical liver damage in a small percentage. In 2 patients the responsible drug could not be pinpointed.

raw_record.support_text: This retrospective cohort study states that all first-line anti-tuberculosis drugs isoniazid (INH), rifampicin (RMP) and pyrazinamide (PZA) are hepatotoxic and increase the risk of hepatotoxicity when used together, citing references. Hepatotoxicity was defined as symptomatic elevation of liver transaminases ≥3× ULN (or ≥5× if asymptomatic).
raw_record.extra_details: In 926 adult PTB patients, 111 (12.0%) developed hepatotoxicity after a median 38 days. Hepatotoxicity incidence 3.71/100 person-months for PZA. More days with PZA in the last 8-14 days before hepatotoxicity was an independent risk factor on time-dependent Cox regression. Conclusion: PZA is the most common causative drug. Around 3.5% overall had severe hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Pyrazinamide-induced centrolobular necrosis with slight inflammatory cellular reactions (Fig. 6), in the section on toxic liver injury. In the tuberculostatic-treated group receiving pyrazinamide, 8 of 43 cases (18.6%) had abnormal transaminase activities.
raw_record.extra_details: Pyrazinamide-induced centrolobular necrosis with slight inflammatory cellular reactions on biopsy (Fig. 6). In the tuberculostatic group treated with pyrazinamide, 8 of 43 cases (18.6%) showed abnormal transaminase activities.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity was fatal in patient 74, and pyrazinamide was the drug incriminated. Cases were assessed with the Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences (CIOMS) scale, yielding a diagnosis of definite or highly probable in 96 cases and probable in 53 (149 ratings because of multiple drugs).
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal hepatotoxicity in patient 74 of a 140-patient cohort of drug-induced liver disease; pyrazinamide was the drug incriminated. Cohort cases were graded with the CIOMS causality scale.

raw_record.support_text: In a 59-year-old woman, pyrazinamide (1500 mg/d) reintroduction during antituberculous therapy produced acute hepatitis with hypersensitivity symptoms (fever, pruritus, arthralgia, malaise) within 2 hours, marked transaminase elevation (ALT 3,240 U/l, AST 4,140 U/l) and eosinophilia; symptoms resolved after withdrawal. The authors note that acute hepatitis associated with pyrazinamide has been described as dose-related direct (intrinsic) toxicity, but conclude that in this case the liver injury was secondary to a hypersensitivity mechanism and that hypersensitivity hepatitis should be included among the causes of pyrazinamide-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 59-year-old woman with tuberculosis. Pyrazinamide 1500 mg/day was reintroduced (day 28) after ethambutol and rifampicin had been resumed and tolerated; a positive rechallenge occurred 2 hours after the pyrazinamide dose with acute malaise, fever 40°C, generalized pruritus, arthralgia, perioral paresthesia, vomiting, eosinophilia (859 x 10^6/l eosinophils) and transaminase elevation (ALT 3,240 U/l, AST 4,140 U/l); values fell after withdrawal (ALT 720 U/l, AST 120 U/l, eosinophils 280 x 10^6/l within 6 days). Initial episode had fever and hypereosinophilia. Patient remained healthy with normal laboratory data at 1-year follow-up. Authors note acute hepatitis with pyrazinamide is usually a dose-related predictable direct toxic mechanism, but attribute this case to a hypersensitivity mechanism involving antibodies and cytotoxic T-lymphocytes directed against hepatocyte proteins modified by reactive metabolites.

raw_record.support_text: Within a series of 9 patients with drug-induced hepatitis and bridging necrosis at Shinko Hospital, Kobe, Japan, pyrazinamide was the causative drug in one patient. Causality was identified by cautious rechallenge, and the patient had complete clinical and biochemical recovery within 6 months after withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: One case in a series of 9 patients with drug-induced hepatitis and bridging necrosis. Causality identified by cautious rechallenge. Complete clinical and biochemical recovery within 6 months of withdrawal; repeat biopsy showed minor fibrosis.

raw_record.support_text: As input probabilities for a decision analysis of chemoprophylaxis for isoniazid- and rifampin-resistant tuberculosis, the authors compiled published human data on pyrazinamide hepatotoxicity. In three single-agent pyrazinamide studies (Phillips, Schwartz and Moyer, Yeager; total 73 patients), four patients (4/73=0.055) had therapy discontinued because of evidence of hepatitis; when pyrazinamide was used at 25 mg/kg with isoniazid in a US Public Health Service trial, hepatic toxicity was 0.025 in 16 patients. The combined major-toxicity estimate for pyrazinamide was 8/233=0.0343, and a probability of death due to pyrazinamide toxicity of 0.003 was derived from the Yeager study.
raw_record.extra_details: Drug-induced hepatitis requiring therapy discontinuation reported in 4/73 (0.055) patients across three single-agent pyrazinamide studies using higher-than-current doses; hepatic toxicity 0.025 in 16 patients when administered at 25 mg/kg in combination with isoniazid (US Public Health Service trial); combined major-toxicity estimate 8/233=0.0343; probability of death due to pyrazinamide toxicity 0.003 derived from the Yeager study. The hepatic-toxicity figure in the isoniazid-combination trial may reflect co-attribution with isoniazid, which is not separately implicated here.

raw_record.support_text: In a study undertaken by the United States Public Health Service (1958) with pyrazinamide, hepatic toxicity developed in 21 of 645 patients: there were 6 cases of clinical jaundice, and 4 of these occurred after the twelfth week (from the nineteenth to twenty-third week).
raw_record.extra_details: US Public Health Service (1958) study: hepatic toxicity in 21 of 645 patients; 6 cases of clinical jaundice, 4 occurring between the nineteenth and twenty-third week, i.e., beyond the 12-week observation window of the present series.

raw_record.support_text: In this retrospective single-center study of tuberculosis patients, adverse effects that led to interruption or discontinuation of medication occurred in 16.4% of patients, and pyrazinamide (PZA) was the most common causative drug. Among the serious adverse events, hepatotoxicity was substantially more common than other types of adverse events, and hepatotoxicity was not related to age. PZA was confirmed as a causative drug by de-challenge alone.
raw_record.extra_details: PZA was the most common drug causing serious adverse events (SAEs) requiring interruption or discontinuation of anti-tuberculosis medication; hepatotoxicity was the most common SAE type and was not related to age. PZA was confirmed as the causative drug by de-challenge alone, which the authors note may reflect preferential discontinuation of PZA because it is not a maintenance drug. In prior studies, old age, female sex, treatment regimen, abnormal liver function test at baseline, and previous hepatitis history were reported risk factors for PZA-associated hepatotoxicity. The exact mechanism is not fully understood; an animal study implicated the metabolites pyrazinoic acid and 5-hydroxypyrazinoic acid, whereas studies measuring serum PZA levels found hepatotoxicity not significantly related to drug concentration. In a multivariate analysis, age was a risk factor for SAEs overall (OR 1.013, 95% CI 1.004-1.023, p=0.007) but hepatotoxicity per se was not associated with age.

raw_record.support_text: Pyrazinamide may be the most hepatotoxic antituberculous medication. Its mechanism of hepatotoxicity has been considered dose related, although a case report of rechallenge after an initial reaction to a combination regimen led to an increase in serum aminotransferase levels to 80 times the upper limit of normal with associated eosinophilia, suggesting a hypersensitivity reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Described as potentially the most hepatotoxic antituberculous medication; mechanism considered dose related; one rechallenge case after an initial combination-regimen reaction produced aminotransferases 80 times the upper limit of normal with eosinophilia, suggesting a hypersensitivity reaction.

raw_record.support_text: Among 35 patients with drug-induced hepatitis seen at Shinko Hospital, nine had a severe hepatic lesion with bridging necrosis confirmed in liver biopsy during the acute episode. Drugs were identified by cautious rechallenge in eight and by an in-vitro test in one; pyrazinamide was the causative drug in one patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Causative drug for severe drug-induced hepatitis with bridging necrosis in 1 of 9 affected patients; identified by cautious rechallenge or in-vitro test; complete clinical and biochemical recovery within 6 months of drug withdrawal; repeat biopsies showed normal lobular structure with minor fibrosis; female preponderance (7 of 9) in this severe hypersensitivity-type group.

raw_record.support_text: Among 98 patients with isoniazid-resistant tuberculosis, 31 (32%) experienced adverse events prompting treatment alteration and 9 (9%) experienced elevated liver enzymes/hepatotoxicity. Six of these nine hepatotoxicity events were attributed to pyrazinamide, which abbreviated its use to a maximum of 1 month. Regimen tables (p:32, p:37) record pyrazinamide stopped early for hepatotoxicity in several patients, including one who died.
raw_record.extra_details: Six of nine patients (9%) with elevated liver enzymes/hepatotoxicity were attributed to pyrazinamide, prompting abbreviated use capped at 1 month; pyrazinamide was continued ≥6 months in a subset (n=9) with no hepatotoxicity reported. In the unsuccessful-outcomes table, pyrazinamide was stopped for hepatotoxicity at 0.2-0.9 months in two patients, one of whom died (death not specifically attributable to hepatotoxicity).

raw_record.support_text: Among 430 patients treated for active TB between 1990 and 1999, side effects resulting in modification/discontinuation of therapy or hospitalization were attributed based on resolution after withdrawal and/or recurrence with rechallenge. The incidence of all major adverse effects was 1.48 per 100 person-months (95% CI, 1.31-1.61) for pyrazinamide. The paper concludes that the incidence of pyrazinamide-induced hepatotoxicity and rash during treatment for active TB was substantially higher than with other first-line anti-TB drugs and higher than previously recognized.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of all major adverse effects 1.48 per 100 person-months (95% CI 1.31-1.61) among 430 patients treated 1990-1999 at Montreal Chest Institute; attribution based on resolution after withdrawal and/or recurrence with rechallenge. Pyrazinamide-associated adverse events (hepatotoxicity and rash) associated with age over 60 years (adjusted HR 2.6; 95% CI 1.01-6.6) and birthplace in Asia (adjusted HR 3.4; 95% CI 1.4-8.3).

raw_record.support_text: The most serious toxic effect of pyrazinamide is upon the liver. The U.S. Public Health Service Tuberculosis Therapy Trial (1959) reported, in a series of 780 patients, an incidence of hepatic toxicity of 2-6%, depending upon the dosage employed. A summary by the Committee on Therapy of the American Trudeau Society covering 13 published clinic reports on 1,070 patients showed 33 (3.1%) instances of jaundice and 43 (4%) instances of increased bromsulphthalein excretion without clinical jaundice.
raw_record.extra_details: Antituberculous agent; recommended dosage 30-40 mg/kg body weight (total daily dose not exceeding 3 g). US PHS Tuberculosis Therapy Trial (1959) reported hepatic toxicity incidence of 2-6% in 780 patients depending on dosage. Trudeau Society summary of 13 published clinic reports on 1,070 patients: 33 (3.1%) instances of jaundice and 43 (4%) of increased bromsulphthalein excretion without clinical jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: Among patients on the short and individualized regimens, 46 patients had 124 adverse-event episodes, 14 of which were severe. Four severe adverse events were due to hepatotoxicity. The culprit drugs for hepatotoxicity were pyrazinamide (two patients), high-dose isoniazid (one patient) and bedaquiline (one patient). Culprit drugs were stopped and regimens adapted; no patient had to definitively stop treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as culprit in 2 patients among 4 severe hepatotoxicity episodes in a cohort of 112 RR-TB patients; culprit drug stopped and regimen adapted; no definitive treatment stop; no AE was life-threatening.

raw_record.support_text: Among 35 patients with drug-induced hepatitis at Shinko Hospital, 9 had a severe hepatic lesion with bridging necrosis on liver biopsy. In these patients, pyrazinamide was identified as the causative drug in one case; drugs were identified by cautious rechallenge in eight and by an in-vitro test in one. The patient had complete clinical and biochemical recovery within 6 months after drug withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: Causative in one of 9 patients with severe drug-induced hepatitis; bridging necrosis on liver biopsy; causality identified by cautious rechallenge or in-vitro test; complete recovery within 6 months after withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: Among nine patients with severe drug-induced hepatitis and bridging necrosis, pyrazinamide was the causative drug in one patient, with the drug identified by cautious rechallenge in eight of nine cases and an in-vitro test in one.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as causative in 1 of 9 patients with severe drug-induced hepatitis with bridging necrosis. Complete clinical and biochemical recovery within 6 months after withdrawal; repeat biopsy at 3-34 months showed normal lobular structure with minor fibrosis. Described as a severe hypersensitivity response; female preponderance (7 of 9).

raw_record.support_text: Among nine patients with severe drug-induced hepatitis with bridging necrosis, pyrazinamide was identified as the causative drug in one patient. The patient recovered clinically and biochemically within 6 months of drug withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as causative in 1 of 9 severe cases with bridging necrosis; identified by cautious rechallenge or in-vitro test. Complete clinical and biochemical recovery within 6 months; paper characterizes injury as a severe hypersensitivity response.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 563 patients treated with confirmed hepatotoxic tuberculostatics (isoniazid, protionamide, pyrazinamide, cycloserine, p-aminosalicylic acid), icterus was observed in 29 cases. The damages generally occur dose-independently and with variable latency, in the sense of indirect toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among 'gesichert hepatotoxische Tuberkulostatika' (confirmed hepatotoxic tuberculostatics); icterus occurred in 29 of 563 patients in the study group receiving these agents; damage generally dose-independent with variable latency.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of 9 patients with severe drug-induced hepatitis with bridging necrosis at Shinko Hospital, Kobe, Japan, pyrazinamide was identified as the causative drug in one patient. Drugs were identified by cautious rechallenge in eight patients and by an in-vitro test in one, and all nine patients recovered clinically and biochemically within 6 months after drug withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: Identified as the causative drug in 1 of 9 patients with severe hepatic lesion with bridging necrosis during the acute episode.

raw_record.support_text: DILI-inducing antituberculotics included INH, RFP, PZA (pyrazinamide) and ethambutol (EMB), mostly in combinations, among 72 antituberculotic DILI patients (17.0%).
raw_record.extra_details: Antituberculotic, listed as PZA. Antituberculotics accounted for 72 patients (17.0%). Mostly used as combinations INH+RFP+PZA+EMB, INH+RFP+EMB and INH+EMB.

raw_record.support_text: In a consecutive series of patients with acute liver failure (ALF) and tuberculosis admitted to a liver intensive care unit between 1986 and 2008, 14 of 16 patients had an established diagnosis of anti-TB drug-induced ALF. The paper states that hepatitis was caused by pyrazinamide (PZA) in 10 patients and by isoniazid (INH) treatment in 4. Mean time from initiation of anti-TB treatment to the development of jaundice was 3.5 ± 3.1 months.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis attributed to PZA in 10 of 14 patients with anti-TB drug-induced ALF. Patients were receiving anti-tuberculosis treatment (ATT) for tuberculosis, initial regimens including combinations of RIF, INH, PZA, ETH, and sometimes streptomycin; some patients were immunosuppressed (renal transplant recipients, HIV infection).

raw_record.support_text: In a 6-year series of 35 patients with drug-induced hepatitis at Shinko Hospital, Japan, nine had severe hepatic lesions with bridging necrosis; drugs were identified by cautious rechallenge in eight and by in-vitro test in one. Pyrazinamide was the causative drug in one of these patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as causative drug in 1 of 9 severe drug-induced hepatitis patients with bridging necrosis. Causality identification by cautious rechallenge or in-vitro test. Complete clinical and biochemical recovery within 6 months of withdrawal; repeat biopsies showed normal lobular structure with minor fibrosis.

raw_record.support_text: In the series of 35 patients with drug-induced hepatitis, nine had a severe hepatic lesion with bridging necrosis; pyrazinamide was the causative drug in one patient, identified by cautious rechallenge or an in-vitro test.
raw_record.extra_details: Causative drug in one of nine patients with severe bridging-necrosis hepatitis; causality identified by cautious rechallenge or in-vitro test. Complete clinical and biochemical recovery within 6 months of withdrawal; normal lobular structure with minor fibrosis on follow-up biopsy.

raw_record.support_text: Pyrazinamide is listed among the drugs involved in the viral-hepatitis-type (Group IV) drug-induced hepatic injury (61 cases), a lesion resembling viral hepatitis with spotty, zonal, and massive/submassive necrosis patterns.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among drugs involved in the viral-hepatitis-type (Group IV) hepatic injury (61 cases).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that hepatotoxicity is the most common adverse effect of anti-TB treatment that leads to interruption of therapy, and frames the reintroduction of isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide therapy after hepatic injury as involving the risk of additional morbidity, attributing drug-induced hepatitis to these anti-TB drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: Anti-TB drug whose therapy is reintroduced after drug-induced hepatitis resolves; recurrence of DIH was observed on reintroduction, with approximately 11% recurrence in this study. A prior Turkish trial (Tahaoglu et al) found a 24% DIH risk when reintroduction included pyrazinamide from day 1 versus 0% with gradual sequential introduction excluding pyrazinamide; the present study found comparatively lower recurrence when the original regimen including pyrazinamide was given from day 1.

raw_record.support_text: Among nine patients with severe drug-induced hepatitis with bridging necrosis, pyrazinamide was the causative drug in one patient, identified among 8 cases by cautious rechallenge (and one by in-vitro test). The patient recovered completely clinically and biochemically within 6 months of drug withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: Causative drug in 1 case; drug-induced hepatitis with bridging necrosis on acute-phase liver biopsy; causality by cautious rechallenge; complete recovery within 6 months of withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: The paper records one fatal case of liver toxicity due to pyrazinamide (not in the study series) and refers to the incidence of hepatotoxicity from reported series, concluding that although liver toxicity is a hazard, pyrazinamide may still have a place as short-term therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: One fatal case of liver toxicity recorded (outside the study series). In the study series, 2 patients had abnormal liver function tests necessitating discontinuance of treatment (temporary in 1); treatment was stopped after two months in one patient because of abnormal liver function tests. Reference made to the incidence of hepatotoxicity from reported series. Pyrazinamide considered for short-term therapy to cover surgery or long-term in combination with isoniazid for isoniazid-sensitive bacilli.

raw_record.support_text: A group of eight patients with drug-induced cholestasis caused by drugs other than tiopronin was analyzed (Table 3). Patient 1, F/60, received pyrazinamide for tuberculosis with a maximum bilirubin of 12 mg/dl and jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is described as the most severe side effect of antituberculosis medications including pyrazinamide. In the Lee et al. raw_record.support_text: In the Loch Raven Veterans Administration Hospital, which contributed 618 patients to the present study, no cases of hepatitis unrelated to transfusion, except several attributed to treatment with pyrazinamide, were recognized during the time of the study.

raw_record.support_text: In the authors' prior study of 210 patients treated with the drugs of Regimen I (first-line antituberculosis drugs), pyrazinamide was the principal drug responsible for hepatotoxicity, with 76% of cases attributed to pyrazinamide, 18% to rifampin, and 6% to isoniazid; alcoholism was the risk factor related to this side effect, and hepatotoxicity predominated in the 2nd month of treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Principal drug responsible for hepatotoxicity in a prior cohort of 210 patients treated with Regimen I antituberculosis drugs; 76% of hepatotoxicity cases attributed to pyrazinamide; adverse reaction predominated in the 2nd month of treatment; alcoholism was the related risk factor. A separate study of severe side effects from first-line antituberculosis medications also found pyrazinamide toxicity greater than rifampin and isoniazid, with major side effects (hepatotoxicity and exanthema) three times greater: 1.48/100 patients/month for pyrazinamide vs 0.43 for rifampin and 0.49 for isoniazid.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that the major disadvantage of isoniazide-PZA therapy is the hepatic toxicity of PZA (pyrazinamide), which manifests in most cases only through abnormal laboratory tests. Across 114 patients treated for 1-25 months, evidence of hepatic toxicity was found in 15% of cases only through an abnormal liver function test, clinical liver involvement occurred in 4% of cases, and one death from jaundice occurred whose relationship with PZA was considered doubtful. Hepatic toxicity appeared sporadically during the first ten months of treatment, and no toxicity was seen in 12 cases treated with PZA for 10-25 months.
raw_record.extra_details: Among 114 tuberculosis patients treated with isoniazide-PZA combination for 1-25 months: hepatotoxicity evidence in 15% of cases via abnormal liver function test only; clinical liver involvement in 4% of cases; one death by jaundice whose relationship to PZA was doubtful (not counted at highest severity); toxicity arose sporadically during the first ten treatment months; no toxicity in 12 cases treated 10-25 months. Hepatic toxicity attributed specifically to the PZA component, not the combination.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective observational cohort of 52 adult patients with pulmonary drug-susceptible TB on PZA-containing first-line regimens, 6 (11.5%) had to discontinue PZA due to hepatotoxicity (outcome defined as an increase in liver enzymes leading to discontinuation of PZA). By CTCAE grade, 2 (33.3%) had grade 2, 3 (50.0%) had grade 3, and 1 (16.6%) had a grade 4 hepatotoxic adverse event. Hepatotoxicity occurred at a median of 22 days (IQR 11-43 days) after starting TB treatment, and female patients had a significantly higher risk of PZA-associated hepatotoxicity (OR 10.4, 95% CI 1.2-135.8).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adult patients with pulmonary drug-susceptible TB treated with PZA-containing first-line regimens; in one of the six cases isoniazid was also not reintroduced after treatment interruption.
raw_record.extra_details: The paper states PZA is associated with the highest risk of hepatotoxicity among first-line TB drugs, with reported incidence ranging from 5-58%. Cohort results: 6/52 (11.5%) discontinued PZA due to hepatotoxicity; CTCAE (v5.0) grades 2 (n=2), 3 (n=3), and 4 (n=1); median latency 22 days (IQR 11-43); female sex risk OR 10.4 (95% CI 1.2-135.8). Mechanism proposed to involve PZA metabolic intermediates. Main study aim was to identify differentially expressed genes predictive of PZA-hepatotoxicity. General context notes hepatotoxicity can present as asymptomatic elevation of liver enzymes, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase and GGT and can escalate to life-threatening acute liver failure.

raw_record.extra_details: 35-year-old male with first episode of pulmonary tuberculosis; RHEZ fixed combination 150/75/400/275 mg, 3 tablets/day (dose adjusted to 41 kg). Symptoms (rash, jaundice, facial edema, fever 40°C, diarrhea) appeared ~20 days after treatment start. Liver tests rose after treatment resumed: AST 94->406->2011 UI/L, ALT 69->501->1437 UI/L (ALAT >10x ULN), conjugated bilirubin 3.28 mg/dl, total bilirubin 5.46 mg/dl, prothrombin 33%, albumin 14.2 g/L, alkaline phosphatase 488 UI/L; eosinophilia 4790/µL. RegiSCAR and DiHS diagnostic criteria met. Antitubercular treatment stopped; systemic corticosteroids 1 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks led to hepatic normalization, but patient died at home 2 weeks after discharge from severe hepatic failure.

Cited in the Discussion as an example of animal models' lack of human relevance; the human Liver-Chip accurately modeled the hepatotoxicity. The paper separately notes that since January 2022 at least eleven clinical trials have reported drug-induced liver injury and some deaths (no specific agent named for that claim).

raw_record.support_text: Serious hepatotoxicity developed in 7 of 15 patients given the nucleoside analogue fialuridine for 8 to 12 weeks; five of these patients died. Cell-culture studies showed fialuridine is incorporated into nuclear and mitochondrial DNA, causing marked mitochondrial dysfunction, and it contains a free 3'-hydroxyl group. These findings are presented as contrast to lamivudine, for which no serious hepatotoxicity and no mitochondrial effects were observed.
raw_record.extra_details: Serious hepatotoxicity developed in 7 of 15 patients given fialuridine for 8-12 weeks as an investigational nucleoside analogue; 5 of these 15 patients died. Supporting cell-culture findings: fialuridine is incorporated into nuclear and mitochondrial DNA causing marked mitochondrial dysfunction, attributed to its free 3'-hydroxyl group permitting inter-nucleotide incorporation. Presented in contrast to lamivudine (which lacks a 3'-hydroxyl group and is not incorporated into DNA).

raw_record.support_text: The letter discusses fatal hepatotoxicity in patients treated with fialuridine (FIAU), noting that among patients enrolled in the National Institutes of Health's three treatment protocols, five died and two were rescued by emergency liver transplantation, and that fulminant hepatic failure developed in all, several weeks to 4 months after termination of FIAU administration. Clinical, pathological, and experimental findings strongly suggested the cause of the hepatic failure was mitochondrial toxicity resulting from incorporation of the thymidine analogue into mitochondrial DNA.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal hepatotoxicity (fulminant hepatic failure) reported in patients treated with fialuridine (FIAU), a thymidine analogue, in the NIH's three treatment protocols. Five patients died and two were rescued by emergency liver transplantation. Onset delayed and abrupt, occurring several weeks to 4 months after termination of FIAU administration. Etiology attributed to mitochondrial toxicity from incorporation of the analogue into mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), with delayed onset postulated to reflect progressive replicative segregation toward homoplasmy and a critical mtDNA concentration threshold. FIAU undergoes enterohepatic recirculation, with highest concentrations in hepatic DNA, and small amounts are excreted in feces for many weeks after withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: On June 25, 1993, a 44-year-old man in trial 3 of flaluridine (FIAU) presented with multiple organ failure and lactic acidosis; the NIH stopped the trial. A 1991 theory by Dr Yung-Chi Chang proposed that FIAU damaged mitochondrial DNA, giving rise to delayed toxicity. By July 16, 3 patients had died (2 after liver transplants, the third while waiting), and by August 1993, 2 more patients had died from liver failure and 2 others were gravely ill, requiring liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Investigational nucleoside analog (FIAU) given in NIH trial 3 for chronic hepatitis B therapy; injury included lactic acidosis, multiple organ failure and acute liver failure with delayed onset. 3 patients died by July 16, 1993 (2 after liver transplants, one while awaiting), and 2 additional patients died of liver failure by August 1993, with 2 others requiring liver transplantation. Proposed mechanism: FIAU damage to mitochondrial DNA causing delayed toxicity; attempts made to counteract mitochondrial loss with thymidine and uridine. FDA later sent warning letters over protocol violations during these trials.

raw_record.support_text: The paper notes that about 50% of drugs that caused significant DILI in humans produced minimal or no toxicity in animal studies, and cites fialuridine (FIAU) as a striking example of an unexpectedly fatal DILI: fatalities occurred in 7 of 15 human subjects in a Phase II clinical trial caused by fialuridine, a toxicity that was not predicted by toxicology studies using multiple animal species.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II clinical trial setting; fatal DILI occurred in 7 of 15 human subjects; the hepatotoxicity was not predicted by toxicology studies using multiple animal species. Cited as an example of human DILI that animal testing failed to predict.

raw_record.support_text: In the paper's context, fialuridine toxicity was mentioned as an example: although fialuridine hepatotoxicity was not detected in any preclinical study (including 2D primary hepatocyte cultures and rat, mouse, dog, and cynomolgus monkey in vivo studies), in clinical trials severe hepatotoxicity was observed after multiple weeks, and 7 of 15 patients developed progressive lactic acidosis and worsening jaundice, 5 of whom died.
raw_record.extra_details: In clinical trials severe hepatotoxicity was observed after multiple weeks of dosing; 7 of 15 patients developed progressive lactic acidosis and worsening jaundice, 5 of whom died. Notably, the hepatotoxicity was not detected in any preclinical study, including primary hepatocyte 2D cultures and rat, mouse, dog, and cynomolgus monkey in vivo studies.

raw_record.support_text: In two patients with fialuridine toxicity from the Hepatix ELAD pilot trials (23 patients total), fialuridine is described as an agent that causes mitochondrial damage, and affected patients present with acute liver failure and lactic acidosis. ELAD therapy provided the liver function needed to control lactate levels, although cartridge function was overwhelmed toward the end of treatment. The same two patients (nos. 8 and 10) had received liver transplantations.
raw_record.extra_details: Fialuridine causes mitochondrial damage; patients present with acute liver failure and lactic acidosis. Two affected patients (nos. 8 and 10) were treated with the Hepatix ELAD (single cartridges, 200 g of metabolic function each); serum lactic acid decreased at onset of ELAD therapy but rose when cartridge capacity was overwhelmed. Both received liver transplantations.

raw_record.support_text: The PHH 3D spheroid platform is presented as a predictive model for human drug response, exemplified by fialuridine (FIAU), which caused the deaths of 5 of 15 participants in a clinical trial by inducing acute liver failure. Toxicity was not detected in any preclinical model (rat, mouse, dog, cynomolgus monkey), yet the PHH spheroid system indicated that FIAU toxicity was already present at therapeutic exposure levels (spheroid EC50 = 100 nM; FIAU serum Cmax = 639 nM).
raw_record.extra_details: FIAU caused acute liver failure leading to death in 5 of 15 clinical trial participants; the therapeutic-use setting was highlighted because spheroid-predicted toxicity occurred at therapeutic exposure levels (spheroid EC50 = 100 nM; FIAU serum Cmax = 639 nM). FIAU hepatotoxicity was not detected in rat, mouse, dog, or cynomolgus monkey preclinical models. Agent referenced with alias FIAU.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that fialuridine caused acute liver failure during clinical trials: 7 of 15 patients treated with fialuridine developed acute liver injury, of which 5 died, an outcome not observed in preclinical toxicology studies. Damaged liver tissue showed steatosis, cholestasis, cytoplasmic fat droplets and swollen mitochondria with reduced cristae, and mitochondrial toxicity and intracytoplasmic lipid droplets were also reported as mechanisms related to fialuridine hepatotoxicity. The authors conclude that fialuridine-induced hepatotoxicity has several underlying mechanisms.
raw_record.extra_details: 7 of 15 patients treated with fialuridine developed acute liver injury, of which 5 died, during clinical trials; injury not observed in preclinical toxicology studies. Histological marks in damaged liver tissue: steatosis, cholestasis, cytoplasmic fat droplets, swollen mitochondria with reduced cristae. Mitochondrial toxicity and intracytoplasmic lipid droplets reported as mechanisms; the paper states fialuridine-induced hepatotoxicity has several underlying mechanisms. In the in vitro DIC assay fialuridine gave borderline DICI 0.80 ± 0.08 with high safety margins for both DIC and general cytotoxicity, and it was found to cause ATP depletion.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine, an antiviral agent, resulted in 5 deaths and 2 cases of liver transplantation in 15 volunteers, and only exhibited severe hepatotoxicity a few weeks after initiating therapy. This is cited as an example of delayed-onset DILI that takes weeks to appear, contrasting with short-term acute in vitro experiments.
raw_record.extra_details: Antiviral agent; administered to 15 volunteers (therapy setting); resulted in 5 deaths and 2 liver transplantations; severe hepatotoxicity appeared only a few weeks after initiating therapy, illustrating delayed-onset DILI; example used to argue for long-term human cell-based liver models. Cited from Vorrink et al. 2018.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes fialuridine-induced hepatotoxicity and discusses its mechanisms, including inhibition of mitochondrial DNA replication by fialuridine and its metabolites, and pyruvate oxidation inhibition. Five of the seven patients with severe hepatotoxicity also reported paresthesias, dysesthesias, and muscle pain or weakness.
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanisms: fialuridine and its metabolites inhibit mitochondrial DNA replication, leading to decreased mitochondrial DNA and mitochondrial ultrastructural defects; another suggested mechanism is pyruvate oxidation inhibition. Of the seven patients with severe hepatotoxicity, five also had mild-to-moderate peripheral nerve injury (paresthesias and dysesthesias in feet/toes) and two reported muscle pain or weakness.

raw_record.support_text: In clinical trials, 7 of 15 patients developed severe hepatotoxicity several weeks after beginning fialuridine treatment, and five of them died. No indication of fialuridine hepatotoxicity was observed in any pre-clinical testing, and the in vitro PHH spheroid model described here predicted fialuridine toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: In the referenced clinical trials, 7 of 15 patients developed severe hepatotoxicity several weeks after beginning fialuridine treatment, and five of the 15 patients died. No hepatotoxicity was observed in pre-clinical testing; toxicity was later reproduced in chimeric TK-NOG mice carrying human hepatocytes and in long-term PHH spheroid cultures (cytotoxicity only after long-term dosing, EC50 > 100 uM at 48 h vs. 0.1 uM at 28 days).

raw_record.support_text: A six-month fialuridine course began in March 1993 and was terminated on an emergency basis 13 weeks later when hepatic failure and lactic acidosis occurred in one of 15 patients; three patients had already discontinued therapy between weeks 10 and 12. Seven of the 15 patients showed varying degrees of hepatic failure and lactic acidosis, with symptoms including fatigue, nausea, constipation, abdominal pain, worsening jaundice, decreasing hepatic synthetic function, worsening prothrombin times, and rising serum ammonia and lactate.
raw_record.extra_details: 7 of 15 trial patients developed hepatic failure with lactic acidosis. Two patients with rapidly progressive hepatic failure died 22 and 36 hours after emergency liver transplantation; two others died of hemodynamic collapse due to pancreatitis and lactic acidosis before transplantation; one died of pancreatitis complications after transplantation; the remaining two underwent successful liver transplantation and survived with only little residual toxicity over 24 months follow-up. The seven patients with severe hepatotoxicity had biochemical evidence of pancreatitis, and all five who died showed pancreatitis at autopsy. Earlier-reported side effects included crampy abdominal pain, foot paresthesia, fatigue, nausea, numbness/tingling of feet or hands, lower abdominal pain, constipation, and mild thrombocytopenia.

raw_record.support_text: Patients 8 to 10 were treated for FIAU (fialuridine) toxicity, described by the authors as a previously undescribed cause of fulminant hepatic failure (FHF). FIAU is a nucleoside analogue that becomes incorporated into mitochondrial DNA, affecting many organs, and the liver is unable to clear the lactic acid generated throughout the body; serial lactate levels were measured in Patients 8 and 10.
raw_record.extra_details: FIAU is a nucleoside analogue incorporated into mitochondrial DNA and described as a mitochondrial toxin; toxicity was dominated by multisystem disease and lactic acidosis with the liver unable to clear lactic acid. All 3 affected patients (Patients 8-10) were treated for fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) and were eventually transplanted, as their mitochondria did not recover once FIAU was withdrawn. The FIAU patients had higher baseline hepatic galactose elimination capacity (GEC) than expected in advanced FHF.

raw_record.support_text: Seven of 15 clinical trial participants treated with the nucleoside analogue fialuridine (FIAU) developed acute liver failure. Five treated participants died, and two required a liver transplant. Preclinical toxicology studies in mice, rats, dogs, and primates had not indicated that FIAU would be hepatotoxic in humans, and the authors investigated whether the toxicity could be detected in chimeric TK-NOG mice with humanized livers.
raw_record.extra_details: 7 of 15 clinical trial participants developed acute liver failure; 5 died and 2 required liver transplant (1993). Clinical features included liver failure and lactic acidosis. Preclinical toxicology in mice, rats, dogs, and primates did not indicate hepatotoxicity. In chimeric TK-NOG mice with humanized livers, oral FIAU 400 mg/kg/d for 4 d produced clinical and serologic liver failure with lactic acidosis, steatosis confined to human (not mouse) hepatocytes, and lipid and mitochondrial abnormalities on electron microscopy; dose-dependent toxicity was seen at 100, 25, and 2.5 mg/kg/d for 14 d, with toxicity detected even at a dose only 10-fold above the human dose.

raw_record.support_text: The paper cites fialuridine as an example that animal studies fail to predict human DILI: in a phase II clinical trial, acute liver toxicity induced by fialuridine led to the deaths of five subjects, in contrast to its safe use in animal studies. This is presented as evidence that determining DILI potential is challenging because animal models do not efficiently predict human DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II clinical trial; acute liver toxicity led to the deaths of five subjects. Cited by the authors as an example of hepatotoxicity induced by a drug that was safe in animal studies, illustrating poor animal-to-human concordance in DILI prediction.

raw_record.support_text: The nucleoside analogue fialuridine (FIAU) reached Phase II trials before its toxic side effects were discovered. The study was terminated as an emergency at week 13 when seven of 15 patients were discovered to have developed severe hepatotoxicity and progressive lactic acidosis that progressed despite the drug being stopped. Three other patients showed mild hepatotoxicity; of the seven worst affected, only two survived following orthotopic liver transplantation, three died despite receiving a transplant, and two succumbed before transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Experimental anti-HBV nucleoside analogue evaluated in a Phase II clinical trial; study terminated at week 13 when 7/15 patients developed severe hepatotoxicity with progressive lactic acidosis that worsened after drug discontinuation; other adverse events included pancreatitis, myopathy and neuropathy; 3 additional patients showed mild hepatotoxicity; 5 of 15 were symptom-free (short exposure); of the 7 severe cases, 2 survived after orthotopic liver transplantation, 3 died after transplant, and 2 died before transplantation; outcome progressed despite stopping the drug.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine, a nucleoside analogue used for the treatment of hepatitis B virus infection, caused acute liver failure in several clinical trial participants. Preclinical toxicology studies in conventional mice, rats, dogs, and non-human primates provided no indication of hepatotoxicity, whereas chimeric TK-NOG mice with humanized livers were able to mirror the hepatotoxicity seen in humans.
raw_record.extra_details: Nucleoside analogue used for treatment of hepatitis B virus infection; caused acute liver failure in several clinical trial participants. Preclinical toxicology in conventional mice, rats, dogs, and non-human primates showed no hepatotoxicity, but chimeric TK-NOG mice with humanized livers mirrored the human hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In a 1993 Phase II clinical trial of fialuridine (FIAU), a nucleoside analogue for treatment of hepatitis B, 7 of 15 subjects unexpectedly developed hepatic failure with lactic acidosis and pancreatic failure and subsequently died by week 13. Liver histology revealed steatosis and cholestasis, and electron microscopy showed hepatocytes with cytoplasmic fat droplets and swollen mitochondria with a reduced number of cristae.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II trial conducted in 1993 in 15 subjects with HBV infection; trial terminated by week 13. 7 subjects developed hepatic failure with lactic acidosis and pancreatic failure and died. Histology: steatosis and cholestasis; electron microscopy: cytoplasmic fat droplets and swollen mitochondria with reduced cristae. Preclinical toxicology in mice, rats, dogs, and monkeys provided no indication of such toxicity; rats tolerated 510 mg/kg-day (2,000-fold the maximum human dose) for 10 weeks. The paper concludes FIAU has a direct toxic effect on human hepatocytes that does not require a comorbidity (e.g., viral infection) and is not immune mediated.

raw_record.support_text: The paper cites Fialuridine as an example of a drug that failed in human trials despite working in animal models: this experimental hepatitis B drug led to the death of five patients in a clinical trial due to liver toxicity, a severe adverse effect that had not been seen in prior animal studies.
raw_record.extra_details: Experimental hepatitis B (antiviral) drug; the drug led to the death of five patients in a clinical trial due to liver toxicity. This severe hepatic adverse effect was not observed in prior animal studies, cited as an example of divergence between murine-model predictions and human outcomes.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine, an experimental drug for hepatitis B, is cited as a highlight of the need for in vivo and bridging in vitro test systems to predict secondary pharmacological adverse effects in humans. In June 1993, during phase II trials, 5 out of 15 patients died while two others required emergency liver transplantation for liver and kidney failure; this effect had not been observed in four animal species, and in vitro studies in cultured hepatoblasts suggested the toxicity may be due to inhibition of mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma by fialuridine and its metabolites.
raw_record.extra_details: Experimental nucleoside-analog drug for hepatitis B. During phase II trials (June 1993), 5 of 15 patients died and 2 required emergency liver transplantation for liver and kidney failure. The effect was not observed in four animal species. Based on in vitro studies in cultured hepatoblasts, the toxicity may be due to inhibition of mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma by fialuridine and its metabolites. Presented as a secondary pharmacological (type A) adverse reaction.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine, developed as a treatment for chronic hepatitis B virus infection, passed various pre-clinical safety assessments but its clinical trial failed due to the identification of human-specific chronic hepatotoxicity. The hepatotoxicity was not predicted at the preclinical stage because conventional in vitro models such as PHHs were designed primarily to assess acute drug toxicity. This chronic human-specific hepatotoxicity is cited as rationale for developing long-term in vitro models; fialuridine toxicity is attributed to mitochondrial dysfunction, and the time-dependent toxicity at high concentration observed in the authors' organoid model appears shallow compared to previously published data.
raw_record.extra_details: Developed as a treatment for chronic hepatitis B virus infection; passed pre-clinical safety assessments but clinical trial failed due to human-specific chronic hepatotoxicity that was not predicted by conventional preclinical models. Toxicity attributed to mitochondrial dysfunction. Indication: chronic hepatitis B. No specific histologic or biochemical pattern stated in this text.

raw_record.support_text: In the phase II fialuridine trial, 15 patients with chronic hepatitis B received oral fialuridine 0.10 or 0.25 mg/kg/day in 2 or 3 divided doses. After 13 weeks one patient developed sudden-onset hepatic failure, shock and lactic acidosis, and the study was terminated; during follow-up 7 patients exhibited varying degrees of hepatic failure, jaundice, lactic acidosis and biochemical signs of pancreatitis. Five patients died and the other 2 survived after emergency liver transplantation, with severe toxicity attributed to the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral pyrimidine nucleoside analogue [1-(2'-deoxy-2'-fluoro-1-β-D-arabinofuranosyl-5-iodo)-uracil] for chronic hepatitis B; dosed 0.10 or 0.25 mg/kg/day in 2 or 3 divided doses; toxicity developed after 9-13 weeks of treatment (p0). 7 of 15 patients affected; 5 died and 2 survivors required emergency liver transplantation; signs of hepatic failure, jaundice, lactic acidosis and pancreatitis. Histology of liver explants showed microvesicular and macrovesicular steatosis and cholestasis, and electron microscopy showed swollen, misshapen mitochondria with fewer cristae and fat droplets, suggesting multisystem mitochondrial injury; steatosis appeared to be an early sign. Patients receiving <4 weeks (cumulative dose 200 mg) showed no overt toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine (FIAU), a uracil nucleoside analogue, was evaluated in a clinical trial (NCT01337466) with fifteen HBV patients. The paper states that FIAU caused hepatic toxicity owing to mitochondrial damage, resulting in the death of five patients, which led to discontinuation of the trial.
raw_record.extra_details: Uracil nucleoside analogue originally developed as an anti-herpes drug; FIAU monophosphate is converted intracellularly to FIAU triphosphate, which enters viral DNA causing HBV DNA chain termination, and showed antiviral properties in the woodchuck model. In the clinical trial with 15 HBV patients, hepatic toxicity was attributed to mitochondrial damage and resulted in the death of five patients, leading to discontinuation of further trials.

raw_record.support_text: The fluorinated nucleoside analogue fialuridine (FIAU) yielded serious toxicity and was linked to several deaths in an aborted clinical trial for chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV). Toxic manifestations of FIAU treatment included profound lactic acidosis, hepatic failure, fat accumulation in the liver, coma, skeletal and cardiac myopathy, pancreatitis and peripheral neuropathy.
raw_record.extra_details: Aborted clinical trial for chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV). FIAU is a fluorinated nucleoside analogue (1-(2'-deoxy-2'-fluoro-β-D-arabinofuranosyl)-5-iodouridine). Other toxic manifestations reported included profound lactic acidosis, coma, skeletal and cardiac myopathy, pancreatitis and peripheral neuropathy. No dose, latency, or case counts specified in the provided text.

raw_record.support_text: The paper notes that human micropatterned co-cultures (MPCCs), but not conventional primary human hepatocyte monolayers, detected the toxicity of fialuridine, a nucleoside analog drug used for hepatitis B viral infection. The text states that fialuridine caused liver failure and the deaths of 5 patients in clinical trials, and that these deaths resulted from lactic acidosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Nucleoside analog drug for hepatitis B viral infection; attributed injury manifested as liver failure with lactic acidosis, resulting in the deaths of 5 patients in clinical trials. In the in vitro component, human MPCCs, but not conventional PHH monolayers, detected fialuridine toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine (FIAU), a nucleoside analogue developed for treatment of hepatitis B, was removed from the market after several reported cases of fatal microvesicular steatosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Nucleoside analogue (FIAU) developed for hepatitis B; removed from the market after several reported cases of fatal microvesicular steatosis (McKenzie et al., 1995).

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine (FIAU), a nucleoside analog for therapy of hepatitis B infections, did not show toxicity in preclinical test systems, yet in clinical trials 7 of 15 participants developed severe hepatic dysfunctions, five of whom died.
raw_record.extra_details: Indicated for hepatitis B. 7 of 15 trial participants developed severe hepatic dysfunctions; 5 died. No toxicity seen in preclinical test systems.

raw_record.support_text: In 1993, 15 participants in a phase II trial received the nucleoside analogue fialuridine to treat hepatitis B virus infection. Seven participants developed liver failure and lactic acidosis; analysis of liver tissue revealed steatosis (fatty degeneration), intracellular fat droplets, and swollen mitochondria. Five participants subsequently died, and two required liver transplantation. The paper states that human-specific mitochondrial toxicity underlies fialuridine's human hepatotoxicity, which was not predicted by preclinical animal testing.
raw_record.extra_details: Two hepatotoxins: 7 of 15 phase II participants (treated for hepatitis B virus infection) developed liver failure and lactic acidosis; histology showed steatosis with intracellular fat droplets and swollen mitochondria; 5 died and 2 required liver transplantation. Toxicity attributed to human-specific mitochondrial toxicity of the nucleoside analogue. Preclinical testing in mice, rats, dogs, and primates gave no indication of hepatotoxicity, and a 1,600-fold dose over 4 days produced liver failure and lactic acidosis only in chimeric TK-NOG mice with humanized livers (toxicity in human-hepatocyte regions).

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine (FIAU), an antiviral nucleoside analogue tested against chronic hepatitis B virus infection, halted HBV in Hep G2 cells and in animals. However, in 1993, patients with chronic HBV infection treated with FIAU for 9.5 to 13 weeks developed signs of severe and, in some cases, fatal hepatotoxicity associated with lactic acidosis and multiple organ failures. Histopathology showed clear microvesicular steatosis in the liver and pancreas, now known to be due to mitochondrial DNA damage disturbing the electron transport chain; this outcome was not seen in preclinical studies in mice, rats, woodchucks, dogs, or cynomolgus monkeys.
raw_record.extra_details: Antiviral nucleoside analogue (1-[2-deoxy-2-fluoro-beta-D-arabinofuranosyl]-5-iodouracil) tested for chronic HBV infection; injury attributed to mitochondrial DNA damage disturbing the mitochondrial electron transport chain. Microvesicular steatosis in liver and pancreas; lactic acidosis and multiple organ failure; fatal in some cases. Treatment duration 9.5-13 weeks. Outcome was not seen during preclinical animal studies in mice, rats, woodchucks, dogs, and cynomolgus monkeys.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a 1993 phase II clinical trial (Eli Lilly Trial H3X-MC-PPPC, NIH protocol #93-DK-0031) evaluating fialuridine as an anti-HBV antiviral drug. Although the preliminary results reduced HBV DNA in patients, the study was terminated on an emergency basis by week 13 because of serious hepatotoxicity in seven patients, of whom five died and two required emergency liver transplantation. The paper attributes the human-specific toxicity to mitochondrial toxicity through a nucleoside transporter expressed in human mitochondria, and notes fialuridine toxicity was recapitulated in human liver organoids but not in HepG2 cells.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II trial (Eli Lilly Trial H3X-MC-PPPC, NIH protocol #93-DK-0031) terminated emergently at week 13; serious hepatotoxicity in 7 patients, 5 deaths and 2 emergency liver transplants. Mechanism attributed to human-specific mitochondrial toxicity via a nucleoside transporter expressed in human mitochondria. Fialuridine passed preclinical toxicity studies; its toxicity was significant and quantifiable in primary human liver organoids but not observed in HepG2 hepatoma cells.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine was developed as antiviral therapy for hepatitis B infection. In a phase II study, fialuridine caused severe toxicity: irreversible acute hepatic failure in 7 out of 15 patients, myopathy, myoglobinuria, severe lactic acidosis, and neuropathy after 9–13 weeks of treatment. Five out of 7 participants with severe hepatotoxicity died and two survived after liver transplantation. Preclinical toxicology studies in mice, rats, dogs, and primates gave no indication that FIAU would be hepatotoxic in humans.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II study in hepatitis B patients; irreversible acute hepatic failure in 7/15 patients, with myopathy, myoglobinuria, severe lactic acidosis, and neuropathy after 9–13 weeks of treatment; 5 of 7 patients with severe hepatotoxicity died, 2 survived after liver transplantation. Histology showed prominent microvesicular fat with chronic active hepatitis and variable macrovesicular steatosis, little hepatocellular necrosis, without substantial serum aminotransferase elevations; electron microscopy showed markedly swollen mitochondria with loss of cristae, matrix dissolution, and vesicular inclusions. Mechanism (mechanism 1, mitochondrial impairment): inhibition of mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma by the triphosphate metabolite leading to mtDNA depletion. Preclinical toxicology in mice, rats, dogs, and primates showed no hepatotoxicity signal.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine (1-(2-deoxy-2-fluoro-1-d-arabinofuranosyl)-5-iodouracil or FIAU), a nucleoside analogue developed as a potential therapy for viral hepatitis B, caused lactic acidosis and acute liver failure in a phase I human clinical study. Despite no hepatotoxic indications in preclinical animal studies (rat, mouse, dog, cynomolgus monkey), 7 of the 15 enrolled volunteers developed lactic acidosis and acute liver failure a few weeks into the trial at doses 100 times lower than the preclinical animal doses; 5 patients died and 2 survived only after receiving liver transplants. A later US National Academy of Sciences retrospective analysis of all preclinical studies confirmed none indicated the drug would cause human liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Nucleoside analogue (FIAU) developed for viral hepatitis B. Phase I clinical study with 15 volunteers; 7 developed lactic acidosis and acute liver failure within a few weeks, at doses 100-fold lower than the preclinical animal doses. Five of the 7 died and 2 survived only after liver transplantation. Preclinical studies in rat, mouse, dog, and cynomolgus monkey showed no hepatotoxicity; a later retrospective US National Academy of Sciences analysis of all preclinical toxicity studies found no indication the drug would cause human liver failure, though a humanised-liver mouse model could recapitulate the toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The paper cites fialuridine as an anti-hepatitis B drug developed in the 1990s, tested in five animal models yet failing during 9-week human clinical trials due to unexpected induction of liver failure, with the trial terminated following the deaths of five volunteers, and elsewhere describes fialuridine as a discontinued anti-hepatitis B drug known for causing severe liver toxicity in humans.
raw_record.extra_details: Anti-hepatitis B drug discontinued; developed in the 1990s and extensively tested in mice, rats, dogs, monkeys, and woodchucks; failed during a 9-week clinical trial with unexpected induction of liver failure; trial terminated following deaths of five volunteers.

raw_record.support_text: Five patients died in a small 1993 clinical trial of an experimental hepatitis B drug, fialuridine (FIAU), and the resulting committees blamed the drug's toxicity rather than the researchers, because earlier animal studies had failed to show the drug was toxic. The paper states this represents 'the first definitive example of a human-specific, drug-induced toxicity,' and a humanized-liver mouse model was built to detect this liver toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Experimental hepatitis B drug; five patient deaths occurred during a small 1993 clinical trial; the article presents this as the first definitive example of a human-specific, drug-induced toxicity and describes a humanized-liver (chimeric) mouse developed to detect the drug's liver toxicity, which prior animal studies had failed to reveal.

raw_record.support_text: A 1993 trial of the antiviral nucleoside analogue fialuridine (FIAU) for chronic hepatitis B was halted after 13 weeks when several patients developed severe hepatotoxicity, lactic acidosis and pancreatitis. Of the seven patients with severe hepatotoxicity, five died and two required transplantation. The toxic reaction was believed to be caused by marked accumulation of hepatic microvesicular and macrovesicular fat as well as widespread mitochondrial damage.
raw_record.extra_details: 1993 trial in chronic hepatitis B treatment halted after 13 weeks; 7 patients with severe hepatotoxicity, 5 died and 2 required transplantation; concurrent lactic acidosis and pancreatitis; attributed to marked accumulation of hepatic microvesicular and macrovesicular fat and widespread mitochondrial damage.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that fialuridine hepatotoxicity manifests through mitochondrial dysfunction, and that liver biopsies of the affected patients participating in the phase II clinical trial presented with signs of lactic acidosis, steatosis, and mitochondrial damage, which can reasonably be linked to mitochondrial dysfunction. This attributes human liver injury (steatosis/steatohepatitis with lactic acidosis and mitochondrial damage) to fialuridine in treated patients.

Pancreatitis, neuropathy, and myopathy often accompanied the syndrome, and liver histologic findings showed macrovesicular and microvesicular steatosis and abnormal mitochondria.

raw_record.support_text: Kosar et al. documented the first case of ornidazole-induced autoimmune hepatitis, which recurred after re-exposure despite previous corticosteroid-induced remission. A separate study of eight similar cases explored whether ornidazole triggers or unmasks autoimmune hepatitis; all but one patient was treated with prednisolone (30 mg/day) and azathioprine (50 mg/day). No cases progressed to acute liver failure, supporting the conclusion that ornidazole can trigger autoimmune hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: First documented case of ornidazole-induced autoimmune hepatitis (Kosar et al.) recurred after re-exposure despite prior corticosteroid-induced remission. A study of eight similar cases explored whether ornidazole triggers or unmasks autoimmune hepatitis; treatment employed prednisolone (30 mg/day) and azathioprine (50 mg/day) on a standardized two-year regimen. No cases progressed to acute liver failure. ANA positivity observed in 17 patients (mean titer 1:240), significantly higher among corticosteroid users (36%, n=9) than non-users (10.5%, n=8; p=0.011).

raw_record.support_text: A case series reported ornidazole-induced hepatic injury across three new patients: Case 1 (38/F, ornidazole 1.5 g/day for 7 days then 1 g/day for 4 days) had chronic autoimmune hepatitis and improved in 20 weeks; Case 2 (50/F, 1 g/day for 3 days) had total bilirubin 47.9 mg/dl, ALT 3042 U/l, AST 1665 U/l, with mild cholestasis, focal and bridging parenchymal necrosis and moderate portal inflammation, improving in 7 weeks; Case 3 (25/F, ornidazole 1 g/day for 3 days for vaginitis) presented with jaundice (bilirubin 10.1 mg/dl, ALT 1160, AST 790) and biopsy showing mild cholestasis with focal and confluent necroses, improving in 4 weeks. Case 2 also had a history of a previous reaction following ornidazole use, consistent with rechallenge recurrence.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases were adult women; indication vaginitis in Case 3; prior ornidazole reaction (rechallenge recurrence) in Case 2; negative viral/autoimmune serology; MR cholangiography normal in Case 3; all three improved without liver failure or death. The authors describe DILI features of absence of baseline liver abnormality, temporal relationship to drug use, and improvement upon withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: In a multicenter case series, final diagnoses included ornidazole-induced liver injury (OILI) in 90.1% of cases (n=91), ornidazole-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis in 5.0% (n=5), and ornidazole-induced autoimmune hepatitis in 5.0% (n=5). Overall recovery occurred in 87.7% of cases, liver transplantation was required in 7.9% (n=8), one patient developed chronic DILI (1.0%), and four died (4.0%).
raw_record.extra_details: Severe acute liver injury developed shortly after starting ornidazole (mean latency 16.9 days), with improvement upon cessation, meeting established DILI criteria; recurrence upon re-exposure was noted. Liver biopsy in 47 patients (47%) showed pericentral hepatocyte necrosis (Zone 3), lobular/interface activity, lymphocytic infiltration with eosinophils and plasma cells, single-cell necrosis, Councilman bodies, and hepatocyte ballooning, with no significant fibrosis; one case showed massive necrosis with lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates. Outcomes: recovery 87.7%, liver transplantation 7.9% (8 cases, all females), chronic DILI 1.0% (1 case), deaths 4.0% (4; male 10.0%, female 2.4%). Plasmapheresis used in 17.8% and corticosteroids in 24.8% of cases (mean use 67.3 days; clinical relapse in 20% after discontinuation). Paper cites AASLD 2023 recommendation to evaluate all drugs taken within 180 days prior to hospitalization when assessing for DILI.

raw_record.support_text: The patient's condition and laboratory tests gradually improved on symptomatic treatment after the drug was discontinued, indicating pantoprazole-induced hepatitis. The case describes hepatitis triggered by pantoprazole after 8 days of use; serology largely excluded infectious, autoimmunological, and metabolic causes, and duplex sonography showed no bile obstruction or Budd-Chiari syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: Single 46-year-old female with cramping upper abdominal pain and reduced general condition; hepatitis suggested by abnormal liver function tests; onset after 8 days of pantoprazole for suspected reflux disease; improved on symptomatic treatment after drug discontinuation (dechallenge); serology excluded infectious/autoimmunological/metabolic cause; duplex sonography excluded bile obstruction and Budd-Chiari syndrome. Other potentially hepatotoxic substances (alcohol, analgesics, oral contraceptives) denied. Conclusion notes proton pump inhibitors are a rare cause of hepatitis of uncertain etiology.

raw_record.support_text: In the reported case, the RUCAM score was 9, which made the diagnosis of acute pirfenidone-induced liver injury highly probable (Table 1), while the RECAM score was 3, making the diagnosis possible. The R-factor was calculated as 15.16, indicating a hepatocellular pattern, with ALT ⩾5x ULN. Pirfenidone was used therapeutically for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Present case: DILI occurred 6 months after pirfenidone introduction; R-factor 15.16 (hepatocellular); RUCAM score 9 (highly probable); RECAM score 3 (possible, losing points for unprocessed HCV PCR and ANA titer >1/80); ALT ⩾5x ULN; fully recovered after discontinuation. Liver biopsy showed lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate consistent with an immunogenic reaction; ANA titer 1/320 left an autoimmune-like reaction not excluded. Large RCTs: ALT >3x ULN in 4% of pirfenidone patients, mostly asymptomatic with rapid normalization, drug withdrawn in ~1%; monthly ALT monitoring recommended for first 6 months. A 2018 published case of idiosyncratic pirfenidone DILI occurred 1 month after exposure and led to acute liver failure and death on day 4 of hospitalization. In 2020 the EMA warned of several severe cases of DILI associated with pirfenidone and recommended close monitoring. Pirfenidone is metabolized by CYP1A2 and, to a lesser extent, CYP2C9, 2C19, 2D6, 2E1, with 5-carboxy-pirfenidone as main minimally active metabolite; concurrent simvastatin (CYP3A4) with no known interaction.
