raw_record.support_text: The paper reports an unusual case of idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (DILI) due to pirfenidone presenting as acute liver failure (ALF). A 77-year-old man with Parkinson's disease and IPF had been taking pirfenidone 200 mg three times daily for 1 month; he presented with jaundice, hepatic encephalopathy, and ALF. Other etiologies were ruled out, and a RUCAM score of 7 suggested possible DILI-ALF; the postmortem liver biopsy revealed centrizonal confluent hepatic necrosis and bridging necrosis consistent with DILI, with a final RUCAM score of 10 (highly probable). The patient died on day 4 of illness.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly 77-year-old man with IPF and Parkinson's disease; concomitant levodopa/carbidopa considered incompatible on timing with reaction onset; no pre-existing liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose pirfenidone 200 mg three times daily for 1 month without liver function monitoring. RUCAM score 7 initially (possible DILI-ALF) and final RUCAM score 10 (highly probable). Labs: total/conjugated bilirubin 12.8/7.5 mg/dL, AST 1260 U/L, ALT 526 U/L, ALP 434 U/L, INR 2.1. Postmortem biopsy: centrizonal confluent hepatic necrosis, bridging necrosis, Kupffer cells/macrophages with lipofuscin, portal lymphocytic infiltrate with eosinophils. ALF with grade III hepatic encephalopathy, MELD 31, King's College criteria; liver transplant declined; patient died on day 4.

Notably, in comparison with other PI3Kδ inhibitors, no cases of hepatotoxicity or colitis were observed among the patients; in the combination trial with ublituximab, no hepatotoxicity or grade 3/4 toxicities were reported. These statements explicitly rule out hepatotoxicity for this agent.

In a separate phase I trial combining TGR-1202 with ublituximab (anti-CD20 mAb) in B-cell malignancies, no hepatotoxicity or grade 3/4 toxicities were reported.

Single-agent raltitrexed was used at higher mean weekly dose intensity (0.9 vs 0.8 mg/m2/week) and cumulative dose (14.0 vs 11.2 mg/m2) than the combination.

Adverse event frequencies did not differ significantly between groups; only a non-significant trend toward mild-to-moderate anemia was noted among ribavirin recipients.

raw_record.support_text: A 33-year-old man with surgically corrected congenital transposition of the great vessels and atrial fibrillation was restarted on dofetilide for rate and rhythm control after presenting with elevated liver enzymes (ALT 121 U/L, AST 9 U/L, total bilirubin 2.9 mg/dL, INR 3.2). After restarting dofetilide, AST and ALT rose and peaked at 1026 and 734 U/L respectively, and total bilirubin peaked at 5.4 mg/dL with INR peaking at 6.63 despite warfarin discontinuation. After discontinuing dofetilide, all values returned to normal, and the Naranjo score estimating the probability of an adverse drug reaction was 10. The authors present this as a case of dofetilide-induced severe hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo causality score = 10 (definite). Patient had a history of surgically corrected congenital transposition of the great vessels and atrial fibrillation, and was on warfarin 5 mg which was discontinued. Dofetilide was restarted and stopped after a total of 5 doses; patient was treated with N-acetyl cysteine. Baseline ALT 3 months prior was 24 U/L. Peak values: ALT 734 U/L, AST 1026 U/L, total bilirubin 5.4 mg/dL, INR 6.63. Infectious and autoimmune workup unrevealing; no alcohol use; no other hepatotoxic medications. Dofetilide is a class III antiarrhythmic (I_Kr blocker) FDA-approved for atrial fibrillation/flutter; the mechanism of dofetilide DILI requires further study.

raw_record.support_text: The DILIN identified 10 cases of amiodarone hepatotoxicity. Amiodarone toxicity occurred after a longer latency than dronedarone (387 vs 119 days), and amiodarone patients were more likely to be symptomatic, with nausea and abdominal pain most frequent. Cases were attributed to the drug by DILIN adjudication.
raw_record.extra_details: DILIN case series, N=10, median age 70 (range 59-89). Daily dose 100 mg BID to 200 mg BID PO. Days from drug start to DILI onset median 388 (21-3112). Latency 387 days. Pattern at onset: cholestatic 4/9, mixed 4/9, hepatocellular 1/9; R value median 2.1 (0.2-13.8). Peak ALT median 229 U/L, peak alkaline phosphatase 402 U/L, peak total bilirubin 8.6 mg/dL. Jaundice in 80%. Biopsy (5 cases): fibrosis/advanced bridging fibrosis or cirrhosis (3), steatosis, numerous Mallory-Denk bodies (one periportal), one burned-out cirrhosis. 9 hospitalized, 5 died (1 liver-related) at median 32 days, 3 fatal DILI, 0 liver transplants, chronic DILI 1/6.

raw_record.support_text: Amiodarone was listed among the other single agents cited as the cause of DILI (affecting only one or two patients) in the DILIN series of 74 patients with acute non-acetaminophen drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Cited as a single causative agent affecting one or two of 74 acute non-acetaminophen DILI patients in the DILIN series.

raw_record.support_text: Of 189 patients treated with amiodarone, 29 developed amiodarone-induced toxicity to one or more organs (a prevalence rate of 15%). The paper reports 'amiodarone-induced toxicity' across organs including hepatic toxicity: Table I lists 5 total cases of liver toxicity (2 alive, 3 dead), and paragraph 14 states that 3 patients had hepatic toxicity and 2 had combined pulmonary and hepatic toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver toxicity was defined as fibrolamellar changes with fibrosis on liver biopsy or abnormal serum liver enzymes (>3 times normal), with no evidence for pneumonia or congestive heart failure required for attribution. In this cohort, 5 of 189 patients developed liver toxicity (2 alive, 3 dead); 2 patients had combined pulmonary and hepatic toxicity. Liver toxic patients received amiodarone for an average duration comparable to the overall cohort (mean ~2.5 years across all patients).

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a patient with severe amiodarone hepatotoxicity who also manifested symptoms and signs of pancreatitis with persistent, albeit mild, elevation of amylase and lipase in serum and ascitic fluid; no other etiology for his pancreatitis was evident. They suggest that patients on amiodarone with abnormal liver enzymes or nausea/vomiting/abdominal pain be evaluated for toxic liver and pancreas side effects, and that cessation of amiodarone and substitution with other antiarrhythmic agents be considered.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient on amiodarone as an antiarrhythmic who developed severe hepatotoxicity accompanied by symptoms/signs of pancreatitis and persistent mildly elevated amylase and lipase in serum and ascitic fluid; no other etiology for pancreatitis was evident. The authors note fulminant hepatotoxicity may be accompanied by hyperamylasemia and lipasemia suggesting concomitant pancreatic damage, and recommend evaluating amiodarone patients with abnormal liver enzymes or nausea/vomiting/abdominal pain for hepatic and pancreatic toxicity, with cessation of amiodarone.

raw_record.support_text: In 189 of 198 validated certain/probable IH cases the drug relationship per the updated CIOMS scale was at least 'possible'; 177 different drugs/herbs were identified as related to liver injury. In nine patients there was unintentional reexposure with the suspected drug, leading to a positive rechallenge in five, for amiodarone, ramipril, acetylsalicylic acid, tamoxifen, and mesalazine.
raw_record.extra_details: Positive rechallenge on unintentional reexposure with the suspected drug; the case was among those with at least 'possible' drug relationship on the updated CIOMS scale. Exact causality grade within the study was not reported.

raw_record.support_text: The case report notes that a notable point in the patient was amiodarone-induced hepatotoxicity, alongside hypocalcaemia, which caused further disturbances of the blood clotting mechanism in a patient being managed for retroperitoneal hemorrhage with renal insufficiency and anticoagulant therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported in a patient with retroperitoneal hemorrhage, uremia/renal insufficiency requiring reduced heparin dosing, and acute kidney injury; amiodarone-induced hepatotoxicity and hypocalcaemia were cited as further disturbing the blood clotting mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: Among the 48 DILI cases requiring liver biopsy, amiodarone was reported as one of the most common causes of DILI (Table 2: 4/48, 8.3%).
raw_record.extra_details: 4/48 (8.3%) of DILI cases in this liver biopsy series.

raw_record.support_text: Amiodarone was among the drugs implicated as a cause of hepatic injury in a follow-up study of 44 patients with drug-induced hepatotoxicity; patients with abnormal hepatic evaluation at follow-up had previously taken amiodarone.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported in the 44-patient drug-induced hepatotoxicity cohort followed a median of 5 years; residual disease found at follow-up included chronic hepatitis, fibrosis, and ductopenia in some analyzed biopsies.

raw_record.support_text: In the study of 106 cases of severe adverse drug reactions (SADR), four patients died; one of these deaths was caused by a serious hepatitis induced by amiodarone. The other fatal cases were anaphylactic shock from noramidopyrine and a contrast media, and a Lyell syndrome from phenobarbital.
raw_record.extra_details: One fatal case of serious hepatitis attributed to amiodarone in a hospital study of 106 SADR cases; the patient was one of four fatalities in the study. The paper did not report the intrinsic imputation score specifically for this amiodarone case (overall score distribution was doubtful 19%, probable 55%, likely 24%, very likely 3%).

raw_record.support_text: Analysis of liver specimens from 17 individuals with suspected amiodarone (AD) liver disease showed changes similar to alcoholic liver injury: macrovesicular and microvesicular steatosis (most frequent), hepatocyte ballooning, Mallory bodies, and fibrosis. Lamellar lysosomal inclusion bodies (phospholipidosis) were found in 2 of 14 specimens studied ultrastructurally. These pseudoalcoholic hepatitis and/or phospholipidosis changes occurred both in asymptomatic patients with only mild aminotransferase or alkaline phosphatase elevations and in patients with clinically overt hepatotoxicity. The cytotoxic pseudoalcoholic changes appeared to be an independent phenomenon in susceptible patients who may have been less able to metabolize AD through normal pathways.
raw_record.extra_details: Paper describes 17 cases of suspected amiodarone liver disease; histopathologic spectrum includes pseudoalcoholic hepatitis (steatosis macro/microvesicular, hepatocyte ballooning, Mallory bodies, fibrosis, cirrhosis) and phospholipidosis (lamellated lysosomal inclusions in 2 of 14 EM specimens). A number of deaths have been reported due to AD-induced hepatic failure. Hepatic tissue levels of amiodarone and its metabolite desethyl amiodarone can be detected months after stopping treatment and may account for persistent injury. Amiodarone is a cationic amphophilic, iodinated benzofuran derivative used for refractory ventricular tachyarrhythmias. Changes were seen in patients with hepatomegaly, mild serum aminotransferase/alkaline phosphatase elevations, and clinically overt hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Nine of the 68 primary-role DILI fatality cases died of chronic liver failure more than 26 weeks after DILI onset. Amiodarone, known to cause insidious fibrosis, accounted for one of these chronic liver failure fatalities.
raw_record.extra_details: Amiodarone is described as known to cause insidious fibrosis leading to chronic liver failure; it accounted for one of 68 primary-role DILI fatalities in the DILIN cohort, with death occurring more than 26 weeks after DILI onset.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report one case of acute hepatitis induced by an acute loading dose of amiodarone, with a positive accidental rechallenge test, adding to previously reported cases of cytolytic and cholestatic hepatitis and cirrhosis during chronic amiodarone therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute hepatitis was induced by an acute 1200 mg amiodarone IV infusion in saline over 24 hr given to restore sinus rhythm in a 59-year-old man with ischemic heart disease and atrial fibrillation. ASAT rose from 15 to 145 IU/l and ALAT from 25 to 265 IU/l within 24 hr, then peaked at 1470 and 2090 IU/l three days later; total bilirubin rose to 22 µmol/l. Values declined after amiodarone withdrawal. Three years later an inadvertent rechallenge with amiodarone infusion (1200 mg over 24 hr) produced the same liver-function changes, confirming causality. Liver biopsy 13 days after rechallenge showed major parenchymal damage with hepatocyte atrophy and peliosis-like sinusal ectasia, polymorph portal infiltrate with eosinophilic lymphocytes; electron microscopy was normal. Viral hepatitis, cytomegalovirus, mononucleosis, herpes, non-A/non-B hepatitis markers, tissue antibodies, and stool cultures were negative on both episodes.

raw_record.support_text: This prospective study of 104 patients compares the prevalence of apparent amiodarone-related hepatic injury with literature reports. Approximately one-fourth of patients had asymptomatic elevation of serum aminotransferases; symptomatic 'hepatitis' developed in 3% of this series and in less than 1% of literature cases. Hepatic phospholipidosis and pseudoalcoholic liver injury are attributed to the drug's biochemical effects and possible metabolic idiosyncrasy, respectively, and several instances of cirrhosis and occasionally fatal injury attest to the drug's hepatotoxic potential.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective cohort of 104 patients taking amiodarone orally longer than 2 weeks at Georgetown University Hospital (1982-1986); 25 (24%) had serum aminotransferases more than 2x baseline and above the upper limit of normal (mean peak AST 89 IU/L, range 44-230; mean peak ALT 104 IU/L, range 54-337), alkaline phosphatase less than 3-fold elevated, bilirubin rarely exceeding 3 mg/dl. Mean dose 400 mg (200-800); mean duration to enzyme elevation 10.4 months; mean cumulative dose 104 g. Symptomatic hepatitis in 3%; severe liver injury estimated at 1-3%. Literature mentions elevated hepatic enzymes in 14-82% of patients, instances of cirrhosis and occasionally fatal injury. Hepatic phospholipidosis (biochemical effects) and pseudoalcoholic liver injury (possible metabolic idiosyncrasy) are proposed mechanisms. Extrahepatic organ toxicity more frequent in patients with elevated enzymes (76% vs 37%, p<0.001).

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents a case series titled 'Amiodarone Hepatotoxicity' describing five patients who developed drug-induced liver injury while on therapeutic amiodarone. In Patient 1, biopsy showed moderate to marked panlobular steatosis with occasional hepatocellular degenerative changes and no fibrosis or Mallory bodies; liver tests improved after amiodarone was discontinued, and upon rechallenge with amiodarone 400 mg/d, anorexia returned and ALT rose to 61 U, resolving again after drug withdrawal. Patient 2 developed rising aminotransferases during amiodarone 800 mg/d with biopsy showing mild focal steatosis and minimal hepatocellular degeneration, followed by enzyme improvement after dose reduction. These findings explicitly attribute hepatic steatosis-associated injury to therapeutic amiodarone use in humans.
raw_record.extra_details: Five patients (58/M, 51/M, 73/F, 64/M, 63/M) developed amiodarone hepatotoxicity after 2-18 months of therapy at usual daily doses of 400-800 mg. Liver biopsies showed moderate-to-marked panlobular steatosis (Patient 1) and mild focal steatosis with minimal hepatocellular degeneration (Patient 2), with occasional sinusoidal monocyte aggregates and portal round-cell infiltrates, and no Mallory bodies, fibrosis, or cirrhosis. Elevated AST/ALT and alkaline phosphatase (e.g., Patient 2 ALT 5x normal, ALP 1.5x ULN; Patient 4 AST 500, ALT 1320, ALP 234) and hepatomegaly in Patients 3 and 5; bilirubin, PT, and PTT normal in all five. Patient 1 showed positive dechallenge/rechallenge (ALT 61 U on rechallenge), with clinical and biochemical recovery after withdrawal. Concurrent cardiac/other medications included digoxin, furosemide, KCI, propylthiouracil, dyazide, warfarin, thyroxine, and lubricant eye drops. Indications: coronary artery disease, cardiomyopathy, aortic valve disease. No specific biochemical R-based pattern classification is stated.

raw_record.support_text: The hepatic lesions produced by amiodarone (AD) include phospholipidosis, Mallory bodies and steatosis (a lesion referred to as pseudoalcoholic liver disease), and cirrhosis. Amiodarone and its metabolite desethylamiodarone accumulate in the lipid-rich liver, and the paper attributes these human liver injuries to amiodarone therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Elevated serum aminotransferase values are generally mild, mostly subclinical, transient, and normalize after dose lowering or stopping, and may normalize despite continued therapy; currently considered the most common laboratory abnormality with amiodarone. Symptoms referable to liver disease reported in 40% and hepatomegaly in 68% of patients with histologic liver injury. In the authors' series, 25 patients developed elevated aminotransferases (latent period 1-28 months, mean 10.4 months; daily dose 200-800 mg, mean 400 mg; cumulative dose 17-470 g, mean 104 g); only 3 of 25 developed clinical manifestations. Hepatic lesions: phospholipidosis, Mallory bodies, steatosis (pseudoalcoholic liver disease), and cirrhosis. AD and desethylamiodarone accumulate in liver (up to 890 mg/kg and 6,500 mg/kg in humans); iodine (~37% of AD molecule by weight) in hepatocytes increases CT density. Mean elimination half-life of AD 52 days; high hepatic tissue levels persist up to 10 months after discontinuation. No clear dose-duration relationship with injury observed.

raw_record.support_text: The editorial describes liver toxicity caused by intravenous amiodarone, typically developing within 24 hrs (occasionally 2–3 days), with rapid rise in liver transaminases exceeding ten times the upper normal limit, less frequent increases in bilirubin, creatinine, and alkaline phosphatase, prolongation of prothrombin time, and centrilobular necrosis on liver biopsy. Manifestations are usually reversible after discontinuation of amiodarone but may occasionally progress to a fatal outcome. The authors reference the three cases from Ratz Bravo and colleagues, including unpublished cases reported to the Swiss Agency for Therapeutic Products.
raw_record.extra_details: Intravenous route. Liver toxicity typically develops within 24 hrs, occasionally 2–3 days, after IV amiodarone. Transaminases rise rapidly to >10x upper normal limit; bilirubin, creatinine, and alkaline phosphatase increase less frequently; prothrombin time prolongs; biopsy shows centrilobular necrosis. Manifestations usually reversible after drug discontinuation but occasionally fatal. Evidence includes three cases presented by Ratz Bravo and unpublished cases reported to the Swiss Agency for Therapeutic Products. Note: editorial later questions whether the specific presented cases were amiodarone toxicity versus ischemic hepatitis given their heart-failure/post-cardiac-surgery setting.

raw_record.support_text: Amiodarone, commonly used for arrhythmias, causes adverse effects in up to 55.3% of patients, and hepatotoxicity is described as a known but uncommon complication of amiodarone treatment. The authors report a fatal case of severe hepatic failure due to prolonged amiodarone treatment in a 62-year-old woman who had taken amiodarone 800 mg/day for one year for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, with no history of alcoholism or previous hepatitis; histology showed micronodular cirrhosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case: 62-year-old woman treated with amiodarone 800 mg/day for one year for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (resistant to digoxin, verapamil, and quinidin); no alcoholism or prior hepatitis. Presented with jaundice, enlarged tender liver (span 20 cm), ankle edema; labs included bilirubin 3.9-5.4 mg%, SGOT 520 U/L, SGPT 131 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 329 U/L, gamma-GT 1493 U/L, prolonged prothrombin time. Histology showed regenerative nodule with fibrosis (micronodular cirrhosis). Fatal outcome from severe hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: In this case report, amiodarone was suspected as the cause of drug toxicity and the dosage was decreased to 200 mg daily; other causes of hepatitis were investigated and excluded by serology. Liver biopsy showed marked fibrosis, lobular disarray, swollen hepatocytes with foamy cytoplasm, focal hepatocellular necrosis with inflammatory infiltrates, Mallory's bodies, proliferated bile ductules, and portal inflammatory infiltrate, with lysosomal phospholipid inclusions on electron microscopy. After amiodarone was discontinued the patient's condition deteriorated, and he died on day 21 of hospitalization; a postmortem biopsy showed micronodular cirrhosis with amiodarone and metabolite tissue levels of 180 and 1060 µg/g.
raw_record.extra_details: Elderly patient with arrhythmia treated with amiodarone; serum amiodarone and N-desethylamiodarone levels on admission were 3.0 mg/L (normal 1.0-2.5 mg/L) and 2.6 mg/L, respectively (were 2.0 and 1.6 mg/L 2 months after initiation of therapy in November 1986, when hepatic enzymes were normal). Laboratory findings at admission: total bilirubin 2.7 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 1.6 mg/dl, AST 223 IU/L, ALT 124 IU/L, GGT 738 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 459 IU/L, prothrombin time 39 sec (control 12.1 sec). Histology: marked fibrosis, lobular disarray, swollen foamy hepatocytes, focal necrosis, Mallory bodies, proliferated bile ductules, portal inflammation, lysosomal phospholipid inclusions in hepatocytes, Kupffer cells and bile duct epithelium; postmortem micronodular cirrhosis. Hepatitis B surface/core antibodies positive with no active disease; hepatitis A IgG positive. Amiodarone discontinued on admission; patient transferred to ICCU, given encainide which was stopped for negative inotropic effects, developed congestive heart failure, and died on day 21. Discussion notes amiodarone commonly causes asymptomatic liver enzyme elevations (15-55% frequency) and rarely clinically apparent hepatic disease (symptomatic hepatotoxicity in 6/2122 patients, 0.28%, treated mean 13 months); symptoms such as hepatomegaly, jaundice, cirrhosis, or chronic hepatitis generally subside on discontinuation, with reversal time 20 days to 17 months. Six deaths have been attributed to amiodarone-induced liver toxicity (patients aged 8-76 years; dosages 400 and 600 mg/day; durations 2 months to 4 years). Case presented at ASHP 45th annual meeting.

raw_record.support_text: Among 60 long-latency DILI cases (>365 days) in the DILIN study, amiodarone (n=3) was among the most commonly implicated agents.
raw_record.extra_details: Long-latency DILI (>365 days); n=3 cases in the DILIN Prospective Study cohort.

raw_record.support_text: The discussion addresses amiodarone-induced hepatotoxicity, noting it may occur even without abnormalities in liver enzymes and that amiodarone toxicity can be a cause of marked hepatic hyper-density on CT scan in long-term amiodarone users. Prior reports of amiodarone toxicity showed abnormally high liver density with normal enzyme results, and a previous case at 200 mg amiodarone once daily for 2 years progressed to hepatic cirrhosis. Three presented patients (Cases 1-3) were long-term amiodarone users evaluated for hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Long-term amiodarone users showed marked hepatic hyper-density on non-enhanced CT (e.g., 69 HU at 120 kVp in Case 1); liver enzymes returned to reference ranges in Case 1, while Case 2 died of multiple organ failure after rapidly progressive pneumonia (not attributed to hepatic injury). A cited prior case at a low dose of 200 mg once daily for 2 years progressed to hepatic cirrhosis. Plasma/serum amiodarone levels may be poorly correlated with toxicity and may be normal despite hepatotoxicity; normal liver enzymes may not exclude amiodarone-induced hepatotoxicity. No evidence-based standards exist for monitoring amiodarone-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports two contrasting cases of amiodarone hepatotoxicity. In one, perivenular collections of swollen granular cells (probably macrophages) with high iodine content in lysosomes (presumptive evidence of amiodarone or a metabolite) were seen in an otherwise nearly normal liver, representing the early stage. In the second, there was micronodular cirrhosis with similar iodine-containing granular cells in fibrous tissue, representing the late/terminal stage of amiodarone liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Two case reports of therapeutic amiodarone use. Case 1: 64-year-old man, amiodarone 200 mg three times daily for ventricular arrhythmia post-myocardial infarction; developed RUQ discomfort, nausea, anorexia, weight loss, fever to 38 C, raised AST (54 IU/l then 141 IU/l then 575 IU/l), raised ESR (78 mm/h) and globulins; lung toxicity (basal reticular shadowing) also present; liver function returned to normal within two months of stopping amiodarone (positive dechallenge); prednisolone given for suspected collagen disease without sustained effect, and symptoms recurred/worsened on steroid withdrawal. Case 2: micronodular cirrhosis with iodine-containing granular cells in fibrous tissue. Early-stage lysosomal phospholipidosis documented in hepatocytes, Kupffer cells, bile duct epithelium, and endothelial cells; dose-related accumulation in lysosomes proposed as the mechanism; high iodine content in lysosomal bodies by X-ray energy/wavelength spectroscopy supporting amiodarone or metabolite presence.

raw_record.support_text: Under adverse effects of amiodarone therapy for arrhythmia control, two patients developed hepatic toxicity: one had hepatitis and the other had biopsy-proven nonalcoholic steatosis, and both recovered after amiodarone withdrawal. These hepatic effects were reported among 19 patients (15%) who developed amiodarone-related side effects, with a cumulative incidence of 5.8 per 100 patient years.
raw_record.extra_details: Two of 123 amiodarone-treated arrhythmia patients developed hepatic toxicity: one with hepatitis and one with biopsy-proven nonalcoholic steatosis; both recovered after drug withdrawal. Reported within 19 patients (15%) with amiodarone-related side effects, cumulative incidence 5.8 per 100 patient-years; side effects followed a mean treatment duration of 25 ± 20 months. Amiodarone was withdrawn in 12 patients overall for adverse effects.

raw_record.support_text: A patient presented with amiodarone-induced liver injury, which led to liver failure. Computed tomography revealed a gradual increase in hepatic density over a long period following initiation of amiodarone. Despite discontinuation of the drug, the patient developed hepatic encephalopathy and subsequently died, which the authors attribute to the drug's extended half-life causing persistent end-organ damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Vaughan-Williams class III antiarrhythmic used for atrial fibrillation. The molecular structure includes iodine; hepatic accumulation increases hepatic density on CT, which correlates with blood level of desethyl-amiodarone metabolite. 74-year-old woman; oral amiodarone 200 mg started perioperatively (after mitral valvuloplasty for severe mitral regurgitation) and continued after discharge; referred ~6 years later for elevated liver enzymes. Also taking atorvastatin (10 mg), vonoprazan (20 mg), diltiazem (90 mg), and warfarin (1 mg); no drinking/smoking. Patient progressed to liver failure and hepatic encephalopathy and died despite drug discontinuation, reflecting amiodarone's extended half-life; authors recommend lowest effective dose and annual liver function monitoring.

raw_record.support_text: In this cohort of 427 patients treated with amiodarone for ventricular arrhythmias, the authors state that amiodarone was always discontinued when cardiac or pulmonary toxicity, severe peripheral neuropathy, clinically significant hepatitis or optic neuritis became evident, and report that amiodarone was discontinued because of side effects in 1% of patients at 1 month and 8% at 6 months, with 83 patients total discontinuing for side effects over follow-up.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as clinically significant hepatitis, listed among predefined amiodarone side effects requiring drug discontinuation (together with cardiac and pulmonary toxicity, severe peripheral neuropathy and optic neuritis). In this cohort of 427 patients (83% with ejection fraction measured before therapy), overall side-effect discontinuation was 1% at 1 month, 8% at 6 months, and cumulative 14%/22%/26%/32%/37% at 1-5 years; 83 of 462 intention-to-treat patients discontinued amiodarone due to side effects. Total mortality was 9% at 1 month, 24% at 1 year, 43% at 3 years and 62% at 5 years. Hepatitis phenotype not further subtyped (acute/chronic not specified).

raw_record.support_text: Human evidence for amiodarone hepatotoxicity is cited: in 104 patients treated with amiodarone and followed prospectively, 25 developed an increase in serum transaminases and 3 of these 25 patients developed symptomatic liver injury (Lewis et al., 1989). At therapeutic dosages amiodarone reaches plasma concentrations of ~2µM, with hepatic concentrations 10-20 times higher than plasma, which the authors cite as making their in vitro mitochondrial toxicity findings clinically relevant.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective cohort of 104 amiodarone-treated patients: 25/104 had elevated serum transaminases and 3/25 of those had symptomatic liver injury (Lewis et al., 1989). Therapeutic plasma concentrations ~2µM; hepatic concentrations 10-20x higher than plasma.

raw_record.support_text: A case report describes the onset of hepatic enzyme elevations (GGT and alkaline phosphatase increased to 412 and 238 U/L) on day 397 of amiodarone therapy, with a liver biopsy showing small ill-defined nodules, ballooned hepatocytes with Mallory bodies, and perisinusoidal collagen deposits compatible with alcoholic hepatitis and liver cirrhosis. Amiodarone therapy was considered the suspected toxicity and was later discontinued. On readmission the patient had deteriorated with portal hypertension, micronodular cirrhosis, hepatorenal syndrome, and died 69 days after amiodarone cessation.
raw_record.extra_details: Amiodarone dosage decreased to 200 mg/d for suspected toxicity then returned to 400 mg/d; enzyme elevations first documented 363 days after start of therapy and continued despite cessation; cumulative dose approximately 213 g; onset of liver enzyme abnormalities in a separate 104-patient cohort averaged 10.4 months after a mean cumulative dose of 104 g; reversal of toxicity can range from 14 days to 2.5 years; amiodarone plasma terminal half-life averages about 40 days so elimination of amiodarone and N-desethylamiodarone may take 4-6 months longer after cessation of chronic therapy. Histology showed micronodular cirrhosis consistent with alcoholic hepatitis; patient developed hepatorenal syndrome and died 69 days after cessation; plasma and tissue amiodarone/N-desethylamiodarone concentrations were not measured.

raw_record.support_text: Analysis of 39 amiodarone-induced liver injury case reports published between 1984 and 2007 found that 19 (49%) developed cirrhosis attributed to amiodarone, with low ALT, AST and TB values observed in these patients but no statistically significant differences versus non-cirrhotic patients; the cumulative amiodarone dose was significantly higher in patients who developed cirrhosis (p = 0.01). A Likelihood Ratio model was constructed comparing these published cases with LFT abnormalities of any other etiology in a general population.
raw_record.extra_details: 39 published amiodarone-induced liver injury case reports (1984-2007); 19 (49%) developed cirrhosis, 15 patients died (20 did not, 4 not registered). Mean age 68.77 y (SD 11.15), mean latency period 1021 days, mean cumulative dose 300.70 g. Cirrhotic patients had significantly higher cumulative dose (382.8 vs 222.7 g, p=0.01). Likelihood-ratio model compared published cases with LFT abnormalities of any other cause in a general population; LRs >1 for AST 1-3×ULN (1.98), ALT 1-3×ULN (1.70), age >65 y (2.27), and AP >8×ULN (4.42) categories.

raw_record.support_text: Patient number 9, a 58-year-old woman with monomorphic ventricular tachycardia who had been taking a maintenance oral dose of 300 mg amiodarone (AMD) for over 3 years, was found to have abnormal liver tests compatible with cholestatic liver injury. Alcohol consumption and injection drug abuse were excluded; hepatitis A, B and C tests were negative, and antinuclear, anti-LKM and anti-mitochondrial antibodies were not detected. The serum amiodarone concentration was 1012 ng/mL (therapeutic range 500-1000 ng/mL). The patient was diagnosed with AMD-induced hepatotoxicity, the drug was discontinued, and a liver biopsy two weeks later showed moderate fibrosis and steatosis with periportal Mallory bodies. Liver enzymes gradually returned to normal after about three months, and amiodarone was not resumed.
raw_record.extra_details: 58-year-old woman with monomorphic ventricular tachycardia; maintenance oral dose 300 mg amiodarone for over 3 years before detection. Laboratory values: total bilirubin 1.9 mg/dL (normal 0.7-1.1), AST 160 U/L (normal 19-35), ALT 174 U/L (normal 7-45), gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase 105 U/L (normal 6-29). Serum amiodarone concentration 1012 ng/mL (therapeutic range 500-1000 ng/mL). Alcohol and injection drug abuse excluded; hepatitis A/B/C negative; ANA, anti-LKM and anti-mitochondrial antibodies absent. Liver biopsy 2 weeks after discontinuation showed moderate fibrosis and steatosis and periportal Mallory bodies. Dechallenge led to gradual normalization of liver enzymes within about 3 months; drug not resumed.

raw_record.support_text: In the discussion of amiodarone side effects, Dr. Podrid reported that a biopsy was taken from their patient who had hepatitis, and that this patient had a typical drug-reaction hepatitis indistinguishable from any other type of drug reaction. This attributes the hepatitis to the administered antiarrhythmic amiodarone.
raw_record.extra_details: Described as a typical drug-reaction hepatitis indistinguishable from any other type of drug reaction; a biopsy specimen was taken. In the same discussion, the patient also exhibited a Coumadin (warfarin) interaction, and another patient had an intracerebral hemorrhage, neither of which is a liver-injury attribution.

raw_record.support_text: A 61-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation taking clopidogrel and amiodarone presented with elevated liver tests (total bilirubin 0.71 mg/dL, AST 358 U/L, ALT 177 U/L, prothrombin time 27.1 s) and diffuse increased liver intensity on CT. The authors diagnosed amiodarone-induced hepatic, pulmonary, thyroid, and ophthalmologic toxicity, and liver function was restored after cessation of amiodarone. The same narrative states that amiodarone causes liver damage ranging from asymptomatic serum aminotransferase elevation to hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: 61-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation; concurrent clopidogrel use; presented with general weakness, nausea, visual disturbance, heat intolerance, and non-productive cough. Baseline liver tests: total bilirubin 0.71 mg/dL, AST 358 U/L, ALT 177 U/L, prothrombin time 27.1 s; CT showed diffuse increased liver intensity. Liver function restored after amiodarone cessation. Multi-system toxicity also involved lungs (fibrinoid interstitial inflammation with atypical type II pneumocytes and intra-alveolar foamy macrophages), thyroid (TSH <0.008 μIU/mL, free thyroxine 4.67 ng/dL, treated with methimazole), and eyes (bilateral vortex corneal deposits). Amiodarone is an iodine-containing benzofuran derivative, class III antiarrhythmic. Narrative notes liver damage range up to hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: A 60-year-old male with atrial fibrillation was given amiodarone 150 mg bolus followed by continuous infusion of 900 mg over 24 h. Blood work 24 h later showed a sudden rise in aminotransferases (AST 3,254 U/L, ALT 1,643 U/L), lactate dehydrogenase 2,234 U/L, direct bilirubin 5.12 mg/dL, and INR 2.53, while gamma-GT and alkaline phosphatase were normal. Extensive workup (abdominal ultrasonography, viral hepatitis serologies, autoimmune markers) was unremarkable, and no alcohol or other hepatotoxic drug besides amiodarone was found. The case narrative identifies amiodarone-induced liver injury as the primary diagnostic hypothesis, and the liver enzymes improved and normalized within 7 days after amiodarone was discontinued about 50 h after starting.
raw_record.extra_details: Intravenous amiodarone (150 mg bolus then 900 mg over 24 h) given for atrial fibrillation; onset of acute liver injury 24-36 h after starting amiodarone. Peak labs: AST 3,254 U/L, ALT 1,643 U/L, LDH 2,234 U/L, direct bilirubin 5.12 mg/dL, INR 2.53; gamma-GT and alkaline phosphatase normal. Viral, autoimmune, and ultrasound workup negative; no other hepatotoxic drug or alcohol identified retrospectively. Amiodarone discontinued ~50 h after initiation; liver enzymes improved and normalized within 7 days. The article notes intravenous amiodarone acute hepatotoxicity is a rare but potentially fatal complication, and lists amiodarone among causes of drug-induced liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: The study developed a novel scoring system to differentiate amiodarone induced liver injury (AILI) from alcoholic steatohepatitis (ASH). Patients with AILI had mean amiodarone use of 20.4 months at a mean dose of 300 mg. Histologically, compared with ASH, AILI was less frequently associated with ductular reaction, macrovesicular steatosis, abundant ballooning degeneration, neutrophilic lobular inflammation, satellitosis, megamitochondria, and hepatocellular/canalicular cholestasis, with a trend for Mallory hyalines restricted to periportal hepatocytes and periportal-predominant pericellular fibrosis. The scoring system correctly classified 100% of cases, all AILI cases scoring <8 and all ASH cases >11.
raw_record.extra_details: Amiodarone induced liver injury (AILI) at a mean dose of 300 mg over a mean duration of 20.4 months. Histology resembled alcoholic steatohepatitis: macrovesicular steatosis, hepatocyte ballooning without degeneration, Mallory hyalines, satellitosis, periportal pericellular fibrosis, and lamellar lysosomal inclusions on transmission electron microscopy; less ductular reaction, cholestasis, and megamitochondria than ASH. A novel biochemical+histologic scoring system (score <10 suggests AILI, >10 ASH) correctly classified 100% of cases, with all AILI cases scoring <8.

raw_record.support_text: In the presented case, hepatic enzyme levels and CT density of the liver normalized after cessation of amiodarone, and the authors attribute hepatotoxicity to amiodarone-induced inhibition of mitochondrial fatty-acid β-oxidation with subsequent production of reactive oxygen species, causing apoptosis and necrosis of hepatocytes that can lead to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis. They note hepatic function is generally reversible if amiodarone is withdrawn early and cite a previous case report in which long-term amiodarone administration induced liver cirrhosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient on amiodarone for refractory supraventricular/ventricular arrhythmias showing abnormally high liver density on unenhanced CT and hepatic enzyme elevation that normalized after drug cessation, supporting dechallenge recovery. Authors propose amiodarone-induced inhibition of mitochondrial β-oxidation and reactive oxygen species production leading to hepatocyte apoptosis/necrosis and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis. They note a previous case report of long-term amiodarone use inducing liver cirrhosis and recommend periodic liver-function monitoring/biopsy before an irreversible stage is reached.

raw_record.support_text: Amiodarone hepatotoxicity most commonly manifests as mild asymptomatic elevations of serum aminotransferases, but more severe injury can occur simulating alcoholic liver disease with steatohepatitis, Mallory bodies, and cirrhosis, and four fatal cases of hepatotoxicity had been reported. Phospholipid-laden lysosomal lamellar bodies on electron microscopy are a characteristic feature of amiodarone hepatotoxicity, and latency from treatment start to recognition ranges from several weeks to several years.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of the reported fifth fatal amiodarone hepatotoxicity: mild asymptomatic serum aspartate aminotransferase elevation appeared 5 months after starting amiodarone; liver tests not repeated until 3 years later when hospitalized with massive ascites and apparent pancreatitis. Liver biopsy (micro-nodular cirrhosis, bile ductular proliferation, hepatocyte destruction, polymorphonuclear infiltrate, Mallory bodies; electron microscopy showed multilamellated lysosomal inclusion bodies) was consistent with severe amiodarone-induced liver disease. Ascites attributed primarily to severe cirrhosis. Phospholipidosis and oxygen free radical damage proposed as pathogenic mechanisms. Postmortem studies show high amiodarone and metabolite concentrations in adipose tissue, liver, lung, and pancreas. Competing cause considered but no evidence of a common duct stone.

raw_record.support_text: 17 cases of amiodarone induced liver injury (AILI) confirmed by transmission electron microscopy from 1990-2020 were identified, with a mean amiodarone usage of 20.4 months and a mean dose of 300 mg. AILI histologically mimics alcoholic steatohepatitis and can be definitely diagnosed by identifying characteristic lamellar lysosomal inclusions on transmission electron microscopy.
raw_record.extra_details: 17 EM-confirmed AILI cases (1990-2020); mean usage 20.4 months at mean dose 300 mg. Histology: steatohepatitis with ballooning degeneration, periportally located Mallory hyalines, satellitosis, periportal pericellular fibrosis, sinusoidal Kupffer cell lipidosis (1 case); less frequently ductular reaction, macrovesicular steatosis, hepatocellular and canalicular cholestasis than ASH. A histologic scoring system (score <10 suggestive of AILI) correctly classified 100% of cases, with all AILI cases scoring <8. Diagnosis confirmed by characteristic lamellar lysosomal inclusions on transmission electron microscopy.

She was diagnosed with drug-induced steatohepatitis and urea cycle abnormalities caused by long-term amiodarone use. The authors state amiodarone may cause drug-induced steatohepatitis and urea cycle abnormalities that could induce hyperammonemia.

raw_record.support_text: A 75-year-old man with normal baseline liver function had been given amiodarone 400 mg orally once daily for 17.8 months for atrial fibrillation and heart failure and developed nausea, vomiting and muscle weakness. Liver biopsy showed microvesicular steatosis, foam cells in the hepatic sinusoids and Mallory bodies in the periportal hepatocytes with features of chronic hepatitis, and electron microscopy showed pleomorphic mitochondria with crystalloid inclusions; the authors state both findings strongly suggested amiodarone-induced hepatotoxicity. Liver enzymes improved by day 3 after amiodarone withdrawal (AST 31, ALT 27 IU/L) and the patient fully recovered at 1 month.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 75-year-old man with atrial fibrillation and heart failure; prior alcohol intake (40 g/day for 20 years, abstinent for 4 months before admission); concurrent carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, diltiazem 30 mg twice daily and triflusal 300 mg once daily; history of pulmonary tuberculosis treated 30 years prior.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 400 mg orally once daily for 17.8 months. Admission labs: AST 123 IU/L, ALT 146 IU/L, albumin 2.5 g/dL, bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 99 IU/L, platelets 212,000/uL, hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL; hepatitis B/C/A and VDRL negative; ANA positive with other autoantibodies negative. Liver biopsy: microvesicular steatosis, foam cells in sinusoids, Mallory bodies, chronic hepatitis features (grade 2 lobular, grade 1 porto-peripheral, stage 1 portal fibrosis); electron microscopy showed pleomorphic mitochondria with crystalloid inclusions and concentric membranous arrays. Dechallenge: liver enzymes improved by day 3 after withdrawal (AST 31, ALT 27 IU/L); full recovery at 1 month. Sural nerve biopsy showed demyelination; nerve conduction showed mixed sensorimotor polyneuropathy.

raw_record.support_text: A 76-year-old woman who had received an average daily dose of 200 mg of amiodarone since December 1979 for recurrent supraventricular tachycardia developed progressive liver enzyme elevations (alkaline phosphatase, then aspartate aminotransferase), hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, abdominal pain, anorexia, and wasting. While still on amiodarone she died of hepatic encephalopathy; autopsy showed cirrhosis with prominent fibrosis, bile duct proliferation, severely damaged hepatocytes, and widespread Mallory bodies. The authors interpret this as evidence that asymptomatic amiodarone-induced liver function disturbance, especially with prolonged treatment, can herald irreversible liver damage.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 76-year-old woman; prolonged (approximately 3-year) amiodarone treatment; recurrent supraventricular tachycardia indication
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 200 mg/day from December 1979; asymptomatic two- to three-fold increases in alkaline phosphatase (195 U/L) and aspartate aminotransferase (85 U/L, later 225 U/L) noted from 1982-1983; 2 weeks after referral patient died of hepatic encephalopathy while still on amiodarone. Autopsy: cirrhosis, scant fatty infiltration, prominent fibrosis, bile duct proliferation, severely damaged hepatocytes, widespread Mallory bodies. Authors note hepatotoxicity appears concentration-dependent and that amiodarone induces alcohol-like changes (lamellar osmiophilic lysosomal inclusions); Rotmensch and associates held the traditional view that hepatic enzyme elevation is transient and clinically insignificant.

raw_record.support_text: In this case report, the diagnosis of amiodarone-induced hepatitis is based on drug history, temporal relationship, time course of liver dysfunction, exclusion of other causes, and rapid improvement after amiodarone withdrawal. Although no bioptic or autoptic features of liver damage were obtained, the cause-effect relationship between amiodarone infusion and hepatitis was rated 'probable' according to the Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability score (total score +7). A peculiarity was the very short latency between infusion and transaminase elevation, and the authors advise monitoring liver function during the first hours of intravenous amiodarone loading in critically ill elderly patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Critically ill elderly patient with intravenous amiodarone loading; the authors call for heightened alertness and liver-function monitoring in this population.
raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability score total +7, classified as probable. Very short latency between intravenous amiodarone infusion and transaminase elevation (earlier reports showed intervals of a day or more with lower transaminase elevation). Rapid improvement after amiodarone withdrawal; no biopsy or autopsy confirmation of liver damage. Intravenous loading route.

raw_record.support_text: Case report of an 80-year-old woman whose volume overload was determined to be amiodarone-induced acute and chronic liver injury leading to submassive necrosis and bridging fibrosis consistent with early cirrhosis. The histopathology was uniquely absent of steatosis and phospholipidosis, which are commonly seen in amiodarone-induced cirrhosis (AIC). The authors concluded the histological findings with the clinical presentation were most consistent with an amiodarone-induced acute and chronic drug reaction, and the patient died 2 days after discharge to hospice care.

raw_record.support_text: The case presents severe cholestatic jaundice induced by amiodarone in an elderly patient, illustrating the rarity of this complication after extensive diagnostic testing ruled out biliary or pancreatic malignancy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly patient; low-dose amiodarone with a total cumulative dose of 100 g; onset of jaundice more than 8 weeks after drug intake.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe cholestatic jaundice attributed to amiodarone; only seven cases of amiodarone-induced cholestatic jaundice have been reported worldwide, with total doses ranging from 4.2 to 648 g, and only five of the seven patients had severe cholestatic jaundice. Other causes of cholestasis were excluded by serologic, histologic, and imaging studies. Extrahepatic manifestations included corneal deposits, constipation, and dysthyroidism. Slow resolution of hepatotoxicity occurred after ursodeoxycholic acid administration. Amiodarone is an iodinated benzofuran derivative metabolized to desethylamiodarone by hepatic cytochrome P450; amiodarone and desethylamiodarone may accumulate in human liver at concentrations up to 800 and 6500 mg/kg respectively. Lysosomal lamellar bodies occur in almost all amiodarone-treated patients and denote drug exposure, not toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents descriptive parameters of published amiodarone-induced liver injury case reports, comparing 20 cases that did not develop cirrhosis with 19 cases that did develop cirrhosis. Reported values include cumulative dose, total bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, AST, ALT, latency period, and recovery (period of remission) after amiodarone withdrawal, indicating these are published human cases of amiodarone hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings derived from published case reports of chronic amiodarone therapy; cirrhosis developed in 19 of 39 cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Amiodarone-induced liver injury among 39 published cases (20 non-cirrhotic, 19 cirrhotic). Non-cirrhotic group: cumulative dose mean 222.7 g (median 189, range 4-1051.2), latency period mean 873.0 days, recovery 98.83 days on average. Cirrhotic group: cumulative dose mean 382.8 g (median 285), latency mean 1117.3 days. Recovery data available for 12 reversible cases: 2 within 15-30 days, 8 within 31-180 days, 2 within 6-9 months after withdrawal. ALT altered below 8x ULN in a majority; TB above 8x ULN in 3/36 (8%) of cases, about four times the general-population frequency. AP below 8x ULN in most cases, consistent with the non-cholestatic (hepatocellular) injury pattern most commonly described. Likelihood ratios favored age >65 years (2.27), ALT 1-3x ULN (1.98), and AP 3-8x ULN (2.55).; confidence_note: Overall relationship treated as established amiodarone-induced liver injury; one sentence (p:49) frames amiodarone as 'a possible cause' specifically for rare high-bilirubin cases.

raw_record.support_text: Dr. Ratz Bravo and colleagues present three cases of liver toxicity caused by intravenous amiodarone, including unpublished cases reported to the Swiss Agency for Therapeutic Products. Liver toxicity typically develops within 24 hrs (may take 2-3 days) of IV amiodarone, with liver transaminases rising rapidly to exceed ten times the upper normal limit; less frequently bilirubin, creatinine, and alkaline phosphatase increase and prothrombin time prolongs. Liver biopsy reveals centrilobular necrosis, and manifestations are usually reversible after discontinuation but may occasionally progress to a fatal outcome.

raw_record.support_text: Acute elevation of liver enzymes following IV amiodarone use ranged from mild asymptomatic to severe life-threatening and frequently necessitated drug discontinuation; in most reported cases the liver injury occurred within 24–48 h of therapy and reversed within 2–3 weeks of discontinuation. This describes acute hepatotoxicity attributed to intravenous amiodarone.

raw_record.extra_details: Acute hepatic injury following IV amiodarone ranged from mild asymptomatic to severe life-threatening and frequently required drug discontinuation; injury typically occurred within 24–48 h of therapy and reversed within 2–3 weeks of discontinuation. Mechanism is controversial (possible ischemic injury, or immune-mediated alteration of hepatocellular membrane by solubilizers such as polysorbate 80); acute IV injury differs from chronic oral amiodarone hepatotoxicity. Study described: 180 ICU/CCU patients receiving IV amiodarone, with 90 AILI cases defined as acute rise in serum aminotransferase levels by at least 2-fold of baseline within 24–48 h of IV amiodarone, versus 90 controls without AILI.

raw_record.support_text: A 79-year-old woman treated with intravenous (IV) amiodarone for atrial flutter abruptly developed coagulopathy, altered mental status and liver enzyme derangement, and was diagnosed with acute liver failure (ALF) secondary to an amiodarone adverse drug reaction, with a Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale score of 7. Amiodarone was withheld and N-acetylcysteine (NAC) was initiated; clinical improvement was seen within 48 hours of holding the drug and complete recovery was reported at follow-up.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intravenous amiodarone administration (IV push then infusion) for atrial flutter in a 79-year-old woman; N-acetylcysteine co-administered as treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Received 150 mg amiodarone IV push followed by an IV infusion totalling 930 mg over 24 hours, then transitioned to oral amiodarone 200 mg twice daily. Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale score of 7 supports a probable causal relationship. Clinical improvement within 48 hours of holding the drug and within 24 hours of initiating NAC; complete recovery at post-hospital follow-up, making this the only reported survivor among seven total cases of amiodarone-induced ALF (the prior six reported cases were all fatal). Chronic oral amiodarone is noted to be associated with asymptomatic hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Long-term amiodarone administration causes hepatotoxicity in patients on chronic oral amiodarone therapy, attributed to iodine accumulation in the liver. Three clinical cases of amiodarone-induced hepatotoxicity are presented. The paper also reports that hepatotoxicity and elevated transaminase levels occur in 15% to 50% of patients with long-term amiodarone use.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term (chronic) oral amiodarone therapy at low dose for the prevention of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients underwent dual-energy computed tomography (DECT); iodine accumulation in the liver was proposed as the mechanism of hepatotoxicity. Liver enzymes were elevated in all three; abdominal DECT without contrast showed highly increased attenuation and increased hepatic iodine concentration. Case 1 showed a reversible course of liver function and decreased CT values after amiodarone discontinuation. Case 2 had increased hepatic iodine concentration and liver damage but died of multiple organ failure after rapidly progressive pneumonia (death not attributed to liver injury). Case 3 had increased hepatic iodine concentration and elevated liver enzymes, continued oral amiodarone, and required routine liver function tests every 3-6 months. The paper states hepatotoxicity/elevated transaminases occur in 15%-50% of patients on long-term use.

raw_record.support_text: Case 2: a 68-year-old man receiving intravenous amiodarone (bolus 450 mg then constant infusion and oral therapy) for refractory symptomatic ventricular tachycardia developed, 36 hours after starting amiodarone, a considerable rise in serum transaminases, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin with icterus and pruritus. Hepatitis A/B markers and viral and immunologic studies were negative and ultrasonography excluded obstructive biliary disease. Toxic cholestatic hepatitis was suspected; liver function returned to normal within 2 weeks along with gradual reduction of amiodarone dosage. The discussion states the clinical course, together with absence of known causes of acute liver damage, strongly suggests amiodarone as the cause of hepatic dysfunction.

raw_record.support_text: A 76-year-old woman who had received an average daily dose of 200 mg of amiodarone for recurrent supraventricular tachycardia since December 1979 developed progressive liver enzyme elevations (alkaline phosphatase up to 317 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 225 U/L), ascites, and varices, and died 2 weeks after referral due to hepatic encephalopathy while still on amiodarone. At autopsy the liver showed histologic findings consistent with cirrhosis, with scant fatty infiltration, prominent fibrosis and bile duct proliferation, severely damaged hepatocytes, and widespread Mallory bodies. The authors report this as a case of fatal cirrhosis in a patient treated with amiodarone for over 4 years, adding evidence that asymptomatic liver dysfunction with prolonged amiodarone treatment may herald irreversible liver damage and that cessation of amiodarone should be considered.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Prolonged amiodarone therapy (over 4 years) at an average daily dose of 200 mg in a 76-year-old woman with recurrent supraventricular tachycardia and no pre-existing liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity presented as initially asymptomatic twofold alkaline phosphatase rise (195 U/L; normal 90 U/L), later aspartate aminotransferase rise (85 U/L then 225 U/L; normal 40 U/L), albumin 2.9 g/dL, normal bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase, negative hepatitis B surface antigen and VDRL. Clinical findings included hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, and esophageal varices; death from hepatic encephalopathy. Autopsy histology: cirrhosis with prominent fibrosis, bile duct proliferation, damaged hepatocytes, widespread Mallory bodies. Authors also note amiodarone induces alcohol-like hepatic changes, electron microscopy shows lamellar osmiophilic lysosomal inclusions even without clinical disease, and hepatotoxicity is suggested to be concentration-dependent in contrast to pulmonary toxicity.

raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Study population consists of hospitalized cardiac patients (including those with cardiomyopathy, congestive heart failure, congestive hepatomegaly, and on inotropic support); AILI developed in the setting of therapeutic amiodarone use for cardiac indications.
raw_record.extra_details: 90 patients developed AILI among the cohort. Liver injury grades: 77.8% grade 4, 21.1% grade 3, 1.1% grade 2 (mean grade 3.76 ± 0.45). Grade 4 AILI showed mean ALT and AST rises of 8.53 ± 4.33 and 7.67 ± 5.12 fold from baseline. Predictors of severe (grade 4) AILI on multivariate analysis: inotropic support (OR 4.03, P=0.034), congestive hepatomegaly (OR 2.69, P=0.012), increasing baseline total bilirubin (OR 2.02, P=0.001), and increasing dose of amiodarone (OR 1.002, P=0.002). ROC: total bilirubin >1.3 mg/dl predicted AILI (AUC 0.72, 95% CI 0.64-0.79); >1.6 mg/dl predicted severe AILI (AUC 0.67, 95% CI 0.6-0.74). Post-amiodarone ALT/AST correlated with baseline ALT, AST, total and direct bilirubin, and ejection fraction.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents 2 cases of antihistamine-induced hepatitis with autoimmune features caused by loratidine (10 mg daily). Case 1 was a 49-year-old male diagnosed with loratidine-induced hepatitis with autoimmune features after extensive exclusion of other causes; biopsy showed panacinar and portal hepatitis with lymphocytic infiltrate (grade 4/4) and no fibrosis, and liver biochemistries remained normal for 10 years after discontinuation. Case 2 was diagnosed with loratidine-induced hepatitis, confirmed by rechallenge (resuming loratidine 10 mg daily promptly raised ALT to 1,800 U/L, AST to 1,027 U/L, bilirubin to 3.9 mg/dL), resolving after rechallenge discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases at 10 mg daily oral therapeutic dosing. Case 1 (49y male): ALT 675 U/L, AST 305 U/L, bilirubin 2.9 mg/dL, INR 1.2, biopsy showed panacinar/portal hepatitis with lymphocytic infiltrate sparing bile ducts, grade 4/4 hepatitis with zone necrosis but no fibrosis; positive antismooth muscle antibody (1:40) and circulating immune complexes; both recovered after loratidine discontinuation (normal biochemistries for 10 years). Case 2 (50y male): jaundice/fatigue, bilirubin 9.1 mg/dL, ALT 2,495 U/L, ALP 189 U/L; biopsy showed chronic hepatitis with lymphocytic infiltrate, eosinophils, plasma cells and portal fibrosis; positive anti-F1 actin (1:31) and anti-mitochondrial antibody (1:88); rechallenge confirmed causality; treated with prednisone and ursodeoxycholic acid, normal biochemistries for 1.5 years. Authors suggest loratidine triggered immune-mediated injury resembling overlap between autoimmune hepatitis and primary biliary cirrhosis; no other medications, alcohol, or herbs taken.

raw_record.support_text: The AKRENDO1 clinical trial, which assessed the efficacy and safety of the AKR1C3 inhibitor BAY1128688 as a potential treatment for endometriosis-related pain symptoms, was prematurely terminated by the sponsor due to cases of hepatotoxicity. Increases in serum ALT were detected after 12 weeks of treatment or thereafter, and individual bile acid levels were increased at isolated early time points; the in vitro BSEP inhibitory IC50 was 3.6 µM while total BAY1128688 concentration in human plasma was approximately 10 µM, and increases in androsterone and bilirubin were observed.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Trial population comprised patients with endometriosis-related pain symptoms; treated with BAY1128688 at 60 mg BID.
raw_record.extra_details: Trial prematurely terminated by sponsor due to hepatotoxicity cases. ALT increases detected after 12 weeks of treatment or thereafter (from visit 7 onward). Proposed mechanism: BSEP inhibition (in vitro IC50 3.6 µM) with total human plasma concentration ~10 µM, leading to toxic bile acid accumulation; increases in androsterone (AKR1C3 inhibition pharmacodynamic biomarker) and serum bilirubin observed. Bile acid measurements had limited value for predicting ALT increases; biomarkers MCSFR, androsterone and six candidate biomarkers could not consistently predict ALT increases. Preclinical 13-week animal study showed transient bilirubin increases without liver enzyme or microscopic liver findings.

raw_record.support_text: In pooled analyses of the ENLIVEN trial and phase 1 extension (N=130, median follow-up 39 months), 92% of pexidartinib-treated patients experienced aminotransferase elevations (dose-dependent, resolved with treatment interruption), and 4 (3%) cases of mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity occurred within the first 8 weeks of treatment, all recovering within 1-7 months after discontinuation. A further pooled analysis of the clinical program (N=140) found 91% with dose-dependent aminotransferase elevations (66% of ALT/AST increases were 1 to <3x ULN) and 5 (4%) cases of mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity, all recovering after discontinuation. The US prescribing information includes a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity, and a retrospective analysis of 3-year hepatic safety data from the tREMS program (N=451) found 21 (4.7%) patients met criteria for a hepatic AE or laboratory abnormalities suggestive of a serious and potentially fatal liver injury, with event onset within 2 months of starting pexidartinib.
raw_record.extra_details: Pooled analyses of ENLIVEN (phase 3 trial) + phase 1 extension (N=130; median follow-up 39 mo): 92% aminotransferase elevations, 4 (3%) mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity within first 8 weeks, recovered within 1-7 months after discontinuation. Clinical program pooled analysis (N=140): 91% dose-dependent aminotransferase elevations resolved with interruption, 66% of ALT/AST increases were 1 to <3x ULN, 5 (4%) mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity recovered after discontinuation. Final ENLIVEN analysis (median follow-up 31 mo, cutoff April 2021): no new safety signals, no additional mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity cases. Indication: diffuse-type tenosynovial giant cell tumor. USPI carries a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity; drug available only through the TURALIO REMS (tREMS) program. tREMS retrospective hepatic safety analysis (N=451): 21 (4.7%) met criteria for hepatic AE or laboratory abnormalities suggestive of serious and potentially fatal liver injury; onset within 2 months; treatment interrupted in 1, permanently discontinued in 20. Both ALT (UMLS:C0151905) and AST (UMLS:C0151904) elevations reported.

raw_record.support_text: Pexidartinib is only available in the US through a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) program due to the risk of hepatotoxicity. During the ENLIVEN trial, 3 patients had hepatotoxicity per laboratory assessment (ALT and AST ≥3 times the ULN plus total bilirubin and ALP ≥2 times ULN); each had started on 1000 mg/day pexidartinib and recovered after discontinuation, with onset within the first 8 weeks of treatment. The paper states pexidartinib is associated with two types of hepatotoxicity: dose-dependent, reversible, generally low-grade aminotransferase elevations without concurrent total bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase elevations, and mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity that can be nonreversible, both occurring in the first 2 months of treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Data from the ENLIVEN trial in tenosynovial giant cell tumor. Three patients with hepatotoxicity per laboratory assessment (ALT and AST ≥3x ULN plus total bilirubin and ALP ≥2x ULN), each started on 1000 mg/day pexidartinib and recovered after discontinuation; onset within the first 8 weeks. Pexidartinib available only via US REMS due to hepatotoxicity risk. Two attributed hepatotoxicity types: dose-dependent, reversible, generally low-grade aminotransferase elevations without concurrent bilirubin/ALP elevation; and mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity that can be nonreversible. Both types occur in the first 2 months of treatment, supporting close monitoring in early treatment.

raw_record.support_text: Cumulatively through June 2024, 45 (5.7%) patients receiving pexidartinib in the tREMS Program met criteria for AEs or laboratory abnormalities suggestive of serious and potentially fatal liver injury; 32/45 (71.1%) recovered, 6/45 recovering, 6/45 not yet recovered, and 1/45 status unknown. Of 158 liver adverse event report forms for 114 patients, there were 19 (12.0%) hospitalizations due to liver AEs. Pexidartinib was discontinued in a VBDS-suspect case.
raw_record.extra_details: tREMS Program (FDA-mandated REMS for pexidartinib in adult TGCT patients), data through June 2024; 45/785? (5.7%) patients with serious/potentially fatal liver injury; 158 LAERFs for 114 patients, 22 hepatology referrals, 27 liver ultrasounds, 1 liver biopsy, 19 liver-AE hospitalizations, 7 medically managed, 59 resolved/88 ongoing/1 resolved with sequelae/10 missing. Frequency and pattern of liver injury consistent with ENLIVEN trial and prior 3-year REMS assessment; no irreversible liver injury and no new safety signals identified.

raw_record.support_text: The paper introduces pexidartinib, an orally administered small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor of CSF1R, KIT, and FLT3-ITD, used to treat tenosynovial giant cell tumor. It states that pexidartinib can cause serious and potentially fatal mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity. In July 2019 the US FDA determined a favorable benefit/risk for patients with no surgical options and approved pexidartinib, whereas the EMA's CHMP considered the safety and efficacy balance not sufficiently demonstrated, based largely on a negative assessment of the balance between the risk of life-threatening liver toxicity and the nonmetastatic nature of the disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Pooled analysis of the phase 3 ENLIVEN study (NCT02371369) and the phase 1 PLX108-01 extension (NCT01004861) TGCT cohort, with median follow-up of 39 months (range 32-82 months); dosing 1000 mg/d then 800 mg/d (split dose). Hepatotoxicity described as 'serious and potentially fatal' mixed or cholestatic; EMA CHMP cited 'life-threatening liver toxicity' risk in declining approval, while the US FDA approved pexidartinib in July 2019 as first systemic therapy for TGCT.

raw_record.support_text: In part 1 of the ENLIVEN phase 3 trial in tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT), serious adverse events occurred in 8 of 61 (13%) patients in the pexidartinib group. Three patients experienced ALT and AST ≥3×ULN with total bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase ≥2×ULN, described as mixed and cholestatic hepatotoxicity; in one 75-year-old woman hyperbilirubinemia lasted about 7 months, required two liver dialysis procedures, and a liver biopsy showed significant ductopenia and severe cholestasis, while in the other two cases hyperbilirubinemia recovered within 1–2 months of pexidartinib discontinuation. No additional cases of mixed and cholestatic hepatotoxicity were reported with longer pexidartinib treatment through the January 31, 2018 data cutoff.
raw_record.extra_details: Serious AEs: 8/61 (13%) pexidartinib vs 1/59 (2%) placebo in part 1. Three patients had ALT and AST ≥3×ULN with total bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase ≥2×ULN (mixed and cholestatic hepatotoxicity). First case: 75-year-old woman, hyperbilirubinemia ~7 months, required two liver dialysis procedures, biopsy showing significant ductopenia and severe cholestasis; other two cases recovered within 1–2 months of pexidartinib discontinuation. No additional mixed/cholestatic hepatotoxicity cases through the January 31, 2018 cutoff. In the part 2 crossover pexidartinib group (30 patients, open-label, 800 mg/d), no bilirubin increases or signs of drug-induced cholestatic hepatotoxicity were seen.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that pexidartinib has generally manageable side effects in TGCT patients but 'also causes serious hepatotoxicity that may be fatal', and advises close monitoring for signs of liver toxicity particularly during initial treatment. Supporting data in the safety/executive sections report that in TGCT clinical studies five patients had serious hepatic adverse reactions, all within the first 2 months (reversible with discontinuation, four resolving within 2 months, one case of ductopenia and severe cholestasis resolving after 7 months); across the clinical program there were two irreversible cases of cholestatic liver injury, with one patient dying with ongoing liver toxicity and one requiring a liver transplant. These support pexidartinib as an established human cause of cholestatic drug-induced liver injury at therapeutic use (approved dose 400 mg orally twice daily / 1000 mg/day in trials).
raw_record.extra_details: Pexidartinib is a CSF1R inhibitor approved in the USA for symptomatic TGCT with severe morbidity/functional limitations not amenable to surgery, available only under a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) program; dose 400 mg orally twice daily, taken on an empty stomach at least 1 h before or 2 h after a meal. Administering with a high-fat meal approximately doubles plasma exposure and may increase hepatotoxicity risk. In ENLIVEN, Grade 3/4 events higher in pexidartinib than placebo were increased AST (10 vs 0%), ALT (10 vs 0%), ALP (7 vs 0%); any-grade AST increase 39%, ALT increase 28%. Five serious hepatic adverse reactions occurred within the first 2 months of treatment; four resolved within 2 months of discontinuation, one ductopenia/severe cholestasis resolved after 7 months. Two irreversible cases of cholestatic liver injury across the clinical program: one patient died with advanced cancer and ongoing liver toxicity, one required a liver transplant.

raw_record.support_text: Pharmacovigilance analysis identified hepatic injury signals for pexidartinib under the Investigations SOC, including Aspartate Aminotransferase Increased (ROR 28.34, 95% CI 24.76–32.43), Alanine Aminotransferase Increased (ROR 24.17, 95% CI 20.89–27.97), Gamma-Glutamyltransferase Increased (ROR 18.92, 95% CI 15.23–23.49), and Hepatic Enzyme Increased (ROR 15.64). Clinical trial data corroborated this, with 95% (133/140) of pexidartinib-treated patients experiencing hepatic adverse events, predominantly reversible low-grade dose-dependent transaminase elevations (91% of cases). However, 4% (5 cases) developed severe mixed/cholestatic liver injury requiring treatment discontinuation, critical cases necessitating liver transplantation have been documented, and FDA-mandated REMS was implemented for risk management. Mechanisms proposed include reactive intermediates from CYP3A4/UGT1A4 metabolism and CSF-1R-inhibition-related Kupffer cell dysfunction.
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated in hepatic injury in TGCT patients treated for Tenosynovial giant cell tumor. FAERS disproportionality signals (Investigations SOC): AST Increased ROR 28.34 (95% CI 24.76–32.43), ALT Increased ROR 24.17 (95% CI 20.89–27.97), GGT Increased ROR 18.92 (95% CI 15.23–23.49), Hepatic Enzyme Increased ROR 15.64 (95% CI 12.89–18.97). Clinical trial: 95% (133/140) patients had hepatic AEs; 91% reversible low-grade dose-dependent transaminase elevations; 4% (5 cases) severe mixed/cholestatic liver injury requiring treatment discontinuation; liver transplantation cases documented; FDA-mandated REMS implemented. Mechanism not fully elucidated; pexidartinib metabolized by CYP3A4 and UGT1A4 generating reactive intermediates that may directly damage hepatocytes or trigger immune responses; CSF-1R inhibition may impair Kupffer cell function promoting cholestasis/inflammation; concomitant CYP3A4 inducers/inhibitors may alter PK and exacerbate hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Among 24 patients with liver AEs suggestive of serious and potentially fatal liver injury in the current reporting period, one patient had vanishing bile duct syndrome (VBDS) considered most likely related to pexidartinib. At last follow-up, this patient showed improvement in liver function transaminases and liver transplant was not required.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case of vanishing bile duct syndrome (VBDS) attributed to pexidartinib within the TURALIO REMS liver adverse event reporting forms (LAERFs). At last follow-up the patient showed improvement in transaminases and no liver transplant was required; no death or transplant reported for this patient.

raw_record.support_text: Long-term treatment with pexidartinib was reported to have a predictable effect on hepatic aminotransferases and an unpredictable risk of serious cholestatic or mixed liver injury. Prolonged pexidartinib treatment may be associated with hepatic laboratory abnormalities, including hepatic adverse reactions, of two clinically distinct types: frequent isolated aminotransferase elevations (>90%), which were reversible with dose interruption and dose dependent, and mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity (<5%), which in clinically significant cases presented as increases in alkaline phosphatase and total bilirubin with aminotransferase elevations. All cases of serious liver toxicity presented in the first 8 weeks of treatment and all resolved in patients with TGCT.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings restricted to patients with tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT); open-label uncontrolled study with liberal dose reductions and holidays due to the non-life-threatening disease course and long cumulative therapy duration.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic adverse reactions fell into two clinically distinct types: isolated aminotransferase elevations (>90% of hepatic ARs), frequent, reversible with dose interruption and dose dependent; and mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity (<5%), which in clinically significant cases presented as increased alkaline phosphatase and total bilirubin with aminotransferase elevations. Serious liver toxicity occurred within the first 8 weeks and all cases resolved in TGCT patients. Study is open-label and uncontrolled with centralized time-blinded TVS assessment; long-term pexidartinib showed tolerable safety with no late-emerging toxicity, most frequent TEAE being hair color change.

Readministration of a small test dose reproduced the clinical and laboratory manifestations of hepatic injury, confirming the drug's hepatotoxic effect in this patient. The features conformed to the generally accepted criteria for drug-induced hepatic injury on the basis of acquired hypersensitivity, except for the absence of rash.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report with positive rechallenge: oral test dose of sulfamethoxazole (4 doses of 250 mg over 24 h) reproduced generalized malaise, nausea, back pain, chills, fever (102°F), blood eosinophilia, and elevated serum bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and transaminases; symptoms resolved within 2 days and laboratory abnormalities within 12 days. During the original episode both transaminases exceeded 200 Karmen units (glutamic pyruvic transaminase rose to 500 units after test dose), alkaline phosphatase was in the range generally seen in obstructive jaundice, and biopsy showed multiple focal areas of parenchymal necrosis and prominent bile casts. The jaundice was designated 'mixed hepatocellular' type. History of prior exposure without adverse effect, prompt recurrence on rechallenge, blood eosinophilia, and hepatic eosinophilic infiltration supported an acquired-hypersensitivity mechanism. Administered as Gantanol (Roche).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that sulfamethoxazole has occasionally been described as inducing hepatic injury. Two detailed case reports (Case no. 1, a 60-year-old woman treated with sulfamethoxazole 500 mg four times daily; Case no. 2, a 38-year-old man given sulfamethoxazole 500 mg four times a day) show drug-induced hepatitis with positive rechallenge to sulfamethoxazole, confirming sulfamethoxazole as the causal agent.
raw_record.extra_details: Case no. 1 (Fries and Siraganian): 60-year-old woman, sulfamethoxazole 500 mg with phenazopyridin-HCl 100 mg four times/day for urinary infection; hepatitis with bilirubin 8.4 mg/dl, GOT 110 IU, GPT 360 IU, alkaline phosphatase 28.0 K-A units, rash, fever, arthralgia; biopsy resembling drug hepatitis; rechallenge with sulfisoxazole (related substance) provoked recurrence, attributed to cross-allergy. Case no. 2 (Dujovne): 38-year-old man, sulfamethoxazole 500 mg four times/day before cystoscopy; developed scleral icterus, elevated alkaline phosphatase (30 B.U.), bilirubin and transaminases, liver biopsy with bile casts and focal hepatocellular necrosis; rechallenge with sulfamethoxazole 250 mg four times/day reproduced symptoms and laboratory abnormalities. Allergic features (eosinophilia) present in both.
