raw_record.support_text: A 45-year-old male was admitted to the Regional Poison Center after inadvertently ingesting a toxic resin-curing dimethyl aniline-based formulation (dimethyloaniline/dimethylaniline) at work. During hospitalization he developed massive intravascular hemolysis requiring blood products and showed signs of liver dysfunction with cholestatic liver damage and jaundice; the case is presented as evidence that severe organ damage can result from even a small amount of this toxicant. The patient stayed in the Toxicology Clinic for 3 weeks.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Occupational poisoning with inadvertent oral (peroral) exposure to a resin-curing dimethyl aniline-based formulation; treated with methylene blue, the classic antidote in such cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of an occupational intoxication; patient also had massive intravascular hemolysis requiring blood products; stayed 3 weeks in the Toxicology Clinic; jaundice attributed to cholestatic liver damage. Keywords also carry 'liver failure'. The vedant antidote methylene blue and its metabolites were not implicated as the cause.

raw_record.support_text: Triazolam (Halcion), a benzodiazepine used widely in Japan for insomnia, is reported to rarely cause hepatotoxicity identified as cholestasis. The authors describe an idiosyncratic hepatic injury attributed to triazolam, reporting a single case of fulminant hepatic failure associated with this agent.
raw_record.extra_details: 64-year-old woman with insomnia occasionally took 0.25 mg/day oral triazolam; presented with appetite loss, fatigue, jaundice (total bilirubin 6.1 mg/dl, AST 1066 IU/l, ALT 1272 IU/l), progressing to hepatic encephalopathy grade III and fulminant hepatic failure. Viral serology and autoantibodies negative (ASMA faintly positive 40-fold); drug lymphocyte stimulation test (DLST) for triazolam positive (stimulation index 287%). Underwent plasma exchange and continuous hemodiafiltration, then living-related donor liver transplant 31 days after symptom onset; recovered with nearly normal liver function at 2 years. Explanted liver (520 g, no cirrhosis) showed submassive and extensive coagulative necrosis, inflammatory cell infiltration, and pseudobileduct proliferation. Authors note cholestasis is a rare triad recorded hepatotoxicity pattern for triazolam.

raw_record.support_text: A patient with proved multiple myeloma treated with urethan at 2 to 4 gm daily for 10½ months died of hepatic failure; autopsy showed massive acute centrilobular liver necrosis resembling previously reported cases of urethan toxicity, which appeared to result from the toxic effects of this compound.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had multiple myeloma and received co-exposures including triethylene melamine, cortisone, and penicillin for pneumococcal meningitis; urethan dose 1 gm/daily restarted after interruption and raised to 4 gm daily.
raw_record.extra_details: Urethan used since 1946 for multiple myeloma with palliative response in somewhat more than 50% of cases; five cases of acute massive centrilobular liver necrosis in the prior five years; at autopsy the liver weighed 1350 gm with extensive centrilobular and midzonal necrosis; marked renal tubular injury also attributed to urethan.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that the clinical, biochemical, and histologic observations in its group of patients support the view that enflurane-associated hepatic injury does occur and may be associated with a fatal outcome in some instances, although the incidence is lower than that of halothane jaundice. The character and presumably the mechanism of the injury are stated to be similar to those of halothane, and cross-reactivity/cross-sensitization may exist for enflurane, so the authors recommend not administering halothane, methoxyflurane, or enflurane to a patient who developed evidence of hepatic injury after prior exposure to any haloalkane anesthetic.
raw_record.extra_details: Enflurane-associated hepatic injury has a centrilobular type of necrosis similar to halothane and a lower incidence than (the rare) halothane jaundice; fatal outcome possible in some instances. Comparison table lists 7 accepted published cases/10 years in clinical use for enflurane. Enflurane has little intrinsic hepatotoxic potential: in >1800 volunteers/surgical patients few hepatic abnormalities seen, though transient mild elevations of AST, ALT, LDH or GGTP were recorded in up to 58% of subjects; multiple-exposure results were conflicting (Allen/Downing reported no significant enzyme changes; Dundee reported ALT/GGTP/LDH/cholinesterase elevations in almost 25%), but hepatic toxicity was never severe. Risk of cross-reactivity/cross-sensitization with halothane and methoxyflurane.

raw_record.support_text: Based on this case report of a patient who developed hepatotoxicity following repeated enflurane anesthesia for surgery, the authors conclude it is reasonable that enflurane, like halothane and methoxyflurane, can probably rarely cause hepatotoxicity, and that patients with a history of hepatotoxicity to the latter two agents should avoid enflurane anesthesia.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient (Mrs. M.S.) had normal liver tests (SGOT, LDH, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin) in 1973, 1974, and 1976 before first enflurane exposure; tests returned to normal between exposures. After the second exposure (12/5/77) peak values included SGOT 1215, LDH 265, alkaline phosphatase 268, bilirubin 10.9; after third exposure (1/3/79) SGOT 750, bilirubin 2. Viral serologies (mono spot, HBsAg, HBs antigen, HA antibody, antibody core) were negative; no history of viral hepatitis, other hepatotoxic medication/chemical exposure, transfusions, or excessive alcohol. Liver biopsy findings resembled mild halothane or methoxyflurane hepatitis. Evidence cited: normal pre-exposure tests with return to normal between exposures, earlier symptom onset after each exposure, negative viral hepatitis workup, no other toxic exposure, and hepatitis-like biopsy; rechallenge with enflurane considered too dangerous. Postulated mechanisms include a hypersensitivity reaction and/or direct hepatotoxic effect of metabolic breakdown products. Authors recommend avoiding enflurane in patients with a history of halothane or methoxyflurane hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that triacetyldiphenolisatin is probably responsible for the adverse hepatotoxic effects observed in man, based on 21 cases reported to the Australian Registry of Adverse Reactions to Drugs, which featured active chronic hepatitis and were predominantly in middle-aged females.
raw_record.extra_details: Component of laxative preparations (e.g., Bekunis-Dragees, triacetyldiphenolisatin 14 mg, marketed since 1960). Portion of the aggregated 21-case registry series comarked to oxyphenisatin/diacetoxydiphenolisatin; injury spectrum includes active chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis; one case had a fatal outcome. Committee concluded the case 'cannot be said to be completely proven' but benefit/risk ratio compelled market withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: In a patient with chronic aggressive hepatitis, drug history revealed 15 years of intake of phenolisatin-containing 'Kissinger Pillen' (not the phenolisatin-free preparation previously assumed). After tapering azathioprine and prednisolone, serum enzymes fell to normal. On re-exposure in March 1974 with 2 days of 2×1 Laxagetten (10 mg triacetyldiphenolisatin per dragee), there was a prompt rise of bilirubin (82.1 µmol/l), GOT (155 U/l), GPT (120 U/l) and GLDH (18.6 U/l), which promptly fell again and fully normalized by day 5 after stopping the preparation. In a second patient (Example 2), regular intake until 1970 of Bekunis-dragees (which then contained triacetyldiphenolisatin) was associated with chronic active hepatitis progressing to cirrhosis; phenolisatin re-exposure produced a marked reaction (GOT 130 U/l, GPT 80 U/l, GLDH 18.6 U/l) with subsequent rapid normalization.
raw_record.extra_details: Phenolisatin-containing laxative (triacetyldiphenolisatin) associated with chronic aggressive/active hepatitis. Case 1: 15 years of 'Kissinger Pillen'; after taper of concomitant azathioprine/prednisolone enzymes normalized; diagnostic rechallenge with 2 days of 2×1 Laxagetten (10 mg triacetyldiphenolisatin/dragee) caused prompt rise in bilirubin (82.1 µmol/l, 4.8 mg/100 ml), GOT 155 U/l, GPT 120 U/l, GLDH 18.6 U/l, with prompt normalization by day 5 after stopping. Case 2: chronic active, partially necrotizing hepatitis with transition to micronodular cirrhosis and portal hypertension; intake of Bekunis-dragees (containing triacetyldiphenolisatin) until 1970; later laparoscopy showed marked liver fibrosis without portal hypertension; rechallenge gave marked reaction (GOT 130 U/l, GPT 80 U/l, GLDH 18.6 U/l) and rapid normalization. Both patients were treated with corticosteroids (and azathioprine in case 1) for the hepatitis; the rechallenge isolated the phenolisatin effect.

raw_record.support_text: In the authors' prior study of 210 patients treated with Regimen I drugs, 18% of the hepatotoxicity cases were due to rifampin.
raw_record.extra_details: 18% of hepatotoxicity cases attributed to rifampin in a prior cohort of 210 patients treated with Regimen I antituberculosis drugs; major side effects (hepatotoxicity and exanthema) incidence of 0.43/100 patients/month, consistent with lower toxicity than pyrazinamide.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 105 patients receiving rifampicin-containing anti-tuberculosis treatment, 14 developed elevated serum bilirubin. In Case 12, after liver function tests had returned to normal, isoniazid 300 mg daily for 1 week caused no upset, whereas rechallenge with rifampicin 600 mg daily raised serum bilirubin to 2.2 mg/100 ml within 1 day, directly attributing the liver injury to rifampicin. In Case 10, a shock-like hypersensitivity reaction with liver enlargement and elevated SGPT (330 units/ml) and bilirubin (3.8 mg/100 ml) recurred after rechallenge with the rifampicin–isoniazid combination, but a subsequent isoniazid-only challenge provoked no reaction, again implicating rifampicin. Overall 8 of 105 patients had skin rashes and 10 of 14 bilirubin-elevation cases had a coincident rise in alkaline phosphatase.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 12: isoniazid 300 mg/day for 1 week uneventful, then rifampicin 600 mg/day raised serum bilirubin to 2.2 mg/100 ml after 1 day; Case 10: hypersensitivity/shock reaction (SBP 80 mm Hg, rigors, fever 39.4°C) with liver enlargement, SGPT 330 units/ml, bilirubin 3.8 mg/100 ml, bile in urine, recovered with i.v. hydrocortisone; rechallenge with isoniazid 300 mg + rifampicin 300 mg reproduced the reaction (without LFT disturbance) while isoniazid-only challenge was negative; isoniazid+ethambutol then uneventful. Cases 11 and 14: rifampicin re-added later without disturbance of liver function. Liver biopsy (Cases 7, 12, 13) showed mild portal inflammatory infiltration, centrilobular Kupffer cell swelling/pigmentation, cell pleomorphism and patchy fatty change - nonspecific changes compatible with drug toxicity. Overall 14/105 patients had raised serum bilirubin; 10 of those 14 had a coincident alkaline phosphatase rise (exceeding 20 K.A. units/ml in 3). Indication: tuberculosis chemotherapy; SGPT was the more sensitive marker than SGOT.

raw_record.support_text: In the study cohort, non-viral acute liver failure (ALF) cases were caused by rifampicin in 1 patient (along with α-methyldopa in another and 3 cryptogenic cases). Rifampicin was attributed as the cause of drug-induced acute liver failure in this individual patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as the cause of 1 non-viral acute liver failure case among the ALF cohort (n=16 total).

raw_record.support_text: Rifampicin is described as relatively non-toxic, but abnormalities of liver function tests have been described, and Scheuer et al. (1974) recently reported the clinical picture and hepatic histology in 11 patients with 'rifampicin hepatitis', attributing symptomatic hepatitis to therapeutic rifampicin exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Scheuer et al. (1974), 11 patients with 'rifampicin hepatitis' including hepatic histology; liver function test abnormalities also described. Flu-like syndrome and thrombocytopenia previously seen with intermittent high-dose regimens.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that hepatotoxicity is the most common adverse effect of anti-TB treatment that leads to interruption of therapy, and frames the reintroduction of isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide therapy after hepatic injury as involving the risk of additional morbidity, attributing drug-induced hepatitis to these anti-TB drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: Anti-TB drug whose therapy is reintroduced after drug-induced hepatitis resolves; recurrence of DIH was observed on reintroduction. In this study 156/175 (89%) patients tolerated reintroduction of isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide without recurrence of DIH.

raw_record.support_text: Among 136 patients (120 treated with INH and RIF and 16 who received RIF) only 2 had RIF toxicity; one had vomiting and the other had urticaria, jaundice and drug fever. Both were readily detectable with clinical monitoring and symptoms were entirely reversible. The incidence of RIF toxicity in this experience was 1.5% (2 of 136).
raw_record.extra_details: Case of rifampicin (RIF) toxicity presenting with jaundice (icterus) together with urticaria and drug fever; symptoms entirely reversible. One of a 2-of-136 RIF toxicity case series (1.5% incidence) in an Arkansas pediatric/patient cohort; the other case had vomiting. Liver manifestation is reported as jaundice within a broader rifampicin toxicity presentation rather than a specifically characterized hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective cohort of TB patients, 38 developed DILI due to anti-TB drugs, with rifampicin identified as the causative drug in 14 patients. Patients with rifampicin-induced liver injury showed no association with mitochondrial DNA variants.
raw_record.extra_details: In 38 TB patients who developed DILI during anti-TB therapy, rifampicin was the attributed causative drug in 14. DILI defined as ALT >=5x ULN, or ALT >=3x ULN with total bilirubin >=2x ULN. No association with mitochondrial DNA variants was found for rifampicin-induced liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that of the first-line anti-tuberculosis drugs, isoniazid (INH), rifampicin (RMP) and pyrazinamide (PZA) are all hepatotoxic and increase the risk of hepatotoxicity when used together. Hepatotoxicity was defined as symptomatic elevation of liver transaminases ≥3× ULN (or ≥5× if asymptomatic).
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity incidence 0.69/100 person-months for rifampicin (RMP) in 926 adult PTB patients, of whom 111 (12.0%) developed hepatotoxicity after a median 38 days. Fewer days with RMP in the last 15-21 days before hepatotoxicity was an independent risk factor on time-dependent Cox regression. Around 3.5% overall had severe hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In this case series of 26 patients treated with daptomycin plus ceftaroline salvage therapy, characteristic antibiotic-related adverse effects requiring alternative therapy were observed, and these included hepatotoxicity and interstitial nephritis attributed to rifampin, thrombocytopenia from linezolid, eosinophilic pneumonitis from daptomycin, and hypersensitivity reactions from trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity was severe enough to require alternative (alternative antimicrobial) therapy. Rifampin was used within a daptomycin plus ceftaroline salvage regimen context; the hepatotoxicity is a separate adverse effect attributed to rifampin itself.

raw_record.support_text: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is described as the most severe side effect of antituberculosis medications including rifampin. In the Lee et al. (2019) study of 38 tuberculosis patients who experienced DILI, 14 cases were attributed to rifampin, and patients presenting with rifampin-induced liver injury were explicitly identified.
raw_record.extra_details: Lee et al. (2019) case-control study (38 TB patients with DILI, 14 attributed to rifampin, vs 38 matched non-DILI TB controls) using PacBio SMRT sequencing. No mitochondrial DNA variant associations were found in the patients presenting with rifampin-induced liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: After the patient's antituberculous treatment was switched to the first-line regimen, he coincidentally developed rifampicin-induced hepatotoxicity with aspartate aminotransferase 848 IU/L (range 15–48 IU/L), alanine aminotransferase 1067 IU/L (range 10–40 IU/L), total bilirubin 6.4 mg/dL (range 0.2–1 mg/dL) with direct bilirubin 3.5 mg/dL (range 0–0.2 mg/dL), and normal serum gamma-glutamyl transferase and alkaline phosphatase levels. This necessitated replacement of rifampicin with moxifloxacin.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case report during first-line antituberculous therapy for tuberculosis. Liver tests showed markedly elevated aminotransferases (AST 848 IU/L, ALT 1067 IU/L) and elevated bilirubin (total 6.4 mg/dL, direct 3.5 mg/dL) with normal GGT and alkaline phosphatase. Hepatotoxicity necessitated replacement of rifampicin with moxifloxacin in the subsequent non-rifampicin based regimen (isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, moxifloxacin). Rifampicin resistance genotypically suspected (rpoB S512T / Xpert probes A and B) but phenotypically pan-susceptible on DST.

raw_record.support_text: During therapy, 27 of 1,028 tuberculosis patients had hepatitis as a major toxicity, 20 during daily and seven during twice-weekly therapy. Of these hepatitis cases, 8 were attributed to rifampin and 14 to isoniazid; in five the drug could not be identified. Attribution was based on the impressions of treating physicians, with single-drug challenge confirming the offending drug in 59 of 106 total side-effect patients.
raw_record.extra_details: 8 of 27 hepatitis cases attributed to rifampin during antituberculosis therapy (table breakdown: daily therapy - jaundice 3, hepatitis/increased enzymes 4; twice-weekly therapy - jaundice 1). Attribution by treating-physician impression with selective single-drug challenge. No deaths were attributed to rifampin-associated hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: One of the more frequent adverse effects of rifampicin is liver damage. In patients with severe liver damage, the degree of tritiated thymidine incorporation in cultures to which rifampicin was added significantly increased more than in cultures with isoniazid or ethambutol, indicating a delayed hypersensitivity-type reaction and suggesting the liver damage is a hypersensitivity reaction to rifampicin. Hepatic damage due to rifampicin has been reversible in most instances.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver damage was part of 20 liver-damage cases during antituberculosis therapy (overall onset 41.3 ± 33.2 days). Liver damage noted more often with rifampicin plus isoniazid than with rifampicin plus other antitubercular drugs; rifampicin hepatotoxicity reportedly more frequent in slow acetylators of isoniazid. DLTR highest for rifampicin (mean 181 ± 38) among liver-damage cases, supporting delayed-type allergic hypersensitivity. Hepatic damage reversible in most instances and frequency relatively low compared with other drugs.

raw_record.support_text: DILI-inducing antituberculotics included INH, RFP (rifampicin), PZA and ethambutol (EMB), mostly in combinations, based on a ranking of 424 DILI patients (antituberculotics 72 patients, 17.0%).
raw_record.extra_details: Antituberculotic, listed as RFP. Antituberculotics accounted for 72 patients (17.0%). Mostly used as combinations INH+RFP+PZA+EMB, INH+RFP+EMB and INH+EMB.

raw_record.support_text: Rifampicin was among the specific drugs implicated as a cause of hepatic injury in a follow-up study of 44 patients with drug-induced hepatotoxicity; patients with abnormal hepatic evaluation at follow-up had previously taken rifampicin.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported in the 44-patient drug-induced hepatotoxicity cohort followed a median of 5 years; continuation of the implicated drug >6 months after an abnormal index biopsy was the factor most associated with abnormal follow-up.

raw_record.support_text: In the exposure-safety analysis of the S31/A5349 trial, 5 participants (<1%, n=722) with increased rifampicin exposure had serum total bilirubin of 3×ULN or greater. The authors explicitly note that rifampicin is known to affect bilirubin uptake or clearance, which typically is not associated with hepatotoxicity, and caution that the association is driven by a small subset of participants.
raw_record.extra_details: In 5 participants (<1%, n=722) of the S31/A5349 trial, increased rifampicin exposure was associated with serum total bilirubin ≥3×ULN; this bilirubin elevation is attributed to rifampicin affecting bilirubin uptake or clearance and is stated to typically not be associated with hepatotoxicity. Standard treatment context of 600 mg daily rifampicin within a 6-month regimen for tuberculosis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that the most important rifampicin toxicity is liver impairment, although serious hepatic toxicity is rare (< 1% of patients). Study drug (rifampicin/placebo) was withdrawn without unblinding if significant liver toxicity was observed (blood AST/ALT > 5x ULN without other probable causes) and for grade 4 liver toxicity (blood AST/ALT > 10x ULN) regardless of probable cause, with dose reduction for less severe liver dysfunction. Rifampicin-related hepatic toxicity requires no specific treatment other than withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: Description from a randomized trial of oral/i.v. rifampicin. Serious hepatic toxicity reported rare (<1% of patients). Liver toxicity monitoring/withdrawal criteria cited: withdrawal for AST/ALT >5x ULN without other probable causes and for grade 4 liver toxicity (>10x ULN) regardless of cause; dose reduction for less severe liver dysfunction. No specific treatment needed other than drug withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses rifampin hepatotoxicity in humans, noting that the mechanism of rifampin toxicity in the liver is unknown and referencing one published study that reported lymphocytic infiltration in a patient who died of rifampin hepatotoxicity. This is put in the context of the authors' in vitro finding that rifampin augments production of the proinflammatory mediators NO and IL-8 in HepG2 cells, which they propose may partly underlie rifampin-related liver toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Human attribution rests on a cited case report of a patient who died of rifampin hepatotoxicity with lymphocytic infiltration; the mechanism of rifampin liver toxicity is stated to be unknown. The paper's primary data are in vitro: rifampin increased cytokine-induced NO and IL-8 and constitutive IL-8 and IL-1beta in human hepatic HepG2 cells, with iNOS mRNA/protein upregulation. In rats, co-administration of rifampin with isoniazid produced hepatotoxicity accompanied by increased total liver nitrite.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that Cases 1 and 2 demonstrate good evidence of liver damage due to rifampicin. In Patient 1 (a 30-year-old woman treated for tuberculous peritonitis with streptomycin, isoniazid, rifampicin and prednisolone), jaundice developed after 2 weeks of therapy with bilirubin 7.0 mg/100 ml and A.S.T. 240 I.U./litre; a second biopsy showed hepatitis with cholestasis closely resembling viral hepatitis, and liver-function tests returned to normal within a week after rifampicin was stopped. In Patient 2, a second biopsy showed widespread liver-cell swelling, acidophilic bodies, increased mitoses and mild fatty change with raised serum bilirubin and A.S.T.; rifampicin was resumed uneventfully later.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Anti-tuberculosis combination therapy with co-administered streptomycin, isoniazid, prednisolone, ethambutol and pyridoxine.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient 1: 30-year-old woman, jaundice after 2 weeks, bilirubin 7.0 mg/100 ml, A.S.T. 240 I.U./litre, biopsy showed hepatitis with cholestasis resembling viral hepatitis with a few fat vacuoles; recovered within a week of stopping rifampicin. Patient 2: 64-year-old man drinking 25-30 pints of beer weekly, raised bilirubin and A.S.T., biopsy showed liver-cell swelling, variation in nuclear size/staining, increased mitoses, many acidophilic bodies, mild fatty change; rifampicin resumed on Nov 16, 1971 with no complications.

raw_record.support_text: In this case series of 6 HIV/TB coinfected patients with rifampicin-associated DRESS, rechallenge reactions to rifampicin produced hepatitis with eosinophilia in cases 1-3, 5, and 6 (4 of 6 cases), with initial DRESS presentations showing ALT >5x ULN in most cases. Isoniazid rechallenge produced hepatitis in cases 1, 2, and 4; moxifloxacin produced hepatitis in case 2; and in case 6 hepatitis was attributed to moxifloxacin and/or terizidone and/or ethionamide with unresolved co-attribution.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: DRESS syndrome hypersensitivity reaction; HIV/TB coinfected patients; rechallenge setting with clinical/laboratory monitoring for 96 h.
raw_record.extra_details: Rechallenge reactions to rifampicin: rash 6/6, itch and eosinophilia 5/6, hepatitis 4/6, edema 3/6, fever/hypotension/diarrhea once; CTCAE severity mild-moderate-severe across cases; 19/88 (22%) reacted to rifampicin in the parent RCT; all 6 successfully switched to therapeutic-dose rifabutin. Initial DRESS presentations included ALT >5x ULN in 5/6 cases. Discussion references prior reports of rifampicin-associated hepatotoxicity with successful switch to rifabutin.

raw_record.support_text: A 62-year-old woman developed combined hepatic and renal toxicity after three intermittent doses of rifampicin, having previously taken rifampicin 450 mg daily and sodium aminosalicylate regularly for 16 months. The authors state this is apparently the first report of combined hepatic and renal toxicity due to rifampicin and the first to incriminate rifampicin taken alone, concluding that intermittent rifampicin therapy can cause acute hepatic and renal failure and that both toxic effects are reversible.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intermittent (non-continuous) rifampicin dosing taken after 16 months of regular daily therapy; co-medication sodium aminosalicylate had been stopped 6 days earlier and was not implicated; no pre-existing renal or liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Case in a 62-year-old woman with active pulmonary tuberculosis. Rifampicin was taken as three intermittent doses (three tablets each); first intermittent dose produced chills, nausea, vomiting within 2 hours resolving after 24 hours; subsequent doses produced nausea/malaise and acute right loin pain with nausea/vomiting. On admission: jaundice, fever 38 C, bilirubin 4.3 mg/100 ml, prothrombin time 60%, alkaline phosphatase 165 IU, SGOT 1,450 IU/ml, indicating hepatocellular damage and early acute renal failure without haemolysis. Liver function returned to normal after 5 days; hepatic and renal effects reversible. Paper notes possible immune mediation via circulating antirifampicin antibody; influenza-like syndrome with anuric acute tubular necrosis reported. Comment section states intermittent rifampicin therapy can cause acute renal and hepatic failure. Clinical phenotype = acute hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of studies of rifampin for latent tuberculosis, the paper reports the absence of hepatotoxicity: in the Hong Kong randomized trial none of the patients who discontinued due to adverse reactions developed hepatotoxicity; in the homeless Boston cohort there were no reports of hepatotoxicity; among 157 adolescents, 18 interrupted temporarily and two discontinued permanently; in a recent randomized comparison, 2/58 (3%) rifampin recipients permanently discontinued due to adverse events and none developed hepatitis; and in another observational study there were no cases of drug-induced hepatotoxicity among the 261 patients who received rifampin.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Latent tuberculosis infection treated for latent infection; tolerability assessments in general adult populations (HIV-seronegative).
raw_record.extra_details: Multiple cohorts: Hong Kong randomized trial (patients discontinuing due to adverse drug reaction, none developed hepatotoxicity); homeless cohort in Boston (7/49 discontinued due to adverse effects, no hepatotoxicity reported); 157 tuberculin skin-test positive adolescents (18 interrupted temporarily, 2 discontinued permanently); randomized comparison of 4 months rifampin vs 9 months isoniazid (2/58, 3%, permanent discontinuation, none developed hepatitis); retrospective observational study where hepatotoxicity rates were 0.08% for rifampin vs 1.8% for isoniazid (p<0.001); another observational study with no drug-induced hepatotoxicity among 261 rifampin recipients.

raw_record.support_text: This single centre report describes three cases of significant hepatitis associated with rifampicin therapy used as an antipruritic agent in patients with primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC), a cholestatic liver disease. Two patients developed significant impairment of hepatic synthetic function, necessitating liver transplantation in one case. The authors report that rifampicin caused significant hepatitis in 7.3% (95% CI 2.5-19.4%) of patients treated for cholestatic liver disease in their centre, and note that prior reports of rifampicin hepatitis in tuberculosis patients were confounded by concurrent hepatotoxic antitubercular therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with cholestatic liver disease (primary biliary cirrhosis) receiving rifampicin as second-line antipruritic therapy; two of the three affected patients had significant impairment of hepatic synthetic function.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis occurred in 7.3% of 41 patients treated with rifampicin (95% CI 2.5-19.4%); three cases identified via a 50% increase in liver function tests (bilirubin, ALT, or ALP). One case required liver transplantation due to impaired synthetic function. Authors state these are the first reports of impaired hepatic synthetic function due to rifampicin monotherapy; prior tuberculosis-treatment reports were confounded by concurrent hepatotoxic antitubercular drugs.

raw_record.support_text: In a real-world cohort of patients with cholestatic pruritus treated with rifampicin, 95% of patients did not develop any liver injury, while 5% developed rifampicin-associated hepatitis. All patients who developed hepatitis recovered after drug cessation with only one patient requiring further intervention (corticosteroids and hospital admission); none developed life-threatening complications despite some having advanced liver disease at baseline.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with cholestatic liver disease receiving rifampicin for cholestatic pruritus; many had advanced liver disease and marked baseline jaundice (bilirubin >100 μmol/L); concurrent nonrifampicin medications (median 5) including long-term antibiotics, so drug-drug interactions could not be excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: 105 patients in cohort; median time to onset of hepatitis was 70 days (longer than the ~15-30 days reported in TB cohorts); two cases occurred after the period of biochemical monitoring suggested by recent guidelines; two of three rifampicin-induced hepatitis cases reported by Prince et al occurred at 11 and 14 months after initiation; no protocol liver-biochemistry monitoring, so subclinical cases may have been missed, potentially underestimating the rate; oral vitamin K co-prescribed for icteric patients; one patient required corticosteroids and hospital admission; no life-threatening complications or deaths.

raw_record.support_text: In a recent issue, Webb et al evaluated rifampicin-associated hepatotoxicity in a real-world cohort of 105 patients with established liver disease of mixed aetiology. With a median treatment duration of 131 days, 5 (4.8%) patients developed rifampicin-induced hepatitis at a median of 97 days after commencing the drug, and in all cases the hepatitis resolved after drug cessation. The accompanying editorial notes rifampicin is used as a second-line agent for cholestatic pruritus and that a main clinician concern is its potential and unpredictable hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A 76-year-old woman with Parkinson's disease developed hepatotoxicity associated with entacapone use. She had been started on entacapone (200 mg five times/day) 3 weeks before admission because of falls, and developed nausea, anorexia, and malaise. On admission she had scleral icterus and mild right upper quadrant tenderness, with total bilirubin 40 mmol/L (normal 2–20), ALT 104 U/L, GGT 328 U/L, ALP 238 U/L, and LDH 1,565 U/L; viral, autoimmune, and metabolic serology and abdominal ultrasound were normal. Entacapone was discontinued on the 4th hospital day and liver function tests improved, with ALT normalizing on day 14 and ALP/GGT 4 weeks later. She refused a supervised rechallenge test.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported case of entacapone-induced hepatotoxicity; 76-year-old woman, entacapone 200 mg five times/day for ~3 weeks; jaundice (scleral icterus), epigastric symptoms; peak GGT 487 U/L, ALT 116 U/L, ALP 293 U/L on day 4; resolution on dechallenge (dose halved for 2 days before stopping); no rechallenge. Concurrent medications included levodopa 200 mg/benserazide 50 mg, amiloride/hydrochlorothiazide, verapamil, and rofecoxib. Background: significant liver toxicity not reported among ~80,000 entacapone-treated patients and entacapone reported not to cause hepatotoxicity in experimental studies, human trials, and postmarketing surveillance.

raw_record.support_text: The paper highlights flupirtine's hepatotoxic potential: a 2011 international multi-centre study in patients with overactive bladder syndrome was prematurely discontinued due to unexpected liver enzyme elevation in 14 of 84 flupirtine-exposed patients, and a 2011 publication reported six patients with flupirtine-induced liver injury (FILI), one of whom underwent liver transplantation due to acute liver failure. The present study adds seven FILI patients from the Berlin Case-control Surveillance Study (FAKOS, 2002–2011, standardized causality assessment, RUCAM applied) and reviews severe flupirtine-associated hepatotoxicity cases in the BfArM ADR database; EMA has requested risk minimisation measures including a maximum treatment duration of 2 weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: 2011 trial (overactive bladder) discontinued for liver enzyme elevations in 14/84 flupirtine-exposed patients; six published FILI cases with one liver transplantation for acute liver failure; study adds 7 FAKOS patients and reviews severe cases from the BfArM ADR database; EMA requested risk minimisation (max treatment duration 2 weeks). RUCAM causality scoring and R-ratio-based pattern classification are described as methods but specific per-case scores/patterns are not given in this window.

raw_record.support_text: The analgesic flupirtine has been linked to cases of severe idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (sFILI). The authors retrospectively examined whether N-acetylcysteine (NAC) and glucocorticoid therapy are effective in managing sFILI.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe flupirtine-induced idiosyncratic liver injury (sFILI) described in a retrospective cohort of 21 sFILI cases treated with combined NAC-infusion and oral prednisolone, compared with an external cohort of 30 sFILI cases not receiving the antidote. On admission, patients had ALT, AST and bilirubin elevations up to 90-, 35- and 30-fold of ULN, respectively; average INR was 2.2 and 50% of patients had a high MELD score of >=25, including 5 cases with MELD 28-32. Combined NAC/prednisolone treatment was well tolerated and led to significant ALT, AST and INR improvements within 2 [days].

raw_record.support_text: This case series consists of seven patients with drug-induced hepatotoxicity, where the flupirtine causality was judged as at least 'probable' using the RUCAM scale, contributing information on flupirtine-induced liver injury (FILI). The paper also reports 248 reports of severe flupirtine-associated hepatotoxicity in the BfArM ADR database from 1991 until March 2012, with jaundice the most common symptom (n=69), acute liver failure in 38 cases, and death in eight. The hepatocellular pattern of liver injury was described as a key feature of FILI.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 7 patients from the Berlin Case-control Surveillance Study with flupirtine hepatotoxicity, causality at least 'probable' on RUCAM; hepatocellular liver-injury pattern (R ratios 20.3-79.6, all HC type); jaundice and ALF common; 3 patients had elevated autoantibody titres but immune-mediated toxicity was considered unlikely given absence of hypersensitivity symptoms, normal eosinophils, and long time to onset. BfArM ADR database (1991 to March 2012): 248 severe flupirtine-associated hepatotoxicity reports, 199 female (80.2%), approx. 4:1 female-to-male ratio (vs ~2:1 intake ratio, so female sex may be a partial risk factor), age 40-69 predominant; time to onset <1 week in 9% (n=13) of 148 reports with data; symptoms: jaundice 69 (27.8%), ALF 38 (15.3%), nausea 35 (14.1%), fatigue 14 (5.6%); death in 8 cases (3.2%). Corroborates Puls et al.

raw_record.support_text: The review cites a 2018 retrospective cohort (Borlak, 2018) comparing patients with flupirtine-induced liver injury who received combined NAC plus prednisolone versus those who did not, concluding the combined treatment resulted in significant improvements in ALT, AST, and INR within 2 weeks and that treated patients resolved more rapidly than those receiving standard of care.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective cohort of 51 patients (Borlak, 2018). Patients with flupirtine-induced drug-induced acute liver injury treated with combined NAC + prednisolone showed significant improvements in ALT, AST, and INR within 2 weeks and resolved more rapidly than those on standard of care.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that in 10 cases of idiosyncratic DILI (IDILI) caused by the centrally acting non-opioid analgesic flupirtine, the use of which has been restricted by the EMA because of hepatotoxicity, MCSFR1 levels were considerably higher than in 19 cases of APAP-induced DILI, despite ALT levels being markedly higher in APAP-induced DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: Flupirtine (centrally acting non-opioid analgesic) caused 10 cases of idiosyncratic DILI (IDILI). Its use has been restricted by the EMA because of hepatotoxicity. In these cases MCSFR1 levels were considerably higher than in 19 APAP-induced DILI cases, despite markedly higher ALT in the APAP group. SAFE-T Consortium data.

raw_record.support_text: In the genetic-association table (Table 4), flupirtine is listed with DILI as the adverse reaction for HLA-DRB1*1601 in Germans (OR 18.7, 6 DILI cases/39,689 general population, Nicoletti et al., 2016). Paragraph 40 reiterates the flupirtine association with the DRB1*1601-DQB1*0502 haplotype and OR 18.7 as a notable HLA biomarker for idiosyncratic DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: HLA-DRB1*1601 association with DILI (OR 18.7, 6 DILI cases/39,689 general population; Nicoletti et al. 2016). Described in paragraph 40 as the DRB1*1601-DQB1*0502 haplotype with OR 18.7.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 154 DILI patients, flupirtine was one of six drugs with more than 5 cases analyzed specifically and showed 16 significant test differences, tied with APAP for the highest number among the drug groups.
raw_record.extra_details: Flupirtine cases had the lowest ApoA1 (median 0.27 g/L) and haptoglobin (0.10 g/L) and the highest bilirubin (335 umol/L) and FibroTest (0.99) compared with the other drug classes; 16 significant (Bonferroni) baseline test differences.

raw_record.support_text: The authors concluded that, after excluding other potential aetiologies, DILI due to flupirtine was the most probable cause of acute liver failure in this case. The RUCAM score for flupirtine as the potential DILI trigger was 6 (5–90 days time frame, other causes ruled out, reaction labelled), making it a probable cause (between 6 and 8).
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report culminating in acute liver failure. RUCAM score 6 for flupirtine as DILI trigger (points for 5-90 days time frame, other causes ruled out, reaction labelled), graded probable (6-8). Flupirtine-induced DILI shows a hepatocellular-type pattern (R values commonly higher than 20) with extensive perivenular necrosis; histological extent of necrosis correlates with serum transaminase levels. Latency from drug intake to injury ranges from 11 days to 24 months. HLA-DRB1*16:01-DQB1*05:02 was recently identified as a risk factor for flupirtine-induced DILI (genotyping not available in this case). Prognosis usually favourable, but ALF requiring liver transplantation has been described. Co-medication with Hypericum perforatum was considered an unlikely primary injury trigger (RUCAM of 2), though its role in interfering with other medication could not be completely excluded. Patient consent obtained.

raw_record.support_text: Within the HLA study comprising 11 RUCAM-based cases of iDILI caused by flupirtine, the proposal was made that the liver injury likely involves an inappropriate T cell response within the liver, supporting the concept that the adaptive immune system is involved in the pathogenesis of this iDILI.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 RUCAM-based iDILI cases; causality assessed via RUCAM; proposed mechanism is an inappropriate T cell response within the liver, indicating involvement of the adaptive immune system.

raw_record.support_text: Six cases of flupirtine-associated liver injury (4 female, 2 male, aged 48-78) were described. One patient on flupirtine monotherapy presented with jaundice, hepatic encephalopathy and coagulopathy, requiring orthotopic liver transplantation for acute liver failure. Three presented with jaundice and mild coagulopathy without encephalopathy, and two were asymptomatic with elevated aminotransferases on routine controls. After discontinuation of flupirtine, aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin normalized. None had preexisting liver disease. One patient was accidentally re-exposed to flupirtine after 4 years and again developed elevated aminotransferases.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Six adults aged 48-78 (mean 56); five of six were taking concurrent medications with flupirtine the only common agent; one patient received flupirtine monotherapy; no preexisting liver disease.

raw_record.support_text: A 68-year-old man was started on dapagliflozin (together with atorvastatin). Both drugs were held at discharge from a first admission and serum ALT and total bilirubin rapidly improved; resumption of atorvastatin and dapagliflozin led to a second episode of hepatitis with higher serum ALT. After discontinuation, liver biochemistries again improved and atorvastatin was safely reintroduced with no recurrent hepatitis, indicating dapagliflozin as the culprit.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 68-year-old man; RECAM (Revised Electronic Causality Assessment Method) total score 9 interpreted as 'highly likely/highly probable' (R-value 25, Domain 1A time-to-onset 4, dechallenge 3, Liver Tox Likelihood 1, exclusion of other causes -6, additional optional data 7). Rechallenge reproduced hepatitis with a higher serum ALT; atorvastatin co-suspect was safely reintroduced without recurrent hepatitis, leaving dapagliflozin as the sole attributed cause. Mechanism unclear; proposed via glucuronidation by UGT1A9 and/or binding to SGLT1 receptors in the liver; low incidence noted.

raw_record.support_text: The clinical presentation of propafenone hepatotoxicity was cholestatic hepatitis in the paper's two patients and in seven previously reported cases (case series of eight total). The injury affected both sexes, presented with jaundice in most patients, had latency periods of 2-6 weeks (28 weeks in one patient), and liver disease faded gradually after drug discontinuation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: null
raw_record.extra_details: Eight cases of propafenone hepatotoxicity presented (2 new patients plus 7 previously reported). Presents as cholestatic hepatitis with jaundice in most; latency 2-6 weeks except one case at 28 weeks; injury resolved progressively after drug discontinuation. ALT ranged 22-501 IU/L, ALP up to 1512 IU/L, gamma-GT up to 890 IU/L; eosinophilia (2-11%) in most cases suggested a hypersensitivity reaction as the pathogenic mechanism, though neither of the paper's two patients had eosinophilia. One patient had transient ANA positivity. Liver biopsies showed portal tract enlargement with mononuclear infiltrates, bile duct proliferation with injury, ballooning of hepatocytes, and cholestasis with biliary thrombi. Clinical abnormalities improved after propafenone discontinuation even while the patient continued digitoxin and enalapril, supporting propafenone as the cause. Authors note relatively low frequency, making routine ALT monitoring unnecessary, but abdominal symptoms or jaundice should prompt hepatotoxicity consideration.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report an acute cholestatic syndrome temporally associated with administration of the antiarrhythmic drug propafenone, believing the drug was involved due to a close time relationship between drug administration and onset of liver injury and because rechallenge with propafenone after partial recovery elicited a new significant increase in serum GGT and alkaline phosphatase activities.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report of acute cholestatic syndrome with jaundice. Onset after 2-4 weeks latency from starting the drug; positive rechallenge after a 2-week course produced a new rise in serum GGT (to 901 IU/L) and alkaline phosphatase (to 615 IU/L). Liver tests reverted to normal within 5 months. Patient also continuously took antidiabetic drugs and enalapril during the whole period. Authors note propafenone hepatotoxicity is very rare (only three prior published cases) and suggest accumulation of toxic hepatic metabolites and enterohepatic recirculation may account for the injury.

raw_record.support_text: Our patient developed cholestatic liver injury approximately 2 weeks after starting propafenone, with development of jaundice and pruritus within 3 to 4 weeks thereafter. Three months after withdrawal, the patient was asymptomatic and all liver tests had normalised. The paper frames propafenone as a very rare cause of hepatotoxicity (DILI) and recommends discontinuing the drug when cholestatic and/or hepatocellular injury is suspected.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic liver injury with jaundice and pruritus, latency approximately 2 weeks from drug initiation; jaundice/pruritus developed 3-4 weeks after start; complete resolution ~3 months after withdrawal; RUCAM causality assessment performed (criteria tabulated: onset 5-90 days +2, ALT decrease >=50% within 8 days of withdrawal +3, age >=55 +1, all-cause exclusion +2); positive dechallenge; concurrent C. freundii gastroenteritis with sepsis/hypotension and meropenem use were evaluated and excluded as causes. Prior case reports show cholestatic injury with jaundice, latency generally 2-8 weeks; liver biopsies described portal tract enlargement with lymphocytic/monocyte/macrophage/granulocyte infiltrates, bile duct proliferation, hepatocyte ballooning, and macrovesicular steatosis; proposed mechanism includes hepatic toxic metabolite accumulation (p-quinone intermediates) and enterohepatic recirculation.

raw_record.support_text: The clinical picture observed in 1979 and 1981 after propafenone treatment (Propafenon) is described as speaking for a drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis. A drug-allergic hepatitis was considered compatible with the liver enzyme patterns; other potentially hepatotoxic drugs, alcohol, extrahepatic obstruction, and viral hepatitis were excluded. Lymphocyte stimulation tests performed 2 weeks later using therapeutically effective propafenone serum concentrations showed a clear proliferation rate, which the authors state confirms this diagnosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report (events in 1979 and 1981). Liver enzyme patterns compatible with drug-allergic hepatitis; chronic active hepatitis with cholestatic component and chronic non-destructive cholangitis excluded by course; alcoholic liver damage and extrahepatic obstruction ruled out; viral hepatitis excluded serologically. In-vitro lymphocyte stimulation (metabolite serum or propafenone) of patient lymphocytes yielded 3.6-fold and 2.9-fold proliferation rates versus a control person, supporting the drug-allergic diagnosis. Propafenone has high affinity for lung and liver tissue. The reaction is rare but should be considered in differential diagnosis of unclear cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: A 76-year-old male developed a cholestatic hepatitis and an unusual pacing-threshold elevation of about 425%, coincidentally 5 weeks after VVI-pacemaker implantation. Lead dislocation, myocardial infarction, metabolic disorder, biliary obstruction, and liver infection were excluded as causes. Most probably both disorders were caused by propafenone (450 mg/day); withdrawal of the drug resulted in normalization of elevated enzyme and threshold levels.

The present retrospective study, as well as other retrospective analyses, suggests that the risk of clinically significant hepatotoxicity from caspofungin is low, and concurrent use was not observed to pose a clinically significant hepatotoxicity risk.

The authors concluded that fondaparinux was considered the probable cause of hepatotoxicity, and in the discussion stated that the role of fondaparinux was highly likely since signs occurred soon after introduction and disappeared rapidly after drug withdrawal.

raw_record.extra_details: Fondaparinux (Arixtra) 2 mg/day given for a left-sided axillary veno-lymphatic malformation-related thrombosis. Onset of nausea and vomiting ~30 h after first fondaparinux dose. Hepatotoxicity evidenced by a 15-fold increase in ALT (509 IU/L) and AST (720 IU/L), and 5-fold increase in GGT (161 IU/L); ALP (278) and bilirubin (10 umol/L) remained normal. Signs resolved within 5 days after discontinuation with return to baseline ALT/AST. Viral serology (Hep A/B/C, herpes, adenovirus, enterovirus, parvovirus B19, HHV6, HHV8) negative; liver ultrasound normal without hepatic thrombosis.

raw_record.support_text: In 189 of 198 validated certain/probable IH cases the drug relationship per the updated CIOMS scale was at least 'possible'; 177 different drugs/herbs were identified as related to liver injury. In nine patients there was unintentional reexposure with the suspected drug, leading to a positive rechallenge in five, for amiodarone, ramipril, acetylsalicylic acid, tamoxifen, and mesalazine.
raw_record.extra_details: Positive rechallenge on unintentional reexposure with the suspected drug; case rated at least 'possible' on the updated CIOMS scale. Exact causality grade within the study was not reported.

raw_record.support_text: The patient developed raised liver enzyme activity, chronic hepatitis lesions, raised serum IgG, and anti-nuclear and anti-smooth muscle autoantibodies after 21 months of mesalazine treatment; idiopathic autoimmune hepatitis was reasonably excluded. Liver tests and serum IgG became normal and autoantibodies disappeared without immunosuppressive therapy, and the liver disease never relapsed. The authors conclude mesalazine probably caused chronic hepatitis and autoimmune manifestations in this patient; no other cause of liver disease was detected. Simvastatin was withdrawn without improvement, and the five remaining drugs did not prevent recovery once mesalazine was discontinued.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported after 21 months of mesalazine treatment. Raised liver enzymes, chronic hepatitis lesions, elevated serum IgG, anti-nuclear (peak 1:500) and anti-smooth muscle (peak 1:200) autoantibodies. Liver biopsy at three weeks after mesalazine discontinuation showed portal and periportal fibrosis, mild cholangiolar proliferation, mild perisinusoidal fibrosis, mononuclear portal infiltrates with some neutrophils and rare eosinophils, piecemeal necrosis around portal fibrosis, and acidophilic bodies surrounded by inflammatory cells; mild iron deposits in Kupffer cells; wedge-free hepatic vein gradient moderately increased (6 mm Hg; N 1-4). Liver tests improved quickly after mesalazine withdrawal and returned to normal by 12 Aug 1997 without relapse; autoantibodies declined and disappeared, IgG normalized. Patient had received six other drugs; simvastatin was withdrawn earlier without improvement and the remaining five drugs continued did not prevent recovery after mesalazine cessation. Patient never had inflammatory bowel disease.

raw_record.support_text: Mesalazine is itself capable of causing serious liver injury, so continuing it during an IBD flare may worsen the clinical course; chronic liver damage can develop, and adverse drug reactions should be considered in patients with persistent fever and clinical deterioration despite standard treatment. The associated case report described mesalazine-induced granulomatous hepatitis in which the associated fever disappeared within 3 days, both on initial cessation and again after rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Used for inflammatory bowel disease; case reported as mesalazine-induced granulomatous hepatitis with associated drug fever that resolved within 3 days on cessation and recurred after rechallenge; authors advise discontinuing mesalazine once liver dysfunction occurs to prevent permanent liver damage and note that chronic liver damage can develop.

raw_record.support_text: The authors performed a PubMed literature review (January 2023) for case reports of liver dysfunction, hepatotoxicity, or liver injury caused by 5-ASA (mesalazine), excluded cases not associated with 5-ASA-induced liver injury, and identified 7 published case reports plus their own case (8 total). All events occurred after initiation of 5-ASA, with onset ranging from 1 week to 8 months; one case was classified as idiosyncratic DILI (allergic type) and the others as idiosyncratic DILI (metabolic type). The paper concludes that although mesalamine is generally safe, serious 5-ASA-related liver injury can occur and regular monitoring of liver function is needed.
raw_record.extra_details: 8 human case reports of DILI attributed to 5-ASA (mesalazine) at therapeutic doses (800-4,000 mg/day); onset 1 week to 8 months after initiation. One case classified as idiosyncratic DILI (allergic type; Hautekeete et al., CTCAE grade 4), the rest as idiosyncratic DILI (metabolic type). CTCAE grades ranged 3-4. Patients had ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease; treatment included withdrawal of 5-ASA, PSL, UDCA, and SNMC. Literature search limited by small number of reports suggesting possible publication bias; pathogenesis and timing not well understood. Authors note 5-ASA-related DILI is typically classified as a blood-test abnormality with a median onset of about 55 days (~2 months), but can present in various ways including mimicking IBD exacerbations or lupus-like symptoms.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that, despite the long duration of mesalazine therapy before the reaction, the jaundice, eosinophilia, and thrombocytopenia in their patient were adverse reactions of mesalazine therapy. They did not rechallenge the patient with mesalazine because of the fear of inducing a severe reaction, and liver function tests returned to normal and remained normal over the following 3 years.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: a patient (with previously described colitis, subsequently controlled on azathioprine) developed jaundice, eosinophilia, and thrombocytopenia as concurrent adverse reactions to 5-ASA (mesalazine) therapy with onset many years after starting the drug; believed to be the first reported case of concurrent hepatotoxicity, thrombocytopenia, and eosinophilia from 5-ASA with such a delayed onset. Not rechallenged due to fear of severe reaction; liver tests improved over the following week and returned to normal, remaining normal 3 years later. In other published case reports the duration of therapy before an adverse reaction varied from a few days to 2 years. The authors advise considering 5-ASA-induced toxicity in any patient taking 5-ASA irrespective of treatment duration.

raw_record.support_text: Mesalazine (a slow release formulation of 5-aminosalicylic acid) caused liver dysfunction and hepatitis in humans. In a randomised trial of coated mesalazine (115 patients) versus sulphasalazine (105 patients), mesalazine caused liver injury in three patients and sulphasalazine in four. Across 11 published clinical trials reporting liver test abnormalities, the global incidence of mesalazine-induced liver dysfunction was 2.8%.
raw_record.extra_details: Slow release formulation of 5-aminosalicylic acid. In the randomised trial mesalazine total ADR incidence was 14% vs 24% for sulphasalazine. Eight published individual cases of mesalazine-induced hepatitis (three biopsy-proven) occurred 6 days to 1 year after treatment onset; among seven assessable patients the liver profile was cytolytic in four, mixed in one, and cholestatic in two; two cases had associated immunoallergic manifestations. All previously reported patients had acute hepatitis; the presenting patient developed chronic liver disease because mesalazine was continued for eight months after initial detection of injury. Higher 5-aminosalicylic bioavailability with mesalazine than with sulphasalazine may increase adverse-effect probability; the mechanism is undetermined but possibly involves metabolic activation to covalent binding species.

raw_record.support_text: The case report describes a patient with ulcerative colitis who developed biopsy-proven hepatic injury (granulomatous hepatitis) following systemic therapy with mesalazine. After mesalazine was discontinued, the fever resolved completely and liver enzymes declined and subsequently normalized; the granulomatous hepatitis was treated with a tapered steroid course (prednisone 40 mg/day initial). A systemic rechallenge was not performed to avoid harming the patient, but the patient tolerated mesalazine suppositories later, remaining well with normal liver enzymes over 12 months of follow-up.
raw_record.extra_details: Biopsy-proven granulomatous hepatitis; fever, elevated liver enzymes and inflammatory signs; dechallenge led to complete resolution and normalization of liver enzymes over 12 months of follow-up; treated with tapered prednisone (initial 40 mg/day) over 6 weeks; systemic rechallenge not performed; subsequent mesalazine suppository therapy tolerated without recurrence. Patient had ulcerative colitis (IBD indication). Mechanism of injury not clearly understood.

raw_record.support_text: A case report by Watanabe et al. described a patient with ulcerative colitis who, on day 98 of mesalazine (5-ASA) therapy at 2.4 g/day, developed an increase of transaminases >5 times normal and a significant increase in cholestasis indices. After discontinuing 5-ASA and excluding all other causes of DILI, the case was defined as 5-ASA-induced DILI, and liver enzymes normalized 24 days after drug suspension.
raw_record.extra_details: Also known as 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA); most prescribed aminosalicylate for ulcerative colitis/Crohn's disease. Hepatic effects range from mild asymptomatic increase in hepatic cytolysis to idiosyncratic cholestasis, mostly resolving on discontinuation; incidence low because the drug is minimally absorbed. In 0-4% a rise in liver enzymes is detected; in an RCT 1% of patients on 1.5 g/day had hypertransaminasemia that resolved on discontinuation and recrudesced on rechallenge 4 weeks later. Case report: day 98 of 2.4 g/day, transaminases >5x normal plus elevated cholestasis indices, defined as 5-ASA-induced DILI after excluding other causes, with normalization 24 days after withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: This case report presents a patient with Crohn's disease who developed severe but fully reversible cholestatic hepatic injury following the prescription of mesalazine. The diagnosis is the most probable one, since other causes leading to the observed histomorphological alterations of the liver could be excluded. After long-term mesalazine therapy was halted, the patient's nausea and abdominal pain disappeared, and all liver tests returned to normal within 6 weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report in a patient with Crohn's disease on long-term mesalazine therapy. Liver biopsy 6 days after admission showed well-preserved lobular architecture with prominent perivenous canalicular and cytoplasmic hepatocellular cholestasis, occasional acidophil bodies, frequent hepatocellular mitosis, Kupffer cell hyperplasia, minimal focal mononuclear infiltrate, mild portal edema, moderate mononuclear portal infiltration with few eosinophils, and mild degenerative changes in small bile duct epithelium. Medication halted at admission; neither 5-ASA nor acetylated 5-ASA detectable in plasma at that time. Nausea and abdominal pain resolved rapidly, discharged at 2 weeks, liver tests returned to normal within 6 weeks. Other potential causes excluded by laboratory investigations. Mesalazine = 5-ASA. Authors note 70-90% of patients with sulfasalazine side effects tolerate new preparations.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a patient with Crohn's disease who suffered severe hepatic injury after high-dose mesalazine. Laboratory findings were consistent with cholestasis associated with mesalazine therapy: on admission, total bilirubin 6 mg/dl, ALT 393 IU/l (normal <23), GGT 166 IU/l (normal 6-28), and alkaline phosphatase 201 IU/l (normal 50-190), all returning to normal 6 weeks later. The patient, a 30-year-old man with ileal Crohn's disease, received 4 g mesalazine daily as the only medication; hepatitis/cytomegalovirus/EBV/herpes/HIV serology and autoimmune liver antibodies were negative, and he had no evidence of gallstones, gallstones, inflammatory or rheumatic disease, or alcohol abuse.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose (4 g daily) mesalazine used as monotherapy for ileal Crohn's disease; single case.
raw_record.extra_details: 30-year-old man with 9-month history of abdominal pain; Crohn's disease diagnosed endoscopically and histologically. No evidence of liver dysfunction before therapy; symptoms (nausea, fatigue, jaundice, severe right-upper-quadrant pain, 4 kg weight loss) developed 4 months after starting mesalazine. No other concomitant medication. Viral serology (anti-HAV IgM, HBs-Ag, anti-HBs, anti-HBc, anti-HCV, HCV-PCR, CMV IgM, EBV IgM, HSV IgM, HIV) and liver-kidney-microsomal, anti-mitochondrial, anti-nuclear, anti-cytoplasmic antibodies all negative; no gallstones, no alcohol abuse, no eosinophilia (4% eosinophils). Labs returned to normal 6 weeks after stopping mesalazine.

raw_record.support_text: A 57-year-old man with ALK-positive, EML4-ALK fusion lung adenocarcinoma (stage IVB) treated with alectinib 600 mg/day as first-line therapy developed serum AST and ALT elevation to CTCAE grade 3 on day 79. The injury was determined to be alectinib-induced hepatotoxicity of the cholestatic type (Digestive Disease Week Japan 2004 scale and R value), with hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, and EBV excluded. After recovery with UDCA and glycyrrhizin, rechallenge with reduced alectinib (150 then 300 mg/day) caused recurrent grade 2 and then grade 3 elevations, requiring discontinuation and a switch to lorlatinib on day 235.
raw_record.extra_details: ALK-positive NSCLC patient. Onset of AST/ALT elevation on day 79 (CTCAE v5.0 grade 3), readmitted on day 107 for alectinib-induced hepatotoxicity; abdominal CT/ultrasonography showed no liver abnormality; cholestatic-type injury by Digestive Disease Week Japan 2004 scale and R value; treated with oral UDCA 600 mg/day and IV glycyrrhizin (SNMC), improving to grade 1; positive rechallenge at 150 mg/day (day 128) then 300 mg/day (day ~149) with recurrence to grade 2 on day 191 requiring discontinuation, then grade 3 on day 219 requiring readmission and IV SNMC; switched to lorlatinib on day 235. Paper notes approximately 1-5% of patients experience alectinib-induced liver damage.

raw_record.support_text: A 57-year-old Japanese man with ALK-positive NSCLC received first-line alectinib and developed hepatotoxicity, leading to discontinuation after 79 days. Rechallenge at 150 mg/day induced hepatotoxicity again after 64 days, confirming alectinib as the cause of drug-induced liver injury in this patient.
raw_record.extra_details: First-line therapy for ALK-positive NSCLC in a 57-year-old Japanese man; hepatotoxicity appeared after 79 days, and rechallenge at a reduced dose of 150 mg/day reproduced the injury after 64 days. The patient was subsequently switched to lorlatinib.

raw_record.support_text: A 35-year-old woman with ALK-rearranged lung adenocarcinoma achieved complete response to first-line Alectinib 600 mg twice daily but the treatment was permanently discontinued after 6 months due to persistent hepatotoxicity grade 3 (CTCAE v5.0). She developed elevation of ALAT (219 U/L) and subsequently ASAT (243 U/L) first after 6 months of Alectinib treatment, without bilirubin elevation; re-exposure at reduced doses (450 mg then 300 mg BID) reproduced ALAT elevation up to 474 U/L, requiring permanent treatment stoppage, and a liver biopsy 3 months after discontinuation still showed biopsy-verified drug-induced hepatitis with lymphocytic, histiocytic and ceroid-laden Kupffer cell infiltration, mild fibrosis and bile ductular reaction. The patient took no other drugs (notably no statins) that could have contributed.
raw_record.extra_details: Grade 3 hepatotoxicity (CTCAE v5.0) in first-line therapy at 600 mg BID, first noted after ~6 months of treatment. ALAT 219 U/L then ASAT 243 U/L, bilirubin never elevated. On rechallenge after a 6-week break at reduced doses (450 mg BID; then 300 mg BID) ALAT rose to 252 U/L and then 474 U/L, prompting permanent discontinuation. Liver biopsy 3 months after stopping showed drug-induced hepatitis with subcapsular/periportal/centrilobular infiltration of lymphocytes, histiocytes and ceroid-laden Kupffer cells, mild fibrosis and bile ductular reaction; hepatotoxicity biochemically resolved later. No statins or other contributory drugs were taken.

raw_record.support_text: On clinical and paraclinical grounds the authors oriented towards the diagnosis of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) manifested by acute liver failure, attributed to a history of alectinib intake. Alectinib was stopped, supportive measures and treatment with N-acetylcysteine and corticosteroids were given, with favorable clinical evolution; the hepatotoxicity gradually improved to grade 1.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report. Differential diagnosis of hepatocellular injury excluded viral hepatitis, ischemic hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, NAFLD, alcohol hepatitis, biliary disease, malignancy, and herbal hepatotoxicity. DILI manifested as acute liver failure and improved to grade 1 after alectinib withdrawal; treated with N-acetylcysteine and corticosteroids with favorable evolution.

raw_record.support_text: A 56-year-old male with stage IV ALK-positive NSCLC on alectinib 600 mg twice daily (119 days of treatment) presented with jaundice, pruritus and fatigue. Laboratory tests showed TBIL 315.0 μmol/L, DBIL 260.7 μmol/L, ALP 374 U/L, GGT 47 U/L with near-normal aminotransferases (AST 34, ALT 42 U/L). A diagnosis of alectinib-induced grade 4 hyperbilirubinemia (>10×ULN) was considered, and alectinib was held due to hepatotoxicity. No liver metastases were present and viral hepatitis assessment was unrevealing, supporting drug attribution.
raw_record.extra_details: Alectinib 600 mg twice daily for ALK-positive (EML4-ALK variant 2) stage IV NSCLC. Elevated TBIL 59.2 μmol/L noted on May 5, 2020 (after 119 days on alectinib); on May 29 presented with jaundice/pruritus/fatigue, KPS 60, TBIL 315.0 μmol/L, DBIL 260.7 μmol/L, IBIL 54.3 μmol/L, total bile acid 179.9 μmol/L, ALP 374 U/L, GGT 47 U/L, AST 34 U/L, ALT 42 U/L. Grade 4 hyperbilirubinemia (>10×ULN, CTCAE v5.0). Hepatoprotective treatment with ursodeoxycholic acid, glycyrrhizin and glutathione for one week did not improve bilirubin; drug-induced liver failure diagnosed. Treated with ALSS (DPMAS) on June 5 and 8, 2020, with continuous bilirubin decrease; alectinib discontinued for more than two months, later switched to ensartinib 225 mg once daily. Competing causes excluded: no liver metastases at baseline or follow-up, viral hepatitis assessment unrevealing.

raw_record.support_text: In the reported patient, liver injury occurred after initiation of rivaroxaban therapy and resolved after dechallenge, with a strong chronologic relationship between rivaroxaban and hepatocellular injury resulting in a RUCAM score of 8 (time to onset, course, risk factors, concomitant drugs, exclusion of other causes, previous information of hepatotoxicity, and response to readministration). The authors additionally note that in daily practice hepatotoxicity is a rare unpredictable adverse effect of rivaroxaban highlighted by post-marketing spontaneous reporting systems.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report. RUCAM score of 8 (probable causality), with components including time to onset (+2), course (+2), risk factors (+1), concomitant drugs (0), exclusion of other causes of liver injury (+2), previous information of hepatotoxicity of the drug (+1), and response to readministration (0). Liver injury resolved after dechallenge. Post-marketing spontaneous reporting systems highlight hepatotoxicity as a rare unpredictable adverse effect; authors advise hepatic enzyme monitoring during the first weeks of treatment because asymptomatic forms are the most common expression.

raw_record.support_text: A report of 14 postmarketing cases of liver injury associated with rivaroxaban, including two with liver biopsy. Formal causality assessment classified rivaroxaban as the 'probable' cause in 7 patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Among 14 postmarketing cases, 7 patients classified as 'probable' by formal causality assessment; 2 cases had liver biopsy; cases reported to a regional pharmacovigilance center for thromboembolic disorder treatment.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 2 cases of rivaroxaban-induced DILI in patients, with alanine aminotransferase >5x ULN and serum bilirubin >2x ULN, most symptomatic, who recovered after discontinuing rivaroxaban. It cites a Swiss Regional Pharmacovigilance Center series of 14 rivaroxaban-induced DILI cases (10/14 with ALT >5x ULN, 9 with bilirubin >2x ULN, 13 recovered), stating the similarity strengthens the conclusion that rivaroxaban was causing liver injury. The conclusion states that treatment with rivaroxaban can be associated with severe hepatocellular liver injury, with some patients fulfilling Hy's law criteria, and complete recovery after discontinuation; renal reexposure is discouraged.
raw_record.extra_details: 2 index cases plus reference to a separate Swiss series of 14 rivaroxaban-induced DILI cases; 10/14 had ALT >5x ULN, 9/14 had serum bilirubin >2x ULN, most symptomatic, 13 recovered after discontinuation. Some patients fulfilled Hy's law criteria. Rapid clinical and biochemical improvement and complete recovery after discontinuation; authors recommend rapid discontinuation for symptomatic liver injury and avoiding reexposure, and propose a symptomatic-liver-injury warning in drug labels.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that after clinical investigation in thousands of patients, rivaroxaban appears to have no significant hepatotoxicity and a bleeding risk comparable to other conventional anticoagulants. This is an explicit negative conclusion regarding human drug-induced liver injury for rivaroxaban based on clinical trial data.
raw_record.extra_details: Claims of no significant hepatotoxicity arise after clinical investigation in thousands of patients (extensive Phase II and emerging Phase III trial data). Rivaroxaban (BAY 59-7939) is a novel oral direct Factor Xa inhibitor.

raw_record.support_text: In the Strasbourg registry, among the five rivaroxaban-attributable liver injury cases, two patients had a RUCAM score of 6 (probable). All recovered after rivaroxaban cessation.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM score 6 (probable) in two patients; rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily; recovery after cessation.

raw_record.support_text: A publication describes five patients with possible, probable, or highly probable liver injury associated with rivaroxaban. Only one of them had symptomatic liver injury; three had a hepatocellular and two a cholestatic pattern. The onset of liver injury was 2 to 3 days after treatment initiation in all patients, and all recovered without sequelae.
raw_record.extra_details: Causality grades reported across the five patients as possible, probable, or highly probable; three hepatocellular and two cholestatic patterns; onset 2-3 days after treatment start; only one patient symptomatic; all recovered without sequelae.

raw_record.support_text: In a patient presenting with jaundice, competing etiologies of intrahepatic cholestasis were excluded by serology and imaging, and all the patient's drugs were examined. It was concluded that the jaundice can be a very rare adverse reaction of rivaroxaban, so rivaroxaban was stopped and enoxaparin was substituted; the patient showed rapid biochemical and clinical recovery within one day, with liver function tests nearly normal after two weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of rivaroxaban-induced intrahepatic cholestasis causing severe, long-lasting jaundice. Authors state the most probable diagnosis is rivaroxaban-induced intrahepatic cholestasis based on exclusion of other causes and dramatic resolution after drug cessation (dechallenge). Lab values after 2 weeks off drug: ALT 24, AST 28, GGT 36, ALP 168 U/l, total bilirubin 4.5 mg/dl, conjugated bilirubin 4.3 mg/dl; skin and scleral icterus not fully resolved 6 weeks after discontinuation. Labeled adverse reactions of rivaroxaban include jaundice and increased transaminases, ALP, and total and conjugated bilirubin. Mechanism stated as unknown, possibly immune-mediated; rechallenge not described; no cross-reactivity among anticoagulants suspected.

raw_record.support_text: New oral anticoagulants accounted for 2 DILI cases, with rivaroxaban as the attributed causative agent in one case.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as the causative new oral anticoagulant in 1 of 22 DILI cases.

raw_record.support_text: A publication described 14 patients with rivaroxaban-associated liver injury reported to a Swiss regional Pharmacovigilance Center. Patients had a median age of 71 years (9 female, 5 male), treated for atrial fibrillation (n=4) or after knee/leg surgery (n=10); median dose was 10 mg/day, and median latency was 15.5 days. All but one were symptomatic and 11 were jaundiced; ALT exceeded 2x ULN in all (median 7.8x ULN). Eight had hepatocellular, four cholestatic and one mixed liver injury; median bilirubin was 6.6x ULN. RUCAM causality was highly probable in 4, probable in 7 and possible in 3 patients; one patient died, all others recovered. Author database searches found rivaroxaban as a suspected DILI cause in WHO (179 reports), EMA (375) and FDA FAERS (87) databases. A second Swiss case report described two further patients (10 mg rivaroxaban after surgery) presenting with jaundice 1-2 months later; one had hepatocellular and one mixed injury, causality probable/possible, with full recovery 2 weeks after stopping.
raw_record.extra_details: First series of 14 patients: median age 71 y (range 41-91), 9 female/5 male; indications AF (n=4) and knee replacement/leg surgery (n=10); median dose 10 mg/day (range 10-20); latency 15.5 d (range 3-62); 13/14 symptomatic, 11 jaundiced; ALT >2x ULN in all (median 7.8x, range 2.5-53.7); ALP <2x ULN in 5 and >2x ULN in 9 (median 2.5x); 8 hepatocellular, 4 cholestatic, 1 mixed; bilirubin in 10 patients median 6.6x ULN (range 1-21.6); RUCAM: highly probable 4, probable 7, possible 3; one death, others recovered. Two patients biopsied showed cholestatic injury with centroacinar cholestasis, focal hepatocyte ballooning, portal lymphocytic/eosinophilic infiltration and biliary epithelial alterations. Pharmacovigilance database searches: WHO VigiBase 179 DILI-compatible reports, EMA EudraVigilance 375 events, FDA FAERS 87 cases with rivaroxaban as suspected cause. Second case series (2 patients, 52 y man and 73 y woman, 10 mg after surgery): jaundice 1-2 months later, massively raised transaminases with slight ALP rise; 1 hepatocellular and 1 mixed injury; causality probable/possible; full recovery ~2 weeks after stopping; biopsy in the hepatocellular case showed confluent centroacinar hepatocyte necrosis with macrophage infiltration and minimal portal lymphocytic infiltrate.

raw_record.support_text: A 74-year-old male with CAD who had undergone CABG developed non-valvular atrial fibrillation and was started on rivaroxaban 20 mg daily for stroke prophylaxis. He presented 8 days later with elevated AST (136 IU/L), ALT (164 IU/L), ALP (78 IU/L) and INR 3.1, which had been normal before starting rivaroxaban. Over the next 2 days his liver enzymes rose dramatically with encephalopathy and multi-organ failure; he was treated with N-acetyl cysteine for probable drug-induced liver injury and died on day 8 of hospitalization. Autopsy showed nutmeg liver, severe centrilobular necrosis of zones 2 and 3 with a rim of viable periportal cells, plus mild steatosis and intra-hepatic cholestasis, indicating a possible DILI. This is reported as the first case of acute liver failure associated with rivaroxaban in the absence of underlying liver disease, with the CIOMS/RUCAM score of 5 suggestive of DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 20 mg daily for stroke prophylaxis for non-valvular atrial fibrillation; latency ~8 days from start. Labs on admission AST 136 IU/L, ALT 164 IU/L, ALP 78 IU/L, prothrombin time 35.5s (INR 3.1), all normal before rivaroxaban. Patient also on atorvastatin, metoprolol and aspirin (stable for 5-6 years prior). Autopsy: nutmeg liver, severe centrilobular necrosis of zones 2 and 3 with rim of viable periportal cells (zone 1), mild steatosis and intra-hepatic cholestasis. Treated with N-acetyl cysteine; developed encephalopathy and multi-organ failure; died on day 8 of hospitalization. CIOMS/RUCAM score 5 suggestive of DILI. Paper notes prior reports of hepatitis and/or cholestasis associated with rivaroxaban with incidence appearing less than 1%.
