raw_record.support_text: The commentary states that lumiracoxib, a selective COX-2 inhibitor, joins the list of NSAIDs withdrawn due to their association with DILI, and reports that lumiracoxib has the potential for rare but serious hepatotoxicity. Worldwide at least 20 cases of severe DILI associated with lumiracoxib have been reported, including 14 with acute liver failure, two deaths, and three liver transplants; most cases occurred several months after starting lumiracoxib, many at daily doses exceeding 100 mg, but severe DILI was also reported at 100 mg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: Selective COX-2 inhibitor developed for osteoarthritis and acute pain; hepatotoxicity contributed to withdrawal/nonapproval in most major markets. At least 20 reported cases of severe DILI, including 14 with acute liver failure, 2 deaths, and 3 liver transplants. Most cases occurred several months after starting lumiracoxib, with early presentations also noted; many cases involved daily doses exceeding 100 mg, but severe DILI also occurred at 100 mg/day.

raw_record.support_text: A GWAS on 41 cases of DILI resulting from the NSAID lumiracoxib found a highly significant association (p=6.8×10^-25; allelic OR 5.0; 95% CI 3.6–7.0) with an HLA class II haplotype that includes DRB1*1501, and the association was replicated in a further 98 lumiracoxib DILI cases. No independent HLA class I association was found, and lumiracoxib shows good clinical utility apart from rare incidences of DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug. GWAS of 41 DILI cases with allelic OR 5.0 (95% CI 3.6–7.0), p=6.8×10^-25, associated with HLA class II haplotype including DRB1*1501; replicated in 98 additional cases. No independent HLA class I association. Pattern of liver injury generally differs from that of amoxicillin-clavulanate. Consideration of genotyping for DRB1*1501 to exclude at-risk patients.

raw_record.support_text: Lumiracoxib, a COX-2 inhibitor, was found to cause idiosyncratic DILI in clinical trials. In the TARGET trial 2.6% of 9,117 randomized patients developed ALT elevations >3x ULN versus 0.6% in the naproxen/ibuprofen arms, with nine cases consistent with Hy's law. It was not approved in the United States; in 2007 Australia's TGA received eight reports of serious liver injury including two deaths and two liver transplants, and several countries withdrew approval in 2007-2008.
raw_record.extra_details: COX-2 inhibitor; TARGET trial 9,117 patients, 2.6% ALT>3x ULN vs 0.6% in naproxen/ibuprofen arms; nine Hy's law cases; cases with ALT increases >5x, 8x, 10x, 15x, 20x ULN. Not approved in the United States; approved and marketed abroad; 2007 Australia TGA received 8 reports of serious liver injury including 2 deaths and 2 liver transplants; approval withdrawn in several countries in 2007-2008.

raw_record.support_text: Detectable titres of serum autoantibodies, mostly antinuclear antibodies, were present in 3 cases of lumiracoxib-induced hepatotoxicity, suggesting an immune-mediated mechanism in the pathogenesis of coxib-induced DILI. A genome-wide association study in 41 cases of lumiracoxib-induced DILI and 176 drug-tolerant lumiracoxib-exposed controls found a strong association with HLA class II markers, with HLA-DQA1*0102 being the most sensitive (73.6%) in predicting risk.
raw_record.extra_details: Three reported cases of lumiracoxib-induced hepatotoxicity had detectable antinuclear antibodies, suggesting an immune-mediated/immune mechanism in the pathogenesis. Genetic susceptibility is supported by a GWAS of 41 lumiracoxib-induced DILI cases versus 176 drug-tolerant lumiracoxib-exposed controls, with strong association to HLA class II region markers; HLA-DQA1*0102 was the most sensitive (73.6%) in predicting risk. Proposed mechanisms include reactive metabolites generating antigenic drug-protein adducts presented by HLA complexes triggering a T-cell-mediated immune response, or direct interaction of lumiracoxib with the HLA complex.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that Lumiracoxib, a Cox-2 selective inhibitor anti-inflammatory drug, was withdrawn from market because of hepatotoxicity, and that a GWAS with only 41 cases uncovered HLA-DRB1*15:01 as the genetic underpinning of the toxicity (OR~5).
raw_record.extra_details: Cox-2 selective inhibitor anti-inflammatory drug withdrawn from market because of hepatotoxicity; GWAS of 41 cases mapped the toxicity to HLA-DRB1*15:01 (OR~5) [38].

raw_record.support_text: Pillans et al. report three women who developed severe hepatotoxicity with lumiracoxib, a recently introduced COX-2 inhibitor, all with histologic evidence of significant hepatocellular necrosis. One patient died from acute liver failure, another needed a liver transplant. Five further cases have been reported to the Australian TGA, of which two patients died and two underwent liver transplantation. Drug dose or duration of use was not predictive of liver toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Three reported index cases, all with significant histologic hepatocellular necrosis; one died from acute liver failure, one required liver transplant. Five additional cases reported to the Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration, with two deaths and two liver transplants. Anti-nuclear antibodies noted in all three cases. GWAS of 41 lumiracoxib-induced liver injury cases vs 176 exposed controls found association with HLA class II markers; HLA-DQA1*0102 had highest sensitivity (73.6%). Health regulators called for withdrawal of lumiracoxib from clinical use. Structurally similar to diclofenac, sharing proclivity for forming reactive hepatotoxic metabolites and glutathione adducts.

raw_record.support_text: The FDA issued a nonapprovable letter for lumiracoxib in 2007, and postmarketing surveillance identified serious instances of DILI not foreseen in clinical trials. In the large TARGET trial, 2.6% had aminotransferase elevations >3× ULN, with six cases of probable or possible clinical hepatitis that all resolved on drug cessation and no reports of liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: FDA nonapprovable letter (2007); postmarketing surveillance identified serious DILI not foreseen in trials. TARGET trial: 2.6% AT >3× ULN; six cases of probable/possible clinical hepatitis all resolved; no liver failure. Pharmacogenetic GWAS (Affymetrix 6.0, >900,000 SNPs) in 41 cases (ALT/AST >5× ULN) vs 176 matched controls, validated in 98 cases vs 405 lumiracoxib-exposed controls (ALT/AST >3× ULN), associated lumiracoxib DILI with MHC class II SNPs on chromosome 6 (leading rs9270986, P = 2.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) and extended haplotype HLA-DRB1*1501-HLA-DQB1*0602-HLA-DRB5*0101-HLA-DQA1*0102 (most significant allele P = 6.8 × 10⁻²⁵, OR 5.0; 95% CI 3.6-7.0). No similar relationship seen in ibuprofen (n=18) or naproxen (n=9) DILI control cases. All patients with ALT >20× ULN and all three Hy's law (ALT/AST >3× ULN, bilirubin >2 ULN) cases carried the implicated haplotype. HLA-DQA1*0102 had best negative predictive value (99%) and sensitivity (73.6%). Curated table lists HLA-DQA1*0102 OR 6.3 (4.1-9.6) for lumiracoxib DILI.

raw_record.support_text: Pillans et al. report three women who developed severe hepatotoxicity with lumiracoxib, a recently introduced COX-2 inhibitor. All had histologic evidence of significant hepatocellular necrosis; one patient died from acute liver failure and another needed a liver transplant. A further five cases of liver injury were reported to the Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration, of which two patients died and two underwent liver transplantation. Drug dose or duration of use was not predictive of liver toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Three women with severe hepatotoxicity and histologic evidence of significant hepatocellular necrosis; one died from acute liver failure and another needed a liver transplant. A further five liver-injury cases were reported to the Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration, of which two patients died and two underwent liver transplantation. Lumiracoxib is a cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) inhibitor; drug dose or duration of use was not predictive of liver toxicity, and many affected individuals were women (noted as not unusual in DILI case series).

raw_record.support_text: In the TARGET clinical trial the proportion of patients with liver function test abnormalities was significantly higher with lumiracoxib than with conventional NSAIDs (hazard ratio 3.97; 95% CI 2.96–5.32), though these abnormalities resolved on cessation of treatment. Clinical hepatitis was rare regardless of drug: six cases were adjudicated to lumiracoxib (0.07%), two to ibuprofen (0.05%) and one to naproxen (0.02%).
raw_record.extra_details: TARGET trial (chronic osteoarthritis therapy). Proportion of patients with liver function test abnormalities significantly higher with lumiracoxib than with conventional NSAIDs (HR 3.97; 95% CI 2.96–5.32), resolving on cessation of treatment. Six cases of clinical hepatitis adjudicated to lumiracoxib (0.07%).

raw_record.support_text: In the TARGET trial (52-week, double-blind outcomes trial), nine cases of serious liver abnormalities were judged to be probable drug-induced hepatitis: six (0.07%) were associated with the use of lumiracoxib, two (0.05%) with ibuprofen and one (0.02%) with naproxen. The difference between lumiracoxib and the NSAIDs was not statistically significant, and in all cases raised transaminase levels reversed after the drug was stopped.
raw_record.extra_details: Six of nine adjudicated cases of probable drug-induced hepatitis in the TARGET trial (0.07%); raised transaminase levels reversed after drug discontinuation; difference versus NSAIDs not statistically significant. Commentary notes lumiracoxib was studied at a supratherapeutic dose.

raw_record.support_text: In this patient case, a percutaneous liver biopsy (August 2008) showed preserved lobular architecture without necrosis, mild portal-tract expansion with ductular proliferation and occasional ductopenia, and heavy portal inflammatory infiltrates of neutrophils, lymphocytes, occasional eosinophils, and plasma cells, with no piecemeal necrosis or granulomas. The biopsy was consistent with a cholestatic drug-induced liver injury correlating with a predominantly cholestatic liver function test, and the drug-use chronology with complete normalisation of liver function tests after discontinuation suggested a probable hepatotoxic reaction to lumiracoxib.
raw_record.extra_details: Biopsy showed ductular proliferation, occasional ductopenia, damaged bile duct, and inflammatory infiltrate; chronology of drug use and complete normalisation of LFTs after drug discontinuation support causality; no granulomas or piecemeal necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: Lumiracoxib, a selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitor developed for osteoarthritis, was shown to be superior to nonselective NSAIDs at reducing ulcer complications, but data from the phase 3 clinical trial showed hepatotoxicity in 2.6% of individuals receiving lumiracoxib. The drug was withdrawn from the market due to rare but fulminant hepatitis. A GWAS carried out in a subgroup of the pivotal efficacy trial identified a significant association between an HLA haplotype (HLA-DRB1*1501-DQB1*0602-DRB5*0101-DQA1*0102) and lumiracoxib-induced hepatotoxicity (P = 2.8 × 10⁻¹⁰).
raw_record.extra_details: Selective COX-2 inhibitor for osteoarthritis; hepatotoxicity in 2.6% of individuals in the phase 3 clinical trial; withdrawn from market due to rare but fulminant hepatitis. GWAS in a subgroup of the pivotal trial found HLA-DRB1*1501-DQB1*0602-DRB5*0101-DQA1*0102 haplotype association (P=2.8e-10); DRB1*1501 OR 5.0 (95% CI 3.6-7.0); DQA1*0102 screening sensitivity 74%, negative predictive value 99%; predicted hepatotoxicity incidence would fall to 1.0% for non-carriers.

raw_record.support_text: RUCAM causality assessment rated topiramate as a probable causal agent for acute liver failure in this patient. The timing of the elevated topiramate level, rapid decrease in ALT after discontinuation, and lack of a concomitant drug trigger supported the link; the total RUCAM score of 8 points placed the case on the border between 'probable' and 'highly probable' topiramate causally related hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single-patient case with chronic 10-year topiramate exposure; the drug level was >4-fold higher than it had ever been, with no medication or supplement changes, hypothesized to mimic a 'new drug' idiosyncratic-like effect.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM total score 8 (border of 'probable' and 'highly probable'); elevated ammonia level (ammonia >1300) also cited as supporting topiramate-induced hepatic toxicity, proposed via inhibition of type V mitochondrial carbonic anhydrase and reduced carbamyl phosphate synthesis in the urea cycle; both ALF and topiramate can cause hyperammonemia independently. Histology showed a hepatocellular and cholestatic pattern with microvesicular steatosis, consistent with DILI; no well-established characteristic pathology for topiramate hepatotoxicity exists. Three prior case reports of DILI attributed primarily to topiramate: Bjoro et al. (adult ALF requiring liver allograft 4 months after topiramate added to carbamazepine and days after a dose increase), Doan et al. (ALF in a young adult with topiramate added to valproate, liver tests corrected after discontinuation), and del Val Antonana et al. (hepatotoxicity in a 16-year-old male on topiramate monotherapy with elevated transaminases and coagulopathy but no hyperammonemia, resolving 2 weeks after discontinuation). Topiramate is an antiepileptic/metabolism inducer of CYP3A4; DILI mechanism not well understood.

raw_record.support_text: A patient treated with Fingolimod developed acute liver failure. Hepatic encephalopathy developed on the 7th day of follow-up, and a cadaveric liver transplant was performed on the 9th day, 44 days after initiation of Fingolimod treatment. Massive necrosis was detected in the pathological examination of the explanted liver.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of fingolimod (Gilenya)-treated MS patient. Duration of treatment 15 days; onset of symptoms on 12th day; laboratory abnormalities on 14th day; R ratio 11.4 (hepatocellular pattern) at first application; modified RUCAM +8 (Probable); severity grade 5+ (Fatal). Initial labs: ALT 517 U/L, AST 646 U/L, total bilirubin 36.7 mg/dL, INR 3.7, creatinine 0.66 mg/dL. Hepatic encephalopathy developed on day 7; cadaveric liver transplant on day 9 (44 days after therapy initiation); explant pathology showed massive necrosis with bile duct proliferation and perivascular connective tissue. Patient survived and complies with liver transplant outpatient follow-up. Therapeutic plasmapheresis was performed; patient had not received steroids before transplant.

raw_record.support_text: The commentary reports 33 published cases of severe propylthiouracil (PTU)-related liver failure in adults and 14 in children, plus 16 liver transplants in adults and seven in children due to PTU-induced liver failure reported by UNOS between 1990 and 2007. FDA AERS data detail severe liver injury in 22 adults over 20 yr, nine of whom died and five received liver transplants, and 12 pediatric patients who sustained severe liver injury resulting in three deaths and six liver transplants. The average daily dose of PTU associated with liver failure was approximately 300 mg in both children and adults, with liver failure occurring after 6 to 450 d (median 120 d) of treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Antithyroid drug for hyperthyroidism/Graves' disease; also inhibits T4 to T3 conversion. Published reports: 33 severe liver failure cases in adults, 14 in children. UNOS reported 16 liver transplants in adults and seven in children (1990-2007) due to PTU-induced liver failure; one to three PTU-related liver transplants per year over 17 yr. AERS: severe liver injury in 22 adults (9 died, 5 transplanted) and 12 pediatric cases (3 deaths, 6 transplants) over 20 yr. Two reports of serious maternal liver injury during pregnancy and two reports of liver injury in fetuses whose mothers took PTU. Average daily dose associated with liver failure ~300 mg in children and adults; latency 6-450 d (median 120 d). Estimated incidence of severe hepatic damage ~0.1% in adults; projected liver-failure (transplant or death) incidence ~1:10,000, giving 1-2 deaths/transplants per year in U.S. adults. Children: ~1 in 1000 incidence of liver failure. US PTU prescriptions: 101,000 patients in 2008, >340,000 prescriptions.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that while propylthiouracil (PTU) may cause hepatocellular inflammation and, in severe cases, focal necrosis, methimazole (MMI) typically results in cholestatic dysfunction, and both are considered rare. It reports 22 cases of PTU-related liver failure over 20 years in the US resulting in 9 deaths and 5 liver transplants among adults, and 12 children who developed liver failure resulting in 3 deaths and 6 transplants, estimating a risk of 1 in 10,000 adults and 1 in 2000 children. The FDA has voiced concern regarding routine use of PTU. A separate paragraph notes recent case reports of fulminant hepatitis and liver failure in young adults treated with PTU.
raw_record.extra_details: PTU may cause hepatocellular inflammation and, in severe cases, focal necrosis; recent case reports of fulminant hepatitis and liver failure in young adults. Over 20 years in the US, 22 cases of PTU-related liver failure caused 9 deaths and 5 liver transplants among adults, while 12 children developed liver failure with 3 deaths and 6 transplants; estimated risk of 1 in 10,000 adults and 1 in 2000 children. The US FDA has voiced concern regarding routine PTU use. Antithyroid drug hepatotoxicity is described as rare (Arab et al. 1995).

raw_record.support_text: Twenty-nine cases of PTU-induced liver failure have been reported in individuals aged 6 to 62 years. Recovery without transplant occurred in 18 individuals, transplantation occurred in 3 persons, and 9 deaths were reported; 14 of these cases were pediatric patients, with 3 deaths and 5 children who underwent liver transplantation reported in the PTU-treated pediatric subset.
raw_record.extra_details: Indication: Graves' disease/hyperthyroidism. Of 29 reported cases of PTU-induced liver failure (ages 6-62 y): 18 recovered without transplant, 3 underwent liver transplantation, 9 died; 14 cases were pediatric.

raw_record.support_text: The paper's summary describes propylthiouracil (PTU)-associated hepatotoxicity occurring during antithyroid therapy, stating that significant hepatic enzyme abnormalities require immediate drug discontinuation, that hepatic failure can progress despite discontinuation of PTU, and that early recognition of the need for liver transplantation may be lifesaving. It emphasizes that PTU should not be reinstituted because of recurrence of hepatotoxicity with drug rechallenge and a possible autoimmune etiology of the injury. Earlier text notes patients who succumbed (died) from PTU hepatotoxicity and details two presented cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Report includes two cases of PTU-associated hepatotoxicity in hyperthyroid patients (Graves' disease vs suspected toxic multinodular goiter). Hepatic failure can progress despite drug discontinuation; liver transplantation may be lifesaving; some patients died of PTU hepatotoxicity. PTU should not be reinstituted due to recurrence of hepatic injury with rechallenge and a possible autoimmune nature of the hepatotoxicity. Baseline liver enzyme elevations present in both patients prior to PTU; up to 72% of hyperthyroid patients may have ≥1 elevated hepatic enzyme.

raw_record.support_text: A patient with Graves' disease was on levothyroxine with PTU added for the previous 10 months; approximately 3 weeks before emergency admission her PTU dose was increased. No liver-toxic co-medication, alcohol abuse, or travel was found. The etiological work-up for hepatitis A/B/C and autoimmune hepatitis was negative, and the case was reported to the pharmacovigilance system, which designated the PTU-related hepatic complications as 'highly probable'. Liver biopsy showed hepatocellular insufficiency with cytolysis and cholestasis, and the patient decompensated to cirrhosis requiring orthotopic liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: PTU used concurrently with levothyroxine and phloroglucinol (recently added for abdominal pain, not implicated as cause). PTU dose increased ~3 weeks before admission. Labs showed Quick test 18%, ALAT 310 U/L, ASAT 650 U/L, PAL 540 U/L; liver biopsy demonstrated cytolysis and cholestasis with hepatocellular insufficiency. Etiology negative for hepatitis A/B/C and autoimmune disease. Referred for pre-transplant assessment and registered for decompensated cirrhosis; orthotopic liver transplantation performed 5 days after admission, followed by thyroidectomy; cytolytic hepatitis decreased 3 days post-surgery and the patient returned home 20 days after transplantation. Causality designated 'highly probable' by the EU pharmacovigilance system.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses propylthiouracil-induced hepatotoxicity, noting that when the association is recognized and propylthiouracil therapy is discontinued, the clinical course typically shows improvement and eventual resolution, as illustrated by 'our patient's course.' Biochemical abnormalities begin to improve immediately but often do not resolve completely for 2–3 months or as long as 7 months.
raw_record.extra_details: Propylthiouracil, an antithyroid drug, was used to treat hyperthyroidism. A rechallenge case is described in which hepatotoxicity redeveloped 5 days after rechallenge once liver function tests had returned to normal. Some reported propylthiouracil-induced hepatitis cases showed circulating autoantibodies, suggesting a possibly immunologically mediated mechanism for the liver damage. Hepatotoxicity improved/resolved after drug discontinuation; recovery of biochemical abnormalities could take up to 7 months. Paper recommends avoiding re-use of propylthiouracil and discusses methimazole substitution, radioactive iodine, or surgery as alternatives.

raw_record.support_text: Among US patients with drug-induced acute liver failure who underwent transplantation, propylthiouracil ranked after isoniazid as a causative drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed after paracetamol and isoniazid among US drug-induced acute liver failure transplant cases; 7.3% in the USA 1990-2002 series (Russo et al.).

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that PTU (propylthiouracil) causes severe DILI with a higher prevalence than MMI (6.3% vs 1.4% severe cases; 0.68% vs 0.08% most-severe cases), supporting that PTU is associated with a higher risk of severe liver injury. In 2010 the FDA added a Black Box warning to the PTU label for the risk of severe liver failure and recommended its use only in patients who cannot tolerate other treatments.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe DILI prevalence 6.3%, most-severe cases 0.68% (higher than MMI). No age-dependency in PTU-related DILI prevalence (p=0.1163); no one in the 70s-80s age group developed DILI with PTU. Of 35 patients who continued the suspected ATD with dose reduction, 12 were treated with PTU (median daily dose 275 mg, range 100-300 mg), all hepatocellular-type DILI, no hospitalization. FDA 2010 Black Box warning for risk of severe liver failure; PTU recommended only when other treatments are not tolerated. Per cited previous report, PTU is the third most common cause of DILI in patients under age 20, resulting in liver transplantation in about 10% of Graves' disease patients in that age group who developed liver failure. No fatalities in the present cohort.

raw_record.support_text: Using the Hanson conditions and CIOMS criteria, the authors concluded that their two cases matched the parameters for propylthiouracil to be causative of fulminating hepatitis. Viral hepatitis was ruled out via negative hepatitis A, B, and C markers, autoimmunity tests were largely negative, and neither patient had congestive heart failure or other extrathyroidal risk factors; fulminating hepatitis was diagnosed based on jaundice, severe clinical evolution like viral hepatitis, encephalopathy, terminal multiple organ failure, and autopsy-confirmed histologic hepatic injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients (case series). Case 1: varying intermittent dose of propylthiouracil over 4 months, jaundice onset 92 days after start, death 30 days after icterus onset. Case 2: propylthiouracil 200 mg/day for 5 months plus constant 150 mg/day for 15 days, jaundice onset at 162 days, death 50 days after icterus. Hepatitis A/B/C ruled out; CMV and EBV not tested (optional per CIOMS). Autoantibody testing largely negative except low-titer antinuclear antibodies. Histology: extensive areas of necrosis with hemorrhagic infiltration, widened portal triads with edema and incipient fibrosis, perilobular cholestasis, slight ductal proliferation, lymphoplasmocytic portal infiltrate, centrolobular hepatocyte lysis, moderate cholestasis. No laboratory tests before propylthiouracil intake. Indication: thyrotoxicosis (mild to moderate).

raw_record.support_text: In the UNOS liver transplant cohort of drug-induced acute liver failure recipients, propylthiouracil was implicated in 13 of 137 (9.5%) non-acetaminophen cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Second most frequently implicated non-acetaminophen drug. 13 of 137 non-APAP cases (9.5%). Diagnosis at transplant was acute hepatic necrosis from an implicated drug.

raw_record.support_text: A 19-year-old female with Graves' disease initiated propylthiouracil (PTU) therapy; three months later she presented with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and jaundice with markedly elevated liver enzymes (total bilirubin 6.5 mg/dl, AST 1747 IU/L, ALT 1589 IU/L). She progressed to acute liver failure with coagulopathy and stage II encephalopathy and was the only medication taken; all serologic, autoimmune, and metabolic studies were negative. She underwent orthotopic liver transplant on hospital day 7 but succumbed to tonsillar herniation immediately after surgery; explant pathology revealed marked necrosis and collapse consistent with acute liver failure. The paper states PTU-associated hepatotoxicity is a well-recognized serious adverse effect, with PTU-related liver injury ranging from asymptomatic ALT elevations to fatal acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: 19-year-old African American female treated for hyperthyroidism/Graves' disease; PTU started at 50 mg twice daily then increased to 100 mg three times daily; symptoms appeared about 3 months after starting PTU. Pretreatment liver enzymes normal; no routine liver-associated enzyme (LAE) monitoring was performed, consistent with 1995 US/ATA guidelines that deemed PTU hepatic necrosis rare enough to not require routine LAE monitoring. Presenting labs: total bilirubin 6.5 mg/dL, AST 1747 IU/L, ALT 1589 IU/L; on arrival INR 3.01, albumin low, total bilirubin 25.3 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 13.3 mg/dL, AST 1092 IU/L, ALT 1039 IU/L. Acute hepatitis/failure: admitted for acute hepatitis, transferred to tertiary center, listed status 1 for liver transplant, developed stage II encephalopathy, intubated, intracranial pressure reached 51 mm Hg; underwent orthotopic liver transplant on hospital day 7 but died of tonsillar herniation (brainstem herniation) immediately after surgery. Explant pathology showed marked necrosis and collapse. Excluded alternative etiologies include autoimmune, viral, and metabolic causes; acetaminophen and supplements not taken. Paper urges reconsideration of US monitoring guidelines for LAEs during PTU therapy and notes pediatric endocrinology centers recommend against PTU as first-line therapy due to liver failure risk.

raw_record.support_text: Propylthiouracil is reported as a cause of drug-induced liver injury: Yang et al analyzed 90 cases of severe DILI induced by antithyroid drugs in China over 13 years and found no substantial disparity in the types of severe DILI caused by methimazole and propylthiouracil. There is evidence that propylthiouracil-induced liver injury side effects are more severe, including cases of liver failure and death.
raw_record.extra_details: Yang et al analyzed 90 cases of severe antithyroid drug-induced DILI in China over a 13-year period; no substantial disparity in types of severe DILI vs methimazole. Additional evidence indicates propylthiouracil-induced liver injury can be more severe with cases of liver failure and death.

raw_record.support_text: All six patients in the study showed clinical evidence of hepatic injury with onset of hepatitis definitely related to PTU administration and hypersensitivity symptoms, occurring within 2 months after the start of PTU therapy. The study suggests most symptomatic hepatic injury develops in the first few months of PTU therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Six patients with hepatitis definitely related to drug administration; onset within 2 months after starting PTU. Mechanism attributed to host idiosyncrasy rather than direct toxicity (hypersensitivity symptoms such as itching and jaundice developed in five patients; fever, rash, arthralgia uncommon; variable onset, dose-independent, unpredictable). All patients recovered after PTU withdrawal; no fatal cases in this series, but several case reports have implicated PTU as the cause of severe hepatocellular injury, hepatic failure, or death. Authors recommend monitoring LFTs regularly in patients receiving PTU.

raw_record.support_text: Propylthiouracil for thyrotoxicosis accounted for five (combined with disulfiram, part of nine) cases of drug-induced liver injury acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Five cases.

raw_record.support_text: Research found that propylthiouracil (PTU)-induced liver injury is mainly characterized by varying degrees of hepatocyte necrosis; both PTU and MMI can manifest as increased bilirubin or transaminase, and the incidence of ATD-related drug-induced liver injury is low, ranging from 0.1% to 0.2%. In Wang's observational study of 71,379 cases of hyperthyroidism initially treated with antithyroid drugs, PTU had a liver injury risk of 1.19‰ and an acute liver failure risk of 0.68‰.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver injury characterized by varying degrees of hepatocyte necrosis with increased bilirubin or transaminase; ATD-related DILI incidence 0.1%-0.2%; from Wang's study of 71,379 ATD-treated hyperthyroidism cases: PTU liver injury risk 1.19 per mille and acute liver failure risk 0.68 per mille; compared with MMI (MMI higher liver injury risk, large-dose risk, but lower ALF risk).

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a patient with propylthiouracil (PTU)-induced acute liver failure that was successfully managed with an artificial liver support system (ALSS), concluding that although PTU-induced liver failure is rare, liver function should be monitored during PTU treatment. The discussion attributes to PTU a spectrum of liver injury including PTU-induced hepatitis, severe liver injury, acute liver failure, and classic histologic changes of chronic lobular hepatitis with cholestasis and centrilobular necrosis; FDA data describe PTU-treated patients progressing to ALF, several of whom died or required liver transplantation, and a Taiwan cohort showed PTU-associated hepatitis at 1.19/1000 person-years.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of PTU-induced acute liver failure treated with four sessions of ALSS (plasma exchange plus plasma bilirubin adsorption); total bilirubin improved from 442.8 to 122.1 µmol/L and liver function normalized after 4 months; no biopsy obtained. Estimated ATD-associated hepatotoxicity incidence 0.1-0.2%; PTU-induced severe liver injury ~0.1% of ~15,000 treated adults/year in USA; Taiwan cohort (71,379 hyperthyroid patients) PTU hepatitis 1.19/1000 person-years; FDA report: of 32 PTU patients (22 adults, 10 children) who developed ALF, 13 died (12 adults, 1 child) and 11 required liver transplantation; children appear at higher risk for PTU liver injury; classic histology preserved architecture, chronic lobular hepatitis with cholestasis, centrilobular necrosis. Mechanism: inhibits thyroperoxidase and 5'-deiodinase.

raw_record.support_text: Propylthiouracil (PTU) contributed 5 of the 133 non-APAP drug-induced acute liver failure cases in the Acute Liver Failure Study Group registry.
raw_record.extra_details: 5 ALF cases attributed to propylthiouracil.

raw_record.support_text: In 2004, drug-induced liver injury accounted for 15% of liver transplants in the OPTN and UNOS database. PTU was the third most common cause of drug-induced liver failure, accounting for 10% of drug-related transplants; PTU-related transplant recipients ranged in age from 6 to 69 years.
raw_record.extra_details: PTU is reported as the third most common cause of drug-induced liver failure, accounting for 10% of drug-related liver transplants in the OPTN/UNOS 2004 data. Additional OPTN/UNOS data as of September 22, 2008 showed 23 PTU-related liver transplants from 1990 to 2007, with 30% of recipients being pediatric patients; transplant recipient age range was 6 to 69 years.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of patients diagnosed with ATD-induced severe hepatotoxicity, 39 patients were being treated with propylthiouracil (PTU) at diagnosis, with a mean PTU dose of 212.8±105.0 mg/d at the onset of severe hepatotoxicity. The attributed injury showed hepatocellular, cholestatic, and mixed patterns in 56.4%, 17.9%, and 25.6% of PTU patients, respectively.
raw_record.extra_details: Antithyroid drug (ATD) treated hyperthyroidism patients in China. Severe hepatotoxicity occurred within 4, 8, and 12 weeks in 63.3%, 75.6%, and 81.1% of patients across both groups. Female:male ratio 2.2:1; mean age 41.6±12.5 years.

raw_record.support_text: Propylthiouracil was listed among the other agents causing idiosyncratic drug-induced acute liver failure (≥2 cases).
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as a cause of idiosyncratic drug-induced acute liver failure with at least 2 cases in this series. These patients typically presented subacutely with low aminotransferases, high bilirubin, and more frequent ascites.

raw_record.support_text: Of 104 cases of acute hepatic failure in two steroid trials, 12 were attributable to a drug; propylthiouracil was implicated in one of those patients. Propylthiouracil is also listed among drugs for which anecdotal cases show benefit from drug withdrawal and steroid treatment in allergic-type DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated in 1 of 12 drug-attributable acute hepatic failure cases among 104 acute liver failure cases in two steroid trials. Also reported as an anecdotal DILI cause benefiting from drug withdrawal and steroid treatment in the allergic/hypersensitivity type.

raw_record.support_text: At the time the ATA/AACE 2011 hyperthyroidism guidelines were being formulated, heightened awareness emerged of the association between the use of propylthiouracil (PTU) and severe hepatotoxicity. A review of US liver transplant registries showed PTU was the third most common drug linked to a need for liver transplantation, with 1 to 3 cases of liver failure per year between 1990 and 2007 linked to PTU use.
raw_record.extra_details: US liver transplant registry review found PTU was the third most common drug linked to a need for liver transplantation; 1 to 3 cases of liver failure per year linked to PTU over 1990-2007. Context: antithyroid drug used to treat Graves' disease hyperthyroidism. This association helped drive selection of methimazole (MMI) over PTU in the 2011 ATA/AACE guidelines.

raw_record.support_text: A 46-year-old woman who was taking propylthiouracil died due to hepatic failure. Her laboratory results met the criteria for Hy's law. In the expired/transplanted patient table, propylthiouracil is given as the cause, with peak AST 781, ALT 1118, TB 28.6, ALP 989, and a RUCAM score of 6; she expired.
raw_record.extra_details: 46-year-old woman; died of hepatic failure; peak values AST 781 IU/L, ALT 1118 IU/L, TB 28.6 mg/dL, ALP 989 IU/L; RUCAM score 6; case met Hy's law criteria; propylthiouracil also appears in Table 4 among the 'Medications' (n=111) causal agents of DILI.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that propylthiouracil (PTU)-induced acute liver failure may develop at any age and that the exact mechanism is unrecognized, with idiosyncrasy or immunological mechanisms held responsible for pathogenesis. It further notes that although this is a case-related report, the present case represents a PTU-related asymptomatic acute liver damage, supporting the significance of liver function test monitoring to detect liver damage and reduce fatality.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of PTU-related acute liver failure/acute liver damage presenting asymptomatically; ALT fell from 575 U/L at admission to 35 U/L by day 25, AST from 253 to 47 U/L. No defined risk factor for hepatotoxicity; liver damage is independent of treatment duration; liver function tests normalized in most patients 16-145 days after PTU discontinuation, though liver damage can be irreversible in some cases. No estimated prognostic factor. Two-thirds of PTU-induced ALF patients are women, attributed to Graves' disease dominance. Pathogenesis attributed to idiosyncrasy or immunological mechanisms, exact mechanism unrecognized. Management is LFT monitoring and drug discontinuation upon detection.

raw_record.support_text: In the summary, of 21 observed patients with non-mechanical obstructive jaundice, 10 had drug jaundice, attributed to Megaphen, Arsenobenzol, Propycil and methyltestosterone. The drug jaundice showed intense prolonged icterus with pruritus, elevated serum alkaline phosphatase and cholesterol, and often blood eosinophilia, with cholestasis on biopsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Called Propycil in the paper. The patient of observation #8 had a previous jaundice from Propycil 3 years before the current illness (recurrent reaction to the same agent).

raw_record.support_text: Published case reports show that PTU (propylthiouracil) was discontinued in all cases once hepatotoxicity was detected; patients were subsequently treated with radioactive iodine, surgery, or MMI after discontinuation. Earlier guidance (American Thyroid Association) notes that patients with PTU who develop hepatic injury signs should have liver function tested, and PTU should be discontinued if liver tests remain elevated 2-3× the upper limit of normal with no improvement within a week.
raw_record.extra_details: Antithyroid drug used to treat hyperthyroidism. Management guidance: discontinue PTU when liver function tests are elevated to 2-3× the upper limit of normal with no improvement within a week; monitor liver tests weekly and refer to gastroenterologist/hepatologist if no resolution. Signs of hepatic injury listed include jaundice, pruritus, rash, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, dark urine, and light-colored stool. Alternative treatments after PTU discontinuation: radioactive iodine, surgery, or MMI.

raw_record.support_text: In a UNOS analysis of liver transplants performed for ALF due to drug-induced hepatotoxicity (1990-2002), propylthiouracil was responsible in 9.5% of the 258 single-drug cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Third most common single drug (9.5%) responsible for drug-induced hepatotoxicity-related liver transplants for ALF in the UNOS analysis (1990-2002).

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of hepatotoxicity caused by propylthiouracil in a 64-year-old hyperthyroid woman who received 250 mg/day for 1 year and developed hepatitis. Alcohol and illicit drug use were ruled out, serologies for hepatitis A, B, and C were negative, Epstein-Barr and cytomegalovirus infections were excluded, and antinuclear, anti-mitochondrial, and anti-smooth-muscle antibodies were negative. Symptoms included nausea, vomiting, and jaundice; liver biopsy ruled out chronic active hepatitis, and the patient subsequently developed cirrhosis.
raw_record.extra_details: 64-year-old hyperthyroid female; dose 250 mg propylthiouracil daily for 1 year. Presented with hepatitis-like clinical picture (nausea, vomiting, jaundice). Alcohol and illicit drug intake eliminated; hepatitis A/B/C serologies negative; EBV and CMV infections excluded; ANA, anti-mitochondrial, and anti-smooth-muscle antibodies negative. Liver biopsy ruled out chronic active hepatitis; patient later developed cirrhosis (permanent liver damage).

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that major side effects of antithyroid drugs include hepatitis and that hepatitis is associated with propylthiouracil (PTU), but apparently not with other antithyroid drugs. Reporting agreement with Han son regarding toxic hepatitis associated with PTU (but not methimazole), they note a higher frequency in their own hospitalized-patient series (6% vs the reported 0.5-1%).
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective study of hospitalized hyperthyroid patients in Albania. Frequency of toxic hepatitis in this study was 6%, compared with a reported 0.5-1%; the authors suggest higher figures may reflect the quality of antithyroid drugs used in Albania and patient selection bias (serious side effects more likely hospitalized). Cited as a major side effect and classified as toxic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 4,287 patients treated with propylthiouracil (PTU), 272 (6.3%) developed PTU-induced DILI, with overall incidence 1.43% in male and 6.51% in female patients (females significantly higher, p=0.015). Median PTU dose at DILI diagnosis was 300 mg/day (range 50-500 mg), median time to DILI was 33.5 days (significantly longer than MMI-DILI, p<0.001), and 98.9% had hepatocellular type injury; 7 patients required hospitalization. There was no correlation between PTU dose and severity of liver injury. Prevalence of DILI was significantly higher with PTU than MMI (6.3% vs 1.4%, p<0.001).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adults treated for Graves' disease (hyperthyroidism); marked female predominance with significantly higher incidence in females; no PTU dose-severity correlation observed.
raw_record.extra_details: 272/4,287 cases (6.3% overall); median age 33 years (range 17-66); median PTU daily dose 300 mg (range 50-500 mg); median peak T-bil 0.8 mg/dL (range 0.4-18.6), peak ALT 240 U/L (range 32-1329); median time to DILI 33.5 days (range 8-314), longer than MMI (p<0.001); hepatocellular 98.9%, mixed 0.7%, cholestatic 0.4%; 7 hospitalized; alternatives included RAI, MMI switch, surgery, potassium iodide; 12 continued PTU.

The authors note PTU-induced hepatitis is a recognized drug reaction with a small but potentially serious risk of hepatic failure, and they describe it as the first reported case of occurrence in the second trimester with a subsequent successful outcome following best supportive care and carbimazole (CBZ) therapy.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity is described as the second major, occasionally lethal side effect of antithyroid drugs. In an analysis of 18,558 Japanese patients with Graves disease treated with antithyroid drugs, severe liver injury (alanine aminotransferase >8-fold or total bilirubin >3-fold the upper limit) was significantly higher in the propylthiouracil (PTU)-treated group (6.3%) than in the methimazole (MMI)-treated group (1.4%); median time to development of antithyroid-drug-induced hepatic injury was 30 (range 7-314) days and no deaths were reported. Recent data from Taiwan and China are noted to challenge the older concept of a more hepatocellular injury pattern with PTU versus a more cholestatic pattern with MMI.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with Graves disease; no deaths reported in the cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: Japanese cohort of 18,558 patients; severe liver injury (ALT >8x ULN or total bilirubin >3x ULN) in 6.3% of PTU-treated patients; median latency 30 (range 7-314) days; no deaths. Recent Taiwan and China data challenge the older concept of a predominantly hepatocellular injury pattern with PTU.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that ATD-induced severe hepatotoxicity, attributed to propylthiouracil (PTU) as well as methimazole, was identified in 90 patients with Graves' disease. PTU-induced hepatotoxicity is described as taking the form of allergic hepatitis accompanied by laboratory evidence of hepatocellular injury, and the hepatocellular, cholestatic, and mixed types of severe hepatotoxicity were present at approximately equivalent rates in the MMI and PTU groups.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with Graves' disease treated for hyperthyroidism; female predominance; greater susceptibility in the 20-50 year age group.

Mean treatment duration before severe hepatotoxicity was 10 weeks for PTU; more than 60% of patients developed severe hepatotoxicity within 4 weeks and more than 80% within 12 weeks. PTU-induced hepatotoxicity is described as allergic hepatitis with hepatocellular injury, markedly elevated aminotransferases, and pathological findings ranging from hepatocellular inflammation to submassive or massive hepatic necrosis; cholestatic type frequency was 17.9% in the PTU group.

Their manifestations ranged from a benign course after drug withdrawal in one patient, a longstanding course in another suggesting drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis, and a more severe clinical condition with acute liver failure in a third patient that required liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: A 12-year-old girl with Graves disease developed fatigue, fever, diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting after 4 weeks of therapy with PTU 300 mg/day (100 mg thrice daily), followed several days later by jaundice, hepatic tenderness, and dark urine. On admission, SGOT was 2312 IU/L, SGPT 1435 IU/L, ALP 171 IU/L, total bilirubin 12.7 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 7.6 mg/dL, and prothrombin time 23.2 s, with negative serology for hepatitis A and B.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (12-year-old girl) treated for Graves disease; PTU 300 mg/day administered orally as 100 mg three times daily for 4 weeks before symptom onset.
raw_record.extra_details: Diagnosis of PTU-induced hepatitis was established. PTU was discontinued and prednisone 50 mg/day plus vitamin K were given; hepatic function returned to normal ~4 weeks after admission. Elevated transaminases (SGOT 2312, SGPT 1435 IU/L) with mild ALP rise (171 IU/L), conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (total 12.7, direct 7.6 mg/dL), prolonged prothrombin time (23.2 s). Ultrasonography showed increased liver size with patchy areas, no intrahepatic biliary dilatation. Symptoms included jaundice, hepatic tenderness, dark urine, fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea.

raw_record.support_text: A 12-year-old girl with hyperthyroidism who had started treatment with propylthiouracil (PTU) 100 mg tid developed hepatitis. The drug was stopped and the clinical and laboratory findings of hepatitis disappeared within a week; she received no other hepatotoxic drugs and viral investigations were negative. The authors report this as the ninth reported case of PTU-induced hepatitis, with a clinical picture similar to viral hepatitis, noting that recovery usually follows drug withdrawal but that two fatal cases of PTU-induced hepatitis have been reported.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (12-year-old girl); indication of hyperthyroidism; prior urticarial rash with initial PTU exposure that resolved and recurred on rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose PTU 100 mg tid. Onset of urticarial rash on day 3 after first administration; symptoms (diarrhea, fever, headache, nausea, vomiting) developed within days of the second administration. Dechallenge led to resolution of hepatitis within one week. Mild jaundice appeared two days after admission; enlarged liver and spleen. No other drugs used and viral investigations negative. Ninth reported case of PTU-induced hepatitis; two fatal cases previously reported; recovery usually follows withdrawal of the drug. Clinical picture similar to viral hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Propiltiouracil (PTU) is widely used to treat hyperthyroidism, and hepatotoxicity is among the rarest but most serious side effects associated with it. The paper reports a case of acute cholestatic hepatitis in a 15-year-old boy on PTU, in which viral, metabolic, and autoimmune causes were excluded and liver biopsy showed findings suggestive of drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis. Withdrawal of the drug led to remission of symptoms and progressive normalization of liver function tests; the paper notes that patients on PTU can rarely develop severe liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (15 years old) treated for hyperthyroidism; recent acetylsalicylic acid use noted as an additional (excluded) potential factor; propylthiouracil was withdrawn.
raw_record.extra_details: PTU 100 mg/day for 15 months; onset ~7 days before first consultation with asthenia, myalgia, coluria, pale stools, and jaundice; exclusion of hepatitis A/B/C, EBV, CMV, Wilson disease, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, and autoimmune hepatitis (only FAN 1:160 granular nuclear positive). Laboratory: ALT 1070 UI/L, AST 1060 UI/L, total bilirubin 25.1 then 39 then 46.7 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 14.9-31 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 1319 UI/L, prothrombin activity reduced to 50%. Liver biopsy showed portal widening with mononuclear infiltrate, rare eosinophils, mild fibrosis, bile duct proliferation, hepatocyte ballooning with bilirubin pigment, and centrilobular congestion with subendothelial edema. Treated with prednisone (60 mg/day, tapered); full normalization of liver tests 2.5 months later; PTU hepatotoxicity has a known potential, with ~30 published cases up to 1996, some fatal, including severe cholestasis and submassive necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: Un niño de 12 años y 10 meses, diagnosticado de enfermedad de Graves 2 años antes, desarrolló una hepatitis tóxica por propiltiouracilo 4 meses después de comenzar el tratamiento. Se había indicado este fármaco porque el paciente había presentado exantemas urticariformes con metimazol y con carbimazol. El cuadro clínico cedió de manera progresiva tras suspender el tratamiento e iniciar corticoterapia en dosis altas, y una vez controlada la hepatopatía la enfermedad de Graves se trató con radioyodo. Este fue el único efecto secundario grave detectado en la serie de 20 pacientes.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (boy aged 12 years 10 months) with Graves disease; propylthiouracil was selected because the patient had previously developed urticarial skin rashes with methimazole and carbimazole.
raw_record.extra_details: Toxic hepatitis developed 4 months after starting propylthiouracil treatment; it resolved progressively after drug discontinuation and high-dose corticosteroid therapy, after which Graves disease was treated with radioiodine. This was the only severe adverse effect among the 20 antithyroid-drug-treated patients.

raw_record.support_text: A 32-year-old pregnant woman with Graves' disease, started on a reducing regime of propylthiouracil (PTU), developed jaundice at week 20 of gestation. Bloods showed bilirubin 91 µmol/l, ALT 1,796 IU/l, ALP 200 IU/l, INR 1.2 and albumin 33 g/l. A presumptive diagnosis of PTU-induced hepatitis was made; PTU was immediately discontinued, and the bilirubin peaked at 378 before improving over the following two weeks. Autoimmune and viral hepatitis markers, ultrasound, ferritin and caeruloplasmin were normal, supporting PTU as the cause.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnancy; jaundice developed at week 20 of gestation while on a reducing PTU regime for Graves' disease.
raw_record.extra_details: PTU used as first-line anti-thyroid drug in pregnancy. Initial labs: bilirubin 91 µmol/l, ALT 1,796 IU/l, ALP 200 IU/l, INR 1.2, albumin 33 g/l; bilirubin peaked at 378 after PTU discontinuation, then fell (dechallenge improvement). After PTU cessation she became thyrotoxic and was started on carbimazole (not attributed as a cause); liver function tests improved and carbimazole was stopped at week 32; healthy baby delivered at 38 weeks. Reported as the first case of PTU-induced hepatitis in the second trimester with successful outcome.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a case of propylthiouracil (PTU)-induced fulminant hepatic failure in a pregnant patient who required liver transplantation and thyroidectomy, noting the case reflects a very rare complication of a presumed safe drug and echoes the FDA warning on propylthiouracil. Therapy for the condition involved immediate cessation of PTU with expectant management of hepatic-failure complications, and a fatality rate of 25% to 50% has been reported in these patients, with liver transplantation required in severe cases.

raw_record.extra_details: FDA warning exists on the drug (propylthiouracil). A fatality rate of 25% to 50% has been reported in patients with PTU-induced hepatic failure. Severe cases may require liver transplantation; 12 cases of liver transplantation for fulminant hepatic failure between the 13th and 27th weeks of pregnancy have been reported, with a fetal survival rate of 36%.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 36-year-old pregnant Kenyan woman with Graves' disease (started on propylthiouracil/PTU therapy 3 months prior) who, at 19 weeks' gestation, developed acute liver failure attributed to propylthiouracil hepatotoxicity, requiring liver transplantation. This is framed as the first case of propylthiouracil-induced acute liver failure in a hyperthyroid second-trimester patient resulting in LT.

raw_record.extra_details: Latency of ~3 months after starting PTU. Presenting labs: total bilirubin 19.6 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 17.5 mg/dL, albumin 2.2 gm/dL, INR 2.99 (peak 5.64), PTT 60.2 s, ALP 217 U/L, AST 2549 U/L, ALT 1427 U/L, ammonia 104 umol/L. Grade 3 hepatic encephalopathy requiring intubation; intraparenchymal pressure monitoring within normal limits. Attempted plasmapheresis and high-dose IV steroids before emergency listing for LT. Serologic workup for viral, autoimmune, and metabolic etiologies was unrevealing.

raw_record.support_text: The authors attribute prolonged cholestasis in their patient to amitriptyline based on: absence of biliary tract disease (normal retrograde cholangiography and ultrasound), no serologic or circumstantial evidence of viral hepatitis, negative serum antitissue antibodies, and discontinuation of other drugs 2 weeks before jaundice onset without reported hepatotoxicity. The clinical presentation (jaundice after 5 weeks of amitriptyline, transient eosinophilia, initial centrilobular cholestasis) resembled previously reported amitriptyline-induced acute cholestatic hepatitis. Despite stopping amitriptyline, cholestasis was markedly protracted, with pruritus and jaundice lasting 19 and 20 months and abnormal liver tests persisting at 2 years; three liver biopsies showed progression from centrilobular cholestasis to portal inflammation, ductular proliferation, moderate fibrosis, and partial disappearance of interlobular bile ducts.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case report. Jaundice onset 5 weeks after starting amitriptyline, accompanied by transient blood eosinophilia. Outcome remarkable for protracted cholestasis: pruritus for 19 months and jaundice for 20 months; liver tests still abnormal 2 years after jaundice onset. Three serial liver biopsies documented initial centrilobular cholestasis progressing to portal inflammatory infiltration, ductular proliferation, moderate fibrosis, and partial loss of interlobular bile ducts. Competing causes excluded (no biliary disease, no viral hepatitis, negative antitissue antibodies). Hepatitis suggested to be immunoallergic; a reactive-metabolite/immune mechanism analogous to imipramine/amineptine was hypothesized. Debrisoquine/dextromethorphan oxidation phenotyping showed an extensive metabolizer phenotype (metabolic ratio 0.009), indicating amitriptyline hydroxylation was not deficient.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 5 published patients plus one new patient (6 total) with amitriptyline-induced jaundice. Hepatitis occurred 24-430 days after starting amitriptyline at 30-150 mg daily. Hypersensitivity manifestations (fever, rash, hypereosinophilia) were seen in 3 patients. Serum ALAT was markedly increased in 4 patients; alkaline phosphatase was usually increased. Liver histology showed necrosis, cholestasis, or both. The jaundice induced by amitriptyline is classified as 'mixed' with the hepatocellular component usually predominating. Two of the 3 patients with fulminant hepatitis died; our patient survived; patients without hepatic encephalopathy recovered in 53-128 days.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Most reported patients took concurrent psychotropic/sedative medications (diazepam, furosemide, amobarbital, secobarbital, chlordiazepoxide, perphenazine, sulpiride); the index patient received amitriptyline plus perphenazine (Mutanxion) before both episodes, clobazam only before the first episode and sulpiride only before the second, with amitriptyline reasonably assumed responsible.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency 24-430 days at 30-150 mg daily; fulminant hepatitis with hepatic encephalopathy in 3 patients (2 died); rechallenge led to recurrence sooner after second administration. Liver histology showed necrosis, cholestasis, and inflammation. Index patient had deep jaundice, asterixis, mild ascites, 9 mm Hg wedged-free hepatic vein gradient, and massive centrilobular/mediolobular necrosis on biopsy, with slow but complete recovery.

raw_record.support_text: In this double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of rimegepant 75 mg oral tablet versus placebo for acute migraine treatment, the authors state: 'No signal of drug-induced liver injury due to rimegepant was identified.' The conclusion reiterates that tolerability and safety were similar to placebo with no evidence of hepatotoxicity. This is an explicit agent-specific negative conclusion about human drug-induced liver injury for rimegepant.
raw_record.extra_details: Rimegepant 75 mg oral tablet, a small molecule CGRP receptor antagonist, in acute migraine treatment. Double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled phase trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03235479); 1485 enrolled, 1162 randomized (rimegepant n=582; placebo n=580), mostly female (85.5%), mean age 41.6 years. Coprimary endpoints: pain freedom and most bothersome symptom freedom at 2 h postdose. No DILI signal and no evidence of hepatotoxicity reported.

raw_record.support_text: The discussion states that no new safety issues for rimegepant were identified and that 'no evidence of drug-induced liver injury' was found. During the double-blind treatment phase, hepatic-related adverse events occurred in 1.2% (n=3) of rimegepant participants (preferred terms included hepatic enzyme increase, liver function test increase, hepatic function abnormal, and hepatic steatosis, n=1 each) versus 1.6% (n=4) in the placebo group, and no participants had AST or ALT levels >3×ULN or total bilirubin >2×ULN.
raw_record.extra_details: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of rimegepant 75 mg for preventive treatment of migraine in Japan (DBT safety analysis set rimegepant n=247, placebo n=249). Hepatic-related AEs by SMQ were 3 (1.2%) rimegepant vs 4 (1.6%) placebo; MedDRA version 26.1. Liver function test data available for 241 rimegepant and 246 placebo participants; no participant had AST or ALT >3×ULN or total bilirubin >2×ULN during the DBT phase. AEs related to study drug occurred in 24 (9.7%) rimegepant vs 11 (4.4%) placebo participants; SAEs related to study drug 0 in both.

raw_record.support_text: In this randomized controlled trial of a single 75 mg rimegepant oral tablet for the acute treatment of adults with migraine, the authors state that safety and tolerability with rimegepant were excellent and that liver function testing showed no evidence of hepatotoxicity. Transaminase elevations comparing rimegepant (serum AST or ALT >ULN in 2.0%, 11/546) versus placebo (3.6%, 20/549) showed no signal, one participant in each group had levels >3x ULN, none >5x ULN, and no bilirubin elevations >2x ULN were observed.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase safety assessment of rimegepant 75 mg oral tablet for acute migraine. Serum AST or ALT >ULN: 2.0% (11/546) rimegepant vs 3.6% (20/549) placebo; >3x ULN in 0.2% each group; none >5x ULN; total bilirubin >2x ULN in 0.0% both groups. Authors explicitly concluded liver function testing showed no evidence of hepatotoxicity. Most common AE was nausea (0.9% vs 1.1% placebo).

raw_record.support_text: In the pivotal phase III trials of rimegepant (75 mg) for acute migraine treatment, no serious adverse events related to treatment occurred and no hepatotoxicity was described; nausea and urinary tract infections were the most common adverse events. A companion open-label study (NCT03266588) with up to 75 mg rimegepant taken as needed for up to 52 weeks likewise reported that hepatotoxicity was not observed with long-term and high-frequency dosing.
raw_record.extra_details: NURTEC ODT 75 mg; approved by the US FDA for acute migraine treatment in February 2020. In phase III trials (NCT03235479, NCT03237845, NCT03461757) no hepatotoxicity was described; in the long-term open-label study (NCT03266588) hepatotoxicity was not observed with high-frequency dosing up to one tablet per day for 52 weeks. Use should be avoided in severe hepatic impairment due to higher plasma rimegepant concentrations, but no DILI-related injury is attributed.

raw_record.support_text: The use of dabigatran did not show hepatotoxic effects like its sister drug ximelagatran, and in the RE-LY trial (18,113 patients with AF) no evidence of hepatotoxicity was found with dabigatran etexilate 110 or 150 mg twice daily.
raw_record.extra_details: Prodrug of dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor evaluated in the RE-MODEL, RE-NOVATE, RE-MOBILIZE, RE-COVER, and RE-LY trials for VTE prevention and stroke prevention in AF; more dabigatran patients had dyspepsia than warfarin, but no hepatotoxicity or hepatotoxic effects were observed in the RE-LY trial.
