raw_record.support_text: In a case report, the patient presented with cytolytic hepatitis 117 days after initiation of crizotinib treatment. Other potential causes of liver failure (viral hepatitis, hepatic metastasis, alcoholic liver disease, other drug-induced liver injuries) were excluded, and relapse rapidly occurred after re-initiation of crizotinib despite oral methylprednisolone. This supports crizotinib-associated hepatotoxicity with a rechallenge-confirmed relapse.
raw_record.extra_details: Cytolytic hepatitis appearing 117 days after crizotinib initiation; relapse rapidly after re-initiation despite oral methylprednisolone. Competing causes excluded (viral hepatitis, hepatic metastasis, alcoholic liver disease, other drug-induced liver injuries). Patient had primary lung SRCA with EML4-ALK NSCLC. Crizotinib metabolized by CYP3A4; liver injury hypothesized to involve accumulation of toxic metabolites or immune-related mechanisms. No cross-toxicity seen with lorlatinib.

raw_record.support_text: The paper cites a case report by Kreitman et al. describing a patient in whom crizotinib caused acute liver failure (ALF), and notes that treatment with the ROS scavenger N-acetylcysteine partially restored liver function tests to normal and partially relieved the crizotinib-induced ALF. This is presented as supporting the oxidative-stress mechanism for crizotinib-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Attribution rests on a single cited case report by Kreitman et al. N-acetylcysteine partially restored liver function tests and partially relieved crizotinib-induced acute liver failure. The paper otherwise relies on animal-model and HepG2/HL7702 cell data, which are not human DILI evidence.

raw_record.support_text: The paper references a published report of two patients with successful Ceritinib treatment after Crizotinib-induced hepatitis, using the induced-injury phrase 'Crizotinib-induced hepatitis' and noting liver injury is a class effect of ALK inhibitors that appears less frequent and less severe with Ceritinib or Alectinib than Crizotinib.
raw_record.extra_details: Crizotinib-induced hepatitis supported by a reference to a case report of two patients successfully treated with Ceritinib afterward; hepatitis framed as a class effect of ALK inhibitors, reported less frequent and less severe with Ceritinib or Alectinib.

raw_record.support_text: Crizotinib hepatotoxicity was reported at an incidence of 6% to 11%, with a fatality rate of 0.1% [18]. In a single clinical study, neither CYP3A4 inducers nor inhibitors showed any hepatotoxicity, although concurrent use of H2-antagonists and proton pump inhibitors enhanced hepatotoxicity [74]. Additional in vitro findings (mitochondrial oxygen-consumption inhibition, ROS overproduction, cytochrome c release, ATP depletion, caspase activation, and necrosis in rat/HepG2/primary rat-human hepatocytes) were not themselves human DILI evidence.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported incidence of hepatotoxicity 6%-11% with fatality rate 0.1% [18]. In a clinical study, CYP3A4 inducers/inhibitors showed no hepatotoxicity, while concurrent H2-antagonists and proton pump inhibitors enhanced hepatotoxicity [74]. Companion in vitro data (inhibited oxygen consumption, ROS overproduction, cytochrome c release, ATP depletion, caspase activation, necrosis at 20-100x blood levels) are preclinical and do not constitute human DILI.

raw_record.support_text: A 62-year-old female with non-small-cell lung cancer treated with crizotinib presented with acute liver failure after 24 days of therapy. AST and ALT rose from normal to 2053 IU/L and 6194 IU/L, total bilirubin and PT-INR increased up to 443 µmol/L and 5.33, and hepatic encephalopathy and hepatorenal syndrome emerged. Despite crizotinib discontinuation and supportive therapy, the patient died 40 days after treatment initiation due to acute liver failure with massive liver cell necrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of fatal fulminant acute liver failure due to liver cell necrosis in a Caucasian patient with ALK-positive stage IV NSCLC, described as the first such reported case. Dose 250 mg twice daily; onset of fulminant failure ~24 days after start. Peak ALT 6194 IU/L, AST 2053 IU/L, total bilirubin up to 443 µmol/L, PT-INR 5.33; coagulation factor V 11%; ferritin 10756 µg/L; hepatic encephalopathy and hepatorenal syndrome; MELD 36; met King's College criteria for poor prognosis but not a transplant candidate due to poor cancer prognosis; died on day 40. Other causes excluded (biliary obstruction, viral hepatitis A/B/C, alcohol, concomitant medication). Plasma crizotinib levels within expected range after discontinuation; estimated t1/2 ~50 h. No autopsy/biopsy. Authors note crizotinib-induced fatal hepatotoxicity occurs in 0.2% of patients and grade 3-4 ALT elevations in ~15% in pivotal phase III trials.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that crizotinib caused drug-induced hepatitis in the present case and describes three previously reported cases of crizotinib-induced hepatitis, all occurring within a few months after crizotinib introduction. In one reported case, rechallenge with half-dose crizotinib failed because hepatitis recurred. The present case was non-dose-dependent, which the authors interpreted as partly an allergic reaction to crizotinib or its metabolites, and oral desensitization with crizotinib (with co-administered oral steroids) permitted continued treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Present case plus three previously reported cases of crizotinib-induced hepatitis, all within a few months of starting treatment; half-dose rechallenge failed in one case due to hepatitis recurrence; present case was dose-independent, suggesting an allergic reaction to crizotinib or metabolites; successful oral desensitization to crizotinib (with oral steroids) allowed further treatment; patient had ALK-rearranged NSCLC and received crizotinib as second-line and fifth-line therapy.

raw_record.support_text: In the PROFILE 1005 study of crizotinib in patients with previously treated ALK-positive NSCLC, 15 patients died due to treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs). Hepatotoxicity was reported as the cause of death in two of these patients, alongside ILD in four patients, pneumonia in three, and other causes in single patients. Crizotinib-related hepatotoxicity was thus attributed as a fatal treatment-related adverse event in human patients.
raw_record.extra_details: In the PROFILE 1005 trial, 15 patients died due to treatment-related adverse events overall; hepatotoxicity caused death in 2 of these patients. At data cut-off 709/1059 patients (67%) had died (any causality); disease progression (n=640) was the most common cause of death. Elevations in transaminases were also TRAEs associated with dose reductions (5%) and dosing interruptions (5%) but were not themselves framed as DILI.

raw_record.support_text: Crizotinib received FDA accelerated approval for ALK-positive NSCLC in August 2011. A meta-analysis of clinical trials showed the dose had to be reduced or treatment discontinued in 6.5% of patients because of toxicity, and the most clinically significant toxicities of crizotinib included hepatotoxicity. One case of fatal drug-induced hepatotoxicity occurred in a crizotinib-treated patient following closure of the FDA safety database, prompting investigation of the mechanism of crizotinib-induced hepatotoxicity. The paper presents this as established human hepatotoxicity and studies its mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: Indication: ALK-positive NSCLC. A meta-analysis of clinical trials reported crizotinib dose reduction or treatment discontinuation in 6.5% of patients because of toxicity. Severe hepatotoxicity is observed with most receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors in clinical applications. One case of fatal drug-induced hepatotoxicity occurred in a crizotinib-treated patient after the FDA safety database closed. The paper's mechanistic work (HL-7702 cells and human primary hepatocytes) indicates ALK, ROS1 and MET are not targets of crizotinib-induced hepatocyte death/apoptosis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 54-year-old woman treated with 400 mg/day of crizotinib for advanced ALK-positive lung adenocarcinoma who developed severe acute hepatitis on Day 29 that progressed to fulminant hepatitis and death from liver failure on Day 36. After excluding biliary abnormalities, viral/autoimmune hepatitis, alcohol, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease and hemodynamic liver disease, and ruling out the co-administered sitagliptin and rabeprazole (taken >2 years without adverse effect), they concluded using international criteria and scoring systems that the fulminant hepatitis was caused by crizotinib.
raw_record.extra_details: 54-year-old Japanese woman with concurrent dermatomyositis (on prednisolone 10 mg), steroid-induced diabetes (on sitagliptin), and rabeprazole; started crizotinib 400 mg/day (reduced dose for low body weight, 155 cm/40 kg) as first-line therapy. On Day 29: AST 3236 IU/l, ALT 5201 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 506 IU/l, gamma-glutamyltransferase 86 IU/l, total bilirubin 46.2 µmol/l, prothrombin time <10%, NH3 153 µg/dl; abdominal CT suggested acute hepatitis. Progressed to hepatic encephalopathy and fulminant hepatitis (Inuyama Symposium criteria); treated with steroid pulse, plasma exchange, continuous hemodiafiltration, lactulose, fosphenytoin and midazolam; died of liver failure on Day 36. Co-administered sitagliptin and rabeprazole were explicitly excluded as guilty drugs. Biochemical values are consistent with an acute hepatocellular-type injury (not explicitly labeled in the paper).

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes a 62-year-old woman with ALK-rearranged NSCLC who developed severe lobular hepatitis with submassive parenchymal dropout while on crizotinib, with a predominantly lymphohistiocytic infiltrate, sparing of the bile ducts, marked canalicular/hepatocellular cholestasis, and hyperbilirubinemia. The marked cholestasis paralleled the biochemical hyperbilirubinemia.
raw_record.extra_details: The 62-year-old woman had ALK-rearranged NSCLC. Crizotinib was discontinued 8 days after admission (2 days after initiation) and the patient's serum transaminases precipitously declined after cessation. She developed edema and ascites post-discharge requiring furosemide 40 mg daily and spironolactone 100 mg daily for 3 weeks; never developed hepatic encephalopathy. All liver chemistries normalized by follow-up 79 days after admission; CT showed improved liver radiography. Histology showed severe lobular hepatitis with submassive parenchymal dropout, lymphohistiocytic inflammation without frank granulomata, neutrophils outnumbering eosinophils and plasma cells, and proliferating residual hepatocytes, plus marked mostly canalicular and hepatocellular cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: In the safety database of the crizotinib clinical trial in ALK-positive NSCLC, the most clinically significant toxicities of crizotinib were hepatotoxicity, bradycardia, interstitial lung disease (ILD) or pneumonitis, and QT-interval prolongation. Alanine transaminase elevation (17%) based on laboratory evaluation in crizotinib-treated patients was the most common grade 3–4 adverse event. Following safety database closure (March 2012), one case of drug-induced fatal hepatotoxicity occurred in a crizotinib-treated patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Crizotinib is FDA-approved for ALK-positive NSCLC. Elevated transaminases were among the most common adverse drug reactions (>25%). Alanine transaminase elevation (17%) was the most common grade 3–4 adverse event. One case of drug-induced fatal hepatotoxicity occurred in a crizotinib-treated patient after safety database closure (March 2012). In the discussion, crizotinib's tolerability included a low frequency of clinically significant adverse reactions such as ILD and hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Acute hepatitis in this patient was ascribed to crizotinib. There was no history of liver disease, liver tests were normal before starting the drug, there was no other cause of acute hepatitis (no viral hepatitis serology, negative anti-tissue antibodies, no alcohol abuse or metabolic syndrome), and the role of acetylsalicylic acid was excluded because it had been used for years without liver reaction. Crizotinib had been administered for 2 months before acute hepatitis, withdrawal was followed by prompt recovery, and rechallenge with the drug caused a transient recurrence of liver abnormalities. Using international drug causality assessment criteria and scoring systems, the role of crizotinib in this case of hepatitis was judged highly probable.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report. Crizotinib administered for 2 months before onset of acute hepatitis; withdrawal followed by prompt recovery; rechallenge with the drug at low dose led to relapse with ALT elevation within 13 days. Causality assessed as highly probable using international criteria and drug causality scoring systems [7–9,12,13]. Acetylsalicylic acid ruled out as a cause (used for years without liver reaction). No signs of biological cholestasis or hypersensitivity; isolated Grade 3/4 transaminase elevations without cholestasis during clinical use normalized after crizotinib dose reduction, consistent with a dose-dependent hepatocellular metabolic reaction [2,4,7–10]. Mechanism unknown; crizotinib is predominantly metabolized by CYP3A enzymes and moderately inhibits them in vivo. Rapid relapse on rechallenge may be compatible with an immune reaction, but an idiosyncratic metabolic reaction remains possible given absence of drug hypersensitivity hallmarks.

raw_record.support_text: Crizotinib, an oral small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting ALK, ROS1 and MET, is the FDA-approved first-line treatment for ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer. Nearly 0.1% of crizotinib-treated patients experienced fatal hepatotoxicity across clinical trials. Per FDA adverse events, 11.2% and 5.7% of patients had ALT and AST elevations >5x ULN, respectively, after crizotinib treatment, and 1.0% required permanent discontinuation due to elevated transaminases, generally within the first 2 months. A reported case involved a 62-year-old patient who presented with acute liver failure after 24 days of crizotinib therapy and died after 40 days despite crizotinib discontinuation and intensive supportive therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: In ALK-positive NSCLC therapeutic use. Nearly 0.1% fatal hepatotoxicity across clinical trials; FDA adverse events showed 11.2% ALT and 5.7% AST elevations >5x ULN; 1.0% permanent discontinuation due to elevated transaminases, generally within the first 2 months of treatment. Case: 62-year-old patient with acute liver failure after 24 days of crizotinib therapy, died after 40 days despite discontinuation and intensive supportive therapy (van Geel et al., 2016). Cell-based mechanistic work in HL-7702 and human primary hepatocytes showed crizotinib-induced hepatocyte apoptosis independent of ALK/ROS1/MET involving MMP decrease, DNA damage and ROS generation, stated as consistent with clinical cases.

raw_record.support_text: During crizotinib therapy in a patient with ROS1-rearranged pleomorphic pulmonary carcinoma, grade 4 treatment-related hepatotoxicity was observed, with peak AST and ALT of 865 U/L and 2451 U/L, respectively, while total bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase remained within normal limits. Her liver enzymes returned to normal levels at day 39 after crizotinib discontinuation (AST 19 U/L, ALT 20 U/L), after which treatment was changed to ceritinib.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report within a serial-ROS1-TKI treatment narrative for ROS1-rearranged pulmonary pleomorphic carcinoma (PPC), young non-smoker female. Grade 4 (CTCAE) treatment-related hepatotoxicity; peak AST 865 U/L and ALT 2451 U/L with normal total bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase; enzymes normalized by day 39 after crizotinib discontinuation (AST 19 U/L, ALT 20 U/L) with no rechallenge; treatment then switched to ceritinib.

raw_record.support_text: In the crizotinib group, four hepatic events led to permanent treatment discontinuation: three involved elevated aminotransferase levels only, and one was a grade 2 drug-induced liver injury that met Hy's law criteria (elevated aminotransferase and total bilirubin levels without evidence of cholestasis, i.e., no elevated serum alkaline phosphatase). An additional Hy's law case occurred in a patient in the chemotherapy group after crossover to crizotinib. Grade 3 or 4 aminotransferase elevations occurred in 24 patients (14%) in the crizotinib group versus 4 (2%) in the chemotherapy group. No deaths from hepatic dysfunction occurred.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase trial of crizotinib versus chemotherapy (platinum-based) for ALK-positive non-small-cell lung cancer; as-treated populations crizotinib N=171, chemotherapy N=169 before crossover. Four hepatic events led to permanent crizotinib discontinuation: three aminotransferase-elevation-only events and one grade 2 DILI meeting Hy's law; an additional Hy's law DILI case occurred in a chemotherapy patient after crossover to crizotinib. Grade 3/4 aminotransferase elevations in 24 (14%) crizotinib patients vs 4 (2%) chemotherapy, managed by dose interruption/reduction. No deaths from hepatic dysfunction. Median treatment duration 10.9 months (range 0.4-34.3) in the crizotinib group.

The authors describe this as crizotinib-induced hepatotoxicity and note the precise mechanism and risk factors remain unknown.

raw_record.support_text: A 37-year-old Asian patient with anaplastic lymphoma kinase-rearranged lung adenocarcinoma was started on crizotinib 250 mg twice daily as first-line therapy. On day 55 he was admitted with elevated AST (402 IU/L), ALT (215 IU/L) and total bilirubin (145 μmol/L) and was diagnosed with crizotinib-induced fulminant liver failure. Despite discontinuation and supportive therapy, enzymes continued to rise (AST 1075 IU/L, ALT 240 IU/L, bilirubin 233 μmol/L) and he died on day 60.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had ALK-rearranged lung adenocarcinoma with hepatic metastasis; 37-year-old Asian male.
raw_record.extra_details: First-line dose 250 mg twice daily; no adverse effects until day 46; admitted day 55 with elevated AST 402 IU/L, ALT 215 IU/L, total bilirubin 145 μmol/L; despite crizotinib discontinuation and supportive therapy levels rose to AST 1075 IU/L, ALT 240 IU/L, bilirubin 233 μmol/L and the patient died on day 60. Authors note crizotinib hepatotoxicity is rare and non-specific and may progress to fatal liver failure, and recommend King's College Criteria and weekly liver enzyme monitoring.

raw_record.support_text: Ten cases of crizotinib-induced liver toxicity have been reported since 2013, including the present case; all except the present case were hepatocellular-type liver toxicity in eight ALK-rearranged and one ROS1-rearranged NSCLC, and four cases were fulminant hepatitis including three fatal cases. Crizotinib was initially administered at 200-500 mg/day, and the onset of liver enzyme abnormalities ranged from 10 to 70 days (median 29.5 days), with a shorter median onset of 17 days for the three fatal cases. The authors conclude most crizotinib-induced liver toxicity is hepatocellular type, is not associated with initial prescribed dose, and that onset of liver enzyme abnormalities is shorter for fatal cases.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Reported in patients with ALK- or ROS1-rearranged NSCLC treated therapeutically; individual reported risk factors include pre-existing liver disease or HBV carrier status and concurrent H2-antagonist/PPI use, but no definite risk factors were confirmed for the present case, whose HBV serology showed resolved infection.
raw_record.extra_details: Initial doses 200-500 mg/day were not associated with injury risk; onset of liver enzyme abnormalities 10-70 days (median 29.5 days); 4 of 10 cases fulminant hepatitis with 3 fatal (median onset 17 days for fatal cases); the present case was ROS1-rearranged lung adenocarcinoma with fever and eosinophilia, interpreted as immune/adaptive-immune-related injury; rechallenge cases: successful desensitization only when starting at ≤50-100 mg/day (two cases), failures at 200-250 mg/day; crizotinib metabolized largely via CYP3A4; liver function tests every two weeks during the first two months recommended.

raw_record.support_text: A 51-year-old Japanese woman with relapsed ALK-rearranged NSCLC received crizotinib (250 mg twice daily) as second-line treatment. On day 15-16, she developed fever and rising AST/ALT (peak AST 437 IU/l, ALT 1,096 IU/l), with increased gamma-glutamyltransferase and total bilirubin but no rise in alkaline phosphatase; hepatocellular injury was suspected and hepatitis A/B/C, Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus were excluded. Crizotinib was discontinued and symptoms and laboratory abnormalities resolved. The paper frames this as crizotinib-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single-patient case report in a 51-year-old non-smoking Japanese woman with relapsed ALK-rearranged NSCLC treated with crizotinib as second-line systemic chemotherapy following carboplatin/pemetrexed.
raw_record.extra_details: Crizotinib 250 mg twice daily; first dose held on day 2 for abdominal pain, nausea and grade 3 diarrhea, then re-introduced at 250 mg once daily with dexamethasone 3 mg daily. On the second exposure the patient developed fever and nausea on day 15, crizotinib was stopped on day 16; peak AST 437 IU/l on day 18 and peak ALT 1,096 IU/l on day 19; gamma-glutamyltransferase and total bilirubin rose to grade 2, alkaline phosphatase did not increase; contrast-enhanced CT and ultrasonography showed no other cause; hepatitis A, B, C, EBV and CMV excluded. Abnormalities resolved fully without increase of steroids after 1 month. Later the patient was rechallenged with desensitized oral crizotinib starting at 50 mg/day (capsule contents dissolved in sterile water and diluted) with betamethasone 2 mg; grade 1 hepatotoxicity on day 12 of desensitization, then ursodeoxycholic acid and glycyrrhizic acid started and no further hepatotoxicity observed; achieved partial response.

raw_record.support_text: The established diagnosis was 'Acute toxic (drug, imatinib-induced) drug-induced liver disease with cholestatic, cytolytic syndromes' in a patient with Philadelphia-chromosome-positive chronic myeloid leukemia in early chronic phase. The liver injury (imatinib-induced DILI with both cholestatic and cytolytic patterns) developed during imatinib therapy, resolved after imatinib discontinuation, steroid (prednisolone) therapy, and hepatoprotective treatment, with recovery after about three and a half months.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report in a CML (Ph-positive, early chronic phase) patient. Injury described as acute toxic drug-induced liver disease with cholestatic and cytolytic syndromes; bilirubin rose to ~400 µmol/L (23.40 mg/dL) on day 27 with severe jaundice and hepatic encephalopathy; AST/ALT elevated (peak AST 978.6 U/L day 16, ALT 1155 U/L day 0). Managed by imatinib cessation, prednisolone 40 mg/day IV, ursodeoxycholic acid 750 mg, ademetionine, and detoxification; recovered and switched to nilotinib 200 mg twice daily. No reported drug dose for imatinib in the provided window.

raw_record.support_text: Imatinib, an oral small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for chronic myeloid leukaemia and GIST, rarely causes severe liver injury. In two large multicentre GIST studies (147 and 946 patients), abnormal liver function tests were observed in 5.4% of treated patients (including grade 3-4 toxicity in 2.7%), and fatal liver disease occurred in 3%. In chronic myeloid leukaemia, imatinib was found to cause grade 2 or higher serum aminotransferase elevations in 8% of treated patients and grade 3-4 elevations in 1-5%; grade 3-4 serum bilirubin elevations were reported in 0.4-3.5% of patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Imatinib is an oral small-molecule BCR-ABL/KIT/PDGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for chronic myeloid leukaemia and GIST. Cases of severe liver injury are rare. In two large multicentre GIST studies (147 and 946 patients) abnormal liver function tests occurred in 5.4% (grade 3-4 toxicity in 2.7%), fatal liver disease in 3%. In CML, grade 2+ serum aminotransferase elevations in 8%, grade 3-4 in 1-5%; grade 3-4 serum bilirubin elevations in 0.4-3.5%.

raw_record.support_text: The case report describes drug-related liver toxicity during STI571 (imatinib) administration in a single chronic myelogenous leukemia patient who took STI571 alone with no interacting agents, foods, or supplements affecting CYP3A4. The authors attribute severe liver damage to STI571 and state it is unclear whether it results from immunologic idiosyncrasy (hypersensitivity) or injury from a toxic metabolite (metabolic idiosyncrasy); a significant serum STI571 level was still detected 7 days after drug cessation, suggesting metabolic idiosyncrasy in the liver. The authors also note that severe liver damage caused by STI571 involved females in all cases reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Imatinib (reported as STI571), a BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor; therapeutic dose 400 mg for chronic myelogenous leukemia. Severe liver damage/nephrotoxicity event attributed to the drug; the authors could not distinguish immunologic idiosyncrasy (hypersensitivity) from toxic-metabolite (metabolic) idiosyncrasy but suggested metabolic idiosyncrasy given significant serum STI571 detectable 7 days after stopping. Note that all described cases of severe STI571-related liver damage were in females. STI571 is metabolized by CYP3A4, CYP2C9 and CYP2D6 and competitively inhibits CYP3A4; concurrent CYP3A4 inhibitors (erythromycin, clarithromycin, itraconazole, grapefruit juice) raise STI571 serum concentrations and enhance toxicity—not applicable to this patient, who took STI571 alone.

raw_record.support_text: In the NOVEL trial of nilotinib in imatinib intolerant/resistant CML, one patient with imatinib-induced liver toxicity required a switch of therapy to nilotinib, which resulted in DILI resolution. Imatinib was also implicated in the DASISION trial, where therapy discontinuation was required among 400 mg imatinib-treated patients due to ALT or AST increases (n=1 each out of 258) and in one case of toxic hepatitis (n=1); DILI was a rare event in the 5-year follow-up.
raw_record.extra_details: Toxic hepatitis and drug-induced liver injury attributed to imatinib 400 mg daily in CML trials. DASISION: discontinuations due to ALT or AST increases (n=1 each of 258) and one case of toxic hepatitis (n=1). NOVEL: one patient with imatinib-induced liver toxicity required switch to nilotinib with DILI resolution (dechallenge-recovery). DILI was a rare event in the 5-year DASISION follow-up.

raw_record.support_text: A 40-year-old female with Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic myelogenous leukemia in chronic phase was treated with imatinib mesylate (STI571) 400 mg/day after interferon resistance. Six months after starting STI571 she developed severe liver damage with no evidence of active viral hepatitis; serum STI571 was still 107 ng/ml six days after the last dose, and liver biopsy showed massive hepatic necrosis consistent with drug-induced hepatitis. The authors conclude that both the severe hepatitis and the complete molecular response were caused by STI571. On percutaneous biopsy the injury was described as severe centrolobular hepatic necrosis without veno-occlusive disease, consistent with drug-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 40-year-old female with Ph1-positive CML in chronic phase treated with imatinib mesylate (STI571) at 400 mg/day starting January 2, 2003. Liver damage developed ~6 months after starting therapy (May 2003: AST 96 U/l, ALT 152 U/l; June: AST 406 U/l, ALT 559 U/l, total bilirubin 2.7 mg/dl rising to max 9.98 mg/dl, prolonged prothrombin time 69%, impaired coagulation factors requiring 72 units of fresh frozen plasma). Serum STI571 measured by LC-MS/MS: 107.0 (Jun 13), 13.8 (Jun 16), 7.4 (Jun 18), 3.6 ng/ml (Jun 20). Liver biopsy showed severe centrolobular hepatic necrosis without veno-occlusive disease. Drug lymphocyte-stimulating test for STI571 was negative. Viral hepatitis (A, B, C, G, E, TT, EBV, CMV) and autoantibodies excluded. Patient recovered and was discharged; no rechallenge was performed.

raw_record.support_text: A 36-year-old woman treated for chronic myeloid leukemia with imatinib mesylate (selective Bcr-Abl tyrosine kinase inhibitor) for 6 months developed imatinib-induced liver failure and subsequently underwent a successful liver transplant for acute liver failure. The authors also reviewed PubMed literature through September 2017 on imatinib-induced acute liver failure and highlight the role of liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Imatinib mesylate taken continuously for 6 months after delivery of a baby in a 36-year-old woman with chronic myeloid leukemia. The patient's acute liver failure resolved after a successful liver transplant. Literature review (PubMed, through September 2017) identified that severe hepatotoxicity occurs in 1-4% of imatinib-treated patients but fulminant liver failure is rare, with only 8 known cases; all but one involved CML, most were fatal, and liver transplant was performed in four (one postoperative death). Dasatinib and nilotinib are mentioned only as alternative/sequential therapies after imatinib-associated liver failure, not as DILI causes.

raw_record.support_text: Imatinib-related severe acute hepatitis has been described in 11 cases with favorable outcome after drug interruption in all cases and use of prednisolone in four cases. Nine patients were female, two male, aged 22 to 64 years; nine had CML and two had GIST, and the time from imatinib start to hepatotoxicity ranged from less than 2 weeks to 77 weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 cases: 9 female, 2 male, age 22-64 years; 9 CML and 2 GIST; time from imatinib start to hepatotoxicity <2 weeks to 77 weeks; favorable outcome after drug interruption in all cases with prednisolone used in four cases.

raw_record.support_text: In a 2008 analysis of 259 CML patients treated in 3 imatinib first-line studies at MD Anderson (400 mg/day in 50 patients, 800 mg/day in 209 patients), mild-to-moderate liver dysfunction was seen in 38 patients (15%), and only 3 of these 38 (8%) developed grade 3/4 liver toxicity while on imatinib and required dose reduction. The paper presents imatinib hepatotoxicity as a recognized adverse effect requiring management, recommending that imatinib be withheld if bilirubin rises >3-fold the institutional ULN or transaminases rise >5-fold the ULN, and resumed at a reduced dose once values fall.
raw_record.extra_details: 2008 MD Anderson analysis of 259 CML patients across 3 imatinib first-line studies (400 mg/day n=50; 800 mg/day n=209). Mild-to-moderate liver dysfunction (total bilirubin <1.5 mg/dL with AST >ULN, up to 3.0 mg/dL with AST any) seen in 38 patients (15%; n=7 in 400-mg arm, n=31 in 800-mg arm); 3 of 38 (8%; 1 in 400-mg, 2 in 800-mg arm) developed grade 3/4 liver toxicity requiring dose reduction. Dose-reduction schedule: 400→300, 600→400, or 800→600 mg/day; withhold imatinib if bilirubin increase >3-fold IULN or transaminase increase >5-fold IULN; resume at reduced dose when bilirubin <1.5-fold IULN and transaminases <2.5× IULN; withhold for hepatic toxicity grade >2 until grade <1; consider 25-33% dose reduction; evaluate other hepatotoxic drugs; consider switching to a second-generation TKI.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 60 chronic-phase CML patients treated with imatinib, one patient was primarily resistant and two were intolerant with grade 3 hepatic toxicity; imatinib was then discontinued in those patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Two of 60 chronic-phase CML patients developed grade 3 hepatic toxicity attributed to imatinib and had imatinib discontinued; one other patient was primarily resistant. Patients had prior therapy with Hydrea (53) or Hydrea plus IFN (7).

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of a 72-year-old man with CML treated with imatinib mesylate who subsequently developed severe hepatotoxicity, leading to submassive hepatic necrosis and liver failure; close biochemical monitoring and consecutive liver biopsies documented the evolution of hepatic damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatotoxicity progressed to submassive hepatic necrosis and liver failure in a 72-year-old male with CML on imatinib mesylate 400 mg/day; findings contrasted with previously described cases.

raw_record.support_text: A 53-year-old woman with advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumors developed hepatotoxicity while receiving imatinib mesylate and subsequently acute liver failure. Ten weeks after commencing imatinib, hepatotoxicity was determined, and imatinib was immediately ceased; a week later hepatic encephalopathy, jaundice, and coagulopathy occurred. Liver biopsy showed sinusoidal congestion, necrosis of hepatocytes, inflammation, and hepatocyte drop out around the hepatic venule, consistent with drug toxicity. Her liver tests normalized after nine weeks of prednisolone; the authors refer to the event as imatinib-induced acute hepatitis and note that several cases of hepatotoxicity, including fatal liver failure, have been reported with long-term imatinib use.
raw_record.extra_details: Imatinib 400 mg/day for advanced GISTs. Hepatotoxicity determined 10 weeks after starting treatment; after imatinib was discontinued liver tests worsened (AST rose to 1,072 U/l, ALT 1,234 U/l, total bilirubin 7.78 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 5.24 mg/dl). Hepatic encephalopathy, jaundice, and coagulopathy developed; treated with prednisolone (40 mg/day) with normalization of liver function over ~9 weeks; patient discharged and liver enzymes remained normal. Liver biopsy showed sinusoidal congestion, hepatocyte necrosis, inflammation, and hepatocyte drop out around the terminal hepatic venule consistent with drug toxicity. No competing causes (no alcohol, drugs, herbal remedies, or viral hepatitis risk factors). Abstract notes several hepatotoxicity cases including fatal liver failure have been reported with long-term imatinib use; hepatotoxicity generally resolves after imatinib discontinuation. Authors suggest prednisolone may allow reintroduction of the drug without recurrence.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that imatinib mesylate caused the acute cytolytic hepatitis observed in their patient because other potential causes were carefully excluded and a compatible chronological sequence with shortening of the exposure time after rechallenge was observed, giving the maximum likely causality score. In the absence of immunoallergic manifestations, an idiosyncratic type of drug-induced liver disease was judged probable, especially since rechallenge at only 2.5% of the usual therapeutic dose (10 mg/day) again produced an increase in aminotransferase activities.
raw_record.extra_details: Imatinib mesylate given at 400 mg/day for a pelvic mass (indication) starting 22 Oct 2003; cytolytic hepatitis with markedly elevated ALT (up to 66.3 x ULN) and AST (30.1 x ULN), serum bilirubin rising to 56 µmol/l, and prothrombin time nadir of 76%. Other drugs (pentoxifylline, naftidrofuryl, omeprazole, ketoprofen, paracetamol 1–3 g/day, aspirin 75 mg/day, atorvastatin, irbesartan/hydrochlorothiazide) taken >1 year were excluded as causes; viral, autoimmune, and metabolic serologies were negative. Liver function normalized after drug cessation. Rechallenge with 300 mg/day (24–27 Feb 2004) and 10 mg/day (17–20 Mar 2004; 2.5% of usual dose) caused immediate biochemical relapse. Liver biopsy showed periportal necrosis, portal and periportal fibrosis with septa and bridging fibrosis, mild lymphocytic/neutrophilic infiltrate, and Councilman bodies, without steatosis or granuloma. Patient subsequently treated with sunitinib malate without detectable liver toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a 46-year-old woman with advanced GISTs who developed hepatotoxicity 11 days after initiation of imatinib mesylate (400 mg daily). Before therapy her liver function tests were normal; she had no risk factors for viral or alcoholic liver disease, imatinib was her only regular medication, and she had not used acetaminophen or over-the-counter medications. One week after imatinib discontinuation her liver function tests improved significantly, and the report confirms early-onset imatinib mesylate-induced liver failure in patients treated for GISTs.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of 46-year-old woman with advanced (relapsed) c-kit-positive GIST treated with imatinib mesylate 400 mg daily; hepatotoxicity developed 11 days after starting therapy, presenting with 2 days of nausea and weakness (no jaundice, fever, or abdominal pain). Labs: ALT 2520 UI/L, AST 1845 UI/L, alkaline phosphatase 192 UI/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, albumin 3.3, INR 1.6. Abdominal CT showed mild diffuse fatty liver changes; ultrasound normal. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, C all negative; no acetaminophen or herbal/OTC use. Liver tests began to decrease after imatinib discontinuation and were nearly normal 1 week later. Paper frames this as acute fulminant hepatitis/acute liver failure. Background context supplied: hepatotoxicity observed in ~2%–5% of patients in clinical trials (mostly mild transaminase elevation; grade 3–4 transaminase elevation in 1%–5%, grade 3–4 bilirubin elevation 0.4%–3.5%, usually resolving after dose reduction/interruption within 1–4 weeks); 5 deaths from hepatic failure reported (4 during CML treatment, 1 during polycythemia vera treatment); in the Demetri et al phase 2 trial of 147 GIST patients, abnormal liver function tests occurred in 5.4% and fatal liver disease in 0.3%. Reported histopathology varies from periportal necrosis with mixed lymphocyte/neutrophil/plasmocyte infiltration to massive hepatic necrosis or cytolytic acute hepatitis. Authors recommend early and continued surveillance of liver function tests.

raw_record.support_text: A newly diagnosed chronic-phase CML patient developed grade 3 hepatotoxicity with transaminases peaking approximately 3 weeks after imatinib discontinuation (AST 711 IU/l, ALT 999 IU/l, TB 1.3 mg/dl). Liver histology showed zonal centrilobular necrosis, acidophilic bodies, hepatocyte dropout, lymphocyte/neutrophil infiltration, Mallory bodies, and piecemeal necrosis, which suggested drug-induced liver injury. Rechallenge with imatinib at 100 mg/day caused transaminase values to double within one week, which the authors state strongly supports that the liver damage was caused by imatinib.
raw_record.extra_details: Newly diagnosed Philadelphia-chromosome-positive chronic-phase CML; no concurrent medications, no infection, negative serologies for hepatitis A/B/C, EBV, CMV, HSV. Grade 3 non-hematological toxicity led to imatinib discontinuation; transaminases kept rising, peaking ~3 weeks after discontinuation (AST 711 IU/l, ALT 999 IU/l, TB 1.3 mg/dl). Drug lymphocyte-stimulating test was negative. Liver biopsy (11 Jan 2005) showed zonal centrilobular necrosis, acidophilic bodies, hepatocyte dropout, lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltration, Mallory bodies, and piecemeal necrosis. Injury persisted after discontinuation and required prednisolone 30 mg/day; rechallenge at 100 mg/day doubled transaminases within a week, confirming causality, and was managed with PSL while imatinib was tapered up to 400 mg/day; patient recovered and achieved complete cytogenetic remission. Authors speculate high imatinib plasma concentration / metabolic idiosyncrasy (Kikuchi reference found high plasma imatinib 7 days after cessation); phase III trial of imatinib in chronic-phase CML reported 5.1% grade 3-4 transaminitis. Four prior histologically assessed case reports all involved prior CML/PV treatment.

raw_record.support_text: One patient with imatinib-induced liver injury was included in this Icelandic DIAIH study among 18 patients who developed immune-mediated liver injury; 93% of the cohort had hepatocellular injury and 8 (53%) had jaundice but none coagulopathy. Causality was assessed with RUCAM and simplified AIH criteria were calculated.
raw_record.extra_details: 1 patient; single attributed case of drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis (DIAIH). RUCAM causality across the cohort: 12 probable, 1 highly probable, 2 possible. 93% of cohort hepatocellular, 53% jaundice, none coagulopathy.

raw_record.support_text: Imatinib-induced acute liver failure is reported as a rare and serious complication of imatinib therapy; the case shares features with 13 other reported cases (three in male patients) from eight case reports, with patient ages 22-79 years and imatinib treatment durations before toxicity recognition of 8 weeks to 1 year. Coagulopathy or encephalopathy was associated with poor outcome: of five patients with coagulopathy, only one survived without liver transplantation, and that survivor's presentation was associated with an alcohol binge and paracetamol consumption. Successful liver transplantation for imatinib-induced hepatic failure in CML is described, and the paper reports the first use of dasatinib for CML after liver transplantation for imatinib-induced liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of imatinib-induced acute liver failure/fulminant hepatic failure in a CML patient who required liver transplantation within 24 hours of developing fulminant hepatic failure; the report aggregates 13 other reported cases (three male) in eight case reports. Coagulopathy or encephalopathy associated with poor outcome; of five patients with coagulopathy, only one survived without liver transplant (that survivor's presentation was associated with an alcohol binge and paracetamol consumption, but this is a separate patient, not the index case). Six cases without coagulopathy received steroids and recovered; three other non-coagulopathic cases recovered without steroids. Duration of imatinib before recognition of toxicity 8 weeks to 1 year; age range 22-79 years. Dasatinib was subsequently used for CML after liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 20-year-old CML patient who developed recurrent hepatotoxicity with the use of imatinib, a frontline tyrosine kinase inhibitor. They note that severe hepatotoxicity, although uncommon, can occur with imatinib, tends to subside with dose reduction or cessation but can recur upon reintroduction, and recurrent severe hepatotoxicity mandates permanent discontinuation of the drug. Successful reintroduction of imatinib was achieved by adding corticosteroids.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 20-year-old woman with chronic-phase CML on oral imatinib 400 mg daily for 2 weeks at presentation. Elevated ALT 2364 IU/l, AST 1406 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 97 IU/l, total bilirubin 1.0 mg/dl; viral hepatitis profile negative. Hepatotoxicity is severe and uncommon, subsides with dose reduction or cessation, and recurs with reintroduction; recurrent severe hepatotoxicity requires permanent discontinuation. Corticosteroids (prednisone) enabled successful reintroduction of imatinib. Patient initially on hydroxyurea before imatinib.

raw_record.support_text: DILI-inducing antineoplastics were methotrexate, nedaplatin, cisplatin, carboplatin, pemetrexed, gefitinib and imatinib; antineoplastics accounted for 13 patients (3.07%).
raw_record.extra_details: Antineoplastic; antineoplastics accounted for 13 patients (3.07%) of DILI cases.

raw_record.support_text: A 34-year-old woman with chronic myeloid leukemia treated solely with imatinib 400 mg/day developed asthenia, jaundice, coluria, acholia, nausea and vomiting after 8 months of treatment, with progressive worsening despite imatinib discontinuation. The authors present this as a case of fulminant hepatitis due to imatinib with survival after liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient with chronic myeloid leukemia treated with imatinib 400 mg/day for 8 months; symptoms of asthenia, jaundice, coluria, acholia, nausea and vomiting with progressive worsening despite imatinib discontinuation; liver transplantation with post-transplant survival. The paper also notes several previously reported cases of reversible acute hepatitis after imatinib dose reduction/discontinuation with occasional corticosteroid treatment, six published cases of imatinib-attributed fulminant hepatitis (good outcome in only one), and fulminant hepatitis from HBV reactivation.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes patients who developed imatinib-induced hepatotoxicity: Spataro introduced nilotinib in a patient who had developed imatinib-induced hepatotoxicity, and a successful switch to sunitinib was made in a patient whose imatinib-induced hepatotoxicity was confirmed by two rechallenges. This constitutes explicit attribution of human DILI to imatinib.
raw_record.extra_details: Tyrosine kinase inhibitor. Switch to nilotinib and to sunitinib was successful; one patient's imatinib-induced hepatotoxicity was confirmed by two rechallenges. Separate paragraph (p53) describes conflicting data on co-administration of imatinib with acetaminophen: a patient (Ridruejo) experienced exacerbations of hepatic toxicity upon co-administration with acetaminophen, animal models showed increased irreversible hepatotoxicity with co-administration, whereas a Korean clinical study found acetaminophen pharmacokinetics similar to control and the combination well tolerated.

raw_record.support_text: A 64-year-old woman with chronic myeloid leukemia developed acute cytolytic hepatitis attributed to imatinib mesylate. Liver tests rose to ASAT 20xN and ALAT 28xN with GGT 8.5xN, alkaline phosphatase 3xN, bilirubin 98 Pmol/L and prothrombin 68%, while viral (hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV, HSV), autoimmune, and other etiologies (hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency) were excluded. The paper's title frames this as 'acute cytolytic hepatitis induced by imatinib mesylate' (hépatite aiguë cytolytique induite par l'imatinib mesylate).
raw_record.extra_details: 64-year-old female with chronic myeloid leukemia previously treated with interferon alpha. Imatinib mesylate given at 400 mg/day, later restarted at 200 mg/day (July 22, 2002); cytolysis appeared about 3 weeks later (August 14, 2002) with asthenia, ASAT 7.5xN and ALAT 10xN, GGT, ALP and bilirubin not elevated initially; worsened by September 2, 2002 (ASAT 20xN, ALAT 28xN, GGT 8.5xN, ALP 3xN, bilirubin 98 Pmol/L, prothrombin 68%) with mild eosinophilia (750/mm3). Concurrent Deroxat (paroxetine) and Hexaquine were discontinued while imatinib was continued during the worsening cytolysis. Competing causes excluded: viral hepatitis serologies (hepatitis A IgM, HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM, anti-HCV, HCV RNA PCR, HSV, CMV, EBV), borreliosis/Lyme, rickettsia, autoimmunity (ANA, LKM, smooth-muscle, AMA, circulating immune complexes, rheumatoid factor, complement), iron/copper overload, and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

raw_record.support_text: This report describes a clinical case of acute, toxic imatinib-induced hepatitis in a 56-year-old woman with chronic myeloid leukemia and concomitant sulfa allergy and rheumatoid arthritis. The patient developed acute imatinib-induced hepatitis after three months of imatinib treatment and three days after increasing the dose from 400 mg/day to 600 mg/day, resolving within three months after imatinib discontinuation and prednisolone administration. The paper notes the drug can cause hepatic failure and death in rare cases, and that approximately 25 clinical case reports of imatinib-induced hepatitis have been published.
raw_record.extra_details: 56-year-old woman with CML, early chronic phase, intermediate risk group (Sokal 1.14, Hasford 1286), concomitant sulfadimezine allergy and rheumatoid arthritis. Imatinib 400 mg/day for 3 months then increased to 600 mg/day; hepatitis developed 3 days after dose increase and resolved within 3 months after imatinib discontinuation with prednisolone administration. Baseline ALT 12 U/L, AST 18 U/L, total bilirubin 0.33 mg/dL. Nausea after dose increase; fever of unknown cause during first two months of therapy. Paper states approximately 25 case reports of imatinib-induced hepatitis published and that imatinib can cause hepatic failure, acute liver failure, and death in rare cases; predisposing factors not identified.

raw_record.support_text: A patient treated with imatinib mesylate developed hepatotoxicity including an increase in total bilirubin to a maximum of 513.4 µmol/l on hospital day 7, with normalization after 6 weeks following discontinuation of imatinib and short steroid therapy. After resuming imatinib mesylate at a reduced dose of 400 mg daily, the patient experienced no further hepatotoxicity. The authors attribute the liver abnormalities to imatinib mesylate.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of imatinib mesylate-induced hepatotoxicity in a patient with Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic myeloid leukemia. Transaminase activity and bilirubin increased after 10 days of imatinib use; levels normalized after interruption for 6 weeks with minimal corticosteroid use. Bilirubin level and ALP activity reached grade 4 toxicity, aminotransferase and γ-glutamyltransferase activities grade 3. Liver biopsy (day 4) showed portal tract inflammation with cholestasis, acute hepatocyte injury, scattered acidophilic bodies, occasional ballooning degeneration, canalicular cholestasis, moderate inflammatory infiltration of lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils and many eosinophils, and eosinophil infiltration of interlobular bile ducts with ductal epithelial damage. Associated skin rash and hypereosinophilia (max 2.47 x 10^9/l, ~40% WBC) resolved after stopping imatinib. Rechallenge at reduced dose 400 mg daily produced no further hepatotoxicity and patient continued imatinib for 18 months. Authors concluded the single dose of a Korean ginseng herbal remedy did not cause the hepatic function abnormalities.

raw_record.support_text: A case report describes what the authors state is the first case of liver cirrhosis developing during adjuvant imatinib treatment in a patient with GIST. MRI one month after discontinuing the adjuvant treatment showed clearly cirrhotic changes of the liver parenchyma, and the conclusion states that chronic liver disease can be a consequence of imatinib-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adjuvant imatinib treatment in a gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) patient who had previously received neoadjuvant treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported case of liver cirrhosis during adjuvant imatinib in GIST. Transaminases rose under adjuvant treatment (shown in figure); MRI one month after discontinuation showed cirrhotic parenchymal changes. Authors recommend careful follow-up, especially for patients with grade 3 or 4 hepatic toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Two patients treated with imatinib developed hepatic dysfunction; both had an imatinib 're-challenge' immediately followed by recurrence of biochemical abnormalities, reinforcing the implication of imatinib as the cause of the hepatic injury. The authors note that because imatinib inhibits CYP3A4/5, CYP2C9 and CYP2D6, the co-administered roxithromycin (case 1) would be expected to increase imatinib levels and thus its toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Case 1 had concomitant roxithromycin, which is expected to raise imatinib levels via CYP inhibition; case 2 had no concomitant medication.
raw_record.extra_details: Two female cases (aged 58 and 35) plus a prior case from Ohyashiki. Onset of hepatic dysfunction at 22 and 49 weeks; Case 1 peaked ASAT 3230 U/l, ALAT 2430 U/l, total bilirubin 84 µmol/l with normal AP; Case 2 ASAT 487 U/l, ALAT 159 U/l. Biopsy Case 1: acute severe cytolytic hepatitis with necrosis and mild cholestasis (13 days post-discontinuation); Case 2: acute cytolytic hepatitis with spotty and piecemeal necrosis and some fibrosis (3 months). Both patients had positive rechallenge with recurrence of biochemical abnormalities; both recovered after discontinuation. Histology showed diffuse inflammation without lymphoid follicles, distinguishing it from viral acute hepatitis. Imatinib is an anticancer agent for CML and GIST.

raw_record.support_text: A 32-year-old woman with CML-CP developed histology-confirmed imatinib-induced liver toxicity after 6 months of treatment with standard-dose imatinib (400 mg/day). She presented with jaundice, nausea, and epigastric pain; lab tests showed acute liver dysfunction (ALT 1638 U/l, AST 1182 U/l, GGT 69 U/l, ALP 94 U/l, total bilirubin 2.8 mg/dl, INR 1.33). Viral and autoimmune hepatitis and a vascular event were ruled out. Early corticosteroid therapy led to rapid and complete hepatic recovery, and treatment was resumed safely with dasatinib.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic myeloid leukemia in chronic phase; rapid and complete hepatic recovery following early corticosteroid therapy; TKI therapy subsequently resumed with dasatinib.

raw_record.support_text: In late 2018 the authors observed a case of acute imatinib hepatotoxicity in a 32-year-old woman with CML. Grade III hepatotoxicity (ALT 354 u/l, AST 183 u/l) developed after six months of imatinib treatment. The hepatotoxicity resolved within two weeks of imatinib withdrawal on 20 mg prednisolone tapered and withdrawn after 45 days; viral hepatitis by PCR was negative and no offender concomitant drug causing interaction was identified. Imatinib was restarted at a reduced dose of 300 mg/day with simultaneous prednisolone after the hepatitis resolved, and liver tests stayed within normal range during four months of the restart, after which imatinib was increased to 400 mg/day.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic myeloid leukemia patients; therapeutic use for CML; one grade III case and a previously reported case; a previously reported case had absent early molecular response (3-month BCR-ABL1IS 17.241%) and was switched to nilotinib rather than restarted.
raw_record.extra_details: 32-year-old woman: grade III hepatotoxicity (ALT 354 u/l, AST 183 u/l) after six months of imatinib; resolved within two weeks on prednisolone (20 mg, tapered and withdrawn after 45 days); restarted at 300 mg/day then increased to 400 mg/day after four months with normal liver tests. Prior reported case: grade III hepatotoxicity with absent early molecular response led to imatinib withdrawal and switch to the second-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitor nilotinib. Imatinib-induced liver cirrhosis was not identified.

raw_record.extra_details: Case report: 57-year-old woman with chronic-phase CML treated with imatinib mesylate 400 mg/day. The paper states that olanzapine rarely may induce clinical and/or biological hepatic toxicity, that mostly transient, asymptomatic increases in hepatic enzymes are reported, but that substantial and lasting changes may result in symptomatic hepatitis. This is presented as the first reported case of serious symptomatic liver enzyme increase three years after starting olanzapine.
raw_record.extra_details: 44-year-old female with Bipolar Disorder Type I. Paper describes olanzapine hepatotoxicity as mostly transient, asymptomatic, and dose-unrelated, with rare progression to symptomatic hepatitis. Reported as first case of serious symptomatic liver enzyme increase after three years of olanzapine treatment.

raw_record.support_text: Olanzapine is reported as the cause of acute hepatocellular-cholestatic liver injury in a 78-year-old woman. A diagnostic validation scale for drug-induced hepatitis scored the case 16 out of 20, favoring a diagnosis of olanzapine-induced liver injury. The patient recovered and liver function tests normalized at 4-week follow-up; the authors found no prior reports of olanzapine-related acute hepatitis in a MEDLINE search.

raw_record.extra_details: Olanzapine 10 mg/d; hepatitis onset 13 days after start, with fever, malaise, arthralgia, upper abdominal pain, anorexia, and nausea. Initial AST 361 U/L, ALT 204 U/L, total bilirubin 22 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 189 U/L; on hospital day 3 AST 964 U/L, ALT 965 U/L, total bilirubin 156 µmol/L (conjugated 7.9), alkaline phosphatase 488 U/L; symptoms resolved by day 4 and tests normalized by 4 weeks. Diagnostic validation scale score 16/20. Authors reasoned acute hepatitis is probably not dose dependent because of absence of hepatitis in overdose reports. Serology for hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV, antimitochondrial and antinuclear antibodies negative.

raw_record.support_text: In a post-marketing case series of 14 cases of clinically significant DILI associated with dimethyl fumarate (DMF), causality was assessed as probable for 11 cases. No cases resulted in transplant or death, but 10 cases resulted in hospitalization; severity was moderate/moderate-severe in eight and mild in six. The pattern of liver injury was categorized as hepatocellular for 12/14 cases based on an R value ≥5.
raw_record.extra_details: Causality assessed as probable for 11 of 14 clinically significant DILI cases. Severity moderate to moderate-severe in eight and mild in six; 10 cases resulted in hospitalization; no transplant or death. Mean time to event onset 101 days (median 83.5, range 4 to 302 days); seven cases occurred within 1 month of DMF initiation. DMF discontinued in all cases; ALT/bilirubin returned to normal within days to weeks. Two cases had liver biopsies consistent with DILI; hepatocellular pattern in 12/14 cases (R value ≥5), two cases lacked AP so R value not calculated but ALT exceeded 20x ULN. Seven cases met ATs >3x ULN with TBili >2x ULN; five fulfilled Hy's law criteria. Reported DILI mechanisms include hypersensitivity, autoimmune hepatitis, or infection; four cases had eosinophil elevations including one probable DRESS. Demographics: 12 female, 2 male, ages 25-56, mean/median age 42.

raw_record.support_text: Nine patients received 49 courses of 4-aminopyrazolo[3,4-d]pyrimidine (4-APP) by oral and intravenous routes as part of antitumor therapy studies. The limiting evidence of toxicity in man was hepatic damage; a daily dose of 0.1-0.15 mg/kg was safe and a single intravenous dose of 0.75 mg/kg produced no toxicity. The first sign of hepatic toxicity was elevation of prothrombin time, with factor VII and factor V deficiencies at lower doses and depression of prothrombin concentration at higher doses; vitamin K1 failed to reverse these deficits, and the coagulation deficits were believed to represent hepatocellular damage by 4-APP.
raw_record.extra_details: Antitumor study in 9 patients over 49 courses (oral and IV). Daily dose 0.1-0.15 mg/kg considered safe; single IV dose of 0.75 mg/kg produced no toxicity. First sign of hepatic toxicity was prothrombin time elevation; lower doses caused deficiency of factor VII and factor V, higher doses depressed prothrombin concentration; vitamin K1 (phylloquinone) failed to reverse deficits. Coagulation deficits interpreted as hepatocellular damage by 4-APP. 4-APP metabolized to pyrazoloisoguanine in man; rapid urinary excretion of 4-APP with none detectable after 6 hours, pyrazoloisoguanine excretion continuing beyond 12 hours; no antitumor effects seen.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a case of a 60-year-old male with MET exon 14-mutated non-small cell lung cancer who developed grade 4 liver injury after starting the oral MET-kinase inhibitor capmatinib. The injury did not respond to capmatinib discontinuation, but eventually responded to N-acetyl cysteine plus ursodeoxycholic acid (ursodiol) therapy, and the paper frames the case as capmatinib-induced hepatotoxicity with scarce published data on its management.
raw_record.extra_details: Grade 4 hepatotoxicity in a 60-year-old male NSCLC patient with MET exon 14 skipping mutation. Supportive trial data from the GEOMETRY mono-1 study (373 patients, 400 mg twice daily) reported ALT/AST elevation in 14% of patients, about half (7%) grade 3 or 4 (defined as >5x and >20x ULN), with median time to onset of grade 3+ ALT/AST elevation of 1.8 months (range 0.5-46.4 months). FDA label (Tabrecta) instructs holding or permanently discontinuing capmatinib for grade 3 or 4 ALT/AST elevation with or without bilirubin elevation. Injury did not improve with drug discontinuation but showed significant improvement one day after N-acetyl cysteine plus ursodeoxycholic acid, near-resolution in two months. Mechanism relevant to MET/HGFR pathway.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that on 29 June 2006 the US FDA announced labelling changes for telithromycin to warn about the risk of hepatotoxicity, citing serious liver injury and liver failure with four deaths and one liver transplant. A case series by Clay and colleagues describes three cases of severe telithromycin-related hepatotoxicity: one patient spontaneously recovered, one required orthotopic liver transplantation, and one died; the autopsy showed hepatomegaly, substantial liver necrosis, and a lymphocytic inflammatory response.
raw_record.extra_details: Three severe telithromycin-related hepatotoxicity cases by Clay and colleagues: one recovered, one required orthotopic liver transplantation, one died; autopsy showed hepatomegaly, substantial liver necrosis, and lymphocytic inflammatory response. FDA product labelling changes (29 June 2006) warned of the risk of hepatotoxicity, citing serious liver injury and liver failure, four deaths and one liver transplant. Telithromycin-related hepatotoxicity described as rare, precise incidence unclear.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude by reporting 3 cases of severe drug-induced liver injury secondary to telithromycin, stating it includes, to their knowledge, the first related death and need for orthotopic liver transplantation, and advise caution in prescribing this drug pending further postmarketing surveillance data.
raw_record.extra_details: 3 cases of severe drug-induced liver injury reported by the authors, including the first related death and orthotopic liver transplantation. Pharmacovigilance (FDA AERS) described 10 postmarketing hepatic adverse events with telithromycin, severity from serious to fatal (2 patients died), involving cholestatic hepatitis, abnormal aminotransferase levels, increased bilirubin, liver disorder, cholestatic jaundice, and hepatocellular damage; duration of use 1-30 days, patient ages 35-85 years. Phase III data (Sanofi-Aventis) described 7 cases of hepatitis or hepatocellular damage, with alcohol use, baseline aminotransferase elevations, and hepatitis B virus infection as confounders in 4 cases; all but 1 resolved without sequelae. Prescribing information: ALT>3x ULN in 1.6% and reversible hepatitis with or without jaundice in 0.07%; labels advise caution in patients with a hepatitis or jaundice history. Postmarketing reports of infrequent hepatocellular or cholestatic hepatitis with and without jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: A 25-year-old male patient presented with jaundice, malaise, and vomiting shortly after receiving telithromycin, and reported similar complaints 11 months prior when he was diagnosed with telithromycin-related toxic hepatitis. At the second occurrence the diagnosis was confirmed by liver biopsy, and the Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale gave a score of 8, indicating telithromycin was the probable cause of acute hepatitis in this patient. Viral, autoimmune, and metabolic causes were excluded, and histology showed hydropic degeneration, hepatic necrosis around the central vein, and hepatocellular and canalicular bile cholestasis; the patient recovered after telithromycin was discontinued.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of a 25-year-old male; dechallenge-rechallenge (two separate exposures to telithromycin) with hepatic event recurred on rechallenge ~11 months later, supporting causality. Telithromycin 400 mg/d was used for an upper respiratory tract infection and for community-acquired pneumonia. Naranjo score 8 = probable cause of acute hepatitis. Liver biopsy at second event showed hydropic degeneration, hepatic necrosis around the central vein, and hepatocellular and canalicular bile cholestasis, suggesting drug-induced toxic hepatitis. Viral (hepatitis A/B/C, mononucleosis, HIV), autoimmune (ANA, AMA, ASMA, liver-kidney microsomal) and metabolic (ceruloplasmin, iron, ferritin) causes excluded; abdominal ultrasound showed a benign hemangioma. Lab peaks at second exposure: AST 71 U/L, ALT 98 U/L, TB 20.08 mg/dL, DB 14.75 mg/dL, ALP 513 U/L, GGT 32 U/L; recovery of bilirubin within ~2 months. Patient also had jaundice, malaise, and vomiting.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states telithromycin has been reported to cause significant hepatotoxicity shortly after its April 2004 approval, and that three recently published case reports of telithromycin-induced hepatotoxicity each involved patients who developed severe liver dysfunction.
raw_record.extra_details: Three published case reports of telithromycin-induced hepatotoxicity, all with severe liver dysfunction. In two of the three published cases the patients completed a five-day course and experienced the most severe hepatotoxicity; two of those patients regularly consumed alcohol (reported to increase drug-induced hepatotoxicity risk).

raw_record.support_text: In the Galan et al. retrospective series, telithromycin was reported as a cause of a single case of confirmed acute drug-induced liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case of non-fulminant drug-induced hepatitis among the 32 confirmed acute DILD cases; hepatocellular or mixed injury pattern.

raw_record.support_text: Telithromycin is the first and only ketolide approved for clinical use. In Phase III trials mild-to-moderate ALT increases occurred at higher frequency than placebo. After US launch, three cases of serious liver injury with jaundice and significantly elevated liver enzymes occurred in patients given telithromycin for minor upper respiratory infections; one recovered, one required liver transplantation, and one died. The FDA issued a boxed warning and drastically restricted the indication to community-acquired pneumonia.
raw_record.extra_details: Serious liver injury with jaundice and significantly elevated liver enzymes (>10x ULN in one case) in three patients treated for minor upper respiratory infections; one recovered, one required liver transplantation, one died. An analysis of 12 cases showed a rare unusual form of hepatotoxicity with short latency, systemic symptoms and, in some cases, significant ascites. FDA boxed warning and restriction to community-acquired pneumonia; EMA added alterations in hepatic enzymes, severe hepatitis, and liver failure to Special warnings. Designed against macrolide-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae; mild-to-moderate ALT increases more frequent than placebo in Phase III trials.

Liver biopsy revealed toxic hepatitis of minor grade with periportal fibrosis and intrahepatic cholestasis. raw_record.extra_details: An 81-year-old African American male with metastatic prostate cancer started bicalutamide 3 weeks before presenting with nonspecific symptoms and 1-day jaundice; physical exam showed scleral icterus; workup showed acutely elevated transaminases (>5x ULN), elevated alkaline phosphatase, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and coagulopathy. The authors conclude fulminant hepatotoxicity is a rare but potentially fatal adverse effect of bicalutamide.

raw_record.support_text: Phase II clinical data in 878 patients with HCV G1 infection demonstrate that the unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia arising from faldaprevir administration is benign and not associated with hepatotoxicity. The frequency of hyperbilirubinemia was 47.8% and 83.8% in the 120- and 240-mg q.d. dose groups, respectively; discontinuation due to hyperbilirubinemia and/or jaundice was ≤1%. In phase III studies, hyperbilirubinemia was predominantly unconjugated, rapidly reversible, and determined not to result from liver injury based on prospectively defined criteria. Toxicology studies in rhesus monkeys showed a dose-dependent increase in unconjugated bilirubin not associated with microscopic evidence of hepatotoxicity, elevations in liver enzymes such as ALT, or hemolysis.
raw_record.extra_details: Faldaprevir (an HCV NS3/4A protease inhibitor) dose-dependently increased unconjugated bilirubin, but this hyperbilirubinemia was explicitly determined to be benign and not to result from liver injury or hepatotoxicity. In phase II data (878 HCV G1 patients, 120 or 240 mg q.d. plus Peg-IFN/RBV, 24 weeks), hyperbilirubinemia frequency was 47.8% (120 mg) and 83.8% (240 mg) with ≤1% discontinuation due to hyperbilirubinemia/jaundice; not associated with ALT elevations, microscopic hepatotoxicity, or hemolysis; rapidly reversible on cessation of therapy. Proposed mechanism is reversible inhibition of bilirubin uptake (OATP1B1/OATP1B3), glucuronidation (UGT1A1), and biliary efflux (MRP2), with UGT1A1 inhibition considered likely most important.

raw_record.support_text: The case emphasises azathioprine's potential for hepatotoxicity and that clinicians should suspect azathioprine as the culprit for any patient's liver failure regardless of when azathioprine therapy was initiated, noting this rare but potentially life-threatening hepatotoxicity. The learning points state azathioprine can cause life-threatening hepatotoxicity, that hepatotoxicity can occur years after initiation of use, and that patterns of liver injury include hepatitis, cholestasis, or a mixed (hepatitis and cholestasis) pattern; clinical recovery typically occurs with discontinuation of azathioprine and supportive treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Life-threatening hepatotoxicity framed as rare but potentially fatal liver failure. Injury can occur years after initiation of azathioprine therapy. Reported biochemical/injury patterns include hepatitis, cholestasis, or a mixed (hepatitis and cholestasis) pattern. Levels of 6-methylmercaptopurine nucleotide, described as a hepatotoxic metabolite of azathioprine, can be measured as supportive evidence for drug-induced liver injury, but this metabolite is not independently assigned as the injuring entity. Clinical recovery typically follows azathioprine cessation and supportive treatment. Reported as a case report with the learning-point framing that hepatotoxicity can occur regardless of when therapy was initiated.
