raw_record.extra_details: AZA-induced hepatotoxicity diagnosed in 8/293 patients (about 2.7%), none progressing to liver failure or liver transplantation; spectrum reported to range from asymptomatic elevated liver enzymes to cholestasis and nodular regenerative hyperplasia; in some patients hepatotoxicity was dose-independent; context is inflammatory bowel disease patients.

raw_record.support_text: Azathioprine is described as having hepatotoxicity as another serious side effect, likely connected to the effect of AZA metabolites or reactive oxygen species formed during metabolism by XDH. In the study's experimental group, only four individuals (of the 44 who developed ADRs) experienced hepatotoxicity in connection with azathioprine treatment. The authors report that their results do not confirm a correlation between TPMT, XDH, and ITPA genotypes and the occurrence of hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity occurred in 4 of 44 azathioprine-treated patients who developed ADRs in the study cohort. The proposed mechanism involves AZA metabolites or ROS generated during metabolism by XDH; no correlation with TPMT, XDH, or ITPA genotypes could be shown for hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A male patient receiving azathioprine for discoid lupus erythematosus developed severe cholestatic hepatitis 14-21 days after starting treatment, with a peak bilirubin of 62.4 mg/dL. Viral hepatitis and other causes of hepatic dysfunction were clinically and serologically excluded, and liver biopsy showed cholestatic hepatocellular damage. Liver function began to improve 14 days after azathioprine was stopped, although alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase remained elevated after 4 months. The authors conclude the case argues for an idiosyncratic cholestatic hepatocellular damage caused by azathioprine.
raw_record.extra_details: 67-year-old male treated for discoid lupus erythematosus; latency 14-21 days after initiation; peak bilirubin 62.4 mg/dL; liver biopsy revealed cholestatic hepatocellular damage; onset of improvement in transaminases and bilirubin 14 days after discontinuation, with alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase still elevated after 4 months; viral hepatitis and other causes of hepatic dysfunction excluded; patient also had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, gastroesophageal reflux, hip arthrosis, smoking (~20 cigarettes/day) and moderate alcohol intake. The named hepatic phenotype is cholestatic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Two patients developed cholestatic jaundice with only mild elevations of ALT, and liver biopsy was suggestive of AZA-induced cholestasis rather than an autoimmune hepatitis flare. In one patient the AZA dose had been escalated to 3.2 mg/kg/day for poorly controlled disease, and his TGN and MeMPN concentrations rose during hospital admission as he developed jaundice; the second patient was on a stable AZA dose with a high mean MeMPN concentration (18,879 pmol/8 x 10^8 RBCs). Both had high TPMT activity, and withdrawal of AZA resulted in clinical and biochemical improvement in both.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients with autoimmune hepatitis on azathioprine developed cholestatic jaundice with mild ALT elevation; liver biopsy suggestive of AZA-induced cholestasis, not an AIH flare. One patient's dose had been escalated to 3.2 mg/kg/day; TGN rose 150 to 254 and MeMPN 1,698 to 9,675 pmol/8 x 10^8 RBCs in that patient during admission. The avMeMPN concentration was higher in the 2 cholestasis patients than in those without (14,277 versus 1,416 pmol/8 x 10^8 RBCs). Both had high TPMT activity (12.7 and 13.7 IU/mL); withdrawal of AZA led to clinical and biochemical improvement in both.

raw_record.support_text: As a possible explanation for AZA-induced hepatotoxicity, increased levels of the methylated inactive metabolite 6-methylmercaptopurine (6-MMP) have been incriminated. Dubinsky et al. reported that hepatotoxic events (n = 16) in IBD patients under AZA/6-MP were associated with higher median 6-MMP levels (P < 0.05), with a 3-fold increased risk for hepatotoxicity at 6-MMP levels above the third quartile (> 5700 pmol/8x10^8 erythrocytes); none of these patients showed TPMT heterozygosity. The paper further states that AZA-induced hepatotoxicity cannot generally be attributed to a homozygous mutant or heterozygous TPMT genotype, and in the present study all cases with hepatotoxicity displayed TPMT wildtype.
raw_record.extra_details: AZA (azathioprine) used for IBD therapy induced hepatotoxicity. Hepatotoxic events (n=16) in IBD patients on AZA/6-MP were associated with higher median 6-MMP levels (P<0.05), with a 3-fold increased risk at 6-MMP > 5700 pmol/8x10^8 erythrocytes; none were TPMT heterozygous. The paper's own patients with hepatotoxicity displayed TPMT wildtype. A dose-dependency of methylated metabolites (such as 6-MMP, an inactive metabolite not independently causal) may underlie hepatotoxicity. In a cited study of ALL children receiving 6-MP/6-thioguanine plus methotrexate, four heterozygous carriers of TPMT*3A developed severe hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A 55-year-old male with pemphigus foliaceus and azathioprine-induced hepatotoxicity, unresponsive to prednisolone, was successfully treated with mycophenolate mofetil 1 g twice daily. Elsewhere the paper lists patients intolerant of azathioprine due to hepatotoxicity or nausea, explicitly attributing hepatotoxicity to azathioprine.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported in a 55-year-old male with pemphigus foliaceus; also cited as a reason for azathioprine intolerance (hepatotoxicity or nausea) among pemphigus vulgaris patients who improved on mycophenolate mofetil (Nousari's studies, doses 400-2500 mg/d).

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity (n = 5) was observed only in patients receiving azathioprine (group 1) and is described together with anemia/leukopenia and gastrointestinal symptoms as a well-known side effect of azathioprine. Eight of the 13 patients in group 1 who did not complete 6 months of therapy due to side effects discontinued for drug-related reasons; overall, major side effects were more frequent in the azathioprine group (17 patients, 16.8%, vs 6, 5.7%, in group 2; P = 0.01).
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity (n=5) was reported only in the azathioprine (group 1) arm of a comparative trial in which patients were followed for 6 months of therapy; anemia/leukopenia (n=3) and gastrointestinal symptoms (n=3) were also attributed only to azathioprine. Thirteen patients in group 1 discontinued prematurely due to side effects versus 1 in group 2 (discontinuation risk 14.9% vs 2.8%, P=0.002). No deaths were considered directly related to study drugs.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective multicenter study of 220 Slovak IBD patients treated with azathioprine, adverse drug reactions to AZA therapy were observed, including hepatotoxicity in 10.9% of patients. The hepatotoxicity was attributed to AZA therapy, with the high frequency partly explained by meticulous monitoring including regular hepatic enzyme biochemistry.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective multicenter study of 220 Slovak IBD patients treated with azathioprine; hepatotoxicity occurred in 10.9% of patients (myelotoxicity 14.5%, dyspepsia 3.2%, pancreatitis 2.7%, allergic reactions 0.9%). High frequency partly due to meticulous monitoring including regular hepatic and pancreatic enzyme biochemistry; analysis of TPMT genotype effects on ADRs. Concomitant mesalazine (5-ASA) use did not affect occurrence of ADRs (73.9% of ADR patients vs 66.3% of AZA patients without ADRs, p=n.s.).

raw_record.support_text: A 67-year-old patient with primary polymyositis and no prior liver disease developed clinical and biochemical features of severe cholestasis 3 months after initiation of azathioprine therapy. Liver biopsy showed cholestasis with both cytological and architectural alterations of interlobular bile ducts. Azathioprine withdrawal resulted after 7 weeks in resolution of the clinical and biochemical abnormalities, and the authors state this is the first reported case of reversible azathioprine-induced cholestasis with histologic evidence of bile duct injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 67-year-old man with primary polymyositis; presented with jaundice of 2 weeks duration; developed cholestasis 3 months after azathioprine reintroduction on June 27, 1988 (100 mg/day p.o., increased to alternate 100 and 150 mg/day on August 17, 1988). Liver biopsy showed cholestasis with cytological and architectural alterations of interlobular bile ducts. Azathioprine withdrawal led to complete resolution within 7 weeks. Reported as the first case of reversible azathioprine-induced cholestasis with histologic bile duct injury. Concurrent medications (corticosteroids/prednisolone, ranitidine) were not implicated. Elevated total serum bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase (N <= 60 IU/l) and ALT were documented.

raw_record.support_text: Azathioprine is among the top ten drugs in the Icelandic prospective DILI registry and among the drugs most strongly associated with DILI in GPRD, with a crude incidence of 1 per 1,103 users and the highest Icelandic incidence of 1 of 133 users among potentially hepatotoxic drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: Immunosuppressive agent; top-ten drug in Icelandic registry; strongly associated with DILI in GPRD (crude incidence 1 per 1,103 users); highest Icelandic incidence of 1 of 133 users; listed in Table 1 with >100 reported DILI cases (LiverTox).

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of mixed hepatitis induced by azathioprine, described as the third such case in the literature, which caused a severe acute hepatitis (the first severe form described in relation to inflammatory intestinal disease, Medline 1986-2000). It notes that in 7-10% of patients azathioprine produces occasionally serious adverse effects, with hepatotoxicity showing varied clinical, analytical, and histologic expression.
raw_record.extra_details: 38-year-old man with Crohn's disease (ileocolonic involvement); azathioprine added at 100 mg/24h; onset of hepatitis approximately 3 months after starting treatment. On admission: prothrombin activity 21%, AST 136 U/l, ALT 652 U/l, GGT 331 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 281 U/l, total bilirubin 1.9 mg/dl, subicterus, leucocytosis. Viral, autoimmune, and metabolic causes excluded. Azathioprine withdrawn; within 48 h prothrombin rose to 50% and enzymes fell (AST 38, ALT 250, GGT 204, FA 198), normalized by day 8 and remained normal at 1 month. No liver biopsy was performed because the causal relationship was considered sufficiently proven. Presented as third mixed-hepatitis case and first severe form in inflammatory intestinal disease. Azathioprine hepatotoxicity incidence cited as 0.3-3%, with latency reported as 2 weeks to 33 months.

raw_record.support_text: Azathioprine has been associated with intrahepatic cholestasis in renal-allograft recipients and in patients treated for immune-mediated conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus. The cholestasis occurred 3 weeks to 18 months after initiation of therapy, and liver function improved after drug withdrawal. In one study, all patients were rechallenged, with a recurrence of cholestasis.
raw_record.extra_details: Intrahepatic cholestasis in renal-allograft recipients and patients with immune-mediated conditions (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus); latency 3 weeks to 18 months after therapy initiation; cholestasis recurred on rechallenge in one study.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 181 patients under azathioprine (AZA) therapy, 74 reported AZA-related adverse drug reactions (ADRs). Among 166 TPMT*1/*1 wild-type patients who experienced ADRs, hepatotoxic reactions occurred in 29 (43.2%), alongside hematological (22), gastrointestinal (29), and hypersensitivity (17) reactions. These non-hematological ADRs manifested within a few months of therapy start and led either to AZA dose adjustment or to stopping AZA, indicating that azathioprine caused clinically relevant human hepatic injury (hepatotoxicity) at therapeutic exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: AZA doses ranged from 0.5 mg/kg/day to 2.5 mg/kg/day. Hepatotoxic ADRs (29/67 in wild-type patients with ADRs, 43.2%) manifested within a few months of starting therapy and led to either dose adjustment or treatment interruption. One heterozygous TPMT*2 allele carrier developed hepatotoxicity (with leucopenia and nausea) resolved by AZA dose reduction. Genotyping focused on TPMT variants; ADR prevalence did not differ significantly between variant carriers and wild-type patients overall (p=0.78).

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective, single-center, blind, case-control study of 200 IBD patients, 60 cases suspended azathioprine due to toxicity, with reasons including leukopenia, pancreatitis, hepatitis, and nausea or vomiting, while 140 controls continued treatment without adverse events. The paper states that azathioprine use results in adverse events at a rate of 5% to 20%, with hepatitis listed among the azathioprine-associated toxicities.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis listed as one of several azathioprine toxicity adverse events (with leukopenia, pancreatitis, nausea/vomiting) in IBD patients with steroid-dependent Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis; adverse event rate 5-20%; 60/200 patients discontinued azathioprine for these toxicities. The paper found no significant difference in TPMT allelic variants (TPMT*2, *3A, *3B, *3C) between patients who tolerated azathioprine and those with adverse events (OR=0.77, 95% CI 0.08-7.72, p=0.82). Background discussion notes that overproduction of the 6-MMPr metabolite could lead to hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In this sarcoidosis cohort, all patients received corticosteroids and azathioprine; three patients who switched to mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) from azathioprine due to hepatotoxicity showed satisfactory responses. The immunosuppression dose was modified based on clinical and biochemical responses, and methotrexate was not used in patients with renal sarcoid.
raw_record.extra_details: Unqualified attribution that azathioprine caused hepatotoxicity, prompting 3 patients to switch to mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), after which they showed satisfactory responses. Context: renal sarcoidosis treatment; azathioprine used together with corticosteroids; severity of the hepatotoxicity not specified.

raw_record.support_text: Among seven patients with recalcitrant vasculitis or steroid-induced side effects treated with azathioprine 150 mg/day, all had a good clinical response within four to eight weeks, but azathioprine-induced hepatitis developed in one of these patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 150 mg/day; injury described as azathioprine-induced hepatitis in one of seven treated patients, used for recalcitrant disease or steroid-induced side effects.

raw_record.support_text: Over the initial ten-year period of the prospective DILIN cohort study, 1434 cases of drug-induced liver injury were enrolled and underwent causality assessment, of which 27 were attributed, at least in part, to a thiopurine, including 15 to azathioprine (Aza), 12 to 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP), and none to 6-thioguanine (6-TG). After excluding 5 cases in which liver injury was considered only possibly related to the thiopurine, 22 cases (12 attributed to Aza and 10 to 6-MP) fulfilled the predefined inclusion criteria and were analyzed.
raw_record.extra_details: 12 of 22 included DILIN cases were attributed to azathioprine (10-year prospective DILIN cohort, total 1434 DILI cases). Combined Aza/6-MP expert DILIN causality was definite in 2 (9%), very likely in 12 (54%), and probable in 8 (36%); RUCAM median 6.5 with 4 highly probable, 14 probable, and 4 possible. Most patients were adults with autoimmune conditions; most common indication was inflammatory bowel disease (55%). Presenting features included symptoms attributable to liver injury in all but one patient (jaundice 73%, nausea 64%, fatigue and abdominal pain 50%); viral serologies for HAV/HBV/HCV/HEV were negative except one patient with stable pre-existing chronic hepatitis C; imaging showed no biliary obstruction. Ten patients (46%) were receiving corticosteroids when liver injury developed.

raw_record.support_text: The authors diagnosed azathioprine hypersensitivity based on macular erythema with chills, fever, hepatotoxicity, leucocytosis and increased C-reactive protein, plus the short interval between an oral azathioprine challenge and symptom onset. The patient had received cumulative azathioprine doses up to 150 mg via 1.5, 15, 30, 45 and 60 mg doses at 30-min intervals, and six hours after challenge liver-specific enzymes were above normal (aspartate aminotransferase 24 U/L, gamma-glutamyltransferase 99 U/L). Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity was normal, supporting hypersensitivity rather than TPMT-deficiency toxicity, and all serological markers returned to normal after corticosteroid treatment. The paper notes this is a rare complication reported in only about 50 published cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity occurred as part of an acute systemic hypersensitivity reaction (macular erythema, eyelid edema, chills, fever up to 39 °C, blood pressure 230/110 mmHg, leucocytosis 17.5 x 10^9/L, CRP 104 mg/L) reproducing on diagnostic oral challenge. Six hours after the oral challenge AST was 24 U/L and GGT 99 U/L; enzymes returned to normal within 2 weeks of oral methylprednisolone. TPMT activity was normal. Mechanism proposed: nitroimidazole ring split from 6-mercaptopurine in vivo may form a hapten-protein adduct triggering hypersensitivity. Azathioprine is rapidly converted to 6-mercaptopurine, metabolized by xanthine oxidase (to thiouric acid), HGPRT (to 6-thioinosinic acid), or TPMT. The paper recommends identifying patients with non-functional TPMT before azathioprine therapy and documenting hypersensitivity to avoid rechallenge.

raw_record.support_text: In a case report of a woman in her twenties with myasthenia gravis who benefited from mycophenolate mofetil, the patient's prior history recorded that she had previously tried azathioprine but had to discontinue it due to liver toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as prior immunosuppressive therapy in a myasthenia gravis patient; azathioprine was discontinued because of liver toxicity. No further laboratory, histologic, or latency details are given. This was mentioned in the context of a case report describing benefit from later mycophenolate mofetil therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A liver biopsy in four patients (three treated with infliximab) indicated a probable DILI in 3/4 patients; of the three with established DILI, one was on azathioprine, one on infliximab (which was discontinued), and one on a combination of infliximab and 6-MP (6-MP was subsequently discontinued).
raw_record.extra_details: Biopsy-proven DILI in a patient with IBD and ALT ≥ 3 ULN; azathioprine was discontinued. Histopathology indicated a probable DILI.

raw_record.support_text: In the chronic actinic dermatitis cohort, one patient treated with azathioprine (1.0–2.5 mg/kg/day) developed reversible azathioprine-induced hepatotoxicity that necessitated cessation of the drug; the patient subsequently responded well to cyclosporin. The paper explicitly attributes the hepatotoxicity to azathioprine in a human patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient in a retrospective study of 44 chronic actinic dermatitis patients; the azathioprine-induced hepatotoxicity was reversible, required drug cessation, and the patient subsequently responded well to cyclosporin. Azathioprine was dosed at 1.0–2.5 mg/kg/day and was used in 12 patients overall with partial to good clinical response.

raw_record.support_text: The development of anorexia, vomiting and hepatocellular jaundice with eosinophilia after two weeks of treatment with azathioprine, and prompt subsidence on withdrawal of the drug, strongly suggest a hypersensitivity reaction to azathioprine.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient with rheumatoid arthritis treated with azathioprine for two weeks; anorexia, vomiting, hepatocellular jaundice and eosinophilia developed, with prompt subsidence on withdrawal (dechallenge). Liver ultrasound normal; technetium scintigraphy showed patchy uptake suggestive of moderate hepatocellular damage; biopsy showed normal architecture with marked lipofuscin deposition, no necrosis or cholestasis, confirmed by electron microscopy. Azathioprine was withdrawn while ketoprofen (continued) was not implicated. Jaundice and biochemical hepatic dysfunction resolved completely within two weeks; eosinophilia settled to <1%.

raw_record.support_text: Among 180 patients treated with azathioprine (AZA), the incidence of azathioprine adverse reactions was tabulated: hepatic reactions occurred in 23 patients (45.1%), comprising high transaminase levels in 15 (29.4%), cholestasis in 1 (1.96%), and 'not specified' hepatic reactions in 7 (13.74%). These hepatic adverse reactions are attributed to azathioprine treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Study cohort of 180 azathioprine-treated patients (124 female, 56 male). Hepatic adverse reactions: 23/51 intolerant patients or ADR subgroup (45.1%), of which high transaminase levels 15 (29.4%), cholestasis 1 (1.96%), and not-specified hepatic reactions 7 (13.74%). Gastrointestinal (19.6%), hematological (19.6%), and allergic rash (1.96%) adverse reactions also reported. ADR type was missing for 7 patients (13.74%).

raw_record.support_text: Azathioprine was attributed to 11 DILI cases with a predominantly cholestatic pattern (64%). No cases met nR-based Hy's law criteria.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 of 843 registry DILI cases; Hep 9.1%/Chol 64%/Mix 27%; female 54%, lymphopenia 20%, eosinophilia 36%; 0 fulfilled nR-based Hy's law.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of 53 human DILI cases with liver biopsy, azathioprine was listed among the causative DILI drugs in the immunomodulator/immunosuppressor category, with a necroinflammatory (N) histological pattern. It was also among the drugs related to ANA positivity in one DILI case (p:39).
raw_record.extra_details: Histological pattern: necroinflammatory (N). One of 53 biopsy-confirmed DILI cases in the series.

raw_record.support_text: In 17 cases, the patient was receiving an excessive dose of azathioprine (6-TGN >450 pmol/8 × 10⁸ RBCs) or the drug was metabolised via an alternative pathway (6-TGN <230 and 6-MMP >5700 pmol/8 × 10⁸ RBCs). However, the authors explicitly state that there was no evidence of hepatotoxicity or myelotoxicity in any of the patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of pediatric IBD patients (Crohn disease n=47, ulcerative colitis n=25) treated with azathioprine; 17 cases had supratherapeutic exposure (6-TGN >450 or high 6-MMP >5700 pmol/8 × 10⁸ RBCs) yet no hepatotoxicity or myelotoxicity was observed in any patient.

raw_record.support_text: Patient 3, a 38-year-old man with pan-colonic and ileal Crohn's disease, had previously been treated with azathioprine, which was ceased due to hepatotoxicity. He was then unable to tolerate mercaptopurine because of nausea and was changed to infliximab and later adalimumab. Because of this previous hepatotoxicity, azathioprine was later restarted at 25 mg together with 100 mg of allopurinol.
raw_record.extra_details: Crohn's disease patient; azathioprine was ceased due to hepatotoxicity and subsequently restarted at a low dose of 25 mg/day together with 100 mg/day allopurinol, with a 6-thioguanine nucleotide level of 918 and 6-methylmercaptopurine level of 0 pmol/8x10^8 red cells.

raw_record.support_text: In Table 5, listing the main adverse effects of azathioprine (AZA) in 35 ulcerative colitis patients, hepatotoxicity was reported in 8 patients (23%). All 5 patients with AZA hepatotoxicity who were shifted to 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP) were 6-MP-tolerant, indicating the hepatotoxicity was attributed to AZA rather than 6-MP. A separate patient case noted that AZA was discontinued due to hepatotoxicity after which the patient tolerated 6-MP.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity was a main adverse effect of AZA in 8 of 35 (23%) ulcerative colitis patients (Table 5). Five of the 8 were shifted to 6-MP and all tolerated it (5 6-MP-tolerant). In one illustrative case, a patient discontinued AZA due to hepatotoxicity and was successfully treated with 6-MP with improved endoscopic findings. No biochemical pattern, histology, or severity grade beyond hepatotoxicity requiring drug discontinuation is reported.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective cohort of inflammatory bowel disease patients, azathioprine monotherapy (AZAm) was discontinued due to hepatotoxicity in three patients (3/118, 3%) and due to elevated liver function tests without hepatotoxicity in two patients (2/118, 2%).
raw_record.extra_details: Conducted in an IBD cohort receiving thiopurine-based therapy. Hepatotoxicity was distinguished from elevated LFTs without hepatotoxicity; the latter led to AZAm discontinuation in a further 2 patients (2%). A low-dose allopurinol+azathioprine combination (LDAA) cohort separately reported hepatotoxicity (2/166 discontinued, 6 continued on escalated allopurinol dose), but causality there was attributed to the combination regimen, not to azathioprine specifically.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity results in the withdrawal of thiopurine drugs, azathioprine (AZA) and mercaptopurine (MP), in up to 10% of patients with inflammatory bowel disease. The study enrolled unselected patients with acute thiopurine hepatotoxicity who were offered allopurinol co-therapy with low-dose AZA or MP, implying thiopurine therapy itself caused the hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity led to withdrawal of AZA in up to 10% of inflammatory bowel disease patients; 11 unselected patients (3 Crohn's disease, 8 ulcerative colitis) with acute thiopurine hepatotoxicity were treated with allopurinol co-therapy plus low-dose AZA/MP; 9/11 (82%) remained in long-term remission (median 42 months) with normal liver tests; one stopping patient had abnormal liver function with steatosis on biopsy.

raw_record.support_text: Case report of a 53-year-old man with Crohn's disease who developed azathioprine-induced nodular regenerative hyperplasia of the liver. Diagnosis was suspected after abnormal liver function tests and signs of portal hypertension on transabdominal ultrasonography and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, and confirmed by liver biopsy showing the characteristic alterations in liver architecture. Outcome was favorable after treatment discontinuation, with complete normalization of liver function tests within a year.
raw_record.extra_details: 53-year-old man with Crohn's disease treated with azathioprine (thiopurine) for maintenance of remission. Presentation: abnormal liver function tests with echographic and endoscopic signs of portal hypertension; diagnosis confirmed by liver biopsy showing characteristic alterations in hepatic architecture. Complete resolution of laboratory abnormalities within one year after drug discontinuation (dechallenge). In the discussion, thiopurine hepatotoxicity is classified into hypersensitivity syndrome, idiosyncratic cholestatic reaction, and dose-dependent hepatotoxicity secondary to endothelial injury, the latter encompassing nodular regenerative hyperplasia, veno-occlusive disease, and hepatic peliosis; hepatotoxicity observed in up to 3.3% of thiopurine-treated patients.

condition_group: exposure=therapeutic_use+population=human+population_context=psoriasis

raw_record.support_text: AZA-related hepatotoxicity is defined in three groups: hypersensitivity, idiosyncratic cholestatic reaction, and endothelial cell injury (veno-occlusive disease or peliosis hepatis). In the Du Vivier study of 29 patients with psoriasis treated with AZA, hepatotoxicity was seen in nine patients by long-term monitoring (two patients had cholestasis and the other patients had portal fibrosis).
raw_record.extra_details: AZA hepatotoxicity grouped as hypersensitivity, idiosyncratic cholestatic reaction, and endothelial cell injury (veno-occlusive disease or peliosis hepatis). In the Björnsson/DILIN prospective analysis, 12 AZA cases were among 22 with liver damage (also 10 6-MP); all but one had symptoms, most commonly jaundice (73%), nausea (64%), fatigue (50%) and abdominal pain (50%), with the two general patterns being transient mildly symptomatic aminotransferase elevation and cholestatic hepatitis with modest ALT and Alk P elevation and moderate-to-severe jaundice. Different injury types (hepatocellular, cholestatic or mixed) may occur; for AZA histology showed bile duct canaliculus distortion, focal hepatocellular necrosis, ground glass hepatocytes and portal infiltration with lymphocytes, neutrophils and histiocytes, with a case of cholestatic hepatitis shown at week 6 of treatment resolving after 2 months of drug cessation. Learning point: peak AZA-induced injury is usually self-limited cholestatic hepatitis, but severe cholestasis may occur.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 8451 patients taking azathioprine (AZA) for prevention of renal transplant rejection and treatment of inflammatory conditions, 1503 (17.8%) stopped AZA due to intolerable adverse drug events that included hepatotoxicity, with hepatitis in 4.6% of patients. The paper groups these as AZA-induced adverse events (also including leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, GI discomfort, alopecia, and allergy), and notes that concomitant use of allopurinol increased the risk of adverse-event development.
raw_record.extra_details: AZA is described as having a high potential for adverse drug effects including hepatotoxicity (para 24). In the cohort of 8451 AZA users, 17.8% (1503 patients) discontinued treatment due to intolerable ADEs, with hepatitis accounting for 4.6% of patients. Indications included renal transplant rejection and inflammatory conditions (SLE, Sjogren's syndrome, RA, other connective tissue disorders, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, severe atopic dermatitis). Concomitant allopurinol increased ADE risk. Hepatotoxicity was not analyzed for biochemical pattern or restriction in this evaluation.

raw_record.support_text: Azathioprine, a cytotoxic agent that blocks DNA synthesis, is well established in rheumatoid arthritis management. Cholestatic hepatitis is an important but uncommon complication of azathioprine treatment, while its association with hepatocellular necrosis is considered less clear. The authors describe a case in which azathioprine was clearly implicated as the cause of an idiosyncratic hepatitis on biochemical grounds, with liver biopsy showing no abnormality beyond marked lipofuscin deposition.
raw_record.extra_details: Azathioprine given orally 50 mg twice daily, started two weeks before admission, in a 58-year-old man with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis (previous failed trials of indomethacin, phenylbutazone, gold sodium thiomalate, and D-penicillamine due to rash/ulceration). Presented with anorexia, nausea, vomiting, myalgia, night sweats, icterus and 3 cm tender hepatomegaly; bilirubin 39 mmol/l (NR 0-17), alkaline phosphatase 898 IU/l (NR 100-300), aspartate transaminase >300 IU/l (NR 32-50); eosinophils 0.83 x 10^9/l. Hepatitis B surface antigen, Monospot, and serology for hepatitis A, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasma and mycoplasma were negative. Also on ketoprofen 200 mg daily at the time. Liver biopsy showed no abnormality beyond marked lipofuscin deposition.

raw_record.support_text: A 61-year-old obese male with subacute spongiotic dermatitis developed jaundice after 16 days of azathioprine therapy (50 mg twice daily). Liver function tests revealed a cholestatic type of liver injury; work-up for viral and autoimmune liver disease was negative. Liver biopsy showed moderate canalicular and intrahepatocytic cholestasis with maintained lobular architecture. RUCAM score was 9, indicating highly probable/definite drug-induced liver injury. The patient improved clinically and biochemically after azathioprine cessation and ursodeoxycholic acid supplementation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 61-year-old obese male (BMI 32 kg/m²); indication subacute spongiotic dermatitis; treated with concurrent ursodeoxycholic acid 600 mg/day after onset
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 50 mg twice daily; jaundice after 16 days of therapy; RUCAM score 9 (highly probable/definite); liver biopsy showed moderate canalicular and intrahepatocytic cholestasis with maintained lobular architecture, portal tracts and bile ducts; serial LFTs showed bilirubin up to 21.6/12 mg/dL (total/conjugated) on 26.09.2010, ALP up to 3x ULN, AST 215 IU/L, ALT 210 IU/L; recovered after azathioprine cessation with ursodeoxycholic acid supplementation.

raw_record.support_text: The conclusion states that, given the pharmacological adverse effects of azathioprine therapy and the increasing descriptions of morphological liver changes in the form of nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH), patients on chronic azathioprine therapy should have regular laboratory monitoring of hepatic parameters so that a 'transaminitis', which may be an early marker of NRH, is detected early. In the case, the patient on 4 years of azathioprine for Crohn's disease developed NRH confirmed by liver biopsy with consequent portal hypertension and variceal bleeding; azathioprine was discontinued.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic (4-year) azathioprine maintenance therapy for Crohn's disease (disease duration 18 years) leading to nodular regenerative hyperplasia and portal hypertension.
raw_record.extra_details: 45-year-old patient presented with hematemesis and melena; EGD showed grade III esophageal varices and signs of fundus variceal bleeding; thrombocytopenia and mildly elevated serum bilirubin and GOT/ASAT; MRI showed a splenorenal venous convolution with a patent portal vein and splenomegaly, indicating an intrahepatic cause of portal hypertension; liver biopsy showed low-grade non-active hepatitis with mild fibrosis consistent with NRH; treated with sclerotherapy of fundus varices, azathioprine was discontinued and beta-blocker therapy started; patient remains asymptomatic. NRH is noted as an increasingly described liver morphology change under azathioprine, with transaminitis as a possible early marker.

raw_record.support_text: A 51-year-old man treated for sympathetic ophthalmia with prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day) and azathioprine (1.4 mg/kg/day) developed jaundice and diffuse abdominal pain with elevated liver enzymes (ALT 282, AST 105, ALP 230, GGT 992 U/L and bilirubin 35 µmol/L). Percutaneous liver biopsy showed a portal inflammatory infiltrate with granulomatous aspects and destruction of bile ducts, consistent with destructive cholangitis. After azathioprine was changed to Endoxan, abdominal pain resolved within 2 days and liver function tests normalized within 8 weeks. The authors judged the diagnosis of azathioprine-related liver toxicity likely because liver tests were normal before therapy, other causes of cholangitis (no stones, no antibodies, no other drug-induced cholestasis) were excluded, symptoms appeared 4 weeks after starting azathioprine, and symptoms/biochemistry resolved after azathioprine withdrawal.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Concurrent prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day) co-medication; indication sympathetic ophthalmia; azathioprine dose 1.4 mg/kg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: Jaundice and diffuse abdominal pain with posterior irradiation; LFTs: ALT 282 (N=60 U/L), AST 105 (N=50), ALP 230 (N=110), GGT 992 (N=50), bilirubin 35 µmol/L, prothrombin time normal; liver biopsy showed portal tract granulomatous mononuclear infiltrate without eosinophils and bile duct destruction (destructive cholangitis); latency ~4 weeks after starting azathioprine; dechallenge: pain resolved in 2 days, LFTs normalized at 8 weeks after substitution with Endoxan (cyclophosphamide); azathioprine is hepatically metabolized to 6-mercaptopurine; author hypothesis of idiosyncratic reaction of the metabolite type.

raw_record.support_text: Azathioprine (AZA), a corticosteroid-sparing treatment for Crohn's disease, can be associated with varying forms of hepatotoxicity, and nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH) of the liver can arise 1 to 5 years after starting azathioprine. The presented 53-year-old man with Crohn's disease developed NRH after azathioprine exposure, with portal hypertension and esophageal varices; multiple case reports have documented NRH as an adverse effect of AZA.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Crohn's disease patient; co-treatment with 5-ASA and subsequently MTX/infliximab; azathioprine dose 150 mg/day; no prior liver disease or alcohol abuse.
raw_record.extra_details: Biochemical markers (albumin, GGT, ALP, bilirubin, AST, ALT) were within normal limits at diagnosis; NRH presented with new anemia and thrombocytopenia, portal hypertension, and esophageal varices (controlled by beta-blocker); high-dose thiopurine NRH frequency reported up to 62% vs low-dose, with dose-dependent, irreversible portal hypertension; hepatic function preserved after elective surgery.

raw_record.support_text: Azathioprine-induced peliosis hepatis is reported as idiosyncratic in humans. The authors describe a Crohn's disease patient who developed peliosis hepatis during azathioprine therapy most likely due to concomitant alcohol binging; the patient improved after azathioprine was stopped, with peliosis hepatis diagnosed by liver biopsy showing sinusoidal ectasia in zones II and III. Alcohol binging was concluded to be an additional risk factor via hepatic glutathione depletion increasing azathioprine endothelial toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Crohn's disease patient; concomitant episodic alcohol binging identified as most likely precipitating co-factor; required combination immunosuppression with steroids (prednisolone) and prior mesalazine/metronidazole; male gender noted as a possible azathioprine-peliosis risk factor.
raw_record.extra_details: Azathioprine dosed at 2.5 mg/kg/day. Hepatic toxicity only appeared after three episodes of alcohol binging (800 g over 3 d followed by two episodes of 20 g/day); liver enzymes were normal in April 2006 under azathioprine alone. Presenting features: progressive fatigue, abdominal discomfort, pruritus, pancytopenia, portal hypertension. Lab values: GGT 121 U/L, ALP 220 U/L, total bilirubin 4.03 mg/dL, transaminases normal, hyaluronic acid 166 ng/mL, TPMT 44 nmol/g Hb x h. Liver biopsy: sinusoidal ectasia zone II/III without venous obliterations, minimal portal tract fibrosis, no cirrhosis, no bile duct alterations. Syndrome grouped among azathioprine liver reactions (hypersensitivity, idiosyncratic cholestatic reaction, endothelial cell injury). Improvement after azathioprine withdrawal; proposed mechanism (murine in vitro) is glutathione depletion in sinusoidal endothelial cells increasing azathioprine toxicity; alcohol binging depletes hepatic glutathione ~60%.

raw_record.support_text: In this study of azathioprine (AZA)-intolerant inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients, the authors conclude that a trial of mercaptopurine (MP) should be considered in all AZA-intolerant patients, and note that patients who have reacted with hepatotoxicity and arthralgia/myalgia during AZA treatment might benefit more from the switch than patients with other adverse events. This attributes hepatotoxicity to AZA treatment. The paper also reports that about 70% of adverse events occurred during the initial 3 months of therapy and that hepatotoxicity, like myelotoxicity, has been associated with increased thiopurine metabolite (TGN and meTIMP) levels.

raw_record.extra_details: Patients who reacted with hepatotoxicity (and arthralgia/myalgia) during AZA treatment may benefit most from switching to mercaptopurine; about 70% of adverse events occurred during the initial 3 months of therapy; hepatotoxicity has been associated with increased thiopurine metabolite (TGN and meTIMP) levels. The paper does not state severity or biochemical pattern for the AZA-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The thiopurines 6-MP and AZA are useful for IBD but have significant hepatotoxicity. In a study of almost 3500 patients, AZA/6-MP-induced hepatotoxicity occurred in 3.4% of patients, with an overall incidence of about 1% per patient-year in IBD patients on 6-MP/AZA, with no difference between AZA and 6-MP. Most mild thiopurine-induced liver injury occurs in the first few months of therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings in IBD patients on thiopurine therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: AZA/6-MP-induced hepatotoxicity occurred in 3.4% of patients in a study of almost 3500 patients; overall hepatotoxicity incidence approximately 1% per patient-year. No difference in hepatotoxicity incidence between AZA and 6-MP. Most mild thiopurine-induced liver injury occurs in the first few months of therapy. Serious thiopurine hepatotoxicity grouped into three categories: hypersensitivity (arises 2-3 weeks after initiation, cholestatic profile with elevated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase), dose-dependent endothelial cell injury (manifesting at 3 months to 3 years as peliosis hepatis, nodular regenerative hyperplasia, veno-occlusive disease, sinusoidal dilatation and/or fibrosis), and idiosyncratic cholestatic reaction with severe jaundice that may not resolve after drug withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that Aza (azathioprine) and 6-MP (6-mercaptopurine) caused liver injury in humans, with frequent injury after dose escalation (59% of patients, including 11 of 16 jaundiced and 2 of 6 anicteric cases), indicating partial dose-relatedness and intrinsic hepatotoxicity at higher doses, while the authors conclude that Aza and 6-MP should be added to a growing list of agents with both idiosyncratic and intrinsic hepatotoxic potential.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Includes dose escalation within therapeutic use; prognosis generally favorable except in patients with pre-existing liver disease; concurrent corticosteroid use and underlying immune-mediated diseases are common in this population.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective DILI case-series study with well characterized patients and good follow-up; injury most often occurs within 3 months of exposure or dose escalation, often in women, with non-specific symptoms followed by jaundice; two patterns: transient mildly symptomatic aminotransferase elevation and cholestatic hepatitis with modest ALT and Alk P elevations and moderate-to-severe jaundice (cholestasis verified by biopsy, low serum Alk P); occurrence of sinusoidal obstruction syndrome and nodular regeneration supports intrinsic hepatotoxicity; possibility of cross-sensitivity with 6-MP cholestatic liver injury (recurrence of injury in a prior azathioprine case); serum enzyme pattern distinct from anabolic steroid injury.

raw_record.support_text: Three patients who received a cadaveric kidney transplant and were maintained on the immunosuppressant azathioprine (2.0-2.3 mg/kg) plus prednisone (10 mg) developed liver disease 16-24 months after grafting. They had no previous hepatic disease, normal pre-transplant liver function, no alcohol use, and no hepatotoxic drug other than azathioprine; HBsAg/HBsAb remained negative and serologic tests (CMV, brucellosis, toxoplasmosis, mononucleosis, syphilis, hepatitis A and B) failed to show an infective cause. Liver biopsy showed sinusoidal dilatation progressing to cirrhosis, with improvement after azathioprine dose reduction, implicating azathioprine as the cause of the hepatic injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Kidney transplant recipients maintained on azathioprine with prednisone (10 mg) as second immunosuppressant; onset 16-24 months after grafting.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 3 transplant patients (patients 1-3: ages 48, 37, 33; azathioprine doses 2.3, 2.0, 2.1 mg/kg/day). Injury featured hepatic sinusoidal dilatation progressing to cirrhosis, with splenomegaly, ascites, esophageal varices, increased wedged hepatic pressure, and marked 99mTc uptake reduction. Laboratory findings of frank hemolysis (increased reticulocytes, no detectable serum haptoglobin, elevated LDH first fraction, elevated bilirubin), macrocytic anemia, leuco- and thrombocytopenia; SGPT/SGOT, alkaline phosphatase and gamma-GT only slightly elevated in patients 1 and 2 and normal in patient 3; serum albumin decreased. Congestive heart failure and infective causes excluded. Improvement after azathioprine dose reduction in all 3 patients.

raw_record.support_text: A 40-year-old patient with pemphigus foliaceus, previously on corticosteroids, was started on azathioprine 100 mg daily (2 mg/kg per day). Three weeks after initiation he developed jaundice, dark urine and pruritus; laboratory investigations revealed severe hepatitis and cholestasis, with other hepatitis aetiologies negative. After azathioprine was withdrawn the jaundice regressed and hepatic tests normalised slowly; a low thiopurine methyltransferase activity (0.48 IU/mL red blood cells; normal 9.3–17.6) was found. The paper frames this as a severe case of azathioprine-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.extra_details: Dose 100 mg daily (2 mg/kg/day); latency 3 weeks after therapy onset; jaundice, dark urine and pruritus; severe hepatitis and cholestasis on laboratory tests; other viral/aetiologic causes of hepatitis negative; dechallenge led to regression of jaundice and slow normalization of hepatic tests; TPMT activity 0.48 IU/mL red blood cells (normal 9.3-17.6). raw_record.support_text: The paper reports, to the authors' knowledge, the first case of hepatic peliosis caused by azathioprine (AZA) in a non-transplanted patient, a case that allows eliminating the transplantation factor and strongly incriminates AZA as an agent capable of inducing hepatic vascular lesions of the peliotic type. This is supported by Degott and colleagues, who found 12 cases of hepatic peliosis among 55 patients with hepatic alterations out of 500 renal transplant patients treated with AZA and corticosteroids.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Non-transplanted patient; intercostal shingles (zona) appeared simultaneously with the revealing hepatic pain and the authors cannot exclude that the herpes infection played a cofactor role with AZA; in transplanted patients the role of transplantation itself could always be discussed.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported case of AZA-induced hepatic peliosis in a non-transplanted patient. Peliosis is characterized by intralobular blood cavities distributed inhomogeneously; typical associated biologic findings include elevation of alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl-transferase, isolated or with moderate transaminase elevation, frequent subicterus, almost constant hepatomegaly sometimes painful; lesions may regress, stabilize, or progress to fibrosis, cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and death by hepatic failure or intraperitoneal hemorrhage. AZA hepatotoxicity was previously only invoked in renal transplant patients.

raw_record.support_text: A 53-year-old man with Crohn's disease, on mesalazine, azathioprine and steroids, developed altered liver tests with a cholestasis pattern seven months after his azathioprine dose was increased to 2.5 mg/kg/day (200 mg daily). Values showed AST 113 U/l, ALT 61 U/l, FA 284 U/l, GGT 462 U/l and total bilirubin 2.2 mg/dl, with thrombocytopenia (79,000/mm³), and abdominal ultrasound showed signs of portal hypertension (spleen 15 cm, portal vein 14 mm) and chronic hepatopathy; upper endoscopy showed small esophageal varices.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Occurred after azathioprine dose increase to 2.5 mg/kg/day in a patient with Crohn's disease (ileocolic L3, fistulizing B3) also receiving mesalazine and steroids; features of chronic hepatopathy and portal hypertension present.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency ~7 months after the dose increase. Liver biopsy showed moderate architectural alteration with portal and sinusoidal fibrosis, regenerative nodules (reticulin staining) with lightly enlarged hepatocytes, perivenular fibrosis, sinusoidal congestion and areas of hepatocyte atrophy, compatible with nodular regenerative hyperplasia. After stopping azathioprine, aminotransferases, cholestasis enzymes and bilirubin improved and platelets normalized about one year later; follow-up ultrasound showed disappearance of portal hypertension signs (portal vein 12 mm, spleen 11.5 cm). Viral, autoimmune, alpha-1-antitrypsin, iron and copper workup were normal.

raw_record.support_text: A 26-year-old female patient with CD and high TPMT activity stopped 2 mg/kg and then 1 mg/kg azathioprine (AZA) because of drug-induced hepatitis. She was then prescribed 0.5 mg/kg/day (25 mg/day) AZA concurrently with 200 mg/day allopurinol, which generated a satisfactory level of TGNs (350 pmol/8 x 10^8 erythrocytes) with no hepatotoxicity, and she remained asymptomatic with normal liver function tests for 5 years.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient with Crohn's disease and high TPMT activity.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis attributed to AZA, prompting drug discontinuation at 2 mg/kg then 1 mg/kg. Subsequently AZA 0.5 mg/kg/day (25 mg/day) plus 200 mg/day allopurinol produced a satisfactory TGN level (350 pmol/8 x 10^8 erythrocytes) without hepatotoxicity and with normal liver function tests over 5 years; 6TU excretion was undetectable (<1% of AZA dose).

raw_record.support_text: Of the 150 renal-transplant patients included, azathioprine (AZA) therapy was reduced or withdrawn in 30 patients (20%) because of side effects. Among those 30, 18 patients showed hepatotoxicity (12 developed hematological toxicity such as leucopenia or pancytopenia, and none had both). These side effects, including the hepatotoxicity, resolved in all intolerant patients after azathioprine dose reduction or withdrawal, attributing the hepatotoxicity to azathioprine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients following renal transplantation treated with azathioprine as immunosuppressive therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Among the 30 patients whose azathioprine was reduced or withdrawn due to side effects, 18 showed hepatotoxicity and 12 showed hematological toxicity (leucopenia or pancytopenia); no patient had both simultaneously. Hepatotoxicity resolved in all intolerant patients after azathioprine dose reduction or withdrawal. Overall 20% (30/150) of cases had azathioprine reduced/withdrawn for side effects.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that hepatotoxicity is a well-known side-effect of thiopurines (azathioprine) and describes patients who stopped AZA treatment due to liver dysfunction. In their cohort, five patients developed liver dysfunction on AZA: one of the two NUDT15 R139C homozygous patients and four other patients who carried no SNP. The authors note that thiopurine-induced liver dysfunction was not associated with NUDT15 gene polymorphisms and may be due to other unknown genetic factors. Table 2 lists 'Liver dysfunction' as an adverse effect of AZA occurring in 4 patients with no SNP, with a mean duration of AZA intake of 34.0 ± 11.5 days before the liver dysfunction (average AZA dose 1.64 ± 0.41 mg/kg/day).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients receiving AZA for severe/steroid-resistant dermatological diseases (connective tissue disease, autoimmune bullous disease, ANCA-associated vasculitis, polyarteritis nodosa); indication-restricted cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: Five patients in the cohort stopped AZA due to liver dysfunction (4 with no SNP and 1 NUDT15 homozygous), occurring at a mean of 34.0 ± 11.5 days of AZA intake at average dose 1.64 ± 0.41 mg/kg/day. Hepatotoxicity was not associated with NUDT15 gene polymorphisms; the authors state thiopurine-induced liver dysfunction may be due to other unknown genetic factors. Reported in a small single-institution study of 15 AZA-treated patients.

raw_record.support_text: A number of reports have suggested an association between azathioprine therapy and veno-occlusive disease, especially in renal-transplant recipients. Of 16 reported cases, 10 presented with jaundice as a predominant symptom, 5 had hepatomegaly, 3 ascites, and 1 splenomegaly. All patients became symptomatic 6 months to 9 years after renal transplantation; 8 had hepatic failure, 3 had progressive portal hypertension, 3 died of nonhepatic causes, 1 improved after azathioprine withdrawal, and 1 improved after a portacaval shunt.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Renal-transplant recipients on continuous azathioprine therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Veno-occlusive disease characterized by non-thrombotic concentric luminal narrowing of sublobular hepatic veins without large hepatic vein obstruction. 16 reported cases; symptoms 6 months to 9 years after renal transplantation (11 between 12-24 months); among 16: 8 hepatic failure, 3 progressive portal hypertension, 3 died of nonhepatic causes, 1 improved on withdrawal, 1 improved after portacaval shunt. Some acute, some insidious progression to chronic liver disease.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective study of Chinese patients with neuromyelitis optica treated with azathioprine (2 mg/kg) plus a low-dose corticosteroid, the most common side effects observed using the protocol were hepatotoxicity and neutropenia. Adverse effects were reversible with adjustment of AZA dose. The paper relates AZA metabolism by the TPMT enzyme and genetic TPMT*3C polymorphisms to higher likelihood of adverse effects, and excluded patients with the TPMT mutation from the cohort.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Retrospective cohort of Chinese patients with neuromyelitis optica and normal TPMT genotypes; AZA given at 2 mg/kg in combination with a low-dose corticosteroid; patients with TPMT mutation excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity and neutropenia were the most common side effects of the AZA plus corticosteroid protocol; adverse effects were reversible with AZA dose adjustments. AZA is metabolized by TPMT and its activity is affected by genetic polymorphisms; about 5-10% of the Chinese population carries the TPMT*3C heterozygous or homozygous mutation and is more likely to experience adverse effects.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that 'Hepatotoxicity and/or myelosuppression are well-established adverse effects associated with the use of AZA,' and describes the study as evaluating characteristics of AZA-associated hepatotoxicity and myelosuppression in myasthenia gravis (MG).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Retrospective cohort of myasthenia gravis patients treated with azathioprine.
raw_record.extra_details: Overall prevalence of AZA-associated hepatotoxicity was 15.2%. GGT-predominant elevation was the most common pattern, seen in 67.8% of patients with hepatotoxicity; isolated GGT elevation was seen in 6.9%. Hepatotoxicity and/or myelosuppression occurred relatively early (mean 5.3-6.0 weeks, median 3.5-6.0 weeks after initiation). AZA was discontinued in 53 patients (88.3%) with isolated hepatotoxicity, and 84.9% had normalization of test abnormalities after discontinuation; mean time to normalization was 5.8 weeks (median 5.0 weeks). The paper recommends monitoring liver enzymes, especially GGT, weekly for the first 6-8 weeks after AZA initiation.

raw_record.support_text: Azathioprine (Aza), a prodrug of 6-mercaptopurine, is a thiopurine used as an immunosuppressive agent for prevention of transplant rejection and therapy of autoimmune diseases such as IBD and autoimmune hepatitis. Reports of liver injury, sometimes fatal, appeared shortly after its introduction, and more than 100 cases of liver injury attributed to Aza and 6-MP have been reported. In large prospective and retrospective studies on drug-induced liver injury, Aza and 6-MP are frequently listed as common causes, and in a population-based study from Iceland Aza was associated with the highest risk of hepatotoxicity, occurring in 1 of 133 persons prescribed it.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Veno-occlusive disease and nodular regenerative hyperplasia are reported with higher doses and long-term treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Aza is a prodrug of 6-MP; both are blamed jointly. In many cases the association was confirmed by prompt recurrence of injury upon readministration (rechallenge). Both Aza and 6-MP are associated with transient, usually mild and self-limited serum enzyme elevations. Both are implicated in clinically apparent hepatotoxicity that can be severe, leading to prolonged intrahepatic cholestasis or acute liver failure, as well as veno-occlusive disease and nodular regenerative hyperplasia at higher doses/long-term use. In a population-based Iceland study Aza was associated with the highest risk of hepatotoxicity, 1 of 133 persons. The current DILIN prospective cohort analysis enrolls cases adjudicated as probable, very likely, or definite.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 70 young inflammatory bowel disease patients treated with azathioprine (15 of whom developed side effects), a correlation was found between the wild-type GST-M1 genotype (high activity) and an increased probability of developing adverse effects and leukopenia during treatment. The paper states that individuals with high GST activity are apparently predisposed to azathioprine side effects, which are listed as pancreatitis, hepatitis, myelosuppression, arthralgias and neuropathy, and these results require confirmation before GST testing can predict azathioprine side effects.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Young patients with inflammatory bowel disease; GST-M1 wild-type (high-activity) genotype as a susceptibility factor for side effects.
raw_record.extra_details: Based on the Stocco et al. study of 70 young IBD patients treated with AZA (15 developed side effects); hepatitis is listed among azathioprine side effects together with pancreatitis, myelosuppression, arthralgias and neuropathy. Proposed mechanisms include high 6MP formation leading to accumulation of active/toxic compounds and glutathione depletion causing cell damage; results require confirmation before GST testing can be used to predict side effects.

raw_record.support_text: The paper introduces the salient features of quinidine-induced liver injury from earlier reports: fever, a mixed type of hepatic injury, rapid return of enzyme tests to normal on withdrawal of quinidine, and a shortening of the latency period on reexposure with fever and disordered liver function appearing sooner and after progressively smaller doses; these features resemble those of a hypersensitivity type of liver injury caused by other hepatotoxic agents. The authors describe a patient whose clinical course after quinidine ingestion showed all of these features and additionally prolonged hepatocellular damage on sulfobromophthalein (Bromsulphalein) testing.
raw_record.extra_details: Quinidine sulfate 0.4 g three times daily, prescribed for frequent ventricular premature beats in a 65-year-old man with mild diet-regulated diabetes; fever (38.8 C) appeared a few days after starting the drug. Laboratory findings at admission: bilirubin 1.5 mg/100 ml, SGPT 180 Karmen units (rising to 290 on day 6), SGOT 123 Karmen units (136 on day 6), alkaline phosphatase 5.5 Bessey-Lowry units (normal up to 2.5; 4.0 on day 6), prothrombin time 100%. Serology negative for brucellosis, infectious mononucleosis, and leptospirosis; blood cultures and thick smear negative. Features match hypersensitivity-type liver injury, including prolonged hepatocellular damage on sulfobromophthalein testing and anticipated rapid enzyme normalization with drug withdrawal and shortened latency with rechallenge.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 487 patients receiving quinidine, quinidine hypersensitivity occurred in 32 (6.5%) and liver involvement was demonstrated biochemically and histologically in 10 patients (2% of the total). Liver involvement was reversible and disappeared after discontinuation of the drug but reappeared when the drug was readministered.
raw_record.extra_details: Granulomata were found in all 4 patients who underwent liver biopsy, and probable in the remaining 6 of the quinidine liver group; 9 of 10 patients with liver involvement had fever. Elevated SGOT (up to 370 mU/ml), alkaline phosphatase (up to 460 mU/ml), and bilirubin (up to 5.0 mg/100 ml) with normal prothrombin time and albumin. Liver-function abnormalities reversed after discontinuation and reappeared on rechallenge (5 patients rechallenged). Duration of quinidine treatment before symptoms ranged from 4 to 180 days. The reaction was interpreted as an immune-mediated granulomatous hepatitis distinct from Klatskin's hepatocellular and cholestatic groups.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that hepatic toxicity secondary to quinidine is an uncommonly reported event. In the author's series, serial liver function tests were available in 5 of 11 patients with fever, and in one of these patients granulomatous hepatitis was demonstrated after biopsy (case 6). The authors also cite four previously reported cases of quinidine-related hepatic abnormality, including one with chemical evidence of both cholestatic and hepatocellular injury, and two cases with biopsy evidence of reversible noncaseating hepatic granulomas. The current case had similar histology during fever with resolution of granulomas one year later. The paper supports routine hepatic function testing in all patients with quinidine fever to clarify the frequency of quinidine-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: One patient in the current series had biopsy-demonstrated granulomatous hepatitis (Appendix, case 6), which resolved one year later. Four previously reported cases of quinidine-related hepatic abnormality include one with chemical evidence of both cholestatic and hepatocellular injury and two with biopsy evidence of reversible noncaseating hepatic granulomas. Serial liver function tests were available in 5 of 11 patients with quinidine fever. The paper describes hepatitis occurring in association with quinidine fever and allergic origin.

raw_record.support_text: A 58-year-old male commenced quinidine (Kinidin Durules) twice daily for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation; ten days later he developed fever, lethargy, nausea and upper abdominal discomfort, and at 15 days abnormal liver function tests were noted (total bilirubin 27.36 µmol/L, SGOT 124 u/L, SGPT 208 u/L, GGT 297 u/L). Quinidine was stopped after a further 11 days and within 48 hours nausea lessened markedly, with transaminases and GGT largely normalizing; the patient was on no other medication and a liver biopsy was not performed.
raw_record.extra_details: Case: 58-year-old male with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation on quinidine (Kinidin Durules). Onset of fever and symptoms at 10 days, abnormal LFTs at 15 days; resolution after cessation. No jaundice reported. Mechanism attributed to hypersensitivity reaction based on delay in onset and prompt recurrence of symptoms upon re-exposure. The paper notes rare jaundice, and that other probable quinidine hepatotoxicity reports show granulomatous hepatitis and nonspecific focal hepatocellular necrosis or transient liver enzyme abnormalities without biopsy. No reported cases of chronic liver injury due to quinidine therapy. No other medication taken during the illness.

raw_record.support_text: A 65-year-old woman taking quinine sulphate for nocturnal leg cramps presented with episodes of malaise, fever, nausea, vomiting, and polyarthralgia, and granulomatous hepatitis was diagnosed with no common cause found. Upon rechallenge with quinine sulphate her temperature rose and symptoms returned within hours, transaminase activities rose within 48 hours along with erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and after withdrawal symptoms abated and transaminase activities returned to normal. The paper concludes that the biochemical response to quinine challenge implicates the drug as the cause of the liver disturbances and that quinine should be added to the list of drugs known to cause granulomatous hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported case of quinine-induced granulomatous hepatitis (case report of a 65-year-old woman). Administered as quinine sulphate for nocturnal leg cramps; four episodes of malaise, fever, nausea, vomiting, and polyarthralgia over five months, each spontaneously subsiding after 3-28 days. No common cause for granulomatous hepatitis found. Rechallenge with quinine sulphate reproduced fever within hours and returned symptoms; transaminases and ESR rose within 48 hours; dechallenge led to symptom resolution and normalization of transaminases. Concurrent daily medications (pindolol, methyclothiazide) and rare alcohol use were noted but not implicated. Granulomatous hepatitis is the attributed specific phenotype, recorded under other_specific_phenotype. Related optical isomer quinidine was noted as a previously reported cause of granulomatous hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a 58-year-old man with repeated episodes of thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, lymphocytopenia, and a typical picture of granulomatous hepatitis after ingestion of quinine, following prior reports of quinine-induced granulomatous hepatitis. The association between the episodes and quinine ingestion was established by a quinine challenge that reproduced the complete clinical picture, with liver biopsy during an attack showing granulomatous hepatitis. Multiple quinine-dependent antibodies to platelets, neutrophils, and lymphocytes were detected, indicating an immune-mediated mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: 58-year-old man with recurrent attacks over a 2-year period; liver biopsy during an attack showed a typical picture of granulomatous hepatitis; GPT and GOT 4-6 times normal during attacks; quinine challenge reproduced fever, vomiting, and diarrhea with profound platelet and leukocyte diminution within hours; quinine-dependent IgG antibodies to platelets, neutrophils, T lymphocytes, and B lymphocytes detected by flow cytometry; specific phenotype is granulomatous hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Reference 24 cites Farber and Lanvin (Ann Pharmacother 1999) titled 'Quinine-induced hepatotoxicity.'
raw_record.extra_details: Quinine-induced hepatotoxicity (Farber DK, Lanvin MN, Ann Pharmacother 1999, 33:32-34).

Laboratory values included ALT 184 IU/L (0-55), AST 264 IU/L (10-60), GGT 697 IU/L (1-50), ALP 192 IU/L (30-117), LDH 385 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL. Hepatitis A/B/C serologies, EBV, CMV, blood/urine cultures, monospot, Legionella, Mycoplasma and Leptospira antibodies were negative; ANA 1:160 homogenous. Case report notes only four published reports of quinine-induced hepatotoxicity, and emphasizes sudden symptom onset with one dose and markedly elevated enzymes with continued use.

raw_record.support_text: The hepatotoxicity of troleandomycin was first discovered in the 1960s and, although no longer used in many countries, one additional case of reversible cholestatic hepatitis and a case of prolonged cholestasis following acute cholangitis in a 62-year-old woman have been reported. The later biopsy showed marked cholestasis, marked biliary duct abnormalities, abundant inflammatory infiltrates, and significant ductopenia with moderate portal fibrosis, with complete recovery 2 years after onset.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity known since the 1960s; additional case of reversible cholestatic hepatitis reported. Prolonged cholestasis following acute cholangitis in a 62-year-old woman: biopsy at 2 months showed marked cholestasis, marked biliary duct abnormalities and abundant interlobular and portal inflammatory infiltrates; biopsy at 1 year showed significant ductopenia and moderate portal fibrosis, with complete recovery 2 years after symptom onset. Cholestatic hepatitis was frequently reported in the late 1970s in French women taking oral contraceptives plus troleandomycin; the suggested ethinyl estradiol metabolism interaction (troleandomycin inhibits ethinyl estradiol 2/4-hydroxylase in rat liver microsomes, unlike erythromycin and roxithromycin) was not confirmed as the cause of human cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: A case report describes a 62-year-old woman in whom troleandomycin-induced acute hepatitis was followed by prolonged anicteric cholestasis. Jaundice occurred after 7 days of troleandomycin administration and was associated with hypereosinophilia; jaundice disappeared within 3 months but was followed by prolonged anicteric cholestasis with pruritus and high alkaline phosphatase and gammaglutamyltransferase activities. Pruritus disappeared at 19 months and liver tests returned to normal 27 months after the onset of hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Troleandomycin given at 2 g/day for 7 days (Aug 19-25, 1982); jaundice and pruritus with dark urine began on Aug 26 (after 6 days of therapy). Hypereosinophilia (10% eosinophils); normal prothrombin time; negative HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HAV IgM, Paul-Bunnell-Davidsohn, and autoantibody panels. Liver biopsy (Oct 1982) showed normal lobular architecture with marked centrilobular cholestasis, mild panlobular hepatocyte necrosis, and moderate mixed inflammatory infiltration; no small bile duct lesions or fibrosis. Prolonged anicteric cholestasis marked by pruritus and high serum ALP and gammaglutamyltransferase; second biopsy ~14 months later nearly normal with mild portal fibrosis. Dechallenge with eventual recovery: pruritus resolved at 19 months, liver tests normalized 27 months after hepatitis onset, normal at 19 and 31 months follow-up. Co-administered drugs (amoxicillin, betamethasone, penicillin G, streptomycin) were considered and excluded as causes because their administration had been discontinued a week or more before onset and their hepatotoxicity is unreported or very uncommon. General literature cited: troleandomycin increases serum aminotransferases in 30% and induces hepatitis in 4% of patients, with mixed cholestatic/hepatocytic-necrosis patterns and frequent hypereosinophilia [refs 1-3].

raw_record.support_text: Antiorganelle antibodies were absent or rare in hepatitis due to troleandomycin, with at least four cases examined. The text attributes drug-induced hepatitis to troleandomycin.
raw_record.extra_details: Drug-induced hepatitis in which LKM-type antiorganelle antibodies were absent or rare; at least four cases examined.

raw_record.support_text: This is a case report of a patient who developed acute hepatitis induced by troleandomycin. Jaundice disappeared within 3 months and serum alanine aminotransferase activity markedly decreased, but anicteric cholestasis (pruritus with high serum alkaline phosphatase and gammaglutamyltransferase activities) persisted after drug discontinuation; pruritus resolved within 19 months and liver tests returned to normal within 27 months.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute hepatitis followed by prolonged anicteric cholestasis marked by pruritus and elevated serum alkaline phosphatase and gammaglutamyltransferase; jaundice resolved within 3 months, pruritus within 19 months, and liver tests normalized within 27 months despite discontinuation. The authors propose that, like several other listed drugs, troleandomycin may induce acute hepatitis through an immune mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: A case is reported in which a second episode of severe cholestasis was shown by the macrophage inhibition factor test to have been caused by inadvertent rechallenge with cloxacillin. The report notes that hepatic damage by cloxacillin, congeneric to oxacillin, had not been reported before. The patient, a 69-year-old woman, had earlier been treated with nitrofurantoin and given ampicillin and cloxacillin, then developed cholestatic jaundice with pruritus.
raw_record.extra_details: 69-year-old woman; first episode of cholestatic jaundice followed treatment with nitrofurantoin, ampicillin and cloxacillin; second episode confirmed as caused by inadvertent rechallenge with cloxacillin using the macrophage inhibition factor test. Jaundice, pruritus, enlarged liver (span 15 cm). Hepatic damage by cloxacillin not previously reported. Confirmed by rechallenge.

raw_record.support_text: Severe intrahepatic cholestasis occurred in a patient after she took nitrofurantoin, ampicillin, and cloxacillin. Because only nitrofurantoin was known to cause cholestasis, she was given cloxacillin again two years later, and the cholestasis reappeared at once. A macrophage inhibition factor test confirmed that cloxacillin was the offending drug, and the authors concluded that cloxacillin should be added to the growing list of drugs causing cholestasis.
raw_record.extra_details: 69-year-old woman; initial episode followed therapy with nitrofurantoin (urinary tract infection), ampicillin, and cloxacillin (suspected pneumonia); inadvertent rechallenge with cloxacillin alone two years later reproduced cholestasis at once; positive macrophage inhibition factor (MIF) test confirmed cloxacillin as the cause. Presentation: pruritus beginning two weeks before admission then jaundice. Hepatic histology on wedge biopsy showed portal round-cell infiltration with scattered liver-cell necrosis, bile plugs in canaliculi, swollen Kupffer cells, and anisocytosis. Authors state this is the first reported hepatic damage due to cloxacillin, which is congeneric with oxacillin.
