raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN registry there were 8 cases of DILI attributed to amoxicillin only. These cases were younger than AC-DILI cases (51 vs 60 years, P=0.03) and more likely to present with rash (63 vs 22%, P=0.02). Amoxicillin DILI onset tended to be abrupt (median 17 vs 29 days) and resolution (50% reduction in TB) was more rapid (median 5 vs 8 days, P=0.02). Three of the eight amoxicillin cases received a severe DILIN Severity score; none were fatal or required liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: 8 adjudicated DILI cases attributed to amoxicillin alone in the DILIN registry, distinct from amoxicillin–clavulanate cases. Three of eight received a severe DILIN Severity score; none fatal and none required liver transplantation. Median latency 17 days; more likely than AC cases to present with rash.

raw_record.support_text: A 42-year-old woman presented with a 4-week history of malaise and jaundice after receiving hydrocodone/ibuprofen 7.5/200 mg per day and amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 6 days following dental work. Admission labs showed AST 1189 IU/L, ALT 521 IU/L, bilirubin 23.0 mg/dL, INR 1.4. She developed progressive hepatic encephalopathy, was listed for liver transplant on day 18 for drug-induced acute liver failure, and received an orthotopic liver transplant on day 19; her explanted liver showed submassive hepatic necrosis with confluent central zone necrosis, collapse, and neocholangiogenesis consistent with a drug reaction. She recovered and was alive as of 9/04.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 2 causality: CIOMS score 9 ('definite/highly probable') and CDS score 9 ('unlikely'). Liver biopsy on hospital day 4 showed portal tract expansion with lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, eosinophils, and mild ductular proliferation suggestive of a drug reaction. Patient developed ALF (ALT 766 IU/L, AST 2075 IU/L, bilirubin 26.9 mg/dL, INR 2.0 at listing), underwent orthotopic liver transplant on hospital day 19. Co-suspect hydrocodone/ibuprofen was also taken; competing causes (hepatitis A/B/C, ANA, anti-smooth muscle antibody, ceruloplasmin) were negative. No rash, fever, or eosinophilia.

raw_record.support_text: In this cohort of 501 patients with liver disease, drug-induced liver injury (DILI) was most often caused by NSARs, amoxycillin, other antibiotics or phenprocoumon. Patients were diagnosed using stringent criteria, with 9.2% of unclear cases classified as cryptogenic.
raw_record.extra_details: Spelled 'amoxycillin' in the paper. Listed among the agents most often causing drug-induced liver injury in a cohort of 501 patients with liver disease; DILI was most often caused by NSARs, amoxycillin, other antibiotics, or phenprocoumon. No specific phenotype, severity, or biochemical pattern is attributed to amoxicillin in this passage.

raw_record.support_text: A 42-year-old Caucasian female presented with ALF 21 days after receiving amoxicillin and underwent successful liver transplantation on hospital day 19. All competing causes were excluded, liver pathology was consistent with drug-induced hepatitis, and the case was deemed 'definite/highly probable' using causality assessment.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient was 42-year-old female; ALF with coagulopathy and encephalopathy; latency 21 days after amoxicillin; successful liver transplantation on hospital day 19; all competing causes excluded; pathology consistent with drug-induced hepatitis; causality scored definite/highly probable (CIOMS).

raw_record.support_text: A 39-year-old woman was diagnosed with abdominal actinomycosis and received amoxicillin treatment. She displayed hepatocellular and bile-duct injury with elevated liver enzymes and was diagnosed with amoxicillin-induced cholestatic hepatitis. When amoxicillin was discontinued, her symptoms improved and liver enzyme levels reduced toward normal.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of a 39-year-old woman given oral amoxicillin 2 g/day for abdominal actinomycosis. Hepatocellular and bile-duct injury with elevated liver enzymes; diagnosed as cholestatic hepatitis; symptoms and enzyme levels improved/dechallenge response on amoxicillin discontinuation. Also described elsewhere in the paper as a very low-rate complication of amoxicillin with benign course typically resolving within months.

raw_record.support_text: In long-term liver biopsy follow-up of 63 patients, three developed chronic rejection. One patient, who had been transplanted because of amoxycillin-related acute liver failure, was retransplanted at day 70 because of chronic rejection; the second graft was also lost to chronic rejection despite reinforced triple-drug tacrolimus-based immunosuppression.
raw_record.extra_details: The patient was transplanted for amoxicillin-related acute liver failure, indicating ALF with transplantation need. After transplantation the patient was retransplanted at day 70 due to chronic rejection and the second graft was also lost to chronic rejection despite reinforced triple-drug tacrolimus-based immunosuppression. Amoxicillin appears in the text as 'amoxycillin'.

raw_record.support_text: The clinical course and laboratory data are compatible with a diagnosis of severe acute cholestatic hepatitis, probably due to amoxicillin. Symptoms appeared 6 days after stopping amoxicillin treatment; symptoms reappeared after the drug was discontinued and taken again, interpreted as a positive rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: patient presented 6 days after stopping amoxicillin with jaundice and malaise; laboratory showed increased direct bilirubin, ALP, and GGT. Viral hepatitis serology (HAV, HBV, HCV) and antinuclear/antismooth muscle antibodies negative; antimitochondrial antibodies positive but anti-M2 negative; abdominal ultrasound normal. Liver biopsy (4 weeks after jaundice onset) showed pronounced centrolobular cholestasis with inflammatory infiltrates and focal portal inflammatory infiltrate involving biliary epithelium, compatible with both toxic hepatitis and PBC. Bilirubin and ALP decreased after 1 month of jaundice and later normalized; patient well with no signs of liver damage at 2 years follow-up. Differential diagnosis of primary biliary cirrhosis considered but drug-mediated toxic hepatitis favored based on positive rechallenge.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports two cases of acute ductopenia, one attributed to ingestion of amoxycillin (amoxicillin) and the other to flucloxacillin. In attributing ductopenia to a drug reaction, other possible causes of liver damage were excluded; neither patient had a history of recent liver disease, autoantibodies and all other serological investigations were negative, and the temporal relationship between drug ingestion, disease onset and disease course was fully consistent with a drug-induced aetiology.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1: acute ductopenia with cholestasis and hepatocyte ballooning present from a very early stage, confirmed with H&E and AE1 staining; serial biopsies showed evolution of secondary biliary features with portal fibrosis, ductular proliferation and persistent cholestasis, with incomplete restoration of bile ducts and development of chronic damage (fibrosis and copper-associated protein accumulation). Clinical course was protracted and severe; serum albumin fell to 25 g/l and liver transplantation was considered. Prednisolone was ineffective and cyclosporin was also given without benefit. The paper notes amoxycillin alone is an exceedingly rare cause of liver damage.

raw_record.support_text: Among the 12 antibiotics-associated DILI cases, amoxicillin accounted for 2 cases. The antibiotics DILI group showed cholestatic (16.7%), hepatocellular (50%) and mixed (33.3%) patterns, with causality RUCAM-adjudicated.
raw_record.extra_details: n=2 of the 12 antibiotics-associated DILI cases. RUCAM across cohort: possible 41.3%, probable 52.5%, highly probable 6.2%. Antibiotics DILI group patterns: cholestatic 16.7%, hepatocellular 50%, mixed 33.3%.

raw_record.support_text: Amoxicillin was among the drugs implicated as a cause of hepatic injury in a follow-up study of 44 patients with drug-induced hepatotoxicity; patients with abnormal hepatic evaluation at follow-up had previously taken amoxicillin.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed separately from the Augmentin combination in the 44-patient drug-induced hepatotoxicity cohort; antibiotics and analgesic NSAIDs together accounted for more than half of the cases.

raw_record.support_text: Among 81 patients with fulminant hepatitis, 11 (14%) were classified as fulminant drug-induced hepatitis. The cause was attributed to amoxicillin in 1 case.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed cause of fulminant drug-induced hepatitis in 1 of 11 drug-induced cases in a Japanese cohort (1980-1999).

raw_record.support_text: In this cohort of 80 patients with chronic DILI/HILI, synthetic drugs were the causative agents in 27/80 (33.7%) cases. The commonly implicated synthetic drugs were amoxicillin (12 cases), clarithromycin (7 cases), and enalapril (2 cases), alongside TCM/herbal agents that were implicated in 52.5% of the cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated as a causative agent of chronic DILI/HILI in 12 of 80 cases. Cohort-level analysis: RUCAM scores 6-8 in 74 patients and >=9 in 6; R value distribution was hepatocellular (R>=5) in 71.2%, mixed in 20.0%, cholestatic in 8.8%; DILI severity was mild (41.2%) or moderate (58.8%) with no severe, fatal, or transplantation outcomes; histology showed inflammatory necrosis and fibrosis.

raw_record.support_text: Amoxicillin was implicated in two cases of drug-induced liver injury acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases; one rechallenge case involved amoxicillin-clavulanic acid followed by amoxicillin.

raw_record.support_text: CB 3717-induced hepatotoxicity, although relatively mild and reversible, has been a frequent problem in man, with commonly associated malaise. Prolonging the infusion to 12 h at doses of 200-400 mg/m² did not significantly alter the incidence or severity of hepatitis, and peak plasma CB 3717 levels of about 20 µM were associated with hepatic dysfunction.
raw_record.extra_details: Antifolate antineoplastic agent in early (phase-I) clinical trials for antitumor effect. Hepatotoxicity described as relatively mild and reversible but frequent; associated with malaise. Prolonging infusion to 12 h at 200-400 mg/m² did not alter hepatitis incidence or severity. Peak plasma CB 3717 concentrations of ~20 µM were associated with hepatic dysfunction (1-h infusions). Weak positive correlation between peak plasma CB 3717 concentrations and subsequent elevation of serum transaminase levels after 1-h infusion; authors conclude the phenomenon is a direct toxic manifestation rather than an idiosyncratic reaction. In 13 patients receiving more than four courses, transaminase values normalized after five or six courses.

raw_record.support_text: In this pharmacokinetic study of CB 3717 in cancer patients, the CB 3717 peak plasma levels were about three times greater than in the earlier study (Alison et al.) because similar doses were given over shorter infusions, yet the incidence of hepatic toxicity was similar in both studies, confirming a lack of correlation between maximal plasma concentrations of CB 3717 and the drug-related hepatic toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Cancer patients receiving CB 3717 as an investigational thymidylate synthase inhibitor antimetabolite.
raw_record.extra_details: CB 3717 is a thymidylate synthase inhibitor (PDDF-class antimetabolite). An earlier study (Alison et al.) reported a weak correlation between CB 3717 peak plasma levels and GPT peak levels when the drug was given as a 1 h infusion; the authors failed to confirm this correlation. Peak plasma levels here were about three times greater than the prior study because similar doses were given over shorter (bolus) infusions, while the incidence of hepatic toxicity was similar in both studies. The paper notes hepatic toxicity is not correlated with maximal plasma concentration and suggests the mechanism of hepatic (and renal) toxicity differs from that underlying antitumoral activity, arguing that non-hepatotoxic analogs should be developable.

raw_record.support_text: The report concludes a probable case of acute hepatic injury induced by linagliptin. The patient's Naranjo probability scale score of 6 was consistent with a possible adverse drug reaction, while the more specific CIOMS/RUCAM scale score of 7 was consistent with probable drug-induced hepatotoxicity. Other causes such as HBV or HCV infection, autoimmune hepatitis, alcohol consumption and concomitant hepatotoxic drugs were excluded, and the patient was only taking linagliptin at the time, with resolution of symptoms and decline of hepatic parameters after discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Adult female diabetic patient on linagliptin monotherapy. Symptoms (nausea, fatigue, jaundice) began ~4 weeks after starting linagliptin (1 May 2013); marked elevations in AST, ALT, ALP, GGT and serum T-Bil with normal renal function. HBV, HCV and ANA serology negative; ultrasound showed no biliary or ductal abnormalities but slight fatty changes in the liver. Symptoms resolved and transaminases declined (slowly) after discontinuation; biliary parameters briefly increased then normalized ~8 weeks after stopping. Naranjo scale score 6 (possible ADR), CIOMS/RUCAM score 7 (probable DILI). Slow recovery attributed to linagliptin's exclusively biliary excretion route and long half-life (>100 h) among DPP-4 inhibitors.

raw_record.support_text: The article reports a probable case of hepatitis secondary to linagliptin: a 58-year-old Japanese woman developed fatigue, nausea, and jaundice with a marked elevation of liver enzymes 4 weeks after starting linagliptin 5 mg/day, without any other concomitant treatment. Viral serology and antibody tests were negative. Symptoms disappeared and liver enzyme concentrations progressively returned to normal after discontinuation of linagliptin, the slow normalization possibly reflecting the drug's very long half-life.
raw_record.extra_details: Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitor for type 2 diabetes; dose 5 mg/day; latency ~4 weeks; fatigue, nausea, jaundice (icterus) and marked elevation of liver enzymes; no concomitant medications; negative viral serologies and antibodies; clinical and biochemical recovery after drug discontinuation, with slow normalization attributed to the long half-life; presented as the first probable case of hepatic alterations secondary to linagliptin.

raw_record.support_text: A 41-year-old woman receiving 200 mg/day tolrestat (Alrestin) died 80 days after starting treatment and 30 days after drug suspension due to first hepatic symptoms (abdominal pain and jaundice). Hepatitis A, B, C and EBV tests were negative, with no alcoholism or prior hepatic illness; last laboratory values showed prothrombin time 13%, total bilirubin 447 µmol/L and ALT 2169 U/L, and the hepatic biopsy showed massive hepatic necrosis. This hepatic necrosis case with fatal outcome was reported to the manufacturer, and two further fatal tolrestat hepatic-necrosis cases (Canada, Italy) plus poor efficacy in trials led to worldwide market suspension.
raw_record.extra_details: First serious hepatic case reported to the manufacturer; also two other fatal hepatic-necrosis cases (Canada and Italy) prompting worldwide market suspension (October 1996, letter to physicians and pharmacists). Patient was on 200 mg/day tolrestat (Alrestin, John Wyeth Laboratory); death 80 days after start, 30 days after drug suspension; initial symptoms abdominal pain and jaundice; prothrombin time 13%, total bilirubin 447 µmol/L, alanine aminotransferase 2169 U/L; hepatic biopsy showed massive hepatic necrosis. Viral hepatitides (A, B, C) and EBV excluded; no alcoholism, prior hepatic illness, or prior liver-enzyme increase. Reported via the National Pharmacovigilance System of Argentina and confirmed via the WHO Collaborating Centre for International Drug Monitoring in Uppsala; tolrestat marketed in Argentina, Chile, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Mexico, Philippines and Uruguay.

raw_record.support_text: Sebode et al. published a case series on metamizole-induced DILI, analyzing 154 cases of DILI based on RUCAM scoring (median score 7, probable) at a hospital in Hamburg, Germany from 2008 to 2017. Of these, 23 (14.9%) cases were attributed to metamizole, with a predominantly hepatocellular injury pattern; 17 underwent biopsy, 76.5% had moderate-to-severe inflammatory histologic activity, and 35.3% had severe centrilobular necrosis (>30%). Two cases progressed to acute liver failure and required liver transplantation. The authors concluded metamizole is a frequent and underrated cause of DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: Analgesic commonly prescribed in Germany, Russia, and South America; withdrawn in USA/UK/Scandinavia for agranulocytosis. 23/154 (14.9%) DILI cases attributed; RUCAM median 7 (probable); 17 biopsies: 76.5% moderate-to-severe inflammatory activity, 35.3% severe centrilobular necrosis (>30%); 2 cases progressed to ALF requiring liver transplant; not listed on EMA drug label; Björnsson found ~17 other reported cases and suggests it may be a rare cause with increased use.

raw_record.support_text: A patient experienced four episodes of a systemic inflammatory syndrome with markedly elevated liver enzymes following metamizole intake hours to several days before symptom onset. Extensive work-up found no infectious, rheumatological, or haematological cause; the medical history, laboratory, and histological findings were suggestive of first grade (mild) DILI with a RUCAM score of 11, and the presumed diagnosis was metamizole-induced liver injury. The temporal correlation across four episodes, including one observed dechallenge, made metamizole-induced liver injury very likely.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report (dipyrone), a non-opioid analgesic/spasmolytic/antipyretic. Four recurrent episodes with temporal correlation between metamizole intake and onset of symptoms/elevated liver enzymes, including one observed dechallenge. RUCAM causality score 11; DILI graded as first grade (mild) based on transaminases, bilirubin, INR. Presentation resembled a systemic inflammatory syndrome without rash or eosinophilia (DRESS considered less likely). Diagnosis of exclusion. Metamizole undergoes extensive hepatic CYP metabolism; described as a very rare and poorly recognised cause of severe DILI with inflammatory syndrome, with only a few published case reports; pathomechanism unclear, some reports suggest immunoallergic (idiosyncratic) mechanisms. Also noted for rare serious agranulocytosis.

raw_record.support_text: Metamizole is increasingly recognized as hepatotoxic at normal doses and without concomitant hepatotoxic treatment, based on published case reports and case series of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) following metamizole. Four patients required liver transplantation; reported RUCAM scores ranged 3-11, with at least 13 cases considered probable or highly probable (RUCAM ≥6); a positive rechallenge was recorded in nine patients; and some 18 cases were supported by a positive monocyte-derived hepatocyte-like (MH) cell test. The authors conclude there is growing evidence that metamizole can cause DILI and it has been proposed that metamizole qualifies as a medicine with definite hepatotoxic potential.
raw_record.extra_details: At normal therapeutic doses and in the absence of concomitant hepatotoxic treatment. Reported RUCAM scores varied between 3 and 11; at least 13 cases had RUCAM ≥6 (probable or highly probable). Positive rechallenge in 9 patients. ~18 cases supported by positive MH cell test (sensitivity 92%, specificity 100% for causative agent in DILI patients with positive rechallenge). Positive LTT in a few further cases suggesting immune-mediated reaction. Proposed to qualify as a medicine with definite hepatotoxic potential.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of patients with metamizole-induced DILI, clinical characteristics showed a slight female predominance, a median age at onset of 41 years, a mostly hepatocellular pattern of injury, and a relatively large proportion presenting with necrosis and eosinophilic cell infiltration (85% respectively) on histopathology.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 32 patients with metamizole-induced DILI; metamizole suspected as cause in 13% of all DILI patients; slight female predominance; median age at onset 41 years; jaundice in 66% and acute liver failure in 22%; 22% reported mostly unintentional positive rechallenge; histology showed necrosis and eosinophilic cell infiltration (85% respectively) and immune cell infiltration in all specimens; high ANA and AMA positivity; cholestasis and higher fibrosis frequency associated with more severe/jaundiced cases; latency of ~2-3 months from initiation of metamizole associated with more severe evolution; causality assessed by RUCAM (probable/highly probable >=6 vs possible 3-5); proposed immune-mediated mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: Metamizole sodium was adjudicated as a single causative agent in 3 DILI cases in the Pro-Euro DILI Registry.
raw_record.extra_details: 3 adjudicated single-cause cases (metamizole sodium); ATC N02BB02; most cases came from Germany.

raw_record.support_text: In the authors' cohort of metamizole DILI patients, the characteristic metamizole DILI pattern showed a relatively long latency from the start of drug intake until DILI recognition of 48 days. 43% of patients with the characteristic metamizole DILI had discontinued the drug before DILI onset, with a median time from drug discontinuation to appearance of liver injury of 17 days. Longer post-withdrawal latencies were also noted for other agents such as minocycline or nitrofurantoin, a consideration incorporated into the revised electronic causality assessment method (RECAM).
raw_record.extra_details: Characteristic metamizole DILI signature included Hy's law positivity in the majority of cases, coagulopathy in 72% of patients, acute liver failure (ALF) in 37%, and high peak serum transaminases with rapid reversal after drug discontinuation (biochemically similar in some respects to acetaminophen overdose). Necrosis was highly present on histopathology, though histology differed from typical acetaminophen-induced injury. Recovery rates remained high at 74%. Mean latency from drug start to DILI recognition ~48 days; 43% of patients discontinued the drug before DILI onset (median 17 days from discontinuation to injury appearance). In the signature subgroup, baseline ALT ≥29 × ULN or TBIL ≥5.2 × ULN and a TBIL increase of ≥0.1 × ULN within 3 days after onset were associated with metamizole DILI. 30% of metamizole cases had RUCAM <6, yet baseline/peak liver parameters and dynamics were comparable to RUCAM ≥6 cases, arguing against RUCAM as a reliable discriminator for metamizole DILI; polymedication and severe cases (ALF) were proposed to lower RUCAM scores. Suggested diagnosis threshold: marked transaminase elevation with a secondary bilirubin peak and ~7–8 week latency.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 44 patients (22 with DILI as final diagnosis), the causative agents of the DILI episodes included NSAIDs in 6 cases, with metamizole in 3 cases and diclofenac in 3 cases. DILI was established as the final diagnosis, supported by RUCAM scoring.
raw_record.extra_details: Metamizole was the attributed NSAID cause in 3 of 22 DILI cases in this cohort; median maximum RUCAM of the DILI group was 6 (3-10).

raw_record.support_text: A 66-year-old male was hospitalized with generalized exanthema and elevated liver enzymes after taking metamizole for flu-like symptoms. Liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis with perivenular non-bridging confluent necrosis and granuloma formation consistent with drug-induced hepatitis; a metamizole-induced process was suspected. Lymphocyte transformation test confirmed sensitization to metamizole and three of its four metabolites (4-methylaminoantipyrine, 4-acetylaminoantipyrine, 4-formylaminoantipyrine), other drugs could be excluded with high probability, and the patient improved with steroid treatment, leading the authors to conclude that metamizole induced an allergic reaction of the skin and liver.
raw_record.extra_details: 66-year-old male; single 250 mg oral dose for flu-like symptoms; histology: acute hepatitis with perivenular non-bridging confluent necrosis and granuloma formation consistent with drug-induced hepatitis; lymphocyte transformation test positive for metamizole and metabolites 4-methylaminoantipyrine, 4-acetylaminoantipyrine and 4-formylaminoantipyrine; other drugs excluded with high probability; treated successfully with high-dose steroids, with improvement and decreasing liver enzymes; transient liver disease; generalized exanthema concomitantly. Described in abstract and title as allergic cholestatic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective analysis of 154 DILI cases admitted to a tertiary care centre in Hamburg (2008-2017), metamizole was the second most frequent putative agent causing DILI, accounting for 23 of 154 cases (14.9%, after phenprocoumon). The biochemical pattern on admission was hepatocellular, with median ALT 779 U/L (64-3532 U/L) far exceeding median ALP 131 U/L (42-578 U/L). Liver biopsy in 17/23 cases showed moderate-to-severe inflammatory activity and severe centrilobular necrosis (>30%) in 76.5% and 35.3%, respectively. Metamizole was involved in 2 DILI cases progressing to acute liver failure that received liver transplantation and were alive at assessment; re-exposure supported causality in 4 patients. A search of the EMA database identified about 300 reports of suspected metamizole-induced DILI in Europe.
raw_record.extra_details: Analgesic frequently prescribed in Germany, Russia and South America; off-market in the UK, USA and Scandinavia due to side effects including agranulocytosis. Liver side effects are not mentioned in the German drug label. Second most frequent putative DILI agent after phenprocoumon in the series (23/154, 14.9%). Infiltration of immune cells on liver histology; 2 cases progressed to acute liver failure and received liver transplantation, alive at assessment; causality supported by re-exposure in 4 patients. EMA (European Medicines Agency) database search identified about 300 reports of suspected metamizole-induced DILI in Europe.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a 50-year-old patient who, after accidental re-exposure to metamizole, developed a cholestatic liver disease within a few hours with a rapid and strong rise in bilirubin and elevations of transaminases (GOT 147, GPT 222, γ-GT 380, alkaline phosphatase 497 U/l; total bilirubin 43.9 mg/dl). Using metamizole and its four known metabolites (4-aminoantipyrine, 4-methylaminoantipyrine, 4-acetylaminoantipyrine, 4-formylaminoantipyrine) in the lymphocyte transformation test, circulating lymphocytes specifically sensitized against the metabolite 4-methylaminoantipyrine were demonstrated, indicating that allergic mechanisms can with high probability be considered the cause of the liver damage.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single 50-year-old patient with prior metamizole exposure (about 30 tablets of Dolo-Attritin 450 mg in 1984, plus 1986 Dolo-Neurobion (paracetamol) and Imbun 500 (ibuprofen)); current reaction followed accidental re-exposure within 5 hours, consistent with prior sensitization (allergic idiosyncratic reaction).
raw_record.extra_details: Allergic (immune-mediated) genesis demonstrated by lymphocyte transformation test performed five times over 232 days; first three tests positive with stimulation indices up to 2.3, showing sensitization to the metabolite 4-methylaminoantipyrine (formed first within 1-1.5 hours and representing about 40% of the four plasma metabolites). Case report title: 'Allergic origin of acute hepatitis demonstrated by lymphocyte transformation test.' Peak values: total bilirubin 43.9 mg/dl, GOT 147 U/l, GPT 222 U/l, γ-GT 380 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 497 U/l.

raw_record.support_text: In this case, dacomitinib-induced grade 3 hepatotoxicity along with disease progression revealed by CT led to the permanent withdrawal of dacomitinib and a switch to afatinib. The authors conclude that this is the first case report of DILI caused by dacomitinib monotherapy in a real-world setting, and note that the mechanism of dacomitinib-induced liver injury remains unclear.
raw_record.extra_details: EGFR-TKI (epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor). Reported as dacomitinib-induced cholestatic-type DILI; jaundice prompted readmission after discharge with normal liver function; injury occurred while the patient took only dacomitinib outside the hospital. Grade 3 hepatotoxicity led to permanent withdrawal and switch to afatinib. Drug interactions of concern: dacomitinib is metabolized by CYP2D6 to O-desmethyl dacomitinib; concomitant CYP2D6 inhibitors (e.g. paroxetine) or substrates (e.g. trazodone) should be avoided; it is a substrate/inhibitor of P-gp and BCRP. Authors note lack of pathological examination and EBV/CMV/HEV serological testing limits DILI diagnosis, and mechanism of injury remains unclear.

raw_record.support_text: A 59-year-old man with stage IV NSCLC was prescribed dacomitinib (45 mg daily, oral); 37 days after administration he was admitted with jaundice and elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin. After dacomitinib discontinuation liver enzymes decreased but bilirubin continued to rise, peaking at 18-fold on day 26 after termination and normalizing on day 146. A 'probable' cause of DILI by dacomitinib was determined by the Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method, and the DILI severity was assessed as acute liver failure. The paper reports this as the first case of DILI caused by dacomitinib monotherapy in a real-world setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral dacomitinib 45 mg daily; latency 37 days after start. Jaundice on admission; elevated serum liver enzymes and bilirubin. Total bilirubin peaked at 18-fold on day 26 after dacomitinib termination and normalized on day 146 after discontinuation. Causality assessed as 'probable' by the Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method. Severity assessed as acute liver failure. Reported as the first case of DILI caused by dacomitinib monotherapy in a real-world setting. Patient also received a single dose of cisplatin (40 mg, intrapleural perfusion) but injury attributed to dacomitinib monotherapy.

raw_record.support_text: A letter to the editor reports that hepatic toxicity from spironolactone (Aldactone) is extremely rare, with only one previously reported case (by Shuck et al in 1981), and states that the authors recently observed another patient with hepatic toxicity from spironolactone in France.
raw_record.extra_details: Spironolactone (Aldactone, G. D. Searle & Co) is an aldosterone-antagonist diuretic in worldwide use for more than 30 years. Hepatic toxicity considered extremely rare; only one prior case (Shuck et al, 1981) had been reported. This letter adds a second case observed in France. No biochemical pattern, histology, or severity is described in this excerpt.

raw_record.support_text: A 74-year-old man treated for 7 weeks with spironolactone (50 mg/d) for moderate lower-limb edema developed jaundice; liver biopsy showed cholestatic lesions with biliary thrombi, overloaded centrolobular cells, some hepatocyte damage, and foci of lobular necrosis, with infectious and biliary causes excluded. All liver function abnormalities (both cytolytic and cholestatic) normalized 3 months after stopping spironolactone. The paper states this case strongly suggests drug-induced liver disease and concludes that spironolactone has potential to cause hepatotoxicity, noting the diagnosis should be considered in patients developing hepatic damage while taking the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: 74-year-old man; spironolactone 50 mg/d for 7 weeks for moderate lower-limb edema; presented with cutaneous and mucosal icterus; no other treatment, no history of liver/biliary disease or transfusion, alcohol <30 g/day; normal biliary ultrasound; biopsy showed cholestatic lesions with biliary thrombi, overloaded centrolobular cells, somewhat damaged hepatocytes, and a few foci of lobular necrosis; infectious hepatitis excluded serologically. Both cytolytic and cholestatic abnormalities normalized 3 months after drug discontinuation (dechallenge). Evolution benign, without liver failure or encephalopathy. Contrasted with a prior case reported by Shuck et al of moderate hepatocellular abnormalities that regressed in 6-8 weeks. Proposed possible mechanism of interference with biliary secretion, similar to steroids. Paper states risk is unknown.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of drug-induced hepatitis in a 50-year-old woman using spironolactone for the treatment of androgenetic alopecia. Six weeks after commencement of spironolactone the patient became unwell with extensive itch but no icterus or jaundice, and liver function tests found abnormally elevated bilirubin and enzyme levels; after withdrawal of spironolactone, symptoms resolved and liver function improved. The authors note only one other prior report of spironolactone-induced hepatitis.

Symptoms and liver function improved after withdrawal (positive dechallenge); no rechallenge reported. Authors cite only one other prior report of spironolactone-induced hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of prolonged cholestasis and vanishing bile duct syndrome (VBDS) attributed to tenoxicam, a member of the oxicam family of NSAIDs, ingested at a therapeutic dose. Responsibility was based on no prior biliary disease, symptoms starting shortly after drug administration, an associated cutaneous hypersensitivity reaction (Lyell syndrome), and exclusion of other causes of liver disease. Serial liver biopsies confirmed persistent ductopenia (VBDS) up to 3 years later.
raw_record.extra_details: Prolonged cholestasis with elevated alkaline phosphatase (1140 IU/l) and gamma glutamyl transferase (410 IU/l). Initial biopsy (Dec 1998) showed enlarged inflammatory portal tracts with non-suppurative cholangitis and polymorphous infiltrate; subsequent biopsies showed ductopenia (ILBD in one portal tract over 6, then over 4) with minimal portal fibrosis, confirmed by anti-cytokeratin 7 immunostaining. Patient asymptomatic and anicteric under ursodeoxycholic acid at follow-up; no liver failure reported. Associated cutaneous hypersensitivity (Lyell syndrome). Other causes of liver disease ruled out. Tenoxicam described as classically responsible for minor/asymptomatic hepatic enzyme elevations with rare cholestatic hepatitis mentioned in the literature.

raw_record.support_text: In a clinical trial of LY3031207, all six cases of DILI were judged to be related to LY3031207 dosing based on negative viral hepatitis serologies, negative serology for autoimmune hepatitis, limited alcohol consumption during the trial, and denial of use of medications with known hepatotoxicity (including acetaminophen). A retrospective analysis showed that females and older subjects were more susceptible to DILI than males and younger subjects.
raw_record.extra_details: Six cases of DILI in the trial; five showed a hepatocellular pattern (R ratio 10-38) and one a mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic pattern (R ratio 4); eosinophilia 6-21% (normal 0-6%) in all; 2 patients had generalised urticaria; 4 patients female and all but one aged >50 years. Three patients developed DILI symptoms after 225 mg daily dosing was stopped early (Patients 3-5: urticaria, abdominal pain, nausea, loss of appetite); Patient 6 completed 28 days of 75 mg daily with modest ALT increases and remained asymptomatic. Total dose ranged from 2100 mg over 28 days (Patient 6) to 4950 mg over 22 days (Patient 3). Dose-dependent increase in likelihood of DILI; plasma concentrations in DILI patients were comparable with subjects in the same dose group without DILI and lower than the NOAEL exposure in both dog and rat. Patients were monitored as outpatients until liver tests returned to predose ranges. Females and older subjects were more susceptible (P ≤ 0.05).

raw_record.support_text: Drug candidate 1 (LY3031207), an mPGES-1 inhibitor, was evaluated in a multiple ascending dose clinical trial (25, 75, and 225 mg per day for one month). Several human subjects experienced significantly increased ALT levels (5–45× ULN) and DILI-related symptoms such as hepatocellular injury and hypersensitivity. These clinical observations led to its termination from clinical development due to the emergence of liver safety signals.
raw_record.extra_details: mPGES-1 inhibitor (inhibition of PGE2 formation in human whole blood IC50 = 0.24 µM); phase 1 multiple ascending dose trial at 25, 75, and 225 mg/day for one month; ALT elevations 5–45× ULN; DILI-related symptoms included hepatocellular injury and hypersensitivity; clinical development terminated due to liver safety signals; 2-aminoimidazole-based agent.

raw_record.support_text: In a Phase 1 trial, 27 healthy subjects received LY3031207 once daily at 25, 75, or 225 mg. Administration of the 225 mg dose was discontinued according to protocol-defined stopping criteria, and based on the clinical DILI definition of Aithal et al., DILI was identified in 2 patients taking the 225 mg dose. All nine subjects in the 225-mg group discontinued, two due to DILI and seven due to early trial discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: DILI defined per Aithal et al. On the Day 19 safety visit, two female subjects on 225 mg had AST elevations of 14- and 20-fold ULN and ALT elevations of 17- and 27-fold ULN. After discontinuation, AST/ALT increases were noted in three additional subjects on 225 mg (Patients 3-5), and one subject completing 28 days of 75 mg had a solitary ALT increase (Patient 6). Viral and autoimmune serology negative in all six. Patients 1 and 2 had low-grade fever, nausea, abdominal pain, and loss of appetite ~2 days before enzyme increases, were admitted to hospital, and received N-acetylcysteine. Liver biopsies showed acute portal and lobular inflammation with numerous eosinophils and microgranulomas, Zone 3 cholestasis, and prominent lobular hepatocyte necrosis consistent with DILI. Both biopsy patients were discharged ~1 week later and recovered to predose liver test ranges.

raw_record.support_text: In clinical trials, treatment with the nonspecific MTP inhibitor lomitapide (formerly AEGR-733) induced an increase in hepatic steatosis in patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia. The liver-fat effect was highly variable (some patients had no change in liver content, others a large increase); liver-fat content returned to normal within a few months of drug discontinuation, and the drug was thereafter studied only at higher dosages in these patients. Separately, in 56 hypercholesterolemia patients studied by Samaha et al., hepatic fat was not assessed, but transaminase elevation occurred in 32% (18/56) and resulted in drug discontinuation in 9 patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Studied in patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia; after the initial trial the higher doses were reserved for these patients where LDL-C reduction was judged to outweigh potential steatosis; in some trials lomitapide was given alongside other lipid-modifying medication (including LDL apheresis in a phase III study).
raw_record.extra_details: MTP inhibitor (formerly AEGR-733). Hepatic steatosis by MRI ranged from <10% to 40% (normal <1%) and was consistent with animal findings. MTP inhibition attenuates hepatic VLDL output, resulting in hepatic lipid accumulation and consequently hepatotoxicity. Variable effect (some patients no change in liver fat, others large increase); alcohol use in some cases may have influenced the effect, and liver fat returned to normal within a few months of discontinuation. Initial dose-escalation study: 6 patients, 0.1 mg/kg/day gave ~50% LDL-C reduction; subsequent trial: 10 patients up to 60 mg/day (~44% LDL-C reduction); Samaha et al.: 56 patients on lomitapide monotherapy (5.0/7.5/10 mg daily) with LDL-C reductions of 19%/26%/30%; transaminase elevation occurred in 32% (18/56) with discontinuation in 9. Authors raised the concern that lifelong accumulation of hepatic fat could progress to hepatic fibrosis.

Diagnosis was based on temporal relationship between drug use and altered liver enzymes, subsequent improvement of liver enzymes upon discontinuation, and liver biopsy findings suggestive of drug-induced liver injury. DILI is noted as a rare, potential consequence of DPP-4 inhibitors.

Attribution based on temporal relationship of drug with altered liver enzymes, resolution of enzymes after drug discontinuation, and liver biopsy findings suggestive of drug-induced liver injury. Hepatocellular and cholestatic injury patterns were observed across the two cases.

Other etiologies (acute viral hepatitis, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, alcohol, and other hepatotoxic drugs) were ruled out, and symptoms disappeared with liver enzymes returning to baseline after sitagliptin was discontinued.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that during the first year tolcapone was marketed, a fulminant and fatal hepatopathy was documented in 3 patients, with an estimated 60,000 patients having received tolcapone by the time of the third fatal hepatopathy. Because of this hepatotoxicity, tolcapone was relegated to a secondary-choice adjunctive therapy, with pharmaceutical-company directives requiring monitoring of serum aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase values at baseline and at regular intervals during treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant and fatal hepatopathy documented in 3 patients during tolcapone's first year on the market; estimated 60,000 exposed by the time of the third fatal case (suggesting a rare problem). Tolcapone relegated to secondary-choice adjunctive therapy. Pharma directives mandate monitoring of serum aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase at baseline, every 2 weeks for the first year, every 4 weeks for the next 6 months, and every 2 months thereafter. Context: adjunctive treatment of levodopa-related fluctuations in Parkinson's disease.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that potential hepatotoxicity is the most serious safety issue associated with COMT inhibitors and that liver toxicity has been observed with tolcapone. In clinical trials elevations of liver enzyme levels were reported for 1-3% of tolcapone-treated patients, and soon after tolcapone's market introduction four cases of fulminant liver failure were reported, three of which resulted in death, in patients who had received tolcapone for 2-4 months. These reports led to a temporary withdrawal of tolcapone from the market in Europe and Canada and a black box warning in the USA; tolcapone was later reintroduced in the EU and now requires prior failure of other COMT inhibitors and regular liver enzyme monitoring.
raw_record.extra_details: COMT inhibitor used to treat Parkinson disease. Liver enzyme elevations in 1-3% of treated patients in clinical trials; four cases of fulminant liver failure reported soon after market introduction, three fatal, after 2-4 months of treatment. Led to temporary European/Canadian market withdrawal and US black box warning; reintroduced in EU with requirement to try other COMT inhibitors first and regular liver enzyme monitoring. Mechanism open, possibly uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation or toxic metabolite accumulation in genetically prone patients; less likely COMT inhibition per se since not seen with entacapone.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses tolcapone's hepatotoxicity in Parkinson's disease patients, noting it can produce predictable liver injury based on dose-dependent serum aminotransferase elevations (higher in the 200-mg than 100-mg group within the first 6 months of clinical trials) and 4 initial reports of severe hepatocellular injury occurring after 2-4 months of treatment. The paper concludes that clinical experience since the 1998 labeling change suggests patients susceptible to severe liver injury are rare and the risk of irreversible liver injury can be minimized by monitoring.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose-dependent ALT elevation within the first 6 months of treatment; 4 initial reports of severe hepatocellular injury after 2-4 months. Mechanism not precisely known: histopathology in affected patients was characteristic of idiosyncratic toxicity, yet the dose-related, first-6-month ALT pattern supports predictable (intrinsic) toxicity; predictable toxicity may initiate idiosyncratic injury in susceptible individuals who fail to adapt. Indication: Parkinson's disease as adjunct to levodopa/carbidopa. Post-marketing experience suggests the risk of severe/irreversible liver injury is low when the drug is appropriately administered and monitored. FDA relaxed liver monitoring in February 2006; discontinuation recommended if SGPT/ALT or SGOT/AST exceed 2x ULN or signs/symptoms of hepatic dysfunction.

raw_record.support_text: The COMT inhibitor tolcapone is an effective adjunctive agent for motor fluctuations in levodopa-treated patients. In clinical trials, elevated liver enzymes were notable in tolcapone-treated patients and regulatory agencies required frequent liver enzyme testing as a condition for drug approval. After approximately one year on the market, three cases of fatal hepatotoxicity and one case of reversible severe liver injury were attributed to tolcapone. Later reports described three additional cases of severe hepatocellular liver injury (including one with hepatocellular jaundice, one after 3 years of treatment, and one developing 17 months after starting), as well as less severe cases with SGPT/ALT or SGOT/AST elevations three times the upper limit of normal; the majority of these elevations were transient, asymptomatic, and resolved spontaneously (median time to elevation 81 days, median duration 22 days).
raw_record.extra_details: Adjunctive agent for motor fluctuations in levodopa-treated patients with Parkinson disease. Clinical trials showed elevated liver enzymes, and regulatory agencies required frequent liver enzyme monitoring as a condition of approval. After ~1 year on market, three fatal hepatotoxicity cases and one reversible severe liver injury were attributed to tolcapone. In these four cases recommended liver-monitoring guidelines were not followed, and in two cases the drug was continued despite clear clinical evidence of hepatic dysfunction. Consequence: 7-year marketing suspension in Europe and Canada and a US black box warning; tolcapone currently carries a black box warning in all countries on the risk of hepatotoxicity. Over a decade later, no further tolcapone-induced hepatic fatalities, but three additional reports of severe hepatocellular injury: one case of hepatocellular jaundice (duration unknown), one severe hepatocellular injury after 3 years, one developing hepatotoxicity 17 months after starting. Olanow and Watkins reported less severe cases with SGPT/ALT or SGOT/AST three times ULN; majority transient, asymptomatic, spontaneously resolved; median time to elevated levels 81 days, median duration 22 days.

raw_record.support_text: Four case reports from 1998 describe liver failure in Parkinson's disease patients treated with tolcapone with no antecedents of liver dysfunction, which led to tolcapone's marketing suspension. A 74-year-old woman on tolcapone 100 mg/day bid with levodopa/benserazide developed severe liver failure in 9 weeks and died in hepatic coma; a 73-year-old woman on tolcapone 200 mg t.i.d. with comorbidities (including sepsis, aortic regurgitation) developed liver failure 12 weeks after starting and died after tolcapone was not discontinued; a 74-year-old woman on levodopa/carbidopa and tolcapone 100 mg t.i.d. developed liver failure 11 weeks after starting and died; and a 66-year-old woman on tolcapone 200 mg t.i.d. recovered after discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Concomitant antiparkinsonian treatment included levodopa/benserazide or levodopa/carbidopa in most cases; one fatal case had sepsis, aortic regurgitation, weight loss and depression as competing factors and tolcapone was not discontinued; another had cirrhosis context with coffee-ground emesis and ARDS; a 66-year-old woman recovered in a week with vitamin K, fresh frozen plasma and prednisone, with no cirrhosis on biopsy. These cases led to the marketing suspension of tolcapone.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that COMT inhibitors harbor the potential for liver toxicity, and that in the case of tolcapone—but not entacapone—this constitutes a safety risk. Following tolcapone's market authorization in 1997, three patients died from acute liver failure, which led to withdrawal of the drug from the European market; after further safety evaluations it was re-approved in 2004, and it is now considered a second-choice COMT inhibitor for advanced Parkinson's disease with fluctuations, with regular liver enzyme monitoring mandated.
raw_record.extra_details: Market authorized 1997; three patients died from acute liver failure leading to European market withdrawal; re-approved 2004 after safety evaluation; considered second-choice COMT inhibitor for advanced Parkinson's disease with motor fluctuations; regular liver enzyme monitoring mandated. Causal claim is presented as a known safety risk documented by the fatal cases and attendant regulatory action.

raw_record.support_text: Tolcapone undergoes methylation and oxidization to form amine and acetylamine metabolites that are further metabolized to reactive intermediates forming covalent adducts to hepatic proteins, resulting in damage to liver tissue. In clinical trials, 3.1% of tolcapone patients had ALT elevation >3-fold (RD 0.03, 95% CI 0.02-0.05), and 1.7% discontinued treatment due to liver toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Clinical trial: 587/592 patients; ALT >3xULN 3.1/0 (RD 0.03, 95% CI 0.02-0.05); >5x 1.2/0; >8x 0.3/0; withdrawal due to liver toxicity 1.7/0 (RD 0.02, 95% CI 0.01-0.03); liver failure 0/0. Mechanism: methylation/oxidation to amine/acetylamine metabolites further metabolized to reactive intermediates forming covalent adducts to hepatic proteins; oxidative phosphorylation uncoupling.

raw_record.support_text: Tolcapone (Tasmar) was associated with severe hepatotoxicity leading to the EMEA recommendation to suspend its marketing authorization. Three cases of acute, unpredictable hepatitis with fatal outcome had been reported, including a fulminant hepatitis in a 74-year-old woman 9 weeks after starting tolcapone as add-on therapy for Parkinson's disease (liver biopsy showed severe centrolobular necrosis and a lobular inflammatory infiltrate mostly of plasma cells and eosinophils) and a US patient who died from hepatic necrosis. A third case of fulminant hepatitis related to tolcapone occurred in a patient already under close liver-enzyme monitoring. The underlying mechanism was considered possibly a severe idiosyncratic reaction, similar to that seen with isoniazid or diclofenac.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Add-on therapy for Parkinson's disease; mechanism described as unpredictable, with possible genetic/environmental susceptibility, but no required co-exposure or restricted population is specified.
raw_record.extra_details: Three fatal human cases of acute unpredictable hepatitis reported after tolcapone marketing (approximately 100,000 patients worldwide treated). Index case: 74-year-old woman, fulminant hepatitis 9 weeks after starting tolcapone, biopsy showing severe centrolobular necrosis with lobular inflammatory infiltrate of plasma cells and eosinophils; a US patient died from hepatic necrosis. EMEA mandated liver-function monitoring (ALT threshold of 3x upper normal for discontinuation) before mandating suspension of EU marketing authorization on 12 November 1998; FDA did not suspend but revised the label to adjunctive use only with monitoring (baseline then every 2 weeks for year 1), discontinuing if ALT/AST exceeds upper limit. In Phase II/III double-blind placebo-controlled trials, asymptomatic aminotransferase elevations (ALT more often than AST) occurred in 1.76% (16 of 906) patients, were reversible, and were considered not of significance. Possible immune-mediated/mixed mechanism and role of hepatic COMT inhibition/catabolism (glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, CYP oxidation) considered unknown.

raw_record.support_text: Tolcapone toxicity problems became apparent soon after its market introduction: three patients taking tolcapone died of hepatic failure, which was attributed to the use of the drug, leading to suspension of tolcapone in the EU and a black box warning in the US. Three deaths from fulminant hepatic failure in 40,000 patient-years is 10-100 times higher than the expected incidence in the general population, and the manufacturer's own information indicates the number is probably underestimated due to under-reporting.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: General adult Parkinson's disease population on therapeutic dosing; no co-exposure restrictions reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Three deaths from fulminant hepatic failure in 40,000 patient-years, 10-100x higher than expected population incidence and probably under-reported. Phase III trials showed serum ALT increases ≥3x ULN in 1% of patients at 100mg three times daily and 3% at 200mg three times daily versus placebo, with some patients reaching serum ALT levels eight times above ULN; ALT was taken as an index of hepatocyte turnover/death, prompting routine ALT monitoring. One fatal case showed mitochondrial swelling, loss of cristae and reduced matrix density. Preclinical toxicology (rat, plasma AUC 14x human) confirmed rat liver toxicity and mitochondrial uncoupling, but these are supportive animal findings; entacapone showed no rat hepatotoxicity (AUC up to 21x human) and lacked the uncoupling activity.

raw_record.support_text: The paper recounts the benoxaprofen saga: in 1982 an extensive review of benoxaprofen side effects in 300 patients reported mainly dermatologic lesions, but within a few months several serious and some fatal benoxaprofen-induced hepatotoxicities were reported. By August 1982, sixty-one fatalities had been reported in Great Britain and benoxaprofen was subsequently withdrawn from the market; unofficially the death toll numbered about ninety-six in the UK and about forty-six in the US.
raw_record.extra_details: Several serious and some fatal hepatotoxicities reported shortly after an initial review described mainly dermatologic side effects in 300 patients; by August 1982, 61 fatalities in Great Britain led to market withdrawal; unofficial death toll ~96 in the UK and ~46 in the US.

raw_record.support_text: The drug Opren (benoxaprofen), thought to be a uniquely beneficial anti-inflammatory drug, was found to have serious hepatotoxicity. This was reported initially in a case report from Glasgow and followed by a case series from Belfast. The paper notes that the main adverse reaction in the South of England was phototoxicity while in the duller northern part of Britain, liver disease was found.

raw_record.support_text: In the study cohort of 18 patients with drug-induced liver injury related acute liver failure (DILI-ALF), one patient's DILI was attributed to Flutamide (n=1). The RUCAM causality category for the cohort as a whole was highly probable in 6 patients and probable in the remainder.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed cause in 1 of 18 DILI-ALF patients who underwent living donor liver transplantation. Cohort-level RUCAM was highly probable in 6 patients and probable in the rest (causality grading per-patient for this agent not specified).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that flutamide causes hepatotoxicity with a frequency ranging from 0.36% to 8.82% depending on authors, and that severity ranges from asymptomatic transaminase elevations to severe acute hepatitis that can lead to death. It notes the toxicity mechanism is unknown, with most characteristics pointing to an idiosyncratic mechanism caused directly by the drug or through CYP450-mediated metabolite formation. This is in the setting of flutamide use to treat prostate cancer.
raw_record.extra_details: Case: 74-year-old man on flutamide plus an LHRH analog for prostate adenocarcinoma with bone metastases; presented with 20-day icteric syndrome ~6 months after starting treatment; laboratory findings included total bilirubin 11.1 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 8.5 mg/dl, GOT 809, GPT 806, GGT 689, LDH 1356 mU/ml, Quick index 47%; hepatotropic virus serology negative; ultrasound showed enlarged liver and spleen without focal lesions. Toxic hepatitis with cholestasis. Dechallenge: favorable course after flutamide withdrawal, with improvement at 4 months (total bilirubin 1.8, direct bilirubin 0.9 mg/dl, GOT 186, GPT 138, GGT 186 mU/ml). Reported hepatotoxicity frequency 0.36-8.82%; spectrum spans subclinical hypertransaminasemia with or without cholestasis to fulminant/severe acute hepatitis leading to death. Mechanism unknown; most features suggest idiosyncratic toxicity via the parent drug or CYP450-mediated metabolites. Suspected hepatic metastases were ruled out; competing causes excluded.

raw_record.support_text: In their patient cohort the authors observed an increase in liver enzymes in two patients, including one case of acute hepatic failure, attributing both to flutamide and suggesting the incidence of flutamide-induced hepatotoxicity may be higher than previously reported, while noting the patient numbers were too limited for a meaningful incidence estimate. Both affected patients showed a cholestatic type hepatitis, and the paper notes hepatotoxicity associated with flutamide may be fatal but also appears completely reversible.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 2 patients on flutamide therapy: one had liver enzyme elevation only and one acute hepatic failure; both showed a cholestatic-type hepatitis. Authors suggest incidence of flutamide-induced hepatotoxicity may be higher than in the literature. Literature cited reports cholestatic hepatitis with or without eosinophilia and cholestatic jaundice, hepatocellular injury with marked transaminase elevation while bilirubin remained normal, and hepatocellular necrosis speculated to be idiosyncratic/immunologic; necrosis could not be determined in these patients. Hepatotoxicity may be fatal but appears completely reversible; close LFT (LF T_s) monitoring at weeks 0,2,4,6,8 recommended and discontinuation advised on symptomatic or asymptomatic enzyme elevation. Alfuzosin/flutamide prostate-cancer therapy context implied clinically but not explicitly stated in the provided text.

raw_record.support_text: A patient developed cholestatic hepatitis after surgery, with the paper concluding that flutamide was the most likely cause of the hepatic injury. Total parenteral nutrition had not been given and no halothane had been administered, and the 5-week interval between surgery and symptom onset made a surgical causal relation unlikely. Viral and extrahepatic causes of jaundice were excluded, there was no hemolysis, and non-A, non-B hepatitis was considered less likely because the biochemical pattern suggested a predominantly cholestatic pattern. The authors state 'We think that flutamide was the cause of cholestatic hepatitis in our patient', noting repeated eosinophilia (10% to 16%) compatible with an immunoallergic reaction and speculating on an androgen-related effect via increased testosterone.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis with jaundice; onset about 5 weeks after surgery; no total parenteral nutrition and no halothane administered; viral and extrahepatic causes of jaundice excluded (no hemolysis, normal cardiac function, no metastases); non-A, non-B hepatitis considered a less likely cause because no transfusions were given and the pattern was predominantly cholestatic. Repeated eosinophilia (10%-16%) suggested an immunoallergic reaction; the authors also speculated that cholestasis could be an androgen-related effect because flutamide may increase blood testosterone levels.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that flutamide, a first-generation antiandrogen used in the management of prostate cancer, can cause acute liver failure (ALF) as a rare but potentially fatal side effect that must be taken into account whenever the drug is used. Its dangerous toxicity profile, scarce oncological benefit, and better alternatives lead the authors to consider flutamide a drug of the past with minimal indications. This is drawn from a submitted patient case report (informed consent obtained, patient follow-up described).
raw_record.extra_details: Flutamide is described as a first-generation antiandrogen. ALF is characterized as a rare but potentially fatal side effect; indication was prostate cancer management. Paper is a patient case report (informed consent signed, pathology analyses and radical prostatectomy, patient follow-up reported).

raw_record.support_text: The only serious side effect encountered during flutamide treatment was a case of reversible liver toxicity. Occasional hepatic abnormalities, although rare events, have been reported using twice the dose given in the study. Patients all had prostate cancer and received breast irradiation prior to the study.
raw_record.extra_details: Indication: prostate cancer. Reported as a reversible serious side effect in one patient in a flutamide treatment study; occasional hepatic abnormalities have been reported by others at twice the dose used in this study.

raw_record.support_text: The letter reports that a 20-year-old woman given flutamide for hirsutism, who had no other known causes of liver disorder and recovered after withdrawal of the drug, developed serious hepatotoxicity, and the authors call this confirmatory evidence that flutamide can cause serious hepatotoxicity. They also cite their earlier case series of two 58-year-old men treated with flutamide for benign prostatic hypertrophy who developed serious hepatotoxicity, noting the estimated incidence of this disorder is less than 1%.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases: a 20-year-old woman treated with flutamide for hirsutism (an unapproved indication) who recovered after drug withdrawal, and two 58-year-old men treated for benign prostatic hypertrophy; incidence of this 'serious hepatotoxicity' estimated at less than 1%. Letter advises patients to immediately report nausea, vomiting, fatigue, discolored urine, jaundice, and other signs of liver injury so the drug can be withdrawn promptly.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report that in 2007 they reported 28 cases of DILI, with flutamide accounting for 10.7% of the cases (i.e., about 3 of 28 cases) among named causative agents in their human DILI case series.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed in 10.7% (about 3) of 28 human DILI cases reported by the authors in their 2007 series.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 65 patients with prostate cancer receiving a total androgen suppression (TAS) regimen, flutamide was discontinued because of liver function test (LFT) elevations in 14 patients (22%), and hepatotoxicity contributed to discontinuation in others. ALT elevation was the most sensitive finding (37/60 evaluable patients had ALT ≥41 U/L), and grade 3-4 toxicity with ALT >5 times normal occurred in 4/60 patients. AST and ALT were significantly elevated relative to baseline during flutamide therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: 65 prostate cancer patients on a TAS regimen; flutamide discontinued for LFT elevation in 14 (22%); median time to discontinuation 8 weeks (range 1-16). ALT elevation most sensitive: 37/60 (62%) ≥41 U/L; grade 3-4 toxicity (ALT >5x normal) in 4 (7%) of 60. AST: 24/61 (39%) ≥41 U/L. Median AST/ALT rose from 21/25 to 35/50 U/L; no rise in alkaline phosphatase. Baseline only 4/65 had AST/ALT ≥41. P<.02 for AST, P<.005 for ALT. In 12/14 discontinued patients transaminase elevation noted; one isolated alkaline phosphatase elevation; one patient had pruritus with bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL and GGT 112 U/L with normal transaminases.

raw_record.support_text: A 20-year-old woman given flutamide for hirsutism, with no other known causes of liver disorder, developed serious hepatotoxicity and recovered after drug withdrawal; the authors describe this as confirmatory evidence that flutamide can cause serious hepatotoxicity. They also cite their prior case series in which two 58-year-old men treated with flutamide for benign prostatic hypertrophy developed serious hepatotoxicity, and note the incidence of this disorder has been estimated at less than 1%.
raw_record.extra_details: New case: 20-year-old woman treated for hirsutism (an unapproved/off-label indication) who recovered after drug withdrawal; supporting prior case series of two 58-year-old men treated for benign prostatic hypertrophy with serious hepatotoxicity. Incidence of serious hepatotoxicity estimated at less than 1%. Letter recommends caution in off-label prescribing and instructing patients to report nausea, vomiting, fatigue, discolored urine, and jaundice. Views are those of the authors and not necessarily those of the Food and Drug Administration.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case series of 3 patients who developed moderate flutamide-induced hepatic dysfunction during flutamide therapy for prostate cancer, with plasma levels of flutamide, hydroxyflutamide (OH-Flu), FLU-1 (4-nitro-3-(trifluoromethyl)phenylamine) and FLU-2 measured at 0.5 h and 3 h. The authors state that hepatic dysfunction appeared in almost all studied patients after the examination period, and that two additional patients developed clinically significant hepatic dysfunction with considerably higher plasma FLU-1 concentrations irrespective of flutamide or OH-Flu levels.
raw_record.extra_details: Patients were on flutamide therapy for prostate cancer. Three patients developed moderate flutamide-induced hepatic dysfunction; plasma concentrations of flutamide, OH-Flu (hydroxyflutamide), FLU-1 (4-nitro-3-(trifluoromethyl)phenylamine) and FLU-2 were measured at 0.5 h and 3 h after intake. Plasma FLU-1 levels were considerably higher in 2 patients with clinically significant hepatic dysfunction, irrespective of flutamide or OH-Flu concentrations. Hepatic dysfunction appeared in almost all patients after the examination period, so plasma data were not influenced by the hepatic injury itself. Metabolism of flutamide to OH-Flu mainly by cytochrome P450 1A2, and to FLU-1 by carboxyesterase, were discussed as pathways.

raw_record.support_text: Gomez et al. analyzed flutamide-related liver toxicity in 1,091 consecutive stage C or D prostate cancer patients treated with flutamide combined with LHRH agonist LHRH ethylamide. An increase in ASAT and ALAT at least 4 times the upper limits was seen in 4 patients (0.36%), of whom only 2 (0.18%) developed clinical symptoms of liver disturbance. All clinical and biologic signs of liver toxicity disappeared after discontinuation of flutamide, with no sequelae at 18, 22, 31 and 62 months follow-up.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 1,091 prostate cancer patients; 4 (0.36%) had ASAT/ALAT elevation ≥4x ULN, 2 (0.18%) had clinical liver symptoms; biochemical and clinical signs resolved on flutamide withdrawal, no long-term sequelae; remaining 1,087 had no or mild (below 4x ULN) transient aminotransferase elevation within first 6 months of treatment, normalizing later. Reported incidence estimates of hepatic disorders in such studies range from <1% to about 5%.

raw_record.support_text: Flutamide, a nonsteroidal antiandrogen, was associated with 19 severe hepatotoxicity cases reported in the US by the FDA (published 1993). Hepatitis developed 56-80 days after starting therapy and was mainly cytolytic. Fatal outcome from massive hepatic necrosis at autopsy occurred in four cases. The mechanism was considered to be direct hepatotoxicity; the only hypersensitivity sign was eosinophilia (plus antinuclear antibodies in one case).
raw_record.extra_details: 19 severe hepatotoxicity cases reported to the FDA, summary published 1993; onset 56-80 days after start; mainly cytolytic hepatitis; 4 fatal cases with massive hepatic necrosis at autopsy; antinuclear antibodies in one case; eosinophilia as the only sign of hypersensitivity.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series, the compatible sequence of events, absence of other causes of liver disease or other drug-induced causes, and positive rechallenge in two patients provided convincing circumstantial and biologic evidence that flutamide was responsible for the liver changes observed.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of flutamide-induced liver toxicity reported as very low (0.36%); the clinical picture is a mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic pattern of an idiosyncratic nature; injury is reversible and discontinuation of flutamide is recommended. Positive rechallenge test in two patients; recommendation that aminotransferase serum levels be measured before starting flutamide and repeated at 2 and 4 weeks of treatment to promptly detect and manage the reversible drug-induced liver toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A 79-year-old man on flutamide therapy (unknown dose) presented with jaundice, choluria, and 2 weeks of asthenia/anorexia. At admission, liver tests showed total bilirubin 20.9 mg/dL, AST 739 IU/mL, ALT 262 IU/mL, AP 103 IU/mL, GGT 200 IU/mL, and a prothrombin index of 35%. Acute hepatitis with severe hepatocellular insufficiency was suspected to result from flutamide, which was withdrawn; viral, autoimmune, thyroid, iron, and tumor etiologies were excluded. Bilirubin peaked at 23.2 mg/dL and liver tests recovered to near normal before discharge after 20 days. In the discussion, the CIOMS causality scale yielded 9 points for this episode (highly probable drug-induced liver injury), with 90 days from treatment start to symptom onset.
raw_record.extra_details: Prostate cancer indication. Latency 90 days; recovery 20 days. CIOMS scale 9 points. Prothrombin index 35% (low). Acute hepatitis with severe hepatocellular insufficiency; other causes of liver injury excluded. Abdominal ultrasound showed increased liver echogenicity with normal gallbladder and biliary tract. No dose stated in the window.

raw_record.support_text: In this case report, a 79-year-old man with prostatic adenocarcinoma developed jaundice 5 weeks after starting oral flutamide (750 mg/d) post-transurethral prostatectomy. Laboratory findings showed elevated bilirubin (74 µmol/L), AST (120 U/L), ALT (158 U/L), alkaline phosphatase (1070 U/L), and GGT (405 U/L); hepatotropic viral causes were excluded, and liver enzymes and bilirubin declined rapidly after flutamide was discontinued, with all values returning to normal within 3 weeks. The authors concluded that 'Flutamide was the most likely cause of hepatic injury in this patient' and that flutamide caused cholestatic hepatitis, noting a predominantly cholestatic biochemical pattern, peripheral eosinophilia possibly compatible with an immunoallergic reaction, and uncertainty about the exact mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: Flutamide (4'-nitro-3'-trifluoromethyl-isobutyranilide), a nonsteroidal antiandrogen without estrogenic, antiestrogenic, progestational, antiprogestational, androgenic, adrenocortical, or antigonadotropic activity, used for prostate adenocarcinoma. Dose 750 mg/d oral; jaundice appeared after 5 weeks. Laboratory values: bilirubin 74 µmol/L (normal <20); AST 120 U/L; ALT 158 U/L; alkaline phosphatase 1070 U/L (normal <110); GGT 405 U/L. Peripheral eosinophilia (16% of leukocytes, with 10%–16% reported) disappeared on dechallenge; full clinical and laboratory recovery within 3 weeks with unremarkable follow-up at 4 months, 1 year, and 18 months. Viral (hepatitis A/B, cytomegalovirus, infectious mononucleosis), extrahepatic, hemolytic, and metastatic causes excluded; non-A non-B hepatitis considered less likely. Authors unsure of mechanism, speculating androgen-related cholestasis or immunoallergic reaction.

raw_record.support_text: Flutamide was attributed to 22 DILI cases, predominantly hepatocellular (64%). Of these, 12 (57%) met nR-based Hy's law criteria and 4 patients (33%) died or required liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: 22 of 843 registry DILI cases; Hep 64%/Chol 9.1%/Mix 27%; female 14%, lymphopenia 5.6%, eosinophilia 4.8%; 12 (57%) fulfilled nR-based Hy's law, 4 (33%) died or required liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: Flutamide is reported to cause drug-induced hepatopathy in treated patients. In the authors' series, simultaneous administration of UDCA (ursodeoxycholic acid) significantly decreased the incidence of flutamide-induced hepatopathy from 32.4% to 11.4%.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective study comparing patients with and without UDCA (70 vs 111 patients). UDCA prophylaxis reduced flutamide-induced hepatopathy incidence from 32.4% to 11.4%. Risk factors identified by Wada et al. via multivariate logistic regression included a history of liver disorders and elevated alanine aminotransferase levels. Hepatotoxic parameters monitored were GOT and GPT. UDCA is a cholic acid derivative used to treat drug-induced hepatopathy.

raw_record.support_text: The paper's patient developed jaundice after 6 months of treatment with flutamide, a non-steroidal anti-androgen used in advanced prostate cancer. The liver toxicity was attributed to flutamide after excluding viral hepatitis, liver autoantibodies, liver metastasis/bile duct obstruction, and vasculitis relapse, and the temporal relationship between flutamide administration and symptom onset plus gradual normalization of liver enzymes after flutamide discontinuation were consistent with drug-induced liver injury. The paper further notes increasing evidence that flutamide may cause serious hepatotoxic reactions in susceptible individuals, with severe liver failure and death reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Flutamide is metabolized mainly in the liver; its incidence of liver toxicity was claimed to be very low (0.18%). Clinical manifestations of flutamide-induced liver injury appear 5 days to 10 months after treatment (average 3 months). In the Andalucian Registry of drug-induced liver disease (Garcia Cortes et al.), 9 of 185 patients (4.9%) had liver injury due to flutamide; mean therapy duration 151 days (4-443 days), all with overt liver injury (asthenia, anorexia, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, jaundice), no hypersensitivity features, and two patients evolved to fulminant liver failure (one liver transplantation, one death). In a Turkish series of 22 prostate cancer patients treated with flutamide plus goserelin or orchiectomy, severe hepatotoxicity occurred in 2 (9%) and one died of acute liver failure. Pathology from flutamide-induced hepatotoxicity showed hepatocellular necrosis and cholestasis. The patient in this paper developed jaundice after 6 months and renal insufficiency due to vasculitis, which the authors speculate could contribute via raised metabolite levels. Mechanism: direct hepatotoxicity cannot be excluded, but features resemble an idiosyncratic reaction possibly caused by flutamide or a metabolite; rat studies showed cytochrome P450-mediated formation of toxic metabolites and inhibition of mitochondrial respiration and ATP formation.

raw_record.support_text: Among the 36 enrolled patients with biopsy-proven cirrhosis of mixed aetiologies, two had cryptogenic cirrhosis, two had autoimmune hepatitis and drug-induced cirrhosis as a result of flutamide use, respectively. This attributes the drug-induced cirrhosis in one patient directly to flutamide use.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient among a 36-patient cirrhotic cohort whose cirrhosis was attributed to flutamide use; clinical details of the flutamide-induced injury (e.g., dose, latency) are not provided in this study.

raw_record.support_text: For flutamide, the major adverse effects include gastrointestinal disorders, hematological disorders, muscle cramps, and gynecomastia, with acute liver failure highlighted as the most relevant adverse effect due to high mortality and frequent need for liver transplantation. A 14-year retrospective observational study observed 10 cases of acute and fulminant hepatitis induced by flutamide; two of these patients were treated for acne vulgaris and developed fulminant flutamide-induced hepatitis that responded well after discontinuation. A separate retrospective study of 230 patients on flutamide for acne and seborrhea initiated at 250 mg daily (annually halved to a minimum of 62.5 mg daily) found that only 5% discontinued due to increased liver enzymes at 250 mg daily, with no enzyme elevation at 125 mg and 62.5 mg.
raw_record.extra_details: In a 14-year retrospective observational study, 10 cases of flutamide-induced acute and fulminant hepatitis were observed; 2 of the 10 cases were patients treated with flutamide for acne vulgaris, both developing fulminant hepatitis with good response after discontinuation. In another retrospective study of flutamide tolerability in 230 patients with acne and seborrhea (started at 250 mg daily, annually reduced by half to a minimum of 62.5 mg daily), only 5% discontinued at 250 mg daily due to increased liver enzymes, and no enzyme elevation was seen at 125 mg and 62.5 mg daily. Acute liver failure from flutamide is associated with high mortality and necessity of liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: A 20-year-old East Indian woman treated with flutamide, 250 mg orally twice daily, for hirsutism developed severe jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, and pale stools about 6 weeks after starting the drug. Laboratory results included bilirubin 263 µmol/L (peaking at 480 µmol/L), INR 1.9, alkaline phosphatase 180 IU/L, and alanine aminotransferase 1481 IU/L. Other causes of liver disease were excluded, flutamide was discontinued, and her condition improved with return of liver enzyme levels to normal within 6 weeks. Liver biopsy near the height of illness showed changes typical of drug toxicity, including zonal hepatic necrosis with cholestasis and ballooning degeneration of surviving zone 1 hepatocytes. The authors report this as the first association of flutamide with serious hepatotoxicity in a woman using the drug for hirsutism, saying the features of the case are quite conclusive.

raw_record.support_text: A 91-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia treated with flutamide (250 mg every 8 hours) and triptorelin (3.75 mg every 3 months) developed severe icteric hepatitis 6 months after starting treatment, with disorientation, asterixis, and elevated liver tests (GOT 496 U/L, GPT 342 U/L, GGT 223 U/L, total bilirubin 160 µmol/L with direct fraction 125 µmol/L, ammonia 420 µmol/L) and CA 19-9 359 KU/L, while hepatitis/pregnancy/cancer serologies, immunologic studies, and imaging were negative/normal. On suspicion of toxic hepatitis, flutamide was withdrawn; jaundice and encephalopathic signs resolved within 15 days and all parameters normalized by 6 weeks. The case is framed as severe toxic hepatitis caused by flutamide.
