raw_record.extra_details: Dose 250 mg every 8 h; hepatitis onset about 6 months after starting treatment. Initial labs GOT 496 U/L, GPT 342 U/L, GGT 223 U/L, total bilirubin 160 µmol/L (direct 125), ammonia 420 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 194 U/L; CA 19-9 elevated to 359 KU/L and fell to 103 KU/L by 3 weeks and 55 KU/L by 6 weeks after discontinuation (dechallenge). Jaundice and encephalopathic signs resolved 15 days after stopping, all parameters normalized by 6 weeks. Flutamide is a nonsteroidal antiandrogen; proposed mechanism mitochondrial respiration inhibition; mild (<2x normal) transaminase elevation reported in ~30% (Rosenthal), and in the Gomez series 4 of 1091 prostate adenocarcinoma patients on flutamide 250 mg/8 h showed markers of severe hepatic toxicity, only 2 with clinical manifestations. The authors note severe flutamide hepatotoxicity causing acute liver failure may present with elevated CA 19-9.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 1,091 prostate cancer patients all treated with the antiandrogen combination of flutamide and an LHRH agonist with serial liver-function monitoring, only 4 patients (0.36%) developed liver toxicity: 2 with clinical signs of liver toxicity and 2 with hepatic enzyme levels at least fourfold above upper normal limits without symptoms. raw_record.extra_details: Incidence 0.36% (4/1,091) of flutamide-related liver toxicity; 2 patients with clinical signs and 2 with asymptomatic enzyme elevations (transaminases up to 60-fold above pretreatment, one ~2-fold alkaline phosphatase rise, normal bilirubin in those three). One patient had a mainly cholestatic pattern with overt jaundice, fatigue, nausea, no pruritus; peak bilirubin >120 µmol/L, 6-fold alkaline phosphatase, 16-fold ALT, 5-fold AST; biopsy showed acute cholestatic hepatitis with mixed cytotoxic (spotty necrosis, acidophilic bodies) and cholestatic (bile plugs, bile pigment, feathery degeneration, periportal inflammation) findings, no zonal necrosis or portal fibrosis. The other three showed a 'pure' hepatocellular-type pattern. All patients recovered rapidly and completely within 2 to 8 weeks after flutamide discontinuation. Classified as an idiosyncratic response without signs of hypersensitivity, assumed toxic-metabolite dependent. Liver function tests remained within normal limits in almost all 1,091 patients during the 36-month observation. Upper normal values: ALT/AST 24 IU/L, γ-GT 28 IU/L, bilirubin 20.5 µmol/L.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses flutamide-induced hepatotoxicity in prostate cancer patients, proposing that clinical flutamide hepatotoxicity occurs when CYP1A2 inhibition, reactive-metabolite production by extensive metabolizers, and lowered GSH content coincide. Preliminary clinical results from 11 prostate cancer patients showed that those who developed severe hepatitis with flutamide had lower CYP1A2 enzyme activity than the normal population, and higher flutamide and lower OH-flutamide plasma concentrations have been reported in patients with flutamide-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Prostate cancer patients taking flutamide as an antiandrogen; susceptibility proposed to involve lower CYP1A2 activity (assessed by caffeine test), concurrent CYP1A2-inhibiting medication, and lowered glutathione content due to poor nutritional status and aging.
raw_record.extra_details: Referenced clinical findings: lower CYP1A2 enzyme activity in the 11 patients who developed severe hepatitis; higher flutamide and lower OH-flutamide (4-hydroxyflutamide) plasma concentrations in patients with flutamide-induced hepatotoxicity; higher FLU-1 plasma concentration in patients with flutamide-induced hepatic disorders. Proposed mechanism involves CYP1A2-mediated reactive-metabolite (originating from FLU-1) formation and glutathione (GSH) depletion; caffeine test (urinary caffeine metabolites) proposed as noninvasive CYP1A2 assessment.

raw_record.support_text: Both patients in this report developed hepatic failure following flutamide treatment, and neither had been exposed to known hepatotoxins; the authors conclude that an unpredictable reaction caused by flutamide seems plausible. For patient 1, previous case descriptions also noted severe liver damage with jaundice, ascites, impaired coagulation and hepatic coma following flutamide, while in the present second patient jaundice resolved and liver function improved after flutamide cessation, with a liver biopsy read as drug-induced.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Two patients with prostatic cancer; patient 1 additionally received Zoladex and dextropropoxyphene, though Zoladex was argued unlikely to contribute, and had renal impairment possibly raising metabolite levels.
raw_record.extra_details: Two case reports. Case 1: severe liver damage with jaundice, ascites, impaired coagulation and hepatic coma; developed after therapeutic flutamide during period of therapeutic Zoladex. Case 2: serum alkaline phosphatase 1202 U/l, ALAT 56 U/l, bilirubin 255 µmol/l; liver biopsy showed slight portal lymphocytic/histiocytic infiltrate without obstruction, scattered focal necroses, and centrilobular cholestasis with bile thrombi and bile pigment in Kupffer cells, interpreted as drug-induced; liver tests improved and jaundice disappeared ~2 months after flutamide cessation; the patient died 1 year later from prostatic cancer. Flutamide is metabolized to hydroxyflutamide plus minor metabolites; renal impairment hypothesized to raise metabolite levels, though animal toxicology showed no serious hepatotoxicity. Prior reports described only slight transaminase elevations that normalized despite continued therapy.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the first association of flutamide with serious hepatotoxicity in a woman using the drug for the treatment of hirsutism. Flutamide hepatotoxicity had previously been considered infrequent and had been reported by Wysowski and colleagues in 19 patients treated for prostatic diseases.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Used for the treatment of hirsutism (a benign condition) in a 20-year-old woman, not for prostatic disease; the patient also continued taking an oral contraceptive pill (Demulen-30) concurrently.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose: flutamide 250 mg orally twice daily. Onset: therapy started in late January 1993; gastrointestinal symptoms appeared in early March and she presented on 13 March with severe pruritus, dark urine, and pale stools, deeply jaundiced. Labs: bilirubin 263 µmol/L (normal 3-20), INR 1.9, alkaline phosphatase 180 IU/L (normal 40-130), ALT 1481 IU/L (normal 5-55). History and viral serology excluded other causes of liver disease; ultrasound normal with non-dilated biliary tree. Bilirubin peaked at 480 µmol/L. Liver biopsy near the height of illness showed changes typical of drug toxicity, including zonal hepatic necrosis with cholestasis and ballooning degeneration of surviving zone 1 hepatocytes. On flutamide discontinuation, enzymes normalized within 6 weeks and bilirubin returned to normal by early June; pruritus controlled with subcutaneous naloxone. Authors state the features of the case are quite conclusive and note the potential for a life-threatening adverse effect.

raw_record.support_text: In the reported clinical series, all severe cases of flutamide-induced acute liver failure (ALF) occurred in young women (mean age 29, range 20-44) treated with flutamide for benign pathologies (acne, hirsutism, alopecia). Histopathological study of 5 cases through the explanted liver confirmed ALF with massive or submassive hepatic necrosis, excluding other conditions such as autoimmune diseases, and severe cases required liver transplantation, with favorable evolution in 4 of the 5 cases. The authors attribute this to a hyper-acute inflammatory response through immunologic mechanisms and warn of a potential lethal complication.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that the most likely cause of death was an idiosyncratic allergic reaction to sorafenib manifesting as hepatotoxicity with associated renal impairment, supported by a RUCAM causality score of 7 consistent with sorafenib being the probable cause. They note idiosyncratic drug reactions typically take 2-8 weeks to manifest and may demonstrate ongoing progression despite drug withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient with resected renal cell carcinoma enrolled in the SORCE phase III trial (NCT00492258) receiving sorafenib 400mg BD. Symptom onset at week 4 (fatigue), worsening through week 7 with jaundice; treatment withdrawn but jaundice and deterioration progressed. Liver tests: ALT 6935 IU, bilirubin 288 μM, alkaline phosphatase 577 IU, prothrombin time 18.2s, LDH 1226 IU; acute hepatitis with hepatic failure, encephalopathy, hypoglycaemia, lactataemia; treatment withdrawn by day 7 with death. Post-mortem liver histology showed lobular hepatitis with mononuclear cell infiltrate and hepatocyte necrosis; kidneys showed acute tubular necrosis. RUCAM causality score 7. Viral (CMV, EBV, hepatitis viruses) and autoimmune (ANA/ANCA) screens negative; no other co-medications or alcohol.

raw_record.support_text: Reports for sorafenib-induced hepatotoxicity are rare and demonstrate consistent hepatocellular necrosis, with variation in timing and type of inflammatory infiltrate. In one 2010 report hepatocellular necrosis with an eosinophilic infiltrate occurred within 5 days of treatment initiation and resolved quickly after drug withdrawal, consistent with hypersensitivity DILI; in another series 3 patients developed symptoms within 3-8 weeks with persistence after drug withdrawal, and all 3 died. The one fatal case with biopsy showed hepatocellular necrosis with a lymphocytic infiltrate consistent with immune-mediated DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: Rare reports of sorafenib-induced hepatotoxicity; consistent hepatocellular necrosis but variation in timing and inflammatory infiltrate. First 2010 report: hepatocellular necrosis with eosinophilic infiltrate within 5 days, resolving after withdrawal (hypersensitivity DILI); second case symptomatic within 4 days of treatment with rapid resolution; 3 patients had symptoms within 3-8 weeks persisting after withdrawal, with death of all 3; the 1 fatal case with biopsy showed hepatocellular necrosis with a lymphocytic infiltrate consistent with immune-mediated DILI.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that in TKI treatment including sorafenib, serum aminotransferase elevation occurs in 20-50% of patients, that the liver injury caused by sorafenib is mild in most cases and improves with drug discontinuation, but that some fatal cases have been reported. The present case's DILI was attributed to sorafenib, which was discontinued due to its severe adverse events including liver injury; DILI here is considered idiosyncratic.
raw_record.extra_details: In the index case sorafenib was discontinued due to severe adverse events including liver injury and fever; the DLST for sorafenib was negative at one month after recovery from the liver injury, suggesting a metabolic rather than hypersensitivity mechanism. Serum aminotransferase elevation occurs in 20-50% of TKI-treated patients; liver injury is mild in most cases and improves with discontinuation, though some fatal cases have been reported. Because the DLST was negative, the liver injury might have been associated with a metabolic mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: In this open-label phase II trial, 30 patients with metastatic, iodine-refractory thyroid carcinoma received sorafenib 400 mg orally twice daily. Toxicity was consistent with other sorafenib trials, although a single patient died of liver failure that was likely treatment related.
raw_record.extra_details: Open-label phase II trial in 30 patients with metastatic, iodine-refractory thyroid carcinoma; sorafenib 400 mg orally twice daily. One patient died of liver failure that was described as likely treatment related; otherwise toxicity consistent with other sorafenib trials. Trial also reported 7 partial responses (23%; 95% CI 0.10-0.42), 16 with stable disease (53%; 95% CI 0.34-0.72), and median PFS of 79 weeks.

raw_record.support_text: The paper cites a clinical case report (Murad et al., 2014) indicating that Sorafenib can cause lethal hepatotoxicity in humans. Separately, the authors note that in the present study Sorafenib increased AST levels in a HepG2 xenograft model, which they interpret as potential hepatotoxicity, but that finding is preclinical (xenograft model) and not human evidence.
raw_record.extra_details: Causal claim rests on a published clinical case report (Murad et al., 2014) describing lethal (fatal) hepatotoxicity. The paper's own AST elevation in the HepG2 xenograft is a preclinical model finding and not human evidence. General cancer-chemotherapy context noted that liver-enzyme elevations resolve in ~90% of patients after stopping hepatotoxic drugs and are sometimes accompanied by severe thrombocytopenia.

raw_record.support_text: A 65-year-old female on sorafenib (third-line for advanced follicular thyroid carcinoma) developed acute on chronic liver failure with a rapid rise in serum transaminases (AST 1,724 U/L), bilirubin (22 mg/dL), and INR 2.9. Liver biopsy demonstrated severe drug-induced necrotic hepatitis, prompting treatment with prednisolone at 1 mg/kg, which led to normalization of AST (to 70 U/L) and INR (to 1.36). The authors call this the first patient reported with sorafenib-induced liver failure, and note the patient had previously unknown well-compensated Child Pugh A cirrhosis, likely from nonalcoholic steatohepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had pre-existing, previously undiagnosed well-compensated Child Pugh A liver cirrhosis, likely due to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report, claimed first report of sorafenib-induced liver failure. Female, 65 yr, third-line treatment of advanced follicular thyroid carcinoma; dose reduction after 10 days due to skin rash, stomatitis, and diarrhea; treatment stopped after flu-like symptoms and fever about 1 week later; liver enzymes continued rising over the next 20 days until admission with beginning liver failure. Histology: severe drug-induced necrotic hepatitis with underlying fatty liver disease and early cirrhosis. Allergic-type immune-mediated liver injury was suspected. Prednisolone 1 mg/kg led to rapid recovery of liver function; bilirubin declined to 1.3 mg/dL under steroid taper. The patient later died from gastric ulcer perforation (not the liver injury). Pulmonary metastases regressed 50%.

raw_record.support_text: In this cohort of 17 AML patients treated with sorafenib before and/or after allogeneic stem cell transplantation (target dose 800 mg/day, median actual dose 600 mg), toxicity leading to dose reduction or transient stop of therapy included diarrhea (n=4), nausea/vomitus (n=2), cytopenias (n=1), hepatotoxicity (n=2), hand-foot syndrome (n=1), and exanthema (n=1). Hepatotoxicity is therefore directly attributed to sorafenib as a therapy-limiting adverse effect in 2 patients.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report that liver biopsy findings and resolution of the patient's jaundice after sulindac withdrawal suggest another case of reversible hepatotoxicity secondary to sulindac. They also note that alterations in hepatic enzymes have been observed during Merck Sharp & Dohme clinical trials of sulindac and that hepatotoxicity has recently been reported with the drug. The case involved therapeutic sulindac use, toxic hepatitis on liver biopsy, and jaundice that resolved after discontinuation (18 d later bilirubin fell to 2.3 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase to 183 mU/mL, GOT to 249 mU/mL).
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: patient developed jaundice and toxic hepatitis on liver biopsy while on therapeutic sulindac; surgical/ultrasound workup showed a portahepatis defect but intraoperative cholangiogram was normal. After sulindac discontinuation and over 18 d, total bilirubin fell to 2.3 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase to 183 mU/mL, and glutamic-oxalacetic transaminase (GOT) to 249 mU/mL; repeat abdominal ultrasound was normal, and the patient recovered without jaundice at 2-week and 2-month follow-up. Authors note elevated hepatic enzymes have been reported in Merck Sharp & Dohme clinical trials of sulindac and cite a prior report of sulindac hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Liver biopsy findings and resolution of the patient's jaundice after sulindac withdrawal suggest this is another case of reversible hepatotoxicity secondary to sulindac. Alterations in hepatic enzymes had been noted during clinical trials of sulindac by Merck Sharp & Dohme, and hepatotoxicity had recently been reported with sulindac.
raw_record.extra_details: A 46-year-old white man developed jaundice 2 weeks after beginning regular use of sulindac 200 mg twice daily (had taken <100 tablets over 15 weeks irregularly; occasional aspirin ≤4/d). Hospitalized with jaundice, 12-cm nontender liver; total bilirubin 10.2 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 7.7 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase >350 mU/mL, glutamic-oxalacetic transaminase 249 mU/mL, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase 1897 mU/mL; prothrombin time, amylase, leukocyte count and urinalysis normal; HBsAg, hepatitis B antibody, antismooth muscle and antimitochondrial antibodies negative. Imaging showed possible pancreatic mass effect/ductal dilatation; surgery and intraoperative cholangiogram were unremarkable; liver biopsy showed toxic hepatitis. After sulindac discontinuation, total bilirubin fell to 2.3 mg/dL, ALP to 183 mU/mL, GOT to 249 mU/mL by 18 d; patient recovered without jaundice on follow-up. Reversible, dechallenge-responsive hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: There have been numerous reports of liver damage associated with the use of sulindac, with some fatalities. Most, but not all, patients were female, many had underlying collagen diseases, and there was no predilection for the elderly. Typically nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fever, skin rash and jaundice developed within a few days or weeks of starting sulindac in doses of 300 to 400 mg daily; liver function tests showed moderate to severe elevations of plasma aminotransferases, bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase, and liver biopsies revealed hepatic necrosis with portal infiltration and cholestasis.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 300-400 mg daily; latency of days to weeks; symptoms included nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fever, skin rash and jaundice; lab showed moderate to severe elevation of plasma aminotransferases, bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase; biopsy showed hepatic necrosis with portal infiltration and cholestasis; most patients were female and many had underlying collagen diseases, with no predilection for the elderly; some fatalities reported.

raw_record.support_text: The paper's summary of 'Published Cases of Sulindac Hepatitis' and the three cases reported in the present study attribute hepatotoxicity (hepatitis presenting with anorexia, nausea, vomiting, malaise, fever, rash, pruritus, jaundice, hepatomegaly, and abdominal pain) to sulindac given at therapeutic doses (200 mg b.d. for musculoskeletal pain). Ceasing sulindac led to resolution of symptoms and falling liver enzymes (e.g., within 24 hours in case 1; within two weeks in case 2), and rechallenge was positive in several of the published cases, supporting sulindac as the causal agent; one published case (Park et al. 1982) died. Case 2's liver biopsy showed canalicular bile plugs and portal eosinophil infiltration.
raw_record.extra_details: Sulindac 200 mg b.d. for pain (back pain, neck pain, cervical spondylosis, MCTD, JRA, SLE, OA, bursitis). Latency from onset typically days to 3 months. Symptoms included anorexia, nausea, vomiting, malaise, fever, rash, pruritus, jaundice, hepatomegaly, abdominal pain. Dechallenge resolved symptoms over about 2-24 days; rechallenge positive in several published cases. One published case (Park et al. 1982) died. Case 2: liver biopsy showed normal lobular architecture, slight portal tract expansion, patchy eosinophil infiltration, centrilobular Councilman bodies, lipofuscin-laden macrophages, hepatocyte anisonucleosis with nuclear vacuolation, binucleated cells, occasional canalicular bile plugs; AP elevation of liver origin, bilirubin 32 µmol/l, GGTP 92 U/l. Case 2 had a prior misdiagnosis of allopurinol hepatitis that did not resolve on withdrawing allopurinol. Case 3 had alcohol intake 30 g/day (heavier previously) and liver biopsy showed thickened hepatocyte plates and binucleated cells. Entry into the present-study cases was in the setting of varying underlying rheumatic diseases; these do not constrain attribution to sulindac.

raw_record.support_text: Sulindac is an NSAID; two patients developed painless jaundice while taking sulindac, which caused hepatotoxicity. It is associated with cholestatic, hepatocellular and mixed injury patterns and, among the NSAIDs, with the highest risk for liver injury in human patients. It was very recently reported that idiosyncratic liver injury may occur through synergistic interplay with the toxic sulindac sulfide metabolite.
raw_record.extra_details: NSAID; two patients developed painless jaundice attributed to sulindac. Associated with cholestatic, hepatocellular and mixed biochemical patterns; reported to carry the highest risk for liver injury among NSAIDs in humans. Idiosyncratic injury proposed to occur via synergistic interplay with the toxic sulindac sulfide metabolite (mechanism, not an independent causal entity).

raw_record.support_text: Sulindac (SLD) is associated with an increased incidence of liver toxicity and serious hepatic reactions (5-10 times) when compared with other NSAIDs. In a series of 91 documented cases reported to the FDA, a predominantly cholestatic pattern was present in 43% while hepatocellular-related changes were found in 25%; a hypersensitivity mechanism of liver injury was present in 60% of cases. Sulindac-induced hepatotoxicity was more frequently encountered among people over 50 years old.
raw_record.extra_details: NSAID (also used in colonic polyposis for antiapoptotic effect); increased incidence of liver toxicity and serious hepatic reactions 5-10 times vs other NSAIDs; FDA series of 91 documented cases: cholestatic pattern 43%, hepatocellular 25%; hypersensitivity mechanism in 60%; more frequently encountered in people over 50. Animal-mechanistic context (excluded from human evidence): SLD sulfide hypothesized central in idiosyncratic injury with LPS/TNF-alpha in rats.

raw_record.support_text: This report and the package insert describe sulindac-induced hepatic injury that is usually mechanism-driven by hypersensitivity; the analysis of 91 cases indicates the idiosyncratic injury is immunologically mediated, supported by hallmarks of hypersensitivity, correlation with brief exposure before injury, and positive responses to challenge doses. Some cases without hypersensitivity hallmarks suggest metabolic idiosyncrasy, tending to appear after longer exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Analysis of 91 cases of sulindac-associated hepatic injury. Death occurred in 4 of 91 cases; 3 fatal outcomes appeared due to severe hypersensitivity reactions rather than the hepatic injury itself (cholestatic in 3 of the 34 cholestatic cases; one with toxic epidermal necrolysis, one with complicating renal failure), and the fourth died of fulminant hepatocellular failure with complicating renal failure (1 of the 17 hepatocellular (HCELL) cases). Histology from 15 cases was predominantly hepatocellular in 9 (spotty/panacinar in 8, zonal in 1; one severe case with zone-3 bridging and multiacinar necrosis) and predominantly cholestatic in 6 (some with acute cholangitis/cholangiolitis, one with alcoholic-hepatitis-like changes, one with α-1-antitrypsin globules). Sulindac-associated injury can be cholestatic, hepatocellular, or mixed; cholestatic pattern is the most characteristic and almost twice as frequent as hepatocellular and mixed combined. Cases without hypersensitivity hallmarks tended to have longer exposure. Significant difference in incidence of eosinophilia between hepatocellular and cholestatic-type injury. Four possible cases of pancreatitis noted. Positive responses to 'challenge doses' reported.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report two women who developed reversible hepatic dysfunction with sulindac. Sulindac had been started one month before admission for back pain and was stopped one week after developing jaundice. Case 1 was similar to previous reports in biochemical presentation, while Case 2 demonstrated a predominantly cholestatic picture. The authors note three prior cases of hepatitis associated with sulindac use.
raw_record.extra_details: Two female patients; sulindac started one month before admission for back pain, stopped one week after jaundice developed (dechallenge). Clinical jaundice without chronic liver disease stigmata; liver enzymes took seven months to return to normal (recovery). Case 2 showed a predominantly cholestatic picture; Case 1 similar to previous reports. Labs (case presented): SGOT 65 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 278 IU/l, bilirubin 213 µmol/l (12.6 mg/dl), normal albumin and thyroid indices, negative hepatitis markers, normal ultrasound/ERCP. Liver biopsy showed zone III (centrilobular) hepatocellular damage with acidophil bodies, focal hepatocyte drop-out with mononuclear infiltrates, mild small and large droplet steatosis, pigmented Kupffer cells, and dilated bile canaliculi with bile plugs. NSAID therapeutic indication.

raw_record.support_text: Early clinical trials reported increased serum alkaline phosphatase, and in 1979 the first report of sulindac hepatitis appeared, followed by eleven further published cases of acute sulindac hepatitis plus the three cases in the present report. In five published cases sulindac was definitely implicated on the basis of rechallenge; in the others it was implicated by association of drug administration with symptom onset, resolution on cessation, and exclusion of other causes. The present cases were implicated on the same grounds, with rechallenge considered unjustifiable due to a report of a potentially life-threatening reaction on inadvertent re-exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Sulindac (Clinoril, Charles E. Frosst) is a substituted indene structurally related to indomethacin; the parent drug is metabolised in the liver to the sulphide analogue, the major pharmacologically active anti-inflammatory agent. Reacts at recommended dosages of 200-400 mg/day; two reports described intermittent non-usual dosing for four to six months with reaction only after recommended dosing, indicating some degree of dose dependency. Initial symptoms occurred within one week to one month of commencement: anorexia, nausea, vomiting, malaise, then fever and jaundice; some cases had diffuse pharyngitis or stomatitis, facial swelling, or generalised rash; tender hepatomegaly occasionally present. 14 published cases plus 3 present cases are tabulated; one published case (Park et al. 1982) died. Histology showed focal lobular hepatitis with lipofuscin-laden macrophages in centrilobular regions, canalicular bile plugging in a predominantly cholestatic case, and hepatocyte regeneration (thickened plates, binucleated hepatocytes) in a late-resolution biopsy; sulindac hepatitis did not progress to irreversible structural injury. Reaction independent of age, sex, and underlying rheumatic disorder, and independent of prior adverse reactions to other NSAIDs including aspirin; lack of reactions to other NSAIDs (naproxen, aspirin, indomethacin) did not preclude sulindac hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Sulindac-associated DILI case reports were analyzed for liver-injury pattern, eosinophilia, hepatic necrosis, inflammatory reaction, and death/liver transplantation outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: 23 individual case reports; median age 51 y; 18 female/5 male; median treatment duration 3 weeks; HC 10%, Cs/mixed 90%; peripheral eosinophilia present in 12% (17/23 reported); hepatic eosinophilia present in 40% (19/23 reported); hepatic necrosis 22%; inflammatory reaction 82%; death or liver transplant 4%; liver biopsy reported in 12/23 cases.

raw_record.support_text: The patient, diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis, had previously used aspirin and fenoprofen without improvement; these were discontinued and sulindac 200 mg was started approximately six weeks before the first episode of acute hepatitis. Sulindac was stopped during the first hospitalization, but three days after discharge she self-administered one 200 mg sulindac tablet and was readmitted within 24 hours with a recurrence of signs and symptoms of acute toxic hepatitis (positive rechallenge).
raw_record.extra_details: Toxic hepatitis with recurrence within 24 hours of rechallenge with a single 200 mg sulindac tablet, supporting causality. Patient treated with sulindac 200 mg for rheumatoid arthritis; prior aspirin and fenoprofen had been discontinued. Abnormal liver tests included gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase 815 IU/L and elevated alkaline phosphatase, LDH, SGOT, and SGPT on admission, with improvement after 3 days and return to normal one week after hospitalization; supportive care only. The discussion notes three patients previously reported with acute hepatitis following sulindac, of whom two plus this patient were 18 years of age or younger, in contrast to the virtual absence of hepatitis in that age group with isoniazid.

raw_record.support_text: The paper derives a drug-specific DILI phenotype for cefazolin using 19 cefazolin-induced liver injury cases (n=19), scored with a cefazolin-specific DILI-CAT. The cases are treated as confirmed cefazolin DILI, and cefazolin's phenotype (median latency 20, R-value 20, AST/ALT ratio 20; weighted scores all 60) is distinguished from cyproterone (no overlap in latency, U=0, p<0.001; median latency weighted score 60 vs -12.5) and from Polygonum multiflorum (R-value, p<0.001).
raw_record.extra_details: Cefazolin DILI phenotype derived from 19 cases. DILI-CAT median subscores: latency 20, R-value 20, AST/ALT ratio 20; weighted scores all 60. Latency differed from cyproterone (U=0, no overlap, p<0.001; median latency-weighted score 60 vs -12.5); R-value differed from Polygonum multiflorum (U=17, p<0.001; median R-value-weighted score 60 vs 7.5).

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN prospective registry, cefazolin accounted for 20 of 899 adjudicated DILI cases, and mortality for DILI caused by cefazolin was 0-1%.
raw_record.extra_details: 20 adjudicated DILI cases; mortality for cefazolin DILI 0-1%.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN Prospective Study cohort, cefazolin was implicated as a cause of DILI, and cases attributed to it showed a higher frequency of increased eosinophil counts (30%). The paper notes that cefazolin is known frequently to cause immuno-allergic liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated among the ten most frequent prescription drugs causing DILI in the DILIN cohort; increased eosinophil count frequency 30%; described as a known cause of immuno-allergic liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that cephalosporins appear to be a relatively common cause of antibiotic-associated liver injury, with a latency of typically 1-3 weeks, and that a single infusion of cefazolin can lead to DILI. The course of cefazolin-induced DILI is usually a mild-to-moderate, self-limited cholestatic injury, although severe and even fatal DILI may occur in a small number of patients, and some cases may be followed by evidence of chronic injury.
raw_record.extra_details: DILIN adjudicated case series of 19 patients with cefazolin-induced DILI following single prophylactic infusion. Latency from administration to symptom onset: <1 week in 16%, 2-4 weeks in 68%, >4 weeks in 16%; jaundice 95%, itching 100%, nausea 79%, rash 32%, fever 47%, eosinophilia 26%, hospitalization 69%. Severity distribution: mild 5%, moderate 32%, moderate and hospitalized 53%, severe 11%, fatal 0. DILIN causality: probable 5%, highly likely 84%, definite 11%. Persistent abnormal liver tests >6 months in 16%. Histology shows cholestatic hepatitis with mild portal/lobular inflammation and prominent canalicular cholestasis (zone 3). ALT/AST/ALP/bilirubin at onset and peak values reported per patient; disease site as ulceration (DILIN score: definite >95%, very likely 75-95%, probable 50-75%). Immuno-allergic features often present but usually transient and mild; DRESS syndrome uncommon; rapid recurrence upon re-exposure common.

raw_record.support_text: In the ongoing prospective Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network (DILIN) study, cephalosporins were relatively common causes of DILI, and the first-generation parenteral cephalosporin cefazolin ranked highly among implicated single agents. The paper describes 19 patients with DILI attributed to cefazolin, who had a distinctive clinical phenotype, and cefazolin was frequently overlooked as the putative cause.
raw_record.extra_details: 19 patients from the US DILIN prospective multicenter registry (8 centers) with DILI attributed to cefazolin. DILI developed following a single dose with a latency period of 1-3 weeks after exposure, marked cholestasis, and a self-limited moderate to severe clinical course. Other cephalosporins can cause a similar but more severe injury. Cephalosporins accounted for only 4/461 (0.9%) episodes in a Spanish Registry, 1/77 (1.2%) in a Swedish study, and 1/96 (1%) in an Icelandic survey. DILIN enrollment criteria included AST or ALT >5x ULN, alkaline phosphatase >2x ULN, total bilirubin >=2.5 mg/dL with any enzyme elevation, or INR >1.5 with enzyme elevations; patients with autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cirrhosis, or sclerosing cholangitis were excluded.

Nineteen of these patients developed clinically apparent DILI after a single intravenous dose of cefazolin, with all developing self-limited liver injury 3-23 days after receiving cefazolin during surgery, often during a minor outpatient procedure.

Injury appeared 3-23 days after dosing with a reported latency period of 20 days. Clinical features included itching, jaundice, nausea, fever, and rash. raw_record.support_text: The patient's alkaline phosphatase and aminotransferase levels steadily decreased over the following 4 weeks. Dapsone was determined to be the most likely cause of her hepatic granulomas and liver injury, and she was advised to stop dapsone permanently.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient presented with jaundice 4 days after prednisone cessation and 7 weeks after dapsone initiation (100 mg). Liver biopsy showed well-formed non-necrotizing periportal granulomas without bile duct involvement; Grocott methenamine silver and acid-fast bacilli stains negative. Infectious and autoimmune etiologies ruled out; improvement in jaundice after stopping dapsone. Dapsone 100 mg held at admission. Broad DIH (dapsone-induced hepatitis) spectrum ranges from mild liver injury to acute liver failure, usually presenting within 4-6 weeks of starting the medication; in the largest (n=44) retrospective study only 17% showed a cholestatic pattern. Prednisone (60 mg tapered by 10 mg/week) was administered before presentation.

raw_record.support_text: The 'dapsone syndrome' developed in a 44-year-old woman treated for pyoderma gangrenosum with 100 mg/day dapsone for about 5 weeks. Symptoms included fever, malaise, jaundice with hepatic dysfunction, lymphadenopathy, mononucleosis and dermatitis; these resolved after oral prednisolone. A lymphocyte stimulation test with dapsone was positive, and the delayed-type intradermal skin test with dapsone in saline was positive. Immunohistochemistry showed the dominant infiltrating T cells in the upper dermis were of the Leu 2a+ cytotoxic/suppressor-type rather than Leu 3a+ helper-type.
raw_record.extra_details: Dapsone syndrome, recognized as a severe hypersensitivity side-effect of dapsone. Dose 100 mg/day for about 5 weeks (45 days) for pyoderma gangrenosum in a 44-year-old woman. Also described as suspected hepatitis on admission, with fever (39°C), generalized erythema multiforme exudativum progressing to erythroderma, icterus, hepatosplenomegaly with slightly tender palpable liver edge, and enlarged cervical lymph nodes. Abnormal values included glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase 112 IU/l, glutamic-pyruvic transaminase 232 IU/l, lactic dehydrogenase 1852 IU/l, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 59 IU/l, total bilirubin 9.83 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 7.83 mg/dl, and urine bilirubin 3+. The symptoms resolved with 30 mg/day oral prednisolone. Positive lymphocyte stimulation test and positive delayed-type intradermal skin test with 0.5 and 0.05% dapsone in saline; T cells in upper dermis predominantly Leu 2a+ cytotoxic/suppressor-type.

raw_record.support_text: Other drugs such as allopurinol, dapsone, and nevirapine were also identified as offending drugs in definite DRESS/DIHS cases. Patient 7 received dapsone for acne and developed DRESS with hepatitis (ALT 476 U/L, AST 891 U/L). Hepatitis was the most common visceral involvement, present in 23 patients (85.1%).
raw_record.extra_details: Dapsone identified as culprit drug in definite RegiSCAR-scored DRESS/DIHS cases; patient 7 (acne, latency 21 days) had MPE and purpuric lesions with ALT 476 U/L, AST 891 U/L; patient 26 (aphtae) also dapsone-attributed; hepatitis was the most common visceral involvement (23/27 patients, 85.1%).

raw_record.support_text: A 27-year-old woman treated for linear IgA disease with oral dapsone 100 mg once daily reported 4 weeks later with fever, extensive erythematous maculopapular rash, and icterus. Investigations showed serum bilirubin 3.3 mg/dL, ALT 162 IU/L, AST 92 IU/L, absolute eosinophil count 1383 cells/cm3, and hepatosplenomegaly on ultrasound; she was diagnosed with dapsone-induced hypersensitivity syndrome and dapsone was stopped.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the hepatotoxicity caused by dapsone in their patient, with liver biopsy showing focal destruction of bile ducts and intraepithelial neutrophils, features suggestive of acute cholangitis. They state this is the first report of dapsone as a cause of cholangitis, and describe the case as a dapsone syndrome with hepatic involvement in the form of acute cholangitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (dapsone syndrome) with hepatic involvement manifesting as acute cholangitis; liver biopsy showed focal destruction of bile ducts and intraepithelial neutrophils, not previously reported in dapsone syndrome. The patient had also received one dose of rifampicin, which the authors deemed unlikely to have caused such a severe reaction. Prior dapsone syndrome biopsy literature describes hepatitis, cholestasis, or granuloma formation. Indications noted: leprosy, AIDS, and dermatitis herpetiformis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a near fatal case of the dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (DHS) in a patient with urticarial vasculitis. Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome is described as well recognized, occurring in less than 1% of patients treated with dapsone, with symptoms including fever, haemolytic anaemia, lymphocytosis and hepatitis. The authors conclude that DHS should be remembered in any patient who becomes unwell while taking dapsone.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: 55-year-old Caucasian woman with urticarial vasculitis, previous subtotal thyroidectomy on thyroxine. Treated with oral dapsone 100 mg once daily; also on cetirizine and short courses of hydroxychloroquine, methylprednisolone, and hydrocortisone/crotamiton cream (none attributed as DILI cause). Near fatal outcome; DHS reported in <1% of dapsone-treated patients; symptoms of DHS include fever, haemolytic anaemia, lymphocytosis and hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: A single-hospital registry in Bangalore, India (1997-2008) identified 313 DILI cases; dapsone (used for leprosy) accounted for 5.4% of cases, while anti-TB drugs (one or more of four) were the most common cause (58%) and anti-epileptics accounted for 11%. Overall mortality was 17.3%, driven mostly by ALF from the anti-TB agents, since liver transplantation was not available at the center.
raw_record.extra_details: 5.4% of 313 DILI cases in Bangalore, India registry, indication leprosy. Mortality 17.3% overall driven by ALF from anti-TB agents; transplantation unavailable.

raw_record.support_text: The paper attributes hepatotoxicity to dapsone as part of dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (DHS), describing hepatic dysfunction in which hepatocellular injury is less common than cholestatic injury. The mechanism of injury, including the hepatotoxicity in dapsone syndrome, is described as a hypersensitivity reaction, and a review reported a DHS incidence of 1.4% with an overall case-fatality of 9.9%. The reported case presented with icterus due to a predominantly cholestatic pattern of hepatic injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (DHS) typically begins 3-5 weeks after starting therapy (range 7-10 days to 6 months); most common signs include sudden fever, generalized rash, hepatitis, lymphadenopathy, nausea/vomiting, eosinophilia, and mucosal involvement; other manifestations include hemolysis, agranulocytosis, methemoglobinemia, lymphocytosis, and toxic epidermal necrolysis. In DHS hepatic dysfunction, hepatocellular injury (elevated transaminases, eosinophilic lobular/portal infiltration) is less common but more severe than cholestatic injury (high alkaline phosphatase, modest transaminase rise, possible granuloma). Mechanism appears to be a hypersensitivity reaction (combination of type I, type IV, and possibly type III; or graft-versus-host-like). DHS incidence 1.4% and overall case-fatality 9.9% (review). Reported case showed a predominantly cholestatic pattern with icterus, plus leukemoid reaction and thrombocytosis. Dapsone is hepatically metabolized via N-acetylation and N-hydroxylation; age and pre-existing liver disease reduce toxic-metabolite production, lowering adverse-event risk.

raw_record.support_text: This is a case report of dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (DHS). Dapsone is described as one of the commonly implicated drugs in drug-induced systemic hypersensitivity syndrome, and DHS is a rare dose-independent adverse effect reported with dapsone use. Manifestations include hepatitis with mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic features, coagulopathy, encephalopathy, and shock. In the presented patient, the diagnosis of DHS with hepatitis was made after typical clinical manifestations following 3 weeks of dapsone intake, after excluding other drug exposures and close differential diagnoses, and was supported by prompt response to systemic steroids.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (DRESS syndrome). DHS is a rare dose-independent adverse effect; latency several weeks to up to 6 months after treatment initiation; reported incidence 0.5%-3%. The patient had severe systemic manifestations including hepatitis with mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic features, coagulopathy, encephalopathy, shock and exfoliative dermatitis. Diagnosis followed 3 weeks of dapsone intake after excluding viral hepatitis, rickettsial infection, CMV, EBV, complicated malaria and leptospirosis; supported by prompt response to systemic steroids (prednisolone or methylprednisolone). Rechallenge not recommended. Mortality as high as 12%-23% reported in severe DHS. Pathogenesis proposed to involve dapsone metabolites (hydroxylamines via hepatic microsomal cytochrome P-450). Dapsone used for leprosy, Pneumocystis jirovecii infection, toxoplasmosis, malaria, dermatological conditions and immune thrombocytopenic purpura.

raw_record.support_text: Use of the Naranjo probability scale indicates that sulfone syndrome associated with dapsone was probable in our patient. The patient had primarily a cholestatic type of liver injury with exfoliative dermatitis, fever, malaise, and methemoglobinemia. One month after discontinuation of dapsone, all symptoms resolved and laboratory values began to normalize, supporting the diagnosis of sulfone syndrome.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 42-year-old HIV-infected man; no pre-existing liver disease reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Sulfone syndrome (dapsone hypersensitivity) developed 4 weeks after dapsone was started. Naranjo probability scale rated the association as probable. Features included predominantly cholestatic liver injury with exfoliative dermatitis, fever, malaise, and methemoglobinemia; liver biopsy was not performed. Symptoms resolved and laboratory values began to normalize ~1 month after dapsone discontinuation. Sulfone syndrome is described as not dose-related, resolving within 1-14 days (time course) after stopping dapsone; fatal reactions have been reported in the literature. Peak labs at 11 weeks on dapsone: ALP 2078 U/L, AST 533, ALT 127, total bilirubin 5.7 mg/dL (conj. 4.7), methemoglobin 5.0%. Prednisone used for symptomatic relief.

raw_record.support_text: A 34-year-old HIV-infected woman with no other opportunistic infections presented a classic sulfone syndrome manifested by fever, rash, hemolytic anemia, and fulminant hepatitis due to a dapsone hypersensitivity reaction, with a fatal outcome. This is described as the first reported fatal complication of dapsone in an HIV-infected patient.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: HIV-infected patient receiving dapsone for Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia prophylaxis; co-medication zidovudine (AZT) as the only other medication; normal G6PD level.
raw_record.extra_details: Case occurred ~1 month after starting dapsone. Sulfone syndrome: fever, exfoliative dermatitis, hepatitis, hemolytic anemia; 15% eosinophils, markedly elevated liver enzymes, bilirubin peaked at 23 mg/dL, prothrombin time peaked at 36.2 seconds, hypocomplementemia. Hepatitis A, B, and C, infectious mononucleosis, syphilis serologies negative; drug-related hypersensitivity. Dapsone is a diaminodiphenylsulfone used for leprosy and dermatitis herpetiformis, now used for PCP prophylaxis.

raw_record.support_text: A 12-yr-old girl was prescribed dapsone for PPD. Twenty days later she developed high fever, followed by a skin rash, and required hospitalization; dapsone was discontinued on HD 1. Laboratory findings showed elevated total bilirubin (1.8 mg/dL), ALT (141 IU/L) and AST (158 IU/L). Her liver function subsequently deteriorated with rising bilirubin, AST and ALT and coagulopathy, and she developed fulminant hepatic failure, hepatic encephalopathy (grade 3) and hepatorenal syndrome.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (12-yr-old girl); treated for PPD; associated dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome with hemolytic anemia, fever, rash and multi-organ failure; no infection identified.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report titled 'Dapsone hypersensitivity induces fulminant liver failure'. Latency ~20 days from dapsone start; high fever up to 40 �C, body skin rash; laboratory evolution (HD 12: total bilirubin 11.6 mg/dL, AST 737 IU/L, ALT 372 IU/L, prothrombin time 15.0 s/1.4 INR; HD 14: bilirubin 19.6 mg/dL, AST 1146 IU/L, ALT 199 IU/L, PT 26.8 s/2.58 INR; HD 15: grade 3 hepatic encephalopathy, hepatorenal syndrome, ammonia 124 µg/dL). Positive direct Coombs test, low C3/C4, elevated IgG/IgM, negative FANA/anti-dsDNA/anti-cardiolipin. Treated with steroids, rituximab and plasmapheresis; registered UNOS status 1; emergent LDLT on HD 17 (Child-Pugh 11, MELD 38, donor cousin).

raw_record.support_text: After excluding glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, therapy with dapsone 1 mg/kg daily and prednisolone was initiated in a 15-year-old girl with linear IgA bullous dermatosis. Within 3 weeks of treatment, liver enzymes and cholestasis parameters rose up to 10-fold above normal and dapsone was discontinued; after normalization, reintroduction of dapsone again markedly increased liver enzymes, requiring withdrawal. The authors state this confirmed its causative role.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (15-year-old girl) with concurrent prednisolone treatment; dapsone reintroduction after normalization of liver parameters repeated the liver-enzyme increase.
raw_record.extra_details: Dapsone given at 1 mg/kg daily initially, then 0.5 mg/kg daily on reintroduction. Liver enzymes and cholestasis parameters rose up to 10-fold above normal within 3 weeks; parameters normalized after withdrawal and increased again upon rechallenge. Authors note hepatotoxicity is a very rare side-effect of dapsone that may occur as part of a hypersensitivity reaction ('dapsone syndrome'), mostly when combined with antimalarial or antileprosial agents. Skin disease relapsed upon dapsone discontinuation; patient also developed septicaemia.

The paper explicitly states that no drug-related adverse events were shown to have a causal association with azithromycin therapy, and the discussion reiterates that standard azithromycin treatment was well-tolerated with no liver injury detected.

The authors concluded no drug-related adverse events had a causal association with azithromycin therapy and that standard treatment was well-tolerated with no liver injury detected.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of 53 human DILI cases with liver biopsy, azithromycin (histological pattern N, 3 cases; C, 1 case) was listed among the causative DILI drugs in the anti-infectious category. Causality was assessed by the CIOMS/RUCAM scale, with most cases scored as definitive or probable DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: Histological pattern reported: necroinflammatory (N) in 3 cases and cholestatic (C) in 1 case. Drug was also among those related to ANA positivity in one DILI case (p:39). One of 53 biopsy-confirmed DILI cases in the series.

raw_record.support_text: Azithromycin was one of the macrolide antibiotics associated with DILI (the macrolides as a group accounted for three cases). In addition, a separate azithromycin-attributed jaundice case was documented with bilirubin 4.8 ULN, AST 8.4 ULN and ALT 8.4 ULN.
raw_record.extra_details: Part of the three macrolide cases (2 hepatocellular/1 mixed) with grouped duration mean 7 (4-10) days; separate jaundice case (58-year-old female, 10 days treatment, bilirubin 4.8 ULN, AST 8.4 ULN, ALT 8.4 ULN, ALP 1.9 ULN, resolution 60 days). Spelled Azitromycin in tables.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a patient initially suspected of having autoimmune hepatitis who was later confirmed by liver biopsy to have acute hepatitis secondary to drug-induced liver injury with a temporal relationship to azithromycin. The conclusion highlights azithromycin-induced liver injury as a rare but potentially fatal side effect of this otherwise safe antibiotic.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report. The patient had no personal or family history of liver disease before admission. She had been taking atorvastatin (which has hepatotoxic potential) but stopped 11 months prior, with baseline liver function tests normal six months prior, so atorvastatin was not considered the culprit. Acute hepatitis was confirmed by liver biopsy as secondary to DILI with a temporal relationship to azithromycin; autoimmune hepatitis was initially suspected but ruled out. A cited previous study noted azithromycin DILI in a higher proportion of patients with pre-existing liver disease. Azithromycin-induced liver injury is described by the authors as a rare and potentially fatal side effect.

raw_record.support_text: In a DILIN-causality adjudicated cohort of 345 patients, 37 were classified as probable-DILI using a DILIN expert opinion causality score of 1, 2, or 3. The most commonly identified individual agents were all antibiotics and included trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (8%), ceftriaxone (8%), amoxicillin-clavulanate (5%), isoniazid (5%), and azithromycin (5%).
raw_record.extra_details: One of the most commonly identified individual agents (5%) among 37 probable-DILI cases. Cohort-level: probable-DILI more often hepatocellular at onset (57% vs 32.5%, p=0.01); DILIN severity index up to fatal (6/37 fatal).

raw_record.support_text: After excluding other causes of liver disease, drug-induced hepatotoxicity was considered, and a temporal relationship between azithromycin initiation and onset of clinical signs was observed. In the absence of another cause of liver injury, the patient's cholestatic hepatitis was attributed to the four doses of azithromycin she received after her initial arrival at the ER.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient who received azithromycin 1000 mg orally once followed by 500 mg orally daily for four of seven days for community-acquired pneumonia, after which cholestatic hepatitis was attributed to the drug. Peak total and direct bilirubin reached 18.5 and 10.9 mg/dL; peak ALT 4068 IU/L and AST 2001 IU/L; INR rose to 3.07; patient was intubated and admitted to the intensive care unit. Liver function tests began improving nine days after initial azithromycin exposure and returned to normal at clinic follow-up. The paper notes five previously described cases of azithromycin-induced hepatotoxicity. The paper contains conflicting reaction-type statements: it states that because liver damage occurs within hours/days of initiation azithromycin's effect is thought to be intrinsic, while it also concludes the evidence suggests the liver damage is idiosyncratic, immunologically mediated, and unrelated to dose and duration. Mechanism described as hypersensitivity-mediated with immunologic alterations and metabolite-dependent lesions leading to ductal cholestasis. Macrolide class; histologic/laboratory features included pruritus and jaundice in 4 of 5 prior cases.

raw_record.support_text: The study prospectively identified and adjudicated 18 cases of clinically apparent liver injury as probably, highly likely, or definitely owing to azithromycin. Hepatocellular injury outnumbered cholestatic injury, latency to onset was 1 to 3 weeks (recognized 2 weeks after stopping azithromycin in 16 patients), typical symptoms were fatigue, nausea and abdominal pain followed by itching and jaundice, and recovery usually was prompt (2 to 5 weeks) with complete resolution.
raw_record.extra_details: 18 prospectively identified, adjudicated cases of clinically apparent DILI (probable, highly likely, or definite). Latency 1-3 weeks after azithromycin; onset typically after completing the course (only 2 of 18 developed jaundice while taking it). Typical regimen 250-500 mg once daily for 4-7 days. At 6-month follow-up for 14 patients, 8 recovered, 4 had chronic injury, 1 died of multi-organ failure, 1 underwent liver transplantation. Four patients (1, 3, 6, 11) met chronic DILI definition; 3 had initial hepatocellular injury with jaundice and later mild-moderate ALT/Alk P increases. Histology showed ductopenic portal areas, zone 3 cholestasis with hepatocellular and canalicular bile accumulation, chronic hepatitis with perivenular inflammation and hemorrhage, and mild veno-occlusive changes. Recovery usually prompt, resolving in 2-5 weeks; median time to 50% reduction of peak bilirubin 12 days (8-27 d) and to normalization 35 days (25-46 d).

raw_record.support_text: Azithromycin was among the agents associated with bile duct loss in the DILI registry cohort, accounting for 2/26 (8%) of bile duct loss cases versus 10/363 (3%) of all biopsied subjects. It was also named as a primary implicated agent in 2 subjects with poor outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: Agent attributed as causing DILI with bile duct loss in the DILIN registry; primary implicated agent in 2 poor-outcome subjects.

raw_record.support_text: A 67-year-old female admitted with new onset jaundice, yellow skin and conjunctiva, diffuse pruritus, and elevated hepatic enzymes had her acute jaundice ultimately attributed to an azithromycin-related, drug-induced liver injury that resolved with conservative management; she was discharged three days after admission.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented with jaundice, yellow skin and conjunctiva, diffuse pruritus, and elevated hepatic enzymes; injury resolved with conservative management. Occurred in context of a non-urologic diagnostic workup causing incidental detection of a ureteral mass.

raw_record.support_text: In the multivariate analysis of the AC genetic risk score and risk of DILI due to other agents, azithromycin was listed among causal drugs with DILI cases (N=17). Mean GRS 0.92, 6% with GRS > 1.58, OR 0.89 (0.48-1.65), P = 0.72.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed as a causal DILI drug with 17 DILI cases in the AC-GRS comparator analysis (below the stated 20-case threshold).

raw_record.support_text: Martinez et al. defined the clinical, histological features and outcome of azithromycin-induced liver injury based on 18 patients in the current DILIN registry. The injury was mostly hepatocellular and occurred within 1–3 weeks of exposure; outcomes were typically favorable but azithromycin caused chronic injury and associated cutaneous reactions, and in some cases resulted in liver transplantation or death.
raw_record.extra_details: 18 DILIN registry patients; onset 1–3 weeks after exposure; chronic injury and cutaneous reactions also reported; cases resulted in liver transplantation or death.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN prospective registry, azithromycin accounted for 18 of 899 adjudicated DILI cases, one of the top 10 individual agents.
raw_record.extra_details: 18 adjudicated DILI cases in the DILIN registry.

raw_record.support_text: Among 41 short-latency DILI cases (<7 days) in the DILIN study, the most commonly implicated agents were moxifloxacin (n=4), azithromycin (n=3), ciprofloxacin (n=3), rifampin (n=2), and levofloxacin (n=2).
raw_record.extra_details: Short-latency DILI (<7 days); n=3 cases in the DILIN Prospective Study cohort.

raw_record.support_text: Azithromycin was listed among the top 10 implicated individual agents causing definite, highly likely, or probable drug-induced liver injury in the DILIN registry cohort, attributed to 2% of Caucasian cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated agent in a DILIN cohort of definite, highly likely, or probable DILI (Caucasians 2%). Separately noted as one of the agents in a case with severe cutaneous reaction.

raw_record.support_text: Azithromycin has had accumulating reports of hepatotoxicity, some with serious consequences. In the DILIN study, 18 azithromycin cases were identified among patients enrolled 2004-2013: 89% presented with jaundice, 67% with abdominal pain and 56% with pruritus; mean duration of therapy was 4 days and median time to onset was 17 days. More than half had hepatocellular injury, with cholestatic and mixed patterns also observed; histology demonstrated veno-occlusive changes and ductopenia in a few patients. At 6-month follow-up, one patient required liver transplantation, one died of multi-organ failure and four had chronic biochemical injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 18 cases in DILIN 2004-2013; 89% jaundice, 67% abdominal pain, 56% pruritus; mean therapy duration 4 days (range 4-7), median onset 17 days; longer half-life than erythromycin; >half hepatocellular with cholestatic and mixed patterns; histology showed veno-occlusive changes and ductopenia; two reactions with severe hypersensitivity cutaneous reactions; at 6 months 1 transplant, 1 death from multi-organ failure, 4 chronic biochemical injury. Can be associated with severe cutaneous reactions, liver-related death and chronic injury.

raw_record.support_text: A previously healthy 33-year-old woman presented with jaundice and pruritus after a 5-day course of azithromycin followed by one day of erythromycin for a flu-like syndrome. She was diagnosed with azithromycin-induced cholestasis, treated with cholestyramine and six courses of plasmapheresis, with normal biochemical liver tests at her 4-year follow-up.

Treated with cholestyramine and six plasmapheresis courses; bilirubin and transaminases normalized within two months and remained normal at 4-year follow-up. raw_record.support_text: An 83-year-old male admitted for possible community-acquired pneumonia received azithromycin and ceftriaxone. After 2 doses of azithromycin, AST and ALT exceeded 3 times the upper limit of normal and continued rising with subsequent doses; total bilirubin stayed within normal limits and abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly. Liver enzymes, INR, and aPTT continued to climb until hospital day 5, when azithromycin was discontinued, after which all values decreased over days 6-8. The authors conclude a potentially serious liver injury occurred with azithromycin initiation and began resolving quickly after discontinuation, describing it as the third reported case of direct hepatocellular injury (cholestatic injury being well described with azithromycin).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly 83-year-old male; indication of possible community-acquired pneumonia; concurrently received ceftriaxone; rosuvastatin and fenofibrate were held on admission and not resumed; rivaroxaban held for renal function.
raw_record.extra_details: After 2 doses: AST and ALT >3x ULN, rising with subsequent doses; total bilirubin remained normal; hepatomegaly on ultrasound; INR, aPTT, and LDH climbed until hospital day 5 then decreased over days 6-8 after azithromycin discontinuation (dechallenge improvement). Hepatitis serologies negative. Paper states it is the third reported case of direct hepatocellular injury with azithromycin, whereas cholestatic injury is well described.

raw_record.support_text: The 2 individuals with a fatal/liver transplant outcome within 6 months after DILI onset were elderly, had pre-existing chronic liver disease, and presented with jaundice and a hepatocellular pattern of liver injury. Patient 15, a 60-year-old woman with underlying nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, was treated with azithromycin for 3 days for a respiratory tract infection and underwent liver transplantation 1 month after initial presentation; patient 18, a 76-year-old man with daily alcohol abuse and COPD treated with a 4-day course for acute bronchitis, died 1 week later of multi-organ failure. Hepatocellular necrosis/damage with jaundice was the pattern in these fatal outcomes.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly patients with pre-existing chronic liver disease (nonalcoholic steatohepatitis in one case; daily alcohol abuse with COPD in the other); treated for respiratory tract/bronchial infections.

Patient 18: 76-year-old man, 4-day course, nausea then jaundice 1 week later; bilirubin 7.2 mg/dL, ALT 8787 IU/L, Alk P 130 IU/L; small heterogeneous liver on imaging; died 1 week later of multi-organ failure.

raw_record.support_text: Based on the Maria and Victorino clinical scale for diagnosing DILI, the initial diagnosis of azithromycin-induced liver injury was confirmed, reaching a score of 15 (probable). After anamnestic discovery that an episode of transient dark urine and hypocholic stools occurred following a 3-day azithromycin treatment for an upper respiratory tract infection a few months earlier, the current jaundice was considered a positive rechallenge test, giving a total score of 18 corresponding to a 'definite' diagnosis of DILI. Liver biopsy revealed cholestatic hepatitis with severe reduction of native biliary ducts.

raw_record.support_text: The patient described in this case report had a severe episode of acute liver failure following monochlorobenzene ingestion. Although factor V decreased to 14% of normal (a value seen in fatal fulminant hepatitis B), encephalopathy did not develop and the patient ultimately recovered. Prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) was administered, but no beneficial effect could be demonstrated.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Ingestion/poisoning case; chronic alcohol consumption may have contributed to severity of the liver lesions.
raw_record.extra_details: Erythema was noted and was likely related to monochlorobenzene ingestion, not phototoxic (face uninvolved). Factor V fell to 14% of normal; no encephalopathy developed and the patient recovered. Treated with prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) with no demonstrable benefit. Proposed mechanism: metabolism likely similar to bromobenzene, via cytochrome P450 to a reactive epoxide causing reactive-metabolite formation and glutathione depletion; alcohol-induced CYP2E1 induction may have exaggerated hepatotoxicity. Monochlorobenzene blood concentrations exceeded benzene concentrations in exhaled breath.

raw_record.support_text: A single patient developed hepatocellular jaundice among 2517 patients treated with zileuton in phase II/III clinical trials; in a long-term study of 2458 zileuton-treated patients there were no cases of jaundice, but one patient met a conservative definition of Hy's law. For the total zileuton experience in over 6000 patients, these two cases were used to predict a risk of liver failure of approximately 1 in 30,000 treated patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Zileuton-associated liver injury signature defined as a hepatocellular injury generally occurring within 3 months of starting therapy and resolving within 1 month of discontinuing therapy; generally asymptomatic, with treatment often continued under monitoring in asymptomatic patients with enzyme elevations between 3 and 5 × ULN. A single treatment-arm patient developed hepatocellular jaundice (total bilirubin >3 mg/dL). Predicted risk of liver failure ~1:30,000 over 6000 treated patients per Hy's law, but true risk is uncertain because incidence as a function of treatment duration is unknown. Paper notes monitoring (stopping when ALT >5 × ULN) likely prevented progression to clinically important liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: A single 28-year-old woman developed severe liver injury and jaundice after treatment with zileuton 400 mg four times daily for approximately 6 weeks. At discontinuation she was jaundiced with AST 19×ULN, ALT 33×ULN, alkaline phosphatase 1.3×ULN and total bilirubin 6.6×ULN; all viral hepatitis serology was negative and no alternative aetiology was identified. Total bilirubin reached 12.8×ULN 8 days after stopping zileuton; within 35 days ALT and AST returned to normal and bilirubin fell to 2.6×ULN, and the patient fully recovered with normal bilirubin after 70 days. This case was the basis for a long-term liver surveillance study.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adult female (28 years old); no pre-existing liver disease noted; no alternative aetiology identified.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency approximately 6 weeks; dose 400 mg four times daily; symptoms fatigue, nausea, itching, influenza-like symptoms; AST 19×ULN, ALT 33×ULN, ALP 1.3×ULN, total bilirubin 6.6×ULN at discontinuation, rising to 12.8×ULN 8 days after stopping; ALT/AST normalized within 35 days, bilirubin normal after 70 days; full recovery; viral hepatitis serology negative; no alternative aetiology identified; motivated a 12-month surveillance study of zileuton liver safety.

raw_record.support_text: Rare pediatric reports of vancomycin-induced DRESS syndrome describe a life-threatening condition with acute liver failure, aggravated encephalopathy, and azotemia, necessitating liver transplantation in one case and causing frank and refractory shock in another case. The patient in the present study developed vancomycin-induced DRESS fulfilling all RegiSCAR and Japanese Consensus Group criteria, with a benign outcome after prompt withdrawal of the culprit drug.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients; DRESS syndrome as the presenting systemic hypersensitivity drug reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: DRESS is a drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome whose systemic manifestations include acute liver failure; reagents: pediatric case series reported one case requiring liver transplantation and another with refractory shock. In the present case ALT rose from 72 to 353 U/L and AST from 32 to 341 U/L, with resolution after vancomycin discontinuation (ALT 88, AST 56); total bilirubin and ALP remained near baseline. Patch test to vancomycin was positive. Diagnosis fulfilled European Registry of Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions (RegiSCAR) Study Group and Japanese Consensus Group inclusion criteria. A prior study at Massachusetts General Hospital found vancomycin involved in 5 of 6 inpatient DRESS cases over 18 months.

raw_record.support_text: 26 patients met the inclusion criteria for vancomycin-associated DRESS, all probable or definite cases of vancomycin-induced DRESS per the Naranjo algorithm (>5). The mean vancomycin dosage was 1,628.8 mg/day and the duration to DRESS onset after the first day of treatment ranged from 14 to 62 days; 6/26 subjects were concomitantly receiving other medicines when prescribed vancomycin. Hepatitis with GPT >3-fold elevation was present in 13 (50.0%) of the 26 patients, and 10 (38.5%) had acute renal failure. Lactate-based lymphocyte activation tests (LAT) on the 6 concurrently medicated cases confirmed vancomycin as the culprit drug (granulysin expression 4.7±3.7 fold, exceeding the cutoff), while the concomitant medicines showed no increase, so all 6 DRESS cases were attributed to vancomycin.
raw_record.extra_details: 26 patients with vancomycin-associated DRESS, all probable/definite (Naranjo algorithm >5). Mean vancomycin dose 1,628.8 ± 584.2 mg/day (range 250–2400 mg/d); duration to DRESS onset 14–62 days (mean 20.6 ± 12.9 d). Hepatitis defined as GPT elevation >3-fold of upper normal limit (36 U/L): present in 13/26 (50.0%). Acute renal failure in 10 (38.5%); 2 deceased (7.7%) overall. HLA associations with DRESS: HLA-A*32:01 (OR 7.8), HLA-B*07:05 (OR 32.3), HLA-B*40:06 (OR 4.7), HLA-B*67:01 (OR 44.8) vs general population. LAT confirmed vancomycin as culprit in the 6 concurrently co-medicated cases (amoxicillin, ceftriaxone, teicoplanin, valproic acid, diclofenac, esomeprazole).

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 59-year-old male on peritoneal dialysis for KDIGO stage 5 chronic kidney disease who developed DRESS, including hepatic involvement with elevated liver enzymes and eosinophilia, 25 days after initiating intraperitoneal vancomycin for bacterial peritonitis. The diagnosis was confirmed with the RegiSCAR scoring system and supported by skin biopsy showing lymphocytic and eosinophilic inflammation. The patient improved after vancomycin withdrawal and systemic corticosteroids. The paper states that although vancomycin is a known DRESS causative agent, DRESS associated with intraperitoneal vancomycin is extremely rare and highlights intraperitoneal vancomycin as a potential DRESS trigger, particularly in patients with impaired renal clearance.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intraperitoneal route of administration (unusual/formulation-route departure); patient with end-stage chronic kidney disease on peritoneal dialysis (impaired renal clearance) treated for bacterial peritonitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency of 25 days after starting intraperitoneal vancomycin. DRESS diagnosis confirmed by RegiSCAR scoring and supported by skin biopsy showing lymphocytic and eosinophilic inflammation. Hepatic involvement characterized by hepatitis with elevated transaminases/elevated liver enzymes. Patient improved after drug withdrawal and systemic corticosteroid therapy. Background: type 2 diabetes, benign prostatic hyperplasia, systemic arterial hypertension. DRESS carries an estimated 10-20% mortality but no liver failure/death was reported in this patient.
