raw_record.support_text: Ciprofloxacin was involved as an idiosyncratic drug reaction in one DILI case. The cohort was adjudicated with the RUCAM method (highly probable 3, probable 7, possible 4 of 14 scored patients), with per-agent scores not reported.
raw_record.extra_details: One idiosyncratic DILI case; RUCAM assessment applied in the cohort but per-agent score not disclosed.

raw_record.support_text: An 84-year-old nursing-home woman developed acute cholestatic jaundice while taking ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for a urinary tract infection. On the sixth day of treatment a pruritic erythematous rash appeared on the chest and abdomen and ciprofloxacin was stopped because of a suspected allergic reaction; three days later she developed yellowish discoloration of skin and conjunctivae with abnormal liver function tests, elevated plasma cholesterol but normal prothrombin time and albumin. Liver function tests normalized within one month and remained normal at three months. The discussion and conclusions state this is considered a probable hepatic injury attributable to ciprofloxacin and, reportedly, the first case of an acute cholestatic reaction caused by ciprofloxacin.
raw_record.extra_details: 84-year-old woman in a nursing home; indication urinary tract infection; ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily; erythematous pruritic rash on chest and abdomen on day 6 prompted drug cessation; jaundice appeared 3 days later with disturbed liver function tests; elevated plasma cholesterol with normal prothrombin time and albumin; supportive fluids given; liver function normalized within one month and remained normal at three months; patient asymptomatic; authors call it probable hepatic involvement (atteinte hépatique imputable) and the first reported acute cholestatic reaction caused by ciprofloxacin; causality mechanism unknown.

raw_record.support_text: Several other patients were diagnosed with DILI, including 1 treated with ciprofloxacin (ages 64-80); resolution of liver function test abnormalities eventually occurred in all patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Patients aged 64-80; eventual resolution of liver function test abnormalities.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN Prospective Study cohort, ciprofloxacin was implicated as a cause of DILI, and cases attributed to it showed a higher frequency of increased eosinophil counts (33%). The paper notes that ciprofloxacin is known frequently to cause immuno-allergic liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated among the ten most frequent prescription drugs causing DILI in the DILIN cohort; increased eosinophil count frequency 33%; described as a known cause of immuno-allergic liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: A 44-year-old woman developed severe hepatitis 3 weeks after starting a 7-day ciprofloxacin (ciprofloxacina) therapy; liver biopsy showed submassive hepatic necrosis, other possible causes of liver damage were ruled out, and liver function tests returned to normal 4 months after jaundice appeared. The temporal relationship between ciprofloxacin administration and the adverse event, and the absence of other causes of hepatotoxicity, suggest ciprofloxacin was the causative agent. The stated objective describes this as a probable case of ciprofloxacin-induced hepatotoxicity, and the conclusion states that clinical and causal evaluation suggests ciprofloxacin can cause severe liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: 44-year-old woman developed severe (submassive) hepatic necrosis 3 weeks after initiating a 7-day ciprofloxacin course; icterus appeared and liver function tests normalized 4 months later; other causes of hepatic toxicity excluded. Evidence cited that two drugs of the same family (fluoroquinolones) have caused hepatic toxicity, and several unpublished hepatotoxicity cases associated with ciprofloxacin were reported to the manufacturer.

raw_record.support_text: The patient was diagnosed with ciprofloxacin-induced cholestatic liver injury after excluding other causes of cholestasis (hepatitis A/B/C/E serology and autoimmune antibodies were negative). The onset of symptoms and liver enzyme derangements following ciprofloxacin use, improvement in clinical and biochemical parameters after cessation, and liver biopsy findings (centrivenular cholestasis with focal mixed steatosis) all suggested ciprofloxacin-induced cholestatic liver injury. The RUCAM causality assessment scored the case as "highly probable." The discussion further states ciprofloxacin can cause dose-independent idiosyncratic DILI and that most ciprofloxacin-induced liver injury cases manifest within two to three weeks of therapy, usually with a hepatocellular or cholestatic LFT pattern, rarely mixed.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a woman with ciprofloxacin-induced cholestatic liver injury manifesting with deep jaundice and widespread excoriations. On admission: total bilirubin 16.7 mg/dL (direct 13.3, indirect 3.4), ALT 172 U/L, ALP 866 U/L, INR 1.6; LFTs and INR normalized by 6 weeks. Liver biopsy showed centrivenular canalicular and hepatocellular cholestasis with focal macrovesicular steatosis, fibrosis score 0/6, favoring drug-induced cholestasis. RUCAM "highly probable." Other possible culprits fosfomycin and cefixime were used three months prior and deemed unlikely to contribute. Ciprofloxacin-associated injury is dose-independent and idiosyncratic; symptoms typically begin within 2-3 weeks of initiation. Phenotype: drug-induced cholestasis/cholestatic liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: The prospective DILIN study enrolled DILI cases attributed to four fluoroquinolones available in the US during the study period: ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, and gatifloxacin. Attribution by expert opinion scored 9 of 12 (75%) cases as definite or very likely and 3 as probable.
raw_record.extra_details: One of 12 prospectively enrolled DILIN cases attributed to fluoroquinolones at therapeutic doses; spectrum ranged from cholestatic (high AP 603 U/L, bilirubin 33.4 mg/dL, prolonged jaundice, vanishing bile duct syndrome, Case 3) to hepatocellular (ALT 1684 U/L leading to hepatic failure and death, Case 12); 6 cases without jaundice of which 4 had mixed enzyme pattern and self-limited course; histology showed eosinophils in all 4 and increased plasma cells in 2; short latency and immunoallergic features suggest hypersensitivity; Case 8 had repeated reactions to ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin (ALT up 1680 IU/L); 2 cases had competing co-suspects (amoxicillin/clavulanate and metronidazole) deemed unlikely/possible.

raw_record.support_text: Ciprofloxacin was among the antibiotics most often responsible for DILI with four cases in the series. The pattern distribution was two hepatocellular, one cholestatic and one mixed; three of the cases involved jaundice (bilirubin ≥2 ULN).
raw_record.extra_details: Four of 77 DILI cases; pattern 2 hepatocellular/1 cholestatic/1 mixed; duration of treatment median 7 (2-7) days, time to biochemical resolution 32 (26-45) days. Three jaundice cases listed (listed as Ciproxin), bilirubin 2.2-9.6 ULN.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that although fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin are rarely implicated, it is a cause of idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (DILI), and describes two cases of idiosyncratic DILI following ciprofloxacin treatment. In Case 1 (35-year-old man, periorbital cellulitis), elevated AST and ALT developed on the second day of treatment with abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting; exclusion of other causes and cessation of ciprofloxacin led to clinical improvement and normalization of liver function tests. In Case 2 (82-year-old man, osteomyelitis), jaundice and elevated AST, ALT, ALP and total bilirubin developed on the tenth day; exclusion of other causes and cessation of ciprofloxacin again led to improvement and normalization of LFTs.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1: 35-year-old man, ciprofloxacin for periorbital cellulitis, liver-test abnormality (elevated AST and ALT) with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting on treatment day 2; infectious hepatitis, autoimmune disease and structural liver disease excluded; dechallenge produced improvement and normalization of LFTs. Case 2: 82-year-old man, ciprofloxacin for osteomyelitis, jaundice with elevated AST, ALT, ALP and total bilirubin on treatment day 10; other DILI causes excluded; dechallenge produced improvement and normalization of LFTs. Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic described as a rarely reported cause of DILI.

raw_record.support_text: A 74-year-old female with unremarkable past medical history was treated with ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BID for 3 days for a urinary tract infection. One week later she re-presented with aspartate transaminase 1106 U/L, alanine transaminase 789 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 338 U/L, and total bilirubin 2.75 mg/dL; over 3 days she developed worsening cholestasis and coagulopathy (INR rising from 1.0 to 2.5). Liver biopsy showed mild to moderate cholestatic changes with multifocal chronic inflammation. The CIOMS/RUCAM causality score was 8, indicating a high or definite probability that ciprofloxacin caused the patient's hepatotoxicity. A one-week prednisone course was unsuccessful and the patient died shortly thereafter. The authors conclude that, although rare, ciprofloxacin may be associated with severe cholestatic induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 74-year-old female with unremarkable past medical history treated for urinary tract infection; ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BID for 3 days. Re-presented ~1 week later: AST 1106 U/L, ALT 789 U/L, ALP 338 U/L, total bilirubin 2.75. Worsening cholestasis and coagulopathy with INR rising from 1.0 at presentation to 2.5 at day 3. Liver biopsy: minimal fatty infiltration, mild-moderate cholestatic changes, multifocal chronic inflammation with rare intermixed neutrophils, no plasma cells or granulomas, few ballooned hepatocytes, no hepatocellular necrosis, focal mild periportal fibrosis on reticulin/trichrome stains. CIOMS/RUCAM score 8 (high or definite probability). One-week prednisone trial for possible hypersensitivity unsuccessful; palliative care consulted and patient died. Competing causes excluded (negative serology/nucleic acid for HAV, HBV, HCV, HEV, CMV, HSV, EBV; non-reactive autoimmune markers; negative toxicology and acetaminophen level; no herbal or other prescription co-medications).

raw_record.support_text: In the three cases observed by the authors, the temporal relation and short latency (median 2 days) between use of ciprofloxacin (or levofloxacin) and liver damage, the absence of other hepatotoxic drugs, exclusion of other causes of hepatitis, and a compatible liver histology in case 3 supported the diagnosis of fluoroquinolone-associated liver injury. Dechallenge was positive in all cases and rechallenge was not performed. RUCAM classified the cases as probable or highly probable and the Naranjo algorithm as possible or probable.
raw_record.extra_details: Diagnosis of fluoroquinolone-associated liver injury in 3 cases; median latency 2 days; patients were not taking other hepatotoxic drugs; other causes of hepatitis (viral, autoimmune, alcohol) excluded; compatible liver histology in case 3; dechallenge positive, no rechallenge; RUCAM probable/highly probable, Naranjo possible/probable. SPC lists hepatotoxicity as a rare adverse reaction of ciprofloxacin related to both oral and intravenous administration.

raw_record.support_text: In a DILIN adjudicated cohort (383 DILI cases, causality definite/highly likely/probable), 99 drugs belonging to BDDCS classes 1–4 were responsible for the DILI episodes. Four compounds—ciprofloxacin, nitrofurantoin, cefdinir, and levonorgestrel/ethinylestradiol—accounted for all DILI cases belonging to BDDCS class 4. Class 4 DILI cases had a significantly lower percentage of jaundiced patients (P<.001), lower rate of absolute eosinophilia >500/µL (P=.008), lower peak ALT (P=.001) and aspartate aminotransferase (P<.001), and lowest hospitalization rate (45%, P=.01) compared with other classes.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed as one of four agents that accounted for all BDDCS class 4 DILI cases in the DILIN cohort (383 eligible cases, 107 drugs, inclusion required causality score 1/2/3=definite/highly likely/probable, oral administration, known daily dose). Class 4 aggregate features (not drug-specific): lower jaundice (P<.001), lower eosinophilia>500/µL (P=.008), lower peak ALT (P=.001) and AST (P<.001), lowest hospitalization rate 45% (P=.01).

raw_record.support_text: The report describes a case of cholestatic jaundice induced by ciprofloxacin, an antimicrobial agent.
raw_record.extra_details: 47-year-old white man treated with ciprofloxacin 500 mg po twice a day for occult pyuria; jaundice and pruritus appeared after three doses and ciprofloxacin was discontinued 24 hr later. Peak labs: total bilirubin 10 mg/liter (normal 0.0-0.3), direct bilirubin 6.5 mg/liter, alkaline phosphatase 163 IU/liter, AST 109 IU/liter, ALT 308 IU/liter; prothrombin time prolonged 5 sec then normalized with parenteral vitamin K. Hepatitis A/B/C serology and PCR negative; ultrasound normal (single small gallbladder stone on CT). Liver biopsy showed mild to moderate intracellular and intracanalicular cholestasis, scattered necrotic hepatocytes with foci of chronic inflammatory cells, and mild macro- and microvesicular steatosis, without fibrosis or cirrhosis. Jaundice/severity improved and liver tests returned to normal over 12 weeks; patient was evaluated for possible fulminant liver failure but did not develop it.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN prospective registry, ciprofloxacin accounted for 16 of 899 adjudicated DILI cases. DILI caused by ciprofloxacin had a 19% mortality rate, the highest among the compared agents, versus 0-1% for minocycline, cefazolin, and amoxicillin-clavulanate.
raw_record.extra_details: 16 adjudicated DILI cases; DILI-caused mortality 19%, the highest among compared agents.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN analysis by Vuppalanchi et al, all drugs causing liver injury did so as single agents and were assessed as being at least probably related or higher using standardized scoring criteria and expert opinion. Class 4 agents (low solubility, poor metabolism) included nitrofurantoin, ciprofloxacin, cefdinir, and levonorgestrel with ethinyl estradiol, representing 40 of the 372 cases of DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: Class 4 BDDCS agent (low solubility, poor metabolism) in the DILIN analysis of 383 instances of DILI caused by 99 single agents; classified as at least probably related.

raw_record.support_text: The CIOMS/RUCAM scale was assessed to be 8, defining the suspicion of ciprofloxacin as the cause of the patient's hepatotoxicity as highly probable. Factors included time of onset between medication use and symptoms, course of injury, risk factors, concomitant drug administration, potential non-drug origins of hepatic failure, documented information on ciprofloxacin hepatotoxicity, and response to readministration of the antibiotic. The patient presented with worsening fatigue, jaundice, ascites, and rising bilirubin (TBIL 22.6, INR 1.8). The background section states the background states that ciprofloxacin-induced hepatotoxicity proved fatal.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 74-year-old female treated with ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection; onset of nausea/vomiting on day 4-5 of first course; drug discontinued day 5; patient rechallenged with three days of ciprofloxacin during a later admission before ciprofloxacin was suspected. Liver biopsy showed active chronic hepatitis with cholestasis and portal and periportal fibrosis. Labs included AST 1,106-1,263, ALT 789-870, ALP 338-496, TBIL up to 22.6, INR 1.8. CIOMS/RUCAM score 8 (highly probable). Concurrent medications simvastatin (discontinued during workup), pantoprazole, levothyroxine were considered; competing causes (viral hepatitis A-E, HSV, CMV, EBV, autoimmune, alpha-1 antitrypsin, ceruloplasmin, malignancy) were ruled out. Fatal outcome from ciprofloxacin-induced liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that Ciprofloxacin, though generally well tolerated, may cause idiosyncratic hypersensitivity reactions presenting as liver injury or life-threatening toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). The authors emphasize that early recognition and prompt treatment of the patient in their reported case help prevent fatal outcomes, attributing the liver injury to ciprofloxacin exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report from Nepal. Liver injury occurred in the context of an idiosyncratic hypersensitivity reaction that also manifested as life-threatening toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), which carried risk of fatal outcome. Authors note easy over-the-counter availability of antibiotics in WHO-SEARO countries and recommend antibiotic stewardship to prevent such undetected complications.

raw_record.support_text: A letter by Lucena et al. attributed 14 cases of hepatotoxicity up to 1998 to ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, enoxacin and ofloxacin. Quinolone-associated hepatotoxicity has been reported as hepatocellular damage, cholestatic damage, ductopenia, and acute liver failure and death, with biopsy findings of central-zone necrosis and mixed inflammatory infiltrates with abundant eosinophils, implying an immuno-allergic mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: One of four quinolones (with norfloxacin, enoxacin, ofloxacin) to which 14 hepatotoxicity cases up to 1998 were attributed (Lucena letter). Quinolone-class reports: hepatocellular damage, cholestatic damage, ductopenia, acute liver failure and death; biopsy showed central-zone necrosis and mixed inflammatory infiltrates with abundant eosinophils (immuno-allergic mechanism); jaundice could begin up to several weeks after end of treatment, complicating causality assessment.

raw_record.support_text: A 41-year-old male presented with pruritus, rash, nausea, and diarrhea after taking ciprofloxacin (4 days prior) for a recent urinary tract infection, and was found to have acute renal failure and hepatic dysfunction. Labs showed total bilirubin 2.9, alkaline phosphatase 351, AST 832, ALT 959, with LFTs peaking on hospital day 3 (bilirubin 3.6, AP 493, AST 1059, ALT 1231) and INR 2.04. After gastrointestinal workup, viral (EBV, CMV, HIV, Hepatitis A-C) and autoimmune (SMA, ANA) etiologies were negative, and the patient was diagnosed with ciprofloxacin-induced liver injury (CILI). Given deteriorating hepatic failure he was treated with N-acetylcysteine and steroids with rapid improvement in hepatic and renal function.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Case patient had dilated cardiomyopathy, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, gout, obesity, concurrent acute renal failure, and was taking multiple co-medications (spironolactone, allopurinol last dose 4 weeks earlier, lisinopril, furosemide, metolazone); DRESS due to allopurinol was considered in the differential but excluded because the patient met only 2 of 3 RegiSCAR and 2 of 5 DIHS criteria.
raw_record.extra_details: Ciprofloxacin taken for urinary tract infection, exposure 4 days before presentation. R-ratio of 5.83 suggested hepatocellular injury. Symptoms included pruritus, rash, nausea, diarrhea; LFTs peaked on hospital day 3 (bilirubin 3.6, AP 493, AST 1059, ALT 1231), INR 2.04. Mechanism thought to be a hypersensitivity response to fluoroquinolones; steroid and N-acetylcysteine therapy led to rapid improvement (AP 97, AST 298, ALT 341, INR 1.2, Cr 1.5). Discussion states CILI carried a 15% mortality rate in one study, consistent with 10-80% mortality for DILI with acute liver failure. CT showed hepatic steatosis, normal triglycerides/ceruloplasmin/iron saturation.

raw_record.support_text: A 22-year-old male developed generalized pruritus and fluid-filled bullous skin lesions 2 days after taking Ciprofloxacin (obtained over-the-counter) for a surgical site infection, along with scleral icterus, markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase (1390 U/L), conjugated bilirubin (13.7 mg/dl), and transaminases. Based on clinical findings, biopsy, and laboratory values he was diagnosed with toxic epidermal necrolysis and drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis. The Naranjo ADR probability scale gave a score of 6, implicating a probable adverse drug reaction caused by Ciprofloxacin.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Young adult male on over-the-counter Ciprofloxacin; prior/co-exposure to paracetamol taken for fever before Ciprofloxacin onset; surgical site infection context.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of toxic epidermal necrolysis with cholestatic hepatitis; Naranjo ADR probability score 6 (probable, 5-8 range); lab findings SGOT 283 U/L, SGPT 246 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 1390 U/L, total bilirubin 14 mg/dl, conjugated bilirubin 13.7 mg/dl, INR 2.70; skin biopsy consistent with epidermal necrolysis secondary to ciprofloxacin; normal hepatobiliary ultrasonography; no dose reported.

raw_record.support_text: The abstract states that amongst recreational drugs, cocaine, amphetamines and ecstasy (methylenedioxymethamphetamine) have been known to cause acute liver failure (ALF) as a complication, and presents a single case of ALF secondary to amphetamine ingestion, which recovered rapidly after intravenous N-acetylcysteine.
raw_record.extra_details: 20-year-old male with no significant past medical history ingested 2 g of methamphetamine and developed ALF. On admission urine toxicology was positive for amphetamines; labs showed AST 121 IU/L, ALT 32 U/L, PT 19.4 s, PTT 36.5 s, INR 1.61, and normal bilirubin. Patient was obtunded, hyperthermic (42 °C), hypertensive then hypotensive, and recovered rapidly after intravenous N-acetylcysteine. Clinical phenotype is acute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: In a single case, a 38-year-old male with a six-year history of chronic methamphetamine addiction died from complications of prolonged substance abuse. Histopathological examination of his liver tissue, stained with hematoxylin and eosin, showed cholestasis with degeneration of hepatocytes and inflammatory cellular infiltrates; representative images showed hepatocyte cholestasis with bile salt accumulation, minimal portal mononuclear/lymphocyte inflammation, and no significant fibrosis. The discussion characterizes this as METH-induced hepatocellular damage and hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic methamphetamine (METH) substance abuse/addiction in a single male patient who died; findings based on one autopsy case only.
raw_record.extra_details: 38-year-old male with a 6-year history of chronic methamphetamine addiction who died; liver histology showed cholestasis (bile salt accumulation inside hepatocytes), hepatocyte degeneration, minimal portal inflammation with mononuclear lymphocytes, and no significant fibrosis. Study also reported elevated liver enzymes including GGT (with diagnostic accuracy assessed via AUC and a meaningful cut-off value, interpreted with caution as GGT can rise with alcohol, medications, hepatitis or bile duct obstruction) and elevated blood urea as a sensitive marker of METH-related metabolic disturbance reflecting disrupted protein metabolism and impaired liver processing (METH-induced hepatotoxicity).

raw_record.support_text: The authors state it is exceedingly difficult to assess the importance of azaserine in the production of hepatic injury, since many patients were in poor general condition, had received multiple blood transfusions, and often had liver involvement by neoplastic cells. Despite jaundice in some patients, there was no histological evidence of drug toxicity in the liver parenchyma, and in children treated with azaserine there was no evidence of hepatic injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with advanced Hodgkin's disease, poor general condition, prior multiple blood transfusions, and liver involvement by neoplastic cells; pre-existing hepatic damage possible.
raw_record.extra_details: No histological evidence of drug toxicity in liver parenchyma even among patients who became jaundiced, so jaundice was not attributed to azaserine; attributable to disease progression, transfusions (possible homologous serum jaundice), and hepatic neoplastic involvement. Fifteen children treated with azaserine showed no evidence of hepatic injury. The authors report that azaserine cannot be stated with certainty to produce serious systemic intoxication and recommend caution and prompt stopping in debilitated or pre-existing hepatic dysfunction patients.

raw_record.support_text: A 31-year-old woman treated with fluindione for deep venous thrombosis developed abdominal pain, pruritus, anorexia and asthenia two weeks after starting treatment, with severe hepatic cytolysis (TGO 160 UI/l, TGP 421 UI/l) and negative viral (A, B, C, E, CMV, EBV) and autoimmune markers. A mixed hepatitis with cholestatic predominance was diagnosed and fluindione was suspected; after discontinuation, her general state improved and liver tests became almost normal in one month. The case was reported to the pharmacovigilance unit, and the French causality assessment gave an imputability score likely in favor of fluindione (C2, S2), consistent with drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: 31-year-old woman treated for deep venous thrombosis (prior episode of phlebitis treated with fluindione 2 years earlier; only other drug was a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system). Injury appeared 2 weeks after starting fluindione; severe hepatic cytolysis with TGO 160 UI/l and TGP 421 UI/l; viral (A,B,C,E, CMV, EBV) and autoimmune markers negative; diagnosis of mixed hepatitis with cholestatic predominance; attributed to drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome (DHS), which may also cause cutaneous reaction and nephropathy; French causality assessment imputability C2,S2 (likely); improved after drug discontinuation, liver tests almost normal in 1 month; reported to pharmacovigilance unit; sensitization occurred at first fluindione exposure in 2006; authors conclude fluindione and all indane-dione derivatives are contraindicated due to allergic cross-reactivity risk.

raw_record.support_text: Eleven episodes of hepatitis reported to the regional monitoring center of Bordeaux in 1985 involved patients treated with fluindione, an oral anticoagulant. The number of patients treated in the area was estimated as T = 2,000 with an annual background incidence of similar liver injury of 1/2,500. The drug, which is pharmacologically different from other indane-dione derivatives, was considered possibly hepatotoxic, and this risk was subsequently confirmed by the French National Board for Drug Safety.
raw_record.extra_details: Eleven episodes of hepatitis reported to the regional monitoring center of Bordeaux during 1985 involving patients treated with fluindione, an oral anticoagulant; estimated treated patients T = 2,000 from prescription data; annual background incidence of similar liver injury estimated at 1/2,500; calculated m = I·T = 0.8 with critical number Xcr below 11 for alpha ≤ 30%; Poisson P(X ≥ 11 | H0) < 0.0001. Initial classification as 'possibly hepatotoxic' (pharmacologically different from other indane-dione derivatives) was subsequently confirmed by the French National Board for Drug Safety.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective cohort study of approximately 300 subjects, initial therapy with ritonavir, a protease inhibitor approved by the FDA in 2000, resulted in hepatotoxicity in 30% of patients (95% confidence interval 17.9–44.6%). Hepatotoxicity was assessed by monitoring aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) activity, and the odds ratio for hepatotoxicity following full-dose (400 mg) ritonavir was 6.2 (95% CI 2.8–13.7). Hepatotoxicity manifested through non-specific gastrointestinal symptoms (upper and lower abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea), as well as jaundice and hepatomegaly.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity occurred in 30% of patients (95% CI 17.9–44.6%) in an initial-therapy prospective cohort (~300 subjects); odds ratio for hepatotoxicity at full dose 400 mg was 6.2 (95% CI 2.8–13.7). Assessed by AST and ALT monitoring; manifestations included unspecified GI symptoms (abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea), jaundice and hepatomegaly.

raw_record.support_text: Belinostat, a new HDACI, was studied as a single agent in refractory/relapsed lymphoma as daily infusions on days 1–5 every 21 days. Adverse effects were nausea, fatigue, and fever; severe reactions included acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia, and toxic liver failure, with 7.8 % of patients dying of drug reaction. Fatalities were attributed to drug-related tumor lysis syndrome, hepatic failure, and ventricular fibrillation from QTc prolongation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Use as a single agent in refractory/relapsed lymphoma (AITL constituted 10 of 22 patients); indication-restricted population.

raw_record.support_text: In the DDI stage of this phase 1 study, all nine participants receiving GDC-2394 with midazolam experienced at least one AE, and two participants experienced SAEs of grade 4 drug-induced liver injury (DILI) on days 18 and 20 that were considered related to study treatment and met Hy's law criteria (AST or ALT >3x ULN and total bilirubin >2x ULN or clinical jaundice). The sponsor halted all further enrollment, and both participants recovered, one receiving oral ursodeoxycholic acid. Additionally, three participants experienced events consistent with hepatic injury after completing GDC-2394 dosing, including one participant with a grade 2 ALT increase on day 11 considered related to study drug that resolved by day 20.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Occurred in the drug-drug interaction stage where GDC-2394 was co-administered with midazolam in healthy participants; study enrollment was halted after these events.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase 1 first-in-human SAD/MAD/FE/DDI study (NCT, 2021-2022). Two SAEs of grade 4 DILI reported on days 18 and 20, both meeting Hy's law criteria (AST or ALT >3x ULN and total bilirubin >2x ULN or clinical jaundice), considered related to study treatment; both participants recovered, one treated with oral ursodeoxycholic acid. Seven (78%) DDI participants reported events considered related (fatigue and DILI most frequent). Three participants had events consistent with hepatic injury after completion of dosing; one had a grade 2 ALT increase on day 11 (related) resolving to grade 1 by day 20. No deaths. DILI was the reason the DDI stage (planned n=15) was halted at n=9.

raw_record.support_text: Phenindione jaundice, which has been reported previously, is a combination of hepatocellular and cholestatic jaundice, usually presenting in the 5th week of therapy. Pyrexia is the presenting feature, and a rash may appear without constant relation to the onset of jaundice. Serum-transaminase levels were greatly raised during the pre-icteric period in the two cases the author described (Perkins 1962), and liver biopsy in one case showed eosinophil infiltration of the portal tracts and increased lipochrome pigmentation with increased mitoses, mostly arrested in metaphase.
raw_record.extra_details: Jaundice described as a combination of hepatocellular and cholestatic jaundice, usually presenting in the 5th week of anticoagulant therapy; resembles chlorpromazine jaundice, especially when cholestasis is prominent. Pyrexia is the presenting feature; a rash may appear without constant relation to jaundice onset. Serum-transaminase levels greatly raised in the pre-icteric period in two cases (Perkins 1962). Liver biopsy in one case showed eosinophil infiltration of the portal tracts, increased lipochrome pigmentation, and increased mitoses mostly arrested in metaphase, possibly reflecting increased regenerative activity after hepatic necrosis or a dinitrophenol-like mitotic-poison action of phenindione. Phenindione (2-phenyl-1,3-indanedione). Context: anticoagulant, long-term therapy.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports two further cases of phenindione jaundice, together with serum-transaminase studies; liver biopsy was performed in the second case. Phenindione may cause hepatocellular jaundice with cholestasis, usually in the 5th week of therapy, and cholestasis may predominate, resembling chlorpromazine jaundice. Improvement was rapid when phenindione was stopped and steroids instituted, though relapse occurred when the steroid dose was reduced; 133 such cases have been reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases of jaundice reported with serum-transaminase studies; liver biopsy performed in the second case. Onset typically in the 5th week of phenindione anticoagulant therapy. Cholestasis may predominate, closely resembling chlorpromazine jaundice. Pyrexia during therapy with serum-transaminase estimation and daily urine testing for bile may detect early liver involvement. Improvement rapid after stopping phenindione and instituting steroids, with possible relapse on steroid dose reduction. A total of 133 phenindione jaundice/sensitivity cases reported (Bingle and Shine 1959 reviewed thirteen).

raw_record.support_text: Ditercalinium, a 7H-pyridocarbazole dimer designed as a bisintercalator, showed promising antitumor activity (NSC366241) and had been introduced in phase 1 clinical trial until it proved to be highly hepatotoxic, possibly as a strong inhibitor of the electron-transport chain in the mitochondrion inner membrane, and was hence withdrawn from human testing.
raw_record.extra_details: Antitumor anticancer agent (NSC366241), 7H-pyridocarbazole dimer designed as a bisintercalator; introduced in phase 1 clinical trial; proved highly hepatotoxic and was withdrawn from human testing; suggested mechanism is strong inhibition of the electron-transport chain in the mitochondrial inner membrane (as an investigative hypothesis).

raw_record.support_text: Ditercalinium was originally designed to bis-intercalate into DNA with high affinity and displayed strong cytotoxicity on experimental tumor cells. However, it turned out after a clinical trial that irreversible hepatotoxicity is a dose-limiting side-effect. The reagent specifically accumulates in mitochondria, depletes mtDNA, and the drug was ultimately abandoned as a clinical anticancer drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Irreversible hepatotoxicity was a dose-limiting side-effect; ditercalinium is a DNA bis-intercalator that specifically accumulates in mitochondria and depletes mtDNA; the drug was ultimately abandoned as a clinical anticancer drug. The cardiotoxic doxorubicin and myopathic AZT (mtDNA depletion) are mentioned in the same paragraph but are not attributed to liver injury, so no records are made for them.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes valproate (VPA), a widely prescribed antiepileptic drug, as a therapy that 'is associated with hepatotoxicity, a fatal and idiosyncratic adverse drug reaction,' with reported incidences of about 1/40,000 in adults, 1/5000 in children, and 1/500 in high-risk populations. It further states that 2-propyl-4-pentenoic acid (4-ene-VPA) and 2-propyl-2,4-pentadienoic acid (2,4-diene-VPA) are considered the main hepatotoxic metabolites of VPA, and frames the goal of the study as identifying risk factors for VPA-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: VPA is a first-generation antiepileptic drug. The paper studied 279 Chinese epilepsy patients on valproate monotherapy, of whom 79 had abnormal liver function (ANLFT group) and 200 had normal liver function (NLFT group). Serum 4-ene-VPA and 2,4-diene-VPA concentrations were significantly higher in the ANLFT group. Logistic regression identified CYP2C9 and CYP2A6 as significant risk factors for hepatotoxicity (7.50-fold and 5.13-fold increased risk, respectively); the paper reports hepatotoxicity incidence of ~1/40,000 in adults, 1/5000 in children, and 1/500 in high-risk populations, and characterizes the reaction as fatal and idiosyncratic.

raw_record.support_text: The letter presents a case of an HIV-infected man who developed acute hepatitis due to valproic acid (VPA) given concurrently with cytochrome P450 active drugs (ritonavir, nevirapine). The authors note that hepatotoxicity due to valproic acid is a known event and that VPA's use in psychiatry has enlarged the at-risk population; pediatric epilepsy risk factors include neurological disease, male gender, and concomitant use of hepatic P450-inducing drugs.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 51-year-old HIV-infected man with multidrug-resistant HIV and bipolar disorder; concurrent antiretroviral therapy (ritonavir 400 mg BID, saquinavir 400 mg BID, stavudine 40 mg, nevirapine 200 mg) with unresolved possible enhancement by P450 inhibitor ritonavir or inducer nevirapine; low serum carnitine.
raw_record.extra_details: VPA used for mood stabilization; VPA serum level remained therapeutic throughout. On Day 5 ascites and pleural effusions developed; all drugs discontinued on Day 5. Infectious workup (hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV serology; urine, blood, CSF cultures) negative; LP negative. Liver-associated enzymes trended downward on Day 7 after levocarnitine (1 gm tid) started on Day 6; patient discharged on Day 11. LAEs later remained normal after antiretrovirals resumed with efavirenz replacing nevirapine. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (added for suspected UTI) was discontinued and its role as a competing cause was not implicated; rash deemed secondary to the sulfa drug.

raw_record.support_text: The paper clinically characterizes fatal cases of hepatic dysfunction associated with valproic acid (VPA), dividing them into a chronic progressive form (4-6 week course of lethargy, vomiting, nausea, anorexia, jaundice and edema, mostly in older patients, with unimpressive histology except cholestasis in a few cases) and an acute fulminating form usually occurring in children under 12 years of age, with abrupt onset of coma, markedly abnormal coagulation, elevated SGOT and ammonia, microvesicular fatty changes in hepatocytes with mitochondrial dissolution on biopsy, and all reported patients in this category dying.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute fulminating form is restricted to children under 12; chronic progressive form occurs mostly in older patients; severe cases may involve predisposing factors such as inborn partial deficiencies of mitochondrial enzymes, added stress of an acute viral illness, or concomitant use of other drugs metabolized by mitochondrial enzyme systems.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic form: 4-6 week course of slowly increasing lethargy, vomiting, nausea, anorexia, jaundice and edema; recovery if VPA stopped early; histology unimpressive except cholestasis in a few cases. Acute fulminating form: sudden onset of coma with signs of increased intracranial pressure, jaundice absent, marked coagulation abnormalities and elevated SGOT and ammonia at symptom onset, renal failure in some patients, liver biopsies showing microvesicular fatty changes and mitochondrial dissolution; all reported patients in this category died. Mechanism: VPA (2-n-propylpentanoic acid), a short-chain fatty acid; Haas et al (1981) showed VPA inhibits oxidative phosphorylation in isolated rat liver mitochondria; hypothesized mitochondrial decompensation spectrum from transient SGOT/ammonia elevations to chronic progressive hepatic dysfunction to acute generalized mitochondrial failure, hepatic failure, cerebral edema, coma and death.

raw_record.support_text: Of 470 epileptic patients with measured VPA serum metabolites, 170 asymptomatic subjects served as a reference. Among 11 patients with early symptoms and signs of possible fatal VPA-associated hepatotoxicity, reversible or irreversible fulminant liver failure occurred in 5 children, and 4 children had a fatal outcome (3 with massive lactic acidosis). The paper states that VPA hepatotoxicity is considered dose-independent and idiosyncratic, and that the most toxic compound could be VPA itself, possibly unmasking an inborn or acquired metabolic defect in fatty-acid processing.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric epileptic patients; suspected underlying inborn or acquired defect in fatty-acid metabolism that VPA may unmask.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 470 epileptic patients; 11 patients with symptoms/signs of possible fatal VPA-associated hepatotoxicity, 5 with fulminant liver failure, 4 fatal (3 with massive lactic acidosis). Benign presentations included unusually severe side effect at initiation, high VPA dosage, reversible coagulation impairment with bleeding and slight transaminase increase (1 child), and reversible liver dysfunction with febrile illness (7 patients). Affected patients showed impaired VPA beta-oxidation and increased metabolites of omega- and omega1-hydroxylation and dehydrogenation; 2-PGA (omega-oxidation end product) was found in some children in prior reports. Pathogenesis described as dose-independent and idiosyncratic.

raw_record.support_text: A synopsis of 16 German patients, all children, describes liver failure while receiving VPA (valproate). Clinical signs of impending liver failure appeared >8 weeks before death in 6 of 16 patients, and pathological symptoms were seen in all patients 2-4 weeks before death. Reversible cases of VPA hepatotoxicity were noted, and the fatal outcome of liver failure might be avoided if nonspecific early symptoms are recognized as potentially dangerous side effects of VPA. Liver dystrophy leading to hepatic failure and coma hepaticum was the cause of death in all autopsy cases, and a hepatogenic cause of death was strongly suggested in the remaining patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients (children treated for epilepsy with VPA), representing 16 German cases
raw_record.extra_details: 16 patients with fatal VPA-associated liver failure; all died of hepatic failure/coma hepaticum (autopsy) or strongly suspected hepatogenic death. Liver histology was uniform: hepatocellular damage with cellular ballooning and microvesicular steatosis in all patients, acidophilic single-cell or cell-group necrosis mostly in central lobular areas, pseudoglandular hepatocyte arrangement with bile thrombi, destruction of liver architecture (cirrhosis criterion) in 9 of 10 examined patients, and striking bile duct proliferation; one case showed only microvesicular steatosis and cholesteatosis without bile duct proliferation. Associated findings included pneumonia (4), sepsis (3), shock (4), cerebral edema, and hemorrhagic necrotizing pancreatitis (patients 2, 7, 10). VPA treatment durations 6-22 weeks; maximum VPA doses 24-55 mg/kg; discontinuation of VPA within ≤1 week after first symptoms did not change the rapid fatal outcome in patients 1, 2, 6, 7.

raw_record.support_text: The study compared L-carnitine-treated and untreated children who developed valproate-induced hepatotoxicity (92 total patients, 42 treated with L-carnitine and 50 untreated). After onset of toxicity, valproate was stopped after a median of 7 days in the L-carnitine group and 8 days in the untreated group. The children often had poor nutrition and chronic illness, and 69% were below the 25th percentile for weight.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients treated for epilepsy (two with bipolar disorder); polytherapy with other anticonvulsants (phenobarbital, carbamazepine, phenytoin, clorazepate, clonazepam) or lithium was common; many had pre-existing chronic illness/poor nutrition.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 92 children with valproate-induced hepatotoxicity collected from US, German, and other centers; valproate median dose 39 mg/kg/d (treated) and 43 mg/kg/d (untreated), duration median 81 vs 72 days. Hepatic survival was 47% (20/42) in L-carnitine-treated vs 10% (5/50) in untreated patients (p < 0.001), indicating substantial mortality from valproate-induced hepatic failure; three patients who received prophylactic L-carnitine (stopped 60-100 days before the event) had this hepatic event delayed. L-carnitine is framed as a treatment/preventive measure, not the causal agent.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe human hepatocyte injury produced by valproic acid in children treated with the drug. Liver-biopsy tissue from two additional valproic-acid-treated children with abnormal liver-function tests (not in hepatic failure), along with one of the two children in the prior case report (whose late-biopsy and autopsy tissues showed hepatocyte injury), showed ultrastructural abnormalities of parenchymal cells, including alterations of mitochondria, Golgi apparatus, peroxisomes, and pericanalicular cytoplasm. The authors state that neither the mitochondrial injury nor the overall hepatocyte injury produced by valproic acid is similar to that in Reye's syndrome or to that produced by hypoglycin or 4-pentenoic acid.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children being treated with valproic acid as an antiepileptic).
raw_record.extra_details: Evidence from ultrastructural examination of liver-biopsy and autopsy tissue in valproic-acid-treated children, including two with abnormal liver function but not hepatic failure and two from the earlier case report with late-biopsy and autopsy tissue. Findings: alterations in hepatocyte mitochondria, Golgi apparatus, peroxisomes, and pericanalicular cytoplasm. The authors explicitly conclude valproic acid causes hepatocyte injury, and that this injury is not similar to Reye's syndrome or to injury from hypoglycin or 4-pentenoic acid.

raw_record.support_text: Valproic acid (VPA) is used to treat epilepsy; its hepatotoxicity is a major concern. In epileptic children, targeted metabolomics of serum acylcarnitines showed that VPA-induced abnormal liver function resulted in accumulation of serum long-chain acylcarnitines and reduced expression of beta-oxidation genes (CPT1, CPT2, LCAD), indicating disruption of fatty acid beta-oxidation. The introduction states VPA hepatotoxicity is the most common and life-threatening adverse drug reaction, has been associated with secondary carnitine deficiency, and intravenous carnitine has been used to treat severe symptomatic hepatotoxicity caused by VPA.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (epileptic children) receiving long-term therapeutic VPA; abnormal liver function context.
raw_record.extra_details: Proposed mechanism: disruption of fatty acid beta-oxidation with accumulated serum long-chain acylcarnitines and reduced CPT1, CPT2, LCAD expression; association with secondary carnitine deficiency; hepatic steatosis and reduced beta-FAO demonstrated in VPA-exposed mice; fenofibrate (PPARalpha agonist) showed a protective effect by reversing fatty acid metabolism. Introduction notes VPA hepatotoxicity is described as the most common and life-threatening adverse reaction limiting its use.

raw_record.support_text: Valproate-induced hepatotoxicity is described as rare, but often fatal, and is attributed to direct disruption of mitochondrial processes. It is heralded by nonspecific symptoms such as lethargy, nausea/vomiting, or worsening seizures, and occurs more frequently in at-risk populations such as mentally retarded individuals, young children, and those taking multiple drugs. One proposed mechanism is drug-induced carnitine deficiency.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Reported more frequently in at-risk populations including mentally retarded individuals, young children, and patients taking multiple drugs; most children appeared malnourished (69% <25th percentile for weight, 38% <5th percentile).
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective inception cohort from the International Registry for Adverse Reactions to Valproate; 92 patients with severe, symptomatic, valproate-induced hepatotoxicity (90 with epilepsy, 2 with bipolar disorder); outcome was hepatic survival (deceased and liver transplant combined as terminal hepatic failure). Valproate stopped after a median of 7 days in L-carnitine-treated and 8 days in untreated patients. 48% of 42 L-carnitine-treated patients survived vs 10% of 50 treated with supportive care only (p < 0.001).

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes valproate-induced hepatotoxicity, noting that shortly after its introduction cases of severe and occasionally fatal hepatotoxicity in treated patients were reported, with fatal damage frequency roughly 1:10,000 in children and 1:40,000 in adults and higher with antiepileptic polytherapy; microvesicular steatosis is the principal histological finding and is attributed to decreased mitochondrial β-oxidation.

raw_record.extra_details: 39-year-old woman with fatal valproate-induced hepatotoxicity; valproate 2400 mg/day with serum concentrations in therapeutic range. Frequency of fatal valproate-induced liver damage averages roughly 1:10,000 in children and 1:40,000 in adults and is higher with antiepileptic polytherapy. Microvesicular steatosis named as the principal histological finding in valproate-induced hepatotoxicity, attributed to decreased mitochondrial β-oxidation. Case showed bilirubin 145 µM, ALAT 35 U/l, ASAT 95 U/l, prothrombin ratio 39%, ammonia 75 µM, thrombocytopenia, disseminated intravascular coagulation and hepatorenal syndrome, ending in multiorgan failure and death five days after admission. Plasma and liver free/total carnitine decreased with increased short-chain acylcarnitine ratios; liver total CoA decreased by 84% with reduced CoASH, acetyl-CoA and long-chain acyl-CoA and increased succinyl-CoA and propionyl-CoA.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the first detailed electron microscopic analysis of pure acute valproic acid (VPA)-induced hepatotoxicity in a patient recovering from severe VPA-induced biopsy-proven microvesicular steatosis with liver failure, documenting that the [1-¹³C]methionine breath test may monitor mitochondrial function in such patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Pure severe valproic acid overdose-induced microvesicular steatosis with acute liver failure, biopsy-proven, in a single recovering patient. Microvesicular steatosis attributed to acquired mitochondrial dysfunction. Electron microscopy showed small/medium lipid droplets and swollen mitochondria with decay of mitochondrial matrix and disorganized cristae. The initially abnormal [1-¹³C]methionine breath test (reflecting hepatic mitochondrial α-ketobutyrate decarboxylase activity) improved along with recovery from liver failure; results in 10 healthy volunteers trended toward the lower range. A possible negative interaction of the neuroleptic olanzapine on the breath test was considered unlikely because olanzapine has no recognized mitochondrial toxicity. The authors note hepatic tissue damage simply from excessive VPA ingestion is unlikely based on epidemiological data in acute VPA poisoning.

raw_record.extra_details: Acute biopsy-proven reversible VPA-associated hepatic failure. Liver biopsy showed diffuse massive panlobular clarification with focal hepatocellular necrosis and predominant microvesicular steatosis (oil red O); electron microscopy showed swollen mitochondria with disorganized cristae and fluffy matrix. Peak ALT 174x normal, PT 28%, factor V 24%, blood lactate 3.8 mmol/l, blood valproate 1380 µmol/l (therapeutic range 350-700). Patient recovered without liver transplantation; valproic acid was not reintroduced.

raw_record.support_text: Patient 1's condition was diagnosed as fulminant hepatitis from VPA (valproic acid) intoxication. After withdrawal of VPA and glucagon-insulin therapy, consciousness returned to normal, and SGOT, SGPT, and blood ammonia levels returned to normal within 12 days. Two patients with acute encephalopathy due to VPA intoxication were described; the liver injury was attributed to VPA intoxication.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: VPA intoxication (overdose) in two patients with acute encephalopathy
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatitis diagnosed from VPA intoxication; SGOT, SGPT, and blood ammonia normalized within 12 days after VPA withdrawal plus glucagon-insulin therapy, and consciousness returned to normal within 10 days. In patient 2 a lymphocyte stimulation test was positive with a stimulation index of 49.2 vs standard 2.0. Liver histology differed from Reye's syndrome: mitochondria were not swollen and matrix granules did not disappear; enlarged mitochondrial matrix granules (111 ± 22 nm in patient 1, 80 ± 22 nm in patient 2 vs ~32-40 nm in five chronic-hepatitis controls) and calcium content detected by energy-dispersive X-ray microanalysis in patient 1 (not patient 2).

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a young man with a previously unrecognized POLG-1 mutation who developed valproic acid-associated acute liver failure and was treated successfully with liver transplantation. It also notes that patients with POLG-1 gene mutations have an increased risk of valproic acid-induced acute liver failure, that severe valproate hepatotoxicity most commonly arises in children within the first 3 months of treatment with an estimated incidence of 1 in 40,000 treated patients, and that many experts consider valproic acid-induced acute liver failure in patients with mitochondrial disorders a contraindication to liver transplant due to high mortality among transplanted children.

These drugs were chosen because they have characteristic signatures in clinical presentation.
