Drug was selected due to its characteristic clinical-presentation signature.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 25 patients on valproic acid therapy, an elevation of hepatic enzymes was observed in four patients at three months. All of these patients responded to a reduction in valproic acid dosage, and Dr. Wilder noted that one patient had what he described as 'toxic hepatitis.'
raw_record.extra_details: Reported among 25 seizure patients treated with valproic acid; 4 patients had elevated hepatic enzymes at 3 months, all responding to valproic acid dose reduction; one patient developed 'toxic hepatitis.' Other reported side effects included nausea/vomiting, somnolence (mostly with concomitant phenobarbital), alopecia, and weight gain.

raw_record.support_text: In the UNOS liver transplant cohort of drug-induced acute liver failure recipients, valproate was implicated in 10 of 137 (7.3%) non-acetaminophen cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Tied with phenytoin at 10 of 137 non-APAP cases (7.3%). Diagnosis at transplant was acute hepatic necrosis from an implicated drug.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 29-year-old patient who developed liver failure during valproic acid (VPA) therapy; the patient tested negative for hepatitis viruses A, B, and C, Epstein-Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus, and the valproate level was 97.1 µM (below the therapeutic range of 350-700 µM). Autopsy showed subacute liver dystrophy with an organ weight of 860 g, microvesicular steatosis and bridging hepatocellular necrosis predominantly in the centrolobular zone, signs of cholestasis, and marked fibrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 29-year-old patient with Friedreich's disease on VPA therapy who died. Laboratory abnormalities included bilirubin 14.3 mg/dl conjugated at admission, AST 113 U/L, ALT 109 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 221 U/L, GGT 34 U/L, NH3 150 µM; before death bilirubin 33.7, AST 50, ALT 63, ALP 182, NH3 281. Autopsy: subacute liver dystrophy (860 g), microvesicular steatosis, bridging hepatocellular necrosis in centrolobular zone, cholestasis, marked fibrosis, plus generalized hemorrhage, bronchopneumonia, aspiration, and pancreatitis. Viral hepatitis (A,B,C), EBV, and CMV excluded.

raw_record.support_text: The conclusion states that this case report adds to the evidence behind treatment of valproate-induced acute liver failure (ALF) with NAC and L-carnitine, and illustrates a rare association between ALF and posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES). The report attributes the ALF to valproate.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report. Valproate-induced ALF was treated with NAC and L-carnitine. The report illustrates a rare association between ALF and PRES; NAC and L-carnitine were given as treatment for the valproate-induced ALF and are not themselves attributed as causes of liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: A retrospective review by Bohan et al. (2001) described 92 patients with severe, symptomatic valproate-induced hepatotoxicity, reporting a survival rate of 50% in patients treated with carnitine compared with 10% in those given supportive care alone; early intervention with intravenous rather than enteral L-carnitine was associated with the greatest hepatic survival. This explicitly attributes severe human hepatotoxicity to valproate (valproic acid).
raw_record.extra_details: Aliases: valproate, VPA. Severe, symptomatic valproate-induced hepatotoxicity in a retrospective cohort of 92 patients; 50% survival with carnitine vs 10% with supportive care alone. L-carnitine is described as a treatment/protectant for VPA-induced toxicity, not a cause. An associated 1996 case report of acute VPA overdose (4000 mg, ~400 mg/kg) in a comatose child showed decreased beta-oxidation, increased omega-oxidation, and elevated 4-en-VPA (an intermediate suspected of causing hepatotoxicity), with complete recovery after L-carnitine; 4-en-VPA is only a suspected mechanistic intermediate and not independently established as a human causal entity.

raw_record.support_text: Patients developed illness a mean of 4 (1.5-15) months after starting valproic acid therapy; in 4 of 13 adequately documented cases valproic acid was the only drug prescribed. The full picture was characterized by acute liver failure with disturbance of consciousness up to coma, frequent bleeding, thrombocytopenia, and prolonged prothrombin time; only 2 of 13 cases survived after valproic acid was withdrawn. Histology showed centrilobular necrosis with microvesicular fat deposition in hepatocytes and signs of toxic hepatitis with severe hepatocellular destruction. The author regards acute liver failure as a very rare complication of valproic acid therapy, favoring an idiosyncrasy or hypersensitivity reaction over dose-dependent damage because patients did not have very high plasma valproic acid concentrations.
raw_record.extra_details: 13 documented patient cases with valproic acid-induced acute liver failure; in 4 of these valproic acid was the sole agent. Latency mean 4 months (range 1.5-15). Presenting features: malaise, vomiting, edema, weight loss, not always marked icterus, sometimes dizziness, facial swelling, nystagmus/ataxia. Early liver enzymes could be normal; during illness SGOT and SGPT rose, bilirubin (direct and indirect) rose, alkaline phosphatase and lactate dehydrogenase rose variably; thrombocytopenia and prolonged prothrombin time; elevated blood ammonia in 2 cases; hepatitis B surface antigen negative. Histology: centrilobular necrosis with microvesicular fat, toxic hepatitis signs, severe hepatocellular destruction with loss of lobular architecture, marked fibrosis, scant mononuclear infiltration, pseudoductular proliferation, and small/medium vacuole steatosis. 2 of 13 survived after drug withdrawal. Pathogenesis unresolved; possible link to hypoglycin structural similarity considered but hypoglycemia usually not part of the picture; role of hyperammonemia/hyperglycinemia and encephalopathy open; valproic acid-induced hepatitis vs toxic necrosis debated by Ware and Millward-Sadler.

raw_record.support_text: In the reported patient, valproic acid (VPA) was immediately stopped, leading to normalization of laboratory findings and rapid resolution of neurological symptoms. The case describes altered mental status, hyperammonemia, and deranged liver function tests (LFTs) as presenting signs of drug-induced liver injury (DILI), distinguishing it from valproate hyperammonemic encephalopathy (VHE).
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report; Naranjo ADR likelihood score of 9 (definite) for VPA causing the reaction; transaminases increased >100x after drug administration, improved on discontinuation, reappearance on re-administration contributes to score; presenting signs of DILI were altered mental status, hyperammonemia, and deranged LFTs, distinguishing it from valproate hyperammonemic encephalopathy (VHE); withdrawal of valproate led to normalization of laboratory findings and rapid resolution of neurological symptoms; paper emphasizes early diagnosis given high DILI mortality (11.7%-17.3%); text notes evaluation for renal function, serum glutamate, serum carnitine, and urea cycle disorders, and possible benefit of carnitine-pantothenic acid in VPA-induced DILI.

raw_record.support_text: Plasma concentrations of valproate and its metabolites were described in three adults who developed hepatotoxicity during treatment of epilepsy with sodium valproate; one patient also developed reversible renal insufficiency, and another may have had associated infectious mononucleosis. All three cases showed evidence of impaired mitochondrial beta-oxidation of valproate, diverting its metabolism into alternative pathways, while plasma concentrations of the suspected hepatotoxic metabolite 4-en-valproate were normal in all cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Valproic acid (2-n-propylpentanoic acid), given as sodium valproate for epilepsy. At least 112 deaths from valproate-associated hepatotoxicity were known worldwide to 1988; instances typically occur in infants or young children on multiple anticonvulsants in the first weeks/months of exposure, beginning with worsening seizures, clouding of consciousness, biochemical/clinical liver failure, often thrombocytopenia, and microvesicular steatosis and/or hepatic cell necrosis at biopsy/necropsy; some recover after cessation, others fatal. The three reported adult cases (all on multiple anticonvulsants: patient 1 on sodium valproate 1400 mg/day with phenytoin, carbamazepine and clonazepam) showed impaired mitochondrial beta-oxidation of valproate (at fatty acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase, and enoyl-CoA hydratase stages respectively), with metabolism diverted to alternative pathways; plasma 4-en-valproate (suspected hepatotoxic metabolite) was normal. Patient 1 recovered after valproate cessation; liver biopsy showed oedematous portal tracts with inflammatory infiltrate, bile duct proliferation and canicular cholestasis with bile retention in centrilobular hepatocytes. Suggestive of valproate overload on limited mitochondrial beta-oxidation capacity causing accumulation of a toxic product of endogenous branched-chain amino acid metabolism.

raw_record.support_text: Eighteen days after starting valproic acid (VPA) prophylactic treatment and 11 days after discharge, the 58-year-old patient was admitted with massive elevations of liver enzymes (AST 8747 U/L, ALT 7184 U/L, GGT 153 U/L), elevated creatinine, INR 2.4 and a VPA serum level of 81 mg/L. Hepatitis serology and auto-antibodies were negative, and the diagnosis of an acute toxic liver failure most likely due to treatment with VPA and duloxetine was made. The patient developed progressive hepatic encephalopathy and underwent urgent liver transplantation, followed by a second transplant after primary graft dysfunction; she died of sepsis and multi-organ failure five months later.
raw_record.extra_details: VPA given as Ergenyl chrono prophylactic treatment (300 mg OD day 1, 300 mg three times day 2, then 300 mg 1-0-2-0). Liver function tests were normal on day 7 of VPA (serum level 73 mg/L); on admission VPA level was 81 mg/L. Histology showed massive necrosis with less than 5% of liver tissue preserved, plasma cell infiltration and slight fatty degeneration, consistent with acute drug-induced liver failure due to VPA. Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale scored the causative role of valproate as probable. Possible cytochrome P450 polymorphism was not tested. Generalized toxicity attributed to toxic metabolites such as 4-en VPA via impaired beta-oxidation. Co-suspect duloxetine was initially mentioned ('most likely due to treatment with VPA and duloxetine') but the final diagnosis and histology attributed the liver failure to VPA. Multi-organ involvement included renal failure, pancolitis and lymphadenopathy. Patient died of sepsis and multi-organ failure five months after transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 367 epilepsy patients, liver dysfunction (ALT or AST > fivefold the upper limit of normal) during VPA (valproate) monotherapy was reported in three of 33 (9.1%) POLG1 p.Q1236H/p.E1143G variant-group patients and one of 28 (3.6%) nonvariant patients (P=0.62); transaminases normalized after VPA discontinuation in one variant and one nonvariant patient, and in two variant patients normalized without changing treatment. Apart from four previously described VPA-ALF (acute liver failure) patients with juvenile-onset Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome (AHS) and one patient with single heterozygous p.Q1236H variant and AHS phenotype, no severe liver injury was identified. Mild-to-moderate transaminase elevations were seen in both groups with medians of highest ALT/AST within the normal range.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of POLG1 p.Q1236H and p.E1143G variants and VPA hepatotoxicity in epilepsy patients. Liver dysfunction defined as ALT or AST >5x ULN on VPA monotherapy: 3/33 (9.1%) variant vs 1/28 (3.6%) nonvariant, P=0.62. Normalization after VPA discontinuation in one variant and one nonvariant patient; two variant patients normalized without treatment change. Medians of highest ALT, AST, GGT and plasma amylase within normal range; no substantial differences between groups in peak-baseline changes or time to peak. Previously described VPA-ALF cases occurred in juvenile-onset AHS (Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome) patients. No other severe liver injury identified in this cohort.

raw_record.support_text: The observations recorded in this study of 23 patients with fatal valproate toxicity strongly suggest that valproate can lead to a characteristic form of hepatic injury. Microvesicular steatosis was found in 80% of the cases, accompanied in most instances by necrosis or cirrhosis, and most of the necrosis was centrilobular.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal valproate toxicity in 23 patients. Microvesicular steatosis was the most frequent lesion (recorded in 17 of 21 autopsied cases), accompanied in most instances by necrosis (centrilobular in seven cases, nonzonal in three) or cirrhosis (micronodular in three, macronodular in one); four patients had necrosis without steatosis. Cholestasis was prominent in 9 of 16 cases whose sections were studied. Serum ammonia levels were elevated in all nine patients with recorded values (above 300, 200, or 100-200 µg/dl); most had azotemia. One liver showed venoocclusive changes; ballooning degeneration and sinusoidal acidophilic bodies were noted in nonnecrotic areas. Authors conclude valproate can lead to a characteristic form of hepatic injury.

raw_record.support_text: Bohan et al analyzed the association of L-carnitine treatment with hepatic survival in 92 patients with severe, symptomatic, VPA-induced hepatotoxicity, reporting that prompt intervention with intravenous rather than enteral L-carnitine was associated with the greatest hepatic survival. Because enteral L-carnitine has low (15%) bioavailability, the better survival with i.v. treatment may be related to higher blood levels.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 92 patients with severe, symptomatic, valproic-acid-induced hepatotoxicity; i.v. L-carnitine treatment (versus enteral, with 15% bioavailability) was associated with the greatest hepatic survival.

raw_record.support_text: A study in 17 patients with valproate hepatotoxicity found that heterozygous genetic variation within the POLG gene correlated significantly with valproate-induced liver injury. In vitro analyses showed therapeutic concentrations of valproate suppressed hepatocyte proliferation and high doses led to non-apoptotic cell death.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of 17 patients with valproate hepatotoxicity; heterozygous genetic variation in the POLG gene correlated significantly with valproate-induced liver injury. In vitro, therapeutic concentrations of valproate suppressed hepatocyte proliferation while high doses caused non-apoptotic cell death.

raw_record.support_text: Sodium valproate (VPA) has been associated with acute, not rarely fatal hepatotoxicity. Two types are distinguished: Type I, a dose-dependent elevation of serum liver enzymes and low plasma fibrinogen that normalize after VPA discontinuation, and Type II, a rare but usually lethal, irreversible idiosyncratic reaction. Histologically, microvesicular steatosis, sometimes accompanied by liver cell necrosis, was described in affected patients.
raw_record.extra_details: German survey (1994-2003, mailed questionnaire to members of the German Section of the International League Against Epilepsy) found 31 cases of reversible hepatotoxicity and 9 cases of lethal hepatopathies; outcome of severe hepatotoxicity is better than in the past; risk is not limited to patients younger than 2 years, polytherapy, or congenital/acquired metabolic diseases. Histology: microvesicular steatosis, sometimes with liver cell necrosis. Type II described as idiosyncratic reaction; Type I as dose-dependent enzyme elevation and low plasma fibrinogen normalizing after discontinuation. i.v. carnitine recommended upon onset.

raw_record.support_text: The DILIN retrospective study is a nationwide registry that includes patients who experienced liver injury within the past 10 years after consuming one of 8 drugs: phenytoin, isoniazid, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid, valproic acid, nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, minocycline, and quinolone antibiotics. The goals include establishing a database of patients with severe DILI due to any of these medications.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among 8 drugs included in the DILIN retrospective registry for patients with severe DILI due to these medications.

raw_record.support_text: Among the well-known hepatotoxic agents the study lists the antiepileptic drug valproic acid, with ALI in around one case in 7,000-9,000 patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Antiepileptic; ALI around 1 in 7,000-9,000 exposed patients; described as a well-known hepatotoxic agent.

raw_record.support_text: The first detailed report of valproate-induced hepatotoxicity included one patient with symptomatic hepatic dysfunction and three patients with biochemical changes only. Clinical trial data showed altered liver enzymes in 11% of 1197 monitored patients, and transient dose-related hepatotoxicity was later followed in 1979 by reports of fatal outcomes associated with valproate treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose-related hepatotoxicity described as transient. First report included one patient with symptomatic hepatic dysfunction and three with biochemical changes only; trial data reported altered enzymes in 11% of 1197 monitored patients.

raw_record.support_text: A 19-year-old previously healthy woman with myoclonic epilepsy was treated with valproate (VPA) 2 g daily (40 mg/kg) for 1 month, after which nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain developed. Laboratory findings included hyperammonaemia, increased serum transaminases (AST 200 IU/L, ALT 280 IU/L) with normal γ-glutamyltranspeptidase and alkaline phosphatase, increased bilirubin, and impaired coagulation. VPA was discontinued. Although the patient had pancreatitis treated and received carnitine, liver function declined with jaundice, hepatoencephalopathy and bleeding diathesis; liver transplantation was proposed but the patient died from cardiovascular failure. Liver examination showed prominent centrolobular necrosis without regeneration, large amounts of microvesicular fat, areas of intrahepatic cholestasis, balloon degeneration of hepatocytes, and periportal fibrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Epilepsy treatment; valproate given at 2 g daily (40 mg/kg) for 1 month before symptom onset; severe hypoglycaemia, hyperammonaemia, amylasuria 2000 IU/L and amylasaemia 200 IU/L, AST 200 IU/L, ALT 280 IU/L with normal GGT and ALP, bilirubin 440 mmol/L, coagulation impairment. Concurrent acute pancreatitis confirmed surgically with peritoneal petechiae and cytosteatonecrosis; treated with carnitine. Died of cardiovascular failure before liver transplant. Histology: centrolobular necrosis, microvesicular fat, intrahepatic cholestasis, balloon degeneration of hepatocytes, periportal fibrosis; electronmicroscopy showed lipid droplets and normal mitochondria. Discussion notes VPA hepatotoxicity may be related to mitochondrial β-oxidation impairment in children, with possibly a different mechanism in adults.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that hepatotoxicity is a rare complication of valproate (VPA) therapy and that it is related to mitochondrial dysfunction. It further reports that VPA therapy leads to serum carnitine deficiency, which may be related to VPA hepatotoxicity. Carnitine metabolism was studied in patients during VPA hepatotoxicity and in patients at risk for it. A separate paragraph notes that carnitine levels/profiles were obtained in 5 patients during VPA hepatotoxicity, compared with 8 previously reported patients, and periodically in patients beginning VPA therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity described as a rare complication of VPA therapy and related to mitochondrial dysfunction; VPA leads to serum carnitine deficiency which may be related to the hepatotoxicity. Carnitine levels/profiles measured in 5 patients during VPA hepatotoxicity and compared with 8 previously reported patients with VPA hepatotoxicity, and measured periodically in patients beginning VPA therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A 19-year-old female patient with Friedreich's ataxia and grand-mal epilepsy died after therapy with valproic acid (valproate) from acute liver failure with massive lactacidosis. Clinical symptoms were hyperventilation, increasing loss of consciousness and shock, leading to treatment-resistant hepatic coma. Pathoanatomy showed extensive confluent lytic necroses of the liver acini (centrolobular and intermediary accentuation) and small-to-medium droplet fatty degeneration increasing from periphery to centre. The paper states the disease picture is quite characteristic for being caused by valproic acid.
raw_record.extra_details: 19-year-old female with Friedreich's ataxia and grand-mal epilepsy; died of acute liver failure with massive lactacidosis; hyperventilation, loss of consciousness, shock and treatment-resistant hepatic coma; histology: extensive confluent lytic necroses with centrolobular/intermediary accentuation plus small-to-medium droplet fatty degeneration increasing from periphery to centre; authors recommend monitoring liver function with prodromal symptoms (anorexia, weakness, apathy), dose reduction or drug discontinuation, and keeping serum valproate in the lower half of the therapeutic range. Paralanguage note: valproate considered a relatively complication-free drug despite known side effects; prior reported cases of acute liver failure after valproate (18 published with detail, 11 fatal).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that although valproic acid (VPA) is generally very well tolerated, very rarely VPA-associated liver failure has occurred, and even more rarely acute pancreatitis and coagulation disorders with spontaneous bleeding tendency. The paper separately concludes that a benign, reversible transaminase elevation under VPA reflects a harmless direct pharmacodynamic effect.
raw_record.extra_details: VPA-associated severe liver injury is very rare (also described as reversible severe liver insufficiency and irreversible fulminant liver failure). Analysis based on 177 patients with liver failure under VPA; the first symptom could be determined in 101, and clinical signs were leading in 80 of 101. In 14 of 101, transaminase rise or coagulation disorder coincided with clinical signs; a febrile infection preceded in over half of cases; one patient had subarachnoid hemorrhage. In 5 of 101 documented deceased patients pathological lab values preceded clinical symptoms: one had asymptomatic transaminase rise under VPA and developed liver failure only after switching to the also potentially hepatotoxic phenytoin; in 3 of the 5 transaminases were already elevated at least 3-fold before VPA therapy; 3 of 5 had neurodegenerative disease or unclear familial deaths with Reye-like symptoms. The consensus concluded that laboratory monitoring was not suitable for early detection of valproate-associated liver failure, and no patient was shown to have liver failure detected earlier by lab values than by clinical monitoring, including via valproate metabolites in serum and urine.; global_identifier: SMILES:4674104

raw_record.support_text: Jinjuvadia and colleagues used ICD-9 codes to identify DILI cases in a University of Michigan database, attributing DILI cases secondary to valproic acid among the four drugs of special interest (Augmentin, Dilantin, valproic acid, isoniazid), which together accounted for 51 of 119 DILI cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Valproic acid is one of four drugs (with Augmentin, phenytoin, isoniazid) to which 51 of 119 DILI cases were attributed in an ICD-9 coded hospital database study (1994-2000).

raw_record.support_text: The ILIAD reliability study enrolled its first 40 patients including 11 cases of valproate hepatotoxicity. The paper describes these as cases of drug-induced liver injury used to test RUCAM causality score reliability.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 of 40 DILI cases in the ILIAD study cohort; patients with a diagnosis of valproate hepatotoxicity. Cohort-wide median time to onset was 42.5 days, 73% hospitalized, 15% overall required liver transplantation (not drug-specific).

raw_record.support_text: Valproic acid is described as causing induced hepatotoxicity, with the mechanism that valproate inhibits carnitine biosynthesis by affecting beta-oxidation of fatty acids. Intravenous carnitine has been shown useful in valproic acid induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Valproate-induced hepatotoxicity (DILI). Mechanism: valproate inhibits carnitine biosynthesis by affecting fatty acid beta-oxidation; carnitine supplementation increases valproate beta-oxidation. In a case-controlled study of 92 patients with valproate-induced hepatotoxicity, 42% of the 42 patients treated with L-carnitine survived versus 10% of the 50 patients on supportive care (p<0.001); intravenous administration was associated with greatest survival. Steroids generally not useful unless features of drug-induced hypersensitivity are present.

raw_record.support_text: The study included 15 cases of DILI, 30 VPA-tolerant controls, and 15 controls with mild liver injury, all on VPA therapy. The DILI cases had major presence of seizures as the indication, more severe drug interactions, hepatocellular hepatitis more common than in the mild-injury group, shorter time to onset of liver injury, and more deaths in the cases group.
raw_record.extra_details: Valproate (VPA) DILI study; 15 DILI cases compared with 30 VPA-tolerant and 15 mild-injury controls. Indication predominantly seizures (86.7% of cases). Deaths were more frequent in the DILI case group. Time from VPA start to liver-injury onset was shorter in cases (61.6 vs 304 days, p<0.01) and DILI duration until laboratory recovery was shorter in cases (18.7 vs 204.4 days, p=0.02). Drug interactions were more severe in DILI patients (46.7% vs 13.3% vs 13.3%, p<0.01); among possible CYP interactions only rufinamide and phenytoin are inducers and clobazam a weak inhibitor.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 43 juvenile myoclonic epilepsy patients, VPA therapy was changed in 2 patients because of side effects that included hepatotoxicity (along with alopecia), after which they were switched to LTG (lamotrigine). The hepatotoxicity is attributed to valproic acid therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported in 2 of 43 juvenile myoclonic epilepsy patients treated with valproic acid; hepatotoxicity occurred together with alopecia as side effects prompting change of therapy to lamotrigine (LTG).

raw_record.support_text: The first case is a 24-year-old woman who developed a reversible hepatic lesion attributed to valproate (VPA) treatment, described as 'liver lesion due to VPA treatment.' Liver biopsy showed liver tissue with drug-induced changes. The authors recommend stopping VPA if symptoms of hepatic toxicity appear to prevent irreversible injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 24-year-old woman on valproate for primary generalized epilepsy with absences and tonic-clonic seizures; medication changed from carbamazepine and primidone to carbamazepine and VPA; VPA 900 mg daily, serum level 220 (350-450) µmol/l just below therapeutic range; liver parameters normal one month after starting VPA; both cases were reversible; indication: epilepsy.

raw_record.support_text: The DILIN Retrospective Study establishes a nationwide registry of patients who had suffered in the past severe idiosyncratic liver injury associated with the administration of valproic acid (valproate). Paragraph 59 lists valproate as one of the implicated medications for DILI cases enrolled into the retrospective protocol (7 cases).
raw_record.extra_details: 7 DILI cases enrolled in the DILIN retrospective protocol; synonymous with valproate.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the case of a 23-year-old patient with liver failure associated with the use of valproic acid (AV) successfully treated with orthotopic liver transplantation. They note that hepatic failure is a rare but often fatal adverse effect associated with valproic acid use, whose mechanism is not clearly established but is postulated to involve formation of toxic metabolites; risk factors include age under two years and concurrent use of more than one anticonvulsant.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 23-year-old female with valproic acid-associated hepatic failure successfully treated with orthotopic liver transplantation. Liver failure described as a rare but often fatal adverse effect. Mechanism postulated to involve formation of toxic metabolites. Reported risk factors include age under two years and concomitant use of more than one anticonvulsant. Authors advise caution when initiating valproic acid therapy and recommend clinicians be familiar with the clinical presentation and risk factors of this reaction.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the occurrence of fulminant hepatic failure, pancreatitis, acute renal failure, and rhabdomyolysis in a healthy 52-year-old adult taking valproic acid (as divalproex sodium) for migraine prophylaxis. The patient presented with altered mental status and jaundice; liver function tests 3 months earlier were unremarkable and the divalproex dose was doubled at that time to 500 mg twice a day. He was also using dihydroergotamine nasal spray and, rarely, naproxen and acetaminophen with codeine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 52-year-old adult; migraine prophylaxis; co-exposure to dihydroergotamine nasal spray and occasional naproxen and acetaminophen-with-codeine; divalproex dose doubled to 500 mg twice a day 3 months before presentation; no history of liver or kidney disease or alcoholism.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of multiorgan failure attributed to valproic acid toxicity, comprising fulminant hepatic failure, pancreatitis, acute renal failure, and rhabdomyolysis; patient survived. Presented with 24 hours of altered mental status and jaundice; reported by the authors as an occurrence of this multisystem toxicity not previously described in an adult taking valproic acid.

Hepatic dysfunction resolved after VPA discontinuation (3 patients) or VPA dosage reduction (4 patients).

raw_record.support_text: The author describes a case of ALF due to drug toxicity of the antiepileptic valproic acid in a 17-year-old girl, reported as the first case of heterotopic auxiliary liver transplantation for ALF (performed March 1980). After initial recovery, the patient developed agranulocytosis requiring withdrawal of immunosuppression and died of graft rejection on postoperative day 22.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adolescent female patient (17 years old) undergoing antiepileptic treatment for an unstated indication; ALF provided the context for heterotopic auxiliary liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Case performed in March 1980; first published in French in 1982 and in English in 1985 as part of the first series of partial liver grafts. The patient died of graft rejection at postoperative day 22 from agranulocytosis after immunosuppression withdrawal; the acute liver failure itself was the attributed valproic-acid injury, not the cause of death. Mechanistic details (e.g., intrinsic vs idiosyncratic mode) and biochemical pattern not stated.

raw_record.support_text: A prospective study revealed that a single heterozygous variant in POLG (p.Gln1236His) was strongly associated with VPA-induced hepatotoxicity (odds ratio 23.6, p=5.1×10^-7), attributed to non-apoptotic cell death not mediated through mtDNA defect or impairment of fatty acid oxidation. Additional iPSC-derived hepatocyte work with the POLG p.Ala467Thr variant showed that VPA led to increased apoptosis via a mitochondrial permeability-transition pore-opening pathway, with carnitine or N-acetylcysteine supplementation seeming to rescue VPA-induced toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Association observed in the context of POLG-related mitochondrial disease; strong association reported specifically for carriers of a heterozygous POLG p.Gln1236His variant.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective study reported an odds ratio of 23.6 (p=5.1x10^-7) for the POLG p.Gln1236His variant with VPA-induced hepatotoxicity; toxicity was described as non-apoptotic cell death not mediated through mtDNA defect or impairment of fatty acid oxidation. Supporting iPSC-derived hepatocyte data (POLG p.Ala467Thr) indicated VPA increased apoptosis via a mitochondrial permeability-transition pore-opening pathway; carnitine or N-acetylcysteine appeared to rescue VPA-induced toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Two patients on valproic acid (Divalproex) therapy developed acute hepatic dysfunction; patient 1 presented with hepatic failure and concurrent rhabdomyolysis leading to acute renal failure, while abdominal CT on patient 2 suggested hepatosteatosis. Their ARDS was deemed secondary to community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), which is considered a predisposing factor for hepatic dysfunction by VPA, and VPA therapy was continued in both patients because the treating team did not realize it could contribute to the hepatic failure and rhabdomyolysis. Patient 1's serum VPA level of 38 µg/mL was subtherapeutic with home Divalproex ER 500 mg oral twice daily. The calculated Naranjo score for both patients was 5, indicating probable adverse drug events.

raw_record.extra_details: Two case reports of acute hepatic dysfunction with VPA; patient 1 had hepatic failure with hyperammonemia postadmission, patient 2 had hepatosteatosis on abdominal CT with normal serum ammonia; Naranjo score 5 (probable) for both; cause of acute conditions stated as unknown per treating medical teams; patient 2 discharged on previous home medications including Divalproex DR.

raw_record.extra_details: Presenting illness was valproate-associated hepatic encephalopathy with hyperammonaemia (serum ammonia rising from 43 to 215 umol/l, normal <33 umol/l) and low carnitine (free 7.6, total 15.4 umol/l) despite normal routine liver function tests; delirium and asterixis resolved within three days after valproate reduction (3 g to 2.75 g/day) and oral L-carnitine 330 mg four times daily. raw_record.support_text: The paper states that hepatotoxicity due to valproate often necessitates discontinuation of the drug, and reports a patient with unstable epilepsy in whom valproate was an irreplaceable anticonvulsant. Hepatic encephalopathy in this patient was reversed and remained controlled by combining L-carnitine supplementation with an essentially unchanged valproate schedule, framing valproate as the cause of the hepatotoxicity-related encephalopathy. The patient, a 35-year-old previously healthy woman, developed delirium with asterixis and hyperammonemia (serum ammonia rising to 215 µmol/l) with low serum carnitine while on a valproate 3 g/day regimen together with phenobarbitone; the encephalopathy resolved after valproate reduction to 2.75 g/day and addition of L-carnitine 330 mg four times daily.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Co-exposure to phenobarbitone as part of a multidrug anticonvulsant regimen; patient had viral encephalitis with status epilepticus and prior withdrawal of carbamazepine for abnormal liver function tests.
raw_record.extra_details: 35-year-old woman; hepatic encephalopathy with delirium, asterixis, and hyperammonemia (serum ammonia rising from 43 to 215 µmol/l; normal <33 µmol/l) while serum liver function tests were normal and valproate concentration was therapeutic (83 mg/l); low serum free carnitine 7.6 µmol/l (normal 19.0-60.0) and total carnitine 15.4 µmol/l; valproate reduced from 3 g to 2.75 g/day with L-carnitine 330 mg four times daily; encephalopathy resolved over three days with normal serum ammonia (25 µmol/l) and therapeutic valproate (93 mg/l). Paper also notes valproate can cause reduced serum carnitine and hyperammonemia in children, especially with multidrug regimens and within a few months of starting, and that carnitine has been used/reported to reverse such hepatotoxicity in children.

raw_record.support_text: The report attributes fatal liver failure to valproic acid (VPA) therapy in a 21-year-old patient on VPA for seizures/status epilepticus; no other cause of the hepatic injury could be substantiated, and necropsy showed hepatic steatosis, necrosis, fibrosis, and destroyed hepatic architecture. The paper states that pancreatitis associated with hepatic failure under VPA has a poor prognosis mainly because of the VPA hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Concurrent antiepileptic co-medications (clonazepam, phenobarbital) present; phenytoin failed initially; patient was a 21-year-old mentally retarded male with seizures evolving into status epilepticus.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal liver insufficiency 18 weeks after starting VPA; initial dosing 25.5 mg/kg/day increased to 39.2 mg/kg/day; VPA serum level remained within therapeutic range (50-100 mg/L; 350-700 µmol/L). Elevated AST, ALT, GGT (max 600 IU/L), alkaline phosphatase (max 665 IU/L), bilirubin (up to 50 µmol/L), and persistent severe coagulopathy. Necropsy: hepatic steatosis, necrosis, fibrosis, destroyed architecture; coexistent pancreatitis, pancreatic pseudocyst, 5 L serous icteric peritoneal fluid, ascites. Literature review: until March 1991, 24 cases of isolated pancreatitis and 6 cases of pancreatitis with hepatic failure under VPA published; overall pancreatitis mortality approaching 21%; pancreatic side effects range from asymptomatic hyperamylasemia to fatal pancreatitis.

raw_record.extra_details: Combined data on 67 fatal/assessed cases (23 from Zimmerman and Ishak 1982 plus 35 other sources, 9 with no information). Presenting features included jaundice (15/23 and 21/35 cases), vomiting, drowsiness/malaise, fever, oedema, haemorrhage. Laboratory findings: abnormal SGOT in 56 cases, abnormal SGPT in 40, abnormal bilirubin in 40, coagulation disorder in 41, raised ammonia in 16/20 tested. Histology in 67 cases: necrosis only 20, steatosis only 8, cirrhosis only 1, steatosis and cirrhosis 4, steatosis and necrosis 22, unknown 12. Reversible hepatotoxicity: 21 patients recovering after valproate withdrawal (age 12 months to 73 years; 11 females, 6 males; 11 published cases).

raw_record.support_text: The review compiles reported cases of acute pancreatitis associated with fatal liver failure in patients receiving valproic acid (VPA) for epilepsy (Sugimoto, Scheffner, Dickinson, and the present study), with VPA doses of about 20-55 mg/kg/day and serum VPA levels around 32-100 mg/L and latency from days to about 1.5 years; most patients either died or died after exploratory laparotomy. Separately, the text notes that the hepatic side effects of VPA, like the pancreatitis, appear to meet criteria of both toxic and idiosyncratic reactions, consistent with Eadie's view of a continuum of liver (or pancreatic) injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients were predominantly children/young adults with epilepsy, several with mental retardation, treated with VPA at 20-55 mg/kg/day; several were concurrently on other antiepileptic co-medications (carbamazepine, ethosuximide, phenobarbital, primidone, clonazepam, phenytoin).
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal liver failure cases: Sugimoto 13F, VPA 20 mg/kg/day, serum level 37 mg/L, death; Scheffner 3.6F (55 mg/kg/day, 21 wk), 6.6F (30 mg/kg/day, 3 mo), 5.1M with CMZ/ETH/PB/PRM; Dickinson 25M; present study 21M with CL/PB, 39.2 mg/kg/day, serum VPA 91.1 mg/L, serum amylase 2.6x, death. Onset latency roughly 1 month to 1 year. The primary focus of the paper is VPA-associated pancreatitis, with the associated fatal hepatic failure documented during VPA therapy; hepatic side effects also discussed as meeting criteria of both intrinsic and idiosyncratic reactions.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that patients with POLG1 gene mutations have an increased risk of valproate-induced liver failure, and that these patients often suffer from intractable seizures. The study retrospectively identified five patients with valproate-induced liver failure associated with POLG1 mutations, examined POLG1 and mtDNA depletion, and assessed their prognosis after liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with POLG1 gene mutations (mitochondrial disease) treated with valproate for epilepsy/intractable seizures; valproic acid should be avoided in these patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Five patients with valproate-induced liver failure retrospectively identified. Four patients homozygous for POLG1 p.W748S and p.E1143G had hepatic mtDNA depletion; one of these died prior to anticipated transplantation and the other three survived 4-19 years after liver transplantation. One patient with a heterozygous POLG1 p.Q1236H mutation but no mtDNA depletion died suddenly two years after transplantation. Three patients had been suspected to have Wilson's disease. POLG1 analysis recommended before introducing valproate therapy.

raw_record.extra_details: CIOMS causality score 8 (probable). Injury is dose-independent and mediated by an idiosyncratic metabolic-predisposition mechanism, in contrast to the hypersensitivity mechanism of other anticonvulsants. Causes hepatocellular injury with GPT increase ~2 times the upper limit of normal. Lipids reversed/declined and the patient was asymptomatic on follow-up; carbamazepine was replaced by phenobarbital during management. Clinical manifestations of valproate hepatotoxicity range from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to fulminant toxic hepatitis. L-carnitine treatment was considered but omitted as the patient had no risk factors and favorable evolution.

raw_record.support_text: A boy with delayed psychomotor development, attention deficit disorder, and therapy-resistant epilepsy was treated with valproate. The patient died of liver failure after 4 months of valproate treatment. Postmortem investigation of cultured fibroblasts suggested medium chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, an unexpected finding since the boy had not presented typical manifestations of this disease. Because MCAD is important in fatty acid beta-oxidation, the patient probably had a genetically reduced tolerance to valproate, and the drug should be omitted in treating seizures in patients with possible MCAD deficiency.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (10-year-old boy). Possible underlying medium chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency, an inborn error of fatty acid beta-oxidation, was detected postmortem and is proposed as a genetically reduced tolerance/susceptibility to valproate. The patient had prior/ concurrent antiepileptic polypharmacy (phenobarbital, phenytoin, carbamazepine) and therapy-resistant epilepsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal fulminant hepatic failure occurred after 4 months of valproate treatment. Valproate-induced fatal hepatotoxicity has been regarded as an idiosyncratic reaction; risk factors noted include young age, polypharmacy, high valproate serum levels, and inborn errors of metabolism. Reduced MCAD activity was detected postmortem in cultured skin fibroblasts. Authors recommend omitting valproate in patients with possible MCAD deficiency.

raw_record.support_text: A diagnosis of vanishing bile duct syndrome was made in an 8-year-old girl with unresolved jaundice and pruritus 5 months after beginning treatment with VPA. Severe interlobular bile duct loss and eosinophil-dominant mixed inflammatory infiltration with canalicular and hepatocellular cholestasis were found. Elevated total bilirubin (20.2 mg/dL), direct bilirubin (12.9 mg/dL), gamma-GTP (1531 IU/L), ALP (2787 IU/L), total cholesterol (1398 mg/dL), AST (209 IU/L) and ALT (118 IU/L) were present; cholestasis and liver enzymes normalized after ursodeoxycholic acid.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (8-year-old girl); onset 5 months after starting VPA.
raw_record.extra_details: Ultrasound showed slight hepatomegaly and splenomegaly without biliary tree dilatation; severe interlobular bile duct loss in portal areas with no interlobular bile ducts seen; eosinophil-dominant mixed inflammatory infiltration. No signs of chronic liver disease. Resolved after ursodeoxycholic acid treatment. Latency 5 months.

raw_record.support_text: A 10-year-old girl with Alpers syndrome (POLG1 mutations, c.248T>C p.L83P and c.2662G>A p.G888S) and refractory seizures was treated with valproic acid (VPA) among other antiepileptics. VPA was used for 2.5 months and then terminated due to acute liver failure after she developed edema and coagulopathy 52 days after starting VPA, followed 3 weeks later by jaundice and hepatomegaly with abnormal ALT, AST, total and direct bilirubin, total protein, albumin, and fibrinogen. After VPA was stopped, liver function improved and was near normal 6 months later.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient with Alpers syndrome due to POLG1 mutations (c.248T>C p.L83P, c.2662G>A p.G888S), i.e., underlying mitochondrial hepatocerebral disease; VPA given for refractory seizures as part of a multidrug antiepileptic regimen (phenobarbital, carbamazepine, topiramate, lamotrigine, clonazepam).
raw_record.extra_details: VPA used for ~2.5 months. Acute liver failure developed with edema and coagulopathy 52 days after starting VPA; jaundice and hepatomegaly appeared 3 weeks later. Laboratory values: ALT 64 U/L (nl 0-40), AST 215 U/L (nl 0-45), total bilirubin 145.6 µmol/L (nl 1.7-20), direct bilirubin 113.1 µmol/L (nl 0-6), total protein 44.35 g/L, albumin 28.8 g/L, fibrinogen 0.64 g/L (earlier decreased fibrinogen 1.56 g/L). Liver function improved and was near normal 6 months after VPA was discontinued (dechallenge). Patient had known POLG1 genotype; VPA-triggered liver failure in setting of mtDNA polymerase gamma deficiency.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that the patient's acute liver failure was due to VPA hepatotoxicity: "It may be concluded that liver failure in our patient was due to VPA hepatotoxicity." The patient was diagnosed with liver failure 4 days after VPA administration, and more than 100 patients with VPA-associated liver failure have been reported worldwide. VPA-associated liver failure was reported to have occurred 2 or 3 days after initiation of VPA treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient with pre-existing neonatal asphyxia brain damage and myoclonic epilepsy with status epilepticus, suspected to have (likely) Alpers–Huttenlocher syndrome; no histological examination of the liver was performed.
raw_record.extra_details: VPA given as antiepileptic therapy. Liver failure diagnosed 4 days after VPA administration; VPA-associated liver failure reported generally at 2-3 days after VPA initiation; >100 VPA-associated liver failure cases reported worldwide. Supportive care after VPA cessation included nutrition and fresh-frozen plasma; patient survived but with severe neurological sequelae (cerebral atrophy, generalized seizures). Authors advise deferring VPA therapy in patients with status epilepticus/myoclonic epilepsy until Alpers–Huttenlocher syndrome is excluded.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents histologic findings in the liver of 10 cases of valproate-induced hepatotoxicity, consistently showing microvesicular steatosis, vacuolar steatosis, ductular proliferation, necrotic areas, and fibrosis, with the architecture of the liver destroyed. In a larger series of 16 patients who died during valproate therapy, none had progressive neuronal degeneration of childhood (PNDC), and histologic findings clearly indicated a hepatogenic cause of death, supporting valproate as the cause of fatal hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients with epilepsy treated therapeutically with valproate; some had underlying diseases such as urea cycle defects or were discussed as having carnitine deficiency as susceptibility factors.
raw_record.extra_details: Sixteen patients died during valproate (VPA) therapy; histology was evaluated in 10 cases (biopsy/autopsy). The most constant feature was microvesicular steatosis attributed to inhibited mitochondrial beta-oxidation of fatty acids, with swollen mitochondria and damaged cristae on electron microscopy; findings also included intracellular cholestasis, hepatocyte single-cell necrosis, ductular proliferation, necrotic areas, fibrosis, and destroyed liver architecture. Histology was Reye-like in appearance. VPA is described as 2-propyl-pentanoic acid. All pediatric cases were explicitly checked and none had progressive neuronal degeneration of childhood (PNDC), which some authors argued could confound attribution.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes valproic acid (VPA)-associated liver failure and hepatotoxicity as a known side effect of VPA therapy, citing the 1988 German series of 16 patients with VPA-associated hepatotoxicity. Patient 13 in that series had normal laboratory tests initially with severe apathy 6 weeks after VPA initiation, recovered, but died of fatal liver failure 9 weeks later; 5 of the 16 patients showed apathy as the initial symptom of VPA-associated hepatotoxicity, 3 of whom had no pathologic laboratory tests at that time.

raw_record.extra_details: Fatal VPA-associated liver failure cases described (patients F1-F8) showed marked transaminase elevations (e.g., AST up to 20,850 U/L, ALT up to 6,900 U/L), hyperammonemia, impaired coagulation (low PT/PTT, DIC), elevated bilirubin, lactic acidosis and coma; VPA serum levels ranged from 15 µg/ml to 268 µg/ml. The 1988 German series included 16 patients with VPA-associated hepatotoxicity, and 5 of 16 had apathy as initial symptom. Also noted: stupor/coma during VPA therapy in 2-21% of patients with reversible encephalopathy and unaltered liver tests; mild transaminase/GGT elevations (pathologic GGT in up to 12% of VPA-treated patients) are usually transient and reversible. raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a patient with symptoms of impending hepatotoxicity during the second week of valproic acid (VPA) therapy, in whom fatal liver failure was a concern, and cites a report of a child who developed hepatotoxicity after only three doses of VPA. Serious signs were considered possibly attributable to comedication with phenobarbital (PB) and VPA, though serum concentrations of both antiepileptic drugs were within therapeutic ranges and no explanation of the severe clinical reaction was found.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients; several cases had polytherapy (e.g., with phenobarbital) and acute viral/bacterial febrile illnesses; one child had hereditary 3-methylglutaconic aciduria; patients belonged to a high-risk group (age <2 years, multiple antiepileptic drugs, neurologic deficits).
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 16 children on VPA with hepatotoxicity. Reported outcomes include reversible liver dysfunction during febrile illness in 7 children, reversible liver failure, reversible impairment of coagulation with bleeding manifestations, and fatal liver failure (autopsy findings included microvesicular steatosis, marked/acute diffuse severe/multifocal necroses, cholangiolar proliferation). Fatal cases showed elevated AST (up to 12,300 U/L) and ALT (up to 6,989 U/L), hyperammonemia, low prothrombin time. In one fatal case there was prior aspirin therapy; VPA-associated severe hepatotoxicity may be reversible if VPA is discontinued early. Some patients had increased 4-ene-VPA levels suggesting diversion of VPA metabolism to omega-oxidation.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity occurred in patients receiving valproate therapy. The median valproate dose was 39 mg/kg/day (range 14-92) for L-carnitine-treated patients and 43 mg/kg/day (range 12-108) for untreated patients, with median duration of valproate therapy of 81 and 72 days, respectively. Three L-carnitine-treated patients had received prophylactic L-carnitine to prevent toxicity, stopped 60 to 100 days before the hepatotoxic event.

raw_record.extra_details: In this cohort of 92 patients with valproate-induced hepatotoxicity, hepatic survival was 20/42 (47%) for L-carnitine-treated patients vs 5/50 (10%) for untreated patients (p<0.001). Survival was better when valproate was stopped early (<5 days) and L-carnitine was given IV. Deaths attributable to the hepatotoxic event occurred in both groups. Initial symptoms included nausea/vomiting, anorexia, lethargy, increased seizures, and infection.

raw_record.support_text: In 102 patients with POLG-related mitochondrial disease and valproic acid (VPA) exposure from 46 articles, adverse drug reactions occurred in 91 patients (89%) and hepatotoxicity was reported in 87 patients (85%). There was no pre-existing liver disease in 92/102 (90%). Fatal outcomes occurred in 53/102 (52%), 8 unrelated to VPA (e.g., intractable seizures); liver transplant was required in 15 patients, 6 (40%) of whom died post-transplant. All patients with reported genotypes (97/102) had recessive POLG variants, with compound heterozygotes having worse outcomes than homozygotes (p<0.01).

raw_record.support_text: Valproate-induced liver failure arises after a therapy duration of 6 weeks to 6 months and is not accompanied by hyperergic signs. Leading subjective symptoms include loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, weakness, lethargy and somnolence, together with various neurological symptoms, shock, kidney failure and signs of hepatic insufficiency. Transaminases are moderately elevated (mostly below 400 U/l), bilirubin is variably elevated, platelets are often decreased and prothrombin time is prolonged. Histology shows variably expressed, preferentially centrilobular steatosis and inflammatory infiltrates. Of 18 patients with more detailed case history, 11 died within a few days as a consequence of liver failure; only three of the 18 were older than 20 years.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Predominantly pediatric population (only 3 of 18 detailed cases older than 20 years).
raw_record.extra_details: Valproate-induced liver failure latency 6 weeks to 6 months; no hyperergic signs; symptoms: anorexia, nausea, vomiting, weakness, lethargy, somnolence, various neurological symptoms, shock, renal failure, hepatic insufficiency; transaminases moderately elevated (mostly <400 U/l), bilirubin variably elevated, platelets often decreased, prothrombin time prolonged; histology: variable, preferentially centrilobular steatosis with inflammatory infiltrates; 11 of 18 cases died within days of liver failure. Patient case showed marked metabolic (lactic) acidosis with anion gap 53 mval/l, resembling Reye syndrome with mitochondrial damage and disturbed fatty-acid beta-oxidation; mitochondrial swelling, reduced matrix and cristae disorganization observed in two children treated with valproate, which regressed after discontinuation; acidosis noted in 3 of the 18 cases.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a 23-year-old woman with valproic acid (VPA)-associated hepatic failure that was successfully treated with orthotopic liver transplantation. It states that hepatic failure is a rare, often fatal adverse effect of VPA, with most cases occurring within several months of initiation of therapy; initial symptoms often include nausea and vomiting, lethargy, or loss of seizure control. The exact mechanism is not clearly established but is postulated to involve toxic metabolite formation, and major risk factors include age less than two years and concomitant treatment with more than one anticonvulsant, with other significant risk factors being underlying metabolic or serious neurologic disorders.

raw_record.support_text: Four patients aged 3–18 years of multiple ethnicities developed VPA-induced hepatotoxicity, all having received VPA for intractable partial seizures (three with epilepsia partialis continua). The time from VPA exposure to liver failure was 2–3 months, and liver failure was reversible in one patient. Molecular studies revealed homozygous p.R597W or p.A467T POLG mutations in two patients and compound heterozygous mutations (p.A467T/p.Q68X and p.L83P/p.G888S) in the other two; clinical findings and POLG mutations were diagnostic of Alpers–Huttenlocher syndrome. The authors conclude VPA dosing at any stage of Alpers–Huttenlocher syndrome can precipitate liver failure.

raw_record.extra_details: Four patients across multiple ethnicities. Latency from VPA exposure to liver failure 2–3 months. Liver failure reversible in one patient. Molecular findings: homozygous p.R597W or p.A467T POLG mutations in two patients; compound heterozygous p.A467T/p.Q68X and p.L83P/p.G888S in the other two. Authors propose POLG gene testing consideration before VPA dosing in children/adolescents presenting with intractable seizures, particularly with psychomotor regression, given VPA dosing can precipitate liver failure in Alpers–Huttenlocher syndrome.

raw_record.support_text: Tamoxifen-induced hepatic injury most characteristically presents as fatty liver disease, but chronic and panacinar hepatitis have also been described; one patient treated with tamoxifen in this study showed both hepatitis and mild steatosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatty liver disease is the most characteristic pattern of tamoxifen-induced hepatic injury; chronic and panacinar hepatitis also described. One patient exhibited both hepatitis and mild steatosis.

raw_record.support_text: Applying the Karch-Lasagna algorithm and Paris Consensus criteria, the causal relationship between the liver injury in this 56-year-old woman and treatment with tamoxifen is classified as probable, based on a compatible chronological relationship between drug administration and altered liver enzymes, absence of other potential causes of liver disease (alcohol, prior chronic hepatopathy, hepatotropic viruses), and persistence of the liver changes when all other medications except tamoxifen were withdrawn. The probability was not upgraded to 'definite' because there are no data on enzyme changes after tamoxifen discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: 56-year-old woman treated with oral tamoxifen 10 mg/12 h since 1996 after right mastectomy for intracystic papillary carcinoma. Presented with right hypochondrial pain, vomiting, coluria and slight mucosal jaundice; liver biopsy showed chronic active hepatitis with marked portal inflammation and moderate macrovesicular steatosis. Lab values: total bilirubin 2.5 mg/dl, AST 199 U/l, ALT 184 U/l; later GGT 331 U/l and alkaline phosphatase 483 U/l. No alcohol intake or blood transfusions; hepatitis B surface antigen, HCV, ANA, AMA, anti-smooth muscle and ANCA all negative. Other potential hepatotoxic drugs (fluvastatin, lansoprazole, ofloxacin, omeprazole, metamizole) were withdrawn and re-introduced without any change in liver values, supporting tamoxifen as the cause. Biopsy findings concordant with a chronic hepatitis resembling a previously published case of tamoxifen hepatotoxicity; steatosis component and active chronic hepatitis pattern imply a mixed mechanism of metabolic idiosyncrasy and autoimmune phenomena. Discussion notes that published tamoxifen hepatotoxicity cases show two predominant injury patterns: cholestasis with or without cytolysis and steatohepatitis, including cholestatic jaundice without cytolysis, cholestasis with cytolysis, a case of hepatic peliosis, a case of fatty liver with liver failure and death, and several cases of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis; additional cases collected by pharmacovigilance systems with little detail.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report that the imputability of a 46-year-old patient's hepatic alterations to tamoxifen was established using criteria of drug-induced liver disorders, after exclusion of hepatic metastasis and bile duct obstruction and following normalization of bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and aminotransferases upon tamoxifen discontinuation. They note tamoxifen hepatotoxicity is uncommon, previously reported as essentially steatosis and cholestatic syndrome, and that severe hepatotoxicity is a rare complication that can occur at any time of tamoxifen therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: 46-year-old woman with no history of hepatic disease, treated with tamoxifen as adjuvant hormonal therapy after mastectomy, four courses of doxorubicine and cyclophosphamide chemotherapy, and adjuvant radiation for lobular breast carcinoma; not taking other medicines. Jaundice appeared four weeks after tamoxifen initiation with elevated bilirubin, aminotransferase, and alkaline phosphatase consistent with acute hepatic injury; no hepatomegaly, no hepatic metastasis or main bile duct obstruction on ultrasound and CT. Negative serologic and immunologic tests. Bilirubin normalized one month after tamoxifen discontinuation; alkaline phosphatase and aminotransferases returned to baseline in ~6 weeks. Rechallenge not attempted. Patient remained free of cancer relapse and hepatic disorders at 10 months. Paper notes previously reported tamoxifen-induced liver diseases are essentially steatosis and cholestatic syndrome, and severe hepatotoxicity is a rare complication.

raw_record.support_text: In 189 of 198 validated certain/probable IH cases the drug relationship per the updated CIOMS scale was at least 'possible'; 177 different drugs/herbs were identified as related to liver injury. raw_record.support_text: The patient had evidence of tamoxifen-induced nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), as evidenced by an ALT/AST ratio greater than 1, steatosis on liver ultrasound, and normalization of these tests after discontinuing tamoxifen. The paper also states that hepatitis A, B, and C serology were negative and alcohol and other known hepatotoxin intake were excluded. Tamoxifen is N-demethylated in the liver by CYP3A4, generating reactive metabolites capable of damaging protein and DNA.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of a patient on tamoxifen. Evidence of tamoxifen-induced NASH included ALT/AST ratio greater than 1 (ALT 48 U/L, AST 42 U/L, normal 0-31), steatosis on liver ultrasound, and normalization of liver toxicity tests after stopping tamoxifen. Paper notes six cases of tamoxifen-induced NASH have been reported, two progressing to cirrhosis. Hepatitis A/B/C serology negative; alcohol and other known hepatotoxins excluded. Proposed mechanisms: partial estrogenic activity and CYP3A4-mediated N-demethylation generating reactive metabolites (binding irreversibly to and damaging protein/DNA). Tamoxifen also implicated in porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) in this patient (urinary uroporphyrins 25,200 nmol/L, falling from 1570 to 359 nmol/mmol creatinine after stopping tamoxifen); PCT itself is not treated as a liver-injury phenotype here.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that acute liver failure is a rare but potentially life-threatening complication of etodolac, and that presentation may be delayed (in this case 6 months after treatment onset). They propose regular monitoring of liver function in all patients receiving etodolac to facilitate early identification of adverse hepatic effects.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report. Patient presented with severe jaundice, bilirubin 525 µmol/L (<21), ALT 1,400 IU/L (5-38), ALP 274 IU/L (25-140), prothrombin time 16.7 s (9.8-12.6), and grade II encephalopathy early in admission. Percutaneous liver biopsy showed findings compatible with drug-induced liver injury. Acute IgM serologies and PCRs for hepatitis A, B, C, E, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and toxoplasma were negative. Spontaneous recovery with liver function returning to normal within 3 months of drug cessation and stable for 2 years. Mechanism unclear; etodolac is a weak CYP2C9 inhibitor. Injury developed as a delayed event 180 days after initiation (6 months), and the absence of rash or eosinophilia makes a hypersensitivity reaction unlikely. Acute liver failure described as a rare but potentially life-threatening complication, with authors recommending liver function monitoring starting within 1 month of initiation.

raw_record.support_text: In the ALFSG, 1 of 133 cases with drug-induced acute liver failure was attributed to etodolac.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed to 1 of 133 drug-induced ALF cases in the ALFSG.

raw_record.support_text: Etodolac, a COX-2 selective NSAID of the pyranocarboxylic acid group, causes liver impairment, though severe liver impairment is exceedingly rare (<0.3%); three cases of etodolac-induced liver failure have been described in literature, one in the DILI-ALF study by Reuben et al. (2010).
raw_record.extra_details: COX-2 selective NSAID of the pyranocarboxylic acid group; severe liver impairment exceedingly rare (<0.3%). Two cases reported in this paper met RUCAM criteria for etodolac-induced DILI, both presenting as ALF after short exposure with extreme transaminase elevation, hyperbilirubinemia, coagulopathy, and cerebral edema within 24-48h of ingestion; surviving patient showed rapid recovery of liver function on drug cessation. Pattern consistent with acute hepatic necrosis (latency 1-14 days). Hepatotoxicity may present within days to months after therapy; warrants immediate discontinuation and close monitoring.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the first case of etodolac-induced acute liver failure without confounding factors such as chronic liver disease or concomitant hepatotoxic agents. In the described 73-year-old patient, extensive laboratory, histopathological and radiological investigations, together with spontaneous recovery following etodolac withdrawal, strongly support a diagnosis of etodolac-induced acute liver failure, defined as hepatic impairment associated with encephalopathy and coagulopathy.
raw_record.extra_details: Etodolac 600 mg twice daily was the patient's only medication, started 6 months prior and discontinued 1 week before admission. 73-year-old female with inflammatory polyarthritis presented with worsening jaundice, malaise and abdominal pain; developed grade II encephalopathy. Admission labs: bilirubin 525 µmol/l, ALT 1400 IU/l, ALP 274 IU/l, prothrombin time 16.7 s. Viral, autoimmune, metabolic, radiological and Doppler work-up negative. Liver biopsy showed severe acute portal and lobular hepatitis with confluent necrosis and bridging collapse, compatible with drug-induced liver injury. Spontaneous recovery, liver function normalized within 3 months and stable at 2 years. Prior hepatic impairment reported in <0.3% of patients; one prior liver failure report was confounded by alcohol-related chronic liver disease and cocaine abuse.

A number of deaths in pregnancy among women taking nevirapine-containing ART have also been reported to the Food and Drug Administration.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 235 nevirapine-exposed individuals, nevirapine-associated reactions included hepatitis (n = 9) and fever (n = 11), with 14 patients experiencing a multisystem or hepatotoxic reaction in addition to 21 with rash. Hepatic/systemic (hepatotoxic) nevirapine reactions were associated with a higher percentage of CD4 T cells (optimal threshold ≥25%, OR 5.5, P = 0.003) and with carriage of HLA-DRB1*0101 (OR 4.8, P = 0.01), the risk being best explained by an interaction between these two risk factors (Pc = 0.001).
raw_record.extra_details: Nevirapine-associated hepatitis occurred in 9 of 235 exposed individuals; 14 patients had multisystem or hepatotoxic reactions. HLA-DRB1*0101 carriage (15.3% of cohort) was associated with hepatic/systemic reactions (OR 4.8, P = 0.01, Pc = 0.14). Risk of hepatic/systemic reactions was most significantly associated with an interaction between HLA-DRB1*0101 and CD4 T-cell percentage ≥25% (Pc = 0.001 for interaction); neither variable was independently significant after adjustment. Presence of both ≥25% CD4 T cells and HLA-DRB1*0101 (n = 15, six cases) gave OR 17.7 vs the remaining cohort (Pc = 0.0006), with positive and negative predictive values of 40% and 96%. No associations for isolated rash or at HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C, or HLA-DQ loci. Cohort was 81% male, 83% Caucasian, HIV-infected. Study supported by NHMRC project grant IDs 194808 and 237408.

raw_record.support_text: The label states that severe, life-threatening, and in some cases fatal hepatotoxicity, including fulminant and cholestatic hepatitis, hepatic necrosis and hepatic failure, have been reported in patients treated with VIRAMUNE (nevirapine), and cites controlled clinical trial data on symptomatic hepatic events.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal hepatotoxicity reported. Symptomatic hepatic events regardless of severity occurred in 4% (range 0% to 11.0%) of VIRAMUNE-treated patients and 1.2% of controls in controlled clinical trials; presentations included fulminant and cholestatic hepatitis, hepatic necrosis, and hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: A case report was published on a patient who suffered nevirapine-induced hepatitis and had peripheral mononuclear cells that were activated by nevirapine in vitro. This human case is cited in the context of a mechanistic review of nevirapine idiosyncratic reactions. The paper further notes separately that patients with a history of nevirapine hypersensitivity reactions had peripheral mononuclear cells that responded to nevirapine by producing IFN-γ, consistent with the p-i hypothesis.
raw_record.extra_details: Human case report of nevirapine-induced hepatitis cited in a review of the mechanism of nevirapine idiosyncratic reactions; the patient's peripheral mononuclear cells were activated by nevirapine. The paper also notes (as a poster/Keane et al. 2007) that patients with a history of nevirapine hypersensitivity produced IFN-γ in response to nevirapine, consistent with the p-i hypothesis. The surrounding review centers on the nevirapine rat model of skin rash, which is animal-only and not related to liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: A South African study reported a 17% incidence of serious hepatotoxicity, defined as alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase levels >5 times the upper limit of normal, among 385 patients receiving nevirapine-based regimens, with no cases among 83 patients on efavirenz-based regimens; female patients with a BMI <18.5 had a 50% incidence. A retrospective analysis of prior studies found a 12-fold increased risk of severe hepatotoxicity in women with CD4 cell counts >250 cells/µL versus <250 cells/µL, resulting in a black-box warning for nevirapine, with the risk for men increasing at CD4 counts >400 cells/µL; Thai and Zambian studies did not reproduce the CD4-cell-count association.
raw_record.extra_details: Serious hepatotoxicity defined as ALT and AST >5x ULN (17% in South African cohort; 50% in females with BMI <18.5). Black-box warning for nevirapine reflecting 12-fold increased risk of severe hepatotoxicity in women with CD4 >250 cells/µL; risk for men increased at CD4 >400 cells/µL. Thai/Zambian studies did not find the CD4 association; authors attributed the high rate to race and BMI (decreased nevirapine clearance with low BMI, black race, particular pharmacogenetic profiles; Thai ethnicity also a possible risk factor). Female sex, high CD4 at initiation, low BMI, low albumin, HBV/HCV coinfection, ATT use and possibly race/ethnicity are cited as risk factors.

raw_record.support_text: The 'Acute liver failure' review list cites a report of nevirapine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and fulminant hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation (Jao J, Sturdevant M, Martin JD, Schiano T, et al., Am J Transplant 2010).
raw_record.extra_details: Case of nevirapine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome with fulminant hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation (Jao et al., Am J Transplant 2010;10:1713-1716).

raw_record.support_text: A 2002 study of 568 patients found the frequency of hepatotoxicity was 15.6% with nevirapine and 8.5% with efavirenz; a 2005 South African study of 468 patients using either nevirapine or efavirenz as the NNRTI showed a 17% hepatotoxicity rate with nevirapine and 2 deaths due to hepatic failure, with high body mass index identified as a risk factor. Nevirapine-based ART was also associated with cases of severe hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity frequency 15.6% (2002 study, 568 patients) vs 8.5% for efavirenz; HCV and HBV coinfection 43.0% and 7.7%, respectively; presentation within first 12 weeks occurred in 50.0% of the nevirapine group; 17% hepatotoxicity rate (2005 South African study, 468 patients) and 2 deaths due to hepatic failure with high body mass index as a risk factor; efavirenz suggested as preferred NNRTI with perceived lower rates of hepatotoxicity; case of severe hepatitis with marked portal inflammation including eosinophils, ductular reaction, and zone 1 steatosis.

raw_record.support_text: Rash and hepatotoxicity are described as the most frequent toxicities associated with nevirapine (NVP), with 6%-7% of patients starting NVP needing to stop therapy because of such hypersensitivity reactions (HSRs). NVP-associated symptomatic hepatitis resulting in hepatic failure is rare but potentially lethal. The paper frames these as established hepatotoxic reactions of NVP that occur within the first 18 weeks of therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: NVP-associated symptomatic hepatitis resulting in hepatic failure is rare but potentially lethal; life-threatening rashes occur in <1% of patients. In the ATHENA cohort of 3752 patients on NVP-based combination therapy, 231 (6.2%) discontinued NVP because of HSRs (rash and/or hepatotoxicity) within 18 weeks; independent risk factors were female sex and Asian ethnicity; an undetectable viral load at start reduced HSR risk (adjusted OR 0.52; 95% CI 0.38-0.71). Pretreated patients with low pre-ART and high current CD4 cell counts and a detectable VL when switching had higher HSR risk versus treatment-naive low-CD4 starters (adjusted OR 1.87; 95% CI 1.11-3.12). NVP package insert carries a black-box warning to avoid starting NVP in women with CD4 cell counts >250 cells/µL and men with CD4 cell counts >400 cells/µL. Most HSRs occur within the first 18 weeks of NVP therapy.

raw_record.support_text: In a genome-wide association study of nevirapine-induced hypersensitivity, the authors considered five nevirapine-induced hypersensitivity phenotypes for analysis, namely nevirapine-induced rash (NIR), hypersensitivity syndrome (HSS), Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN), and drug-induced liver injury (DILI), plus an overall hypersensitivity group, in a discovery cohort of 333 samples (151 cases, 182 controls) of 352 passing QC. The DILI phenotype (n=21 cases in the discovery cohort) was analyzed by logistic regression without covariates.
raw_record.extra_details: Nevirapine-induced DILI was one of five hypersensitivity phenotypes in a case-control pharmacogenomics (GWAS) study. Discovery cohort DILI cases n=21; candidate DILI SNPs included rs147773805 (NTNG1, P=4.47e-6, OR 11.05), rs114693001 (intergenic chr9, P=8.82e-6, OR 9.35), rs142213069 (5' of MYCBP2, P=6.64e-6, OR 14.42), and rs6139258 (RNF24, P=6.64e-6, OR 14.42). Combining discovery and replication cohorts strengthened the RNF24 rs6139258 association [P=5.7e-7, OR 13.62 (95% CI 4.90-37.84)]; replication DILI cases n=42. No variant reached genome-wide significance.

raw_record.support_text: In the 2NN trial (first randomized controlled trial comparing efavirenz with nevirapine), there were two drug-related deaths in the nevirapine arm, including one from liver failure and one from methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus septicaemia in a patient with Stevens-Johnson syndrome. The nevirapine-arm liver failure death is explicitly attributed as drug-related.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported in the 2NN trial (randomized controlled trial comparing efavirenz with nevirapine) during antiretroviral therapy with nevirapine. One drug-related death in the nevirapine arm was from liver failure; a second drug-related death in that arm was from MRSA septicaemia in a patient with Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Effi�cacy comparison: HIV-RNA < 50 copies/ml in 65.4% for nevirapine vs 70% for efavirenz.

raw_record.support_text: Among the 734 patients who, after using a 200 mg twice-daily nevirapine (NVP)-based regimen for some time, switched to a 400 mg once-daily regimen, only 3 (0.41%) had to discontinue NVP within 18 weeks after the switch because of a hypersensitivity reaction, comprising 2 rashes and 1 hepatotoxicity. This attributes nevirapine as the cause of hepatotoxicity that required drug discontinuation in that patient.
raw_record.extra_details: 1 case of hepatotoxicity requiring NVP discontinuation within 18 weeks after switching from a 200 mg twice-daily to a 400 mg once-daily NVP-based regimen, among 734 patients switched (0.41% total HSR discontinuations; 2 rashes and 1 hepatotoxicity). Occurred in HIV-infected patients on combination antiretroviral therapy.

raw_record.support_text: In the 2NN comparative study of NNRTI-based initial regimens (efavirenz versus nevirapine), there were two deaths attributed to nevirapine: one with fulminant hepatic failure and the other with a staphylococcal septicemia secondary to a severe Stevens-Johnson syndrome. The authors note Boehringer Ingelheim (nevirapine manufacturer) found enhanced mortality in controlled trials among women with CD4 count >250 cells/mm3 and men with CD4 count >400 cells/mm3.
raw_record.extra_details: A death in the 2NN randomized controlled study was attributed to nevirapine with fulminant hepatic failure (a second attributed death was from staphylococcal septicemia secondary to severe Stevens-Johnson syndrome). Manufacturer (Boehringer Ingelheim) analysis of controlled trials found enhanced mortality associated with women with CD4 count >250 cells/mm3 and men with CD4 count >400 cells/mm3.
