raw_record.support_text: A 40-year-old HIV-positive woman who received nevirapine (a nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor) together with azidothymidine and lamivudine as antiretroviral therapy responded initially, but 4 weeks later presented with acute fulminant liver failure. A liver biopsy showed massive hepatic necrosis, and she underwent successful orthotopic liver transplantation. The paper identifies the acute fulminant liver failure as secondary to nevirapine.
raw_record.extra_details: 40-year-old HIV-positive woman; antiretroviral therapy included nevirapine with azidothymidine and lamivudine; presented with acute fulminant liver failure 4 weeks after an initially good response; liver biopsy showed massive hepatic necrosis; underwent orthotopic liver transplantation in May 2000. The remainder of the report concerns a pharmacokinetic drug interaction between nelfinavir and sirolimus in this transplant patient, not a DILI attribution to either drug.

raw_record.support_text: During therapeutic use for HIV, nevirapine was associated with serious hepatic toxicity: in the FTC 302 trial there was a 17% incidence of severe hepatotoxicity including two deaths among patients randomized to the nevirapine arm versus 0% in the efavirenz arm; in the 2NN trial severe hepatotoxicity occurred in 13.2% (nevirapine 400 mg daily), 7.8% (nevirapine 200 mg twice daily) and 4.5% (efavirenz 600 mg daily), with one hepatotoxicity-related death on nevirapine. EuroSIDA registry data showed liver failure in 0.3 cases per 100 patient-years (14/1648; 95% CI 0.1-0.6) among nevirapine-treated patients, with 11 of the 14 patients dying.
raw_record.extra_details: Section framing is 'nevirapine-induced hepatotoxicity'. EuroSIDA: liver failure 0.3 cases/100 patient-years (14/1648; 95% CI 0.1-0.6), 11/14 died. FTC 302: severe hepatotoxicity 17% (two deaths) nevirapine vs 0% efavirenz. 2NN: severe hepatotoxicity 13.2% (nevirapine 400 mg daily), 7.8% (nevirapine 200 mg twice daily), 4.5% (efavirenz 600 mg daily); one hepatotoxicity-related death on nevirapine. African HIV-infected women study: early hepatitis in 17% (66/385) nevirapine vs 0% (0/83) efavirenz. Risk factors: HCV/HBV co-infection, female sex with CD4>250 or male sex with CD4>400 cells/mm3, nevirapine+PI or nevirapine+efavirenz co-administration, alcohol/isoniazid/methadone, abnormal baseline liver enzymes, HLA DRB1*0101 with CD4%>25, female BMI<18.5.

raw_record.support_text: Candidate gene studies identified HLA associations for DILI resulting from the anti-HIV drug nevirapine: an Australian study found HLA-DRB1*0101 significantly interacting with high CD4 T-cell counts in liver or multisystem toxicity cases, and in 57 European-ethnicity DILI cases the HLA allele DRB1*01 occurred frequently (OR 3.02; 95% CI 1.66–5.49 for allele carriage), remaining significant after Bonferroni correction.
raw_record.extra_details: Anti-HIV drug. Australian study linked HLA-DRB1*0101 with high CD4 T-cell counts in liver or multisystem toxicity; 57 European-ethnicity DILI cases had DRB1*01 OR 3.02 (95% CI 1.66–5.49) after Bonferroni correction (two-digit typing, treated with caution). No significant associations in a small number of African and Asian cases.

raw_record.support_text: In a case-control pharmacogenetic study of nevirapine (NVP)-treated patients in Mozambique, the ABCB1 c.3435C>T polymorphism was analyzed comparing 78 patients who experienced NVP hepatotoxicity against 78 controls; the 3435T allele was significantly associated with reduced risk of NVP hepatotoxicity (p=0.038, OR 0.42). The paper frames NVP hepatotoxicity as the studied adverse outcome of NVP-based combination antiretroviral therapy, occurring at roughly 5% frequency.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: HIV patients receiving NVP-based combination antiretroviral therapy in Mozambique with pharmacogenetic susceptibility assessed.
raw_record.extra_details: Case-control study with 78 NVP-hepatotoxicity cases and 78 controls; hepatotoxicity frequency about 5%; ABCB1 c.3435C>T T allele associated with reduced hepatotoxicity risk (OR 0.42, p=0.038); c.1459C>T (rs3211371) CYP2B6 SNP not polymorphic in this population; ABCB1 c.2677G>T/A not detected. Genetic/HLA markers themselves are not DILI-causal agents.

raw_record.support_text: Among 119 patients (29.1% of the total) with either hepatic or rash toxicities of any grade, NVP-related hepatotoxicity was reported, including grade III/IV and/or symptomatic hepatotoxicity in 13 adults. Hepatotoxicity led to NVP discontinuation in 4.2% of patients, and some patients continued NVP despite ALT/AST values above 2.5 times ULN. The paper frames these as NVP-related hepatic toxicities in HIV patients on NVP-containing antiretroviral therapy.

raw_record.support_text: In 522 HIV-infected pregnant women initiating triple antiretroviral prophylaxis, 14 (3%) developed severe hepatotoxicity (grade 3 or 4 ALT elevation), including 12 women who initiated nevirapine (NVP). Median time from ART initiation to severe hepatotoxicity was 68 days (IQR 35-127); symptomatic in 8 of 14 cases (rash n=7, jaundice n=4, fever n=3, abdominal pain n=2, nausea n=2). No deaths were attributed to severe hepatotoxicity. Nevirapine was discontinued in 11 of 12 severe hepatotoxicity cases and ALT elevations resolved in 10 of 11 women who switched to nelfinavir (NFV); one woman had persistent ALT elevations.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: HIV-infected pregnant women receiving triple ART prophylaxis (NVP/3TC/ZDV or NFV/3TC/ZDV) in Kisumu, Kenya; 12 of 14 cases occurred in women who initiated NVP.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatotoxicity defined as grade 3 or 4 ALT elevation. Median total bilirubin 43 umol/L (IQR 23-93), with 4 women having total bilirubin >210 umol/L (>5 x ULN). Rash preceded hepatotoxicity by median 8 days in 6 of 7 cases with rash. HBsAg negative in all 13 tested. HBV (hepatitis B surface antigen) negative. ALT resolved in 10 (91%) of 11 women switched to NFV; one woman had persistent ALT elevation. Regimens included lamivudine (3TC), zidovudine (ZDV), nelfinavir (NFV).; dose: None

raw_record.support_text: Rash-associated hepatotoxicity (rash with grade 2-4 ALT elevation) occurred in 9 (2%) of 522 women, all of whom were receiving nevirapine (NVP). Median time from NVP initiation to rash-associated hepatotoxicity was 47 days (IQR 36-66), and rash preceded hepatotoxicity in 7 of 9 cases. No deaths were attributed to this toxicity. Nevirapine was discontinued in 8 (89%) of 9 cases and ART reintroduced with a single drug substitution with NFV; ALT elevations resolved in 7 (89%) of 8 women who switched to NFV, while one woman had persistent ALT elevations.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: HIV-infected pregnant women receiving triple ART prophylaxis in Kisumu, Kenya; all cases were in women receiving the NVP-containing regimen (NVP/3TC/ZDV).
raw_record.extra_details: Rash-associated hepatotoxicity defined as rash with grade 2-4 ALT elevation. All 9 cases were on NVP. One woman with rash-associated hepatotoxicity continued NVP because her rash and ALT elevation had resolved on repeat testing. NVP discontinued in 8 of 9 cases; ALT resolved in 7 (89%) of 8 women switched to NFV; one woman had resolution of rash but persistent ALT elevations despite switching to NFV. Regimen also included lamivudine (3TC), zidovudine (ZDV), nelfinavir (NFV).; dose: None

raw_record.support_text: In HIV-infected South African patients receiving a blinded regimen of lamivudine or emtricitabine, stavudine, and either nevirapine or efavirenz, early hepatotoxicity (grade 3 or greater increase in serum aminotransferases within the first 12 weeks) occurred in 17% of the nevirapine group versus 0% of the efavirenz group, and was balanced between the lamivudine and emtricitabine arms. Two subjects died of hepatic failure, and independent risk factors included BMI<18.5, female sex, serum albumin<35 g/L, MCV>85 fL, HIV-1 RNA<20,000 copies/mL, AST<75 IU/L, and LDH<164 IU/L. The paper notes that the acute hepatic toxicity of nevirapine led to a product label change in the US and EU and that enrollment in the nevirapine stratum was terminated by health authorities.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: HIV-infected, antiretroviral-naive subjects with CD4+ cells >=200/mm3; given in fixed combination antiretroviral therapy with stavudine (30 or 40 mg twice daily) plus lamivudine (150 mg twice daily) or emtricitabine (200 mg once daily); female sex and low BMI identified as risk factors; nevirapine dosed 200 mg once daily for 2 weeks then 200 mg twice daily.
raw_record.extra_details: Early hepatotoxicity defined as treatment-emergent grade 3 (5-10x ULN) or grade 4 (>10x ULN) increase in serum ALT or AST within the first 12 weeks; observed in 17% of the nevirapine arm versus 0% in the efavirenz arm; 2 subjects died of hepatic failure; nevirapine acute hepatic toxicity led to US and EU product label change and termination of enrollment in the nevirapine stratum (trial put on hold). Independent risk factors: BMI<18.5, female sex, serum albumin<35 g/L, mean corpuscular volume>85 fL, plasma HIV-1 RNA<20,000 copies/mL, AST<75 IU/L, lactate dehydrogenase<164 IU/L. Nevirapine brand Viramune; marketed by Boehringer Ingelheim.

raw_record.support_text: Among 117 HIV-infected Malawian adults with nevirapine hypersensitivity identified for an HLA genetic association study, the hypersensitivity phenotypes included 15 cases of drug-induced liver injury (DILI), 33 SJS/TEN, 20 hypersensitivity syndrome, and 46 nevirapine-induced rash, plus 3 cases with both DILI and SJS phenotype. The cases were matched to nevirapine-exposed controls, indicating that the DILI cases were attributed to nevirapine exposure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Malawian HIV-infected adults receiving nevirapine-containing regimens, identified as cases of nevirapine hypersensitivity.
raw_record.extra_details: Nevirapine is a nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor. 18 of 117 hypersensitivity cases involved DILI (15 DILI only, 3 with both DILI and SJS phenotype). Study focus was HLA genotyping (A, B, C, DRB1, DQB1) to identify predictive markers for nevirapine hypersensitivity, not causality classification of DILI.

raw_record.support_text: Thirty non-HIV-infected individuals who received short-term nevirapine as postexposure prophylaxis (PEP) after HIV exposure developed hepatotoxicity after a median of 20.5 days (range 8-35 days). Findings included ECOG grade 3-4 hepatotoxicity (n=14), fevers (n=11), skin rashes (n=8), eosinophilia (n=6), and fulminant hepatic necrosis requiring orthotopic liver transplantation (n=1); no other causes for severe hepatotoxicity were identified. After nevirapine discontinuation most improved within a median of 21.5 days, though one case required liver transplant and one resolved after corticosteroids. Liver biopsies showed extensive hemorrhagic central zonal necrosis with portal eosinophils and lymphocytes in one case and central zonal cholestasis with bile canalicular plugs without hepatocyte necrosis in another.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Non-HIV-infected individuals (health care workers, sexual contacts, clinical trial participants, and others) receiving short-term nevirapine as postexposure prophylaxis after potential HIV exposure (off-label use).
raw_record.extra_details: MedWatch FDA passive reports (n=19), HIV-specialist queries (n=6), pharmaceutical supplier (n=8), and published reports (n=9); severe hepatotoxicity defined as ECOG grade 3 or 4 (>5x normal ALT/AST, Alk Phos, and/or >1.5x normal total bilirubin). Grade 3-4 hepatotoxicity in 14 of 30; onset median 20.5 days (range 8-35); improvement after discontinuation in median 21.5 days (range 14-60); 1 patient had fulminant hepatic necrosis and coma requiring liver transplant 14 days after discontinuation; 1 case improved with corticosteroids after 2 months of persistent hepatotoxicity. Biopsy showed hemorrhagic central zonal necrosis with portal eosinophils and lymphocytes (patient 15) and central zonal cholestasis with bile canalicular plugs, no hepatocyte necrosis (patient 17). No positive HIV or hepatitis C serology.

raw_record.extra_details: Case report of one patient with TEN, hepatotoxicity and leucopenia attributed to nevirapine. Also present were maculopapular rash, targetoid lesions and extensive skin erosions. Liver enzyme abnormalities normalized about four weeks after nevirapine discontinuation (dechallenge), and the authors cite reports that nevirapine-related liver function test abnormalities are reversible upon discontinuation. raw_record.support_text: In the report, non-HIV-infected healthcare workers developed severe hepatic toxicity, attributed to nevirapine, after use of a nevirapine-containing post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) regimen; the toxicity occurred in conjunction with hypersensitivity reactions, and 2 workers did not improve until high-dose prednisone was administered. The paper concludes that non-HIV-infected individuals who receive nevirapine are at risk for severe and potentially life-threatening hepatic toxicity, with risk appearing higher than in HIV-infected persons.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Population restricted to non-HIV-infected adults receiving multiple-dose nevirapine-containing post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) regimens; findings explicitly do not apply to single-dose nevirapine use for prevention of perinatal HIV transmission.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatic toxicity described in non-HIV-infected healthcare workers after a nevirapine-containing PEP regimen, occurring with hypersensitivity reactions; 2 cases did not improve until high-dose prednisone was given (corticosteroid use is otherwise controversial). Risk for severe hepatotoxicity appears higher than in HIV-infected persons and may be associated with higher CD4 counts. The report concludes non-HIV-infected individuals should not receive PEP or other prophylaxis regimens including multiple doses of nevirapine.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports severe nevirapine-related hepatotoxicity and rashes among pregnant women. Kramer and colleagues described 14 cases of mild-to-moderately severe hepatotoxicity and 11 cases of mild-to-moderately severe rash among 125 pregnant women who received nevirapine. A second prospective, randomized, open-label study comparing nelfinavir/zidovudine/lamivudine versus nevirapine/zidovudine/lamivudine in pregnant women was stopped early because 5 of 17 women on nevirapine had events leading to treatment discontinuation, and one of the five experienced fulminant hepatic failure and death. Nevirapine prescribing information was subsequently changed and initiation of nevirapine is now contraindicated in women (pregnant or not) with a CD4+ cell count greater than 250/mm³ due to a greater risk of adverse events.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnancy; increased risk in women with a CD4+ cell count greater than 250/mm³ (initiation now contraindicated); nevirapine given as part of a combination regimen (nevirapine/zidovudine/lamivudine).
raw_record.extra_details: Severe nevirapine-related hepatotoxicity and rash described in pregnant women. Kramer study: 14 cases of mild-to-moderately severe hepatotoxicity (1/35 African-American, 13/86 non-African-American) and 11 cases of rash among 125 pregnant women. Second prospective randomized open-label trial stopped early: 5/17 women on nevirapine had adverse events leading to discontinuation, 1 of 5 experienced fulminant hepatic failure and death. Led to changes in nevirapine prescribing information; initiation contraindicated in pregnant or non-pregnant women with CD4+ count >250/mm³.

raw_record.support_text: At least eight cases of fulminant hepatitis culminating in maternal death related to antiretroviral therapy containing nevirapine in pregnancy have been reported. Six cases in one of the series shared fulminant hepatic failure presenting four to five weeks after starting therapy, in treatment-naive women with normal pre-therapy ALT and no hepatitis B or C history. All cases occurred in women with baseline CD4 counts above 250 cells/µL, and hepatitis progressed rapidly to hepatic failure despite nevirapine discontinuation and intensive clinical and laboratory monitoring.

raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure (fulminant hepatitis) appearing 4-5 weeks after therapy start; normal pre-therapy ALT; no hepatitis B or C history; progressed to maternal death despite nevirapine interruption. Immune-mediated toxic liver effect hypothesis noted in the paper.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents a case series of nevirapine-associated adverse events in pregnant HIV-infected women. Patient 1 (starting NVP-based ART at 27 1/7 weeks gestation) developed fever, diffuse urticarial rash, eosinophilia, clinical hepatitis, and renal failure; NVP was discontinued, and laboratory parameters returned to baseline 4 months after delivery. Patient 2, who added NVP at the 27th week of gestation, presented with pruritus, urticarial rash, and elevated ALT/AST with eosinophilia; after NVP discontinuation, repeat LFTs returned to baseline.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnant HIV-infected women on nevirapine-containing antiretroviral therapy (third-trimester initiation); accompanies urticarial rash and eosinophilia.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient 1: ALT 235 U/L (grade 2), AST 309 U/L (grade 3), GGT 233 U/L at onset with fever, eosinophilia, and renal failure; improved after NVP discontinuation, resolved after cesarean delivery ~4 months postpartum; patient also on Combivir and treated with prednisone. Patient 2: ALT 295 (grade 3), AST 152 (grade 2) at onset; LFTs returned to baseline 4 weeks after stopping NVP; also on Combivir. Dechallenge supported by LFT return to baseline after NVP discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: Among 107 pregnant women initiating HAART in the MTCT-Plus Program, eight developed grade 3 or 4 adverse events attributed to HAART. Two women developed grade 4 liver toxicity attributed to nevirapine (NVP), with alanine aminotransferase levels over 50 times and over 5 times the upper limit of normal, respectively. All events resolved with drug changes and no deaths were reported. In the short-course ARV (PMTCT) cohort, no grade 3 or 4 toxicities were observed.

raw_record.extra_details: Two cases with grade 4 liver toxicity attributed to NVP; alanine aminotransferase over 50x and over 5x upper limit of normal in the two respective women; events resolved with drug change (switched to nelfinavir); no deaths. raw_record.support_text: Among women who initiated nevirapine (NVP), 2 of 42 pregnant women (4.8%) and 43 of 211 nonpregnant women (20.4%) developed either rash or hepatitis after starting NVP (rate ratio 0.234 pregnant vs nonpregnant, 95% CI 0.0516-0.797). One pregnant woman developed grade 2 hepatitis and one grade 1 rash; both resolved upon NVP discontinuation. Two nonpregnant women with time to AE >90 days both had hepatitis, one also with lactic acidosis, and both normalized their transaminases upon medication discontinuation. None of the cohort developed fulminant hepatic failure or died.

raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 21 pregnant and 211 nonpregnant women. Onset within the first 30 days for 31 of 41 nonpregnant women with known onset, days 31-60 for 8, and day 408 and 487 for 2. Package insert notes female gender and CD4 >250 associated with greatest hepatotoxicity risk.

raw_record.support_text: In a South African randomized study of HIV-infected patients, early hepatotoxicity (grade 3 or greater increase in serum aminotransferase levels within the first 12 weeks) occurred in 17% of patients in the nevirapine group. Fatal drug-related liver failure occurred in two of 385 women receiving nevirapine. The study population consisted of a high proportion of women with relatively high baseline CD4 cell counts (mean 398 cells/µl), and stavudine was part of the NRTI backbone of the regimen.

raw_record.extra_details: Randomized comparison with efavirenz; early hepatotoxicity (grade 3 or greater aminotransferase rise within 12 weeks) in 17% of the nevirapine group versus 0% in the efavirenz group; fatal drug-related liver failure in 2 of 385 women. A separate study reported that among HIV patients one-third of all liver toxicities leading to hospital admission were associated with nevirapine use, and 80% of these occurred in patients with underlying chronic HCV infection.

raw_record.support_text: Before marketing nevirapine, Boehringer-Ingelheim ran a series of clinical trials that concluded nevirapine can lead to both skin rash and liver toxicity in HIV patients. With a 200 mg/day lead-in dose for the first 2 weeks followed by 400 mg/day, liver toxicity was detected in 1% of the tested population. Postmarketing reports gathered by Boehringer-Ingelheim indicated the incidence of liver toxicity was greater than before approval, increasing from 1% to 3%.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Treatment of HIV-1 infection; nevirapine used with a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor or protease inhibitor (not monotherapy).
raw_record.extra_details: FDA-approved June 1996 (marketed as Viramune); 200 mg/day lead-in for 2 weeks then 400 mg/day. Clinical-trial liver toxicity in 1% of patients; postmarketing (pharmacovigilance) incidence rose to 3%. Abstract reports rare life-threatening liver failure associated with nevirapine therapy; first 6 weeks of therapy are most critical for adverse drug reactions with close clinical/laboratory monitoring urged during the first 12 weeks.

raw_record.support_text: Researchers at the Hospital for Sick Children reported the case of a previously healthy 14-year-old boy with ADHD who had received pemoline 37.5 mg/day for 16 months together with methylphenidate 20 mg/day for 2 months. He was hospitalized due to jaundice, which progressed into acute liver failure; a liver biopsy was suggestive of drug toxicity. He underwent liver transplant, which failed, and the child died. All known causes of liver failure (infection, metabolic disease, tumour, chemical exposure) were ruled out.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (14-year-old boy); co-medication methylphenidate 20 mg/day as a possible co-exposure; therapeutic dose (pemoline 37.5 mg/day for 16 months).
raw_record.extra_details: Case progressed from jaundice to acute liver failure; liver biopsy suggestive of drug toxicity; liver transplant failed and child died. A crude relative risk of developing liver failure was estimated at 45.3 (95% CI 4.1, 510), based on three reported cases and an assumption of 80,000 exposed children in North America and a 1:10^6 rate of fatal paediatric liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of pemoline-induced hepatic failure that resulted in the need for a liver transplant. A 9-year-old boy diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and treated with pemoline developed signs and symptoms consistent with liver failure; pemoline therapy was discontinued but hepatic function continued to deteriorate, and the patient ultimately required a liver transplant. Pemoline was associated with the development of hepatotoxicity, mostly in pediatric patients, and this is reported as the second case of pemoline-induced hepatic failure resulting in liver transplant.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (9-year-old boy)
raw_record.extra_details: Indication: attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Hepatic function continued to deteriorate after pemoline discontinuation. Reported as the second known case of pemoline-induced hepatic failure resulting in liver transplant; most reported cases occurred in pediatric patients. Mechanism of the adverse effect is unknown; hypotheses proposed include hypersensitivity reactions, dose-related phenomena, and autoimmune reactions. Authors advise against pemoline as first-line ADHD treatment and recommend liver function testing before and during therapy.

raw_record.support_text: These cases fit the reported spectrum of pemoline hepatitis. Hepatocellular injury is prominent. Pemoline hepatotoxicity is more common in children than in adults, and occurs late in the course of treatment; drug-induced hepatitis usually resolves after withdrawal. In our patients, treatment with pemoline lasted an average of 16 months before hepatotoxicity was evident. Liver biopsy specimens from children with jaundice or more severe symptoms showed hepatocellular necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Reported case series skewed to children (more common in children than adults) and males; one reported case with preexisting cholestatic liver disease; the most severe case involved concurrent use of methylphenidate, an unresolved co-exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Treatment averaged 16 months before hepatotoxicity; injury occurs late in the course of treatment; biochemical recovery was slow and aminotransferases could take months to normalize; biopsy in jaundiced or more severely symptomatic children showed hepatocellular necrosis; the most severe patient had fulminant hepatic failure and required liver transplantation. Mechanism speculation includes metabolic idiosyncrasy and decreased pemoline metabolism with chronic use (half-life increases with chronic use and age); hypersensitivity considered less likely due to lack of fever/rash, though eosinophilia may occur and rechallenge caused rapid aminotransferase rises in only some patients. Chemical: phenylisohydantoin, an oxazolidinone derivative.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 43 cases of hepatic injury in patients treated with pemoline, in whom pemoline was the only drug and serological markers of viral disease (hepatitis A, B, CMV, EBV) were negative, with one of two rechallenge attempts positive. The authors conclude that the 43 cases support the reality of pemoline-induced hepatic injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 43 reported cases, all with pemoline as the only drug and negative serology for hepatitis A, hepatitis B, CMV and EBV (NANB hepatitis could not be excluded); rechallenge was positive in 1 of 2 patients who received a month-long readministration, with recurrence of AST and bilirubin elevation; the injury appeared hepatocellular based on high serum aminotransferase values; case fatality rate was 1 out of 13 jaundiced patients (7%); one 9-year-old boy had persistent liver-enzyme elevations for over 8-9 months after drug discontinuation, judged probably to represent other disease (possibly NANB hepatitis); in remaining cases symptoms and biochemical markers regressed after stopping the drug; clinical presentation included elevated AST, hyperbilirubinemia (peak bilirubin 26 mg/dL in the fatal case with late AST of 42) and hepatocellular necrosis; pemoline continues to be prescribed in the adolescent population.

raw_record.support_text: The abstract reports the first report of hepatotoxicity due to pemoline, a CNS stimulant used in Great Britain and Europe, describing two patients who developed reversible liver abnormalities while receiving pemoline during a prospective US efficacy and safety study and following rechallenge with the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases among approximately 600 patients on chronic therapy in a prospective efficacy and safety study; first report of pemoline hepatotoxicity despite about 10 years of prior use; liver abnormalities were reversible on withdrawal and recurred on rechallenge; liver biopsy, serum bilirubin, SGOT, alkaline phosphatase, BSP storage capacity (S) and transport maximum (Tm), and estimated hepatic blood flow were assessed; 'Drug hypersensitivity' is listed among the key words.

The paper titles and develops this as a case of pemoline-induced hepatotoxicity, reporting that the patient developed acute hepatitis with submassive necrosis and required orthotopic liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Off-label use for overweight; dose 75 mg/day (within recommended dosages for its primary indication).
raw_record.extra_details: Therapy recently modified with introduction of pemoline; liver dysfunction progressed rapidly (grade II encephalopathy, INR 2.6, bilirubin 28.4 mg/dl, glucose 49 mg/dl) and patient listed for transplant at UNOS status I; surgical biopsy and explant showed acute hepatitis with submassive necrosis and focal cirrhosis; underwent orthotopic liver transplantation on day 20. Discussion states pemoline-induced hepatotoxicity is supported by a large body of evidence: about 50 published cases of liver enzyme increases of variable entity reversible after withdrawal, at least 4 cases of acute liver failure leading to liver transplantation, and 3 fatal cases. Cases mostly paediatric because of the primary indication in attention/hyperactivity deficit disorders. Steroids (methylprednisolone 60 mg/day) tried but did not change disease course.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports its own case series of 4 patients who developed significant liver injury while receiving pemoline, with ALT values of 1060–5000 U/L, elevated total/direct bilirubin, prolonged prothrombin time, and jaundice, malaise, fever, or hepatosplenomegaly. Patients 1 and 2 required orthotopic liver transplantation, while patients 3 and 4 resolved, with normalization of liver chemistries taking 3 months after discontinuing pemoline.

Rechallenge in one patient brought relatively rapid hepatic inflammation, suggesting sensitization; autoantibodies (positive ANA in all three tested, antiparietal cell and antihistone antibodies in others) suggested possible drug-induced autoimmune activation.

raw_record.support_text: Nitrofurantoin is identified among the most common single implicated antimicrobial agents causing DILI in the DILIN cohort and appears in the top ten drugs of the DILIN, Icelandic, and Spanish prospective studies (in at least two of the three studies).
raw_record.extra_details: Antibiotic; among most common single implicated antimicrobial agents in DILIN (with amoxicillin–clavulanate, isoniazid, trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole); listed in Table 1 with more than 100 reported DILI cases (LiverTox).

raw_record.support_text: The paper identified 24 patients with drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis (DIAIH), of whom 11 had nitrofurantoin-induced AIH and 11 had minocycline-induced AIH. Nitrofurantoin AIH patients (n=11) had a median age of 61 years, all female, duration of therapy 24 months (8-36), ANA positive in 73%, typical histology in 45%, compatible histology in 55%, and jaundice at presentation in 73%; all required immunosuppressive therapy and 100% of those tried discontinued treatment successfully.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 cases of drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis attributed to nitrofurantoin; median age 61 years, all female, median therapy duration 24 months (8-36). ANA positive 8/11 (73%), SMA positive 6/11 (55%), simplified AIH score probable or definite 7/9 (78%), typical histology 5/11 (45%), compatible histology 6/11 (55%), jaundice at presentation 8/11 (73%). Liver tests at presentation (median): AST 827 U/L, ALT 778 U/L, ALP 426 U/L, total bilirubin 7.0 mg/dL. Immunosuppressive therapy in 11/11; steroids alone 8/11, steroids plus azathioprine 3/11; trial of discontinuation successful 9/9 (100%). Confluent necrosis on histology; gamma globulin levels unavailable in 2 cases.

raw_record.support_text: The study characterized clinical and autoimmune features of liver injury caused by nitrofurantoin, minocycline, methyldopa, or hydralazine, using 88 cases of DILI attributed to these agents in the DILIN prospective study (2004-2014).
raw_record.extra_details: 82% of cases attributed to nitrofurantoin had an autoimmune phenotype (autoimmune score >= 2). 74% of all 88 cases had hepatocellular injury and 25% had severe injury; 91% of cases were women. Autoimmune features (ANA, SMA, IgG) decreased with recovery; no association with HLA-DRB1*03:01 or *04:01 vs controls.

raw_record.support_text: A severe but transient bleeding disorder and liver dysfunction followed oral ingestion of nitrofurantoin (Furandantin). The liver disorder appeared to be toxic hepatitis rather than intrahepatic cholestasis, and the bleeding was attributed to deficiencies of prothrombin and factor VII caused by the hepatitis. Spontaneous bleeding into the neck necessitated tracheostomy after exchange transfusion.
raw_record.extra_details: 65-year-old male treated orally with 150 mg/day nitrofurantoin for dysuria for one month; nausea from the start. Liver disorder was toxic hepatitis (the paper explicitly favored toxic hepatitis over intrahepatic cholestasis); resulting prothrombin and factor VII deficiencies caused a severe but transient, life-threatening hemorrhagic state (nose, neck, hemoptysis, hematuria) requiring exchange transfusion and tracheostomy. The paper notes development of toxic hepatitis following nitrofurantoin ingestion appears to be quite rare.

raw_record.support_text: Nitrofurantoin was among the agents whose liver injury was analyzed in the DILIN cohort, with no significant difference in severity or outcomes between African-Americans and Caucasians.

The patient developed erythema multiforme, cholestatic hepatitis, and acute pulmonary toxicity secondary to nitrofurantoin administration, culminating in death. The authors recommend promptly discontinuing nitrofurantoin when evidence of skin, lung, or liver adverse reactions manifests.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of cholestatic hepatitis attributed to nitrofurantoin administration; the patient also developed erythema multiforme and acute pulmonary toxicity and died. Authors advise prompt discontinuation of nitrofurantoin when skin, lung, or liver adverse reactions appear.

raw_record.support_text: A 49-year-old woman developed acute granulomatous hepatitis while receiving nitrofurantoin for recurrent urinary tract infections; nitrofurantoin was the reported causative agent. She had received nitrofurantoin in the month preceding and up to admission.
raw_record.extra_details: 49-year-old woman with recurrent urinary tract infections on nitrofurantoin (therapeutic use); presented with fever (rectal 39 C) and malaise, no jaundice; elevated alkaline phosphatase 255 mU/ml, SGOT 160 mU/ml, SGPT 100 mU/ml; liver biopsy showed granulomatous hepatitis (negative for organisms on Gomori methenamine silver and AFB stains and culture); symptoms resolved (defervescence, normal liver function) on nitrofurantoin withdrawal, and patient was well 4 months later.

raw_record.support_text: A 50-year-old woman developed jaundice and right upper quadrant pain after taking nitrofurantoin 50 mg once daily for 12 months. Tests showed bilirubin 132 µmol/L, ALT 747 IU/L, ALP 294 IU/L, and elevated IgG 22.2 g/L with negative autoantibodies. Liver biopsy revealed autoimmune chronic active hepatitis with mild fibrosis, consistent with immune-mediated drug-induced liver injury. After nitrofurantoin was suspended and prednisolone started, ALT declined and liver function normalized within two months.
raw_record.extra_details: Prolonged therapeutic prophylaxis; nitrofurantoin 50 mg once daily started 12 months prior to admission. Described as severe acute on chronic hepatitis with jaundice. ALT began to rise 5 months before admission despite previously normal liver function. History included type 2 diabetes and numerous co-medications (pioglitazone, metformin, amitriptyline, paroxetine, lansoprazole, chlorphenamine, buprenorphine, morphine sulfate, temazepam, lactulose). Viral serology negative; gallstones on ultrasound but otherwise unremarkable; MRCP excluded biliary obstruction. Treatment with prednisolone 20 mg daily led to recovery with normal liver function tests.

raw_record.support_text: The patient had only been treated with nitrofurantoin in the year before liver disease appeared, so nitrofurantoin is judged the most likely cause of the liver damage; a rechallenge ('provocation test') was considered but deemed unethical given the severe initial liver reaction. The case was presented with a laboratory picture resembling chronic active hepatitis, with SGOT up to 930 U/l, raised SGPT and γ-globulin, and high titres of ANF and smooth-muscle antibodies, resolving after withdrawal (SGOT fell to 19 U/l by Aug-74).
raw_record.extra_details: Long-term nitrofurantoin treatment; single-patient case report with a chronic-active-hepatitis-like picture and no pulmonary involvement (unlike three previously reported similar cases that also showed lupus-like syndrome with pulmonary fibrosis). SGOT rose to 930 U/l during treatment and normalized (19 U/l) after discontinuation; ANF titre fell from >=1/1600 to 1/25. An immunological (immune-mediated) reaction mechanism was proposed. Provocation test withheld as unethical.

raw_record.support_text: Among 13 cases (5.3%) with a drug-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis (DI-AILH) phenotype, infliximab and nitrofurantoin were each responsible for five cases.
raw_record.extra_details: One of the most frequent causes of the DI-AILH phenotype (5 of 13 cases).

raw_record.support_text: Nitrofurantoin was implicated in 3 cases of mixed (2<R<5) reaction DILI ALF. Separately, high ANA titers (1:80-1:640) were seen in 3 DILI cases attributed to nitrofurantoin, and the anti-smooth muscle antibody-positive subjects took nitrofurantoin or sulfasalazine.
raw_record.extra_details: 3 cases of mixed reaction DILI ALF; 3 DILI cases with ANA titers 1:80-1:640 attributed to nitrofurantoin.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN prospective study of 300 patients, nitrofurantoin was the second most frequently implicated agent after amoxicillin-clavulanate in adjudicated cases of drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort causality adjudication: definite 32%, highly likely 41%, probable 14%, possible 10%, unlikely 3%.

raw_record.support_text: In a DILIN adjudicated cohort, nitrofurantoin was one of four agents (with ciprofloxacin, cefdinir, and levonorgestrel/ethinylestradiol) that accounted for all DILI cases belonging to BDDCS class 4. Class 4 DILI cases had a significantly lower percentage of jaundiced patients (P<.001), lower rate of absolute eosinophilia >500/µL (P=.008), lower peak ALT (P=.001) and aspartate aminotransferase (P<.001), and lowest hospitalization rate (45%, P=.01).
raw_record.extra_details: Listed as one of four agents accounting for all BDDCS class 4 DILI cases in the DILIN cohort (383 eligible cases, 107 drugs, causality 1/2/3=definite/highly likely/probable, oral, known daily dose). Class 4 aggregate features (not drug-specific) as described.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a patient with nitrofurantoin-induced pancreatitis, the first reported case in the literature, confirmed by rechallenge. The authors propose that nitrofurantoin-induced jaundice is not always due to cholestatic hepatitis but can result from obstruction of the common bile duct due to edema of the pancreatic head secondary to nitrofurantoin pancreatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: 79-year-old woman took nitrofurantoin 400 mg daily for a suspected urinary tract infection; nausea and anorexia from start of therapy, jaundice and epigastric pain 5 days later. Laboratory findings included total bilirubin 150 µmol/L, conjugated bilirubin 129 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 1325 U/L, GOT 226 U/L, GPT 214 U/L, GGT 1925 U/L, LDH 647 U/L, serum amylase 371 U/L, urinary amylase 500 U/L. Diagnosis of nitrofurantoin-induced pancreatitis confirmed by rechallenge; clinical and biochemical picture cleared rapidly after drug discontinuation. Differential diagnoses included nitrofurantoin-induced cholestatic hepatitis and pancreatic carcinoma. Authors conclude jaundice resulted from common bile duct obstruction due to edema of the pancreatic head, an alternative to cholestatic hepatitis; the paper notes allergic nitrofurantoin reactions mainly cause lung reactions and cholestatic jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: Nitrofurantoin was implicated 12 times in the US ALFSG analysis, with 11 individual cases and 1 in combination with a statin, among the most common antimicrobial causes of drug-induced ALF.
raw_record.extra_details: ALFSG: 12 drug-induced ALF cases (11 individual, 1 in combination with a statin). DILIN: n=13 suspected single-agent DILI. UNOS: n=12 causes of emergency liver transplant for drug-induced ALF.

raw_record.support_text: Nitrofurantoin was implicated in two DILI cases in the series, one hepatocellular and one cholestatic. One of the nitrofurantoin cases was jaundiced (bilirubin 12.8 ULN).
raw_record.extra_details: Two of 77 cases, both female; pattern 1 hepatocellular/1 cholestatic; duration of treatment median 189 (7-370) days; time to biochemical resolution 120 (60-180) days. One jaundice case with bilirubin 12.8 ULN, AST 18.6 ULN, ALT 17.1 ULN.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 20 patients with acute hepatitis, of which eight cases were of drug-induced hepatitis due to a variety of agents, one patient had nitrofurantoin-induced hepatitis. In this patient, both bilirubin and ALT fell in close association with the liver stiffness measurement.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as one of eight drug-induced hepatitis cases among 20 patients studied with acute hepatitis; the patient had elevated ALT and bilirubin that fell in close association with the liver stiffness measurement (LSM). Part of a study of the effect of acute necroinflammatory activity on transient elastography, in which LSM in the cirrhotic range did not predict fibrosis in acute hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Nitrofurantoin is listed among the main 10 drugs leading the Latin American DILI Registry with n = 11 cases, with RUCAM-based causality assessment.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 cases in the Latin American DILI Registry; RUCAM-based causality assessment used.

raw_record.support_text: De Boer et al. characterized autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) secondary to nitrofurantoin, minocycline, methyldopa, or hydralazine in DILI cases, defining an autoimmune phenotype as an autoimmune score ≥2. For nitrofurantoin, an autoimmune phenotype was present in the majority of cases (83%), and the typical AIH HLA alleles HLA-DRB1*03:01 and HLA-DRB1*04:01 were found at rates similar to the general population.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases from the US DILIN prospective study; autoimmune phenotype (score ≥2 based on ANA, SMA, SLA, IgG) present in 83% of nitrofurantoin cases; AIH-associated HLA-DRB1*03:01 and HLA-DRB1*04:01 allele frequencies similar to the general population. Nitrofurantoin is one of the drugs for which the modified lymphocyte transformation test was found not reliable for diagnosing DILI.

raw_record.support_text: Nitrofurantoin was among the top 10 drugs involved in LA DILI Registry cases, with n = 11 cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Among the top 10 drugs in the LA DILI Registry, n=11 cases.

raw_record.support_text: In a population-based Icelandic study of drug-induced liver injury, the most commonly implicated agents included nitrofurantoin (4% of 51 cases). Cases were adjudicated by RUCAM with 94% classified as highly probable (n=18) or probable (n=30).
raw_record.extra_details: ~2/51 (4%) of DILI cases attributed (nitrofurantoin listed as a commonly implicated agent with 4%); causality per RUCAM (94% of all cohort cases highly probable or probable). All cohort cases recovered with median time to resolution of liver tests 67 days.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that commonly used drugs like diclofenac and nitrofurantoin are frequently reported to cause DILI, and that the Björnsson Iceland prospective population-based study implicated nitrofurantoin and diclofenac as common agents linked to DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated as a common agent linked to DILI in the Björnsson Iceland prospective population-based study; frequently reported to cause DILI; Likelihood score category A (well-known cause, >50 published cases); antibiotic with a higher DILI risk than ulipristal acetate; SMPC advises hepatic function monitoring with prolonged use and/or signs of hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: A 40-year-old woman developed hepatic failure after receiving nitrofurantoin 200 mg po bid for one month for urinary-tract infection prophylaxis; symptoms began after two weeks of therapy. After other causes of hepatic failure (viral infection, autoimmune disorder, concomitant medications, cancer, Wilson's disease, ethanol abuse, pregnancy) were ruled out, the authors concluded that she appeared to have developed hepatic failure secondary to nitrofurantoin, ultimately requiring orthotopic liver transplantation. Acute and chronic hepatic injury has previously been reported with nitrofurantoin use.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 200 mg po bid for one month; symptoms after two weeks; progressed to stage I hepatic encephalopathy; orthotopic liver transplantation two days after admission; liver histology showed extensive hepatocyte necrosis, moderate cholestasis, and bridging necrosis; lab values: AST 17.7, ALT 19.7, alkaline phosphatase 4.1, total bilirubin 436 umol/L, GGT 3.0 ukat/L, ammonia 156 umol/L. Nitrofurantoin has been associated with acute and chronic liver injury at a rate of 0.02-0.035%; reaction described as idiosyncratic or hypersensitivity, not dose related, proposed mechanism immunoallergic or metabolic; small number of fatalities previously reported.

raw_record.support_text: The DILIN retrospective study is a nationwide registry that includes patients who experienced liver injury within the past 10 years after consuming one of 8 drugs: phenytoin, isoniazid, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid, valproic acid, nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, minocycline, and quinolone antibiotics. The goals include establishing a database of patients with severe DILI due to any of these medications.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among 8 drugs included in the DILIN retrospective registry for patients with severe DILI due to these medications.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports nitrofurantoin (Furadantine®)-induced hepatic injury based on a series of 34 cases, with acute cases recovering within 1 to 3 months following discontinuation and chronic cases taking longer, some showing signs of irreversible damage. Chronic cases were consistent with chronic active hepatitis, often with nuclear and smooth muscle antibodies, and HLA B8 was not more frequent in these patients than in controls.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 34 hepatic injury cases attributed to nitrofurantoin (Furadantine®); incidence was higher in females (88.1%) and in patients over 64 years (47% of female cases), versus prescription figures. Acute reactions appeared almost invariably within the first 6 weeks of therapy with an accelerated reaction to rechallenge; chronic injury involved chronic active hepatitis with autoantibodies. Two cases showed signs of irreversible damage. Reported incidence of nitrofurantoin-induced hepatic injury estimated at 0.0003% and 0.00073% (the latter with other hepatotoxins); the authors' own estimate based on Dutch sales (1977-1986) with correction for ~80-90% underreporting suggests approximately 0.020-0.035% symptomatic cases (23 probable, 32 probable+possible cases). Mechanism considered immunoallergic or metabolic idiosyncrasy; direct toxicity unlikely since reaction is not dose-dependent and relatively rare and unpredictable. One case of cross-sensitivity to furazolidone and nifuroxime, and possible liver damage after ingestion of milk from a nitrofurantoin-treated cow noted as supporting evidence. HLA B8 was not increased in chronic patients (33% vs 23% controls).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that the cases described in this and other reports show the development of chronic active hepatitis in some patients who have taken nitrofurantoin for long periods, and that the hypergammaglobulinemia and serologic abnormalities are those of the 'autoimmune' ('lupoid') type of that condition. The reaction is described as rare and as a hypersensitivity reaction, and continued drug administration after hepatic injury has become apparent could lead to cirrhosis or death.
raw_record.extra_details: Series of 20 patients with nitrofurantoin-associated chronic liver disease. Two deaths (Patients 3 and 4) occurred in patients who continued the drug after jaundice onset; one showed massive acute hepatic necrosis, the other chronic active hepatitis with submassive necrosis, fibrosis and collapse. Histology was autoimmune/lupoid type. Laboratory findings: elevated transaminase 20/20, elevated bilirubin 12/17, low albumin 13/15, elevated gamma globulin 14/17, positive antinuclear antibody 11/16, positive antismooth muscle antibody 11/12, negative HBsAg 12/12. Authors recommend monthly monitoring during long-term therapy; continued administration after apparent liver injury could lead to cirrhosis or death.

raw_record.support_text: The DILIN acute DILI series (74 patients) reported that nitrofurantoin was causative in three patients, attributing human DILI to nitrofurantoin as a single agent in this registry.
raw_record.extra_details: Causative single agent in three of 74 acute non-acetaminophen DILI patients in the DILIN series.

raw_record.support_text: Three patients with nitrofurantoin-induced liver injury were included in this Icelandic DIAIH study, among 18 patients who developed immune-mediated liver injury; 93% of the cohort had hepatocellular injury and 8 (53%) had jaundice but none had coagulopathy. Causality was assessed with RUCAM, and the new simplified AIH criteria were calculated.
raw_record.extra_details: 3 patients; hepatic injury classified as drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis (DIAIH) with positive ANA and/or elevated IgG. RUCAM causality across the cohort: 12 probable, 1 highly probable, 2 possible. 93% of cohort hepatocellular, 53% jaundice, none with coagulopathy.

raw_record.support_text: Nitrofurantoin was among the drugs implicated as a cause of hepatic injury in a follow-up study of 44 patients with drug-induced hepatotoxicity; patients with abnormal hepatic evaluation at follow-up had previously taken nitrofurantoin.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported in the 44-patient drug-induced hepatotoxicity cohort followed a median of 5 years; some follow-up biopsies showed residual chronic hepatitis, fibrosis, and ductopenia.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of a healthy 24-year-old female who presented with epigastric abdominal pain, found to be drug-induced liver injury (DILI) secondary to her recent nitrofurantoin use. Nitrofurantoin is described as having idiosyncratic drug-induced liver toxicity as a rare but significant side effect that can present with abdominal pain and elevated liver enzymes, and can cause either an acute or a chronic hepatitis-like syndrome that may be severe and lead to liver failure or cirrhosis. In this patient, nitrofurantoin (50 mg every six hours for the past three days) was discontinued and symptoms subsided with liver enzymes trending toward normal over three days.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of a 24-year-old obese female with GERD taking famotidine and ibuprofen as needed, not taking herbal products. Nitrofurantoin 50 mg q6h for 3 days for a urinary tract infection; normal liver enzymes at PCP one week prior. Admission labs: direct bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, total bilirubin 1.9 mg/dL, AST >717 U/L, ALT 476 U/L, alkaline phosphatase and INR normal (hepatocellular biochemical picture). Viral hepatitis (A/B/C/E), autoimmune (ANA, anti-smooth muscle, anti-mitochondrial, anti-LKM-1) and toxicology (ASA, acetaminophen, alcohol) workups negative. Gallbladder ultrasound showed stones without cholecystitis. Dechallenge: nitrofurantoin stopped, symptoms subsided after 3 days, enzymes trended toward normal (ALT 331 U/L, AST 135 U/L). No rechallenge. Abstract also notes nitrofurantoin hepatotoxicity can be severe, causing liver failure or cirrhosis, but that outcome is not attributed to this case.

raw_record.support_text: In Case 2, a woman with an abnormal autoimmune screen (ANA 1:640, smooth muscle antibodies 1:320) and a liver biopsy showing marked chronic portal inflammation, extensive fibrosis and some features of cirrhosis was treated with oral steroids, and nitrofurantoin was stopped. Her liver biochemistry improved rapidly after a few weeks of corticosteroid medication, and two years after diagnosis she remained well with entirely normal liver biochemistry on prednisolone 7.5 mg daily, implicating nitrofurantoin exposure as the cause of this autoimmune hepatitis with fibrosis/cirrhosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Autoimmune markers included ANA 1:640, smooth muscle antibodies 1:320, anti-mitochondrial antibodies 1:320, positive anti-Rho/ENA/rheumatoid factor, and elevated IgG 22.8 g/L. Biopsy showed marked chronic portal inflammation, extensive fibrosis and some features of cirrhosis. Treated with prednisolone (initial 40 mg daily, maintenance 7.5 mg daily) after stopping nitrofurantoin, with rapid biochemical improvement; azathioprine postponed for pregnancy.

raw_record.support_text: A series of 23 nitrofurantoin-induced DILI cases is described, with causality assessed by RUCAM ('Highly probable' in 3, 'Probable' in 16, 'Possible' in 4) and RECAM ('Probable' in 7, 'Possible' in 16). The main indication was long-lasting therapy for prophylaxis of recurrent lower UTI (91%), with 11 patients prescribed for more than six months; only two patients received it as first-line treatment for less than three weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 23 cases, 22 (96%) women, mean age 61 years (SD 14). Indication mostly long-term prophylaxis of recurrent lower UTI; median duration of therapy 175 days (IQR 96-760), median latency to DILI 143 days (IQR 83-757); hepatotoxicity developed in <30 days (13%), 30-180 days (39%), and >180 days (48%). Median dose 100 mg/day (range 50-450). Hepatocellular pattern most frequent (83%), mixed or cholestatic in 8.7% each. Jaundice in 48%, hospitalization 39%, fever 8.7%, arthralgia 20%. Positive autoantibodies in 65% (ANA 64%, ASMA 18%, LKM-1 8.3%); drug-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis (DI-AILH) in 5 patients (22%). Severity: mild 52%, moderate 44%, severe 4%. Median time to resolution 81 days (IQR 57-141). Liver parameters at recognition (xULN, median): total bilirubin 1.5, AST 11, ALT 13, ALP 1.4. No skin rash, asthenia, abdominal pain, or pruritus.

raw_record.support_text: In this case series of acute hepatitis patients, toxic (drug-induced) hepatitis was attributed to intake of nitrofurantoin, efavirenz, amphetamine, prophylthiouracil, sirolimus, flumatid, lamictal (lamotrigine), and opipramol. All patients underwent ultrasound, liver stiffness measured by FibroScan at diagnosis, and biopsy in some cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among drugs causing toxic (drug-induced) hepatitis in a case series of acute hepatitis patients in which liver stiffness was measured with FibroScan at diagnosis; fibrosis staged by METAVIR.

raw_record.support_text: Among non-sulfa-containing antibiotics causing non-APAP drug-induced acute liver failure in the Acute Liver Failure Study Group registry, 11 of 19 cases were nitrofurantoin. Of 19 nitrofurantoin or sulfasalazine patients who underwent biopsy, 13 lacked autoimmune hepatitis features, 12 had massive or submassive necrosis and 1 had microvesicular steatosis.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 of 19 non-sulfa antibiotic ALF cases were nitrofurantoin. Biopsy findings pool nitrofurantoin with sulfasalazine: 13 of 19 lacked autoimmune hepatitis features, 12 had massive/submassive necrosis, 1 microvesicular steatosis.

raw_record.support_text: Among 1198 ALFSG subjects over 10 years, DILI caused ALF in 11% of cases and 61 unique agents were implicated, alone or in combination. Antimicrobials were the commonest cause, in particular isoniazid, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, nitrofurantoin, and antifungal agents.
raw_record.extra_details: Named among antimicrobials as a commonest cause of DILI-induced ALF in the ALFSG cohort (61 unique implicated agents; DILI caused 11% of ALF). Latency of implicated agents 1-2 weeks to 8 months; 65% of subjects did not stop the drug until or after jaundice developed.

raw_record.support_text: Chronic active hepatitis is described as a recognized complication of treatment with nitrofurantoin; the letter reports the first case in a man. A 65-year-old man had taken nitrofurantoin 100 mg at night for 12 months for recurrent urinary tract infections and was admitted for nonresolving jaundice and developing liver failure. Biopsy showed severe architectural disturbance with extensive liver cell necrosis, reported as chronic active hepatitis with bridging hepatic necrosis. After nitrofurantoin was stopped (and prednisolone started), liver function tests returned to normal within 4 weeks and ascites and oedema resolved.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported case in a man; all previously described cases occurred in women. Dose 100 mg at night for 12 months for recurrent urinary tract infections. Bilirubin 55 mmol/L with moderately raised transaminase and alkaline phosphatase; total protein 92 g/L, albumin 28 g/L; fourfold increase in IgG, IgA, and IgM; hepatitis B surface antigen negative; antinuclear factor and smooth-muscle antibody titers 1:640. Biopsy: severe architectural disturbance, extensive liver cell necrosis, chronic active hepatitis with bridging hepatic necrosis. After nitrofurantoin was stopped and prednisolone started, liver function tests returned to normal within 4 weeks and ascites/oedema resolved.

raw_record.support_text: The letter reports chronic active hepatitis related to nitrofurantoin treatment, first reported in 1975 and now totaling 24 reported cases. In all cases hepatitis B surface antigen has been negative, and raised immunoglobulin levels and antinuclear factor suggest the "lupoid" form of chronic active hepatitis. All reported cases have been in women, but the author argues this reflects greater drug use by women rather than differential sex susceptibility; a Swedish 10-year adverse-reaction analysis found an 86% preponderance of female patients. The single reported male case is taken as evidence that females are not preferentially susceptible to this toxic effect.
raw_record.extra_details: 24 cases of chronic active hepatitis reported since 1975; all hepatitis B surface antigen negative; raised immunoglobulins and antinuclear factor suggest 'lupoid' autoimmune form; all earlier cases occurred in women (86% female preponderance in a Swedish 10-year adverse-reaction analysis), attributed to greater use in women; the presented single male case suggests females are not preferentially susceptible.

raw_record.support_text: Analysis of 26 RUCAM-based cases of idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (iDILI) caused by nitrofurantoin was described; no mechanistic proposals were presented for these cases.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM-based iDILI cases, n = 26; no mechanistic proposals presented; study citation [58].

raw_record.support_text: A 72-year-old woman taking nitrofurantoin for recurrent urinary sepsis presented with breathlessness, abdominal discomfort, and abnormal liver function tests. Drug toxicity secondary to nitrofurantoin was diagnosed, and cessation of the drug plus a course of steroids markedly improved her condition.
raw_record.extra_details: 72-year-old woman with recurrent urinary sepsis; presented with breathlessness (pulmonary toxicity), abdominal discomfort, and abnormal liver function tests; concomitant pulmonary and hepatic toxicity; condition markedly improved after drug cessation and a course of steroids. Disease entity 'Hepatotoxicity' (UMLS:C0235378).

raw_record.support_text: In the initial 300 patients in the DILI Network (DILIN) registry of non-acetaminophen DILI causes, nitrofurantoin was among the most common individual agents found responsible, accounting for 4.3% of cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Represented 4.3% of the first 300 non-acetaminophen DILI cases in the DILIN registry.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN prospective registry, nitrofurantoin was the third most common individual DILI agent, accounting for 42 of 899 adjudicated cases. It was a predominant cause (16 cases) among the 60 cases with latency greater than 1 year.
raw_record.extra_details: 42 adjudicated DILI cases; predominant cause (n=16) among cases with latency >1 year.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 28 drug-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis (DI-AILH) patients, nitrofurantoin was the most frequent implicated drug (n=7) followed by tetracycline antibiotics (minocycline n=4 and lymecycline n=2). The commonest drug classes were antibiotics (n=18), biologics (n=4, comprising infliximab and adalimumab), and herbal products (n=4). Most patients scored RUCAM 6-8 (probable DILI) and the rest 3-5 (possible DILI).
raw_record.extra_details: Most frequent drug implicated (n=7 cases, patients 5,13,14,15,16,17,18); doses 50-100 mg with durations up to 1843 days; RUCAM scores 6-8 (probable DILI); RUCAM ≥9 highly probable, 6-8 probable. Biopsies showed autoimmune hepatitIS features whereas simplified and new histology criteria were typical/compatible (and one atypical case, patient 14). Median exposure to presentation across cohort was 116 days (IQR 31-762).

raw_record.support_text: The letter discusses drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis (DIAIH) cases (n=24) reported by Björnsson et al., contrasting them with classical AIH (n=237). The author specifically addresses nitrofurantoin-induced DIAIH, noting that these cases presented acutely as DIAIH with stage 0 fibrosis histologically, centrilobular necrosis (65%), confluent necrosis (30.4%), and a median aminotransferase increase >10 times the upper limit of normal; the author suggests these nitrofurantoin-induced DIAIH cases were acute and severe (though not fulminant) in presentation, and that a 'cirrhotic' radiologic appearance was likely due to sampling variability or radiologic mimics of cirrhosis rather than true fibrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis (DIAIH) described in Björnsson et al. series of 24 DIAIH patients; nitrofurantoin-induced cases were acute and severe (unlikely fulminant) in presentation, with centrilobular necrosis (65%) and confluent necrosis (30.4%), stage 0 fibrosis histologically, and median aminotransferase increase >10x ULN. The author attributes an apparent 'cirrhotic' liver appearance on radiology to confluent necrosis, fibrosis sampling variability, or radiologic mimics (e.g., severe/fulminant hepatitis), not confirmed histologically.

raw_record.support_text: Shortly after admission, a diagnosis of nitrofurantoin-induced hepatic and pulmonary toxicity was entertained, and administration of Macrodantin (nitrofurantoin) and erythromycin was discontinued. A liver biopsy showed moderate portal infiltration by lymphocytes, plasma cells, acute inflammatory cells, and eosinophils, piecemeal necrosis, mild fibrosis, extensive hydropic changes of hepatocytes, and focal acidophilic degeneration, interpreted as severe chronic active hepatitis with a significant acute component. ANA (homogeneous) and anti-smooth muscle antibody were positive, while hepatitis A, hepatitis B, and infectious mononucleosis markers were negative.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report; brand Macrodantin. Admission labs: total bilirubin 130 µmol/L (7.6 mg/dL), direct 106 µmol/L; SGOT 1124 IU/L; SGPT 1184 IU/L; alkaline phosphatase 203 IU/L; γ-glutamyl transferase 305 IU/L; prothrombin time 13.5 s. CT showed normal liver without biliary dilatation; liver-spleen scan suggested hepatic dysfunction. Biopsy: portal infiltration with lymphocytes/plasma cells/eosinophils, piecemeal necrosis, mild fibrosis, hydropic hepatocyte changes. ANA (homogeneous) >1:640, anti-smooth muscle 1:40. Co-medication erythromycin was also discontinued at the same time; viral hepatitis and mononucleosis screens negative.

raw_record.support_text: In a US DILIN cohort of 300 subjects with suspected drug-induced liver injury, a single prescription medication was implicated in 217 subjects. The most common single implicated agents included nitrofurantoin, implicated in 13 cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated in 13 of 300 DILI cases; listed among the most common single implicated prescription medications in a prospective DILIN registry (causality assessed by expert opinion and RUCAM across the cohort).

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN analysis by Vuppalanchi et al, all drugs causing liver injury did so as single agents and were assessed as being at least probably related or higher using standardized scoring criteria and expert opinion. Class 4 agents (low solubility, poor metabolism) included nitrofurantoin, ciprofloxacin, cefdinir, and levonorgestrel with ethinyl estradiol, representing 40 of the 372 cases of DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: Class 4 BDDCS agent (low solubility, poor metabolism) in the DILIN analysis of 383 instances of DILI caused by 99 single agents; classified as at least probably related.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that among the DILI cases in the GWAS, nitrofurantoin was a causative drug with 64 cases, the second most common after diclofenac.
raw_record.extra_details: DILI GWAS (862 European ancestry DILI cases); nitrofurantoin was a causative drug with 64 cases.

raw_record.support_text: In this case, the prior hepatitis episode upon the first introduction of nitrofurantoin in the 1990s constituted a major element supporting the attribution of the antibiotic as the cause of the drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis (HAI). The patient met the 1999 IAIHG simplified criteria for definite HAI with a score of 8/8 (ANA 1/640, anti-smooth-muscle antibodies 1/80, IgG 28.2 g/L, no viral hepatitis, and typical histology with lymphocytic infiltrate and significant necroinflammatory activity).
raw_record.extra_details: Case of definite drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis (IAIHG simplified score 8/8): ANA 1/640, anti-smooth-muscle antibodies 1/80, IgG 28.2 g/L, no viral hepatitis, histology with lymphocytic infiltrate and significant necroinflammatory activity. Key causality element was a prior hepatitis on first nitrofurantoin exposure in the 1990s (rechallenge-like history). Second liver ultrasound showed atrophy of the left lobe. Björnsson et al. retrospective analysis of 261 HAI patients reported 22 (9.2%) drug-induced HAI, of which 11 (4.6%) were linked to nitrofurantoin, with more frequent liver atrophy (73% vs 24%, p=0.0089) than non-drug HAI and no relapse at 6-month follow-up after drug discontinuation vs 65% in non-drug HAI (p<0.0001).

raw_record.support_text: In an ALFSG cohort, which categorized patients into DILI-ALF and APAP-ALF groups, nitrofurantoin was named among the causative drugs responsible for non-APAP hepatotoxicity progressing to acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among causative drugs for non-APAP hepatotoxicity in the ALFSG DILI-ALF cohort (this study subgroup N=39; larger study N=52).

raw_record.support_text: DILI-inducing antibiotics included nitrofurantoin, ketoconazole, tretinoin and terbinafine; antibiotics accounted for 11 patients (2.59%) of DILI cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Antibiotic; antibiotics accounted for 11 patients (2.59%) of DILI cases.

raw_record.support_text: Among 60 long-latency DILI cases (>365 days) in the DILIN study, the most commonly implicated agents were nitrofurantoin (n=16), minocycline (n=10), statins (n=4), amiodarone (n=3), mercaptopurine (n=3), atomoxetine (n=2), tamoxifen (n=2), oxaliplatin (n=2), and interferon-beta (n=2).
raw_record.extra_details: Long-latency DILI (>365 days); n=16 cases in the DILIN Prospective Study cohort.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 23 nitrofurantoin-induced liver injury cases from the LATINDILI network, 91% of patients received long-term treatment (>3 weeks), consistent with prior reports that long-term treatment is more likely to produce DILI. Cases showed hepatocellular, cholestatic, and mixed biochemical injury patterns, jaundice, hospitalization, and a severity spectrum ranging from mild to severe; where causality was assessed, most cases scored 'Probable' on RUCAM while the majority scored 'Possible' on RECAM. Liver biopsy in seven patients showed interphase hepatitis, lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltrate, ductal damage, and fibrosis. Nitrofurantoin was restricted in Spain (2016 AEMPS) to curative treatment of acute cystitis for a maximum of seven consecutive days.
raw_record.extra_details: 23 cases from LATINDILI network (Latin America and Spain); 91% long-term treatment (>3 weeks); 48% exposure time >1 year; 43% latency >1 year; mean age 61 years; female predominance (100% in the >=180-day group); p<0.001 longer latency in >=180-day group (median 761 vs 103 days); biochemical patterns hepatocellular (7/10 vs 10/11), cholestatic, and mixed; jaundice in 3-7 cases; hospitalization in 3-4 cases; severity mild/moderate/severe (one severe case in >=180-day group); DI-AILH (drug-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis) in 2-3 cases; positive autoantibodies in 5-10 cases; liver biopsy in 7 patients showing interphase hepatitis, lymphocytic/eosinophilic infiltrate, ductal damage, lobular necrosis, fibrosis and incipient cirrhosis; RUCAM mostly 'Probable' vs RECAM mostly 'Possible'; a retrospective study cited reported 25/3400 (0.7%) elderly patients with hepatic or pulmonary adverse effects; 2016 Spanish AEMPS restriction to 7 days for acute cystitis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 67-year-old woman who developed fulminant hepatitis related to the use of nitrofurantoin taken for prophylaxis of recurrent urinary tract infection. The Naranjo probability scale determined a probable cause-effect relationship between nitrofurantoin and liver disease, and the patient died of liver failure due to continued use of nitrofurantoin despite jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports two patients who developed chronic active hepatitis secondary to prolonged nitrofurantoin therapy, resembling cases reported in Scandinavian patients. The presence of severe necroinflammatory liver disease with hypergammaglobulinemia and high titers of antinuclear and smooth muscle antibodies initially suggested the lupoid form of chronic active hepatitis. Discontinuation of nitrofurantoin therapy resulted in immediate clinical improvement, and laboratory values became normal in 4 to 6 weeks without specific treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic/prolonged nitrofurantoin therapy; both patients recovered with resolution of laboratory values in 4-6 weeks after drug discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients (Cases 1 and 2). Features of chronic active hepatitis with hypergammaglobulinemia, high titers of antinuclear and smooth muscle antibodies, and biopsy showing chronic aggressive hepatitis suggestive of the lupoid form. Case 1 biopsy: moderate hepatocellular unrest, spotty centrilobular necrosis, focal acidophilic degeneration, portal/periportal inflammation and piecemeal necrosis with prominent plasma cells, minimal fibrosis. Repeat biopsy showed progression possibly evolving into cirrhosis. Case 2 showed marked enhancement of lymphocyte transformation by nitrofurantoin (ratio 13.8) at first study, gone in follow-up (ratio 1.4); Case 1 showed no enhancement. Discontinuation led to clinical improvement.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes 23 cases of nitrofurantoin-induced liver injury from the Latin American DILI Network (LATINDILI) and the Spanish DILI Registry, with causality assessed using the RUCAM and RECAM scales. Hepatocellular damage was the most frequent biochemical pattern (83%), and 5 patients (22%) developed nitrofurantoin-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis (NI-AILH), of whom two had persistent transaminase increases requiring immunosuppressive treatment. Neither death nor liver transplantation was documented in this series; the median time to resolution was 81 days.

raw_record.extra_details: 23 DILI cases from LATINDILI and the Spanish DILI Registry; causality assessed with RUCAM and RECAM; mean age 61 years; hepatocellular damage 83%; 52% asymptomatic; 65% positive autoantibody titres; median time to resolution 81 days (IQR 57-141), 83% recovered within 6 months; 5 patients (22%) developed nitrofurantoin-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis (NI-AILH), 2 of whom required immunosuppressive treatment for persistent transaminase increase. General spectrum of nitrofurantoin DILI ranges from transient liver enzyme increases, icteric hepatitis, acute liver failure to death. Incidence reported as 1 in 1,369 patients (Iceland population study); nitrofurantoin accounts for 4.2-4.7% of DILI cases in prospective registries; paraphernalia: high ALT with increased gamma globulin and positive ANA/ASMA titres mimicking AIH.

raw_record.support_text: Four patients are described in whom anicteric hepatitis appeared to be related to the use of nitrofurantoin. All had increased serum transaminase levels, hypergammaglobulinaemia, and liver biopsies suggestive of chronic active hepatitis; three showed cirrhotic features and two had circulating albumin-IgG-complexes ('tailing-albumin'). Serum transaminases became normal within weeks of drug withdrawal, while hypergammaglobulinaemia and biopsy findings persisted during 2-6 months of observation. One patient was re-challenged with nitrofurantoin, which resulted in recurrence of elevated serum transaminases after nine weeks of medication.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that long-term use of nitrofurantoin in moderate doses in patients with normal kidney function may cause or trigger chronic hepatitis. They cite a challenge (rechallenge) with the drug in patient no. 1 and rapid normalization of serum transaminases in all patients after withdrawal, together with no elevated transaminase levels in a well-matched control group, as strong evidence. Liver biopsies in all four patients showed chronic aggressive hepatitis with piecemeal necrosis and mononuclear/eosinophilic infiltration, with signs of developing cirrhosis in three patients; none were jaundiced and alkaline phosphatase was normal.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term (chronic) use in moderate doses in patients with normal kidney function; exact dose not specified; none of the patients were jaundiced and clinical picture was not severe.
raw_record.extra_details: Four patients; biopsies taken at maximal transaminase increase; first biopsies showed enlarged portal tracts with mononuclear and eosinophilic polymorphonuclear infiltration, piecemeal necrosis, irregular lobular margins, and swollen/eosinophilic hepatocytes; three patients (nos. 2, 3, 4) also showed lobular architectural irregularity with fibrous septa and signs of developing cirrhosis; patient no. 1 showed chronic aggressive hepatitis in follow-up biopsies 3 and 6 months after withdrawal. Rapid normalization of serum transaminases after drug withdrawal; rechallenge with drug in patient no. 1 confirmed the association; matched control group had no elevated transaminase levels. Hypoalbuminemia and hypergammaglobulinemia developed during treatment; normal eosinophile counts peripherally but eosinophilic granulocytes in liver biopsies. All but patient no. 2 (who had pulmonary infiltrates) had hepatic reaction without other obvious toxic manifestations.

raw_record.support_text: Nitrofurantoin can lead to a broad spectrum of liver injury with mild liver test abnormalities, acute liver failure with fatal outcome, or need for liver transplantation, and also liver cirrhosis. It was recently found to be one of the most common single agents associated with drug-induced liver injury (DILI) in a prospective study in the United States, and has been documented to induce autoimmune hepatitis (DIAIH). Zone 3 necrosis was observed in the DIAIH cohort. All current-series DIAIH cases with laboratory parameters scored at least 'probable' by the new simplified AIH criteria.

raw_record.extra_details: Broad spectrum includes mild liver test abnormalities, acute liver failure with fatal outcome, need for liver transplantation, and liver cirrhosis. Zone 3 necrosis observed in DIAIH cohort. Identified as one of the most common single agents associated with DILI in a recent prospective US study. Severe imaging abnormalities (low attenuation patches, confluent fibrosis and massive fibrotic bands) seen in 8/11 (73%) nitrofurantoin DIAIH cases. Inadvertent rechallenge reported to induce chronic liver injury and severe liver injury 17 years after an initial hepatitis-like illness. Cases scored at least 'probable' by simplified AIH criteria. Favorable prognosis in current DIAIH series; no cirrhosis found at presentation or on follow-up.; qualifying_conditions_note: None

raw_record.support_text: In a 55-year-old female with lichen simplex chronicus and an autoimmune disposition (mesangioproliferative glomerulonephritis and hypothyroidism), chronic nitrofurantoin therapy was implicated as the cause of autoimmune hepatitis-type 1. The positive ANA and ASMA results, hypergammaglobulinemia, histological chronic active hepatitis on liver biopsy, and clinical response to immunosuppressive drugs were strongly suggestive of nitrofurantoin-triggered autoimmune hepatitis. The Naranjo algorithm score was 6, indicating a probable drug-induced reaction. The patient was treated with drug withdrawal and parenteral glucocorticosteroids; azathioprine was considered if steroids failed.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had a pre-existing autoimmune disposition (mesangioproliferative glomerulonephritis and hypothyroidism); chronic nitrofurantoin therapy for UTI; 55-year-old female.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver biopsy showed chronic active hepatitis with lymphoplasmacytic portal infiltrate and interface hepatitis. Positive ANA and ASMA, hypergammaglobulinemia. Naranjo algorithm score 6 (probable DIR). WHO-method rechallenge test considered confirmatory but not performed due to severity. Treatment: drug withdrawal and parenteral glucocorticosteroids; azathioprine if steroids fail. The paper also notes nitrofurantoin has been linked to autoimmune hepatitis (mostly single case reports/small series) and estimates nitrofurantoin-induced hepatic injury incidence at about 3 cases per 1,000,000 from Dutch and Danish national adverse-drug-reaction monitoring agencies.
