raw_record.support_text: A 31-year-old primigravida was treated with nitrofurantoin 100 mg/day in the 36th week of gestation for dysuria with enterococcus in urine culture. After induced delivery, repeated labs showed elevated AST and ALT with negative hepatitis C and B markers, and the patient was subicteric. Nitrofurantoin was discontinued, and discontinuation plus methylprednisolone therapy significantly lowered liver enzyme levels. The authors concluded this was probably toxic liver damage caused by nitrofurantoin. The case is described as a rare case of acute toxic hepatitis in pregnancy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnant patient (31-year-old primigravida, 36th week of gestation); delivery was induced near term because of hypertension, which coexists with the exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 100 mg/day for treatment of dysuria from enterococcus urinary tract infection. Elevated aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase, negative hepatitis C and B markers, patient subicteric, normal coagulation and complete blood count, slight hepatomegaly on ultrasound without focal or diffuse lesions. Nitrofurantoin was discontinued and methylprednisolone therapy was introduced; liver enzymes significantly decreased to near normal. Authors described the injury as 'acute toxic hepatitis' (toxic drug-induced hepatitis).

raw_record.support_text: Sotorasib had a manageable tolerability profile in 359 patients with solid tumours treated with sotorasib 960 mg once daily in the CodeBreaK 100 trial. Increased ALT, increased AST and drug-induced liver injury (all 1%) were the most common ADRs leading to discontinuation of sotorasib. For the drug-induced liver injury portion of paragraph 40: DILI was reported as an adverse drug reaction and was among the most common ADRs leading to sotorasib discontinuation (1% of 359 patients). 26% of patients who had hepatotoxic reactions were treated with corticosteroids.
raw_record.extra_details: Sotorasib (KRAS G12C inhibitor, 960 mg orally once daily) for solid tumours/NSCLC. CodeBreaK 100 (n=359 solid tumour patients): drug-induced liver injury was an ADR leading to discontinuation in 1%; increased ALT (6%), increased AST (6%) and DILI (1%) were the most common ADRs leading to dose modification/discontinuation; increased ALT/AST elevation was transient with median time to onset of 8 weeks; 26% of patients with hepatotoxic reactions were treated with corticosteroids. Phase II CodeBreaK 100 (n=126 KRAS G12C-mutant NSCLC patients): grade >=3 liver-related TRAEs included ALT increase 6.3%, AST increase 5.6%, GGT increase 2.4% and drug-induced liver injury 1.6%; dose modification due to all-grade TRAEs 22.2%, discontinuation due to all-grade TRAEs 7.1%.

raw_record.support_text: In autopsy specimens from patients who developed jaundice after intake of iproniazid, cases were divided into groups including acute massive and submassive necrotic hepatitis (cases 1, 3, 6, 10, 13, 24, 26, and 27) with whole-lobule loss of epithelial cells, collapsed framework, and mixed inflammatory infiltrate, as well as subacute hepatitis with massive collapse (cases 2, 14, 15, 21, 22, 25B) showing degeneration, necrosis, collapse, and regeneration. Biopsy material from a subset of iproniazid-treated patients showed spotty necrotic hepatitis, subsiding hepatitis, and subacute hepatitis with bile stasis, hepatocellular degeneration/necrosis, and perilobular fibrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of patients who developed jaundice after iproniazid therapy, examined by liver biopsy and autopsy. Reported histopathology included spotty necrotic hepatitis, subsiding hepatitis, subacute hepatitis with bile stasis and perilobular fibrosis, acute massive and submassive necrotic hepatitis, and subacute hepatitis with massive collapse; a fulminant massive necrotic hepatitis was observed 10-12 days after the onset of jaundice. In one case (case 5) with the smallest total dose and shortest therapy, possible infectious hepatitis was raised as a competing cause.

raw_record.support_text: Anti-M6 antibodies were found in two cases of iproniazid-induced hepatitis in a series of 157 drug-induced hepatitis cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Anti-M6 antibodies were detected in two cases of iproniazid-induced hepatitis. From a 157-case series of drug-induced hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The occurrence of jaundice in a small fraction of patients receiving iproniazid (Marsilid) made necessary the study of biochemical features of the syndrome and evaluation of the incidence of hepatic dysfunction in patients receiving the drug. The paper explicitly frames this jaundice as a drug toxicity reaction, consistent with human iproniazid-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 86 patients developed jaundice while receiving iproniazid (data on 82 from manufacturer-submitted physician protocols, 4 from the Chicago, Ill. area). Jaundice was intense: 45% had bilirubin above 20 mg%, with values up to 60 mg%; in three quarters the direct-reading fraction was 40-65% of total bilirubin. Thymol turbidity was abnormal in 83% (range 4-41 units) and cephalin flocculation abnormal in 85%. Among substudies: serum iron elevated in all 6 patients; prothrombin time prolonged in 21/24; cholesterol esters below 60% of total in 9/13; serum albumin below 3 gm% in 8/27; globulins elevated (related table 1). GOT available in 50, GPT in 22 patients; 18 sera analyzed centrally. Iproniazid also known as Marsilid (Hoffmann-La Roche).

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses reports of severe hepatic necrosis in patients receiving iproniazid (Marsilid) phosphate medication, stating that no known mechanism for this toxicity has been demonstrated and that no definite relationship between dosage and extent or severity of hepatic damage appears to exist. The liver damage was histologically and biochemically indistinguishable from acute fulminating viral hepatitis, with patients showing diffuse parenchymal hepatic disease usually without fever; hepatomegaly was common and terminally patients developed hepatic coma. The mortality rate for cases of liver damage attributed to iproniazid medication approaches 20 per cent, markedly higher than that for viral hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Two additional recovering patients (Case 1, M.B., a 57-year-old male with depression, treated with iproniazid 25 mg 3x/day for one week then 10 mg 3x/day until onset of icterus; total dose 945 mg; also received promazine and secobarbital) are presented with serial liver function studies and needle biopsies. Popper studied liver tissue from 27 patients (needle biopsy or autopsy) with jaundice associated with iproniazid therapy. A previous fatal case of massive hepatic necrosis following iproniazid was reported by Shay and Sun. Damage was described as dissimilar to liver damage from chemical hepatotoxins or chlorpromazine sensitivity; Popper suggested iproniazid may activate existing subclinical viral hepatitis in a serum hepatitis carrier. Case 1 presented with icterus, nontender hepatomegaly, dark brown urine, decreased appetite, 6% eosinophilia, and bile pigments/bilirubin in urine.

raw_record.support_text: Iproniazid, a monoamine oxidase inhibitor introduced in 1952 for tuberculosis and later used for depression and intractable angina, is described as a good example of a drug associated with a hepatitis-like picture. Patients were reported to develop acute hepatic necrosis while receiving the drug, with hepatocellular damage on biochemical tests. The complication seems unrelated to total dose, may appear up to 20 days after cessation of therapy, may be more frequent after a second course, and the most seriously affected patients develop a shrinking liver and die of liver failure; mortality may be as high as 20 percent.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence very low; unrelated to total dose; onset can be up to 20 days after stopping therapy; possibly more frequent after a second course; preicteric gastrointestinal symptoms resembling acute hepatitis followed by jaundice with pale stools, dark urine, and enlarged tender liver; maximum serum bilirubin reached 2-3 weeks after recovery; shrinking liver and fatal liver failure in the most severely affected; mortality up to 20%. Pathology virtually indistinguishable from acute virus hepatitis; electron microscopy shows endoplasmic reticulum damage.

raw_record.support_text: Case 4 concerns a 48-year-old man who took iproniazid 150 mg daily for two months (total dose 9.0 g) for depression and developed jaundice, dark urine, and evident diffuse liver damage. The comment states there is no positive evidence in this case to suggest any etiology for the patient's evident diffuse liver damage other than iproniazid therapy, attributing the injury to iproniazid.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient took 150 mg iproniazid daily for two months (total 9.0 g) for depression prior to admission; presented with jaundice and dark urine of one week's duration plus mild abdominal cramps; on admission: total serum bilirubin 9.5 mg%, total cholesterol 209 mg%, cephalin flocculation 4+, thymol turbidity 8.0 units, alkaline phosphatase 11.5 Bessy-Lowry units, SGOT (serum glutamic oxalacetic transaminase) 1,300 units; no prior hepatic, biliary, or GI disease; no history of transfusion, injections, or exposure to hepatotoxic agents other than iproniazid; patient remained icteric at follow-up two weeks after discharge.

raw_record.support_text: Study of additional cases confirmed that the histological changes in the liver in patients who developed jaundice following the intake of iproniazid represent different stages and degrees of a diffuse hepatic parenchymal disease, with a picture similar to viral hepatitis. Multiple biopsy and autopsy specimens from patients who received iproniazid showed acute severe hepatitis and massive, submassive, or zonal necrotic hepatitis (14 biopsy and 19 autopsy cases in the tabulated material), and the authors note the mortality rate after iproniazid jaundice appears higher than in viral hepatitis, consistent with the greater severity of the histological changes.
raw_record.extra_details: Histology of jaundice after iproniazid intake was similar to viral hepatitis (spotty, contiguous, massive, submassive and zonal necrotic hepatitis); tabulated cases: 14 biopsy acute severe hepatitis, 5 biopsy others, 11 autopsy acute and 8 autopsy subacute or chronic necrotic hepatitis. Mortality reported higher after iproniazid jaundice than in viral hepatitis; higher-age group, particularly women, noted for worse prognosis, interpreted as possibly reflecting the age mix. No pre-existing liver disease encountered in the studied cases; authors raised the possibility of a hypersensitivity mechanism and that iproniazid itself produces the alterations in very few exposed patients.

raw_record.support_text: In the viral-hepatitis-type group (61 cases of drug-induced hepatic injury), the drugs involved were iproniazid, metahexamide, B-phenyl-isopropyl hydrazine, isocarboxazid, amidosalicylic acid, pyrazinamide, and zoxazolamine. The histology resembled the acute icteric spotty necrotic form of viral hepatitis, with single-cell necrosis, mononuclear infiltrates, balloon cells, acidophilic bodies, and cholestasis prominent in half of the spotty necrosis cases; the group also included extensive zonal necrosis and massive/submassive necrosis (acute atrophy, subacute atrophy, transition to postnecrotic cirrhosis, postnecrotic cirrhosis).
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among drugs involved in the viral-hepatitis-type (Group IV) drug-induced hepatic injury (61 cases). Histology included spotty necrosis (13 cases, acute icteric form with cholestasis prominent in half), extensive zonal necrosis (9 cases), and massive/submassive necrosis (39 cases: 13 acute atrophy, 15 subacute atrophy, 7 transition to postnecrotic cirrhosis, 4 postnecrotic cirrhosis). Monoamine oxidase inhibitor.

raw_record.support_text: The three patients observed developed hepatitis with jaundice while taking iproniazid therapeutically; the daily dose ranged from 30 to 75 mg and the drug was taken for 2 to 6 months before jaundice appeared. Jaundice appeared in all reported cases while the drug was still being taken, and the reported daily dose in other cases ranged from about 25 to 150 mg. The hepatic derangement in all three patients was characteristic of diffuse hepatocellular disease rather than the cholestatic type induced by chlorpromazine; liver biopsy in one case showed a histologic picture of toxic hepatitis with no significant bile stasis or eosinophilic infiltration. Clinical improvement was fairly rapid after stopping the drug, though the paper notes reported occurrences of fulminant jaundice ending with fatal necrosis of the liver.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 3 new patients plus previously reported cases; onset insidious with jaundice the outstanding symptom, hepatomegaly in 2 patients, no fever and no eosinophilia; laboratory findings included total bilirubin 25.4 mg/100 ml, direct 13.9, SGOT 920 units, serum alkaline phosphatase 6 Bodansky units, prolonged prothrombin time 21.8 s (control 10.2); liver biopsy showed toxic hepatitis without bile stasis or eosinophilic infiltration; improvement fairly rapid after drug cessation; some reported cases of fulminant jaundice ending with fatal necrosis of the liver. Contrasted with the cholestatic-type alteration induced by chlorpromazine. Fatal case of Frantz and that of de Verteuil and Lehmann cited.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 230 cases of hepatitis associated with iproniazid therapy, with 51 deaths among them, and states that a cause-and-effect relationship has been well established and accepted. The estimated incidence is one per 3,000 to 4,000 patients treated with iproniazid, with death occurring in 20 to 25 per cent of the afflicted. The hepatotoxicity has an insidious onset and a particularly fulminant course, is not readily differentiated pathologically from infectious hepatitis, and no relationship of dose to incidence appears to exist.
raw_record.extra_details: 230 reported cases of hepatitis with 51 deaths. Estimated incidence 1 per 3,000-4,000 patients treated; fatality in 20-25% of the afflicted. Insidious onset and particularly fulminant course; not readily differentiated pathologically from infectious hepatitis other than by severity. No dose-incidence relationship evident; hepatotoxic effects occurred only rarely within the first few weeks of therapy. Predictive susceptibility factors not identified; routine liver-function testing did not predict impending disease; course not immediately reversible after drug discontinuation. Iproniazid (Marsilid) was used in selected patients with mental depression and as adjunctive therapy in terminal malignancies and advanced collagen diseases.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports histologic changes in the liver in patients with iproniazid jaundice, describing necrosis, stromal collapse, and diffuse mononuclear cellular infiltrates with some neutrophils and eosinophils, plus bile stasis; the authors' observations in five patients were similar, and these pathologic features are indistinguishable from those of viral hepatitis. The hepatotoxicity of iproniazid is stated to be apparently unrelated to the dose or duration of therapy, and iproniazid-associated jaundice is described as more severe than that of viral hepatitis with a relatively high mortality rate.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver histology showed hepatic parenchymal necrosis, stromal collapse, and diffuse cellular infiltrates predominantly of mononuclear cells with some neutrophils and eosinophils, and bile stasis, indistinguishable from viral hepatitis (confirmed by Popper in 27 patients and by the authors in 5). Onset was insidious with anorexia and dark urine, without a febrile prodrome. Jaundice from iproniazid appeared more severe and deeper than in viral hepatitis, not explained by patient age. The hepatotoxicity appeared unrelated to dose or duration of therapy; in 15 patients jaundice developed after the drug had been discontinued, possibly because pharmacologic effects persist up to three weeks after a single dose. There were 86 patients with 'iproniazid jaundice'; a relatively high mortality rate was noted, and the intensity/severity may be inflated because severe cases are more likely reported to the manufacturer.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses the laboratory features of 'iproniazid jaundice' and compares them with viral hepatitis (Table 6), and illustrates the similarity of viral hepatitis and jaundice associated with iproniazid administration through case histories. One case (CASE I) involved a 69-year-old woman given iproniazid (75 mg/day for 5 days, then 50 mg/day for 10 days, then 25 mg/day) for severe depression who developed deep jaundice, hepatic coma, and died; a liver biopsy showed extensive necrosis, mild inflammation, and cholestasis, and serum transaminase levels suggested hepatic necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 69-year-old woman with prior myocardial infarction and cerebrovascular accident on anticoagulant (bishydroxycoumarin/Dicumarol) therapy; advanced age and co-medication present as non-default context.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented as 'iproniazid jaundice', a syndrome with laboratory features compared to viral hepatitis across multiple patients (e.g., increased serum iron in 6 patients, prolonged prothrombin time in 23, low cholesterol ester fraction in 14, decreased albumin in 9, increased globulin in 17). CASE I: iproniazid dosed 75 mg/day x5 days, 50 mg/day x10 days, then 25 mg/day for depression; onset of anorexia/weakness/dark urine/icterus; liver palpable 5 cm below costal margin; deep jaundice, stupor, flapping tremor, hepatic coma and death; biopsy showed extensive necrosis, mild inflammation, and cholestasis; serum transaminases suggested hepatic necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: A 51-year-old female with NTRK2 fusion-positive NSCLC was treated with first-line larotrectinib 200 mg daily orally. From week 9 to week 18 therapy had to be interrupted due to a grade 3 elevation of transaminases (ALT > AST); serum bilirubin and coagulation were normal. Hepatopathy screening showed no viral or autoimmune etiology, with mild hepatic steatosis on ultrasound and a normal FibroScan. After a 2-month break the patient recovered to grade 1 hepatitis. Re-exposure to larotrectinib at 50% dosage at week 18 produced a recurrence of grade 3 hepatitis within 9 days, and after a renewed start at 20% of dose a consecutive ALT increase occurred, leading to permanent discontinuation of larotrectinib.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 51-year-old female, never-smoker, with SQSTM1(exon4)-NTRK2(exon16) fusion-positive NSCLC; larotrectinib given first-line at 200 mg daily orally. Grade 3 transaminase elevation (ALT > AST) with normal bilirubin and coagulation; hepatopathy screening excluded viral and autoimmune etiology; mild hepatic steatosis on ultrasound with normal FibroScan. Recovery to grade 1 hepatitis after a 2-month treatment break. Positive rechallenge: recurrence of grade 3 hepatitis within 9 days upon re-exposure at 50% dose, and an ALT increase on rechallenge at 20% dose, leading to permanent discontinuation and switch to entrectinib.

raw_record.support_text: The authors investigated liver biopsy specimens from patients with hepatotoxicity due to five drugs not previously listed for peroxisomal ultrastructural changes: aprindine (N-[3-(diethylamino)propyl]-N-phenyl-2-indanamine), amitriptyline, clomipramine, phenytoin and methimazole (thiamazol, 1-methylimidazole-2-thiol). Six patients with drug-induced hepatitis were studied, and each drug is reported as the cause of that patient's hepatotoxicity, with the abstract noting catalase-activity loss in amitriptyline, aprindine, clomipramine and methimazole hepatitis and peroxisomal proliferation in aprindine, methimazole and phenytoin hepatitis livers.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as one of five drugs causing drug-induced hepatitis in six patients. Peroxisomal changes attributed in this case included decreased catalase activity, peroxisomal proliferation (number increased 1.5 to 4.2 times), shape changes, and surface density exceeding the upper control value. Chemical name: N-[3-(diethylamino)propyl]-N-phenyl-2-indanamine.

raw_record.support_text: Viral-hepatitis-like hepatic damage ('aprindin hepatitis') developed in a 50-year-old woman after taking aprindin, the cause of the jaundice being confirmed by the same signs recurring when the drug was taken again after initial withdrawal. A rechallenge confirmed the drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 50-year-old woman; viral-hepatitis-like hepatic damage termed 'Aprindin-Hepatitis'; jaundice present; injury reproduced on re-administration after initial withdrawal (positive rechallenge). Aprindin (Amidonal) is an oral antiarrhythmic of the local-anesthetic class; no hepatotoxic side effects had been observed in prior clinical testing.

raw_record.support_text: A 63-year-old man developed granulomatous hepatitis probably due to the administration of aprindine (200 mg/day for paroxysmal supraventricular arrhythmia). Evidence of hepatitis appeared within 6 weeks of initiating aprindine therapy and resolved rapidly when the drug was withdrawn; six months later, fibrosis but no granulomata were found in the expanded portal tracts. The authors conclude that granulomatous hepatitis can occur during aprindine therapy. Biopsy 5 days after withdrawal showed granulomata in portal tracts and lobules with an infiltrate of eosinophils, plasma cells and lymphocytes and no caseous necrosis; HBsAg, PPD, CMV and EBV tests were negative, and serum aprindine concentration was not determined.
raw_record.extra_details: Granulomatous hepatitis presented within 6 weeks of aprindine at 200 mg/day; symptoms included abdominal discomfort, right hypochondrium pain, rigor, fever (38°C), nausea, vomiting, fatigue, headache, pruritus and jaundice; marked elevation of serum bilirubin and moderate aminotransferase abnormalities; liver resolved on withdrawal; second biopsy at 6 months showed portal tract fibrosis without granulomata.

raw_record.support_text: In this phase 2, open-label study, participants with HCV GT1 infection and Child-Pugh class B (CP-B) decompensated cirrhosis received elbasvir (EBR) 50 mg plus grazoprevir (GZR) 50 mg for 12 weeks. The authors state the regimen was well tolerated, with no evidence of hepatotoxicity. AE data (paragraph 46) showed minor grade 1 ALT/AST increases and mild transient grade 3 bilirubin elevations but no clear drug-related liver injury.

raw_record.extra_details: Grade 1 ALT increase (1 participant) and grade 1 AST increase (2 participants); no ALT/AST increases >2.5x baseline or >5x ULN; grade 3 bilirubin increases 2.6-5.0x ULN in 4 participants that were mild, transient, and resolved with ongoing therapy. Authors explicitly concluded no evidence of hepatotoxicity. The approved EBR/GZR FDC (GZR 100 mg) is noted to be contraindicated in CP-B/C due to elevated GZR concentrations and consequent increased risk of ALT elevations.

raw_record.support_text: In this case series, three young women (aged 17-30 years) from rural India ingested the rodenticide Rattol (yellow phosphorus) in suicidal attempts, in approximate quantities of 20, 10, and 5 grams. Two of the women developed toxic hepatitis and acute liver failure, while one had no organ damage. All three recovered within a mean hospital stay of 17 days.
raw_record.extra_details: Rodenticide brand Rattol sold as paste and powder; quantities ingested were approximately 20, 10, and 5 grams; time lag between ingestion and first healthcare was 6, 18, and 1 hours, respectively; major symptoms were vomiting, abdominal pain, and headache; significantly altered biological markers included total bilirubin, alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, creatinine, prothrombin time, international normalized ratio, and MELD score; two of three cases (Case 1 and Case 2) had toxic hepatitis and acute liver failure while one had no organ damage; all recovered within a mean hospital stay of 17 days; no specific antidote is known and treatment remains supportive care; the paper also notes that rodenticide-containing yellow phosphorus is a more frequent cause of drug-induced acute liver failure than paracetamol in India.

raw_record.support_text: In India many rodenticides contain hepatotoxic drugs leading to acute liver failure, of which yellow phosphorus (in 3% yellow phosphorus rodenticide paste) is most lethal. A consecutive series of 101 patients admitted with alleged yellow phosphorus rodenticide paste poisoning was analyzed; 42 (41%) developed acute liver injury, 21 (21%) developed acute liver failure, and the overall mortality was 19%. Conclusion states that a lethal dosage and late presentation led to development of acute liver failure and mortality.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Deliberate suicidal (para-suicide) ingestion of 3% yellow phosphorus rodenticide paste; no specific antidote; underlying liver disease ruled out.
raw_record.extra_details: 101 consecutive patients over 6 months; 62% female, 38% male; age 15-65 yr (peak 20-30 yr); ingestion mode: 34% raw, 30% with water, 20% with alcohol, 17% with food; first symptom <6h in 41%, 6-12h in 42%, >12h in 17%; care sought within 3h in 46%, 3-10h in 41%, after 10h in 13%. Liver injury spectrum: acute liver injury 42 (41%), acute liver failure 21 (21%), acute kidney injury 19%, multiple organ failure 19%, 3 acute pancreatitis, 2 myocarditis, 1 atrial fibrillation. INR <2 in 69, 2-3 in 11, >3 in 21; MELD <10 in 9, 11-20 in 30, 21-30 in 35, >30 in 27; all MELD >40 died. Overall mortality 19% (22% females, 13% males); 82 recovered (mean stay 8.88 days). Standard of care plus N-acetylcysteine administered.

raw_record.support_text: In an observational study (n=48, mean age 29) of rat killer compound (yellow phosphorus) poison consumption, all patients developed acute liver failure; 29 (60%) underwent therapeutic plasma exchange based on the presence of acute liver failure and bone marrow toxicity. Despite plasma exchange, mortality was 18%. Factors associated with poor outcome included no gastric lavage within 2 hours, hemodynamic instability, hepatic encephalopathy, high toxin dose, higher admission lactate (>4), delayed presentation (>72 hours), and worsening liver/renal function despite plasma exchange. Case formulation of the toxin appeared less toxic than paste.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intentional rat killer (yellow phosphorus) poison consumption; overdose/supratherapeutic exposure setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Rat killer compound (yellow phosphorus) is a protoplasmic poison causing multiorgan failure; dose >1 mg/kg is stated as nearly always fatal. Mean age 29; 50% (n=24) presented within 24 hours of consumption; 19% (n=9) had bone marrow toxicity at presentation (most commonly neutropenia with increased absolute monocyte count). 29 (60%) patients underwent therapeutic plasma exchange for acute liver failure and bone marrow toxicity; 3 developed hypotension during the procedure; number of sessions was based on LFT and coagulopathy. 18% mortality despite plasma exchange. Indication for exchange: acute liver failure and bone marrow toxicity; new-onset diabetes insipidus seen in 4 patients. Cake formulation appeared less toxic than paste.

raw_record.support_text: Rodenticide-induced hepatotoxicity (yellow phosphorus as the toxic protoplasmic agent) is described as a major cause of acute liver failure in southern and western India. Yellow phosphorus is a protoplasmic toxin with no specific antidote; management is supportive and may require liver transplantation. The Tamil Nadu Chapter of the Indian Society of Gastroenterology reported a retrospective series of 685 patients consuming rodenticide, of whom 450 developed hepatotoxicity; 396 were managed conservatively, 54 required plasma exchange and 1 patient additionally required a liver transplant. 35% had an adverse outcome with 131 deaths and 28 discharged in a moribund state.

raw_record.support_text: The editorial states that hepatotoxicity due to yellow phosphorus poison (YPP) is being increasingly recognized as a cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in parts of the Indian subcontinent, largely from southern and western India, analogous to paracetamol overdose causing toxic liver necrosis and death in the West.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Rodenticide-poison ingestion (non-therapeutic poisoning exposure) in parts of the Indian subcontinent (southern and western India).
raw_record.extra_details: A statewide multicenter survey across 6 districts in Tamil Nadu (Jan-Jun 2019) on causes of toxic hepatitis found a rodenticide (yellow phosphorus) ingestion to paracetamol overdose ratio of 75:1; among 450 YPP-induced hepatotoxicity cases, 131 (31%) died and 28 (6%) were discharged moribund; extrapolation to all 35 districts estimated a six-month case burden of 1584 rodenticide-induced hepatotoxicity patients (95% CI 265-6119) with ~554 projected poor outcomes. Only 1 of 450 (0.2%) underwent urgent liver transplantation. Plasma von Willebrand factor (vWF) levels predicted survival with AUC 0.92 vs MELD score 0.66 in 24 patients with YPP-induced hepatotoxicity (20 ALI, 3 ALF, 1 uncomplicated acute hepatitis).

raw_record.extra_details: The report demonstrates a YP poisoning case presenting with predominant clinical and biochemical cholestasis. After self-limiting nausea/vomiting on the day of ingestion, patient was asymptomatic for 4 days, then developed dark urine and severe pruritus (visual analogue score 8/10) on day 5, jaundice noted by day 8. Examination showed jaundice with excoriation marks from pruritus, firm liver palpable 4 cm below the costal margin, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, splenomegaly, ascites, or hepatic encephalopathy. The authors note this is the first documented case of clinical cholestasis in YP toxicity, though biochemical evidence of cholestasis had been reported previously.

raw_record.support_text: In a randomized trial of hepatic arterial infusion (HAI) after resection of liver metastases, a significantly higher rate of biliary sclerosis was noted in the HAI group than in the non-HAI group. Six of 17 patients receiving HAI therapy (35%) developed persistently elevated serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase levels indicative of biliary sclerosis; five underwent cholangiography documenting a pattern of stricturing consistent with this diagnosis, and four were managed with chronic indwelling stents. In the five patients with available treatment plans, the dose of FUDR given did not exceed 0.2 mg/kg/d. Three of the six patients received concomitant systemic chemotherapy (two with 5-FU/LV and one with CPT-11).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Delivery by hepatic arterial infusion (local/unusual route) in patients with resected hepatic metastases; three of the six affected patients also received concomitant systemic chemotherapy as part of adjuvant therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Biliary sclerosis (bile-duct stricturing injury) developed in 6/17 (35%) of HAI-treated patients, significantly more than controls; 5 confirmed by cholangiography, 4 managed with chronic indwelling stents, and 1 (patient 4) required intrahepatic Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy for a dominant hilar stricture. FUDR dose did not exceed 0.2 mg/kg/d in the five patients with available plans. One patient (paragraph 33) died of cirrhosis and subsequent liver failure associated with HAI therapy. raw_record.support_text: In a pilot study, 24 patients with hepatic metastases from colorectal cancer received hepatic artery infusion of floxuridine (FUDR) plus leucovorin (LV) through an implantable pump. Sclerosing cholangitis developed in 2 of 8 patients treated with FUDR 0.3 mg/kg/d plus LV 30 mg/m²/d for 14 days within 4 months, and in 3 of 9 patients treated with FUDR 0.3 mg/kg/d plus LV 30 mg/m²/d for 7 days; no biliary sclerosis occurred at the lower FUDR dose (0.2 mg/kg/d). The authors concluded that hepatic toxicity with FUDR and LV appeared to be greater than that previously reported with FUDR alone.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Given by hepatic artery infusion via an implantable pump (unusual regional route); co-infused with leucovorin (LV) as biochemical modulator; sclerosing cholangitis occurred at FUDR 0.3 mg/kg/d dose levels but not at the 0.2 mg/kg/d level, indicating a dose-related effect.
raw_record.extra_details: Pilot dosing study for hepatic metastases from colorectal cancer. Regimen 1: FUDR 0.3 mg/kg/d + LV 30 mg/m²/d for 14 days alternating with 2 weeks saline, sclerosing cholangitis in 2/8 patients within 4 months. Regimen 2: FUDR 0.2 mg/kg/d + LV 30 mg/m²/d for 14 days, no biliary sclerosis. Regimen 3: FUDR 0.3 mg/kg/d + LV 30 mg/m²/d for 7 days alternating with 1 week saline, sclerosing cholangitis in 3/9 patients. Overall response rate 72%; 18/25 patients alive at 1 year; median survival >27 months. Hepatic toxicity appeared greater than previously reported with FUDR alone.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of 34 patients receiving hepatic arterial infusion pump (HAIP) chemotherapy after resection/ablation of colorectal liver metastases, delayed complications were predominantly pump infections, chemotherapy-induced hepatitis, and biliary sclerosis. Biliary sclerosis developed in 6 (18%) patients, usually after the second or third dose of FUDR (floxuridine); all affected patients discontinued HAIP chemotherapy. Two patients had bilirubin levels of 3.3 and 2.9 mg/dL with diffuse sclerosis on cholangiogram that was not amenable to stenting, while 4 others underwent biliary stenting, with bilirubin normalization in 3 and a decline to 2.9 mg/dL in the fourth.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy (HAIP) with FUDR in patients with resectable/ablated colorectal liver metastases; non-systemic route of administration; all affected patients discontinued therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: FUDR = 5-fluoro-2'-deoxyuridine (floxuridine). Biliary sclerosis developed in 6 of 34 (18%) patients, usually after the second or third dose. Two patients had bilirubin 3.3 and 2.9 mg/dL with diffuse cholangiogram sclerosis not amenable to stenting; 4 underwent biliary stenting (bilirubin normalized in 3, declined to 2.9 mg/dL in one). Comparison with published series showed biliary sclerosis rates of 0.5-35% across studies.

Across 61 untreated and treated patients, 11 (18%) had bilirubin >3 mg/dL by 3 months, increasing to 28 (46%) beyond 6 months, with 3% developing biliary sclerosis. raw_record.support_text: In a prospective randomized trial of hepatic arterial (I.A.) versus intravenous (I.V.) FUDR (floxuridine) for colorectal liver metastases, I.A. FUDR was associated with major hepatobiliary toxicity, described as chemical injury to normal hepatocytes and ductal structures. Chemical hepatitis occurred in 79% (19/24) of I.A. patients versus 7% (2/29) on I.V. therapy, and biliary sclerosis occurred in 21% (5/24) of I.A. patients. raw_record.support_text: Floxuridine (FUDR) administered by continuous hepatic artery infusion through a totally implantable pump for hepatic metastases is described as causing chemical hepatitis as one of its major complications. At the City of Hope National Medical Center, 75 patients received continuous hepatic artery infusion of FUDR as part of a prospective protocol for treating hepatic metastases; the complications are tabulated, with all except chemical hepatitis and diarrhea requiring surgical intervention.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Regional continuous hepatic artery infusion via totally implantable pump for the indication of hepatic metastases (unusual route of administration).
raw_record.extra_details: 75 patients received continuous hepatic artery infusion of FUDR via implantable pump at the City of Hope as part of a prospective protocol; chemical hepatitis (drug-induced hepatitis) and diarrhea were the only major complications considered not to require surgical intervention. As of June 1985 more than 11,000 pumps had been implanted in the US, mostly for hepatic metastases from colorectal cancers treated with continuous hepatic artery FUDR.

raw_record.support_text: Nineteen patients with hepatic tumors were treated with hepatic artery infusion chemotherapy using an implantable pump delivering floxuridine (FUDR), starting at 400 mg for 2 weeks with 2 weeks of rest. Reported toxicity included dyspepsia, elevated liver function tests in all patients, gastric ulcer in 2, cholecystitis in 2, and sclerosing cholangitis in 3, attributing these liver injuries to the FUDR regional infusion regimen.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Regional hepatic artery infusion route of delivery; patients had colorectal adenocarcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, or carcinoid with liver involvement.
raw_record.extra_details: 19 patients treated; floxuridine (FUDR) 400 mg for 2 weeks with 2 weeks rest via implantable Infusaid pump; elevated liver function tests in all patients; sclerosing cholangitis in 3 patients; gastric ulcer in 2; cholecystitis in 2; dyspepsia in all. FUDR delivers high hepatic concentrations with near complete hepatic clearance.

raw_record.support_text: In this clinical trial, hepatic arterial FUDR therapy was associated with hepatobiliary toxicity, defined as a ≥2-fold increase in alkaline phosphatase, ≥3-fold increase in AST, or serum bilirubin ≥3 mg/dL in the absence of tumor progression. Patients with bilirubin elevations that did not return to baseline underwent ERCP to distinguish biliary sclerosis from extrahepatic obstruction, and patients with documented biliary sclerosis were never retreated with hepatic arterial FUDR, implicating FUDR as the cause of this cholangiopathy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Unusual regional route: hepatic arterial infusion rather than systemic use; colorectal cancer patients with liver metastases.
raw_record.extra_details: Given with leucovorin (LV) 15 mg/m2/d and dexamethasone 20 mg; initial FUDR dose 0.3 mg/kg/d as a 14-day continuous infusion (actually delivered ~0.21 mg/kg/d due to ~15 mL pump dead space) followed by a 14-day rest period. Hepatic toxicity defined as ≥2-fold increase in alkaline phosphatase, ≥3-fold increase in AST, or bilirubin ≥3 mg/dL absent tumor progression. Persistent bilirubin elevations prompted ERCP to distinguish biliary sclerosis from extrahepatic biliary obstruction; documented biliary sclerosis precluded retreatment with hepatic arterial FUDR. Dexamethasone (Dec) was used to treat hepatobiliary toxicity and may hasten recovery via anti-inflammatory properties.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of 53 human DILI cases with liver biopsy, allopurinol was listed among the causative DILI drugs in the drugs-acting-in-the-rheumatologic-system category, with a necroinflammatory (N) histological pattern. It was also among the drugs related to ANA positivity in one DILI case (p:39).
raw_record.extra_details: Histological pattern: necroinflammatory (N). One of 53 biopsy-confirmed DILI cases in the series.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a single patient who developed hepatic granulomatosis (granulomatous hepatitis) as an idiosyncratic adverse reaction to allopurinol, tel with no other cause identified despite physical, skin, microbiological, biochemical, and radiological investigation. After re-exposure to the drug the patient showed a prompt exacerbation of previous symptoms and abnormal liver function values; the reappearance of a dose-independent reaction when medication was resumed after a drug-free interval was considered consistent with a 'definitive' adverse allergic reaction, and the authors conclude the hepatic adverse effect of allopurinol in susceptible hosts is probably immunologically mediated.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report. Hepatic granulomas consisted of multinucleated giant cells (up to 50 nuclei) surrounded by epithelioid cells and mononuclear infiltrate, located in portal tracts and throughout the three zones of Rappaport's acinus, with readily shown eosinophils; mild large-droplet fatty change but no focal necrosis; special stains for acid-fast bacteria and fungi negative. Latency of 6 years before allergic symptoms (fever, malaise, eosinophilia, granulomas) became manifest. On re-exposure there was prompt exacerbation of symptoms and abnormal liver function values, interpreted as a 'definitive' allergic reaction. Liver function and eosinophilia returned to normal 16 days after allopurinol discontinuation; follow-up liver biopsy at 6 months showed no granulomas or inflammatory infiltrate; patient well at 10 months. Hypothesis of oxypurine (hypoxanthine/xanthine) crystal deposition considered unlikely since no crystalline material seen.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report 6 cases of granulomatous hepatitis in which a causal relationship with the intake of allopurinol was probable. The temporal relationship, the absence of other possible causes, and the characteristic pattern suggested that allopurinol was causative, and control biopsies in 2 cases showed disappearance of granulomas after discontinuation of allopurinol. Histology in all 6 cases showed granulomas (n=3) or granuloma-like reactions (n=3), with minimal to mild steatosis in most specimens, cholestasis in 1 case, and significant cholangitis in 1 case.
raw_record.extra_details: Granulomatous hepatitis in 6 patients. Histologically all cases showed granulomas (n=3) or granuloma-like reactions (n=3); epithelioid cells accompanied by lymphocytes, mixed with neutrophils or eosinophils; ill-defined granulomas/granuloma-like lesions with focal histiocyte/lymphocyte accumulations, ballooning, focal sometimes confluent necrosis and acidophilic degeneration. Minimal to mild steatosis in most specimens; cholestasis in 1 case; significant cholangitis in 1 case. Eosinophilic infiltration most prominent in cases with peripheral eosinophilia. None contained fibrin rings or fibrinoid material; 2 cases had vacuolated granulomas. Control biopsy in 2 cases showed disappearance of granulomas after allopurinol discontinuation; in one case a biopsy was done 17 days after discontinuation with no fibrin rings. Authors conclude fibrin-ring granulomas are uncommon in allopurinol-induced granulomatous hepatitis. Reference (5) cited as Vanderstigel et al.

raw_record.support_text: A 70-year-old man with gout, chronic renal failure, and hypertension was treated with allopurinol and presented after 3 months with fever, jaundice, dyspnea, and generalized maculopapular rash; blood analysis showed eosinophilia, elevated liver enzymes (ALT 429 IU/L, AST 369 IU/L, GGT 481 IU/L, ALP 773 IU/L), hyperbilirubinemia, and elevated IgE. Skin biopsy was consistent with drug-induced hypersensitivity and he was diagnosed with DRESS syndrome. Allopurinol was stopped and steroids started; acute renal failure and acute liver failure developed, and the patient died on day 24 of admission. The text states that allopurinol can cause DRESS syndrome and that DRESS involves hepatitis/liver involvement.
raw_record.extra_details: Allopurinol prescribed for gout (hyperuricemia); rash and liver involvement appeared after 3 months of therapy (paper notes allopurinol can cause DRESS typically 2-6 weeks after initiation). Diagnosed as DRESS with hepatitis and acute liver failure; eosinophilia 7300/mm3; skin biopsy consistent with drug-induced hypersensitivity; allopurinol stopped and steroid treatment initiated; acute renal failure and acute liver failure developed; hemodialysis performed; patient died of DRESS/multiple organ failure on day 24. Comorbidities: chronic renal failure and hypertension. Viral, autoimmune, and brucella work-up negative; ERCP and abdominal ultrasound (grade-2 hepatosteatosis, gallbladder sludge) not mechanistic.

raw_record.support_text: Of nine acute liver failure cases considered hepatotoxicity, one case was attributed to allopurinol and one case was attributed to isoniazid in the study cohort of 40 patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Single attributed case among 9 hepatotoxicity cases in a retrospective cohort of 40 acute liver failure patients; acute liver failure (ALF) was the reported phenotype.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN Prospective Study of 2220 enrolled cases, 2027 had undergone 6 months of follow-up and formal adjudication for causality. Allopurinol was potentially implicated in 17 cases, of which 11 were judged definite (n = 4), highly likely (n = 4), or probable (n = 3) related to allopurinol; the other six were considered possible (n = 4) or unlikely (n = 2) and were excluded from analysis.
raw_record.extra_details: Eleven confirmed cases of allopurinol hepatotoxicity from the DILIN Prospective Study (2003-2020). Median time from drug start to liver-injury onset was 52 days (range 12-89); daily dose ranged 100-600 mg/day (median 200 mg/day). Other prescription drugs were implicated in four cases but none were considered probable. Hypersensitivity features: rash in 91%, fever in 45%, eosinophilia in 45%. Comorbidities included type 2 diabetes in 46%. Median baseline eGFR was 70 ml/min, below 50 ml/min in three patients. Cases: six men and five women, median age 60 years (range 27-74), median BMI 33.7 kg/m², with seven African Americans, three European Americans, one White Hispanic. HLA candidate analysis for allopurinol-induced DILI was performed in the African-American subset.

raw_record.support_text: This case provides direct evidence for an allopurinol-associated granulomatous reaction: after being re-exposed to the drug the patient showed a prompt exacerbation of his previous symptoms and abnormal liver function values. The reappearance of a dose-independent drug reaction when medication is resumed after a drug-free interval is consistent with a 'definitive' adverse allergic reaction to that drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Rechallenge after a drug-free interval produced prompt exacerbation of symptoms and abnormal liver function values, with a three-week latent period between readministration and symptom onset; the dose-independent reaction was classified as a definitive allergic reaction. Liver biopsy (March 1977) showed many granulomas in portal tracts and in all zones of the liver acinus, with no histopathologic evidence of hepatitis; serum transaminase and alkaline phosphatase were mildly raised with normal bilirubin. Clinical and biochemical abnormalities resolved within three weeks of permanent drug discontinuation, and at six months laboratory values were normal with no granulomas. Haematological reactions to allopurinol have also been reported after months or years of medication. No serological or antibody evidence of an allergic mechanism was obtained.

raw_record.support_text: Seventy-one patients with idiosyncratic drug-induced hepatitis were described and the causative drug for each patient was tabulated.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases 24-25. No histologic annotation. Max bilirubin 9-10 µmol/l; max ALT 2.7-3x ULN.

raw_record.support_text: Allopurinol was identified as a major cause of DILI among African-Americans in the DILIN Prospective Study, representing 43% of allopurinol cases, and is associated with immune-allergic type of injury commonly presenting a mixed pattern; allopurinol is also known to cause severe cutaneous reactions linked to HLA-B*5801.
raw_record.extra_details: African-Americans represented 43% of allopurinol DILI cases; known to cause severe cutaneous reactions, with higher risk in Asians and blacks associated with HLA-B*5801 frequency.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of 16 DRESS patients, allopurinol was incriminated as causative in n=2 cases. The cohort had severe liver involvement including hepatic encephalopathy (median ALT 1693 IU/L, INR 2.74), hepatic necrosis, and 2 patients required liver transplantation; none had prior liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Incriminated in n=2 cases of a 16-patient DRESS cohort (RegiSCAR probable/definite). Cohort-level severe liver injury: hepatic encephalopathy, confluent necrosis (up to 90%), 2 liver transplantations.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that allopurinol can cause severe cholestasis as well as hepatocellular necrosis, with strong evidence that immunological mechanisms can be involved in allopurinol-induced hepatitis. Lymphocyte proliferative responses to allopurinol were found in 4 out of 6 patients tested and in none of the studied controls, and the lymphocyte transformation test is described as helpful in drug-induced liver injury diagnosis, particularly in identifying the culprit drug when patients have been exposed to multiple drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: Allopurinol-induced injury manifested as severe cholestasis and hepatocellular necrosis. Strong evidence for involvement of immunological mechanisms; lymphocyte proliferative responses to allopurinol found in 4/6 patients and in none of the controls. Lymphocyte transformation test described as helpful in DILI diagnosis and in identifying the culprit drug in multidrug-exposed patients.

raw_record.support_text: Allopurinol-induced hepatotoxicity is believed to be related to immunoallergic reactions, such as severe allopurinol hypersensitivity skin reactions, which are closely associated with the HLA B*58:01 allele, commonly seen with drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) or Stevens Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis. An included study showed hepatobiliary disorders were experienced in allopurinol groups only for cholestasis (0.6%) and hepatotoxicity (0.6%) and were assessed as severe in intensity; these liver abnormalities did not appear in the febuxostat groups. Additionally, product labeling states transient and minor liver test abnormalities are associated with allopurinol therapy in 2-6% of patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Immunoallergic mechanism associated with HLA B*58:01; seen in the setting of DRESS syndrome or SJS/TEN. In an included clinical trial for gout, hepatobiliary disorders occurred in allopurinol groups as cholestasis (0.6%) and hepatotoxicity (0.6%), each assessed as severe in intensity. Product labeling reports transient and minor liver test abnormalities in 2-6% of patients. These liver abnormalities were not observed in febuxostat groups.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective cohort of 15 patients with severe DRESS, allopurinol was the culprit drug in patients 4, 7, 8, and 10; hepatitis was reported in patients 4, 8, and 10, with renal failure and pneumonitis in several cases. The paper states allopurinol (4 patients) was already established as a trigger for DRESS.
raw_record.extra_details: Four allopurinol cases: patient 4 (F/71, hepatitis, renal failure, pneumonitis), patient 8 (M/71, hepatitis, renal failure; died from DRESS), patient 10 (M/44, hepatitis, renal failure, pneumonitis), and patient 7 (F/65, alcoholic cirrhosis, no hepatitis). Intervals from first drug intake to ICU admission were 6, 25, 7, and 17 days. DRESS was the cause of death in patient 8.

raw_record.support_text: A 39-year-old man was diagnosed with allopurinol-induced hepatic injury. He developed severe cholestatic liver failure without hepatic encephalopathy, and because medical treatment was transiently effective and his renal function and coagulation deteriorated, a living-donor liver transplantation (LDLT) with a right lobe graft was performed four months after onset. The explanted liver was severely enlarged (2,480 g) and cholestatic, and microscopically compatible with drug-induced cholestatic liver injury. He was discharged 55 days after LDLT, with persistent renal dysfunction at 6 months. The authors note allopurinol hepatotoxicity is rare but can be severe and even fatal.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 39-year-old man with hyperuricemia who started allopurinol 2 months before onset of jaundice; after detailed examination no cause of liver dysfunction other than allopurinol-induced hepatic injury was found (nondrinker, no hepatitis virus infection, no blood transfusion). Serum TB reached >40 mg/dL; MELD score 31 at transfer (AST 382 IU/L, ALT 238 IU/L, TB 60.9 mg/dL, creatinine 1.74 mg/dL). Histology showed severe cholestasis around the central vein, hepatic cord atrophy, sinusoidal/pericentral venous fibrosis, atypical bile ductule proliferation, and lymphocyte infiltration, compatible with drug-induced cholestatic liver injury. Bilirubin adsorption and corticosteroid therapy were ineffective. Living-donor LT performed; discharged 55 days post-LT with TB 2.8 mg/dL; renal dysfunction remained at 6 months. Authors state allopurinol hepatotoxicity is rare but can be severe and fatal; reported as first case of successful LDLT for allopurinol-induced cholestatic liver failure without DRESS syndrome.

raw_record.support_text: A 74-year-old man developed DRESS (drug hypersensitivity) syndrome after allopurinol was prescribed for asymptomatic hyperuricaemia. Diagnosis was based on clear exposure to allopurinol, a time frame with cutaneous rash 14 days after medication start, clinical signs including fever and acute hepatocellular injury with abnormal liver enzymes (ALAT 474 IU/L, ASAT 350 IU/L, earlier ASAT 212 U/L, ALAT 280 U/L), worsened renal function, adenopathy, rash and leucocytosis, and lack of exposure to another drug. Hepatic cytolysis with vesicular lithiasis and febrile hepatic failure (cholestatic jaundice, cytolysis, coagulation abnormalities, prothrombin time 34%) were diagnosed, and a favourable clinical evolution followed allopurinol withdrawal.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 74-year-old male patient; prescribed for asymptomatic hyperuricaemia; allergic/hypersensitivity (DRESS) reaction
raw_record.extra_details: DRESS (drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms) syndrome; DRESS is an uncommon but potentially life-threatening idiosyncratic drug reaction with lethal visceral involvement in 6-10% of cases. Cutaneous rash appeared 14 days after starting allopurinol; hepatic cytolysis, febrile hepatic failure with cholestatic jaundice, coagulation abnormalities (prothrombin time 34%), elevated liver enzymes (ALAT 474 IU/L, ASAT 350 IU/L), high serum creatinine (171 µmol/L) and leucocytosis (18.1 × 10⁹/L). HBV, HCV, HIV, CMV, Epstein-Barr virus, syphilis and Toxoplasma serologies negative. Favourable clinical evolution after allopurinol withdrawal; allopurinol was initially suspected but not halted, after which the patient deteriorated.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report 3 cases of allopurinol-induced hypersensitivity syndromes admitted with fever, generalized exanthematous rash, eosinophilia and liver dysfunction shortly after starting allopurinol for non-symptomatic hyperuricemia. Case 2 (34-year-old female) presented with severe liver dysfunction and recovered only after 9 weeks of corticosteroid therapy; case 3 (66-year-old male) developed severe liver dysfunction and renal failure and ultimately died with liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Cases occurred in patients treated for non-symptomatic asymptomatic hyperuricemia; patients with liver dysfunction and renal impairment appear at greater risk for allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS) is described as an infrequent but potentially lethal adverse reaction of allopurinol therapy, with features resembling EBV infection including fever, exanthematous rash, leukocytosis, eosinophilia, impaired renal function, hepatocellular injury, and severe reactions such as toxic epidermal necrolysis and acute vasculitis. Reactions are considered cell-mediated immunity directed toward allopurinol and, more importantly, to its oxypurinol metabolite, which has a markedly longer half-life. One fatal case also complicated by iatrogenic diabetes, oropharyngeal and esophageal candidiasis, and severe ethmoidal rhinomucormycosis, with death due to liver failure from amphotericin B therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A 38-year-old woman under allopurinol therapy for hyperuricemia was admitted with fever and a diffuse cutaneous erythematous eruption and shortly developed rapidly progressive signs of acute liver and kidney failure. Histologic findings from skin and liver biopsies were consistent with a toxic drug reaction, and the case was characterized as drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome; the patient completely recovered.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient was also receiving losartan and low-dose hydrochlorothiazide, all of which were withdrawn together; adult female with newly diagnosed hypertension and hyperuricemia.
raw_record.extra_details: DRESS syndrome with fever (peaks up to 38°C), diffuse erythematous eruption on light-exposed regions, arthralgia, mild eosinophilia (12%), acute kidney failure and rapidly progressive acute liver failure with very high AST/ALT and declining serum proteins/albumin. Liver biopsy showed hepatocytic ballooning and scattered acidophilic bodies with moderate lymphohistiocytic infiltrate and few eosinophils; skin biopsy showed focal parakeratosis with necrotic keratinocytes and perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate. Treated with prednisone (1 mg/kg) and later high-dose steroids; complete recovery, healthy at five years. No formal causality scoring instrument reported.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 11 cases of well-documented acute liver injury associated with allopurinol use enrolled in the DILIN Prospective Study over a 16-year period, with all cases developing liver injury within the first 3 months of treatment and being severe (all 11 required hospitalization, the majority developing jaundice). Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor commonly used to treat and prevent gout and hyperuricaemia, and there was an overrepresentation of African Americans compared with the overall DILIN cohort (60% vs 13%).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Population overrepresented among African Americans (60% vs 13% of overall DILIN cohort); severe cases all required hospitalization; DRESS/hypersensitivity presentation occurred in a subset of cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 adjudicated DILIN cases of acute liver injury; latency within the first 3 months of treatment; majority developed jaundice. Most patients had a mixed or cholestatic biochemical profile at presentation, with prominent hypersensitivity features (rash in 10, fever in 5, eosinophilia in 5); four patients presented with DRESS features with initially normal liver biochemistries that rose after hospital admission, and two were confirmed as DRESS by skin biopsy. Histopathology showed a spectrum including granulomatous hepatitis, cholestasis with mild inflammation, ductopenia, and acute hepatitis with necrosis. Nine patients were treated with corticosteroids; three patients died 38, 45, and 182 days after DILI onset, with two deaths considered liver-related. HLA associations (HLA-B*58:01, potential HLA-B*53:01 and HLA-A*34:02) reported as risk factors, not causal molecules.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a life-threatening toxicity syndrome consisting of an erythematous, desquamative skin rash, fever, hepatitis, eosinophilia, and worsening renal function in 78 patients receiving allopurinol. In a majority of cases the syndrome was associated with use of standard (200 to 400 mg per day) allopurinol doses in patients with renal insufficiency. Avoidance of allopurinol or use of reduced doses in patients with renal insufficiency is recommended to reduce the incidence of life-threatening allopurinol toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Syndrome most commonly occurred with standard (200-400 mg/day) allopurinol doses in patients with renal insufficiency; earlier reports also associated the syndrome with concurrent thiazide diuretic use.
raw_record.extra_details: 78 patients with a hypersensitivity-like syndrome including some or all of vasculitis, rash (usually toxic epidermal necrolysis), eosinophilia, hepatitis, and progressive renal failure, described as life-threatening. Allopurinol (4-hydroxypyrazolo pyrimidine), a xanthine analogue used for hyperuricemia, is converted to oxipurinol, its pharmacologically active metabolite; oxipurinol clearance correlates with creatinine clearance, and long-term 300 mg/day dosing produces elevated steady-state serum oxipurinol concentrations in renal insufficiency. Dose-reduction guidelines proposed for renal insufficiency may reduce life-threatening toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The authors ascribe the acute hepatitis in this patient to norfloxacin, citing no past history of liver or biliary tract disease, normal liver tests 2 days before therapy, no serologic evidence of viral, toxoplasmic, or rickettsial hepatitis, and a histologic pattern consistent with drug-induced hepatitis. They note digoxin was the only other regular drug but that liver tests were normal on admission and remained normal, supporting norfloxacin as the cause.
raw_record.extra_details: A 72-year-old woman with chronic atrial fibrillation (on digoxin) was given norfloxacin 800 mg/day for 7 days for a urinary tract infection. Aminotransferases peaked at 25 times the basal value about 3 weeks after therapy and slowly fell after drug withdrawal. Liver biopsy showed normal architecture with moderate steatosis, small foci of centrilobulillar necrosis, scattered eosinophilic bodies and ceroid-laden macrophages, without fibrosis, portal inflammation, or bile duct lesions. Serologies for viral, toxoplasmic, and rickettsial hepatitis and autoantibodies (except ANA 1:80, borderline) were negative. Patient was asymptomatic with normalized liver tests 16 months later. The paper notes mild aminotransferase elevations had been reported in about 0.1% of patients taking norfloxacin but no prior true hepatitis report.

raw_record.support_text: The paper mentions that NAC is beneficial for norfloxacin-induced acute liver injury (Elliott et al., 2016), explicitly attributing norfloxacin as a cause of acute drug-induced liver injury in humans.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as norfloxacin-induced acute liver injury; NAC reported to be beneficial (Elliott et al., 2016).

raw_record.support_text: Among the control sera were six patients with hepatitis induced by drugs other than carbamazepine: three due to lofepramine, one due to sulphasalazine, one due to phenytoin, and one due to norfloxacin.
raw_record.extra_details: Mentioned as one control patient with drug-induced hepatitis used for comparison with the index carbamazepine case; no further clinical, laboratory or outcome details reported.

raw_record.support_text: A 70-year-old man developed acute cholestatic jaundice after norfloxacin treatment. The authors state that a causal relationship between norfloxacin and hepatic injury can confidently be established because of a temporal relationship between drug administration and the onset and resolution of signs and symptoms, and because alternative explanations were ruled out; rechallenge was not attempted for ethical reasons.
raw_record.extra_details: 70-year-old male, UTI indication, norfloxacin 400 mg/12 h for 12 days, onset at 7 days; bilirubin 171 µmol/L, ALT 78 U/L, AP 443 U/L; acute cholestatic jaundice; absence of hypersensitivity symptoms suggested a metabolic idiosyncrasy; rechallenge not attempted. Our case (1997) in Table 1.

raw_record.support_text: The paper is a case report of severe norfloxacin-induced hepatotoxicity leading to acute liver failure (ALF), with causality assessed using the liver-specific validated CIOMS scale for DILI. Liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis with centrilobular hepatocyte drop-out, ceroid-laden macrophages, pericholangitis/cholangitis, and parenchymal and portal inflammation with eosinophilia. The learning points state that norfloxacin can, rarely, cause acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Causality assessed with the liver-specific Council for International Organisation of Medical Sciences (CIOMS) scale for DILI. Liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis with centrilobular hepatocyte drop-out, ceroid-laden macrophages, pericholangitis/cholangitis, parenchymal and portal inflammation with eosinophilia. Liver function tests during the clinical course were consistent with hepatitis and acute liver failure after norfloxacin treatment, with slow resolution after N-acetylcysteine (NAC) administration. The paper notes only five previously published cases of severe norfloxacin-induced hepatotoxicity and proposes a likely class effect for fluoroquinolones with short latency to DILI and prominent eosinophils on biopsy.

raw_record.support_text: Norfloxacin accounted for 1 (2.9%) of the 35 fluoroquinolone-related cases of acute/subacute liver damage. The single reported case, a 71-year-old female treated for urinary tract infection with a 14-day latency, was classified as cholestatic, showed necrotising granulomatous hepatitis on histology, and resulted in full recovery.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case, 71-year-old female, urinary tract infection indication, 14-day latency, cholestatic pattern with necrotising granulomatous hepatitis on histology, outcome full recovery.

raw_record.support_text: A letter by Lucena et al. attributed 14 cases of hepatotoxicity up to 1998 to ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, enoxacin and ofloxacin. Quinolone-associated hepatotoxicity has been reported as hepatocellular damage, cholestatic damage, ductopenia, and acute liver failure and death, with biopsy findings of central-zone necrosis and mixed inflammatory infiltrates with abundant eosinophils.
raw_record.extra_details: One of four quinolones (with ciprofloxacin, enoxacin, ofloxacin) to which 14 hepatotoxicity cases up to 1998 were attributed (Lucena letter). Quinolone-class reports: hepatocellular damage, cholestatic damage, ductopenia, acute liver failure and death; biopsy showed central-zone necrosis and mixed inflammatory infiltrates with abundant eosinophils (immuno-allergic mechanism).

raw_record.support_text: A 48-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis developed acute hepatitis, probably due to orodispersible prednisolone (Solupred), which was started at 40 mg/d after intravenous methylprednisolone. Liver tests worsened after readministration of orodispersible prednisolone and improved after its withdrawal and replacement with oral prednisone, supporting causality. The case is titled prednisolone-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Orodispersible (Solupred) formulation; patient with ulcerative colitis receiving concurrent enoxaparine, hydroxyzine, cholecalciferol, and low-dose paracetamol.
raw_record.extra_details: At day 14 after starting prednisolone: ALT 165 U/L (3.3 N), AST 73 U/L (1.5 N), Alk Phos 369 U/L (3.2 N), GGT 706 U/L (12.8 N), bilirubin normal. Values improved on withdrawal and worsened on rechallenge (day 27: ALT 730 U/L (14.6 N), AST 313 U/L, Alk Phos 393 U/L, GGT 1097 U/L), then resolved after switch to oral prednisone (Cortancyl). Isolated antismooth muscle antibody (1/160); HBsAg, HCV, HIV, and EBV serologies negative; no alcohol. Liver function tests normal 3 months later.

raw_record.support_text: Propofol is commonly used as an anesthetic agent for invasive procedures. The paper reports a case of idiosyncratic drug induced liver injury (DILI) in a 39-year-old female after a brief exposure to propofol during routine endoscopy. Within 48 hours of discharge she was hospitalized with abdominal pain, nausea, and laboratory abnormalities consistent with hepatocellular injury; serologic workup for viral and autoimmune etiologies was negative, and the transaminase abnormalities improved by hospital day three and resolved by two week follow up. The RUCAM score was highly suggestive of an adverse drug reaction, and this was described as only the fourth case report of propofol-related DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: 39-year-old female; brief exposure during routine endoscopy; hospitalized within 48 hours with abdominal pain and nausea; serologic workup for viral and autoimmune etiologies negative; transaminase abnormalities improved by hospital day three and resolved by two week follow up; Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) score highly suggestive of an adverse drug reaction; reported as the fourth case report of propofol-related DILI; INR was 1.5 on day of admission then ranged from 1.1 to 1.2 throughout hospital stay.

raw_record.support_text: A 75-year-old woman who had been on ezetimibe (Zetia) 10 mg/d for 6 months presented with elevated serum total bilirubin, AST, ALT, and alkaline phosphatase and decreased albumin. Percutaneous liver biopsy revealed hepatitis with an inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells and some eosinophils, findings compatible with DILI, along with portal and periportal inflammation and early fibrosis (stage 2/4). Liver function tests decreased by 50% two weeks after ezetimibe was discontinued and normalized four months later, which the authors state strongly suggests ezetimibe as the offending agent.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of DILI with ezetimibe given alone. Patient also took long-term aspirin, furosemide, and calcium acetate (PhosLo) and had long-standing polycystic kidney disease, hypertension, and reported no prior liver disease. Peak labs on day 1: AST 694 U/L, ALT 731 U/L, ALP 149 U/L, total bilirubin 0.9-1.4 mg/dL, albumin 3.2 g/dL; ANA titer 1:320, normal antimitochondrial antibody, no viral hepatitis. Liver biopsy hepatitis with lymphocytic/plasma-cell/eosinophil infiltrate and portal and periportal fibrosis stage 2/4; liver sonogram showed mild enlargement with multiple small cysts. LFTs fell 50% by day 17 and normalized by day 120 after discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: Case 1: a 30-year-old male began cefamandole 1 g IV q6h perioperatively for seven days after esophageal perforation and acute mediastinitis. On day 5 dark urine was noted followed by increasing jaundice; laboratory tests on days 3–7 showed moderate cholestatic jaundice with alkaline phosphatase rising from 51 IU (day 3) to 85 IU (day 9), total bilirubin 2.2 mg% (day 8), slight transaminase elevation, and negative hepatitis A/B serology. TPN and other causes were ruled out. Within 48 hours of cefamandole discontinuation (day 8) the jaundice cleared and transaminases began decreasing; the patient recovered fully by day 14.
raw_record.extra_details: Cefamandole 1 g IV q6h given for 7 days; jaundice and dark urine appeared day 5–7; ALP 51→85 IU, total bilirubin 2.2 mg%, WBC 10900 with eosinophils <7%, low-grade fever; chronic hepatitis A/B serology negative; jaundice cleared within 48 h of discontinuation with full recovery by day 14. Paper suggests a possible hypersensitivity reaction resembling penicillin liver toxicity. Cholestatic jaundice phenotype.

raw_record.support_text: The described hepatic injury is attributed to amineptine: an anicteric acute hepatitis developed 15 days after the onset of amineptine (300 mg daily for depression) and improved rapidly after its cessation, with no other cause of liver disease. Multiple cases of amineptine-induced hepatitis with similar features (abdominal pain, fever) had been reported, and at therapeutic dose amineptine hepatotoxicity is described as likely immuno(activating) — a hypersensitivity pattern.
raw_record.extra_details: Tricyclic antidepressant given at 300 mg daily for depression in a 39-year-old woman. Anicteric acute hepatitis appeared 15 days after amineptine start, with nausea, abdominal pain, chills, fever (40°C), dark urine, tender 12 cm hepatomegaly. Labs on admission: ALT 1360 U (N 5-40), AST 560 U (N 5-30), GGT 205 U (N 10-40), AP 5.5 U (N 2-5), 6% eosinophils; HBsAg/HBV markers/HCV and M-, SM-, nuclei-, DNA-autoantibodies negative; normal biliary ultrasound. Improved after amineptine interruption (bilirubin 7 µmol/l, ALT 426 U, AST 120 U, GGT 152 U). Authors note several previously reported amineptine-induced hepatitis cases.

raw_record.support_text: The study subjects are patients with amineptine hepatitis, i.e., humans who developed hepatitis from therapeutic use of amineptine. The paper further discusses 'amineptine hepatotoxicity' throughout, and reports that this susceptibility was constitutional and inherited based on in vitro lymphocyte testing of 9 patients (8 tested after complete recovery) and their relatives.
raw_record.extra_details: About 9 patients with amineptine hepatitis; hepatotoxicity attributed to a reactive amineptine metabolite (cytochrome P-450/NADPH dependent, detoxified by glutathione/epoxide hydrolase). Susceptibility was constitutional and inherited, not related to debrisoquine/dextromethorphan (CYP2D6) poor-metabolizer phenotype, and not due to impaired glutathione synthesis (basal lymphocyte glutathione and acetaminophen-metabolite cytotoxicity were similar to controls). In vitro lymphocyte cytotoxicity test (amineptine 1-2.5 mM) positive in first-degree relatives, some never exposed to amineptine. Phenotype reported as hepatitis (acute/chronic not specified).

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 71 Caucasian patients with idiosyncratic drug-induced hepatitis, HLA-A11 was present in 6 of 12 patients (50%) with hepatitis caused by tricyclic antidepressants, including four of seven patients with amineptine hepatitis. Amineptine is thereby attributed as a cause of drug-induced hepatitis in these patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Four of seven patients with amineptine hepatitis carried HLA-A11 vs 12% prevalence in controls (p<0.01 uncorrected; not significant after correction). Reported among 71 Caucasian patients with idiosyncratic drug-induced hepatitis; five patients in the overall cohort had fulminant or subfulminant hepatitis. Amineptine is a tricyclic antidepressant.

raw_record.support_text: Among the 51 patients with drug-induced hepatitis, the great majority had the extensive metabolizer phenotype, in particular for the causative drugs amineptine and amodiaquine; later text notes 8 cases of hepatitis were attributed to amineptine.
raw_record.extra_details: Causative drug of drug-induced hepatitis in 8 of 51 patients (n=8); none were CYP2D6 poor metabolizers. The paper discusses hepatotoxicity likely related to formation of a reactive metabolite.

raw_record.support_text: A 45-year-old woman treated with ulipristal acetate (Esmya®, Laboratoire Gedeon Richter) for 25 days for uterine fibroids developed elevated liver enzymes, jaundice, and rapid liver failure with encephalopathy, requiring liver transplantation at Day 27. Following exclusion of viral etiologies (including HHV-6, which was determined to be inherited chromosomal integration rather than active infection), a final diagnosis of fulminant drug-induced hepatitis due to ulipristal acetate was made.
raw_record.extra_details: Treated 25 days for uterine fibroids; presented asthenia, nausea, vomiting, pruritus, dark urine, jaundice. ALT 1312 IU/L (rising to 1600 IU/L), total bilirubin 330 µmol/L, prothrombin ratio 57% then <25%, factor V 72%. Liver biopsy showed subacute hepatitis with lobular and periportal necrosis involving 20% of parenchyma and marked lymphocytic infiltrate. Hepatic encephalopathy and fulminant hepatic failure led to liver transplant at Day 27; posttransplant course straightforward with ALT normalization. Initial immunosuppression with corticosteroid, mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus. HHV-6A/HHV-6B DNAemia was attributed to inherited chromosomal integration (iciHHV-6) rather than active infection, supporting drug-induced etiology.

raw_record.support_text: After ruling out other possible causes of acute liver injury, a diagnosis was made based on the timing of Ligandrol administration, the improvement of total bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and aminotransferases after the patient stopped the drug (dechallenge), and liver biopsy findings. The authors concluded that they reported a severe Ligandrol (LGD-4033)-induced hepatotoxicity, and noted that despite an FDA warning, Ligandrol and other SARMs continue to be sold over the counter and via the internet as body-building products, requiring higher regulation to prevent life-threatening hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient self-administered LGD-4033 10 mg daily, 10 to 100 times higher than the doses (0.1, 0.3, 1.0 mg) used in a 21-day placebo-controlled clinical trial; purchased as an over-the-counter/internet body-building SARM product; possibility that the Ligandrol the patient took contained other different unapproved drugs was not excluded; genetic testing for hepatic transporter gene abnormalities was not performed.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of severe Ligandrol (LGD-4033)-induced hepatotoxicity with acute liver injury. Diagnosis based on timing of administration, dechallenge improvement of total bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase and aminotransferases, and liver biopsy findings, after ruling out other causes. A placebo-controlled randomized trial of LGD-4033 in 76 healthy men showed no serious adverse effects and no significant change in serum aminotransferases at 0.1, 0.3, and 1 mg daily over 21 days. Authors noted hepatotoxicity can be intrinsic (dose-dependent) or idiosyncratic, suggesting the patient's DILI was either intrinsic or idiosyncratic with a dose-dependent component. FDA warning exists for Ligandrol and SARMs.

raw_record.support_text: A 32-year-old man developed severe drug-induced liver injury after using Ligandrol (LGD-4033), a selective androgen receptor modulator available over the counter. The diagnosis of DILI was confirmed by a liver biopsy that showed cholestatic hepatitis with mild portal, periportal, and perisinusoidal fibrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Unapproved over-the-counter use as a muscle-building supplement in a previously healthy 32-year-old man; single-agent exposure with no other supplements or medications reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Ligandrol (LGD-4033), also known as VK5211, chemical name 4-((R)-2-((R)-2,2,2-Trifluoro-1-hydroxyethyl)pyrrolidin-1-yl)-2-(trifluoromethyl)benzonitrile. Patient took 1 mL (10 mg) daily for approximately 2 weeks (~15 mL total) starting ~50 days before presentation. Symptoms: fatigue, pruritus, weight loss (40 lbs), jaundice, acholic stool, nausea, intermittent abdominal pain. Lab values at our hospital: AST 33 IU/L, ALT 45 IU/L, ALP 425, total bilirubin 35.0 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 26.8, INR 1.1; hepatic patients negative for viral/serologic/autoimmune markers (ANA, AMA, ASMA, anti-LKM). Transjugular liver biopsy showed cholestatic hepatitis with canalicular bile plugs, mild portal inflammation, mild portal, periportal and perisinusoidal fibrosis, no ductopenia; no clinical liver failure, transplantation, or death reported.
