raw_record.support_text: In a prior treatment series, 47 patients with echinococcosis received mebendazole (MBZ) 100 mg orally twice a day for 5 days, repeated after intervals; although the cure rate was 100%, liver injury was observed in 48.9% of the patients. In a subsequent study the MBZ (powder; 100 mg twice a day) was given in reduced 4-day courses repeated after a 3-day interval and then once more after 10 days (group 1).
raw_record.extra_details: Used for treatment of echinococcosis. In the earlier series (100 mg twice daily for 5 days, repeated) cure rate was 100% but liver injury occurred in 48.9% of patients. In the reduced 4-day-course schedule, liver injury appeared frequently (68.9% after 4 courses totaling 16 days vs 13.3% after 2 courses totaling 8 days), with deworming rate 97.8% after 2 courses; no difference in liver-injury frequency between powder and tablet formulations.

raw_record.support_text: During this study treating strongyloidiasis with mebendazole (MBZ), liver injury appeared, prompting a reduction in dosage. Even with a regimen of 4-day courses with 3-day rest periods between them, liver injury occurred in 25% of patients. The authors recommend dosing MBZ in 4-day courses consisting of 3 courses, or 3-day courses of 3-4 courses, with 1-2 week inter-course rest periods, while monitoring liver function.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver injury appeared during MBZ treatment of strongyloidiasis, prompting a dose reduction. In subjects given 4-day courses (2 courses with 3-day inter-course rest), liver injury occurred in 25%. The authors considered side effects and laboratory abnormalities and recommend dosing with a 4-day schedule of 3 courses or a 3-day schedule of 3-4 courses with 1-2 week rest intervals between courses while monitoring liver function.

raw_record.support_text: The study states that IV dilmapimod was generally well tolerated in severely injured subjects at risk for ARDS, and that at the dose levels tested there was no evidence of hepatotoxicity in trauma patients. The lack of drug-related clinically significant increases in transaminase levels suggested the risk of a future subject experiencing them lies below 16% when dosed with 10-mg dilmapimod IV for 24 hours over 3 days, and below 6% if the mechanism causing such transaminase increases is unrelated to dose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Severely injured trauma subjects at risk for ARDS (critically ill population); finding limited to the dose levels tested (up to 10 mg IV infused over 24 hours for 3 days).
raw_record.extra_details: IV dilmapimod, a p38 MAPK inhibitor. No drug-related clinically significant transaminase increases were observed; authors note this is important because other p38 MAPK inhibitors have been discontinued for causing liver transaminase increases. Upper confidence bound of the risk of future transaminase-increase events estimated below 16% (dose-related) or below 6% (dose-unrelated mechanism). Comparison with placebo arms supported that abnormal safety laboratory results were related to critical illness and injury rather than study drug; no study-drug-related SAEs or significant ECG findings were reported.

raw_record.support_text: One of the 35 cases of acute liver failure or injury in the cohort, who was exposed to tolazamide, was definitely ascribed to use of a hypoglycemic agent. For the other 34 cases there was insufficient evidence to ascribe a specific cause other than use of a hypoglycemic agent, and 27 could possibly be caused by concomitant drug use (e.g., diclofenac sodium or lovastatin) or concomitant medical conditions.
raw_record.extra_details: Single adjudicated case among 35 outcomes in a population-based diabetes cohort; indication type 2 diabetes mellitus; outcome category acute liver failure or acute liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: Reviewing the literature, the authors found only 3 cases of tolazamide-induced liver disease, of which only one became chronic. They conclude that tolazamide may be added to the list of agents that may cause chronic hepatic dysfunction, although its occurrence is rare. In the present case, the patient developed jaundice and intrahepatic cholestasis after 3 weeks of tolazamide use, with dechallenge leading to gradual improvement but persistence of cholestatic liver tests, cholangiopathy on ERCP, and development of portal fibrosis with bridging on follow-up biopsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of chronic cholestatic hepatic dysfunction: jaundice developed after ~3 weeks of tolazamide (peak total bilirubin 22.0 mg/dl, direct 18.0 mg/dl, alkaline phosphatase 357-425 U/L, ALT/AST elevated). Dechallenge produced gradual improvement over 4 months but alkaline phosphatase, ALT, and AST remained elevated. Second liver biopsy (Feb 1984) showed intrahepatic cholestasis with ductular proliferation, marked portal inflammation and fibrosis with occasional portal-to-portal bridges; ERCP showed decreased caliber of biliary radicals, focal decrease in duct caliber, and decreased arborization. Patient asymptomatic and not jaundiced by March 1984. Literature: only 3 prior tolazamide-induced liver-disease cases, only one chronic.

raw_record.support_text: In a phase 1 clinical trial, DWP14012, a new potassium-competitive acid blocker under clinical development, showed rapid and sustained suppression of gastric acid secretion, was safe and well tolerated, and the authors explicitly state that no hepatotoxicity was observed.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Phase 1 clinical trial in healthy volunteers; exposure as an investigational acid suppressant, not ordinary marketed use.
raw_record.extra_details: DWP14012 is a potassium-competitive acid blocker (P-CAB) whose inhibition is dose-dependent; intragastric pH maintained above 4 for 24 h; gastric holding time pH>4 80.5±8.4% (80 mg) and 91.3±4.1% (160 mg); Cmax at 1–4 h, AUC>1000 µg.h/L, t1/2 9 h; serum gastrin lower than vonoprazan and normalized within 48 h of cessation. The no-hepatotoxicity observation is an explicit negative statement, not an inferred absence.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 51 patients with drug-induced hepatitis caused mainly by drugs undergoing oxidative metabolism, compared with 103 control subjects, dextromethorphan oxidation capacity was similar between patients and controls across phenotype prevalence, distribution of log metabolic ratio, and mean urinary outputs. The authors concluded that hepatotoxicity of several drugs, including amineptine, amodiaquine and Plethoryl®, is related neither to an impairment in dextromethorphan oxidation capacity nor to an unusually high capacity to oxidize this drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Authors conclude amodiaquine hepatotoxicity is related neither to impaired dextromethorphan (debrisoquine-type) oxidation nor to unusually high oxidation capacity; phenotype prevalence in patients was 5.9% poor metabolizer vs 3.9% in controls. Study included 51 patients with drug-induced hepatitis and 103 controls using metabolic ratio after 40 mg dextromethorphan hydrobromide.

raw_record.support_text: The review reports that antibodies against amodiaquine (AQ) were detected in patients with liver injury induced by AQ, suggesting that AQ-induced idiosyncratic reactions represent an immune-mediated reaction against AQ-modified proteins. This attributes human AQ liver injury to an immune mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: Anti-AQ antibodies detected in patients with AQ-induced liver injury (Christie et al., 1989), supporting an immune-mediated reaction against AQ-modified proteins.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that the patient's course incriminates amodiaquine as the cause of the fatal hepatic injury: hepatitis appeared 5 weeks after beginning amodiaquine, regressed when the drug was stopped, and the symptoms (asthenia, pruritus, vomiting, worsened jaundice) recurred only 3 days after readministration of 600 mg amodiaquine, progressing to hepatic encephalopathy and death with massive hepatic necrosis on autopsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a fatal fulminant hepatitis in a patient who developed hepatitis 5 weeks after starting treatment with amodiaquine (600 mg rechallenge dose). Injury regressed on drug withdrawal and recurred sharply 3 days after rechallenge, with worsening jaundice, hepatic encephalopathy, respiratory disturbance, and death on March 12. Autopsy showed massive hepatic necrosis with isolated lymphocytic clusters. Laboratory findings at the time of repatriation: total bilirubin 372 µmol/L, conjugated bilirubin 280 µmol/L, SGPT 965 IU/L, SGOT 1180 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 313 IU/L (N 30-120), prothrombin 20%, factor V 23%, fibrinogen 1.5 g/L. No competing etiology found (no alcohol, no other medications, negative viral A and B hepatitis serology, no reason to suspect non-A, non-B hepatitis).

raw_record.support_text: The drug amodiaquine, a 4-aminoquinoline antimalarial, became of importance when some P. falciparum strains resistant to chloroquine retained sensitivity to amodiaquine. In 1986 it was shown that 1 in 2000 subjects taking amodiaquine for prophylaxis of malaria developed neutropenia or hepatotoxicity, or both, illustrating idiosyncratic (Type B) drug toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Used for prophylaxis of malaria; 1 in 2000 subjects developed neutropenia or hepatotoxicity, or both. Mechanism attributed to an unstable reactive quinoneimine metabolite formed in liver and white cells that acts as a hapten, and high titres of specific antibodies to the reactive metabolite were found in the blood of patients who developed myelotoxicity or hepatotoxicity, giving evidence for an immunological basis. Whereas chloroquine retained sensitivity in resistant strains, amodiaquine was toxic.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of seven patients with amodiaquine-induced agranulocytosis treated therapeutically for malaria, five patients presented with concomitant icterus or signs of liver damage, or both. Necropsy in one of these patients (case 2) showed mild predominantly centrilobular cholestasis with bile pigment droplets in hepatocytes and Kupffer cells, scanty bile thrombi in minimally dilated canaliculi, moderate sinusoidal dilatation, and mild perivenular steatosis, with swollen vacuolated epithelium of interlobular bile ducts and ductules. The patients reported no known risk factors for liver damage or a history of pre-existing liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Series of 7 patients (cases 1-7) with amodiaquine-induced agranulocytosis; 5 had icterus or signs of liver damage. Amodiaquine total dose 1.8-6.0 g over 34-63 days. Case 2 necropsy: cholestasis, bile thrombi, sinusoidal dilatation, perivenular steatosis, interlobular bile duct epithelial swelling. Associated complications: septicaemia, abscesses, orbital infection, gangrene; cases 1 and 2 died of pseudomonas septicaemia.

raw_record.support_text: In a comparison of the fixed-dose AS/AQ formulation with separate tablets in malaria patients, of 10 patients with desethylamodiaquine blood levels above 600 ng/ml after the third dose, only one had evidence of hepatocellular injury that was probably amodiaquine-related and was resolving by day 28. The authors state that transient, amodiaquine-induced hepatocellular liver toxicity is well described and is probably a type II immune reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: One of 10 patients with desethylamodiaquine levels >600 ng/ml post 3rd dose showed hepatocellular injury resolving by day 28; injury described as transient, AQ-induced, probably a type II immune reaction. No relationship between high blood concentrations of either drug (AQ/AS) and adverse effects overall. Desethylamodiaquine is the active metabolite of amodiaquine.

raw_record.support_text: Three patients suffered from fulminant hepatitis within 23, 59 and 22 weeks after having ingested a total dose of 16, 26 and 15 g, respectively, of amodiaquine for the prophylaxis of malaria. Amodiaquine administration was continued for 44, 21 and 25 days after the onset of jaundice. One patient underwent emergency orthotopic liver transplantation and survived; the other two died. The report states that fulminant hepatitis threatens patients in whom amodiaquine administration is protracted for several months and not interrupted when jaundice occurs.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Occurred during protracted amodiaquine prophylaxis of malaria with administration continued 21-44 days after jaundice onset, which the authors link to the fulminant course.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients (including a 12-year-old girl, Case 1) with no prior liver disease or co-medication; serology negative for HAV, HBV, HSV, CMV, EBV; no pyrexia; normal leukocyte counts. Fulminant hepatitis attributed to severe liver cell necrosis. Total ingested doses 16, 26 and 15 g; onset at 23, 59 and 22 weeks. One patient (Case 1) underwent emergency orthotopic liver transplantation and survived; two died. Case 1 whole blood amodiaquine (AD) and monodeethylamodiaquine (MAD) 3 days after withdrawal were 173 and 725 ng/ml (normal ranges 0-5 and 75-92 ng/ml); hepatic tissue AD 27 and MAD 98 mg/g wet tissue. The authors note prior reports that amodiaquine is responsible for acute hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: A 65 year old man had acute hepatitis, thought to be caused by exposure to 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid (2,4-D), a selective weedkiller. The patient ingested 2,4-D as a result of habitual licking of his golf ball. Clinical and histological data together with a challenge test confirmed the diagnosis of 'golf ball liver'.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Ingestion via habitual licking of golf ball (oral herbicide exposure, not therapeutic use); 65-year-old retired consultant engineer; no other drugs, alcohol, travel, or infection.
raw_record.extra_details: Two-month history of lethargy, two-week history of dark urine and upper abdominal discomfort, jaundice. Liver function at admission: bilirubin 142 µmol/l, AST 205 U/l, ALT 380 U/l, γ-GT 210 U/l, ALP 412 U/l. Liver biopsy showed preserved architecture with pronounced canalicular and intracellular cholestasis plus acute hepatitis features (lobular and portal inflammation, periportal oedema, mixed infiltrate with mononuclear cells and eosinophils). Viral, bacterial, and parasitic serology negative. Dechallenge: after ceasing golf ball licking, liver function tests returned to normal within two months. Labelled 'golf ball liver'.

raw_record.support_text: After exclusions, a total of 50 patients (19 from category 1 controlled trials and 31 from category 2 postmarketing) who developed liver injury during dantrolene therapy were analyzed. Hepatic adverse reactions were categorized into four groups: transaminase elevation only; transaminase elevation with mild hyperbilirubinemia (1-2.5 mg/100 ml); icteric hepatitis (bilirubin above 2.5 mg/100 ml) with recovery; and fatalities caused by acute or subacute hepatic failure.
raw_record.extra_details: 50 patients with liver injury during dantrolene therapy (19 from category 1 premarketing controlled efficacy/safety trials including up to 7 years of follow-up, covering 2191 trial patients; 31 from category 2 postmarketing, an estimated 30,000 long-term users). Hepatic reactions included transaminase elevation only; transaminase elevation with mild hyperbilirubinemia (1-2.5 mg/100 ml); icteric hepatitis (bilirubin >2.5 mg/100 ml) with recovery; and fatalities from acute or subacute hepatic failure. Hepatic tissue available from 9 patients (6 liver biopsy, 3 autopsy). Indication: spasticity; drug used as dantrolene sodium (talc crystal evidence and alcoholism and baseline SGOT elevation were exclusion reasons in some patients).

raw_record.support_text: Dantrolene was implicated in two cases (patients 22 and 23) of non-paracetamol drug-induced fulminant hepatic failure; neither met KCH criteria and both survived without transplant.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure (acute liver failure); patient 22 latency unknown, PT 23, ALT 211, bilirubin 505; patient 23 latency 2 months, PT 97, ALT 5094, bilirubin 269; both survived without transplant.

raw_record.support_text: Reported cases of fatal hepatic injuries induced by dantrolene have prevented its widespread use. Dantrolene-related hepatic dysfunction ranges from slight elevation in liver enzyme levels to fatal hepatic injury, with reported incidences of hepatic dysfunction and fatal hepatic injury of 1.8% and 0.35%, respectively. US researchers reported 122 cases of dantrolene-related hepatic dysfunction until 1987, 27 of which were fatal; the dantrolene dosage in fatal cases was 582 mg/d administered for 13.8±12.0 months, and most deceased patients were adults. Suggested mechanisms include direct hepatotoxicity, a drug-induced idiosyncratic reaction, and an autoimmune-mediated reaction, but the exact mechanism is not established.
raw_record.extra_details: Dantrolene-related hepatic dysfunction ranges from slight elevation in liver enzymes to fatal hepatic injury; incidence of hepatic dysfunction 1.8% and fatal hepatic injury 0.35%. 122 reported cases of hepatic dysfunction related to dantrolene until 1987, of which 27 were fatal. Dantrolene dosage in fatal cases was 582 mg/d with administration period 13.8±12.0 months; most deceased patients were adults. Suggested mechanisms include direct hepatotoxicity, drug-induced idiosyncratic reaction, and autoimmune-mediated reaction, though exact mechanism not established. Dantrolene is currently used cautiously in adults with recommended daily dose 12.5-400 mg. The agent is dantrolene sodium, administered orally.

raw_record.support_text: The patient, a 38-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis who had taken dantrolene sodium 400 mg/day for 16 weeks (stopped on Aug 13, 1974, after which she became jaundiced), was believed to have a cholestatic hepatitis secondary to dantrolene therapy and was simply observed; her jaundice slowly abated, taking more than three months for serum bilirubin to return to normal. In the discussion the authors attributed a severe, prolonged hepatic dysfunction to dantrolene, noting that rechallenge was not carried out.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 38-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis taking dantrolene sodium 400 mg/day for 16 weeks for skeletal muscle spasticity (structured as hydantoin derivative). Jaundice, anorexia, and nausea appeared two days after drug cessation; biopsy showed swollen/vacuolated/ballooned pericentral hepatocytes, enlarged portal triads with inflammatory cells and eosinophils, loss of the limiting plate, and frank cholestasis without bile duct damage. Peak total serum bilirubin 32.8 mg/dl (direct 19.8), SGOT up to 415 IU, serum alkaline phosphatase up to 225 IU, serum albumin 1.8 gm/dl. HBsAg negative, antimitochondrial and anti-smooth-muscle antibody negative. Authors stated other causes of cholestasis/hepatitis were unlikely and that a rechallenge with the drug was not performed. Recovery over more than three months. Prior to this report only minor liver-function abnormalities had been observed, but the manufacturer had recently added a hepatic-toxicity warning to the package insert.

raw_record.support_text: In a report of a large population of patients who had received dantrolene for long periods, biochemical abnormalities of liver function (including moderate elevations of serum transaminases, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin) occurred in about 1.8% of patients, with symptomatic hepatitis in 0.6% and fatal hepatitis in 0.3%. The risk of hepatic injury appears about 2-fold greater in females, in patients receiving doses over 300 mg/day, and in those treated for over 60 days. The major histological pathology was subacute hepatic necrosis or chronic active hepatitis, although cholestasis has been reported; the reactions were considered unlikely to be due to hypersensitivity or autoimmune reactions. Reduced dosage recommendations for long-term use resulted in a marked decrease in severe hepatic disease reports.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term oral use; risk about 2-fold greater in females, in patients receiving doses over 300 mg/day, and in those treated for over 60 days.
raw_record.extra_details: Biochemical liver-function abnormalities (moderate elevations of serum transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin) in about 1.8% of patients; symptomatic hepatitis in 0.6%; fatal hepatitis in 0.3%. Histology: subacute hepatic necrosis or chronic active hepatitis; cholestasis also reported. Reactions considered unlikely to be due to hypersensitivity or autoimmune reactions. Following reduction of long-term dose recommendations, the number of severe hepatic disease reports markedly decreased. Reference: Utili et al. 1977; data on file, Norwich Eaton.

raw_record.support_text: In the discussion, the obstructive jaundice seen in this (the 1st) patient is attributed only to the gold therapy, with supporting evidence including normal liver function tests before gold injections, a liver biopsy at the height of illness showing centrilobular cholestasis as the major abnormality, and failure of challenges with isoniazid and acetaminophen to worsen liver function. raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient with rheumatoid arthritis/inflammatory polyarthritis on gold therapy who developed jaundice with pruritus and excoriations, urine bile, total bilirubin 12.0 mg/100 ml (direct 6.2), SGOT 83 U, alkaline phosphatase 498 U; serum gold 150 µg/100 ml and 24-h urine gold 1944 µg. raw_record.support_text: In AFCAPS/TexCAPS, treatment with lovastatin 20 to 40 mg daily was explicitly not associated with hepatotoxicity. Small increases in mean liver transaminase levels were observed, but data from nearly 7,000 participants receiving placebo or lovastatin in EXCEL and AFCAPS/TexCAPS showed no significant differences in frequency of confirmed AST or ALT elevations >3×ULN. Among over 100,000 liver transaminase tests in AFCAPS/TexCAPS, only 18 lovastatin-treated participants had clinically important confirmed elevations >3×ULN, no cases of lovastatin-induced hepatitis were identified, and the risk of transaminase elevation was independent of treatment, indicating lovastatin does not increase the risk of clinically important transaminase elevations.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: CHD primary-prevention cohort (AFCAPS/TexCAPS) with average cholesterol and no symptomatic CHD; long-term lovastatin 20-40 mg daily in a trial setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Randomized controlled trial AFCAPS/TexCAPS. No significant differences vs placebo in confirmed AST/ALT elevations >3×ULN across nearly 7,000 participants (EXCEL + AFCAPS); only 18 lovastatin participants with clinically important elevations among >100,000 transaminase tests; no cases of lovastatin-induced hepatitis; half of elevations occurred in the first year, as did half the tests; risk of elevations independent of treatment; ~30% sporadic elevations >1×ULN in both arms. Small increases in mean transaminases observed with statins generally. Also no new drug-related adverse experiences and no clinically important increase in muscle side effects.

raw_record.support_text: A 75-year-old man with severe aplastic anemia was treated with cyclosporin A, steroid pulse therapy, and metenolone acetate. Marked transaminase elevation appeared after starting metenolone acetate, followed by hepatic failure and death. Autopsy findings were compatible with drug-induced liver injury, and metenolone acetate was considered the most likely causative agent. Metenolone acetate was given at 25 mg/day beginning July 18 for less than 1 month; on August 14 AST rose to 1609 IU/l, ALT to 2173 IU/l, gamma-GTP to 126 IU/l, and total bilirubin to 6.5 mg/dl. After discontinuation transaminases decreased immediately, but the patient fell into hepatic coma on August 15 and died on August 28. The authors caution that liver impairment from this drug, usually regarded as mild, reversible, and infrequent, warrants extreme caution in debilitated patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 75-year-old man with severe aplastic anemia (debilitated state); prior treatment with cyclosporin A and steroid pulse therapy; co-administered cimetidine and antibiotics; the authors caution on use in debilitated patients.
raw_record.extra_details: MA given 25 mg/day for <1 month (from July 18). Liver tests normal until MA; on Aug 7 AST 108 and ALT 163 IU/l (cimetidine discontinued), on Aug 14 AST 1609, ALT 2173, gamma-GTP 126 IU/l, total bilirubin 6.5 mg/dl; MA discontinued, transaminases fell immediately (AST 1355, ALT 1248) but hepatic coma Aug 15; died Aug 28. Autopsy liver 1550 g with marked degeneration/regeneration of hepatocytes, lymphocytic infiltration and pseudo-bile-duct formation in portal areas, compatible with drug-induced liver injury. Lymphocyte stimulation test for MA was negative; IgE normal; patient positive for hepatitis-B virus antibodies but negative for anti-HCV and anti-CMV. Liver impairment from metenolone acetate had been considered mild, reversible, and infrequent. Plasma exchange with glucose-insulin therapy (10 times) was ineffective.

raw_record.support_text: In a case report of a single patient, the diagnosis of trazodone-induced hepatotoxicity was supported by a liver biopsy showing no significant inflammation or fat and, more importantly, by the biochemical response to inadvertent rechallenge with trazodone (given on 8/10/98 and 8/11/98). Viral and serological markers were negative, there was no biliary radiographic abnormality, and the liver tests essentially normalized approximately 2 weeks after discontinuation of trazodone and again after stopping the inadvertent challenge. The atypical rapid rise in AST on rechallenge was considered consistent with (but not diagnostic of) an idiosyncratic mechanism, described as an idiosyncratic, possible immune reaction. The reaction occurred almost 18 months after drug initiation.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case proven by inadvertent rechallenge (2 days of drug, 8/10-8/11/98); onset ~18 months after drug initiation. Liver biopsy showed bile plugs with intracanalicular cholestasis and modest periportal lymphocytic infiltrate without interface, with feathery degeneration and ballooning of hepatocytes. Lab values at hospitalization: total bilirubin 11.0 mg/dL, AST 625 U/L, ALT 1092 U/L, Alk Phos 206 U/L; values rose on rechallenge (AST 824, ALT 1476) then normalized. Patient hospitalized 8/2/98, all drugs stopped, discharged after 3 days, no other meds taken. Five prior reports of trazodone hepatotoxicity noted (latencies from 14 days to 8 months); one reported fatal hepatic necrosis (Hull et al.) occurred in a patient concurrently taking a neuroleptic drug. Patient was on low-dose steroids and still had a severe idiosyncratic reaction. Trazodone bears structural similarity to fluorobutyrophenone antipsychotics; major metabolite is m-chloro-4-phenylpiperazine.

raw_record.support_text: Six cases of hepatotoxicity secondary to trazodone have been well described, one confirmed by inadvertent drug rechallenge. Three cases occurred within 9 weeks of starting treatment with a mixed cholestatic and hepatocellular histological pattern; two other cases developed jaundice after 7-8 months of use with liver function tests increased until 6 months after withdrawal (one showing a chronic active hepatitis pattern on histology); and one occurred after 18 months of use while on low-dose steroids. Liver injury was self-limited upon discontinuation. The mechanism seems immunoallergic/hypersensitivity given associated exanthema/rash or leukonychia, positive antimitochondrial antibody, eosinophils in liver specimens, and a rapid response on rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Six well-described cases; one confirmed by inadvertent drug rechallenge. Latency 9 weeks to 18 months. Histology mixed cholestatic and hepatocellular; one case chronic active hepatitis (jaundice after 7-8 months, LFTs elevated up to 6 months post-withdrawal); one case after 18 months of use on low-dose steroids. Immunoallergic/hypersensitivity mechanism (exanthema, leukonychia, antimitochondrial antibody, eosinophils, rapid response on rechallenge). Liver injury self-limited on discontinuation. p49: main psychoactive metabolite is mCPP via CYP3A3/4 hydroxylation, further metabolized by polymorphic CYP2D6; poor metabolizers have higher mCPP steady-state concentrations; thioridazine (CYP2D6 inhibitor) increased mCPP plasma concentrations ~50%; the only fatal liver failure case involved combined trazodone and trifluoperazine (neuroleptic) treatment.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that the chronic active hepatitis in their patient was caused by trazodone. Hepatitis B serology was consistent with remote past exposure but not ongoing viral infection (confirmed by negative immunostains), which effectively ruled out other causes of chronic hepatitis. The authors note the temporal relation of the symptoms and liver enzyme abnormalities to starting and stopping the drug strongly implicates trazodone as the cause, and suggest clinicians be alert to the possibility of hepatic injury in patients taking trazodone.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report of chronic active hepatitis. The authors report being 'confident' the chronic hepatitis was caused by trazodone based on ruling out other causes (hepatitis B serology consistent with remote past exposure but not ongoing infection; negative immunostains on biopsy) and the temporal relation of symptoms and liver enzyme abnormalities to starting and stopping the drug. Trazodone is framed as an antidepressant medication.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a case of mixed cholestatic-hepatocellular liver injury in a patient on trazodone at the recommended starting dose. They state: 'We believe our patient also had an idiosyncratic drug reaction to trazodone, characterized by both a cholestatic and hepatocellular resemblance and profound hyperbilirubinemia.' The reaction peaked 2 weeks after drug discontinuation and resolved over 8 weeks, and they advise monitoring liver enzymes and bilirubin during the first 4 weeks in patients starting trazodone, regardless of dosage.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of a patient presenting with what appeared to be obstructive jaundice with hepatocellular inflammation; extensive evaluation was negative. Liver biopsy showed intrahepatic cholestasis and inflammatory response consistent with a drug reaction. Bilirubin peaked at 29 mg/dL two weeks after drug discontinuation; aspartate transaminase and alkaline phosphatase decreased to 235 IU/L and 152 IU/L, respectively, and all liver enzymes and bilirubin returned to normal eight weeks after trazodone was discontinued. The reaction occurred at the recommended starting dose. A prior published case (Chu et al., reference 1) of a mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic reaction at trazodone 500 mg/d was the first published case of liver toxicity. Trazodone is a triazolopyridine derivative (nontricyclic antidepressant); its primary side effects are drowsiness and dizziness. Authors recommend monitoring liver enzymes and bilirubin for the first 4 weeks in patients starting trazodone.

raw_record.support_text: A patient developed liver disease after beginning trazodone; liver tests returned to normal after she stopped the drug, and no other etiology was evident, which the authors state strongly suggests drug-induced hepatotoxicity. The authors also attribute her leukonychia to trazodone based on timing of onset and resolution, but this is not a liver-injury claim.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: liver disease developed after starting trazodone, resolved on dechallenge, with no other evident etiology. Two previously reported cases of trazodone-induced hepatotoxicity are noted: one patient developed a rash and elevated hepatic enzymes without jaundice 3 weeks after starting the drug, and the other became jaundiced 2 weeks after starting trazodone; both recovered within several weeks of stopping the drug. Leukonychia was also attributed to the drug but is not a liver-injury finding. Authors advise that physicians be aware that hepatotoxicity can be caused by trazodone.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report that their patient had an idiosyncratic drug reaction to trazodone characterized by both cholestatic and hepatocellular features and profound hyperbilirubinemia, occurring at the recommended starting dose of trazodone. The reaction peaked 2 weeks after discontinuation of the drug and resolved over 8 weeks. A liver biopsy showed intrahepatic cholestasis and an inflammatory response consistent with a drug reaction, and the authors advise monitoring liver enzymes and bilirubin for the first 4 weeks in patients started on trazodone.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of a patient who presented with what appeared to be obstructive jaundice along with hepatocellular inflammation while on the recommended starting dose of trazodone; liver biopsy showed intrahepatic cholestasis and inflammatory response consistent with a drug reaction. Bilirubin peaked at 29 mg/dL two weeks after trazodone discontinuation, with aspartate transaminase decreased to 235 IU/L and alkaline phosphatase to 152 IU/L; all liver enzymes and bilirubin returned to normal eight weeks after discontinuation. The paper cites Chu and associates' earlier report of a mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic reaction in a patient receiving trazodone 500 mg/d as the first published case of trazodone liver toxicity. Trazodone is a triazolopyridine derivative and nontricyclic antidepressant; primary side effects are drowsiness and dizziness. Authors recommend monitoring liver enzymes and bilirubin for the first 4 weeks in patients started on trazodone regardless of dosage.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of acute reversible liver injury with the use of trazodone in a 38-year-old woman, who had taken trazodone for about 18 months while on corticosteroids. The diagnosis of trazodone-induced liver injury was confirmed by an inadvertent rechallenge with trazodone (taken for 2 days while off all other medications), after which bilirubin and transaminases rose again, and the patient improved upon stopping. The authors describe this as a well documented instance of trazodone-induced liver injury.

Peak labs: bilirubin 11.0 mg/dl (conjugated 7.1), AST 625 U/L, ALT 1092 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 206 U/L, albumin 3.5 g/dl. Biopsy showed zone 3 feathery degeneration and ballooning, modest lymphocytic inflammation, and cholestasis (no fat, fibrosis, or iron). On rechallenge (2 consecutive days of trazodone), bilirubin rose to 10.3 mg/dl, AST 824 U/L, ALT 1476 U/L; tests normalized ~14 days after last dose. Serologies for hepatitis A/B/C negative. One prior report of five cases of trazodone hepatotoxicity exists (one chronic; others acute cellular and cholestatic injury).

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 28 prior case reports plus 3 from the current study of ticlopidine-induced cholestasis. Patients presented with anorexia, vomiting, itching, fever, chills, abdominal pain, and jaundice one week to three months after starting ticlopidine (≤ recommended 250 mg twice daily). Liver tests showed moderate elevation of bilirubin (0.7–26.4 mg/dl) and alkaline phosphatase (5–10x normal, mean 749 IU/liter) with mild transaminase elevation; jaundice resolved and enzymes normalized over 10 days to over a year after discontinuation, with no fatalities or chronic liver disease. Biopsies showed pure cholestasis or mixed cholestasis and hepatocellular injury, and epitheloid granulomas were reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Ticolpidine-induced cholestatic hepatitis; 28 published case reports plus 3 in current study. Latency 1 week to 3 months after starting therapy. Serum bilirubin 0.7–26.4 mg/dl (mean 9.6 mg/dl); alkaline phosphatase 5–10x normal (mean 749 IU/liter); transaminases 41–2661 IU/liter (mean 425 IU/liter). All cases resolved; 7 cases had prolonged cholestasis lasting >6 months after withdrawal; no fatalities or chronic hepatic injury. Biopsies showed pure cholestasis or mixed cholestasis/hepatocellular injury; epitheloid granulomas reported. Temporal relationship observed in the 3 current cases, with normalization 6 weeks to 4 months after discontinuation; biliary obstruction ruled out (US/CT/ERCP); hepatitis and autoimmune serologies negative. TRIALS: CATS reported 4.4% abnormal liver tests (alkaline phosphatase most common finding), while TASS reported no hepatotoxicity. Mechanism uncertain; drug hypersensitivity proposed but a direct cholestatic mechanism was also suggested.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents ticlopidine as a recognized cause of drug-induced hepatotoxicity, analyzing 49 reports of ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity patients (47 previously published cases described in table I plus two new cases described in this paper). A Bayesian causal-assessment method based on analytical and demographic traits was applied to attribute abnormal liver function to ticlopidine.
raw_record.extra_details: Ticlopidine was given at 250 mg twice daily. Case 2 (76-year-old man) had abnormal liver function emerging after 21 weeks and severe enzyme elevations (AST 91 IU/L, ALT 134 IU/L, GGT 1029 IU/L, ALP 754 IU/L) with total bilirubin rising to 11.5 mg/dl by week 28; enzymes and bilirubin improved after ticlopidine discontinuation at week 64. The Danan causality assessment gave a suggestive relationship, and the Bayesian method assigned ticlopidine a posterior probability (PsP) of 87.30% at week 21 and 81.89% at week 64. The analytical profile emphasized alkaline phosphatase (ALP >720 IU/L had a likelihood ratio of 109.50); alcohol, viral hepatitis, mononucleosis, and drug-associated/uncertain etiologies had statistically different PsP from ticlopidine. Published ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity cases (47 in table I plus the 2 new cases) were used to build the model.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude the patient's clinical picture can be explained as an adverse reaction to ticlopidine that caused cholestatic hepatitis, based on the sequence of events and their compatibility with ticlopidine's reported reactions, noting no published cases of hepatic nodular lesions from this drug. Additional supporting text describes that acute cholestatic hepatitis from ticlopidine can occur weeks to months after starting treatment, with jaundice and pruritus resolving after drug withdrawal and liver tests returning to normal within several months (sometimes over a year), and centrilobular cholestasis characteristically on biopsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of acute cholestatic hepatitis attributed to ticlopidine. Features included jaundice and pruritus resolving after drug withdrawal. Transaminases normalized at 10 months, but GGT and alkaline phosphatase remained elevated and abnormal liver tests persisted beyond 1.5 years. Onset reported as weeks to several months after starting ticlopidine. Liver biopsy characteristically shows centrilobular (centroacinar) cholestasis. Novel observation: non-neoplastic hepatic nodules appeared during the acute phase, resolved by 6 months after recovery from the acute illness, and were suggested to relate to the ticlopidine hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors concluded that this patient was likely to have ticlopidine-induced cholestatic hepatitis because of the temporal relationship with commencement of the medication and resolution with its withdrawal; the liver biopsy was consistent with a drug-induced phenomenon, and there was an absence of other possible aetiologies on laboratory testing and imaging. They recommended that ticlopidine be considered as a cause of intrahepatic cholestasis in patients presenting with jaundice.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of cholestatic hepatitis attributed to ticlopidine in a patient presenting with jaundice. Causality was based on temporal relationship to drug start, resolution (dechallenge) on withdrawal, a liver biopsy consistent with a drug-induced phenomenon (portal tract fibrosis, inflammation, and florid bile ductule proliferation highlighted by cytokeratin 7, with mixed inflammation including eosinophils and neutrophils), and exclusion of other aetiologies. The paper notes hepatotoxicity has been reported in up to 4.4% of cases, mainly as asymptomatic elevations of alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase, and that cholestatic hepatitis is a rare side-effect; typically jaundice appears after a latent period of about 6 weeks and lasts approximately 4 months, and the condition is generally benign with resolution after drug withdrawal. Pathogenesis is unknown, with both direct intrinsic hepatotoxicity and immuno-allergic mechanisms proposed.

raw_record.support_text: In this case report, the authors attribute hepatic injury to ticlopidine: the strict temporal correlation between use of the drug and alteration of hepatic tests is cited as the reason for the causal link, further supported by a stable medication regimen before ticlopidine was added, no recent alcohol consumption, and normalization of laboratory values after ticlopidine was suspended. Calcium heparin, added recently, was considered an unlikely cause because it was continued after ticlopidine discontinuation while liver function tests normalized. The paper notes ticlopidine hepatotoxicity resolves with drug suspension and that cholestasis is a constant characteristic, with an immunologic reaction to the drug considered as a possible mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of cholestatic hepatotoxicity attributed to ticlopidine. Laboratory findings on day 18 after ticlopidine suspension had normalized (bilirubin not tested; AST 24, ALT 30, alkaline phosphatase 260, GGT 58); hepatic tests remained normal four months later. Liver-injury signs typically arise 1-2 months after drug initiation and resolve 1-10 months after suspension; mechanism unknown, immunologic reaction considered; advanced age (69 y in reported cases) and interaction with other drugs (e.g., cardiovascular drugs) suggested as possibly contributory, with no clear gender prevalence. Calcium heparin co-medication deemed an unlikely cause since it was continued while tests normalized. Phenotype: cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: A 69-year-old man presented with malaise, anorexia, jaundice and pruritus after being given ticlopidine for a cerebral infarction. Blood chemistries showed liver dysfunction and hyperbilirubinemia (ALT 455 IU/L, AST 190 IU/L, total bilirubin 8.2 mg/dl, γ-GTP 806 IU/L), with negative viral and autoimmune serologies. He was diagnosed with acute intrahepatic cholestasis induced by ticlopidine, and liver enzymes and bilirubin improved after ticlopidine was discontinued. The patient later developed pure red cell aplasia, and on day 43 a laparoscopy-guided liver biopsy showed intrahepatic cholestasis. He was diagnosed with acute intrahepatic cholestasis associated with pure red cell aplasia due to ticlopidine.
raw_record.extra_details: Intrahepatic cholestasis diagnosed by biochemistry and confirmed on liver biopsy showing centro-acinar-compatible intrahepatic cholestasis; dechallenge (ticlopidine discontinuation) led to improvement. Concomitant pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) attributed to ticlopidine. Paper notes ticlopidine-induced mild serum liver enzyme elevations with 1-2% incidence and severe hepatitis incidence estimated at 0.0013%; only a few cases of a severe cholestatic pattern have been reported.

raw_record.support_text: A 69-year-old man developed jaundice, pruritus, and liver dysfunction (ALT 455 IU/L, AST 190 IU/L, total bilirubin 8.2 mg/dl, gamma-GTP 806 IU/L) after starting ticlopidine for a cerebral infarction. Serology for hepatitis B and C and ANA were negative, and abdominal ultrasound showed a normal liver without obstruction, so the patient was diagnosed with acute intrahepatic cholestasis induced by ticlopidine. After ticlopidine discontinuation liver enzymes and bilirubin improved; a later liver biopsy showed intrahepatic cholestasis and the case was reported as acute intrahepatic cholestasis associated with pure red cell aplasia due to ticlopidine.
raw_record.extra_details: Ticlopidine was given for cerebral infarction. Markers for HBsAg, HBsAb, HBeAg, HBeAb, IgM-HBc Ab, HCV Ab and IgM-HA Ab were negative; anti-nuclear antibody negative; ultrasound showed no obstructive jaundice. Dechallenge led to improvement of liver enzymes and T-bilirubin. Liver biopsy on day 43 showed intrahepatic cholestasis compatible with drug-induced liver damage. The case was accompanied by pure red cell aplasia (PRCA), whose etiologic attribution to ticlopidine was raised. The text also notes ticlopidine-induced mild serum liver enzyme elevations at 1-2% incidence in some studies and an estimated 0.0013% incidence of severe hepatitis, with only a few reported cases of a severe cholestatic pattern of liver injury showing centro-acinar cholestasis on biopsy.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity in three patients in whom clopidogrel was successfully used as a substitute, with hepatic symptoms disappearing when switching from ticlopidine to another thienopyridine, suggesting a specific immune response.
raw_record.extra_details: Ticlopidine hepatotoxicity reported in three patients; hepatic symptoms resolved when switching to clopidogrel, supporting a specific immune response; HLA-A*33:03 linked to ticlopidine cholestatic injury.

raw_record.support_text: From 1982, the year of the first ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity case report, to 1999, 47 reports of ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity cases have been indexed on Medline. The demographic and clinical information from these 47 cases is described in table I, whose data include age (mean 69.3 years), dose (250-500 mg/day), total bilirubin (mean 10.2 mg/dl) and ALT (mean 364.3 IU/L).
raw_record.extra_details: 47 published ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity cases indexed on Medline 1982-1999; mean age 69.3 ± 13.2 years, 33 female/13 male cases tabled; dose 250-500 mg/day; mean total bilirubin 10.2 ± 8.0 mg/dl, alkaline phosphatase 783.5, AST 228.9, ALT 364.3 IU/L; mean latent period 6.2 weeks.

raw_record.support_text: A 69-year-old man on ticlopidine for a cerebral infarction developed malaise, anorexia, jaundice and pruritus with marked liver dysfunction and hyperbilirubinemia (ALT 455 IU/L, AST 190 IU/L, total bilirubin 8.2 mg/dL, γ-GTP 806 IU/L). Hepatitis serologies (HBV, HCV, HAV) and ANA were negative, and ultrasound showed no obstruction. He was diagnosed with acute intrahepatic cholestasis induced by ticlopidine; enzymes improved after discontinuation, and he also developed pure red cell aplasia. Liver biopsy on day 43 showed intrahepatic cholestasis compatible with drug-induced liver damage, and he was diagnosed with acute intrahepatic cholestasis associated with pure red cell aplasia due to ticlopidine.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 69-year-old man with acute intrahepatic/acute cholestatic hepatitis plus pure red cell aplasia (PRCA), both attributed to ticlopidine. Ticlopidine was given for cerebral infarction. Liver biopsy showed intrahepatic cholestasis; liver enzymes and bilirubin improved after drug discontinuation. Serologies for HBV/HCV/HAV and ANA negative; ultrasound showed normal liver and no obstruction. The paper notes ticlopidine causes mild serum liver enzyme elevations in ~1-2% in some studies, with severe hepatitis incidence estimated at 0.0013% and only a few cases of a severe cholestatic pattern, with biopsies showing centro-acinar cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: A 69-year-old man developed general malaise, anorexia, jaundice and pruritus after being given ticlopidine for a cerebral infarction. Blood chemistries showed liver dysfunction and hyperbilirubinemia (ALT 455 IU/L, AST 190 IU/L, total bilirubin 8.2 mg/dL, γ-GTP 806 IU/L) with negative viral and autoimmune serology and a normal ultrasound. The patient was diagnosed with acute intrahepatic cholestasis induced by ticlopidine; after ticlopidine was discontinued liver enzymes and bilirubin improved. Liver biopsy on day 43 showed intrahepatic cholestasis, and the patient was diagnosed with acute intrahepatic cholestasis associated with pure red cell aplasia due to ticlopidine.
raw_record.extra_details: 69-year-old man with a cerebral infarction; presented with general malaise, anorexia, jaundice and pruritus; ALT 455 IU/L, AST 190 IU/L, total bilirubin 8.2 mg/dL, γ-GTP 806 IU/L; serology negative for HBsAg, HBsAb, HBeAg, HBeAb, IgM-HBc Ab, HCV Ab, IgM-HA Ab; ANA negative; ultrasound showed no obstructive jaundice; liver biopsy showed acute intrahepatic cholestasis; injury improved after ticlopidine discontinuation (dechallenge with recovery); the patient simultaneously developed pure red cell aplasia (PRCA). Phenotype described as acute intrahepatic cholestasis / acute cholestatic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: A patient presenting with jaundice, cholestatic liver tests, and marked hyperlipidemia (total cholesterol 1,666 mg/dl) had a liver biopsy showing moderate spotty necrosis, moderate steatosis and slight bile stasis compatible with drug-induced cholestasis. The drug-induced leukocyte stimulating test (DLST) was positive for ticlopidine hydrochloride, and the liver damage and hyperlipidemia were diagnosed as ticlopidine hydrochloride-induced cholestatic hepatitis with associated abnormal lipidemia (LP-X). Values increased even after withdrawal of the causative drug, then declined.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report. Admission labs: total bilirubin 7.8 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 5.5 mg/dl, GOT 94 IU/l, GPT 243 IU/l, ALP 842 IU/l, γ-GTP 2,418 IU/l, LAP 156 IU/l; LP-X test positive; total cholesterol rose from 257 mg/dl before onset to 1,682 mg/dl with cholestasis. DLST positive for ticlopidine hydrochloride. Liver biopsy (Dec 12) showed moderate spotty necrosis, moderate steatosis and slight bile stasis, compatible with drug-induced cholestasis. Phenotype: cholestatic hepatitis with associated abnormal (LP-X) lipoproteinemia. Total bilirubin peaked at 30.2 mg/dl and took 80 days to normalize; GPT and γ-GTP remained elevated ~140 days after jaundice. Patient recovered without transplantation or death. Structural pattern: cholestasis/bile stasis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a biopsy-proven case of granulomatous hepatitis attributed to ticlopidine, a platelet aggregation inhibitor. A 75-year-old man developed asthenia, anorexia, weight loss and painless hepatomegaly four weeks after starting ticlopidine 250 mg bid; liver biopsy revealed epithelioid granulomas affecting all areas of the hepatic lobule with eosinophilic inflammatory infiltrates. Ticlopidine was discontinued while amlodipine was maintained, and he became asymptomatic within ten days with normal serum alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyltransferase and liver scintigraphy at six months. The authors note granulomatous hepatitis had not previously been reported as an adverse effect, and that ticlopidine was not rechallenged but other causes of granulomatous hepatitis were excluded; according to the Naranjo algorithm, ticlopidine seemed the more likely etiology.
raw_record.extra_details: Biopsy-proven granulomatous hepatitis with eosinophilic infiltrates; first reported case of this phenotype. Dose 250 mg bid for 4 weeks (cerebrovascular accident) before symptom onset; asthenia, anorexia, 4 kg weight loss, fever 37.6 C, painless hepatomegaly. Labs: alkaline phosphatase 1526 U/L (normal 30-120), gamma-glutamyltransferase 886 U/L (normal 0-30), AST 41 U/L, ALT 50 U/L, total bilirubin 12.2 umol/L (normal), platelets 693 x 10^6/L eosinophils. Negative serologies for hepatitis A/B/C, Brucella, Echinococcus, CMV, herpes, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Legionella, Coxiella; negative acid-fast stains/cultures, normal ACE and calciuria. Dechallenge led to clinical recovery within 10 days and normalization of liver tests/scintigraphy at 6 months; no rechallenge. Causality assessed by Naranjo algorithm ('ticlopidine seems the more likely etiology'). Concurrent amlodipine 10 mg/d was maintained and not implicated. Presentation with elevated alkaline phosphatase and GGT with mild transaminases suggests cholestatic-biochemical features but the paper does not classify a canonical biochemical pattern.

raw_record.support_text: A percutaneous liver biopsy performed on day 54 after the first Ticlopidine intake showed preserved liver architecture with edema of the portal fields and mild lymphocytic/granulocytic infiltrates containing eosinophils, an excessive cholestasis with dilated canaliculi filled with bile thrombi, vacuolar cytoplasmic transformation of hepatocytes, and small focal parenchymal necroses. The overall pattern of severe intrahepatic cholestasis with mild parenchymatous hepatitis was interpreted as drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report. Cholestatic hepatitis: severe intrahepatic cholestasis with bile thrombi and mild parenchymatous hepatitis on biopsy. Clinically presented with icterus and pruritus (controlled by antihistamines). Transaminases normalized rapidly after discontinuation, while cholestasis parameters returned to normal only 79 days after stopping Ticlopidine. No rechallenge was performed. Biopsy also showed vacuolar hepatocyte transformation, small focal parenchymal necroses, mild parenchymal siderosis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a rare case of agranulocytosis associated with hepatic toxicity, probably related to the use of ticlopidine, a platelet inhibitor. More serious but less frequent adverse effects of ticlopidine are hematological dyscrasia and cholestatic hepatitis. In the presented patient, ticlopidine 250 mg twice daily was given after a vertebrobasilar stroke, and about four weeks later she developed agranulocytosis and hepatic toxicity; after ticlopidine was discontinued, liver tests progressively normalized.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient was a 70-year-old Caucasian woman with no prior hematological or liver disease and no prior history of blood or liver disorders. Hepatic toxicity and agranulocytosis developed about 4 weeks after starting ticlopidine 250 mg twice daily; ticlopidine was discontinued and she was treated with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, with rapid rise in white blood count and progressive normalization of liver tests. Cholestatic hepatitis is described as a recognized serious, less frequent ticlopidine adverse effect. The paper recommends monitoring complete blood count and liver function tests in the first three months of ticlopidine therapy for early detection of serious and unpredictable side effects.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reviews published cases of ticlopidine hepatotoxicity in humans, defining a clinical profile in which patients develop jaundice, usually without fever, eosinophilia, or pain, between 10 days and 12 weeks after starting therapy. Laboratory tests show cholestasis and elevated transaminase concentrations; improvement and complete biochemical recovery typically follow ticlopidine withdrawal within 1-11 months, although hepatic damage was occasionally permanent. The authors' own case (para 13) attributes a cholestatic hepatitis to ticlopidine because obstructive cholestasis was excluded and laboratory parameters improved after ticlopidine withdrawal despite continued enalapril, hydrochlorothiazide, and amiloride therapy and discontinuation of pipemidic acid.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series includes 18 tabulated reported cases (Table 1, refs 2-17 plus present case) of ticlopidine hepatotoxicity; doses 250-500 mg/day; onset 2-12 weeks; jaundice without fever, eosinophilia, or pain; cholestasis and elevated AST/ALT; recovery usually within 1-11 months, with occasional permanent damage and one death (Girardin and Cordonnier 1982); alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, and AST/ALT values recorded per case. The authors recommend periodic hepatobiliary monitoring during ticlopidine therapy. Present case: F/51, 500 mg, onset 7 weeks, bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL, ALK PHOS 1069 U/L, AST/ALT 47/163, recovery 3.5 months; causality attributed to ticlopidine after excluding obstructive cholestasis and pipemidic acid and noting improvement after ticlopidine withdrawal despite continued enalapril, hydrochlorothiazide, and amiloride.

raw_record.support_text: A group of eight patients with drug-induced cholestasis caused by drugs other than tiopronin was analyzed (Table 3). Patient 5, M/62, received panaldine (ticlopidine) for cerebral infarction with a maximum bilirubin of 8.9 mg/dl and jaundice.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported in Table 3 as 'panaldine', a brand of ticlopidine; drug-induced cholestasis with jaundice; M/62 given for cerebral infarction; maximum total bilirubin 8.9 mg/dl.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report two patients who developed prolonged cholestatic hepatitis after receiving the antiplatelet agent ticlopidine following percutaneous coronary angioplasty, with complete remission on follow-up. An objective causality assessment revealed that the adverse drug event was probably related to the use of ticlopidine. The hepatitis may develop weeks after drug discontinuation but resolved after withdrawal, and complete remission was seen in all reported cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients developed jaundice with clinical and laboratory characteristics of cholestatic hepatitis after ticlopidine therapy for post-coronary angioplasty stent/PTCA; hepatitis resolved after drug discontinuation with complete remission during follow-up; hepatitis may develop weeks after discontinuation and run a prolonged course. An objective causality assessment scored the event as probably related. In vitro T-cell stimulation by therapeutic concentrations of ticlopidine was demonstrated in the patients but not healthy controls, suggesting a possible immune-mediated mechanism. Ticlopidine is an antiplatelet agent used 14-21 days with aspirin after PTCA with stenting or long-term for cerebrovascular prevention.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that with the increasing use of Ticlopidine, which is approved in more than 60 countries and used mainly for stroke prophylaxis, adverse effects must be anticipated. It explicitly attributes liver function disorders, and in individual cases even more severe cholestatic liver damage, to Ticlopidine treatment, noting these can occur within the first 4 months of therapy. The paper recommends monitoring liver values every two weeks and considering pre-existing liver disease and drug interactions.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported dosing was 2×250 mg daily (two cases had no dose data). Time from therapy start to onset of clinical symptoms averaged 30.1 days (range 7-84 days); in the authors' own case 28 days. Time from drug discontinuation to near-normalization of liver values averaged 146 days (range 11 days to 1 year); the own case took 77 days for cholestasis parameters and bilirubin to largely normalize. The mechanism of liver injury is described as currently unclear; the paper hypothesizes possibly rather toxic mechanisms from accumulation of Ticlopidine or its metabolites than allergic-hyperergic reactions causing cholestasis, supported by isolated perfused rat liver studies. Injury predominantly involves the cholestatic pattern with elevated cholestasis parameters and bilirubin. Liver damage may occur especially within the first 4 months of treatment.

raw_record.support_text: In a preliminary study, 3 patients with cholestatic hepatitis due to ticlopidine were genotyped for CYP2C19 and evaluated for T cell reactivity and cytokine levels after therapy withdrawal. All patients carried 'slow metabolizer' CYP2C19 genotypes (CYP2C19*2/CYP2C19*2 and CYP2C19*2/CYP2C19*3), and T cell reactivity to ticlopidine was present in all patients during follow-up, with a positive correlation between decreasing ticlopidine-specific responses, decreasing Th1 cytokine serum concentrations, and clinical markers of liver damage.

raw_record.extra_details: 3 patients with cholestatic hepatitis due to ticlopidine. Genotyping for CYP2C19*1/*2/*3 by PCR-RFLP; T cell reactivity assessed by proliferation assay on days 0, 90, 150 and 210 after therapy withdrawal; serum INF-γ, IL-2, IL-4, IL-10, TNF-α, sFas, sFasL measured by ELISA. T cell reactivity present throughout follow-up; positive correlation between decline in ticlopidine-specific responses, decline in Th1 cytokines, and clinical markers of liver damage. Authors attribute pathogenesis to Th1-type immune reactivity and note a direct association between metabolic (CYP2C19) and immunological mechanisms in drug-induced cholestatic liver damage.

Recovery occurs within 3 to 6 months of discontinuing ticlopidine but may occasionally take longer than 1 year.

raw_record.support_text: In post-marketing surveillance in Japan, ticlopidine-induced liver injury characteristically occurred within two months of treatment initiation and included pruritus, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and more rarely marked progression of jaundice. In the present study (62 Cases), most patients developed liver function abnormalities within 30 days, and the disease type was cholestatic in the majority according to the ICM and DDW Japan 2002 criteria; effects of aging and dose were not significant, whereas pre-existing renal functional abnormalities tended to increase risk. The paper recommends monitoring ALT, ALP, and γ-GTP for at least 30 days to prevent serious ticlopidine hydrochloride-induced liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with pre-existing liver or renal function abnormalities at initiation of ticlopidine therapy tended to develop abnormal liver function; risk was increased in those with pre-existing renal abnormalities, particularly for the cholestatic type.
raw_record.extra_details: Among 62 cases of liver function abnormalities on ticlopidine: 11 hepatocellular-type, 29 cholestatic-type, 11 mixed-type, 11 non-classified type (cholestatic >50%). Most (88.7%) abnormalities occurred within 30 days of treatment start; all abnormal LFTs normalized on discontinuation (or spontaneously with continued administration) except 7 with unknown outcome. Post-marketing surveillance: cholestatic injury within 2 months with pruritus, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, rarely marked jaundice. CYP1A2, 2B6, 2C9, 2C19, 3A4, 2D6 associated with ticlopidine metabolism; concomitant CYP2C9 substrate/inhibitor use significantly reduced cholestatic-type risk; no dose or age dependence. Dosing of UDCA (used as preventive) not effective.

raw_record.support_text: The study identified 22 Japanese patients with ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity (cases) and 85 ticlopidine-treated patients with no adverse reactions (controls). The diagnosis of ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity was based on clinical history and laboratory findings (serum bilirubin >1.5 mg/dL or serum AST/ALT at least twice the upper limit of normal), and cases were divided into cholestatic (n=14), mixed (n=5), and hepatocellular (n=3) damage categories per Danan's criteria. There were no differences in age, gender, or ticlopidine dosage between groups; all subjects were Hondo Japanese.

raw_record.support_text: During the 12-week sitaxsentan study, asymptomatic elevations in serum transaminases were observed in seven patients. In an extension trial, two patients had significant increases in liver function enzyme values after 4 months of sitaxsentan treatment; in both, liver biopsy findings were consistent with acute hepatitis. Despite dose reduction and eventual discontinuation of study drug, one patient died from liver failure, while the other's liver function values returned to normal after discontinuation. The authors subsequently discontinued all patients from the study drug after these hepatitis episodes. A subsequent passage frames the injury as more likely direct hepatotoxicity than immune-mediated, since no anti-liver-kidney microsome autoantibodies were found, and notes that drug accumulation from nonlinear pharmacokinetics may increase toxicity risk.
raw_record.extra_details: Aliases used in paper: sitaxsentan; an ET-A receptor antagonist studied for pulmonary hypertension. 12-week study: asymptomatic transaminase elevations in 7 patients. Extension trial: 2 patients with significant LFT increases after 4 months of treatment; liver biopsy consistent with acute hepatitis; one died from liver failure despite dose reduction/discontinuation, the other normalized after discontinuation. All patients were then withdrawn from study drug. Mechanism: direct hepatotoxicity suggested as more likely than immune-mediated given absence of anti-liver-kidney microsome autoantibodies; accumulation from nonlinear pharmacokinetics may increase toxicity risk. Sitaxsentan is a potent CYP2C9 inhibitor and moderate CYP2C19/3A4 inhibitor, altering warfarin clearance (lower warfarin doses needed to maintain therapeutic INR). Nonclinical toxicology in rats and dogs at higher/longer exposure showed no hepatotoxicity or elevated liver enzymes.

raw_record.support_text: Pfizer announced voluntary worldwide withdrawal of sitaxsentan from the market after 2 cases of fatal hepatotoxicity during the Sitaxsentan Efficacy and Safety Trial With Randomized Prospective Assessment of Adding Sildenafil (SR-PAAS) clinical trial (NCT00795639). This attribution of fatal hepatotoxicity to sitaxsentan precipitated the market withdrawal and forced transition of stable PAH patients from sitaxsentan to other ERAs.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases of fatal hepatotoxicity occurred during the SR-PAAS clinical trial (NCT00795639), leading to Pfizer's voluntary worldwide market withdrawal on December 15, 2010. Agent is a highly selective ET-A antagonist used for pulmonary arterial hypertension; patients were transitioned to bosentan or ambrisentan after withdrawal. Specific hepatic histopathology, biochemical pattern, and causality-instrument scores were not reported.

raw_record.support_text: Sitaxentan significantly inhibits organic anion transport, considered the cause of the observed severe toxicity. In clinical trials, 7% of sitaxentan patients had ALT >3xULN (RR 1.4), seven patients developed combination ALT and bilirubin elevation, and one patient developed liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Clinical trial: 899 patients; ALT/AST >3xULN 7.0/5.0 (RR 1.4); >5x 4.0/0.7; combination ALT and bilirubin elevation 7; liver failure 1/0. Mechanism: inhibition of organic anion transporter considered the cause of the observed severe toxicity; nonclinical centrilobular hypertrophy (occasional necrosis), increased prothrombin time and coagulopathy in rats and dogs at high dose.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present two patients who suffered severe liver injury attributed to sitaxentan therapy for pulmonary arterial hypertension. Transaminases peaked above 30 times the upper limit of normal, and the pattern of hepatic injury was mixed with significant elevation of both bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase. Both cases occurred within the first 12 weeks of treatment and resulted in a protracted period of jaundice; the authors conclude that these were two cases of fulminant hepatic failure from sitaxentan therapy, emphasizing the importance of monthly liver function testing.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients on sitaxentan for pulmonary arterial hypertension. Transaminases peaked at >30x ULN; mixed hepatic injury with significant elevation of bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase; onset within first 12 weeks of treatment; protracted jaundice. Liver biopsy of patient 2 showed moderate portal and parenchymal lymphocytic infiltrate with scattered eosinophils and extensive active hepatocyte injury (H&E). Authors conclude both cases were fulminant hepatic failure and recommend monthly liver function monitoring.

raw_record.support_text: In the extended treatment of the Canadian STRIDE-1/1X cohort (n=11) with sitaxsentan, one case of gallstone hepatitis, resolving after 3 days, was reported; increased hepatic transaminases (>3-fold the upper limit of normal) were not observed in any of the patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Gallstone hepatitis (cholestatic, gallstone/obstructive injury) reported as one case in extended STRIDE-1/1X cohort, resolving after 3 days; 11 Canadian patients continued on sitaxsentan; no patient showed transaminase elevation >3x ULN at 1 year.

raw_record.support_text: Seven cases of severe hepatitis-like drug reactions have been described in association with sitaxentan. Five of these were treated with the currently approved dose of 100 mg once daily: one patient died from liver failure, one underwent heart, lung and liver transplantation, one recovered after prednisone treatment, and two recovered after standard treatment. An additional two cases of fatal liver injury related to the use of sitaxentan in PAH patients have also been reported, and in all these cases liver function deteriorated despite drug discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: ERA approved for pulmonary arterial hypertension. Five approved-dose cases: 1 death from liver failure, 1 heart+lung+liver transplantation, 1 recovery after prednisone, 2 recoveries after standard treatment; plus 2 additional fatal cases. In all cases liver function deteriorated despite drug discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: Sitaxentan (Thelin), an endothelin receptor A antagonist used to treat pulmonary arterial hypertension, was withdrawn from the market due to an idiosyncratic risk of drug-induced liver injury identified from emerging clinical trial data and clinical case reports. The paper reports its preclinical (animal) safety profile and notes the human DILI risk as the reason for market withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: Endothelin receptor A antagonist withdrawn from the market for pulmonary arterial hypertension (Thelin) due to idiosyncratic DILI risk identified from emerging clinical trial data and clinical case reports; marketed with a presumably positive benefit:risk at approval. Preclinical findings (covered elsewhere in the paper) included coagulopathy in rats and dogs, increased serum alkaline phosphatase in mice and dogs, hepatic hypertrophy in all species, decreased albumin/erythrocyte/hemoglobin/hematocrit, increased coagulation times and liver weight, generally at systemic exposures above human AUC; no carcinogenicity and low hepatic toxicity potential in animals.

raw_record.support_text: A case of a 61-year-old female with sitaxsentan-induced acute severe liver failure is presented. Despite withdrawal of therapy, her liver tests failed to improve, and after six weeks of monitoring she was given high-dose corticosteroids with a good clinical and biochemical response. The paper notes endothelin receptor antagonists are postulated to cause hepatitis by inhibition of a bile salt transporter pump, but an immune-mediated or idiosyncratic mechanism should be considered.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adult patient with pulmonary arterial hypertension and a background of atrial septal defect repair, atrial flutter, atrioventricular node ablation and pacemaker insertion, with no known liver disease; unclear contribution of concomitant medications (warfarin, diltiazem, furosemide, vitamin D, calcium).
raw_record.extra_details: Sitaxsentan given at 100 mg/day for 16 weeks; liver enzymes became abnormal after 8 weeks and sitaxsentan was discontinued 6 weeks later; dechallenge was negative (continued worsening of all liver parameters over the next 6 weeks and admission); treated with high-dose corticosteroids with good clinical and biochemical response. Baseline near-normal liver tests (ALT 24 U/L, AST 28 U/L, ALP 112 U/L, bilirubin 11.6 µmol/L). Postulated mechanism: inhibition of a bile salt transporter pump; immune-mediated or idiosyncratic mechanism considered. Sitaxsentan is a selective endothelin A receptor antagonist.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe admitting two patients with severe hepatotoxicity on sitaxentan sodium, an endothelin receptor antagonist approved for pulmonary arterial hypertension, to their Pulmonary Hypertension Unit. Both patients developed severe acute drug-induced liver injury attributed to sitaxentan that resolved following drug discontinuation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Both patients had severe pulmonary arterial hypertension treated with sitaxentan 100 mg once daily; patient 2 was also concurrently taking aspirin, doxazosin XL, valsartan/hydrochlorothiazide, and frusemide.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient 1 (47-yr male, PAH with congenital heart disease) developed nausea, vomiting, anorexia and icterus ~4 months after starting 100 mg q.d.; LFTs worsened after discontinuation; INR peaked at 1.6 on vitamin K; transjugular biopsy consistent with severe acute drug-induced liver injury showing ballooning degeneration of hepatocytes, bile stasis and eosinophilic infiltration; no other hepatotoxic medications; recovered on ursodeoxycholic acid. Patient 2 (70-yr female, idiopathic PAH) had AST and ALT peak at 1,198 and 1,040 IU, bilirubin peak 426 umol/L, INR 1.6 off anticoagulation ~3 months after starting; biopsy showed moderate portal and parenchymal lymphocytic infiltrate with scattered eosinophils, extensive active hepatocyte injury and confluent necrosis; recovered from acute liver injury then died of respiratory failure from lobar pneumonia. Both had positive parietal cell antibodies; viral/autoimmune serologies otherwise negative. Authors note initial 300 mg sitaxentan studies showed potential for liver injury following the death of one patient, whereas a follow-up 100 mg study caused no significant liver enzyme elevation; they attribute delayed injury and prolonged recovery to nonlinear-pharmacokinetics-related drug accumulation.

raw_record.support_text: In the phase 2 211 study of sitaxsentan (doses 100-500 mg b.i.d. p.o.), elevation of hepatic transaminases (>3x ULN) occurred in 7 of the 20 patients in the 12-week study; in the extension phase following the 12-week study, 2 cases of acute hepatitis occurred with 1 death, both with the 300 mg b.i.d. dose. These hepatic events are consistent with the liver abnormalities recognized as a class effect associated with ET receptor antagonists.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High exploratory sitaxsentan dose of 300 mg b.i.d. in the phase 2 211 study; these were dose-ranging doses above the eventual therapeutic 100 mg/day dosing.
raw_record.extra_details: 2 cases of acute hepatitis occurred in the extension phase of the 211 study, leading to 1 death; both cases occurred with the 300 mg b.i.d. dose. Sitaxsentan selective endothelin receptor A antagonist for pulmonary arterial hypertension in STRIDE-1/-2/-4.

raw_record.support_text: In the extension phase of an open-label pilot study of sitaxsentan (doses 100-500 mg twice daily) in patients with PAH, 2 patients developed severe hepatitis resulting in 1 death despite stopping the drug. The text attributes this hepatic toxicity to the non-linear pharmacokinetics of sitaxsentan at high doses, and states that subsequent studies used doses up to 300 mg once a day.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Interpreted as dose-dependent, related to non-linear pharmacokinetics at high doses (100-500 mg twice daily); deaths occurred in the extension phase of the pilot study.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases occurred in the extension phase of an open-label pilot study in adults and children with idiopathic and associated PAH (congenital heart disease, collagen vascular disease). Severe hepatitis occurred with 1 death despite drug discontinuation. The paper links toxicity to non-linear pharmacokinetics at high doses, prompting later trials to use 300 mg once daily (STRIDE-1). Separately, elevated hepatic transaminases >3x ULN were 0% at 100 mg and 10% at 300 mg in STRIDE-1, and 5% and 21% respectively by 26 weeks in STRIDE-1X.

raw_record.support_text: The report of two additional cases of fatal liver injury related to the use of sitaxentan (Thelin; 100 mg sitaxentan tablets) in pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) patients enrolled in a randomised controlled study prompted Pfizer to voluntarily discontinue all ongoing clinical trials with this compound and to withdraw the commercial drug from the market worldwide. Thelin had been authorised in the EU since 2006 for treatment of PAH and marketed in 16 EU member states, Australia and Canada. The EMA advised patients taking Thelin to consult their physician to review treatment, and the ESC/ERS 2009 PH guidelines recommended no de novo initiation of Thelin and transitioning existing patients to another ERA (bosentan or ambrisentan) or to prostanoids/phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pulmonary arterial hypertension indication; cases occurred in a randomised controlled study population.
raw_record.extra_details: Two reported additional fatal liver injury cases led to Pfizer voluntarily discontinuing all ongoing clinical trials and global market withdrawal of Thelin (100 mg sitaxentan tablets). Drug authorised in the EU since 2006 for PAH, marketed in 16 EU member states, Australia, and Canada. ESC/ERS 2009 PH guidelines recommended against de novo Thelin initiation and advised transition to bosentan (Tracleer) or ambrisentan (Volibris) or other PAH drug classes (prostanoids, phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors) in cases of prior adverse reactions to those ERAs. Paper notes two types of ERA liver injury: a common dose-dependent, reversible toxic type, and a rare possibly idiosyncratic/immunologically mediated type that can result in severe liver failure.
