raw_record.support_text: The authors report that ponatinib can cause hepatotoxicity including fulminant hepatic failure and even deaths. They describe a 30-year-old man with chronic myeloid leukaemia and a BCR-ABL T315I mutation who developed ponatinib-induced hepatotoxicity after 6 months of treatment with ponatinib 45 mg once daily: alanine aminotransferase rose to 5 times the upper normal limit with normal bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase, then progressed to conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, intense pruritus and deep jaundice; liver biopsy was consistent with mild steatohepatitis. Liver function improved markedly after 2 weeks of oral prednisolone 40 mg daily and normalised within 1 month, and rechallenge with ponatinib at a lower dose was tolerated well without adverse events.
raw_record.extra_details: Third-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitor used in CML with BCR-ABL T315I mutation; case: ALT 5x ULN, normal bilirubin and ALP initially, then conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia within 2 weeks, jaundice and intense pruritus; hepatobiliary ultrasound and endoscopic ultrasonography normal; autoimmune and viral hepatitis screening negative; biopsy mild steatohepatitis; response to oral prednisolone 40 mg daily (improvement at 2 weeks, normalisation within 1 month); successful lower-dose rechallenge with gradual escalation over 6 months. Paper also states ponatinib can cause fulminant hepatic failure and even deaths; hepatotoxicity mechanism not fully understood, histology of steatohepatitis and corticosteroid response suggested an inflammatory response. Trial-derived incidence of ALT and AST elevations reported as 56% for all grades and 8% for Grades 3 or 4 (NCI CTCAE v4.0); aminotransferases >3x ULN should prompt dose reduction or temporary cessation with resumption at lower dose; discontinue in clinically apparent liver injury with jaundice. Phase I trial reported dose-dependent, mostly self-limiting hepatotoxicity; subsequent lower-dose rechallenge generally successful, Grade 4 events warranted cessation in some patients.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of liver injury induced by warfarin in a 64-year-old woman taking long-term warfarin 4.5 mg/day for anticoagulation after mechanical mitral valve replacement. Stopping warfarin (with vitamin K1, artificial liver support, and antioxidant/anti-inflammatory liver therapy) improved the elevated liver enzymes and hyperbilirubinemia. The discussion refers to 'warfarin-induced liver failure' and notes that warfarin-induced acute liver injury has rarely been reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 64-year-old woman after mechanical mitral valve replacement on warfarin 4.5 mg daily for about 10 years. Presented with ecchymosis and black stool; INR exceeded 10.0 and rose to 3.48; elevated ALT, AST, total/direct/indirect bilirubin, and total bile acids. Injury improved after warfarin discontinuation with vitamin K1, glutathione, polyene phosphatidylcholine, ademetionine 1,4-butanedisulfonate, ursodeoxycholic acid, and artificial liver support; patient transferred to ICU. Warfarin was restarted (2.5-3.75 mg qd) with no significant enzyme/bilirubin elevation, and the patient discharged on day 24. Authors note warfarin-induced acute liver injury is rarely reported and recommend timely warfarin discontinuation and INR adjustment to reduce warfarin-induced liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present the case of a patient with Stevens-Johnson syndrome and severe liver injury in which warfarin was confirmed as the culprit drug; they report this as the first case of warfarin-induced SJS/TEN in an adult. Using the RUCAM score they confirmed the diagnosis of warfarin-induced DILI, and the MELD score verified seriously impaired liver function.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adult patient with concurrent SJS/TEN; reported as the first adult case of warfarin-induced SJS/TEN.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe liver injury with significantly elevated transaminase values. Diagnosis of warfarin-induced DILI confirmed with the RUCAM score; the MELD score was applied to evaluate the degree of liver injury and verified seriously impaired liver function. Warfarin causality for SJS/TEN was also confirmed by ALDEN score and IFN-γ ELISPOT assay, and its discontinuation was essential for patient recovery. The authors note that in a retrospective study of 748 patients with DILI, only 36 (4.8%) presented with both SJS/TEN and DILI, with a higher mortality rate of 22%, though this does not specifically attribute those cases to warfarin.

raw_record.support_text: Trabectedin was also administered at 0.3-1.9 mg/m²/cycle divided over 5 days every 21 days in a study of 42 patients, with MTD of 1.625 mg/m² over 5 days. Transient hepatotoxicity was seen, but the dose-limiting toxicity was neutropenia, thought to be due to delayed drug clearance from dose accumulation on day 5.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-agent Phase I study of trabectedin given daily 1-h infusion over 5 days (0.3-1.9 mg/m²/cycle) every 21 days in 42 patients; MTD 1.625 mg/m² over 5 days; transient hepatotoxicity observed but DLT was neutropenia attributed to delayed clearance due to dose accumulation on day 5; objective responses in three leiomyosarcoma and two ovarian cancer patients.

raw_record.support_text: In a pharmacogenomic patient cohort treated with trabectedin, the ABCG2 intron 1 promoter variant rs7699188 was associated with hepatotoxicity: 30% of patients were heterozygous, 63.2% of them had a severe increase of AST/ALT, and T allele carriers had a 3.4-fold enhanced risk of toxic cytolysis when treated with trabectedin (p=0.034). The surrounding text likewise refers to trabectedin-related liver toxicity and overall hepatotoxicity as an outcome of trabectedin treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Pharmacogenomic cohort of trabectedin-treated patients; hepatotoxicity manifested as toxic cytolysis with severe AST/ALT increase. Genetic modifiers: ABCB1 rs2032582 (c.2677G>T, A) associated with lower risk of overall hepatotoxicity (p=0.027, OR=0.22 (0.05-0.91)); ABCC3 rs2072365 (p=0.003, OR=5.92) and rs4148415 increased overall hepatotoxicity risk, especially severe cytolysis (p=0.046, OR=2.99); ABCC4 rs9516519 decreased overall hepatotoxicity (p=0.048, OR=0.31); ABCG2 rs7699188 T allele increased toxic cytolysis risk 3.4-fold. Functional biliary transporters (P-gp, MRP2, MRP3, MRP4, BCRP) implicated in trabectedin elimination.

raw_record.support_text: In a clinical trial, combination therapy with dexamethasone, a known inducer of CYP-enzymes, increased hepatic clearance and reduced hepatotoxicity of ET-743 (trabectedin), indicating that ET-743 produces hepatotoxicity in treated patients that is modulated by dexamethasone.
raw_record.extra_details: ET-743 is an anti-cancer agent (trabectedin). In a clinical trial, combination therapy with dexamethasone (a CYP-enzyme inducer) increased hepatic clearance and reduced hepatotoxicity of ET-743. Main paper content concerns in vitro CYP-mediated biotransformation (CYP3A4 as major isozyme, ~95% contribution; minor roles of CYP2C9, 2E1, 2D6, 2C19), which is mechanistic/preclinical and does not by itself establish a human DILI relationship.

raw_record.support_text: The combination of I3C and ET-743 is cited as an example where a chemopreventive is used with a chemotherapeutic regime to prevent unwanted side-effects without compromising antitumour efficacy. ET-743 has shown promising activity against sarcomas and mammary carcinomas in early clinical evaluation, but hepatotoxicity is described as a consistent unwanted side-effect of this agent.
raw_record.extra_details: Trabectedin (ET-743) is an investigational chemotherapeutic showing promising early clinical activity against sarcomas and mammary carcinomas; hepatotoxicity is described as a consistent unwanted side-effect. Related animal findings: I3C given with the diet was reported as a potent hepatoprotectant in rats given a hepatotoxic dose of ET-743, without compromising and possibly enhancing antitumour activity in a mammary carcinoma model; DIM did not appear protective in that rat system.

raw_record.support_text: The authors characterize trabectedin's safety profile, based on their long-term clinical experience and prior reports (RetrospectYon, TrObs, Y-IMAGE), as being associated with myelosuppression and hepatic toxicities; in this study over 40% of patients received ≥6 cycles and up to 44 cycles of trabectedin.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic toxicity is noted as a characteristic toxicity of trabectedin's safety profile alongside myelosuppression, supported by prior reports (RetrospectYon: 34.4%; TrObs: 36.5%; Y-IMAGE: 56.9% of patients received ≥6 cycles). The statement is presented without a named biochemical pattern, syndrome, or severity.

raw_record.support_text: In a phase II randomized trial of trabectedin in pretreated relapsed ovarian cancer, two treatment-related deaths occurred: one patient (arm A, 24-h 1.5 mg/m²) developed unrelated renal insufficiency and drug-related grade 3 hepatic toxicity (per laboratory data) before dying of acute myocardial infarction, and one patient (arm B, 3-h 1.3 mg/m²) died of multiorgan failure after presenting drug-related laboratory abnormalities including severe pancytopenia (febrile neutropenia, grade 4 thrombocytopenia, grade 3 anemia, grade 4 leukopenia) plus grade 3 toxic hepatitis. Hepatotoxicity was also listed as a trabectedin-related adverse event (grade 2 in 1 patient and grade 3 in 4 patients in arm A; grade 3 in 1 patient in arm B).
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II randomized trial in pretreated relapsed ovarian cancer; both schedules (arm A 1.5 mg/m² 24-h, arm B 1.3 mg/m² 3-h, every 3 weeks) attributed drug-related hepatic toxicity. Arm A case: drug-related grade 3 hepatic toxicity per laboratory data, death due to acute myocardial infarction (not liver). Arm B case: drug-related grade 3 toxic hepatitis as part of severe pancytopenia and multiorgan failure; death due to multiorgan failure. Hepatotoxicity adverse events (NCI-CTC v2.0): arm A grade 2 in 1 patient (2%) and grade 3 in 4 patients (7%); arm B grade 3 in 1 patient (2%). Related laboratory abnormalities: ALT grade 3/4 elevations (arm A 48%/7%; arm B 53%/6%), AST grade 3/4 and occasional bilirubin grade 3 were seen; AP only grade 1/2.

raw_record.support_text: Among 15 patients (23.4%) who experienced 25 adverse events leading to dose reduction, several liver-related events of grade 3 were reported (hepatitis, hepatotoxicity, and hypertransaminasaemia, each n=1). The text states that all these events, except pyrexia grade 2, were related to trabectedin treatment given at 1.5 mg/m2 BSA as a 24-h IV infusion every 3 weeks, and 10 (15.6%) patients had trabectedin withheld at least once.
raw_record.extra_details: Three separate grade 3 liver events attributed to trabectedin (hepatitis n=1, hepatotoxicity n=1, hypertransaminasaemia n=1) among 15 patients with 25 events leading to dose reduction; trabectedin withheld at least once in 10 (15.6%) patients. Dose: 1.5 mg/m2 BSA IV over 24 h every 3 weeks. Patients had prior chemotherapy (mostly anthracyclines, ifosfamide, docetaxel, gemcitabine, pazopanib).

raw_record.support_text: A 79-year-old male with radiation-induced sarcoma received trabectedin (1.5 mg/m² over 24 h, dose-reduced to 1.2 mg/m²). He developed progressive hepatic and renal failure during a 2-week hospitalization. Viral hepatitis and ischemic hepatitis were ruled out, ultrasounds showed no focal abnormality. Gastroenterology and nephrology consults concurred that his liver failure was most likely due to his trabectedin treatment. The patient died on Day 54 from irreversible hepatic and renal insufficiency, with causes of death ruled as fulminant hepatic failure and acute renal failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 79-year-old male; concurrent as-needed acetaminophen use; dose reduction from 1.5 to 1.2 mg/m² per product recommendations; concurrent acute renal failure requiring hemodialysis; liver biopsy not performed due to thrombocytopenia.
raw_record.extra_details: Trabectedin is an orphan chemotherapy for soft-tissue sarcoma used when patients are not candidates for ifosfamide or anthracyclines. Clinical trials report hematological and hepatic toxicities as dose-limiting; in trials trabectedin-induced hepatic failure is described as transient and reversible, with transaminase increases within 2-5 days, peaking days 5-9, resolving within 3-4 weeks. Laboratory findings included rising total bilirubin (2.4 on Day 39 to 12.0 mg/dL on Day 54), AST up to 1053 U/L, ALT up to 502 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 473 U/L. Death occurred Day 54.

raw_record.support_text: An early report of a phase II trial in patients with advanced soft tissue sarcomas described 3 toxicity-related deaths among 59 patients treated with 1500 µg/m² ET-743 (trabectedin) as a 24-h infusion; in two patients death was due to neutropenic fever, renal insufficiency and liver failure, and the third died of neutropenic sepsis with elevated creatine kinase. A statistical analysis identified intercycle elevations of alkaline phosphatase and AST, and elevated baseline bilirubin or alkaline phosphatase, as prognostic factors for multi-organ toxicity in subsequent cycles.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with advanced soft tissue sarcomas; 1500 µg/m² as a 24-h infusion every 3 weeks
raw_record.extra_details: 3 toxicity-related deaths in 59 patients; 2 attributed to neutropenic fever, renal insufficiency and liver failure; a fourth patient later died of multi-organ toxicity; protocol amended to require normal bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase at entry and dose reduction to 1200 µg/m² for intercycle elevations, which improved safety.

raw_record.support_text: In the ATREUS trial safety population, hepatotoxicity (hepatobiliary disorders) was the most frequent adverse event attributable to trabectedin therapy, occurring at any grade in 127 of 132 patients (96.2%), including 78 patients (59.1%) with grade 3 or 4 hepatotoxicity (17 G1, 32 G2, 71 G3, 7 G4). At the 1.3 mg/m2 trabectedin starting dose, grade 3-4 hepatotoxicity occurred in 59 of 84 patients (70.2%), and no grade 4 events occurred at the 1.1 mg/m2 dose (19/48, 39.6% G3).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with unresectable malignant pleural mesothelioma (epithelioid and nonepithelioid); trabectedin given as single agent at starting doses of 1.3 or 1.1 mg/m2 in the ATREUS trial.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatotoxicity was reported in 70% of patients treated at 1.3 mg/m2 and in 40% at the lower 1.1 mg/m2 dose. The observed relevant liver toxicity, together with a small survival benefit, precluded additional development of trabectedin in MPM as a single agent at the investigated schedule. One toxic death due to multiorgan failure occurred in the trial.

raw_record.support_text: Iprindole (Prondol) is a commonly used antidepressant. The authors report two patients treated with iprindole for depression who developed a hepatic reaction, with liver biopsies (light and electron microscopy) in one, plus 19 other patients who had a hepatic reaction to iprindole; the summary states that 21 such patients developed evidence of liver damage (15 jaundiced, five with bilirubinuria, one with pruritus) between 4 and 21 days after first drug exposure, and all recovered.
raw_record.extra_details: Antidepressant taken at 15 mg three times daily. Latency of hepatic reaction 4-21 days after initial exposure. Of 21 patients: 15 jaundiced, 5 bilirubinuria, 1 pruritus; all recovered. Liver biopsy of one patient (Case 1, a 36-year-old woman) showed cholestasis without inflammation on light and electron microscopy, with elevated total bilirubin (7.6 mg/100 ml at 8 weeks), alkaline phosphatase and aspartate transaminase; pruritus of the patient was managed with cholestyramine. Jaundice was associated with pruritus, dark urine, and pale stools; hepatitis-associated antigen absent.

raw_record.support_text: A 35-year-old housewife treated with iprindol 15 mg three times daily developed jaundice eleven days after starting the drug; jaundice cleared on stopping but recurred after only three tablets when she restarted. Liver-function tests confirmed hepatocellular damage (serum bilirubin 3.8 mg/100 ml, alkaline phosphatase 30 K.A. units/100 ml, S.G.P.T. 124 units/ml) and 30% of her 6,000/mm³ white cells were eosinophils; recovery was rapid and liver-function tests were normal a week later. The case is presented as iprindol-associated hepatotoxicity with an allergic (eosinophilic) feature.
raw_record.extra_details: Tricyclic antidepressant (trade name Prondol). Administered at 15 mg three times daily for a depressive illness (indication). Jaundice first occurred after 11 days of treatment and recurred within 24 hours of rechallenge after only three tablets; recovery was rapid after dechallenge with normal liver-function tests within a week. Laboratory values: bilirubin 3.8 mg/100 ml, alkaline phosphatase 30 K.A. units/100 ml, S.G.P.T. 124 units/ml; eosinophilia of 30% (total white cell count 6,000/mm³) that fell to 2% on recovery. No personal or family history of allergy. The authors frame the mechanism as allergic (hypersensitivity) though this was questioned in correspondence.

The summary reports that CyA was effective in inhibiting rejection but that there was clear evidence of both nephrotoxicity and hepatotoxicity; a cyclophosphamide analogue was added to CyA in six of the patients.

raw_record.extra_details: Prospective pilot study of 7 patients with first cadaveric renal allografts from mismatched donors; CyA dosed 25 mg/kg, given intramuscularly in 'Miglyol' for the first 2-3 days then orally in olive oil (changed to Sandoz capsules in two cases in the third postoperative month); liver and renal function carefully monitored postoperatively. Hepatotoxicity was reported in addition to nephrotoxicity. Outcome: five patients out of hospital with functioning allografts, one allograft nephrectomy for pyelonephritis, one death from systemic aspergillus and candida infection.

raw_record.support_text: Calne in 1978 first introduced cyclosporin A (CyA) in seven patients with renal failure receiving transplants from mismatched cadaver donors. CyA was used initially as the sole immunosuppressive agent; it was effective in inhibiting rejection, but there was clear evidence of both nephrotoxicity and hepatotoxicity. The initial administered dose of CyA was 17 mg/kg and no therapeutic drug monitoring was used.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Renal transplant recipients with renal failure receiving cadaver-donor allografts; CyA given as the sole immunosuppressive agent; no therapeutic drug monitoring; initial dose 17 mg/kg.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported by Calne in 1978 as the first use of CyA in humans; hepatotoxicity accompanied nephrotoxicity; mentioned as evidence that further careful study of the drug would be required before clinical recommendation.

raw_record.support_text: A 42-year-old renal transplant patient was jaundiced with elevated bilirubin (4.5 mg/dl) and liver enzyme abnormalities (AST 50, ALT 335, GGT 132, LDH 492 IU/l); serum cyclosporine (CyA) measured by whole blood RIA was markedly elevated at 1905 ng/ml (normal 250–800 ng/ml), and a diagnosis of CyA hepatotoxicity was made. The CyA dose was reduced, and the liver enzyme abnormalities improved slightly; liver enzyme levels later normalized.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Supratherapeutic cyclosporine trough level (1905 ng/ml vs normal 250–800 ng/ml); complex post-transplant course with competing/relevant conditions including acute rejection, hemolytic uremic syndrome and infection; liver enzyme abnormalities improved slightly after dose reduction and later normalized (dechallenge).
raw_record.extra_details: Jaundice with bilirubin 4.5 mg/dl; liver enzymes AST 50, ALT 335, GGT 132, LDH 492 IU/l; CyA level by whole blood RIA; creatinine 1.4 mg/dl. Dechallenge (CyA dose reduction) produced slight improvement with eventual normalization of liver enzymes along with other therapy (steroids, fresh frozen plasma, HUS management).

raw_record.support_text: Among 81 patients with fulminant hepatitis, 11 (14%) were classified as fulminant drug-induced hepatitis. The cause was attributed to mercazole in 1 case.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed cause of fulminant drug-induced hepatitis in 1 of 11 drug-induced cases in a Japanese cohort (1980-1999).

raw_record.support_text: Thiamazole was among the top 10 drugs involved in LA DILI Registry cases, with n = 4 cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Among the top 10 drugs in the LA DILI Registry, n=4 cases.

raw_record.support_text: Thiamazole is listed among the main 10 drugs leading the Latin American DILI Registry with n = 4 cases, with RUCAM-based causality assessment.
raw_record.extra_details: 4 cases in the Latin American DILI Registry; RUCAM-based causality assessment used.

raw_record.support_text: The background states that liver injury is a side effect of antithyroid drug treatment, and cites a study of drug-induced liver injury across 308 medical centers in China in which methimazole accounted for one among 72 death cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as a side effect of standard first-line antithyroid therapy. Evidence: methimazole accounted for one among 72 death cases in a DILI study covering 308 medical centers in China (Shen et al., 2019). As a mechanism note, the cytotoxic intermediate glyoxal from methimazole metabolism may induce oxidative stress and cell dysfunction.

raw_record.support_text: In this DILI cohort, the 118 other-DILI patients included 65 cases mainly induced by Chinese herbal medicines and 53 by Western medicines. The top 6 causative agents in the other-DILI group were antibiotics (18), Radix Bupleuri (16), statins (11), Fructus Psoraleae (10), Cortex Dictamni (8), and methimazole (4). Methimazole was therefore one of the agents to which DILI cases in this group were attributed.
raw_record.extra_details: Methimazole accounted for 4 of 118 other-DILI cases in the study cohort; the other-DILI group consisted mostly of cases induced by Chinese herbal medicines (65) and Western medicines (53). DILI was diagnosed in recruited patients classified by injury type (hepatocellular, cholestatic, mixed) and RUCAM scoring; the paper lists methimazole among the top 6 causative agents of the other-DILI group.

raw_record.support_text: The authors highlight that their case also involved an uncommon event, toxic hepatitis due to methimazole (hepatitis tóxica por metimazol). Adverse reactions to antithyroid drugs occur in fewer than 10% of cases and are generally minor (skin rash, arthralgia).
raw_record.extra_details: Case report; the patient improved rapidly after methimazole was discontinued (dechallenge) but developed a cross-reaction when substituted with propylthiouracil, ultimately requiring definitive treatment with radioiodine. In this case the injury presented as dissociated cholestasis (colestasis disociada). The paper states major antithyroid-drug side effects are rare and include agranulocytosis (0.2-0.5%), vasculitis, lupus-like syndrome and hepatotoxicity, generally cholestatic and resolving upon drug withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that, in a Graves disease patient, physical/laboratory evaluation showed liver dysfunction (total bilirubin 26.4 µmol/L, direct bilirubin 10.7 µmol/L, AST 166 IU/L, ALT 226 IU/L, ALP 143 IU/L) with viral hepatitis A-E and other hepadnavirus infections excluded, and the authors reached a diagnosis of acute agranulocytosis and hepatotoxicity attributed to the use of methimazole (MMI). The patient was treated with the hepatoprotective drug reduced glutathione, and liver function recovered to normal range by day 11-14.
raw_record.extra_details: Graves disease patient case report. Hepatotoxicity onset within 6 days of starting MMI (total dose 120 mg, reported to be first reported case of agranulocytosis along with hepatotoxicity within 6 days in an MMI-treated Graves patient). Labs: total bilirubin 26.4 µmol/L (6-20.5), direct bilirubin 10.7 µmol/L (0-7.8), AST 166 IU/L (5-40), ALT 226 IU/L (10-42), ALP 143 IU/L (30-290). Viral hepatitis A/B/C/E and Epstein-Barr, Cytomegalovirus, Varicella zoster, and simple herpes virus excluded; p-ANCA and c-ANCA negative; serum showed polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (elevated IgG 24.23 g/L and IgE 2.87 g/L). Hepatic recovery to normal after treatment with hepatoprotective drug (reduced glutathione); concurrent acute agranulocytosis; ultrasonograph showed normal liver.

raw_record.support_text: A single-patient case report attributes cholestatic DILI to methimazole. The patient presented with signs and symptoms of cholestatic disease with concern for obstructive biliary pathology; malignancy, autoimmune, and infectious etiologies were ruled out, and choledochoscopy showed normal bile duct mucosa. The R-value at symptom onset was 0.64 (cholestatic pattern), the RUCAM score was 8 points, and the temporal relationship between methimazole initiation and symptom onset, together with improvement in symptoms and a downward trend in liver function tests after methimazole discontinuation, argued in favor of DILI. Six months after discontinuation the LFTs remained normal and the patient was symptom-free.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of cholestatic DILI presenting like hepatobiliary obstruction. R-value 0.64 at symptom onset (cholestatic pattern); RUCAM score 8. Endoscopy showed a CBD stricture with distal narrowing and proximal dilation up to 14 mm; sphincterotomy/stenting initially performed; choledochoscopy spyglass showed normal bile duct mucosa within the narrowing; cytology negative for malignancy; autoimmune and infectious etiologies ruled out. Dechallenge: symptoms and LFTs improved after methimazole discontinuation, CBD stent later removed; LFTs remained normal and patient symptom-free 6 months later. Phenotype is cholestatic liver injury mimicking obstructive biliary pathology.

raw_record.support_text: In the comparison table of clinical cases of propylthiouracil-induced interstitial pneumonia, Patient 1 (Miyazono et al., 1984) had previous treatment with methimazole and is recorded as having 'Methimazole side effects: Hepatotoxicity', indicating that this patient experienced methimazole-attributed hepatotoxicity that necessitated switching to PTU.
raw_record.extra_details: Recorded as a 'Methimazole side effect' (hepatotoxicity) in Patient 1 (Asian, male, age 75), attributed in the comparison table; the patient had prior methimazole treatment before being switched to PTU. The paper's primary focus is PTU-induced interstitial pneumonia.

raw_record.support_text: A 28-year-old woman with Graves-Basedow hyperthyroidism was treated with methimazole 30 mg/day and propranolol 40 mg. Within days she developed asthenia, anorexia, nausea and mucocutaneous jaundice, with elevated liver enzymes and hyperbilirubinemia. Liver biopsy showed a well-structured parenchyma with mild cholestasis without apparent histolysis. After ruling out an alcoholic, viral or autoimmune cause, she was diagnosed with toxic hepatitis secondary to methimazole, and use of any thionamide for her hyperthyroidism was contraindicated. The patient's hyperthyroid symptoms recovered within a few days of discontinuing methimazole.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 28-year-old woman; indication Graves-Basedow hyperthyroidism; methimazole 30 mg/day with propranolol 40 mg. Symptoms asthenia, anorexia, nausea, mucocutaneous icterus; elevated liver enzymes and hyperbilirubinemia; liver biopsy showed mild cholestasis without histolysis; alcoholic, viral and autoimmune causes excluded; reversible after drug withdrawal; article notes that antithyroid drug toxic hepatitis can be cytolytic, cholestatic or mixed and that fulminant hepatitis may develop if drug not withdrawn early; any thionamide contraindicated in this patient.

raw_record.support_text: The admitting diagnosis was methimazole-induced hepatitis, and use of the drug was stopped immediately. Despite stopping, the patient's total serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase continued to rise; prednisone therapy (up to 30 mg/day for four weeks) was tried without improvement. Surgical exploration showed a normal biliary system, and open liver biopsy showed cholestasis compatible with drug-induced hepatitis; the jaundice then receded and liver-function tests returned to normal by June 28, 1971.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report. Patient presented with deep jaundice; admission serum total bilirubin 13.6 mg/100 ml (direct 9.2), alkaline phosphatase 270 IµU/ml, with low/normal transaminases (SGOT 30). Total bilirubin rose to a peak of 31.0 mg/100 ml on 6/2 with direct 16.5. Liver biopsy showed marked cholestasis (dilated bile ducts with bile casts). Prednisone (max 30 mg/day for four weeks) was tried without improvement. Laparotomy revealed normal biliary system; open biopsy showed cholestasis compatible with drug-induced hepatitis. Jaundice receded after drug discontinuation and liver tests returned to normal by 6/28/1971. Causal wording uses 'methimazole-induced hepatitis' diagnosis with dechallenge recovery.

raw_record.support_text: The patient, a 67-year-old woman with Graves' disease, was started on methimazole (and propranolol), and she developed fulminant hepatitis, which after extensive workup was determined to be due to the methimazole. Methimazole was withdrawn, and the patient's liver tests had been elevated precipitably at presentation.
raw_record.extra_details: Methimazole was given at 40 mg twice daily for Graves' thyrotoxicosis. LFTs elevated precipitously with features of fulminant hepatitis, and causality was determined after extensive workup. Methimazole was stopped. The patient was subsequently deemed unsuitable for thyroidectomy or radioactive iodine ablation.

raw_record.support_text: Among 171 patients with drug-induced liver injury and liver failure, methimazole accounted for 1.2% of the 'other drugs' cases. Methimazole was attributed as a causal drug in these DILI cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective cohort in Southwest China; methimazole accounted for 1.2% of 171 DILI-associated liver-failure cases; DILI defined as any hepatotoxic drug within 6 months before onset.

raw_record.support_text: In a patient suffering from methimazole hepatitis, peroxisomes showed a preferential localization around the cell nucleus (De Craemer et al 1991a). The passage attributes the patient's hepatitis to methimazole.
raw_record.extra_details: Portion of a review on hepatic ultrastructure; report (De Craemer et al 1991a) described peroxisomes localized around the cell nucleus in a methimazole hepatitis patient.

raw_record.support_text: Methimazole (MMI), the first-line agent for hyperthyroidism, is generally well tolerated but may rarely cause severe hepatotoxicity such as cholestatic jaundice; the authors describe a 49-year-old woman with Graves' disease who developed MMI-induced severe cholestatic jaundice, treated with therapeutic plasma exchange and other supportive measures.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient was a 49-year-old woman with Graves' disease and type 2 diabetes; MMI prescribed at 20 mg/day for hyperthyroidism and discontinued after 3 weeks due to generalized icterus. Presented with worsening jaundice for 2 months; initial evaluation at another hospital revealed hyperthyroidism with acute liver failure, with elevated total bilirubin (322.4 umol/L), direct bilirubin (289.9 umol/L), and alkaline phosphatase (235 U/L). Treatment included ursodeoxycholic acid, ademetionine infusions, therapeutic plasma exchange (3 sessions of 1.5 plasma volumes replaced with 5% albumin), about 3 months of glucocorticoid therapy, and insulin; radioactive iodine ablation plan was dropped and she was started on levothyroxine.

raw_record.support_text: Among patients with Graves' disease treated with methimazole (alone or combined with T₄), 2 patients developed drug-induced hepatitis—1 was severe and the other showed only increasing liver enzymes—and 2 patients dropped out of the study because of hepatitis. Drug reactions were otherwise mostly non-severe (rash/itching, joint or muscle discomfort, metallic taste, gastrointestinal complaints, jaw pain, and 1 case of agranulocytosis).
raw_record.extra_details: Reported drug-induced hepatitis in 2 patients during methimazole treatment for Graves' disease: 1 case was described as severe and the other as increasing liver enzymes only; 2 patients withdrew from the study because of hepatitis. Methimazole was administered daily (7.2–30 mg/day at 18 months) either alone (group 1) or combined with levothyroxine (groups A and B).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that both carbimazole/methimazole (CMZ/MMI) and propylthiouracil carry a risk of mild liver dysfunction in which liver transaminases are elevated to within twice the normal range. A recent Japan study in 476 patients with Graves' disease reported a prevalence of drug-induced liver injury of 1.4% with methimazole (MMI) and a prevalence of the most severe liver injury of 0.08%, with a median time to the development of liver injury of 30 days and all patients recovering.
raw_record.extra_details: Paper presents methimazole and carbimazole as a combined entity (CMZ/MMI). Mild liver dysfunction with transaminases within twice normal. Traditionally associated with cholestatic jaundice; recent studies suggest additional hepatocellular toxicity of varying severity. Taiwan health insurance database (71,379 patients): dose-dependent association with a hepatitis-like picture within the first 30 days, incidence 3.17/1000 person-years (CMZ/MMI) vs 1.19/1000 (PTU); liver failure incidence 0.32/1000 vs 0.68/1000 person-years for PTU. China retrospective analysis of 90 cases of antithyroid drug-induced severe hepatotoxicity over 13 years: severe hepatotoxicity within 90 days, equal frequency for CMZ/MMI and PTU. Japan study (476 Graves' patients): DILI prevalence 1.4%, most severe liver injury 0.08%, median 30 days, no fatalities. Table 3 frequencies: hepatocellular toxicity 0.03-0.08%, cholestatic jaundice 0.02%.

raw_record.support_text: The discussion states that methimazole (MMI) can induce cholestatic hepatitis after drug exposure ranging from 2 days to 3 months, and lists liver injury among MMI-related adverse events, including rashes, urticaria, arthralgias, vasculitis. A Taiwan study of 71,379 hyperthyroid patients reported ATD-induced hepatitis incidence of 3.17/1000 person-years with MMI/carbimazole and a 5.08-fold increased hepatitis risk with high-dose MMI/carbimazole compared with any PTU use; FDA data report that of 5 adult MMI patients who developed acute liver failure, 3 died.
raw_record.extra_details: MMI can induce cholestatic hepatitis with latency 2 days to 3 months; Taiwan cohort hepatitis incidence 3.17/1000 person-years for MMI/carbimazole (CBM) and 5.08-fold increased risk of hepatitis with high-dose MMI/CBM relative to any PTU use; FDA report: of 5 adult MMI patients who developed ALF, 3 died; MMI-related AEs include rashes, urticaria, arthralgias, vasculitis, and liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of patients diagnosed with ATD-induced severe hepatotoxicity, 51 patients were being treated with methimazole (MMI) at diagnosis, with a mean MMI dose of 19.1±7.4 mg/d at the onset of severe hepatotoxicity. The attributed injury showed hepatocellular, cholestatic, and mixed patterns in 43.1%, 35.3%, and 21.6% of MMI patients, respectively.
raw_record.extra_details: Antithyroid drug (ATD) treated hyperthyroidism patients in China; MMI more commonly used than PTU (65.7% overall). Severe hepatotoxicity occurred within 4, 8, and 12 weeks in 63.3%, 75.6%, and 81.1% of patients across both groups; 17 patients developed it after 12 weeks and 5 patients after >1 year (mostly with re-exposure or dose change). Female:male ratio 2.2:1; mean age 41.6±12.5 years.

raw_record.support_text: Drug-induced liver injury is a frequent adverse event associated with antithyroid drugs, and numerous cases of drug-induced liver injury attributed to methimazole have been documented. A retrospective analysis of 71,379 patients treated with antithyroid medications in Taiwan (2004-2008) reported that the incidence of DILI caused by methimazole was higher than that of propylthiouracil and correlated with the dose of methimazole, with occurrence of acute hepatic necrosis and cholestasis similar to propylthiouracil. Although most patients have mild hepatic impairment, a minority may develop life-threatening conditions due to severe liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective analysis by Wang et al of 71,379 patients treated with antithyroid medications in Taiwan from 2004 to 2008; incidence of DILI was higher than for propylthiouracil and correlated with methimazole dose; occurrence of acute hepatic necrosis and cholestasis similar to propylthiouracil. Majority of patients have mild hepatic impairment; a minority may develop life-threatening severe liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: In an institutional case series, five cases of medically refractory severe cholestatic DILI were identified, defined by persistent serum bilirubin >20 mg/dL. Hepatotoxic medications included phentermine, methimazole, OxyElite, and two cases of the anabolic steroid methyl-1-etiocholenololepietiocholanolone. Cholestatic DILI was defined as ALP greater than two times the upper limit of normal secondary to a drug exposure known to cause intrahepatic cholestasis.
raw_record.extra_details: One case of severe cholestatic DILI (persistent bilirubin >20 mg/dL, ALP >2x ULN, >345 U/L) treated with 5 sessions of 8-hour MARS albumin dialysis; patient recovered with normalization of liver tests at outpatient follow-up. No hepatic encephalopathy or extrahepatic organ dysfunction; INR remained <2.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a 27-year-old female with Graves' disease prescribed methimazole at 20 mg/day who developed severe pruritus with cholestatic jaundice 13 days after starting the drug. Concomitant causes of liver disease were ruled out; after methimazole was discontinued, pruritus and jaundice resolved and liver function normalized after about 2 years. The case is described as methimazole-induced cholestatic jaundice, a rare yet severe adverse effect.
raw_record.extra_details: Methimazole dose 20 mg/day for Graves' disease (with propranolol 120 mg/day). Onset of pruritus and jaundice 13 days after initiation. Lab findings: AST 95 U/L, ALT 117 U/L, GGT 103 U/L, ALP 759 U/L, total/direct bilirubin 412/400 µmol/L (predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinemia). Etiologic workup (viral serologies, immunology, Bili-MRI) negative; liver biopsy showed portal/periportal fibrosis with lymphocytic and plasmocytic infiltrate and interface hepatitis, compatible with autoimmune hepatitis or drug-induced liver injury. Dechallenge with gradual resolution; treated with ursodeoxycholic acid 13 mg/kg/day and prednisone 1 mg/kg/day; liver tests normalized by January 2023 (~2 years). Authors note hypersensitivity/allergic reaction as the most widely accepted mechanism, and a potential hepatotoxic metabolite or oxidant/antioxidant imbalance hypotheses. Hepatotoxicity from antithyroid drugs reported to occur in approximately 0.1-0.2% of patients, with female predominance and a selective risk among Asian patients.

raw_record.support_text: An HLA study of 40 RUCAM-based cases of idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (iDILI) due to methimazole was described; docking studies indicated methimazole could bind indirectly to HLA, and the hapten hypothesis was proposed as the mechanism of HLA involvement.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM-based iDILI cases, n = 40; proposed mechanism: hapten hypothesis, indirect HLA binding, drug–peptide adducts presented to T cells; study citation [56].

raw_record.support_text: A 34-year-old female Filipino with Graves' disease on methimazole presented with fever, sore throat and jaundice and was initially diagnosed with methimazole-induced agranulocytosis and drug-induced liver injury. The Authors' abstract states the case presents 3 rare life-threatening complications of methimazole: agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia and hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: methimazole 20 mg three times daily for Graves' disease (hyperthyroidism); hepatitis and agranulocytosis appeared on approximately the 28th day of treatment. Liver tests showed total/direct/indirect bilirubin 6.90/4.03/2.86 mg/dL, ALT slightly elevated at 78 mg/dL (units reported as mg/dL), AST normal at 37; jaundice with icteric sclerae. Patient also developed aplastic anemia on day 4 of admission; treated with antibiotics, G-CSF, steroids, packed red blood cell, ursodeoxycholic acid and eltrombopag; discharged stable at 12th hospital day. Described as a rare life-threatening methimazole complication (hepatitis).

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that this is a case of concurrent occurrence of agranulocytosis and severe hepatotoxicity induced by methimazole (MMI) therapy after 4 weeks of treatment for hyperthyroidism. After discontinuing MMI and switching to hepatoprotective agents, antibiotics, and radioactive iodine (131I) ablation of the thyroid, the patient had a favorable prognosis. The authors describe ATD-induced agranulocytosis together with severe cholestatic hepatotoxicity as clinically significant adverse effects.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report in a hyperthyroid patient treated with MMI (antithyroid drug). Hepatotoxicity appeared after 4 weeks of therapy; patient presented with jaundice and sore throat, concurrent with agranulocytosis. After stopping MMI and using hepatoprotective agents and antibiotics, with 131I thyroid ablation, the patient had a favorable prognosis (recovery). The paper suggests a possible drug-related immune reaction as the mechanism, with hypersensitized lymphocytes producing cholestatic and neutrophil factors on antigen stimulation. Latency ~4 weeks.

raw_record.support_text: The authors investigated liver biopsy specimens from patients with hepatotoxicity due to five drugs, including methimazole (thiamazol outside the United States; 1-methylimidazole-2-thiol), among six patients with drug-induced hepatitis; methimazole is reported as the cause of the hepatotoxicity in its case(s). The abstract notes decreased catalase activity, peroxisomal proliferation, and surface density exceeding the upper control value in methimazole hepatitis livers.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as one of five drugs causing drug-induced hepatitis in six patients. Peroxisomal changes attributed in this case included decreased catalase activity, proliferation (number increased 1.5 to 4.2 times), and surface density exceeding the upper control value. Aliases: thiamazol; chemical name 1-methylimidazole-2-thiol.

raw_record.support_text: DILI-inducing antithyroids were methimazole and propylthiouracil; antithyroids accounted for 11 patients (2.59%) of DILI cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Antithyroid; antithyroids accounted for 11 patients (2.59%) of DILI cases.

raw_record.support_text: For methimazole, cholestasis can occur within a few weeks of initiation, with liver biopsy showing preserved hepatocellular architecture along with intracanalicular cholestasis and mild periportal inflammation. The adverse effects of methimazole are described as dose-related rather than idiosyncratic, with consequent liver injury generally not as severe or potentially life-threatening as with PTU.
raw_record.extra_details: Antithyroid thionamide; cholestasis can occur within a few weeks of therapy initiation with biopsy showing preserved hepatocellular architecture, intracanalicular cholestasis, and mild periportal inflammation; adverse effects are dose-related rather than idiosyncratic, with liver injury generally not as severe or life-threatening as PTU; the paper's Case 2 patient developed drug-induced liver injury on methimazole with marked hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin up to 23.9 mg/dL), mildly elevated AST/ALT (up to 80/114 IU/L), alkaline phosphatase up to 308 IU/L, and normal INR; recommended drug of choice except during the first trimester of pregnancy; even so patients can develop DILI and require vigilance for signs/symptoms of liver disease.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that since the introduction of methimazole in 1949 a total of 20 cases of cholestatic jaundice have been described, 13 of which were caused by methimazole. The present case report describes methimazole-induced cholestatic liver injury mimicking sclerosing cholangitis, where the etiology was proven by a clear chronological relationship and the lack of other causative factors.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of cholestatic liver injury mimicking sclerosing cholangitis (radiological picture of primary sclerosing cholangitis) during antithyroid therapy for hyperthyroidism. Etiology proven by clear chronological relationship and lack of other causative factors. Reported as a rare complication; a total of 13 prior cases of cholestatic jaundice caused by methimazole described in the literature since its introduction in 1949.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 14,271 patients treated with methimazole (MMI) for Graves' disease, severe DILI occurred in 198 patients (1.4%), with incidence 0.26% in male and 1.69% in female patients (females significantly higher, p<0.0001). Median MMI dose at DILI diagnosis was 15 mg/day (range 5-30 mg), median time to DILI was 25 days, and 93.9% had hepatocellular, 2.5% cholestatic, and 3.5% mixed type injury; 7 patients required hospitalization. There was no correlation between MMI dose and severity of liver injury.

Among the 40 MMI-DILI cases, women (57.5%) and cholestatic liver damage (50.0%) predominated, liver damage could occur from days to months after dosing, and RUCAM scored most cases (92.5%) as probably due to MMI rather than other factors.

raw_record.support_text: We report a case of hepatotoxicity induced by methimazole treatment in a 54-year-old hyperthyroid man treated with methimazole (30 mg/day). Fourteen days later he developed scleral icterus, dark urine, and right-upper-quadrant abdominal pain; laboratory tests and liver biopsy led to a diagnosis of cholestatic hepatitis secondary to methimazole usage. The drug was withdrawn, laboratory parameters returned to normal within five days, and the Naranjo probability scale indicated a probable relationship between hepatotoxicity and methimazole therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Indication of hyperthyroidism; antithyroid therapy in a 54-year-old male patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis (confirmed by liver biopsy) with scleral icterus, dark urine, and right-upper-quadrant pain. Dose 30 mg/day; onset 14 days after starting treatment. Methimazole withdrawn and cholestyramine, ursodeoxycholic acid, and chlorpheniramine administered; abdominal pain resolved and laboratory parameters returned to normal within five days. Naranjo probability scale indicated a probable causal relationship. Author conclusion: physicians should be aware of hepatotoxicity risk with methimazole.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity is described as the second major, occasionally lethal side effect of antithyroid drugs. In an analysis of 18,558 Japanese patients with Graves disease treated with antithyroid drugs, severe liver injury (ALT >8-fold or total bilirubin >3-fold the upper limit) was significantly higher in the PTU-treated group (6.3%) than in the methimazole (MMI)-treated group (1.4%). Median time to development of antithyroid-drug-induced hepatic injury was 30 (7-314) days with no deaths. Recent Taiwan and China data challenge the older concept of a more cholestatic injury pattern with MMI.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with Graves disease; no deaths reported in the cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe liver injury (ALT >8x ULN or total bilirubin >3x ULN) in 1.4% of MMI-treated patients vs 6.3% for PTU; median latency 30 (range 7-314) days; no deaths. Recent Taiwan and China data challenge the older concept of a predominantly cholestatic injury pattern with MMI.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 8864 patients treated at a department of nuclear medicine in China, 90 cases of ATD-induced severe hepatotoxicity were identified (incidence 1.0%). Methimazole (MMI) was one of the antithyroid drugs implicated in causing severe hepatotoxicity; one patient was diagnosed with MMI-induced severe cholestatic hepatotoxicity within 9 weeks of initiating 20 mg/d MMI and died one week after radioiodine therapy because of progressively worsening liver function and complications.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with Graves' disease treated for hyperthyroidism; female predominance; greater susceptibility in the 20-50 year age group.
raw_record.extra_details: Among 51 MMI patients, dose at onset of severe hepatotoxicity was 19.1±7.4 mg/d (range 5-30 mg/d). Mean treatment duration before severe hepatotoxicity was 9 weeks for MMI; more than 60% of patients developed severe hepatotoxicity within 4 weeks and more than 80% within 12 weeks. MMI-induced hepatotoxicity is generally considered a cholestatic process with preserved hepatocellular architecture, intracanalicular cholestasis and mild periportal inflammation; cholestatic type frequency was 35.3% in the MMI group. Hepatocellular, cholestatic, and mixed types occurred at approximately equivalent rates in the MMI and PTU groups.

raw_record.support_text: The present report describes a case of acute cholestatic hepatitis occurring in a 39-year-old woman after administration of venlafaxine. Liver biopsy showed cholestatic hepatitis predominantly involving zone 3 of the hepatic lobule with portal inflammation and abundant eosinophils. The clinical course rapidly improved after cessation of venlafaxine and administration of corticosteroid; liver toxicity recurred with a medium dose upon initiation of therapy and with increase of dosage after reinitiation of low-dose venlafaxine. The positive rechallenge clearly supports the association between venlafaxine and liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 39-year-old woman; liver biopsy (Nov 17, 2011) showed cholestatic hepatitis predominantly involving zone 3, perivenular feathery degenerated hepatocytes with cytoplasmic bile pigment, intrasinusoidal lymphocytes, activated Kupffer cells, occasional apoptotic bodies and single liver cell necrosis, portal lymphocytic infiltrate with eosinophils; no bile duct lesions or bile plugs. Diagnosed as venlafaxine-associated cholestatic hepatitis. Positive rechallenge: toxicity recurred with reinitiation of low-dose venlafaxine and dose increase; improved after cessation with methylprednisolone 50 mg/day tapering. Elevated AST 734 U/L, ALT 805 U/L, AP 167 U/L, γGT 102 U/L, bilirubin 11.2 mg/dL on readmission.

raw_record.support_text: A 78-year-old man treated for Parkinson disease and a prior depression episode presented on 15 April 1999 with icteric acute hepatitis. He had begun venlafaxine on 6 March at 37.5 mg/d, increased to 150 mg/d on 9 April, while continuing regular therapy. Admission showed elevated alanine aminotransferase (3.97 µkat/L), aspartate aminotransferase (4.36 µkat/L), γ-glutamyltransferase (12.17 µkat/L), alkaline phosphatase (11.33 µkat/L), total bilirubin (87 µmol/L) and direct bilirubin (86 µmol/L), with negative serology for hepatitis A, B, and C and normal abdominal ultrasonography.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient also had Parkinson disease treated with levodopa and pergolide and a prior major depression treated with electroconvulsive therapy, but the authors excluded all other possible causes of toxic hepatic injury. Venlafaxine was progressively discontinued while other therapy continued; liver function tests returned to normal within 5 weeks (dechallenge recovery). Authors concluded it is well justified to identify venlafaxine as the culprit in the acute liver toxic insult and supported monitoring of liver function in venlafaxine patients. Onset/report: venlafaxine started 6 March at 37.5 mg/d, increased to 150 mg/d on 9 April; presented 15 April 1999.

raw_record.support_text: A 27-year-old Chinese Han woman admitted for depression was diagnosed with hepatocellular acute liver injury (ALI) that was derived from venlafaxine-related adverse events, after abnormal serum liver function indices were observed. The RUCAM causality assessment score was 8 and the R value was 31.18.
raw_record.extra_details: 27-year-old Chinese Han female treated for depression; RUCAM causality score 8; R value 31.18; all medications were stopped and a hepatoprotective strategy with psychological treatment was given; liver function fully recovered as indicated by liver function indices and ultrasound imaging. All antidepressants may induce DILI even at low therapeutic doses.

raw_record.support_text: A 60-year-old woman taking 75 mg of venlafaxine daily for vasomotor symptoms presented one month after starting treatment with abdominal pain, an enlarged liver, and elevated liver enzymes (ALT 372 U/L, AST 99 U/L, GGT 962 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 758 U/L). After all potentially hepatotoxic medications including venlafaxine were stopped, liver function improved markedly; rechallenge at 37.5 mg produced renewed rises (ALT 269, AST 49, GGT 256, ALP 263 U/L) within six days, which resolved when venlafaxine was withdrawn. The authors concluded that an objective causality evaluation revealed a probable causal link between venlafaxine and the adverse effect, describing the hepatotoxic effects as rare and idiosyncratic.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of drug-induced hepatitis at low therapeutic dose: 60-year-old woman, 75 mg/day for vasomotor symptoms; onset ~1 month after start. Positive rechallenge: on rechallenge with 37.5 mg, elevated ALT (269), AST (49), GGT (256), ALP (263) U/L within 6 days. Initial labs: ALT 372, AST 99, GGT 962, ALP 758 U/L, enlarged liver, abdominal pain, nonspecific symptoms. Liver enzymes returned to normal after withdrawal. Hepatotoxicity characterized as rare and idiosyncratic; objective causality assessment deemed the reaction probably due to the drug.

raw_record.support_text: Among danazol-treated patients, one of two patients with severe side effects developed cholestatic hepatitis that led to definitive treatment withdrawal. The authors note these complications, although infrequent, mandate monitoring of liver function and periodic imaging surveillance for possible liver tumours during therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis occurred as a severe side effect in one danazol-treated patient with myelofibrosis with myeloid metaplasia (MMM) and anaemia, leading to definitive treatment withdrawal; authors recommend liver function monitoring and periodic imaging surveillance for possible liver tumours during therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A 73-year-old woman with idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura was switched from prednisone to danazol 600 mg/d because of iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome; before danazol there was no evidence of hepatic dysfunction.
raw_record.extra_details: After 4 weeks of danazol 600 mg/d, AST rose to 57 IU/L and ALT to 45 IU/L; ALP later rose to 619 IU/L and GGT to 553 IU/L while aminotransferases returned to normal. Transjugular liver biopsy 6 weeks after withdrawal showed intrahepatic cholestasis, Kupffer cell hyperplasia, portal and periportal lymphoplasmocytic infiltrate, and scattered fatty change. Pruritus occurred without jaundice; eosinophil count and bile ducts were normal; hepatitis A and B serologies negative; recovery within 3 months. Prior reports of danazol liver damage were mostly isolated transient ALP elevation, plus reports of jaundice, peliosis, and hepatocarcinoma.

raw_record.support_text: A 39-year-old woman taking danazol 400 mg/d for endometriosis developed allergic drug-induced hepatitis. Her ALT rose from a baseline of 9 IU/L to 125 IU/L; on admission AST was 54 IU/L, ALT 154 IU/L and alkaline phosphatase was normal. She was on no other medication. Danazol was suspected as the etiologic agent and discontinued, and the lymphocyte stimulation test (LST) was positive; AST/ALT returned to normal and symptoms resolved.
raw_record.extra_details: 39-year-old female with endometriosis; danazol 400 mg/d from April 8, 1985; ALT increased to 125 IU/L (June 11), then AST 54 IU/L and ALT 154 IU/L on July 29 admission with high fever and abdominal pain; hepatitis B surface antigen negative; eosinophils 0% and no rash; no other medication. Drug discontinued Aug 17; LST positive Aug 22; AST normalized and ALT decreased Aug 27; discharged Aug 29; AST and ALT normal Jan 9, 1986. Authors diagnosed allergic drug-induced hepatitis based on positive LST, although no rash or eosinophilia.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that the time course and histologic changes in a 73-year-old woman treated with danazol 600 mg/d for idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura are compatible with drug-induced liver damage caused by danazol, the only drug being taken at the time. Four weeks into therapy her aspartate aminotransferase rose to 57 IU/L and alanine aminotransferase to 45 IU/L; after drug withdrawal, alkaline phosphatase rose to 619 IU/L and gamma-glutamyltransferase to 553 IU/L, with normal aminotransferases, and a liver biopsy showed intrahepatic cholestasis, Kupffer cell hyperplasia, portal and periportal lymphoplasmocytic infiltrate, and scattered fatty change. Pruritus and laboratory abnormalities resolved within 3 months of withdrawal, with no jaundice.
raw_record.extra_details: Danazol 600 mg/d for idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura in a 73-year-old woman; prednisone had been replaced due to iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome, leaving danazol as the only drug. Initial hepatocellular enzyme rise at 4 weeks (AST 57 IU/L, normal <17; ALT 45 IU/L, normal <23) followed, after danazol withdrawal, by a cholestatic picture: alkaline phosphatase 619 IU/L (normal <190), gamma-glutamyltransferase 553 IU/L (normal <23), with normal aminotransferases, bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time, and no jaundice (pruritus present). Transjugular liver biopsy 6 weeks after withdrawal showed intrahepatic cholestasis, Kupffer cell hyperplasia, portal and periportal lymphoplasmocytic infiltrate, and scattered fatty change. Negative IgM anti-HAV and HBsAg and normal bile ducts on ultrasound excluded infection and obstruction; normal eosinophil count. Pruritus resolved within 2 weeks and liver enzymes normalized within 3 months; uneventful follow-up. Authors note prior reports of danazol liver damage consisting mostly of isolated transient ALP elevation, plus isolated reports of jaundice, peliosis, and hepatocarcinoma.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report that, to their knowledge, there are no published reports of losartan causing acute severe hepatotoxicity, but in their patient the temporal relationship, recurrence of abnormal liver function on reexposure, and improvement on discontinuation strongly suggest losartan was responsible, probably an idiosyncratic-type reaction. They suggest discontinuing losartan in patients who develop abnormal liver function test results while receiving the agent. The companion reply notes this was the first reported case of liver function abnormalities of this magnitude in a losartan-treated patient documented by rechallenge, with reversible test abnormalities after each discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Single described patient with abnormal liver function while on losartan; causality supported by temporal relationship, documented recurrence of abnormalities on rechallenge, and improvement/reversibility upon discontinuation of treatment. Context added by the pharmaceutical response: controlled clinical trials in nearly 3000 patients showed liver function abnormalities at a frequency comparable with placebo/control agents; the prescribing information notes occasional elevations of liver enzymes and/or serum bilirubin; ~80 reports of liver function abnormalities were received among an estimated 2 million losartan users over almost 3 years of marketing.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the seventh case of losartan-associated severe liver injury in a 61-year-old female. After two doses of losartan 100 mg on re-presentation, AST was 5,677 IU/L and ALT 4,137 IU/L (about 75-100 times the upper limit of normal), with hepatocellular injury evident by transaminase elevation about 30 times ULN without increased ALP or bilirubin. The Naranjo algorithm scored the event nine, indicated as 'definite cause' of acute liver injury; alternative causes such as viral hepatitis, acetaminophen toxicity, biliary blockage, sepsis, Wilson's disease, hemochromatosis, and autoimmune hepatitis were considered.
raw_record.extra_details: Authors' case: 61-year-old female, losartan 100 mg, initial injury ~16 days after start, re-exposure to two further 100 mg doses led to AST 5,677 IU/L and ALT 4,137 IU/L (75-100x ULN), highest enzyme elevation reported; Naranjo score 9 = 'definite cause' of acute liver injury; hepatocellular pattern with normal ALP/bilirubin; reported as seventh case of losartan-associated severe liver injury. Six prior losartan case reports (doses 50-150 mg, latency 3 weeks-5 months; AST 115-2,042 IU/L, ALT 272-2,547 IU/L); one prior case had re-exposure and biopsy. Differential diagnoses ruled out: viral hepatitis, acetaminophen toxicity, biliary obstruction, sepsis, Wilson disease, hemochromatosis, autoimmune hepatitis. Discussion notes liver injury may progress to need for liver transplantation, especially on re-exposure.

raw_record.support_text: A 46-year-old man developed acute severe hepatic injury (malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, low-grade fever, jaundice, tender hepatomegaly) while taking losartan, 50 mg/d, for hypertension. Laboratory evaluation showed markedly elevated aminotransferases (AST 2042 U/L, ALT 2574 U/L), alkaline phosphatase 738 U/L, and total bilirubin 164 µmol/L; serologic, viral, autoimmune, iron, and copper studies were negative. Injury resolved after losartan was discontinued and atenolol substituted. On rechallenge with losartan 25 mg/d, hepatotoxicity recurred within 3 weeks (mild jaundice, tender hepatomegaly; AST 206 U/L, ALT 254 U/L, total bilirubin 72 µmol/L), and liver tests normalized after losartan was again stopped. The case is presented under the heading 'Losartan-Induced Hepatotoxicity.'
raw_record.extra_details: Losartan 50 mg/d given for moderate essential hypertension after enalapril was stopped for cough. Initial episode: about 1 month of losartan exposure preceding admission, with 2-week symptom history; AST 2042 U/L, ALT 2574 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 738 U/L, GGT 266 U/L, total bilirubin 164 µmol/L (conjugated 152 µmol/L), moderately prolonged prothrombin time, normal eosinophil count; negative hepatitis A/B/C and other viral serologies, normal/negative iron, copper, and autoantibody tests. Dechallenge with atenolol substitution led to improvement (one month later AST 154 U/L, ALT 218 U/L, bilirubin 39 µmol/L) and full normalization 4 months after admission. Positive rechallenge with losartan 25 mg/d after atenolol was stopped produced recurrence within 3 weeks; losartan was then definitively discontinued and the liver profile normalized 1.5 months later.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that their patient had elevations in liver enzymes after losartan use which returned to normal after discontinuation, re-elevations after rechallenge, no evidence of other hepatic disorders, a biopsy consistent with hepatic damage, and normal liver tests during a 2-year follow-up, and that these data clearly demonstrate the existence of losartan-induced hepatic injury in this patient. The majority of drug-related reactions are described as idiosyncratic and unpredictable.
raw_record.extra_details: 52-year-old female treated with losartan 50 mg/d for 5 months; AST rose to 1,093 U/L, ALT 941 U/L, total bilirubin 8.9 mg/dL after rechallenge; liver biopsy showed chronic hepatitis with a mild-severe inflammatory response and mild fibrosis; enzymes normalized after discontinuation and rechallenge reproduced the injury; 2-year follow-up normal with recovery. A compiled table summarizes 5 reported cases of losartan-induced hepatic injury (additional prior cases from refs 7-9), all of whom improved.

raw_record.support_text: A 77-year-old man being treated for essential hypertension with losartan developed hepatocellular and renal damage. He had been prescribed losartan 50 mg/d but, due to a misunderstanding of directions, took 150 mg/d (50 mg three times a day). Six weeks later he presented with asthenia, anorexia, and weight loss; laboratory tests showed SCr 1.9 mg/dL, total bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL, AST 115 U/L, ALT 410 U/L, and GGT 89 U/L with normal alkaline phosphatase. Losartan was discontinued (other medications continued) and within one month his clinical condition and laboratory results returned to normal; rechallenge was not attempted.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 77-year-old man; actually took 150 mg/d (50 mg tid) due to misunderstanding of prescription, i.e., three times the prescribed 50 mg/d; concomitant ditazole 400 mg/d and almagate; no alcohol use; other medications continued during dechallenge; rechallenge not attempted for ethical reasons.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatocellular pattern with elevated AST 115 U/L, ALT 410 U/L, GGT 89 U/L, total bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL and normal alkaline phosphatase; transient ischemic attack context; renal damage also present (SCr rose from 0.9 to 1.9 mg/dL); viral (HAV, HBV, HCV, CMV, EBV) and autoimmune liver serology negative; symptoms asthenia, anorexia, 5-kg weight loss; recovered within 1 month after discontinuation and remained asymptomatic over 18 months; authors note two 1996 case reports of possible losartan (50 mg/d) hepatotoxicity and that elevation in ALT occurred at 1.9% incidence in controlled trials (not significantly different from placebo); authors conclude mechanism unlikely dose-related given 150 mg/d used in trials and, with absence of hypersensitivity, suggest a metabolic idiosyncrasy; losartan (angiotensin II antagonist) used for hypertension.

raw_record.support_text: Several hours after admission, the patient became hemodynamically unstable with hypotension and hypoglycemia, disorientation, and an ammonia level of 122 µmol/L. The working diagnosis was fulminant acute liver failure with multiorgan dysfunction secondary to staggered supratherapeutic niacin ingestion; investigations for other causes of liver failure (hepatitis screen, ceruloplasmin, autoimmune screen) were negative. She was placed on the liver transplantation list and treated with NAC, inotropes, and later CVVHDF.

raw_record.extra_details: Working diagnosis of fulminant acute liver failure with multiorgan dysfunction secondary to niacin. Biopsy showed subacute necrosis with loss of 90% of sampled hepatocytes; CT showed patchy perfusion. Peak ALT 14,300 U/L (day 1), total bilirubin 134 µmol/L, INR >10, ammonia 122 µmol/L. Other causes excluded (negative hepatitis, ceruloplasmin, autoimmune screens); LFTs one month earlier unremarkable. Treated with NAC infusion, ICU support, inotropes, broad-spectrum antibiotics (meropenem, anidulafungin) and six days of CVVHDF; liver function resolved on outpatient follow-up. Authors note dialysis did not significantly clear niacin.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports niacin-induced liver injury in humans, describing histopathologic features including necrosis, cholestasis, fibrosis, and hepatocyte vacuolization (Table 2), and presents a case of fatal anicteric acute liver failure with diffuse microvesicular hepatic steatosis due to ER or SR niacin, concluding this scenario may be underrecognized. Time-release (SR) niacin is linked to dose-dependent serum aminotransferase elevations in up to 52% of patients, typically with symptoms above 2 g/day and onset from as early as 2 days to months of exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Forms include immediate-release (IR), sustained-release (SR), extended-release (ER), and intramuscular (IM) niacin; time-release formulations have higher liver-injury potential, with dose-dependent aminotransferase elevations in up to 52% of SR users, symptoms usually above 2 g/day, latency from 2 days to months, and hepatotoxicity observed within days of switching from IR to SR. Reported histology includes necrosis, cholestasis (canalicular bile plugging), fibrosis, hepatocyte vacuolization, and microvesicular steatosis. Impaired hepatic synthesis may present with coagulopathy (clotting factor deficiency) and low serum albumin with minimal transaminase elevations. The described index case was fatal anicteric acute liver failure with microvesicular hepatic steatosis as the only pathologic finding (case received ~1.5 g/day ER niacin, lower than most reported ER/SR cases >2 g/day; underlying bullous pemphigoid, steroid use, and diabetes may have increased susceptibility). Schaffellner et al. case was a 22-year-old female on 20 g/day dead with panlobular parenchymal necrosis. Proposed mechanism involves mitochondrial redox (NAD/NADPH) imbalance and dose-dependent metabolism to an unknown toxic intermediate.

raw_record.support_text: Among six patients with drug-induced hepatitis, niacin was an inciting agent. Hepatocellular injury uncommonly complicates niacin use for hypercholesterolemia, manifesting as an acute hepatitis that rarely results in liver failure; all three niacin patients had panacinar hepatitis and cholestasis was present in two of three.
raw_record.extra_details: Used for hypercholesterolemia. All three niacin-induced hepatitis patients had panacinar hepatitis; cholestasis in two of three; HSC hyperplasia and histologic features of massive/submassive lobular collapse and cholestasis have been described. Hepatocellular injury rarely results in liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: The letter argues that the hepatotoxic potential of niacin has been understated and cites three human cases of niacin-induced hepatotoxicity: a 46-year-old man with clinical and biochemical hepatotoxicity on unmodified niacin 3 g/d for one month who, on rechallenge six weeks later, developed fulminant hepatic failure with stage 3 encephalopathy that resolved on discontinuation; a 32-year-old man taking SR niacin 500 mg/d for two months who developed acute liver failure with stage 4 encephalopathy and recovered on discontinuation; and a 44-year-old man on niacin 6 g/d who, three days after being switched to an SR formulation, developed fulminant hepatic failure and coma requiring liver transplantation. The letter concludes that severe hepatotoxicity occurs with both unmodified and sustained-release (SR) niacin.
raw_record.extra_details: Letter responding to an earlier DIAS Rounds column; argues SR niacin offers no adverse-effect profile advantage over unmodified niacin and that hepatotoxic potential is understated. Cases: (1) 46-year-old man, unmodified niacin 3 g/d for 1 month, clinical/biochemical hepatotoxicity; positive rechallenge 6 weeks later leading to fulminant hepatic failure with stage 3 encephalopathy, resolved on niacin discontinuation; (2) 32-year-old man, SR niacin 500 mg/d for 2 months, acute liver failure progressing to stage 4 encephalopathy, recovered on discontinuation; (3) 44-year-old man, niacin 6 g/d, fulminant hepatic failure and coma requiring liver transplantation, onset 3 days after switch to SR formulation. Both unmodified and SR niacin implicated.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes the development of hepatitis as an uncommon adverse effect of niacin that usually occurs only at doses above 3 g/day. Both cholestatic and hepatocellular reactions have been previously described, with liver biopsy findings of parenchymal necrosis and centrilobular cholestasis in the majority of patients. The authors also note prior reports of greater frequency and severity of hepatic toxicity with sustained-release (SR) niacin preparations compared with crystalline niacin, and they previously described three patients who developed hepatitis on SR-niacin but retained normal liver function when switched to R-niacin.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis usually occurs only at doses above 3 g/day, but in this series at least seven of eight hepatitis cases occurred in SR-niacin users, five of them at niacin doses of 1 to 2 g/day, below the dose generally considered hepatotoxic. Both cholestatic and hepatocellular reactions are described, with liver biopsy findings of parenchymal necrosis and centrilobular cholestasis in the majority of patients. Greater frequency and severity of hepatic toxicity has been suggested with SR preparations versus crystalline niacin; three prior patients developed hepatitis on SR-niacin but retained normal liver function on subsequent R-niacin. One additional patient developed hepatitis after switching to a different over-the-counter niacin brand, and an in vitro solubility test suggested that formulation was considerably less soluble than the previously used R-niacin.

raw_record.support_text: The case report attributes hepatocellular injury to niacin, documented by elevations of serum ALT, AST, and ferritin, with alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin not elevated, consistent with hepatocellular rather than cholestatic injury. The paper states niacin hepatitis may be cholestatic, hepatocellular, or mixed and usually resolves after cessation of therapy, and that the temporal sequence suggested improvement of laboratory values corresponded with cessation of niacin use; a confirmatory rechallenge was refused.
raw_record.extra_details: Daily niacin dose 3 gm for 120 months (10 years) before hepatitis onset, the longest reported such interval (prior longest 48, 31, and 30 months). Peak ALT 139 IU and AST 102 IU; ferritin elevated (peak 709 ng/ml on 5/18) then improved after niacin cessation (last use 5/7). Bilirubin 1.1 mg/dl, alkaline phosphatase not elevated. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, C, and HIV negative; no infectious mononucleosis. Transient elevations of ferritin and ALT noted 11 days after cessation. Niacin-associated thrombocytopenia (118,000/mm3) also reported; recovery after cessation. A confirmatory niacin rechallenge was refused by the patient.

raw_record.support_text: A 46-year-old man began taking nicotinic acid, 3 g daily, for hypercholesterolemia. A month later he developed clinical and biochemical evidence of modest hepatocellular injury and therapy was stopped; it was restarted 6 weeks later, and 10 weeks after that he presented with fulminant hepatic failure that resolved rapidly after cessation of nicotinic acid therapy. The authors suggest that nicotinic acid was the cause of his liver disease, noting the short period of therapy before onset and the severity of the hepatic failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Used for hypercholesterolemia at 3 g/day (1 g three times daily). First episode: modest hepatocellular injury, AST 428 IU/L, ALT 413 IU/L, total bilirubin 1.1 mg/dl, PT 14 s, with full normalization over 6 weeks after withdrawal. Rechallenge 6 weeks later led to fulminant hepatic failure with stage 3 encephalopathy about 10 weeks after restart, resolving after drug cessation. Viral etiologies (HBsAg, IgM anti-HAV, EBV, CMV) were negative. Paper notes both cholestatic and hepatocellular reactions have been described for nicotinic acid and general agreement that the mechanism is dose-related hepatotoxicity rather than hypersensitivity.

raw_record.support_text: Nicotinic acid is associated with flushing and pruritus, and liver toxicity is a well-recognized adverse effect of treatment at pharmacologic doses (1.5 to 6 g/day), reported as more common with slow-release than immediate-release (crystalline) nicotinic acid. In the current report, 3 cases of hepatic toxicity induced by treatment of dyslipidemia with crystalline nicotinic acid are described, characterized by signs of generalized synthetic dysfunction of the liver out of proportion to transaminase elevation, manifesting as a striking decrease in apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins and plasma LCAT, and in some cases increased prothrombin time and decreased serum albumin. In 2 of the 3 patients these changes occurred without hyperbilirubinemia and with normal or only mildly elevated transaminases.
raw_record.extra_details: Treatment for dyslipidemia with crystalline (immediate-release) nicotinic acid. Novel presentation of generalized hepatic synthetic dysfunction out of proportion to transaminase elevation: decreased plasma apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins and LCAT activity, increased prothrombin time and decreased serum albumin; in 2 of 3 patients without hyperbilirubinemia and with normal/mildly elevated transaminases. At 3.0 g/d, LCAT activity fell (Patient 1: 320 to 147; Patient 2: 355 to 151; Patient 3: 394 to 133 nmol/h/ml), AST/ALT rose mildly, and recovery of LCAT/transaminases followed dose reduction (1.5 g/d) or cessation. Liver toxicity noted as more common with slow-release than immediate-release nicotinic acid.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a series of patients who developed hepatitis attributed to niacin, particularly following a switch from regular-release (R) niacin to sustained-release (SR) niacin; hepatitis often developed within days or several weeks of the switch. The authors note the mechanism of niacin-induced hepatitis is unknown and speculate that prolonged enzyme-system exposure with SR preparations may lead to shorter recovery and more severe toxicity, and that a sudden R-to-SR switch may be particularly harmful.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis developed within days to several weeks of switching from R-niacin to SR-niacin; various commercial SR-niacin preparations were involved, making a contaminant unlikely; two affected patients were identical twin brothers and two others were sisters, suggesting a possible genetic susceptibility; use of SR-niacin without monitoring of liver function tests can lead to fulminant hepatitis. Mechanism of niacin-induced hepatitis unknown.

raw_record.support_text: A 44-year-old man with hypercholesterolemia taking crystalline nicotinic acid 6 g daily for over a year without side effects developed nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fever, dark urine and gingival bleeding 3 days after switching to sustained-release nicotinic acid (6 g daily). He progressed to fulminant hepatic failure with grade II hepatic encephalopathy progressing to coma, and required successful liver transplantation. The explanted liver showed massive hepatic necrosis with collapse of architecture and cholestasis.
