raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure with grade II hepatic encephalopathy progressing to coma despite 10% dextrose and lactulose; admission labs: serum bilirubin 168 µmol/L (direct 101 µmol/L), ALT 86.20 µkat/L, AST 103.22 µkat/L, alkaline phosphatase 6.42 µkat/L, LDH 31.77 µkat/L, albumin 37 g/L, prothrombin time 64.6 s (control 12.5 s), ammonia 149 µmol/L; bilirubin rose to 333 µmol/L; prothrombin time improved to 19.5 s with fresh frozen plasma and vitamin K; successful liver transplantation and discharge after 3 weeks; explanted liver weighed 890 g with massive hepatic necrosis, collapse, pigment-laden macrophages, prominent cholestasis and minimal fatty change; hepatitis B stains negative; the sustained-release preparation contained on average 950 mg nicotinic acid and 50 mg nicotinamide per 1-g tablet.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report four cases of niacin-induced hepatotoxicity in patients using sustained-release niacin preparations; symptoms and laboratory abnormalities resolved after the patients stopped taking niacin. Two patients had focal fatty infiltration of the liver on imaging, and one patient had a coagulopathy despite only mildly elevated aminotransferase levels. The authors recommend periodic liver-enzyme monitoring and discontinuation if abnormalities develop.

raw_record.extra_details: Four patients; all used sustained-release niacin preparations; symptoms and laboratory abnormalities resolved on discontinuation (dechallenge). Focal fatty infiltration of the liver seen on imaging in two patients, presented as a not previously described presentation of niacin hepatotoxicity. One patient had a coagulopathy despite only mildly elevated aminotransferases (prothrombin time 16.6 s, AST 86 U/L, ALT 86 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 136 U/L, total bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL, albumin 3.3 g/dL) and a factor VII deficiency attributed to liver disease. Niacin is a water-soluble B vitamin used for hyperlipidemia therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A life-threatening ADR, fulminant hepatic failure, has been reported with lamotrigine. A 22-year-old woman developed a maculopapular rash and hepatic failure; lamotrigine was stopped and liver function gradually improved after admission to hospital, but the patient died unexpectedly of a massive pulmonary embolus 2 months after admission. Biopsy confirmed a diagnosis of fulminant hepatic failure and, in the absence of other causes, it was concluded that the fulminant hepatic failure was due to lamotrigine.

raw_record.extra_details: Used for partial and generalized seizures and as adjunctive therapy in treatment-resistant pediatric epilepsy; 6 patients examined including 1 fulminant hepatic failure; onset 2-3 weeks; occasional extrahepatic features (rash, disseminated intravascular coagulopathy, rhabdomyolysis); histology of acute hepatic necrosis or focal hepatitis with mild portal inflammation; 4 recovered completely, 1 had mildly abnormal liver tests, 1 had normalized tests at death from pulmonary embolism; mechanism unclear—immune-mediated (RMS) or interactive toxicity with other antiepileptic drugs producing a toxic metabolite.

raw_record.support_text: It seems highly probable that in the reported patient, lamotrigine was the cause of a mixed liver injury, based on a close temporal relationship between first intake and onset of symptoms, rapid improvement of liver enzymes after lamotrigine withdrawal, and exclusion of alcohol, viral hepatitis, autoimmunity, and extrahepatic bile duct obstruction. Valproic acid was considered an unlikely cause because the patient had taken it for years without side effects.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All three cases, including the index patient, occurred when lamotrigine was added to chronic valproic acid (valproate) administration; valproate blocks lamotrigine elimination and may raise lamotrigine levels.
raw_record.extra_details: Index case: maculopapular rash, hyperthermia, headaches, diplopia, moderate creatinine kinase increase, laboratory signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation. Liver histology showed mild portal inflammation with scant eosinophils and hepatocyte clarification/microvesicular fatty infiltration; AST higher than ALT, suggestive of rhabdomyolysis; suggested immunoallergic rather than direct toxic mechanism. Two prior reported cases: a 22-year-old woman developed fulminant hepatic failure with acute hepatic necrosis three weeks after starting lamotrigine (liver function improved after withdrawal but she died of a massive pulmonary embolism two months later), and an 8-year-old boy developed acute cytolytic hepatitis three weeks after introduction with prompt enzyme decrease and uneventful recovery on withdrawal. Recommended maintenance dose 1-5 mg/kg/day with valproate, 5-15 mg/kg/day without; all three cases followed dose adaptation. Rechallenge should be avoided.

raw_record.support_text: An 8-year-old boy started lamotrigine for seizures and presented with fever, generalized maculopapular rash, facial edema, and enlarged lymph nodes; serum AST and ALT were twice normal. He developed fulminant hepatitis with a fast rise in transaminases within 5 days and required liver transplantation despite glucocorticoid treatment, with histology showing massive hepatic necrosis with dense lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltrates. PCR detected high HHV-6 viremia before transplantation, and both a skin patch test and a lymphocyte stimulation test for lamotrigine hypersensitivity were positive, leading to a diagnosis of lamotrigine-induced hypersensitivity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (8-year-old boy); DIHS with concurrent HHV-6 viremia.
raw_record.extra_details: Given for multiple seizures (indication). Presentation included fever, generalized maculopapular rash, facial edema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia (18%), atypical lymphocytes (8%); transaminases initially two times normal then fulminant hepatitis with fast rise within 5 days; histology showed massive hepatic necrosis with lymphocytes and eosinophils; liver transplantation required despite glucocorticoid therapy; positive lamotrigine skin patch test and lymphocyte stimulation test; diagnosis of lamotrigine-induced hypersensitivity (DIHS/DRESS).

raw_record.support_text: Methasteron, a nutritional supplement used to increase weight or accelerate muscle-mass gain, was studied in 5 cases of hepatotoxicity at tertiary-care medical centers. Five previously healthy patients using methasteron developed jaundice 2 weeks after discontinuation and presented 2 weeks later; bilirubin peaked within another 2 to 3 weeks, and all cases resolved about 12 weeks after initial presentation with no identifiable residual hepatic dysfunction. The authors concluded that methasteron use can result in severe hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Nutritional body-building/muscle-enhancing supplement marketed as safe. Five previously healthy patients developed jaundice 2 weeks after discontinuing methasteron, presenting to a tertiary-care center 2 weeks later; bilirubin levels peaked within another 2-3 weeks and all resolved about 12 weeks after initial presentation with no identifiable residual hepatic dysfunction. Paper states 5 cases of cholestatic liver damage caused by this supplement; hepatotoxicity and liver failure can worsen after initial presentation, especially within 2 weeks, and acute hepatic injury should resolve with close observation and supportive care.

raw_record.support_text: In a phase I study, intoplicine (RP 60475F; NSC 645008), a topoisomerase I/II inhibitor, was administered as a 1 h i.v. infusion at 12-360 mg/m² to 33 patients. Dose-dependent and reproducible hepatotoxicity was dose-limiting in three of four patients at 360 mg/m²; the toxicity was reversible in two of three patients but fatal in one. The study concludes that hepatotoxicity is dose-limiting at 360 mg/m² and sets the phase II recommended dose at 270 mg/m² every 3 weeks with close monitoring of hepatic and cardiac functions.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase I dose-escalation study in 33 cancer patients (31 with prior radiotherapy and/or chemotherapy); 69 courses given as 1 h i.v. infusion. Hepatotoxicity was dose-limiting in 3 of 4 patients at 360 mg/m², reversible in 2 and fatal in 1. Two sudden deaths also occurred at 12 and 48 mg/m² in whom drug implication could not be excluded. No myelosuppression was noted. Phase II recommended dose 270 mg/m² every 3 weeks with close hepatic and cardiac monitoring.

raw_record.support_text: Laboratory studies are reported for 13 children and adolescents who had isoniazid hepatotoxicity during treatment for latent tuberculosis infection. Two additional patients were excluded (1 with Becker muscular dystrophy, 1 with uncertain number of ingested isoniazid doses). At onset, mean ALT was 401 U/L and mean AST 361 U/L, with peak ALT 559 U/L and peak AST 457 U/L; all patients had ALT >3x ULN at onset, with 5 (38%) having ALT >=10x ULN. Mean bilirubin at first or peak was 2 mg/dL. Viral hepatitis testing was negative in 11 (85%). Time for ALT/AST to decrease was 69 days on average.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Children and adolescents (0-18 years) treated for latent tuberculosis infection.
raw_record.extra_details: N=13 patients. ALT at onset 401 +/- 448 U/L (range 100-2690, highest outlier), peak 559 +/- 523 (101-2925); ALT >ULN at onset: 0 <3-fold, 5 (38%) 3- to <5-fold, 3 (23%) 5- to <10-fold, 5 (38%) >=10-fold. AST at onset 361 +/- 580 (26-3589), peak 457 +/- 663 (26-4139); AST >ULN at onset: 5 (38%) <3-fold, 1 (8%) 3- to <5-fold, 3 (23%) 5- to <10-fold, 4 (31%) >=10-fold. Bilirubin first or peak 2 +/- 4 mg/dL (0.2-14.5). Viral hepatitis negative in 11/13 (85%); HBsAg negative only in 1 (8%); not tested in 1 (8%). Time for ALT/AST to decrease 69 +/- 63 days (21-232). One patient with nonalcoholic steatohepatitis had ALT decrease to 33 U/L and AST to 38 U/L after isoniazid discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: In this pediatric case series, INH (isoniazid) was listed among the toxic agents that caused acute liver failure (ALF) in a 4-year-old boy (Case 3) following ingestion as medical treatment; the prodromal period from ingestion to symptom appearance was 2 months. At admission he had grade II hepatic encephalopathy, AST 40–34 IU/mL, ALT 217–23 IU/mL, total bilirubin 22–25 mg/dL and INR 3.9 to >4.5, and the explanted liver showed massive necrosis. He required living-related liver transplantation (from his mother) 8 days after admission and was alive at 9 months follow-up.

The retrospective descriptive study (patients <18 years initiating isoniazid for LTBI) evaluated prevalence of hepatotoxicity caused by isoniazid, defining isoniazid hepatotoxicity as ALT >3x ULN with hepatitis symptoms/jaundice, or ALT >5x ULN without symptoms.

raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective cohort reviewed 1582 patients aged <18 years initiating isoniazid for LTBI (2005–2011, California county). ATS-based definition: (1) ALT >3x ULN (female >93 U/L; male >120 U/L) with hepatitis symptoms or jaundice (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, unexplained fatigue), or (2) ALT >5x ULN (female >155 U/L; male >200 U/L) without symptoms. Literature cited: national sample of 2473 patients <20 years, hepatitis in 1/1000; Seattle study (11,141 patients) no hepatotoxicity in 1468 patients <14 years; San Diego County study no cases in 1277 patients <14 years, 6/1939 (0.3%) in patients aged 15–34 years. Known lower hepatotoxicity frequency in children; however severe outcomes (liver transplant, death) documented.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity is described as a well-known potential adverse effect of INH therapy, most likely due to reactive metabolites including acetylhydrazine and free-radical generation. Serum transaminase elevations were seen in 6.8–13.6% of children receiving INH monotherapy and in 6.4–22.9% of adults, with most patients asymptomatic and liver tests normalizing on discontinuation. Clinically overt hepatitis occurred in 0.1–3% of adults and 0.1–7.1% of children, and a surveillance study of 13,838 patients on INH for latent TB found clinically significant hepatitis in 0.1% of children versus 1.3% of adults.

raw_record.extra_details: INH (isoniazid) monotherapy or therapy for latent TB/active TB. Transaminase elevation incidence 6.8–13.6% (children) and 6.4–22.9% (adults); clinically overt hepatitis 0.1–7.1% (children) and 0.1–3% (adults); clinically significant hepatitis in 0.1% of children vs 1.3% of adults in a 13,838-patient surveillance study. raw_record.support_text: Thirteen of 1582 patients (0.8%) who started isoniazid therapy for latent tuberculosis infection developed isoniazid hepatotoxicity; among 1235 patients who completed the 9-month isoniazid course the frequency of hepatotoxicity was 1.1% (13 of 1235). No significant difference in hepatotoxicity frequency was found between sex, age, or racial groups. All 13 patients were children or adolescents treated at therapeutic isoniazid dosages, and improvement of ALT occurred in all 13 at a mean 69 days after isoniazid discontinuation, with no deaths.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children and adolescents, age range 2-17 years); treatment for latent tuberculosis infection.
raw_record.extra_details: 13 of 1582 patients (0.8%) overall; 1.1% (13/1235) among those who completed the 9-month course. Mean time to hepatotoxicity onset 109 days (range 28-257); in 3 patients detection >6 months after start. Dosages 150-300 mg/d (mean 9 ± 4 mg/kg/d). Most had ALT elevation ≥5 times ULN; onset ALT mean 401 ± 448 U/L (range 100-2690), peak mean 559 ± 523 U/L (range 101-2925). Symptoms most commonly abdominal pain, anorexia, vomiting, nausea; jaundice in 3, hepatomegaly in 1, splenomegaly in 1. ALT improvement at mean 69 days after discontinuation; no deaths. No known viral hepatitis or HIV. Two additional patients excluded (1 with Becker muscular dystrophy, 1 with uncertain isoniazid dose count). Most patients (62%) were female and Hispanic. Half completed therapy with rifampin.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid (INH) therapy for tuberculosis carries a known risk for hepatotoxicity and leads to hepatic failure in a small subset of patients; the study aimed to estimate pediatric referrals for INH-related liver failure and describe outcomes.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Restricted to pediatric patients on prophylactic INH for latent/asymptomatic tuberculosis infection (ages 1.3–17 years; mean age 9.8 years).
raw_record.extra_details: A 10-year survey of 84 U.S. pediatric liver-transplant centers plus UNOS statistics found 20 cases of INH-related liver failure: 4 (20%) recovered spontaneously, 10 (50%) underwent orthotopic liver transplantation (OLT), and 6 (30%) died awaiting OLT. Mean INH therapy duration was 3.3 months (range 0.5–9). Five patients with hepatitis symptoms were initially told not to stop treatment. INH-associated liver failure accounted for 0.2% (8/4679) of all pediatric OLTs and 14% (8/56) of transplants for drug hepatotoxicity. Estimated incidence of liver failure up to 3.2/100,000 among children on prophylactic INH. Case count, incidence, outcomes, therapy duration, and monitoring-context details are recorded here.

raw_record.support_text: In this single-patient case report, isoniazid (INH) toxicity was assessed as the underlying etiology of liver failure: with a Naranjo score of six, the culpability of INH toxicity was described as solidified. A positive anti-smooth muscle titer was hypothesized to be a false positive since the patient did not meet criteria for autoimmune hepatitis. The case occurred in an overdose (accidental or intentional) setting in the US, presenting with a nonspecific toxidrome, and the patient recovered with supportive care and aggressive management of liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case of INH overdose (accidental or intentional) in the US; Naranjo causality score of 6; positive anti-smooth muscle titer was considered a likely false positive as autoimmune hepatitis criteria were not met; nonspecific toxidrome overlapping with other etiologies; patient recovered with supportive care and aggressive management of liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that, besides neurotoxicity, isoniazid (INH) poisoning causes hepatotoxicity, citing human overdose cases: a 2-year-old girl who accidentally received 2 g of INH had abnormal liver function test results; a 26-year-old man who ingested 8 g of INH showed elevated serum aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase activities and prolonged prothrombin time, suggesting INH-induced acute hepatitis; and a 21-year-old woman who ingested 12 g of INH showed 20-fold increases in serum aspartate aminotransferase and lactate dehydrogenase activities. The paper recommends monitoring liver functions and prothrombin time in management of INH poisoning.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose ingestion of isoniazid (INH); one case was a 2-year-old child with accidental ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: Cited human overdose cases: 2 g INH in a 2-year-old girl (abnormal liver function tests); 8 g INH in a 26-year-old man (elevated AST, ALT, GGT and prolonged prothrombin time, consistent with INH-induced acute hepatitis); 12 g INH in a 21-year-old woman (20-fold increases in serum AST and lactate dehydrogenase).

raw_record.support_text: The main toxic side effect associated with isoniazid chemoprophylaxis is the development of hepatitis. A US study of nearly 14,000 persons between 1971 and 1972 (Kopanoff et al., 1978) found an overall rate of isoniazid-induced hepatitis of 1%, which was age-related (no cases in those aged <20 years, 2.3% in those aged >50 years) and also related to alcohol consumption.
raw_record.extra_details: Epidemiologic study of ~14,000 persons on isoniazid chemoprophylaxis (1971-1972, Kopanoff et al.). Overall rate of isoniazid-induced hepatitis 1%; age-related with no cases under 20 years and 2.3% in persons >50 years; development of hepatitis also related to alcohol consumption. Discussed in the context of isoniazid preventive therapy for TB.

condition_group: exposure=therapeutic_use+population=human

raw_record.support_text: Dr. Mitchell described the results of a prospective study of isoniazid plasma concentrations and monthly liver function tests during 1 year of isoniazid preventive therapy for tuberculosis. No correlation was found between isoniazid plasma concentrations and susceptibility to isoniazid liver injury, suggesting a toxic metabolite rather than the drug itself might be responsible for isoniazid hepatitis. In the U.S. Public Health Service trial of isoniazid preventive therapy, Orientals were more susceptible to isoniazid liver injury than other populations, and this was noted to be of interest because over 90% of Orientals are genetically rapid acetylators of isoniazid.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid used as 1-year preventive therapy for tuberculosis. Liver injury spectrum includes acute hepatocellular injury with submassive and massive necrosis, chronic active hepatitis (3 patients) with periportal stellate fibrosis and portal infiltration by plasma cells and lymphocytes, and mixed macronodular-micronodular cirrhosis with active necrosis in a fourth patient. Orientals were more susceptible to isoniazid liver injury (over 90% of Orientals are rapid acetylators vs 45% of black and white Americans). Prospective study found no correlation between isoniazid plasma concentrations and susceptibility, suggesting a toxic metabolite rather than the drug itself is responsible. A third study phenotyped 26 non-Oriental patients recovered from apparent isoniazid hepatitis into rapid and slow acetylator groups by the sulfamethazine method (40 mg/kg oral).

raw_record.support_text: A 17-year-old on INH chemoprophylaxis (300-mg tablets) developed fever, malaise, and jaundice and died on March 23, 1987; autopsy showed massive hepatic necrosis, and because hepatitis A and B antibodies were negative and no other hepatotoxic medication was given, death was attributed to INH toxicity. A second case (Case 3) involved a 66-year-old woman on INH who developed acute nausea, vomiting, and jaundice, progressed to fulminant hepatic failure with renal failure, and died with massive hepatic necrosis at necropsy.
raw_record.extra_details: INH given as latent TB chemoprophylaxis (positive tuberculin test; 300-mg tablets). Case 2: 17-year-old, symptoms (fever, dark urine, malaise, nausea) began ~3 weeks before jaundice; INH stopped March 9, 1987; death March 23, 1987; massive hepatic necrosis at autopsy; no other hepatotoxic medication. Case 3: 66-year-old, N/V/jaundice acute onset, total bilirubin 24, SGOT 869, SGPT 2,373, alkaline phosphatase 195; fulminant hepatic failure complicated by Klebsiella septicemia and renal failure; death August 17, 1990; massive hepatic necrosis at necropsy.

raw_record.support_text: A prospective study of 174 patients receiving isoniazid, examined monthly for SGOT and bilirubin elevations, found that about 20% showed abnormal values that subsided while patients continued the drug. The paper concludes that isoniazid was hepatotoxic in a large proportion of individuals, though most adapted to the insult and recovered rather than progressing to severe hepatic injury; no correlation with slow acetylation or anti-isoniazid antibodies was found.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective study of 174 isoniazid recipients; ~20% had abnormal SGOT/bilirubin that subsided on continued therapy ('adaptation'). A second retrospective USPHS surveillance program on 13,838 isoniazid recipients (224 with possible isoniazid-related hepatic injury) showed the injury was biochemically (SGOT, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase) and morphologically indistinguishable from iproniazid-induced liver damage or viral hepatitis, with no evidence of a hypersensitivity mechanism; ~30% of hepatic reactors were Honolulu residents of Oriental ancestry, so up to 90% would be expected to be fast acetylators. No correlation with acetylation rate or anti-isoniazid antibodies.

raw_record.support_text: Idiosyncratic drug reactions comprised 13% of acute liver failure cases and were important because of the poor outcome. Prominent among these cases were isoniazid, bromfenac, and troglitazone (≥4 cases each), the latter two having subsequently been withdrawn; other agents included trimethoprim/sulfa, phenytoin, disulfiram, and propylthiouracil (≥2 cases each).
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as a cause of idiosyncratic drug-induced acute liver failure with at least 4 cases in this series. These patients typically presented subacutely with low aminotransferases, high bilirubin, and more frequent ascites; more than half received a liver graft.

raw_record.support_text: Treatment of latent TB infection (LTBI) includes isoniazid (INH), a drug that can cause potentially serious hepatotoxicity. The study genotyped NAT2 and CYP2E1 in 170 subjects (23 INH-hepatotoxicity cases and 147 controls); no NAT2 association was significant at p=0.05, though a trend for increasing hepatotoxicity risk across rapid, intermediate and slow acetylators approached significance (p=0.08).
raw_record.extra_details: Used for treatment of latent TB infection (LTBI). Genetic association study: NAT2 and CYP2E1 genotyping in 23 INH-hepatotoxicity cases and 147 controls; NAT2 polymorphism association non-significant but with a trend (p=0.08) for increasing risk across rapid, intermediate and slow acetylator groups. CYP2E1 Rsa1 polymorphism was genotyped by PCR-RFLP.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that about 15–18% of patients treated for tuberculosis with regimens containing isoniazid develop drug-induced hepatitis, and that prospective studies in Japan and Taiwan indicate NAT2 genotyping can identify patients at risk of hepatotoxicity during isoniazid treatment. This is a human liver-injury claim attributing drug-induced hepatitis/hepatotoxicity to isoniazid at therapeutic anti-tuberculosis dosing, with susceptibility modulated by the acetylator phenotype.
raw_record.extra_details: About 15-18% of tuberculosis patients treated with isoniazid-containing regimens develop drug-induced hepatitis. In a Japanese prospective study, NAT2 genotypes predicting the slow acetylator phenotype carried a relative risk of 28.0 (95% CI 26-30) for developing hepatotoxicity versus wild-type NAT2*4 homozygotes (rapid acetylators); in a Taiwan study slow-acetylator NAT2 genotypes increased the risk about four-fold (odds ratio 3.7, 95% CI 1.6-8.5). CYP2E1 polymorphisms may also be associated with antituberculosis drug-induced hepatitis susceptibility, although to a lesser extent than NAT2.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a patient in whom hepatitis developed shortly after he began taking isoniazid (INH) for a recent tuberculin skin-test conversion, and challenge with INH was followed by a recurrence of hepatitis confirmed by histologic study. The paper notes that INH is thought to be a rare cause of jaundice but that its precise role has previously been unclear, as most patients in earlier cases also received para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS), a known hepatotoxin.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 40-year-old merchant seaman with no prior jaundice who took isoniazid 300 mg daily for a positive tuberculin test; hepatitis (with 1 week of anorexia, epigastric pain, loose gray stools, dark urine and jaundice) developed one month after starting INH. Serial SGOT peaked at 1885 U (2/14/68) and bilirubin at 24.2 mg/100 ml; jaundice recurred on INH rechallenge (4/17/68, then again 8/1/68-8/5/68), with elevation confirmed and biopsy performed; INH was stopped on 8/5/68 and SGOT fell to 37 U by 8/16/68. Galbumin 3.5 gm/100 ml, total protein 6.5 gm; no history of blood transfusions or recent injections, only moderate social whiskey drinking. Author affiliation: Alaska Native Medical Center.

raw_record.support_text: At Charity Hospital, 420 tuberculin reactive hospital employees started INH prophylaxis in August 1970; after 6 months, 2 employees developed clinical hepatitis, and within the same period a fatal case of hepatic necrosis occurred in an INH recipient at another agency in New Orleans. Diagnostic laboratory test profiles from all INH recipients in the Charity Hospital program showed 8.7% had abnormal liver function studies, usually elevations of SGOT. The paper further notes that 2 deaths from hepatic disease associated with INH therapy attracted publicity and focuses attention on isoniazid hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: INH chemoprophylaxis for tuberculosis control; hepatitis rarely associated with INH administration. In another series, 10% of asymptomatic patients had elevated transaminase concentrations during the first 2 months of treatment; liver biopsy in 5 of 8 patients showed liver cell damage. Byrd's prospective secondary chemoprophylaxis study found 10% of INH recipients could not complete therapy because of symptomatic reactions, usually with SGOT elevations. At Charity Hospital 2 cases of clinical hepatitis and a separate fatal hepatic necrosis case were reported; 8.7% of recipients had abnormal liver function studies. Paper's own investigation of 12 INH-treated subjects with colorimetric SGOT >100 units/ml established that a diazonium dye colorimetric method falsely elevates SGOT (unlike p-aminosalicylic acid) and that INH does not cause these false elevations, with paired enzymatic measurements shown in a table.

raw_record.support_text: Cases 8-12 describe adults started on isoniazid 300 mg/day for a positive tuberculin skin test who developed jaundice and hepatitis. Liver biopsies showed patchy hepatitis, with multilobular necrosis in Cases 8 and 11 and focal bridging necrosis in Case 12. In Case 9, re-administration of a single 300 mg isoniazid dose caused recurrent fever, weakness, sweating, a rise in SGOT to 650 MIU, and a patchy hepatitis on biopsy, confirming the drug as the cause; the patient recovered fully after isoniazid was stopped. Hepatitis B antigen was negative in the tested cases, attributing the hepatitis to isoniazid therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases 8-12 (L.W., F.R., A.B., J.B., H.P.) each on isoniazid 300 mg/day for latent tuberculosis chemoprophylaxis after a positive tuberculin skin test. Latency varied (approximately 9 weeks, 14 days, 11 days/weeks, 4 months, 6 months). Presenting features included jaundice, dark urine, right upper quadrant pain, nausea, fever, weakness, malaise, and myalgias. Percutaneous liver biopsy findings: patchy hepatitis (cases 8, 9, 10), multilobular necrosis (cases 8, 11), focal bridging necrosis (case 12). Case 9 had a positive dechallenge/rechallenge: symptoms resolved off drug, recurred within hours of a 300 mg rechallenge dose (SGOT rose from 70 to 650 MIU, bilirubin 2.3 mg/100 ml). Case 11 had asterixis and obtundation requiring neomycin/gut cleansing and recovered; a maculopapular rash early on was attributed to co-administered aminosalicylic acid (stopped), not isoniazid. Case 12 also used compazine intermittently. Hepatitis B antigen negative in cases 8, 10, 11; anti-mitochondrial and smooth-muscle antibodies negative in case 10. All patients recovered and did well on follow-up.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses INH (isoniazid) as a cause of human drug-induced liver injury in the context of anti-TB therapy. Clinical studies presented include 224 patients on anti-TB treatment in whom slow acetylators had higher risk of liver toxicity than rapid acetylators (26.4% vs 11.1%, P=0.013); a Brazilian study reporting hepatitis risks of 22% for slow, 9.8% for intermediate, and 2.9% for rapid acetylators; and a multicenter randomized controlled trial in Japanese patients in which a lower INH dose (2.5 mg/kg) in slow acetylators significantly decreased the incidence of INH-induced liver injury versus standard treatment (5 mg/kg). The paper also notes INH hepatotoxicity in INH + rifampicin combination therapy and that INH can bind liver proteins and cause immune-mediated liver injury, while concluding the role of NAT2 acetylator status remains controversial.
raw_record.extra_details: INH used for anti-TB therapy. Acetylator-status studies report conflicting associations: early observations favored rapid acetylators (86% of probable and 60% of possible liver-injury patients rapid; 14/18 with abnormal serum aminotransferase rapid vs 7/18 with normal), whereas later studies favored slow acetylators; several other observations showed no significant difference. NAT2 genotypes have low positive predictive value for identifying liver-injury risk. INH also implicated in INH + rifampicin combination therapy (77 Japanese patients: higher liver-injury risk in slow than intermediate/rapid acetylators). Mechanism: NAT2 and amidase biotransformation; INH hydrolyzed to INA and hydrazine; hydrazine and acetylhydrazine considered hepatotoxic metabolites; INH may bind liver proteins causing immune-mediated injury. Reduced INH dose (2.5 mg/kg) in slow acetylators decreased INH-induced liver injury incidence; outcome granularity not otherwise specified.; confidence: 0.88; needs_more_context: False

raw_record.support_text: Chronic hepatic injury was seen in 4 isoniazid-treated patients. In 3 it resembled chronic active hepatitis with diffuse moderate hepatocellular abnormality, scattered sinusoidal acidophilic bodies, periportal degeneration, periportal stellate fibrosis, and portal infiltrates of plasma cells, lymphocytes, and occasional eosinophils/neutrophils. The 4th patient showed macronodular-micronodular cirrhosis with active necrosis and degeneration and heavy lymphocytic-plasmacytic infiltration.
raw_record.extra_details: Histology: chronic active hepatitis-like findings in 3 patients (periportal degeneration, stellate fibrosis with portal linkage) and macronodular-micronodular cirrhosis with active necrosis in a 4th. Cases described in context of isoniazid preventive/anti-TB therapy.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 1039 patients treated prophylactically for latent TB with isoniazid (6H or 9H regimens), hepatotoxicity requiring discontinuation occurred in 49 (4.7%) on 6H and 54 (5.2%) on 9H, and transient ALT elevation occurred in 39 (3.8%) on 6H and 70 (6.7%) on 9H. Liver toxicity receded when isoniazid was suspended, and normal liver function was confirmed on follow-up after withdrawal; no patient was hospitalised for hepatotoxicity or required liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective cohort of 1039 patients at risk of developing TB; 6H and 9H isoniazid regimens (6 or 9 months). Hepatotoxicity requiring treatment discontinuation: 6H 49 (4.7%, 95%CI 3.4-6.1), 9H 54 (5.2%, 95%CI 3.8-6.6). Transient ALT elevation not causing discontinuation: 6H 39 (3.8%), 9H 70 (6.7%). Liver toxicity receded and liver functions normalized after isoniazid withdrawal; no hospitalization for hepatotoxicity and no liver transplantation. Costs of these adverse effects were maintained based on maximum probable incidence.

raw_record.support_text: Two case reports attribute isoniazid (INH) as the cause of drug-induced hepatitis in humans. In Case 1 (WR, 52-year-old man) fever and liver injury developed during daily 300 mg INH chemoprophylaxis; after INH was discontinued the patient became afebrile within 24 hours, prothrombin time normalized, and liver biopsies showing portal infiltration and granulomas fully resolved, evidence of positive dechallenge. In Case 2 (GM, 56-year-old woman) jaundice, acholic stools, and markedly elevated serum bilirubin (up to 19 mg/100 ml), SGOT (1,340 units), and SGPT (1,430 units) developed during 300 mg INH daily for 2 months; liver biopsy was consistent with acute hepatitis and increased portal eosinophils suggested drug-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: INH given as 300 mg daily chemoprophylaxis for latent tuberculosis exposure: Case 1 for 4 months after a positive tuberculin test, Case 2 for 2 months. Case 1 (52-year-old man): fever, prolonged prothrombin time (46%), elevated alkaline phosphatase (14.4 Bodansky units), SGOT (190 Frankel units), SGPT (125 Frankel units); normal bilirubin; portal infiltration with histiocytes, lymphocytes, eosinophils, neutrophils and granulomas that resolved; afebrile within 24 h and prothrombin 100% by day 4 after INH discontinuation; all tests normal at 6 weeks. Case 2 (56-year-old woman): jaundice, hepatomegaly with tenderness, palpable spleen tip, bilirubin peak 19 mg/100 ml with direct 6.7, SGOT 1,340, SGPT 1,430, absolute eosinophil count 310/mm3; biopsy consistent with acute hepatitis with portal eosinophils; liver tests normalized over ~3 months. Case 2 also received nitroglycerin, conjugated estrogens, meprobamate, and methenamine mandelate; HAA and infectious mononucleosis serology negative; no transfusion, hepatitis exposure, or alcoholism history.

raw_record.support_text: On rehospitalization, the patient presented with vomiting, abdominal pain, and elevated transaminases and was admitted for isoniazid-induced liver injury. Her 4-drug anti-TB regimen was discontinued, and she recovered after 8 additional days in the hospital.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report: a frail 76-year-old woman with COPD and prior TB treated with a 4-drug anti-TB regimen that included isoniazid; presented with vomiting and abdominal pain and elevated transaminases; the regimen was stopped and the patient recovered after 8 additional days in hospital.

raw_record.support_text: The Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network (DILIN) enrolled well-defined cases of hepatotoxicity caused by isoniazid occurring since 1994, adjudicated by three reviewers using RUCAM. A total of 40 DILI cases were enrolled, including nine individuals treated with isoniazid. Cases were classified overall as hepatocellular (44%), mixed (28%), or cholestatic (28%).
raw_record.extra_details: 9 of 40 adjudicated DILI cases in the DILIN cohort; part of a RUCAM test-retest and interrater reliability study (HEPATOLOGY 2008;48:1175-1183). Overall cohort mean age 44.8 +- 19.5 years, 68% female, 78% Caucasian; cases classified as hepatocellular 44%, mixed 28%, cholestatic 28% (aggregate across all four implicated agents, not drug-specific).

raw_record.support_text: In the authors' prior study of 210 patients treated with Regimen I drugs, 6% of the hepatotoxicity cases were due to isoniazid.
raw_record.extra_details: 6% of hepatotoxicity cases attributed to isoniazid in a prior cohort of 210 patients treated with Regimen I antituberculosis drugs; major side effects (hepatotoxicity and exanthema) incidence of 0.49/100 patients/month, consistent with lower toxicity than pyrazinamide.

raw_record.support_text: Three registries from Sweden, Spain, and the United States totaling over 1,500 patients reported 6 to 9% having a severe outcome of death or need for liver transplantation within 6 months. In the Swedish registry, both isoniazid and halothane cases of hepatocellular injury had 40% rates of death or transplantation. Risk of early adverse outcome was highest in those with acute hepatocellular injury (7–13%) and lowest with a mixed pattern (2%).
raw_record.extra_details: In the Swedish DILI registry, isoniazid cases of hepatocellular injury had a 40% rate of death or liver transplantation within 6 months; severe outcome (death/transplantation) rates across three registries (Sweden, Spain, US) totaled over 1,500 patients with 6-9% affected overall; risk of early severe outcome was highest with acute hepatocellular injury (7-13%) and lowest with mixed pattern (2%); elevated bilirubin at presentation was associated with early severe outcome.

raw_record.support_text: The study examined DILI cases arising after anti-tuberculosis treatment involving isoniazid and notes that only one DILI case (a slow acetylator) had received isoniazid alone, while most had not undergone systematic rechallenge with each drug. The authors were therefore unable to reliably assess whether all cases were related primarily to isoniazid, but they repeatedly frame isoniazid as the cause of isoniazid-related hepatotoxicity, noting the risk of hepatotoxicity with isoniazid and the role of NAT2 acetylator status.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of DILI following isoniazid-containing anti-TB regimens; only one case (a slow acetylator) received isoniazid alone, and systematic rechallenge with each drug was not performed in most cases, so certainty that isoniazid was the primary cause is limited. PMID context confirms isoniazid-related DILI; NAT2 slow-acetylator status and rs7845127 tag SNP discussed as genetic risk factors; moderate-to-severe DILI incidence estimated in the study and a Japanese randomized trial of NAT2-genotype-guided isoniazid dosing showed decreased DILI incidence in the slow-acetylator group.

raw_record.support_text: In the mLTT study, samples from 24 subjects enrolled in the U.S. Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network (DILIN) were tested. Robust positive mLTT responses were observed for two of four samples from three DILIN subjects with hepatitis due to isoniazid (INH), and the authors concluded the mLTT may be useful for confirming the role of the adaptive immune response in DILI ascribed to INH.
raw_record.extra_details: Two of four samples from three DILIN subjects with INH-associated hepatitis showed robust positive modified lymphocyte transformation test (mLTT) responses using cytokine and granzyme B production as endpoints on frozen/thawed PBMC. The paper also cites Warrington et al. (1978) reporting 95% positive LTT responses among 20 patients with INH-associated liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 3,377 patients treated with isoniazid (INH) for latent tuberculosis, 19 patients developed hepatotoxicity, defined as serum AST >5 times the upper limit of normal; INH was immediately discontinued. The incidence was 5.63 hepatotoxic events per 1,000 patients started on therapy. The events were attributed to INH therapy, with peak AST elevations peaking 1 to 6 months after treatment start, and some affected patients were icteric with elevated total bilirubin.
raw_record.extra_details: 19/3,377 patients (0.56%) had hepatotoxicity (AST >5x ULN), 5.63 events per 1,000 patients started. Risk factors: age >49 years (bivariate OR 4.814, 95% CI 1.400-16.551, p=0.02; multivariable OR 3.699, 95% CI 1.428-9.584, p=0.008) and baseline AST > ULN (bivariate OR 4.832, 95% CI 1.884-12.394, p=0.0003; multivariable OR 5.398, 95% CI 2.081-13.999, p=0.0005). No association with gender, race/ethnicity, alcohol consumption, or prior liver disease. Only 1 of 19 had prodromal symptoms; two icteric patients had total bilirubin 5.8 and 6.4 mg/dL with malaise/nausea. Peak AST ranged 212-1602 U/L, 1-6 months after starting INH. Population was predominately African-American men <50 years with no reported alcohol use or prior liver disease.

raw_record.support_text: The paper attributes clinically meaningful human liver injury to isoniazid. Scharer and Smith reported that 10% of patients receiving isoniazid alone for preventive tuberculosis therapy developed elevated serum transaminases (SGOT and SGPT) during the first 2 months of treatment, with liver biopsies in 5 patients showing focal hepatic necrosis and transaminases generally returning to normal with continued therapy. In a Capitol Hill cohort, 19 of 2,321 employees given isoniazid developed hepatitis (attack rate 8.2 per 1,000), 13 were jaundiced, and 2 died, versus attack rates of 0.5 per 1,000 in matched non-isoniazid controls and 0 per 1,000 in tuberculin reactors who refused treatment. A subsequent prospective Public Health Service surveillance of 13,838 patients, including 3,196 in Baltimore, recorded 41 isoniazid-associated cases of liver dysfunction with 7 deaths (rate 12.83 per 1,000) and 133 probable/possible hepatitis cases with 1 fatality in the other 20 health departments (rate 12.50 per 1,000). The paper concludes that the new evidence shows isoniazid can produce liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Preventive-therapy setting for tuberculosis. Elevated serum transaminases (SGOT and SGPT) in 10% of patients in the first 2 months, with focal hepatic necrosis on biopsy in 5 patients and enzyme return to normal despite continued isoniazid in most instances. Capitol Hill study: 19/2,321 developed hepatitis, 13 jaundiced, 2 died; hepatitis attack rate 8.2/1,000 vs 0.5/1,000 in matched non-treated controls and 0/1,000 in untreated tuberculin reactors. Symptom onset 3-31 weeks after therapy initiation; 2 fatal cases began at 22 and 30 weeks. Prospective PHS surveillance: 41 isoniazid-associated liver-dysfunction cases with 7 deaths in Baltimore (3,196 patients, rate 12.83/1,000) and 133 probable/possible hepatitis cases with 1 fatality across 20 health departments (10,642 patients, rate 12.50/1,000). CDC Ad Hoc Committee on Isoniazid and Liver Disease recommended continued use with monthly questioning for symptoms of liver damage.

raw_record.support_text: The 74-year-old patient was given 150 mg of isoniazid (INH) daily for tuberculosis prophylaxis. One month later she developed INH-induced hepatic injury, and INH was replaced by rifampicin and streptomycin.
raw_record.extra_details: Given 150 mg daily for pulmonary tuberculosis prophylaxis; hepatic injury developed one month after starting INH and resolved after the drug was replaced by rifampicin (450 mg daily) and streptomycin (1 g intramuscularly twice weekly). No liver-test values, biochemical pattern, or severity level were reported.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that approximately 10% to 20% of isoniazid recipients manifest biochemical evidence of liver injury and that a smaller number develop clinically overt hepatitis. It further describes patients who recovered from probable isoniazid hepatitis and others who showed biochemical evidence of mild isoniazid liver injury, and concludes that release of the hepatotoxic hydrazino moiety (acetylhydrazine) of isoniazid in man is responsible for isoniazid liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: In isoniazid preventive therapy for tuberculosis. 21 non-Oriental patients with probable isoniazid hepatitis and 5 with possible mild isoniazid liver injury were phenotyped: 86% of probable cases and 60% of possible cases were rapid acetylators vs an expected frequency of about 45%. In a USPHS trial of 13,838 patients, 30% of those developing isoniazid hepatitis were residents of Honolulu of Oriental ancestry, and over 90% of Orientals are rapid acetylators. No correlation was seen between isoniazid plasma concentrations and susceptibility to isoniazid liver injury. Mechanism suggested: rapid acetylators hydrolyze more isoniazid to isonicotinic acid and free hydrazine/acetylhydrazine, which animal studies show is converted to a potent acylating agent producing liver necrosis. Probable hepatitis required acute hepatocellular biochemical injury with no other identifiable cause and improvement on withdrawal; possible cases had SGOT <250 Karman units and bilirubin <2.5 mg% or other possible causes.

raw_record.support_text: In one survey of almost 14,000 patients treated with isoniazid, 114 patients developed hepatitis and 13 died from liver failure; symptoms usually developed within three months of starting treatment, and histological studies in 33 patients most often showed acute hepatitis, with three patients having chronic active hepatitis and one having cirrhosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Also listed in the antimicrobial agents that may produce acute hepatitis or cholestasis. Survey of almost 14,000 treated patients: 114 developed hepatitis, 13 died from liver failure. Symptoms usually within three months of starting. Histology in 33 patients most often acute hepatitis; 3 chronic active hepatitis and 1 cirrhosis. Some patients may have had chronic liver disease before isoniazid. Asymptomatic rise in serum transaminases occurs in about one-fifth of patients.

raw_record.support_text: The learning points state that isoniazid, used as protective therapy for tuberculosis prophylaxis, can lead to fulminant liver failure, and that living donor liver transplantation is of vital importance when cadaveric liver transplantation cannot be performed.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient with isoniazid-associated fulminant liver failure requiring living donor liver transplantation; isoniazid was used as protective therapy for tuberculosis prophylaxis.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 89 patients receiving isoniazid therapy, isoniazid-induced hepatitis (INH-H) occurred in 8 patients (9%). Incidence by sex was 5/40 (13%) among females and 3/49 (6%) among males, and by age was 1/29 (3%) for ≤26y, 2/30 (7%) for 27-35y, and 5/30 (17%) for ≥36y; non-parametric tests did not reveal significant differences among groups.
raw_record.extra_details: Patients were treated with isoniazid monotherapy at 300 mg daily (n=89). The study reported a non-significant trend for the CYP2E1 *1A/*1A genotype with INH-H (OR 5.9, 95% CI 0.69-270) and failed to show any significant NAT2 genotype association with INH-induced hepatotoxicity, in contrast to Asian-population studies that used 600 mg INH combined with rifampicin, ethambutol and pyrazinamide.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that isoniazid produces mild hepatic injury in 10 to 20 percent of patients, and not just in a few hypersensitive subjects. In a retrospective study of 112 patients with isoniazid-related clinical hepatitis, no clinical evidence (rash, fever, arthralgias, eosinophilia) of an allergic mechanism was found. The authors conclude that most evidence fails to support idiosyncratic or allergic mechanisms as the cause of isoniazid liver injury in most patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid produces mild hepatic injury in 10-20% of patients; retrospective study of 112 patients with isoniazid-related clinical hepatitis showed no clinical evidence (rash, fever, arthralgias, eosinophilia) of allergy; no circulating antibodies to isoniazid detected. Severe hepatitis mentioned as progression risk in susceptible individuals. Overt hepatitis due to isoniazid therapy reported in 21 non-Oriental patients who had recovered; 18 of 21 (86%) displayed the rapid-acetylator phenotype vs an expected frequency of 45%, supporting rapid metabolism correlation with overt hepatitis, though no direct correlation was found between rapid-acetylator phenotype and subclinical injury. The suspected mechanism is a hepatotoxic acylating metabolite (acetylhydrazine liberated from acetylisoniazid), which directly causes hepatocellular necrosis in rats in vivo; this is a mechanism/proposed hypothesis rather than evidence that the metabolite itself is the human DILI entity.

raw_record.support_text: A 39-year-old woman with isoniazid-implicated acute liver failure required liver transplantation; her peak AST was 797 U/L, ALT 850 U/L, ALP 243 U/L, total bilirubin 7.1 mg/dL, INR 4.5, with 21 days from jaundice to hepatic encephalopathy.
raw_record.extra_details: Single confirmed case; also cited as one of the 2 most common antimicrobial agents leading to drug-induced liver injury and acute liver failure; 21-day interval from jaundice to hepatic encephalopathy.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of healthcare workers receiving latent tuberculosis infection treatment, hepatotoxicity occurred in 17/43 (39.5%) on the 9-month isoniazid (9H) regimen, with hepatotoxicity ≥grade 2 in 8 (18.6%). Hepatotoxicity incidence was higher in 9H than in 3HR (39.5% vs 17.2%). Seven workers had to change or discontinue their LTBI treatment because of hepatotoxicity, all in the 9H group, with LFT (ALT/AST) elevations with or without hepatitis symptoms.
raw_record.extra_details: 9-month isoniazid (9H) LTBI regimen; 43 recipients among healthcare workers. Hepatotoxicity 17/43 (39.5%), ≥grade 2 in 8 (18.6%); median time to hepatotoxicity 102 days (IQR 96-105). Seven cases caused regimen change/discontinuation: LFT elevation ALT grade 1-3 with/without hepatitis symptoms, sample AST/ALT 84/212, 105/126, 129/135, 338/670, 100/106, 102/140, 105/678. Major adverse event hepatotoxicity: ALT >3x ULN with symptoms in 4 (9.3%) and ALT >5x ULN without symptoms in 3 (7.0%).

raw_record.support_text: The study assesses genetic variation in the candidate genes CES1, CES2 and CES4 in subjects with and without INH (isoniazid)-induced hepatotoxicity. The paper repeatedly refers to 'INH-induced hepatotoxicity' as the liver-injury phenotype under investigation, i.e., isoniazid is the molecular agent implicated in causing the hepatotoxicity events, and the pharmacogenetic analyses (e.g., of CES1/CES2/CES4 variants) test whether genetic factors modify this drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: INH (isoniazid) is used as the anti-tuberculosis drug whose hepatotoxicity (INH-induced hepatotoxicity) is the study phenotype. The paper catalogued variants in CES1, CES2 and CES4 in subjects with and without hepatotoxicity (n=170 all subjects for association tests) and found no significant association of genetic variation in CES2, or SNPs and haplotypes in CES1/CES4, with INH-induced hepatotoxicity; no trend P values remained significant after adjustment for multiple testing using the false discovery rate.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid (INH) hepatotoxicity is considered a hepatocellular hypersensitivity reaction that may cause diffuse hepatocellular necrosis. Initial elevation of transaminases occurs in 10-20% of patients undergoing INH therapy and is typically remedied by discontinuation. Once massive necrosis occurs the damage is irreversible and may be fatal, with reported mortality rates from hepatic failure of 23.2/100,000 or 57.9/100,000. In the present case, the patient developed INH-associated massive hepatic necrosis requiring and receiving orthotopic liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of INH hepatotoxicity during antituberculosis therapy resulting in massive, irreversible hepatic necrosis that was fatal without liver transplantation; the patient underwent orthotopic liver transplantation. Initial transaminase elevation occurs in 10-20% of INH-treated patients and resolves on discontinuation. Reported hepatic failure mortality rates of 23.2/100,000 or 57.9/100,000. Resected liver showed extensive necrosis with islands of intact hepatocytes, acute and chronic inflammation, regenerating hepatocytes and proliferating cholangioles, without significant fibrosis.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of employees treated with isoniazid (INH), 32 subjects developed SGOT levels above the upper limit of normal. In one patient (Case 29), marked SGOT and bilirubin elevations developed after four weeks of INH administration, with preceding fatigue and jaundice; she was thought to have developed INH hepatitis and the drug was discontinued, after which bilirubin and SGOT promptly returned to normal. Elevation of SGOT levels in all but two subjects returned to normal within three to eight weeks after discontinuation of the drug, and the discussion notes concern about toxic hepatitis during treatment with INH.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective cohort of employees in a tuberculosis control program treated with INH; 32 of an unstated denominator developed elevated SGOT (>65 Karmen units). Case 29 developed jaundice with SGOT 898 Karmen units, SGPT 200, and bilirubin >10.0 mg/100 ml after 4 weeks of therapy; drug discontinued and tests normalized. INH was stopped in patients with rapid/progressive SGOT rise, bilirubin >1.5 mg/100 ml, or symptoms. Two subjects with persistently elevated SGOT had been drinking alcohol heavily during therapy (competing exposure); SGOT elevations ranged up to 898 units and developed from within 2 months to after 6 months of therapy. No positive HBsAg or rheumatoid factor was found in tested patients; some patients demonstrated antinuclear factor.

raw_record.support_text: Among 663 LTBI participants receiving isoniazid (INH) treatment, 69 (10.4%) reported side effects including gastrointestinal symptoms, of whom 14 had abnormal liver transaminase levels, and 49 completed INH treatment. Drug-related adverse effects were mainly grades 1 and 2, and only one participant had grade 3 hepatotoxicity attributed to INH treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Of 663 participants, 69 (10.4%) reported side effects including gastrointestinal symptoms; 14 had abnormal liver transaminase levels. Adverse effects were mainly grades 1 and 2; one participant had grade 3 hepatotoxicity attributed to INH. LTBI treatment (isoniazid monotherapy) among recent Ethiopian immigrants; 49 of the 69 with side effects completed INH treatment.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid is listed among drugs with very well documented hepatotoxicity with numerous case reports and case series and positive rechallenge (reproduced DILI), and is identified among the most common single implicated antimicrobial agents in DILIN and as a top-ten drug in multiple DILI registries.
raw_record.extra_details: Antituberculosis agent; among the most common single implicated antimicrobial agents in the DILIN cohort (with amoxicillin–clavulanate, nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole); in the ten most frequent drugs of the DILIN, Icelandic, and Spanish registries; rechallenge has reproduced the DILI.

raw_record.support_text: The DILIN retrospective study is a nationwide registry that includes patients who experienced liver injury within the past 10 years after consuming one of 8 drugs: phenytoin, isoniazid, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid, valproic acid, nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, minocycline, and quinolone antibiotics. The goals include establishing a database of patients with severe DILI due to any of these medications.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among 8 drugs included in the DILIN retrospective registry for patients with severe DILI due to these medications.

raw_record.support_text: A correction to the paper 'Isoniazid Hepatitis' (Ann Intern Med 79:1-12, 1973) corrects the figure legends for two photomicrographs. The Figure 3 legend describes a liver biopsy from Case 3 showing bridging necrosis along the lower right corner with a delicate extension across the bottom midportion, and only mild inflammation and hepatocellular damage elsewhere; the Figure 5 legend describes a liver biopsy from Case 2 taken during a first bout of hepatitis with bridging necrosis, chronic intralobular inflammation, and evidence of hepatocellular injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Correction letter refers to the paper 'Isoniazid Hepatitis' (Ann Intern Med 79:1-12, 1973) reporting isoniazid-induced hepatitis with biopsy findings of bridging necrosis and hepatocellular injury in individual patients (Cases 2 and 3).

raw_record.support_text: The ILIAD reliability study enrolled its first 40 patients including nine cases of isoniazid hepatotoxicity. The paper describes these as cases of drug-induced liver injury used to test the reliability of RUCAM causality scores.
raw_record.extra_details: 9 of 40 DILI cases in the ILIAD study cohort; patients with a diagnosis of isoniazid hepatotoxicity. Median time to onset across the cohort was 42.5 days, 73% were hospitalized, and 15% overall required liver transplantation (not drug-specific).

raw_record.support_text: In a letter responding to criticisms, the authors defend the finding that isoniazid preventive therapy causes hepatitis, including fatal disease. They report that in the carefully controlled prospective USPHS surveillance study, 7 deaths occurred among 87 patients with hepatitis (about 12% case-fatality), and state that the risk of hepatitis, including fatal disease, for American populations is well-documented by this surveillance study conducted across 26 health clinics in the United States.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid used for preventive (prophylactic) antituberculosis therapy in adult tuberculin reactors. USPHS surveillance trial: 7 deaths among 87 patients with hepatitis (case-fatality estimated at about 12%, or 8% if 27 additional severely ill patients and the 114 total are considered). The authors note even the surveillance estimates are likely low because more than 50% of patients dropped out during the year of treatment, so the actual isoniazid liver injury risk may be higher. The paper is a letter to the editor responding to comments by Dr. Farer.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes INH-induced hepatotoxicity, which manifests mainly as hepatocellular necrosis, as seen in the present clinical case, and states that INH causes liver injury in an unpredictable, 'idiosyncratic' manner (in contrast to predictable dose-dependent agents such as acetaminophen).
raw_record.extra_details: Index case developed acute liver failure about 20 days after onset of jaundice and presented hepatotoxicity after five months of treatment. Known risk factors cited: advanced age, female gender (not stated as applicable here), alcohol use, cirrhosis or pre-existing liver disease, Asian racial background, chronic viral hepatitis, and concurrent use of other hepatotoxic medications. Genetic susceptibility attributed to slow acetylator status of N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2) combined with cytochrome P450 2E1 (CYP2E1) C/D or C/C genotype. Latency reported as approximately one week to three months in most cases, up to one year or more. A similar cited case (Li et al.) of a 67-year-old man on isoniazid and pyridoxine for latent TB for three months developed acute liver failure and underwent liver transplantation about six weeks after symptom onset.

raw_record.support_text: In 1975, Mitchell et al. prospectively followed psychiatric hospital patients treated with isoniazid (INH) during a tuberculosis outbreak, collecting blood before starting INH and up to 1 week after study termination. INH (isoniazid) resulted in elevated liver enzymes in 38% of patients, which subsided in the majority despite continued INH treatment, including several who developed concomitant hyperbilirubinemia (Hy's Law cases). The text notes that although INH toxicity can result in severe liver injury and even liver failure, no cases of liver failure were reported in this study.
raw_record.extra_details: Classic example of adaptation: 38% of patients developed elevated liver enzymes, resolving in the majority despite continued INH; several developed concomitant hyperbilirubinemia (Hy's Law). Though INH toxicity can cause severe liver injury and even liver failure, no liver failure cases occurred in this study. Patients were psychiatric hospital patients treated during a tuberculosis outbreak; liver enzymes followed every 4 weeks. Figure 1 shows AST and bilirubin trends (AST >60 and bilirubin >1.2 mg/dl, with three Hy's Law cases having bilirubin >2x ULN) plotted by Dr John Senior (FDA).

raw_record.support_text: The study found no significant difference in the frequency of liver injury due to isoniazid between African-Americans and Caucasians (6.2 vs. 3.6%, P=0.16), consistent with isoniazid being a recognized cause of DILI in the DILIN cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: Frequency of liver injury 6.2% in African-Americans vs 3.6% in Caucasians (P=0.16); no significant difference.

raw_record.support_text: The study investigates human patients with INH (isoniazid)-induced liver failure, presenting a series of 20 acute liver failure (ALF) patients attributed to isoniazid therapy. Sera from these patients were analyzed for anti-INH and anti-CYP antibodies; the paper frames the injury as 'INH-induced liver failure' and reports that elevated peak ALT, bilirubin, and INR values occurred in these patients following isoniazid treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: 20 patients with INH-induced acute liver failure were studied; isoniazid dosed typically at 300 mg/day for durations up to ~8 months for tuberculosis prophylaxis/treatment. Peak ALT up to 144 U/L was recorded in milder cases; liver-failure patients showed markedly elevated ALT, bilirubin, and INR. Sera were tested for anti-INH antibodies (positive in patients ALF-2, ALF-3, ALF-7, ALF-9, ALF-10, ALF-14, ALF-18, ALF-19) and for autoantibodies against CYP2E1, CYP3A4, and CYP2C9. Many ALF patients also took concomitant medications (rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, and others), but the paper attributes the liver failure to isoniazid. In vitro covalent binding of INH to CYP2E1, CYP2C9, and CYP3A4 was shown, and patients with liver failure displayed antibodies against INH-modified CYP2E1.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid failed to induce in vitro transformation of peripheral blood lymphocytes from 14 patients in whom hepatic function tests became abnormal while taking isoniazid for chemoprophylaxis of tuberculosis; 12 of the 14 patients had definite clinical and laboratory evidence of hepatitis. The paper frames these cases as liver damage induced by isoniazid, and notes its study lends no support to a previously implied immunologic mechanism for isoniazid-induced liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid used as chemoprophylaxis for tuberculosis. 14 patients developed abnormal hepatic function tests while on isoniazid, 12 with definite clinical and laboratory hepatitis. The paper's own headline finding is a mechanistic negative: isoniazid failed to induce in vitro transformation of peripheral blood lymphocytes, lending no support to an immunologic mechanism of isoniazid-induced liver damage. This mechanistic-negative conclusion concerns the immunologic hypothesis, not a negative DILI-causality verdict for isoniazid itself.

raw_record.support_text: Western drugs ranked by frequency of DILI induction found DILI-inducing antituberculotics included INH (isoniazid), RFP (rifampicin), PZA (pyrazinamide) and ethambutol (EMB), mostly in combinations of INH+RFP+PZA+EMB, INH+RFP+EMB and INH+EMB among 72 patients (17.0%).
raw_record.extra_details: Antituberculotic, listed as INH. Antituberculotics accounted for 72 patients (17.0%) of DILI cases. DILI-inducing antituberculotics were mostly used as combinations INH+RFP+PZA+EMB, INH+RFP+EMB and INH+EMB.

raw_record.support_text: In 2004, drug-induced liver injury accounted for 15% of liver transplants in the OPTN and UNOS database. Acetaminophen accounted for 50% of drug-related transplants, followed by isoniazid (17%).
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid accounted for 17% of drug-related liver transplants in the OPTN/UNOS 2004 data for drug-induced liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: Antiorganelle antibodies were absent or rare in hepatitis due to isoniazid, with at least four cases examined. The text attributes drug-induced hepatitis to isoniazid.
raw_record.extra_details: Drug-induced hepatitis in which LKM-type antiorganelle antibodies were absent or rare; at least four cases examined.

raw_record.support_text: In a consecutive series of patients with acute liver failure (ALF) and tuberculosis admitted to a liver intensive care unit between 1986 and 2008, 14 of 16 patients had an established diagnosis of anti-TB drug-induced ALF. The paper states that hepatitis was caused by isoniazid (INH) treatment in 4 patients and by pyrazinamide (PZA) in 10 patients. Mean time from initiation of anti-TB treatment to the development of jaundice was 3.5 ± 3.1 months.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis attributed to INH in 4 of 14 patients with anti-TB drug-induced ALF. Patients were receiving anti-tuberculosis treatment (ATT) for tuberculosis, some immunosuppressed (renal transplant recipients, HIV infection). Two additional patients (miliary TB presenting as liver failure; carbamazepine-induced ALF in DRESS syndrome) were excluded from the study.

raw_record.support_text: Of nine acute liver failure cases considered hepatotoxicity, one case was attributed to isoniazid and one case was attributed to allopurinol in the study cohort of 40 patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Single attributed case among 9 hepatotoxicity cases in a retrospective cohort of 40 acute liver failure patients; acute liver failure (ALF) was the reported phenotype.

raw_record.support_text: A 59-year-old Asian woman with cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis started on rifampicin, isoniazid and pyrazinamide developed a rash and all three drugs were stopped with normal liver tests; 1 month later isoniazid alone was restarted and 28 days later she presented with a hepatitic picture (bilirubin 310 µmol/L, ALP 314 IU/L, ALT 2175 IU/L), then progressed to grade 3 encephalopathy, coagulopathy (INR 3.0) and increasing jaundice, fulfilling emergency-liver-transplantation criteria for fulminant hepatic failure. She was successfully transplanted and explant histology showed severe confluent necrosis with extensive collapse, consistent with drug-induced hepatotoxicity, and granulomatous infiltration.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid rechallenge-like pattern: restarted alone after a rash led to stopping all three anti-tuberculous drugs; hepatitis appeared 28 days later (ALT rose to 2386 IU/L, bilirubin to 399 µmol/L, ALP 350 IU/L, INR 3.0, grade 3 encephalopathy); fulminant hepatic failure meeting emergency transplantation criteria; successful orthotopic liver transplant; explant showed severe confluent necrosis with extensive collapse and granulomatous infiltration consistent with drug-induced hepatotoxicity. Indication: cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis.

raw_record.support_text: Among the 71 tuberculosis patients, 11 (15.4%) (eight males/three females, mean age 36 ± 17.5 years, range 13 to 72 years) were diagnosed with isoniazid-induced hepatotoxicity (IIH). The mean daily dose of INH in this group was 264.8 ± 78.9 mg (150 to 375 mg) and the mean INH concentration (C3) was 3.6 ± 2.2 µg ml⁻¹ (1.7 to 9 µg ml⁻¹), compared with 2.3 ± 1.1 µg ml⁻¹ in the 60 patients without IIH.
raw_record.extra_details: In a cohort of 71 tuberculosis patients on isoniazid-containing therapy, 11 (15.4%) were diagnosed with isoniazid-induced hepatotoxicity (IIH). IIH patients had higher mean INH concentration (C3 3.6 ± 2.2 µg/ml vs 2.3 ± 1.1 µg/ml in non-IIH). 42/71 (59%) showed a NAT2 slow acetylator (NAT_SA) phenotype, 27 (38%) intermediate, and 2 (3%) rapid.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective cohort of TB patients, 38 developed DILI due to anti-TB drugs. The causative drug was identified as isoniazid in eight patients, rifampicin in 14 and pyrazinamide in 16 per next-generation sequencing analysis framed around the hypothesis that mtDNA variants are risk factors for isoniazid-, rifampicin- or pyrazinamide-induced DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: In 38 TB patients who developed DILI during anti-TB therapy, isoniazid was the attributed causative drug in 8. DILI was defined as ALT >=5x ULN, or ALT >=3x ULN with total bilirubin >=2x ULN. Isoniazid-induced liver injury cases had more variants in complex I NADH subunit 5 and 1 genes, more nonsynonymous mutations in NADH subunit 5, and a higher nonsynonymous/total substitution ratio, consistent with the hypothesis that hydrazine, an isoniazid metabolite and complex II inhibitor, predisposes to injury.

raw_record.support_text: Girling cites the Finnish Riska chemoprophylaxis study with well over 30,000 subjects randomized to isoniazid or placebo, which showed an added risk of hepatitis from isoniazid of 5.2 per 1000 subjects per year on isoniazid alone. He also notes that in the Hong Kong trial of prophylaxis in silicotic patients with isoniazid, rifampicin, both, or placebo, there was a little hepatotoxicity with isoniazid.
raw_record.extra_details: Finnish Riska prophylaxis study randomized over 30,000 subjects to isoniazid or placebo; added risk of hepatitis from isoniazid was 5.2 per 1000 subjects per year on isoniazid alone. In the Hong Kong trial in silicotic patients given isoniazid, rifampicin, isoniazid plus rifampicin, or placebo, there was a little hepatotoxicity with isoniazid alone and with isoniazid plus rifampicin.

raw_record.support_text: In the IUAT study (Thompson 1982), hepatotoxicity was prospectively assessed as the most serious adverse effect of isoniazid (INH) preventive therapy, in which patients took 0, 3, 6, or 12 month INH regimens. The first-year placebo rate of hepatitis was 0.12%, whereas rates for 3, 6, and 12 month INH courses were 0.25%, 0.36%, and 0.52% respectively. A total of 95 of 20,840 patients receiving INH developed hepatitis and 3 died; no serum liver enzyme monitoring or discontinuation for biochemical or clinical hepatotoxicity signs was done in this study.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective hepatitis assessment in the IUAT preventive-therapy trial (0, 3, 6, 12 month INH regimens). Hepatitis rates increased with INH duration: placebo 0.12%, 3-month 0.25%, 6-month 0.36%, 12-month 0.52% in the first year. 95 of 20,840 INH recipients developed hepatitis and 3 died. No serum liver enzyme monitoring or medication discontinuation for biochemical/clinical hepatotoxicity was performed.

raw_record.support_text: The letter discusses isoniazid-associated hepatitis, describing clinically overt hepatic injury in 114 patients reported by Black, Mitchell, and Zimmerman, of whom 13 of 114 (12%) died. Most of the 114 cases came from the U.S. Public Health Service prospective surveillance of 13,838 isoniazid recipients, with the authors adding 27 other patients that accounted for 6 of the 13 fatalities. The author argues these added cases should not be included in calculating the case-fatality rate, and that the expected case-fatality rate for isoniazid-associated hepatitis is probably considerably lower than the article indicated. In a related passage the author states that no one would disagree that hepatic damage can be caused by isoniazid, that it can be serious, and that it can be fatal.
raw_record.extra_details: Letter to the editor critiquing the case-fatality-rate calculation. Black, Mitchell, and Zimmerman series of 114 clinically overt hepatic injury cases: 13/114 (12%) died; the 114 included 87 U.S. Public Health Service prospective-surveillance cases among 13,838 isoniazid recipients plus 27 added cases with unknown denominator accounting for 6 of the 13 fatalities; among the 87 PHS cases there were 7 fatalities, all but 1 in a single city. Author concludes the true expected case-fatality rate is uncertain and probably lower than reported, especially now that the problem is widely recognized. Context: isoniazid used for tuberculosis preventive therapy; fatality is cited as evidence hepatic damage can be serious and fatal.

raw_record.support_text: The DILIN Retrospective Study establishes a nationwide registry of patients who had suffered in the past severe idiosyncratic liver injury associated with the administration of isoniazid, among other named drugs. Paragraph 59 lists isoniazid as one of the implicated medications for DILI cases enrolled into the retrospective protocol (10 cases).
raw_record.extra_details: 10 DILI cases enrolled in the DILIN retrospective protocol.

raw_record.support_text: The editorial reports an analysis of hepatotoxicity from the PREVENT TB study in patients treated for latent tuberculous infection (LTBI). Among 6862 patients who took at least one dose, hepatotoxicity was lower in the once-weekly rifapentine-plus-isoniazid (3HP1) group than in the daily isoniazid for 9 months (9H) group (0.4% vs 1.9%, P<0.001), for both symptomatic and asymptomatic cases. The editorial also states generally that hepatotoxicity limits completion of daily isoniazid LTBI therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Daily isoniazid monotherapy for 9 months (9H) for LTBI preventive chemotherapy. In the PREVENT TB study (6862 patients taking at least one dose), hepatotoxicity was 1.9% in the 9H group vs 0.4% in the 3HP1 (weekly rifapentine+isoniazid) group, P<0.001, seen in both symptomatic and asymptomatic patients; monitoring of liver enzymes varied by site (baseline AST measured for 76% of participants; repeat AST for 40% on 9H and 35% on 3HP1). Multivariable risk factors: abnormal baseline AST (relative risk 5.57, 95% CI 3.31–9.37), increased age, female sex, white race, non-Hispanic ethnicity, history of chronic liver disease; nested case-control identified hepatitis C as a risk factor (OR 3.24, 95% CI 1.12–9.34). Editorial notes hepatotoxicity limits completion rates of daily 6–9 month isoniazid LTBI therapy.

raw_record.support_text: Among 680 trial participants receiving isoniazid preventive therapy, hepatotoxicity resulting in isoniazid discontinuation occurred in 47 (7%) participants. Isoniazid discontinuation due to a grade 3 or higher adverse event occurred in 53 (8%) participants, and there was significant heterogeneity in hepatotoxicity by study site, with one rural site having significantly greater hepatotoxicity rates.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity resulting in isoniazid discontinuation occurred in 47 (7%) of 680 participants during isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT); 53 (8%) discontinued isoniazid due to a grade 3 or higher adverse event overall. No significant association between randomisation group (alcohol reduction and/or isoniazid adherence incentives) and hepatotoxicity leading to isoniazid discontinuation after adjusting for sex and site; significant site heterogeneity, with one rural site showing greater hepatotoxicity rates.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that hepatotoxicity is the most common adverse effect of anti-TB treatment that leads to interruption of therapy, and that retreatment is started only after all biochemical markers of liver injury have returned to normal. It frames the reintroduction of isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide therapy after hepatic injury as carrying a risk of additional morbidity, attributing drug-induced hepatitis to these anti-TB drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: Anti-TB drug whose therapy is reintroduced after drug-induced hepatitis resolves; recurrence of DIH was observed on reintroduction. In this study 156/175 (89%) patients tolerated reintroduction without recurrence of DIH, giving approximately 11% recurrence. Biochemistry used as the trigger for reintroduction (liver injury markers returned to normal).

raw_record.support_text: In group B, sera were taken from 17 patients with acute hepatitis of known etiology, 3 of whom had drug-induced hepatitis. The cases of drug-induced hepatitis were respectively associated with isoniazid, perhexiline maleate, and phenothiazine.
raw_record.extra_details: One of three drug-induced hepatitis cases included as known-etiology control sera in a serological study of NANB hepatitis; part of the group labelled acute hepatitis of known etiology.

raw_record.support_text: The paper notes that although isoniazid was long considered virtually nontoxic, increasing reports of hepatotoxicity have appeared, and the authors collected information on individuals who died when isoniazid was not discontinued after clinical hepatitis became evident.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid hepatotoxicity described as an unpredictable hypersensitivity phenomenon whose frequency is not yet determined but appears to vary between 0% and 1%, differing by location, time, and patient type; deaths occurred when the drug was not discontinued after clinical hepatitis became evident. The paper additionally notes that hepatitis must result from isoniazid to attribute it, and that two patients reported by Kester had liver dysfunction coincidental with isoniazid and not caused by the drug.

raw_record.support_text: In an ALFSG cohort, which categorized patients into DILI-ALF and APAP-ALF groups, isoniazid was named among the causative drugs responsible for non-APAP hepatotoxicity progressing to acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among causative drugs for non-APAP hepatotoxicity in the ALFSG DILI-ALF cohort (this study subgroup N=39; larger study N=52).

raw_record.support_text: In the U.S. Public Health Service-sponsored study of isoniazid preventive therapy, the incidence of hepatotoxicity was 1.2% per year for persons 35 to 49 years of age and 2.3% per year for persons above 50 years of age. The authors note these figures tend to underestimate the actual incidence of isoniazid hepatitis, since roughly half of these patients failed to finish their year of therapy. This attributes isoniazid therapeutic (preventive) use to human hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of hepatotoxicity from the US Public Health Service-sponsored study of isoniazid preventive therapy: 1.2% per year for persons aged 35-49 and 2.3% per year for persons over 50; figures likely underestimate actual isoniazid hepatitis because about half of the patients did not finish their year of therapy. The authors also report giving isoniazid 15 mg/kg (average 900-1000 mg) twice a week with ethambutol or streptomycin to 203 patients (79 aged 35-49, 103 over 50), most completing 18 months, with no hepatotoxicity appearing, and attribute this possibly reduced incidence to the intermittent higher-dose regimen.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective cohort of 1,000 patients receiving isoniazid chemoprophylaxis followed with monthly liver function tests and clinical evaluation, 222 (22.2%) had at least one elevated SGOT level during treatment; 47 asymptomatic persons had isoniazid discontinued for consistent elevations greater than five times normal, and 17 others had symptoms with elevated SGOT and also had therapy stopped. No patient became seriously ill and there were no deaths. The authors conclude that biochemical monitoring should be routine in isoniazid chemoprophylaxis to avoid irreversible hepatic reactions.
