raw_record.extra_details: Prospective cohort at US Air Force Medical Center Scott. 222/1000 (22.2%) had at least one elevated SGOT; 47 asymptomatic patients discontinued for SGOT >5x normal; 17 had symptoms with elevated SGOT and therapy stopped; no serious illness and no deaths in this cohort. Text also notes life-threatening hepatitis develops in a few isoniazid patients. SGOT upper limit of normal 20 IU/ml (Karmen method). Indication: tuberculosis chemoprophylaxis per American Thoracic Society criteria.

raw_record.support_text: A single case of drug-induced hepatitis was attributed to isoniazid after 11 days of use, among 982 patients who received the drug in hospital.
raw_record.extra_details: One case of drug-induced hepatitis attributed to isoniazid after 11 days of use; 982 patients were exposed in hospital. BCDSP monitoring cohort.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid is described as a leading cause of hepatotoxicity and acute liver failure. In a study from the US DILI Network (DILIN), isoniazid was the second most frequently reported hepatotoxic agent in the registry, with cases likely under-reported. Investigators found a significant delay in discontinuing isoniazid after hepatitis-related symptoms developed: over 50% of patients who met criteria that would warrant immediate drug cessation continued isoniazid for more than 7 days, and 24 patients (40%) continued for more than 14 days; 9 of 13 patients who continued for more than 7 days were listed as having died or needing a liver transplant.
raw_record.extra_details: Leading cause of hepatotoxicity and acute liver failure. Second most frequently reported hepatotoxic agent in the US DILIN registry; cases likely under-reported. Self-reported symptom monitoring was relied upon rather than formal ALT testing. Delay in discontinuation: over 50% of patients meeting symptom criteria for immediate drug stop continued isoniazid >7 days, 24 patients (40%) >14 days; 9 of 13 patients continuing >7 days died or needed liver transplant. Symptoms: nausea, abdominal pain, jaundice, unexplained fatigue.

raw_record.support_text: Among adjudicated DILI cases in the Spanish DILI Registry, isoniazid was named as a culprit agent responsible for DILI in one patient (n=1).
raw_record.extra_details: One case within the Spanish DILI Registry cohort of 8 DILI patients.

raw_record.support_text: A table of the top 48 drugs worldwide causing idiosyncratic DILI with verified causality assessed by RUCAM lists isoniazid with 19 RUCAM-based DILI cases, categorized as a CYP substrate (CYP+), referenced to Hopley (99).
raw_record.extra_details: 19 RUCAM-verified DILI cases; CYP substrate (CYP+); HLA pharmacogenetic association noted in some patients (p32).

raw_record.support_text: In this case report of a 49-year-old woman with tuberculous salpingitis, based on clinical follow-up and liver histology, isoniazid (INH)-induced severe hepatotoxicity could be confirmed, and it further contributed to the abdominal symptoms. The paper states that INH hepatic injury is histologically indistinguishable from viral hepatitis and is related to individual susceptibility of patients who hydrolyze the drug to isonicotinic acid at different rates. After adaptation of the standard therapeutic regimen no further complications occurred.
raw_record.extra_details: 49-year-old woman on a standard anti-tuberculosis regimen; INH hepatotoxicity confirmed by clinical follow-up and liver histology, described as histologically indistinguishable from viral hepatitis and related to individual susceptibility based on differing rates of hydrolysis of the drug to isonicotinic acid. The hepatic injury further contributed to the patient's abdominal symptoms. After adaptation of the standard therapeutic regimen no further complications occurred.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 224 cases of fulminant hepatic failure, etiology could be determined in 49 cases. In six cases (3%), drug toxicity was the offending agent: isoniazid (INH) in 4 cases and acetaminophen in 2 cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as the offending drug in 4 of 6 drug-toxicity cases (3% of 224 FHF cases) in a fulminant hepatic failure cohort; etiology was determined in only 49 of 224 cases. The FHF cohort showed multifocal confluent hepatic necrosis with or without regeneration as the dominant histologic pattern, but histology was not separately attributed to individual drugs.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN prospective registry, isoniazid was the second most common individual DILI agent, accounting for 48 of 899 adjudicated cases. Isoniazid is classified under antimicrobials, the class responsible for most cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 48 adjudicated DILI cases in the DILIN registry; second most common individual agent.

raw_record.support_text: A modified version of the lymphocyte transformation test (LTT) measuring granzyme B and cytokines after incubation of PBMCs with possibly causative drugs failed to demonstrate lymphocyte sensitization against the implicated drugs, and positive tests were only observed in two cases of isoniazid DILI. The paper thus explicitly identifies isoniazid as an agent with human DILI cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Mentioned in the context of the modified LTT: a positive test was observed in only two cases of isoniazid DILI out of the implicated-drug cases tested; the modified LTT otherwise failed to demonstrate lymphocyte sensitization. Parent drugs rather than reactive metabolites were noted as a possible cause of false-positive rates.

raw_record.support_text: Jinjuvadia and colleagues used ICD-9 codes to identify DILI cases in a University of Michigan database, attributing DILI cases secondary to isoniazid among the four drugs of special interest (Augmentin, Dilantin, valproic acid, isoniazid), which together accounted for 51 of 119 DILI cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid is one of four drugs (with Augmentin, phenytoin, valproic acid) to which 51 of 119 DILI cases were attributed in an ICD-9 coded hospital database study (1994-2000).

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective study of 113 patients taking preventive isoniazid (INH) for at least 8 weeks, 19 of 101 patients with initially normal liver tests developed significant liver dysfunction, mostly hepatocellular, with three developing overt hepatitis. After excluding 12 patients who drank alcohol, 15 of 89 still developed significant liver dysfunction, 12 of whom were slow acetylators (p<0.05), and age was the only other risk factor. The paper concludes that fast acetylation is not a risk factor for INH-induced liver dysfunction.
raw_record.extra_details: Preventive INH 300 mg orally daily (or 5 mg/kg for children) in outpatients, followed prospectively; the paper cites an ~1% incidence of overt and 10-20% incidence of subclinical liver damage with INH therapy. Among 113 completing 2 months, 19/101 with normal initial tests developed significant liver dysfunction (3 overt hepatitis); excluding 12 alcohol drinkers, 15/89 remained affected, 12 being slow acetylators. Risk of INH-induced liver enzyme elevation by acetylator phenotype and age (alcohol excluded): under 35 fast acetylators 3.7%, slow 13%; over 35 fast 13.2%, slow 37% (p<0.02). Slow acetylation and older age were risk factors; fast acetylation was not a risk factor. Mitchel evidence on monoacetylhydrazine (P-450 mediated acylating agent causing liver necrosis) is discussed as a proposed mechanism, not an independent human DILI claim.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 563 patients treated with confirmed hepatotoxic tuberculostatics (isoniazid, protionamide, pyrazinamide, cycloserine, p-aminosalicylic acid), icterus was observed in 29 cases. The damages generally occur dose-independently and with variable latency, in the sense of indirect toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among 'gesichert hepatotoxische Tuberkulostatika' (confirmed hepatotoxic tuberculostatics); icterus occurred in 29 of 563 patients in the study group receiving these agents; damage generally dose-independent with variable latency.

raw_record.support_text: In the Toxic Hepatitis group (D), three patients had biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis caused respectively by diphenylhydantoin, INH (isoniazid), and methyldopa. Liver biopsies in each case showed hepatobiliary necrosis with eosinophils and occasional fat accumulation, and all three had extremely high GGTP values (1018, 980, and 645 mU/ml) with alkaline phosphatase values of 284, 560, and 251 IU.
raw_record.extra_details: Biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis attributed to INH (isoniazid); histology showed hepatobiliary necrosis with eosinophils and occasional fat accumulation; GGTP 980 mU/ml and AP 560 IU.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of LTBI prophylaxis in patients about to receive anti-TNF therapy, the six patients who developed active TB despite prophylaxis were characterized; the table footnote notes that Patient 1, who received the 9H regimen (9 months of isoniazid), stopped treatment permanently due to hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid was given as the 9H regimen (9 months) for latent tuberculous infection (LTBI) prophylaxis before anti-TNF therapy in Patient 1 (ankylosing spondylitis, male, 34 years). Treatment was permanently interrupted specifically due to hepatotoxicity; no details on laboratory values, histology, or recovery were reported.

raw_record.support_text: A 53-year-old female underwent orthotopic liver transplantation (OLT, May 1997) for fulminant hepatic failure owing to isoniazid hepatotoxicity, establishing isoniazid as the attributed cause of acute liver failure requiring transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure attributed to isoniazid hepatotoxicity in this patient; resulted in orthotopic liver transplantation (OLT, May 1997); this transplant is the reason the patient was later exposed to the immunosuppressants discussed in the report.

raw_record.support_text: In an open-label randomized trial comparing 4 months of daily rifampin with 9 months of daily isoniazid (5 mg/kg, up to 300 mg/day) for latent tuberculosis infection, three patients developed drug-induced hepatitis, and all three were taking isoniazid. Adverse events resulted in permanent discontinuation of therapy for eight (14%) patients taking isoniazid.
raw_record.extra_details: Three of 58 patients randomized to 9 months of daily isoniazid (5 mg/kg, up to 300 mg/day) for latent tuberculosis infection developed drug-induced hepatitis, all in the isoniazid arm; eight (14%) isoniazid patients permanently discontinued due to adverse events.

raw_record.support_text: The study reports that the overall rate of INH-related hepatitis was 0.3%, while that associated with treatment of latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) was 0.1%, attributing episodes of hepatitis to isoniazid (INH) in patients receiving first-line antituberculosis drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: Overall INH-related hepatitis rate 0.3%; rate associated with LTBI treatment 0.1%. Cohort of 764 patients treated for active and latent tuberculosis, of whom 55 (7.2%) had at least one major side effect.

raw_record.support_text: An unexpectedly high incidence of hepatitis occurred among Capitol Hill employees receiving isoniazid chemoprophylaxis, recognized because of 2 deaths and subsequent investigation. Chemical analyses of the pills and manufacturing procedures revealed no recognizable source of hepatotoxicity, and the CDC subsequently received more than 100 additional reports of hepatitis developing in patients taking isoniazid from several different distributors. The paper concludes the problem may be more widespread than previously reported and that close supervision is needed, framing hepatitis as an induced complication of isoniazid therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Capitol Hill outbreak: 2,321 tuberculin-reactive employees started isoniazid chemoprophylaxis in Feb 1970; during the following 9 months 19 developed clinical signs of liver disease, with symptoms of fatigue, anorexia, fever, and GI discomfort; 13 of 19 had icterus and 2 died. Mean age 49.4 years; 10 women and 9 men. No person-to-person or common-association link except prior isoniazid use. Comparison group of 2,154 non-tuberculin-reactive employees not taking isoniazid had only 1 case of hepatitis in the same 9-month period, and none among 260 tuberculin reactors who declined therapy. Chemical analysis of the lots and manufacturing review found no hepatotoxic source; CDC later received over 100 additional reports from several distributors. Authors note causal role of isoniazid remains to be more precisely defined by prospective studies and recommend monthly monitoring during preventive therapy.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that despite the possible inclusion of sporadic viral hepatitis cases, the cases of hepatitis that recurred after rechallenge with the drug provide overwhelming evidence that isoniazid does occasionally cause severe hepatitis, which may be fatal. Among their three fatal cases, death appeared primarily related to the severe hepatitis, though one was complicated by a perforated duodenal ulcer.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid prophylaxis/therapy for tuberculosis. Three fatal cases in the authors' series; death was primarily related to severe hepatitis, though one case was complicated by a perforated duodenal ulcer. Hepatitis recurred after rechallenge with isoniazid, supporting causality. In a separate series reported in the same letter from a United Farm Workers Union clinic (Delano, California), of 249 patients treated with isoniazid, three developed hepatitis (1.2%); 6000 families/60000 patient visits were followed over 2 years. Possible inclusion of sporadic viral hepatitis could not be ruled out.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid (INH)-induced liver injury ranks at place #13 among the drugs most implicated in idiosyncratic DILI with 19 DILI cases assessed for causality using RUCAM to verify the diagnosis. Patients with acute liver failure due to INH use were included in a study, but confirmation of the DILI diagnosis by RUCAM was lacking for that cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: INH; ranked #13 among drugs most implicated in idiosyncratic DILI; 19 DILI cases verified by RUCAM; metabolized preferentially by CYP 2E1, also CYP 3A4 and possibly CYP 2D9; in sera of 15/19 acute-liver-failure patients anti-CYP isoform antibodies were found (11 anti-CYP 2E1, 14 against CYP 2E1 modified by INH, 14 anti-CYP 3A4, 10 anti-CYP 2C9), but RUCAM confirmation was lacking for that cohort.

raw_record.support_text: Of 104 cases of acute hepatic failure in two steroid trials, 12 were attributable to a drug; isoniazid was implicated in one of those patients. Isoniazid is also listed among drugs for which anecdotal cases show benefit from drug withdrawal and steroid treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated in 1 of 12 drug-attributable acute hepatic failure cases among 104 acute liver failure cases in two steroid trials. Anti-tuberculosis drug also highlighted in monitoring recommendations (isoniazid alone in patients older than 35 years) because the risk is significant.

raw_record.support_text: In the multi-center prospective Acute Liver Failure Study Group trial, 133 of 1198 ALF cases were caused by non-APAP hepatotoxins. Among the most commonly implicated agents were anti-tuberculosis drugs (n=25), of which 15 were isoniazid (INH), with causal assessment overall rated 81.2% highly likely, 15% probable and 3.8% possible; 77.8% of the overall registry injuries were hepatocellular.
raw_record.extra_details: 15 of the 25 anti-TB drug ALF cases were isoniazid; ALF defined as INR>=1.5 with hepatic encephalopathy within 26 weeks with no chronic liver disease. Registry-wide causality: 81.2% highly likely, 15% probable, 3.8% possible; 77.8% of registry injuries hepatocellular. Overall ALF mortality ~34%, 42% required transplant, 27.1% spontaneous recovery.

raw_record.support_text: Autoimmune reactions involving CYP2E1 are a feature of DILI induced by halogenated hydrocarbons and isoniazid (INH). From 19 patients enrolled in the Acute Liver Failure Study Group for INH-induced acute liver failure, eight tested positive for anti-INH antibodies; these antibodies were not detectable in patients with only mild INH-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: INH-induced acute liver failure described in 19 patients from the Acute Liver Failure Study Group, of whom 8 had anti-INH antibodies; mild INH-induced liver injury resolves with immune tolerance. CYP2E1 autoimmunity is a feature of INH DILI.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a 40-year-old merchant seaman who developed hepatitis shortly after beginning isoniazid (INH) 300 mg daily for a recent tuberculin skin-test conversion. Challenge with INH was followed by a recurrence of hepatitis that was confirmed by histologic study, and after rises in SGOT each time INH was restarted with return to normal on discontinuation, the authors concluded INH was causing the hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a single patient; INH taken at 300 mg daily starting one month before presentation (February 13, 1968) with anorexia, epigastric pain, gray stools, dark urine and jaundice. Serial SGOT rose to 1885 and 1750 U and total bilirubin to 18.4 and 24.2 mg/100 ml; rechallenge with INH (restarted and stopped) produced recurrent SGOT rises (151, 734, 526 U) with return to normal on discontinuation. Liver biopsy showed moderate mononuclear, rare polymorphonuclear and eosinophilic infiltrate in periportal and centrolobular regions with necrosis and reticulin-fiber collapse. Patient denied fever, skin rash, peripheral eosinophilia, prior jaundice, transfusions and recent injections; consumed only moderate social whiskey. PAS concurrently noted as a well-known potential hepatotoxin in other reported cases, but only INH was administered here.

raw_record.support_text: Among the 55 patients with acute idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (IDILI) studied by blood RNA-Seq, the authors report that isoniazid-induced IDILI demonstrated 25 differentially expressed genes compared to other non-isoniazid IDILI cases, while exploration of DEGs specific for the individual causal agents was largely unsuccessful. These patients had liver injuries attributed to IDILI.
raw_record.extra_details: The study analyzed peripheral blood RNA-Seq from 55 acute IDILI patients; isoniazid-induced IDILI cases showed 25 DEGs versus other non-isoniazid IDILI cases. The paper's focus is transcriptomic biomarkers for IDILI diagnosis/prognosis, not causality assessment.

raw_record.support_text: In the Bronx-Lebanon methadone maintenance program, 58 of 175 patients with positive tuberculin tests discontinued isoniazid chemoprophylaxis for various reasons, such as incarceration, death, or liver toxicity attributed to isoniazid. This explicitly attributes human liver toxicity (hepatotoxicity) to isoniazid in the setting of tuberculosis chemoprophylaxis.
raw_record.extra_details: In a methadone maintenance program cohort, 58 of 175 tuberculin-positive patients discontinued isoniazid chemoprophylaxis for reasons including incarceration, death, or liver toxicity to isoniazid. Isoniazid was given for 6 months in HIV-negative patients and 12 months in HIV-positive patients with positive tuberculin tests.

raw_record.support_text: Among 60 isoniazid (INH) hepatotoxicity patients, patterns of liver injury at presentation were predominantly hepatocellular, with 55 (92%) patients having an R ratio greater than 5, and 4 (7%) having a mixed pattern (R ratio 2-5); no patient had a cholestatic pattern. The mean days from INH initiation to increased ALT was 97 days, and from DILI onset to peak ALT was short (mean 6.6 days).
raw_record.extra_details: 60 INH hepatotoxicity patients from the DILIN registry. 55/60 (92%) hepatocellular (R ratio >5); 4 (7%) mixed (R ratio 2-5); none cholestatic. Mean days INH initiation to increased ALT 97 d (SD 64); to ALT ≥5x ULN 103 d (SD 59); DILI onset to peak ALT mean 6.6 d (SD 9). DILIN Severity Index scores reported; 12 patients required liver transplant (1 died post-transplant) and another patient died without transplant; 37 (62%) hospitalized; 14 (23%) encephalopathy. Mean peak ALT 1385 IU/L, bilirubin 12.7 mg/dL, INR 2.6. Delay in stopping INH after ATS stopping criteria correlated with higher SIS (P=.05); among those continuing INH >1 week, 49% had severe/fatal course vs 22% stopping within 7 days; higher BMI correlated with increased SIS (P=.02).

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes immunohistochemical staining of a liver slide from a patient (patient number 2) with INH-induced liver failure, attributed to isoniazid (INH) treatment. The paper further frames isoniazid as a well-known cause of idiosyncratic liver injury, stating 'The basis for the idiosyncratic nature of INH-induced liver injury is unknown' and that INH treatment is well known to cause a lupus-like syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: A patient (patient number 2) with isoniazid (INH)-induced acute liver failure was studied. Serum from eight patients positive for anti-INH antibodies was phenotyped; IgG antibodies dominated, and the IgG3 subtype predominated, implicating an immune mechanism. IgG3 and IgM can activate complement and antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity and can bind hepatocytes and induce cell necrosis. The paper proposes a Th1 (IFN-γ-driven) immune mechanism for INH-induced liver injury and notes INH treatment is well known to cause a lupus-like syndrome, though liver injury is not considered autoimmune.

raw_record.support_text: Within the 18 cases of fulminant hepatic failure in the course of orthotopic liver transplantation, the study lists 1 case of isoniazide toxicity as the cause of the fulminant hepatic failure.
raw_record.extra_details: 1 of 18 fulminant hepatic failure cases undergoing orthotopic liver transplantation was attributed to isoniazide toxicity; the paper's focus was progenitor-cell/regenerative-cluster histology, not a DILI outcome study.

raw_record.support_text: Of 8 patients who died of isoniazid hepatotoxicity in New York State between 1991 and 1993, 7 had continued to take isoniazid for at least 10 days after the onset of symptoms (nausea, vomiting, fatigue, abdominal pain) before jaundice developed. Fatal isoniazid hepatotoxicity is explicitly attributed to continued isoniazid use despite early warning symptoms.
raw_record.extra_details: 8 patients died of isoniazid hepatotoxicity in New York State, 1991-1993; 7 continued isoniazid for at least 10 days after symptom onset. Accompanying narrative discusses drug-induced hepatitis; jaundice described as a late sign.

raw_record.support_text: In six patients taking INH for chemoprophylaxis, temperatures between 39.2 and 40.8°C were reported to have developed between the eighth and 20th days after initiation of INH therapy. The paper explicitly states that no hepatotoxicity or other untoward effects were seen, and all patients improved when INH was discontinued.
raw_record.extra_details: The paper reports febrile reactions in six patients receiving INH 300 mg/day for tuberculosis chemoprophylaxis (fever onset between days 8 and 20; temperatures 39.2-40.8°C), and independently asserts that no hepatotoxicity or other untoward effects were seen. The two presented cases (CASE 1, CASE 2) likewise had no hepatotoxicity, with fever resolving on INH discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that INH causes a mild, evanescent focal hepatitis associated with asymptomatic aminotransferase elevation in 10-20% of users and clinical hepatitis in about 1% of patients, with a spectrum from mild acute hepatitis to early hepatic failure or a more prolonged subacute course resulting in chronic active hepatitis. It reports that progressive hepatic failure developed secondary to INH in one patient, who underwent successful liver transplantation after submassive necrosis was found in the explant.
raw_record.extra_details: INH hepatotoxicity ranges from mild acute hepatitis to early hepatic failure to chronic active hepatitis; asymptomatic aminotransferase elevation in 10-20% of users and clinical hepatitis in about 1% of patients; therapy is drug discontinuation and supportive care, with liver transplantation as a potentially curative option for hepatic failure. Case 1: 49-year-old man on INH 300 mg/day for ~4 months (positive tuberculin test, no active TB) developed jaundice, ascites, and confusion; total bilirubin 16.1 mg/dl rising to 30.9 mg/dl, AST 2882 to 505 units/liter, ALT 500 units/liter, PT prolonged to 17.9 sec, factor V 26%; explant liver showed submassive necrosis; he underwent transplantation and was doing well 14 months later. INH with rifampin produces hepatotoxicity more frequently than either drug alone.

raw_record.support_text: In a DILIN-causality adjudicated cohort of 345 patients, 37 were classified as probable-DILI using a DILIN expert opinion causality score of 1, 2, or 3. The most commonly identified individual agents were all antibiotics and included trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (8%), ceftriaxone (8%), amoxicillin-clavulanate (5%), isoniazid (5%), and azithromycin (5%).
raw_record.extra_details: One of the most commonly identified individual agents (5%) among 37 probable-DILI cases. Cohort-level: probable-DILI more often hepatocellular at onset (57% vs 32.5%, p=0.01); DILIN severity index up to fatal (6/37 fatal).

raw_record.support_text: Among 133 drug-induced liver injury acute liver failure (DILI ALF) cases adjudicated by site investigators and expert opinion, isoniazid was the only drug used in nine cases, attributing isoniazid as the cause of these DILI ALF cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Nine DILI ALF cases used isoniazid as the only medication. Cohort: 133 DILI ALF subjects among 1198 ALF subjects; expert-opinion causality was highly likely in 108 (81.1%), probable in 20 (15.0%), and possible in 5 (3.8%) overall. Isoniazid was also part of 2-4 drug antituberculosis combinations in three cases.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 240 patients receiving anti-TNF-α therapy in Turkey, one patient developed a drug reaction attributed to etanercept and another patient demonstrated hepatotoxicity attributed to isoniazid, during follow-up of latent tuberculosis treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case of hepatotoxicity; isoniazid was given for latent tuberculosis infection (tuberculin skin test positive) in a patient from a cohort of 240 receiving anti-TNF-α therapy, with 12-month follow-up. The paper's main focus was tuberculosis risk from anti-TNF-α therapy, not DILI characterization.

raw_record.support_text: In a US DILIN cohort of 300 subjects with suspected drug-induced liver injury, a single prescription medication was implicated in 217 subjects. The most common single implicated agents included isoniazid, implicated in 13 cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated in 13 of 300 DILI cases; listed among antituberculosis antimicrobial agents and among the most common single implicated prescription medications in a prospective DILIN registry (causality assessed by expert opinion and RUCAM across the cohort).

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of fatal isoniazid-induced acute liver failure in a 53-year-old Japanese man being treated for latent tuberculosis infection. INH was given at 300 mg/day, and 70 days later the patient developed jaundice and general malaise; INH was continued 10 more days despite hepatitis symptoms. He was hospitalized, INH was stopped, and he died four months later. On admission his AST was 1,581 IU/L and ALT was 2,540 IU/L, and a drug-induced lymphocyte stimulation test for isoniazid was positive (249 S.I.).
raw_record.extra_details: 300 mg/day for latent tuberculosis infection prophylaxis; symptoms (jaundice, general malaise) appeared 70 days after starting, and INH was continued an additional 10 days despite hepatitis symptoms. Admission labs: AST 1,581 IU/L, ALT 2,540 IU/L, ALP 724 IU/L, T-Bil 7.82 mg/dL. Drug-induced lymphocyte stimulation test for INH positive (249 S.I.). Patient was previously healthy, no chronic liver disease, no other medications/supplements, not a heavy alcohol user, not at risk of viral hepatitis. Died four months after hospitalization.

raw_record.support_text: In the European American subset, 32 DILI patients were due to isoniazid, two of whom carried HLA-B*14:01 (carriage frequency 0.063). The paper groups these as DILI patients attributed to isoniazid in the DILIN cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: DILIN registry DILI cohort; 32 European American isoniazid DILI patients (2/32 carrying HLA-B*14:01, CF=0.063); 19 African American isoniazid DILI patients (2/19 carrying HLA-B*35:01, CF=0.105).

raw_record.support_text: In the US Acute Liver Failure Study Group (ALFSG) analysis of non-acetaminophen drug-induced ALF, isoniazid (INH) was implicated in 21 cases, 15 as monotherapy and 6 when used in combination, as one of the most common antimicrobial causes.
raw_record.extra_details: ALFSG 1998-2007: 21 drug-induced ALF cases (15 INH monotherapy, 6 in combination). US DILIN registry: n=13 suspected single-agent DILI. UNOS database: n=48 INH alone and n=2 with another antituberculosis drug as causes of emergency liver transplant for drug-induced ALF. Spain (n=9) and Sweden (n=7) also list INH as an implicated antimicrobial.

raw_record.support_text: Among 182 reported adverse events in both the DOT and SAT groups, 29 were severe enough to warrant permanent treatment termination. There were five subjects with grade III isoniazid hepatotoxicity in the SAT (self-administered therapy) group compared with none in the DOT (directly observed therapy) group. The authors note the absence of grade III hepatitis in the DOT group may reflect early identification of drug-related hepatitis symptoms by the supervising nurse prompting prompt treatment discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Five cases of grade III isoniazid hepatotoxicity among newly arrived Ethiopian immigrants (EIs) receiving latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) treatment in the SAT arm; none in the DOT arm. The study compares directly observed therapy (DOT) vs self-administered therapy (SAT) for LTBI treatment completion. Grade III hepatitis described as drug-related; the paper suggests early detection of hepatitis symptoms led to prompt treatment discontinuation in the DOT group. A 4-month rifampin course was offered to the 29 subjects whose adverse events led to permanent treatment termination.

raw_record.support_text: Among 1198 ALFSG subjects over 10 years, DILI caused ALF in 11% of cases and 61 unique agents were implicated, alone or in combination. Antimicrobials were the commonest cause, in particular isoniazid, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, nitrofurantoin, and antifungal agents.
raw_record.extra_details: Named among antimicrobials as the commonest cause of DILI-induced ALF in the ALFSG cohort (61 unique implicated agents; DILI caused 11% of ALF). Latency of implicated agents ranged from 1-2 weeks to 8 months; most subjects (65%) did not stop the drug until or after jaundice developed.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid is described as a well-known hepatotoxin in the Acute Liver Failure Study Group series (1998-2003) and was, after acetaminophen, the next most common agent among cases of drug-induced ALF leading to emergency liver transplantation in the UNOS database (1990 through October 2002).
raw_record.extra_details: Also listed in Table 5 among drugs with known hepatotoxicity that remain allowed on the market; was the next most common cause of drug-induced ALF leading to emergency transplantation after acetaminophen.

raw_record.support_text: Of 249 patients treated with prophylactic isoniazid, three (1.2%) developed hepatitis. All three cases had elevated SGOT, negative hepatitis B antigen tests, and resolved abnormal laboratory values after isoniazid was withdrawn (dechallenge), consistent with isoniazid-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Prophylactic use (indications prioritized as close contact, recent conversion, positive PPD in child/adolescent, inadequately treated TB, reinfective X-ray with positive PPD, positive PPD with risk factors). Incidence 3/249 (1.2%). Latency: Patient 1 after ~2 years on isoniazid (then 300 mg/day; lethargy, 6 kg weight loss, SGOT 450 Karmen units [normal 8-40], LDH 600 IU, normal bilirubin, negative HBsAg; enzymes normal within a month after withdrawal and weight regained within 3 months). Patient 2: 6 weeks after starting, dark urine, abdominal discomfort, jaundice; SGOT 1600 Karmen units, bilirubin 9.0 mg/100 ml, negative HBsAg; lab values normalized within a month after withdrawal. Patient 3: 7 weeks after starting, jaundice and itching; SGOT 2000 Karmen units, bilirubin 26 mg/100 ml, negative HBsAg; values normal 6 weeks after withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: In contrast to most other drugs causing hepatic injury, the risk of INH (isoniazid) DILI is clearly age related, with older patients at higher risk. Kunst and Khan found INH risk related to age with a rate of 1.7% for those older than 35 years versus 0.2% for a younger population; a large public health department study of 1100 individuals reported hepatotoxic events (AST >5 times the upper limit of normal) per 1000 patients of 4.4 (ages 25-34), 8.54 (ages 35-49), and 20.83 (ages 50 and older).
raw_record.extra_details: INH DILI risk is clearly age related: 1.7% for those older than 35 years vs 0.2% younger population (Kunst and Khan); 1100-person study hepatotoxic events (AST >5x ULN) per 1000 patients: 4.4 (25-34 yr), 8.54 (35-49 yr), 20.83 (50+ yr). No apparent gender difference except pregnant and postpartum women. Alcohol abuse is a significant risk factor; hypoalbuminemia (<3.5 g/dL) predicts ~3-fold higher DILI risk; weight loss of 2 kg or more within 4 weeks of treatment start is a risk factor. ATS recommends ALT monitoring only for high-risk patients: chronic alcohol users, HIV-positive, chronic viral hepatitis or other cause of elevated liver enzymes, and pregnant/postpartum females within 3 months of delivery; patients older than 35 years considered higher risk. Of 10 severe adverse events (2004-2008) among patients treated with INH for latent TB, all were prompted by symptoms rather than laboratory abnormalities; several patients delayed evaluation until jaundice, eventuating in need for liver transplant in some cases.

raw_record.support_text: The study reports that hepatotoxicity, a major concern for patients and clinicians, was uncommon in the study population: only 1.6% of patients who initiated isoniazid (INH) therapy developed treatment-limiting hepatotoxicity. This rate was higher than the 0.1% and 0.3% rates reported in larger studies in Seattle-King County and San Diego, respectively, which the authors attribute to differences in case definitions, patient ages, and therapy duration (9 vs 6 months).
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective cohort of patients treated with INH for latent tuberculosis infection; 1.6% of patients who initiated INH therapy developed treatment-limiting hepatotoxicity; this was compared to reported rates of 0.1% (Seattle-King County) and 0.3% (San Diego) in larger studies using older treatment guidelines; the authors attribute the higher rate to differences in case definitions, patient ages, and duration of therapy (9 vs 6 months). Patients with LTBI who were young, pregnant and/or postpartum, uninsured, or reported treatment side effects were at risk for poor adherence. The study population was largely foreign-born, and findings may not apply to US-born persons with LTBI.

raw_record.support_text: The paper recounts the Baltimore experience with isoniazid-induced hepatitis, reporting 14 patients who developed hepatitis while taking isoniazid. Three died of fulminant hepatic failure, and 8 of 11 survivors showed hepatic necrosis with bridging or multilobular damage on liver biopsy. In three cases, reinstitution of isoniazid therapy was followed by recurrence of hepatitis, and the report identifies isoniazid as the cause of hepatitis that may develop after 4 to 6 months of therapy as well as in the first 2 months.
raw_record.extra_details: 14 patients developed hepatitis while taking isoniazid; 3 died of fulminant hepatic failure; 8 of 11 survivors had hepatic necrosis with bridging or multilobular damage on liver biopsy; in 3 cases reinstitution of isoniazid was followed by recurrence of hepatitis (shown by liver biopsy in 2 and by a prompt and striking SGOT rise in the third). Hepatitis could develop after 4 to 6 months of therapy, not only in the first 2 months. Duration of hepatitis symptoms was longer (mean 4.6 weeks) in patients with bridging or multilobular necrosis than in those with only diffuse hepatitis (mean 2.2 weeks). Prodromal period of fatigue, weakness, anorexia, and malaise preceded jaundice in all patients. The paper notes isoniazid hepatitis is worsened by continuing isoniazid in the face of symptoms.

raw_record.support_text: During therapy, 27 of 1,028 tuberculosis patients had hepatitis as a major toxicity, 20 during daily and seven during twice-weekly therapy. Of these hepatitis cases, 14 were attributed to isoniazid and 8 to rifampin; in five the drug could not be identified. Attribution was based on the impressions of treating physicians, with challenge with one drug at a time confirming the offending drug in 59 of 106 total side-effect patients.
raw_record.extra_details: 14 of 27 hepatitis cases attributed to isoniazid during antituberculosis therapy (table breakdown: daily therapy - jaundice 4, hepatitis/increased enzymes 5; twice-weekly therapy - jaundice 3, hepatitis/increased enzymes 2). Attribution by treating-physician impression with selective single-drug challenge. Two deaths occurred among moribund patients in the unidentified-drug jaundice group and were not attributed to isoniazid.

raw_record.support_text: The paper identifies hepatitis as the risk of greatest concern from isoniazid chemoprophylaxis. A CDC cooperative surveillance study following 13,838 people in 21 health departments found 82 possible and 92 probable isoniazid hepatitis cases, with the authors judging the true incidence best approximated by the probable cases. Age-specific rates (per 1000 persons) were used: one possible and no probable for those under age 20 years; seven possible and three probable for ages 20-34; 11 possible and 12 probable for ages 35-49; 18 possible and 23 probable for ages 50-64; and 18 possible and eight probable for those over 64 years. The probability of terminating chemoprophylaxis because of hepatitis used combined possible and probable rates.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid given as tuberculosis chemoprophylaxis, assumed 70% effective in preventing activation (varied 30%-90% in sensitivity analysis). Hepatitis led to termination of prophylaxis in the analysis. In a CDC cooperative surveillance study of 13,838 people in 21 health departments there were 82 possible and 92 probable isoniazid hepatitis cases; incidence rates per 1000 persons by age (possible/probable): under 20 y: 1/0; 20-34 y: 7/3; 35-49 y: 11/12; 50-64 y: 18/23; over 64 y: 18/8. Rates varied by 75%-125% in sensitivity analysis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper documents isoniazid hepatotoxicity in humans during therapeutic prophylaxis. It reports that enzyme elevations occur in approximately 10% of patients during early weeks of isoniazid administration and are usually transient, but hepatocellular damage was confirmed by liver biopsy in some asymptomatic patients. A report from Johns Hopkins Hospital documented 14 instances of isoniazid hepatitis including 3 deaths in persons taking isoniazid for prophylaxis, and clinical hepatitis appears to occur in close to 1% of patients. In 427 hospital employees receiving isoniazid prophylaxis, 3% showed clinical hepatitis or elevations of bilirubin or alkaline phosphatase (or both) requiring drug discontinuation; a Baltimore series reported 7 deaths among 3000 patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid used for tuberculosis prophylaxis. Clinical hepatitis rate approximately 1%. Enzyme elevations in early weeks in ~10% of patients, usually transient; hepatocellular damage confirmed by liver biopsy in some asymptomatic patients. Johns Hopkins report: 14 instances of isoniazid hepatitis including 3 deaths. Baltimore series: 7 deaths among 3000 patients (USPHS communication). In 427 hospital employees, 3% showed clinical hepatitis or elevated bilirubin/alkaline phosphatase requiring drug discontinuation. Authors note difficulty distinguishing isoniazid toxicity from viral hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Peroxisomes with a condensed matrix were reported in the liver of a patient with isoniazid hepatitis (Sternlieb and Quintana 1977). This review of hepatic ultrastructure attributes the hepatitis in the patient to isoniazid.
raw_record.extra_details: Portion of a review on hepatic ultrastructure; the report (Sternlieb and Quintana 1977) described condensed peroxisomal matrix in the liver of a patient with isoniazid hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Among 14 patients with fulminant hepatitis, the etiologies included drug-induced hepatitis in 4 cases, attributed to acetaminophen (2 cases), isoniazid (1 case), and halothane (1 case).
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as cause of drug-induced fulminant hepatitis in 1 of 14 patients in the study cohort; the study assessed plasma CEA levels in patients with maximum hepatic dysfunction.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN proteomic study of 74 patients with acute non-acetaminophen drug-induced liver injury, the most commonly reported single causative agents were isoniazid and herbal preparations (five patients each); isoniazid is therefore explicitly cited as causing DILI in this human case series, with nearly two-thirds of all cases adjudicated as very likely or definitely drug-related.
raw_record.extra_details: Most commonly reported single causative agent in a DILIN acute DILI series, affecting five of 74 patients; series restricted to acute non-acetaminophen DILI; severity of cases overall rated moderate or severe in 88% and nearly two-thirds assessed very likely or definitely drug-related.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN Prospective Study cohort (1198 participants with definite, highly likely, or probable DILI), the frequency of liver injury due to isoniazid was not different between the heavy alcohol consumption group and those without alcohol consumption (6.3% vs 5%, p=0.8). The text attributes isoniazid as a cause of DILI in these adjudicated human cases.
raw_record.extra_details: From the DILIN Prospective Study; frequency of isoniazid-attributed DILI was 6.3% in the heavy alcohol consumption group (n=80 heavy drinkers) versus 5% in those without alcohol consumption, p=0.8. Part of adjudicated DILI cases (definite, highly likely, or probable).

raw_record.support_text: Of the 690 patients (81.6% of 845 eligible) who initiated INH therapy for latent TB infection at the RISE TB Clinic in Rhode Island in 2003, INH therapy was discontinued in 18 patients (2.6%) overall, of whom 11 patients discontinued because of hepatotoxicity. The study population figure notes therapy was discontinued by the clinician because of hepatotoxicity in 11 patients. This attributes hepatotoxicity to isoniazid therapy in these patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective review of medical records of 873 persons evaluated for LTBI at RISE TB Clinic (Rhode Island, 2003); 690 patients initiated INH therapy, of whom 426 (61.7%) completed and 246 (35.7%) were lost to follow-up. Two-point-six percent (18/690) discontinued therapy: 11 for hepatotoxicity, 4 for pregnancy, 2 for transfer out of state, 1 death unrelated to INH. Age-based monitoring protocol included baseline and serial AST checks (monthly for ages >80, months 1-5 for ages 61-80, baseline+2 mo for 35-60, baseline+2 mo for 20-34, clinical monitoring only for <20) and clinical monitoring every 2 mo.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that the most important adverse effect of isoniazid is hepatitis, and reports hepatotoxicity risk of 0.5% to 1% in the International Union Against Tuberculosis trial (20,840 subjects) and the US Public Health Service (PHS) multicentre study (13,838 persons). Increasing age and daily alcohol consumption are important risk factors, and hepatotoxicity usually occurs in the first 3 months of treatment. PHS data showed isoniazid-associated hepatitis in 0% under 20 years, 0.3% from 20-34, 1.2% from 35-49 and 2.3% from 50-64 years, with hospitalization rates up to 5.0 per 1000 treatment initiations and a mortality rate of 0.6 per 1000 persons (with liver cirrhosis possibly confounding).
raw_record.extra_details: Given at 5 mg/kg daily (max 300 mg) or 15 mg twice weekly (max 900 mg) for 6-12 months of LTBI treatment. Hepatotoxicity risk 0.5-1% (IUAT trial), usually within first 3 months. Age-dependent incidence (0% <20 y, 0.3% 20-34 y, 1.2% 35-49 y, 2.3% 50-64 y). Hospitalization up to 5.0/1000; recent symptomatic hepatitis estimated 1-3/1000, hospitalization 0.1-0.2/1000, mortality 0.0-0.3/1000. Risk factors: increasing age and daily alcohol consumption.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid causes mild liver injury (increased serum transaminases) in approximately 10% of persons taking it, usually transient and asymptomatic, and occasionally clinically apparent hepatitis that mimics acute viral hepatitis, often with severe hepatitis showing bridging and/or multilobular necrosis. In a study of 14 patients with isoniazid hepatitis, 3 died with fulminant hepatic failure and bridging/multilobular necrosis was found in 8 of the 11 survivors; one patient who died after 6 months of drug had cirrhosis at postmortem.
raw_record.extra_details: Mild transaminase elevations occur in ~10% of users, generally unassociated with clinical symptoms and usually subsiding despite continued administration; clinically apparent hepatitis is infrequent and mimics acute viral hepatitis; severe hepatitis with bridging and/or multilobular necrosis common among clinically apparent cases. In a study of 14 isoniazid hepatitis patients, 3 died of fulminant hepatic failure and 8 of 11 survivors had bridging/multilobular necrosis; one 6-month-treated fatal case had cirrhosis at postmortem; no clinical or biochemical evidence of continuing disease in surviving patients, with follow-up biopsy in 2 showing mild residual scarring but no ongoing necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: In the folic acid nutritional-intervention row, a human study involving 3,302 isoniazid-induced liver injury patients is reported; folic acid intervention reduced the frequency of liver event reporting in these patients. The phrase 'isoniazid-induced liver injury patients' explicitly attributes human liver injury to isoniazid.
raw_record.extra_details: 3,302 isoniazid-induced liver injury patients were studied in the context of a folic acid nutritional intervention; folic acid reduced liver event reporting frequency. The attribution of liver injury to isoniazid is provided as study context rather than as the paper's primary claim.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid causes hepatitis with extensive liver necrosis which may be fatal. Scharer and Smith (1969) reported raised SGOT and SGPT in 9 out of 90 patients given isoniazid 300 mg daily for 2 months; serum bilirubin remained normal in all and liver biopsies revealed a hepatocellular pattern of injury without bile stasis. Hyperglycaemia, glycosuria and gynaecomastia have also been described with isoniazid administration.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid 300 mg daily for 2 months; raised SGOT and SGPT in 9 of 90 patients; serum bilirubin remained normal in all; liver biopsies showed hepatocellular pattern without bile stasis; hepatitis with extensive liver necrosis which may be fatal; associated hyperglycaemia, glycosuria and gynaecomastia. Antitubercular use. Source: Scharer and Smith (1969).

raw_record.support_text: Among 20 patients with acute liver failure, drug-induced liver injury was the attributed etiology in 5 (25.0%), including isoniazid in 2 patients. The paper therefore attributes ALF/DILI to isoniazid in these two adult patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as the DILI etiology in 2 of 20 ALF ICU patients; ALF course could be hyperacute, acute, or subacute (2/20 patients had this quantity only per cohort listing). Clinical phenotype is acute liver failure leading to coma/HE severity assessment in this ONSD study.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid (INH) causes human drug-induced liver injury with a delayed onset; anti-INH and/or anti-P450 antibodies were found in 15 of 19 patients with INH-induced liver failure, and covalent INH binding was identified in a human liver biopsy from a patient with INH-induced liver failure. In five patients with mild INH-induced liver injury there was an increase in Th17 cells and IL-10-producing cells, whereas patients taking INH without liver injury showed none of these findings. The authors conclude the mechanism is immune-mediated idiosyncratic injury rather than 'metabolic idiosyncrasy.'
raw_record.extra_details: Delayed-onset liver injury; mild injury can resolve despite continued treatment. Anti-INH and/or anti-P450 antibodies detected in serum of 15/19 patients with INH-induced liver failure, but no anti-drug or anti-P450 antibodies in patients who received INH without severe liver injury. Increased Th17 and IL-10-producing cells in 5 patients with mild INH-induced liver injury. Covalent binding of INH identified in a human liver biopsy from a patient with INH-induced liver failure. Authors reject prior 'metabolic idiosyncrasy' mechanism attributed to acetylhydrazine (AcHz) bioactivation.

raw_record.support_text: Among patients with acute liver failure resulting from drugs in the US who underwent liver transplantation, paracetamol was the most common causative drug, followed by isoniazid.
raw_record.extra_details: Second most common drug after paracetamol among US drug-induced acute liver failure patients who underwent liver transplantation; also 17.5% in the USA 1990-2002 series (Russo et al.).

raw_record.support_text: The patient had a febrile reaction to isoniazid and para-aminosalicylic acid, but it was felt that isoniazid was the drug responsible for her liver destruction. When the drugs were next received there was no doubt that clinical jaundice progressed with isoniazid administration and subsided with its discontinuance. Para-aminosalicylic acid was not considered to be the offender.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of fatal isoniazid hepatotoxicity framed as drug allergy. Jaundice progressed with isoniazid administration and subsided on discontinuance (dechallenge); an earlier hospitalization illness construed as infectious hepatitis or post-transfusion jaundice was reinterpreted as a probable isoniazid reaction. Patient died of massive hemorrhage from esophageal varices secondary to cirrhosis on May 15, 1957; autopsy showed a 1000 gm liver with marked scarring, fibrosis with persistent bile ducts, diffuse lymphocytic infiltration, and acute necrosis probably related to death from exsanguination, plus splenomegaly and tuberculous osteomyelitis of thoracic vertebrae. Febrile reaction and hepatocellular disease (rising serum bilirubin and thymol turbidity) were observed.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is the most severe side effect associated with antituberculosis medications such as isoniazid, and describes a study by Lee et al. (2019) in which 38 patients with tuberculosis who had experienced DILI (16 attributed to pyrazinamide, 14 to rifampin, 8 to isoniazid) were compared with 38 sex- and age-matched non-DILI TB-positive controls. Patients presenting with isoniazid-induced hepatotoxicity were explicitly identified, making isoniazid the attributed liver-injuring agent.
raw_record.extra_details: Lee et al. (2019) case-control study (38 TB patients with DILI, including 8 isoniazid-attributed cases, vs 38 matched non-DILI controls) using PacBio SMRT sequencing of the mitochondrial genome. The paper's focus was mtDNA variant associations: patients with isoniazid-induced DILI had more mtDNA variants in complex I ND1 (p=0.025) and ND5 (p=0.028), more non-synonymous ND5 mutations (1.5±1.6 vs 0.7±0.8; p=0.033), and a higher ratio of non-synonymous to total substitutions than non-DILI controls. The authors hypothesized variation in complex I subunits predisposes to isoniazid-induced DILI via the primary metabolite hydrazine, a complex II inhibitor.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 154 DILI patients, isoniazid was one of six drugs with more than 5 cases analyzed specifically and showed no significant test signatures (0 significant differences).
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid DILI cases had no significant (Bonferroni) baseline test differences compared with the other drug classes (n = 0).

raw_record.support_text: In a population-based cohort study of 11,141 persons starting isoniazid preventive therapy for latent tuberculosis infection (1989-1995), the study identified 11 cases of hepatotoxicity attributable to isoniazid, a rate of 1.0 per 1000 persons starting therapy. The authors observed an increasing risk of isoniazid hepatotoxicity with increasing age and a greater frequency in women than in men, and a borderline association with white race. They concluded that isoniazid is less toxic than previously believed.
raw_record.extra_details: Population-based cohort, 1989-1995, 11,141 persons starting isoniazid preventive therapy for latent TB; 11 cases of hepatotoxicity (rate 1.0 per 1000). Rates by subgroup: males 0.5 (3/6066), females 1.6 (8/5075, adjusted OR 3.30, 95% CI 0.87-12.45); age 15-34 0.8 (reference), 35-64 2.1 (OR 3.17, 0.94-10.70), >=65 2.8 (OR 3.62, 0.43-30.42), 0-14 0 cases; white 2.2 (OR 2.60, 0.75-8.95), nonwhite 0.8. Authors note these findings were based on a small number of cases (n=11).

raw_record.support_text: Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network (DILIN) cases adjudicated as definite, highly likely, or probable for isoniazid injury from 2004 through 2013 were analyzed. Isoniazid was the second most commonly reported agent in the DILIN, with 69 cases, of which 60 met inclusion criteria. Thirteen patients died or underwent liver transplantation, and 62% were hospitalized.
raw_record.extra_details: 69 DILIN cases (second most commonly reported agent in DILIN, 2004-2013), 60 met inclusion criteria; median age 49 y (range 4-68), 70% female, 97% latent TB, 62% hospitalized. Patients took a median of 9 days to stop isoniazid after ATS stopping criteria were met; delay in stopping associated with more severe injury (P<.05). 13 patients died or underwent liver transplantation, of whom 9 (70%) continued isoniazid >7 days after meeting stopping criteria. Only 1 of 25 cases eligible for CDC reporting was reported. ATS criteria: for ALT >3x ULN stop if symptomatic; stop for ALT >5x ULN if asymptomatic. Elevation of ALT >5x ULN occurs in 3%-5% of patients and severe injury in <1%.

raw_record.support_text: Seven livers came from patients with the clinical diagnosis of drug hepatitis attributed to the contraceptive pill (two cases), methyldopa (two), indomethacin (one), chlorpromazine (one), and isoniazid (one). The biopsy findings confirmed the drug hepatitis diagnosis and each patient was negative for HBsAg.
raw_record.extra_details: One of seven drug hepatitis cases in the series; clinical diagnosis of drug hepatitis confirmed by liver biopsy; patient negative for HBsAg.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 755 patients with latent tuberculosis infection treated with isoniazid for 9 months, 94 patients (12.4%) had adverse effects, and treatment was withdrawn in 50 (6.6%): 2 for hypersensitivity and 48 for hepatic toxicity. Of these, 25 (3.3% of the total) met the criteria for isoniazid withdrawal due to hepatotoxicity. Viral hepatitis markers were negative and liver function normalized in all cases. Table 4 tabulates hepatic toxicity by grade: grade I 49 (6.50%), grade II 23 (3.04%), grade III 5 (0.66%), and grade IV 11 (1.45%).
raw_record.extra_details: Nine-month isoniazid therapy (270 doses) for latent tuberculosis infection in a retrospective cohort of 755 patients. Hepatic toxicity grades (n, %): grade I 49 (6.50), grade II 23 (3.04), grade III 5 (0.66), grade IV 11 (1.45). Adverse effects occurred in 94 (12.4%; 95% CI 10.1-14.7%); treatment withdrawn in 50 (6.6%), 2 for hypersensitivity and 48 for hepatic toxicity, of whom 25 (3.3%; 95% CI 2.0-4.6%) met explicit isoniazid-hepatotoxicity withdrawal criteria. Viral hepatitis markers negative; liver function normalized in all; 47 of 48 patients with hepatic toxicity discontinued before 6 months.

raw_record.support_text: Recent reports suggest that liver injury with isoniazid (INH) therapy is due to a metabolite of INH, not hypersensitivity, occurring more often in rapid acetylators. Studies in volunteers show INH is converted to the toxic acetylhydrazine and that the rate of conversion depends on the rate of INH acetylation, and clinical data reportedly support this (claiming Orientals, more likely rapid acetylators, are more susceptible to INH hepatic injury, and that 86% [18 of 21] of patients with evident INH hepatotoxicity were rapid acetylators).
raw_record.extra_details: Liver injury is attributed to a metabolite of INH (acetylhydrazine) rather than hypersensitivity, with conversion rate depending on acetylation rate; the paper disputes whether Orientals are unusually susceptible (Black study: 55/5190 whites, 36/6140 blacks, and 23/2608 Orientals developed INH hepatotoxicity, i.e., rates per 1000 of 10.6, 5.9, and 8.8, which does not suggest unusual Oriental susceptibility). A separate claim that 86% (18 of 21) of INH-hepatotoxicity patients were rapid acetylators is also presented.

raw_record.support_text: In the initial 300 patients in the DILI Network (DILIN) registry of non-acetaminophen DILI causes, isoniazid (INH) was among the most common individual agents found responsible, accounting for 4.3% of cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Represented 4.3% of the first 300 non-acetaminophen DILI cases in the DILIN registry.

raw_record.support_text: Guidelines for isoniazid administration aim to identify hepatotoxicity as early as possible; at the first suggestion of hepatitis-like symptoms isoniazid should be discontinued and liver function tests performed. A reported series of 14 cases of isoniazid-associated hepatitis showed prodromal fatigue, weakness, and anorexia, and the severity of subsequent hepatitis was related to the duration of continued isoniazid consumption: patients with histologic patchy hepatitis continued isoniazid an average of 2.2 weeks, while those with multilobular or bridging necrosis continued it an average of 4.6 weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: 14 cases of isoniazid-associated hepatitis (Maddry and Boitnott report); prodromal symptoms fatigue, weakness, anorexia; severity proportional to duration of continued isoniazid intake despite symptoms; histologic patchy hepatitis observed after ~2.2 weeks continued use versus multilobular or bridging necrosis after ~4.6 weeks; severity of isoniazid-induced hepatitis judged best by onset of hepatitis-like symptoms; routine LFT monitoring considered impractical.

raw_record.support_text: In the UNOS liver transplant cohort of 270 drug-induced acute liver failure recipients, isoniazid was the most frequently implicated non-acetaminophen drug, accounting for 24 of 137 (17.5%) non-APAP cases. The authors conclude four drugs (including isoniazid) were implicated in 42% of patients undergoing liver transplantation for acute liver failure due to drugs other than APAP.
raw_record.extra_details: Most frequently implicated non-acetaminophen drug in the UNOS liver transplant database cohort (1990-2002). 24 of 137 non-APAP cases (17.5%). Diagnosis at transplant was acute hepatic necrosis from an implicated drug.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that of the first-line anti-tuberculosis drugs, isoniazid (INH), rifampicin (RMP) and pyrazinamide (PZA) are all hepatotoxic and increase the risk of hepatotoxicity when used together. Hepatotoxicity was defined as symptomatic elevation of liver transaminases ≥3× ULN (or ≥5× if asymptomatic).

raw_record.support_text: Among people receiving tuberculosis preventive therapy in Tibetan schools in Himachal Pradesh, India, 11 schoolchildren (1.4%) and 1 staff member (1.0%) experienced hepatotoxicity attributed to isoniazid, with elevated liver enzymes and symptoms that regressed after the drug was discontinued. raw_record.extra_details: Recipients were schoolchildren and staff with latent TB infection receiving TB preventive therapy in Tibetan boarding/day schools in Himachal Pradesh, India, 2017. Of those treated, 227 (25%) people developed at least 1 treatment side effect, almost all attributed to isoniazid; fatigue, drowsiness, and gastrointestinal complaints were reported by 8%-10% of schoolchildren and 5%-13% of staff. Isoniazid-attributed hepatotoxicity occurred in 11/799 (1.4%) schoolchildren and 1/101 (1.0%) staff, with elevated liver enzymes and symptoms regressing after drug discontinuation; preventive therapy was permanently stopped in 2 people. One of 20 (44%) HBV-coinfected latent TB individuals receiving isoniazid + rifampicin developed hepatotoxicity requiring discontinuation. Isoniazid was used both as part of a regimen with rifampicin (isoniazid-rifampicin) and alone for 4-6 months in some individuals.

raw_record.support_text: A previously healthy 44-year-old female developed anorexia, nausea, and jaundice after six months of isoniazid (INH) monotherapy for latent tuberculosis. Other causes of liver injury were ruled out, and liver biopsy showed submassive necrosis, hepatocellular dropout, and lobular inflammation with no fibrosis; she also had acute portal hypertension. She was diagnosed with drug-induced liver injury (DILI), treated with NAC, ursodiol, and vitamin K, and recovered without liver transplantation. The paper notes severe hepatitis occurs in up to 1% of INH patients and supports monitoring of liver tests during INH therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Case of a 44-year-old female also taking pantoprazole for gastroesophageal reflux disease; latent TB prophylaxis monotherapy setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Six months of INH monotherapy for latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis before symptom onset (~2 weeks of anorexia, right-sided abdominal pain, jaundice). Labs on day 1: ALT 651 U/L, AST 1134 U/L, ALP 186 U/L, total bilirubin 14.1 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 7.7 mg/dL, INR 1.75, MELD-Na 24; subacute liver failure with concurrent acute portal hypertension; biopsy showed submassive necrosis, hepatocellular dropout, lobular inflammation, no fibrosis; treated with N-acetyl cysteine, ursodiol, and vitamin K; recovered without liver transplant. Paper also cites up to 20% asymptomatic aminotransferase increases and severe hepatitis in up to 1% of INH patients.

raw_record.support_text: In 14 patients with isoniazid-associated hepatitis, clinical signs and symptoms of hepatitis had developed in 12 of them, and all had increased serum SGOT (AST) concentrations ranging from 140 to 1,640 IU. raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid introduced in 1952 for tuberculosis treatment/chemoprophylaxis; hepatic damage generally reported, usually after excessive dosages. Immunologic hypersensitivity was suggested as pathogenesis based on occasional fever, rash, urticaria, and rarely eosinophilia. In the 14 study patients, in vitro lymphocyte transformation to INH showed A/C ratios <2 (no sensitization), failing to support an immunologic basis. All patients lacked hepatitis-associated antigen (cross immunoelectrophoresis, hemagglutination, complement fixation), no injection/narcotic/transfusion history.

raw_record.support_text: In a Japanese randomized, parallel, multicenter, controlled trial, NAT2 genotype-guided dosing stratification of isoniazid improved the tolerability of the standard 4-drug 6-month TB regimen. The incidence of isoniazid-associated DILI was 78% among slow acetylators in the standard treatment group versus none in the NAT2 genotype-guided treatment group. A Taiwan study also showed patients with NAT2 slow acetylator genotypes were more likely to develop TB DILI than rapid acetylators (26.4 vs 11.1%; OR 2.87; 95% CI 1.32–6.23).

raw_record.extra_details: Japanese RCT: 172 patients with confirmed pulmonary TB (9.3% slow, 53.5% rapid acetylators); isoniazid-associated DILI was 78% in slow acetylators on standard dosing versus 0% in genotyping-guided arm. Taiwan study OR 2.87 (95% CI 1.32-6.23) for TB DILI in slow versus rapid acetylators. Also reported: HLA-B*52:01 associated with isoniazid-induced hepatotoxicity among Europeans (OR 2.67, 95% CI 1.63-4.37); GSTM1/GSTT1 gene deletion linked to isoniazid-induced hepatotoxicity risk and severity, with GSTT1 possibly increasing risk only among NAT2 slow acetylators; CYP2E1 allele associations with INH DILI risk in slow acetylators were inconsistent across reports.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective cohort of 318 tuberculosis patients treated with a standard antituberculosis regimen, 49 (15.4%) were diagnosed with drug-induced hepatotoxicity. The paper states that most cases with antituberculosis drug-induced hepatitis have been attributed to isoniazid, and that isoniazid is the main drug to induce hepatotoxicity among antituberculosis regimens.

raw_record.extra_details: 49/318 (15.4%) patients diagnosed with drug-induced hepatotoxicity; CYP2E1 c1/c1 genotype raised hepatotoxicity risk (20.0% vs 9.0% for c1/c2 or c2/c2; OR 2.52, P=.009; adjusted OR 2.38, P=.017), and risk rose from 3.94 (c1/c1 with rapid acetylator) to 7.43 (c1/c1 with slow acetylator) relative to the c1/c2/c2 rapid reference. Isoniazid withdrawn when aminotransferases exceeded 3-5x ULN with gradual rechallenge after normalization. Mechanism: isoniazid metabolized by hepatic NAT and CYP2E1; metabolic intermediates (e.g., acetylhydrazine oxidized to hepatotoxic intermediaries) rather than isoniazid per se are incriminated.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective study of 95 patients with active tuberculosis treated with isoniazid (INH) 10 mg/kg, rifampicin (RMP) 10 mg/kg, and ethambutol (EMB) 25 mg/kg, the authors investigated the influence of acetylator phenotype on isoniazid hepatotoxicity. They found a 12.6% incidence of isoniazid hepatitis (SGOT, SGPT >200 U/l) and a significantly higher risk of isoniazid-induced hepatotoxicity in slow acetylators (p <0.01): 26/56 slow acetylators (≈46.4%) vs 4/30 rapid acetylators (≈13.3%) had transaminases >50 U/l, and all 12 patients with the most severe hepatotoxic side effects (SGOT/SGPT >200 U/l) were slow acetylators. Women developed severe hepatic injury more often than men (p <0.05). In isoniazid hepatitis cases therapy was stopped or reduced to RMP+EMB; transaminases normalized within 2-4 weeks and no new elevation occurred upon resuming full therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Confirmed active pulmonary tuberculosis; triple therapy with rifampicin and ethambutol as co-medication; slow acetylator phenotype carries higher risk; women affected more often than men.
raw_record.extra_details: Doses: isoniazid 10 mg/kg, rifampicin 10 mg/kg, ethambutol 25 mg/kg (INH 10 mg/kg mentioned). Isoniazid hepatitis defined as SGOT/SGPT >200 U/l, incidence 12.6% of treated. Transaminase elevations >50 U/l in 46.4% of slow vs 13.3% of rapid acetylators. Onset constant in the 2nd-4th week (19 +/- 7 days); transaminases normalized within 2-4 weeks; no new transaminase elevation on rechallenge with full triple therapy. Authors propose an interaction between rifampicin and isoniazid metabolism limited to the early phase of chemotherapy.

raw_record.support_text: In three of the diabetic patients who had recovered from jaundice after Neoteben (INH) was stopped and liver-function tests normalized, cautious rechallenge with small doses of Neoteben for a few days rapidly reproduced intolerance symptoms (fullness, belching, loss of appetite, inner restlessness) together with deterioration of carbohydrate tolerance with pronounced glycosuria. In one case the Takata-Ara fell from 80 to 60 mg%, and the Ehrlich urobilinogen test became positive in the others. The medication was promptly withdrawn and symptoms disappeared. The authors conclude that this behavior indicates liver damage, possibly a hypersensitivity reaction, rather than homologous serum hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Diabetic patients with tuberculosis; authors state the diabetic liver reacts more readily with damage than that of non-diabetic tuberculous patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Five jaundice cases among 15 Neoteben-treated diabetic patients (case series); rechallenge in 3 reproduced symptoms. Weicksel is cited as observing jaundice in 3 additional diabetics. The decrease of the glucose equivalent under Neoteben in 4 of these patients was attributed to hepatogenic insulin resistance from toxic liver damage. Animal experiments were conflicting (Freerksen: marked glycogen depletion of liver cells in rabbits fed high INH doses; Emmerich & Petzold: no regeneration inhibition or liver fatty change in rat liver regeneration test). Alias: INH.

raw_record.extra_details: DIH is drug-induced hepatitis, the study outcome attributed to INH-containing treatment; DIH frequency 11.76% in the cohort; AcINH AUC0-6h significantly lower in patients with DIH and AcINH plasma level proposed as a DIH biomarker; metabolites proposed to cause INH-induced liver injury: acetylhydrazine (AcHz), hydrazine (Hz), and an INH bioactivation metabolite (Metushi et al., 2011) - described only as proposed mechanism, not independently confirmed injuring entities; GSTM1-null genotype (59% of cohort) showed no effect on DIH; CYP2E1*6 (rs6413432) associated with INH pharmacokinetic changes but no direct demonstration of contribution to DIH.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid (INH) preventive treatment is associated with hepatotoxicity. The 1977 Public Health Service (PHS) Cooperative Surveillance Study showed increasing age was associated with increasing risk of INH toxicity up to age 64, with a fall in risk thereafter, and a rate of eight probable hepatotoxicity cases per 1000 individuals over 65 was used as a high limit for serious toxicity. The International Union Against Tuberculosis (IUAT) study of 28,000 people under age 65 found 5.2 cases of hepatitis per 1000 in those receiving INH for 12 months.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly (over 65) preventive-treatment setting; monthly serum AST (SGOT) monitoring model assumed; decision-analysis context
raw_record.extra_details: PHS 1977 Cooperative Surveillance Study: risk rose with age to 64 then fell; 8 probable hepatotoxicity cases per 1000 individuals over 65 used as high limit; PHS did not monitor liver enzymes routinely, only on symptom. IUAT study (~28,000, age <65): 5.2 hepatitis cases per 1000 with 12-month INH. Death from toxicity: 8 deaths among 174 hepatitis cases (case fatality 4.6%, 0.58 deaths per 1000 taking medication); none in people over 65, 7 of 8 in Baltimore; most had other conditions such as severe alcoholism or other hepatotoxic medications.

raw_record.support_text: The paper treats anti-TB drug-induced hepatitis as caused by isoniazid (INH) during anti-TB treatment, noting the association of INH with hepatitis has already been reported and that the study's findings corroborate the hypothesis that acetylator status is a risk factor for the hepatic side effects of INH. Slow acetylators acetylate not only INH but also acetylhydrazine (the precursor of toxic intermediates) more slowly, and the study concludes that slow acetylators are prone to INH-induced hepatitis; the incidence of elevated serum transaminases was significantly higher in slow acetylators than in rapid/intermediate acetylators.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Finding applies to slow NAT2 acetylator phenotype/genotype individuals (slow acetylation was the only risk factor after multivariate adjustment); patients were treated with 400 mg INH in the anti-TB regimen.
raw_record.extra_details: 26 hepatitis cases among 167 patients; slow acetylation associated with anti-TB drug-induced hepatitis, OR 3.59 (95% CI 2.53-4.64, p=0.02), confirmed with three-phenotype analysis OR 3.47 (95% CI 2.43-4.47, p=0.02). Slow acetylator phenotype OR 2.86 (95% CI 1.06-7.68) vs rapid/intermediate reference. Mechanistic basis: slow acetylation of INH and acetylhydrazine (precursor of toxic intermediates) to harmless diacetylhydrazine, with hydrazine production via direct INH hydrolysis as another route to hepatic injury; NAT2 is the main hepatic enzyme in INH metabolism. Age, sex, CYP2E1, GSTM1 and GSTT1 genotypes were not independent risk factors; CYP2E1*5/*5 rare (0.6%).

raw_record.support_text: In a randomized trial comparing NAT2 genotype-guided (PGx) with conventional standard (STD) dosing of isoniazid (INH) for drug-sensitive tuberculosis, isoniazid-related liver injury (INH-DILI) occurred in 7 of 9 slow acetylators receiving STD INH (5 mg/kg) within the first 4 weeks, versus 0 of 7 slow acetylators in the PGx group during the first 8 weeks (attributable risk difference 77.8%, p=0.003). Multivariable analysis showed the NAT2 slow acetylator genotype was associated with INH-DILI in the STD treatment. Few rapid acetylators had INH-DILI (4.2% STD, 4.6% high-dose PGx), equivalent to intermediate acetylators (4.7%). Standard-dose INH was concluded to be too much for slow acetylators. One slow acetylator required INH withdrawal after standard treatment was interrupted due to INH-DILI.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Finding is genotype-restricted: NAT2 slow acetylator genotype at standard INH dose (5 mg/kg/day) within a first-line anti-tuberculosis combination regimen; association with slow-acetylator genotype in STD treatment only, not seen with genotype-guided lower dosing or in rapid/intermediate acetylators.
raw_record.extra_details: Randomized controlled trial (n=155 evaluable patients) comparing NAT2 genotype-guided (PGx) vs conventional standard (STD) INH dosing for drug-sensitive tuberculosis. INH-DILI incidence: 77.8% (7/9) in slow acetylators on STD vs 0% (0/7) on PGx (p=0.003); 4.2% (2/48) rapid acetylators STD, 4.6% (2/44) rapid acetylators high-dose PGx, 4.7% (3/64) intermediate acetylators. INH doses: STD 5.5 mg/kg, PGx slow acetylators 2.6 mg/kg, PGx rapid acetylators 8.8 mg/kg. One rapid acetylator with INH-DILI showed no clinical improvement by week 8; 2 of 9 slow acetylators with INH-DILI on STD showed no improvement and INH was withdrawn in one. Derived from prior study assumptions of INH-DILI incidence 65% (control) vs 15% (test) in slow acetylators; combined unfavorable-event endpoint (INH-DILI or early treatment failure) reduced with PGx dosing (RR 0.354, 95% CI 0.177-0.707).

raw_record.support_text: In this prospective study, the authors report that (1) milder hepatotoxic reactions are more common under combination therapy with isoniazid, rifampicin and ethambutol (Myambutol) than previously described; (2) isoniazid hepatitis occurs more frequently with the rifampicin-isoniazid combination than with isoniazid alone and probably also depends on the isoniazid dose; and (3) patients who are phenotypically slow acetylators of isoniazid significantly more often (P<0.01) develop isoniazid hepatitis than fast acetylators.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings concerning slow versus fast acetylator phenotype; isoniazid administered for tuberculosis treatment, including in combination with rifampicin (and with ethambutol/Myambutol in the milder-reaction finding).
raw_record.extra_details: Milder hepatotoxic reactions were more common in prospective observation under combination therapy with isoniazid + rifampicin + myambutol than previously described; isoniazid hepatitis was more frequent in the rifampicin-isoniazid combination than with isoniazid alone and was considered probably dose-dependent; slow acetylators had a significantly higher frequency of isoniazid hepatitis than fast acetylators (P<0.01). Ongoing biochemical and pharmacokinetic investigations (Musch et al. 1981) aim to make the tuberculosis treatment with isoniazid safer.

Patient education about hepatitis symptoms (nausea, vomiting, yellow eyes, dark urine, fatigue, abdominal pain) and monthly monitoring were recommended.

raw_record.support_text: In a randomized trial of 36-month continued isoniazid preventive treatment versus placebo in HIV-infected adults, there were nine cases of hepatitis (one with jaundice) in the continued isoniazid group, one of which (jaundice with disseminated herpes zoster) progressed to death from hepatic encephalopathy 9 months after enrolment; the participant stopped isoniazid 3 days after becoming jaundiced. A second death from hepatic encephalopathy attributed to isoniazid occurred during the open-label period. From enrolment there were 29 cases of severe isoniazid-associated hepatitis in more than 3100 person-years of isoniazid use: 8 (28%) had symptoms (including the two hepatic encephalopathy cases), 4 (14%) had jaundice, and 26 (90%) occurred during the first 9 months of therapy. Overall, 29 (1%) of 1995 participants had severe isoniazid-associated (biochemical) hepatitis (rate 14.5 per 1000 participants), 8 had clinical hepatitis (4.0 per 1000), and 2 had hepatic encephalopathy (1.0 per 1000).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: HIV-infected adults receiving continued (36-month) isoniazid preventive treatment with antiretroviral therapy in some participants; tuberculosis-endemic setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Nine hepatitis cases (one with jaundice) in the continued isoniazid group versus six hepatitis cases in placebo controls. One jaundiced continued-isoniazid participant died of hepatic encephalopathy with concomitant disseminated herpes zoster and lymphocytic pleiocytosis on CSF analysis, stopping isoniazid 3 days after becoming jaundiced. A second isoniazid-attributed death from hepatic encephalopathy occurred in the open-label period. Aggregate rates: severe biochemical hepatitis 14.5 per 1000 participants, clinical hepatitis 4.0 per 1000, hepatic encephalopathy 1.0 per 1000; 26 of 29 cases (90%) occurred within first 9 months of therapy.

Across trials there were no deaths attributed to study drug in the Soweto or Chennai trials. raw_record.support_text: In a 7-year Seattle-King County cohort study, rates of isoniazid hepatotoxicity were derived by comparing hepatotoxicity cases from a 1989-1995 register with the number of patients who began isoniazid alone or in multiple-drug regimens. During the study, 11 patients experienced hepatotoxic reactions while receiving isoniazid (median age 34 years, range 27-67; 73% female; median latency 9 weeks, range 19 days to 5 months). All 11 had highly elevated serum hepatocellular enzymes, 9 (82%) were hyperbilirubinemic, 1 (9.1%) was hospitalized, and all recovered without sequelae.
