raw_record.extra_details: 11 hepatotoxicity cases among the cohort; median age 34 (range 27-67), 73% female; median interval to diagnosis 9 weeks (range 19 days to 5 months), with 10/11 (91%) within 3 months; all had highly elevated hepatocellular enzymes and 9/11 (82%) hyperbilirubinemia; 1 patient (9.1%) hospitalized; all 11 recovered without sequelae. Rates computed per persons beginning therapy and per persons completing isoniazid single- or multiple-drug therapy; subgroup rates by sex, race, and age (0-14, 15-34, 35-64, ≥65); logistic regression odds ratios adjusted for sex, age group, and race.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective study of 415 long-term drug users treated with isoniazid 300 mg daily for latent tuberculosis infection, hepatotoxicity occurred in 20 patients (4.8%), including 6 (1.4%) with clinical hepatotoxicity; 34 patients (8.2%) had ALT and/or AST elevations to 3–5 times the upper limit of normal, and 71 (17.1%) abandoned or changed therapy. raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity occurred in 20/415 patients (4.8%); clinical hepatotoxicity in 6 (1.4%); ALT/AST elevation to 3–5x ULN in 34 (8.2%); 71 (17.1%) abandoned or changed therapy. Diagnostic/drug-withdrawal criteria: symptomatic hepatitis with AST and/or ALT >5x ULN, or asymptomatic elevations >5x ULN on two consecutive weekly determinations or a single elevation >250 IU/L, with transaminases returning to baseline within 3 weeks and exclusion of viral hepatitis and other drug causes. Mean treatment duration 154.1 ± 51.4 days.

raw_record.extra_details: Nine reported cases (ages 8-56 years) of isoniazid jaundice at doses 150-900 mg/day for 9 days to 7 weeks. raw_record.support_text: The paper reports isoniazid (INH)-associated hepatitis observed in a Philadelphia tuberculosis chemoprophylaxis and treatment program. A table of annual surveillance data (1969-1973) shows 7-9 annual cases of INH-associated hepatitis among the INH-treated population (rates of 0.12%-0.22% of the total INH population), including cases arising during both treatment and prophylaxis. The paper states that with proper surveillance isoniazid-associated hepatitis is readily reversible and shows no permanent defect on follow-up, and that the relatively low incidence of isoniazid-associated hepatitis does not preclude prophylactic use when there is a significant community problem.

raw_record.support_text: In the analysis of toxicity attributable to treatment of latent tuberculosis infection (TLTBI) with isoniazid, elevated transaminase levels were found in 83.3% of oncohematological patients versus 37.3% of the control group (RR: 2.23; 95% CI: 1.56–3.20), and treatment had to be discontinued for severe hepatotoxicity in 3 patients (16.7%) with hematologic malignancies and 7 patients (9.3%) in the control group (RR: 1.79; 95% CI: 0.51–6.24). Severe hepatotoxicity was defined as a transaminase increase attributable to isoniazid greater than 5 times the upper limit of normal (ULN), or between 3 and 5 times ULN together with attributable symptoms.

raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatotoxicity defined as transaminase increase >5x ULN or 3-5x ULN with attributable symptoms. Elevated transaminases in 15/18 (83.3%) oncohematological vs 28/75 (37.3%) control patients (RR 2.2, 95% CI 1.6-3.2); severe hepatotoxicity in 3/18 (16.7%) vs 7/75 (9.3%) (RR 1.8, 95% CI 0.5-6.2). Overall discontinuation of TLTBI for any toxicity-related reason in 16.7% of hematologic patients vs 14.7% controls (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.35-3.66). raw_record.support_text: In a prospective cohort of 224 tuberculosis patients treated with an isoniazid-based antituberculosis regimen, 33 (14.7%) were diagnosed with drug-induced hepatitis by the International Consensus Meeting definition. During isoniazid rechallenge, 14 of these patients (6.3%) developed serum ALT >3x ULN, which the authors classified as clinically significant isoniazid-induced hepatitis, prompting replacement of isoniazid with streptomycin or ofloxacin; the other 19 had transient hepatic dysfunction. Slow acetylator NAT2 status and older age were significant risk factors for isoniazid-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with pulmonary tuberculosis on isoniazid-based antituberculosis therapy; predominantly elderly cohort; age was a significant independent risk factor.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid rechallenge confirmed causality: 14 patients (6.3%) had ALT >3x ULN during rechallenge and were classified as clinically significant hepatitis; 19 (8.5%) had ALT <=3x ULN (transient hepatic dysfunction) and continued isoniazid safely. Peak ALT 393.6 ± 353.9 U/L (range 98-1609) and peak total bilirubin 3.25 ± 3.57 mg/dL (range 0.5-20.2) in hepatitis cases. Hepatitis risk was higher in slow acetylators (26.4% vs 11.1%; OR 2.87, 95% CI 1.32-6.23), and slow acetylators had higher peak ALT/AST and were more likely to exceed 3x ULN on rechallenge (64.3% vs 26.3%; P=.040). Multivariate OR for slow acetylator 3.66 (1.58-8.49) and age OR 1.09 (1.04-1.14). Rapid acetylator was protective (OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.16-0.76).

raw_record.extra_details: Case of INH-related fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) with grade III encephalopathy requiring mechanical ventilation; histology showed acute massive hepatocellular necrosis with spared portal tracts and marginal ductular proliferation. Treated with APOLT; the graft failed on post-transplant day 22 due to hepatic artery kinking and thrombosis, requiring urgent re-transplantation; recovered with signs of hepatic regeneration; patient healthy with normal liver function tests 24 months after APOLT. Authors note the risk of INH-related liver injury increases with older age, female gender, and Oriental ethnicity, but this case occurred in a child.

raw_record.support_text: The paper recognizes that isoniazid (INH), shortly after its introduction, was known to cause toxic hepatitis and, rarely, death. A U.S. Public Health Service surveillance study (1971-1973) among 13,838 persons recorded eight deaths attributed to INH-associated hepatitis, and a 1989 California cluster reported 20 such deaths. The investigation focused on deaths attributable to INH-associated hepatitis in persons taking INH alone for preventive therapy within the United States.

raw_record.extra_details: USPHS surveillance study (1971-1973) of 13,838 persons in 21 health departments reported eight deaths (seven in one city, six female of whom five were black). A 1989 California cluster comprised 20 deaths (16 in women, 10 Hispanic). Literature search (Medline 1965-1989) identified 48 deaths among persons on INH alone for preventive therapy; FDA Adverse Reaction Reporting System (reports dating from 1970) added 17 deaths not cited in the literature; state/territorial epidemiologists and TB control officers identified a further 59 cases. INH-associated 'toxic hepatitis' can progress to death.

raw_record.support_text: A retrospective cohort study analyzed isoniazid (INH) hepatitis morbidity and mortality among patients at a U.S. prenatal clinic, comparing 3,681 pregnant/postpartum women in the 1981 INH preventive therapy program with an unmatched comparison group of 3,948 women aged 15-44 from the 1971 PHS multicenter INH hepatitis surveillance study. Two expert panels determined possible cases of INH hepatitis: five cases in the prenatal group and 10 in the non-pregnant group. Two Hispanic women aged 24 and 27 died at 3 and 5 months postpartum in the preventive therapy group, and one 38-year-old non-pregnant black woman died in the PHS group. The analysis raised the possibility of an association of pregnancy/post-partum state with INH hepatitis (risk ratio 2.5, 95% CI 0.8-8.2) and fatal hepatotoxicity (rate ratio 4, 95% CI 0.2-258), though groups were unmatched, followed a decade apart, and underpowered due to rarity of events.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnancy and post-partum state examined; cohorts were unmatched, followed a decade apart, and the analysis was underpowered because of the rarity of the events.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective cohort comparing 3,681 pregnant/postpartum women in the 1981 INH preventive therapy (LTBI) program with 3,948 women aged 15-44 from the 1971 Public Health Service multicenter INH hepatitis surveillance study. Five possible INH hepatitis cases in the prenatal group and 10 in the non-pregnant group. Two Hispanic women aged 24 and 27 died at 3 and 5 months postpartum; one 38-year-old non-pregnant black woman died in the PHS group. Association of pregnancy/post-partum state with INH hepatitis risk ratio 2.5 (95% CI 0.8-8.2) and with fatal hepatotoxicity rate ratio 4 (95% CI 0.2-258).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states there is now no doubt that isoniazid can occasionally produce liver damage, though the exact mechanism is unknown. It notes a relatively high incidence of biochemically demonstrable hepatic damage (10 per cent in Sharer and Smith's series and 13.3 per cent in the Public Health Service surveillance study), argues this argues against a hypersensitivity or idiosyncratic reaction, and suggests hepatic metabolic products of isoniazid may be responsible for hepatic necrosis. Concomitant drugs, preexisting liver disease, and inactivation rates of isoniazid are being explored as influences.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Preventive (prophylactic) therapy in tuberculin reactors/hospital employees; liver damage is rare in children and young adults but the incidence increases significantly in older adults, and it was predicted that preventive therapy would no longer be recommended for tuberculin reactors over age 35 without other risk factors.
raw_record.extra_details: In one study, 37 of 427 (9 per cent) hospital employees on isoniazid preventive therapy developed elevated SGOT; 5 had symptomatic hepatitis, isoniazid was stopped in 8 others with elevated SGOT plus abnormal total bilirubin and/or alkaline phosphatase, and in 5 others with SGOT greater than 100 on 2 occasions or greater than 250 on 1 occasion. Maddrey and Boitnott reported hepatitis attributed to isoniazid in 14 patients over 5 years, with 3 dying of fulminant hepatitis; rechallenge caused recurrent hepatitis in 2 patients and abnormal serum transaminases in a third; duration of symptoms before stopping ranged from 1 to 10.5 weeks, with longer duration associated with more severe hepatitis. Mechanism unknown; metabolic products of isoniazid may cause hepatic necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: A 59-year-old Asian woman with tuberculous cervical lymphadenitis started triple therapy (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide); all were stopped after a rash. One month later isoniazid was restarted and 28 days later she presented with nausea, abdominal pain, and jaundice and a hepatitic picture (bilirubin 310 µmol/L, ALP 314 IU/L, ALT 2175 IU/L). Isoniazid was stopped again, but she was readmitted 3 days later with grade 3 encephalopathy, coagulopathy (INR 3.0), and rising jaundice; she met criteria for emergency liver transplantation for fulminant hepatic failure and was successfully transplanted. Explanted liver showed severe confluent necrosis with collapse and granulomatous infiltration, consistent with drug-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Rechallenge exposure: isoniazid restarted after a prior triple-therapy course; indication was tuberculous cervical lymphadenitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1 of four reported cases of fulminant hepatic failure caused by rifampicin, isoniazid, or both. Hepatitic laboratory picture (ALT 2175 then 2386 IU/L; bilirubin 310 then 399 µmol/L; ALP 314 then 350 IU/L; INR 3.0); grade 3 encephalopathy; successfully transplanted, discharged well at 7 weeks. Explanted liver histology: severe confluent necrosis with extensive collapse and granulomatous infiltration consistent with drug-induced hepatotoxicity. The paper notes isoniazid is among three potentially hepatotoxic anti-tuberculous drugs (with rifampicin and pyrazinamide).

raw_record.support_text: A renal allograft recipient on isoniazid 300 mg daily prophylaxis (given because of tuberculin reactivity and a Ghon complex) developed malaise, fever, epigastric tenderness, and bilirubinuria with markedly abnormal liver function about 2½ months after starting isoniazid. Isoniazid was immediately discontinued, and clinical and chemical recovery rapidly followed its withdrawal, supporting isoniazid as the cause of the hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Renal allograft recipient with chronic glomerulonephritis who had received a cadaveric renal transplant and was on immunosuppression (antithymocyte globulin, prednisone, azathioprine; azathioprine later replaced by cyclophosphamide); on concomitant Maalox, hydralazine, and chlorothiazide.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid 300 mg daily started May 1973 as prophylaxis; injury appeared after about 2½ months and on 26 July isoniazid was discontinued. SGOT rose from 65 (20 July) to 1830 IU/ml (26 July) and bilirubin to 5.9 mg/100 ml (28 July); alkaline phosphatase rose to 9.7 Bodansky units/ml. Percutaneous liver biopsy showed moderate diffuse hepatitis with ballooned hepatocytes, acidophilic bodies, mixed inflammatory infiltrate, hyperplastic Kupffer cells, small centrolobular zones of collapse without bridging, and moderate cholestasis. Hepatitis-associated antigen was negative; globulins and prothrombin time normal. Recovery followed isoniazid withdrawal. Authors note that the extreme hyperbilirubinemia and marked intrahepatic cholestasis without inflammatory reaction reported after azathioprine were absent here.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid is described as virtually the only drug implicated in drug-induced liver injury in developing countries. Fifteen to 20% of individuals receiving isoniazid as a single agent for tuberculosis prophylaxis may develop increased transaminases, which usually stabilize or improve, so that <1% may develop severe hepatic necrosis; a large tuberculosis public health clinic recently estimated severe liver injury at 1:1000, with 11 of 11,141 patients developing isoniazid-induced liver disease.

raw_record.support_text: Among 3,377 adults (aged ≥25 years) started on isoniazid (INH) therapy for latent tuberculosis infection in a public health TB clinic over a 7-year period, 19 patients developed isoniazid hepatotoxicity defined as aspartate aminotransferase (AST) >5 times the upper limit of normal (ULN), a rate of 5.6 per 1,000 patients. Only 1 of 19 patients had prodromal symptoms. Age >49 years (p<0.02) and baseline AST >ULN (p<0.0003) were identified as risk factors for INH hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Study restricted to adults aged ≥25 years; exclusion criteria included pregnancy, INH initiation within 3 months postpartum, baseline AST >3 times ULN, and history of INH allergy.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined as AST >5 times ULN; 19 events among 3,377 patients (5.6/1000). Events per 1000 patients were 2.75 at 1 month, 7.20 at 3 months, and 4.10 at 6 months of therapy. Age-specific events per 1000: 4.40 (25-34 y), 8.54 (35-49 y), 20.83 (≥50 y). Risk factors: age >49 years (p<0.02) and baseline AST >ULN (p<0.0003). Moderate-to-severe hepatotoxicity frequently occurred without symptoms, supporting value of AST monitoring. Authors note INH is well documented to cause liver adverse effects ranging from mild transient aminotransferase elevations (approximately 10-20% of patients) to overt hepatitis; risk factors include age >35 years, female gender, and concurrent ethanol use, with some data suggesting African-American and Hispanic women at greater risk. Consistent with earlier trials, INH hepatotoxicity is age related.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports the proportion of patients developing significant liver dysfunction from isoniazid (INH) therapy, attributed on the basis of a multiple logistic regression analysis of a prospective cohort. Age over 35 years and slow acetylation phenotype were the primary risk factors: in those ≥35 with slow acetylation 37.5% developed significant liver dysfunction versus 3.7% in rapid acetylators under 35. The discussion further states that INH is associated with overt hepatocellular disease, subclinical and overt hepatitis, with historical fatalities from INH-induced liver damage.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: The analysis was restricted to patients on INH chemoprophylaxis; the 12 patients who drank an excess of alcohol were excluded from the main risk-factor model, and patients with normal baseline laboratory studies were used for the prediction analysis.
raw_record.extra_details: Multiple logistic regression equation: log_e(theta/(1-theta)) = -1.90434 + 1.37376X1 - 1.35344X2, where X1=1 if age >35 and X2=1 if rapid acetylation (chi^2=10.5, d.f.=3, p=0.015). Observed rates of significant liver dysfunction: age<35 rapid 4.2% (1/24), age<35 slow 12.5% (3/24), age≥35 rapid 12.5% (2/16), age≥35 slow 37.5% (9/24). Historic evidence cited: Garibaldi et al. 2321 patients, 19 overt hepatocellular disease with 2 deaths; Bailey et al. 471 patients, 8.7% subclinical and 1% overt hepatitis, no deaths; Maddrey & Boitnott 14 overt biopsy-documented hepatitis cases ascribed to hypersensitivity; Black et al. 13,838 patients, 114 (0.82%) overt liver damage with 13 fatalities (11.4%). Discussion of proposed mechanism via acetylisoniazid, acetylhydrazine, and hydrazine metabolites (mainly animal evidence) that the paper notes is not clearly documented in humans prospectively.

raw_record.support_text: Severe hepatocellular damage occurred during isoniazid therapy in 114 patients reported here and in 60 or more additional patients reported by others. The authors conclude that isoniazid-related hepatic injury in humans results from the formation in the liver of a hepatotoxic metabolite, consistent with an occasional allergic mechanism involving acetylation of hepatic macromolecules by acetylhydrazine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Therapy for chemoprophylaxis of tuberculosis; increased mortality noted in patients presenting late in their course of isoniazid therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: 114 patients with severe hepatocellular damage reported here; 60 or more additional cases reported by others. Severe liver damage incidence rises with age: rare under 20 years, up to 0.3% at ages 20-34 years, up to 1.2% at 35-49 years, and up to 2.3% at 50 years and over; rates may underestimate due to dropout. Moderate serum transaminase abnormalities occur in 10-20% of isoniazid recipients, mostly subsiding despite continued therapy. Mechanism attributed to a hepatotoxic metabolite (acetylhydrazine-related acylation of hepatic macromolecules), with an allergic mechanism in occasional patients. Authors recommend discontinuing isoniazid in patients over 35 whose liver function tests do not improve within a few weeks.

raw_record.support_text: In a DILIN (Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network) registry cohort of latent TB patients, 13 patients experienced fatal liver injury or required liver transplantation linked to isoniazid (INH) treatment. Of these, 4 (31%) stopped INH quickly (within 7 days of meeting stopping criteria), while 2 continued INH for more than 3 weeks yet had mild injury. One patient showed adaptation despite continued INH, with ALT peaking above 1000 U/L before decreasing; the paper refers to this as 'INH injury' and notes ALT level alone cannot fully predict serious INH liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Treatment of latent tuberculosis infection (preventive therapy); patients were otherwise healthy before therapy. Patients harmed by suboptimal adherence, prolonged drug exposure, and delayed drug stoppage.
raw_record.extra_details: DILIN registry data for latent TB patients on isoniazid. Of 13 fatal or transplanted patients, 4 (31%) stopped INH within 7 days of meeting stopping criteria; 2 continued INH >3 weeks yet had mild injury; one patient showed adaptation with ALT peaking >1000 U/L that decreased despite continuing INH. Authors note under-reporting makes the true incidence larger than captured, and state ALT level alone cannot reliably predict serious injury. INH for 3-9 months DOT is a recommended latent TB option; point-of-care ALT and automated text reminders proposed.

raw_record.support_text: INH (isoniazid) and its metabolic intermediates are indicated to be the cause of hepatotoxicity. INH is inactivated in the liver by NAT2, and slow acetylators may accumulate toxic intermediates and are prone to isoniazid-induced hepatitis, as supported by the present study and previous studies. In a Tunisian study, the incidence of INH-induced hepatitis was 21.2%, and one TB patient with a slow-acetylator profile (NAT2*5B/5B) died of acute fulminant hepatitis; slow acetylators with NAT2*6A/*6A and NAT2*5/*5 genotypes had a significantly higher risk of INH drug-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Tuberculosis (TB) patient population; slow-acetylator NAT2 genotypes (NAT2*6A/*6A, NAT2*5/*5, NAT2*5B/5B) associated with higher risk; possible concurrent anti-tuberculosis drugs (e.g., rifampicin) in the regimen are co-exposures.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of INH-induced hepatitis in this study was 21.2%. One patient with slow-acetylator NAT2*5B/5B profile died of acute fulminant hepatitis. Slow acetylators dispose about 10 times more isoniazid via direct hydrolysis to hydrazine (a potent hepatotoxin), a pathway enhanced by rifampicin. Cytochrome P450 2E1 oxidation of monoacetylhydrazine yields toxic intermediates (acetyldiazene, acetylonium ion, acetylradical, ketene). Findings support NAT2 genotyping to pre-screen patients at high risk of INH-induced hepatotoxicity in the Tunisian population.

raw_record.support_text: Among 18 tuberculosis patients with INH (isoniazid)-related hepatotoxicity during anti-tuberculosis treatment, 11 (61%) were slow acetylators and 3 (17%) were fast acetylators. A significant association was observed between the slow acetylation profile and hepatotoxicity (P = 0.009, OR 3.71, 95%CI 1.38–9.93). This patient cohort in Belem, Brazil was studied for NAT2 and CYP2E1 polymorphisms as susceptibility factors for INH-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Tuberculosis patients on combination anti-tuberculosis therapy in Belem, Brazil; NAT2 slow/slow acetylator genotype associated with higher risk (alcohol-abuse adjusted OR 3.05, 95%CI 1.07–8.64, P = 0.036), while no individual NAT2 SNP or CYP2E1 polymorphism reached significance.
raw_record.extra_details: 18 patients with hepatotoxicity among 270 tuberculosis patients. A significant association was observed between slow acetylation profile and hepatotoxicity (P = 0.009, OR 3.71, 95%CI 1.38–9.93). Slow/slow genotype vs other genotypes crude OR 3.71 (95%CI 1.38–9.93); alcohol-abuse adjusted OR 3.05 (95%CI 1.07–8.64). No individual NAT2 SNP was associated with hepatotoxicity; no significant CYP2E1 association (full wild-type haplotype 1A/7632A/1C homozygotes, P = 0.098, OR 2.92, 95%CI 0.82–10.37). Acetylator classification: fast, intermediate, and slow genotypes defined by NAT2 alleles.

raw_record.support_text: In tuberculous meningitis (TBM) patients with drug-induced hepatotoxicity (DIH) there was evidence of oxidative and ER stress compared to controls and baseline values. The paper attributes INH (isoniazid) hepatotoxicity to oxidative and nitrosative stress, with peroxynitrite (ONOO-) generation and mitochondrial dysfunction; acetyl isoniazid is metabolized to monoacetyl hydrazine (MAH) and other metabolites, and NAT2 acetylator polymorphism (fast/slow/intermediate) affects drug exposure. Isoniazid hepatotoxicity is described as resulting in non-zonal necrosis simulating viral hepatitis, which may be massive in 10% of patients, with severe fulminant and sub-acute necrosis reported in 30% of patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Tuberculous meningitis patients treated with an isoniazid-containing anti-tuberculosis regimen; co-exposure to other anti-TB agents in the regimen.
raw_record.extra_details: DIH occurred after a median duration of 11 (3-48) days; significant alterations in oxidative and ER stress markers (P < .001). Of 36 DIH patients, 58.3% had poor outcome (mRS>2) and 33.3% of poor-outcome patients died in hospital; 14 (39%) DIH patients died during follow-up. Massive necrosis may occur in 10% of patients and severe fulminant/sub-acute necrosis in 30%. Mechanistic support: acetyl isoniazid converted to monoacetyl hydrazine (MAH) and nontoxic diacetyl hydrazine; NAT2 polymorphism (slow/intermediate/fast acetylators) affects exposure; long half-life extends exposure. Supporting rat data: isoniazid reduced free-radical-scavenger thiols, glutathione peroxidase and catalase, increased glutathione reductase activity, and N-acetylcysteine pretreatment reduced injury; isoniazid also inhibits certain cytochrome P450 enzymes, raising levels of hepatotoxic drug.

raw_record.support_text: The discussion concludes that a toxic hepatitis occurred twice in this patient after ingestion of psoralen (methoxsalen) during PUVA therapy. The rapid onset of symptoms 4-5 hours after methoxsalen ingestion on treatment days and rapid defervescence and resolution of liver enzymes with symptomatic therapy strongly suggest a toxic drug reaction rather than a viral origin or extrahepatic biliary pathology; a viral origin was considered unlikely due to negative HAA testing and repetition of the reaction after readministration of methoxsalen, and other medications were excluded because they were continued without recurrence.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient with psoriasis undergoing PUVA photochemotherapy; after a scheduled PUVA treatment she ingested 50 mg oral methoxsalen and received UVA (4 joules) 2 hours later. Four hours after ingestion temperature rose to 39.5 C, LDH to 905, SGOT to 870, and alkaline phosphatase to 111; she defervesced within 24 h and enzymes returned to normal over 5 days. HAA was negative; intravenous cholangiogram unsuccessful because liver function was too poor to excrete dye; no liver biopsy. The reaction recurred after repeat methoxsalen readministration (rechallenge), supporting causality. The same patient later used topical methoxsalen with no similar reaction. Note: the discussion heading refers to 'methotrexate-induced toxic hepatitis,' but the attributed administered causal agent throughout is methoxsalen (psoralen).

raw_record.support_text: In the discussion the authors state: 'We believe that the submassive necrosis in these two patients was caused by piroxicam', with metabolic and infectious causes deemed unlikely given negative biochemical and serological tests, including negative hepatitis C serology. Supporting cases: Case 1 (elderly woman) developed severe hepatitis with submassive/multiacinar necrosis, encephalopathy, and renal impairment, and died three months after illness onset; Case 2 (48-year-old man) started piroxicam (Feldene 10 mg) for joint stiffness, developed jaundice six weeks later, had submassive necrosis on histology, progressed to grade IV hepatic encephalopathy, and required orthotopic liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1 (elderly woman): biopsy showed severe hepatitis with multiacinar (submassive) necrosis with lymphocytic, plasma-cell and eosinophilic infiltration; bilirubin 426 umol/l, AST 1854 U/l, AP 187 U/l, GGT 36 U/l, prothrombin time 20 s; encephalopathy and renal impairment; died 31 May, necropsy showed small liver (620 g) with submassive necrosis. Case 2 (48-year-old man, piroxicam/Feldene 10 mg): bilirubin 243 umol/l, AST 1860 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 87 U/l; grade II then grade IV hepatic encephalopathy and ascites; orthotopic liver transplantation on 28 February 1988 with submassive necrosis histology; recovered after ganciclovir for post-transplant CMV; alive 30 months later. Competing causes (hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV, autoimmune, copper/iron studies) excluded; stored serum negative for hepatitis C antibody (RIBA).; supporting_animal_or_cell_evidence: None

raw_record.support_text: Two of the three previously reported cases of severe hepatitis caused by piroxicam occurred in women in their 60s; corticosteroid treatment was unsuccessful in each, with death occurring 105 and 53 days respectively after the onset of jaundice. The paper's first patient, also in her 60s, survived three months after jaundice onset without corticosteroids, and the authors note a report of successful liver transplantation in a 36-year-old man with acute hepatic failure related to piroxicam usage and a 48-year-old man who underwent liver transplant. Liver transplantation is recommended as the only treatment likely to succeed in drug-related submassive necrosis of the liver.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases of severe hepatitis/submassive necrosis caused by piroxicam; two prior cases in women in their 60s died 105 and 53 days after jaundice onset despite corticosteroids; the authors' first patient survived 3 months; one reported case treated by successful liver transplantation (36-year-old man with acute hepatic failure) and a 48-year-old man who underwent liver transplant. Authors recommend liver transplantation for drug-related submassive necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: Two patients with piroxicam-induced liver toxicity were admitted to the authors' liver unit over three decades. Case 1 was a 44-year-old woman with clinical and histological submassive necrosis, who developed ascites and liver failure after 28 d of piroxicam intake and recovered without transplantation in 95 d. Case 2 was a 42-year-old man on piroxicam as the single medication for 58 d who presented severe cholestasis, with histology showing hepato-canalicular cholestasis with ductopenia; he progressed to prolonged cholestasis with asthenia, anorexia and intolerable itching, and showed complete biochemical recovery 120 d after onset. raw_record.support_text: The paper reports piroxicam hepatotoxicity. It describes a patient who presented with features of acute hepatocellular injury that progressed to fatal subacute hepatic necrosis despite withdrawal of the drug, with piroxicam identified as the offending agent.
raw_record.extra_details: 66-year-old woman treated with piroxicam 40 mg/day (total dose 120 mg) for plantar fasciitis developed jaundice, dark urine and pale stools three days after starting the drug; drug was immediately stopped. No history of blood transfusion, recent injection, contact with jaundice, or other drugs or alcohol. Laboratory values: bilirubin 325 µmol/l (19.0 mg/100 ml), aspartate transaminase 430 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 190 IU/l (24 KA units), protein 74 g/l (albumin 38 g/l), prothrombin time 16/12 seconds. Negative hepatitis A and B virus and antinuclear, smooth muscle, and mitochondrial antibody tests. Liver biopsy two weeks after jaundice onset showed acute hepatitis with spotty necrosis. Injury progressed to fatal subacute hepatic necrosis despite drug withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: The authors discuss clozapine-related hepatotoxicity as an idiosyncratic adverse drug reaction, noting that abnormal liver transaminase levels often remain asymptomatic, that onset generally occurs in the first 3 months, and that there is a known risk of acute fulminant hepatic failure. They raise the question of whether routine LFT monitoring at 3 months should be performed for all patients on clozapine, and call for clearer guidelines on managing clozapine-related hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases are reported in the letter. Onset of abnormal liver transaminase levels generally occurs within the first 3 months and patients often remain asymptomatic. The paper notes a known risk of acute fulminant hepatic failure with clozapine and debates routine LFT monitoring at 3 months. There are conflicting reports on whether hepatotoxicity is dose-related: a 4-year follow-up study (Marinkovic et al) concluded dose-related hepatotoxicity because dose reduction normalized liver function, while more recent studies found dose reduction had no effect on normalization time; the authors' 2 cases also argue against a dose relation.

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes 2 patients who developed hepatotoxicity on clozapine. The first patient's clozapine was discontinued and later rechallenged with similar hepatotoxicity, while the second patient remained on clozapine with the liver abnormalities resolving spontaneously.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported hepatic adverse effects of clozapine include increased liver enzymes affecting 30-50% of patients, with AST and ALT most commonly involved; 60% of increases resolve within the first 13 weeks of treatment. Two cases of mortality due to hepatic failure and 1 due to hepatitis secondary to clozapine have been reported. Monitoring guidelines suggest baseline LFTs and 6-monthly thereafter. Patient 1 (52-year-old woman with paranoid schizophrenia) developed hepatotoxicity on clozapine within about 1 week (dose 25 mg morning/75 mg evening) with ALT 75 IU/L and AST 198 IU/L; after discontinuation LFTs rose further (ALT 308, AST 119, GGT 78) then normalized. On rechallenge at 100 mg morning/250 mg evening, elevations recurred (AST 44, ALT 107, GGT 37), persisted despite dose reduction, and normalized after withdrawal. Patient 2 remained on clozapine with abnormalities resolving spontaneously.

raw_record.support_text: Among the medications taken by the patient leading up to ICU admission, clozapine was determined to be the most likely culprit for drug-induced liver injury: the Naranjo nomogram indicated a possible relationship (score of 3), RUCAM indicated clozapine as a probable cause of liver injury (total score 6), and LiverTox suggests clozapine as a very likely cause of clinically apparent liver injury. Lithium and risperidone were determined to be unlikely causes.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of clinically apparent liver injury with hepatic encephalopathy requiring ICU admission; AST and ALT ~5x upper limit of normal at admission (AST 225, ALT 364 IU/L) rising to peak ALT 1313 IU/L after NAC, with subsequent recovery after clozapine discontinuation. Naranjo score 3 (possible); RUCAM score 6 (probable); LiverTox classifies as very likely cause. Discussion states serum enzyme elevations occur in up to 60% of patients on clozapine while clinically apparent ALI with liver enzyme elevations and jaundice occurs in ~1 of 2000 patients; mechanism unknown, possibly a clozapine toxic metabolite. Concurrent lithium and risperidone were taken but ruled out as culprits.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe clozapine-related hepatotoxicity as an idiosyncratic adverse drug reaction that generally begins within the first 3 months, often with asymptomatic abnormal liver transaminase levels, and note the known risk of acute fulminant hepatic failure. Manufacturer guidelines recommend discontinuation when any LFT exceeds 3x the upper reference limit or when any bilirubin elevation, hepatitis, or jaundice develops, with cautious rechallenge possible once liver function normalizes.

raw_record.support_text: Clozapine has been related to liver enzyme increase in 30%-50% of patients, though they were asymptomatic. Icteric hepatitis occurs in 0.06% of those on clozapine, compared with a more fulminant form occurring rarely at a rate of 0.001%. In a vignette about allergic hepatotoxicity, the patient became clinically symptomatic with abnormal enzymes that improved after discontinuing the drug.

Icteric hepatitis occurs in 0.06%; a more fulminant form occurs rarely at 0.001%. 37% of cases showed a twofold or greater aminotransferase increase. raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses clozapine-induced liver damage, noting the mechanism is unclear and may result from a metabolic idiosyncrasy or an immunoallergic reaction. Given the absence of fever, rash, or eosinophilia, the authors speculate this reaction may represent a metabolic idiosyncrasy, and clozapine is mainly metabolized in the liver in a cytochrome P450-dependent manner. The paper further notes a known risk of acute fulminant hepatic failure and that many patients with abnormal liver transaminase levels remain asymptomatic, with onset generally in the first 3 months, and describes clozapine-related hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Occurs in the first 3 months of treatment; authors speculate a metabolic idiosyncrasy (absent fever/rash/eosinophilia); mechanism is cytochrome P450-dependent hepatic metabolism. Highest reported increases were a 22-fold ALT rise and a 12-fold AST rise with no clinical sequelae; liver enzyme elevations are usually transient and resolve after the first 13 weeks. Manufacturer guidelines advise discontinuing clozapine if any LFT exceeds 3x the upper reference limit or if bilirubin rises, and immediate cessation and medical referral if hepatitis or jaundice develops; cautious rechallenge may be attempted after liver function normalizes. Conflicting evidence on dose-relatedness: a 4-year follow-up study (Marinkovic) concluded the hepatotoxicity was dose-related, while more recent studies found dose reduction had no effect on normalization time; the authors' 2 cases argue against a dose relation. There is a known risk of acute fulminant hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: The mechanism of clozapine-induced liver damage is unclear and may result from a metabolic idiosyncrasy or an immunoallergic reaction. Given the absence of fever, rash, or eosinophilia, the authors speculate the reaction represents a metabolic idiosyncrasy; clozapine is mainly metabolized in the liver and is cytochrome P450-dependent.

Liver enzyme elevation with clozapine is described as common, usually transient and clinically insignificant, resolving after the first 13 weeks of treatment; highest reported increases are a 22-fold ALT and 12-fold AST elevation with no clinical sequelae. There are conflicting reports on whether the effect is dose-related (a 4-year follow-up by Marinkovic et al concluded hepatotoxicity was dose-related since dose reduction normalized liver function, whereas later studies and the authors' 2 cases found no dose relation). Manufacturer guidelines recommend discontinuing clozapine if any LFT is >3x upper reference limit or bilirubin elevates, and immediate discontinuation and physician referral if hepatitis or jaundice develops; cautious rechallenge may be attempted after LFT normalization. Mechanism speculated to be metabolic idiosyncrasy (no fever/rash/eosinophilia); clozapine metabolized in the liver, CYP450-dependent.

raw_record.support_text: The authors identified 20 cases of clozapine induced hepatitis among 42 patients who developed a clozapine associated systemic inflammatory disorder (hepatitis, nephritis, or pancreatitis), collected from 41 qualifying case reports. Hepatitis is one of the clozapine-associated inflammatory organ injuries framed as causally induced by clozapine.
raw_record.extra_details: Among 42 patients with a clozapine-associated systemic inflammatory disorder (from 41 qualifying case reports), 20 had clozapine induced hepatitis; 11 had nephritis and 11 had pancreatitis. The broader case series included predominantly White (48%) and Asian (44%) patients, mostly with schizophrenia (76%), schizoaffective disorder (14%), bipolar affective disorder, or psychosis in Parkinson's disease. Data collected included timing of onset, clozapine dose, plasma clozapine and norclozapine concentrations, concurrent medications, and outcome.

raw_record.support_text: Clozapine is associated with a spectrum of human drug-induced liver injury in therapeutic use. The most common abnormality is an isolated asymptomatic increase in aminotransferase levels (ALT increased in 53% and AST in 39% of 164 clozapine-treated patients; an increase in one enzyme in 61% of 125 patients). Icteric hepatitis has been reported twice, with biopsy-confirmed zone 3 (piecemeal) necrosis in one case and normalization of bilirubin and aminotransferases within 4 weeks. Cholestatic or mixed hepatitis has been reported in two cases, with jaundice within 8 weeks and confirmed cholestatic hepatitis on biopsy. Fulminant hepatitis with encephalopathy and coagulopathy is very rare, with only 2 cases (0.001%) among 136,000 patients in the manufacturers' database over 6 years. The mechanism is unclear, but the drug is hepatically metabolized via cytochrome P450 and reactive metabolites are presumed to mediate the damage, with insufficient evidence to distinguish toxic from immunoallergic hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Common isolated asymptomatic aminotransferase elevation: ALT increased in 53% and AST in 39% of 164 patients; in 125 patients an increase in one of AST, ALT, GGT, alkaline phosphatase, lactic dehydrogenase in 61%, with ≥2-fold increase in 31%; no jaundice reported in that cohort; regulatory data reported aminotransferase increase in 30%. Icteric hepatitis reported twice, associated nausea within 4 weeks, biopsy-confirmed zone 3 necrosis in one case, bilirubin/aminotransferase normalized in 4 weeks; manufacturers reported icteric hepatitis in 84/136,000 (0.06%). Two cases of cholestatic or mixed hepatitis with jaundice within 8 weeks and biopsy-confirmed cholestatic hepatitis; liver tests normalized upon discontinuation. Fulminant hepatitis with encephalopathy and coagulopathy: 2 cases (0.001%) among 136,000 patients over 6 years, including the present case. Mechanism unclear; predominantly hepatic cytochrome P450-dependent metabolism; reactive metabolites presumed, insufficient evidence to distinguish toxic vs immunoallergic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: In this case report, a patient on clozapine 250 mg/day developed marked liver test abnormalities (ALT 1914, AST 830, bilirubin 76, gamma-GT 99 U/L, albumin 35 g/L, WCC 21.4, Hb 107). Clozapine was stopped immediately and the patient was transferred to a gastroenterology unit for observation. The authors describe the case as illustrating the treacherous nature of a rare fulminant hepatotoxic reaction, with no pre-existing liver disease or indicator of vulnerability, and rapid progression of liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Young male treated for a first psychotic episode; described as the youngest such case in the literature with good recovery. Peak transaminases (ALT 2282, AST 1056) occurred the day after clozapine cessation, gamma-GT peaked at 164, bilirubin peaked at 112 on day 3, INR raised to 1.3 for 5 days, albumin below normal for 2 weeks, CRP peaked at 45.5 mg/L. All enzymes returned to normal 3-4 weeks after cessation, bilirubin last to normalise; recovery so complete that liver transplant, otherwise to be considered, was not needed. Patient was subsequently restarted on amisulpride 200 mg twice daily with normal liver function tests. Clinical course included only sedation despite severe injury; no pre-existing liver disease or vulnerability indicator identified.

raw_record.support_text: A case report described a 45-year-old woman with schizophrenia on a cross-titration from Olanzapine 2.5 mg daily to Clozapine 125 mg daily. After 12 days she presented fever, elevated white blood cell count, and elevated AST, ALT, and C-reactive protein, and was diagnosed with Clozapine-induced hepatitis, recovering after drug discontinuation. Reintroduction of Clozapine at 100 mg daily again altered liver function, indicating a strong connection between the hepatitis and Clozapine.
raw_record.extra_details: 45-year-old woman with schizophrenia; clozapine-induced hepatitis after 12 days on clozapine 125 mg daily during cross-titration from olanzapine 2.5 mg daily; presented fever, leukocytosis, elevated AST, ALT, and C-reactive protein; resolved after discontinuation; positive rechallenge - reintroduction of clozapine 100 mg daily re-altered liver function.

raw_record.support_text: A systematic review (literature up to December 2017) identified 20 case reports of clozapine-induced hepatitis among 42 inflammatory reactions to clozapine treatment. Mean clozapine dose was 252.4 mg (SD 133.7); time to onset of hepatitis was 34.2 days (SD 20.1, range 12-90 days), mean time to recovery was 25.9 (SD 16.5) days, and three hepatitis cases died. Three hepatitis cases had a clozapine rechallenge, two of which were successfully rechallenged.

Mean patient age 38.8 (SD 11.9) years; mean clozapine dose 252.4 (SD 133.7) mg; time to onset 34.2 (SD 20.1, range 12-90) days; mean time to recovery 25.9 (SD 16.5) days. Three hepatitis cases died. Three hepatitis cases were rechallenged with clozapine, two successfully. Clozapine used for treatment-resistant schizophrenia.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the case of a 44-year-old woman with chronic paranoid schizophrenia given clozapine, 400 mg/day, as monotherapy. During the fifth week of treatment her previously unremarkable transaminase levels dramatically rose to 675 U/liter for ALT and 369 U/liter for AST, with only a slight increase in gamma-glutamyltransferase (67 U/liter) and unremarkable bilirubin and cholestatic parameters; she developed 28% eosinophilia, and serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, and C, Epstein-Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus were negative. This case is presented as toxic hepatitis caused by clozapine treatment in a letter titled 'Toxic Hepatitis by Clozapine Treatment'. A previously reported clozapine case of toxic hepatitis accompanied by jaundice and bone marrow damage showed enzymes increased to 133 (ALT) and 268 (AST) U/liter.
raw_record.extra_details: Clozapine given at 400 mg/day as monotherapy; toxic hepatitis developed during the fifth week of treatment. raw_record.support_text: A close temporal relationship between the first intake of risperidone and liver enzyme elevations, deterioration under continued risperidone treatment, a considerable decrease in liver enzyme abnormalities after switching to haloperidol, and exclusion of other causes make it highly probable that risperidone caused the initial hepatic injury. The liver biopsy result was consistent with drug-induced hepatotoxicity. The authors conclude that the possibility of risperidone-induced cholestatic hepatitis must be borne in mind.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of risperidone-induced cholestatic hepatitis. Liver needle biopsy was performed and was consistent with drug-induced hepatotoxicity; an excess of eosinophils in the liver supported a possible immunoallergic reaction, while CYP2D6-dependent pharmacokinetic differences were discussed as possibly increasing risk of toxic liver injury. Rechallenge was not attempted due to the severity of the reaction. Elevations in AST, ALT, and γGT (γ-glutamyltransferase) resolved considerably after switching to haloperidol. Olanzapine caused deterioration of the hepatic injury in this case.

raw_record.support_text: A 34-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder and insulin-dependent diabetes, maintained on risperidone 6 mg at night for 8 years (with lithium 900 mg twice daily, enalapril 5 mg daily, and insulin as needed), developed cholestasis that resolved when risperidone was withdrawn. The Naranjo probability scale indicated that the atypical antipsychotics (risperidone and quetiapine) were the probable cause of the cholestasis.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic therapeutic dosing of risperidone 6 mg nightly for 8 years; cholestasis (signs and symptoms) resolved upon drug withdrawal; Naranjo probability scale judged risperidone as a probable cause. Patient concurrently received lithium, enalapril, and insulin. A prior publication (Whitworth et al.) reported moderately elevated liver enzymes that normalized at an unchanged risperidone dose in one case and with a 1 mg decrease in another.

raw_record.support_text: In a 41-year-old man (Mr. A) on outpatient risperidone monotherapy, elevated serum AST (83 U/L) and ALT (123 U/L) were noted after 7 weeks; levels rose during week 8 (AST=139 U/L, ALT=522 U/L) with nausea, vomiting, and epigastric pain, prompting hospitalization and risperidone discontinuation. Viral hepatitis A/B/C serology, ultrasound, ceruloplasmin/copper, and autoimmune (ANA, AMA, LKM, SLA) tests were negative, but eosinophilia (850 cells/mm3) and anti-smooth-muscle antibodies (titer 1:640) were present, which resolved after discontinuation. Excluding other causes, the authors classified the case as probable risperidone-induced hepatotoxicity according to the Naranjo scale.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of an adult on risperidone monotherapy for a psychiatric indication. Off-therapy AST/ALT normal on haloperidol 4 years earlier; AST/ALT returned to normal within 3 weeks of treatment with loxapine (200 mg/day) and oxazepam (200 mg/day), and remained normal on haloperidol (20 mg/day). Naranjo causality scale classified as probable. Laboratory highlights: cholestatic serum tests, WBC, RBC, and coagulation normal; negative hepatitis A/B/C serology, normal abdominal ultrasound, normal ceruloplasmin/copper; eosinophilia (850 cells/mm3) and anti-smooth-muscle antibodies (1:640, decreasing to 1:100) without actin/vimentin specificity; negative anti-LKM, anti-soluble liver antigen, ANA, and AMA.

raw_record.support_text: A 23-year-old man with schizophrenia developed a sharp rise in liver enzyme levels during 13 days of treatment with risperidone, interpreted as hepatotoxicity, after which antipsychotic therapy was switched to paliperidone. Scoring with the Naranjo algorithm indicated a probable association between risperidone use and hepatotoxicity, with a score of 7. This is reported as the first case of a patient who developed hepatotoxicity during risperidone use that did not remit with a switch to paliperidone therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver enzyme levels rose sharply during 13 days of risperidone therapy in a schizophrenic patient; therapy was then switched to paliperidone. Naranjo causality score 7 (probable). Hepatotoxicity resolved approximately 4 weeks after discontinuation of antipsychotics, with haloperidol initiated. First reported case of risperidone hepatotoxicity not remitting upon switch to paliperidone.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of risperidone-induced cholestatic hepatotoxicity in a 37-year-old male who developed a rapid increase in liver enzymes and cholestatic parameters after starting risperidone for paranoid psychosis. Work-up for other aetiologies was negative, and a percutaneous liver biopsy was consistent with drug-induced liver injury and cholestasis. Liver function tests returned to near-normal values over one month after discontinuance of all anti-psychotic agents.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single case with a history of inactive Crohn's disease; subsequent exposure to haloperidol (10 mg/day) and later olanzapine also worsened the already-pathological liver tests, though risperidone is the designated culprit.
raw_record.extra_details: Risperidone (Risperdal) dosed 2 mg/day titrated to 6 mg/day within a week for paranoid psychosis; elevated AST (42 U/l), ALT (77 U/l), γGT (367 U/l) noted after 3 days, increasing over 10 days until discontinuation. On admission: AST 96, ALT 209, γGT 254, alkaline phosphatase 634 U/l, bilirubin 1.6 mg/dl, serum lipase 239 U/l. Percutaneous liver biopsy consistent with drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis: bile pigments in hepatocytes, portal and peri-cholangiolar inflammatory infiltrates, excess eosinophils; no autoimmune hepatitis, fibrosis, or cirrhosis. Viral and other aetiologies excluded; values returned near-normal over one month. Authors recommend monitoring cholestatic parameters plus liver enzymes at initiation and during the first weeks of risperidone intake.

raw_record.support_text: In a phase I clinical study comparing liposomal paclitaxel (LEP) with Taxol (paclitaxel), the paper states that symptoms including diarrhea, anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, hepatotoxicity and chest pain became more severe in the patients treated with Taxol, while these symptoms were mild after intrapleural LEP application. Taxol (paclitaxel) is thereby explicitly attributed as causing hepatotoxicity, which was more severe than with LEP, along with anaphylaxis and peripheral nerve toxicity as the major side-effects.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity was more severe in Taxol-treated patients than with intrapleural LEP. Anaphylaxis and peripheral nerve toxicity were the major side-effects with Taxol; standard paclitaxel (cremophor-based) formulation.

raw_record.support_text: In a clinical study (Case 6), fluconazole (400 mg/day) was assessed by physicians as having caused the patient's liver injury (causality 'Yes'), whereas prochlorperazine, acetazolamide, and cimetidine were assessed as non-causal. Separately, the paper states that clinically dose-dependent hepatotoxicity of fluconazole (a potent CYP2C19 and moderate CYP2C9/CYP3A inhibitor) was observed, and the results suggest clinically observed DILI may occur when P450 inhibitors are given at high daily doses.
raw_record.extra_details: Physician-assessed causality 'Yes' in clinical DILI case (Case 6) at 400 mg/day; predicted DILI-positive; separately reported clinically dose-dependent hepatotoxicity as a potent CYP2C19 inhibitor (moderate CYP2C9/CYP3A inhibitor) (Wells and Lever, 1992).

raw_record.support_text: A 39-year-old previously healthy male ingested two therapeutic 150 mg doses of fluconazole one week apart, then developed jaundice, scleral icterus, a pruritic erythematous rash, fever, mild eosinophilia (810 cells/µl), and markedly elevated transaminases (ALT 4192 U/l, AST 2267 U/l) with total bilirubin 31.5 mg/dl. Liver biopsy showed portal and lobular inflammation with cholestasis and apoptosis. He had negative serologies for viral and autoimmune hepatitis and took no other medications apart from 1 g total acetaminophen over two days. The authors made a diagnosis of fluconazole hypersensitivity and, in a following paragraph, state that the absence of pre-existing liver disease and the presence of eosinophilia, rash, and fever support an immunoallergic reaction to fluconazole.
raw_record.extra_details: Healthy 39-year-old male without pre-existing liver disease or alcohol use. Two 150 mg fluconazole doses taken 1 week apart; jaundice, rash, and fever developed about 4 days later. Alanine aminotransferase 4192 U/l (normal 0-42), aspartate aminotransferase 2267 U/L (normal 0-48), alkaline phosphatase 141 U/l, total bilirubin 31.5 mg/dl with conjugated 9.9 mg/dl; mild eosinophilia 810 cells/µl; PT/PTT normal; abdominal sonogram normal. Liver biopsy showed portal and lobular inflammation with cholestasis and apoptosis; dermatologic biopsy showed necrotic keratinocytes. Negative serologies for hepatitis A/B/C, toxoplasmosis, CMV, HSV, parvovirus, EBV, and autoimmune hepatitis (ANA, anti-smooth muscle). Concomitant acetaminophen 1 g total was taken but not attributed as cause. Treated with IV methylprednisolone 60 mg BID and IVIG 1 g/kg; liver parameters declined next day and normalized ~3 months after ingestion, consistent with dechallenge. The paper notes fluconazole-induced liver injury is less common than ketoconazole and previously reported mainly in HIV or underlying liver disease patients.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that data associating hepatic injury with fluconazole are convincing. Trends toward increased frequency of severe hepatic adverse events were consistently observed in large randomized controlled trials, and in one placebo-controlled trial mean ALT increased by 100 IU/L in patients assigned fluconazole versus 35 IU/L in placebo (P=0.024). They conclude that 'fluconazole can cause hepatic injury' and clinicians should be aware of its potential serious toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Commonly used antifungal agent. Trends toward increased frequency of severe hepatic adverse events consistently observed in large randomized controlled trials. In one placebo-controlled trial, mean ALT increased by 100 IU/L with fluconazole versus 35 IU/L with placebo (P=0.024).

raw_record.support_text: Given the close temporal relation between initiation of fluconazole therapy (400 mg orally daily from March 12, 1992) and the acute increase in serum hepatic transaminases, the previously reported association of fluconazole with abnormal transaminase elevations, and exclusion of other potential causes of acute hepatic necrosis, the authors conclude the report most likely represents a case of fatal fluconazole-induced hepatotoxicity. The patient died on April 6, 1992.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report in an AIDS patient. Fluconazole 400 mg orally daily initiated March 12, 1992; acute rise in transaminases (ALT up to 1,825 IU/L, AST up to 2,770 IU/L), bilirubin up to 28.6 mg/dL, prothrombin time up to 33.0 s. Histology showed massive hepatic necrosis with portal lymphocytic infiltrate and spared hepatocyte islands; viral, Amanita phalloides, and acetaminophen-overdose causes excluded; prochlorperazine differential not consistent because hepatocellular necrosis was not reported for it. Patient died April 6, 1992. Authors note fatal hepatotoxicity also reported with related azole ketoconazole and recommend transaminase monitoring during fluconazole therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A 39-year-old male ingested two 150 mg fluconazole doses one week apart and 4 days later developed weakness, jaundice, scleral icterus, and a pruritic erythematous rash, with eosinophilia (810 cells/µl), ALT 4192 U/l, AST 2267 U/l, total bilirubin 31.5 mg/dl, and a liver biopsy showing portal and lobular inflammation with cholestasis and apoptosis; viral and autoimmune serologies were negative, and the presentation was attributed to fluconazole-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Therapeutic 150 mg fluconazole taken twice (one week apart) after suggested use for recurrent candidiasis of his wife; jaundice appeared 4 days later. Labs: eosinophilia 810 cells/µl, ALT 4192 U/l (normal 0-42), AST 2267 U/l (normal 0-48), alkaline phosphatase 141 U/l (normal 20-125), albumin 4.1 g/dl, total bilirubin 31.5 mg/dl with conjugated 9.9 mg/dl; PT/PTT normal; normal abdominal sonogram. Biopsy: portal and lobular inflammation with cholestasis and apoptosis; dermatologic biopsy showed numerous necrotic keratinocytes. Also took 500 mg acetaminophen for two consecutive days (1 g total) before symptoms; no other medications, no alcohol use. Negative viral hepatitis (A, B, C), CMV, HSV, parvovirus, EBV and autoimmune hepatitis serologies. Temperature 100.0 F.

raw_record.extra_details: 42-year-old black man, a veterinarian's assistant, admitted to Houston VA Hospital on March 7, 1975. Two weeks before admission he developed nausea, vomiting, and vague intermittent midabdominal pain with temperature of 101-102 F (38.3-38.9 C) and chills. He admitted sniffing methoxyflurane for the two months before admission, confirmed by his family and employer. Methoxyflurane (Penthrane) is a fluorinated agent sharing the basic chemical structure of halothane; a hypersensitivity reaction has been implicated in the pathogenesis of halothane- or methoxyflurane-induced hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: In the described case series, fever was present within twenty-four hours after the operation, and in a given patient repeated exposures to the anesthetic produced a similar duration of febrile response. Seven patients had jaundice, most had moderate hepatomegaly, and several had shaking chills. The hepatic dysfunction, characterized by cellular damage, was attributed to repeated exposure to the anesthetic, methoxyflurane, given as surgical anesthesia (as in the case undergoing gastrectomy under methoxyflurane and nitrous oxide anesthesia, who developed fatal hepatic necrosis).
raw_record.extra_details: Fever developed within 24 hours after anesthesia, with duration from 1 to 23 days. Seven of the patients had jaundice; most had minimal to moderate hepatomegaly. Hepatic function studies indicated cellular damage: transaminases elevated in every patient (often strikingly), and alkaline phosphatase and prothrombin time elevated in all but one. Cephalin flocculation and thymol turbidity were negative or only weakly positive in all but one case. Three cases had leukopenia (1750-3550) and three had eosinophilia (6-8%), suggestive of an allergic process; one had atypical lymphocytes resembling infectious mononucleosis. Liver function abnormalities commonly resolved slowly over several months. In the illustrative case, marked hepatic necrosis with hemorrhage, fatty change, bile-duct proliferation, and cholestasis were found at autopsy; the patient lapsed into coma and died on the 11th postoperative day in shock.

raw_record.support_text: Among fifteen patients with diagnoses of drug-induced hepatitis made following anesthesia, one patient's hepatitis followed methoxyflurane anesthesia. The paper presents this in the context of halothane-related sensitization data, with no additional methoxyflurane-specific detail.
raw_record.extra_details: One of 15 patients carrying a diagnosis of drug-induced hepatitis had hepatitis following methoxyflurane anesthesia; it is mentioned only in passing within a study focused on halothane-induced lymphocyte stimulation, and the patient's lymphocyte stimulation was assessed in the presence of halothane.

raw_record.support_text: Case 3 is presented under the heading "Severe hepatotoxicity to benzoarene." The first liver biopsy showed fibrosis with proliferation of bile ductules, inflammatory infiltrate, and piecemeal necrosis on the edges of the remaining parenchyma, attributed to the drug benzoarene (benzarone).
raw_record.extra_details: Case 3 presented with jaundice, palmar erythema, spider naevi, ascites and a nodular dysmorphic liver; serum ALT 819 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 164 IU/l, bilirubin 188 µmol/l (113 µmol/l direct), prothrombin level 35% of normal; ANA and anti-smooth-muscle antibodies positive; HBV, HCV and HAV markers absent, AFP normal. First biopsy showed extensive hepatic collapse, bile ductule proliferation and marked piecemeal necrosis; electron microscopy showed no lysosomal lipid inclusions. Patient treated with methylprednisolone 24 mg/day, spironolactone 150 mg/day and lactulose; a second biopsy 1 month later showed cirrhosis with extensive fibrosis and hepatocyte rosettes. Patient became comatose and died at home approximately 1 week after discharge. Chemical identity: 2-ethyl-3-(4-hydroxybenzoyl)benzofuran, a noniodinated benzofuran derivative.

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes chronic active hepatitis caused by benzarone, a benzofuran derivative used in Europe for peripheral venous disorders. The patient developed jaundice with elevated serum ALT while on the drug, which decreased upon discontinuation, and liver lesions were those of chronic active hepatitis with anti-smooth muscle antibodies present.
raw_record.extra_details: 61-year-old woman treated for capillary fragility/peripheral venous disorder at 200 mg/day (two tablets). Jaundice and ALT (up to 38x ULN, then 27x and 34x ULN) recurred on rechallenge on three occasions and subsided on discontinuation, demonstrating positive dechallenge/rechallenge. Serum bilirubin rose to 103 µmol/l; alkaline phosphatase 1.5x ULN. Liver biopsy showed extensive portal fibrosis, bridging necrosis, mild inflammatory infiltration, and a single lymphohistiocytic granuloma. Anti-smooth muscle antibodies (titer 1:500) disappeared ~8 months after withdrawal. Reported as the first case of benzarone-induced chronic active hepatitis; drug's structure is close to amiodarone.

raw_record.support_text: A 44-year-old woman presented with icterus for 2 months and markedly elevated hepatocellular-pattern liver function tests (T-BIL 6.61 mg/dL, AST 1043 U/L, ALT 1187 U/L, ALP 186 U/L, GGT 48 U/L). A diagnosis of acute hepatitis was made; viral, autoimmune, iron and ceruloplasmin work-ups were negative, and liver biopsy showed active hepatitis with bile stasis, focal confluent necrosis, hepatocyte apoptosis, and portal/lobular inflammation.
raw_record.extra_details: Benzarone taken as 2 tablets (total 200 mg) per day without prescription since 4 months prior; Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Model (RUCAM) score 7, indicating probable attribution. Patient was hospitalized, received supportive care, and liver tests normalized in 50 days. Competing causes excluded; one case only, first in Asia.

raw_record.support_text: In the current report, two clinically apparent cases of grade 4 hepatotoxicity were observed among 43 patients treated with ribociclib. In both cases ALT and AST remained elevated for a long period despite discontinuation of therapy; although the patients did not have elevated autoimmune markers such as ANA, the clinical and biochemical phenotype was similar to that of seronegative drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis. Liver tests improved promptly after a course of corticosteroids and completely normalized at last follow-up, and both patients later tolerated palbociclib without further elevation of liver enzymes.
raw_record.extra_details: Two of 43 ribociclib-treated patients developed grade 4 hepatotoxicity; ALT/AST stayed elevated for a long period despite drug discontinuation; no elevated ANA (seronegative picture); treated with corticosteroids tapered over eight weeks with prompt improvement and complete normalization; both patients tolerated palbociclib without liver enzyme elevation, arguing DILI is not a class effect of CDK4/6 inhibitors but specific to ribociclib.

raw_record.support_text: Causality assessment for ribociclib-induced liver injury used an R-factor of 20.73 (hepatocellular pattern, R≥5), a RUCAM score of ~10 (highly probable association with ribociclib), and a Naranjo score of 7 (probable ADR), together with histologic confluent centrilobular necrosis, supporting ribociclib as the source of acute hepatic injury in a postmenopausal woman with HR+/HER2- metastatic invasive lobular carcinoma who developed severe hepatocellular DILI 8 weeks after starting ribociclib with anastrozole.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of biopsy-confirmed submassive, zone-3-predominant confluent hepatocyte necrosis without significant inflammation, cholestasis, steatosis, or fibrosis (DILIN histopathology instrument; trichrome/reticulin showed collapsed reticulin framework). Laboratory: ALT 1825 U/L (ULN 40), ALP 278 U/L (ULN 120) yielding R=20.73; RUCAM ~10 (highly probable); Naranjo ~7 (probable). Onset ~8 weeks after start; liver tests improved with IV N-acetylcysteine (NAC) despite initial worsening after withdrawal; rechallenge with another CDK4/6 inhibitor deemed unsafe; treatment continued with anastrozole monotherapy, stable disease at 13 months. Patient was treated with ribociclib plus anastrozole with causality attributed to ribociclib (alternative causes excluded). Supporting trial/registry data cited: MONALEESA-2/-3/-7 grade 3-4 ALT elevations up to 9.3%, 8.5%, 5%; real-world transaminitis in 9.4% (Buller, median time to onset grade>3 hepatotoxicity 85 d) and 5.9% (Abdel-Razeq, 21.4% of drug cessation attributed to hepatotoxicity).

raw_record.support_text: In this patient series, ribociclib was one of the two CDK4/6 inhibitors mainly involved in CDK4/6 inhibitor-induced liver injury (alongside abemaciclib). The predominant liver-injury type was hepatocellular, and 32% of patients had autoimmune features such as positive anti-nuclear antibodies and/or elevated serum IgG at diagnosis. Corticosteroid treatment was initiated in 40% of patients and allowed resolution of liver injury that had not improved spontaneously. No patient experienced fulminant hepatitis or death secondary to anti-CDK4/6-induced liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Paper argues CDK4/6 inhibitors should be included in the drug-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis (DI-ALH) category based on autoimmune features (ANA and/or elevated IgG in 1/3 of patients), consistent biopsy/histology, and corticosteroid response without hepatitis recurrence after discontinuation. Corticosteroids started about 1 month after hepatitis onset; corticosteroid-treated patients improved more slowly. Management recommendation: discontinue treatment at hepatitis grade 3 or 4. Small, heterogeneous series; no fulminant hepatitis or death.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a real-world experience of rechallenging with abemaciclib after a prior reaction of grade 4 liver toxicity to ribociclib, describing high transaminase values of more than 27 times the upper limit of normal (ULN) that occurred while the patient was receiving ribociclib for HR+/HER2- metastatic breast cancer. After switching to abemaciclib the patient later had grade 3 neutropenia and diarrhea, but after two years hepatic enzymes and complete blood count were normal with stable oncological disease.
raw_record.extra_details: 67-year-old female with HR+/HER2- metastatic (inflammatory) breast cancer on CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy; grade 4 hepatic toxicity with transaminases >27x ULN while on ribociclib. She was subsequently rechallenged by switching to abemaciclib, which caused grade 3 neutropenia and diarrhea but not liver injury; after two years hepatic enzymes and complete blood count normalized and oncological disease was stable.

raw_record.support_text: A 41-year-old female with metastatic HR-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer developed liver enzyme elevation under ribociclib treatment. Ribociclib was withdrawn 8 weeks after initiation due to enzyme elevation. A liver biopsy performed after further enzyme increase (peak ALT 2836 U/l), jaundice (peak bilirubin 353 µmol/l) and coagulopathy (INR 1.8) revealed acute hepatitis with 30% parenchymal necrosis; the RUCAM score was 7 points (probable).
raw_record.extra_details: Severe idiosyncratic hepatocellular DILI grade 3 (International DILI Expert Working Group) in a 41-year-old female with primary metastatic HR-positive HER2-negative breast cancer. Ribociclib withdrawn 8 weeks after initiation. Liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis with 30% parenchymal necrosis; peak ALT 2836 U/l, peak bilirubin 353 µmol/l, INR 1.8. RUCAM score 7 (probable). Managed with prednisone 60 mg and N-acetylcysteine (Prescott regimen); liver enzymes normalized within 8 weeks with prednisone tapering. Peak ALT, bilirubin, and INR values and treatment details recorded.

raw_record.support_text: After one month of treatment with the CDK4/6 inhibitor ribociclib, the patient developed grade 2 liver toxicity with alanine and aspartate aminotransferases four times the upper limit of normal (ULN). Liver enzyme values returned to baseline after stopping the drug, but the patient again developed grade 2 liver toxicity upon re-administration, prompting a first ribociclib dose reduction (200 mg twice daily orally). After four months on 400 mg ribociclib daily the patient developed grade 3 liver toxicity (transaminases 12x ULN), and subsequently grade 4 liver toxicity (transaminases >27x ULN) in February 2022, requiring complete discontinuation of ribociclib. Other probable causes of hypertransaminasemia were excluded (no infectious disease, no liver metastases, no concomitant hepatotoxic medications, negative viral serology for hepatitis A, B, and C). Total bilirubin remained within normal limits, and it took about 5 months for AST and ALT to return to baseline, with corticosteroid therapy required after the grade 4 episode.
raw_record.extra_details: Female patient on ribociclib for metastatic breast cancer (treated alongside letrozole/aromatase inhibitor and zoledronic acid); the liver toxicity was attributed specifically to ribociclib. Timing: grade 2 after ~1 month; grade 3 after 4 months on 400 mg/day; grade 4 in February 2022. Dechallenge resolved transaminases, rechallenge reproduced grade 2 toxicity. Dose reductions: first to 200 mg twice daily, later to 200 mg/day, then full stop. Total bilirubin within normal limits throughout. Recovery to baseline took ~5 months; corticosteroid therapy required after grade 4 hypertransaminasemia. Other causes excluded (infection, liver metastases, viral hepatitis A/B/C, concomitant hepatotoxic drugs). No acute liver failure, transplant, or death reported.

raw_record.support_text: The study reports analysis of 22 cases of CDK4/6 inhibitor-induced liver injury; according to Table 3, 19 of these cases involved ribociclib (10 without and 9 with corticosteroid treatment). All patients exhibited CTCAE grade 3 or 4 hepatitis, with DILI network severity mild in 18, moderate in 3, and severe in 1 patient, with no hepatitis-related deaths. The one severe case leading to hospitalization may be explained by the concomitant use of pembrolizumab and ribociclib.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Breast cancer patients on concomitant hormonal therapy; in the single severe case leading to hospitalization, co-exposure to pembrolizumab and ribociclib may explain the severity.
raw_record.extra_details: 19 of 22 total cases of CDK4/6 inhibitor-induced liver injury involved ribociclib. All patients had CTCAE grade 3-4 hepatitis; DILI network severity mild (18), moderate (3), severe (1); no hepatitis-related deaths. Hepatitis improvement was significantly slower in corticosteroid-treated patients (106.62 +/- 54.75 vs 49.36 +/- 40.74 days, p=0.009). Liver biopsies showed acute centrilobular hepatitis with foci of necrosis and lymphocytic infiltrate.

raw_record.support_text: Actinomycin D (administered with vincristine) is reported as a cause of hepatopathy in children receiving chemotherapy for Wilms' tumour. In NWTS 4, 5 of 37 children receiving a single 60 µg/kg dose per 3-week course developed hepatic toxicity, while none of 63 children on the divided-dose regimen did; dose reduction to 45 µg/kg followed. In SIOP 9, 64 children suffered at least one episode of hepatotoxicity, with 41 of 511 (8%) classed as 'H-VOD', supporting a steep dose/toxicity relationship between 1.5 and 1.8 mg/m².
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Children with Wilms' tumour; administered together with vincristine (and in some cohorts with abdominal radiation, which increases risk); infants and younger/lower-weight children appear more vulnerable, and right-sided tumours are associated with higher risk; dose and scheduling varied across study protocols.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic veno-occlusive disease ('H-VOD') was the reported syndrome. Dose/schedule data: NWTS 4 single dose 60 µg/kg per 3 weeks (approx 1.8 mg/m²) versus same total fractionated over 5 days; dose later reduced to 45 µg/kg. UKW1/UKW2 used pulsed 1.5 mg/m² 3-weekly, with 6/355 (1.7%) developing hepatopathy. SIOP 9 used 0.45 mg/m²/day x 3 days (later 15 µg/kg/day x 3) in weeks 1-2, repeated in weeks 4-5 for the 8-week arm; infants received 66% of doses; 64 children had at least one episode, 41/511 (8%) H-VOD. SIOP series: abdominal irradiation produced hepatopathy in 11/68 (16%) versus 30/443 (6.7%), multivariable P=0.001. Right-sided Wilms' tumour associated with more hepatopathy (5.6% vs 1.2%, P=0.0002); of 33 H-VOD cases from four series, 27 were right-sided. A newborn with fatal hepatopathy after 75 µg/day x 5 days (approx 100 µg/kg if ~3 kg) and one fatal hepatopathy in 5/9 infants on UKW3 new dosing were reported. A convincing case in a 3.8-year-old with rhabdomyosarcoma after 2.25 mg/m² in divided doses is also cited.

raw_record.support_text: Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS) is described as a well-known serious complication, and the paper states that chemotherapeutic agents such as Act-D, as well as radiation, can damage small hepatic venules and sinusoids, recapitulating SOS in non-HSCT patients. The reported incidence of SOS ranges from 1.2% to 8% in children treated for Wilms' tumor, and this study describes a single-center experience where children with WT developed SOS during neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy that included Act-D.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients (children) treated for Wilms' tumor/clear cell sarcoma of the kidney under the SIOP-WT2001 protocol; SOS developed during neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy; one patient expired before surgery.
raw_record.extra_details: 5 of 104 children (4.8%) developed SOS while on Act-D therapy; median age 3.3 years (range 6 months-5 years); median interval from start of therapy to SOS diagnosis was 6 weeks (range 4-13); median 2 doses of Act-D received before SOS (range 2-6); Act-D given as single dose slow IV bolus of 45 mcg/kg, reduced to two-thirds in children <12 kg and half in children <6 months. SOS diagnosed clinically by modified McDonald criteria (jaundice with total bilirubin >2 mg/dL, tender hepatomegaly and/or right upper quadrant pain, 5% weight gain with/without ascites). All 5 had tender hepatomegaly and fluid accumulation; clinical jaundice, fever and recurrent vomiting in 4; CNS drowsiness/altered sensorium in 3; respiratory distress with bilateral infiltrates in 3; hypotensive shock requiring inotropes in 3; acute renal failure requiring dialysis in 1. All had significant thrombocytopenia and prolonged PT and aPTT; 4 each had conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, hypoalbuminemia, and transaminases >5x ULN. Viral hepatitis serology negative in all; no reversed/attenuated portal venous flow on Doppler. None of the patients received radiation. Papal (abstract) notes re-challenge of ACT-D can be performed in gradually escalating doses under close monitoring.

raw_record.support_text: The authors discuss the frequency of severe hepatotoxicity in Wilms' tumor patients treated with actinomycin D, noting that single-dose actinomycin D caused severe hepatotoxicity in the UK Children's Cancer Study Group and American National Wilms Tumor Study (NWTS-4), which led to the dose being reduced from 60 µg/kg to 45 µg/kg.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric Wilms' tumor (nephroblastoma) patients receiving actinomycin D chemotherapy as part of cooperative-group treatment schedules.
raw_record.extra_details: On the 60 µg/kg single-dose schedule, raised liver function tests occurred in 4 of 33 patients (12%) with no case of severe hepatotoxicity; on the standard schedule (15 µg/kg daily ×5 days), 1 of 32 patients had severe hepatotoxicity and 2 others had raised liver function tests without ascites. Frequency of severe hepatotoxicity was 0/33 versus 1/32. A reduced single dose of 45 µg/kg was reported as well tolerated. Severe hepatotoxicity was previously reported in NWTS-4. The Brazilian study administered doses every six weeks rather than every three weeks as in NWTS-4, which the authors suggest may explain the lower frequency of severe hepatotoxicity with the 60 µg/kg regimen. Ascites was noted in the severe hepatotoxicity case.
