raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that hepatopathy-thrombocytopenia syndrome (HTS) is observed in patients with Wilms tumor undergoing actinomycin D (dactinomycin) treatment, describing it as a rare and often unrecognized syndrome. Actinomycin D-induced HTS is characterized as a rare syndrome, and the case study presents a 3.5-year-old pediatric Wilms tumor patient with actinomycin D-related HTS and multiple *MDR1* (ABCB1) gene mutations.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (3.5-year-old girl) patient receiving actinomycin D as chemotherapy for Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma).
raw_record.extra_details: Actinomycin D (dactinomycin) is an antitumor agent used in the treatment of Wilms tumor for the past 40 years. The hepatopathy-thrombocytopenia syndrome (HTS) is described as rare and often unrecognized. This case study reports that the girl carried the following MDR1 (ABCB1) gene mutations: (−)1G>A, 1236C>T, 2677G>T, 3435C>T, and 61A>G; the authors hypothesize the mechanism underlying HTS may differ with individual MDR1 genotype, though MDR1 genotype is a susceptibility/mechanistic factor rather than an independently causal hepatotoxic agent.

raw_record.support_text: In the Brazilian Cooperative Group Wilms' Tumor Study, patients treated with a 60 µg/kg single dose of actinomycin D showed raised liver function tests in 4 of 33 patients (12%) with no case of severe hepatotoxicity; in the standard 15 µg/kg-for-5-days schedule, 1 of 32 patients had severe hepatotoxicity and two others had raised liver function tests without ascites. raw_record.extra_details: Two regimens compared: 60 µg/kg single dose every 6 weeks gave raised LFTs in 4/33 (12%) and no severe hepatotoxicity; standard 15 µg/kg/day for 5 days gave severe hepatotoxicity in 1/32 plus raised LFTs without ascites in 2. After the US NWTS-4 group noted severe hepatotoxicity at 60 µg/kg, its dose was reduced to 45 µg/kg. Pritchard reported the frequency of severe hepatotoxicity with single-dose actinomycin D in the UK Children's Cancer Study Group Wilms' Tumour Study.

raw_record.support_text: Dactinomycin (Act-D) was implicated as the cause of sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS) during treatment for Wilms tumor (WT), described as a life-threatening complication that is reversible in most cases with supportive care and diagnosis supported by blood count, liver function tests, and abdominal ultrasound. In the study, two patients were safely re-exposed to Act-D after complete recovery while a third patient's further Act-D doses were consciously replaced with doxorubicin; the authors note re-exposure can start at 50% dose and gradually escalate to full dose, though some physicians avoid re-exposure after severe, life-threatening episodes.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients receiving dactinomycin as part of treatment for Wilms tumor (indication-restricted); re-exposure context after recovery from SOS with 50% starting dose escalation in some cases, while some physicians avoid re-exposure after severe life-threatening episodes.
raw_record.extra_details: Act-D refers to dactinomycin/actinomycin D. SOS was described as life-threatening but reversible in most patients with supportive care; diagnosis is clinical, supported by blood count, liver function tests, and abdominal ultrasound. In the study, two patients were safely re-exposed to Act-D following complete recovery, and one patient's further Act-D doses were replaced with doxorubicin (doxorubicin is not itself implicated as a DILI cause here).

raw_record.extra_details: Single-dose schedule 60 µg/kg (identical to dose in American National Wilms Tumor Study-4, which was later reduced to 45 µg/kg after severe hepatotoxicity was noted); standard schedule 15 µg/kg for 5 days. Raised LFTs 4/33 (12%) on single-dose arm; 1 case severe hepatotoxicity plus 2 cases of raised liver function tests without ascites on standard schedule. Authors believed the lower frequency of severe hepatotoxicity with 60 µg/kg may relate to the longer (6-week vs 3-week) interval between doses.

raw_record.support_text: 4-Ipomeanol (IPO, 4-IM), a naturally occurring furanoterpenoid evaluated as an anticancer agent, is activated by CYP enzymes to a DNA-reactive electrophilic furan epoxide. It was clinically evaluated in a phase I study in lung cancer patients and, due to the induction of hepatotoxicity in these studies, was subsequently evaluated in a phase II clinical trial in liver cancer patients, where it was unsuccessful with no antitumor response.

raw_record.support_text: Of 17 patients known to have developed jaundice while receiving chlorpropamide, eight developed a generally pruritic macular rash considered characteristic of an allergic drug reaction, six had drug fever, and three showed eosinophilia. In the following paragraph the paper states that the majority of patients developed jaundice two to five weeks after starting chlorpropamide and that the jaundice was of a benign reversible type; liver biopsy revealed intracanalicular bile stasis.
raw_record.extra_details: 17 patients developed jaundice while receiving chlorpropamide; 8 had a generally pruritic macular rash considered characteristic of an allergic drug reaction, 6 had drug fever, and 3 had eosinophilia. Most developed jaundice 2-5 weeks after starting treatment; fever and rash resolved rapidly after steroid administration. Jaundice was of a benign reversible type; liver biopsy showed intracanalicular bile stasis (intrahepatic cholestasis). Side effects otherwise included anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, skin rashes, alcohol intolerance, leukopenia and prolonged hypoglycemia; doses above 1 g/day produced high, sustained blood levels and the daily dose was reduced to 500 mg or less, with prolonged hypoglycemia still occasionally encountered (including a case of severe hypoglycemia with spinal fluid sugar 20 mg/100 ml and blood sugar 18 mg/100 ml).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that a significant number of patients with jaundice of cholestatic type have been and will continue to develop from chlorpropamide therapy, and the author observed two patients with jaundice due to chlorpropamide in which the picture resembles cholestasis. One case was a 67-year-old woman with diabetes who, three weeks after receiving chlorpropamide 250 mg daily, developed obstructive jaundice lasting almost 3 months; biopsy revealed hyperergic cholangiolitis, severe cholestasis (biliary calculi), and focal liver cell injury suggestive of a drug reaction. Table 1 lists chlorpropamide as positive for liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients with jaundice due to chlorpropamide resembling cholestasis observed by the author; a significant number of cholestatic-type jaundice cases reported from chlorpropamide therapy. Illustrative case: 67-year-old woman with diabetes for 15 years, chlorpropamide 250 mg daily, obstructive jaundice developing ~3 weeks after start and lasting almost 3 months, biopsy showing hyperergic cholangiolitis, severe cholestasis (biliary calculi), and focal liver cell injury suggestive of a drug reaction.

raw_record.support_text: The paper identifies chlorpropamide as a drug implicated in inducing liver injury, being the causative agent in 8 of 53 patients with drug-related liver disease. Chlorpropamide produced hepatocanalicular cholestasis in 5 cases and diffuse necrosis in 3.
raw_record.extra_details: Chlorpropamide was the causative agent in 8 of 53 patients; produced hepatocanalicular cholestasis in 5 cases and diffuse necrosis in 3.

raw_record.support_text: Chlorpropamide is estimated to produce cholestatic hepatitis in some 0.5% of patients, and signs of hypersensitivity with eosinophilia frequently accompany this reaction; it is presented as an example of idiosyncratic, non-dose-dependent drug hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: A 42-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes developed rash, pruritus, jaundice, shivering and cholestatic hepatitis after 4 weeks on chlorpropamide (Diabinese, 500 mg daily); marked improvement on dechallenge and abrupt exacerbation on rechallenge; liver tests indicated a cholestatic type of injury with elevated alkaline phosphatase, GGTP and bilirubin; eosinophilia rose to 31%; estimated population incidence of cholestatic hepatitis about 0.5%; hypersensitivity with eosinophilia frequently accompanies the reaction.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports chlorpropamide side-effects including jaundice occurring within 2 to 5 weeks of therapy start, with elevation of serum alkaline phosphatase. Two patients reported by Dolger had jaundice with a cholestatic picture: obstructive jaundice lasting 3 months, with biopsy showing hyperergic cholangiolitis, severe cholestasis (biliary calculi), and focal liver cell injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Jaundice occurred within 2 to 5 weeks of therapy initiation and was associated with a skin rash and elevation of serum alkaline phosphatase. In the Dolger patients, obstructive (cholestatic) jaundice lasted 3 months; biopsy revealed hyperergic cholangiolitis, severe cholestasis (biliary calculi), and focal liver cell injury. Accompanying findings included leukopenia, eosinophilia, lymphocytosis, and decreased blood platelets. Note: the case report's main subject was toxic amblyopia (visual complaint after one hour of dosing, variable over 6 weeks), which is not a liver event.

raw_record.support_text: A 54-year-old woman with adult-onset diabetes mellitus had received chlorpropamide, 750 mg/day, for 15 months and developed malaise, pruritus, and painless jaundice of several weeks' duration. Chlorpropamide-induced jaundice was suspected and the drug was discontinued; her bilirubin rose from 14 mg/dl to 20.5 mg/dl during the first week after admission. She denied alcohol and exposure to any drug other than chlorpropamide.
raw_record.extra_details: Chlorpropamide 750 mg/day for 15 months for adult-onset diabetes in a 54-year-old woman. Percutaneous liver biopsy showed intraductal, intracanalicular, and intracellular cholestasis with mild portal inflammation, feathery degeneration and regeneration of hepatocytes, compatible with cholestatic hepatitis. Initial laboratory findings suggested intrahepatic cholestasis. Symptoms resolved and hepatic tests rapidly improved during the week after drug discontinuation (dechallenge). Bilirubin rose from 14 to 20.5 mg/dl. No other drugs were involved.

raw_record.support_text: The patient had not started any prescribed or over-the-counter medication other than lisinopril during the year before admission, so the author concluded that the derangement in liver function tests due to cholestasis was most probably caused by lisinopril, reporting a second case of lisinopril liver injury with a cholestatic liver enzyme pattern that did not resolve and was fatal.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as the second case of lisinopril liver injury; cholestatic liver enzyme pattern did not resolve, and the patient died. Histology in the reported series (five patients including this case) showed lymphocytic or monocytic portal or peri-portal hepatitis, histological cholestasis in four, portal fibrosis in three, and centrilobular necrosis in one, with no eosinophilic infiltration; three patients resolved, three died, and one developed chronic liver disease. No new medication other than lisinopril was started in the year before admission.

raw_record.support_text: A case of fulminant hepatitis in a patient taking lisinopril (20 mg daily) for 5 weeks for arterial hypertension is reported. Jaundice, fever, myalgia, and marked increases in serum aminotransferase activities occurred after 2 weeks of treatment. Continuing lisinopril for 3 weeks after onset of jaundice was associated with grade III encephalopathy and decreased prothrombin and proaccelerin levels. The authors state this case strongly suggests that lisinopril may induce acute hepatitis and that continued administration after jaundice onset can lead to life-threatening hepatic failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 55-year-old man treated with lisinopril 20 mg daily for arterial hypertension. Jaundice/fever/myalgia appeared ~2 weeks into treatment (September 15-19, 1988); lisinopril continued until October 10 (5 weeks total), when grade III encephalopathy and marked decreases in prothrombin (20%) and proaccelerin (30%) developed. Fulminant hepatitis with acute liver failure (peak bilirubin 1200 µmol/L, ALT 2561 U/L). Liver biopsy showed extensive hepatocyte necrosis predominating in centrilobular area with cholestasis and inflammatory infiltration; no fibrosis or iron overload. Liver function progressively improved after lisinopril withdrawal (dechallenge), but the patient died on December 7, 1988, after surgery for a perforated duodenal ulcer followed by bacterial infections and gastrointestinal bleeding. Viral hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV, HSV, HIV, rickettsial, and spirochetal infections excluded; no prior liver/biliary disease or alcohol abuse. Enalapril had been discontinued 2 weeks before jaundice; furosemide and bisoprolol (not known hepatotoxic) had been used 11 and 6 months without adverse reaction, so lisinopril was the only recently started drug.

Hepatic function rapidly declined to grade III encephalopathy and acute liver failure (MELD 33 on day 10), and she expired on admission day 13 following bowel perforation and septic shock.

raw_record.extra_details: Drug-induced hepatotoxicity/ALF case; Naranjo criteria for drug-induced reaction probability applied, concluding lisinopril is the probable cause of her ALF. Only few prior reports of ACE inhibitor hepatotoxicity (enalapril, captopril) and only 3 prior reports of lisinopril-induced hepatotoxicity. Laboratory values (day 1): AST 702, ALT 790, Alk phos 269 IU/L, total bilirubin 21.3, direct bilirubin 12.4 mg/dl; INR 1.5. Negative tests: acetaminophen, ethanol, illicit drugs, viral hepatitis, EBV, CMV, HSV, VZV PCR, AMA/ASMA/ALKA, HFE mutation; ferritin 6554 ng/ml. Biopsy: hepatocellular injury without cholestasis, moderate reactive iron deposition in Kupffer cells and hepatocytes, negative copper stain. Outcome: grade III encephalopathy, ALF (MELD 33 day 10), ileus with bowel perforation, septic shock, death on day 13.

raw_record.support_text: Two patients (33 and 55 years old) who were chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) carriers were treated with buprenorphine for addiction and hospitalized with clinical hepatitis and jaundice after intravenous administration. Aminotransferase rose to 100 and 21 times normal. Co-factors included alcohol consumption in the first patient and high-dose aspirin in the second. After discontinuing IV buprenorphine, hepatitis did not recur with oral buprenorphine. Using the Naranjo adverse-event criteria, and also the CIOMS and Maria-Victorino (M&V) scales, the relationship between buprenorphine and acute hepatitis was categorized as probable in both cases. Acute hepatitis was followed by HCV RNA disappearance.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic HCV carriers; misuse of buprenorphine by intravenous route; co-factors included alcohol consumption (patient 1) and high-dose aspirin (patient 2); competing co-exposures unresolved.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases (ages 33 and 55). Aminotransferase increased to 100 and 21 times normal; severe hepatitis with jaundice. Causality scored probable by Naranjo, CIOMS, and Maria-Victorino (M&V) scales. Hepatitis was followed by HCV RNA clearance. Suggested mechanism is a mitochondrial defect aggravated by co-factors (HCV, alcohol, drugs). Patients tolerated buprenorphine well at recommended sublingual doses; risk of acute hepatitis applies to IV intravenous misuse. Drug intended for treatment of opioid addiction.

raw_record.support_text: A letter to the editor reports two patients who had received phenelzine (a monoamine oxidase inhibitor for depression) for 4 months at 22.5 mg and 60 mg twice daily, respectively, and who required emergency orthotopic liver transplantation because of fulminant hepatic failure. Phenelzine-induced fulminant hepatic failure was diagnosed after biochemical, serologic, immunologic, hematologic, and histologic studies ruled out other known causes of liver damage. The cases fit the pattern of hydrazine-derivative-induced hepatotoxic injury: delayed toxic effect, no evidence of hypersensitivity-mediated injury, and predominantly hepatocellular rather than cholestatic damage. The paper states the mechanism by which a hydrazine derivative such as phenelzine causes hepatic injury appears to be idiosyncratic, and notes that advanced age, simultaneous enzymatic induction by alcohol or other drugs, and coincident viral infection may play roles, while the relation with the rapid acetylator phenotype remains controversial.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients treated with phenelzine for 4 months at 22.5 mg and 60 mg twice daily, respectively; both required emergency orthotopic liver transplantation for fulminant hepatic failure (reported as the first two such cases successfully treated by transplant with other causes ruled out). Presented as severe phenelzine-induced hepatitis; pattern matches hydrazine-derivative-induced injury: delayed toxic effect, no hypersensitivity, predominantly hepatocellular (rather than cholestatic) histology. Potential contributing roles of advanced age, enzymatic induction by alcohol/other drugs, and coincident viral infection proposed; possible relation with rapid acetylator phenotype noted as controversial.

raw_record.support_text: The liver injury in a 56-year-old man on zanubrutinib 160 mg twice daily for relapsing Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia was hepatocellular with an R-value of 63.2, and the updated RUCAM causality assessment score for zanubrutinib was 7, indicating 'probable drug-induced liver injury'. A liver biopsy showed patchy necrosis, cholestasis and moderate to severe lobular and portal inflammation suggestive of DILI with no evidence of alcohol-related liver disease. His liver enzymes improved after drug cessation and normalised 28 days after discharge.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 56-year-old Caucasian man with Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia randomised to the zanubrutinib arm of a phase 3 BeiGene trial comparing zanubrutinib with ibrutinib; took zanubrutinib 160 mg twice daily with aciclovir and co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. After 28 months of treatment he developed an asymptomatic transaminase and total bilirubin rise, followed 8 weeks later by pale stools, dark urine, pruritus and jaundice; admission labs ALT 2474 (ULN 45 IU/L), AST 1257, ALP 114, TB 141 (ULN 21 umol/L), PT 14 sec, R-value 63.2. Full liver screen negative excluding other causes; ultrasound showed echo-bright texture in keeping with fatty changes. Biopsy showed patchy necrosis, cholestasis and moderate/severe lobular and portal inflammation; immunohistochemistry showed reactive CD3-positive T-cell-predominant infiltrate with no light chain restriction. Zanubrutinib was withheld as suspected cause and permanently stopped; discharge after 9-day admission, liver profile normalised 28 days later. No clinical signs of liver failure at admission.

raw_record.support_text: A case report attributes cholestatic jaundice with rash and eosinophilia to aminoglutethimide, reasoning that the presentation, occurring after several weeks of sensitization, likely represents a systemic hypersensitivity reaction to the agent. The authors state there was no evidence of infectious hepatitis or other hepatotoxin administration, and the mechanism is believed to be an idiosyncratic hypersensitivity reaction, possibly indicating a latent direct hepatotoxic potential of aminoglutethimide. They conclude the report illustrates a probable additional feature of aminoglutethimide hypersensitivity.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient was not rechallenged with aminoglutethimide and did not undergo liver biopsy. Presentation included rash, eosinophilia, and cholestatic jaundice after several weeks of sensitization. Mechanism is considered similar to that of phenytoin and sulfa compounds (idiosyncratic hypersensitivity, possibly indicating latent direct hepatotoxicity). The authors consider a toxic effect of androgenic precursors androstenedione and testosterone less likely, noting these lack the 17-alkyl group thought necessary for hepatotoxic effect. Aminoglutethimide inhibits aromatase leading to increased androstenedione and testosterone.

raw_record.support_text: A case report attributes cholestatic jaundice, rash, and eosinophilia to aminoglutethimide, appearing after several weeks of sensitization, as a systemic hypersensitivity reaction. The authors state there was no evidence of infectious hepatitis or another hepatotoxin administration, and propose an idiosyncratic hypersensitivity mechanism similar to phenytoin and sulfa compounds, possibly indicating a latent direct hepatotoxic potential of aminoglutethimide.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient presented with rash, eosinophilia, and cholestatic jaundice after several weeks of sensitization, suggesting an idiosyncratic hypersensitivity reaction similar to that seen with phenytoin and sulfa compounds; the case was not rechallenged with aminoglutethimide and no liver biopsy was performed. The authors consider a toxic effect of the androgenic precursors androstenedione and testosterone (increased via aromatase inhibition) less likely, noting these compounds lack the 17-alkyl group thought needed for hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Although the patient was not rechallenged with aminoglutethimide and did not undergo liver biopsy, the authors concluded the case likely represents a systemic hypersensitivity reaction to aminoglutethimide causing cholestatic jaundice after several weeks of sensitization. The presence of rash and eosinophilia along with the cholestatic jaundice suggested an idiosyncratic hypersensitivity mechanism, similar to phenytoin and sulfa compounds, with a less likely contributing role considered for the aromatase-inhibited androgenic precursors androstenedione and testosterone. The patient's icterus and liver tests resolved after aminoglutethimide was discontinued and hydrocortisone was tapered.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the first two cases of mirtazapine leading to prolonged jaundice with a hepatitic picture on liver biochemistry, and note that withdrawal of the drug led to improvement in liver function in both patients. One 49-year-old woman taking mirtazapine 45 mg/day for 1 year presented with malaise, progressive jaundice, and tea-colored urine, with ALP 140 U/L, ALT 550 U/L, AST 434 U/L, bilirubin 140 µmol/L, and PT 18 seconds; liver function only returned to normal 3 months after discontinuation. raw_record.extra_details: Two case reports of depression patients on therapeutic oral mirtazapine. Case 1: prior episode with liver function recovering over about 5 months after discontinuation (albumin 40 g/L; bilirubin 30 µmol/L; ALP 86 U/L; ALT 21 U/L; AST 39 U/L; PT 14 s). Case 2: 49-year-old woman, mirtazapine 45 mg/d for 1 year, malaise, progressive jaundice, tea-colored urine; labs albumin 40 g/L; bilirubin 140 µmol/L; ALP 140 U/L; ALT 550 U/L; AST 434 U/L; GGT 57 U/L; PT 18 s; negative for HAV IgM, HBsAg, HCV Ab, HEV IgM, EBV, HSV, CMV, autoimmune markers (AMA, ASMA), normal IgA/IgG/IgM, copper/ceruloplasmin/iron/transferrin normal, normal liver ultrasound. After stopping mirtazapine her liver function deteriorated for 2 weeks (bilirubin 329 µmol/L; ALP 200 U/L; ALT 852 U/L; AST 654 U/L; PT 23.1 s) then returned to normal by 3 months after discontinuation. Mirtazapine is known to cause elevations in hepatic transaminases; short-term US studies showed ALT elevations up to 3x normal in 2% of patients, mostly without hepatic decompensation, some normalizing despite continuation. Mechanism unknown; paper states it is uncertain whether hepatotoxicity is dose-dependent or idiosyncratic. Paper represents the first reported cases of mirtazapine-related prolonged jaundice with hepatitic picture, more severe than previously reported.

raw_record.support_text: A 48-year-old woman with severe atopic dermatitis and allergic contact dermatitis was started on mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) 500 mg three times daily as a corticosteroid-sparing agent. After a month she developed a biochemical hepatitis with ALT rising from 22 to 418 IU/L and AST from 20 to 139 IU/L; after dose reduction to 500 mg twice daily, ALT and AST rose to 821 and 203 IU/L. Viral hepatitis serologies were negative, ANA was positive (speckled 1:160), and she denied alcohol or herbs; hydroxyzine was taken only intermittently. The hepatology consult agreed with MMF-induced hepatitis, and liver enzymes were normal 1 month after stopping MMF.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report. Dose 500 mg three times daily, reduced to 500 mg twice daily. ALT rose from 22 to 418 IU/L then to 821 IU/L; AST rose from 20 to 139 IU/L then to 203 IU/L. Paper frames MMF-associated hepatitis as rare and as hepatitis due to drug hypersensitivity; authors conclude MMF is relatively safe but physicians should monitor for rare hepatitis. References supporting MMF-induced transaminase elevation: Balal et al (79 transplant patients, 11 with modest liver enzyme elevations, median onset 28 days, resolution 16 days after withdrawal or 50% dose reduction), Hantash and Fiorentino (2 atopic dermatitis patients), a toxic hepatitis case (AST/ALT up to 750 IU/L) in ANCA-positive vasculitis.

After fluoxetine was discontinued, both patients had prompt symptomatic improvement and steady normalization of liver biochemistry test results. raw_record.support_text: A 41-year-old female presented with a skin rash and abnormal liver function tests after the recent initiation of fluoxetine. Skin and liver biopsies showed features of Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and drug-induced liver injury (DILI), respectively. Fluoxetine was stopped, after which her liver function tests and skin rash improved without progression to fulminant hepatic failure. The authors present this as the first described case of fluoxetine-induced SJS and DILI, noting that fluoxetine is associated with an asymptomatic increase in liver enzymes in 0.5% of cases and that only a handful of prior case reports describe isolated fluoxetine-induced DILI presenting as an acute hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: First described case of concomitant DILI and SJS secondary to fluoxetine in a 41-year-old female. Skin and liver biopsies showed features of SJS and DILI, respectively. Fluoxetine was discontinued with subsequent improvement in liver function tests and skin rash, without progression to fulminant hepatic failure. Fluoxetine is associated with an asymptomatic increase in liver enzymes in 0.5% of cases, but is rarely associated with FHF or SJS; a handful of prior case reports describe isolated fluoxetine-induced DILI presenting as an acute hepatitis. DILI is described as an idiosyncratic, dose-independent reaction dependent on age, sex, and genetic polymorphisms of drug-metabolizing enzymes such as cytochrome P450.

raw_record.support_text: In the Mayo Clinic therapeutic trial of CDCA for gallstone dissolution, liver toxicity assessed by plasma aminotransferase activity was not present in most patients, and at doses up to 4 g/day there was no evidence of hepatotoxicity. A large NIH-sponsored multicenter placebo-controlled double-blind study (NCGS) and large French and Italian studies confirmed the safety of CDCA in gallstone subjects; a small percent developed elevated aminotransferase levels that returned to normal when CDCA was discontinued, with the mild toxicity attributable to CDCA per se.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Gallstone patients treated for gallstone dissolution; doses up to 4 g/day in some Mayo instances; NCGS used 10 mg/kg-day CDCA.
raw_record.extra_details: Explicit negative conclusion on human hepatotoxicity: no evidence of hepatotoxicity at Mayo and NCGS/large European trials confirmed safety of CDCA. A small percentage developed elevated plasma aminotransferase levels that returned to normal upon discontinuation; this mild toxicity appeared attributable to CDCA per se rather than to lithocholic acid (Fisher et al., 1991). British studies with liver biopsies showed only minor histological changes. Acute severe hepatotoxicity observed in fetal Rhesus monkeys is animal data and excluded from this human record.

raw_record.support_text: In a randomized double-blind trial, 44 patients with radiolucent gallstones were randomly allotted to ursodeoxycholic acid (600 mg/day), ursodeoxycholic acid (150 mg/day), or placebo. After six months, gallstone dissolution occurred in 8 (26%) of the 31 patients treated with ursodeoxycholic acid but not in the placebo group. The paper explicitly states that ursodeoxycholic acid had no hepatotoxicity as assessed by standard liver-function tests.
raw_record.extra_details: Randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial in patients with radiolucent gallstones and radiologically visible gallbladders; ursodeoxycholic acid given at 600 mg/day or 150 mg/day for six months; gallstone dissolution in 8 of 31 treated patients (26%), none in placebo group; no hepatotoxicity found on standard liver-function tests. Ursodeoxycholic acid is the 7beta-epimer of chenodeoxycholic acid, synthesized by Tokyo Tanabe Company (>99% pure); patients excluded those with obstructive hepatic dysfunction or drug allergy.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), a hydrophilic bile acid described as not hepatotoxic to humans, used in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial in patients with symptomatic primary biliary cirrhosis.

raw_record.support_text: In this case report, the patient was readmitted with new-onset transaminitis and developed acute liver failure after receiving remdesivir for COVID-19. The Naranjo algorithm was used and the case was deemed a 'probable' adverse drug reaction with a score of 5, supporting remdesivir as the likely cause of the DILI with subsequent ALF in the absence of other causes.
raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo causality score 5 ('probable'). New-onset transaminitis two days after initial discharge consistent with a mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic pattern of liver injury, progressing to acute liver failure. Other potential sources (lamotrigine, duloxetine) considered but deemed unlikely given normal LFTs before remdesivir. Exact mechanism unknown; proposed direct hepatocyte toxicity via mitochondrial RNA polymerase inhibition; remdesivir is a CYP 3A4 substrate and substrate of OATP1B1 and p-glycoprotein transporters, suggesting drug-drug interaction potential.

raw_record.support_text: In this patient with COVID-19, liver enzymes were elevated only after 48 hours of remdesivir use; the known in vitro toxicity of remdesivir, the time relation, and automatic resolution after discontinuation of the drug together indicate a causal relation between elevated liver enzymes and remdesivir. No other drug in the patient's treatment could be related to hepatotoxicity, and viral, hypoxic, and autoimmune etiologies were excluded. The biochemical pattern of the injury was hepatocellular (R=ALT/ALP >= 5), and transaminases and INR declined starting 24 hours after remdesivir discontinuation, returning to normal nine days later.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of remdesivir-associated liver injury during treatment of COVID-19. Liver enzymes elevated 48 hours after remdesivir start; transaminases and INR (coagulopathy) declined within 24 hours of discontinuation and returned to normal nine days later. R ratio ALT/ALP >= 5 indicated hepatocellular injury. Patient remained ambulatory with no altered consciousness (EASL acute liver injury without encephalopathy). Viral, hypoxic (no hypotension), and autoimmune causes excluded; alcohol use ~2 units/week. No competing drug co-suspect in the regimen. Discharged on day eleven, recovered; course complicated by nonsevere Clostridium difficile infection treated with metronidazole and vancomycin.

raw_record.support_text: Administration of remdesivir (RDV) was associated with AST and ALT elevation, though in most cases these elevations did not progress to severe liver injury. Liver injury caused by RDV occurred in two patients, manifested with increased transaminases, coagulopathy, and hepatic encephalopathy occurring between days 3 and 10 of RDV administration; practitioners used N-acetyl cysteine and discontinued RDV to stop progression of acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Associated with AST and ALT elevation; in most cases enzyme elevations did not progress to severe liver injury; two patients with RDV-caused liver injury showed increased transaminases, coagulopathy, and hepatic encephalopathy between days 3 and 10; treated with N-acetyl cysteine and RDV discontinuation to stop acute liver failure progression; stopping criteria ALT >5x ULN or ALP >2x ULN and total bilirubin >2x ULN, or coagulopathy/clinical decompensation; acetylcysteine suggested as beneficial in RDV-induced acute liver failure

raw_record.support_text: Remdesivir (RDV) usage is associated with elevations of AST and ALT; in most instances the enzyme elevations did not progress to severe liver damage, but cases of acute liver failure suspected as due to RDV have been reported. In two patients with RDV-induced acute liver failure, significant transaminase increases occurred between day 3 and day 10 of RDV use, associated with coagulopathy and hepatic encephalopathy. Using the Naranjo algorithm, both cases scored as 'probable' adverse drug reactions with a score of 6 each; after stopping the drug and treatment with N-acetyl cysteine infusion there was marked improvement in transaminases and liver function.

raw_record.extra_details: Two patients with RDV-induced acute liver failure; significant transaminase increases between day 3 and day 10 of use, associated with coagulopathy and hepatic encephalopathy; Naranjo algorithm 'probable' adverse drug reaction with score 6 each; marked improvement after drug discontinuation and N-acetyl cysteine infusion. RDV suggested to be stopped if ALT >5x ULN or ALP >2x ULN and total bilirubin >2x ULN or in presence of coagulopathy or clinical decompensation; authors did not use RDV in decompensated cirrhosis patients.

raw_record.support_text: The conclusions state that SJG-136 was associated with dose-limiting VLS and hepatotoxicity when administered by short injection every 21 days. In the phase I study, other unexpected drug-related adverse events included elevated liver function tests, and the liver toxicity had delayed onset and increased in severity with subsequent cycles.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase I dose-escalation study in 16 patients with advanced solid tumors; SJG-136 (BN2629/NSC 694501/SG2000) is a sequence-selective pyrrolobenzodiazepine dimer. Doses 15-240 µg/m2 given as 10-min i.v. infusion every 21 days; dose reduced to 45 µg/m2 due to unexpected toxicity, which was the maximum tolerated dose. Hepatotoxicity had delayed onset and increased in severity with subsequent cycles and was dose-limiting. Also seen: vascular leak syndrome (hypoalbuminemia, pleural effusions, ascites, peripheral edema) and fatigue; no DNA interstrand cross-linking by comet assay but DNA damage noted in circulating lymphocytes at all dose levels by γ-H2AX assay.

raw_record.support_text: A case report by Kleiner 2011 described an 82-year-old man on simvastatin who developed jaundice with peak bilirubin 5.2, AST/ALT 1,919/1,737, ALP 260 after 4 months, with liver biopsy, reported as statin-induced cholestatic hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case (Kleiner 2011), 82-year-old male, simvastatin (dose not provided), jaundice at 4 months, liver biopsy performed, no rechallenge.

raw_record.support_text: In the US DILIN prospective study, after formal adjudication only 22 of 1188 suspected DILI cases were accepted as true statin-induced DILI; injury was mostly mild-moderate and self-limited, and the paper describes statin DILI as a likely class effect with idiosyncratic timing of onset. Simvastatin accounted for 5 of these 22 adjudicated cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Adjudicated simvastatin DILI cases: US DILIN n=5; Iceland study n=1; Swedish total for statins with jaundice 1970-2004 n=8 and 1988-2010 n=28 simvastatin; Spanish Registry n=13 (27.7%). DILIN aggregate (all statins) showed hepatocellular pattern in 12/22 (54%), cholestatic in 9/22 (41%), 4 severe and 1 fatal case, latency 34 days to >10 years.

raw_record.support_text: Atorvastatin was significantly more commonly associated with DILI than simvastatin in the Swedish statin DILI case series, indicating that simvastatin is a recognized cause of statin-associated DILI but reported less frequently than atorvastatin.
raw_record.extra_details: Less commonly associated with DILI than atorvastatin in the series; included among statins with DILI reports.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 270 patients undergoing liver transplantation for acute liver failure, 3 of the liver recipients had acute liver failure attributed to a statin, with 1 attributed to simvastatin over the 12-year study period.
raw_record.extra_details: 1 of 3 liver recipients with statin-attributed acute liver failure had simvastatin-attributed acute liver failure during the 12-year transplant cohort study; this patient underwent liver transplantation for acute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: In the Icelandic prospective population study, 1 of 96 DILI patients had liver injury associated with simvastatin. During the 2-year Icelandic period, 27845 patients were treated with simvastatin and one was diagnosed with liver injury. Statins as a class accounted for 5.5% (47/858) of Spanish Registry DILI cases and 1.9% (22/1188) of DILIN cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 1 simvastatin DILI case among 27845 treated users in the Icelandic study (~1/3700 risk; ~1 per 11,000 when combined with atorvastatin cases). Cholestatic/mixed pattern occurred in only 24% of simvastatin injury cases (vs 56% for atorvastatin, p=0.018), indicating predominantly hepatocellular injury. Documented positive rechallenge reported for simvastatin.

raw_record.support_text: In case 1, after stopping simvastatin, a needle liver biopsy showed preserved architecture, chronic inflammation of portal tracts with mild piecemeal necrosis and mild focal periportal fibrosis, with mild necroinflammatory activity, consistent with but not diagnostic of drug-induced chronic active hepatitis with fibrosis. The patient's only significant long-term drug exposure was simvastatin, and liver enzymes dropped within a week of stopping the drug. The patient had no recurrence of hepatitis over 6.5 years.
raw_record.extra_details: Recurrent acute symptomatic hepatitis episodes with elevations of ALT, AST, ALP and total bilirubin; liver enzymes returned toward normal within a week after discontinuing simvastatin; biopsy 14 days after stopping showed chronic active hepatitis with mild piecemeal necrosis, mild focal periportal fibrosis, mild necroinflammatory activity, incidental lipogranulomata and mild siderosis; elevated IgM (12.10 g/L) with negative HBsAg, anti-HCV, anti-EBV IgM and normal ceruloplasmin, C3, C4, IgA and IgG; symptoms self-treated with acetaminophen for 1 week as a co-medication (not attributed as cause); no recurrence of hepatitis over 6.5 years; statins never re-introduced.

raw_record.support_text: In this prospective U.S. drug-induced liver injury study, statin-associated liver injury showed prolonged latency in some cases, with 5 of 22 patients having taken the agent for a year or more before onset of acute injury. Prolonged latency was seen with most types of statins, including atorvastatin, simvastatin, fluvastatin, and rosuvastatin, presenting with both hepatocellular and cholestatic patterns of liver injury; other causes of liver disease were systematically excluded and liver test elevations resolved with statin discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: From the Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network prospective study: statins initially implicated in 61 cases, with careful adjudication finding 22 (36%) convincing (>50% likelihood). All major statins were implicated at rates similar to their relative U.S. use. Prolonged latency up to >1 year seen in 5 of 22 patients; both hepatocellular and cholestatic biochemical patterns occurred; some cases had autoimmune hepatitis-like features with ANA/SMA positivity, and 2 of 6 autoimmune cases developed self-sustained autoimmune hepatitis requiring long-term immunosuppression. Histology included cholestatic hepatitis, confluent necrosis, and steatosis (often pre-existing fatty liver). One fatal case of acute-on-chronic liver failure occurred in the statin series. Study systematically excluded other liver disease causes and liver tests resolved on drug discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: Simvastatin is listed at position 6 in the RUCAM-based ranking of drugs causing DILI with verified causality (Table 10).
raw_record.extra_details: Ranked #6 in the RUCAM-based top-ranking of drugs causing DILI with verified causality (Teschke, 2018d).

raw_record.support_text: The Swedish DILI register reported statin-related DILI with simvastatin implicated in 28/73 (38%) of cases, showing most commonly a cholestatic/mixed pattern, with 2 deaths due to acute liver failure and 1 liver transplantation among the 73 statin DILI cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated in 28/73 (38%) of statin-DILI cases in the Swedish DILI register (statin DILI incidence 1.2/100,000 users); register statin DILI showed most commonly a cholestatic/mixed pattern, with 2 deaths from acute liver failure and 1 liver transplantation across the 73 cases (not attributable to a specific statin).

raw_record.support_text: One case each of liver transplantation for suspected drug-induced liver injury was associated with simvastatin, nefazodon, and enalapril, each with a highly probable causal relationship.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case among 17 transplant patients with a highly probable causal relationship.

raw_record.support_text: Among 120 cases of symptomatic drug-induced eosinophilia, eosinophilic hepatitis was detected in 3 cases attributed to amoxicillin/clavulanate, atorvastatin, and simvastatin (one case each), within a hospital-based case series of drug-induced eosinophilia.

raw_record.extra_details: Phase 2a, prospective, open, uncontrolled trial; 30 patients; simvastatin 20 mg/day for 2 weeks then 40 mg/day up to 1 year. raw_record.support_text: This case represents the fourth published case describing drug-induced hepatitis temporally related to ingestion of celecoxib. A 41-year-old man developed jaundice and cholestasis after taking 2 doses of celecoxib 200 mg for knee trauma pain; histology showed bile plugs in the bile canaliculi and a mild portal infiltrate suggesting drug-induced cholestasis. The patient denied alcohol, natural products, or other medications, and per the Naranjo algorithm the causal relationship between the cholestatic hepatitis and celecoxib administration appears probable.
raw_record.extra_details: 41-year-old man hospitalized for jaundice after 2 doses of celecoxib 200 mg for right knee trauma pain. Laboratory findings: hyperbilirubinemia, cholestasis, and moderate transaminase elevation; abdominal imaging showed no bile duct dilatation. Histology: bile plugs in bile canaliculi and a mild portal infiltrate suggesting drug-induced cholestasis. Fourth published case of drug-induced hepatitis temporally related to celecoxib; patient denied alcohol, natural products, or additional medications. Causal assessment by Naranjo algorithm: probable. The paper notes celecoxib is considered to have low potential for hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 7 DILI patients due to non-antibacterial sulfonamides, comprising 3 celecoxib, 3 sulfasalazine, and 1 zonisamide DILI patients, none of whom carried HLA-B*14:01.
raw_record.extra_details: DILIN registry; 3 European American DILI patients attributed to celecoxib (non-antibacterial sulfonamide subset); none carried HLA-B*14:01.

raw_record.support_text: Celecoxib is a widely prescribed nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug that has been associated with rare instances of idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (DILI). The paper reviews and analyzes published cases of celecoxib DILI reported from 2000 through June 2016, totaling 18 patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Celecoxib DILI reported in 18 patients, median age 54 (range 29-84), 15 (88%) female; median daily dose 200 mg (range 200-533); median duration and latency 13 days (1-730) and 17 days (2-730) respectively; 15 (83%) cases after short treatment (median 12 days) with rash and immunoallergic features, eosinophilia in 6 (40%); 3 cases after prolonged exposure (152-730 d) without immunoallergic features. Pattern of injury: hepatocellular 6, mixed 5, cholestatic 4, unknown 3. Outcomes: 2 (11%) required liver transplantation, 4 (22%) chronic liver injury, 12 (67%) recovered. NSAID class; women overrepresented.

raw_record.support_text: The United States DILIN registry (899 patients) found coxib-induced liver damage in only 4 patients, caused by either celecoxib (n = 3) or valdecoxib (n = 1). Separately, a retrospective prescription-based study in Umbria reported only 1 case of celecoxib-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 3 of 4 coxib-attributed DILIN registry cases; the Umbria (Italy) retrospective study (1997-2001) reported 1 celecoxib-induced liver injury case amid an overall NSAID liver-injury incidence of 1.7 per 100,000 exposed individuals. No biochemical pattern, phenotype, or severity reported.

raw_record.support_text: Celecoxib was implicated in three cases, two with short latency (16 and 23 days), usually with a mixed pattern of liver enzyme elevations and without immunoallergic features. One patient developed a severe cholestatic hepatitis and ultimately recovered clinically, but had continued evidence of cholestatic injury 6, 12 and 24 months after onset, compatible with some degree of vanishing bile duct syndrome. The comparison table lists 3 celecoxib cases (1 definite, 1 very likely, 1 probable).
raw_record.extra_details: 3 implicated cases; two with short latency (16 and 23 days); usually mixed enzyme pattern without immunoallergic features; one patient with severe cholestatic hepatitis and persisting cholestatic injury at 6, 12 and 24 months compatible with some degree of vanishing bile duct syndrome. Initial ALT 656 U/L, Alk P 319 U/L, bilirubin 7.4 mg/dl (peak 11.1 mg/dl). Causality: 1 definite, 1 very likely, 1 probable.

raw_record.support_text: This study provides detailed information of 18 reported cases of celecoxib-induced liver injury, noting that it was most often reported in females (83%) with variable presenting liver injury patterns and immunoallergic features in 40%. The paper attributes DILI to therapeutic celecoxib exposure (articulate the causal relationship via the unqualified 'celecoxib-induced liver injury' framing), distinct from diclofenac-related hepatocellular injury, and notes all 4 steroid-treated patients were female and that 3 male subjects all presented with cholestatic injury and fully recovered.
raw_record.extra_details: 18 published cases of celecoxib-induced liver injury (83% female; median age 53-57 y); indications arthritis/musculoskeletal pain and postprocedural analgesia; daily dose typically 200 mg (range 100-400 mg). Latency: median 12 d; DILI reported after longer courses (152-730 d) in 3 patients without immunoallergic features. Immunoallergic features in ~40-50%: rash in 2, peripheral/histologic eosinophilia in ~half, fever in 2. Liver injury patterns: mixed in 4 (44%), hepatocellular in 3 (30%), cholestatic in 2 (22%). Outcomes: acute liver failure requiring liver transplantation in 2 cases (vanishing bile duct syndrome in one; severe centrilobular necrosis in another), no deaths; resolution of injury in 67% of cases within 6 weeks in half; all reported cases met at least moderate grade on DILIN severity scale. AERS query identified 100 cases with celecoxib as primary suspected drug (10% death, 20% hepatic failure/comatose, 11% cholestatic, 31% hepatocellular). No patients had detectable autoantibodies and histology not suggestive of autoimmune hepatitis; proposed mechanism includes CYP2C9 metabolism and hapten/immune (HLA-mediated hypersensitivity) response.

raw_record.support_text: A 70-year-old man developed malaise after receiving celecoxib, with elevated hepatobiliary enzymes, and was transferred to hospital after no response to medical treatment. A liver biopsy revealed severe bile duct injury and mild cholestasis, and he was diagnosed with celecoxib-induced vanishing bile duct syndrome (VBDS). Despite bilirubin adsorption therapy, his condition deteriorated and he died; autopsy showed poor liver regeneration and exacerbated bile duct loss, consistent with VBDS.
raw_record.extra_details: 70-year-old man with unremarkable medical history; received celecoxib, a selective COX-2 inhibitor, for shoulder pain a few days before consultation. Labs: AST 124 U/L, ALT 136 U/L, ALP 1,485 U/L, γ-GTP 486 U/L, total bilirubin 10.0 mg/dL. Negative for HBsAg, HCV, CMV, EBV, HAV, HEV; no alcohol history; AMA-M2, ANA, IgG and IgM not elevated. Presented with one-week general malaise; CT showed edematous thickening of gallbladder. Liver biopsy: severe bile duct injury with mild cholestasis and lymphocytic infiltration. Considered steroid-resistant; treated with bilirubin adsorption therapy but deteriorated and died. Presented as a case report; reported as rare NSAID liver injury progressing to death.

raw_record.support_text: Among the five consecutively diagnosed cases of NSAID-induced fulminant hepatitis, one case was related to celecoxib at a dose of 100 mg/day, and the patient was successfully treated by orthotopic liver transplantation. Diagnosis was based on exclusion of other potentially hepatotoxic medications and causes of liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: 1 of 5 cases of NSAID-induced acute liver failure; dose 100 mg/day; treated by orthotopic liver transplantation for fulminant hepatitis. In the introduction celecoxib is described as a COX-2 inhibitor 'likely exhibiting less potential for hepatotoxicity'.

raw_record.support_text: A 77-year-old woman on stable celecoxib 200 mg twice daily for a gout attack developed fatigue, abdominal discomfort, and low-grade fever 12 days after initiation. She denied alcohol and over-the-counter/herbal use and had no history of liver/kidney disorders; sonogram and liver/kidney function tests 3 months earlier were normal.

raw_record.extra_details: Celecoxib 200 mg twice daily; latency 12 days. Naranjo probability scale suggested a probable association with hepatorenal syndrome. Hepatorenal syndrome with jaundice, pitting edema, elevated AST (576), ALT (396), GGT (140), ALP (696), bilirubin (2.4 mg/dL), INR (5), and creatinine; GFR 15 mL/min/1.73 m². Viral/autoimmune/iron/copper/α1-antitrypsin workup negative; biopsy refused. Dechallenge led to rapid symptomatic and biochemical improvement; rechallenge not done for safety; no known interaction with co-medications. Discussion notes rare reported celecoxib-induced hepatitis/hepatorenal syndrome and states celecoxib-induced hepatotoxicity may show hepatocellular, cholestatic, or combined pattern; allergic or idiosyncratic mechanism considered probable.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that drug-induced hepatitis and drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis are recognized complications of NSAIDs, and that COX-2 inhibitors have been implicated in prior case reports of AIN and hepatitis, but simultaneous presentation of both with a single therapeutic agent had previously been reported once with clometacin and never with a COX-2 inhibitor. Given the temporal sequence, clinical findings, and liver and renal biopsy histology, they believe there is good evidence to implicate rofecoxib as the causative agent of this combined drug-induced hepatitis and acute interstitial nephritis in the patient. The liver biopsy demonstrated zone 3 cholestasis, a mixed periportal infiltrate of neutrophils and eosinophils, and mild bile duct proliferation; hepatic dysfunction and cholestasis resolved over weeks and liver function tests fully recovered within months.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report. Simultaneous combined drug-induced hepatitis (zone 3 cholestasis, mixed periportal neutrophil/eosinophil infiltrate, mild bile duct proliferation on liver biopsy) and drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis attributed to rofecoxib. Hepatic dysfunction produced a coagulopathy (returned to normal within ~4 weeks, permitting renal biopsy), persistent leucocytosis with eosinophilia (1.8e9/L), and cholestasis that resolved over 4 weeks; liver function tests fully recovered over ~3 months and remained normal at 12 months. Patient also developed renal failure requiring haemodialysis, heavy proteinuria and acute tubular necrosis. Authors note this combined presentation had previously been reported once with clometacin and never with a COX-2 inhibitor.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of acute severe cytolytic and cholestatic hepatitis probably attributable (probablement imputable) to rofecoxib in a 69-year-old woman hospitalised for cutaneous-mucous jaundice. She had taken rofecoxib 12.5 mg per day for three days, four weeks before admission, for left shoulder pain. Liver tests showed cytolysis (ASAT 38x ULN, ALAT 42x ULN), cholestasis (alkaline phosphatase 4x ULN, γGT 40x ULN) and hyperbilirubinaemia (310 µmol/L total, 157 conjugated); prothrombin was reduced to 55% and factor V to 73%. Liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis compatible with drug-induced hepatitis. Her liver tests and prothrombin normalised within 6 months of rofecoxib discontinuation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient also used irbesartan (3 years, hypertension), zopiclone (insomnia), and self-medicated 1–2 g paracetamol daily for 4 months, representing concurrent co-medications; rofecoxib was taken intermittently at 12.5 mg/day for 3 days and was judged probably responsible.
raw_record.extra_details: Rofecoxib (Vioxx®), a selective COX-2 NSAID, was being self-medicated for left shoulder pain. Presented acute hepatitis with jaundice, hepatomegaly; no splenomegaly, ascites, or hepatic encephalopathy. Hypereosinophilia 0.49 g/L; positive anti-nuclear antibodies (1/320, homogeneous+cytoplasmic) at admission, negative at 6 months; viral, autoimmune and metabolic work-up otherwise negative. Biopsy showed acute hepatitis without portal/periportal fibrosis, centrilobular destruction, mixed portal-periportal-lobular inflammatory infiltrate with moderate cholangiolar proliferation. Prothrombin 55% with factor V 73%; improved to 65% at 1 week, normal 80% at 2 months, liver panel fully normal at 6 months. Adverse event reported Feb 2004 to Merck Sharp & Dohme-Chibret pharmacovigilance. Paper also notes four previously published cases of acute hepatitis in patients treated with rofecoxib.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective case series of seven patients (five pediatric, two adult, aged 2–39 years) treated with molecular adsorbent recirculating system (MARS) therapy for acute liver failure (ALF), the cause of ALF was indeterminate in five cases, with one case of viral ALF driven by varicella infection and one case of acetaminophen toxicity. Patient 7 (39-year-old female) had acetaminophen toxicity as the ALF etiology, was listed for liver transplant, and was transplanted successfully; overall transplant-free survival was 71.4% and one patient died of irreversible neurologic injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen toxicity was identified as the cause of acute liver failure in one patient (patient 7, 39-year-old female, weight 68 kg, PELD/MELD score 33). Mechanical ventilation and inotropic support were required in 43% of the overall cohort. Patient 7 was listed for liver transplant and successfully transplanted. The paper frames acetaminophen toxicity as a 'hepatotoxic ingestion'/'hepatotoxic intoxication,' an FDA-approved indication for MARS therapy.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol at the therapeutic dose (up to 4 g/day for adults and 50–75 mg/kg/day in children) has a safety profile, but an overdose can induce life-threatening adverse reactions like acute hepatic failure. In overdose (≥150 mg/kg or >10 g in an adult), liver glucuronidation capacity is saturated, more of the reactive intermediate N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI) binds covalently to hepatocyte proteins and causes hepatic necrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Overdose threshold stated as ≥150 mg/kg or >10 g in an adult; single massive dose with delayed presentation (serum paracetamol level within therapeutic range at admission). Reactive metabolite NAPQI detoxified by glutathione conjugation at normal doses; CYP450-formed. Paper notes paracetamol is one of the most commonly reported products causing drug-induced liver injury. Case report of a patient; ALT and AST monitored since admission.

raw_record.support_text: The study reported results for patients experiencing liver toxicity following acetaminophen (APAP) overdose, with adduct elimination kinetics measured; comparison with a pediatric/adolescent APAP overdose cohort showed a broader range of liver toxicity, and similarity in APAP adduct elimination across disease severities was taken to indicate broad clinical relevance across the spectrum of APAP toxicity, from early NAC-treated patients to those developing severe liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Study measured serum APAP-protein adducts (APAP-CYS) as a biomarker of APAP toxicity in adults after acute overdose; adduct elimination half-life ~1.5 days, similar to a children/adolescent cohort (James et al., 2008) in which 15% had ALT >1000 IU/l, no deaths occurred, and two patients required liver transplantation. Liver injury severity was indexed by ALT elevation, with encephalopathy, transplant listings, and severe liver failure noted across overdose populations (deliberate suicidal vs unintentional). Chronic/multiple supratherapeutic APAP overdose and combination APAP/opioid preparations were not reflected in the PK data.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol (acetaminophen), widely regarded as a safe analgesic/antipyretic at recommended doses, is in overdose one of the leading causes of acute liver failure worldwide, especially from intentional self-poisoning. The toxic threshold for hepatic injury is generally considered above 7.5-10 g in adults within 24 hours (approximately >150 mg/kg body weight) and above 200 mg/kg in children as a single dose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure; single-agent ingestion with no reported co-ingestion in the presented case.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented case: 32-year-old woman, 54 kg, intentional ingestion of 15 g (~278 mg/kg), admitted ~6 h post-ingestion; liver function tests markedly elevated with classical signs of hepatotoxicity; treated with N-acetylcysteine. Toxic threshold for hepatic injury ~7.5-10 g in adults within 24 h (>150 mg/kg) and >200 mg/kg in children (single dose). Cardiotoxicity (transient second-degree AV block, bradycardia) also occurred but is outside this DILI record. N-acetylcysteine SMILES:1304762 used as antidote.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen overdose caused clinically significant hepatotoxicity. Among patients with acetaminophen levels in the toxic range after long-term (multiple-dose) ingestion, the mortality rate was high: 11 died and 2 underwent liver transplantation. N-acetylcysteine was given to nine patients, of whom four survived. The case series included accidental pediatric overdosage, with 21 of 47 patients aged 2 years or younger and 14 of 21 receiving excess dosing of pediatric acetaminophen formulations.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Accidental and intentional overdosage; multiple-dose/long-term ingestion; case series included pediatric patients (21 of 47 aged <=2 years, 14 of 21 due to excess dosing of pediatric formulations).
raw_record.extra_details: 11 died and 2 underwent liver transplantation among patients with toxic-range acetaminophen levels; N-acetylcysteine given to 9 patients, of whom 4 survived. Mechanism: saturation of glucuronidation and sulfation with increased P450 metabolism to NAPQI; hepatotoxicity results from covalent binding of NAPQI to hepatocyte proteins after glutathione depletion. Only 7 of 47 took adult preparations.

raw_record.support_text: This retrospective study of children and adolescents with acute acetaminophen overdose aimed to identify the most accurate method of detecting patients without acetaminophen-related hepatotoxicity, using hepatotoxicity defined as AST or ALT levels >100 IU/L, including both mild and severe hepatotoxicity. The best predictor of low risk of hepatotoxicity was normal PT, AST, or ALT values within 48 hours of ingestion, whereas abnormal values were highly sensitive indicators of pending hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol overdose in children causes hepatotoxicity. A British study of 417 children aged 5 years or younger who had taken an overdose of paracetamol found only three had significantly raised plasma concentrations of liver enzymes. A subsequent American study of 322 paediatric patients found that among 140 adolescents who deliberately ingested paracetamol, 26 developed liver toxicity, while only one of 172 young children with accidental ingestion developed elevated liver enzymes only, and one of ten patients with dosing errors developed liver toxicity. The reduced hepatotoxicity in young children is attributed to their greater capacity for sulphation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings in children (ages 5 years or younger and adolescent subgroups); age-dependent susceptibility linked to greater sulphation capacity.
raw_record.extra_details: 417- and 322-patient paediatric overdose cohorts; 26/140 deliberate-ingestion adolescents developed liver toxicity; only 1/172 young children with accidental ingestion had elevated liver enzymes only; 1/10 dosing-error patients developed liver toxicity. Metabolism via glucuronidation and sulphation.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports paracetamol overdose as a cause of acute liver injury (ALI) in humans: circulating miR-122 was about 100-fold higher in patients with established ALI than in healthy controls and overdose patients without ALI, and the marker was used to report liver injury in paediatric paracetamol-overdose patients. In a UK cohort of 129 patients (Edinburgh and Newcastle-upon-Tyne), miR-122 measured a median of 8 h post-overdose in those requiring NAC therapy was significantly higher in patients who developed subsequent ALI and correlated with peak ALT and INR.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (paracetamol/acetaminophen poisoning) context, including a paediatric overdose population; ALI developed in patients requiring N-acetylcysteine (NAC) therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Discussed as a paradigm of acute liver injury for biomarker (circulating miR-122) evaluation; miR-122 AUC 0.93 (95% CI 0.86-1.0, sensitivity at 90% specificity, P<0.0001) for separating ALI from non-ALI at an early time when ALT was still normal; correlated with peak hospital-stay ALT and INR.

raw_record.support_text: In a population-based study of 14,662 Victorian hospital admissions for paracetamol overdose between July 1, 2000 and June 30, 2007, complications were uncommon, with acute liver failure reported in 137 cases (0.9%) and acute renal failure in 163 (1.1%). Overall 30-day mortality was 1.1% (n=154), dropping to 0.2% (n=26) when death was attributed to paracetamol or liver failure on the death certificate; nine of these 26 deaths (34%) were in patients with accidental overdose and none in children under 15. The discussion refers to 'life-threatening paracetamol-induced acute liver failure.'
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (the whole recorded relationship concerns paracetamol overdose, whether intentional or accidental).
raw_record.extra_details: 14,662 hospital admissions for paracetamol overdose over 7 years (mean 2095/year), 71% in women, most aged 15-50. Of overdoses, 9157 (62.5%) intentional, 2149 (15%, 307/year) accidental, remainder unknown. Acute liver failure n=137 (0.9%) and acute renal failure n=163 (1.1%); 0.8% of pediatric (<15 y) overdoses had a complication vs 3.5% in adults. 30-day mortality 1.1% (n=154), but 0.2% (n=26) when death attributed to paracetamol/liver failure. 26% of patients referred to the Victorian Liver Transplant Unit had accidental overdose (P=0.01). Overdose admissions decreased from 46/100,000 (2001) to 39/100,000 (2006), with no reduction in liver transplant unit referrals or mortality.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective study of children and adolescents with acetaminophen overdose (a healthy population with no preexisting liver disease or other comorbidities), the authors observed significant elevations of plasma cytokines that reflect acetaminophen-related liver injury. Patients were stratified by the highest recorded AST and ALT values, and higher levels of IL-6, IL-8, and MCP-1 were found in subjects with the most severe liver injury (ALT >1000 IU/L), with MCP-1 showing the strongest relationship to toxicity. The paper frames acetaminophen overdose as causing hepatotoxicity, referring to 'acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity'.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; pediatric population (children and adolescents); otherwise healthy cohort with no preexisting liver disease or comorbidities.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatoxicity severity stratified by highest AST and ALT; most severe liver injury defined as ALT >1000 IU/L. Elevated IL-6, IL-8, and MCP-1 associated with severity; MCP-1 showed the strongest relationship to toxicity, including correlation with prothrombin time (PT) and with time to initiation of NAC treatment. Reference is made to prior finding of association between IL-8 and severity of acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity, and to a study of adults with acetaminophen overdose (n=58; median age 36 years) reporting higher IL-8 in nonsurvivors than survivors. Supporting experimental findings (glutathione depletion, acetaminophen protein adducts, histologic hepatocellular injury in mice, CCR2 knockout increased toxicity) and hepatoprotective/regenerative cytokine mechanisms are noted.

raw_record.support_text: A 5-month-old child with intussusception received a 10-fold accidental overdose of 90 mg/kg intravenous paracetamol over an 8 h period (case 1). She was not initially treated with an antidote and developed hepatic impairment. The authors conclude that this case demonstrates intravenous paracetamol is a potentially dangerous drug, note that therapeutic errors such as 10-fold overdosing are relatively common in children, and recommend discussing significant overdose with the National Poisons Information Service, which suggests intervention with an antidote above 60 mg/kg.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (5-month-old infant, 6.9 kg) with intussusception; accidental 10-fold overdose; intravenous paracetamol formulation; no initial antidote treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1 received 90 mg/kg IV paracetamol over 8 h and developed hepatic impairment without antidote treatment. A second infant (case 2, 6 months old) received a single 75 mg/kg IV dose, was treated with N-acetylcysteine, and remained well without hepatic impairment. Paper notes the oral overdose concentration-time nomogram should be used with caution after intravenous overdose; NPIS recommends antidote intervention above 60 mg/kg. The assertions on overdose frequency, nomogram caution, and NPIS guidance are considered context rather than independent DILI claims.

raw_record.extra_details: Rectal dose 175 mg/kg on first day exceeded suggested 40 mg/kg followed by 20 mg/kg 6-hourly. raw_record.support_text: Fatal acetaminophen toxicity was reported in a 3½-year-old child who ingested 5 g during 24 hours, preceded by a dose of 0.5 g for the preceding 24 hours; his serum acetaminophen level 14 hours after the last dose was about twice the therapeutic range of 1–3 mg/dL. raw_record.support_text: The paper characterizes adults who were having acute liver failure secondary to acetaminophen (APAP) overdose, and studies children and adolescents presenting to pediatric medical centers with APAP overdose. Two of the 157 pediatric subjects required liver transplantation, 155 recovered spontaneously, and there were no deaths; most overdoses were acute and NAC was administered to 90% of subjects.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients (children and adolescents); overdose exposure. Population included 122 female and 35 male subjects, mostly >12 years old; 94.3% acute overdoses and 9 chronic overdoses.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP protein adducts used as a biomarker of occult APAP toxicity; in adults, adducts persisted up to 12 days after overdose with elimination half-life far exceeding the parent compound (APAP t1/2 in APAP-related ALF: 6.4 h without encephalopathy, 18.4 h with encephalopathy). Mean reported dose in acute overdose patients 633 (±1647) mg/kg; in chronic overdose patients 139 (±30) mg/kg/day. NAC given to 141 (90%) subjects; gastric decontamination used (activated charcoal 65, syrup of ipecac 1, gastric lavage 18). Two subjects required liver transplantation; no deaths; 155 (98.7%) recovered spontaneously. Adduct peak values did not vary by gender, race, ethnicity, age, or reported APAP dose.

raw_record.support_text: In a 10-year study of 322 pediatric patients presenting for acetaminophen overdose, hepatocellular injury developed in 27 patients (8.4%) and hepatic failure in 4 of these; 4 had severe hepatocellular injury and 1 died of multisystem organ failure, none required liver transplantation though 2 were accepted but recovered. Development of hepatocellular injury was associated with presentation more than 24 hours after ingestion (OR 335.0; 95% CI 40.8-275.0), age 10-17 years, intentional overdose, dose greater than 150 mg/kg, and white race.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients (median age 4 years; overdose context including intentional and unintentional ingestions and dosing errors with therapeutic intent).
raw_record.extra_details: 322 patients over 10 years (268 from Kansas City, 54 from Seattle); ingested doses ranged 4-8333 mg/kg (median ~151 mg/kg); 27/322 (8.4%) developed hepatocellular injury, 4 developed hepatic failure, 4 had severe hepatocellular injury, and 1 died of multisystem organ failure; 2 were accepted for transplant but recovered before receiving an organ. Association factors: presentation >24 h after ingestion (OR 335.0; 95% CI 40.8-275.0), age 10-17 y (OR 36.9), intentional overdose (OR 37.2; 95% CI 5.0-278.2), dose >150 mg/kg (OR 17.9; 95% CI 2.3-139.2), white race (OR 2.8). 82 patients (25.5%) received N-acetylcysteine. One dosing-error case (11-year-old, repeated self-medication, ~120 mg/kg) developed hepatocellular injury with peak AST 454 U/L and recovered with N-acetylcysteine; none of the 10 dosing-error patients developed severe hepatocellular injury.

raw_record.support_text: The paper is a retrospective case study of 25 children (aged 11-16 years) with severe acetaminophen poisoning, exploring the dose-response relationship between ingested acetaminophen and hepatotoxicity, early biochemical/clinical predictors, the impact of early N-acetylcysteine treatment on hepatotoxicity, and the incidence of nephrotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients aged 11-16 years with severe acetaminophen poisoning (overdose setting).
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective case study (n=25 children). Hepatotoxicity was assessed by maximum INR and maximum ALT. Early predictors of hepatotoxicity included initial bilirubin (p=0.0003 vs max INR), initial phosphate (p=0.003 vs max INR), initial INR (p=0.0003 vs max ALT), initial creatinine (p=0.002 vs max ALT), prehospital vomiting episodes, and time of N-acetylcysteine initiation. Nephrotoxicity incidence was 12%. No significant relationship between the amount of ingested acetaminophen and degree of hepatotoxicity. The paper states that acetaminophen overdoses may cause hepatotoxicity and fulminant liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: Of the 41 pediatric patients included in the sensitivity and specificity analysis, 16 (39%) had hepatotoxicity after acute acetaminophen (APAP) ingestion: 9 'severe' (APAP dose range 190-819 mg/kg, 1 requiring transplantation, 8 fully recovered) and 7 'mild' (APAP dose range 146-500 mg/kg, all completely recovered). All patients had received NAC within the first 24 hours after ingestion, and 11 patients ingested >250 mg/kg of APAP by history without biochemical signs of hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients; acute deliberate/accidental overdose ingestion; all received N-acetylcysteine within the first 24 hours after ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: 16/41 patients (39%) developed hepatotoxicity; 9 severe (APAP dose 190-819 mg/kg; 1 required liver transplantation, 8 recovered) and 7 mild (APAP dose 146-500 mg/kg, all recovered). 11/41 (44%) ingested >250 mg/kg without biochemical hepatotoxicity. In patients with hepatocellular injury, postingestion APAP concentrations were not predictive of 'probable' toxicity per the Rumack-Matthews nomogram in 14% (mild) and 11% (severe) of cases. NAC administration within the first 9 hours in 11 patients. Mechanism (p10-11): APAP is bioactivated to NAPQI by hepatic cytochromes P450; NAPQI covalently binds protein thiols, disrupting enzymes/regulatory pathways and initiating an inflammatory cascade via interleukin-8, producing hepatocellular injury at the site and time of NAPQI formation.

raw_record.support_text: In a compiled case series of children with repeated accidental overdosage of acetaminophen (dosages estimated at 60–420 mg/kg/day for up to 6 weeks), hepatotoxicity was severe: only 20 of 43 (46.5%) survived, four additional patients survived only because of orthotopic liver transplantation, and 21 of 47 cases had histologic evidence of zone 3 (centrilobular) necrosis on biopsy or autopsy. This indicates that acetaminophen causes dose-related intrinsic hepatotoxicity in the supratherapeutic-exposure setting.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients; repeated accidental supratherapeutic overdosage (estimated 60–420 mg/kg/day for 1 day to 6 weeks) rather than a single acute overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: Compilation of 47 well-documented pediatric cases (20 previously unreported) plus 8 nonoverlapping cases from Rivera-Penera et al., totaling 55 cases. Peak serum AST (n=45) ranged 1,180–30,000 IU/L (median 10,000); peak ALT (n=34) ranged 440 to >22,000 IU/L (median 8,200); these were significantly higher than in non-acetaminophen fulminant hepatic failure. Of 30 cases with timing, 22 had serum levels above the Rumack-Matthews nomogram line associated with hepatotoxicity. 21/47 had zone 3 centrilobular necrosis histology. 9 patients received N-acetylcysteine (44% survived). This is described as the largest collection of liver injury from long-term acetaminophen administration in children; the number likely underrepresents true hepatotoxicity cases.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 25 pediatric patients with acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose treated with N-acetylcysteine (NAC), hepatotoxicity severity was assessed. There were highly significant relationships between maximum ALT and maximum INR (p < 0.0001), maximum AST (p < 0.0001), maximum bilirubin (p < 0.0001) and maximum pH (p < 0.0001), and a significant relationship between maximum ALT and minimum phosphate (p = 0.038). The mean time from acetaminophen intake to NAC initiation was 12.4 h (range 1.5–25.5 h), and multiple prehospital vomiting episodes were proposed as an early predictor of acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity in this pediatric cohort.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (25 children); overdose exposure treated with N-acetylcysteine (NAC).
raw_record.extra_details: Mean time from acetaminophen intake to NAC initiation 12.4 h (range 1.5–25.5 h). Hepatotoxicity severity indicated by maximum ALT, INR, AST, bilirubin, pH, and minimum phosphate relationships. Prehospital vomiting (≥3 episodes in 60%, 15/25) proposed as an early predictor; significant relationship of vomiting episodes with maximum INR (p=0.013), maximum AST (p≤0.0001), maximum ALT (p=0.0005), and other biochemical parameters. Maximum ALT significantly related to maximum INR (p<0.0001), maximum AST (p<0.0001), maximum bilirubin (p<0.0001), maximum pH (p<0.0001), and minimum phosphate (p=0.038). Acetaminophen overdose hepatotoxicity treated with NAC.

raw_record.support_text: A case series of 109 children with acetaminophen supratherapeutic-dose severe hepatotoxicity (86% aged two years old and less) reported an overall case-fatality of 53%. Only 15% did not receive NAC during hospitalization; not receiving NAC was associated with increased hazard (HR 5.24, 95% CI 2.23-12.42), while completing the three-day NAC regimen was associated with survival (HR 0.015, 95% CI 0.005-0.047). No adverse effects were observed among the children.

raw_record.support_text: The clinical characteristics of 51 children (6 males) with paracetamol induced significant hepatotoxicity are described. The median age was 14.7 years, with a bimodal distribution; 6/51 children were less than 7 years. In adolescent patients overdose was usually an impulsive act with female predominance (43/45). The median dose for single paracetamol ingestion was 345 mg/kg (range 91-645). Two patients who took supratherapeutic doses (97 and 127 mg/kg) showed significant hepatotoxicity without encephalopathy and survived. 27% with significant hepatotoxicity received N-acetylcysteine treatment despite paracetamol level being less than the nomogram treatment line.

raw_record.extra_details: 51 children; median single ingestion dose 345 mg/kg (range 91-645); two patients with supratherapeutic doses (97 and 127 mg/kg) developed significant hepatotoxicity without encephalopathy and survived; median time from ingestion to presentation 24 h in group I vs 44 h in group II; severe hepatocellular injury in 41% (10/40 group I, 11/11 group II); group I recovered with conservative management while group II had rapidly progressing encephalopathy ≥grade III; 6/11 underwent OLT with only 33% (2/6) survival, and 5/11 died awaiting OLT; survival 100% for encephalopathy ≤II vs 18% for ≥III; main cause of death was cerebral oedema (8/11, 73%), with 1/11 dying of fungal sepsis; histopathology of explanted/postmortem livers in 9/11 confirmed drug toxicity; peak ALT/AST up to 10000/7500 IU/l.
