raw_record.support_text: In a pediatric study of 88 children, 64 presented with acetaminophen (APAP) overdose (Group C). Patients were evaluated for potential hepatotoxicity risk using the Rumack nomogram based on plasma APAP level versus time since ingestion, plus elevated ALT at presentation and antihistamine co-ingestion. Of the 64 overdose patients, 40 were judged at risk for liver injury by nomogram, bringing the overall proportion of Group C judged at risk for developing liver injury to 73%; there were no deaths or liver transplants. Eleven of 64 (17.2%) overdose subjects had ALT values above 1000 IU/L.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children aged ~1.5-18 years); overdose setting; all overdose patients received N-acetylcysteine (NAC), with timing of NAC stratified (<10 h, 10-24 h, ≥24 h); two patients had antihistamine co-ingestion; one subject had unknown time of ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: 40 of 64 overdose patients at risk by Rumack nomogram; 73% of Group C overall judged at risk for liver injury; 11 of 64 (17.2%) had ALT >1000 IU/L; no deaths or liver transplants in the cohort; peak ALT for Group C median 29 IU/L (range 8-9909), higher than healthy controls (p=0.001) but not higher than Group A after early NAC treatment; serum APAP protein adducts (nmol/mL) differed significantly across all groups and were higher in overdose group, consistent with exposure/metabolism.

raw_record.support_text: Acute APAP (acetaminophen) toxicity is described as the most common identifiable cause of acute liver failure in children aged ≥3 years (21%), with an even higher frequency (40%) in adults. The mechanism involves formation of APAP-protein adducts: when usual APAP metabolism and excretion pathways are exhausted, the reactive APAP metabolite binds to intracellular proteins resulting in cell death; these serum adducts may serve as a biomarker of APAP toxicity. Instances of prolonged or inappropriate dosing (therapeutic misadventures) are noted as not easily captured by the study.

raw_record.support_text: This study demonstrates significant increases in long-chain acylcarnitines (palmitoyl-, oleoyl- and myristoyl-carnitine) in children exposed to acetaminophen (APAP) in therapeutic doses or overdose, extending the preclinical model of APAP-induced hepatotoxicity to the clinical setting. In subjects with significant hepatotoxicity (ALT ≥1000 IU), median peak levels of the three long-chain acylcarnitines were 1.2–2.5-fold above those of the control group, indicating disruption of the fatty-acid β-oxidation pathway and mitochondrial dysfunction.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children); all overdose subjects received N-acetylcysteine (NAC) treatment, with outcomes influenced by time to NAC (early ≤24 h vs late >24 h).
raw_record.extra_details: Significant hepatotoxicity defined as ALT ≥1000 IU in the overdose (group C) cohort. Long-chain acylcarnitines (oleoyl-, palmitoyl-, myristoyl-carnitine) elevated with APAP exposure; acetyl-carnitine decreased; increases indicate disruption of fatty-acid β-oxidation and mitochondrial dysfunction, validated with UPLC-TQ MS. Therapeutic-dose exposure also showed acylcarnitine elevations. No acute liver failure, transplantation, or death reported as outcomes.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen is a drug commonly ingested by children in potentially toxic amounts, and it has been recognized that children are less likely than adolescents or adults to suffer hepatotoxicity from overdose. The paper discusses predicting which children are at risk of hepatotoxicity from acetaminophen overdose and reports that only 0.59% of pediatric acetaminophen exposures in this study produced a potentially toxic serum concentration (patients whose concentrations fell in the probable or possible risk areas of the Rumack-Matthew nomogram).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children, typically age 1-6 years); overdose/supratherapeutic ingestion setting.
raw_record.extra_details: In this retrospective series of 223 patients without GI decontamination, no patient ingesting less than 200 mg/kg (n=104) developed a potentially toxic serum concentration (0/104, upper 95% CL 2.9%); 6 patients (cases 1-6) had potentially hepatotoxic concentrations (probable or possible risk areas of the Rumack-Matthew nomogram), 3 ingesting unknown amounts and 3 greater than 200 mg/kg. No correlation was found between reported dose (mg/kg) and 4-hour acetaminophen concentration in the nondecontaminated group (n=69, R²=0.004, excluding one outlier of 2500 mg/kg with 600 µg/mL). Children are recognized as less likely than adolescents or adults to suffer hepatotoxicity from overdose; adult toxicity standards applied to children yield a low rate of documented toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The study compared a 52-hour regimen of IV-NAC with standard therapy with O-NAC for reducing the incidence of hepatotoxicity after acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose in a pediatric cohort (mean age 15.6 ± 3.2 years). In this cohort, no patients treated within 10 hours and only 9.8% treated between 10 and 24 hours after ingestion experienced hepatotoxicity, whereas other series reported 6.1%/26.4% (oral NAC) and 10%/27.1% (IV-NAC) depending on treatment timing. The hepatic injury is attributed to acetaminophen overdose, with the toxic metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (elaborated by CYP1A2 and CYP2E1) discussed as mechanism.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (mean age 15.6 years); overdose setting; one patient with hepatic encephalopathy reportedly abused ethanol (unresolved co-exposure).
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity incidence in acetaminophen overdose: 0% when NAC begun within 10 hours and 9.8% when begun 10-24 hours after ingestion in this cohort; compared to Smilkstein et al. reports of 6.1%/26.4% (oral NAC) and 10%/27.1% (IV-NAC). One patient developed hepatic encephalopathy: ALT/AST >3000 IU/L by 32 h, peak ALT/AST 10,600/9840 IU/L at 58 h, peak ammonia 138 µg/dl at 106 h, improved by day 6 and discharged without sequelae; O-NAC attempt at 11 h with multiple episodes of emesis. Coagulopathy was clinically apparent in two patients (epistaxis, menorrhagia), neither requiring fresh frozen plasma. Mechanism discussion: N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (initially reported as N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine) produced via CYP2E1/CYP1A2; ethanol induced CYP2E1 and reduced glutathione may increase susceptibility; pediatric sulfation more prominent and possibly greater glutathione regeneration.

The paper also compiles case reports of paracetamol overdose in neonates and infants, including a 7-month-old who received 1565 mg (233 mg/kg) due to inadvertent duplication of prescriptions, developed fulminant hepatic failure with hepatic encephalopathy/Reye's syndrome (ALT 22,235 IU/L, AST 8924 IU/L, PT 75 s) and died, and a 3-month-old with an IV dosing error (1500 mg, 300 mg/kg/day instead of 30 mg/kg) who had transient hepatotoxicity (peak ALT 1946 IU/L, AST 1633 IU/L) with recovery.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population, specifically neonates and infants; all cases are supratherapeutic (overdose) dosing from dosing errors or inadvertent prescription duplication.
raw_record.extra_details: Overdose doses ranged from 60 to 445 mg/kg via oral, IV, and IM routes in neonatal and infant cases tabulated by the authors. Fulminant hepatic failure/encephalopathy/Reye's syndrome case (Ebenezer): 233 mg/kg paracetamol over 36–48 h, ALT 22,235 IU/L, AST 8924 IU/L, PT 75 s, INR 4.7, paracetamol concentration 91.1 mcg/mL; death 24 h later despite intubation and antidote. Transient hepatotoxicity case (Aslan): 3-month-old, 300 mg/kg/day IV dosing error, peak ALT 1946 IU/L and AST 1633 IU/L, normalized after NAC. Most neonatal/infant overdose cases recovered fully with N-acetylcysteine (NAC); some showed only transient enzyme elevations. Liver injury typically peaks 3–5 days after ingestion; moderate-severe overdose may initially show nonspecific vomiting, appetite loss, lethargy, weakness. Renal dysfunction co-occurs with hepatotoxicity (about 25% of adults with significant hepatotoxicity, >50% with hepatic failure).; aliases: acetaminophen

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports on a pediatric population with acetaminophen overdose (suicide attempts) and the resulting hepatotoxicity. It states that the importance of early initiation of NAC treatment in acetaminophen overdose has been proved in several adult studies and that the present study confirmed these findings in a pediatric population, with a highly significant relationship between hepatologically relevant biochemical parameters and the latency time before NAC initiation. The conclusion further frames the outcome as moderate/severe hepatotoxicity in these acetaminophen-overdosed patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population; exposure was deliberate acetaminophen overdose during a suicide attempt (overdose context).
raw_record.extra_details: Outcome described as moderate/severe hepatotoxicity with elevated transaminases (ALT/aspartate aminotransferase) and INR, and reduced coagulation parameters. Retrospective design. Number of prehospital vomiting episodes was a more sensitive risk factor for moderate/severe hepatotoxicity than the amount of acetaminophen ingested (only a sparse relationship between acetaminophen intake and biochemical parameters was found). Treatment with intravenous antidotal NAC (99% of study population received NAC); latency to NAC initiation significantly related to higher transaminases and lower coagulation. Illness prior to the suicide attempt was associated with more affected transaminases and INR.

raw_record.support_text: In response to a question about acetaminophen toxicity in a pediatric acute liver failure series, the authors note that of the nine children who survived, four were not teenage suicide attempts but younger children probably overdosed by their parents from either lack of information or lack of understanding of how to use the drug. Earlier discussion adds that in the Philadelphia experience, 32% of the 26 cases were acetaminophen ingestions.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population; exposure was overdose—four survivors were younger children overdosed by parents who misunderstood drug dosing, while other acetaminophen cases were not teenage suicide attempts.
raw_record.extra_details: In a Philadelphia pediatric acute liver failure experience (26 cases), 32% were acetaminophen ingestions; nine children survived overall, and acetaminophen toxicity was associated with survival, likely due to early recognition and treatment with N-acetylcysteine and other support. Presenting features in this series included elevated transaminases with prolonged prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time; only 9 of 26 patients were clinically jaundiced at presentation.

raw_record.support_text: Rectal administration of acetaminophen was significantly associated with supratherapeutic dosing (mean 20.9 mg/kg, range 16.6-41.7 mg/kg). Previously reported cases of hepatotoxicity secondary to multiple supratherapeutic acetaminophen dosing per rectum included 5 children (ages 7 months to 8 years), with an overdose range of 17 to 70 mg/kg/dose or 102 to 420 mg/kg/d. Death occurred in a 2-year-old child who received 650-mg suppositories every 4 hours for a total of 17 doses. The paper also states that with greater than recommended doses the CYP450 pathway produces NAPQI, and excessive NAPQI leads to hepatic cellular necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population; multiple supratherapeutic doses predominantly via the rectal route; at risk in children receiving >15 mg/kg/dose for more than 5 doses within 24 hours, children younger than 2 years who are ill and acutely malnourished, and children with chronic liver disorders or taking medications that stimulate CYP450 hepatic enzymes.
raw_record.extra_details: Overdose range 17 to 70 mg/kg/dose or 102 to 420 mg/kg/d; mean rectal supratherapeutic dose 20.9 mg/kg (16.6-41.7); death in a 2-year-old given 650-mg suppositories every 4 h, 17 total doses; dosing errors attributed to parents (2), physicians (2), and pharmacists (1). Mechanism: therapeutic doses metabolized by sulfation and glucuronidation, but supratherapeutic doses saturate these pathways and activate CYP450, producing N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), which is detoxified by glutathione conjugation; excessive NAPQI leads to hepatic cellular necrosis. Risk enhanced by CYP450 inducers (phenobarbital, carbamazepine, rifampin, ethanol, isoniazid) and by illness/malnutrition in young children.

raw_record.support_text: Untargeted metabolomic profiling was applied to high dose acetaminophen (APAP) toxicity by comparing the urinary metabolic pattern of 13 APAP-overdosed patients versus 6 controls in a pediatric population. Several identified metabolites belonged to pathways known to be involved in acetaminophen intoxication or were increased in a rat model. A further pediatric study used targeted metabolomic profiling to demonstrate a structure-dependent phospholipid alteration in the serum of acetaminophen-overdosed children. Acetaminophen is thereby treated as causing human liver toxicity in the overdose setting.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population; overdose setting (13 APAP-overdosed patients compared with 6 controls).
raw_record.extra_details: Metabolomic biomarker context: untargeted urinary profiling of overdosed patients identified metabolites in pathways known to be involved in acetaminophen intoxication or increased in a rat model; targeted profiling of overdosed children showed structure-dependent serum phospholipid alterations.

raw_record.support_text: Penna & Buchanan reported seven deaths and 11 cases of hepatotoxicity associated with paracetamol in children. Mortality due to hepatotoxicity was associated with doses greater than 300 mg/day/kg for one to six days, while survival was usually seen in children with hepatotoxicity from paracetamol greater than 150 mg/day/kg for two to eight days.

raw_record.extra_details: Penna & Buchanan case series: 7 deaths and 11 hepatotoxicity cases in children; mortality associated with doses >300 mg/day/kg for 1-6 days; survival usually seen with hepatotoxic doses >150 mg/day/kg for 2-8 days; paracetamol may accumulate in paediatric patients after repeated therapeutic doses combined with adult volunteer evidence of glutathione depletion (0.5 g and 3 g doses separated by 4-10 days); current guidelines recommend not exceeding 90 mg/day/kg.

raw_record.support_text: The study shows that at an early stage of admission it is possible to predict subsequently elevated levels of transaminases, INR, and other hepatologically relevant biochemical parameters. Especially prehospital and in-hospital vomiting, latency time before initiation of NAC treatment, and illness prior to a suicide attempt by means of acetaminophen were identified as important early clinical risk factors of underlying evolving moderate/severe hepatotoxicity in a pediatric population.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population; poisoning after suicide attempt (overdose exposure).
raw_record.extra_details: Early clinical risk factors of evolving moderate/severe hepatotoxicity: prehospital and in-hospital vomiting episodes (highly significant relationship between number of prehospital vomiting episodes and elevated hepatologically relevant biochemical parameters), latency time before initiation of NAC treatment (longer delay associated with higher maximum GGT, maximum INR, initial/maximum AST, initial/maximum ALT), and illness up to 48 hours prior to the suicide attempt (significant relationships with initial/maximum INR, maximum AST, maximum ALT). No relationship between ingested acetaminophen amount (mean 10.01-11.29 g) and biochemical parameters in this pediatric population, unlike some adult studies; adults with severe liver failure may have different cytochrome P450 expression yielding higher hepatotoxic NAPQI at lower doses, and glucuronosyltransferase gene polymorphisms have been linked to acetaminophen-induced liver injury risk. None of the patients were candidates for liver transplantation; only 3 required referral to a tertiary pediatric department specialized in children's liver diseases. Study population: patients admitted to a general secondary-level pediatric department.

raw_record.support_text: The paper opens by stating that paracetamol (acetaminophen), although considered a safe over-the-counter analgesic and antipyretic, can cause liver injury with overdose, and notes that therapeutic misadventure is a unique problem where the acute-poisoning nomogram does not apply. A series of 6 children with this type of paracetamol overdose (unintentional multiple/supratherapeutic dosing) is presented, with early N-acetylcysteine administration.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population; therapeutic misadventure type (unintentional multiple/supratherapeutic dosing); two of the six cases also co-administered mefenamic acid.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 6 children (April-December 2008) hospitalized after paracetamol overdose, doses ~90-367 mg/kg/day for 1-5 days. Introduction states poisoning may cause either isolated elevation of transaminases or acute liver failure (ALF). Three of 6 cases had abnormal LFT and PT, three had normal values; none documented to progress to ALF. N-acetylcysteine (oral or IV loading followed by 17 doses of 70 mg/kg every 4 h) was given empirically before biochemical evidence of liver injury; paracetamol levels 32-142 μg/mL (reference 10-20 μg/mL). Infants/young children noted to be less susceptible to acute paracetamol toxicity due to age-associated differences in drug metabolism.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen hepatotoxicity after unintentional ingestion is dose-dependent in young children. The author critiques a prospective observational case series (1,039 patients) that observed children at home after ingestions below 200 mg/kg with no decontamination. Because 93.4% ingested less than 150 mg/kg and only 68 patients (6.5%) ingested 150-200 mg/kg, the author argues low-dose ingestions are very unlikely to produce hepatotoxicity, whereas the risk in the 150-200 mg/kg subgroup is uncertain (upper 95% confidence limit for an adverse outcome 4.4%, 3/68, vs 0.3%, 3/971, in the low-dose group). The minimum acute hepatotoxic dose of acetaminophen in young children is described as not well defined.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric young children; unintentional acute ingestion (overdose setting); risk considered specifically in the 150-200 mg/kg dose range with no decontamination and home observation.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute overdose doses: <150 mg/kg associated with very low likelihood of hepatotoxicity; 150-200 mg/kg subgroup (n=68) had no reported adverse outcomes but upper 95% CI for an adverse outcome was 4.4% vs 0.3% (3/971) in the low-dose group. Letter discusses proprioac-induced emesis <1 hour after ingestion as a mitigation option and questions whether adult (500-mg) formulations were miscounted. Primary data from Mohler et al. prospective observational case series (n=1,039).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that acetaminophen (APAP) overdose is a common cause of pediatric ingestions and, in severe cases, may result in acute liver failure (ALF). It further reports that APAP overdose is a major cause of ALF in adults (~50% of cases) and accounts for ~13% of ALF cases in children, establishing a human DILI relationship for acetaminophen at overdose. Supporting these claims, the study found that of 157 adolescents and children presenting with APAP overdose at eight pediatric hospitals, two required liver transplantation while the others recovered spontaneously, and peak APAP protein adducts correlated with peak hepatic transaminase values.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric/adolescent population (157 patients at eight pediatric hospitals); overdose exposure setting.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP overdose causes acute liver failure in adults (~50% of ALF cases) and in children (~13% of cases); morbidity in children is generally lower than in adults. In the study cohort, 2/157 patients required liver transplantation and the remainder recovered spontaneously. Peak APAP protein adduct concentrations correlated with peak hepatic transaminases, time-to-treatment with N-acetylcysteine (NAC), and Rumack-Matthews nomogram risk determination; model-derived adduct value at 48 h correlated with adduct Cmax, adduct Tmax, Rumack-Matthews risk, peak AST and peak ALT. Mechanism involves cytochrome P450 (CYP2E1, CYP1A2, CYP3A4) oxidation to the reactive metabolite NAPQI; covalent binding of NAPQI to cysteinyl sulfhydryl groups on cellular proteins (3-(cystein-S-yl)APAP protein adduct) under glutathione depletion underlies toxicity. APAP accounts for ~50% of adult ALF and ~13% of pediatric ALF.

raw_record.support_text: This study of 157 children and adolescents with APAP (acetaminophen) overdose who received timely NAC treatment found that APAP protein adducts correlate with measures of toxicity, and that the elimination characteristics of APAP adducts were similar to those reported for adults with acute liver failure (ALF) following APAP overdose. The paper confirms APAP protein adducts as a clinically relevant and specific biomarker of APAP toxicity, and discusses adults with ALF following APAP overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric/adolescent population (children and adolescents presenting with APAP ingestion); subjects received timely NAC treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen (APAP, paracetamol) overdose leads to acute liver failure (ALF). Study measured APAP protein adducts as a toxicity biomarker; adduct elimination half-life exceeds that of the parent compound. Overdose context in pediatrics often involves inadvertent overdose, adult formulations, and OTC cough/cold remedies; opioid/APAP combination products are a target of adolescent drug abuse. NAC (N-acetylcysteine) was administered as treatment. Enrollment from 157 adolescents and children across eight sites of the Network of Pediatric Pharmacology Research Units.

raw_record.support_text: Bucaretschi et al. (2014) reported a case of APAP-induced acute liver failure in a term neonate: after oral APAP (10 mg/kg/dose every 4 hours) for three consecutive days (total ~180 mg/kg), a 26-day-old boy was admitted with slight liver enlargement, increased serum aminotransferase activity, intestinal bleeding, shock signs, coagulopathy, metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia, and hyperbilirubinemia, highlighting the risk of severe hepatotoxicity in neonates after multiple doses of APAP for more than two to three days.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Neonatal patient (term, 26-day-old boy); therapeutic repeated oral dosing (10 mg/kg/dose every 4 h for 3 days, total ~180 mg/kg); detected rise in serum aminotransferase with multiple systemic features.
raw_record.extra_details: Presenting features: slight liver enlargement, intestinal bleeding, shock, coagulopathy, metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia, hyperbilirubinemia; paper notes neonates/infants differ from older children and adults in APAP pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics, making age important in APAP toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that some children with myopathies receiving recommended doses of acetaminophen (APAP) may be at increased risk for toxicity resulting in acute liver failure (ALF), and note that despite a possible relationship between therapeutic APAP use and ALF in myopathic patients, they do not recommend dose adjustment of APAP.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients with myopathies; critically ill; received recommended (therapeutic) doses; concurrent treatment with other drugs (propofol in both, clarithromycin in patient 2) means a role of other drugs could not be excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Two pediatric patients developed ALF attributed to APAP; causality judged 'more probable' supported by high APAP adduct levels. A separate referenced 12-year-old myopathic patient with carnitine deficiency and severe mitochondrial derangement required emergency liver transplantation. Suggested mechanisms include glutathione depletion, increased CYP2E1 activity, inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and oxidative stress. Authors do not recommend dose adjustment of APAP despite reporting therapeutic-use ALF in myopathic children.

raw_record.support_text: In this case series of seven premature infants undergoing nasogastric paracetamol for PDA closure, none of the patients presented high paracetamol blood levels or significant liver function disturbances, except for mild temporary elevation of GGT in 3 infants (Table 1). The authors note that the potential paracetamol hepatotoxicity concentration is unknown, and in their series no significant liver injury was observed.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Preterm infants with hemodynamically significant PDA; off-label nasogastric paracetamol administration for PDA closure at doses recommended for pain control, with paracetamol blood levels and liver function monitored.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 7 premature infants; none presented high paracetamol blood levels or significant liver function disturbances; mild temporary GGT elevation in 3 infants only (recommended GGT range 12-132 units/l). Recommended plasma paracetamol concentration for analgesia/antipyresis 10-20 mg/ml; two infants had transient elevations of 24.3 and 27.1 mg/ml before dose 9, returning to the recommended range after treatment with normal liver function tests. The paper notes the potential paracetamol hepatotoxicity is attributed to production of N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone-imine by hepatic cytochrome P-450, and that the paracetamol concentration causing such hepatotoxicity is unknown.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen serum concentrations were studied in 21 infants and children with fever after therapeutic single and repeated doses (66-81 mg/kg/day as elixir). Maximum serum concentrations ranged from 9.96 to 19.6 µg/ml after a single 12-14 mg/kg dose and 13.9 to 40.1 µg/ml after a single 22-27 mg/kg dose; ten patients were restudied at steady-state. The authors report there was no evidence of hepatotoxicity in these patients, concluding only that acetaminophen may accumulate after repeated therapeutic doses in children with fever.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Subjects were hospitalized febrile children (n=21, ages 0.5-6.4 years, weight 8.84-22.6 kg) with presumed/proven bacterial or viral infection receiving therapeutic oral acetaminophen elixir 66-81 mg/kg/day (12-14 mg/kg/4h or 22-27 mg/kg/8h) for 1-3 days; patients with abnormal liver or renal function, vomiting, diarrhea, dehydration, or malnutrition were excluded; some patients received concomitant drugs (ampicillin, phenobarbital, diphenhydramine, theophylline, phenytoin, penicillin, cefaclor, moxalactam, gentamicin, nafcillin).
raw_record.extra_details: No evidence of hepatotoxicity or abnormal liver function at these therapeutic doses despite dose-normalized AUC increasing from 0.181 to 0.202 (ml/min/kg)^-1 from first dose to steady-state (p<0.05); five of ten steady-state patients showed 13-44% increase in AUC, one a 10% decrease, and four <6% change; conclusion was possible acetaminophen accumulation after repeated therapeutic doses in febrile children, not hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen hepatotoxicity after acute overdose is well documented in the literature, with more severe signs including hepatic damage. In the reported case a 28-year-old man intentionally ingested up to 250 g of acetaminophen (500-mg tablets) plus an unknown quantity of ibuprofen and developed acute renal and fulminant liver failure; his admission acetaminophen level was 316 µg/ml and liver tests were markedly elevated (AST 3993 U/L, ALT 5731 U/L, INR 5.3), and he underwent liver transplantation on hospital day 3.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Co-ingestion of an unknown quantity of ibuprofen during the intentional overdose; patient had schizophrenia.
raw_record.extra_details: Intentional overdose of up to 250 g of acetaminophen (500-mg tablets); admission acetaminophen level 316 µg/ml (critical value > 40 µg/ml); treated with IV acetylcysteine; acute renal and fulminant liver failure; AST 3993 U/L, ALT 5731 U/L, total bilirubin 2.5 mg/dl, INR 5.3, pH 6.9, lactic acid 13.7 mEq/L; liver transplantation on day 3 with necrotic bowel found at surgery; rhabdomyolysis was a rare co-occurrence and the Naranjo scale indicated a probable acetaminophen-overdose-associated reaction for rhabdomyolysis; the literature does not clearly associate acetaminophen with rhabdomyolysis because of other possible causes.

raw_record.support_text: A 48-year-old female presented with clouded consciousness and weakness after seven days of flu symptoms; she had been taking paracetamol, over-the-counter flu remedies and a relative's Tylex capsules. She was diagnosed with hepato-renal failure secondary to paracetamol overdose, with ALT >10,000, bilirubin 121 micromol/l, INR 6.0 and a low paracetamol level (0.1 mmol/l). Despite resuscitation she died within two hours of admission to ICU; the cause of death was fulminant hepatic failure secondary to inadvertent paracetamol overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Inadvertent paracetamol overdose in a setting of self-medication during flu, with concurrent over-the-counter flu remedies and a relative's Tylex capsules (which also contain paracetamol); hepato-renal failure and fulminant hepatic failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Comorbid decompensation: jaundice, dehydration, rigid abdomen, metabolic acidosis (pH 7.15), hypoglycemia (glucose 0.5 mmol/l), renal impairment (creatinine 251 micromol/l), coagulopathy (INR 6.0, prothrombin time 62.3 s); paracetamol level 0.1 mmol/l; death occurred within two hours of ICU admission. Discussion frames this as danger of self-medication with commonly available over-the-counter drugs.

raw_record.support_text: The study analyzes 198 APAP-ALF (acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure) patients, comparing survivors and non-survivors on study admission. APAP-ALF survivors had significantly lower serum INR (2.7 vs. 3.4), bilirubin (4.1 vs. 5.0 mg/dl), creatinine (1.4 vs. 2.6 mg/dl), lactate (2.8 vs. 7.0 mmol/L) and MELD scores (23 vs. 29) than non-survivors. Among the 99 APAP-ALF non-survivors, the most common causes of death were multiorgan failure (52%) and neurological complications (39%).
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective registry cohort of 198 acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure (APAP-ALF) patients; 99 non-survivors. Causes of death reported as multiorgan failure (52%) and neurological complications (39%), unknown in 9%. Comparisons of admission and day 3-5 (late) clinical parameters; 7% of APAP-ALF survivors and 16% of non-survivors met the King's College Criteria on admission. Admission serum FABP1 levels (238.6 vs 690.8 ng/ml) and ALT were lower in survivors than non-survivors (p<0.0001).

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 16 patients in grade 3 or 4 hepatic coma intubated and mechanically ventilated (mean age 38, range 16-67), admission diagnoses included acetaminophen overdose (5 of 16), viral hepatitis (3), macrodantin (1), postpartum hepatitis (1), halothane (1), and undetermined (5). Acetaminophen overdose is therefore attributed as the cause of fulminant hepatic failure with coma and intracranial hypertension in these patients.
raw_record.extra_details: 5 of 16 patients admitted with acetaminophen overdose as the cause of hepatic coma; all study subjects were in grade 3 or 4 hepatic coma, intubated and mechanically ventilated, managed with ICP monitoring and transcranial Doppler (TCD) cerebral blood flow velocity measurements. Paper is a physiological/ICP study, not a DILI report; exposure context is overdose.

raw_record.support_text: The single-center study of acute liver failure patients classified them into four cohorts by etiology (Acetaminophen overdose or non-acetaminophen-overdose-related acute liver failure) and management strategy (conservative or liver transplantation), and compared long-term outcomes among the cohorts.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen (APAP) overdose was used as the etiologic category for acute liver failure (ALF) patients in a consecutive single-center cohort of 200 ALF patients (1990-2014); 124/200 (62%) were early survivors, of whom 124 were acetaminophen or non-acetaminophen categorized by outcome (APAP ELT, APAP SS, nAPAP ELT, nAPAP SS).

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 887 acute liver failure (ALF) patients, 618 had ALF following acetaminophen overdose compared with 269 with other etiologies; the two groups were comparable with respect to incidence of SIRS on admission (51.6% vs 54%), any confirmed infection (43.6% vs 37.9%), fungal infection (12% vs 9.3%), and mortality (46% vs 40%), and mortality increased with increasing maximum number of concurrent SIRS components in both groups.
raw_record.extra_details: In the described cohort of 887 acute liver failure patients, 618 (70%) had ALF following acetaminophen overdose vs 269 from other etiologies; mortality in the acetaminophen overdose group was 46% (vs 40%, P=.110), and mortality rose with increasing maximum number of concurrent SIRS components during admission.

raw_record.support_text: In a single-center cohort of 50 consecutively recruited patients with severe acute liver injury (78% with hepatic encephalopathy), the stated etiology of acute liver failure was acetaminophen overdose in 50% of patients. Platelet-poor plasma and other laboratory parameters were collected on admission and at day 3/4, and microparticles were detected by ISADE and flow cytometry.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose was reported as the etiology of ALF in 50% of 50 patients with severe acute liver injury; 78% had hepatic encephalopathy. Cohort outcomes: 16/50 (32%) died, 27/50 (54%) recovered without liver transplantation. The paper's focus is circulating microparticles in ALI/ALF; platelet count reduction after admission correlated with poor outcome (higher ammonia, lower pH/bicarbonate, higher lactate and phosphate), SIRS, progression to higher-grade HE, and death or liver transplantation. Admission microparticle concentrations (0.36-0.64 µm) correlated with laboratory predictors of poor outcome, and microparticle levels were higher in those who underwent liver transplantation or died (2.1E8/mL) vs. spontaneous recovery (4.5E7/mL; P=0.0001).

raw_record.support_text: In the study cohort of 34 patients with acute liver failure (ALF) admitted to the ICU, the most common cause of ALF was severe protracted ischaemia (n = 11), paracetamol intoxication (8 patients), and cocaine (1 patient), explicitly attributing paracetamol intoxication as a cause of human acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol intoxication was the cause of ALF in 8 of 34 enrolled patients; ALF defined as transaminases >1,000 IU/l within 48 h of onset and INR >2. Cohort medical histories also recorded addictions to alcohol, cannabis, methadone, heroin and cocaine.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (APAP), commonly used as an analgesic and antipyretic, is easily obtained over the counter. The paper states that easy access to this drug in the United States alone resulted in more than 100,000 APAP intoxication cases due to intentional or accidental intake, and about 500 fatal cases caused by acute liver failure are reported annually. N-acetylcysteine is noted as the current treatment for APAP-induced liver injury, but with a narrow therapeutic window.
raw_record.extra_details: Overdose setting from intentional or accidental intake (annual US population statistics): >100,000 APAP intoxication cases and ~500 fatal cases per year due to acute liver failure. Clinical phenotype is acute liver failure. Mechanism described: hepatotoxicity mediated by the metabolite NAPQI, which depletes glutathione then binds intracellular proteins causing dysfunction. The paper's primary experiments are a mouse (IL-1ra KO) model of APAP-induced liver injury, which are not themselves human-relevant; only this human population claim is extracted.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that at therapeutic doses most acetaminophen is conjugated to non-toxic metabolites, but in overdose the glucuronidation and sulfation pathways become saturated, increasing CYP450 (primarily CYP2E1) metabolism to NAPQI, a toxic metabolite. This metabolite is responsible for hepatocyte necrosis and, in severe cases, liver failure, with plasma acetaminophen concentration typically correlating with dose-dependent toxicity. The paper refers to 'acetaminophen-induced acute liver injury'. In the studied cohort none of the patients developed hepatic encephalopathy, were scheduled for liver transplantation, or died.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose cohort (103 patients) considered at low risk of hepatotoxicity based on the Rumack–Matthew nomogram; median serum acetaminophen at ED presentation 42 (4.5–64.8) µg/ml. Mean ingested dose 8759.71 mg (NAC-treated) vs 5617.25 mg (no NAC). None developed hepatic encephalopathy, required liver transplantation, or died. Pathogenesis: NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine) formed via CYP2E1 after saturation of glucuronidation/sulfation; hepatocyte necrosis and, in severe cases, liver failure; dose-dependent toxicity. Acetylcysteine (NAC) used as treatment.

raw_record.support_text: A 21-year-old woman was admitted with hepatic failure caused by acetaminophen overdose and was declared brain dead 46 hr after admission, after which her organs (heart, lungs, pancreas, kidneys) were retrieved for transplantation. The paper frames the hepatic failure as caused by the acetaminophen overdose in this human patient.
raw_record.extra_details: 21-year-old previously healthy woman with hepatic failure after acetaminophen overdose, declared brain dead 46 hr after admission and used as a deceased organ donor (kidneys transplanted into two male recipients, 47 and 62 years old). Paper also notes approximately 250 deaths in the United States in 2006 caused by overdose of acetaminophen alone or in combination with other drugs, and that these patients are usually young and relatively healthy.

raw_record.support_text: During the study period, 1191 patients presented to hospital after paracetamol overdose; after excluding 106 without baseline urea measurement, the study population was 1085 patients (714 women, median age 33 years). N-acetylcysteine was given to 390 patients (35.9%), and the overall incidence of hepatotoxicity after paracetamol overdose was 5.4%. Hepatotoxicity was defined by prothrombin time ratio >1.3 or alanine transaminase ≥1000 U/l.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective observational cohort of 1085 paracetamol-overdose patients (714 women, median age 33 y). Stated ingested dose 11.0 g (IQR 6.5-17.5 g), median interval ingestion-to-presentation 4.5 h (IQR 4.0-6.7 h). Hepatotoxicity defined as prothrombin time ratio >1.3 or ALT ≥1000 U/l; overall incidence 5.4%. N-acetylcysteine administered to 390 patients (35.9%). 394 patients (36.3%) were at high risk due to chronic alcohol excess (340), malnutrition (40), or enzyme-inducing drugs (14). Baseline serum urea concentration did not independently predict hepatotoxicity in multiple regression; explanatory variables were acute ethanol co-ingestion (inverse), above-normal treatment line, interval, serum paracetamol concentration, equivalent 4 h concentration, male and vomiting (R2=0.173).

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective analysis of 42,781 U.S. hospital admissions for acetaminophen overdose (AO) drawn from the Nationwide Inpatient Sample (1998-2005), the rate of acute liver injury (ALI) was 7.2%. ALI following AO is a well-recognized adverse event, and acetaminophen poisoning is implicated in almost 50% of cases in the US Acute Liver Failure Study Group registry of more than 700 patients. In this cohort, patients with ALI had an overall mortality of 8.6%, and 8% of those who develop ALI may require liver transplantation; mortality is approximately 30% in those developing encephalopathy without transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose is the leading cause of toxic drug ingestions in the US, causing well-recognized acute liver injury. ALI was defined by ICD-9-CM codes 570.0 (acute necrosis), 572.2, 573.3. Among AO admissions, risk of ALI increased with coexistent hepatitis C (aOR 1.80; 95% CI 1.30-2.48), nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (aOR 7.43; 95% CI 3.30-16.7), alcoholic liver disease (aOR 6.46; 95% CI 4.53-9.21), and malnutrition (aOR 3.84; 95% CI 2.61-5.65), after excluding patients with cirrhosis. HCV was associated with greater risk of progression to severe liver failure (aOR 3.55; 95% CI 1.88-6.70). ALI mortality overall was 8.6%; about 8% of ALI patients may need liver transplant; ALF mortality is ~30% without transplant in those with encephalopathy. Risk factors noted include chronic alcohol use, narcotic co-use, multiple acetaminophen products, and drugs such as isoniazid (CYP2E1 induction) or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and zidovudine (glucuronidation competition); time from overdose to N-acetylcysteine is the most important prognostic factor. Authors concluded findings warrant prospective confirmation.

raw_record.support_text: This study is the first to document elevated efflux transporter expression in acute liver failure after ingestion of toxic doses of acetaminophen (APAP). The results demonstrate that mRNA and protein levels of hepatocellular efflux transporters (MRP4, MRP5, P-gp, BCRP) increase during APAP-induced acute liver failure after APAP overdose. The authors state these transporter changes may prevent hepatocyte retention of drug metabolites and mediators of injury generated during drug-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver specimens from APAP overdose patients showing acute liver failure and centrilobular cell loss; study compared APAP overdose and primary biliary cholangitis livers, documenting increased protein/mRNA expression of sinusoidal (MRP4, MRP5) and canalicular (BCRP, P-gp) efflux transporters as a response to toxic drug exposure; no significant change in MRP6 or MRP2 expression.

raw_record.support_text: APAP (acetaminophen) overdose is described as a major clinical problem in the U.S. and U.K.; although most patients with APAP-induced liver injury survive, APAP still accounts for the largest number of acute liver failure-related deaths in the U.S. The paper discusses APAP hepatotoxicity in humans, noting that the primary mode of cell death is oncotic necrosis and evaluating ASS as a biomarker of APAP-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective study of APAP overdose patients grouped by liver function: the Abnormal LT group (peak ALT >1000 U/L, peak PT >18 s) showed plasma ASS of 2027±369 ng/mL versus 1.4±0.9 ng/mL (Normal LT) and 0.4±0.3 ng/mL (healthy volunteers). In humans ASS increased >5000-fold over control versus 156-fold for ALT. ASS appeared to rise and plateau faster than ALT in at least two patients and decreased before ALT in all patients; the small patient cohort precluded correlation with death, survival, or transplant outcome. Mechanistic discussion covers mitochondrial damage, oncotic necrosis, APAP-protein adducts, and liver vs kidney ASS expression (liver ~5-fold higher per mg protein in rats, ~7-fold in humans).

raw_record.support_text: The case report presents a patient with hepatotoxicity and subsequent acute liver failure attributed to acetaminophen overdose, characterized by very delayed absorption and a peak acetaminophen concentration, with two earlier acetaminophen concentrations well below the acetaminophen treatment nomogram line. The cause of liver injury is explicitly assigned to the ingested acetaminophen in an overdose (supratherapeutic) context.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case (overdose of over-the-counter acetaminophen capsules). Patient had a history of chronic alcohol use and an eating disorder, with very delayed drug absorption and peak concentration; two initial concentrations were below the 150 mg/L at 4 hours treatment nomogram line. Acetaminophen metabolite analysis showed nontoxic glucuronide (68%, AUC 8663 μmol/L*hr) and sulfate (22%, AUC 2733 μmol/L*hr) conjugates, and CYP-derived metabolites APAP-Cys and APAP-Mer combined accounting for 10% (AUC 1254 μmol/L*hr). The tablets ingested were a fixed-combination cold/flu product containing acetaminophen, dextromethorphan, and chlorphenamine, but causality was assigned to acetaminophen, not the combination. Metabolite concentrations measured by LC-MS/MS.

raw_record.support_text: Two patients with grade 4 hepatic encephalopathy from acute liver failure due to paracetamol poisoning, treated in the department, became anuric. Both received charcoal haemoperfusion, peritoneal dialysis (and haemodialysis in one case); neither recovered consciousness until liver function recovered, and oliguria lasted 6 weeks before kidney function returned.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients with paracetamol poisoning developed acute liver failure with grade 4 hepatic encephalopathy and anuric episodes; both required charcoal haemoperfusion and peritoneal dialysis (one also haemodialysis), with oliguria lasting 6 weeks before kidney function recovered.

raw_record.support_text: The paper studies CypA/CD147 as mediators of acetaminophen hepatotoxicity. In humans, urinary cyclophilin A (CypA) concentration was significantly elevated in patients with acetaminophen-induced liver injury (the organ-injury group) compared with three other patient groups, both as mass/14 μl of urine and normalized to urinary creatinine. Patients in this group are described as having acetaminophen poisoning, supporting an explicit human DILI relationship for acetaminophen.
raw_record.extra_details: Primary focus is mechanistic: CypA/CD147 signaling mediates acetaminophen toxicity. Acetaminophen injection (350 mg/kg i.p.) in mice increased serum ALT 24 h post-injection and produced liver cell vacuolation and necrosis, more severe in WT than Ppia-/- mice; six of 50 WT mice died within 24 h. In humans, urinary (not blood) CypA was elevated with acetaminophen-induced liver injury, present in both soluble and exosomal urine fractions.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 69 acute liver failure (ALF) patients, 26 were diagnosed with APAP (acetaminophen) poisoning, and the paper states that APAP overdose is the most frequent cause of ALF. The paper also notes APAP toxicity involves a major oxidant component generating reactive oxygen species, with glutathione and CYP2E1 noted as risk factors in this toxic liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 26 of 69 ALF patients had APAP poisoning as their diagnosis. APAP overdose is described as the most frequent cause of acute liver failure. AMA (antimitochondrial antibodies) were found in sera of almost 35% of APAP poisoning subjects (9/26). APAP toxicity involves an oxidant component generating reactive oxygen species; decreased glutathione and CYP2E1 were noted as risk factors in toxic liver injury and both play roles in APAP metabolism.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective analysis of 16 acetaminophen overdose cases, patients were classified into two groups of eight potentially enzyme-induced and eight noninduced patients. Those in the induced group had statistically significantly greater elevations of SGOT, hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase, and bilirubin; two patients died in hepatic coma, and acute tubular necrosis developed in three patients, all being from the induced group. This attributes dose-related acetaminophen hepatotoxicity to overdose exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: 16 overdose cases; retrospective analysis of Wright and Prescott; potentiating role of induced hepatic microsomal enzymes studied; induced group showed significantly greater elevations of SGOT, hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase, and bilirubin; two deaths in hepatic coma and three cases of acute tubular necrosis, all in the induced group.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity following acetaminophen (APAP) overdose is explained by metabolism of APAP by cytochrome P450 enzymes to N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), an electrophile that covalently binds to intracellular proteins, most commonly to cysteine residues, to form APAP-protein adducts. There exists strong support for NAPQI's binding to mitochondrial proteins as being essential for subsequent development of hepatocellular necrosis in animals and man.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP overdose hepatotoxicity is explained by P450-mediated metabolism to NAPQI, which covalently binds cysteine residues forming APAP-protein adducts; NAPQI binding to mitochondrial proteins is considered essential for subsequent hepatocellular necrosis. The study measured serum APAP-CYS (3-cysteinyl-acetaminophen) adducts and ALT in 500 patients with suspected APAP toxicity, classified into definite APAP (N=335, 908 samples), definitely not APAP (N=79, 231 samples), and indeterminate groups. In the definite APAP group, APAP-CYS strongly correlated with ALT over all activities (r=0.93, p<0.001) and when ALT>1000 IU/L (r=0.82, p<0.001, N=144); all definitely not APAP subjects had APAP-CYS <3 µM; non-toxic APAP ingestions in the definitely not APAP group could yield APAP-CYS up to 2.8 µM during ALT elevation from ischemic hepatitis. Background notes: therapeutic, non-hepatotoxic APAP doses give APAP-CYS below about 1.1 µM, and serum APAP-CYS >1.1 µM has been reported to correlate with ALT >1000 IU/L in APAP overdose.

raw_record.support_text: Among 103 patients admitted with fulminant hepatic failure, the cause of their liver damage was paracetamol overdose in 57 patients. This consecutively admitted cohort at the Liver Unit included patients with fulminant hepatic failure, and 22 of the paracetamol-overdose patients recovered.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol overdose was the cause of liver damage in 57 of 103 patients admitted to the Liver Unit with fulminant hepatic failure; 22 of these recovered. Recorded as the aetiology of the hepatic necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: Retrospective analysis of 267 acute liver failure (ALF) patients in Spain (1992-2000) from 17 tertiary-care hospitals. Causes of ALF were viral hepatitis in 98 (37%), unknown in 86 (32%), drug or toxic reactions in 52 (19.5%; including 6 acetaminophen overdose cases), and miscellaneous in 31. The paper states that acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose is a leading cause of ALF in some developed countries (e.g., US, UK) but is a very rare cause in Spain.
raw_record.extra_details: In the Spanish cohort, 6 of 52 drug/toxic-reaction ALF cases (drug or toxic reactions accounted for 19.5% of 267 cases) were attributed to acetaminophen overdose, making it a very rare cause of ALF in Spain. Acetaminophen accounts for 20-75% of ALF cases in the US and UK, whereas in Spain suicide attempts by acetaminophen are anecdotal because the drug is not available over the counter.

raw_record.support_text: Twenty patients with definite acetaminophen toxicity causing acute liver failure were studied in the U.S. ALF Study Group cohort, each confirmed to have had rapid-onset disease typical of acetaminophen-induced injury. The site criteria required history of ingestion exceeding package labeling (>4 g/24 hours, in most cases greatly exceeded) within 7 days, detection of acetaminophen in plasma, and/or ALT ≥3500 IU/L. The paper describes acetaminophen-protein (NAPQI-derived) adduct formation as the initial irreversible step in development of hepatic toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen causes ALF via covalent NAPQI binding to hepatocyte cysteine proteins after glutathione depletion; mechanism mediated by CYP2E1 (CYP450). In 20 acetaminophen-related ALF cases: 85% had history of excessive ingestion, 15 ingested >10 g (median ingestion 21 g; group median 24 g), 75% had detectable plasma acetaminophen, 85% had ALT >3500 IU/L; median ALT 5640 IU/L, AST 4404 IU/L, bilirubin 5.0 mg/dl, INR 3.2, adduct concentration 1.17 nmol acetaminophen-CYS/mg protein; 10% transplanted, 85% alive. 15 patients with intentional overdose but minimal liver injury (median peak ALT 26 IU/L) recovered; 8 judged at toxicity risk by Rumack nomogram, median APAP 108 mg/dL at presentation.

raw_record.support_text: The paper's final diagnosis for a 52-year-old male patient was fatal hepatic failure after an acetaminophen overdose, reported under the specialty of Gastroenterology and Hepatology.
raw_record.extra_details: 52-year-old male patient; outcome was fatal hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol-induced ALF is rare in Finland compared to other Western countries; only three patients had been transplanted due to pure paracetamol (paracetamol) intoxication by 2009 among over 800 transplants. The aetiological profile of transplanted ALF patients is changing towards toxic liver injury, with paracetamol cited as a specific toxic aetiology causing acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients transplanted due to pure paracetamol intoxication in Finland by 2009 among over 800 transplants; paracetamol-induced acute liver failure described as rare in Finland compared to other Western countries. Reported in the context of the Finnish liver transplantation and MARS treatment experience.

raw_record.support_text: In patients with acute liver failure (IHA) of unknown cause, analysis of serum samples from 113 patients detected acetaminophen (paracetamol) protein adducts above a toxic cutoff of 1 nmol/ml in 20 (18%) patients, confirming that acetaminophen intoxication accounts for nearly 18% of IHA cases. These patients had a clinical profile similar to paracetamol overdose (female predominance, very high aminotransferase values, favorable course), and N-acetylcysteine appeared to increase survival (from 42% to 75%).
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen protein-adduct analysis in serum of 113 patients with acute liver failure of unknown cause; toxic-adduct cutoff of 1 nmol/ml found in 20 (18%) patients. Clinical profile resembled paracetamol overdose: female predominance, very high aminotransferases, favorable course. N-acetylcysteine appeared to increase survival from 42% to 75%. Authors recommend N-acetylcysteine when adduct testing is unavailable and the biochemical profile is compatible.

raw_record.support_text: In this cohort of patients with APAP (acetaminophen) overdose, hepatic injury was evident in only one patient (1.5%) treated within 15 hours of ingestion compared to 8 (88%) of 9 patients treated 16 to 24 hours after APAP ingestion. Three patients had a peak ALT level above 1000 U/L, and all began treatment more than 16 hours after APAP ingestion. None of the patients treated within 10 hours showed evidence of hepatic necrosis as manifested by a 3-fold increase in transaminases.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP (acetaminophen) overdose cohort of 74 patients; hepatic necrosis defined as a 3-fold increase in transaminases. First dose of N-acetylcysteine was administered within 8.9 ± 6 hours of ingestion (median 7 h; IQR 5-12). Patients treated within 10 hours showed no hepatic necrosis; peak ALT >1000 U/L occurred in 3 patients, all treated more than 16 hours after ingestion. Early high anion gap metabolic acidosis (EHAGMA) occurred in 30 (41%) patients with isolated APAP ingestions, in the presence of normal transaminases, bilirubin, and coagulation tests, suggesting it was not related to direct hepatocellular necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: In data from the International MARS Registry, 38 adult patients with fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) were analyzed; 80% (n=5) of those with acetaminophen overdose recovered without emergency liver transplantation, while overall FHF survival was 50% (19 patients). The registry describes FHF as resulting from acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose in these patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure (acute liver failure) attributed to acetaminophen/paracetamol overdose. In the International MARS Registry (37 hospitals, Europe and Asia), 5 acetaminophen-overdose patients among 38 adult FHF patients, of whom 80% (n=5) recovered without emergency liver transplantation. Also noted that MARS has been used to treat or bridge patients with FHF due to paracetamol overdose and other acute drug intoxications. Mean MARS sessions 4 ± 2.9 (range 1-12), mean duration 11 hrs (range 3-48 hrs).

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity is described as an uncommon consequence of acetaminophen overdose, with a minimum absorbed dose of approximately 125 mg/kg (about 7.5 g in a 60-kg adult) likely needed to produce hepatic damage, and a threshold of approximately 250 mg/kg for significant hepatic damage. Additional analyses after pack-size restrictions showed reduced overdose doses (median 8 g), lower serum acetaminophen levels on admission, and fewer patients requiring the antidote N-acetylcysteine, while deaths related to acetaminophen alone declined with no increase in deaths from acetaminophen combined with other drugs or alcohol.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity framed as dose-dependent hepatic damage in overdose; minimum absorbed dose for hepatic damage ~125 mg/kg (approx 7.5 g in 60-kg adult); threshold for significant hepatic damage ~250 mg/kg. Analyses of ~1200 overdose patients (Northern Ireland) and >4500 patients (southern England) after pack-size restriction showed reduced consumed dose (median 8 g), lower serum acetaminophen levels on admission, fewer patients requiring N-acetylcysteine antidote, and a 7% reduction in average tablets consumed with a 17% reduction in patients consuming >16 g. Hospital admissions with acetaminophen poisoning as a main diagnosis fell 16% (30,918 to 26,096), while subsidiary-diagnosis admissions rose 16% (7250 to 8385); deaths related to acetaminophen alone declined since September 1998 with no increase in deaths from acetaminophen combined with other drugs or alcohol.

raw_record.support_text: The ALFSG registry included 2149 acute liver failure (ALF) patients, of whom 1951 had known 21-day outcomes: 910 (46.6%) with APAP (acetaminophen)-ALF and 1041 (53.4%) with a non-APAP etiology. The 910 APAP-ALF patients are described as a distinct acetaminophen-attributed acute liver failure cohort, with 801 having psychiatric comorbidity, indicating acetaminophen is established as the cause of this acute liver failure in the registry.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP-ALF cohort of 910 patients from the ALFSG registry with known 21-day outcomes (46.6% of 1951). Presenting ALT mean 3836 IU/L (psychiatric comorbidity) vs 2672 IU/L (without); 54.7% vs 51.0% advanced hepatic encephalopathy; ~90% received NAC; 25.8% of psychiatric-comorbidity group and 23.9% without psychiatric comorbidity died; ~20-24% were listed for transplantation; 33.7% vs 38.5% transplanted. Cohort predominantly female and Caucasian. Phenotype clinically characterized as acute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: In a 3-year series of 73 patients treated for fulminant liver failure (defined as encephalopathy within 8 weeks of symptom onset), the aetiology of liver disease was listed as paracetamol overdose in 33 cases, viral in 26, Budd-Chiari syndrome in 5, drug toxicity in 4, malignant infiltration in 3, pre-eclampsia in 1 and ischaemia in 1. Paracetamol overdose is thereby attributed as the cause of fulminant hepatic failure in these patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol overdose accounted for 33 of 73 patients with fulminant liver failure in a hepatic transplantation referral series; fulminant hepatic failure defined as development of encephalopathy within 8 weeks of symptom onset. Among the 73 patients (26 male, 47 female, median age 33 years), 19 had grade I/II and 54 grade III/IV encephalopathy.

raw_record.support_text: Among the 55 patients with acute liver failure evaluated as candidates for emergency liver transplantation and classified into four study groups, the largest diagnostic categories listed included drug-induced hepatitis (n=12), acetaminophen intoxication (n=11), and acute liver failure of unknown etiology (n=19). This records that 11 patients' acute liver failure was attributed to acetaminophen intoxication.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 patients were diagnosed with acetaminophen intoxication among acute liver failure candidates for emergency liver transplantation; the diagnostic listing also included drug-induced hepatitis (n=12) but no specific causal agent was named for that category.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 55 patients with fulminant hepatic failure who had deteriorated to grade IV hepatic encephalopathy, hepatic necrosis was attributed to paracetamol self-poisoning in 32 patients. The summary additionally reports that circulating immune complexes were found in only five of 32 patients with paracetamol-induced hepatic necrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic necrosis attributed to paracetamol self-poisoning in 32 of 55 patients with fulminant hepatic failure, all having deteriorated to grade IV hepatic encephalopathy; circulating immune complexes (Clq binding assay) were found in only 5 of these 32 patients, not related to severity, renal failure, outcome, or hypocomplementaemia.

raw_record.support_text: By 1971 Prescott published a series of case reports of 30 patients in the Lancet with serial plasma paracetamol measurements, demonstrating that the higher the plasma paracetamol concentration, the greater the risk of liver injury (defined as a rise in serum ALT above 1000 IU/L), and that the plasma half-life was far slower in those with liver injury. These data were the original basis for treatment nomograms.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver injury defined as rise in serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) above 1000 IU/L; dose/concentration-dependent risk. Retrospective data suggested 60% of patients presenting after 4 h above the 200 mg line had a rise in ALT above 1000, rising to over 90% in those presenting later. Paracetamol clearance (plasma half-life) was far slower in patients with liver injury. These Edinburgh data were the original basis for treatment nomograms. Concerns over paracetamol liver effects in overdose dated from 1966 reports from the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh.

raw_record.support_text: In a Swedish 10-year (1994-2003) cohort of 279 patients admitted with acute liver failure (ALF), acetaminophen toxicity was the most common cause, accounting for 118 of 279 cases (42%). The median ingested dosage was 17 g/day (IQR 10-31 g/day), and 115 of 118 patients (97%) had ingested more than 4 g/day. The intoxication was considered suicidal in 58 patients, unintentional in 31, and undetermined in 29.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver failure (ALF) attributed to acetaminophen overdose toxicity; median dose 17 g/day (IQR 10-31 g/day), 97% of cases >4 g/day (maximum package recommendation); suicidal ingestion in 58, unintentional in 31, undetermined in 29; 95% of patients treated with acetylcysteine.

raw_record.support_text: In this consecutive case series (Denmark 1987-1990) of adult patients with acute liver failure treated with high-volume plasma exchange, acetaminophen was attributed as the cause of liver failure based on a history of intake and plasma drug levels. One patient had not received antidote, four had received intravenous N-acetylcysteine more than 24 h after overdosage, and one had received oral L-methionine about 12 h after overdosage.
raw_record.extra_details: Patients presented with acute liver failure in stage 3-4 encephalopathy (Fogarty criteria). Overdose context: one case without antidote, four received intravenous N-acetylcysteine >24h after overdosage, one received oral L-methionine ~12h after overdosage. Study of plasma exchange therapy in fulminant hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: Data from the European Liver Transplant Registry (ELTR) in 4903 adult patients (>16 years) transplanted for acute liver failure show that paracetamol overdose represented merely 12% of the indications. Transplantation for paracetamol-induced acute liver failure increased seven-fold from 2% (1973-1978) to 14.1% (2004-2008).
raw_record.extra_details: Based on ELTR data of 4903 adult patients transplanted for acute liver failure; paracetamol overdose comprised 12% of transplant indications and transplantations for paracetamol-induced ALF rose from 2% (1973-1978) to 14.1% (2004-2008).

raw_record.support_text: The clinical scenario involves a 23-year-old female patient undergoing general anesthesia for liver transplantation due to acute liver failure after paracetamol (acetaminophen) intoxication. The vignette attributes the acute liver failure to the paracetamol overdose in a human patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen is a synonym. The patient was a 23-year-old female whose paracetamol intoxication produced acute liver failure severe enough to require liver transplantation under general anesthesia; subsequent questions addressed intraoperative monitoring and early extubation considerations.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) due to paracetamol overdose, where the patient developed grade IV encephalopathy and severe cerebral oedema. It states that of patients who progress to stage IV coma after a paracetamol overdose, 30-50% will die despite best medical therapy, and that early N-acetylcysteine reduces progression to grade III/IV encephalopathy. The case describes FHF as a consequence of a paracetamol overdose that required liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report: a 20-yr-old female who took 100 g of paracetamol presented with fulminant hepatic failure, acidosis, prolonged prothrombin time (>180 s) and rising creatinine, progressing through grade I to IV hepatic encephalopathy. Despite N-acetylcysteine administration she progressed and required urgent liver transplantation; hypothermia (34°C) was used to manage severely raised intracranial pressure before and after transplantation. Reported outcome includes fulminant hepatic failure with liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of 14 patients with acute liver failure (ALF) requiring ICP monitoring, the most common etiology of ALF was acetaminophen toxicity (n=6, 42.8%), followed by ALF of unknown etiology (n=3). The patient table lists additional cases of ALF attributed to acetaminophen toxicity (patients 3, 4, 10, 11, 12), drug toxicity, hepatitis 2/2 Herpes type 2, HELLP syndrome, and Wilson's disease, with markedly elevated ALT/AST and INR on admission.
raw_record.extra_details: Etiology of ALF in 6 of 14 patients (42.8%) with acute liver failure requiring intracranial pressure monitoring; patients 3, 4, 10, 11, 12, 13 are recorded with acetaminophen toxicity as liver-failure etiology, with admission ALT up to 15,018 IU/L, AST up to 18,970 IU/L, and INR up to 7.3; all patients received invasive ICP monitoring, 11 of 14 had elevated ICP, and multiple received liver transplant.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that tylenol (acetaminophen, APAP) toxicity is the most common indication for liver transplantation in the US and frequently develops with consumption of at least 7.5–10 g/day. Its metabolite NAPQI is described as a hepatic toxin that injures mitochondrial proteins, impairing ATP synthesis, leading to hepatocellular necrosis and ultimately liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Case: 18-year-old male who ingested 125 g of tylenol; 4-hour acetaminophen level 738.6 µg/mL, remained 730 µg/mL after a single 4-hour hemodialysis session. Treated with NAC, fomepizole, and CVVH; tylenol became undetectable 57 hours after ingestion and the patient did not develop permanent liver toxicity. Massive poisoning defined as ≥50 g APAP or APAP level >300 µg/mL at ≥4 h. NAPQI (metabolite) described mechanistically as causing mitochondrial injury, hepatocellular necrosis, and liver failure. Paper notes APAP toxicity is the most common indication for liver transplantation in the US.

raw_record.support_text: One hundred cases of severe paracetamol poisoning were treated with intravenous N-acetylcysteine. There was virtually complete protection against liver damage in 40 patients treated within eight hours after ingestion (mean maximum serum alanine transaminase activity 27 IU/l). Only one out of 62 patients treated within 10 hours developed severe liver damage compared with 33 out of 57 patients (58%) studied retrospectively who received supportive treatment alone. Early treatment with acetylcysteine also prevented renal impairment and death, and treatment after 15 hours was completely ineffective, establishing that paracetamol overdose causes clinically severe, dose-dependent liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe paracetamol poisoning (plasma paracetamol above a treatment line joining 200 mg/l at 4 h and 30 mg/l at 15 h; 'high-risk' cases above 300 mg/l at 4 h / 45 mg/l at 15 h). Without acetylcysteine, 33/57 (58%) developed severe liver damage; treatment within 10 h reduced this to 1/62 and protected against renal impairment and death, while treatment after 15 h was ineffective. Mean age 33 y (range 13-82); some patients also took dextropropoxyphene (Distalgesic), benzodiazepines, or aspirin. Mechanism described as paracetamol hepatotoxicity attributable to reactive-metabolite formation and sulphydryl (glutathione) depletion, treatable with sulphydryl compounds.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol is described as one of the main causes of acute hepatitis and as a prototype of dose-dependent drug-induced hepatotoxicity leading to acute liver failure. The dose required to produce significant hepatic injury is generally 10 g in 24 hours or 150 mg/kg; symptoms appear within 24-48 hours as pure acute cytolytic hepatitis without inflammatory histology, and the higher the dose the more constant and severe the liver injury. A 3-year prospective US survey of more than 300 patients attributed 39% of severe hepatitis cases potentially leading to liver transplantation to paracetamol, far ahead of all other drugs (13%) and acute viral hepatitis A and B (12%). Spontaneous mortality risk in paracetamol-induced severe hepatitis is estimated at about 50%, versus 80-90% for other drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: Significant injury threshold ~10 g/24 h or 150 mg/kg; onset 24-48 h; pure cytolytic acute hepatitis, histologically a 'chemical hepatectomy' with hepatocyte necrosis; hepatotoxic potential after overdose predicted by Rumack-Matthew nomogram of plasma paracetamol vs time; therapeutic plasma paracetamol 10-30 µg/mL. US 3-year prospective survey (>300 patients): paracetamol 39% of severe hepatitis possibly leading to liver transplant vs other drugs 13% and HAV/HBV 12%. Spontaneous mortality ~50% in paracetamol-induced severe hepatitis vs 80-90% with other drugs. Paracetamol is also a major suicidal agent in Anglo-Saxon countries. Mechanism: predominant CYP2E1-mediated (inducible by chronic alcohol), with CYP3A4 and CYP1A/2B families, conversion of <5% of metabolism to reactive NAPBQI normally detoxified by glutathione; excess metabolite covalently binds cell molecules causing hepatocyte necrosis; additional mechanisms include oxidative stress/ROS, lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial alterations, apoptosis, and JNK involvement. Toxicity can also appear below the 10 g/24 h threshold toward the 4 g therapeutic limit when predisposed, e.g., glutathione depletion from prolonged fasting/malnutrition or CYP2E1 induction.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective study of 18 patients (aged 20–70) in hepatic coma grade III–IV, 6 had fulminant toxic hepatitis confirmed by liver biopsy, of which 5 cases were attributed to paracetamol overdose and 1 to an adverse effect of disulfiram; the remaining 12 patients had alcoholic cirrhosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Five of six fulminant toxic hepatitis cases (subjects 9–11, 16–18 as a group) were owing to paracetamol overdose; patients were in hepatic coma grade III–IV and the diagnosis was confirmed by liver biopsy.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective poison-center study of 604 transferred poisoned patients, a reason for inter-facility transfer in 21 (3%) cases was liver transplant evaluation for acetaminophen hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed in the setting of poisoned patients transferred between healthcare facilities; 21 cases required liver transplant evaluation for acetaminophen hepatotoxicity out of 604 transferred cases in the study.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective observational study of approximately 360 patients presenting with acute acetaminophen (APAP) overdose, hepatotoxicity defined as ALT > 1000 U/L or an INR > 1.3 occurred in 15.2% of patients who did not consume alcohol versus 5.1% of those with concurrent acute alcohol ingestion, using the Rumack-Matthew nomogram. The paper describes APAP overdose as causing hepatotoxicity, with chronic alcohol augmenting it by up-regulating CYP 2E1 and decreasing GSH stores, thereby enhancing liver necrosis and worsening prognosis, and notes that chronic alcoholism plus APAP overdose may potentiate liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute acetaminophen overdose hepatotoxicity (ALT > 1000 U/L or INR > 1.3) in ~360 patients; prevalence 15.2% without alcohol vs 5.1% with concurrent acute alcohol ingestion, repeated regardless of time from ingestion to assessment; alcohol co-ingestion may be protective via competitive CYP 2E1 utilization reducing NAPQI formation and possibly by NAD(P)H:quinone reductase activity reconverting quinone metabolites to APAP. Chronic alcohol augments injury via CYP 2E1 upregulation and decreased GSH, enhancing hepatic necrosis, the proposed threshold being blood ethanol > 250 mg/dL (~18+ standard drinks). NAC is the only demonstrated salvage treatment; delayed care prolongs time to NAC.

raw_record.support_text: The study concludes that the increasing size of paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose reported to Australia's largest poisons center is resulting in increasing hospital admissions, need for N-acetylcysteine, and hepatotoxicity, and estimates that approximately 50% of toxic liver disease is due to paracetamol. Over the period 1998-99 to 2014-15, nationwide admissions for toxic liver injury increased 449% (from 65 to 357). The increase in toxic liver injury could not be definitively linked to paracetamol in this analysis.
raw_record.extra_details: Intentional (self-poisoning) overdose. Analysis of 23,772 intentional paracetamol exposure calls to Australia's largest Poisons Information Center, 2004-2017, with an 80% increase in call volume; median number of tablets ingested increased from 15 (IQR 10-24) to 20 (IQR 10-32). Nationwide hospital admissions for paracetamol poisoning increased 51% (4213 to 6372) and average length of stay rose from 2 to 2.7 days, 1998-99 to 2014-15. Admissions for toxic liver injury (ICD-10 K71) increased 449% (65 to 357). Approximately 50% of toxic liver disease estimated to be due to paracetamol; overdose size correlates with risk of hepatotoxicity and need for treatment. Estimated cost of paracetamol admissions was $34 million AUD in 2014-15 versus $17 million in 1998-99. The observed rise in toxic liver injury was noted not to be definitively linkable to paracetamol in this analysis.

raw_record.support_text: Acute Paracetamol poisoning is problematic because of its insidious progression to fulminant hepatitis and even death; the study aimed to draw up the epidemiological profile of acute Paracetamol poisonings.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective descriptive study over 8 years at the Pharmacology Toxicology department of University Hospital of Oran; 400 cases of acute Paracetamol poisoning, mostly from emergency departments (85%). Suicide attempts accounted for 82% (adolescents 69%), accidental poisoning 12% (predominant in small children, 89%). 16 cases had high risk of developing liver injury and required N-acetylcysteine antidote therapy; 8 patients had liver damage and 5 deaths were recorded; evolution was mostly favorable (84%). Poisoning progressed insidiously to fulminant hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: In a French prospective controlled trial of 102 patients with acute liver failure (ALF), of whom 49 were randomized to standard medical treatment and 53 received MARS, the main aetiology of ALF was paracetamol, accounting for 38% of cases. In the subgroup of patients with paracetamol intoxication, MARS showed a possible beneficial effect.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol intoxication was the leading cause of ALF (38%) among 102 patients enrolled in the FULMAR trial; a subgroup analysis suggested a possible beneficial effect of MARS on outcome in paracetamol-induced ALF. Clinical syndrome: acute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: The letter states that paracetamol overdose remains the commonest cause of fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) in the UK and is an important cause in Australia, and discusses management decisions about liver transplantation using the King's College criteria.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol-induced fulminant hepatic failure (FHF). 14 patients treated since 1988; 8 fulfilled King's criteria (arterial pH <7.3; or prothrombin time >100 s plus serum creatinine >300 µmol/L plus grade III/IV encephalopathy). One transplanted patient died of cerebral oedema 24 h later; the other 13 recovered fully under conservative management. Debated applicability of King's criteria; authors advocate N-Acetylcysteine benefit when given up to 36 h after overdose. King's group data (1990-1996) on 129 patients meeting the criteria: 39 transplanted (93% survived) vs 90 not transplanted (11% survived).

raw_record.support_text: In an observational before/after study at University Hospitals Birmingham, UK, prior to pack-size legislation an average of 76 patients per year were admitted to the Queen Elizabeth Hospital liver unit with paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity, falling to an average of 38 per year after the legislation (a 50% reduction). Paracetamol overdose admissions to the trust also fell from 360 to 250 per year (a 31% reduction). The authors concluded that restricting paracetamol pack-size reduced the incidence and severity of paracetamol poisoning.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol (paracetamol) overdose study. Before/after UK 1998 pack-size legislation: average 76/year liver unit admissions with paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity pre-legislation vs 38/year post-legislation (50% reduction); trust paracetamol overdose admissions fell from 360 to 250/year (31% reduction). Legislation restricting paracetamol pack size raised a 75% cut. Paper frames hepatotoxicity as paracetamol-induced and reports reduction in incidence and severity after pack-size restriction; no individual patient adjudication, dose, or outcome data reported.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that acute liver failure (ALF) accounts for about 8% of all liver transplants, with acetaminophen overdose contributing to nearly half of these cases. In a retrospective analysis at the Medical University of Warsaw, 39 patients underwent liver transplantation (LT) for ALF induced by acetaminophen (n=18) or Amanita phalloides (n=21) poisoning.
