raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective cohort of 18 patients who underwent liver transplantation for acetaminophen-overdose-induced acute liver failure; 90-day mortality 22.2% for this group; acetaminophen overdose contributes to nearly half of ALF cases overall. Patients with ALF required liver transplantation as life-saving intervention.

raw_record.support_text: Table 1 lists the aetiology of hepatic necrosis in 10 patients with fulminant hepatic failure; paracetamol is the assigned cause in four patients (patients 5, 8, 9 and 10), all women, who died of hepatic necrosis with maximum prothrombin ratios from 44/13 to 92/14 and maximum serum bilirubin from 103 to 260 umol/l, three of whom had cerebral oedema at necropsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Assigned aetiology (paracetamol overdose) of hepatic necrosis causing fulminant hepatic failure in 4 of 10 studied patients (patients 5, 8, 9, 10); maximum prothrombin ratios 44/13-92/14, maximum serum bilirubin 103-260 umol/l; cerebral oedema at necropsy in 3; all patients died and were studied post-mortem.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (APAP) is a widely used analgesic and antipyretic that is a dose-related toxin and can produce severe hepatotoxicity if used in excess. In the United States and many European countries, nearly half of all drug-related liver injuries are caused by APAP, and there has been an increase in drug-induced acute liver failure due to AILI (acetaminophen-induced liver injury).
raw_record.extra_details: APAP is described as a dose-related toxin causing severe hepatotoxicity when used in excess, and is the leading cause of drug-induced acute liver failure (AILI). In the US and many European countries nearly half of all drug-related liver injuries are attributed to APAP. Pathogenic mechanism: excess APAP is metabolized by CYP2E1 and CYP1A2 to the reactive metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), which depletes glutathione (GSH), forms APAP protein adducts (APAP-AD), and leads to mitochondrial damage and hepatocyte necrosis; oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, ER stress, microcirculatory disorders are implicated. Human serum samples were collected from 40 AILI patients and 20 healthy controls; 3 transplant recipients met APASL AILI diagnostic criteria.

raw_record.support_text: The study evaluated 2-year clinical outcomes in 773 ALF patients who survived their initial illness, a cohort generally representative of the entire ALFSG cohort though with fewer acetaminophen (APAP) patients included compared to the overall cohort. The APAP patients represent cases of acute liver failure caused by acetaminophen overdose; roughly 10% of these APAP initial survivors died during 2 years of follow-up. A separate cited Canadian study of hospitalized adult APAP overdose patients found many died over 5 years of follow-up from preventable causes, and survival of APAP overdose patients was significantly lower than age-matched population controls.
raw_record.extra_details: Patients were APAP overdose survivors of acute liver failure enrolled in the ALFSG cohort; 773 ALF initial survivors studied for 2-year outcomes, with approximately 10% of APAP initial survivors dying during 2 years of follow-up. APAP (acetaminophen) is the cause of ALF in this patient subgroup. Cited Canadian study of hospitalized adult APAP overdose patients reported many deaths over 5 years from preventable causes (trauma, substance abuse) with survival significantly lower than age-matched population controls. In the APAP subgroup, higher serum phosphate at baseline was associated with poorer long-term survival.

raw_record.support_text: In the King's unit's clinical trials of charcoal haemoperfusion (five vs ten hours in grade III and ten hours vs intensive care alone in grade IV encephalopathy, 137 patients entered), overall survival was related to aetiology of fulminant hepatic failure, being best in paracetamol overdose and viral hepatitis A and B, and worst in non-A non-B hepatitis and adverse reactions to drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol overdose listed as a leading aetiology (with best overall survival among the fulminant hepatic failure aetiologies) in the context of 137 patients with grade III or IV encephalopathy entered in the charcoal haemoperfusion trials. Survival was generally good and related to aetiology; non-A non-B hepatitis and adverse drug reactions had the worst survival.

raw_record.support_text: In the same single-center series (2002-2019), 311 of 400 patients admitted with severe acetaminophen-related acute liver injury had taken an overdose. This overdose group served as the comparator; 30-day survival was 94.6±1.3%, with host factors including fasting, excess drinking, and repeated use being less frequent than in therapeutic-dose ALI.
raw_record.extra_details: 311 of 400 patients with severe acetaminophen-related acute liver injury took an overdose. 30-day survival 94.6±1.3%. Host factors: fasting ≥1 day 26%, excess drinking 48.5%, median 1 day of use. Phenotype: acute liver injury (ALI).

raw_record.support_text: The study enrolled acetaminophen (APAP) overdose patients at two medical centers; the diagnosis of APAP overdose was made by a physician based on standard clinical criteria (reported history of APAP overdose, detectable serum APAP, and/or aminotransferase level of ≥1500 IU/l), and patients with liver injury from other causes (e.g., viral hepatitis) were excluded. Plasma samples were collected to assess the time course of circulating bile acids after APAP overdose. The authors frame the cohort as acetaminophen-induced acute liver injury (AALI) and acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure (AALF) patients, confirming that total and individual serum bile acid levels are substantially elevated in APAP-induced ALF patients.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP overdose patients were diagnosed by standard criteria (history of APAP overdose, detectable serum APAP, and/or aminotransferase ≥1500 IU/l); viral hepatitis and other causes excluded. Cohorts described: acetaminophen-induced acute liver injury (AALI) patients and acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure (AALF) patients; AALF samples from the Acute Liver Failure Study Group network included both survivors and non-survivors, with only samples showing evidence of tissue necrosis (peak ALT ≥1000 U/l) used. Non-survivors showed preferential accumulation of glycodeoxycholic acid (GDCA). Reported peak ALT ~4973-5720 U/l, peak bilirubin up to 8.2 mg/dl, peak prothrombin time up to 53.4 s. Reference to serum bile acid elevations in mice and rats given toxic doses of APAP is preclinical and not part of this human claim.

raw_record.support_text: Acute liver failure treatment efforts in 2011 should focus on prevention across etiologic categories; for acetaminophen this includes further education on the risk of acetaminophen liver injury and limitation of over-the-counter use of this harmful agent. The paper identifies acetaminophen as a cause of acute liver failure, with paragraph 82 describing patients with ALF secondary to known acetaminophen overdose, and the ALFSG etiology data (Table 1) listing 787 acetaminophen (APAP) cases versus 202 other drug-induced cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver failure secondary to known acetaminophen overdose; ALFSG registry (1696 patients) with 787 acetaminophen (APAP) cases, median age 37, 76% female, median ALT 3846, median bilirubin 4.4 mg/dL, 9% transplanted, 67% spontaneous survival, 75% overall survival. Acetaminophen-related ALF is considered hyperacute with very high aminotransferases and low bilirubin compared with drug-induced liver injury. Acetaminophen–CYS serum adducts used to identify overdose and indeterminate-etiology cases. Discussion calls for education on acetaminophen liver injury risk and limitation of over-the-counter use.

raw_record.support_text: In the King's College Hospital Liver Failure Unit 1993-94 cohort, 250 of 342 acute liver failure cases were attributed to acetaminophen overdose, constituting the single largest etiology group. Acetaminophen overdose is listed separately under 'Overdose' from the 'Idiosyncratic Drug Reactions' category.
raw_record.extra_details: 250 ALF cases due to acetaminophen overdose admitted 1993-94. Acetaminophen overdose cases with grade 3-4 encephalopathy in the most recent 2-year period had a 64% survival rate. Prognostic indicators in acetaminophen-induced ALF: a rise in INR at day 3-4 associated with only 7% survival (vs 79% if INR fell); factor V <20% had positive predictive value 0.49 for mortality; hyperacute liver failure may cause death before bilirubin rises; metabolic acidosis is the most powerful prognostic indicator.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen liver injury is characterized by a hyperacute biochemical pattern with markedly high ALT (median 4,149 U/L, up to 26,600 U/L) and modest bilirubin elevation (median 4.5 mg/dL). Among a prospective consecutive series of 275 cases of acute liver failure due to acetaminophen overdose, women predominated (74%), median age was 36, and despite better survival acetaminophen-related cases made up the largest number of deaths. Intentional (n=122) and unintentional (n=131) overdose cases showed similar total doses, severity, spontaneous survival (66% vs 64%), transplantation (7% vs 9%), and death without transplantation (27% each).
raw_record.extra_details: Overdose exposure; prospective consecutive series of 275 ALF cases due to acetaminophen overdose. ALT median 4,149 U/L (max 26,600), bilirubin median 4.5 mg/dL, women 74%, median age 36 years. Intentional n=122 vs unintentional n=131; total dose medians 25 g vs 20 g, dose/day 25 g vs 7.5 g; spontaneous survival 66% vs 64%, transplantation 7% vs 9%, death without transplantation 27% vs 27% (all NS). Unintentional cases more often used narcotic compounds (63%) and multiple acetaminophen preparations (38%); alcohol use more common in unintentional cases though its role is unclear. Injury involves the reactive intermediate NAPQI, detoxified by NAC (mercapturic acid path); NAC given within 24 h decreases risk of liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: In a recent published study, 662 cases of acute liver failure were investigated. Overall, 275 (42%) patients had paracetamol-related hepatotoxicity. They had ingested a median total dose of 24 g paracetamol. Nearly half of the patients (48%) reported an unintentional overdose, 44% had taken an intentional overdose; 63% of patients with unintentional and 18% with intentional overdose had taken paracetamol combined with other narcotics, mostly opiates.
raw_record.extra_details: Among 662 acute liver failure cases, 275 (42%) had paracetamol-related hepatotoxicity; median total ingested dose 24 g; 48% unintentional overdose, 44% intentional overdose, remainder unclear; 63% of unintentional and 18% of intentional overdose patients also took paracetamol with other narcotics, most of them opiates. Findings cited as showing the extent of drug-related hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The commentary reports the study's estimate that at least 250 cases of acetaminophen-associated acute liver failure (ALF) present to transplant centers in the United States each year. It notes that while over 112 million people use an acetaminophen-containing product each month, the yearly risk of acetaminophen-associated ALF is less than two per 10 million users, and that the incidence is probably low given the widespread use of these medications.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen-associated ALF cases presenting to US transplant centers; at least 250 cases/year estimated vs >112 million monthly users giving a yearly risk below two per 10 million. Study context is overdose/toxic-dose exposure, with many cases involving opioid/acetaminophen combination products. Confounders discussed include alcohol use/abuse, age (over 40 higher ALF/transplant/death risk), co-morbidities, and other drug use (cocaine, amphetamines, marijuana on toxicology screens); authors caution that some cases may have been misclassified, including therapeutic use detected by serum levels.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (APAP; N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)acetamide) overdose has been identified as a major cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in the United States. Diagnosis of APAP overdose relies on history of a large dose (defined as 7.5 g of APAP in adults) supported by elevated blood APAP; many patients develop ALF rapidly, characterized by encephalopathy and coagulopathy (INR ≥ 1.5).
raw_record.extra_details: APAP-protein adducts (3-(cystein-S-yl)-APAP) formed by hepatic metabolism to the reactive metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine serve as specific biomarkers of APAP toxicity; peak APAP adduct concentrations correlated with peak aminotransferase concentrations (r=0.779) in 53 adults with APAP-related ALF. APAP overdose diagnosis required use >4 g/day within 7 days or detection of APAP on admission or ALT >1000 IU/l with APAP history. Patients had acute liver failure with encephalopathy and coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5); excluded other etiologies. Acute liver failure is the clinical phenotype (characterized by encephalopathy and coagulopathy), recorded here as other_specific_phenotype. Adducts disappeared with first-order kinetics after N-acetylcysteine therapy (mean t1/2 1.72 ± 0.34 days) and were detected up to 12 days postingestion. Single acute suicidal ingestion; 230 samples from 53 subjects.

raw_record.support_text: Prospective data on 662 consecutive patients meeting standard ALF criteria (coagulopathy and encephalopathy) at 22 US tertiary centers identified 275 (42%) cases attributable to acetaminophen liver injury. Median ingested dose was 24 g (48 extra-strength tablets); 131 (48%) were unintentional overdose, 122 (44%) intentional suicide attempts, and 22 (8%) unknown intent. Outcomes were: 178 (65%) survived, 74 (27%) died without transplantation, and 23 (8%) underwent liver transplantation; 71% were alive at 3 weeks. Acetaminophen hepatotoxicity far exceeded other causes of ALF in the US, with the annual proportion rising from 28% in 1998 to 51% in 2003.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute Liver Failure Study Group (ALFSG) registry cohort of 275 consecutive patients, 1998-2003. Median dose 24 g (48 extra-strength tablets). Intent: unintentional 48%, intentional (suicide) 44%, unknown 8%. In the unintentional group, 38% took ≥2 acetaminophen preparations simultaneously and 63% used narcotic-containing compounds; 81% took acetaminophen and/or other analgesics for acute or chronic pain. Susceptible patients had concomitant depression, chronic pain, and alcohol or narcotic use. Outcomes: 65% survived, 27% died without transplantation, 8% transplanted, 71% alive at 3 weeks. Annual percentage of acetaminophen-related ALF rose from 28% (1998) to 51% (2003). Paper notes acetaminophen causes severe hepatic necrosis leading to ALF after suicidal overdoses and after unintentional daily doses exceeding 4 g/day recommendations; N-acetylcysteine can prevent hepatic injury if given within 12 hours of a single ingestion.

raw_record.support_text: During the 10-year study period, 871 patients were admitted with acetaminophen poisoning. A total of 288 galactose elimination capacity (GEC) determinations were performed in the 220 patients (25%) included in the study. GEC was performed in 70% of patients (102 of 146) who developed hepatic encephalopathy and in 68% of patients (50 of 74) who died or were transplanted. In the 102 patients with hepatic encephalopathy the mean GEC was 14.5 ± 5.6 µmol/min/kg, and it was significantly higher in the 52 spontaneous survivors than in the 50 patients who died or were transplanted (16.8 ± 5.6 vs 12.2 ± 4.7 µmol/min/kg). Thirty of the 38 patients who died without transplantation died directly from liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen poisoning (overdose) cohort of 871 admitted patients over 10 years; 220 patients studied with galactose elimination capacity (GEC), range 4.2-41.1 µmol/min/kg, mean 19.2 ± 7.6 µmol/min/kg. Liver failure outcomes included hepatic encephalopathy (102 patients) and 74 deaths or liver transplantations. GEC strongly inversely correlated with INR (R=-0.64), bilirubin (R=-0.65), and creatinine (R=-0.48). Independent risk factors for low GEC were high age, long time to N-acetylcysteine, and regular alcohol abuse. GEC >16.5 µmol/min/kg unlikely to die from liver failure; GEC <10 µmol/min/kg appeared incompatible with survival.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose is described as a leading cause of acute liver failure (ALF), and when patients fulfill the King's College criteria for acetaminophen-induced ALF (AALF) they have a poor prognosis for survival without liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of a 41-year-old female with no documented history of liver disease who presented with acute acetaminophen toxicity and developed hepatic encephalopathy, coagulopathy and lactic acidosis; she met King's College criteria for liver transplantation based on pH and INR but was deemed not suitable due to psychosocial comorbidities. Treated with single-pass albumin dialysis (SPAD) starting day 3 of ICU admission for five consecutive daily runs (~77 hours) as a bridge to recovery; course complicated by cerebral edema requiring mannitol. Native liver function recovered by hospital discharge (day 46), with bilirubin <100 mmol/L; no long-term neurological sequelae.

raw_record.support_text: In this overdose-patient cohort, serum APAP-CYS concentrations in patients with hepatic injury following acetaminophen overdose were generally much higher than those observed during therapeutic dosing, with the exception of subjects who received early N-acetylcysteine treatment or were sampled late during resolution of injury. The paper attributes these ALT elevations to acetaminophen overdose injury, including both acute overdose and repeated supratherapeutic ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: Includes acute acetaminophen overdose (treated within and beyond 8 hours of ingestion), repeated supratherapeutic ingestion, and indeterminate-timing cases. Case series of overdose patients with elevated peak ALT (e.g., up to 9903, 8880, 7979 IU/L) treated with N-acetylcysteine. Patient SH-04 developed marked ALT elevation and high APAP-CYS consistent with acetaminophen-induced liver injury. One acute-overdose subject (D-07) had concurrent hepatitis C, and one repeated-ingestion subject (UCH-09) had CMV hepatitis on liver biopsy. Serum APAP-CYS was undetectable in non-acetaminophen hepatotoxin patients, supporting adduct specificity for APAP. Peak APAP-CYS correlated modestly with peak ALT (Spearman rho=0.68, 95% CI 0.36-0.85).

raw_record.support_text: Case no. 7, an 18-year-old female, ingested 60 g of acetaminophen 2 days prior to admission. She developed fulminant hepatic failure with grade IV coma, decerebrate posturing, disconjugated gaze, dilated pupils with sluggish reactivity, and cerebral edema on CAT scan, with intracranial pressure up to 28 mmHg. BAL was used three times; during the last treatment she underwent end-to-side portocaval shunt, total hepatectomy (anhepatic phase 14 h, body temperature lowered to 34.5°C), and OLT with an ABO-incompatible organ that was rejected a week later, at which time she was re-transplanted with an ABO-compatible organ.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-case overdose: 60 g acetaminophen ingested 2 days before admission in an 18-year-old female. Course: fulminant hepatic failure with grade IV coma, decerebrate posturing, disconjugated gaze, dilated pupils with sluggish reactivity, ICP 28 mmHg, CAT scan showing cerebral edema. Treated with bioartificial liver (BAL) three times, end-to-side portocaval shunt, total hepatectomy (14 h anhepatic phase, body temperature lowered to 34.5°C), then orthotopic liver transplantation with an ABO-incompatible organ that was rejected a week later and re-transplanted with an ABO-compatible organ.

raw_record.support_text: This retrospective cohort study compared outcomes after acute acetaminophen poisoning in 4,048 patients treated with either a 20-hour intravenous or 72-hour oral acetylcysteine protocol. The primary outcome was hepatotoxicity (aminotransferase levels >1,000 IU/L), which occurred in 13.9% of the 20-hour group and 15.8% of the 72-hour group. One patient in the 20-hour group received a liver transplant and died because of acetaminophen toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute acetaminophen overdose poisoning; hepatotoxicity defined as aminotransferase levels >1,000 IU/L; incidence 13.9% (20-hour i.v. acetylcysteine group, n=2,086) versus 15.8% (72-hour oral acetylcysteine group, n=1,962), absolute difference -1.9% (95% CI -4.2 to 0.3); one liver transplant followed by death in the 20-hour group attributed to acetaminophen toxicity versus no transplants and 3 deaths in the 72-hour group; relative risk of hepatotoxicity depended on time to acetylcysteine initiation (<12 h favored 20-hr protocol, >18 h favored 72-hr protocol); anaphylactoid reactions to i.v. acetylcysteine in 148/2,086 (7.1%). Acetylcysteine was the antidote, not a cause of the injury.

raw_record.support_text: The study examines patients admitted to a tertiary referral liver intensive therapy unit with paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity, and states that paracetamol overdose can cause hepatotoxic effects. Between 2000 and 2007, 302 patients with paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity (after excluding 54 who received a liver transplant) were evaluated; the cohort had 25% overall mortality.
raw_record.extra_details: Patients with paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity requiring admission to a tertiary referral liver intensive therapy unit (LITU) between 2000 and 2007; 54 transplant recipients excluded leaving 302 patients; overall 25% mortality in the cohort (outcome focus is acute kidney injury, so mortality/severity is not specifically graded for the liver injury). Also known as acetaminophen.

raw_record.support_text: In patients with acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure (AALF), abundant CCR2⁺ and S100A9⁺ pro-inflammatory monocyte-derived macrophages were found in portal tracts. These findings were obtained from AALF patients who required liver transplantation, corroborating that monocyte-derived macrophage-related pro-inflammatory responses contribute to detrimental liver injury. Increased serum CCL2 levels in ALF patients were also reported to predict an unfavorable prognosis (death or need for emergency liver transplantation) following APAP intoxication.
raw_record.extra_details: AALF patients analyzed required liver transplantation; APAP intoxication (overdose) resulted in acute liver failure with unfavorable prognosis (death or need for emergency liver transplantation) predicted by increased serum CCL2. Portal tracts showed abundant CCR2⁺/S100A9⁺ pro-inflammatory monocyte-derived macrophages, in contrast to CD163⁺ and CD68⁺ resident macrophages not restricted to portal tracts. NAC administration is the only pharmacological strategy for APAP-induced liver injury, dampening initial metabolic injury but without benefit at later stages. Mechanism of action in mice and men: MoMF enhance hepatic inflammation after extravasation early after injury and contribute to resolution/repair at later times via maturation into restorative Ly-6C<sup>low</sup> MoMF; neutrophils and HMGB1-TLR4-IL23a-IL17a axis are involved in early injury.

raw_record.support_text: A 30-year-old woman was hospitalized with nausea and abdominal discomfort after an acetaminophen overdose of 15 g. Laboratory results included serum bilirubin 67 µM/L (normal 3 to 20), alanine aminotransferase 2598 U/L (normal 0 to 36), prothrombin time 59.3 s, and plasma ammonia 220 µM/L. She developed fulminant hepatic failure with hepatic encephalopathy and, after Ro 15-1788 administration failed to produce clinical improvement, progressed to coma and died.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-agent intentional overdose of 15 g acetaminophen leading to fulminant hepatic failure with hepatic encephalopathy; bilirubin 67 µM/L, alanine aminotransferase 2598 U/L, prothrombin time 59.3 s, plasma ammonia 220 µM/L; Ro 15-1788 (GABA-benzodiazepine receptor antagonist, 0.5-1.0 mg IV doses) was given to reverse the comatose state but produced no clinical improvement; the patient developed hypotension, anuria, status epilepticus and died. Neusea and abdominal discomfort were presenting symptoms.

raw_record.support_text: Treatment of coagulation disturbances developing with hepatic damage following a paracetamol overdose was assessed in a controlled trial of 22 patients. Two-thirds of the patients had evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation, and a severe coagulation defect was present; the authors attribute this to paracetamol-induced hepatic necrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Refers to hepatic necrosis following paracetamol overdose, with hepatic failure and hepatic coma (some patients in grade IV hepatic coma). Study was a controlled trial of 24 consecutive patients (aged 17-48) admitted with prothrombin time ratio >2.2, treated with fresh frozen plasma ± heparin; 22 patients reported. Trial assessed speed of correction of coagulation defect and clinical outcome; two-thirds had evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation and significant bleeding occurred in only five patients. Coagulation defect may be of shorter duration than in viral hepatitis because paracetamol injury is not a continuing process.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that one Class II study and multiple Class III reports have demonstrated that repeated supratherapeutic ingestions of acetaminophen, at doses ranging from just over 4 g per day to greater than 15 g per day, may result in hepatotoxicity, hepatic failure, and even death.
raw_record.extra_details: Repeated supratherapeutic ingestions with doses from just over 4 g/day to >15 g/day cause hepatotoxicity, hepatic failure, and death. In the prospective analysis by Daly et al (2004, Class II), patients presenting with hepatotoxicity (AST 50-1000 IU/L) had mean acetaminophen dosing of 12 g/day over a median duration of 72 h, with 15% developing severe hepatotoxicity and 1 patient (2%) dying of liver failure; patients presenting with severe hepatotoxicity (AST >1000 IU/L) had mean dosing of 12.6 g/day over a median duration of 72 h, with 5 (14%) dying and 1 undergoing liver transplant. NAS serum concentration thresholds (>=10 µg/mL) and AST/ALT >50 IU/L were used in the management algorithm; no patient with normal AST at presentation developed hepatotoxicity, but 50% had received at least some NAC therapy.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective cohort of 52 patients with fulminant hepatic failure (FHF), the cause of FHF was acetaminophen overdose in 17 cases. Acetaminophen-induced FHF had a significantly higher survival rate compared to the non-acetaminophen group (82% vs 57%, p=0.04).
raw_record.extra_details: 17 of 52 FHF cases were attributed to acetaminophen overdose; 14 of 17 (82%) survived versus 57% in the non-acetaminophen group; 2 of the 2 survivals with grade IV encephalopathy were acetaminophen patients who had undergone liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: Case 2 is listed in Table 1 with the cause of hepatic failure given as 'Acetaminophen toxicity,' and in the text (Case 2) a 64-year-old male with acetaminophen overdose became comatose with significant cerebral edema and electrocerebral silence on EEG. He was treated with mannitol and hypothermia and improved gradually over 2 weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose in a 64-year-old male. Acute liver failure with hepatic encephalopathy: comatose with poorly reactive pupils and absent corneal and vestibulo-ocular reflexes; MRI showed moderate edema with diffusion restriction in cortex and globus pallidus; EEG suppression ~48 h. Treated with mannitol and hypothermia; at 2-month follow-up in inpatient rehabilitation, independent in activities of daily living but with some disorientation and inappropriate jocularity.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes acetaminophen as one of the most commonly used analgesics whose well-known major adverse effect is massive hepatic necrosis with potentially fatal consequences, noting that such complications can occur from intentional overdose or in the presence of certain predisposing factors, and frames the condition as acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity. The presented patient, after an acetaminophen overdose, declined into multiorgan failure and died after support was withdrawn (p:23).
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose case culminating in massive hepatic necrosis, multiorgan failure and death; the patient had ongoing alcohol use and was declined for liver transplantation. Background discussion: ~5% of a dose is metabolized by CYP (primarily CYP2E1, CYP1A2, CYP3A4) to the reactive metabolite NAPQI, considered likely involved in hepatotoxicity; NAPQI is normally conjugated with glutathione but its formation exceeds conjugation capacity at increased doses. Most authorities regard doses <6 g/d as non-toxic with recommended daily cumulative doses not exceeding 4 g/d, and 2 g/d for those with long-term excessive alcohol exposure or other hepatic dysfunction. Whether therapeutic doses increase the risk of massive hepatic necrosis in patients with long-term excessive alcohol exposure is controversial; a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial of repeated 4 g/d dosing in chronic alcoholics reported no evidence of liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes the use of MARS albumin dialysis in treating paracetamol-induced liver failure and paracetamol-induced acute liver failure, framing paracetamol as a cause of human acute liver failure. One report notes a possible enhanced paracetamol clearance with MARS, with drug half-life decreasing from 3.4 h without albumin dialysis to 1.2 h after initiation.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol poisoning/overdose causing acute liver failure (ALF). Helsinki study treated 113 ALF patients with MARS between 2001-2007 vs a historical 46-patient control group (1995-2001); toxic etiology in 63/113, 32 secondary to paracetamol poisoning (controls n=6). MARS group had lower baseline MELD; 6-month survival 84% vs 67% (not significant); liver recovery 81% vs 33% (p=0.031); 1 MARS patient received liver transplantation vs 2 controls, all three survived; only significant predictor of survival in the paracetamol subgroup was grade of hepatic encephalopathy at treatment start. In a separate report paracetamol half-life fell from 3.4 h to 1.2 h after MARS initiation. Paracetamol clearance associated with liver failure, encephalopathy, and hemodynamic/biochemical disturbances.

raw_record.support_text: In the analysis of human acetaminophen (APAP) datasets, GSE74000 contains gene-expression data from liver biopsies of healthy patients and patients with APAP-induced acute liver failure (ALF), addressing differential gene expression in end-stage APAP-induced liver injury. GSE70784 contains blood gene-expression data from patients receiving a daily 4 g APAP dose or placebo, comparing responders (patients with ALT >2 times the upper limit of normal during days 4-9 after starting APAP) to non-responders and placebo after 1 and 8 days of dosing.
raw_record.extra_details: GSE74000: microarray gene-expression data from liver biopsies of 3 APAP-induced ALF patients compared to 2 healthy liver samples; analyzed with GEO2R using FDR-adjusted p-values. Mentions acetaminophen overdose/toxicity as the causal context of the acute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 105 patients with acute liver failure, patients who developed ALF due to APAP overdose (N-acetyl-p-aminophenol, the active compound of acetaminophen) had the highest median plasma osteopontin levels (3603 ng/mL, range 54–19,127). APAP overdose was classified as one of the etiologies causing ALF, with OPN levels in this group significantly higher than all other etiologies (p<0.007).
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen is identified as N-acetyl-p-aminophenol, the active compound of acetaminophen. APAP overdose was one of the adjudicated etiologies of acute liver failure in a 105-patient ALF cohort. Median plasma osteopontin in the APAP-overdose group was 3603 ng/mL (range 54–19,127), the highest among ALF etiologies; comparison of APAP (and shock) OPN levels with all other groups gave p<0.007.

raw_record.support_text: A 16-year-old female adolescent presented to the emergency department 4 hours after ingesting acetaminophen 15 g following a breakup. She complained of nausea without vomiting or abdominal pain; vital signs and physical examination were unremarkable.
raw_record.extra_details: Overdose of 15 g oral acetaminophen; 4 hours between ingestion and emergency department arrival. Acetaminophen overdose causes more hospitalizations than overdose of any other drug. Discussion: symptoms vary by amount and time since ingestion; later symptoms of fulminant hepatic failure may dominate. Dose-dependence reflects saturation of hepatic elimination pathways and depletion of glutathione, leaving free NAPQI to produce the clinical effects. The patient's APAP concentration was above the Rumack-Matthew treatment line (treatment threshold 140-150 µg/mL at 4 hours), so she received oral N-acetylcysteine for 72 hours; she did not develop irreversible hepatic failure and recovered completely.

raw_record.support_text: In the ALFSG experience, patients with acetaminophen (APAP) acute liver failure progress to death, transplant, or recovery in a short time interval; virtually all APAP patients reached an endpoint by 4 days after admission, and overall 36% of ALF patients were listed for transplantation, but only 22% of those with APAP ALF vs 56% of the non-APAP group; only 36% of listed APAP patients received a graft, and the very sick APAP patients often die because a liver cannot be found in time.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen (APAP) overdose (both intentional and unintentional phenotypes) causes acute liver failure (ALF); spontaneous resolution occurs with or without N-acetylcysteine in nearly 2/3 of cases. In the US Acute Liver Failure Study Group (ALFSG) experience, virtually all APAP patients reached their endpoint by 4 days following admission, whereas DILI patients continued to die or receive liver grafts over 7-10 days. 36% of ALF patients were listed for transplantation, only 22% with APAP ALF vs 56% non-APAP; only 36% of those listed received a graft vs 74% of non-APAP group. The listed APAP patients were sicker in clinical/biochemical features.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol overdose is described as the commonest cause of acute liver failure in the UK, prompting measures to restrict its sale. Data from patients admitted to the Scottish Liver Transplantation Unit in 1992-98 compared with 1998-2001 showed that the incidence of paracetamol-induced liver failure, severity of illness, and outcome did not differ between groups, but patients with paracetamol-induced acute liver failure had higher Carstairs scores (1.99, 95% CI 1.33-2.65; n=190) than patients with non-paracetamol acute liver failure (0.02, -0.79 to 0.84; n=68), establishing an association between paracetamol-induced acute liver failure and social deprivation.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver failure specifically; paracetamol is commonly taken in overdose. The paper notes acute liver failure has a high mortality rate and that N-acetyl-cysteine is a highly effective antidote only if given within ~15 h to be most effective. Patients were admitted to the Scottish Liver Transplantation Unit; comparison covered 1992-98 versus 1998-2001, and the key finding was an association between paracetamol-induced acute liver failure and social deprivation (Carstairs score).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that acute hepatic injury may occur after ingestion of as little as 10 gm of acetaminophen, and notes a fatality rate secondary to hepatic failure ranging from 2% to 20% following acetaminophen overdose.
