The study examined 209 consecutive patients with single-dose acetaminophen overdose, of whom 44 (21.1%) developed hepatic coma and 20 (43.5%) of these patients died.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 209 consecutive patients with single-dose acetaminophen overdose analyzed by multiple/logistic regression; 57 (27.3%) had chronic alcohol intake and 45 (21.5%) had acute alcohol intake. 44 (21.1%) developed hepatic coma (hepatic encephalopathy) and 20 of these died. Chronic alcohol intake was independently associated with hepatic coma (relative risk 5.3, 95% CI 2.2-12.4) and death (RR 1.4, 95% CI 0.5-3.9), as well as lower prothrombin index, lower platelet count, higher creatinine and higher bilirubin, indicating that chronic alcohol enhances acetaminophen hepatotoxicity. Acute alcohol intake was not significantly associated with any outcome.

raw_record.support_text: The study examined serum activin A levels in 23 patients with acute liver failure (ALF), including 17 patients with ALF due to paracetamol overdose. These paracetamol-overdose patients had higher serum activin A (median 2.87 ng/ml) than non-A to E hepatitis ALF patients, and 10 of the 17 (59%) survived without liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol overdose was the attributed cause of acute liver failure in 17 ALF patients studied for the biomarkers activin A, follistatin, and TGF-beta1; 10/17 (59%) survived without liver transplantation, implicating liver failure requiring transplant or causing death in the remainder. The paper is a biomarker study, not a DILI-diagnosis study, but explicitly attributes ALF to paracetamol overdose.

raw_record.support_text: Human liver samples were obtained from eight patients with APAP-induced liver injury undergoing liver puncture biopsy, along with normal liver tissues from six subjects undergoing hepatic resection for hepatic cysts or colorectal metastasis. This establishes a human drug-induced liver injury record for APAP (acetaminophen).
raw_record.extra_details: Eight patients with APAP-induced liver injury required liver puncture biopsy. Immunofluorescence staining for GLT25D2 (green) was performed in the liver of normal subjects and patients with APAP overdose. The main experimental work is a mouse model (single intraperitoneal APAP 500 mg/kg, assessed at 2-12 h) examining GLT25D2 expression and autophagy in APAP-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 25 patients with acute fulminant hepatic failure, nine (36%) were attributed to acetaminophen overdose (AOD, six were women, aged 17-39 years). Acetaminophen overdose is explicitly listed among the causes of the hepatic failure; one patient died of cerebral edema and herniation and seven died of liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose (AOD) caused acute fulminant hepatic failure in 9/25 patients (36%), six women, aged 17-39 years. In the specific AOD subgroup, CT variables GWD, sulcal narrowing and ventricular size showed significant changes (GWD OR 2.04, 95% CI 1.26-3.31, p=0.004; SN OR 2.01, p=0.004; VS OR 1.44, p=0.037).

raw_record.support_text: The study describes 560 patients with severe acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity admitted to the Liver Failure Unit of King's College Hospital from 1987 to 1993 following acetaminophen overdose. Median acetaminophen dose taken was 40 g (range 5-210 g); mortality was greatest (43%) in patients taking more than 48 g and lowest (29.3%) in those taking 24-48 g. Patients were treated with NAC, and outcomes included liver transplantation and death from uncontrollable cerebral edema.
raw_record.extra_details: 560 admitted patients (1987-1993); median overdose dose 40 g (range 5-210 g); mortality 43% in >48 g group and 29.3% in 24-48 g group (no significant dose-outcome relationship); 45 patients (8%) in an allegedly <12 g low-dose subgroup had questionable dose histories in 78%, with 8 deaths and 4 transplantations; a separate subgroup (45 patients, 8%) claimed inadvertent therapeutic overdose with staggered intake over 8 h to 3 days, many heavy drinkers; patients treated with NAC; deaths attributed to uncontrollable cerebral edema; coproxamol overdoses had 64% mortality with renal failure in 87% of fatal cases.

raw_record.support_text: The study assessed endothelial cell function in 58 patients with severe hepatotoxicity due to paracetamol ingestion, followed for up to 7 days. Serum hyaluronic acid, a marker of hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cell function, was markedly increased on admission (median 6777 ng/ml, range 24–50 967 ng/ml) versus normal controls (n=10, median 21 ng/ml, range 0–50 ng/ml; P<0.001). Non-survivors (n=21) had HA levels peaking on day 2 after admission, and the authors concluded that endothelial function is abnormal in paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity, with greater hepatic sinusoidal endothelial damage in non-survivors.
raw_record.extra_details: 58 patients with paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity studied for up to 7 days. Non-survivors n=21, survivors n=37. Plasma von Willebrand Factor, plasma thrombomodulin and serum interleukin-8 significantly increased vs controls (P<0.001); serum IL-8 significantly higher in non-survivors in the first 2 days. Illness manifests with complications of acute liver failure (abnormal haemodynamics, multi-organ failure, low platelet counts, loss of coagulation factors). Hyaluronic acid used as marker of hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cell function.

raw_record.support_text: In this cohort of 20 adult patients with acute liver failure, the aetiology of ALF was 55% paracetamol overdose (n=11), 20% ischaemic (n=4), 15% seronegative (n=3), and 10% idiosyncratic drug reactions (n=2). The paper explicitly attributes paracetamol overdose as the cause of ALF in these patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver failure (ALF) attributed to paracetamol overdose in 11/20 (55%) of the cohort; study also reports ALF from ischaemic causes (n=4), seronegative (n=3), and idiosyncratic drug reactions (n=2), the latter unnamed. Outcomes in the cohort: 12 survivors, 6 deaths, 3 OLT (transplant-free survival 60%).

raw_record.support_text: Most cases of drug-related fulminant hepatic failure resulted from acetaminophen overdose; the paper states acetaminophen is the most common cause of FHF in the United States, that this drug is directly hepatotoxic and predictably produces hepatocellular necrosis with overdose, and that in the present study acetaminophen (two cases) was one of the two offender drugs responsible for FHF.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases of acetaminophen-induced FHF in the present study; most common cause of fulminant hepatic failure in the United States; directly hepatotoxic and predictably produces hepatocellular necrosis with overdose.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 17 patients with fulminant hepatic failure, 13 had fibronectin concentrations below the normal range on admission. The four patients with concentrations within the normal range had fulminant hepatic failure due to viral hepatitis, and the mean concentration in that group was higher than in patients with fulminant hepatic failure due to paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose (214.0±15.0 v 80.5±17.0 µg/ml; p<0.001). Paracetamol overdose is thus attributed as the cause of fulminant hepatic failure in several patients in this series.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure caused by paracetamol overdose, in patients admitted to a liver unit (17 patients total). Paracetamol-overdose group mean plasma fibronectin 80.5±17.0 µg/ml. Two surviving paracetamol-overdose patients had very low initial fibronectin that slowly returned to normal; one patient who died received fresh-frozen plasma. Fibronectin correlated negatively with aspartate aminotransferase (r=-0.766) and positively with total bilirubin (r=0.654).

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen is described as the most frequent pharmaceutical agent in poison-center inquiries and the most commonly used substance in self-poisoning. The paper describes the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, based on 1971 data on the pharmacokinetics of acetaminophen in 30 adult patients who received only supportive treatment after acute overdose, which indicated a risk for hepatotoxicity if acetaminophen levels fell above the line joining 200 µg/mL at 4 hours and 6 µg/mL at 24 hours; a later lower treatment line (150 µg/mL at 4 h and 30 µg/mL at 12 h extending to 24 h) was labeled 'possible hepatotoxicity'. NAC treatment is described as reducing this liver injury when given within 10 hours of ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute acetaminophen overingestion; nomogram-derived risk of hepatotoxicity above the line joining 200 µg/mL at 4 hours and 6 µg/mL at 24 hours, with a lower 'possible hepatotoxicity' line joining 150 µg/mL at 4 hours and 30 µg/mL at 12 hours (arbitrarily set 25% lower) to accommodate errors in time-of-ingestion and laboratory errors. N-acetylcysteine treatment effectively prevents liver injury when given within 10 hours of ingestion. Study context is a survey of poison-center medical directors on overdose management protocols.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that acetaminophen (APAP) is a dose-related toxin that causes centrilobular hepatic necrosis and renal tubular damage and is currently the most common cause of acute liver failure in the United States, accounting for nearly 50% of all patients in the US Acute Liver Failure Study Group registry.
raw_record.extra_details: Described as a dose-related toxin causing centrilobular hepatic necrosis and renal tubular damage; most common cause of ALF in the US (~50% of patients); 80 of 187 study-group patients had acetaminophen-related ALF. The main paper focus is subclinical myocardial injury in ALF, not new DILI evidence for acetaminophen.

raw_record.support_text: Thirteen patients with acute liver disease of nonalcoholic etiology were studied; the diagnosis was virus hepatitis in 8 patients, paracetamol poisoning in 3, and halothane hypersensitivity in 2. Acute liver disease from paracetamol poisoning is thus explicitly attributed in these patients.
raw_record.extra_details: 3 patients had paracetamol poisoning among 13 patients presenting with acute liver disease of nonalcoholic etiology. Group mean values at first study were serum bilirubin 13.8 +/- 2.4 mg/100 ml and aspartate transaminase 421 +/- 71 IU/liter; 2 of the 13 patients subsequently died from fulminant liver failure (not specifically attributed to paracetamol).

raw_record.support_text: In the SALT study across seven European countries, acute paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdoses caused acute liver failure leading to registration for liver transplantation (ALFT). 111 paracetamol overdoses resulted in ALFT (19.0% of all-cause ALFT), with overdose patients mostly female (61.3%), mean age 33.6 (SD 10.9) years, and 72.8% eventually transplanted. Most overdoses (63.0%) were intentional suicide attempts.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver failure leading to registration for transplantation (ALFT); 111/114 overdose ALFT cases due to paracetamol. Mean age 33.6 years, 61.3% female, 72.8% eventually transplanted; 63.0% intentional (suicide attempts). Per-ton event rates varied by country (overall 5.99 per 1000 tons, 95% CI 4.93-7.22; Ireland 48.8, UK 10.0, France 3.09). Overdose contributed 19.0% of all-cause ALFT overall (Ireland 52%, UK 28%, France 18%, Netherlands 8%, Italy 1%); no events in Greece or Portugal. Overdose ALFT risk per ton sold was significantly higher in Ireland (RR 8.07) and UK (RR 1.67).

raw_record.support_text: Among 148 consecutive admissions to the West Midlands Poisons Unit with paracetamol overdose, there was no biochemical evidence of hepatic toxicity (AST <45 IU/L) in 90 patients, while 58 patients had evidence of liver damage (AST >45 IU/L) attributed to the overdose: 49 without hepatic encephalopathy (group 3) and 9 with hepatic encephalopathy (group 4). Two patients in group 4 developed acute renal failure requiring dialysis. Patients were treated with N-acetylcysteine when indicated.
raw_record.extra_details: 148 consecutive admissions to West Midlands Poisons Unit; hepatic toxicity defined as AST >45 IU/L. 90 patients had no biochemical evidence of hepatic toxicity (AST <45) (71 took insufficient paracetamol to warrant N-acetylcysteine; 19 given N-acetylcysteine). 58 patients with liver damage (AST >45) split into group 3 (n=49, no hepatic encephalopathy) and group 4 (n=9, with hepatic encephalopathy); 2 patients in group 4 had acute renal failure requiring dialysis. Patients treated with N-acetylcysteine if indicated per protocol or up to 48 h post overdose. Acute renal failure is an extra-hepatic manifestation and does not define liver-injury severity.

raw_record.support_text: In a human phase 1/2 study of safety and tolerability, 24 patients with an acute paracetamol overdose meeting UK treatment criteria (plasma paracetamol ≥100 mg/L at 4 h) received IV calmangafodipir after an acetylcysteine loading infusion or acetylcysteine alone, with liver injury assessed by ALT and INR measurements. The paper frames paracetamol overdose as the cause of the hepatotoxicity that these antidotes are intended to treat and, in the accompanying mouse study, attributes ALT elevation and hepatic necrosis to paracetamol 300 mg/kg.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol overdose causes hepatotoxicity (ALT elevation and hepatic necrosis); mitochondrial toxicity from superoxide free-radical formation is invoked for extremely large paracetamol overdoses. A UK phase 1/2 study enrolled 24 patients with acute paracetamol overdose meeting the treatment threshold (≥100 mg/L at 4 h); about half would not have been treated under the 150-line threshold, only 2 patients had initial concentrations above the high-risk 300 line, and 7 presented more than 8 h after overdose, so most were low risk of hepatotoxicity. A mouse study used paracetamol 300 mg/kg to produce ALT elevation and hepatic necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 100 patients presenting to Sri Lankan hospitals, a history of ingested paracetamol dose had poor discriminatory power (area under the ROC curve 0.58) as a diagnostic test for toxicity; a reported dose >150 mg/kg had 89% sensitivity but only 5% specificity, meaning many patients judged at risk based on reported dose were not actually at risk of hepatotoxicity once their plasma paracetamol concentration was plotted on the nomogram. This reflects that acute paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose can cause hepatotoxicity, though the reported ingested dose alone is a poor predictor of that risk.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute single-event paracetamol overdose; risk of hepatotoxicity depends on plasma paracetamol concentration and time since ingestion. In 1571 acute overdose presentations to an Australian regional toxicology centre there was a positive correlation between reported ingested dose and measured plasma paracetamol concentration; based on the 150 mg/L treatment line there was a 10% chance of requiring antidote treatment after a reported dose of 13-16 g, 50% of patients were above the treatment line after 30-34 g, and 90% after 48-50 g. NAC is considered highly effective when given within 8 h of ingestion but is often given empirically when reported dose >=10 g, which would have led to unnecessary NAC administration in over 50% of early presenters (<8 h).

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective study of 308 consecutive acute liver failure patients admitted over 41 months at 17 tertiary-care centers in the US, paracetamol overdose was the most common apparent cause, accounting for 39% of cases, supporting the view that drugs have replaced viral hepatitis as the most frequent cause of acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol overdose accounted for 39% of 308 consecutive ALF cases admitted over a 41-month period in 17 tertiary-care centers in the US. Acute liver failure defined as massive sudden liver cell dysfunction in a previously healthy person with clotting-test alteration and hepatic encephalopathy.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes human patients with acetaminophen (APAP)-induced acute liver failure (ALF), analyzing a reanalysis of the GEO dataset GSE8075 containing gene array data of blood monocytes from APAP-induced ALF patients who survived versus those who died (6 patient samples per group). This frames acetaminophen as the cause of acute liver failure in overdose-exposed patients, a drug-induced liver injury entity that is the clinical context of the study.
raw_record.extra_details: Mouse model used 600 mg/kg APAP for AALF and 300 mg/kg APAP for AALI. The reanalyzed GSE8075 gene array of peripheral blood monocytes from APAP-induced ALF patients showed 154 mRNAs increased and 37 decreased in patients who died versus those who survived; IL-10 mRNA was 2.43-fold higher in patients who died. The toxic APAP metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) is detoxified by hepatic glutathione; mice treated 24 h after APAP when hepatocyte injury is complete. Primary study focus is IL-10-expressing MDSC-like myeloid cells, not a new APAP DILI causality assessment.

raw_record.support_text: This study examines patients following self-poisoning with paracetamol (acetaminophen). Five patients with paracetamol poisoning developed fulminant hepatic failure requiring successful liver transplantation, and there were three deaths due to liver failure. Patients who fulfilled transplant criteria (n=9) were compared with those who did not (n=9) using hepatic artery resistive index (HARI) measurements; nine patients with fulminant hepatic failure had a pulmonary artery catheter in situ and showed elevated cardiac index.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) self-poisoning/overdose leading to fulminant hepatic failure. Eighteen poisoned patients were studied: nine fulfilled transplantation criteria and nine did not; five paracetamol-poisoned patients underwent successful liver transplantation and three died from liver failure. Hemodynamic assessments (hepatic artery resistive index, cardiac index) were the study focus; no biochemical pattern or reaction type was described.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of severe acetaminophen poisoning in a 23-year-old previously healthy woman who developed acute liver failure complicated by intracranial hypertension. A dose of 49 g of acetaminophen was ingested, and the patient developed acute liver failure, hepatic encephalopathy, and cerebral edema, and was listed for emergency liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Ingestion of 49 g acetaminophen 20 hours before admission; patient developed acute liver failure with grade III hepatic encephalopathy and cerebral edema, was listed for emergency liver transplantation, and was treated with intravenous N-acetylcysteine, plasmapheresis, and hemodialysis. Metabolite/cause of the fatal liver failure; intracranial hypertension was the clinical focus but not the toxic agent.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 62 adult ICU patients with acute liver failure (ALF), just over half of cases were attributed to paracetamol overdose. The study recorded the cause of ALF for each patient through routine clinical data; paracetamol overdose was reported as the etiology in just over half of the 62 ALF patients.
raw_record.extra_details: ALF defined as onset of overt liver failure over less than 8 weeks in the absence of known pre-existing liver disease; paracetamol overdose was the cause in just over half of the 62 ALF patients admitted to adult liver transplant ICUs in ANZ hospitals over a 4-year period. Cohort-level outcomes (60% fulfilled Kings College Criteria for transplantation, 20% underwent emergency liver transplantation, nearly a third died in ICU, only half achieved ELT-free survival) are reported for the whole ALF cohort, not specifically for paracetamol cases.

raw_record.support_text: A retrospective analysis of patients with paracetamol poisoning referred to the Scottish Liver Transplant Unit during 1992–2002 identified 454 patients referred with paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity within the 10-year period; 117 were selected for analysis of phosphate measurements at 48–96 hours post-overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol poisoning/overdose with fulminant hepatic failure; paracetamol is described as the most common cause of acute liver failure in North America and Europe. In the referred Scottish cohort (n=117 with phosphate data), 59 (50.4%) met King's College Hospital criteria, of whom 11 were transplanted and 48 died without transplant; 58 (49.6%) were spontaneous survivors. All patients received intravenous N-acetyl cysteine on hospital arrival. Day-2 (48–72 h) phosphate was significantly higher in nonsurvivors/transplanted patients than survivors (1.32 ± 1.06 vs 0.66 ± 0.26 mmol/L, P<0.001); day-3 difference was not significant. Prior studies referenced: Chung Sitrin Te reported low serum PO4 as a better-prognosis predictor in fulminant hepatic failure; Schmidt and Dalhoff found PO4 of 1.2 mmol/L at 48–96 h after overdose highly specific/sensitive with better predictive value than KCH criteria.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes acetaminophen overdose as a cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in the United Kingdom: only a small proportion of patients taking an acetaminophen overdose are at risk of liver damage, with less than 10% developing severe liver damage and only 1-2% developing ALF. In 1997 more than 38,000 patients were admitted to U.K. hospitals as a result of acetaminophen poisoning, 57 underwent emergency liver transplantation, and 562 deaths were reported in which acetaminophen ingestion was thought to have played a role.
raw_record.extra_details: Overdose (mostly deliberate self-poisoning) is the exposure setting; <10% of overdose patients develop severe liver damage and only 1-2% develop ALF, primarily due to small absorbed doses and early antidotal therapy. U.K. 1997 national data: >38,000 hospital admissions for acetaminophen poisoning, 57 emergency liver transplantations, 562 deaths in which acetaminophen ingestion was thought to play a role. Fatal outcomes were more common in older men and in those consuming acetaminophen/opiate combinations.

raw_record.support_text: Saunders et al. performed aminopyrine breath tests in 30 patients 24-36 hours after ingestion of 10 gm or more of acetaminophen to identify those with the most severe hepatic injury. Plasma acetaminophen half-lives were measured in the same subjects. The aminopyrine breath test correctly identified the 12 patients who developed severe liver injury or died, whereas plasma acetaminophen half-lives overlapped with values from patients who sustained little hepatic injury. The study is cited as evidence that acetaminophen overdose causes severe drug-induced hepatic injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 30 patients evaluated 24-36 hours after ingestion of 10 gm or more of acetaminophen; plasma acetaminophen half-lives measured and found to overlap between patients with little versus severe injury, so half-life was not prognostic; aminopyrine breath test identified the 12 patients who developed severe liver injury or died. Evidence cited from Saunders et al.

raw_record.support_text: In this Acute Liver Failure Study Group series, acetaminophen (APAP) protein adducts were detected in 95% of patients with clinically defined APAP overdose, and nearly one fifth of patients with ALF classified as indeterminate showed evidence of unrecognized acetaminophen toxicity. The paper refers to this as APAP-induced hepatotoxicity and APAP-induced ALF, and cautions that clinical criteria for assigning APAP as the cause of ALF in an emergency setting may over-diagnose APAP-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen hepatotoxicity manifesting as acute liver failure (ALF) in patients presenting to the Acute Liver Failure Study Group. APAP protein-adduct assay (cutoff ~1.0 nmol/mL) detected adducts in 95% of clinically defined APAP overdose patients; ~1/5 of indeterminate ALF cases showed occult acetaminophen toxicity not identified by experienced investigators. Hyper-acute liver injury pattern (low bilirubin, high ALT) was almost exclusively confined to adduct-positive groups. Mean adduct elimination half-life 1.73 days; therapeutic APAP 4 g/day in healthy adults produced a mean Cmax of 0.3 nmol/mL, ~two orders of magnitude below early overdose levels. Spontaneous survival 63.8% in clinically defined overdose group; NAC is the treatment under discussion but is not itself the injuring agent.

raw_record.support_text: In Group 1 (fifteen patients with acute parenchymal liver disease), the liver damage was caused by paracetamol overdose in 10 cases, hepatitis A in three, Epstein-Barr virus hepatitis in one, and an idiosyncratic reaction to pyrazinamide in the remaining case.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose was reported as the cause of acute parenchymal liver disease in 10 of 15 patients in Group 1 (the acute liver disease group).

raw_record.support_text: In the series reported by Schiødt et al (295 patients treated at 13 hospitals during 1994-1996), acetaminophen overdose was found to be the single most frequent cause of acute liver failure (ALF), accounting for 20% of cases in the US. Most instances of ALF caused by acetaminophen in the United Kingdom are the consequence of an overdose of the drug taken with suicidal or parasuicidal intent.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose accounted for 20% of ALF cases in the US nationwide series (Schiødt et al, 295 patients, 13 centers, 1994-1996); UK overdoses were taken with suicidal/parasuicidal intent. Spontaneous survival among acetaminophen-overdose ALF patients was 57%; more than three times as many acetaminophen-toxicity patients died without OLT than underwent OLT. The 20% US figure may underestimate true incidence because some centers contributed data only from transplant databases.

raw_record.support_text: The case report describes a 32-year-old woman who presented to a medical intensive care unit with acute liver failure secondary to an acetaminophen overdose. While awaiting transplant she was started on MARS therapy as a bridge to liver transplant. The paper frames the acetaminophen overdose as the cause of the acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient with acute liver failure secondary to acetaminophen overdose; anuric patient managed with Molecular Adsorbent Recirculating System (MARS) as a bridge to liver transplant. Exact acetaminophen dose not stated.

raw_record.support_text: Aminopyrine breath test values (percentage of administered 14C label excreted) were measured 24-36 hours after paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose in 30 patients, who were grouped according to severity of the ensuing liver damage; the limit of normal in 20 healthy controls and the mean per group are shown.
raw_record.extra_details: Alias: acetaminophen. The aminopyrine breath test was used to predict the extent of liver damage after acetaminophen overdose: mean 14CO2 excretion was 5.5% in patients who escaped hepatic injury, 2.9% in those with mild hepatic injury, and 0.2% in patients with a fatal outcome (30 patients, test performed 24-36 h after overdose).

raw_record.support_text: A 29 year old man admitted after allegedly taking 100 paracetamol tablets (50 g) had a paracetamol level of 0.21 mmol/l. His aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase rose to 3,795 U/l and 6,080 U/l, respectively, 3 days after taking paracetamol, with a maximum recorded bilirubin of 38 µmol/l and an INR of 2.1:1.0, indicating substantial liver injury in the setting of a paracetamol overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: Overdose of 50 g (100 tablets) paracetamol; patient recovered without hepatic encephalopathy. Peak AST 3,795 U/l and ALT 6,080 U/l on day 3 post-ingestion; maximum bilirubin 38 µmol/l and INR 2.1:1.0. Patient was on flupenthixol decanoate for manic depression (not implicated in the liver injury). The paper's primary focus was direct cardiotoxicity with abnormal ECG, not the liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: Among 24 patients with acute liver failure studied in a controlled pilot study of an extracorporeal liver assist device, the causes of acute liver failure were acetaminophen overdose (17 cases), non-A, non-B viral hepatitis (5 cases), and hepatotoxicity from antituberculous chemotherapy (2 cases).
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose was attributed as the cause of acute liver failure in 17 of 24 patients enrolled in a controlled pilot study of an extracorporeal liver assist device (ELAD).

raw_record.support_text: Although acetaminophen (APAP) is considered safe at therapeutic doses, overdoses can cause liver injury and acute liver failure. In the United States, 60,000–80,000 emergency department visits, 30,000–40,000 hospitalizations with more than 5,000 patients developing severe liver injury, and 300–500 deaths occur annually due to APAP overdose, and APAP overdose is the most frequent etiology of acute liver failure in the United States, the United Kingdom, and other mainly western countries.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP considered safe at therapeutic doses; injury is dose-related overdose injury. US annual estimates: 60,000–80,000 emergency department visits, 30,000–40,000 hospitalizations, >5,000 patients with severe liver injury, 300–500 deaths. APAP overdose is the most frequent etiology of acute liver failure (ALF) in the US, UK, and other western countries. N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is approved as a clinical antidote and has saved many overdose patients, though with a narrow therapeutic window and limited efficacy after very high overdoses.

raw_record.support_text: Buckley et al. examined clinical outcomes following single-dose activated charcoal (SDAC) administration in 981 patients with paracetamol overdose, who were treated with SDAC, no treatment, or gastric lavage. Results showed that patients in the AC group were significantly less likely to develop paracetamol hepatotoxicity, and patients who consumed 2.5 grams more of paracetamol received no treatment compared with those receiving gastric decontamination.
raw_record.extra_details: Overdose setting; Buckley et al. study of 981 paracetamol overdose patients comparing SDAC, no treatment, and gastric lavage showed significantly lower likelihood of developing paracetamol hepatotoxicity with activated charcoal; patients who consumed 2.5 g more paracetamol received no treatment compared with those receiving gastric decontamination (paracetamol=acetaminophen).

raw_record.support_text: The study concludes that the clinical outcome of acute liver failure (ALF) due to acetaminophen (AP) poisoning is satisfactory when specific supportive therapy and access to liver transplantation are available in highly specialized toxicology centers. This frames acetaminophen poisoning (overdose) as the cause of the acute liver failure in the studied patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective case series of patients with acute liver failure due to acetaminophen poisoning. Some patients with poor prognosis were listed for liver transplantation; those patients had significantly lower baseline blood pressure, higher serum AST, ALT, total bilirubin, and lactate, lower serum sodium, higher INR, and longer hospitalization, with aminotransferases, bilirubin, and INR rising within 2 days versus patients not listed for LT.

raw_record.support_text: In this study of acetaminophen poisoning patients, 1 patient with toxic hepatitis died of liver failure, and the overall mortality rate was 0.5%. The authors note that in US reports on acetaminophen-related acute hepatitis and liver failure, mortality has been reported at around 19–30%, and 27% of US patients with acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure died within 3 weeks. The paper attributes toxic hepatitis and liver failure to acetaminophen (paracetamol) poisoning.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen poisoning/overdose cohort; onset of toxic hepatitis within hours after exposure; injury attributed to hepatocellular mechanisms only following acetaminophen intoxication (Larson, 2007). The poisoning is managed with detoxification protocols including N-acetylcysteine (used in 78.6% of patients) and gastric lavage/activated charcoal; mortality 0.5% in the study cohort vs 19-30% in US reports, with 27% death within 3 weeks in US acute liver failure cases. Metabolic context: extensive glucuronide and sulfate conjugation with a minor microsomal oxidation route to a hepatotoxic reactive intermediate that undergoes GSH conjugation to cysteine and mercapturate conjugates.

raw_record.support_text: Clinical data from 52 anonymized patients (Remien et al. 2012) who presented to emergency rooms with acetaminophen (APAP) overdose were used; AST and ALT levels, time since ingestion, and initial APAP quantity were recorded. Four illustrative patients were selected based on quantity ingested: Patient A ingested 6.1 g APAP 3.9 days before admission showing low damage, Patient B 10.5 g at 4.7 days (mild damage), Patient C 20.5 g at 3.4 days (medium damage), and Patient D 27.1 g at 4.5 days (severe damage).
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective anonymized clinical data from Remien et al. 2012 (Model for Acetaminophen-induced Liver Damage, MALD; IRB-approved University of Utah); 52 patients, four illustrated here. Ingestion quantities 6.1-27.1 g with ED admission 3.4-4.7 days post-ingestion mapping to low/mild/medium/severe damage; AST and ALT levels and time since ingestion used. Zonal (centrilobular) hepatotoxicity aligns with clinical observations; drug diffusion model with timeframes to peak plasma concentration at t+3 h. Liver injury data reused from a published cohort to validate the Virtual Hepatic Lobule computational model, not newly reported cases.

raw_record.support_text: In referred overdose patients who also took dextropropoxyphene/paracetamol tablets together with 25 g of paracetamol, both patients became unconscious within 24 h and later developed signs of hepatic failure from which they died. The paper as a whole attributes hepatic failure and its mortality to paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose: patients with serum paracetamol levels above the treatment line had substantial mortality (e.g., 16/36 (44%) survival in referred 1982), and the most significant prognostic factor was delay between ingestion and presentation precluding antidote administration.
raw_record.extra_details: Series of local (1982) and referred (1982, 1983) paracetamol overdose patients; referred median presentation 30 h vs 8 h local; overall referred survival 56% (147 patients) with 60% having prothrombin time >50 s and 36% AST >1000 i.u. In local patients taking paracetamol/dextropropoxyphene tablets serum paracetamol never reached toxic levels and PT/AST remained normal. Antidote (N-acetylcysteine, methionine) prevented toxicity when given early; failure of timely antidote was a feature in 11 adverse cases. Concomitant alcohol (>80 g/day) did not significantly alter course or outcome.

raw_record.support_text: Reduced neutrophil adherence was detected in six of the 13 patients with fulminant hepatic failure, in all of whom the cause of hepatic failure was paracetamol overdose. The mean neutrophil adherence in these patients (56.2±8.7%) was significantly lower (p<0.01, Wilcoxon's rank test) than that of the control subjects.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol overdose was the cause of fulminant hepatic failure in all 13 studied patients; 6 of 13 showed reduced neutrophil adherence (mean 56.2±8.7%, p<0.01 vs controls). Direct effects of paracetamol on neutrophils are excluded because residual blood concentrations in these patients were virtually undetectable.

raw_record.support_text: The prognostic accuracy of SIRS and SOFA thresholds was examined in a prospectively collected cohort of 38 paracetamol-induced acute liver injury patients admitted to the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh. Seven patients died or underwent emergency OLT; all manifested a SIRS response, had a SOFA score >7 and a modified SOFA >5 within 96 h of overdose. Four patients were transplanted, three died without transplantation, and 18 (47.4%) were ever encephalopathic (acute liver failure), confirming that paracetamol overdose causes acute liver injury/acute liver failure with death and liver transplantation as outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: Single time point paracetamol overdose setting. In the derivation cohort single time point overdoses were studied; in a validation cohort of 38 paracetamol-induced acute liver injury patients (all received NAC), ALT 5198 (2974-7978) IU/L, bilirubin 81 (32-113) umol/L, PT 41 (29-73) s; 18 (47.4%) ever encephalopathic (ALF), 12 (31.6%) grade 3-4 hepatic encephalopathy; 4 (10.5%) transplanted, 3 (7.9%) died without transplantation, 31 (81.6%) spontaneous survival. Mild/moderate intrinsic direct hepatotoxicity typical of paracetamol overdose, though reaction mode not explicitly labeled. All seven non-survivors (death or OLT) had SIRS, SOFA >7 and modified SOFA >5 by 96 h post-overdose.

raw_record.support_text: In the context of the US Acute Liver Failure Study Group (ALFSG), a prospective study of the etiology and outcomes of adults with acute liver failure (ALF) and severe acute liver injury (ALI), the paper states that acetaminophen overdose is the leading cause of both ALI and ALF, followed by idiosyncratic DILI, autoimmune hepatitis, and indeterminate etiologies.
raw_record.extra_details: Injury is acute liver injury (ALI) and acute liver failure (ALF), defined as new-onset jaundice or hepatitis with INR > 2.0 and no encephalopathy at enrollment; stated as the leading cause of both ALI and ALF within the ALFSG prospective cohort.

raw_record.support_text: Of the 68 DILI cases due to other medications, 36 were attributed to acetaminophen overdose. Among the remaining 32 cases, 17 were due to various antibiotics, 3 due to lipid lowering agents, 2 due to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, 2 due to carbamazepine, and 8 cases due to other individual drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: 36 of 68 non-study DILI cases attributed to acetaminophen overdose.

raw_record.support_text: All four patients were in grade IV coma due to fulminant hepatic failure. Two of them—a 27-year-old male and an 18-year-old female—had liver failure as a result of paracetamol overdose. Each patient had received between 1 and 5 four-hour periods of hemodialysis using a polyacrylonitrile membrane prior to being hemoperfused with albumin-coated resin.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients (27-year-old male, 18-year-old female) in grade IV coma due to fulminant hepatic failure attributed to paracetamol overdose; both were undergoing hemodialysis and resin hemoperfusion for hepatic failure. Paracetamol is also known as acetaminophen.

raw_record.support_text: Among three patients perfused while in coma owing to acute liver failure, the third had liver necrosis owing to paracetamol overdosage. The patient was unresponsive to painful stimuli; improvement in the level of consciousness occurred, and the patient was among the two alive and well 8 months and 4 months, respectively, after treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case of liver necrosis from paracetamol overdosage; patient presented in coma from acute liver failure and unresponsive to painful stimuli; treated with liver perfusion; survived and was alive and well at 8 months follow-up.

raw_record.support_text: All 10 studied acute liver failure (ALF) patients had paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose (POD; abbreviated POD in the table) as the recorded etiology of ALF, fulfilling King's College Criteria for liver transplantation. Six underwent orthotopic liver transplantation, while the other 4 died. The case series reports 10 patients with drug-induced acute liver failure attributed to paracetamol overdose and exceeding therapeutic exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: 10 ALF patients (aged 19-46, 7 female, 3 male) all listed with paracetamol overdose as etiology (POD). All fulfilled King's College Criteria for liver transplantation and required mechanical ventilation and veno-venous hemofiltration; 6 underwent orthotopic liver transplantation and 4 died (2 while awaiting transplant, 2 not listed for psychosocial contraindications). Highest recorded prothrombin times >100-121 s; ALT 2,461-10,460 IU/L; bilirubin 41-145 µmol/L; time delay between poisoning and hospital admission 38-90 h or unknown. Three patients reported additional alcohol abuse.

raw_record.support_text: The study concerns APAP (acetaminophen)-induced liver injury and shows that MCJ is central to this injury in vitro and in vivo; repression of MCJ reduces liver damage triggered by APAP and increases liver regeneration. Human data show higher MCJ levels in livers from patients admitted with life-threatening overdoses of APAP compared with healthy individuals, and the mouse model is described as mimicking the acute liver failure caused by this compound.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP overdose patients had higher liver MCJ levels than healthy individuals; paper identifies MCJ (mitochondrial co-chaperone J-protein) as a druggable target to treat APAP-induced liver injury. Supporting animal data: MCJ KO mice and siMCJ-treated mice were protected from APAP (360 mg/kg) hepatotoxicity, with reduced necrosis, ALT/AST, oxidative stress (ROS), inflammation, and restoration of serum transaminases to normal. Human relevance is limited to the MCJ-level comparison; the APAP-DILI causal relation itself is presented as an induced-injury construction throughout.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol overdose is reported as the main cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in the UK (60.9%) and USA (46%), and has recently become a common cause in other European countries. In the UK, ALF/fulminant hepatic failure is more often due to intentional paracetamol overdose, whereas in the USA paracetamol hepatotoxicity is usually due to accidental overdose (multiple doses for pain relief without suicidal intent).
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol overdose is the main cause of ALF in the UK (60.9%) and USA (46%). Comparison of 122 intentional vs 131 unintentional overdose subjects: unintentional subjects were older (median 38 vs 32 years, p=0.002), more often used multiple paracetamol-containing preparations (38% vs 5%, p<0.0001), less often reported depression (24% vs 45%, p<0.0001), and had severe (grade 3 and 4) hepatic encephalopathy on admission more often than intentional overdose subjects (55% vs 39%, p=0.002). Median paracetamol dose was lower in accidental (12 g) than suicidal-intent (20 g) overdose (p=0.009). Chronic alcohol consumption and malnutrition likely contributed to liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: In this population-based Canadian cohort of patients hospitalized for acetaminophen overdose, acetaminophen-related hepatotoxicity developed in 4.5% of patients. Acetaminophen hepatotoxicity was associated with prolonged median length of stay (8 vs 3 days) and higher hospital costs, and in multivariate models was independently associated with increased LOS and costs. Patients who developed hepatotoxicity were more than 40 times more likely to die in hospital than those without liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Administrative data study (n=1543) of Canadian patients hospitalized for acetaminophen overdose; hepatotoxicity rate 4.5%. Median LOS 3 days (range 1-162) and cost $2,123 overall; hepatotoxicity associated with prolonged LOS (8 vs 3 days) and cost ($5,276 vs $2,010). In multivariate models controlling for age, sex, comorbidities, hepatotoxicity independently associated with increased LOS (P=.01) and costs (P=.001). In-hospital death more common with hepatotoxicity (14.3% vs 0.3%; RR 42.1, 95% CI 14.8-119.8); 15/1543 (1.0%) died during index admission. Predictors of hepatotoxicity included older age, unintentional overdose (OR 5.18), alcohol abuse (OR 2.21), liver disease (OR 3.50), and cirrhosis (OR 2.75). Survival at 5 and 10 years lower in patients with hepatotoxicity (75.5% and 72.1%) versus without (95.9% and 94.1%).

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol is the major metabolite of phenacetin and the paper notes that acute paracetamol overdose may result in hepatotoxicity, referencing the first British report of hepatotoxicity in paracetamol overdose (1966). Four cases of paracetamol overdose are described, and the pharmacodynamic rationale for using dimercaprol as a specific antidote to the hepatotoxic effects is discussed.
raw_record.extra_details: Four overdose cases described; paper frames paracetamol as remarkably safe at therapeutic dosages, with hepatotoxicity occurring only after acute overdose. Dimercaprol, a sulphydryl-containing compound, is proposed as a specific antidote based on paracetamol pharmacodynamics. The first British report of paracetamol-overdose hepatotoxicity was in 1966 (Davidson 1966).

raw_record.support_text: In this single-centre study of 39 therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) treatments in 17 patients with acute liver failure (ALF), the reported causes of ALF were paracetamol toxicity in 13 patients, alcoholic hepatitis in 2, Budd-Chiari syndrome in 1 and herbal remedy ingestion in 1, with 6 patients surviving and 11 dying.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) toxicity was the attributed cause of acute liver failure in 13 of 17 ALF patients in a therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) cohort; patient outcome by liver transplant status shown in Figure 1, with overall 6 survivors and 11 deaths; sufficient data were not available to determine TPE effect on intracranial pressure.

raw_record.support_text: The 47-year-old patient reported taking one to two 500 mg acetaminophen tablets every two to three hours over the past week (6,000-12,000 mg total/day), a repeated supratherapeutic ingestion, after initially well-controlled therapeutic doses. Labs showed AST 1,899 IU/L (normal 8-48) and ALT 533 IU/L (normal 7-56), indicating severe liver damage; the paper presents this as a case of acute liver failure (ALF) caused by repeated supratherapeutic ingestions of acetaminophen, with the patient achieving full recovery.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic/repeated supratherapeutic ingestion (RSTI) of acetaminophen causing ALF; estimated dose 6,000-12,000 mg/day over the past week (therapeutic maximum is 4,000 mg/24 h); AST 1,899 IU/L, ALT 533 IU/L, INR 1.0; managed with N-acetylcysteine when liver transplantation was not a viable option; patient achieved full recovery. Severe liver toxicity defined as peak AST or ALT >1,000 IU/L; toxicity mediated by the toxic metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) formed via CYP2E1, with genetic variants affecting production.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 169 adults with acute liver failure (ALF) admitted to the Victorian Liver Transplant Unit between 2002 and 2017, paracetamol toxicity was the most common aetiology, accounting for 50% of cases with increased incidence compared with a historical 1988-2001 cohort (P = 0.046). Spontaneous recovery occurred in 72% of paracetamol toxicity cases compared with 31% for non-paracetamol ALF (P < 0.001).
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol toxicity (overdose) was the most common aetiology of ALF, 50% of cases, with rising incidence over 30 years; spontaneous recovery in 72% of paracetamol cases. Cohort of 169 adults (>16 years) with ALF from the Victorian Liver Transplant Unit database, 2002-2017, compared with a historical 1988-2001 cohort. Overall transplant-free survival improved to 52% vs 38% (P=0.032); 42 patients (25%) underwent emergency liver transplantation with 1-, 3- and 5-year survival of 81%, 78% and 72%; 9 of 59 waitlisted patients died awaiting transplant. Other aetiologies: viral hepatitis 15%, non-paracetamol drug/toxin liver injury 10% (no specific agents named). Phenotype is acute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: In the discussion of three cases of acute hyperammonemic encephalopathy of different etiologies, the authors describe that in case 2 (the toxic etiology), the patient presented with fulminant acute hepatic failure following an overdose of acetaminophen.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose resulted in fulminant acute hepatic failure complicated by acute hyperammonemic encephalopathy (toxic etiology, case 2 of 3 reported cases). The paper's focus is MRI findings of acute hyperammonemic encephalopathy; no dose, latency, or case-2 outcome details are provided in this window.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective poison center evaluation, 2231 patients with acetaminophen (APAP) exposure were identified. Of these, 537 had a multiplication product <1500 mg/L IU/L (279 with a detectable APAP level, 258 undetectable). One patient became hepatotoxic, giving a negative predictive value of 99.8%. The authors concluded that a multiplication product threshold of 1500 mg/L IU/L had a high negative predictive value, but not 100%, for hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective poison center study (2231 patient exposures). Alias: APAP. Hepatotoxicity outcome predicted by multiplication product of APAP concentration and transaminase level; threshold of 1500 mg/L IU/L yielded a negative predictive value of 99.8% for hepatotoxicity (1 of 537 patients below threshold became hepatotoxic). The threshold was high but not 100% predictive.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 110 patients with fulminant hepatic failure (FHF), the cause was acetaminophen overdose in 88 patients. The paper reports multiple clinical outcomes in this acetaminophen-induced FHF group, including nonsurvival (patients who died had lower factor V levels) and the use of liver transplantation, establishing acetaminophen overdose as the cause of FHF in these patients.
raw_record.extra_details: 88 of 110 FHF patients had acetaminophen-induced hepatic necrosis/FHF; median age 26 years (range 13-60). On admission grades of coma: 45 in grade IV, 7 in grade III, 9 in grade II, 27 in grade I; 23 of 36 patients in grade I/II progressed to deeper coma. Some patients underwent orthotopic liver transplantation; nonsurvivors had significantly lower factor V (median 5%) than survivors (median 10%). Admission labs for the acetaminophen group: INR 6.9 (2.0-17.5), AST 3150 IU/L (100-15000), bilirubin 73 µmol/L, creatinine 257 µmol/L, platelets 101x10^9/L. No single factor V cutoff separated survivors from nonsurvivors; King's criteria (pH, INR, renal failure, coma) were more accurate for transplant selection.

raw_record.support_text: Patients diagnosed at the Universitair Ziekenhuis Leuven between 2011 and 2013 with acute liver failure (ALF) due to acetaminophen (APAP) intoxication were treated by orthotopic liver transplantation, and explant liver samples were obtained for microarray analysis. Liver samples from three patients with ALF due to APAP intoxication and from two individuals deceased from brain damage were used.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients with ALF due to acetaminophen intoxication (diagnosed at UZ Leuven 2011–2013) required and were treated by orthotopic liver transplantation; explant human liver samples were used for whole-genome microarray analysis. Controls were liver samples from two individuals deceased from brain damage. The in vitro MTT/proteomic exposure experiments used hSKP-HPC, HepaRG and HepG2 cells and are cell-assay data, not human DILI evidence.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective cohort of 145 non-transplanted patients with fulminant hepatic failure at the Queen Elizabeth Hospital, Birmingham (1990-1994), acetaminophen overdose was the commonest cause of fulminant hepatic failure, accounting for 120 of 145 cases. The study group had a median age of 31 (range 18-84) years and 85 (59%) were female.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose was the leading cause of fulminant hepatic failure (120 of 145 study-group patients; an additional 22 of 81 transplanted patients); fulminant hepatic failure is defined here as encephalopathy developing within 8 weeks of symptom onset in a patient without previously known liver disease. King's College Hospital (KCH) criteria for acetaminophen-induced FHF include pH <7.3 at 24 h or more following the overdose after correction of hypovolemia, or concurrent serum creatinine >300 micromol/l, grade 3/4 encephalopathy and prothrombin time >100 s.

raw_record.support_text: The paper attributes the first liver recipient's highly urgent liver transplantation to acetaminophen-induced fulminant hepatic failure, describing 'severe acetaminophen intoxication' and 'very severe paracetamol poisonings' whose fatal complications may result from a direct effect of paracetamol metabolites or from raised intracranial pressure. A liver-support device was described as ineffective given brain edema in this fulminant hepatic failure setting.
raw_record.extra_details: The first liver recipient, a 21-year-old woman (etiology Paracetamol in the reported source table), developed acetaminophen-induced fulminant hepatic failure requiring highly urgent liver transplantation, which was complicated by brain death from cerebral hemorrhage/edema; urgent transplantation within 24 h was needed. The paper also cites 'severe acetaminophen intoxication' and up to 33% of very severe paracetamol poisonings having lung complications either from a direct effect of paracetamol metabolites or from raised intracranial pressure.

raw_record.support_text: The paper examines liver injury or hepatotoxicity developing secondary to paracetamol overdose, comparing NACSTOP trial patients given either abbreviated or full acetylcysteine regimens with two comparator groups of non-trial patients who developed liver injury or hepatotoxicity from paracetamol overdose. Acute liver injury (ALI) was defined as ALT >50 U/L and hepatotoxicity as ALT >1000 U/L; affected patients required prolonged acetylcysteine infusions beyond 20 h until ALT peaked and was falling and INR was <2.
raw_record.extra_details: NACSTOP trial context with abbreviated (12-h) vs full (20-h) acetylcysteine regimens and additional non-trial comparator groups. ALI defined as ALT >50 U/L; hepatotoxicity as ALT >1000 U/L. Affected patients received prolonged acetylcysteine until ALT peaked and fell and INR <2. Exclusion criteria included age <16 years, pregnancy, unknown time of ingestion, and modified-release paracetamol overdose. Paracetamol metabolites (APAP-Cys, APAP-Sul, APAP-Glu, APAP-GSH, APAP-Mer, APAP) measured by LC-MS/MS were analysed as predictors of ALI.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that APAP (acetaminophen) overdoses remain the leading cause of acute liver failure (ALF), and that both intentional and unintentional APAP overdoses cause APAP-related acute liver failure (ALF) and acute liver injury (ALI) in humans. Conditions such as depression, alcohol use disorder, substance use disorder, and chronic pain were strongly associated with risk of APAP-related ALF and ALI.
raw_record.extra_details: Registry-based evidence from the Acute Liver Failure Study Group (ALFSG) registry. Acetaminophen overdose is described as the leading cause of acute liver failure in the US, with both intentional and unintentional overdoses associated with ALF and acute liver injury (ALI). Study included 95 APAP overdose cases (median reported dose 10,000 mg/day overall; 6,000 mg/day in unintentional and 20,000 mg/day in intentional overdoses). Depression, alcohol use disorder, substance use disorder, chronic pain, and impulsivity were strongly associated with and may influence APAP-related ALF/ALI risk.

raw_record.support_text: Serum miRNA profiles were compared between a lethal case of acetaminophen overdose, previously measured non-lethal cases of acetaminophen overdose, and healthy controls. Acetaminophen-induced liver injury was corroborated by ALT/AST and TBIL levels; the lethal poisoning case showed the highest ALT and AST at the early time point, and one non-lethal overdose case without elevated ALT was indistinguishable from healthy participants. The degree of PCA shift was proportional to the degree of liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a single lethal acetaminophen (paracetamol) poisoning followed longitudinally from hospitalization to death, compared with previously studied non-lethal acetaminophen overdose cases and healthy participants. Acetaminophen is described as the most commonly used analgesic/antipyretic with frequent supra-therapeutic poisonings. Liver injury was assessed via ALT, AST, TBIL, INR and MELD scores; the lethal case developed acetaminophen-induced lethal acute liver failure (ALF), with severe coagulopathy (INR reaching ~5 within 40 h of admission) and loss of liver function accompanied by rising TBIL and decreasing ALT; one non-lethal case without elevated ALT was indistinguishable from healthy participants. GSE analysis of PC1 implicated pathways related to autophagy, cell-cycle and Notch signaling consistent with molecular mechanisms of acetaminophen hepatotoxicity; PC2-related pathways involved fibrosis, coagulation and thrombosis.

raw_record.support_text: The study reports causes of hyperacute liver failure (HALF) as acetaminophen poisoning (n = 10), fulminant hepatitis B (n = 2), and toxic hepatitis from disulfiram (n = 1). Patients were studied on the day after onset of grade 3-4 hepatic encephalopathy. Ten of the thirteen patients had acetaminophen poisoning as the attributed cause of their liver failure, several fulfilling King's College Hospital transplant criteria.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen poisoning was the cause of hyperacute liver failure (HALF, hepatic encephalopathy grade 3-4 within 7 days) in 10 of 13 patients. Of the 10 acetaminophen patients, patients 1, 3, 8, and 9 died (the remainder survived); patients 1 and 8 fulfilled King's College Hospital criteria. Reported INR 1.9-7.4, creatinine 64-678 µmol/L, HE grade 3-4. Context: study of MARS (Molecular Adsorbent Recirculating System) treatment in HALF.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective analysis of 102 patients with acute liver failure (ALF) treated between 1996 and 2005, the most common causes of ALF were indeterminate liver failure (21%), acute hepatitis B (18%), acetaminophen ingestion (16%), and Budd-Chiari syndrome (9%). Additionally, the paper cites the U.S. Acute Liver Failure Group prospective study in which acetaminophen overdose (39%) was the most common ALF etiology and King's College reported 57% acetaminophen toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Paper's primary focus is prognosis prediction, but acetaminophen is explicitly attributed as a cause of ALF. In this cohort acetaminophen ingestion accounted for 16% of 102 ALF cases; cited U.S. prospective study reported acetaminophen overdose in 39% and King's College Hospital reported 57% acetaminophen toxicity. Acetaminophen is described as the dominant ALF etiology in London (55%) and Copenhagen (74%) in an international survey.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 68 patients admitted with hepatitis associated with coagulation abnormalities, the paper classifies the etiology of hepatitis by cause. There was a higher proportion of subjects with a favorable etiology, which the authors define as including acetaminophen overdose, hepatitis A, and hepatitis B, in the survivor group (58% versus 13% in non-survivors, P<0.04). All 12 patients with acetaminophen overdose survived, with complete resolution of acute hepatitis within 3 weeks of admission.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose was classified among favorable etiologies of hepatitis along with hepatitis A and hepatitis B; 12 acetaminophen overdose patients were all in the survivor group (10 listed under 'Paracetamol' in Table 1 with 0 in non-survivors) and all survived with complete resolution of acute hepatitis within 10-21 days. This was not otherwise detailed as a dedicated DILI characterization.

raw_record.support_text: In the study, causes of fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) among the 16 patients were acetaminophen intoxication (n = 12), unknown (n = 3), and acute hepatitis B (n = 1). All patients were in stage 3 to 4 hepatic encephalopathy on mechanical ventilation. This explicitly attributes acetaminophen intoxication as the cause of acute liver failure in these patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Amid 16 patients with fulminant hepatic failure, 12 were attributed to acetaminophen intoxication (1 to acute hepatitis B, 3 unknown). All were in stage 3 to 4 hepatic encephalopathy on mechanical ventilation; 11 of 16 met King's College liver transplantation criteria. The paper studies cerebral blood flow and hemodynamics; no further clinical characterization of the liver injury is given.

raw_record.support_text: A prospective multicenter study in the United States showed that fulminant hepatic failure in adults was most often caused by an overdose of acetaminophen (in 39% of patients), followed by idiosyncratic drug reactions (13%), acute hepatitis B virus infection (7%), ischemic liver injury (6%), hepatitis A (4%), and autoimmune hepatitis (4%). The incidence of acetaminophen overdosing is lower in many other countries, perhaps because of differences in the selection of medication or in the prevalence of alcohol abuse (which lowers the threshold for acetaminophen overdosing).
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose was the most common cause of adult fulminant hepatic failure (39% of patients) in a prospective US multicenter study. Fulminant hepatic failure is defined as acute hepatitis with encephalopathy developing within 2 to 8 weeks after initial symptoms in a person with no history of liver disease. The incidence of acetaminophen overdosing is lower in many other countries, possibly due to differences in medication selection or the prevalence of alcohol abuse, which lowers the threshold for acetaminophen overdosing.

raw_record.support_text: In a North America series of 308 patients with acute liver failure, paracetamol (acetaminophen) was the most common cause (39% of cases), followed by indeterminate causes (17%), idiosyncratic drug reactions (13%), HBV and HAV infection (7%), and other causes (24%). In an earlier series of 459 patients (Detre et al., 1987-1991), drug- or toxin-induced liver injury accounted for 4.6% (paracetamol) and 10.7% (other drugs) of fulminant hepatitis cases. Prognosis data indicate patients with paracetamol overdose had relatively better spontaneous (transplant-free) survival: 31% (16/52) in a transplant-listed cohort and about 68% short-term survival in American series, whereas survival for non-paracetamol drug-related ALF was <25%.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol is reported as the single most common cause of acute liver failure/fulminant hepatitis in a North American series of 308 patients (39%), and in the Detre series (4.6% of 459). Prognosis passages refer to paracetamol overdose and intoxication; spontaneous transplant-free survival ~31% (16/52) in a transplant-listed cohort, and ~68% short-term survival in American series; patients with paracetamol overdose generally fared better than those with indeterminate cause or non-paracetamol drug-related ALF (<25% transplant-free survival). No biochemical pattern, histology, or reaction type is stated.

raw_record.support_text: Seven of 122 patients presented at least 18 hours after acute acetaminophen ingestions with no acetaminophen detectable in serum. Four manifested minor liver injury (AST >80 but <1,000 IU/L) and two, including one with high-dose alcohol use, experienced severe liver injury (AST >1,000 IU/L). All were hospitalized, six received NAC, all recovered, and none underwent liver transplantation.

raw_record.extra_details: Presented as a case report of a patient who took a paracetamol overdose and died on September 7. Liver weighed 1100 g and post-mortem biopsy showed acute hepatic necrosis with collapse of the reticulin pattern, complete centrilobular necrosis, fatty infiltration, hydropic change, cloudy swelling, and prominent cholestasis, with no cell regeneration. Authors note at least 5 reported cases of hepatic necrosis after paracetamol overdosage in man, 3 fatal; the lowest fatal dose recorded was 'at least 15 g' versus the rat lethal dose of 3.71 ± 0.80 g/kg. Patient also had extreme hypokalemia (1.4 mEq/L), severe hyperglycemia, cardiac arrest, oliguric renal failure and acute tubular necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: A 29-year-old male soldier presented with abdominal pain, vomiting, and sudden-onset jaundice. Initially diagnosed as ischemic liver damage, raised liver function tests and elevated prothrombin time led to detection of acetaminophen in blood and urine by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, and ultrasound evidence of hepatic necrosis gave the final diagnosis of acetaminophen poisoning causing drug-induced liver injury. The paper states acetaminophen hepatotoxicity can occur when the drug is misused or after an overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure; single 29-year-old male patient case
raw_record.extra_details: Toxic effects over 150 mg/kg single dose result in liver failure; ~10% of APAP is oxidized by CYP2E1 to the reactive toxic metabolite NAPQI, which depletes glutathione, causes oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, and depletes ATP stores; toxic metabolite NAPQI identified as the mechanism, not an independently causal entity. Patient's peak lab values included total bilirubin 938 µmol/L (day 4), ALT 7046 U/L (day 1), AST 5035 U/L (day 2), PT 20 sec (day 4), serum ferritin 63433 ng/ml; blood acetaminophen 9874 ng/ml (day 1) declining to undetectable by day 4; HBsAg, anti-HCV, CMV-PCR, and liver kidney microsomal antibodies negative. Four sequential stages of paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity described; Rumack-Matthew nomogram used for management; aminotransferases may rise above 10,000 IU/L.

raw_record.support_text: In a multivariate analysis of 645 cases of single-dose acetaminophen poisoning, the acetaminophen dose was a risk factor for hepatotoxicity, especially in nonalcoholic patients. Doses resulting in death ranged from 15 to 125 g, and 28 cases of severe hepatotoxicity (alanine transaminase level greater than 1,000 U/L) resulted from ingestion of a single dose of less than 12 g. Time to N-acetylcysteine was the most important risk factor for death, hepatic encephalopathy, and liver transplant, with mortality rising from 0.42% (time to NAC <12 h) to 19% (time to NAC >48 h).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single-dose acetaminophen poisoning (overdose); prognostic factors analyzed in 645 cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose of acetaminophen was a risk factor for hepatotoxicity, most importantly in nonalcoholic patients. Doses associated with death ranged from 15 to 125 g; 28 cases of severe hepatotoxicity (ALT >1,000 U/L) followed a single dose <12 g, 21 of them in regular alcohol abusers. Time to N-acetylcysteine was the dominant risk factor: mortality was 0.42% (95% CI 0.05-2.7) when time to NAC <12 h, rising to 6.1%, 13%, and 19% at >12, >24, and >48 h, with corresponding rates of hepatic encephalopathy of 1.3%, 12%, 25%, and 38%. Chronic alcohol abuse was an independent risk factor for HE (OR 4.21; 95% CI 2.42-7.32) and mortality (OR 3.52; 95% CI 1.78-6.97); acute alcohol ingestion was protective for HE (OR 0.40) and mortality (OR 0.12), mainly in chronic abusers. Age was a risk factor for HE and death/orthotopic liver transplantation. No sex-specific differences or effect of other drugs were found.

Paracetamol has been the main cause of DILI in the United States and England, and contributes roughly 10% of acute liver failure cases in European countries such as Portugal and Germany per the European Liver Transplant Registry. A study from Australia reported over 440 deaths from paracetamol in combination with codeine from accidental overdose, with roughly 25% also involving other sedating medications.

raw_record.extra_details: Outcome data across countries, including Australia (440+ deaths from paracetamol with codeine, 25% with other sedating drugs such as antihistamines; 8.8% death in ALF cases, 39 deaths total), UK (2163 cases, 65% of total ALF; 36% deaths, 778 total; 147 transplants), US (120 cases, 39% of ALF; 27% mortality, 6% transplant, 44/120 suicide attempts), Portugal (5 cases/3yr, 11% of ALF; 1 transplant), Germany (10 cases, 9.2% of ALF; 3 transplants, 1 death). raw_record.support_text: The study used high-throughput sequencing to evaluate global profiles of circulating miRNAs in the serum of human subjects with an accidental overdose of acetaminophen (APAP). raw_record.support_text: The paper states that although the liver is well established as the primary site of toxicity after acetaminophen (APAP) overdose, strong clinical evidence also indicates APAP overdose can be nephrotoxic. In the context of overdose, the text notes that acute liver failure after APAP overdose can progress to multi-organ failure if the patient does not spontaneously recover or receive a liver transplant, and reports that data from 375 definitive APAP overdose patients indicate kidney dysfunction after APAP overdose strongly correlates with severe liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen (APAP) overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: Discussed as dose-related direct toxicity initiated by CYP2E1-catalyzed generation of the reactive metabolite NAPQI, which forms protein adducts. Acute liver failure after APAP overdose can progress to multi-organ failure if the patient does not recover or receive a liver transplant. Data from 375 definitive APAP overdose patients show kidney dysfunction strongly correlates with severe liver injury; creatinine (kidney function) is included in the MELD score used for liver transplant decisions.

raw_record.support_text: In this acute liver failure (ALF) registry cohort (1998-2013, n = 2070), 955 patients were classified as having APAP (acetaminophen) toxicity, and approximately 90% of APAP-overdose patients received intravenous or oral N-acetylcysteine. The cohort represents APAP overdose as a cause of acute liver failure, with outcomes at 21 days including liver transplantation and transplant-free survival.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen (APAP) overdose; ALF registry/cohort population.
raw_record.extra_details: 955 patients with APAP toxicity in an ALF registry cohort (1998-2013; n=2070). Approximately 90% of APAP-overdose patients received N-acetylcysteine (88.7% early 1998-2005 vs 91.7% later 2006-2013; P=0.117). Outcomes at 21 d included liver transplantation (461/2070 received transplant), overall survival 1478/2070 (71.4%), and transplant-free survival 1054/2070 (50.9%). N-acetylcysteine is an antidote, not the causal agent.

raw_record.support_text: Patients: 10 patients with severe acute liver failure (ALF) secondary to acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose (mean age 31 yr, range 21-46 yr, 7 female) presenting to Edinburgh Royal Infirmary were included. All fulfilled King's College criteria for poor prognosis, were managed with a standardized protocol, and 8 of 10 were treated for raised intracranial pressure. All underwent continuous veno-venous hemofiltration, were enrolled within the first 48 hours of ICU admission with grade IV hepatic encephalopathy, and required mechanical ventilation. Patients were followed until liver transplantation or death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose setting; patients with severe ALF fulfilling King's College criteria for poor prognosis in the ICU.
raw_record.extra_details: 10 cases; mean age 31 yr (range 21-46 yr), 7 female; grade IV hepatic encephalopathy; all required mechanical ventilation and continuous veno-venous hemofiltration; 8 of 10 treated for raised intracranial pressure; study focused on measuring cytokines, chemokines, and ADMA (asymmetric dimethylarginine), not a causality or mechanism paper. Paper explicates paracetamol as synonym for acetaminophen.

raw_record.support_text: Of 75 retained patients evaluated in the ED with a diagnosis of APAP (acetaminophen) intoxication, 41 with APAP concentrations below the limit for possible risk of hepatotoxicity were excluded; none of these developed hepatotoxicity. The remaining 27 patients (meeting inclusion criteria) were divided into short-, intermediate-, and long-course NAC treatment groups, and hepatotoxicity, defined as a serum aminotransferase (AST or ALT) concentration >1000 IU/L, was the primary outcome measure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen intoxication/overdose; all patients were diagnosed with APAP intoxication and evaluated in the emergency department (24 women, 3 men; mean age 26.7 years, range 12-60).
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity outcome was defined as serum AST or ALT >1000 IU/L. Study comprised 27 patients grouped by NAC therapy duration: short-course (<=36 h, n=17), intermediate-course (37-72 h, n=4), and long-course (>=73 h, n=6). Comparisons were made with historical controls receiving fixed-duration oral NAC for 72 h or intravenous NAC for 20 h. 2 NAC-noncompliant patients recovered; 41 patients with APAP below risk threshold developed no hepatotoxicity. No statistical analysis was performed due to small sample size.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that determination of plasma acetaminophen concentrations and the resulting plasma half-life of elimination serve as prognostic indicators of potential hepatic injury following an acetaminophen overdosage, and that a half-life greater than 4 hr is often associated with liver injury. The report describes two patients who each allegedly ingested greater than 13 gm of acetaminophen (APAP), in whom serial plasma concentrations and half-life were obtained by colorimetric and HPLC methods.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen overdosage; the two patients each allegedly ingested greater than 13 gm of APAP.
raw_record.extra_details: Plasma APAP half-life of elimination is presented as a prognostic indicator of potential hepatic toxicity; a half-life greater than 4 hr is often associated with liver injury. Serial plasma concentrations were measured by a colorimetric (nitrous acid chromophore; Glynn and Kendal) method and HPLC; the colorimetric method overestimates drug concentration below about 50-100 µg/ml, producing falsely prolonged half-lives. The purpose of the report is assay-method comparison rather than establishing the hepatotoxicity itself.

raw_record.support_text: A 20-year-old female presented with acetaminophen overdose (30 g) with more than 24 h elapsed since ingestion, resulting in critical hepatic failure and loss of consciousness (Glasgow Coma Score of 4). Despite passing the golden time for antidote administration, NAC was given (three-bag regimen followed by 3 g q8h); the patient improved, was extubated on day 4, and discharged on day 10 without needing liver transplantation. The report describes hepatic failure and liver injury due to acetaminophen toxicity from the overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen overdose (30 g) with more than 24 h since ingestion; the woman was a liver-transplantation candidate before late NAC administration.
raw_record.extra_details: 20-year-old (60 kg) female; overdose of 30 g acetaminophen; jaundice and abdominal pain after 3 days; Glasgow Coma Score 4; treated with three-bag NAC regimen followed by 3 g q8h despite passing the golden window; improved by day 2, extubated on day 4, discharged on day 10; no liver transplant needed; acetaminophen-induced fulminant hepatic failure. NAC and NAPQI are discussed as antidote and toxic metabolite, not as independent causal entities.

raw_record.support_text: A woman treated for drug-resistant tuberculosis with isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and streptomycin was hospitalized 24 h after ingesting 15 to 20 tablets of acetaminophen (300 mg per tablet; 4.5 to 6.0 g total), complaining of abdominal pain. raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen overdose (ingestion of 15-20 tablets, 4.5-6.0 g); the patient was concurrently receiving antituberculous therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, streptomycin), which was stopped at admission, so co-medication is an unresolved background factor in this susceptible patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Hospitalized 24 h after ingestion with abdominal pain; liver palpable 2 cm below right costal margin. Admission labs: PT 14.1 s, total bilirubin 18.8 µmol/L (1.1 mg/dl), AST 490 U/L, ALT 248 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 58 U/L; blood acetaminophen 11 µg/ml. Worst liver function 24-48 h after admission: bilirubin 18.8 µmol/L, PT 17.2 s, AST 1,200 U/L, ALT 1,616 U/L. Treated with N-acetylcysteine 1.2 g every 4 h for 3 days; recovered and discharged on hospital day 8. Antituberculous therapy resumed with pyrazinamide, ethambutol, ciprofloxacin, capreomycin without further difficulty; treatment completed July 1992.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that hepatotoxicity is a common complication following acetaminophen overdose and can lead to acute liver failure (ALF), noting that acetaminophen is one of the most common causes of ALF in the USA and UK. It reports that without treatment acetaminophen overdose leads to 0.4% mortality and that at least half of people with a blood acetaminophen level above the UK standard treatment line manifest with severe liver damage, with cerebral edema a major cause of death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen overdose (ingestion of 7 g or more of acetaminophen tablets); study cohort restricted to male patients; all patients received standard N-acetylcysteine antidotal treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity described as a common consequence of acetaminophen overdose that may lead to acute liver failure. 64 acetaminophen-overdose patients (age 15-85, all male) studied. Prothrombin time is noted to show the severity of hepatic necrosis; PT rose from 13.9±0.36 s (admission, range 11-21) to 15.7±1.1 s (48 h). Severe liver damage documented in at least half of patients with blood acetaminophen above the UK treatment line; hepatotoxicity accounts for 42% of US acute liver failure cases at tertiary-care centers and one-third of deaths; without treatment mortality is 0.4%; cerebral edema is a major cause of death.
