raw_record.support_text: The report describes cases of severe liver damage and toxic hepatitis in patients who chronically ingested moderately excessive amounts of acetaminophen. The first patient's severe liver damage from chronic ingestion of moderately excessive acetaminophen was attributed to concurrent chronic alcohol abuse (which presumably induced his cytochrome P-450 enzyme system, increasing susceptibility), and a second patient developed toxic hepatitis after ingesting excessive acetaminophen doses on two occasions, with negative nitrogen balance/cachexia and low serum albumin possibly lowering hepatic glutathione stores.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic abuse of moderately excessive acetaminophen doses in metabolically susceptible patients; concurrent chronic alcohol abuse (case 1) or cachexia with low serum albumin and suspected reduced hepatic glutathione stores (case 2).
raw_record.extra_details: Cases of serious liver damage from chronic abuse of acetaminophen in susceptible patients. Reported post-cessation serum acetaminophen levels of 37 and 15 µg/ml more than 24 h after stopping ingestion, described as in the toxic range (normal therapeutic 4-h level <9 µg/ml). In supporting animal work, alcohol and glutathione-depleting agents (diethylmaleate) potentiate acetaminophen-induced hepatic necrosis in mice, and protein restriction depletes glutathione in rats; diethylstilbestrol and ethacrynic acid also deplete glutathione in animals.

raw_record.support_text: Among 27 DILI patients analyzed, a unique case of acute hepatic failure was caused by abusive consumption of paracetamol (APAP) over time, without other relevant comorbidities. The 40-year-old male patient presented with hypotension, drowsiness, peripheral cyanosis, icterus, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and altered laboratory values (AST > 4,600 U/L, creatinine 4.6 mg/dL). Serum APAP at admission (220 μg/mL) indicated possible liver toxicity, N-acetylcysteine was given, and post-mortem liver analysis 2 days after admission showed extensive necrosis, congestion, infiltration, hemorrhage and ischaemia, all signs compatible with a hepatotoxic etiology.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic abusive (supratherapeutic) consumption over time; single male patient (40 years) with several prior suicide attempts; no other relevant comorbidities.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient presented with hypotension (blood pressure 70/40), drowsiness, peripheral cyanosis, conjunctival icterus, right upper quadrant abdominal pain; laboratory values AST > 4,600 U/L, creatinine 4.6 mg/dL, leukocytosis; serum APAP concentration 220 μg/mL at admission (>4 h post ingestion), indicating possible liver toxicity by the Rumack-Matthew nomogram. Treated with N-acetylcysteine. Post-mortem liver examination showed extensive necrosis, congestion, infiltration, hemorrhage and ischaemia.

raw_record.support_text: A 45-year-old man with a history of alcohol abuse and excessive daily use of paracetamol of approximately 20 tablets (500 mg each) for the past 2 months presented with jaundice, fever, hepatomegaly, and acute ischemia of the left leg. Hematology showed prothrombin time 29.0 s, INR 2.90; biochemistry showed severe hepatic enzyme elevation (AST 4840 U/L, ALT 2713 U/L, LDH 4114 U/L, GGT 682 U/L, total bilirubin 7.81 mg/dL). The patient had significant coagulopathy with acquired deficiencies of antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S; after successful thrombectomy and intensive treatment he recovered fully and was discharged on acenocoumarol.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic alcohol consumption co-exposure; excessive daily use of approximately 20 tablets (500 mg each, about 10 g/day) for the past 2 months.
raw_record.extra_details: Alcohol-paracetamol syndrome presenting with hepatic failure and acute limb arterial thrombosis. Jaundice, fever up to 38.8°C, hepatomegaly; transaminases AST 4840 U/L, ALT 2713 U/L, LDH 4114 U/L, GGT 682 U/L, total bilirubin 7.81 mg/dL (4.42 mg/dL direct); co-existing significant coagulopathy (PT 29.0 s, INR 2.90) with acquired deficiencies of antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S. Patient discharged 20 days after admission with complete recovery, on acenocoumarol. Diagnosis ascribed to alcohol-paracetamol syndrome rather than graded by a causality instrument.

raw_record.support_text: A 53-year-old male chronic alcoholic ingesting about 10 g of acetaminophen over two days developed severe hepatotoxicity. On autopsy the liver showed massive hepatic necrosis with only a rim of remaining hepatocytes around the portal areas; these findings were thought to be typical for acetaminophen hepatotoxicity. The patient progressed to hepatic encephalopathy and died on the fourth hospital day.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic alcoholics with a history of heavy alcohol abuse; three patients (case 1 survived, case 2 died, case 3 survived).
raw_record.extra_details: Reported acetaminophen amounts: 10 g/48 hr (case 1), 10 g/24 hr (case 2), 50 g/72 hr (case 3). Case 1 showed severe centrilobular necrosis with preservation of periportal hepatocytes typical of severe acetaminophen liver toxicity; case 2 showed massive hepatic necrosis with residual periportal hepatocytes showing degeneration and microvesicular fat. Peak SGOT values 6,960, 9,940, and 7,720 IU; peak bilirubin 17, 8, and 7 mg/dL. Case 2 developed acute tubular necrosis, oliguria, delirium tremens, progressive hepatic encephalopathy, respiratory arrest, and died on day 4; autopsy additionally showed diffuse petechial myocardial hemorrhages and acute tubular necrosis, both previously associated with acetaminophen toxicity, although other factors (e.g., pancreatitis, shock) may have contributed.

raw_record.support_text: The case is described as APAP-induced acute liver injury with significant elevation in transaminases, in a patient who ingested large/unknown amounts of extra-strength acetaminophen (APAP) over days to weeks for chronic pain, with chronic alcoholism. Laboratory findings included an APAP level of 126.3 ug/ml, AST 2,175 U/l, ALT 896 U/l, total bilirubin 2.6 mg/dl, INR 1.6, and lactate 3.9 mmol/L; hepatic encephalopathy was present and King's College criteria were calculated daily. Treatment included N-acetylcysteine and fomepizole, and liver and kidney function returned to baseline four weeks after admission.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic alcoholism and long-term use of staggering unknown doses of extra-strength acetaminophen for chronic pain; exact ingested amount and time of last ingestion (6-18 h prior) uncertain; co-administration of an N-acetylcysteine rescue regimen; the overdose context is implied by amounts but explicit dose is unavailable.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 58-year-old female. Admission labs: APAP 126.3 ug/ml, ethanol <0.01 gm/dl%, AST 2,175 U/l, ALT 896 U/l, total bilirubin 2.6 mg/dl, INR 1.6, lactate 3.9 mmol/L, CK 151 U/L. Hepatic encephalopathy improved ~one day after admission; acute kidney injury occurred with differential diagnoses including APAP-induced hepatotoxicity, hepatorenal syndrome, and acute tubular necrosis; kidney function improved ~80 h post-admission without hemodialysis. N-acetylcysteine i.v. given (21-hour protocol, then dose increased to 12.5 mg/kg/h then 6.25 mg/kg/h until serum APAP undetectable at ~40 h); one-time fomepizole 15 mg/kg i.v. load then 10 mg/kg every 12 h x4, first dose ~30 h after admission (~36-48 h after last ingestion). King's College criteria did not indicate transplant evaluation. Liver and kidney function returned to baseline four weeks post-admission. Mechanism stated: CYP2E1 forms NAPQI, which depletes glutathione causing hepatocyte necrosis and hepatic failure in overdose.; confidence: 0.9; needs_more_context: False

raw_record.support_text: In the discussion the authors state that acetaminophen, like aspirin and phenacetin, has the potential for chronic abuse, and that all three patients took rather large amounts of acetaminophen during long periods and eventually developed biochemical and histologic evidence of a toxic hepatitis that resolved when acetaminophen use was discontinued.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic heavy-dose therapeutic use (5.2 to 6.5 g/day for weeks, termed chronic abuse); patients had underlying fever/pain (one with neoplasm); no alcohol use reported in Patient 3.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients (Patients 1-3) described. Patient 1 showed very severe pericentral necrosis on liver biopsy; Patient 2 had improved liver tests after initial withdrawal, but rechallenge with 5.2-6.5 g/day for 7 days raised SGOT to 121 IU and total bilirubin to 2.4 mg/dl with biopsy showing moderately severe pericentral necrosis and increased lipofuscin pigment (serum acetaminophen 37 µg/ml 24 h after stopping; SGOT fell to 27 IU in 2 days); Patient 3 had SGOT 400 IU, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dl, mild pericentral necrosis with lipofuscin, improving after withdrawal and normalizing within 4 weeks. Mechanism attributed to saturation of sulfate/glucuronide conjugation and cytochrome P450-dependent reactive electrophilic metabolite with glutathione depletion and covalent binding to hepatocyte membranes; alcohol/barbiturates may induce this pathway (Wright & Prescott retrospective overdose data cited).

The patient ingested approximately 5.0 to 6.5 g of acetaminophen daily for 6 to 8 weeks via multiple medications, with no alcohol abuse, P450-inducing medications, or massive dosing. The report emphasizes that in addition to acute acetaminophen overdose, chronic acetaminophen toxicity should be a concern.

raw_record.extra_details: 54-year-old woman; presented with altered mental status, lethargy, hepatic encephalopathy (asterixis, elevated ammonia up to 131 UM/L), INR 10.4, and severe coagulopathy. Peak AST 7816 U/L, ALT 3066 U/L on day 2, elevated total bilirubin up to 6.5 mg/dL, elevated alkaline phosphatase up to 183 U/L, and elevated creatinine (5.4 mg/dL on admission). Concurrent medications included carisoprodol, citalopram, fexofenadine, celecoxib, estradiol, and gabapentin. Patient denied alcohol use (confirmed by family), smoking, and fasting. Underlying medical history included hypercholesterolemia, depression, rheumatoid arthritis, gastric bypass, and cervical spine fusion.

raw_record.support_text: A case report describes an infant who received a chronic supratherapeutic overdose of acetaminophen (162 mg/kg/day of acetaminophen for several days, due to a maternal dosing error) and developed hepatotoxicity with markedly elevated transaminases (ALT 455 U/L, AST 1907 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 603 U/L), elevated total bilirubin 2.7 mg/dL, ammonia 135 µmol/L, and prolonged PT 53.5 s / INR 2.5. The child was treated with N-acetylcysteine for 18 doses, the liver enzymes returned to near normal by the fifth hospital day, and she made a complete recovery over 3 weeks.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic supratherapeutic dosing (162 mg/kg/day for several days) rather than acute single ingestion, in an infant; overdose resulted from a maternal medication-dose confusion between acetaminophen and amoxicillin. Plasma acetaminophen 78.5 µg/mL ~10 hours after last dose could not be applied to the Rumack-Matthew nomogram because it reflected chronic supratherapeutic dosing.
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism attributed to formation of N-acetyl-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI) via cytochrome P-450 mixed function oxidase pathway. Other labs included total protein 4.6 g/dL, albumin 3.1 g/dL, WBC 29,700/mm3 with 67% neutrophils, platelet 676,000/mm3, glucose 30 mg/dL, hypoglycemia with seizure corrected by IV glucose, BUN 8 mg/dL, creatinine 0.5 mg/dL. Treated with N-acetylcysteine loading dose plus 18 total doses (oral regimen 140 mg/kg then 70 mg/kg q4h for 17 doses); transferred to regional transplant center; complete recovery over 3 weeks. Paper notes acute single-ingestion toxic dose of >140 mg/kg in adults or >150 mg/kg in a child.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a patient with severe acetaminophen-induced acute liver disease who did not volunteer a history of recent acetaminophen ingestion; the diagnosis was established after recognizing that her presentation resembled that of previously reported patients with delayed hospitalization (>24 hr after ingestion). A constellation of metabolic and biochemical findings was deemed highly suggestive of acetaminophen hepatotoxicity in the absence of volunteered ingestion history.

raw_record.extra_details: Presenting picture included low serum bicarbonate, high anion gap, low blood glucose, prolonged prothrombin time, and elevated serum amylase, initially misattributed to alcoholic pancreatitis and ketoacidosis. Serum acetaminophen was 8 µg/ml in a specimen recovered 24 hr after admission (≥28 hr after last ingestion). Peak SGOT 14,500 IU/liter, bilirubin rising to 19.0 mg/dl, PT up to 32.6/12. The diagnosis was only suspected after grossly abnormal liver tests with marked hypoprothrombinemia, hypoglycemia, and acidosis.

raw_record.support_text: Serum samples from 28 transplant-free survivors and 30 nonsurvivors of acetaminophen (APAP)-induced acute liver failure were obtained from the Acute Liver Failure Study Group (ALFSG) biorepository. ALF was diagnosed by ALFSG investigators (INR >= 1.5, hepatic encephalopathy, illness < 26 weeks, absence of chronic liver disease), and APAP toxicity was determined as the etiology based on patient-reported history of APAP overdose, a detectable APAP level documenting ingestion, and aminotransferase levels >= 1000 IU/l. Ten healthy volunteers with reported recent therapeutic APAP exposure served as controls for the effects of APAP itself.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Cohort restricted to APAP overdose-induced ALF patients enrolled in the ALFSG biorepository; the 10 control volunteers had only recent therapeutic APAP exposure and no liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: ALF definition: INR >= 1.5, hepatic encephalopathy, duration of illness < 26 weeks, absence of chronic liver disease. APAP etiology determined from patient-reported APAP overdose history, detectable APAP level documenting ingestion, and aminotransferase >= 1000 IU/l. Study cohorts: 28 transplant-free survivors and 30 nonsurvivors of APAP-induced ALF; 10 healthy volunteers with recent therapeutic APAP exposure. Clinical phenotype: acute liver failure (acute hepatic failure) in the overdose cohort. Paper is a methods/biomarker-discovery proteomics study (dataset PXD029576); APAP is the established causal agent in the studied population.

raw_record.support_text: In this large, single centre cohort study of severe paracetamol-induced acute liver injury, patients with staggered paracetamol overdoses had reduced survival compared with single intentional overdoses, despite ingestion of significantly lower total amounts of paracetamol. Delay to hospital presentation at >24 h following overdose was independently associated with increased mortality or requirement for orthotopic liver transplantation following single time point overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Cohort restricted to severe paracetamol overdoses requiring tertiary-level care at a single liver transplant unit (Scottish Liver Transplantation Unit), representing severe cases (overall mortality 32.7%), with selection bias that may limit generalizability to emergency-department overdose presentations.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospectively defined cohort of 344 paracetamol ALF patients, analysed overall and separately for single time point (n=211) and staggered (n=90) overdoses. King's College poor prognostic criteria (KCC) sensitivity was 89.9% (95% CI 85.8-92.7) for single time point vs 77.6% for staggered overdoses; overall mortality rate 32.7%. Staggered overdoses showed reduced survival despite lower total paracetamol dose ingested. Delayed presentation (>24 h) following single time point overdose was an independent risk factor for death or OLT. Concomitant P450 enzyme inducers or recent fasting were noted to increase hepatotoxicity risk after repeated ingestion.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity, including a case series by Bray et al describing seven cases of acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity in patients (ages 16-29) on phenytoin therapy, of whom six who did not receive NAC died from fulminant hepatic failure and the seventh, who received NAC, survived. Additional reported cases (Minton et al, McClements et al) describe acetaminophen overdose in suicide attempts leading to liver failure, hepatic encephalopathy, and in one case death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Concurrent chronic phenytoin therapy; cases were adolescents and young adults (ages 14-29); overdose by suicide attempt.
raw_record.extra_details: Bray et al: seven cases of acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity on phenytoin therapy; six without NAC died of fulminant hepatic failure, one with NAC survived. Minton et al: 20-year-old male on chronic phenytoin ingested an unknown quantity (serum acetaminophen 94 µg/ml, below toxic threshold on nomogram), developed liver failure, renal failure and hepatic encephalopathy and died. McClements et al: 14-year-old boy on phenytoin ingested 45 g acetaminophen, AST 1630 U/L, treated with cimetidine without NAC, developed hepatic encephalopathy and recovered. Index case lab values: ALT >6600 U/L, AST >8800 U/L, total bilirubin 12 mg/dl, INR 30, pH 7.2. Phenytoin was discussed as a possible enzyme inducer but Rumack concluded it did not enhance acetaminophen hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In a phase I trial, paracetamol was administered at escalating doses up to 20 g/m² in combination with BCNU and NAC. Grade IV AST elevations occurred in two patients and constituted dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) in the 20 g/m² cohort. One of these patients also developed grade III prothrombin time prolongation and grade IV decreased level of consciousness. The paper attributes the persistently elevated paracetamol levels at 24 h (71 µg/ml) to impaired drug clearance secondary to liver injury caused by paracetamol.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Deliberate high-dose investigational (supratherapeutic) use in a phase I trial at doses up to 20 g/m², combined with carmustine (BCNU) and N-acetylcysteine (NAC); one affected patient received numerous concomitant Parkinson's disease medications that may have altered paracetamol metabolism.
raw_record.extra_details: DLT in the 20 g/m² cohort comprised grade IV AST elevation in two patients, one of whom also had grade III prothrombin time prolongation and grade IV decreased consciousness, then aspirated and developed pneumonia requiring intubation (the latter scored as grade IV pulmonary toxicity). Affected patient had peak serum paracetamol 392 µg/ml at 4 h and 71 µg/ml at 24 h post-ingestion with persistently elevated serum levels; another patient also had elevated levels (>20 µg/ml) at 24 h. Mean peak serum paracetamol levels were dose-proportional: 158 µg/ml (10 g/m²), 267 µg/ml (15 g/m²), 319 µg/ml (20 g/m²) (P=0.029).; confidence: 0.75; needs_more_context: False

raw_record.support_text: In Case 190, a 17-year-old girl who was reported to have taken a whole bottle of acetaminophen 4 days earlier presented with altered mental status and markedly elevated liver enzymes (AST 5441 IU/L, ALT 9559 IU/L), bilirubin 4.9 mg/dL, PT 25 s, INR 4.33, and ammonia 183 µmol/L; she developed progressive neurologic deterioration and worsening hepatic dysfunction and was pronounced brain dead within 24 hours. In Case 196 a pregnant woman with a serum acetaminophen concentration of 465 µg/mL died of multisystem organ failure 48 hours after a presumed overdose of up to 100 acetaminophen tablets, and her stillborn infant's death was attributed to massive maternal acetaminophen overdose. In Case 214 a 41-year-old man who ingested an unknown amount of acetaminophen 48 hours earlier had an acetaminophen concentration of 180 µg/mL, total bilirubin 10.6 mg/dL, AST 8272 U/L, ALT 7400 U/L, and PT 46.4 s, and died of hepatic failure on the eighth hospital day despite N-acetylcysteine and bioartificial liver support.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Deliberate or accidental overdose (whole bottle of acetaminophen; up to 100 tablets; unknown amount), not therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 190: 17-year-old girl, reported whole-bottle ingestion 4 days prior; AST 5441 IU/L, ALT 9559 IU/L, total bilirubin 4.9 mg/dL, PT 25 s, INR 4.33, ammonia 183 µmol/L; progressive hepatic dysfunction, brain death within 24 h. Case 196: pregnant woman, serum acetaminophen 465 µg/mL (post-delivery 398 µg/mL), up to 100 tablets for back/labor pain; DIC, multisystem organ failure, death; stillborn infant death attributed to massive maternal overdose. Case 214: 41-year-old man, acetaminophen 180 µg/mL, total bilirubin 10.6 mg/dL, AST 8272 U/L, ALT 7400 U/L, PT 46.4 s, PTT 40.5 s; treated with oral N-acetylcysteine and 5 days of bioartificial liver support; died of hepatic failure on hospital day 8. Overdose cases illustrate intrinsic, dose-related hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective case series of patients requiring tertiary referral after paracetamol overdose, most patients (96.6%) had evidence of acute liver dysfunction defined by a PT≥25 s. The paper frames paracetamol poisoning as a cause of hepatic injury (toxic metabolites generate liver injury monitored by rising hepatic transaminases and prothrombin time) and reports KCHC poor-prognosis criteria (17.6–36.5% across ingestion-to-presentation intervals) and mortality in this overdose cohort.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Deliberate paracetamol overdose (acute single and staggered ingestion); highly selected population with severe poisoning referred to a tertiary liver unit; acute liver dysfunction defined by PT≥25 s (96.6% of the cohort).
raw_record.extra_details: Liver injury monitored by hepatic transaminase rises (referral ALT 1960±264 IU/l presenting ≤24 h up to 7887±875 IU/l presenting >48 h) and prothrombin time; toxicity attributed to toxic paracetamol metabolites generated by local metabolism; KCHC poor prognosis 17.6% (≤24 h), 36.5% (>24–48 h), 26.2% (>48 h); mortality 15.3%, 28.3%, 23.8% by ingestion-to-presentation interval; stated single paracetamol doses ~27–39 g in acute ingestions without a dose-response relation to renal risk. No biochemical pattern classification was stated.

raw_record.support_text: In the discussion of this liver unit series, the authors state that paracetamol poisoning is associated with serious hepatotoxicity when patients who have taken a significant overdose are not treated early, and that early treatment with N-acetylcysteine (within 12 hours) is almost completely successful in averting significant liver damage. This constitutes an explicit human attribution of hepatotoxicity to paracetamol overdose, set against the presented series of 92 consecutive patients admitted with paracetamol poisoning, 10 of whom underwent liver transplantation and 6 of listed-but-not-transplanted patients who died.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Deliberate paracetamol overdose (poisoning) with significant overdose; several patients also had established renal failure requiring dialysis; a number presented late or were not treated early with N-acetylcysteine.
raw_record.extra_details: 92 consecutive patients admitted to the liver unit with paracetamol poisoning. 17 were considered transplant candidates; 10 underwent transplantation (median 79 h from poisoning, range 64-98); 7 were listed but not transplanted, 6 of whom died (median 98 h from poisoning). Early N-acetylcysteine treatment (<12 h) was almost completely successful in averting significant liver damage; only 7 of 92 presented within 12 h of poisoning, and the 3 treated at presentation survived. Hepatotoxicity averted with early treatment, but delayed treatment is associated with increasing severity.

Following treatment with N-acetylcysteine (NAC) and adjunctive therapy, the improvement was marked and transplant was withheld.

raw_record.extra_details: Single case report; presented with elevated serum lactate, INR > 4.5, and persistent shock despite fluid resuscitation, meeting liver transplant candidacy criteria; NAC and adjunctive therapy produced marked improvement so transplant was withheld. NAC (N-acetylcysteine) is the antidote, not an attributed cause of the liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: This case series describes 177 patients hospitalized for acetaminophen deliberate self-poisoning (overdose), all managed with stomach wash, activated charcoal, and intravenous N-acetylcysteine after estimating serum acetaminophen concentrations, which reflects management of acetaminophen hepatotoxicity risk. The study reports that overall two patients were admitted to the intensive care unit, but no patient died or needed a liver transplant as a result of the acetaminophen overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Deliberate self-poisoning (overdose) context; in this cohort no patient died or required liver transplantation as a result of the overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: 177 adults (84.2% female, mean age 23.1 years). Acetaminophen alone in 159 cases and co-ingested in 18. Median reported dose 10 g (IQR 6–15 g), median latency 5 h (IQR 3–10 h), median serum acetaminophen concentration 65 mg/L (IQR 18.5–142.6 mg/L). Two patients admitted to ICU; no liver transplant and no deaths.

raw_record.support_text: In the present series of epileptic patients who took paracetamol overdose, one patient who received NAC 8 h after overdose developed fulminant hepatic failure and died, and two others given NAC 8 and 12 h after ingestion developed fulminant hepatic failure and survived. The effectiveness of NAC as an antidote against paracetamol overdose is described as well established, and the authors note the NAC treatment threshold recommendations for overdose. They report features of evolving hepatic necrosis (rising prothrombin time or development of encephalopathy).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Epileptic patients taking anticonvulsant drugs; some received NAC; acknowledged potentiation by concurrent sodium valproate and barbiturate co-therapy via increased reactive-metabolite formation.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol hepatotoxicity in the overdose setting; one death and two cases of fulminant hepatic failure with survival among NAC-treated epileptics. NAC is well established as an antidote when given within 10 h of overdose. Authors propose NAC for all anticonvulsant-treated overdose patients if plasma paracetamol is detectable or with rising prothrombin time/encephalopathy. Mechanism discussion includes potentiation by enzyme induction, macrophage activation, and competition with glucuronidation.

raw_record.support_text: In a US ALFSG prospective study of 275 consecutive patients with acetaminophen (ACM)-related acute liver failure (ALF), the annual incidence of ALF due to ACM rose from 28% in 1998 to 51% in 2004. Nearly 50% of cases were nonintentional 'therapeutic misadventures', with 48% of ALF-ACM cases nonintentional; most were taking excessive doses, about 50% of the nonintentional group consuming 4-10 g/day and 7% of the entire cohort ingesting less than 4 g/day. The majority (81%) of nonintentional overdose patients had an acute or chronic painful medical condition and 63% were taking a narcotic-ACM analgesic chronically.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Exposure limited to overdose context, including both intentional and nonintentional 'therapeutic misadventure' supratherapeutic doses; some patients taking narcotic-ACM combination analgesics.
raw_record.extra_details: US Acute Liver Failure Study Group (ALFSG) prospective data, 275 consecutive ACM-related ALF patients. Annual ALF incidence due to ACM rose from 28% in 1998 to 51% in 2004. 48% were nonintentional overdose cases; ~50% of these consumed 4-10 g/day and 7% of the entire cohort ingested <4 g/day. 81% of nonintentional patients had acute or chronic painful conditions, 63% used narcotic-ACM analgesics chronically. Nonintentional patients had lower serum ACM (median 106 vs 554 µmol/L, P<0.001), lower ALT (3319 vs 5326 U/L, P<0.001), and more advanced encephalopathy (53% vs 39% grade 3-4). Outcomes: 9% vs 7% required liver transplantation, 28% vs 29% fatal. 87% of intentional and 95% of nonintentional patients received N-acetylcysteine. Reference to 60,000 intentional ACM overdose cases/year in the US with 500 fatalities.

raw_record.support_text: In this retrospective series of 207 patients presenting to the emergency department with acetaminophen overdose, 52 (25%) received hepatology consults due to the severity of their liver injuries, and 36 were transferred to the liver transplant unit. Of 36 LTU patients, 12 were ill enough to be considered for transplant; five were approved, three underwent successful liver transplantation, and two died before they could be transplanted. Across the cohort, liver injury took the form of acute liver injury hepatitis, fulminant liver failure was present in 16 LTU patients (44.4%), and there were two deaths, establishing acetaminophen overdose as a cause of severe human hepatotoxicity including acute liver failure, transplantation, and death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings are restricted to overdose (both intentional, N=158, and unintentional, N=49, ingestions) and include co-exposures such as alcohol, opiates, benzodiazepines, and multiple acetaminophen-containing products; chronic high-dose use in some unintentional pain-management cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 207 acetaminophen overdose patients; NAC was administered to 135 with known ingestion timing (41 first dose within 8 hrs, 31 within 8-24 hrs, 6 within 24-72 hrs, 2 after 72 hrs). LTU vs non-LTU comparisons showed higher tablet amounts (90.7±94.0 vs 39.1±36.2), peak ALT (8235±6344 vs 667±2008), peak AST, acute liver injury hepatitis (94.4% vs 10.3%), fulminant liver failure (44.4% vs 0%), coagulopathy, acute renal failure, and encephalopathy. Three patients received liver transplantation (ALT peaks 8100, 13900, 8720); two patients died (one after 75 g acetaminophen; the other after 150 tablets). One fatal case also ingested alcohol and opiates.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective population-based cohort in Iceland (2010–2017), 542 cases of paracetamol poisoning were identified. Twenty-five (4.6%) patients developed severe paracetamol-induced liver injury and coagulopathy, and six (1.1%) cases were fatal in which paracetamol contributed to the cause of death, with accidental poisoning found in 67% (4/6) of fatal cases.

raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective population-based cohort, 2010–2017, Iceland (only and largest university hospital). 542 cases identified via serum paracetamol concentrations (≥66 µmol/L). Mean annual incidence 27/100,000 (range 22–33). Intentional poisoning in 437/542 (81%), most common in females aged 16–25; accidental overdose more common in males ≥65 years and associated with worse outcomes. 25/542 (4.6%) developed severe paracetamol-induced liver injury and coagulopathy; 6/542 (1.1%) fatal with paracetamol contributing to cause of death (67% accidental). Comparison to a prior 2004–2009 study showing decreased incidence (~16/100,000) during a financial crisis.

raw_record.support_text: This study, from sites representing about 30% of U.S. transplant capability (UNOS data), recorded an average of 49 acetaminophen-related liver failure cases/year over 6 years, and estimates at least 250 cases of acetaminophen-related acute liver failure (ALF) are seen annually at U.S. transplant centers, resulting in approximately 73 deaths. raw_record.extra_details: Estimated 250 acetaminophen-related ALF cases/year and ~73 deaths at U.S. transplant centers; overall mortality ~29%, similar for intentional and unintentional overdose groups; unintentional overdose 50% (vs 31% estimated in Australia); consistent intake of as little as 7.5 g/day may be hazardous (narrow therapeutic margin); 22% used 2 acetaminophen preparations simultaneously (38% of unintentional group); 63% of unintentional group used narcotic combinations; ALT levels and severity similar to suicidal ingestions; >7-day ingestions still showed acute injury, suggesting no chronic form but a threshold; NAC (n-acetylcysteine) referenced as effective early treatment; limited toxicological testing suggested illicit drug use; ethanol may be a co-factor in lower-dose (≤4 g/day) subjects.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of patients with severe paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity managed in intensive care, survival was 63% following a deliberate overdose and 58% after therapeutic misadventure. Acute liver failure complications were frequent: grade III–IV encephalopathy occurred in 58% and 55% of the therapeutic misadventure and deliberate overdose groups respectively, 54% (278/515) of deliberate overdose cases and 56% (21/38) of the therapeutic misadventure group required renal dialysis, and 37 patients fulfilled transplant criteria and received a transplant. Survival, need for inotropic support, transplant criteria fulfilment, and encephalopathy were independent of both the amount of paracetamol taken and the level of alcohol consumption.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings concern a cohort of severe paracetamol (acetaminophen) intoxication cases admitted to intensive care and include both deliberate overdose and therapeutic misadventure; the analysis compares outcomes across nil/light/moderate/heavy alcohol-consumption categories.
raw_record.extra_details: Serum transaminases were invariably recorded as >5000 IU/l or >10 000 IU/l in markedly elevated cases. Peak mean INR and creatinine were 8.9±3.0 and 414±83.8 µmol/l in therapeutic misadventure (INR 8.9 vs 10.2 and creatinine 414 vs 442 µmol/l in deliberate overdose), and minimum mean platelet count was 85±17 x10^9/l in therapeutic misadventure vs 52 x10^9/l in overdose. No significant association of survival, dialysis, inotropic support, transplant-criteria fulfilment, grade III–IV encephalopathy, INR, creatinine, or arterial pH with alcohol consumption was found; heavy drinkers had a lower WBC on day 3 (12.1±0.7) and a lower platelet count over the first 5 days post overdose compared with other categories.

raw_record.support_text: The study concludes that time to NAC, chronic alcohol abuse, quantity of acetaminophen, and age are independent risk factors in the development of severe hepatotoxicity in patients with acetaminophen poisoning (overdose). The acute ingestion of alcohol eliminated the excess risk of chronic alcohol abuse but did not protect against hepatotoxicity in nonalcoholic patients. Multivariate analyses across 157 patients with and 488 without regular alcohol abuse identified time to NAC and dose among risk factors for clinical outcomes including death or liver transplant.

raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of patients with acetaminophen poisoning treated with NAC; analyses covered 157 patients with and 488 without regular alcohol abuse. Independent risk factors for severe hepatotoxicity/clinical outcome (death or liver transplant, hepatic encephalopathy, elevated ALT, bilirubin, creatinine, prolonged prothrombin time) were time to NAC, acetaminophen dose, and age; age as an independent risk factor had not previously been reported except for relative resistance in younger children.

raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol is the most common poisoning in the UK and Ireland; paracetamol-related enquiries accounted for 16% of UK and 15% of Ireland PIC inquiries. raw_record.support_text: The paper examines phospho-JNK expression in human liver tissue from cases of paracetamol-induced acute liver failure (ALF). Compared with a normal control human liver, cytoplasmic and dense nuclear phospho-JNK staining in hepatocytes (around central veins) was markedly increased in paracetamol-induced ALF human livers (n = 8 cases in each group), establishing acetaminophen (paracetamol) as a cause of acute liver failure in humans, consistent with a paracetamol poisoning context.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Human tissue assessment derived from paracetamol-induced ALF cases (n=8), in a paracetamol-poisoning context; the majority of the supporting experiments are in a murine model.
raw_record.extra_details: Synonyms: acetaminophen. Mechanism focus is hepatic JNK (c-Jun N-terminal kinase) activation that precedes onset of hepatocyte death; peak JNK activity 2 h after paracetamol, peak serum ALT 5 h after injection in mice (350 mg/kg IP). JNK inhibitors SP600125 (ATP-competitive) and D-JNKI1 (peptide inhibitor), given 1 h before paracetamol, potently inhibited phospho-JNK, markedly reduced mortality over 72 h, reduced histological liver injury and hepatic necrosis scores, and reduced hepatocyte apoptosis and necrosis in mice. Delayed JNK inhibitor administration was more effective than NAC in limiting liver injury. Human ALF tissue showed increased hepatocyte cytoplasmic and nuclear phospho-JNK.

raw_record.support_text: Prospective data obtained over a 6-year period by the United States observed that APAP overdose was the most common (42%) cause of acute liver failure. Acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure has long been recognized in the United Kingdom as a common etiology for acute hepatic failure for more than 30 years. Unintentional overdoses accounted for 48% of the cases, usually occurring when a narcotic combination was used excessively for several days before the onset of liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Includes both intentional and unintentional overdose; unintentional cases (48%) typically involved excessive multi-day use of a narcotic combination product.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP overdose was the most common (42%) cause of acute liver failure in a US 6-year prospective study. Acetaminophen described as a dose-dependent hepatotoxin; acute hepatic failure recognized in the UK for over 30 years.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that of 71 acetaminophen overdose patients admitted to Parkland Hospital over a 39-month period, 50 were considered suicidal with only one of 50 resulting in acute liver failure (ALF) and death, whereas six deaths occurred among 21 unintentional overdoses; only the seven patients who died had developed acute hepatic failure. Acetaminophen overdose is framed as a cause of drug-induced acute liver failure, with suicidal single overdoses typically treated promptly with N-acetylcysteine while unintentional multi-day overdoses present late after toxicity has developed.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Includes both single suicidal ingestions and unintentional multi-day/chronic overdoses; unintentional group frequently involved concurrent use of multiple acetaminophen-containing preparations and opioid combination products (e.g., hydrocodone plus acetaminophen), often with alcohol, hypnotics, or illicit drugs, and some habituated to up to 40 or more tablets per day.
raw_record.extra_details: Classic hyperacute presentation with very high aminotransferase levels (median ALT 3846 IU/L) and low bilirubin (median 4.4 mg/dL) compared with other drug-induced liver injury. In the US ALFSG cohort of acetaminophen ALF, 38% took more than one acetaminophen-containing product and 62% took an opioid combination. NAC provides protection when given within 12 hours of ingestion and prevents deaths among suicidal patients. Acute liver failure (acute hepatic failure) is the attributed clinical phenotype. Among the 71 overdose patients, 10 of 50 suicidal patients had aminotransferases >= 1000 IU/L; spontaneous survival of APAP ALF patients with encephalopathy was ~64%; transplantation was done in ~7-9%; deaths due to acetaminophen toxicity were the most frequent cause of death in the study. Overall survival in the APAP group was 75%.; note_on_severity: deaths and transplant and ALF are all reported; the highest is death

raw_record.support_text: Of 110 subjects with indeterminate acute liver failure (ALF), 20 (18%) had serum APAP-CYS adduct levels ≥1.0 nmol/mL (median 9.2 nmol/mL), suggesting that the ALF was secondary to an acetaminophen overdose; these 20 (Group 2) were similar to 188 clinically defined acetaminophen-overdose control patients (Group 3), with median ALT values >4,000 IU/L and lower bilirubin concentrations than adduct-negative indeterminates.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Indeterminate ALF patients identified as acetaminophen overdose on the basis of serum APAP-CYS adducts ≥1.0 nmol/mL; in 12 of 20 cases retrospective evidence made APAP a possible or likely ('ill-defined overdose') diagnosis, and 8 were clinically unrecognized acetaminophen overdoses.
raw_record.extra_details: From 1,115 registry cases, 158 (14%) were indeterminate ALF; 110 had day 1-2 sera and 20 (18%) were APAP-CYS positive (median 9.2 nmol/mL; cutoff ≥1.0 nmol/mL, quantitation limit 0.03 µM). Of 199 clinically defined APAP overdose sera, 188 (94.5%) were above the toxicity threshold (median 11.1 nmol/mL). Adduct-positive groups had median ALT 4,025 (Group 2) and 5,156 IU/L (Group 3) with bilirubin <10 mg/dL in 90% and 93%. In a previous study a cutoff ≥1.1 nmol/mL at ALT>1000 IU/L gave 96.8% sensitivity and 95% specificity. Assay: gel filtration, protease digestion, APAP-CYS adducts by HPLC-EC.

raw_record.support_text: A 52-year-old man with a history of chronic analgesics, alcohol, and illicit drug abuse developed acute liver failure in relationship with the ingestion of largely supra-therapeutic doses of acetaminophen over the days preceding admission. The patient received the classical N-acetylcysteine treatment regimen for acetaminophen overdose, but his neurological condition worsened to grade IV encephalopathy with persistent coagulopathy (factor V <10%). He fulfilled criteria for liver transplantation, but this was rejected after psychiatric evaluation; his serum unconjugated bilirubin increased progressively until death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Ingestion of largely supra-therapeutic doses over the days preceding admission; history of chronic analgesics, alcohol, and illicit drug abuse; liver transplantation rejected after psychiatric evaluation.
raw_record.extra_details: Received standard N-acetylcysteine overdose regimen; progressed to grade IV encephalopathy; persistent coagulopathy with factor V <10%; progressive increase in serum unconjugated bilirubin until death without evidence of hemolysis, with Gilbert's syndrome excluded; attributed mechanism is damage to endoplasmic reticulum in relation to centrilobular necrosis caused by toxic metabolism of acetaminophen; the paper notes that a persistent unconjugated bilirubin rise may reflect defective bilirubin conjugation and that the ratio of unconjugated/conjugated bilirubin has insufficient data to serve as a prognostic factor.

raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose was explicitly attributed as the cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in 33 of the 42 enrolled patients (16 men, 26 women, age range 17-64). raw_record.support_text: Two hundred intentional paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose cases were identified (median dose ingested 50 g, IQR 45–60 g, median time to presentation 3.5 h). Twenty-eight (14%) patients developed hepatotoxicity, with a further 9 (5%) having a peak ALT between 150 and <1000 U/L. Those who developed hepatotoxicity had a significantly longer time to treatment (13.9 h) than those who did not (6 h, p<0.001). One patient required a liver transplant despite acetylcysteine being commenced 2.5 h post-ingestion; there was one death unrelated to paracetamol ingestion. The 200 patients were identified across four sites with comparable data.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intentional paracetamol self-poisoning (median dose 50 g, 0.7 g/kg); co-ingestion of ethanol (27%) and gut-slowing medications (33%) in a portion of patients; treated with acetylcysteine in 193 (97%) of cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 28/200 (14%) developed hepatotoxicity and 9/200 (5%) had peak ALT 150–1000 U/L. Median time to treatment 13.9 h in hepatotoxic patients vs 6 h in non-hepatotoxic (p<0.001). raw_record.support_text: This study concerns paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning. Among 16 severely poisoned patients with 4 h paracetamol concentrations above 300 µg/ml who received only supportive therapy, all suffered severe liver damage, 3 died in hepatic failure, and 4 developed acute renal failure. The severity of poisoning was reflected by the average urinary recovery of 18·6 g of paracetamol despite incomplete collections. These findings attribute severe liver injury to paracetamol overdose in humans.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intentional poisonings/overdose (average urinary recovery of 18·6 g paracetamol); among the 16 supportive-therapy-only patients with 4 h paracetamol concentrations above 300 µg/ml, all developed severe liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: 3 of 16 supportive-therapy patients died in hepatic failure and 4 developed acute renal failure. Cysteamine given within 10 h of ingestion protected against severe liver damage; cysteamine, methionine (3 failures in patients treated within 10 h), and penicillamine are discussed as protectants/treatments, not as causal agents.

raw_record.support_text: A 40-year-old woman (patient 1) presented with hyperacute liver failure (HALF) following severe acetaminophen intoxication (15–25 g) 32 h prior to admission, with widespread liver damage and reduced synthetic capacity (ASAT 15 000 U/l; ALAT 10 300 U/l; total bilirubin 63 µmol/l; INR 1.3; factor V 4%). Within 12 h the liver function deteriorated rapidly, the patient was listed for super urgent liver transplantation and developed acute renal failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intentional/severe acetaminophen overdose of 15–25 g ingested 32 h prior to admission; patient was listed for super urgent liver transplantation and underwent grafting.
raw_record.extra_details: Blood group O woman. At presentation: ASAT 15 000 U/l, ALAT 10 300 U/l, total bilirubin 63 µmol/l, INR 1.3, fibrinogen 5.9 µmol/l, factor V 4% of normal. Within 12 h: INR 3.8, fibrinogen 2.3 µmol/l, factor V 1%, bilirubin 96 µmol/l, grade III–IV hepatic encephalopathy, uncontrollable intracranial pressures peaking at 25 mmHg. Treated with MARS liver support (ineffective on ICP), veno-venous haemofiltration for acute renal failure, plasmapheresis and other supportive agents; received an ABO-incompatible split-liver graft perfused ex vivo with Mirococept.

raw_record.support_text: In the Skwarek study, 13 patients with acute liver failure of different etiologies who qualified for very urgent liver transplantation were treated with the Prometheus 4008H device. The reported etiologies included intoxication by amanita phalloides, acetaminophen (acetalminophen) intoxication, Wilson disease, liver insufficiency due to hemihepatectomy, and unknown causes. This explicitly attributes acetaminophen intoxication as a cause of acute liver failure in these patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intoxication (overdose) setting; patients qualified for very urgent liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen (referred to as 'acetalminophen') intoxication was listed as one of several etiologies of acute liver failure in a 13-patient series treated with the Prometheus liver-support device; 7 patients underwent liver transplantation and 4 were discharged without transplantation. Amanita phalloides poisoning and Wilson disease were other etiologies but are not extracted as medicinal DILI agents.

raw_record.support_text: In the setting of paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose, hepatotoxicity was assessed in a single-armed, multicentre US trial of a higher total intravenous acetylcysteine dose (980 mg kg⁻¹ over 48 h). The overall rate of hepatotoxicity (ALT or AST >1000 U L⁻¹) was 18.1% among 309 patients, with a rate of 3.4% in those treated within 10 h of ingestion, indicating that paracetamol overdose causes drug-induced liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: The abstract reports three cases of massive acetaminophen (APAP) overdose with an unusual double-hump APAP concentration pattern. A 38-year-old woman ingested 2 g hydrocodone/65 g acetaminophen, a 25-year-old man ingested 2 g diphenhydramine/26 g APAP, and a 16-year-old boy ingested 5 g diphenhydramine and 100 g APAP; each developed liver injury, with peak AST values of 1603, 1153, and 8686 IU/L and peak INR of 1.6, 2.1, and 5.9, respectively. The paper states that patients with double-hump APAP concentrations may be at risk for liver injury, with AST elevations and peaks occurring later than typical for acute APAP overdoses.

raw_record.support_text: The study states that acetaminophen (APAP) overdose results in hepatic injury, attributed to increased production of the toxic metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), and that N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is highly effective at preventing hepatotoxicity if given within 8 h of acute overdose. In a retrospective cohort of 1425 APAP overdose cases, 104 met the definition of massive APAP overdose (single acute overdose with an APAP concentration exceeding 300 mcg/mL at 4 h post-ingestion); 25 (24%) of these developed hepatotoxicity, and receiving NAC after 8 h carried 5.5-fold higher crude odds of hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive APAP overdose, defined as single acute overdose with APAP concentration exceeding 300 mcg/mL at 4 h post-ingestion, reported to a regional poison center.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective single-center cohort (2010-2019) of 1425 APAP overdoses; 104 met massive overdose criteria; 25 (24%) developed hepatotoxicity while 79 (76%) had no acute liver injury or hepatotoxicity. Of cases receiving NAC within 8 h, 9% (n=4) developed hepatotoxicity and 91% (n=40) were protected. Crude odds of hepatotoxicity were 5.5-fold higher with NAC after 8 h. Mechanism cited as increased production of the toxic metabolite NAPQI. NAC administered at standard IV dose of 300 mg/kg over 21 h.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that acetaminophen toxicity is caused by a highly reactive minor metabolite which is formed by, and damages, the liver, kidneys and certain other vital organs, and that biochemical and symptomatic evidence of acetaminophen toxicity is usually delayed for several days and can be reduced or prevented by early N-acetylcysteine. This is described in the context of a case report of a 28-year-old woman who ingested an estimated 58 g acetaminophen (plus 9 g propoxyphene) 20 h before hospitalization, with a serum acetaminophen concentration of 485 µg/mL at 22 h and complete recovery.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive intentional overdose (estimated 58 g acetaminophen) taken as ~90 Darvocet-N 100 tablets (each containing propoxyphene napsylate 100 mg and acetaminophen 650 mg), with co-ingestion of 9 g propoxyphene; 20 h delay before hospitalization; prior barbiturate exposure (enzyme inducers); patient on methadone maintenance (80 mg/day).
raw_record.extra_details: Serum acetaminophen concentration 485 µg/mL at 22 h, declining with unusually long half-life of 14 h; hemodialysis for 4 h (started at 36 h) reduced concentration from 250 to 32 µg/mL; N-acetylcysteine prevented inorganic sulfate depletion and may have increased acetaminophen sulfate formation; patient recovered completely. Hepatotoxicity attributed to a highly reactive minor metabolite; predictable dose-related overdose mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: A 36-year-old female presented ~72 hours after intentional ingestion of about 200 pills of 500 mg acetaminophen in an overdose. Labs showed severe acidosis (pH 6.9), AST 23,356 IU/L rising to a peak of 28,254 IU/L, and INR 2.8; the patient met King's College Criteria for acidemia and was deemed unfit for liver transplantation. She was treated with N-acetylcysteine and Molecular Adsorbent Recirculating System (MARS, liver dialysis) for 3 days and survived to discharge, recovering from the massive acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure without sequelae.

raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver failure with severe hepatocellular injury (AST peak 28,254 IU/L, initial 23,356 IU/L), INR 2.8, severe metabolic acidosis (pH 6.9 rising to 7.0), initial APAP 28 mcg/mL declining to 14 mcg/mL. MARS (liver dialysis) used for 3 days as extracorporeal therapy; EXTRIP recommendations referenced for ECT when acetaminophen concentrations exceed 800 mg/L or with altered mentation/lactic acidosis at >500 mg/L. Patient survived to discharge without sequelae.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that even if the patient survived the acute CNS depressant effects of propoxyphene, long-term survival appeared questionable because of the likelihood of severe liver damage by acetaminophen. Plasma-acetaminophen concentrations above 400 µg/mL at 4 h after ingestion are associated with very severe intoxication; the patient's concentration was 485 µg/mL at 22 h and probably over 1000 µg/mL at 4 h. Acetaminophen hepatotoxicity is increased by prior exposure to barbiturates and other enzyme-inducing drugs that enhance formation of its hepatotoxic reactive metabolite.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive overdose combined with propoxyphene; patient on methadone maintenance and abused barbiturates prior to ingestion; N-acetylcysteine antidote treatment delayed ~24 h (considered ineffective after 10 h).
raw_record.extra_details: Ingestion of 58.5 g (1.22 g/kg) acetaminophen, among the largest known ingestions; back-extrapolated plasma concentration 1470 mg/L equivalent to 1.40 g/kg. Acetaminophen biologic half-life is 2-3 h at therapeutic doses but averages ~8 h in intoxicated patients, and long half-lives are usually associated with severe liver damage and a high fatality rate. Hepatotoxic reactive metabolite formed by mixed-function oxidase; toxicity increased by barbiturate-induced enzyme induction. Propoxyphene was attributed to coma, respiratory depression, and hypothermia rather than liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: An 18-year-old male presented 1 hour after consuming 125 grams of acetaminophen (APAP) with a peak APAP level of 738.6 µg/mL. He was treated with intravenous N-acetylcysteine, fomepizole, intermittent hemodialysis, and CVVH at a high replacement rate. His AST, ALT, and alkaline phosphatase remained low (AST 50 U/L, ALT 55 U/L, both <100 U/L during hospitalization), and no liver failure developed; the early NAC and fomepizole were credited with protecting him from APAP-induced hepatic injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive overdose of 125 g APAP (single-agent ingestion); no prior liver disease noted.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP level rose from 630.6 to 730 µg/mL despite 4 hours of intermittent hemodialysis, attributed to continued GI absorption and high tissue distribution. Treated with intravenous NAC (initially 150 mg/kg then 12.5 mg/kg/h, with oral NAC 70 mg/kg q4h) and fomepizole (15 mg/kg then 10 mg/kg q6h) during high-rate CVVH (replacement 90 mL/kg/h). Discussion notes APAP toxicity can be fatal if acute liver failure develops; prior massive tylenol ingestion cases delayed beyond the NAC effective window had AST/ALT in the thousands; this patient's AST and ALT remained <100 U/L throughout and liver enzymes returned to normal.

raw_record.support_text: A 59-year-old man ingested 90 g of paracetamol and was admitted 36 hours later. He developed hepatic failure (serum bilirubin 5.2 mg/100 ml, SGOT >2,000 units) as well as hypotension from massive upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage, metabolic acidosis, coagulopathy, an ECG conduction defect, and renal failure. Post-mortem revealed massive hepatic necrosis with preservation of the normal reticulum structure (centrilobular necrosis), and the patient became comatose and died three days after admission.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive paracetamol overdose (90 g ingested); patient had simultaneous massive upper GI haemorrhage with hypotension, metabolic acidosis, coagulopathy, anuria/renal failure, and extensive atheromatous coronary artery disease found at post mortem.
raw_record.extra_details: Admitted 36 hours after ingestion with serum paracetamol 152 µg/ml, fully conscious. Findings: systolic BP 60 mm Hg; pH 7.20, PaCO2 16, base excess -21 mEq/L; prothrombin time 33 s (control 13), partial thromboplastin time 74 s (control 37), thrombin time 9 s (control 7), platelet count 60,000/cmm; gross intraventricular conduction defect; anuria. Hepatic failure with bilirubin 5.2 mg/100 ml; SGOT >2,000 units the next day. Histology: massive centrilobular necrosis with preservation of normal reticulum structure. raw_record.support_text: This study of 'massive' paracetamol overdose highlights prolonged absorption and persistently high concentrations in these patients, with some showing delayed paracetamol peak concentrations out to 60 h suggesting pharmacobezoar formation. Acetylcysteine within hours of the overdose did not prevent severe liver injury in several patients. The paper confirms that very high early paracetamol concentrations are an independent risk factor for hepatotoxicity even when acetylcysteine is given, with hepatotoxicity defined as ALT >1000 U/L in this high-dose cohort.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive paracetamol overdose (ingestion of at least 40 g, high-dose cohort) rather than ordinary therapeutic exposure; some patients had delayed/double peaks out to 60 h suggesting pharmacobezoar formation.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined as ALT >1000 U/L despite IV acetylcysteine given within 8 h of ingestion; high early paracetamol ratio (above the 300 mg/L at 4 h nomogram line) was an independent risk factor for hepatotoxicity even when adjusted for time to acetylcysteine and ratio. In patients presenting within 16 h of ingesting ≥40 g receiving 'standard' treatment (no activated charcoal, standard acetylcysteine dose), hepatotoxicity rate was 11% (n=10/87), vs 5% (n=4/87) with activated charcoal or increased acetylcysteine. Toxic intermediate NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine) discussed as the metabolite acetylcysteine detoxifies; NAPQI not independently blamed as separate causal entity. Activated charcoal within 4 h associated with reduced paracetamol concentrations and reduced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A 78-year-old man reportedly ingested approximately 96 immediate-release acetaminophen 500-mg tablets (48 g) over one hour in an apparent suicide attempt. Following intravenous NAC for 21 hours, therapy was discontinued despite a residual acetaminophen concentration of 116 µg/mL, and the patient experienced hepatotoxicity, coagulopathy, and renal injury. Pharmacokinetic analysis revealed prolonged acetaminophen absorption with a second peak concentration of 228 µg/mL at about 48 hours postingestion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive single overdose (~48 g as ~96 tablets of 500 mg immediate-release acetaminophen) in a 78-year-old patient following a suicide attempt; erratic gastrointestinal absorption with double serum concentration peaks occurred.
raw_record.extra_details: Peak acetaminophen concentration 281 µg/mL at 6.25 h postingestion (264 µg/mL at 2.25 h, residual 116 µg/mL at end of 21-h IV NAC course, second peak 228 µg/mL ~48 h postingestion). Hepatotoxicity and coagulopathy developed despite 21 h of intravenous NAC; renal injury also occurred. Case suggests standard 21-h NAC course may be inadequate in massive ingestion due to erratic absorption.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a case of massive acetaminophen (APAP) ingestion (125 g) associated with GSH depletion, prolonged APAP half-life, increased NAPQI production, and hepatotoxicity, treated with an increased IV NAC regimen (400 mg/kg over 29 hours vs the standard 300 mg/kg over 21 hours). It states that the standard NAC dose may not provide adequate protection against hepatotoxicity in massive APAP ingestion, and discusses predictors of poor prognosis after APAP toxicity (decreased pH, increased lactate, increased PT/INR, increased serum creatinine).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive single-ingestion overdose (125 g ingested by a 70 kg patient; massive ingestion defined as a single APAP intake >40 g), requiring an increased NAC dose and duration.
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism: GSH depletion and increased NAPQI production with prolonged APAP half-life; NAC regimen raised to 400 mg/kg IV over 29 h vs standard 300 mg/kg IV over 21 h because optimal regimen for massive ingestions is uncertain. Chiew et al 2017 retrospective analysis: 79 patients with serum APAP above the 300-line at 4 h treated with NAC within 16 h; clinical_hypothesis the increased NAC dose reduced hepatotoxicity. Predictors of poor prognosis after APAP toxicity: decreased pH, increased lactate, increased PT/INR, increased serum creatinine. Concomitant diphenhydramine may slow GI absorption and prolong APAP half-life.

raw_record.support_text: The case report documents hepatotoxicity occurring after a massive suicidal acetaminophen (APAP) overdose. A 78-year-old man reportedly ingested approximately 96 tablets of APAP IR (each 500 mg) over one hour. IV N-acetylcysteine (NAC) was started 5 hours after ingestion, but was discontinued after 21 hours despite a residual APAP concentration of 116 µg/mL. The patient subsequently experienced hepatotoxicity, coagulopathy, and renal injury, with pharmacokinetic analysis revealing prolonged, erratic APAP absorption and a second peak APAP concentration of 228 µg/mL approximately 48 hours after ingestion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive suicidal overdose in a 78-year-old man; approximately 96 tablets of APAP IR (500 mg each, ~48 g) ingested over one hour; IV NAC started 5 hours after ingestion and prematurely discontinued after 21 hours despite a residual APAP concentration of 116 µg/mL.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP serum concentrations were 264 µg/mL at 2.25 h post-ingestion and 281 µg/mL at 6.25 h; a second peak of 228 µg/mL appeared approximately 48 h post-ingestion. Erratic and prolonged APAP absorption led to toxic serum concentrations persisting beyond the standard 21-hour IV NAC course. The patient also developed coagulopathy and renal injury; re-ingestion was deemed unlikely due to direct hospital monitoring. No specific biochemical pattern (e.g., hepatocellular vs. cholestatic) was reported.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports acetaminophen hepatotoxicity in a moderate-overdose group of patients taking roughly 4 to 10 g of acetaminophen within 24 hours. Sixty percent of the patients in this group who developed severe hepatotoxicity were chronic acetaminophen users, several of whom had taken such amounts for weeks or months without problems; the paper proposes that another factor, such as illness leading to prolonged fasting, precipitated hepatotoxicity, with ample acetaminophen present in the liver to cause hepatocyte necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Moderate-overdose exposure (4-10 g within 24 hours); prolonged fasting (e.g., from illness) proposed as a precipitating factor; chronic alcoholism was much less common in this group and not required; chronic alcohol use or recent alcohol intake alone did not account for most cases.
raw_record.extra_details: This study (see Table, patients 3 and 7) suggests fasting may be an important predisposing factor for acetaminophen hepatotoxicity in the moderate-overdose range. Alcohol may potentiate the effect of fasting by inducing microsomal enzymes; genetic factors such as diminished glucuronidation capacity may increase susceptibility. Benson previously showed patients with chronic liver disease including alcoholic cirrhosis had no ill effects with 4 g/day up to 14 days, and cases of hepatotoxicity at recommended doses (4 g/24 h) in chronic alcoholics are almost absent. Acetaminophen plasma toxic level given as >300 µmol/L (>5.0 mg/dL).

raw_record.support_text: This cohort study reports on modified-release paracetamol overdose treated with acetylcysteine and evaluates the paracetamol × aminotransferase multiplication product as a predictor of hepatotoxicity. Regardless of ingestion type (acute vs. staggered), a product ≥10,000 mg/L × IU/L was associated with a high likelihood of developing hepatotoxicity despite acetylcysteine treatment, while a product <1500 mg/L × IU/L was highly sensitive in excluding the development of hepatotoxicity. The paper frames paracetamol overdose as the cause of the hepatotoxicity and ALI observed in the exposed patients, discussing risk of progression to fulminant hepatic failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Modified-release paracetamol formulation; poisoning context treated with acetylcysteine; includes both single and staggered (staggered) overdose presentations.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of patients with modified-release paracetamol overdose treated with acetylcysteine; 5 patients developed hepatotoxicity (4/5 with calculable serial multiplication products) and 68 did not. Outcome definitions: hepatotoxicity by traditional biochemical criteria; ALI defined as at least a doubling of ALT and >50 IU/L. Paracetamol × ALT multiplication product cut-offs: ≥10,000 mg/L × IU/L (LR 27, 95% CI 4-207 for ALI; LR 28, 95% CI 7-107 for hepatotoxicity with single ingestion), 1500-10,000 (LR 0.9), <1500 (LR 0.3 for ALI; highly sensitive to exclude hepatotoxicity). Product within 8 h of ingestion mildly elevated and fell quickly in patients without ALI/hepatotoxicity; delayed repeat testing improves specificity. Acetylcysteine started within 8 h of overdose prevented hepatotoxicity despite high product. Severity outcome discussed: 'patients are unlikely to develop fulminant hepatic failure unless meeting the traditional biochemical criteria of hepatotoxicity first', with product proposed as an inclusion criterion for trials of intensified acetylcysteine to prevent fulminant hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: The Acute Liver Failure Study Group (ALFSG), examining acute liver failure across 22 academic centres over 6 years, found paracetamol (acetaminophen) accounted for 42% of all ALF cases in the US, increasing from 28% in 1998 to 51% in 2003, and stabilizing at 52% and 46% in 2004 and 2005. ALF mortality was cited at roughly 30%.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Most US paracetamol-associated ALF was from unintentional (48%) or intentional (44%) overdose; only ~10% of paracetamol ALF cases occurred at dosages <4 g/day. Among unintentional-overdose ALF patients, the median paracetamol dose was 7.5 g/day (range 1.0-78 g/day), use was rarely for more than 7 days, and 63% used an opioid-paracetamol product.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol is also known as acetaminophen. ALFSG data: 42% of all US ALF cases attributed to paracetamol; proportion rose from 28% (1998) to 51% (2003), then 52% (2004) and 46% (2005). ALF is rare (~1.4 cases per million per year in Spain) with a mortality rate of ~30%. Among unintentional-overdose ALF patients, 81% reported pain and 62% used a single product. The 2009 FDA Advisory Committee recommended dose limits (3.25 g/day), single-tablet limits (325 mg), and removal of opioid-paracetamol products; in January 2011 the FDA required limiting paracetamol to 325 mg/tablet in opioid-paracetamol products and label revisions on the risk of severe liver damage.

raw_record.support_text: Of the 132 patients identified as having acetaminophen overdose, 22 developed acute liver failure (ALF). Among these patients, hepatic encephalopathy (OR 75.46; 95% CI 8.73–3335) and hepatic necrosis (OR 9.15; 95% CI 2.96–28.46) were the most discriminative liver-related diagnostic codes for identifying ALF. When restricted to patients identified as having acetaminophen hepatotoxicity, the ALF algorithm had sensitivity of 89% (17/19 cases), specificity 63%, PPV 53%, and NPV 93%.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Occurs in the setting of acetaminophen overdose, including patients with multiple time-point (e.g., unintentional) ingestions within a population-based hospitalization administrative database.
raw_record.extra_details: Study validated ICD-9-CM (965.4) and ICD-10 (T39.1) principal codes for identifying acetaminophen overdose (sensitivity 90%, specificity 83%, c-statistic 0.87). Of 132 overdose cases, 59 had hepatotoxicity (n=59 in Table 5) and 22 developed ALF. Hepatotoxicity: hepatic necrosis (570, K71.1) OR 17.16 (4.65–92.85), toxic hepatitis (573.3, K71.2, K71.6, K71.9) OR 7.85 (3.01–21.98). ALF: hepatic encephalopathy (572.2, K72.0, K72.9) OR 75.46 (8.73–3335), hepatic necrosis OR 9.15 (2.96–28.46); diagnostic algorithm requiring hepatic encephalopathy or necrosis code predicted ALF with OR 58.8 (12.5–276.0). Codes for jaundice and hepatorenal syndrome were not recorded in any patient.

raw_record.support_text: A retrospective case series reported that, although the frequency of paracetamol poisoning is lower in older subjects, when paracetamol intoxication does occur it is more frequently associated with fulminant hepatic failure and death, and age is considered an independent risk factor of morbidity and mortality in these cases. The paper also notes there is a lack of good quality clinical evidence that older people have a clinically significant difference in paracetamol metabolism or are at increased risk of toxicity at either therapeutic or supra-therapeutic doses.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Older/elderly people; overdose (intoxication) setting; age is an independent risk factor for morbidity and mortality in these cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure and death are more frequent in older people when intoxication occurs. Metabolism/age data are inconsistent: some PK studies suggest increased toxicity risk with age (prolonged t1/2, reduced clearance, increased oxidation from reduced glucuronidation/sulfation, reduced liver volume), whereas others find no age effect (t1/2, AUC, oral clearance unrelated to age; Cmax not translating to ALT changes). Two population-based studies found paracetamol poisoning rates decrease with age from a peak in adolescence/early adulthood. The paper states there is a lack of good quality clinical evidence that older people have a clinically significant difference in paracetamol metabolism or increased toxicity risk at therapeutic or supra-therapeutic doses.

raw_record.support_text: A 33-year-old pregnant woman (35 weeks) presented 3 days after intentional ingestion of 30 grams of acetaminophen, with elevated ALT (785 IU/L) and AST (630 IU/L), a detectable acetaminophen level of 14 mg/dL, and INR of 1.7, consistent with delayed acetaminophen toxicity. She was treated with n-acetylcysteine, but developed worsening coagulopathy, fulminant hepatic failure with peak AST 6693 IU/L and peak ALT 5566 IU/L, acute renal injury, congestive heart failure, and acute lung injury requiring ventilation. She recovered and was discharged on day 14; the fetus delivered stillborn 72 hours after ingestion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (30 g intentional ingestion) in a 35-week pregnant patient; developed coagulopathy requiring reversal with vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma; treated with n-acetylcysteine; fetal death (stillbirth) occurred.
raw_record.extra_details: Delayed acetaminophen toxicity; fulminant hepatic failure attributed to acetaminophen-induced liver injury; presenting ALT 785 IU/L and AST 630 IU/L, INR 1.7 rising to 3.0; peak AST 6693 IU/L and peak ALT 5566 IU/L; acetaminophen level 14 mg/dL; acute renal injury, congestive heart failure, acute lung injury; n-acetylcysteine continued until hepatic improvement; discharged day 14 after complete recovery. NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine) toxic byproduct forms in fetal liver at a lower rate than adults due to immature P450 system; acetaminophen crosses the placenta with fetal levels approximating maternal levels.

raw_record.support_text: In the authors' single-center series of acute liver failure (ALF), 104 patients underwent liver transplantation, with similar 30-day posttransplant survival in the acetaminophen cohort (69%) and the non-acetaminophen cohort (78%). Mortality on the transplant waiting list was double in the acetaminophen cohort (31.8%) versus the non-acetaminophen cohort (15.7%), and patients with acetaminophen-induced ALF listed for emergency transplantation had an increased incidence of organ failure with cerebral edema, inotropic support, and renal dialysis.

raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose/poisoning causes acute liver failure (acetaminophen-induced ALF), including cases requiring emergency listing for liver transplantation. King's College poor prognostic criteria were used for transplant decisions; lactate was introduced into listing criteria. 327 in-hospital deaths were attributed to acetaminophen overdose in Scotland over 1995-2003 (27-53 deaths/year); ~600 adult (ages 20-69) admissions per quarter followed acetaminophen overdose. In the current cohort (2002-2005), 4 of 81 acetaminophen ALF patients received liver transplant vs 13 of 99 in 1993-1996; transplant waiting-list mortality for the acetaminophen cohort was 31.8%. In 80% of 2002-2005 cases there were contraindications to transplantation, frequently active/resistant alcohol dependence.

It also stresses that a positive history of paracetamol overdose and its temporal relation to symptom onset avoids unnecessary viral serological tests, and that patients with concealed paracetamol overdose may present late.

raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol-induced hepatic necrosis carries a good prognosis once the patient survives the acute episode; survivors do not develop chronic liver disease. The magnitude of the alanine aminotransferase (ALT) rise can help differentiate from viral hepatitis; in the authors' case 2, ALT activity was 13,450 U/l, far exceeding the maximum 5300 U/l (mean 2122 U/l, SD 1565 U/l) recorded in 69 jaundiced patients with proved viral hepatitis in 1981. raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol is frequently taken as an overdose in suicidal attempts, and hepatic damage of all grades of severity, from minor to fulminant hepatic failure, may result, with bleeding often being a major problem and not infrequently the direct cause of death. Low clotting factor levels were attributed in part to impaired hepatic synthesis and increased consumption from intravascular coagulation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (including suicidal overdose) in adults.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic damage of all grades from minor to fulminant hepatic failure. In 66 patients, early coagulation changes included low clotting factors II, V and VII within 24 hours; prothrombin time ratio exceeded 2.2 within 30 hours of overdose in all patients who eventually died (9 deaths in the series), and the ratio was less than this in those developing only moderate hepatic damage. Severe hepatic damage was defined as plasma bilirubin >69 umol/l and was the group from which all 9 deaths occurred. A controlled trial of fresh frozen plasma (300 ml every 6 hr) in 20 patients with prothrombin time ratio >2.2 reduced the maximum prothrombin time ratio abnormality but did not reduce morbidity or mortality. Coagulation disturbance was of short duration, with prothrombin time ratio returning to normal within one week of overdose.

raw_record.support_text: In a 1988 NEJM-based analysis of 11,195 acetaminophen (APAP) poison exposures at our center, hepatotoxicity was minimal regardless of initial APAP plasma concentration when NAC treatment was started within 8 hours of ingestion, with increased frequency of hepatotoxicity when the treatment delay reached 8–16 hours and some retained benefit even beyond 16–24 hours. Paragraph 22 adds that of the 11,195 exposures, 517 had APAP levels below the nomogram line or otherwise did not meet protocol criteria, and an outcome nomogram showed the percentage of toxic cases related to initial plasma level and time of ingestion among patients treated with a full NAC course.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (ingestion) setting from a national multicenter study of 11,195 exposures; outcomes reflect patients treated with NAC (full course in the outcome nomogram); 517 cases with sub-nomogram levels or non-protocol entries were analyzed separately.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity frequency rose with treatment delay (minimal when NAC started within 8 h; increased at 8–16 h; diminished but still present after 16 h). Outcome nomogram (previously unpublished) plots percent toxic cases against initial plasma APAP level and historical time of ingestion. Some patients with initial plasma level below the nomogram line showed toxicity, attributed to inaccuracy of patient histories and time dependence. APAP levels of 300 µg/mL (4 h) referenced in risk analysis nomogram; cases with SGOT ≥ 1000 IU were plotted. Toxicity follows a threshold effect related to plasma level; height above threshold did not further refine severity. Hepatic damage occurs at ~70% glutathione depletion; ~4% of an APAP dose converts to N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), with calculated ~15.9 g APAP absorbed in a 70 kg human to reach threshold toxicity (~0.635 g NAPQI). NAC (N-acetylcysteine) administration discussed as the antidote, not as a cause.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 23 patients presenting more than 15 h after a paracetamol overdose, 20 (87%) developed hepatotoxicity and four died of hepatic failure. The text frames paracetamol poisoning as a cause of hepatotoxicity and of paracetamol-related acute liver failure, describing established hepatotoxicity in overdose. A table of 24 reported paracetamol-poisoning cases lists peak AST/ALT, INR/PT, and outcomes including death from hepatic failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (paracetamol poisoning) context only; many cases involved co-ingested drugs (temazepam, salicylate, codeine, sulphasalazine, aspirin, pine oil, dextropropoxyphene, cinnarizine); some patients received NAC, bicarbonate, haemodialysis/haemofiltration or charcoal treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose causing early lactic acidosis/early metabolic acidosis of uncertain cause and later hepatotoxicity with established hepatotoxicity and paracetamol-related acute liver failure. Reported ingestions up to ~200 g with peak paracetamol concentrations up to 1614 mg/L. In the series of 23 late-presenting (>15 h) overdose patients, median plasma lactate 3.6 mmol/L, 11 (48%) acidotic, 20/23 (87%) hepatotoxicity, 4 died of hepatic failure. In a cohort of 103 with severe paracetamol-related ALF (King's College Hospital 1998-1999), 10 transplanted/excluded, 57 survived, 36 died; early arterial lactate significantly higher in non-survivors (median 8.5 vs 1.4 mmol/L, P<0.0001); pH and lactate were the only independent mortality predictors (cut-offs 3.5 mmol/L admission, 3.0 mmol/L post-resuscitation). King's College criteria for liver transplantation in paracetamol-related ALF: arterial pH <7.3 ≥24h after overdose or creatinine >300 umol/L with grade 3-4 encephalopathy and PT >100 s; modified criteria added lactate-based criteria. Lactate proposed as prognostic marker for transplant decisions.
