raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses the interpretation of aminotransferase abnormalities following APAP (acetaminophen) overdose, and states that very little published information exists regarding the AST:ALT (De Ritis) ratio in 'the most common cause of fulminant hepatic failure, APAP poisoning.' This explicitly attributes fulminant hepatic failure to acetaminophen poisoning in the overdose setting. Additional context from paragraph 40 notes that hepatotoxicity (crossing the 1000 IU/L AST/ALT threshold) followed APAP exposure in this cohort.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (APAP poisoning); findings reflect aminotransferase kinetics in patients presenting after acetaminophen overdose rather than ordinary therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Descriptive analysis of aminotransferase (AST/ALT) rise and fall kinetics following APAP overdose. 55 subjects who received N-acetylcysteine (N-AC) were analyzed; death and a surviving liver-transplant patient are shown. A stopping criterion of aminotransferase decrease to 50% of peak was reached in 43 subjects using AST and 38 using ALT; the AST:ALT ratio half-decay time after N-AC was approximately 24.7 hours. No patient with a normal ALT at presentation developed hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol is being increasingly used as a suicidal agent. About 10 g produces hepatic necrosis but the dose actually ingested is difficult to assess because of the early onset of vomiting and the difficulty in obtaining a reliable history. Shortly after ingestion the patient becomes nauseated and vomits; after about 48 hours recovery seems in progress when the condition deteriorates and jaundice appears on the third or fourth day. Serum transaminase levels and prothrombin times are extremely high, and acute liver failure supervenes. The overall mortality for 201 patients admitted to a district general hospital was 3.5%. Hepatic histology shows centrilobular necrosis, some fatty change and very little inflammation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (increasingly used as a suicidal agent); about 10 g produces hepatic necrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism involves the electrophilic metabolite of paracetamol conjugating with hepatic glutathione; when glutathione is exhausted the metabolite arylates essential nucleophilic macromolecules, producing hepatic necrosis. Clinical course: nausea and vomiting shortly after ingestion, jaundice on approximately the third or fourth day, extremely high serum transaminase and prothrombin times, acute liver failure, prominent myocardial and renal damage and hypoglycaemia. Mortality was 3.5% among 201 patients admitted to a district general hospital. Histology shows centrilobular necrosis, some fatty change and little inflammation; reticulin collapse may be confluent and massive but cirrhosis is not a sequel. Prognostic factors include prothrombin ratio of 20%, hepatic coma, and paracetamol blood levels (normal plasma half-life 2 h; toxicity likely if >4 h, severe damage probable if >12 h; plasma level >300 µg/ml at 4 h gives 100% incidence of hepatic toxicity, <120 µg/ml no danger; >50 µg/ml at 12 h likely toxicity, <50 µg/ml no danger). Cysteamine treatment discussed.

raw_record.support_text: Clinical demonstration of alcohol-exacerbated paracetamol hepatotoxicity was made in 2 studies totaling over 850 patients with paracetamol overdose hepatitis (dose about 25 g). Hepatitis was more severe in heavy drinkers: lower prothrombin time nadir (13% vs 28%) and higher percentage of death or emergency transplantation (26% vs 5.3%), with no difference in ingested paracetamol doses. On multivariate analysis, chronic alcohol intake was an independent prognostic factor for poor outcome with an odds ratio of 3.5 (95% CI 1.78-6.97); the second study showed similar results for hepatic encephalopathy and greater hepatitis severity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (ingested dose about 25 g); chronic alcohol consumption is an independent prognostic factor worsening the course (OR 3.5).
raw_record.extra_details: Two studies totaling >850 overdose patients; hepatitis more severe in heavy drinkers with lower prothrombin nadir (13% vs 28%) and higher death/emergency transplantation rate (26% vs 5.3%) despite identical doses (25 g); multivariate OR 3.5 (95% CI 1.78-6.97); second study showed similar findings for hepatic encephalopathy and severity; these studies did not address impact of therapeutic doses in chronic alcoholics.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) remains the leading cause of acute hepatic failure in the USA. The Acute Liver Failure Study Group's prospective evaluation of 275 consecutive patients (1998-2003) at 22 tertiary care centers found these cases represented 42% of all acute liver failure patients (criteria: acute coagulopathy and encephalopathy, aminotransferases >1000 IU/l, intake of >4 g/day within 7 days, no other cause). Median dose ingested was 24 g (range 1.2-180 g); 44% were intentional (suicidal) overdose (often with a narcotic), 42% unintentional overdose, and 8% of unknown intent. Mortality was 27%, with 8% undergoing liver transplant.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (intake of >4 g/day within 7 days); 44% intentional/suicidal overdose (often combined with a narcotic-containing drug), 42% unintentional overdose (usually for pain control), 8% unknown intent.
raw_record.extra_details: Also referred to as paracetamol; leading cause of acute hepatic failure in the USA. ALFSG prospective study of 275 consecutive patients over 6 years (1998-2003) across 22 tertiary care centers (~30% of transplant facilities). Cases were 42% of all ALF cases (declined from 51% peak in 2003, from 28% in 1998). Median dose 24 g (range 1.2-180 g). Mortality 27%; 8% underwent liver transplant; survival and transplant rates similar between intentional and unintentional overdose.

raw_record.support_text: In this population-based study of paracetamol overdoses in the NUH catchment area of Iceland, the occurrence of acute liver failure (ALF) was very low and more often associated with accidental overdose; N-acetylcysteine (NAC) was used in all patients with clinically significant liver injury and serious outcome was very rare. Among the 7 ALF patients (Table), one patient (case 1) had mortality listed as the liver injury outcome within 2 years of follow-up, and one (case 5) experienced a 2nd ALF.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (intentional and accidental self-poisoning); ALF more often associated with accidental overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: Annual incidence of paracetamol overdose declined from 30 to 16 per 100,000 inhabitants over 6 years (down 47%), with a step-change in 2005 coinciding with removal of paracetamol/codeine combinations as OTC drugs; paracetamol accounted for 18.4% of all drug-related overdoses in the catchment area. 326 patient visits and 182 hospitalized index visits; 7 patients developed ALF (median ALT 7402 IU/l, median peak ALT range 2778-8844 IU/l; peak PT up to 61.4 s; up to 6 days in ICU). ALF patients were older (51 vs 30 years) and more often had accidental overdose (67% vs 7%) and alcohol abuse (100% vs 31%). NAC used in all patients with clinically significant liver injury. One ALF death (case 1) and one recurrent ALF (case 5) within 2-year follow-up. Young females (16-25 years, 75% female) dominated intentional overdoses; no gender difference in accidental overdoses.

raw_record.support_text: Among 182 paracetamol overdose patients, severe hepatotoxicity defined as ALT >1000 IU/l was 10-fold more common in accidental overdose (31%) than intentional overdose (3%, p<0.001). Risk of severe hepatotoxicity increased with age (OR 1.89 per 10 years, 95% CI 1.30–2.73, p=0.001). Paracetamol overdose was thus an attributed cause of dose-related hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (intentional or accidental); all 7 ALF patients had a history of alcohol abuse; one malnourished patient developed ALF after ~4 g paracetamol; only death occurred in a 48-year-old female with a contraindication for liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatotoxicity (ALT >1000 IU/l) in 31% of accidental vs 3% of intentional overdoses (p<0.001); abnormal aspartate/alanine aminotransferases (>50 IU/l) in 31% of males vs 17% of females; 78% of the 182 patients had normal liver tests. Acute liver failure occurred in 7/182 (3.8%) index visits (3 females 2.3%, 4 males 7.8%); 4/16 (25%) accidental vs 2/161 (1.2%) intentional overdoses (p=0.001). Median peak serum paracetamol 83 µmol/l in ALF vs 326 µmol/l in non-ALF (p<0.05); median creatinine 339 vs 68 µmol/l (p<0.001). ALF risk OR per 10 years 1.75 (95% CI 1.14–2.69). All ALF patients received N-acetylcysteine.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatic necrosis is the major manifestation of acetaminophen overdose. In these patients it became clinically evident one to five days after ingestion, with maximal SGOT elevation two to six days after ingestion. Severity varied from mild SGOT elevation to prolonged prothrombin time (four patients) and massive hepatic necrosis with encephalopathy (two patients). Liver biopsies and postmortem examination demonstrated centrilobular necrosis, characteristic of acetaminophen hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The POP Trial's primary objective was to assess adverse events and serious adverse events associated with calmangafodipir co-treatment with the SNAP NAC treatment regime in patients with paracetamol overdose, with a secondary objective of measuring clinical and exploratory biomarkers of acute liver injury. Patients admitted within 24 h of a single acute or staggered paracetamol overdose and deemed to require treatment with NAC were eligible, and NAC continuation depended on ALT activity more than doubling, ALT ≥ 2× ULN (100 U/L), INR > 1.3, or paracetamol > 20 mg/L, indicating hepatotoxicity in the overdose setting.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 645 consecutive patients with single-dose acetaminophen (paracetamol) poisoning admitted from 1994 to 2000, time to intravenous N-acetylcysteine (NAC) treatment was the single most important independent risk factor for acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity and mortality. Mortality was 0.42% (95% CI 0.05-2.7) when time to NAC was less than 12 hours, rising to 6.1%, 13%, and 19% when time to NAC exceeded 12, 24, and 48 hours, respectively. Chronic alcohol abuse was an independent mortality risk factor (OR 3.52; 95% CI 1.78-6.97), whereas acute alcohol ingestion was protective in alcoholic patients (OR 0.08; 95% CI 0.01-0.66).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (single-dose acetaminophen poisoning); chronic alcohol abuse was an independent risk factor for mortality; acute alcohol ingestion was protective against mortality in alcoholic patients but not in nonalcoholics; patient age and quantity of acetaminophen were independent risk factors.
raw_record.extra_details: 645 consecutive acetaminophen poisoning patients (retrospective to 1998, prospective thereafter) at Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen, 1994-2000. Major prognostic factor was time from overdose to NAC treatment. Mortality 0.42% (<12h), 6.1% (>12h), 13% (>24h), 19% (>48h). Chronic alcohol abuse OR 3.52 (95% CI 1.78-6.97); acute alcohol ingestion OR 0.08 in alcoholics (95% CI 0.01-0.66), OR 0.21 in nonalcoholics (95% CI 0.03-1.67). Acetaminophen poisoning is described as the most common cause of acute liver failure in Denmark and the UK. Proposed mechanism: CYP2E1 induction with glutathione depletion; acute alcohol inhibits microsomal acetaminophen oxidation by CYP2E1 reducing synthesis of N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI).

German Federal Statistics Office data for 2010 listed 38 fatal analgesic poisonings, of which only 4 were attributable to paracetamol. The paper treats paracetamol's overdose-related liver toxicity as undisputed.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (suicidal intent or accidental overdose), not therapeutic use; figures reflect German national data.
raw_record.extra_details: Among 155 severe liver failure cases referred to 11 German transplantation centers (2008–2009), paracetamol was involved in 27; 5 underwent transplantation or died. Against roughly 30 million sold packages of the paracetamol monotherapy, the 4 fatal liver cases in 2010 correspond to an incidence of ~0.00001% of applications (packages), comprising suicides, mistaken/avoidable overdoses, and possibly rare damage at normal dosing; such low frequency would not be detectable in typical pre-approval studies of 5,000–10,000 exposed patients. Reported accidental overdoses involved unknown ingredient contents of juices and tablets leading to additive use.

raw_record.support_text: In this cohort of patients with acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure, 19 (7%) reported taking ≤4 g acetaminophen per day before presentation, of whom 16 had ALT levels over 1,000 IU/L and 12 had measurable serum acetaminophen levels. The whole group of 274 studied subjects showed severe liver injury with serum ALT up to 11,240 IU/L, and outcomes included 178 (65%) surviving without transplantation, 74 (27%) dying, and 23 (8%) undergoing transplantation, with 71% alive at the 3-week point.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting that includes unintentional and intentional (suicidal) overdoses; a low-dose subgroup (19 subjects, 7%) reported ≤4 g/day acetaminophen; chronic alcohol use/abuse present in 55%/35% of the group.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 274 patients with acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure; the low-dose subgroup was older (median 46 vs 34 y), more often reported unintentional overdose (74% vs 40%), and used/abused alcohol more often; whole-group ALT range 136-11,240 IU/L; low-dose median ALT 2,949 (range 175-19,826) vs 4,224 (136-11,240) for higher-dose; serum acetaminophen measurable in 12 low-dose subjects; outcomes: 27% died, 8% transplanted, 26% listed for transplant, 71% alive at 3 weeks. Prescription acetaminophen/narcotic compounds (commonly Vicodin, acetaminophen/hydrocodone) were used by 44% of the group, primarily the unintentional group (63% vs 18%), with lower platelets, ALT, and bilirubin but no difference in transplant rate or survival; alcohol abusers had lower acetaminophen levels and less severe encephalopathy.

raw_record.support_text: In this single-patient case report of acetaminophen overdose with markedly delayed absorption, the authors explain that NAPQI is primarily responsible for acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity. They note the patient had a higher fraction of CYP metabolites (10%) compared with therapeutic ingestion (<5%) or acetaminophen overdoses that do not develop liver injury. The associated disease entities in the text describe the resulting acute liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting with markedly delayed acetaminophen absorption; patient was intubated and mechanically ventilated and likely co-ingested a combination product containing dextromethorphan and chlorphenamine, plus clonidine and low-dose fentanyl/propofol, all of which were considered to delay gastric emptying.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case (adult female). True peak acetaminophen concentration occurred between 16 and 39 h post-ingestion; she did not cross the 150 mg/L at 4 h treatment nomogram line until 16 h post-ingestion, so acetylcysteine was not started until hepatotoxicity symptoms developed; no activated charcoal given. Mechanistic detail: NAPQI (reactive metabolite formed from ~5% of a therapeutic dose via CYP) causes hepatotoxicity in overdose by depleting hepatic glutathione and covalently binding cellular proteins; CYP metabolite fraction was higher (~10%) in this patient and higher in those who develop acute liver injury. She developed hepatotoxicity symptoms (clinical liver injury) but acute liver failure is not explicitly reported.

raw_record.support_text: In this case series of modified-release paracetamol (Panadol Osteo®) poisoning, hepatotoxicity was uncommon, with only two patients developing a peak ALT more than 1000 IU/L—one after a 'massive' ingestion (945 mg/kg) and the other a late presenter (9.5 h post-ingestion). Small numbers of cases had mild ALT increases that did not meet the hepatotoxicity criterion (ALT or AST >1000 IU/L). No patients developed acute liver failure as defined by King's College criteria requiring transfer to the specialist liver unit, and no fatalities were noted.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting with modified-release formulation (Panadol Osteo®, 665 mg caplets available in packs of up to 96 caplets, up to 63,840 mg per pack); patients treated with N-acetylcysteine ingested a median reported dose of ~290 mg/kg; one patient had co-ingested ethanol.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined in the paper as ALT or AST >1000 IU/L; patients with these criteria were considered hepatotoxic, whereas smaller ALT rises were not. Treated patients were identified by the Australasian paracetamol treatment nomogram; some later 'line-crossers' had initial concentrations above 500 µmol/L at 4 h and reported doses >10 g. No acute liver failure (King's College criteria) and no fatalities in the cohort. One patient had a 'massive' ingestion of 945 mg/kg and one presented late (9.5 h) with predicted hepatotoxicity despite prolonged NAC infusion.

raw_record.support_text: The patient reported here overdosed on acetaminophen and developed mild-to-moderate hepatotoxicity. She ingested a total of 12 g of acetaminophen over 2 days for dental pain and presented with jaundice; blood chemistry showed alanine aminotransferase 1216 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 1362 U/L, total bilirubin 4.2 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 3.5 mg/dL, and an increased prothrombin time of 19.9 sec. Serologic viral hepatitis markers were negative.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting: 12 g acetaminophen ingested over 2 days for dental pain (supratherapeutic exposure). No acetylcysteine administered; serum acetaminophen 44 µg/mL and <5 µg/mL at 6 and 12 h after last dose.
raw_record.extra_details: Mild-to-moderate hepatotoxicity characterized by jaundice/icterus, ALT 1216 U/L, AST 1362 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 187 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 89 U/L, total bilirubin 4.2 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 3.5 mg/dL, prothrombin time 19.9 sec. Associated unusual hematologic picture of reactive plasmacytosis (70% of nucleated marrow elements) and thrombocytosis (platelets 706 × 10³/mm³) with life-threatening agranulocytosis (WBC 0.5 × 10³/mm³) followed by a leukemoid reaction. 19-year-old white woman; renal function normal; viral hepatitis markers negative.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective analysis of 784 acetaminophen overdose patients (median ingested dose 15,000 mg; median 250 mg/kg), hepatotoxicity occurred in 57 (7.3%) and acute liver injury in 187 (23.9%) of cases. Dose-estimates above 150 mg/kg were associated with hepatotoxicity and acute liver injury, while no hepatotoxicity was found below 150 mg/kg.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting: 784 cases of acetaminophen overdose (single acute ingestion), median ingested dose 15,000 mg and median 250 mg/kg body weight, 642 (81.9%) female, median age 23 years.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity in 57/784 (7.3%); acute liver injury in 187/784 (23.9%). Dose ≥150 mg/kg (n=545): 57 (10.5%) hepatotoxicity, 171 (31.4%) acute liver injury, risk ratio 4.4 (95%CI 2.7-7.1) for acute liver injury vs <150 mg/kg (n=239: 0 hepatotoxicity, 17 (7.1%) acute liver injury). 406 cases (51.8%) had serum concentration ≥150-treatment line. Activated charcoal decontamination associated with risk ratio 0.46 (95%CI 0.38-0.55) for being above 150-treatment line. NAC therapy in 376 (66.9%).

raw_record.support_text: This study of paracetamol poisoning at two hospitals defined paracetamol hepatotoxicity as ALT > 1000 U/L in patients administered acetylcysteine within 8 h post-overdose, and assessed the proportion with an abnormal ALT (above the reference range) attributable to paracetamol toxicity. Complications recorded included death and liver failure (paragraph 20). The paper explicitly attributes the liver enzyme abnormality and hepatotoxicity to paracetamol overdose/poisoning.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting: >4 g paracetamol ingested within 24 h, acute, staggered or chronic ingestion; patients aged ≥16 years admitted to the two study hospitals and treated with acetylcysteine (modified 2-phase or standard 3-phase regimen).
raw_record.extra_details: Secondary outcomes included proportion with paracetamol hepatotoxicity (ALT > 1000 U/L) in patients given acetylcysteine within 8 h post-overdose and proportion with abnormal ALT above reference range attributable to paracetamol toxicity. Specific complications (death, liver failure) were recorded in the first hospital's toxicology database. The acetylcysteine treatment protocol (200 mg/kg then 100 mg/kg infusion) was modified based on a simulation study and a smaller-loading-dose trial.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective observational study of 545 patients with acute non-staggered paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose, ingestions of ≥30 g correlated with higher peak serum aminotransferase and creatinine concentrations (r=0.212, P<0.0001; r=0.138, P=0.002). Acute liver injury, hepatotoxicity and coagulopathy were more frequent when the measured timed paracetamol concentration to nomogram threshold ratio (APAPpl:APAPt) was ≥3, with odds ratios (95% CI) of 9.19 (5.04-16.68), 35.95 (8.80-158.1) and 8.34 (4.43-15.84), respectively (P<0.0001), and heightened risk persisted even when acetylcysteine was given within 8 hours.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting: acute non-staggered paracetamol overdose; massive overdose defined as extrapolated 4-hour plasma paracetamol concentration >250 mg/L or reported ingestion ≥30 g.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective observational cohort (n=545, 2005-2013) from a tertiary care toxicology service. APAPpl:APAPt ratio based on treatment line through 100 mg/L at 4 h. Acute liver injury, hepatotoxicity and coagulopathy ORs (95% CI) 9.19 (5.04-16.68), 35.95 (8.80-158.1), 8.34 (4.43-15.84) at ratio ≥3 (P<0.0001); risk persisted despite acetylcysteine within 8 h. Suggested enhanced therapeutic strategies for APAPpl:APAPt ≥3 patients.

raw_record.support_text: In this comparison of 2,086 patients receiving 20-hour intravenous and 1,962 patients receiving 72-hour oral acetylcysteine after acetaminophen overdose, the unadjusted incidence of hepatotoxicity was 13.9% in the 20-hour group and 15.8% in the 72-hour group (difference not significant). Deaths attributed to acetaminophen-induced hepatic failure occurred (1 in the 20-hour group and 3 in the 72-hour group); one 20-hour-group patient who died had received a liver transplant for persistent coagulopathy and encephalopathy. All patients were treated for acetaminophen overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting: all patients had ingested acetaminophen and all received acetylcysteine (NAC) therapy after ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined as AST or ALT >1,000 IU/L; unadjusted incidence 13.9% (20-h IV group, 289/2,086) vs 15.8% (72-h oral group, 310/1,962), absolute difference -1.9% (95% CI -4.2% to 0.3%). Deaths attributed to acetaminophen-induced hepatic failure: 1 (20-h) and 3 (72-h); the 20-h death had acetylcysteine initiated 20.5 h after ingestion, infusion continued 100 h, and the patient received a liver transplant for persistent coagulopathy and encephalopathy. Median reported acetaminophen dose ingested ~20-22.5 g; median extrapolated 4-h acetaminophen concentration ~260-280 µg/mL.

raw_record.support_text: A 60-year-old woman presented with five days of fever, myalgia, cough and fatigue after influenza contact. Because of disabling flu symptoms she took an estimated eight to ten grams of acetaminophen daily during the preceding week, denied other medications or supplements, and reported no abusive alcohol intake. Her serum acetaminophen level was 358 µmol/L. She subsequently developed acute liver failure and later fatal invasive pulmonary mucormycosis, with abdominal ultrasound showing findings suggesting acute hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting: approximately 8-10 g acetaminophen taken daily during the week preceding onset; concurrent influenza B infection; concurrent medications included lithium, quetiapine, levothyroxine, pregabalin, and clonazepam.
raw_record.extra_details: Serum acetaminophen concentration 358 µmol/L; patient developed acute liver failure followed by invasive pulmonary mucormycosis and died from the infection (death not attributed to the liver injury itself); abdominal ultrasound showed hyperechogenicity of portal triads suggesting acute hepatitis with moderate ascites, and concurrent acute kidney injury with anuria; viral serology negative for hepatitis B, C and HIV and positive for influenza B.

raw_record.support_text: Patients admitted to the University of Kansas Hospital or Banner Good Samaritan Medical Center following acetaminophen (APAP) overdose were studied prospectively, including both acute- and chronic-overdose patients. The diagnosis of APAP overdose was made by a physician; inclusion criteria included a patient-reported history of APAP overdose, high serum APAP levels, and abnormal liver tests based on ALT, AST, PT, and bilirubin, with all participants meeting at least two criteria. Although a toxicology screen detected ethanol, cocaine, antidepressants, or other drugs in some patients, no medication other than APAP could have acutely caused the severe liver injury, and patients with evidence of another cause (viral hepatitis, ischemic liver) were excluded.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting: both acute-overdose and chronic-overdose patients were included; in the abnormal-liver-test group (20 patients) 5 patients took repeated doses in excess of the maximum recommended therapeutic dose of 4 g/day over multiple days.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective cohort of patients admitted to two hospitals after documented APAP overdose; diagnosis confirmed by physician. Liver injury defined by abnormal ALT, AST, PT, and bilirubin; each participant fulfilled at least two inclusion criteria. Ethanol, cocaine, antidepressants or other drugs were detected in some patients but none other than APAP could have acutely caused the severe liver injury; patients with alternative causes (viral hepatitis, ischemic liver) were excluded. All overdose patients received standard-of-care N-acetylcysteine (NAC) treatment.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 60 patients (45 female, 15 male, aged 15-58) admitted after paracetamol overdose, claimed ingested doses ranged from 13 to 100 g but did not correlate with the degree of hepatic damage. There was biochemical evidence of liver damage in all but eleven patients; in seventeen there was clinical evidence of severe liver damage progressing to fulminant hepatic failure with hepatic encephalopathy, deep coma ensued in fifteen, and twelve patients died between days 4 and 18 after ingestion. The paper attributes this hepatic damage to paracetamol overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting: claimed ingested doses of 13-100 g paracetamol; concurrent alcohol or sedatives (barbiturate, nitrazepam, diazepam, chlordiazepoxide) in 19 patients did not alter the severity of liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases of fulminant hepatic failure (acute liver failure) with hepatic encephalopathy (hepatic flap, fetor, mental confusion), deep coma, jaundice, tender liver, and an abnormal prothrombin-time ratio. Biochemical evidence of liver damage in 49 of 60 patients; 7 had isolated raised serum aspartate aminotransferase/S.G.O.T. (range 53-365 IU/L), one a raised serum bilirubin, and one an abnormal prothrombin-time ratio; 17 progressed to fulminant hepatic failure on days 3-5; 12 died (one on day 4, ten on days 6-11, one on day 18). raw_record.support_text: In the Australian Paracetamol Project, a prospective observational study of patients with large paracetamol overdoses and/or paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity, 53 patients were analysed. raw_record.support_text: Among all drug toxicity cases of ALF, acetaminophen overdosing was identified as the most predominant etiology. Sixteen patients (72.7% of these cases or 11.9% of all patients) ingested a median amount of 22 g acetaminophen with suicidal intent, while six patients (27.3%) accidentally intoxicated themselves by ingesting 3-5 g of acetaminophen on a given day. Patients with acetaminophen-induced liver failure were significantly younger than ALF patients of other etiologies (30 vs 43 years) and showed a shorter disease duration, higher serum AST than ALT, and lower bilirubin levels.

raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdosing caused 22 of the 53 drug-toxicity ALF cases (16 suicidal with median 22 g; 6 accidental with 3-5 g/day). Associated with shorter disease duration, higher serum AST than ALT, and lower bilirubin compared to other etiologies. Patients with acetaminophen- or HAV-related ALF had a four-week survival of 82% under conservative therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A 30-year-old woman took 8 g of Dafalgan (paracetamol) per day over two days for acute toothache. On the third day she presented with right upper abdominal pain and nausea and was found to have markedly elevated transaminases and coagulopathy (INR 3.7). She became increasingly somnolent, the diagnosis of acute liver failure was made, and transfer to a center hospital was decided. Acute liver failure criteria are INR>1.5 plus encephalopathy of any grade.

raw_record.support_text: The authors studied drug metabolism in patients with acute hepatic necrosis following paracetamol overdosage. In two patients who eventually died in hepatic failure, the plasma paracetamol half-life increased from a normal value of 2.0 +/- 0.4 (SD) hours to about 25 and 60 hours. In 17 patients recovering from paracetamol-induced hepatic necrosis the antipyrine half-life was 20.6 +/- 7.3 (SD) hours versus a normal of 12.0 +/- 3.5 (SD) hours, measured an average of 3.2 days after overdose when mean SGPT was 891 i.u./l; the antipyrine half-life returned to near normal over 7-21 days. Combined overdosage with paracetamol and barbiturates was reported particularly dangerous with possibly prolonged coma.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; acute hepatic necrosis following paracetamol overdosage in adults.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients died in hepatic failure; in them plasma paracetamol half-life rose from a normal 2.0 +/- 0.4 h to about 25 and 60 h. In 17 patients recovering from paracetamol-induced hepatic necrosis, antipyrine half-life was 20.6 +/- 7.3 h (normal 12.0 +/- 3.5 h) measured ~3.2 days after overdose with mean SGPT 891 i.u./l, recovering to near normal over 7-21 days; significant correlations between antipyrine half-life and paracetamol half-life, SGPT, serum bilirubin, and prothrombin time ratio. Barbiturate and diphenylhydantoin metabolism impaired by paracetamol-induced liver damage; combined paracetamol + barbiturate overdose may prolong coma.

raw_record.support_text: Among 1608 acetaminophen-overdose patients with measured plasma APAP levels, hepatic risk was categorized according to a published nomogram relating APAP concentration to time since ingestion at first admission. 147 patients (9.1%) were categorized as high-risk and 84 (5.2%) as probable-risk for developing hepatotoxicity; 141 high-risk patients received intravenous N-acetylcysteine (IV-NAC). This establishes APAP overdose as a cause of hepatic injury in humans.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; all patients presented for medical care after acetaminophen overdose (therapeutic use not assessed in this cohort).
raw_record.extra_details: Plasma APAP concentration and time since ingestion were used to grade hepatic risk via a published nomogram: high risk = APAP >= 200 mg/L at the 4-hour line; probable = 150-200 mg/L; low risk = <150 mg/L; categories also included early (<4 h), late (>15 h), and unknown timing. Cohort of 1749 overdose patients (1608 with APAP measured). 141/147 high-risk patients received IV-NAC; 2 high-risk patients admitted >15 h after ingestion did not. IV-NAC protocols, activated charcoal co-treatment (151/399), infusion durations, and length of hospital stay (20 min to 111 days) are detailed. No severity (death, transplantation, or acute liver failure) outcomes are stated in this window.

raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; case is a 13-year-old girl; extended-release formulation (Tylenol Extended Relief) rather than immediate-release.
raw_record.extra_details: Tylenol Extended Relief is an extended-release acetaminophen formulation; its dissolution and absorption are slowed with increasing tablet numbers (64% dissolution of 50 tablets at 8 h). Peak levels after supratherapeutic nontoxic doses of the extended-release product were about two-thirds of those after equivalent immediate-release dosing, with nearly identical AUC. Management: serum acetaminophen measured every 2 h from 4 to 16 h post-ingestion, acetylcysteine begun if any value exceeds two-thirds of the potentially toxic level per the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, and treatment discontinued if values stay nontoxic and liver-function tests are normal at 36 h.

raw_record.support_text: In a population-based cohort of 1543 patients hospitalized for acetaminophen overdose, acetaminophen hepatotoxicity (defined using diagnostic codes for hepatic necrosis, toxic hepatitis, and hepatic encephalopathy) was present in 70 patients and strongly predicted in-hospital mortality (14.3% in hepatotoxic patients vs 0.3% in those without; RR 42.1, 95% CI 14.8–119.8; P<.0005). Overall in-hospital mortality for acetaminophen overdose was 1%. Unintentional overdoses, preexisting liver disease, and cirrhosis markedly increased mortality (e.g., cirrhosis in-hospital mortality 54.6%).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; cohort of patients hospitalized for acetaminophen overdose (intentional and unintentional). Higher mortality observed with unintentional overdose, preexisting liver disease, cirrhosis, older age, and lower household income.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity was defined using ICD diagnostic codes for hepatic necrosis, toxic hepatitis, and hepatic encephalopathy. In-hospital mortality overall was 1% (79 deaths, cause available in 92%); acetaminophen hepatotoxicity was an independent predictor of extended-follow-up mortality (median 5.2 years; multivariate HR 2.97, 95% CI 1.62–5.47). Unintentional ('therapeutic misadventure') overdoses occurred in 13% of patients but represented 49% of hepatotoxicity cases, with 5-fold risk of hepatotoxicity and 13-fold risk of in-hospital mortality. U.S. ALF Study Group data cited indicate 50% of acetaminophen ALF cases are unintentional, with ~500 ALF cases and 150 deaths annually. Study used administrative data from 1995–2004.

raw_record.support_text: In patients given supportive therapy only after paracetamol overdosage, liver damage increased dramatically as the four-hour plasma paracetamol concentration rose from <150 to >300 µg/ml. All sixteen patients in the >300 µg/ml group had severe liver damage (mean AST 5,300 iu/l, bilirubin 7.3 mg%, prothrombin time ratio 2.4) and three died in hepatic failure. Patients treated within 10 hours with cysteamine (mean 6.8 hours) had no deaths and only minor liver damage, whereas those treated 10-26.5 hours after overdosage still developed severe liver damage.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; four-hour plasma paracetamol concentrations ranged from <150 to >300 µg/ml, with severe damage concentrated in the higher concentration groups.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver damage evaluated via AST, ALT, bilirubin and prothrombin time ratio. Among 16 patients with 4-hour paracetamol >300 µg/ml given supportive care, all had severe liver damage and 3 died in hepatic failure; supportive-only group overall (n=31, mean 4-hour paracetamol 342 µg/ml) had 71% severe damage and 3 deaths. Cysteamine within 10 hours of ingestion prevented severe damage; when given 12 hours or more after ingestion it did not prevent severe liver damage. Also described in text as 'severe hepatic necrosis' (AST/ALT >1,000 iu/l) among treated patients. Cysteamine is a DILI-protective antidote, not an attributed causal agent.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol is the commonest drug ingested in overdose in the UK. In the early stage of poisoning paracetamol rarely results in specific clinical features, and the risk of liver damage can only be predicted from the plasma paracetamol concentration, so estimation of plasma paracetamol concentrations is important in all patients presenting with a history of a paracetamol overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; in the case series, three patients with a staggered overdose presented more than 24 hours after ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: Risk of liver damage is dose/concentration-related and predicted from plasma paracetamol concentration; three of 26 patients presenting after a staggered overdose developed severe hepatotoxicity and were treated with NAC on arrival, though presentation at >24 h after ingestion reduces NAC efficacy. In 11 of 99 patients presenting within four hours of ingestion with paracetamol levels 150-200 mg/l at four hours, liver function tests, renal function and INR were normal at discharge.

raw_record.support_text: This population-based Swedish study of paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning, defined by laboratory-measured high serum paracetamol levels linked to hospital discharge and causes-of-death data, reports that paracetamol poisoning is the most common cause of acute liver failure in Sweden and elsewhere. Among poisoning cases (830 unintentional, 8841 intentional self-harm, 784 undetermined, 1613 missing intent), hepatic diagnoses occurred in 2-5% within 30 days, liver transplantation in up to 7 intentional self-harm cases within 30 days, and deaths within 30-90 days ranged from 2-6%. The majority of poisonings were intentional overdoses associated with impulsivity, ease of access, and frequent alcohol misuse.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; most cases were intentional self-harm overdoses (8841 of ~12068); a history of alcohol misuse was frequent; cases include unintentional, undetermined, and missing-intent poisonings.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of poisonings rose ~40% after paracetamol became available from non-pharmacy outlets; mortality rate and incidence of high-serum-paracetamol cases remained stable over time. Outcomes: hepatic diagnosis within 30 days 2-5% by intent group; liver transplant within 30 days (0 unintentional, 7 intentional self-harm, 1 undetermined, 2 missing intent); death within 30 days 2-11%, within 90 days 3-12%, within 1 year 4-14%. Paracetamol was prescribed to a comparable proportion of patients prior to events as in prior reports; study based on ICD-based hospital/cause-of-death linkage with case definition confirmed by high serum paracetamol concentration.

raw_record.extra_details: 17 patients with acute hepatic necrosis after paracetamol overdosage; mean maximum SGPT 2639±664 i.u./l, abnormal in all patients; antipyrine half-life significantly prolonged on initial study (20.6±1.8 h) returning toward normal at follow-up (13.3±1.0 h); highly significant correlations between antipyrine half-life and same-day SGPT activity and plasma paracetamol half-life; two patients required Vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma for coagulation problems.

raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; outcomes reported for a patient group in which 11 of 22 patients died (including one death from sepsis 10 days after overdose).
raw_record.extra_details: 22 patients with paracetamol-induced fulminant hepatic failure; factor V ≤10% of normal on admission had highest sensitivity (91%) for predicting adverse outcome, with predictive accuracy 73% and positive predictive value 67%; overall survival after paracetamol overdose in a larger institutional series was 39%. raw_record.support_text: The case report attributes acute liver failure to an acetaminophen (APAP) overdose. The patient arrived in multiorgan failure with irreversible damage to the liver and an acetaminophen level more than 10 times normal; complications such as cardiac arrest, respiratory failure, rhabdomyolysis, and septic shock developed, rendering interventions ineffective. The paper notes that patients lacking glutathione reserves, such as those with chronic alcohol use, are especially at risk and that prompt acetylcysteine administration can effectively prevent acute liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; patient presented in multiorgan failure with irreversible liver damage and an acetaminophen level more than 10x normal. Glutathione-depleted patients (e.g., chronic alcohol use) noted as especially at risk.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of late-stage APAP overdose in an unresponsive patient; NAC antidote given per Rumack-Matthew nomogram (treatment threshold based on APAP level vs time); hemodialysis recommended at extreme plasma acetaminophen (>200 µg/mL at four hours post-ingestion) or with mitochondrial dysfunction (elevated lactate, acidosis); CRRT suggested in severe cases with neurological, respiratory, or circulatory malfunction (encephalopathy/coma) as in this patient; patient developed cardiac arrest, respiratory failure, rhabdomyolysis, and septic shock; liver function normally regained within three months in survivors.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a cohort of acetaminophen overdose admissions: more than 90% of patients consumed in excess of 12 g of acetaminophen, which is stated to be the lowest dose believed capable of producing hepatic damage, and patients who developed severe hepatotoxicity even after alleged ingestion of less than 12 g are singled out, with possible genetically determined increased susceptibility.

raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of acetaminophen overdose admissions 1987-1993 with acute liver failure. Among the 112 patients fulfilling transplant criteria, 62 (55%) were not listed for transplantation (28 due to untreatable sepsis, hypotension, or cerebral edema; 24 due to alcohol/drug/psychiatric history; 10 due to clinical improvement). Among the 50 listed, 21 (42%) died before a donor organ became available and 6 recovered without transplant. Mortality of the 394 patients not fulfilling transplant criteria was 8% (32 patients): 17 died of unresponsive cerebral edema, 11 of sepsis, 4 of cardiovascular failure. Survival of non-transplanted medically managed patients improved from 23% in 1987 to 42% in 1993. Some patients in the low-dose group possibly had genetically determined increased susceptibility; a cited case of chronic 15-20 g/day use with heavy alcohol intake but no hepatotoxicity illustrates variable susceptibility.

raw_record.support_text: In a 17-center registry study of 308 patients with acute liver failure, acetaminophen overdose was the presumed cause in 120 patients (39%). The median ingested dose was 13.2 g/d (range 2.6 to 75 g/d), and 83% of patients ingested more than 4 g/d; 44 (37%) involved suicidal intent and 68 (57%) accidental toxicity. Acetaminophen was the most commonly implicated cause of acute liver failure in this cohort.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; patients ingested a median of 13.2 g/d (range 2.6-75 g/d), with 83% exceeding 4 g/d (maximum package recommendation). Includes suicidal-intent (37%) and accidental (57%) overdoses.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver failure caused by acetaminophen overdose in a multicenter cohort of 308 patients (120 acetaminophen cases). Acetaminophen group had shorter disease duration, higher ALT (mean 4310 U/L, range 136-17670) and AST (mean 4333 U/L), higher creatinine, and lower bilirubin (mean 74 µmol/L) and arterial pH than other causes. Mean INR 2.8; coma grade at admission I-IV distributed across the group. Survival without transplant 68%; overall survival 73%; transplantation received by 6% (7 patients); 56/120 (47%) fulfilled transplant criteria but only 32 (57%) were listed, the rest excluded for psychosocial or medical reasons such as sepsis or cerebral edema.

raw_record.support_text: This trial protocol is designed to assess the benefit of high-dose N-acetylcysteine (NAC) in patients presenting with paracetamol overdose. The primary outcome is the proportion of paracetamol metabolites directly produced by GSH/NAC detoxification of NAPQI (serum %GSH metabolite concentration after 12 hours of NAC), with a higher proportion indicating that additional NAC is reducing the amount of toxic paracetamol metabolites in the body. Standard and novel liver injury markers are measured as secondary endpoints to explore whether higher NAC doses prevent liver injury, establishing paracetamol overdose as the liver-injuring exposure being treated.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; patients presenting to hospital within 24 hours of last paracetamol dose, including single, staggered and therapeutic-excess patterns, accidental or deliberate, paracetamol alone or in mixtures, and judged to need NAC treatment by the clinical team.
raw_record.extra_details: Proposed three-group dose-finding trial (randomised 1:1:1) of NAC at 300 mg/kg (standard care), 450 mg/kg and up to 600 mg/kg for paracetamol overdose; maximum dose 600 mg/kg chosen based on mathematical models predicting efficacy in 98% of patients. Injury is presumed mediated by the toxic paracetamol metabolite NAPQI, which is detoxified by GSH/NAC. Participants receive 12 hours of intervention and are followed for 7 days; recruitment commenced 19 February 2024. ALT and blood paracetamol concentrations are required at enrolment. This is a study protocol without reported human outcomes.

raw_record.support_text: The study demonstrates that the cytochrome P450 enzyme-mediated mechanism of APAP (acetaminophen) toxicity translates to humans, with a higher percentage of circulating CYP metabolites present in patients with APAP overdose and liver injury. APAP overdose is described as a common medical emergency, and the CYP metabolites were superior to both ALT and APAP for early acute liver injury (ALI) risk stratification.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; patients received N-acetylcysteine treatment; the CYP-metabolite-based stratification shows APAP and ALT lacked predictive value for ALI in discovery and validation cohorts.
raw_record.extra_details: CYP metabolites (e.g., APAP-Cys/APAP-Sul) predicted ALI with ROC-AUC 0.83 (0.71-0.94) in validation cohort, superior to APAP (ROC-AUC 0.57, 0.41-0.73) and ALT (ROC-AUC 0.51, 0.35-0.67). In the SNAP trial, post-hoc adjustment for APAP-Cys/APAP-Sul showed ondansetron's reported increase in ALI was no different from placebo (OR 0.465, 0.097-2.226, P=0.338). Modified NAC regimen did not alter APAP half-life or AUC(0-20.25h) CYP/total compared to conventional NAC. Cytochrome P450-mediated mechanism described in rodent models is reported to translate to humans.

raw_record.extra_details: Liver injury was defined by prothrombin time >= 25 s; 96.6% of patients developed significant liver injury. Overall mortality 28.2% (147/522); 34.2% required dialysis; 90% had significant liver injury by SLTU admission. ALT and PT were generally abnormal at initial presentation. Mortality was higher with presentation >24 h after ingestion and with staggered overdose (34.4%, 44/128) vs single overdose (21.5%, 76/354); 33.6% (49/146) presenting after 24 h had poor prognosis by KCHC vs 17.6% (31/176) within 24 h. Stated ingested dose ~30-33.5 g.

raw_record.support_text: The Scottish Liver Transplant Unit (SLTU), a tertiary referral centre, provides clinical management for patients with severe liver disease and those requiring liver transplantation, including patients referred with liver damage due to paracetamol overdose. The study hypothesized that elevated creatinine at first admission or tertiary referral indicates more severe paracetamol poisoning and poorer prognosis in patients transferred to the liver unit, given that renal failure is an important component of severe paracetamol toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; patients referred to a tertiary liver transplant unit for severe paracetamol-induced liver damage; includes acute and staggered overdoses.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective anonymised case study of referrals to SLTU between 1992 and 2004. Data included stated dose ingested, interval between ingestion and presentation, plasma paracetamol concentration, hypotension (SBP <100 mmHg), serum creatinine, ALT, GGT, and PT at admission and referral; outcomes were worst recorded PT, liver transplant, haemodialysis requirement, ITU admission, and death. Severe liver injury was defined by PT >25 s. Renal function categorised by serum creatinine (normal Cr ≤120 µmol/l through severe impairment Cr ≥300 µmol/l). The study examined creatinine as a prognostic marker for severe paracetamol poisoning and poor outcome; paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose is the cause of the liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective study, 79 patients with paracetamol (paracetamol) hepatotoxicity following overdose were stratified by weekly alcohol consumption; 69 of 81 patients admitted with severe liver damage after paracetamol overdose developed fulminant hepatic failure (FHF), and 12 had severe liver damage (coagulopathy) without encephalopathy. raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective study of 81 patients (1987-1988, King's College Hospital Liver Failure Unit); 79 analyzed for clinical features, 74 for survival. raw_record.support_text: The paper describes paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose causing hepatotoxicity in humans. In a study of 30 adult overdose patients, plasma paracetamol concentrations greater than 300 mg/L 4 hours after ingestion were always associated with severe hepatic damage, whereas there was no hepatic damage at concentrations below 120 mg/L. raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; some cases involved co-ingestion of other drugs. Plasma paracetamol >300 mg/L at 4 hours always associated with severe hepatic damage, while <120 mg/L showed no hepatic damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Based on 30 adult overdose patients admitted to a regional poison treatment centre in Scotland (Prescott et al., 1971); 22 female, 10 with co-ingestion. Supportive care only given since no antidote was available at the time. Presence or absence of hepatic damage predicted by plasma paracetamol concentration at 4 hours, with prognosis uncertain for intermediate values; plasma paracetamol half-life cited as most reliable early prognostic guide. The Rumack-Matthew nomogram (1975) later defined 'probable hepatotoxicity' and 'possible hepatotoxicity' treatment lines (200 mg/L at 4 h to 30 mg/L at 15 h, extended to 24 h).

raw_record.support_text: Between 1992 and 2008, 663 patients were admitted with paracetamol-induced severe liver injury, of whom 161 (24.3%) had taken a staggered overdose. Staggered overdose patients were more likely to be encephalopathic on admission and had higher mortality than single time point overdoses (37.3% vs. 27.8%, P=0.025), though the overdose pattern did not independently predict death. The King's College poor prognostic criteria had reduced sensitivity (77.6, 95% CI 70.8-81.5) for this overdose pattern; delayed presentation beyond 24 h post overdose was independently associated with death/liver transplantation (OR 2.25, 95% CI 1.23-4.12, P=0.009).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; staggered repeat supratherapeutic ingestion pattern (frequently for pain relief) compared with single time point overdose; delayed hospital presentation beyond 24 h independently associated with death/liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning described as the major cause of severe acute hepatotoxicity and the commonest cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in the UK. Cohort of 663 patients admitted with paracetamol-induced severe liver injury (1992-2008); 161 (24.3%) staggered overdose. Staggered overdose patients were older and more likely to abuse alcohol, had lower total ingested doses and lower admission serum ALT, but more encephalopathy, renal replacement therapy or mechanical ventilation. Mortality 37.3% (staggered) vs 27.8% (single time point), P=0.025; stagger pattern did not independently predict death. King's College poor prognostic criteria sensitivity 77.6 (95% CI 70.8-81.5) for staggered pattern. Of 396/450 single time point overdoses, 178 (44.9%) presented >24 h; delayed presentation independently associated with death/liver transplantation (OR 2.25, 95% CI 1.23-4.12, P=0.009). Recommendations: consider N-acetyl cysteine treatment irrespective of admission serum paracetamol concentrations; consider early transfer to specialist liver centres.

raw_record.support_text: In this retrospective study of emergency department presentations, cases of unintentional paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose had a significantly higher rate of adverse outcomes in the form of acute liver failure (ALF) than the intentional group. Most unintentional patients had taken paracetamol in supratherapeutic doses over many days with delayed presentation, and the poorer outcome was attributed to staggered intake, postponed presentation, and late initiation of antidote therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; unintentional supratherapeutic dosing over many days predicted worse outcomes than single intentional overdose; two deaths after paracetamol intoxication occurred, of which only one was directly related to paracetamol overdose; no cases required liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: End-points were acute liver failure (ALF) and paracetamol-related death, studied in ED presentations of acute paracetamol intoxication. Unintentional overdose patients were mostly pain patients self-medicating with supratherapeutic paracetamol due to insufficient pain relief; delayed presentation and late NAC initiation contributed to worse outcomes. Available paracetamol packs in Switzerland contain up to 10 g (12 g as suppositories), max 500 mg/pill (750 mg as suppository), with larger amounts available by prescription; only two cases involved a paracetamol–tramadol combination product and none involved multiple paracetamol-containing products. Comparison figures cited: 458 deaths/year in the USA and 100–200/year in the UK from paracetamol-associated overdose, with reports from the Scottish Liver Transplantation Unit indicating about 50% of admitted paracetamol-induced acute liver injury patients developed ALF.

raw_record.support_text: In 22 patients with paracetamol-induced fulminant hepatic failure, demographic and outcome data show that 7 patients died after paracetamol overdose and 4 underwent liver transplantation, while 11 survived. The paper describes 'paracetamol induced fulminant hepatic failure' as a result of paracetamol overdose taken with suicidal intent (median dose 38 g, range 15-50 g, median time to admission 45 h), and states that in the United Kingdom paracetamol overdose is the most common single cause of fulminant hepatic failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose taken with suicidal intent; all 22 paracetamol-overdose patients received N-acetylcysteine as part of late treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose causing fulminant hepatic failure; 22 of 27 consecutive fulminant hepatic failure patients (median age 27 y, range 17-60) were due to paracetamol overdose. Median dose 38 g (range 15-50 g); median time to admission 45 h (range 20-60 h); median admission aspartate aminotransferase 3400 IU/l (range 153-23 000). Outcomes: 7 died, 4 underwent liver transplantation, 11 survived. Study assessed admission coagulation factor V and factor VIII/V ratio as prognostic indicators; factor V ≤10% on admission predicted adverse outcome with 91% sensitivity, and factor V in conjunction with coma grade III/IV and factor VIII ratio >30 gave 95% predictive accuracy, proposed for selecting transplantation candidates in paracetamol-induced fulminant hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: Five hundred sixty patients admitted between 1987 and 1993 with severe acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity were studied retrospectively. Acetaminophen overdose taken with suicidal intent remains the most common cause of acute liver failure in the United Kingdom, with severe cases attributed to acetaminophen, and mortality attributed directly to acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose taken with suicidal intent; in some cases taken as part of a mixed-drug overdose or as a constituent of a formulation containing acetaminophen.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity occurs only when >125 mg/kg is absorbed. Patients with a plasma acetaminophen concentration above the line joining 200 mg/L at 4 h and 30 mg/L at 15 h have a 60% chance of developing severe liver damage (aspartate aminotransferase >1000 IU/L); hepatotoxicity is almost inevitable above a line joining 300 mg/L at 4 h and 45 mg/L at 15 h. 560 patients (56% female, King's College Hospital, 1987-1993); admissions rose from 58 (1987) to 123 (1993) and overall survival improved from just under 50% to 78%. N-acetylcysteine treatment, encephalopathy grades III-IV, cerebral edema, and the number transplanted are detailed; up to ~500 deaths/year are attributed to acetaminophen overdosage in the UK, but only ~150 of these are attributable directly to acute liver failure from acetaminophen.

The paper presents a case of delayed-presentation paracetamol overdose in which the patient presented in fulminant hepatic failure with encephalopathy; the liver injury was attributed to the paracetamol overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose via deliberate self-poisoning (intentional self-ingestion); delayed presentation to Emergency Centre.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of delayed-presentation paracetamol overdose presenting with fulminant hepatic failure and encephalopathy; patient made a full recovery after treatment with N-acetylcysteine (NAC). Liver transplantation may be required in such patients with fulminant hepatic failure to prevent subsequent multi-organ failure and death. Paracetamol is described as the most frequently ingested toxin in intentional self-poisoning in South Africa. The morphological injury is reported as fulminant hepatic failure rather than a canonical biochemical pattern.

raw_record.support_text: Case report of a 27-year-old female who presented with abdominal pain after ingesting 2.6 g acetaminophen on Day 1 and 2.95 g on Day 2, and who had been taking acetaminophen/oxycodone and acetaminophen chronically over several months. On Day 3 her serum acetaminophen was 123 mcg/mL with AST 2,074 and ALT 1,355; transaminases and INR rose (peak AST 7,073; INR > 10) with rising bilirubin, consistent with severe acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity. NAC was given but the patient's family chose comfort measures and she expired on Day 6.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/accumulation from chronic daily consumption of acetaminophen (5 bottles) plus acetaminophen/oxycodone over several months; possible substance abuse and suicidal ideation; history of gastric bypass surgery; concurrent sucralfate, misoprostol, pantoprazole, hydromorphone, and acetaminophen/oxycodone.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver failure (fulminant hepatic failure) with hypoglycemia, possible seizure, acidosis (pH 7.18, HCO3 6.8), rising INR (5.9 on Day 3 to >10 on Day 5), peak AST 7,073 and ALT 3,676, bilirubin up to 5.1, elevated ammonia; N-acetylcysteine started Day 3 (10,500 mg load, 50 mg/kg, then increased to 15 mg/kg/h, later decreased, discontinued Day 6); vasopressors (norepinephrine, vasopressin, phenylephrine) for hypotension; phytonadione given without active bleeding; patient expired on Day 6 after institution of comfort measures.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective observational study of 48 adult patients with acute liver failure (ALF; encephalopathy, INR ≥ 1.5) admitted to the ICU of a hepatic transplant center in Portugal (2016–2024), etiology was unknown in 35.4% of patients, acute viral hepatitis in 14.5%, DILI in 12.5%, autoimmune hepatitis in 10.4%, and paracetamol intoxication in 10.4%. All included patients met the ALF definition, so the paracetamol intoxication cases represent paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose as a cause of acute liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/intoxication setting; adult ICU patients at a liver transplant center in Portugal (2016–2024).
raw_record.extra_details: 10.4% of the 48-patient ALF cohort had paracetamol intoxication. Retrospective observational/epidemiology study; paracetamol intoxication is one of several listed ALF etiologies (unknown 35.4%, acute viral hepatitis 14.5%, DILI 12.5%, autoimmune hepatitis 10.4%). No paracetamol-specific outcome details were reported. The DILI (12.5%) category was not attributed to a specific named agent.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that acetaminophen overdose and idiosyncratic drug reactions have become a more common cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in the U.S., replacing viral hepatitis as the leading cause. It cites 2004 data from the U.S. Acute Liver Failure Study Group registry of >700 ALF patients implicating acetaminophen poisoning in nearly 50% of all ALF cases in the U.S. The accompanying case report concerns a patient with acute liver failure attributed to acetaminophen poisoning who developed hyperammonemia with encephalopathy.

raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient with acetaminophen poisoning causing acute liver failure complicated by hyperammonemia and encephalopathy; plasma glutamine was elevated and declined as the patient recovered, consistent with the osmotic gliopathy theory. Registry context: U.S. Acute Liver Failure Study Group 2004 data (>700 patients) attributed ~50% of U.S. ALF cases to acetaminophen poisoning.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen poisoning is described as the commonest cause of fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) in the United Kingdom; Table 1 lists 307 total cases of acetaminophen poisoning among 552 acute liver failure admissions (287 nontransplanted, 20 transplanted) to the Birmingham Liver Unit between 1984 and 1994, and the text refers to acetaminophen-induced FHF.

raw_record.extra_details: Commonest cause of FHF in the UK. Table 1: acetaminophen poisoning 287 nontransplanted and 20 orthotopic liver transplant (OLT) cases. Poor prognosis when metabolic acidosis with pH <7.3 >24h post-overdose, serum creatinine >300 mmol/L, PT >100 sec (INR >6.5), or encephalopathy grade 3-4; rising INR on days 3-4 after overdose associated with 7% survival vs 79% when INR decreasing. Clichy criteria (factor V-based) less helpful for acetaminophen-induced FHF.

raw_record.support_text: In this series of acute liver failure (ALF) patients at the Victorian Liver Transplant Unit, transplant-free survival (TFS) was significantly higher in patients with paracetamol-induced ALF (74%) than in non-paracetamol aetiologies (31%, P<0.0001). Only three patients with paracetamol-induced ALF underwent liver transplantation (4%).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/poisoning exposure (paracetamol poisoning); patients referred to and managed at a single specialist liver transplant unit for ALF.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol was the most common aetiology of ALF in this cohort (50% overall, 49.7% in 2002-2017 vs 36.3% historical 1988-2001, P=0.046). TFS for paracetamol-induced ALF was 74% vs 31% for non-paracetamol aetiologies; overall survival to hospital discharge 77% vs 67% (P=0.13). Only 4% of paracetamol-induced ALF patients were transplanted. Paracetamol was the cause of ALF in 89% of patients deemed transplant-contraindicated. Significant per-capita increase in paracetamol-induced ALF across 30 years (R2=0.275, P=0.003).

raw_record.support_text: The letter, responding to an external validation study on the paracetamol-aminotransferase multiplication product, discusses the use of this tool to predict hepatotoxicity from paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning, noting that the Rumack-Matthew nomogram is not applicable in scenarios such as repeated supra-therapeutic ingestions. This establishes paracetamol overdose as a cause of human hepatotoxicity across both acute single and repeated supra-therapeutic ingestion settings.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/poisoning setting (acute single and repeated supra-therapeutic ingestions); the risk-stratification data were derived from patients being treated with acetylcysteine.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined by the traditionally accepted criterion of aminotransferase >1000 IU/L; the authors note the great majority of such patients have few significant signs/symptoms, require minimal specialized care, and recover completely without sequelae. Risk-stratification tool (multiplication product of paracetamol × aminotransferase) with >10000 mg/L x IU/L indicating high likelihood and <1500 mg/L x IU/L indicating low likelihood of hepatotoxicity after any type of acetaminophen ingestion; authors caution the tool's use to decide on acetylcysteine administration is unknown because all patients were treated with acetylcysteine.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol poisoning caused hepatotoxicity, with the authors reporting six deaths in hepatic failure due to paracetamol poisoning over 15 months: two in their trial of dextrose with or without cysteamine, and four patients transferred to their hospital more than 72 h after drug ingestion who had received no specific therapy. The paper frames paracetamol's hepatotoxicity and potential hepatic failure in the setting of overdose and notes extrahepatic effects and the lack of evidence that cysteamine prevents paracetamol-induced acute renal failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/poisoning setting (paracetamol poisoning); cases transferred >72 h after ingestion with no specific therapy contributed to mortality.
raw_record.extra_details: Over 15 months, six deaths in hepatic failure due to paracetamol poisoning (two in this trial; four transferred >72 h post-ingestion without specific therapy). Cysteamine, a toxic substance, was studied as an antidote and must be given within 9 h of ingestion if used at all; no controlled trial was carried out (dextrose with or without cysteamine). Methionine incorporated into paracetamol tablets might help, but methionine given after overdose may be harmful due to its hepatogenic/comagenic effect in liver disease. Extrahepatic effects include acute renal failure and acute pancreatitis (not prevented by cysteamine). Authors recommend IV 5% dextrose and no food for at least the first 48 h.

raw_record.support_text: Among 187 patients with acetaminophen poisoning at Chang Gung Memorial Hospital, 15 were grouped according to hepatitis complications and were found to have toxic hepatitis. Patients with toxic hepatitis had higher serum acetaminophen levels (P = 0.007), arrived to the hospital later (P < 0.001), and had a higher prevalence of hepatitis B virus carrier status (P < 0.001) than patients without toxic hepatitis. Acetaminophen-related toxic hepatitis was diagnosed when the alanine aminotransferase (ALT) increase exceeded 1000 U/L.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/poisoning setting among patients with acetaminophen poisoning (patients included only if detectable blood acetaminophen levels); patients with major systemic comorbidities including liver diseases were excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: 15 of 187 (8.0%) patients with acetaminophen poisoning developed toxic hepatitis. Toxic hepatitis was defined as ALT increase >1000 U/L. Serum acetaminophen level was 238.1 ± 300.0 μg/mL in the toxic-hepatitis group versus 114.4 ± 98.6 μg/mL in the no-toxic-hepatitis group; time between ingestion and arrival was 16.1 ± 13.5 h in the toxic-hepatitis group. Hepatitis B virus carrier status (26.6% vs 3.5%) was significantly associated with toxic hepatitis. Treatment included gastric lavage, activated charcoal 1 g/kg, magnesium citrate, and N-acetylcysteine per the Rumack-Matthew nomogram.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that paracetamol poisoning is the most common cause of fulminant liver failure in the United Kingdom, and examined 92 consecutively admitted patients with severe poisoning at a specialist liver unit. In non-transplanted patients, fatal outcome occurred in 26/82 (32%) and was associated with late presentation, coma grade, prothrombin time prolongation, metabolic acidosis, and renal dysfunction; cerebral oedema and sepsis caused most deaths. Seventeen patients were listed for transplantation, 10 received a transplant (7 survived), and 7 listed but not transplanted (1 survived).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/poisoning setting with late presentation; patients admitted to a specialist liver unit with severe poisoning.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning is described as the most common cause of fulminant liver failure in the UK; paracetamol induced hepatotoxicity and paracetamol induced fulminant hepatic failure were managed with N-acetylcysteine (effective in early presenters, and late administration beyond 12 hours improves outcome). 92 patients with severe poisoning; fatal outcome 26/82 (32%) among non-transplanted patients, associated with late presentation, coma grade, prothrombin time prolongation, metabolic acidosis and renal dysfunction; cerebral oedema and sepsis caused most deaths. 17 listed for transplant, 10 transplanted (7/10 survived), 7 listed but not transplanted (1/7 survived). King's College Hospital prognostic criteria (advanced coma grade, acidosis, severe sustained coagulopathy, renal dysfunction) predicted outcome.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol is the most common cause of listing for liver transplant after drug overdose, involved in 96% of such cases in Europe. In patients treated with acetylcysteine, in a recent large UK series, only 10 of 2743 patients with acute single ingestion and 1 of 202 therapeutic excess developed hepatotoxicity (ALT >1000 IU/L), whereas 10 of 452 delayed single (>24 hours) and 13 of 426 staggered (repeated) overdoses developed hepatotoxicity. Untreated paracetamol overdose causes liver injury (ALT >1000 IU/L), renal failure, and death, with risk rising with the paracetamol plasma concentration nomogram line.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/poisoning setting, including acute single ingestion, delayed (>24 h) single ingestion, staggered (repeated) overdoses, and therapeutic excess; data include untreated patients stratified by paracetamol nomogram line, and patients treated with acetylcysteine antidote.
raw_record.extra_details: The Prescott nomogram-derived case data (untreated patients, ALT >1000 IU/L as hepatotoxicity marker): <100 mg/L, 0/9 with liver injury; 100–200 mg/L, 5/22 (23%); 200–300 mg/L, 6/25 (24%) with 1 renal failure; >300 mg/L, 25/27 (93%) with 5 renal failure and 3 deaths. Paracetamol half-life is about 2 h without liver damage; clearance is reduced and half-life prolonged in proportion to liver injury. Paracetamol is involved in 96% of European drug-overdose transplant-listing cases; treated-series hepatotoxicity (ALT >1000 IU/L): 10/2743 acute single, 1/202 therapeutic excess, 10/452 delayed single, and 13/426 staggered overdoses.

raw_record.support_text: The Department of General, Transplant and Liver Surgery of the Medical University in Warsaw reports that liver transplantation for acute liver failure caused by paracetamol poisoning was routinely performed (with extra-corporeal veno-venous bypass because these patients lack hepatic cirrhosis and portal hypertension). This establishes paracetamol overdose as a cause of acute liver failure requiring transplantation in humans.

raw_record.extra_details: Estimated 800-1,000 patients treated per year for paracetamol poisoning across 8 of 10 Polish Toxicology Centres; over 70% of ingestions were suicide attempts; severe cases transferred to S-ICU showed upper gastrointestinal bleeding (managed by esophageal variceal banding, histoacryl injection, or self-expandable stents) and bladder tamponade by blood clots; progressive hepatic failure made patients eligible for liver transplantation (only effective treatment) or albumin dialysis systems (SPAD, MARS, Prometheus); transplantation performed with extra-corporeal veno-venous bypass.

raw_record.support_text: APAP (acetaminophen) hepatotoxicity leading to acute liver failure (ALF) was seen in 2 patients, both fatal. One was a 16-year-old boy with a history of previous drug abuse whose APAP toxicity was associated with concomitant dextropropoxyphene intake; post-mortem liver biopsy showed necrosis with marked sinusoidal congestion. raw_record.support_text: Self-poisoning with acetaminophen (para-acetaminophenol) leads to liver damage that can cause death by fulminant liver failure; of 588 patients admitted to King's College Hospital with acute liver failure between 1976 and 1985, 53% had acetaminophen poisoning, of whom 34% later died.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/self-poisoning context; exposure is supratherapeutic (deliberate self-poisoning) rather than ordinary therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Overdose saturates glucuronidation/sulfation pathways; the remainder is oxidized by cytochrome P-450 to NAPQI, which binds covalently to proteins after glutathione depletion, causing necrosis; NAC replenishes sulfydryl groups and protects if given within 18 hr of overdose. Main study: 18 acetaminophen-poisoning patients examined by 31P MRS; ATP fell to about 20% of normal in severe cases, with parallel fall in phosphodiester signal and increased prothrombin time ratio (INR); of 588 patients with acute liver failure, 53% had acetaminophen poisoning and 34% of those died.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that hepatic damage from paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose has been reported since 1966, and that in 1973 there were sixty-six deaths from fulminant hepatic failure in England and Wales caused by self-poisoning with paracetamol. It also notes that, unlike most other drugs taken in overdose, the toxic effects of paracetamol may not be observed for several days.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/self-poisoning setting (suicide attempts); severity linked to inadequate early intervention.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of clinical/biochemical data from 163 patients after paracetamol overdose to predict severity of ensuing liver damage. Overall severity of hepatic necrosis increased with ingested dose but correlation too weak for individual prognosis; severe damage less likely if patient vomited or had stomach wash-out within 6 hr. Plasma paracetamol concentrations at known times after overdose distinguished those developing hepatic dysfunction from those who did not; early plasma paracetamol half-life (from >=3 samples within 4 hr of admission) greater than 4 hr in all patients developing moderate or severe liver damage, though also in nearly one-third with minimal lesions. Sixty-six deaths from fulminant hepatic failure (England and Wales, 1973) attributed to paracetamol self-poisoning. No completely reliable early prognostic test for individuals; up to 30% selected for treatment with cysteamine (mercaptamine) based on plasma levels would receive it after only trivial hepatic damage.

raw_record.support_text: Our patients demonstrated hepatic injury from acetaminophen (APAP) poisoning, along with extrahepatic involvement; nephrotoxicity was reported to occur in 10% of patients with hepatotoxicity caused by APAP poisoning, and one patient developed rapidly progressive multisystem organ failure with diffuse capillary leak, not previously described from repeated or single-dose APAP. The diagnosis of APAP hepatotoxicity was confirmed by immunochemical detection of the 3-(cystein-S-yl)-APAP (3-Cys-A) protein adduct in serum, which is released from hepatocytes only when hepatic injury occurs and is unique to APAP-related toxic hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/supratherapeutic APAP poisoning following repeated or single-dose ingestion; one of two patients also developed rapidly progressive multisystem organ failure with diffuse capillary leak.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity confirmed via 3-Cys-A (3-(cystein-S-yl)-APAP) protein adduct immunoassay, unique to APAP toxic hepatitis and not elevated in other forms of hepatitis (no other toxic hepatitis elevates the marker). Centrilobar hepatic necrosis described in patients taking supratherapeutic APAP doses. P-450-mediated bioactivation to NAPQI; NAPQI is highly reactive and unlikely to escape the liver, with extrahepatic toxicity (nephrotoxicity ~10%, myocardial toxicity, metabolic acidosis, capillary leak) attributed to P-450 bioactivation elsewhere. Case 2 had a molar 3-Cys-A:protein ratio nearly four times that of Case 1. GSH depletion and local depletion leading to hepatocellular injury discussed (murine-based).

raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose is the leading cause of ALF in the US and UK, accounting for nearly half of all ALF cases annually. Prospective analysis of 113 patients with ALF due to single-time-point acetaminophen ingestions found no relationship between acetaminophen dose and spontaneous survival or clinical prognostic indicators; the most important prognostic factor was coma grade on admission. raw_record.support_text: In the US ALF Study Group cohort (1147 adult patients enrolled 1998-2007), the most common causes of acute liver failure were paracetamol (46%), indeterminate (15%) and idiosyncratic DILI (12%). Spontaneous survival for paracetamol overdose was 63%. A UNOS analysis (1990-2002) found 15% (n=370) of liver transplants for ALF were due to drug-induced hepatotoxicity, with paracetamol the most common culprit (46%).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/supratherapeutic exposure (paracetamol overdose), the dominant context for paracetamol-induced ALF; risk increased by chronic alcohol use, fasting, phenobarbital and isoniazid use.
raw_record.extra_details: Most common cause of ALF in the US ALF Study Group (46%) and most common single drug responsible for DILI-related liver transplants (46%). Spontaneous survival for paracetamol-induced liver failure ~62-63%, better than idiosyncratic cases (26%). NAC is the treatment of choice for paracetamol overdose. Transplant-free survival and transplantation rates are similar between suicidal and unintentional paracetamol-induced ALF.
