raw_record.support_text: The paper reports three patients referred with a diagnosis of viral hepatitis who had actually taken a paracetamol overdose, two of whom had initially concealed it. The authors state that very large doses of paracetamol taken in suicide attempts cause acute hepatic necrosis, that the clinical and biochemical features of paracetamol-induced liver damage may be indistinguishable from viral hepatitis, and that moderate to severe hepatic necrosis due to paracetamol can be accompanied by encephalopathy and acute renal failure. One patient died of hepatic coma with renal failure and pneumonia as contributory causes.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/supratherapeutic exposure involving suicide attempts; in at least two cases the overdose was initially concealed, and in one case multiple analgesics were co-ingested.
raw_record.extra_details: Three case reports: Case 1, a 16-year-old who took 20 paracetamol tablets, presented with jaundice (bilirubin 43 µmol/L, ALT 5390 U/L, ALP 19 U/L) with negative serology for hepatitis A/B, EBV and CMV, and recovered completely. Case 2, a 25-year-old who took 24 Veganin (paracetamol 250 mg, aspirin 250 mg, codeine phosphate 6.8 mg), 20 Panadeine Co (paracetamol 500 mg, codeine phosphate 8 mg) and 26 paracetamol tablets, developed acute hepatitis (ALT 13 450 U/L) and renal failure and recovered. Case 3, a 34-year-old who took about 100 paracetamol tablets, presented jaundiced with hepatic encephalopathy, anuria and acute renal failure, bilirubin 397 µmol/L, ALT 1835 U/L, ALP 239 U/L, rising prothrombin ratio, and died of hepatic coma. raw_record.support_text: In this study of 240 patients presenting after acetaminophen (APAP) ingestion, 36 (15%) developed hepatotoxicity, of whom 25 developed a peak INR ≥ 2.0 and eight had severe coagulopathy (INR ≥ 5.0). There were no deaths, but one patient who ingested 50 g of acetaminophen required liver transplantation. The cohort comprised acute ingestions of immediate-release and modified-release acetaminophen and repeated supratherapeutic ingestions (RSTI), establishing human hepatotoxicity associated with acetaminophen exposure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/supratherapeutic exposure setting (acute ingestion and repeated supratherapeutic ingestion, RSTI); one transplant occurred after a 50 g ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: 36/240 (15%) patients developed hepatotoxicity (28 acute ingestions); 25 had peak INR ≥ 2.0, 8 had INR ≥ 5.0, 5 had severe acute kidney injury (AKIN stage 3); no deaths; one patient ingested 50 g acetaminophen and required liver transplantation. Cohort included acute IR (n=158), MR (n=35), combined, and RSTI (n=36; 24 therapeutic purpose, 8 codeine abusers, 4 staggered acute). Study also evaluated APAP-protein adducts and acetaminophen ratio as predictors of hepatotoxicity and coagulopathy risk.

raw_record.support_text: Among patients treated for paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose, there was no difference in the overall incidence of ALI (183/1300 [14%] vs 115/911 [13%]) or hepatotoxicity (96 [7.4%] vs 76 [8.3%]) comparing the two-bag and three-bag N-acetylcysteine regimens. There were two transfers to a liver transplant unit (one in each group) with both patients surviving, and one death in each group related to fulminant hepatic failure. The liver injury is explicitly attributed to the paracetamol overdose context, which is the focus of the trial.

raw_record.extra_details: Acute single ingestion and other ingestion types (blood tests >24 h, unknown time, staggered). Overall cohort: peak ALT >150 U/L occurred in 183/1300 (14%) two-bag vs 115/911 (13%) three-bag; ALT >1000 U/L in 96 (7.4%) vs 76 (8.3%); peak INR >2 in 63 (4.8%) vs 40 (4.4%); fulminant hepatic failure in 12 (0.9%) vs 11 (1.2%); mortality 2 (0.1%) vs 1 (0.1%). Incidence of ALI stratified by nomogram group at 4-24 h post-ingestion ranged from ~7% at 150-199 mg/L to ~22% at >=500 mg/L. raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of acetaminophen overdose in a 22-yr-old woman who ingested 15 g of acetaminophen and 36 hours later showed biomarker changes (ammonia, glutamine, aspartate aminotransferase) and Glascow Coma Score changes consistent with acute liver failure (ALF) and encephalopathy with increased intracranial pressure. The case is presented under the osmotic gliopathy theory of the common pathway to encephalopathy in ALF from acetaminophen poisoning.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/supratherapeutic exposure: single ingestion of 15 g acetaminophen in a 22-yr-old woman, with biomarker and encephalopathy onset noted 36 hrs after ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report (1 patient) presented as a biochemical demonstration of the osmotic gliopathy theory for the final common pathway to encephalopathy in acute liver failure. Reported biochemical interrelationships between serum ammonia, glutamine, and aspartate aminotransferase and the Glascow Coma Score (surrogate for depth of encephalopathy) with increased intracranial pressure; deep encephalopathy persisted 96-144 hrs after ingestion and neurologic improvement began at ~180 hrs when plasma glutamine normalized. Paragraph 4 reiterates acetaminophen poisoning as one of the listed causes of hyperammonemia and acute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: Ten patients with hepatic toxicity after acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose were characterized at the time of Liver Dialysis treatment. Ingested amounts ranged from 12 g to 50 g (e.g., 100 Extra Strength Tylenol/50 g, 50 Extra Strength Tylenol with ethanol/50 g, >30 Darvocet tablets/>15 g), with markedly elevated AST and ALT (up to AST 9,640; ALT 7,550), prolonged PT, and in several cases altered consciousness including coma; all patients recovered and were discharged. One patient developed fulminant hepatic failure after acetaminophen overdose, with residual plasma acetaminophen concentration near 100 µg/mL at 84 hours.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes acetaminophen hepatotoxicity causing fulminant hepatic failure in an overdose setting. Among 28 patients with fulminant hepatic failure described by Record et al., three had taken an acetaminophen overdose and had a severe anion gap metabolic acidosis with lactic acidosis confirmed in two. A case of a 37-year-old woman who chronically ingested 10 g acetaminophen per day with anion gap acidosis and hypoglycemia is also cited, establishing acetaminophen overdose as a cause of severe human liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/supratherapeutic exposure; the cited cases involved an acetaminophen overdose or chronic ingestion of 10 g per day (a case of chronic high-dose ingestion in a 37-year-old woman).
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity was associated with type B lactic acidosis and hypoglycemia. Record et al. (20) found a markedly reduced lactate elimination rate in patients with liver damage from acetaminophen overdose; another study (21) found mild transient fasting hypoglycemia in four patients with mild-to-moderate liver damage from acetaminophen overdose. The authors note the degree of lactic acidosis and hypoglycemia exceeds that seen with other apparently equally severe liver disease, and suggest impaired gluconeogenesis, though they consider it unlikely that acetaminophen or its metabolites are directly responsible for these metabolic abnormalities.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of paracetamol overdose treated with cysteamine, paracetamol overdose produced mild liver damage. In Case 1, on the third admission the G.O.T. and G.P.T. activities rose to 160 and 288 IU/L respectively, the maximum prothrombin-time ratio was 1.6/1, and plasma bilirubin peaked at 1.8 mg/100 ml 18 hours after admission before falling to normal. raw_record.extra_details: Overdose amounts ranged from 20 g (Cases 2, 3) to 37.5 g (Case 5) plus 25-50 Distalgesic tablets (325 mg paracetamol each) in Case 4. raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol overdose (POD) is described as a major cause of acute liver failure (ALF) requiring liver transplantation in the United Kingdom. Of 127 liver transplants performed for ALF in the Scottish Liver Transplant Unit over 1992–2006, 44 were for POD; post-transplant mortality during the index admission was 30% (13 patients) with five further deaths during follow-up, and actuarial 5-year patient survival was 54.5%.

raw_record.extra_details: The paper states paracetamol is one of the most widely used analgesics with a lack of adverse effects at therapeutic doses, but overdosage can lead to acute liver failure requiring liver transplantation. 44 liver transplants for POD over 14 years (out of 608 POD patients managed; 436 did not meet King's College criteria; 172 assessed; 68 suitable; 44 transplanted). Post-transplant index-admission mortality 30% (13 patients) plus 5 late deaths; 5-year patient survival 54.5%, graft survival 49.5%; 23% re-transplanted (primary nonfunction 1, hepatic artery thrombosis 3, chronic rejection 2). Median age 30 (18–51); median follow-up 7 years; 19 (43.2%) had prior overdose/psychiatric illness.

Using the 100-treatment line instead of the 150-treatment line would increase the number of patients indicated for NAC from 187 (20.9%) to 299 (33.5%), adding 112 NAC courses. raw_record.support_text: Liver-cell necrosis after paracetamol overdose is mediated by a chemically active intermediate metabolite of the drug, which combines irreversibly with hepatic macromolecules. After therapeutic doses of paracetamol (0.5 to 1 g orally up to five times daily) the metabolite is conjugated with hepatic glutathione to form nontoxic mercapturates; only when the dose is large enough to deplete hepatic glutathione reserves does the excess metabolite remain free to exert harmful effects leading to cell death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paracetamol overdose exposure
raw_record.extra_details: Five patients died in acute hepatic failure, all showing subtotal lobular necrosis with only small islets of altered hepatocytes surviving periportally. In survivors, grade III (severe) centrilobular necrotic zones were reconstituted by 3 months with only minor residual changes, including one patient with mild centrilobular fibrosis and reticulin scarring. Injury mechanism: a chemically active metabolite depletes hepatic glutathione, releasing the reactive metabolite to cause cell death; experimental animal data showed a dose threshold for paracetamol-induced centrilobular necrosis. No close dose-damage relationship could be established from stated/estimated overdose size, but plasma paracetamol levels above 400 g/l at 2 h to 30 g/l at 18 h were frequently associated with severe (grade III) damage, while lower admission levels were usually associated with mild (grade I) damage.

Plasma paracetamol concentrations above 1980 µmol/L (300 µg/mL) at 4 h were always associated with severe hepatic toxicity, and hepatic necrosis developed in 16 of 18 patients with a 12 h level greater than 330 µmol/L (50 µg/mL).

raw_record.extra_details: Prescott 1971 study of 30 overdose patients with no antidote (supportive treatment only): severe hepatic poisoning in 17, one death. Plasma concentration >1980 µmol/L (300 µg/mL) at 4 h always associated with severe hepatic toxicity; 12 h level >330 µmol/L associated with hepatic necrosis in 16/18 patients, with no liver damage in 11/12 patients below this; no biochemical evidence of liver damage when 4 h level <793 µmol/L (120 µg/mL); a paracetamol half-life >4 h was the most reliable indicator of hepatic damage. Centrilobular necrosis linked to glutathione depletion. In a survey response, one department reported a specific case of raised transaminases after a 4 h paracetamol level of 770 µmol/L.

raw_record.extra_details: Study population: 746 patients transferred to a specialised unit with severe paracetamol poisoning and 273 unselected patients admitted locally over a 10-year period; partly retrospective chart-based study with multivariate analysis. raw_record.support_text: This multicenter retrospective study characterized acetaminophen (APAP) poisoning in patients weighing >100 kg who were treated with oral or IV N-acetylcysteine (NAC). Among 36 evaluable heavier patients, hepatotoxicity (defined as alanine transaminase >1000 U/L) occurred in 12/36 (33.3%) and death in 4/36 (11.1%), consistent with APAP overdose causing hepatic injury.

raw_record.support_text: A 6-year-old, 18.2-kg boy with cervical adenitis received acetaminophen elixir and acetaminophen-with-codeine elixir over 30 hours, totaling 3.6 g (198 mg/kg) of acetaminophen, which was a subacute overdose (recommended maximum 1.9 g). At presentation he had diaphoresis and emesis, and laboratory testing showed elevated AST (251 IU/L), ALT (175 IU/L), LDH (1507 IU/L) and GGT (84 IU/L) with a prothrombin time of 14.4 seconds; the acetaminophen level drawn 5 hours after the last dose was <10 µg/ml. He was treated with N-acetylcysteine (140 mg/kg loading, then 70 mg/kg every 4 hours for 17 doses) and, per the paper's abstract, manifested stage II hepatic toxicity that resolved and all laboratory values returned to normal within 24 hours.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a case report of a 12-year-old (64-kg) girl with a total estimated ingestion of 1742 mg/kg acetaminophen (paracetamol) and 19 mg/kg diphenhydramine. Despite early treatment with n-acetylcysteine (NAC), she developed hepatic failure with plasma ALT activity peaking at approximately 8000 IU/L around 90 hours after ingestion. This human case attributes hepatic failure/DILI to a massive paracetamol overdose.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic failure developed despite early NAC treatment, with plasma ALT peaking at approximately 8000 IU/L around 90 hours after ingestion; 22 ALT concentration values from 0 to 250 hours were extracted for model fitting. The paper presents the case to demonstrate/validate a mathematical model of ALT biomarker release after paracetamol overdose, and assumed a linear relationship between parent drug concentration and the toxic metabolite NAPQI and that diphenhydramine had no effect on the ALT release profile.

raw_record.support_text: A 12-year-old, 40-kg girl with SMA type II developed postoperative APAP-induced liver injury and acute liver failure after receiving acetaminophen (APAP) rectally at 69 mg/kg/d for 4 days, together with hydromorphine, diclofenac and propofol; APAP and propofol were discontinued once liver injury was detected, N-acetylcysteine was started on day 4, and the acute liver failure with encephalopathy resolved. In a second patient (17-year-old, 55-kg, congenital muscular dystrophy with carnitine deficiency), acetaminophen was given rectally (average 40 mg/kg/d, max 90 mg/kg/d) and acute liver failure developed on day 11 despite immediate discontinuation and N-acetylcysteine; she died of refractory shock on day 14. Serum APAP protein adducts (APAP-CYS) were quantified in both patients to confirm acetaminophen exposure.

raw_record.support_text: An infant presented with hepatomegaly and markedly elevated liver enzymes (ALT 455 U/L, AST 1907 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 603 U/L), total bilirubin 2.7 mg/dL, ammonia 135 µmol/L, PT 53.5 s, and INR 2.5. The child had received an inadvertent acetaminophen overdose: the mother gave 200 mg/dose every 4 hours (~162 mg/kg/day for several days) because a language barrier led her to misuse the acetaminophen and amoxicillin doses. Plasma acetaminophen was 78.5 µg/mL approximately 96 hours after the first dose. The patient was treated with N-acetylcysteine (loading dose plus 18 doses), transferred to a regional transplant center, and made a complete recovery over 3 weeks. The paper states acetaminophen hepatotoxicity is well described in acute overdosage and results from formation of N-acetyl-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI) via the cytochrome P-450 pathway.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric infant; chronic supratherapeutic dosing (~162 mg/kg/day for several days) due to a caregiver medication-dose error (acetaminophen switched with amoxicillin) related to a language barrier; plasma level was from chronic supratherapeutic dosing, not a single acute ingestion, so the Rumack-Matthew nomogram did not apply.
raw_record.extra_details: Plasma acetaminophen 78.5 µg/mL measured ~96 h after the last/first dose; 2 mL of 80 mg/0.8 mL (200 mg/dose) every 4 h. Initial labs: hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, WBC 29,700/mm3, PT 53.5 s, PTT 75 s, INR 2.5, ammonia 135 µmol/L, total bilirubin 2.7 mg/dL (conjugated 1.9), ALT 455 U/L, AST 1907 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 603 U/L. Transferred to regional transplant center; treated with NAC (oral loading 140 mg/kg plus 18 doses) and recovered completely over ~3 weeks with near-normal liver enzymes by hospital day 5. Mechanism attributed to NAPQI formation via cytochrome P-450. The paper notes acute adult ingestions >140 mg/kg (≥7.5 g) or >150 mg/kg in a child are potentially toxic, and prognostic factors for severe liver damage/transplant include PT >37 s, pH <7.3, creatinine >3 mg/dL, and grade 3-4 encephalopathy.

raw_record.support_text: A 3.5-year-old child who received repeated acetaminophen overdose (320 mg, two 160-mg tablets, every 2 hours for at least 48 hours) developed hepatotoxicity, as confirmed by toxic blood acetaminophen concentrations. The dose, about 25 mg/kg every 2 hours, exceeded the recommended therapeutic dose of 10 to 20 mg/kg every 4 hours. Liver enzymes returned to normal by hospital discharge (day 17), and the patient recovered after N-acetylcysteine treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (3.5-year-old child); repeated supratherapeutic dosing (320 mg every 2 hours for at least 48 hours); concurrent acute renal failure requiring peritoneal dialysis.
raw_record.extra_details: Blood acetaminophen 187.2 mg/L at ~22 h from last dose; subsequent 75.0, 41.9, and 6.5 mg/L at 14, 20, and 31.5 h. Peak AST 9,158 U/L and ALT 11,282 U/L (day 1), normalizing by day 17 discharge. Treated with oral N-acetylcysteine (18 doses over 72 h). Also developed pancytopenia with hypoplastic bone marrow (day 6) and acute renal failure; the paper notes no prior report of bone marrow toxicity after chronic acetaminophen overdose in children.

raw_record.support_text: Case 1 describes a 4-year-old girl treated at home for 4 days with unknown quantities of acetaminophen (APAP) given by three caregivers who were unaware of each other's dosing; toxicologic screening revealed a serum APAP level of 450 µmol/L (67.8 mg/L), and hepatic function tests showed markedly elevated AST (6,640 IU/L), ALT (2,926 IU/L), and LDH (5,930 IU/L) with low GGT and near-normal total bilirubin. This APAP intoxication was treated with N-acetylcysteine, and the patient's hepatic function worsened markedly before she improved; the injury was attributed to acetaminophen overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (4-year-old girl); overdose from unknown quantities of acetaminophen administered by three caregivers unaware of each other's dosing.
raw_record.extra_details: Serum APAP 450 µmol/L (67.8 mg/L) on presentation; AST peaked at ~37,820 IU/L, ALT ~16,660 IU/L, LDH ~35,250 IU/L on transfer day; GGT low (24 IU/L then 41 IU/L), alkaline phosphatase 223 IU/L; prolonged prothrombin time (17.6-19.2 s) and elevated serum ammonia; viral hepatitis A/B/C ruled out and ceruloplasmin normal. Treated with oral N-acetylcysteine and vitamin K; transferred for preevaluation for liver transplant but showed marked improvement; complicated by transient renal dysfunction (peak BUN 55 mg/dL, creatinine 4.5 mg/dL), hypertension treated with prazosin, and residual mild renal tubular acidosis. Acetaminophen is also known as paracetamol (APAP).

raw_record.support_text: The report notes that the most common organ affected by acetaminophen intoxication is the liver when the drug is administered in supratherapeutic doses, and that repeated therapeutic doses can also be toxic. In the presented case, a 5-year-old female was treated by her mother with different acetaminophen formulations (250 mg suppositories and 500 mg tablets) every 3 hours for three consecutive days, an approximate dose of 90 mg/kg/24h over 72 hours, and developed fulminant hepatic failure. Acetaminophen poisoning was strongly suspected and confirmed by a blood acetaminophen level of 32.9 mg/l 10 hours after the last dose; viral serologies and blood culture were negative, and the child was treated with NAC.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (5-year-old female); repeated supratherapeutic/repeated dosing via suppositories and tablets every 3 hours for 3 days (about 90 mg/kg/24h over 72 hours) without other concomitant medication.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure with grade II-III encephalopathy, jaundice, hepatomegaly; ALT 5794 U/L, AST 6000 U/L, total bilirubin 3.5 mg/dl, INR 3.86; blood acetaminophen 32.9 mg/l 10 h after last dose; viral serologies (HIV, HEV, HAV, HCV, HBV, Coxsackie, influenza A/B, adeno) negative and blood culture negative; treated with 140 mg/kg NAC loading then 70 mg/kg every 4 h for 18 doses; coagulopathy with melena/hematemesis; suspected acute pancreatitis (hyperamylasaemia 255 U/L, hyperlipasaemia 514 U/L); child recovered with improving liver enzymes. Paper also states risk of toxic reactions is generally lower in children than adults.

raw_record.support_text: The patient presented with acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure, and laboratory investigations corroborated this suspected diagnosis. The patient deteriorated with cerebral edema, was evaluated for liver transplantation and deemed ineligible, but ultimately recovered. The discussion notes acetaminophen is the most common drug taken in overdose and describes classic clinical acetaminophen poisoning progressing through stages to fulminant hepatic failure with cerebral edema as a common cause of death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient; overdose/supratherapeutic exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a pediatric patient with acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure and fulminant hepatic failure with encephalopathy, cerebral edema (CT showing diffuse edema, sulcal/basal cistern effacement and uncal herniation), and elevated liver transaminases. She was evaluated for liver transplantation but deemed ineligible due to poor neurologic prognosis; treated with N-acetylcysteine, mannitol, vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma; recovered with a residual right third and sixth cranial nerve palsy. Discussion frames acetaminophen as the most common drug taken in overdose in pediatric and adult populations, with classic poisoning in 4 stages (nausea/vomiting/abdominal pain, hepatic injury with elevated transaminases, fulminant hepatic failure with encephalopathy/coagulopathy), and cerebral edema leading to herniation as a common cause of death.

raw_record.extra_details: Reported as the lowest acetaminophen dose to date causing fulminant liver failure. Mechanism: small fraction metabolized by CYP450 mixed oxidases to toxic metabolites detoxified by glutathione; hepatonecrosis occurs when glutathione stores are depleted and toxic metabolites accumulate (paragraph 38). Doses of acetaminophen as low as 7500 mg have been shown to cause transient hepatotoxicity. Carbamazepine and fasting induce CYP450; protein-poor diets lower glutathione and increase acetaminophen toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: This population-based study (National University Hospital of Iceland, 2004-2009) reviewed 1913 drug-related poisoning episodes, of which 352 (18%) were paracetamol overdoses. Of 182 hospitalized index visits, ALF occurred in 3.8% (7/182, incidence 0.7/100,000/year); in the intentional group 1.2% (2/163) developed ALF versus 25% (4/16) of the accidental group (p=0.001). Only one patient died from ALF and none underwent liver transplantation. The paper states paracetamol is the most common cause of acute liver failure in the USA and many European countries and emphasizes its dose-dependent hepatotoxicity, with risk factors for hepatotoxicity described.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Population-based study of paracetamol overdoses; findings in intentional (mostly young females) and accidental (mostly older) overdoses; accidental overdose associated with higher aminotransferases and a higher ALF rate.
raw_record.extra_details: Annual incidence of paracetamol overdoses declined from 30.0 (2004) to 16.0/100,000/year (2009), p<0.05; female/male ratio 3.0, largest age group 16-25 years; 26% discharged after initial examination; 182 hospitalized index visits with 16 (9%) accidental overdoses; ALF incidence 0.7/100,000/year; hepatotoxicity described as dose-dependent and paracetamol cited as the most common cause of ALF in the USA and many European countries.

raw_record.support_text: A 22-year-old at 19-20 weeks gestation presented with elevated liver enzymes after self-treating a toothache with approximately 6 g of acetaminophen daily for 2 weeks. Following rapid hepatic decompensation with stage III hepatic encephalopathy, the differential diagnosis excluded viral, HELLP, and acute fatty liver of pregnancy causes, and FHF was deemed secondary to unintentional acetaminophen overdose on the basis of recent ingestion and elevated acetaminophen levels. The patient was listed status 1 and underwent liver transplantation; the previable fetus subsequently expired.

raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure with stage III hepatic encephalopathy. Admission labs: AST 1064 U/L, ALT 1436 U/L, total bilirubin 2.8 mg/dL, pH 6.99, glucose 30 mg/dL, APAP 31.5 µg/mL; later AST>2250 U/L, ALT>3000 U/L, total bilirubin 2.7 mg/dL, INR 3.4, APAP 35 µg/mL. Treated with N-acetylcysteine and bicarbonate. No prior liver disease, IV drug use, or alcohol use. Differential excluded hepatitis A/B/adenovirus, HELLP, acute fatty liver of pregnancy. Reported as the first case of acetaminophen overdose requiring liver transplantation during a second-trimester pregnancy.

raw_record.support_text: A case report of paracetamol intoxication in pregnancy concludes that toxic doses of paracetamol may harm fetal and maternal hepatocytes, and that early antidote (NAC) therapy is crucial. Paracetamol crosses the placenta, and intensive antidote and supportive therapy proved effective even with delayed treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnancy; overdose (paracetamol intoxication) exposure context.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol crosses the placenta and toxic doses may harm both maternal and fetal hepatocytes; N-acetylcysteine (NAC) crosses the placenta and was given as antidote; case report emphasizes efficacy of intensive antidote and supportive therapy even with delayed presentation. NAC itself is the antidote, not an attributed DILI cause.

raw_record.support_text: A 19-year-old at 17-week gestation was diagnosed with acute liver failure secondary to acetaminophen overdose taken for dental pain management. After dental treatment she took over-the-counter Extra Strength Tylenol (500 mg acetaminophen/tablet), 2-3 tablets 10 times per day for 10 days, approximating 20-30 tablets or 10,000-15,000 mg daily. raw_record.support_text: A case of fetal demise and maternal recovery after acetaminophen overdose is presented. Fetal liver and maternal serum concentrations indicated overdose to be the cause of fetal death, and maternal disseminated intravascular coagulation may have been related to maternal acetaminophen-induced liver disease alone or a combination of liver disease and the presence of a dead fetus. The paper is framed as a hepatotoxicity (acetaminophen/paracetamol) case report.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnant patient (27-28 week fetus); overdose ingestion; maternal DIC may reflect liver disease and/or retained dead fetus.
raw_record.extra_details: 24-year-old gravida 2 para 1 woman ingested a total of 29.5 g acetaminophen over less than 24 hours for severe dental pain, followed by impending liver decompensation; maternal recovery occurred. Fetal death attributed to overdose; treatment with oral N-acetylcysteine (9 g, then 4.5 g q8h) began 20 hours after last dose, vomited after each dose; serum acetaminophen 56 µg/mL. Authors state a causal relationship between maternal toxic ingestion and fetal death is very likely.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that liver damage is a major manifestation of acetaminophen overdose and that acetaminophen overdose may also cause acute tubular necrosis, almost always in conjunction with hepatotoxicity. Seven of the thirteen patients ingested acetaminophen in a suicide attempt, and one patient in this suicide group died.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Purposeful ingestion in a suicide attempt; 2/7 patients were alcoholics and 1 was taking another enzyme-inducing drug; 2/7 had nausea/vomiting or starvation.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver damage described as a major manifestation of acetaminophen overdose. In case 1 (suicide attempt), the patient consumed 30 g acetaminophen (60 x 500 mg Datril tablets) with an acetaminophen level of 235 µg/ml at 7 h, SGOT peaking near 8,000 IU/L, and developed acute tubular necrosis with creatinine rising above 16 mg/dl, showing the typical biphasic liver-then-kidney biochemical course. 2/7 patients in this group developed acute tubular necrosis; one death.

raw_record.support_text: Two patients experienced acetaminophen (APAP) toxicity on multiple (3-7) occasions, each time leading to acute liver injury/failure (ALI/ALF), with considerable hospital costs. raw_record.support_text: Repeated supratherapeutic ingestion of acetaminophen is presented as an important cause of acetaminophen-related poisoning, hepatic injury, and death; one study cited estimates that 30% of patients acquired hepatic injury after a repeated supratherapeutic ingestion pattern of misuse. In the poison-center case series (N=249), no patient with an initial aspartate aminotransferase level below 50 IU/L died or developed significant hepatotoxicity, whereas 6 (16%) with an initial aspartate aminotransferase greater than 1,000 IU/L died or required liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Repeated supratherapeutic (chronic, >8 hours) ingestion pattern rather than acute single overdose, representing deliberate misuse/excessive dosing.
raw_record.extra_details: A study estimated that 30% of patients acquired hepatic injury after repeated supratherapeutic ingestion. Of US poison-center acetaminophen deaths in 2002, 31 (16%) were designated as chronic (occurring over >8 hours). In the 18-month poison-center series (N=249), 6/38 (16%) patients with initial AST >1000 IU/L died or required liver transplantation; none with initial AST <50 IU/L died or developed significant hepatotoxicity. Treatment with acetylcysteine noted; the nomogram cannot be applied to repeated-ingestion cases. Variable data collection, recording, and treatment limited definition of precise exposure-therapy-outcome relationships.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 266 patients presenting after repeated supratherapeutic ingestion of paracetamol, 17 (6%) developed hepatotoxicity (ALT >1000 U/L), all of whom also had a peak AST >1000 U/L (median ALT 4127 U/L; two patients had peak INR >5.0). A further 77 (29%) developed a peak ALT between 50 and 1000 U/L during presentation. Hepatotoxicity was attributed to the paracetamol overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Repeated supratherapeutic ingestion (paracetamol overdose); 31 patients (12%) took modified release paracetamol as part of their overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective study of 266 patients (145 female, 55%; median age 43 y, IQR 30-56; median weight 75 kg). Median reported dose 9 g/day (IQR 4-12) over median 2 days (IQR 1-5); median time from last dose to initial blood tests 4.5 h. 192 (72%) had detectable initial paracetamol concentration (median 14 mg/L). Median initial ALT 33 U/L (range 6-6770). Hepatotoxicity defined as ALT >1000 U/L (17 patients, 6%; median ALT 4127 U/L, median peak INR 1.9, two with INR >5.0); all hepatotoxic patients had peak AST >1000 U/L. 77 (29%) had peak ALT 50-1000 U/L. Latency/effects assessed against symptoms and paracetamol-aminotransferase product.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of patients presenting with repeated supratherapeutic ingestion (RSTI) of paracetamol, hepatotoxicity was defined as alanine transaminase (ALT) >1000 IU/L and acute liver injury as ALT ≥50 IU/L. Among 91 paracetamol RSTI presentations, 9 (17%) in the non-abbreviated group developed hepatotoxicity (median peak ALT 3834 IU/L) and 36 had acute liver injury without hepatotoxicity, attributing these liver injuries to paracetamol ingested at supratherapeutic doses.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Repeated supratherapeutic ingestion (RSTI) overdose context; patients presenting after supratherapeutic paracetamol doses, with some receiving an abbreviated or full acetylcysteine treatment regimen.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined as ALT >1000 IU/L (9 of 91 patients, all in the non-abbreviated group; median peak ALT 3834 IU/L, IQR 1973-5171); acute liver injury defined as ALT ≥50 IU/L (36 patients). Median reported paracetamol dose 179-203 mg/kg over 24-48 hours of ingestion. No patients re-presented with developing liver injury or acute liver failure. Paracetamol hepatotoxicity managed with acetylcysteine infusion.

raw_record.support_text: Among 249 patients enrolled after repeated supratherapeutic acetaminophen ingestion, 47 presented with aspartate aminotransferase levels of 50 to 1,000 IU/L; 7 of these (15%) developed hepatotoxicity and 1 (2%) died of fulminant hepatic failure. The mean reported acetaminophen dose in this group was 11.7 g per 24 hours (95% CI 9.6 to 13.8) for a median duration of 48 hours, and all received acetylcysteine after admission.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Repeated supratherapeutic ingestion setting (mean reported doses about 7.6-12.6 g per 24 hours over 34-72 h), not ordinary therapeutic dosing.
raw_record.extra_details: Of 7,298 supratherapeutic ingestion cases received, 277 met inclusion criteria; 249 enrolled. AST <50 IU/L group (n=126) had no hepatotoxicity; AST 50-1,000 group (n=47): 7 (15%) developed hepatotoxicity, 1 died of fulminant hepatic failure; AST >1,000 group (n=37): 5 (14%) died, 1 underwent liver transplantation. Mean acetaminophen level at presentation 19-34 mg/L. All patients received acetylcysteine after admission.

raw_record.support_text: A 17-year-old girl presented 24 h after a voluntary acetaminophen overdose (>10 g, 156 mg/kg), with some alprazolam and cefpodoxime tablets, and the initial work-up revealed severe hepatic insufficiency (prothrombin time 45%, ASAT 240 IU/L, ALAT 430 IU/L). N-acetylcysteine infusion was started, but hepatic cytolysis progressed, with prothrombin time reaching a minimum of 11% at day 3. Her clinical and lab status (including creatinine 70 μmol/L) normalized by 2 months. The abstract and introduction also state that paracetamol is known for its hepatic adverse effects and risk of acute hepatic failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Reported in adolescent patients following voluntary acetaminophen overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: Observation 2: ingestion >10 g (156 mg/kg) with co-ingestion of small numbers of alprazolam and cefpodoxime tablets; severe hepatic insufficiency (prothrombin time 45%, ASAT 240 IU/L, ALAT 430 IU/L) at presentation, hepatic cytolysis progressing with prothrombin time minimum 11% at day 3; treated with intravenous N-acetylcysteine; full recovery by 2 months. Background assertion: paracetamol is known for hepatic adverse effects with risk of acute hepatic failure. Creatinine peaked at 210 μmol/L (creatinine clearance 38 mL/min).

raw_record.support_text: In nine patients with self-administered paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning, plasma levels of glutathione S-transferase B1 subunits, F protein, and ALT were measured. GST exceeded the reference interval in all patients on admission, and F protein was increased in seven, whereas abnormal plasma ALT was seen in only one. Patients whose admission GST exceeded 10 µg/L subsequently developed moderate or severe liver damage despite N-acetylcysteine treatment, leading the authors to conclude that paracetamol poisoning causes acute liver dysfunction with predominantly centrilobular damage, which GST and F protein detect more sensitively than ALT.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Self-administered overdose (poisoning) exposure context; not therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Nine overdose patients studied; admission GST was abnormal in all 9, F protein in 7, but ALT in only 1 (a patient admitted 12 h after poisoning). Post-admission, abnormal GST/F protein/ALT were seen in 9, 8, and 5 patients respectively. GST >10 µg/L on admission predicted moderate or severe liver damage despite N-acetylcysteine treatment. Paper's focus is biomarker performance (GST and F protein vs ALT) for detecting minor degrees of acute liver dysfunction, particularly centrilobular damage, rather than on characterizing paracetamol hepatotoxicity.

One 45-year-old alcoholic patient died 1 day after admission (the only fatality in the series of 10 cases) and was found on admission to have bilateral diffuse cataracts.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol (acetaminophen, N-acetyl p-aminophenol) is described as a commonly used analgesic that is hepatotoxic when taken in overdose. The authors report 220 patients admitted after a paracetamol overdose, of whom 200 showed evidence of liver damage and 29 died from fulminant hepatic failure, with the first case of acute hepatic necrosis related to the drug reported in 1966. The paper describes the histological appearances of the liver damage in 104 patients who had a liver biopsy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Self-poisoning overdose of 10 to 100 g; 25 of the 104 patients had concurrently ingested alcohol or another drug (e.g., barbiturates, nitrazepam, diazepam, chlordiazepoxide), representing unresolved co-exposure in those cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 220 patients admitted to the Liver Unit, King's College Hospital up to 1 Jan. 1974 after paracetamol overdose; 200 showed evidence of liver damage and 29 died from fulminant hepatic failure. In the 104 biopsied patients (65 females, 39 males, aged 15-58 yr), liver function became abnormal in all, 38 developed fulminant hepatic failure with grade 3 or 4 encephalopathy and 27 died. Histological grades: grade 0 (swelling, minor vacuolation/inflammation, no necrosis), grade I (confluent necrosis of centrilobular hepatocytes), grade II (confluent necrosis continuous between adjacent lobules), grade III (massive necrosis leaving a rim of liver cells around portal tracts). Dose-related injury with characteristic delay in appearance of liver damage; plasma paracetamol levels and coagulation disturbance studied.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol is the most common drug used for self-poisoning in the UK and is associated with potentially fatal liver damage. This is an overdose context: patients admitted to hospital because of paracetamol overdoses were studied to determine characteristics and factors that might have deterred them or reduced overdose dangers.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Self-poisoning/overdose exposure setting; patients admitted to hospital following deliberate paracetamol overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver dysfunction occurred in 25 of the 80 studied patients and was associated with consumption of more than 25 tablets (OR 4.46, 95% CI 1.31-17.41, P=0.014). More patients using loose preparations consumed 25+ tablets (69%) than those using blister packs (40%). Only 20 patients thought any warning label would have deterred them. Paracetamol liver damage accounts for over half of cases referred to liver units for fulminant liver failure, is the definite cause of at least 150 deaths per year in the UK, and has become a common reason for liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: This paper reports patients with severe paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning, treated with supportive care, cysteamine and methionine, or acetylcysteine. Among 57 patients given supportive treatment, mean maximum serum ALT activity exceeded 2022 IU/l, mean maximum plasma bilirubin was 56 µmol/l, mean prothrombin-time ratio was 1.9, and 33 (58%) developed severe liver damage (AST or ALT >1000 IU/l). Acetylcysteine given within 10 hours reduced severe liver damage to 1/62 (2%), whereas given 10-24 hours after ingestion it did not prevent it (20/38, 53%). Deaths from hepatic failure occurred in the supportive-treatment group (3/57) and in late-treatment groups. The liver damage is attributed to paracetamol poisoning.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Self-poisoning/overdose in patients with plasma paracetamol concentration exceeding the treatment line (300 mg/l at 4 hours and 45 mg/l at 15 hours); several patients also took alcohol and other drugs including Distalgesic.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe liver damage defined as serum AST or ALT activity exceeding 1000 IU/l. In supportive-treatment patients mean maximum serum ALT >2022 IU/l, plasma bilirubin 56 µmol/l, prothrombin-time ratio 1.9; 33/57 (58%) developed severe liver damage; 6 (11%) had renal impairment (3 requiring haemodialysis); 3 (5%) died from hepatic failure. Acetylcysteine within 8 hours was almost completely protective (serum ALT normal in 89% of 19 high-risk patients treated <8 h); protection declined with treatment at 8-10 h (7% severe damage), 10-12 h (43%), 12-15 h (56%), and was ineffective after 15 h (82%). Comparison groups: acetylcysteine and cysteamine+methionine, which are treatments not causes. High-risk defined by plasma paracetamol concentration.

raw_record.support_text: The study prospectively measured serum phosphate in 125 patients with severe acetaminophen poisoning to evaluate prognosis. Acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity is described, with hyperphosphatemia after acetaminophen overdose seen exclusively in nonsurvivors, predicting nonsurvival; nonsurvivors had significantly higher phosphate than survivors 48-96 h after overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Severe acetaminophen overdose/poisoning requiring tertiary-level care.
raw_record.extra_details: 125 patients with severe acetaminophen poisoning studied prospectively; phosphate threshold 1.2 mmol/L at 48-96 h had sensitivity 89%, specificity 100%, PPV 100%, NPV 98%, accuracy 98%, exceeding KCH criteria and identifying patients earlier (median 1 h vs 12 h). Hyperphosphatemia in nonsurvivors correlated with renal dysfunction (R=.55, P=.02). Acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity is cited as the most common cause of acute liver failure in Denmark, UK, and US.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes the development of the acetaminophen (paracetamol, APAP) nomogram using 30 previously published untreated cases from the Edinburgh Poisons Unit plus 34 additional unpublished untreated cases, plotting initial plasma APAP levels against time to discriminate patients who subsequently developed hepatotoxicity (defined as serum AST > 1000 IU) from those who did not. All 64 cases were untreated with antidotes (NAC, methionine, or cysteamine). The 1971 publication had stated that plasma levels greater than 300 µg/mL at 4 hours and 50 µg/mL at 12 hours were associated with toxicity, and the additional untreated cases led to lowering the 4-hour level to 200 µg/mL, so the nomogram line was drawn from 200 µg/mL at 4 hours to 50 µg/mL at 12 hours (a 4-hour half-life slope). The nomogram was intended to predict whether patients would develop hepatic toxicity after a single acute APAP overdose, based on an initial plasma level obtained 4 or more hours after ingestion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single acute oral overdose with a measured initial plasma level obtained 4 or more hours after ingestion; nomogram not intended for chronic ingestions.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined as serum SGOT/AST greater than 1000 IU at any time during the hospital course. Based on 30 published plus 34 unpublished untreated cases (all untreated with N-acetylcysteine, methionine, or cysteamine). The 1971 publication correlated levels >300 µg/mL at 4 h and >50 µg/mL at 12 h with toxicity, and a half-life >4 h with likely toxicity and >12 h with likely hepatic coma; the revised nomogram threshold was 200 µg/mL at 4 h to 50 µg/mL at 12 h (4-hour half-life slope). Therapeutic oral absorption of APAP is 70-90% with peak plasma values at 20-90 min. Co-ingested propoxyphene was noted to delay gastric emptying, favoring sampling at 4 h or later.

raw_record.support_text: A 22-year-old healthy female presented with a 3-day history of abdominal pain and vomiting and recent-onset confusion; she was jaundiced and confused with right upper-quadrant tenderness. Collateral history revealed she had taken an overdose of an unknown quantity of paracetamol-containing flu tablets three days prior, and a diagnosis of delayed paracetamol overdose (approximately 60 h) with suspected hepatic encephalopathy was made. Laboratory results showed markedly elevated transaminases (ALT 7050, AST 4183 U/L), elevated total bilirubin (82 μmol/L) and INR 11.73, consistent with severe paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In a 26-month period, 171 patients with single-dose paracetamol overdose (defined as intake of ≥5 g) were admitted to the Liver Unit, Rigshospitalet; 10 with hepatic encephalopathy (HE) on admission were excluded, leaving 161 noncomatose patients studied. The study aimed to predict the occurrence of HE, which complicates paracetamol-induced liver injury following overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single-dose paracetamol overdose (intake ≥5 g); all patients received intravenous N-acetylcysteine; chronic alcoholism (≥50 g ethanol/day for ≥5 years) present in a subset; patients with HE on admission were excluded from the analysis.
raw_record.extra_details: 161 noncomatose overdose patients (50 men, 111 women) studied; in the 86-patient learning set, 15 developed hepatic encephalopathy (hepatic coma grade II or more) treated per established guidelines; median dose 25 g (range 9–150 g); delay to N-acetylcysteine and degree of liver dysfunction (ALAT max up to 24,000 IU/l, bilirubin max up to 498 µmol/l, prothrombin index nadir) differed between HE and non-HE groups; the study focused on predicting HE as a complication of paracetamol-induced hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: A 36-year-old woman presented with fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) following an acetaminophen overdose. She was lethargic but arousable, had a King's College Criteria score of 2 for acetaminophen toxicity, MELD score of 36, and an unmeasurably high INR (>8.7). ROTEM (NATEM) parameters were within reference range, but she received cryoprecipitate and FFP prior to central line placement, was started on MARS and CVVHD, and died on day 7.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single-patient case report of FHF following acetaminophen overdose in a 36-year-old woman.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) with elevated PT/INR; INR unmeasurably high (>8.7); King's College Criteria for acetaminophen toxicity = 2; MELD 36; ROTEM NATEM parameters (CT, CFT, alpha-angle, A10, MCF) within reference range; received 5 units cryoprecipitate and 9 units FFP before central venous line placement; started on molecular adsorbent recirculating system (MARS) and continuous venovenous hemodialysis (CVVHD); died on day 7.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of paracetamol-induced acute liver failure (ALF) in an 18-year-old girl who presented 3 days after a paracetamol overdose (30 g) and was treated with intravenous N-acetylcysteine. She met King's College criteria for poor prognosis and, because of uncontrolled intracranial hypertension, underwent hepatectomy, remained anhepatic for 14 h, and was successfully bridged to liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single-patient case; overdose context (30 g paracetamol, 3 days prior) in an 18-year-old female who also subsequently required hepatectomy and transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol overdose of 30 g presented 3 days later; treated with IV N-acetylcysteine 150 mg/kg/day. Laboratory findings on admission: pH 7.3, pCO2 3.9 kPa, bilirubin 119 umol/l, ALT 8756 IU/l, creatinine 190 umol/l, lactate 3.9 mmol/l, WBC 9.7 x 10^9/l. Met King's College criteria for poor prognosis (prothrombin time >100 s, Grade III hepatic encephalopathy, creatinine >300 umol/l). Developed severe uncontrolled intracranial hypertension (ICP >40 mmHg), underwent hepatectomy, was anhepatic for 14 h, and was successfully bridged to orthotopic liver transplantation. Authors noted the necrotic liver may release pro-inflammatory cytokines contributing to intracranial hypertension.

raw_record.support_text: In this overdose case, a 21-year-old man ingested two bottles of acetaminophen along with an unknown amount of bupropion and bleach, with a toxicology screen ruling out other co-ingestants. Liver function tests worsened despite NAC therapy, and the resulting severe liver injury led the intensivist to discuss the patient with hepatology, where he was not considered a candidate for an acute liver transplant. The patient subsequently deteriorated into multiorgan failure and died.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single-patient overdose (two bottles of acetaminophen) with concurrent ingestion of bupropion and bleach; death occurred in the setting of multiorgan failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Peak serum acetaminophen 307 mcg/mL (reference <20 mcg/mL). ALT rose to 5,037 U/L and AST to 5,983 U/L at 48 hours, worsening despite NAC loading (15,560 mg, 200 mg/kg) and only one hemodialysis session. Hepatology consulted regarding acute liver transplant; patient not a candidate, later died. Co-present acetaminophen-induced methemoglobinemia (4.5%) treated with methylene blue 100 mg. Case reported in a paper focused on acetaminophen-induced methemoglobinemia, with liver injury presented as part of the acetaminophen toxicity course.

raw_record.support_text: A 21-year-old female ingested 40 g of immediate release paracetamol 8 h prior to transfer and was treated with N-acetylcysteine infusions, but developed hepatotoxicity with a peak ALT of 13,000 U/l and peak INR of 3.1, followed by renal deterioration. The conclusion states that paracetamol is known to cause acute liver and kidney injuries and that this case highlights considering PRES when treating paracetamol overdose patients who develop hepatorenal toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The first report of hepatic injury resulting from acetaminophen appeared in the British Medical Journal in 1966: two Scottish residents who each ingested 50 or 150 acetaminophen tablets in suicide attempts both died of fulminant hepatic necrosis. Thereafter, severe hepatotoxicity occurring during the course of acetaminophen overdose was increasingly recognized, reaching epidemic proportions in the UK by the early 1970s, with the first US case reported in 1971.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Suicidal overdose ingestion of 50-150 tablets; first two reported cases both died of fulminant hepatic necrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic injury from acetaminophen overdose first reported in 1966 (BMI 1966;3). Recognized increasingly in the UK through the early 1970s, with the first US case report in 1971. Contrasted with the otherwise marketed 'safety' of the compound.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that paracetamol predictably produces acute liver injury when taken in suicidal overdose. After an initial two to three days of irritability, jaundice and other signs of acute liver failure appear; by the fourth day the liver is tender and histologically shows uniformly distributed centrilobular coagulative necrosis with vacuolation of adjacent surviving hepatocytes. Of 200 patients admitted to the Liver Unit at King's College Hospital with signs of liver damage after an overdose of between 10 and 100 g of paracetamol, 29 died in fulminant hepatic failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Suicidal overdose of 10-100 g of paracetamol.
raw_record.extra_details: Centrilobular coagulative necrosis with vacuolation of adjacent surviving hepatocytes in early stages; two to three day initial period of irritability followed by jaundice and signs of acute liver failure by the fourth day; 29 of 200 overdose cases died in fulminant hepatic failure (Portmann et al., 1975).

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective series of 25 paracetamol overdose cases with suicidal intent hospitalized at Clínica Las Condes (2000–2006), the mean ingested dose was 11.7 g (range 5–45 g, 188 mg/kg, range 63–550). Only 3 cases developed acute hepatitis, corresponding to probable toxicity levels per the Rumack and Matthew nomogram; these showed mean peak GOT 1,892 U/L, GPT 3,388 U/L, and prothrombin time 60%. All were treated with N-acetylcysteine with good outcomes. Women mostly co-ingested benzodiazepines, antidepressants, and antipsychotics, and men co-ingested alcohol.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (APAP) overdose is described as the predominant cause of acute liver failure in the United States. Biomarkers of mitochondrial damage and nuclear DNA fragmentation were measured in plasma from APAP-overdose patients, and the authors conclude that mitochondrial damage and nuclear DNA fragmentation are likely critical events in APAP hepatotoxicity in humans, resulting in necrotic cell death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Supertherapeutic exposure (overdose, both accidental and intentional) is required; the paper explicitly notes that APAP is safe at therapeutic doses.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP overdose is stated to be the most common cause of acute liver failure in most Western countries and the predominant cause in the US (~56,000 ER visits, ~26,000 hospitalizations, and nearly 500 deaths per year; about half intentional). Patient cohort (n=40 overdose patients; 20 abnormal LT group with peak ALT >=1,000 U/l and peak PT >=18 s, 20 normal LT controls) plus 6 healthy volunteers. Mechanism: CYP-mediated formation of reactive metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) after saturation of glucuronidation/sulfation, GSH depletion, mitochondrial protein binding, mitochondrial permeability transition and nuclear DNA fragmentation via AIF/EndoG, without caspase activation (necrotic, not apoptotic, cell death) leading to centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis. Plasma biomarkers GDH and mtDNA elevated in abnormal-LT patients; peak ALT up to 8,545 U/l, peak AST up to 26,000 U/l, peak PT up to 374s, peak bilirubin up to 25 mg/dl; 6/20 abnormal-LT patients had encephalopathy grade >=1 and 95% survived.

raw_record.support_text: Case 2: A 28-year-old man developed jaundice, abdominal pain, and oliguria after self-treating with acetaminophen 'extra strength' capsules, taking two to four every 4-6 hours, estimating 10-12 capsules (5-6 g) over a 24-hour period, and denying a single massive dose or suicidal intent. He drank beer daily and frequently abused glutethimide, methaqualone, and nonprescription cough syrups but denied parenteral drug abuse. At admission he was deeply icteric with hepatomegaly. His serum acetaminophen drawn 17 hours after admission was 237 µg/ml, and he experienced hepatic encephalopathy (confusion, asterixis), then cardiac and respiratory arrest after an emesis with aspiration, and died; autopsy was refused.

raw_record.support_text: The infant had received acetaminophen every 4 h since circumcision on the second day of life; dosing was 80 mg (26 mg/kg) every 4 h for the first 24 h, then 40 mg (13 mg/kg) every 4 h for the next 2 days. Acetaminophen concentration measured 16 h after the last home dose was 109.8 µg/ml, well above the therapeutic range of 10 to 30 µg/ml, confirming an oral acetaminophen overdose in this term newborn.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Term newborn (neonatal) infant; oral acetaminophen overdose with supratherapeutic blood concentration; also presented with oliguric renal failure and a presumptive initial diagnosis of sepsis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 4-day-old term male neonate with oral acetaminophen toxicity. Presented with episodic emesis, decreased arousal, hypoglycemia (glucose 27 mg/dl), elevated AST 718 IU/l and ALT 978 IU/l, PT 51.9 s, INR 5.4, factor V 57%, fibrinogen 61 mg/dl, serum bilirubin 9 mg/dl (conjugated 1.4 mg/dl), ammonia 114 µmol/l, creatinine 3.2 mg/dl, and blood-tinged gastric aspirates. Developed hepatic encephalopathy, liver failure, coagulopathy, and oliguric renal failure. Successfully treated with a 20 h intravenous N-acetylcysteine infusion (NAC) without adverse effects. Paper notes acetaminophen toxicity is well documented and can lead to liver failure and death, with risk generally lower in children than adults, and supports NAC treatment for neonatal acetaminophen toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Initial laboratory investigations for the 3 patients with hepatocellular necrosis secondary to acetaminophen ingestion are shown. Across the three patients AST ranged from 7080 to 18012 U/L and ALT from 3540 to 12286 U/L, with acetaminophen concentrations measured at approximately 24, 96, and 48 h after ingestion for patients 1, 2, and 3, respectively (1218, <66, and 78 µmol/L). The paper attributes the hepatocellular necrosis to acetaminophen ingestion in all three patients.

raw_record.extra_details: Patient lab values: patient 1 AST 8330 U/L, ALT 3540 U/L; patient 2 AST 7080 U/L, ALT 12286 U/L; patient 3 AST 18012 U/L, ALT 4119 U/L; LDH levels 8075, 4871, 10147 U/L; lactate 22.5, 1.2, 5.1 mmol/L. The report's focus is spurious ethanol elevation on the Siemens Advia 1650 assay caused by endogenous dehydrogenase interference in these hepatotoxicity samples; patient 3's acetaminophen-toxicity diagnosis and N-acetylcysteine therapy were delayed after a presumptive alcoholic gastritis diagnosis.

raw_record.support_text: Regarding acetaminophen safety for OA pain in older adults, the paper states that acetaminophen toxicity was the leading cause of acute liver failure in the United States from 1998 to 2003, and that unintentional overdose is the leading cause of acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity, with the vast majority of these cases having taken acetaminophen to treat pain. These data led the FDA in January 2011 to recommend capping acetaminophen at 325 mg in prescribed combination products and to run public awareness campaigns focused on the risk of acetaminophen-related liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Unintentional overdose in patients who took acetaminophen to treat pain (OA-related).
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen (up to 4 g daily) modestly effective for OA pain vs placebo (SMD -0.13; 95% CI -0.22 to -0.04); acute liver failure data from 1998-2003 US; FDA January 2011 recommendation to cap prescribed combination products at 325 mg and public awareness campaigns regarding acetaminophen-related liver injury; larger population-based cohort found increased risk of hospitalization for GI events when older adults combined NSAIDs with acetaminophen.

raw_record.support_text: The authors' analysis of 40 poison-center cases found all involved patients taking multiple acetaminophen (APAP)-containing products with a cumulative dose exceeding the FDA maximum daily dose of 4 g per 24 h. The paper concludes that therapeutic exposure to multiple APAP-containing products, alone or with OTC formulations, can lead to severe liver injury and death, calling these unintentional APAP poisonings. The FDA statement cited notes that severe liver injury including acute liver failure resulting in liver transplant and death has been reported with acetaminophen use.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Unintentional overdose/poisoning from taking multiple acetaminophen-containing products concurrently; cumulative daily dose exceeded the FDA maximum of 4 g per 24 h in all 40 cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 40 cases from retrospective poison-center data. FDA recommends not exceeding 4 g/day total daily dose and advises against alcohol use while taking acetaminophen. Acute liver failure resulting in liver transplant and death reported. Authors note imprecise total dose/duration histories and inability to exclude other ingested substances or co-morbidities affecting liver function.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen is a commonly ingested drug, and up to 25% of intentional drug-overdose patients volunteer that they ingested it. Because rapid serum acetaminophen testing is the only way to determine whether NAC antidote treatment is needed and because the ingestion history is often unreliable, many physicians routinely order rapid serum acetaminophen levels in all overdose patients regardless of history.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Unsuspected/overdose exposure setting; applies to patients presenting with drug overdose at a busy urban emergency department.
raw_record.extra_details: In an ED cohort, approximately 1 in 70 drug-overdose patients had unsuspected acetaminophen ingestion and approximately 1 in 500 had unsuspected but potentially hepatotoxic serum acetaminophen levels identifiable only by routine screening. Authors suggest routinely screening all drug-overdose patients for acetaminophen. References document acute liver necrosis following paracetamol overdose and reversal of paracetamol toxicosis with N-acetylcysteine.

raw_record.support_text: A 17-year-old girl with a psychiatric disorder was admitted after voluntary poisoning with 16 g of Paracetamol. A blood Paracetamol assay 5.5 hours after ingestion gave 195.4 mg/L, which on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram indicated a high risk of probable liver injury, prompting N-acetylcysteine treatment. A follow-up level returned to 2.5 mg/L at 48 h, antidote was stopped, and evolution was favorable.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Voluntary drug overdose (16 g) in a 17-year-old girl with a psychiatric disorder; disorder-specific/suicide context.
raw_record.extra_details: Blood Paracetamol 195.4 mg/L taken 5.5 h after ingestion, interpreted on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram as high risk of probable liver injury; follow-up level 2.5 mg/L at 48 h; treated with N-acetylcysteine (loading 150 mg/kg then maintenance); evolution favorable. Paper also notes transaminase increase usually occurs ~24 h after a toxic dose and that transaminase measurement contributes to risk assessment.

raw_record.support_text: In a French multicentre study of acute liver failure (ALF) leading to registration for liver transplantation among 3284 adult patients (2005–2007), 104 drug-exposed ALF cases were found. Of these, 32 (30.8%) were voluntary intoxication, mainly paracetamol (n = 31, 96.9%), identified as the cause of these overdose-related ALF cases.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Voluntary intoxication/overdose setting; cases registered for liver transplantation due to ALF in France.
raw_record.extra_details: 31 of 32 voluntary-intoxication drug-exposed ALF cases were attributed to paracetamol (96.9%). Study period 2005–2007 across 20 French liver transplant centres using the CRISTAL national transplantation list; 181 of 3284 adult patients had ALF.
