raw_record.support_text: The authors report a rare case of acetaminophen-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), vanishing bile duct syndrome (VBDS), and liver failure in a 40-year-old female, which progressed despite withdrawal of the offending drug, supportive care, and immunosuppressants, and ultimately required a living-donor liver transplant. Histology of the explanted liver showed VBDS with severe cholestasis and hepatocyte necrosis, absent small bile ducts (negative cytokeratin 19 in the portal tract), but undamaged large bile ducts.
raw_record.extra_details: 40-year-old female with acetaminophen-related SJS treated with steroid pulse and immunoglobulin therapy in November 2013. Presented with progressive obstructive jaundice and liver failure; labs: WCC=20,580/µL, ALP=895 U/L, GGT=64 U/L, AST=63 U/L, ALT=17 U/L, albumin=1.8 g/dl, total bilirubin=27.9 mg/dl (direct 21.0 mg/dl), normal IgG4, INR=1.28, MELD 18, Child-Pugh 10. Intrahepatic biliary dilatation with normal common bile duct on CT/MRCP; liver and biliary tract normal 3 months prior. Underwent LDLT (daughter's husband donor, ABO-incompatible, rituximab; tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and steroids post-op); explant histology showed VBDS with severe cholestasis and hepatocyte necrosis, CK19-negative small bile ducts, intact large bile ducts. Discharged 68 days after LT with no VBDS recurrence. Histology stains: HE and IHC.

raw_record.support_text: Among 20 patients with acute liver failure, drug-induced liver injury was the attributed etiology in 5 (25.0%), including paracetamol in 1 patient. The paper therefore attributes ALF/DILI to paracetamol in this patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as the DILI etiology in 1 of 20 ALF ICU patients; overdose/supratherapeutic exposure is not specified in the text. Clinical phenotype is acute liver failure in an ONSD study.

raw_record.support_text: In the etiology table for 81 consecutive cases of acute liver failure, drugs and toxins accounted for 22 (27.2%) cases, with acetaminophen listed as the cause in 12 cases, isoniazide in 2, and salazopyrine, erythromycin, azithromycin, cyproterone, naproxen, germander, Amanita verosa, and carbon tetrachloride each in 1 case. The Results section notes that acetaminophen was the most common cause of drug-induced liver injury in this series.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as cause of acute liver failure in 12 of 81 consecutive ALF cases admitted to Hôpital Saint-Luc, Centre Hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal over nine years. Most common cause of drug-induced liver injury in the series.

raw_record.support_text: Among 14 patients with fulminant hepatitis, the etiologies included drug-induced hepatitis in 4 cases, attributed to acetaminophen (2 cases), isoniazid (1 case), and halothane (1 case).
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as cause of drug-induced fulminant hepatitis in 2 of 14 patients in the study cohort; the study assessed plasma CEA levels in patients with maximum hepatic dysfunction.

raw_record.support_text: In the Indian tertiary-care DILI cohort of 80 patients, paracetamol was listed among the other drugs implicated as a cause of DILI at 2% of cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed as a cause in 2% of 80 DILI cases (about 1-2 patients).

raw_record.support_text: Table lists paracetamol among 'other drugs' causing DILI (5 cases total in that category, 6%), with 0 deaths. The narrative (p29) identifies paracetamol as an implicated drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among 'other drugs' (paracetamol, etoposide, pegylated interferon, itraconazole, thalidomide) that together caused 5/82 DILI cases (6%); 0 deaths

raw_record.support_text: A 53-year-old male developed hepatotoxicity after 1 year of chronic treatment with paracetamol 4 g day⁻¹; after the drug was stopped, liver biopsies showed chronic active hepatitis and cirrhosis, and rechallenge with a single 1325 mg dose caused aminotransferase levels to rise 12–18 h later, supporting a hypersensitivity reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic paracetamol 4 g/day for 1 year in a 53-year-old male; liver biopsies showed chronic active hepatitis and cirrhosis after drug cessation; rechallenge with a single 1325 mg dose raised aminotransferase 12–18 h later (hypersensitivity); hepatic glutathione content was higher than controls 1 year after cessation and plasma/urine paracetamol and metabolite kinetics (half-lives, conjugation pattern) were normal.

raw_record.support_text: In the studied acetaminophen (AC) DILI cohort, only two cases developed fulminant hepatic failure, both being B*1801 carriers, one also carrying A*3002. The paper also notes prior HLA genotyping of 140 DILI patients (17% due to AC) and describes AC DILI phenotypes including hepatocellular and cholestatic/mixed types.
raw_record.extra_details: AC accounted for 17% of 140 DILI patients in an earlier HLA genotyping study. DILI phenotype associations: hepatocellular injury enriched in HLA-A*3002 and B*1801 carriers (who were younger, predominantly male, more often hospitalized); cholestatic/mixed injury associated with DRB1*1501-DQB1*0602. 19 cases with R value ≥5 and total bilirubin >2 xULN (Hy's Law-type cases) were enriched in A*3002 and B*1801. Two cases in the cohort developed fulminant hepatic failure, both B*1801 carriers (one also A*3002).

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 224 cases of fulminant hepatic failure, etiology could be determined in 49 cases. In six cases (3%), drug toxicity was the offending agent: isoniazid (INH) in 4 cases and acetaminophen in 2 cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as the offending drug in 2 of 6 drug-toxicity cases (3% of 224 FHF cases) in a fulminant hepatic failure cohort; etiology was determined in only 49 of 224 cases. Exposure setting (therapeutic versus overdose) was not specified in the paper.

raw_record.support_text: Study patients were categorized into DILI-ALF (non-acetaminophen drug-induced liver injury leading to acute liver failure) and APAP-ALF groups, with APAP-ALF representing acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure used as the comparison cohort in this ALFSG study.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP-ALF comparison group in this study (N=110; larger study N=354); median time to death 3.5 days, range mean 5.9 days among those dying within 21 days.

raw_record.support_text: The case report concludes that the patient presented an unusual acetaminophen-induced hepatitis attributed to a probable allergic reaction, with a previously undescribed prolonged clinical course. In the prior discussion, rapid discontinuation of acetaminophen did not prevent late-onset severe hepatitis, and the injury progressed to chronicity with sustained elevation of transaminase, consistent with drug-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis; a positive drug lymphocyte stimulation test (DLST) supported an allergic/immune (adaptive immunity) mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: Positive DLST supported an allergic, adaptive-immune-mediated mechanism. Despite rapid acetaminophen discontinuation, the patient developed late-onset severe hepatitis with sustained transaminase elevation that progressed to chronicity (suggested drug-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis). Chronic course was not favored to be acute-onset autoimmune hepatitis due to absence of perivenular necroinflammatory activity and persistently negative hypergammaglobulinemia and autoantibodies. Authors note that the prolonged course may be under-scored by the Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen accounted for just one case among the 313 human DILI cases.
raw_record.extra_details: One case among 313 DILI cases; no specific exposure (therapeutic vs overdose) or outcome stated.

raw_record.support_text: In this DILI cohort from Southwest Hospital (1096 patients with RUCAM causality assessment), the most common causative agents were medications (462 patients, 42.15%) followed by herbs (391 patients, 35.68%). Among analgesics-caused DILI, only 5 cases were caused specifically by acetaminophen, and among the 172 antimicrobial-agent DILI cases, 103 were caused specifically by antitubercular agents.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen was the specific cause of 5 analgesics-related DILI cases in a cohort of 1096 RUCAM-assessed DILI patients (RUCAM scores 3-14, median 7; causality likely highly probable in 207, probable in 652, possible in 237). Cohort was predominantly Chinese Han adults in Southwest China.

raw_record.support_text: From 1998 to 2003, the ALF Study Group prospectively collected 610 detailed patient histories, including 262 cases of acute liver failure caused by acetaminophen (APAP, N-acetyl-para-aminophenol), an over-the-counter (OTC) drug product. These APAP patients had a median age of 36, median recorded peak ALT of 4310 IU/L, peak serum total bilirubin of 4.3 mg/dL, and 67% survival without transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP = acetaminophen, N-acetyl-para-aminophenol; OTC drug product; 262 of 610 ALF cases attributed to it; median age 36 y, 74% female, jaundice mean 1 day, coma stage 3/4 in 52%, mean peak ALT 4055 IU/L, mean peak bilirubin 4.6 mg/dL, 8% transplanted, 65% spontaneous survival, 71% overall survival.

raw_record.support_text: A 35-year-old male presented with confusion, jaundice, and drowsiness after taking up to 4.2 g of acetaminophen over the previous day for low back pain, and developed acute hepatic failure (AST 3750 U/l, ALT >5000 U/l, INR 12) complicated by hepatic encephalopathy and hepatorenal syndrome. His acute liver failure was attributed to acetaminophen toxicity (Table 1 lists the cause of hepatic failure as 'Acetaminophen toxicity'), and he recovered to baseline after treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Adult male with history of heavy alcohol abuse (none for several months). Dose ~4.2 g/day taken for low back pain. Lab values: acetaminophen 214 µmol/l, AST 3750 U/l, ALT >5000 U/l, ALP 110 U/l, INR 12, creatinine 475 µmol/l, ammonia 141 µmol/l. Developed acute hepatic failure with hepatic encephalopathy (flat EEG, diffusion restriction on DWI) and hepatorenal syndrome; treated with N-acetylcysteine and renal replacement therapy; hypothermia protocol; recovered to normal baseline by discharge on day 12 with normal liver enzymes and INR 1.1.

raw_record.support_text: In this letter responding to comments on their prospective study, the authors state that space did not permit them to expand on cases in which therapeutic doses of acetaminophen caused acute liver failure. They note that each case reported in their prospective trial was diagnosed by the site investigator, an experienced hepatologist, using standard criteria including history of ingestion, plasma acetaminophen levels, and alanine aminotransferase levels exceeding 3500 U/L, with exclusion of other etiologies, and acknowledge that history of ingestion may be inaccurate in patients with altered mental status.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver failure diagnosis based on history of ingestion, plasma acetaminophen levels, and alanine aminotransferase levels exceeding 3500 U/L, with exclusion of other etiologies; diagnosis made by an experienced hepatologist site investigator.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 60 patients with acute hepatitis (19 drug-induced), drug-induced hepatitis was attributed to herb (12 patients), acetaminophen (three patients), ibuprofen (one patient), antituberculosis medication (two patients) and ketoconazole (one patient). The named molecular agents acetaminophen, ibuprofen, and ketoconazole are therefore each reported as a cause of human drug-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as the cause of drug-induced hepatitis in 3 of 19 drug-induced acute hepatitis cases (15.8%) within a 60-patient acute hepatitis cohort; no details on dose, latency, outcomes, or overdose given.

raw_record.support_text: In the cohort of 33 patients with acute hepatic encephalopathy, 1 patient had toxic hepatitis attributed to paracetamol.
raw_record.extra_details: 1 of 16 toxic-hepatitis patients; no dose or overdose details provided.

raw_record.support_text: In a landmark study of 16 patients with acute liver failure (ALF) due primarily to acetaminophen hepatotoxicity, Wright et al. measured proinflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 in arterial and reverse jugular venous blood. The paper explicitly attributes the human hepatotoxicity resulting in ALF to acetaminophen.
raw_record.extra_details: Cited evidence is a study of 16 patients with ALF due primarily to acetaminophen hepatotoxicity; arterial proinflammatory cytokine (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6) levels correlated with intracranial hypertension, with brain cytokine efflux consistent with brain cytokine production. Mentioned in the context of brain neuroinflammation during liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: Jinjuvadia and colleagues used ICD-9 codes to identify DILI cases in a University of Michigan database of 7395 patients between 1994 and 2000, attributing cases to Augmentin, Dilantin (phenytoin), valproic acid, and isoniazid. Among 119 DILI cases, 51 were due to these four drugs; separately listed agents included acetaminophen (36 cases) and carbamazepine (two cases).
raw_record.extra_details: 36 of 119 DILI cases in an ICD-9 coded hospital database (1994-2000) attributed to acetaminophen; overall DILI incidence 1.6%, 0.7% for the four drugs of special interest; mean age 51 years, 51% women; >50% required hospitalization, 10% died of liver failure, one liver transplant (overall cohort, not agent-specific).

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 87 patients with acute liver failure, the etiology was drug-induced in 19 (22%) patients, including acetaminophen-induced ALF in 8 patients. This explicitly attributes acetaminophen as the cause of acute liver failure (DILI) in these patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Among 87 patients with acute liver failure (ALF), drug-induced ALF occurred in 19 (22%), of which acetaminophen was the cause in 8 patients.

raw_record.support_text: DILI-inducing NSAIDs were APAP (acetaminophen), celecoxib and ibuprofen; NSAIDs accounted for 17 patients (4.01%) of DILI cases.
raw_record.extra_details: NSAID, listed as APAP; NSAIDs accounted for 17 patients (4.01%) of DILI cases.

raw_record.support_text: Russo et al. studied more than 51,000 liver transplants in the UNOS database (1990-2002) and identified 270 patients transplanted for documented drug-induced liver failure (15% of all liver transplants). Acetaminophen accounted for nearly half of these patients, either alone or in combination with another medication.
raw_record.extra_details: Identified as cause of ~half of 270 transplants for documented drug-induced liver failure in the UNOS database 1990-2002, alone or in combination with another medication. Of non-acetaminophen causes, leading were isoniazid, propylthiouracil, phenytoin, valproic acid, toxic mushrooms, nitrofurantoin, and herbal therapies.

raw_record.support_text: The paper utilized a previously recruited cohort of 79 DILI patients (assessed by the updated RUCAM) who were treated with 31 different drugs. Among these drugs, epistane, oxaliplatin, and azathioprine consistently led to the same DILI phenotype in all exposed patients, whereas acetaminophen, amoxicillin-clavulanic, and methotrexate exhibited variable, patient-related metabolome features, with different patients displaying different DILI sub-phenotypes that sometimes changed over the course of the event.
raw_record.extra_details: Among a cohort of 79 DILI patients assessed by updated RUCAM, treated with 31 drugs; classified in the second drug category exhibiting variable, patient-related DILI metabolomic phenotypes, with different patients showing different DILI sub-phenotypes that sometimes changed (e.g., hepatocellular to cholestatic or mixed) during the DILI event.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that the 4 leading drug groups causing liver transplantation due to drug-induced acute liver failure (DIALF) in the United States were acetaminophen, antituberculosis drugs, antiepileptics, and antibiotics. Acetaminophen accounts for the largest number of patients transplanted (265 of 661 total, 40%).
raw_record.extra_details: Analysis based on UNOS liver transplantation database for DIALF in the United States. Acetaminophen was the leading drug group causing transplantation (265 patients, 40% of DIALF transplants); drug-induced acute liver failure (ALF) is the named injury phenotype. Recipients transplanted for acetaminophen-induced ALF: mean age 31.66 years, 75% female, serum total bilirubin 9.70 mg/dL, ALT 3777 IU/L, 82% on life support pretransplant.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective population-based study of 62 patients with definite or possible ALF (32 due to acetaminophen or DILI), acetaminophen was implicated in 18 events (56%). In the ALFSG registry (1198 patients, 23 sites over 10 years), acetaminophen toxicity was responsible for 46% of ALF cases.
raw_record.extra_details: ALF is a syndrome whose causes include acetaminophen and idiosyncratic DILI. Acetaminophen implicated in 18/32 (56%) of acetaminophen/DILI ALF events in one retrospective study and in 46% of ALFSG cases. Latency of implicated DILI ALF agents was 1-2 weeks to 8 months; 65% of subjects did not stop the drug until after jaundice developed.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 154 DILI patients analyzed for baseline test signatures, six drugs had more than 5 cases each and were analyzed specifically (APAP, flupirtine, methotrexate, clavulanate, piperacillin, isoniazid), with the remaining drugs combined as 'others'. APAP and flupirtine each showed 16 significant differences versus 9 for methotrexate, 5 for clavulanate, 4 for piperacillin, and no significant signatures for isoniazid.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP DILI cases had the highest ALT (2727 IU/L), AST (647 IU/L) and ActiTest (0.99) and the lowest A2M (1.45 g/L) among the drug groups; 16 baseline tests were significantly (Bonferroni) different from the other drug classes.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) was named among the 'other drugs' that caused DILI in this cohort of 65 patients, in which causality was assessed with RUCAM; DILI was attributed to single prescription medication in 28%, CAM in 9%, and multiple prescription agents in 63% of cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) named among 'other drugs' causing DILI (etoposide, interferon, itraconazole, thalidomide together 8% of cases); median duration of therapy 31 days; overall mortality 10.7% (7 patients), 3 attributed to liver disease but not specified per drug.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that the well-known paracetamol-associated hepatotoxicity is confirmed by a three-fold increase of risk in this case-control study, with an adjusted OR of 2.97 (95% CI 2.09-4.21) for acute serious liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: In a 1992-2006 single-center cohort of 469 ALF patients (104 transplanted), acetaminophen was the most common etiology, and the paper frames acetaminophen as a cause of acute liver failure requiring evaluation for liver transplantation. Acetaminophen-induced ALF was noted to have a distinct clinical course characterized by rapid clinical deterioration, and prior studies were cited highlighting the increasing contribution of acetaminophen as a cause of ALF in the UK, US, and Europe.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-center Scottish Liver Transplantation Unit cohort, 1992-2006; 469 ALF patients of which acetaminophen was the most common etiology. 104 underwent LT: acetaminophen 45/326 (13.8%) vs non-acetaminophen 59/143 (41.3%), P<0.01. King's College poor prognostic criteria fulfilled: acetaminophen 165/326 (50.6%) vs non-acetaminophen 91/143 (63.6%), P<0.01. Contraindications to LT more frequent in acetaminophen cohort (99/165, 60%). Waiting-list survival lower in acetaminophen cohort (45/66, 68.2%). LT proceeded less commonly in acetaminophen ALF in later cohort (2002-2005, 4/81, 5% vs 1993-1996, 16/99, 16.2%), attributed partly to increased psychiatric contraindications (resistant/severe alcohol dependence). Acetaminophen-induced ALF described with rapid clinical deterioration and relatively good prognosis.

raw_record.support_text: The two patients observed by the authors were both in good health with no neoplastic disease or systemic pathology, denied alcohol and drugs that cause CYP induction, were not fasting, and had normal BMIs. They showed asymptomatic elevations of serum ALT and AST (>2 IU/mL), which the authors describe as mild hepatitis consistent with the idiosyncratic drug reaction model. In paragraph 27 the authors state that both cases were idiosyncratic and can be attributed to genetically determined enhancement of cytochrome-P450 enzyme activity, with the mild hepatitis caused by the toxicity of the reactive metabolite NAPQI.
raw_record.extra_details: Two healthy patients without neoplastic disease or other systemic pathology; denied alcohol and CYP-inducing drugs; not fasting; normal BMI; asymptomatic ALT/AST elevations (>2 IU/mL); no eosinophilia or cutaneous rashes; non-allergic idiosyncrasy via a 'danger model'; mild hepatitis attributed to toxicity of the reactive metabolite NAPQI present in larger amounts due to genetically determined upregulation of CYP activity; acetaminophen promptly discontinued upon transaminase elevation; AP (antipyrine) clearance values higher than healthy volunteers and remained high when retested after a 6-month acetaminophen wash-out period.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen is reported to cause hepatotoxicity in humans: a cited recent report describes 69 patients in whom acetaminophen hepatotoxicity developed after taking acetaminophen, nine of whom reported daily alcohol ingestion of 60 g or less (approximately 7 ounces of 80-proof liquor) and five of whom reported acetaminophen ingestion of 4 g or less daily. The paper notes that there has been little reason to suspect that moderate drinkers in good general health are at increased risk of acetaminophen toxicity, though this is characterized as a controversial issue.
raw_record.extra_details: Cited report of 69 patients in whom acetaminophen hepatotoxicity developed; nine reported daily alcohol ingestion of ≤60 g (approximately 7 oz of 80-proof liquor); five of these reported acetaminophen ingestion of ≤4 g daily. raw_record.support_text: Among 171 liver-failure patients classified with drug-induced liver injury (DILI defined as having taken any hepatotoxic drug within 6 months before illness onset), 23 (13.5%) had received 'other drugs' that included acetaminophen (2.3%). raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective tertiary-hospital cohort in Southwest China (2000-2012); 171 DILI-associated liver-failure patients; acetaminophen accounted for 2.3%. raw_record.support_text: A 53-year-old man who rarely drank alcohol and had taken acetaminophen (4 g/day) had evidence of chronic hepatitis on liver biopsy. On several occasions withdrawal of acetaminophen therapy was associated with return of aminotransferase levels to normal, and a deliberate rechallenge with 1,325 mg of acetaminophen was associated with return of injury. A biopsy 23 days after discontinuation showed perivenular (central) necrosis and portal inflammation; a biopsy 5 months later again showed chronic hepatic inflammation.

raw_record.support_text: Two human pharmaco-metabonomics studies attributed mild liver injury to acetaminophen (APAP) at therapeutic dosing. Winnike et al. (2010) administered 4 g of APAP per day for seven days to 35 healthy adults, a regimen stated to produce mild liver injury in about one-third of subjects; urinary profiles obtained shortly after APAP treatment but before ALT elevation predicted development of injury (cysteine and mercapturate conjugates of APAP, glycine, alanine, and acetate tended to be higher in responders). Kim JW et al. (2013) treated 20 healthy subjects with acetaminophen at 3 g/day for seven days and found that AST and lactate dehydrogenase activities were significantly increased seven days post-dosing while all other hepatic biochemical parameters remained within normal range, concluding the urinary metabolome profile could predict hepatotoxicity in humans.
raw_record.extra_details: Winnike et al. (2010): 4 g/day for seven days in 35 healthy adults producing mild liver injury in about one-third of subjects; metabolomics could predict injury before ALT elevation (cysteine and mercapturate conjugates of APAP, glycine, alanine, acetate higher in responders). Kim JW et al. (2013): 3 g/day for seven days in 20 healthy subjects; AST and LDH significantly increased at 7 days, all other hepatic biochemical parameters within normal range; seven endogenous urinary metabolites (TMAO, citrate, 3-chlorotyrosine, phenylalanine, glycine, hippurate, glutarate) separated pre- vs post-dosing; study framed as metabolomics biomarker work for predicting hepatotoxicity in humans.

raw_record.support_text: The summary states that use of acetaminophen by the alcoholic is potentially lethal and warns of the potential hepatocellular damage resulting from the combination of chronic alcoholism and modest increases above therapeutic doses of acetaminophen. Of the seven patients in the series, three died, although in two of the three instances other factors may have contributed to their deaths. The paper frames this as the 'alcohol-Tylenol syndrome' caused by acetaminophen ingestion combined with chronic alcoholism.

raw_record.extra_details: Seven patients with severe acute liver injury; markedly elevated serum transaminases and prothrombin times; AST exceeded 10,000 U/L in four patients and exceeded 4,000 U/L in all; this elevation argues against alcoholic hepatitis (usually <300 U/L). No serologic evidence of acute hepatitis A or B; hepatitis C could not be excluded but such transaminase activity is unusual for viral etiology. Mechanism: acetaminophen partly metabolized by cytochrome P-450 reductase to a toxic intermediate detoxified by glutathione conjugation; alcohol induces P-450 and depletes glutathione, enhancing toxicity; preexisting liver disease may increase risk. Histology from prior reports showed centrilobular necrosis, with some features of alcoholic hepatitis, 'toxic hepatitis,' or chronic hepatitis; established cirrhosis not necessary. Three of seven patients died; in two of three other factors may have contributed. Suggested management: supportive care and acetylcysteine/cimetidine as antidotes within 24 hours.

raw_record.support_text: An epileptic 48-year-old woman treated with phenobarbital (100 mg/d) had been taking acetaminophen (1 g/d) for headaches for 3 months and presented with generalized discomfort and weakness, a palpable liver, and elevated transaminases (AST 170, ALT 456, ALP 131, GGT 498 mIU/mL). Acute hepatitis A/B, cytomegalovirus, herpes, and EBV were excluded, and the dramatic fall of serum transaminases to normal within 2 weeks of acetaminophen withdrawal strongly supported drug-induced liver damage. The authors note only seven prior cases of hepatotoxicity from therapeutic acetaminophen doses and propose that concurrent phenobarbital induced mixed-function oxidase activity, increasing toxic metabolite production beyond glutathione binding capacity, concluding that persons taking phenobarbital with even low therapeutic doses of acetaminophen are at risk of hepatotoxicity.

Lab values: AST 170 mIU/mL (normal <30), ALT 456 mIU/mL, alkaline phosphatase 131 mIU/mL, 5'-nucleotidase 17 mIU/mL, GGT 498 mIU/mL. Seronegative for IgM-HVA, HBsAg, IgM-HBc; persistent low IgM/IgG ruled out CMV, herpes, EBV; sporadic non-A, non-B hepatitis not fully excluded. Transaminases returned to normal within 2 weeks of acetaminophen withdrawal. Authors state only seven previously reported cases of hepatotoxicity from therapeutic acetaminophen doses. Proposed mechanism: phenobarbital-induced mixed-function oxidase, increased toxic metabolites exceeding glutathione binding capacity.

raw_record.support_text: In this single-patient case report, the authors state that the findings in their case are most consistent with acetaminophen-induced liver injury, concluding that acetaminophen protein adducts may aid identification of liver injury due to an adverse drug effect. The patient received therapeutic IV acetaminophen and developed hepatic injury characterized by elevated transaminases, coagulopathy, and elevated serum bilirubin and ammonia.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly patient (>75 years) with limited clinical experience of IV acetaminophen, post-operative and catabolic with NPO status, multiple doses administered over several days, and evidence of prior hepatic disease by ultrasound; the authors consider these uncommon circumstances to limit generalizability to a small number of patients.
raw_record.extra_details: IV route; no monitoring of hepatic transaminases or INR (recommended if IV acetaminophen is continued beyond 48 h); ALT elevation higher than that observed during heparin administration; coagulopathy and elevated serum bilirubin and ammonia; APAP-CYS serum adducts used to identify acetaminophen-induced liver injury; caution advised when acetaminophen is used in patients with prior hepatic disease; report acknowledges inability to draw causal inference inherent to a single case report.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that the patient sustained severe hepatic necrosis from excessive therapeutic use of acetaminophen. They note the histologic features of the liver biopsy are consistent with this proposition, that the patient had a marked decrease in nutritional intake and may have had depletion of hepatic glutathione, and that this, with injudicious doses of the drug, produced a very severe liver lesion and illness. Serum acetaminophen was not measured at admission.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Excessive therapeutic use with injudicious doses; marked reduction in nutritional intake with possible hepatic glutathione depletion; not exposed to a known P-450 inducer.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report. Admission labs: hemoglobin 10.5 g/dl, leukocytes 4600/mm3, serum bilirubin 5.3 mg/dl (2.2 mg/dl direct), alkaline phosphatase 16.8 K-A units, SGOT 1321 Karmen units, prothrombin time 25 s (control 11.5 s), PTT 42.5 s (control 22 s), ammonia 189 ug/dl, HBsAg negative. Initial impression of stage I hepatic encephalopathy with acute fulminant viral hepatitis; biopsy showed centrilobular fibrosis, bridging necrosis, chronic inflammatory infiltrate, moderate fatty metamorphosis, rare coagulation necrosis, and was strongly suggestive of the toxic lesion induced by acetaminophen and atypical for viral hepatitis. Improved with conservative treatment, discharged asymptomatic after 8 days with bilirubin 1.2 mg/dl, alkaline phosphatase 17.4 K-A units, SGOT 17 Karmen units, normal prothrombin time.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that this patient sustained severe hepatic necrosis from excessive therapeutic use of acetaminophen, noting the histologic features of his liver biopsy are consistent with this proposition and that he may have suffered previous, less severe episodes. They reason that his marked decrease in nutritional intake may have depleted hepatic glutathione, which, with injudicious dosages of the drug, produced a very severe liver lesion and illness.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Excessive/injudicious therapeutic dosing rather than overdose; marked reduction in nutritional intake with possible depletion of hepatic glutathione as a contributing susceptibility; no known P-450 system inducer exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: 46-year-old-man (per case narrative) initially considered to have stage I hepatic encephalopathy with suspected acute fulminant viral hepatitis (HBsAg negative). Biopsy showed centrilobular fibrosis with bridging necrosis joining central areas, chronic inflammatory infiltrate, moderate fatty metamorphosis, rare coagulation necrosis of hepatocytes, and regenerative plates; findings deemed 'strongly suggestive of the toxic lesion induced by acetaminophen' and atypical for viral hepatitis. Abnormal labs at presentation: bilirubin 5.3 mg/dl, alkaline phosphatase 16.8 K-A units, SGOT 1321 Karmen units, prothrombin time 25 s (control 11.5 s), ammonia 189 µg/dl. Patient improved and was discharged asymptomatic after 8 days (bilirubin 1.2 mg/dl, SGOT 17 Karmen units, normal prothrombin time). The authors note he may have suffered previous, less severe episodes.

raw_record.support_text: In this prospective pharmacovigilance study of older adults' DILI, paracetamol was the culprit drug for 11% (50/458) of DILI cases, and one case was fatal. Ageing-related changes in liver blood flow and mass can increase paracetamol exposure, causing more frequently acute liver injury with paracetamol given at therapeutic doses, which led to a 2018 recommendation for a maximum paracetamol dose of 3 g per day (previously 4 g) for the elderly, achieving an 80% reduction in paracetamol-related DILI.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Older adult (>65 y) patients from geriatric department cohorts; therapeutic-dose exposure in elderly; 2018 regulatory/clinical recommendation capped paracetamol at 3 g/day for the elderly.
raw_record.extra_details: Culprit for 11% (50/458) of DILI cases, one case fatal; 2018 recommendation lowering maximum elderly dose to 3 g/day (from 4 g) produced ~80% reduction in paracetamol-related DILI after 1 year; aging-related reductions in liver blood flow and mass increase paracetamol exposure and frequency of acute liver injury at therapeutic doses.

raw_record.support_text: Two older patients (83 and 91 years old) developed acute hepatotoxicity with elevated trough paracetamol levels (54 mg/l and 31 mg/l) while receiving a standard European oral dose of paracetamol (2 x 500 mg QDS = 4 g daily) with no risk factors for slowed metabolism (weight <50 kg, interacting medications, hepatic enzyme inducers, history of liver disease), following a recent dose escalation from as-needed to 4 g daily. The authors conclude that even when prescribed appropriately at the usual therapeutic dosage, paracetamol can be hepatotoxic.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Older patients (aged 83 and 91 years); therapeutic standard dose of 4 g daily with no risk factors for slowed metabolism; recent dose escalation from as-needed to 4 g daily; second patient also received co-codamol (paracetamol 500 mg/codeine 30 mg).
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1 (83-year-old female): LFTs rose from normal on Day 4 and peaked Day 6, trough paracetamol 54 mg/l, drug discontinued, treated with N-acetylcysteine, recovered completely with LFTs normalized in 2 weeks. Case 2 (91-year-old nursing home resident): on co-codamol for 3 weeks prior, acute hepatotoxicity with normal LFTs 2 weeks earlier, trough paracetamol 31 mg/l, received N-acetylcysteine but did not respond and died. Paracetamol = N-acetyl-p-aminophenol (acetaminophen).

raw_record.support_text: A patient on zidovudine therapy who took 3.3 g of acetaminophen in less than 36 hours developed severe hepatotoxicity; AST rose to 5,724 U/L, ALT to 3,124 U/L, LDH to 12,675 U/L, alkaline phosphatase was 84 U/L, and total bilirubin 20 µmol/L, with substantial improvement over 4 days. raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen dose ~3.3 g (less than 3.5 g) over 36 hours in a 31-year-old man with AIDS; serum AST 5,724 U/L, ALT 3,124 U/L, LDH 12,675 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 84 U/L, total bilirubin 20 µmol/L; values improved substantially over 4 days; serologies for hepatitis B, hepatitis A, and cytomegalovirus were negative; authors note no prior report of severe acetaminophen-associated hepatotoxicity in zidovudine patients and advise caution in malnourished patients with concurrent hepatic disease.

raw_record.extra_details: Case report from University of Michigan Medical Center. Very high transaminases (peak AST about 209 µkat/L, ALT about 132 µkat/L) unusual for viral hepatitis and consistent with acute toxic liver injury; elevated bilirubin (peak 106 µmol/L); prolonged prothrombin time (up to 20.1 s); complete acute renal failure; initial blood acetaminophen level below the level usually associated with toxicity. Proposed mechanism: isoniazid-induced P450IIE1 conversion of a greater proportion of acetaminophen to toxic metabolites. Patient recovered and was discharged on day 10. Accompanying rat data (Addendum) show isoniazid pretreatment potentiates acetaminophen hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen is well tolerated by patients with chronic liver disease. In a double-blind, two-period, cross-over study comparing acetaminophen, 4 g daily for two weeks, with placebo in 20 patients with stable chronic liver disease, laboratory tests and clinical evaluations revealed no evidence of hepatotoxicity and no adverse nonspecific effect on laboratory abnormalities associated with liver disease, no significant drug accumulation despite modestly impaired metabolism, no enhanced formation of the toxic metabolite as reflected in conjugate excretion, and no glutathione depletion. The authors conclude acetaminophen is preferred to salicylates in patients with chronic liver disease.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with stable chronic liver disease
raw_record.extra_details: Double-blind, two-period, cross-over study of 20 patients comparing acetaminophen 4 g daily for two weeks with placebo; weekly laboratory tests (bilirubin, transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, 5-nucleotidase, gamma glutamyl transpeptidase, serum bile acids, prothrombin/partial thromboplastin time, serum creatinine) showed no adverse effects. No evidence of hepatotoxicity, no drug accumulation, no enhanced toxic-metabolite formation (normal conjugate excretion), no glutathione depletion. Authors frame acetaminophen as preferred antipyretic analgesic over salicylates in chronic liver disease.

The injury may have been favored by pre-existing mitochondrial dysfunction, such as a deficiency in an enzyme of mitochondrial beta-oxidation or the respiratory chain.

raw_record.support_text: A 92-year-old female developed acute hepatotoxicity attributed to intravenous acetaminophen given at 1 g every 6 hours (total 13 g) for postoperative analgesia. On hospital day 5 she had epigastric pain with serum total bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL, ALT 3,914 U/L, AST 4,698 U/L, INR 1.68, and ammonia 60 mcg/dL. The patient had no medication error, no additional acetaminophen source, no other hepatotoxic medications, and no history of shock, alcohol use, malnutrition, or viral hepatitis; serum acetaminophen-protein adducts (APAP-CYS) were elevated (1.79 µM on day 3, 4.81 µM on day 5, 2.92 µM on day 6), supporting acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity. Acetaminophen was discontinued, intravenous acetylcysteine was given, and the patient improved and was discharged.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pre-existing hepatic steatosis and possible cirrhosis documented on ultrasound performed before acetaminophen initiation; advanced age (92 years).
raw_record.extra_details: Intravenous route at 1 g every 6 hours, given hospital days 3-6 for a total of 13 g; elevated serum acetaminophen level 15.3 mcg/mL at 26 h after last dose; APAP-CYS adducts 1.79-4.81 µM (expected <1.1 µM during therapeutic dosing); no acidosis or encephalopathy; treated with intravenous acetylcysteine (standard 21-h protocol) with transaminase improvement and discharge.

raw_record.support_text: A 53-year-old woman with concurrent squamous cell carcinoma of the anus and renal cell carcinoma developed severe hepatotoxicity while receiving paracetamol at recommended dosage (4 g daily) under medical supervision in hospital, without enzyme-inducing agents. She was severely malnourished and had recently fasted. Four days after starting paracetamol her ALT rose to 269 IU/L and AST to 252 IU/L; the next day she had nausea, right upper quadrant discomfort and tender hepatomegaly, with ALT 5920 IU/L, AST 4875 IU/L, bilirubin 30 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 169 IU/L, prothrombin time 20 s (control 13 s) and blood glucose 2.3 mmol/L.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Severe malnutrition, weight loss and a recent ~20 h fasting period at therapeutic exposure; 53-year-old female hospitalized with concurrent anal squamous cell carcinoma and renal cell carcinoma.
raw_record.extra_details: Diagnosis of severe paracetamol-related hepatotoxicity based on highly typical enzyme pattern, with differential diagnosis of ischaemic liver injury excluded (no hypotension) and other medications considered unlikely; treated with N-acetylcysteine and glucose, normalizing over 4 weeks; hepatitis and other viral/metabolic/immune/her metastatic causes excluded. Authors attribute injury to glutathione depletion and shunting of metabolism from glucuronidation to microsomal oxidation producing N-acetyl-p-benzoquinonimine (NAPQI), and conclude the injury is dose-dependent rather than idiosyncratic; a later interval of lower-dose paracetamol (1.3-2.6 g daily up to three times weekly) after a further fasting period produced no liver injury. Patient was not encephalopathic and recovered.

raw_record.support_text: The project's impetus was a recent local case of iatrogenic hepatotoxicity secondary to Paracetamol reported within the trust, prompting a Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) audit cycle. The audit identified two problems with Paracetamol prescribing: patients were not always weighed in a timely fashion leading to incorrect dosing, and healthcare professionals lacked knowledge that IV Paracetamol is dose-adjusted for patients weighing less than 50 kg. Initial audit findings showed 25% of patients were on an inappropriate dose of IV Paracetamol.

raw_record.support_text: An analysis of 1100 cases reported to the Danish Committee of Drug-Induced Hepatic Injury between 1978 and 1987 confirmed that only 18 were due to paracetamol, yet damage did occur in non-alcohol-dependent patients after therapeutic doses of paracetamol. Acute cytotoxic as well as cholestatic reactions appeared after periods ranging from weeks to years, and three patients died. The number of case reports where therapeutic doses of paracetamol were implicated as the sole causative factor in hepatotoxicity is small, and if an unidentified at-risk group exists it must be very small.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Therapeutic (non-overdose) doses; non-alcohol-dependent general population; rare reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Danish Committee of Drug-Induced Hepatic Injury 1978-1987 cohort (1100 cases, 18 attributed to paracetamol). Acute cytotoxic and cholestatic reactions appeared after weeks to years; three patients died. Chronic active hepatitis described in one report; acute biliary pain with cholestasis ascribed to inhibition of prostaglandin production potentially regulating the sphincter of Oddi/biliary duct pressure. The paper notes the mechanism here likely differs from NAPBQI-related toxicity given glutathione conjugation capacity.

raw_record.support_text: A 68-year-old male with adenocarcinoma of unknown primary treated once daily with 8 mg oral gemcitabine was considered to have a toxic death. Nine days after starting the second cycle he developed fever, grade 4 liver and kidney failure with steep rises in ALT (2,424 U/L), AST (2,781 U/L), γ-GT (237 U/L) and LDH (3,360 U/L), and died 5 days later. Obduction revealed severe toxic-induced liver necrosis which was likely related to the study drug. Other possible causes (viral hepatitis B and C, liver metastasis, alcohol abuse) were excluded and an interaction with comedication (simvastatin, irbesartan/hydrochlorothiazide, oxazepam, omeprazol) was deemed unlikely.
raw_record.extra_details: Single fatal case from a phase I trial of oral gemcitabine (30 patients; dose levels 1-8 mg part A, 8-20 mg part B). Onset 9 days after start of second cycle of 8 mg daily oral gemcitabine; grade 4 liver and kidney failure; ALT 2,424 U/L, AST 2,781 U/L, γ-GT 237 U/L, LDH 3,360 U/L; treated with i.v. prednisone 1 mg/kg; died 5 days after deterioration. Autopsy showed severe toxic-induced liver necrosis. Viral hepatitis (B, C), liver metastasis, and alcohol abuse excluded; interaction with comedication judged unlikely.

raw_record.support_text: In the toxicity report of this gemcitabine study, treatment-related nonhematologic side effects included grade 1-2 transient proteinuria, grade 1 hematuria, and grade 3 liver toxicity that occurred in only one patient (Table 3). raw_record.extra_details: Single patient among the treated population developed grade 3 liver toxicity, reported as treatment-related during gemcitabine therapy. raw_record.support_text: In 30 colorectal cancer patients undergoing isolated hepatic perfusion with 200 mg melphalan via hepatic artery infusion, veno-occlusive disease (VOD) occurred in 4 patients and portal hypertension (possibly a result of VOD) in 2 others. Grade 4 biliary toxicity occurred in 5 of 30 patients and 1 patient died of progressive liver failure. Toxic hepatitis was reported as a major complication in 1 patient. The discussion attributes these liver toxicities to the melphalan perfusion exposure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Regional exposure by isolated hepatic perfusion delivered via hepatic artery infusion/perfusion in colorectal cancer patients with liver metastases; not ordinary systemic therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: 200 mg melphalan given as 20-min hepatic artery infusion followed by 40-min perfusion; peak perfusate concentration 93.2 µg/mL, AUC 2841.6 µg·min/mL. Reported liver events: toxic hepatitis in 1 patient, veno-occlusive disease in 4 patients, portal hypertension in 2, grade 4 biliary toxicity in 5 of 30 patients, and 1 death from progressive liver failure. GGT, ALAT, ASAT and bilirubin elevations were graded per NCI CTC across 30 patients. VOD was noted as possibly resulting from accumulative exposure to chemotherapeutic agents; toxicity had a steep concentration-toxicity relationship independent of total melphalan dose (supported by a rat cholangiofibrosis model).

raw_record.support_text: A case series of eleven patients with severe hepatocellular damage attributed to labetalol is reported; all received labetalol in the recommended dose range (average 285 mg/day, range 50-600 mg), median latency to event was 60 days (range 21-189 days), and 3 of 11 patients died (one after liver transplantation) while the other eight were hospitalized and recovered. The paper is presented as a case series of labetalol-induced hepatotoxicity, with careful case-by-case time evaluation excluding alternative drug exposures and viral hepatitis A and B.
raw_record.extra_details: Eleven cases; average age 56 y, 73% white, 82% women; median time to onset 60 d (21-189 d); case fatality 3/11 (27%), one after liver transplantation; 8 hospitalized and recovered. Histology showed severe hepatocellular necrosis in all five available specimens (submassive/massive in cases 1-3 with zone 2/3 tendency; zone 1 and 3 in case 4; case 5 showed chronic active hepatitis pattern with prominent pruritus and more severe cholestasis). Allergic indicators when available: maculopapular rash in 1/11 (case 10), peripheral eosinophilia 8% in 1/7 (case 4), elevated leukocytes 21000/mm3 in case 7, atypical lymphocytes 2% in case 9, elevated temperature 0/8. Case 3 had superimposed alcohol use that may have potentiated an underlying primary toxic effect of labetalol.

raw_record.support_text: The hepatitis evaluation table is titled 'Hepatitis Evaluation in a Patient With Labetalol-Associated Hepatotoxicity,' explicitly attributing the acute liver injury to labetalol. The patient developed jaundice and markedly elevated liver enzymes several months after starting labetalol, and alternative viral, autoimmune, and infectious causes were excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: 51-year-old hypertensive woman; labetalol started at 200 mg PO BID and increased to 300 mg TID. Approximately 3 months after labetalol initiation she reported yellow eyes, nausea, abdominal pain, fatigue, and dark urine. Admitted with diagnosis of acute hepatitis and hypertensive emergency: ALT 1102-4026 IU/L, AST 757-5753 IU/L, total bilirubin up to 24 mg/dL (conjugated 18 mg/dL), PT 22.3 s, INR 2.0, tender hepatomegaly (2 cm below costal margin). Viral (HAV/HBV/HCV, CMV, EBV), autoimmune (ANA, ASMA, AMA), iron/copper studies, and ultrasound unremarkable. Renal insufficiency ruled out as contributing factor. All home blood pressure medications including labetalol were stopped at readmission.

raw_record.support_text: The 11 aggregate cases are far more consistent with labetalol producing severe hepatocellular damage: normal baseline liver function before exposure, development of hepatitis after drug exposure, and marked clinical improvement after discontinuation in 9 of 11 cases (the other two had already evolved to hepatic failure). A documented recurrence after re-exposure in case 2 makes labetalol-induced hepatocellular necrosis the best explanation. The subacute time course (median time to onset ~2 months) and absence of hypersensitivity hallmarks support metabolic idiosyncrasy as the likely mechanism, although pathogenesis is not definitively resolved.
raw_record.extra_details: Eleven cases of labetalol-induced hepatotoxicity reported to the U.S. FDA Adverse Drug Reaction Reporting System, 1985-1989. Average patient age 56 y; predominantly women (9/11, 82%); estimated average daily dose 285 mg; median time to onset 60 d; case fatality rate 3/11 (27%), with 3 deaths (cases 1-3) and 8 hospitalizations (all recovered). Recurrence after re-exposure documented in case 2 (previously described by Douglas et al.). Pathogenesis ascribed to metabolic idiosyncrasy, possibly due to genetically determined cytochrome P-450 isozyme differences; eosinophils were present in two of five pathology reports but fever, eosinophilia, and rash were almost entirely absent (rash 1/11, peripheral eosinophilia 1/7, elevated temperature 0/8). Non-A, non-B hepatitis was considered and largely excluded as an alternative explanation. Laboratory values used were those obtained soonest after clinical diagnosis, expressed as multiples of the upper limit of normal.

raw_record.support_text: The FDA received 11 reports (three fatal) of hepatocellular damage associated with labetalol in the United States. Temporal circumstances strongly implicate labetalol: nine patients improved after cessation of labetalol therapy and one had a recurrence after therapy was restarted. Follow-up with each reporting physician found no historic or laboratory evidence for other viral, toxic, or drug-induced causes, and the series lacked demographic/historic risk factors expected for non-A, non-B hepatitis. Microscopic examinations (5 cases) showed changes consistent with hepatocellular necrosis in four instances and chronic active hepatitis in one. The clinical presentation was most compatible with a metabolic idiosyncrasy mechanism.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Postmarketing cases received as spontaneous reports to the FDA; other pathogenetic explanations could not be entirely excluded; one patient (case 1) also received furosemide, prazosin, and nifedipine.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 US cases, three fatal. Histology showed hepatocellular necrosis in four cases and chronic active hepatitis in one; one case (#1) showed acute massive and submassive hepatic necrosis on explant. Nine patients improved after drug cessation; one had recurrent injury after rechallenge (restart). Case 1 was a 49-year-old black woman on labetalol (stabilized at 300 mg/day) who developed jaundice after ~60 days, with marked AST/ALT elevation, alkaline phosphatase ~2x normal, total bilirubin 308 µmol/L (18.0 mg/dL); negative for hepatitis A IgM, HBsAg, and anti-HBc (anti-HBs positive); no blood transfusion or alcohol history; referred for liver transplant on 20 Dec 1986 and died 4 days post-transplant. Mechanism attributed to metabolic idiosyncrasy.

raw_record.support_text: In this study of 15 patients with MDS treated orally with 13-cis retinoic acid (13-CRA), the agent was well tolerated and all patients completed the prescribed 8-week course. Three patients had transient, reversible asymptomatic elevations of serum triglycerides >50% of baseline. The authors explicitly state that no significant hepatotoxicity or other serious toxicity was encountered.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of 15 adult patients with myelodysplastic syndrome; initial 8-week course at 2.5 mg/kg/d (patient 1 case); 13 of 15 tolerated full-dose escalation to 4 mg/kg/d. The paper's explicit conclusion: no significant hepatotoxicity or other serious toxicity was encountered. Dermatologic toxicity (cheilosis, ichthyosis/dry skin) was invariable; transient asymptomatic serum triglyceride elevations >50% of baseline occurred in 3 patients and were reversible upon drug cessation. Study context also evaluated granulocyte count responses (53% achieved >20% increase).

raw_record.support_text: The authors report two patients, women aged 53 and 65, who developed jaundice and the clinical, laboratory, and pathological picture of chronic active hepatitis after daily use of 5 to 7.5 mg of the laxative Prulets (whose sole active ingredient is oxyphenisatin) for 16 and 8 months respectively. In one patient, liver-function tests and liver biopsy returned to normal within a year of discontinuing the medication, and a rechallenge with Prulets (7.5 mg/day for four days) caused a definite rise in SGOT. In the other patient, liver function markedly improved two weeks after discontinuing Prulets.
raw_record.extra_details: Both patients were women, aged 53 and 65, taking oxyphenisatin as a laxative (Prulets) at 5–7.5 mg daily for 16 and 8 months. In one patient liver-function tests and biopsy returned to normal within a year of discontinuation, and rechallenge with Prulets 7.5 mg/day for 4 days caused a definite rise in SGOT; in the other patient liver function markedly improved two weeks after discontinuation. The patients took laxatives containing only one active ingredient, oxyphenisatin, providing additional proof that oxyphenisatin can be hepatotoxic. The authors note oxyphenisatin has been removed from some laxatives due to a recognized association with jaundice, and that hepatitis as a complication is probably rare, recommending discontinuation of sales of all such laxatives.

raw_record.support_text: Over an 18-month period, development of hepatitis after intake of oxyphenisatin, a laxative, was established in 14 patients by re-exposure (rechallenge) to the drug. Features included non-specific upper abdominal pain, loss of appetite, nausea or vomiting, and pruritus, with biochemical changes of chronic hepatitis of varying severity with biliary stasis and abnormal immunofluorescence. Histology showed acute inflammatory changes in the biliary passages on re-exposure with secondary liver-cell involvement; laparoscopy revealed stages from minor periportal hepatic fibrosis to marked postnecrotic liver scars with portal hypertension and decompensation. The hepatitis regressed completely after stopping oxyphenisatin, and laxatives containing the drug were recommended for withdrawal from the market.
raw_record.extra_details: Laxative (also termed Phenolisatin in German text); 14 female patients (14 Patientinnen) diagnosed via rechallenge (Reexposition). Cases confirmed by re-exposure led to a report citing 162 cases confirmed by Reynolds (1969) and other authors (paras 3-4), with severity ranging up to decompensated liver cirrhosis and subacute necrotizing hepatitis. Notable rise in GLDH activity on re-exposure; abnormal immunofluorescence tests; chronic-hepatitis-like biochemistry with variable cholestasis; acute inflammatory changes centered on the biliary passages with secondary hepatocyte involvement; periportal hepatic fibrosis to postnecrotic scarring with portal hypertension and decompensation at laparoscopy. Complete regression after drug withdrawal. Recommendations to withdraw oxyphenisatin-containing laxatives from the market.

raw_record.support_text: Oxyphenisatin hepatotoxicity was reported in 1970 by Reynolds et al., involving four women who, after prolonged use of the laxative Dialose Plus (containing dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate, carboxymethylcellulose and oxyphenisatin acetate), developed acute hepatocellular disease with jaundice; hepatic disease recurred on rechallenge and abated after drug withdrawal. The 1971 series by Reynolds described seven additional persons taking oxyphenisatin-containing laxatives who developed chronic active 'lupoid' hepatitis with CAH features on biopsy including cirrhosis, which improved after stopping oxyphenisatin.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed in Table 2 among drugs causing CAH; 85 reported cases, 88% female, with associated acute hepatitis. First detailed report (1949, Munthe Fog); 1970 report of 4 women with acute hepatocellular disease with jaundice after Dialose Plus (oxyphenisatin acetate plus dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate and carboxymethylcellulose), recurrence on deliberate/inadvertent rechallenge, improvement after withdrawal. 1971 series of 7 persons (6 established oxyphenisatin, 6 female, laxative use ≥1 year): moderate-to-marked aminotransferase increases, minimal hyperphosphatasemia, hypoalbuminemia, hyperglobulinemia, hyperbilirubinemia in 5/7, positive LE cell test in 2-3 of 5, positive ANA in 2 of 4, SMA in 3 of 5; biopsies showed CAH of varying severity including cirrhosis; all but one improved after discontinuation with loss of LE cells and lessening of biopsy abnormalities. Authors suggested female preponderance reflected greater laxative use by women. Causality originally assigned to oxyphenisatin because the other ingredients were considered minimally absorbed, subsequently supported by reports of oxyphenisatin-alone hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Of 21 cases of active chronic hepatitis (ACH), the disease in 9 was associated with the ingestion of laxatives containing oxyphenisatin. Eight patients took 'Agarolets' containing 10 mg oxyphenisatin plus 25 mg dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate, and one took 'Bekunis Dragees' containing 14 mg oxyphenisatin only, with 1-2 tablets taken daily for 12 months to 4 years before symptoms developed (mean interval 31 months).
raw_record.extra_details: 9 cases of active chronic hepatitis attributed to oxyphenisatin-containing laxative use, all female, mean age 54±3.7 years. Eight patients took 'Agarolets' (10 mg oxyphenisatin + 25 mg dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate) and one took 'Bekunis Dragees' (14 mg oxyphenisatin only); 1-2 tablets/day for 12 months to 4 years, mean symptom latency 31 months. Patients were also on other non-recognized-hepatotoxic drugs (no more than 2 patients on any one). Presenting features included jaundice (9/9), ascites (2), hepatomegaly (7), splenomegaly (6), spider nevi (5); this group had more severe disease (higher jaundice, ascites, splenomegaly) than methyldopa and unknown-etiology groups, though not statistically significant (P>0.05). The oxyphenisatin group had significantly higher bilirubin and SGOT and lower albumin than the ACHUE group.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that in chronic active toxic hepatitis, removal of the offending drug halts progression of liver disease, and this has been true in all of the instances of oxyphenisatin-induced chronic liver disease followed by the author's Liver Unit (about 20 patients). This attributes chronic active toxic hepatitis/chronic liver disease in humans to oxyphenisatin exposure during daily use.
raw_record.extra_details: Descripted as chronic active toxic hepatitis / chronic liver disease in about 20 patients followed by the author's Liver Unit; in the first recognized patient the disease failed to respond to prednisone and azathioprine over three years of daily oxyphenisatin ingestion, with positive nuclear antibody and lupus erythematosus cell test. Removal of the offending drug halted progression of the liver disease.

raw_record.support_text: The discussion reports that in Cases 1 and 2 the liver disease seems definitely to have been due to oxyphenisatin, in Cases 3-6 circumstantial evidence highly favors a relation, and in Case 7 there is only a strong suspicion. Six of seven patients had an illness lasting longer than three months, with depressed serum albumin and mildly increased globulin in five of seven, and all patients except Case 3 achieved complete clinical and biochemical recovery within a few months of discontinuing the oxyphenisatin-containing laxative, with marked histologic improvement on repeat biopsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven-patient case series of chronic liver disease attributed to a chronic oxyphenisatin-containing laxative; initial biopsies interpreted as chronic active hepatitis with cirrhosis. Causal grades varied by case: definite for Cases 1-2, highly favored for Cases 3-6, strong suspicion only for Case 7. Illness exceeded three months in six of seven; serum albumin below 3.0 g/100 ml with mildly increased globulin in five of seven; moderate portal hypertension with elevated wedged hepatic-vein pressure in the two measured. Six of seven recovered clinically and biochemically within months of stopping the laxative; histologic improvement noted in Cases 1 and 7 after several years.

raw_record.support_text: Oxyphenisatin has been reported as the cause of hepatic injury in more than 100 described patients, mostly female. In about one-third the injury resembled acute hepatitis with diffuse hepatocellular necrosis, acidophilic bodies, lobular disarray, Kupffer cell prominence and portal inflammation; the other two-thirds had histologic changes of chronic active hepatitis, many with features of cirrhosis, and a few showed subacute hepatic necrosis. Withdrawal usually produced rapid improvement, while readministration of oxyphenisatin to several patients led to return or increase of abnormal values.
raw_record.extra_details: More than 100 patients with hepatic injury attributable to the drug; a few showed subacute hepatic necrosis; prognosis good with withdrawal, most patients showing rapid improvement and complete or near-complete resolution of biochemical abnormalities; readministration (rechallenge) in several patients led to return or increase of abnormal laboratory values; affected patients were predominantly female, though the paper notes the data do not permit distinguishing disproportionate female susceptibility from greater exposure.

raw_record.support_text: The letter reports two women, aged 53 and 65, in whom jaundice with the clinical, laboratory, and pathological picture of chronic active hepatitis developed after daily use of 5 to 7.5 mg of the laxative Prulets for 16 and eight months. In one, liver-function tests and biopsy returned to normal within a year of stopping the drug, and a challenge with Prulets (7.5 mg/day for four days) caused a definite rise in SGOT; in the other, liver function markedly improved two weeks after discontinuation. The accompanying paragraph states that these patients were taking laxatives with only one active ingredient, oxyphenisatin, providing additional proof that oxyphenisatin can be hepatotoxic.
raw_record.extra_details: Laxative ingredient given as Prulets, 5-7.5 mg/day for 8-16 months. Both patients were women, ages 53 and 65. Jaundice and chronic active hepatitis clinical, laboratory, and pathological picture. In one patient liver-function tests and biopsy returned to normal within a year of discontinuation, and rechallenge with 7.5 mg/day for four days caused a definite rise in SGOT (AST); the other improved markedly two weeks after stopping. Laxative contained oxyphenisatin as the only active ingredient.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 14 female patients with laxative-induced hepatitis (Laxantien-Hepatitis) over the last 18 months, in which the diagnosis was secured by re-exposure (durch Reexposition gesichert) to the incriminated laxative. The hepatic damage is attributed to phenolisatin (phenolisatin-bedingter Leberschaden), framed as continuing phenolisatin-induced hepatitis cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 14 female patients over 18 months; diagnosis confirmed by re-exposure; serum monitoring of GLDH, GOT, GPT and bilirubin; one or more liver biopsies in all cases. Note: section heading on p:8 refers to 'Oxyphenisatin-induced liver disease'.

raw_record.support_text: The laxative (phenolisatin) hepatitis, which runs under the mask of various liver and biliary diseases, is only reliably unmasked by the rechallenge test with phenolisatin. Glutamate dehydrogenase (GLDH) proved a particularly sensitive parameter, and transaminases (GOT, GPT) generally supported the proof by clear activity increases; bilirubin elevation was not obligatory. The paper reports 14 female patients with phenolisatin-induced liver diseases, whose histologic findings ranged from periportal liver fibrosis to advanced postnecrotic liver cirrhosis and scarring liver, with chronic-active hepatitis among the diagnostic forms.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All 14 reported cases were female; onset followed chronic long-term oral laxative use of 2 to 20 years; re-exposure (rechallenge) confirmed the diagnosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Rechallenge with 2 x 10 mg triacetyl-diphenolisatin on two consecutive days produced rises in GLDH (particularly sensitive), GOT and GPT; bilirubin elevation was not obligatory. Histologic spectrum included chronic-aggressive hepatitis (with transition to cirrhosis), acute recurrent and protracted hepatitis, chronic-persistent hepatitis, periportal liver fibrosis, postnecrotic scarring liver/cirrhosis, and one case of chronic-aggressive hepatitis with cholestasis (Fall 10, allegedly on oxyphenisatin-free laxatives). In six of ten examined cases low-titer antibodies against nuclei and smooth muscle were found by immunofluorescence; five of 14 were treated with immunosuppressives and/or glucocorticoids before the final diagnosis. Symptoms resembled acute/chronic liver or gallbladder disease. Before publication all 14 patients were fully investigated in hospital with entirely normal laboratory findings and histologically inactive stage. Reported hospitalizations and estimated total costs (e.g., 150,000 DM in Fall 1); some cases were reported as infectious disease or recognized as occupational disease, and some underwent cholecystectomy.

During stage 2 of the phase 2 trial, three adverse events (chills, muscle rigidity, and hepatotoxicity) were judged to be related to otaplimastat, indicating that a hepatotoxicity adverse event was attributed to intravenous otaplimastat when given as adjunctive therapy to stroke patients receiving rtPA.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity was one of three adverse events judged related to otaplimastat (the others being chills and muscle rigidity) in a phase 2, 2-part multicenter trial. Stage 2 randomized 69 patients (1:1:1) to otaplimastat 40 mg, 80 mg, or placebo; SAEs were 13%, 17%, 14% and deaths were 8.3%, 4.2%, 4.8% across the three groups, respectively; parenchymal hematoma occurred in 0/22, 0/22, and 1/21. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT02787278.

raw_record.support_text: A patient on bupropion SR presented six months after starting the drug with markedly elevated serum aminotransferases and bilirubin, showing a severe acute hepatocellular injury with autoimmune features. Enrolled in the DILIN prospective protocol with all other competing causes of liver injury excluded, the case scored 8 on RUCAM, categorized as a 'highly probable' case of DILI, and also scored 'probable' on a drug-induced hepatitis validation scale. The authors concluded the patient presumably developed fulminant hepatitis with autoimmune features due to bupropion given the temporal course, exclusion of competing etiologies, and compatible histology.
raw_record.extra_details: Index case: bupropion SR 150 mg BID for 180 days, peak ALT 20x ULN, peak bilirubin 37 mg/dl, positive ANA, liver biopsy showing acute hepatocellular injury with autoimmune features; progressed to fulminant liver failure and death with disseminated aspergillosis despite cessation and corticosteroids. RUCAM score 8 (highly probable DILI); scored probable on a drug-induced hepatitis validation scale and probable autoimmune hepatitis on the International autoimmune hepatitis consensus scale. Table 1 lists prior published cases of bupropion hepatotoxicity (Oslin '93: 300-400 mg QD, 54 days, ALT 5.4x ULN, resolution; Hu '00: 200 mg QD, 42 days, ALT 6660 IU/L, bilirubin 3.8, resolution; D. Alvaro '01: 150 mg BID, 20 days, ALT 49x ULN, bilirubin 38, resolution; Humayun '07: 150 mg BID, 180 days, ALT 20x ULN, bilirubin 37, death), all occurring within the first 6 months of use with a hepatocellular injury pattern; this is described as the first reported fatal bupropion hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Bupropion is approved for mood disorders and smoking cessation. It was reported that acute cholestatic hepatitis was induced by bupropion when a 49-year-old female took it to stop smoking; after 20 days she presented a dramatic increase in direct bilirubin (up to 28 mg/dl) and transaminases (up to 68-fold normal). In a case of a 55-year-old man with jaundice and severe hepatic injury about 6 months after starting bupropion for smoking termination, laboratory evaluations confirmed a mixed hepatocellular injury and cholestasis picture, and the patient eventually died. Other controversial studies on bupropion for smoking cessation reported no adverse hepatic events.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Cases were adults using bupropion for smoking cessation (therapeutic use).
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1: 49-year-old female, acute cholestatic hepatitis after 20 days, direct bilirubin up to 28 mg/dl, transaminases up to 68-fold normal. Case 2: 55-year-old man, jaundice and severe hepatic injury about 6 months after start, mixed hepatocellular injury and cholestasis, eventually died. Other 7- and 9-week smoking-cessation studies reported no adverse hepatic events.

raw_record.support_text: The major finding is the high prevalence of moderate to severe sinusoidal lesions (54%) in patients receiving OX-based chemotherapy. Among OX recipients (n=204), sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS) lesions occurred in 77.4% (grade 1: 15.2%, grade 2-3: 62.2%), peliosis was present in 14.6%, nodular transformation in 63.7% (grade 3 NRH 28.9%), and centrilobular/venular fibrosis in 52%, versus essentially none in the no-chemotherapy group (n=111). The study states that toxic liver injury to sinusoidal endothelial cells may manifest as sinusoidal dilation, SOS, perisinusoidal and venular fibrosis, NRH, or peliosis in increasing order of severity.
raw_record.extra_details: Patients received OX-based chemotherapy (colorectal cancer setting) across four centres with similar regimens. OX-related damage spectrum: sinusoidal dilation, sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS)/veno-occlusive disease, centrilobular perisinusoidal and venular fibrosis, nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH), and peliosis, attributed to selective toxicity for sinusoidal endothelial cells over hepatocytes. Prevalence in OX group: SOS 77.4% (grade 1: 15.2%, grade 2-3: 62.2%), peliosis 14.6%, nodular transformation 63.7% (NRH 28.9%), centrilobular/venular fibrosis 52%. SOS also noted not OX-specific, associated with several other drugs at conventional doses.

raw_record.support_text: The paper utilized a previously recruited cohort of 79 DILI patients assessed by the updated RUCAM who were treated with 31 different drugs. Oxaliplatin was classified among drugs that consistently led to the same DILI phenotype in all patients exposed.
raw_record.extra_details: Among a cohort of 79 DILI patients assessed by updated RUCAM, treated with 31 drugs; classified in the first drug category that consistently led to the same DILI phenotype in all exposed patients.

raw_record.support_text: Among 60 long-latency DILI cases (>365 days) in the DILIN study, oxaliplatin (n=2) was among the most commonly implicated agents.
raw_record.extra_details: Long-latency DILI (>365 days); n=2 cases in the DILIN Prospective Study cohort.

raw_record.support_text: The paper notes it is well known that oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy may cause liver injury, such as sinusoidal obstructive syndrome (SOS), and reports a case of oxaliplatin-related SOS mimicking a metastatic liver tumor. The patient had received oxaliplatin plus capecitabine (XELOX) as eight cycles of postoperative adjuvant chemotherapy (oxaliplatin 130 mg/m² per day, 2-h i.v., day 1, every 21 days).
raw_record.extra_details: 40-year-old woman after curative low anterior resection for advanced rectal cancer; received XELOX (oxaliplatin 130 mg/m²/day, 2-h i.v. infusion day 1 plus capecitabine 1000 mg/m²/day twice daily days 1-14, 21-day cycle) for 8 cycles as postoperative adjuvant chemotherapy. Focal sinusoidal obstruction syndrome presented as three hypovascular space-occupying lesions (3.0, 1.5, 1.0 cm) in the right hepatic lobe mimicking metastases; right hepatic lobectomy performed. Histology: peliosis hepatis with sinusoidal dilation, severe congestion outlined by atrophic hepatocyte trabeculae, and dilated space of Disse containing erythrocytes. Splenomegaly observed. Liver tests were within normal limits (AST 34 IU/L, ALT 22 IU/L, ALP 45 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL); reported as first case of focal SOS mimicking metastatic liver tumors.

raw_record.support_text: Nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH) was identified in 20/100 patients (20%) in this prospective series, was significantly more frequent after preoperative chemotherapy (p=0.001), and a correlation was found between Folfox (Oxaliplatin) administration and NRH lesions (p=0.03). The authors state that Oxaliplatin, part of the Folfox regimen, is the chemotherapy mostly incriminated in the development of NRH.
raw_record.extra_details: NRH identified in 20% of resected specimens versus 3% (5/151) in the 2013 series (p<0.001); moderate/severe (grade 2/3) NRH in 12/100; NRH correlated with Folfox/Oxaliplatin administration (p=0.03); strong correlation between NRH and SOS lesions (p<0.001), with grade 2/3 NRH associated with SOS in 9/12 patients; NRH significantly correlated with severe complications (p=0.005, RR=3.31) and postoperative liver failure (p<0.01); one patient with NRH grade 3 (and SOS grade 2) died postoperatively after 9 cycles Folfox without Bevacizumab. NRH detection likely increased by routine reticulin staining.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that Gd-EOB-DTPA-enhanced MRI findings revealed the clinical features of oxaliplatin-induced sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS), proposing the imaging as a biomarker for diagnosing oxaliplatin-induced SOS at an early stage. SOS, previously called hepatic veno-occlusive disease (VOD), is a chemotherapy-induced liver injury whose primary damage occurs in centrilobular (zone 3) sinusoidal endothelial cells.
raw_record.extra_details: SOS, previously called hepatic veno-occlusive disease (VOD), is a chemotherapy-induced liver injury with primary damage to centrilobular (zone 3) sinusoidal endothelial cells. In the retrospective study of oxaliplatin-treated patients, non-tumorous hepatic parenchymal heterogeneity was graded in 57 patients: 21 grade 0, 24 grade 1, seven grade 2, five grade 3; hepatic distribution was diffuse in four (7.0%), peripheral in ten (17.5%), and multifocal in 22 (38.6%). Hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, gallbladder wall thickening, and narrowing of the hepatic vein correlated with heterogeneity grade. Elevated AST, elevated ALT, high AST-to-platelet ratio index, and low platelet count were significantly associated with a high grade (≥2). SOS increases the risk of major hepatectomy and perioperative bleeding. Reticular hypointensity at HBP on Gd-EOB-DTPA-enhanced MRI was proposed as a highly specific indicator of SOS diagnosis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that oxaliplatin's main liver injury consists of sinusoidal dilatation, associated with biliary complications up to liver failure and nodular regenerative hyperplasia. A series of 274 metastatic colorectal cancer patients treated with oxaliplatin-based regimens (Rubbia-Brandt et al.) reported moderate/severe sinusoidal obstruction syndrome in 54%, peliosis in 10.6%, centrilobular perisinusoidal/venular fibrosis in 47%, and nodular regenerative hyperplasia in 24.5%.
raw_record.extra_details: Injury comprises sinusoidal dilatation, biliary complications (up to liver failure) and nodular regenerative hyperplasia [12,13]. In 274 metastatic colorectal cancer patients on oxaliplatin-based regimens (Rubbia-Brandt et al.), moderate/severe sinusoidal obstruction syndrome 54%, peliosis 10.6%, centrilobular perisinusoidal/venular fibrosis 47%, nodular regenerative hyperplasia 24.5%. Hepatic morphologic lesions were less severe with bevacizumab+oxaliplatin vs oxaliplatin alone: moderate/severe sinusoidal obstruction syndrome 31.4% vs 62.2%, peliosis 4.3% vs 14.6%, nodular regenerative hyperplasia 11.4% vs 28.9%, centrilobular/venular fibrosis 31.4% vs 52% [14].

raw_record.support_text: Four patients with metastatic colon cancer receiving oxaliplatin, 5-fluorouracil and elvorin developed a progressive increase in gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase and alkaline phosphatase despite tumour regression. Liver biopsies showed sinusoidal dilatation in all cases, with perisinusoidal fibrosis and centrilobular vein lesions in 3, peliosis in 1 (a patient receiving oxaliplatin by intraarterial hepatic route), and nodular regenerative hyperplasia in 1. The patient with peliosis developed ascites and died from hepatic failure despite drug withdrawal. The patient with nodular regenerative hyperplasia developed jaundice, ascites and severe infection after a right hepatectomy. In the three surviving patients liver function tests improved after oxaliplatin withdrawal, and in one deteriorated again after reintroduction of the drug.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All four patients received combination chemotherapy with oxaliplatin together with 5-fluorouracil and elvorin (leucovorin); one patient received oxaliplatin by intraarterial hepatic route. All patients had metastatic colon cancer.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented as a case series of 4 cases described as 'oxaliplatin-imputable sinusoidal lesions'. Histology: sinusoidal dilatation (all), perisinusoidal fibrosis and centrilobular vein lesions (3), peliosis (1), nodular regenerative hyperplasia (1). Laboratory hallmark was elevated gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase and alkaline phosphatase. One patient died from hepatic failure with ascites; one developed jaundice, ascites and severe infection following right hepatectomy. Dechallenge improved liver tests in all three survivors; rechallenge with oxaliplatin led to deterioration in one. Paper concludes the prevalence of oxaliplatin-induced liver sinusoidal lesions is probably underestimated and recommends GGT and ALP monitoring, especially in adjuvant therapy.
