raw_record.support_text: The paper states that bicyclol can prevent the progression of liver injury caused by anticancer drugs, naming oxaliplatin among them, in cancer patients. It describes a 9-day bicyclol treatment that normalized elevated serum ALT and AST in 58 gastric cancer patients after anticancer treatment with oxaliplatin plus capecitabine had been stopped, and a follow-up 14-day retreatment in which ALT and AST were lower in the bicyclol/oxaliplatin/capecitabine arm than in the oxaliplatin/capecitabine arm (P<0.05).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Cancer (gastric) patients receiving anticancer therapy; oxaliplatin was part of an oxaliplatin plus capecitabine combination in the reported trial.
raw_record.extra_details: Elevated serum ALT and AST after anticancer treatment; bicyclol normalized these and lowered them upon rechallenge with chemotherapy. Reported in the context of bicyclol preventive/hepatic-supportive efficacy.

raw_record.support_text: The study's objective was to evaluate oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy (OBC)-induced hepatic parenchymal heterogeneity detected on contrast-enhanced CT and its influence on liver metastasis response, based on the assumption that such heterogeneity may indicate the presence of chemotherapy-induced sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Colorectal cancer patients with hepatic metastases receiving oxaliplatin-based combination chemotherapy as treatment; SOS presence was inferred from CT hepatic parenchymal heterogeneity rather than confirmed histologically.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective study of 104 patients with hepatic metastases from colorectal cancer (male:female 66:38, age 20-80) treated with OBC and serial CT. Hepatic parenchymal heterogeneity scored on a 5-point scale (interobserver kappa=0.825). Conclusion: post-OBC hepatic parenchymal heterogeneity may indicate the presence of SOS, and more severe SOS predicts worse hepatic metastasis tumor response to oxaliplatin. Suggestion that oxaliplatin-based therapy induces sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (vascular liver injury).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that oxaliplatin has been found to induce hepatic sinusoidal injury (HSI), defined as disruption of the sinusoidal endothelium and collagen deposition in the perisinusoidal space, which may result in portal hypertension, splenomegaly and finally thrombocytopenia.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy for colorectal liver metastases (17 surgically treated patients, mean age 64.3 years, range 48-78); co-administered regimen agents not individually specified.
raw_record.extra_details: SOS described as a fatal hepatic injury occurring after drug/toxin exposure, with abdominal pain, hepatosplenomegaly, portal hypertension, liver enzyme elevations and jaundice. In the cohort, splenic index rose from 25.6±10.4 to 29.6±11.2 cm2 after NAC (P<0.01), platelet counts were lower in the NAC group (16.9±5.5 vs 22.7±8.8 x10^4, P<0.05), and CD42b platelet staining correlated with SOS severity, especially zone III (P=0.009), with hepatocyte destruction in severe cases.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective cohort of patients treated with oxaliplatin at 10 hospitals, the updated Roussel Uclaf causality assessment method (RUCAM) was used to identify cases of oxaliplatin-induced liver injury (OILI). The incidence of OILI was 3.65% with a median RUCAM score of 6 (IQR 4, 9), and ANN and LR models were developed to predict OILI risk.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients receiving oxaliplatin-based combination chemotherapy for cancer; other chemotherapy drugs in the oxaliplatin-based regimen may have different degrees of impact on OILI, leaving co-exposure influence unresolved.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective cohort from 10 hospitals, May to November 2016; incidence of OILI 3.65%; median RUCAM score 6 (IQR 4, 9); RUCAM-based case identification. Predictors of OILI risk included age, chemotherapy regimen and cycles, single and total OXA dose, glucocorticoid drugs, and antihistamine drugs. The paper states the chemotherapy dose factors may be weakly correlated with OILI.

raw_record.support_text: The paper analyzes gene perturbations in drug-induced sinusoidal dilatation (SD) and reports up-regulation of IL16 and CCL2 in CRLM (colorectal cancer liver metastasis) patients with oxaliplatin-induced SD, and a trend towards CCL2 up-regulation (FDR<0.25), citing prior work showing CCL2 up-regulation in CRLM patients with oxaliplatin-induced SD. It frames oxaliplatin as a cause of drug-induced sinusoidal dilatation that may progress to sinusoidal obstruction syndrome/veno-occlusive disease (SOS/VOD).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with colorectal cancer liver metastases (CRLM) receiving oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy; co-treatment with bevacizumab was associated with amelioration (protective effect) of oxaliplatin-induced SD.
raw_record.extra_details: Oxaliplatin causes sinusoidal dilatation (SD) with LSEC dysfunction, ECM remodeling, inflammation and LSEC injury that may progress to SOS/VOD. Associated gene perturbations include up-regulation of IL16, CCL2, TGFB1 (NHP), ERG, CDH5, vWF, MMP2/MMP9 and loss of vascular homeostasis markers (ICAM1, CCND1). Assessment of hepatic lesions attributed to oxaliplatin-induced hepatotoxicity also cited from Rubbia-Brandt et al. and amelioration of SD attributed to bevacizumab from van der Pool et al.; evidence based on a cross-sectional cohort of 65 clinical cases collected 2009-2012.

raw_record.support_text: Oxaliplatin-related sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS) was identified in patients who had received preoperative oxaliplatin for colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) but developed toxic liver injury, compared with controls having histologically normal livers (patients treated with oxaliplatin who did not develop SOS, and patients treated by surgery alone). 913 genes were found differentially expressed in oxaliplatin-related SOS.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with colorectal liver metastases receiving preoperative oxaliplatin as systemic chemotherapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Oxaliplatin-related sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS) considered toxic liver injury; 20 SOS cases compared with 20 oxaliplatin-treated livers without SOS and 10 histologically normal livers. 913 genes differentially expressed; key implicated pathways included acute phase response signaling, coagulation system, hepatic fibrosis/hepatic stellate cell activation, and oxidative stress. CCL20 showed the highest mRNA upregulation, expressed in macrophages (hypoxia-inducible), and upregulation of HIF1 indicated hypoxia; IL-6/STAT (STAT1, STAT2, STAT3) pathways were implicated, with STAT1 contributing to liver inflammation/injury.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 104 patients with colorectal liver metastases who underwent liver resection after neoadjuvant oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy, histopathologic evaluation found sinusoidal dilatation in 59 patients (57%) of the total study group. This finding is presented as chemotherapy-associated liver injury, and the study examined whether adding bevacizumab modified the degree of oxaliplatin-associated sinusoidal dilatation; moderate sinusoidal dilatation was present in 15/51 bevacizumab-treated patients (28%) versus 4/53 in the non-bevacizumab group (8%, P=0.01).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with colorectal liver metastases undergoing hepatic resection after neoadjuvant oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy; histologic assessment of sinusoidal dilatation by two pathologists with substantial inter-observer agreement (kappa 0.77).
raw_record.extra_details: Chemotherapy-associated liver injury; sinusoidal dilatation present in 57% (59/104) overall and not associated with postoperative complications (31% vs 27%, P=0.83). Moderate sinusoidal dilatation 28% in bevacizumab group vs 8% in non-bevacizumab group (P=0.01); severe dilatation in 1 bevacizumab patient vs 0 non-bevacizumab (P=0.45). No significant inter-group differences in perivenular fibrosis, portal inflammation, nodular regenerative hyperplasia, ballooning, lobular inflammation, or steatosis. Findings independent of number of chemotherapy cycles (>=6 vs <6) and of time interval from last dose to resection (<=5 vs >5 weeks).

raw_record.support_text: In a patient who became jaundiced and febrile during malaria chemoprophylaxis, chloroguanide (proguanil) was stopped; a toxic reaction to chloroguanide was considered the most likely cause of the clinical presentation. Because liver enzymes and bilirubin remained elevated, a liver biopsy was performed 3 weeks after admission and showed hepatitis with periportal infiltrates consisting mainly of lymphocytes and eosinophils, indicative of drug-induced hepatitis. Other causes (hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV, leptospirosis, malaria, Salmonella, parasites) were excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient presenting with fever to 39.0 °C, chills, vomiting, mild abdominal cramp, anorexia and jaundice (total bilirubin 4.4 mg/dL, conjugated 3.1 mg/dL; ALT 58 rising to 183 U/L, AST 33 to 45 U/L, GGT 96 U/L, ALP 158 U/L). Differential diagnosis initially considered either a toxic reaction to chloroguanide or a bile-duct infection (e.g., Salmonella); infection was excluded by negative blood/stool cultures, parasite examination, and serology (hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV, leptospirosis, malaria). Chloroguanide was stopped and ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily given for 6 days; patient became afebrile within 3 days, bilirubin normalized after 2 months and aminotransferases after 4 months. Liver biopsy (3 weeks after admission) showed hepatitis with periportal lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltrates indicative of drug-induced hepatitis. Reported as an adverse effect not previously described. Systemic involvement (fever, chills, eosinophilic infiltrate) fits the idiosyncratic pattern discussed in the paper. Patient had a history of hepatitis in 1980 probably due to ketoconazole and consumed 2-4 glasses of beer/wine weekly.

raw_record.support_text: A case report describes omeprazole-induced hepatotoxicity: omeprazole was the only new medication in the patient, and the temporal association between omeprazole therapy and the clinical symptoms and laboratory alterations, together with a positive response to rechallenge, strongly suggests a cause-and-effect relation. On therapy discontinuation liver function returned to normal within 4 weeks, but rechallenge produced acute liver injury (aspartate aminotransferase 954 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 762 U/L). The mechanism is stated to be probably idiosyncratic because an allergic or direct toxic reaction is unlikely.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver injury on rechallenge with aspartate aminotransferase 954 U/L and alanine aminotransferase 762 U/L; liver function returned to normal within 4 weeks of first discontinuation and gradually after stopping rechallenge. Omeprazole was the only new medication; hepatitis serologic testing and immunologic studies were normal. Positive dechallenge and rechallenge responses support causality; mechanism judged probably idiosyncratic.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of recurrent severe acute hepatitis induced by omeprazole. A 30-year-old man with advanced renal failure secondary to diabetic nephropathy, on ranitidine, calcium carbonate, furosemide, and nifedipine, was started on omeprazole 20 mg once daily for erosive gastritis and duodenal ulcer after ranitidine was stopped; nine days later he developed acute liver injury (AST 1788 U/L, ALT 1294 U/L) with hepatomegaly, which resolved within four weeks of discontinuing omeprazole. Six months later, rechallenge with omeprazole produced acute liver injury again (AST 954 U/L, ALT 762 U/L) within one week, which resolved after stopping the drug. Hepatitis and immunologic serologies were negative, supporting omeprazole as the cause of the recurrent hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of recurrent severe acute hepatitis induced by omeprazole in a 30-year-old man with advanced renal failure who was prescribed omeprazole 20 mg once daily. Nine days after starting therapy he developed acute liver injury (AST 1788 U/L, ALT 1294 U/L) with hepatomegaly; after omeprazole was stopped, liver function tests returned to normal within 4 weeks. On rechallenge six months later, acute liver injury recurred (AST 954 U/L, ALT 762 U/L) and again resolved on discontinuation. Viral and immunologic studies were negative, and the authors state the time association, dechallenge/rechallenge response, and omeprazole being the only new medication strongly suggest a cause-and-effect relation, with an idiosyncratic mechanism considered probable.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had advanced renal failure secondary to diabetic nephropathy and had taken ranitidine, calcium carbonate, furosemide, and nifedipine for the previous 4 months; omeprazole was the only new medication. Viral and immunologic etiologies were excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 20 mg once daily; first-onset latency 9 days, rechallenge onset at 1 week; dechallenge led to normalization of liver function within 4 weeks in both episodes; positive rechallenge; prothrombin time normal; negative serology for hepatitis A, B, C, Epstein-Barr, herpes simplex, and cytomegalovirus; normal immunoglobulins, rheumatoid factor, complement (C3 and C4), antinuclear/antineutrophilic/antimitochondrial/anti-smooth-muscle antibodies, ferritin, ceruloplasmin, and alpha-1-antitrypsin. Mechanism believed idiosyncratic because allergic or direct toxic reaction was considered unlikely.

raw_record.support_text: Sudoxicam, an NSAID from the early 1970s, had clinical trials discontinued due to multiple deaths related to hepatotoxicity, so it was never approved for marketing. Studies later implicated thiazole bioactivation as the source of reactive metabolites capable of initiating toxic responses arising from sudoxicam exposure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Clinical trial development setting; the drug was never approved for marketing.
raw_record.extra_details: Multiple deaths related to hepatotoxicity led to discontinuation of clinical trials in the early 1970s; thiazole bioactivation (C4-C5 epoxidation yielding a thioamide protoxin) implicated as source of reactive metabolites initiating the toxic response; structural analog of meloxicam differing only by a methyl group at the C5 position; bioactivation catalyzed by CYP2C8, 2C19, and 3A4, with CYP2C8 dominating.

raw_record.extra_details: Case report of cholestatic liver injury in an adult male. On admission total bilirubin 18.4 mg/dL (peak 26.4 mg/dL at 7 days), direct bilirubin 10.0 mg/dL, ALP 574 U/L, GGT 480 IU/L, ALT 75 U/L, AST 68 U/L. Liver biopsy on day 10 showed intrahepatic cholestasis with portal ductular proliferation and parenchymal cholestasis; normal hepatic parenchyma on ultrasound and MRCP, patent hepatic veins. Scleral icterus and pruritus present; ANA/ASMA/AMA/anti-LKM1, hepatitis A-E, EBV, CMV, HSV, and biliary obstruction excluded. Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability score 7 (probable). Dechallenge with improvement; treated with prednisolone 60 mg/d tapered over 3 months, UDCA, and cholestyramine; jaundice and pruritus resolved within 6 months. NSAIDs account for roughly 10% of total drug-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that the responsibility of erythromycin propionate in causing the hepatic lesions in their two patients can reasonably be established, based on the absence of hepatobiliary history and of other drug intake, normal abdominal ultrasound, negative viral hepatitis markers, and the close parallelism between the clinical and biological signs and the drug intake, its withdrawal, and above all its reintroduction in the first observation.

raw_record.support_text: A 76-year-old man developed fatigue, vomiting and icterus with markedly elevated aminotransferases, bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase while taking montelukast (Singulair) 10 mg/day for 2 years. Singulair and Permixon were stopped, the patient improved, and laboratory values normalized. A lymphocyte transformation test was positive for Singulair (stimulation index 3.6) but negative for Permixon and zafirlukast; liver biopsy showed lymphohistiocytic portal infiltration, piecemeal necrosis and lobular hepatitis. The authors conclude that dechallenge improvement, the positive LTT, histological findings and exclusion of other causes suggest a montelukast-induced acute hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: 76-year-old man; Singulair 10 mg/day for 2 years (long latency); present with fatigue, vomiting, icterus; aspartate aminotransferase 2205 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 2450 U/L (60-fold), total bilirubin 306 µmol/L (18-fold), alkaline phosphatase 446 U/L (2-fold); co-medications included Seretide (salmeterol/fluticasone), Permixon (serenoa repens) and aspirin; both Singulair and Permixon stopped; recovered with normalized values; positive LTT for Singulair with stimulation index 3.6, negative for Permixon and Accolate; liver biopsy showed dense lymphohistiocytic portal infiltration with eosinophils, piecemeal necrosis, ballooned hepatocytes, lobular hepatitis; negative autoantibodies and viral serology; authors propose an immune-mediated mechanism and metabolic idiosyncrasy possibly involving CYP3A4/2C9 metabolism.

raw_record.support_text: A 55-year-old asthmatic woman who had been treated with montelukast 10 mg/day for 4 months presented with pruritus, jaundice, and right hypochondrium pain. Liver tests showed AST 1341 U/l, ALT 1695 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 438 U/l, GGT 166 U/l, and bilirubin 6.5 mg/dl; viral, parasitic, and autoimmune serologies were all negative, and the biliary tree was not dilated. One month after montelukast withdrawal, liver function parameters returned to normal.
raw_record.extra_details: The authors concluded the liver injury 'probablemente' (probably) resulted from montelukast, based on temporal relationship, resolution after dechallenge, and exclusion of other causes of acute hepatitis. Co-administrated omeprazole (20 mg/day) was ruled out as no hepatotoxic effect because liver biochemistry normalized while omeprazole was continued. A post-marketing study of more than 3,000 montelukast patients showed no hepatotoxic effect, suggesting very low incidence. The authors hypothesized an idiosyncratic mechanism, noting montelukast undergoes methylhydroxylation by CYP2C9 and sulfoxidation by CYP3A4 and intermediate metabolites could cause the hepatic damage, accounting for the absence of immunoallergy findings in this case.

Attribution supported by no other causes, normal pre-treatment liver function tests, and normal follow-up liver ultrasonography.

raw_record.support_text: A 37-year-old woman with normal baseline liver function developed jaundice, severe pruritus, and nausea after 3 weeks of montelukast therapy (started after theophylline was stopped). Total bilirubin was 181.3 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 231 IU/L, AST 123 IU/L, ALT 174 IU/L, and GGT 224 IU/L; results for hepatitis A/B/C serology and other tests were negative, with no alcohol or drug use reported. Montelukast was stopped and jaundice and pruritus resolved, with bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and GGT normalizing over 5 months. A liver biopsy at 14 months showed mild chronic portal inflammation without lobular inflammation or fibrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as the first drug-induced hepatitis case attributed to montelukast. Onset after 3 weeks of therapy; dechallenge led to resolution. Labs: total bilirubin 181.3 µmol/L (direct 114, indirect 66.7), ALP 231 IU/L, AST 123 IU/L, ALT 174 IU/L, GGT 224 IU/L; eosinophilia 8%. Liver biopsy (14 months) showed mild chronic portal inflammation without lobular inflammation or fibrosis. Competing causes excluded (negative hepatitis A/B/C serology, anti-smooth-muscle/ANCA/p-ANCA/ANA, normal α-fetoprotein, no alcohol/IV drug/cocaine use). Author suggests possibility of immunologically induced hypersensitivity, hepatotoxic metabolites, drug reaction, or idiosyncratic response, but no mechanism proven.

raw_record.support_text: A 37-year-old woman with aspirin-sensitive asthma and allergic rhinitis began montelukast therapy after baseline liver function tests were normal. After 3 weeks of montelukast, she developed jaundice, severe pruritus, and nausea, with elevated total bilirubin (181.3 µmol/L), alkaline phosphatase (231 IU/L), AST (123 IU/L), ALT (174 IU/L), and γ-glutamyltransferase (224 IU/L); serologic testing for hepatitis A, B, and C was negative. Therapy was stopped and jaundice and pruritus resolved, with most liver test results normalizing over 5 months though aminotransferases remained elevated; a liver biopsy 14 months after starting montelukast showed mild chronic portal inflammation without lobular inflammation or fibrosis. The authors report this as the first case of montelukast-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency ~3 weeks after starting montelukast 10-mg/day (standard therapeutic use); jaundice, severe pruritus, nausea; bilirubin/elevated enzymes normalized over 5 months after dechallenge but aminotransferase levels remained ~2x ULN; eosinophil count 8%; liver biopsy 14 months after start showed mild chronic portal inflammation without lobular inflammation or fibrosis; patient concurrently used inhaled corticosteroids, long-acting inhaled beta-2 agonist, allergy immunotherapy, and occasional oral corticosteroids, with theophylline stopped at montelukast initiation. Clinical trials of montelukast showed no significant difference in liver function abnormalities vs placebo (2.1% of 1955 montelukast vs 2.0% of 1180 placebo recipients had increased ALT; 1.6% vs 1.2% had self-limited transient AST increases).

raw_record.support_text: A patient, approximately 5 weeks after starting thalidomide, developed jaundice with tea-colored urine, mild nausea, abdominal discomfort, fatigue, and decreased appetite. Laboratory tests showed AST 2376 U/L, ALT 2205 U/L, total bilirubin 5.59 mg/dl, stable chronically low albumin 2.0 g/dl, and INR above 15. All home drug therapy including thalidomide was stopped and the patient was transferred for evaluation; after thalidomide discontinuation, liver function test results began to improve toward near-baseline levels, with no hepatic encephalopathy or overt bleeding during the hospital stay.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case report. Jaundice and markedly elevated aminotransferases (~5 wks after starting thalidomide); INR >15 corrected overnight after warfarin held and treatment with fresh-frozen plasma and subcutaneous vitamin K. Liver function tests had been normal before starting the drug and improved after thalidomide discontinuation (positive dechallenge). CT showed diffuse fatty infiltration of the liver parenchyma and scattered hepatic cysts. Serologic work-up (hepatitis A/B/C, EBV, HSV, CMV DNA, autoimmune markers ANA, anti-smooth muscle, anti-mitochondrial) was negative. Patient had chronically low albumin and was on warfarin therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A 76-year-old woman with multiple myeloma developed severe hepatotoxicity attributed to thalidomide while being treated with dexamethasone and daily thalidomide 200 mg/day. By week 6 of therapy her AST and ALT rose to more than 50 times the upper limit of normal, and a liver biopsy showed acute injury with chronic changes of underlying steatosis and bridging fibrosis from previously undiagnosed nonalcoholic steatohepatitis. Her liver tests improved after thalidomide was discontinued (AST/ALT fell to 86 and 165 U/L seven days later). The authors conclude the case demonstrates severe hepatotoxicity as a rare but potentially serious adverse effect of thalidomide therapy.

raw_record.support_text: Of 35 patients with drug-induced hepatitis seen at Shinko Hospital, Kobe, nine had a severe hepatic lesion with bridging necrosis on liver biopsy during the acute episode. N-Methyl carbamate was the causative drug in four of these patients, while mefenamic acid, kanamycin, pyrazinamide, difenamizole, and pyrithioxin hydrochloride were each the causative drug in one patient. Steroids were not prescribed, and all nine patients recovered completely clinically and biochemically within 6 months of drug withdrawal.

Liver tests on admission showed SGPT 2399 U/l, SGOT 1242 U/l, total bilirubin 11.1 mg/dl (conjugated 7.6 mg/dl), and alkaline phosphatase 2020 U/l, with negative viral, autoimmune, ultrasound, and CT evaluations; ropinirole withdrawal led to resolution of symptoms and normalization of all biochemical parameters within 2 months.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 68-year-old woman with hypothyroidism on levothyroxine 150 µg/day; ropinirole used for restless legs syndrome; no other drugs or herbals; no pre-existing hepatic symptoms.
raw_record.extra_details: Symptoms included asthenia, nausea, jaundice, acholic stools, and choluria; normal blood cell count and coagulation; LDH 516 U/l, ferritin 4131 ng/ml; serologies for hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV negative; ANA, AMA, ASMA, LKM negative; abdominal ultrasound and CT normal; resolution within 2 months of dechallenge; RLS subsequently treated with gabapentin 800 mg at night; patient asymptomatic with normal biochemistries over 14 months follow-up.

condition_group: exposure=therapeutic_use+population=human

raw_record.support_text: In the genetic-association table (Table 2), flucloxacillin is listed with DILI as the adverse reaction for HLA-B*5701 in Europeans (OR 80.6, 51 DILI cases/64 tolerant controls, Daly et al., 2009). Paragraph 40 reiterates this as a notable example of an HLA biomarker for idiosyncratic DILI with OR 80.6.
raw_record.extra_details: HLA-B*5701 association with DILI (OR 80.6, 51 DILI cases/64 tolerant controls; Daly et al. 2009). Cited again in the discussion of idiosyncratic DILI (OR 80.6).

raw_record.support_text: The text describes a genome-wide association study of flucloxacillin-induced DILI (Daly et al.) reporting an association in the MHC region with the strongest association at rs2395029, in complete linkage disequilibrium with HLA-B*5701; direct genotyping in 51 cases and 63 drug-exposed controls revealed a strong relationship between HLA-B*5701 and flucloxacillin-induced liver injury (odds ratio 80.6).
raw_record.extra_details: Flucloxacillin is described as a commonly used antibiotic (UK, Australia, Sweden and others); susceptibility associated with HLA-B*5701 (OR 80.6) and marker rs2395029; 51 cases versus 63 drug-exposed controls.

raw_record.support_text: The study found 10 cases of cholestatic hepatitis of uncertain origin diagnosed within 45 days of receiving flucloxacillin that were characteristic of or consistent with a syndrome recently described as associated with this drug. The conclusion states that flucloxacillin is a likely cause of cholestatic hepatitis, with the risk estimated at 7.6 per 100,000 users (95% confidence interval, 3.6-13.9).
raw_record.extra_details: Epidemiologic study; 10 cases of cholestatic hepatitis diagnosed within 45 days of flucloxacillin and 1 case 46-90 days after prescription. Risk estimate 7.6 per 100,000 users (95% CI 3.6-13.9). Cholestatic hepatitis with deep jaundice, highly elevated bilirubin, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and prolonged recovery; onset within a few weeks of starting therapy and possibly up to two or three weeks after completion. ADRAC spontaneous reports accumulated from 17 to 73-77 cases of flucloxacillin-associated liver toxicity. Flucloxacillin is a semi-synthetic penicillinase-resistant penicillin indicated for suspected staphylococcal infections.

raw_record.support_text: PRSgw+ was developed from a GWAS of the original cohort plus 477 patients with DILI due to either amoxicillin–clavulanate or flucloxacillin, so that almost half of the cases used to derive it were due to these two drugs; stronger HLA associations have been demonstrated for these drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed as a cause of DILI among patients in the iDILIC–DILIN clinical cohort (with amoxicillin–clavulanate), for which strong HLA associations have been demonstrated; these cases contributed to the expanded GWAS-derived PRSgw+.

raw_record.support_text: Flucloxacillin accounted for 7 of 28 cases (25%) of drug-induced jaundice presenting to the Jaundice Hotline after application of consensus criteria for DILI. Flucloxacillin cases were mostly cholestatic (6/7) with the remainder mixed, more common in women (M:F 2:5), mean age 76 years, with mean time to normalization of liver function tests of 49 days.
raw_record.extra_details: 7 of 28 DIJ cases (25%); annual incidence of flucloxacillin-induced jaundice 3.2 per million in Cornwall vs 0.6 per million national CSM rate; jaundice onset on average at 20.4 days (range 7–40); marked jaundice, mean peak bilirubin 267 µmol/l; cholestatic pattern in 6/7, mixed in remainder; M:F 2:5; mean age 76 (range 56–81); prescribed mainly for cellulitis (6/7) or one breast abscess.

raw_record.support_text: PBMCs were isolated from six patients who developed cholestatic liver injury following flucloxacillin therapy to characterize the drug-specific T-cell response. PBMC activation with flucloxacillin was detected in five patients (including one HLA-B*57:01-negative individual). Flucloxacillin-responsive CD8+ T-cell clones from four HLA-B*57:01 ELISpot-positive patients and CD4+ clones (in low numbers) were isolated; activation was concentration-dependent and provoked IFN-γ and cytolytic molecule secretion. The authors conclude that immune phenomena contribute to the development of flucloxacillin-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic liver injury phenotype. Six patients with DILI following therapy; five showed PBMC activation (including one HLA-B*57:01-negative patient). Flucloxacillin-responsive CD8+ clones restricted by HLA-B*57:01 and HLA-B*58:01; clones expressed CCR2, CCR4, CCR9, CXCR3. Concentration-dependent activation, peak serum ~60 μM, estimated achievable liver concentration ~100 μM. Clones secreted IFN-γ, granzyme B, FasL, perforin. Flucloxacillin-responsive clones were not activated by abacavir. In p:47 responses were dependent on MHC class I (anti-HLA class I blocking antibody inhibited activation).

raw_record.support_text: Eleven cases of hepatic injury were attributed to the intake of flucloxacillin and reported to the Netherlands Center for Monitoring of Adverse Reactions to Drugs between 1982 and 1992. The biochemical pattern was compatible with cholestatic hepatitis in seven cases, mixed cholestatic-hepatocellular injury in one, hepatocellular pattern in two, and mild liver enzyme elevations in one. Two patients died, one from fatal bleeding from the liver after biopsy and one from combined hepatic and cardiac failure; the rest recovered. In paragraph 9, the causal relationship was assessed as 'probable' in eight cases and 'possible' in three.
raw_record.extra_details: Eleven patients (4 men, 7 women; mean age 57 years) treated for staphylococcal infection; oral flucloxacillin 1500-4000 mg/day for 2-28 days; symptoms appeared about 10-30 days after start. Causal relationship 'probable' in 8 cases (no. 1-8) and 'possible' in 3 (no. 9-11) using temporal-relationship plus exclusion-of-other-causes criteria. Biochemical patterns: cholestatic hepatitis in 7, mixed cholestatic-hepatocellular in 1, hepatocellular in 2, mild liver enzyme elevations in 1; peripheral eosinophilia in 3; autoantibodies absent; hepatitis A/B (and some C), CMV, and infectious mononucleosis serologically excluded; extrahepatic cholestasis excluded by ultrasonography. Histology in 7 cases showed cholestatic hepatitis in 5 (with cholangitis/cholangiolitis in 4), centrilobular cholestasis with bridging fibrosis, and portal-central bridging necrosis in the others. Two deaths: fatal liver bleeding after biopsy, and combined hepatic and cardiac failure; survivors recovered on average 72 days (range 17-180) after peak aminotransferases. Case 4 developed injury on three occasions after flucloxacillin; her second-biopsy hepatocellular damage had initially been attributed to ranitidine and diclofenac before flucloxacillin causality was recognized. Nine patients used other drugs concurrently but, except case 11, continued them without recurrent injury.

raw_record.support_text: A GWAS performed on 51 patients of northern European ancestry with flucloxacillin (Floxacapen)-induced DIHT identified class 1 HLA-B*5701 as the risk factor (OR 80.6; 95% CI 23–285). The paper states that flucloxacillin-induced hepatotoxicity occurs in fewer than 1 in 10,000 patients taking the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Brand names: Floxacapen. GWAS on 51 patients of northern European ancestry identified class 1 HLA-B*5701 as the risk factor (OR 80.6; 95% CI 23–285). Hepatotoxicity occurs in fewer than 1 in 10,000 patients taking the drug.

raw_record.support_text: After numerous individual case reports of flucloxacillin-associated cholestatic liver disease appeared between 1982 and 1993, the association was confirmed by two formal epidemiological studies, which estimated a frequency of flucloxacillin-associated cholestatic liver disease of about 7 per 100,000 first-time users. The current GPRD follow-up study yielded a similar risk estimate of 8.5 per 100,000 users (45-day risk 8.48 per 100,000 users, 95% CI 5.43–12.61, based on 24 cases among 283,097 first-time users).
raw_record.extra_details: British GPRD cohort, 1991–2000; 24 first-time-user cholestatic liver disease cases within 1–45 days (risk 8.48 per 100,000, 95% CI 5.43–12.61) and 5 cases 46–90 days (risk 1.77, 95% CI 0.57–4.12). Cholestatic liver disease with a typically prolonged recovery; first UK marketing in the 1970s with first idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity reports in the mid-1980s. Age >55 years, female sex and treatment duration >14 days had previously been proposed as risk factors; the current study found an approximately six-fold higher risk in patients aged 60 years and older compared with younger patients, whereas female sex was not clearly identified as a risk factor. Study relates only to cholestatic forms of liver disease; oxytetracycline was used as a comparison drug.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that Daly et al, under the DILIGEN and International SAE consortium, performed genome-wide association studies of flucloxacillin DILI (51 cases, 282 matched controls, and 64 drug-exposed controls), finding the strongest association at rs2395029 [G] (P = 8.7 × 10^-33), in complete linkage disequilibrium with HLA-B*5701, with direct genotyping showing a very strong relationship (OR, 80.6), confirmed in 23 replication cases (OR, 100).
raw_record.extra_details: HLA-B*5701 strongly associated with flucloxacillin-induced liver injury (OR 80.6 original, 100.0 replication). Additional SNPs (HLA DRB1*0701, TNF rs361525, TNF rs1799964, HSPAIL rs2227956) were not independent of HLA-B*5701. It was estimated only 1 in 500–1000 HLA-B*5701 carriers develop liver injury on flucloxacillin, with an estimated population attributable fraction of 0.64.

raw_record.support_text: In a DILI registry study, flucloxacillin was implicated as a cause of drug-induced liver injury with 75 cases (9.6%) in the discovery sample and 0 (0.0%) in the replication sample.
raw_record.extra_details: 75 cases (9.6%) in discovery sample, 0 in replication. An additional 8 discovery cases were attributed to 'Flucloxacillin and amoxicillin/clavulanate' (unresolved co-attribution). Known MHC risk variants for flucloxacillin-DILI were conditioned on in the analysis.

raw_record.support_text: In this case series of drug-induced liver injury, flucloxacillin was one of the most common antibiotics responsible, with eight of 77 DILI cases. Among the flucloxacillin-attributed cases the injury was predominantly cholestatic (seven cases) with one mixed case, and seven of the cases were associated with jaundice (bilirubin ≥2 ULN).
raw_record.extra_details: Eight of 77 DILI cases; causality held via highest International Consensus Criteria score. Pattern distribution 7 cholestatic/1 mixed; duration of treatment median 10 (2-21) days; time to biochemical resolution median 120 (2-540) days with some chronic courses. Seven jaundice cases detailed (bilirubin 2.3-11.2 ULN).

raw_record.support_text: Flucloxacillin is a semisynthetic penicillin associated with rare cholestatic jaundice that often persists for more than three months, with abnormal liver function possibly persisting 12 months or more. The study is a retrospective case-control study of flucloxacillin-associated jaundice; cases required jaundice within eight weeks of stopping flucloxacillin with cholestatic liver function tests. Increasing age and prolonged flucloxacillin treatment were risk factors: patients over 55 had an OR of 18.61 (95% CI 5.16-67.17) versus under 30, and treatment over 14 days had an OR of 7.13 (2.90-17.58) versus 14 days or less; dose and route were not related to risk.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic jaundice (DILI) attributed to flucloxacillin; jaundice often persists >3 months and abnormal liver function may persist ≥12 months. Retrospective case-control study: cases required jaundice within 8 weeks of stopping the drug, cholestatic liver function tests, normal bile duct diameter by ultrasound/ERCP, and no other recognized cause of jaundice or hepatotoxic drugs. Risk factors: age >55 vs <30 OR 18.61 (95% CI 5.16-67.17); treatment >14 days vs ≤14 days OR 7.13 (95% CI 2.90-17.58); dose and route not related to jaundice risk. Liver damage first reported in 1982; prior cases reported in Australia (131), Sweden (48), and United Kingdom (21); incidence in Australia paralleled increased use.

raw_record.support_text: Flucloxacillin is listed among the drugs responsible for drug-induced hepatitis, investigated in 2 human hepatitis cases using an ex-vivo drug antigen lymphocyte transformation test after a therapeutic 500 mg dose with blood collected 120 min after intake.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed in 'List of drugs responsible for the hepatitis' in the context of a study evaluating the ex-vivo drug antigen lymphocyte transformation test for diagnosing drug-induced hepatitis; 2 cases; dose 500 mg, blood collected 120 min after intake.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of flucloxacillin-induced liver injury, more than 80% of patients carried the HLA-B*5701 allele compared to 6% of the controls. Only 0.1-0.2% of individuals with the risk allele are likely to develop DILI, and it was estimated that more than 13,000 patients would need to be tested to prevent one case of flucloxacillin-induced liver injury. The text refers to flucloxacillin-DILI and to flucloxacillin toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: >80% of flucloxacillin liver-injury patients carried HLA-B*5701 versus 6% of controls; only 0.1-0.2% of risk-allele carriers are likely to develop DILI; >13,000 patients would need prospective testing to prevent one case; HLA-B*5701 is regarded as more of a diagnostic than predictive marker. T-cell clone properties and in vitro protein binding appear conserved across alternatives oxacillin, cloxacillin and dicloxacillin, so risk may persist with these drugs in HLA-B*5701 carriers.

raw_record.support_text: Flucloxacillin is a narrow-spectrum β-lactam antibiotic of the penicillin class used for Gram-positive infections. The incidence of flucloxacillin-induced hepatotoxicity in the UK is 8.5 per 100,000 patients in days 1 to 45 during treatment. A GWA study with 51 flucloxacillin DILI cases and 282 controls identified HLA-B*5701 as a major genetic risk factor (OR=80.6, P=9.0 x 10^-19), although only 1 in every 500 to 1,000 individuals with this genotype develops flucloxacillin-related hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Narrow-spectrum β-lactam penicillin for Gram-positive bacterial infections. Incidence 8.5 per 100,000 in the UK during days 1-45 of treatment. HLA-B*5701 GWA study: 51 DILI cases vs 282 controls, OR=80.6, P=9.0x10^-19; allele common in Northern Europe, rare in Africa/Asia; only 1 in 500-1,000 carriers develop hepatotoxicity; no significant difference in disease severity between HLA-B*5701-negative and carrier individuals.

raw_record.support_text: Flucloxacillin is the most common reason of idiosyncratic liver injury in Sweden, comprising 16 % of all DILI cases, and is the second most common cause of drug-induced jaundice after amoxicillin–clavulanate in the UK. Female sex, age and high daily doses are associated with higher risk. A total of 7/129 (5 %) died due to reported flucloxacillin liver injury in Sweden from 1970 to 2004, and ductopenia and cholestatic cirrhosis leading to liver transplantation have been reported.
raw_record.extra_details: 16% of all DILI cases in Sweden; second most common cause of drug-induced jaundice in the UK. Risk factors: female sex, age, high daily doses. 7/129 (5%) died from flucloxacillin liver injury in Sweden 1970–2004. Reported phenotypes include ductopenia and cholestatic cirrhosis leading to liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: For flucloxacillin, a rare but potentially serious complication is a cholestatic hepatitis, which affects 1-2 per 1000 individuals treated with the drug. Genetic work included a GWA study using 866,399 markers in 51 patients with flucloxacillin DILI and 282 matched controls, showing that HLA-B*57:01 (rs2395029) carriers have an 80-fold increased risk of DILI when treated with flucloxacillin, a finding replicated in another cohort of 23 cases; an intronic SNP in ST6GAL1 also reached genome-wide significance (OR = 4.1, p = 1.4 x 10^-8).
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence 1-2 per 1000 treated individuals; cholestatic hepatitis; pathogenesis not clear. GWA study (51 cases, 282 sex/ancestry matched controls, 866,399 markers) found strongest association peak in the MHC region on chromosome 6 (p = 8.7 x 10^-33 for rs2395029, in complete linkage disequilibrium with HLA-B*57:01 in Europeans); HLA-B*57:01 carriers have an 80-fold increased risk; replicated in a cohort of 23 cases. rs10937275 intronic SNP in ST6GAL1 on chromosome 3 also genome-wide significant (OR = 4.1, p = 1.4 x 10^-8). Confirmation GWA study of 197 cases and 6835 controls confirmed HLA-B*57:01 (OR = 36.62) as the major risk factor, with HLA-B*57:03 (OR = 79.21) also associated; imputed valine in position 97 of HLA-B was the strongest (OR 38.1). HLA-B*57 was not associated with DILI from other isoxazolyl penicillins (n=6) or amoxicillin (n=15). Positive predictive value of HLA-B*57:01 testing is low (0.12%), making routine testing impractical. Flucloxacillin is a PXR agonist at therapeutic concentrations; PXR C-25385T (rs3814055) CC genotype is a risk factor for flucloxacillin-induced DILI (OR 3.37, 95% CI 1.55-7.30).

raw_record.support_text: Flucloxacillin-associated DILI case reports were analyzed for liver-injury pattern, eosinophilia, hepatic necrosis, inflammatory reaction, and death/liver transplantation outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: 36 individual case reports; median age 54 y; 24 female/12 male; median treatment duration 2 weeks; HC 11%, Cs/mixed 89%; peripheral eosinophilia present in 21% (24/36 reported); hepatic eosinophilia present in 31% (26/36 reported); hepatic necrosis 7%; inflammatory reaction 50%; death or liver transplant 14%; liver biopsy reported in 29/36 cases.

raw_record.support_text: A severe prolonged illness characterized by deep jaundice and debilitating pruritus occurred in five patients after the use of flucloxacillin. Liver biopsy specimens showed severe cholestasis in all cases, with significant bile-duct injury in three cases; in one patient with symptoms persisting nine months, biopsy showed marked bile-duct depletion. Symptoms resolved over at least two months, and liver enzyme activities remained abnormal in all patients after four to nine months' follow-up. The authors concluded that flucloxacillin-induced liver disease is probably underdiagnosed and underreported.
raw_record.extra_details: Five patients seen in a four-month period. Clinical features: deep jaundice and debilitating pruritus; liver disease symptoms took at least two months to resolve; liver enzyme activities remained abnormal in all patients after four to nine months' follow-up. Histology: severe cholestasis in all cases, significant bile-duct injury in three cases, and marked bile-duct depletion in one patient with symptoms persisting nine months. Authors felt flucloxacillin-induced liver disease is probably underdiagnosed and underreported and, given rapidly increasing flucloxacillin use, more cases are anticipated.

raw_record.support_text: Flucloxacillin-induced DILI is studied as an established clinical entity. A genome-wide association study showed that 84.3% of patients with flucloxacillin-induced DILI carry the HLA-B*57:01 genotype, with an 80-fold increased risk (OR 80.6, 95% CI 22.8-284.9), though this yields low positive predictive value because most HLA-B*57:01 carriers treated with flucloxacillin do not develop DILI. Female sex, age over 60 years, and treatment duration longer than 2 weeks have previously been proposed as additional risk factors, and this retrospective case-control study aims to validate and identify new clinical risk factors for flucloxacillin-induced DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: A genome-wide association study showed that 84.3% of patients with flucloxacillin-induced DILI carry HLA-B*57:01 (OR 80.6, 95% CI 22.8-284.9), an 80-fold increased risk; the association implies low positive predictive value because most treated HLA-B*57:01 carriers do not develop DILI. Previously proposed risk factors include female sex, age older than 60 years, and treatment duration longer than 2 weeks. The study is a retrospective case-control study using the SWEDEGENE database of suspected ADR cases (1990-2016) collected from the Swedish MPA spontaneous ADR reports, with TWINGENE controls.

raw_record.support_text: Flucloxacillin, a β-lactam antibiotic used as first-line treatment for Staphylococcal infections, causes drug-induced cholestatic liver injury with an incidence of 8.5 per 100,000 patients and delayed onset of clinical symptoms 1-45 days after starting therapy (and 1.8 per 100,000 following 46-90 days). The cholestasis involves bile duct injury and Vanishing Bile Duct Syndrome (ductopenia); an immune-mediated response with a genetic pre-disposition is generally accepted to account for the DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: β-lactam antibiotic, first-line for Staphylococcal infections; cholestatic liver injury incidence 8.5 per 100,000 patients, delayed onset of clinical symptoms 1-45 days and 1.8 per 100,000 for 46-90 days after starting therapy; cholestasis with bile duct injury and Vanishing Bile Duct Syndrome (ductopenia); small amounts form metabolites via CYP3A4, possibly under genetic control; generally accepted immune-mediated response with genetic predisposition; mechanism 5.

raw_record.support_text: Seven individuals with DILI exposed to co-amoxiclav in addition to flucloxacillin and 16 recently recruited individuals with flucloxacillin DILI were genotyped for HLA-B*5701 for replication; 20 of these 23 additional subjects (87%) were HLA-B*5701 positive (P = 6.62 × 10^-13). The paper is a genome-wide association study of a human DILI cohort that treats flucloxacillin-induced liver injury as an established clinical entity, additionally reporting that HLA-B*5701 did not correlate with pattern of injury and that four subjects with low ICC causality scores were all HLA-B*5701 positive.
raw_record.extra_details: Genome-wide association study of flucloxacillin DILI. Causality supported by Hill causality/HLA cohort with ICC causality scores (four subjects had low ICC scores). HLA-B*5701 genotype did not correlate with pattern of injury. Only 1 in every 500-1000 HLA-B*5701 carriers develops DILI when treated with flucloxacillin; population attributable fraction (PAF) of HLA-B*5701 estimated at 0.64. Additional genetic factors suspected; a chromosome 3 SNP (rs10937275) reached P = 1.4 × 10^-8 (allelic OR = 4.1, minor allele frequency 0.29 vs 0.09) in 48 risk-allele-carrying cases. Most subjects (65%) had at least one extrahepatic manifestation; no common CNV associated with DILI. Co-amoxiclav exposure was present in some subjects as a co-medication.

raw_record.support_text: Daly et al. identified HLA-B*5701 as a potent risk factor for drug-induced liver injury (DILI) owing to flucloxacillin, based on the DILIGEN study of 51 cases and 289 controls. The accompanying table further lists flucloxacillin-DILI associations with HLA-B*5701 (odds ratio 81, PPV 91%, NPV 88%) and TNF-α (-238G/A) (odds ratio 31).
raw_record.extra_details: HLA-B*5701 identified as a potent risk factor for flucloxacillin DILI from the DILIGEN study (51 cases, 289 controls; OR 81, PPV 91%, NPV 88%); additional reported associations for flucloxacillin DILI include TNF-α (-238G/A) (OR 31) and HLA-DRB1*0107-DQB1*0103 (OR 17).

raw_record.support_text: The case report describes a patient who developed fulminant hepatic failure attributed to flucloxacillin, which required orthotopic liver transplantation (the donor became available 48 days after initial admission, at a time when the patient was in grade IV coma on haemodialysis for renal failure). The authors note that the development of aplastic anaemia in association with flucloxacillin-induced liver failure has not previously been reported, using 'flucloxacillin-induced liver failure' as an unqualified causal construction.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of fulminant hepatic failure (grade IV coma with hepatic encephalopathy) attributed to flucloxacillin, managed with orthotopic liver transplant; also complicated by renal failure requiring haemodialysis, severe pancytopenia, and secondary aplastic anaemia that resolved by 2 years post-transplant. The report specifically notes that aplastic anaemia in association with flucloxacillin-induced liver failure has not previously been described. No dose, duration, or biochemical pattern reported.

raw_record.support_text: In an entire cohort of 294 drug-induced liver injury (DILI) cases, 79 were attributed to flucloxacillin as the offending drug; the cohort was analyzed for time to biochemical recovery, with flucloxacillin treated as an established cause of the DILI episode.
raw_record.extra_details: 79 of 294 DILI cohort cases were flucloxacillin-attributed; the paper models time to biochemical recovery, and in this subgroup log_e bilirubin × ULN at DILI onset increased recovery time by 44% per unit (time ratio 1.44, p<0.05).

raw_record.support_text: The paper studied patients with flucloxacillin-induced or amoxicillin-clavulanate-induced liver injury alongside healthy donors, generating flucloxacillin- and β-lactam hapten-specific CD8+ T-cell clones. It also notes that pharmacogenetic studies identified a strong association between expression of HLA-B*57:01 and susceptibility to flucloxacillin liver injury, and that drug-specific T-cell clones from DILI patients were activated via a hapten mechanism in an HLA allele-restricted manner.
raw_record.extra_details: Drug-induced liver injury patients included in the study; pharmacogenetic association with HLA-B*57:01 susceptibility. Mechanism: flucloxacillin forms a hapten that binds covalently to lysine residues on proteins (e.g., human serum albumin), and parent drug activates CD8+ T cells in HLA-B*57:01+ donors without covalent binding, whereas patient T cells were activated via a hapten mechanism in an HLA allele-restricted manner. Peak serum concentrations following therapeutic exposure are 19.4-32.0 µM, whereas in-vitro direct T-cell activation required soluble flucloxacillin concentrations of 100 µM and above.

raw_record.support_text: Flucloxacillin, a semi-synthetic penicillin used for staphylococcal infection, has been known to be associated with cholestatic hepatitis with a prevalence of 10.3 per 100,000 new users in the United Kingdom. A GWAS of 866,399 SNPs in 51 flucloxacillin-related DILI cases vs 282 matched controls found the strongest association with rs2395029 (OR=45, P=8.7e-33), in complete linkage disequilibrium with HLA-B*57:01.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis attributed (prevalence 10.3 per 100,000 new users in the UK). GWAS: strongest association rs2395029 (in complete LD with HLA-B*57:01) OR=45 (P=8.7e-33); ORs vs tolerant controls 80.6 (51 exploration cases) and 100 (23 replication cases); other HLA-region SNPs (e.g., TNF rs361525) not significant after conditioning on HLA-B*57:01; HLA-B*57:01 frequency 0.01–0.03 in Northern Europeans but <0.001 in Japanese; not approved in Japan.

raw_record.support_text: A table of the top 48 drugs worldwide causing idiosyncratic DILI with verified causality assessed by RUCAM lists flucloxacillin with 130 RUCAM-based DILI cases, categorized as a CYP substrate (CYP+), referenced to Dekker (91).
raw_record.extra_details: 130 RUCAM-verified DILI cases; CYP substrate (CYP+); HLA pharmacogenetic associations also noted in some patients (p32).

raw_record.support_text: Flucloxacillin was one of the most commonly implicated conventional drugs in the Pro-Euro DILI Registry, adjudicated as the single cause of liver injury in 23 cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 23 adjudicated single-cause cases in the Pro-Euro DILI Registry; ATC J01CF05; over 90% of cases came from the United Kingdom.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe cases of flucloxacillin-attributed liver injury. Liver biopsy specimens in their patients showed severe cholestasis with relatively mild hepatocytic injury (hepatocanalicular cholestasis), and significant bile-duct lesions in some cases; Patient 4, biopsied at three months with disease persisting for nine months, showed extensive loss of bile ducts. The authors state the hepatotoxic effect of flucloxacillin appears idiosyncratic, is not dose-related, and occurs in a very small proportion of those who receive the drug. In the 15 ADRAC cases reported between 1980 and June 1988, hepatic side-effects were thought to be caused by flucloxacillin.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases showed deep jaundice and debilitating pruritus, prolonged liver-function abnormalities, absence of eosinophilia, and no previous exposure to flucloxacillin. Biopsies showed hepatocanalicular cholestasis, and Patient 4 had extensive loss of bile ducts (drug-induced bile-duct destruction) with a persistent nine-month course; bile-duct destruction had not previously been associated with penicillins. The effect is idiosyncratic, not dose-related, occurring in a small proportion of recipients; rechallenge not recommended. ADRAC spontaneous reports (1980 to June 1988) comprised 15 patients with hepatic side-effects thought caused by flucloxacillin: four with jaundice (two also coded as hepatitis), two other cases of hepatitis, four cases of cholestatic hepatitis, and five cases with abnormal hepatic function. Flucloxacillin became available on prescription in Australia in 1983; use rose from 12,136 (1984-85) to 716,157 (1987-88) prescriptions.

raw_record.support_text: A 62-year-old woman (Table 2) had flucloxacillin as the drug associated with the first DILI (treatment duration 10 days, presentation with jaundice, cholestatic pattern). At follow-up 48 months later she had persistent cholestatic-pattern liver test abnormalities not explained by alternative diagnoses: ALT 1.04 × ULN and GGT 4.6 × ULN, but no jaundice and no itching.
raw_record.extra_details: First DILI treatment duration 10 days; presentation with jaundice and cholestatic pattern; follow-up 48 months. Persistent unexplained abnormalities at follow-up: ALT 1.04 × ULN, GGT 4.6 × ULN; no jaundice or itching.

raw_record.support_text: The paper notes that a strong association between the HLA-B*5701 allele and susceptibility to flucloxacillin-induced liver injury was detected both by direct HLA genotyping and by a genome-wide association study, with a study on flucloxacillin-induced liver injury comprising 51 cases and 487 population controls. This frames flucloxacillin-induced liver injury as an idiosyncratic, immunogenetic-linked adverse drug reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Flucloxacillin-associated liver injury reported as an idiosyncratic adverse drug reaction with an immunogenetic basis. A genome-wide association study on flucloxacillin-induced liver injury compared 51 cases and 487 population controls, and a strong association with the HLA-B*5701 allele was detected both by direct HLA genotyping and by GWAS.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes the first serendipitous discovery of the adverse effects of flucloxacillin due to an inadvertent rechallenge, in which patients developed symptoms of eosinophilia, inflammatory infiltrates and fever (Lobatto et al., 1982). This is cited as support for an immunological basis for drug-induced liver injury, indicating flucloxacillin caused a clinically apparent, immune-mediated DILI reaction upon rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: DILI confirmed by inadvertent rechallenge; accompanied by eosinophilia, inflammatory infiltrates and fever, supporting an immune/hypersensitivity basis (Lobatto et al., 1982).

raw_record.support_text: The analysis used DILI datasets from case-control studies of individuals taking flucloxacillin (77 cases and 288 population controls) and individuals taking co-amoxiclav (201 cases and 532 population controls), with genotyping data generated using the Illumina 1M-duo. The study estimates SNP-based heritability for flucloxacillin-induced and co-amoxiclav-induced DILI cases from these iSAEC datasets.
raw_record.extra_details: Based on iSAEC DILI case-control dataset (77 flucloxacillin-induced DILI cases, 288 population controls). The paper's focus is estimating the proportion of DILI heritability captured by common SNPs using the GCTA algorithm (genome-wide, chromosome 6, and genome-wide without chromosome 6), not on establishing causal attribution.

raw_record.support_text: Patient B, a 53-year-old female, developed DILI with jaundice and pruritus one week after a 3-week course of flucloxacillin. Liver histology showed mild portal inflammation, portal fibrosis, ductopenia, and extensive cholestasis compatible with flucloxacillin-induced liver injury. She had persistent hepatocellular secretory failure and responded to rifampicin 300 mg daily.
raw_record.extra_details: Jaundice and pruritus began 1 week after a 3-week flucloxacillin course; bilirubin 278 µmol/L, AP 298 U/L, γGT 39 U/L, AST 43, ALT 51; AMA positive, ANA/ANCA negative; histology showed ductopenia and portal fibrosis; treated with rifampicin 300 mg od for 4 weeks followed by budesonide; incomplete biochemical recovery possibly due to ductopenia.

raw_record.support_text: A 63-year-old woman developed progressive cholestasis and hyperbilirubinaemia following a course of flucloxacillin, with no other cause demonstrated after comprehensive laboratory, imaging and genetic investigations. Sequential liver biopsies confirmed vanishing bile duct syndrome (VBDS). She developed cachexia and refractory pruritus and was listed for liver transplantation, which she underwent 6 months after the initial drug-induced injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 63-year-old woman with mild psoriasis and no prior liver disease or regular medication; 10-day course of flucloxacillin for a skin infection started 2 weeks before symptom onset, conjunctival icterus 4 days after completing the course. Admission labs: bilirubin 501 mmol/L, ALP 279, AST 83, ALT 60, GGT 36 IU/L, INR 1.0; extended viral, autoimmune and immunoglobulin work-up negative. Sequential liver biopsies confirmed VBDS; refractory pruritus and cachexia led to listing for liver transplantation 6 months after initial injury, with good graft function at 1-year follow-up. Background notes VBDS as a recognised complication of cholestatic DILI with a possibly immunologic (cytotoxic T-lymphocyte) mechanism and HLA DRB1(*04, *11, *15) susceptibility.

raw_record.support_text: During evaluation of the Clinical Diagnostic Scale in 135 hepatotoxic ADR reports, six patients whose hepatotoxicity was considered drug-related on the basis of consensus classification scored < 10 (unlikely). Among these were two patients with flucloxacillin-induced cholestasis that first appeared > 15 days after drug withdrawal, which the authors cite as confirming the limitations of the clinical scale.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients developed cholestasis that first appeared > 15 days after drug withdrawal; cases were drawn from 135 hepatotoxic ADR reports and classified as drug-related by consensus, but scored < 10 (unlikely) on the Clinical Diagnostic Scale, cited as confirming the limitations of that instrument for atypical latency.

raw_record.support_text: An epistasis analysis using data from 51 flucloxacillin DILI cases and 282 country- and gender-matched controls made available by the International Serious Adverse Event Consortium (iSAEC) revealed significant epistasis involving a substantial number of SNPs located outside chromosome 6 that interact with MHC genes, with a restricted network involving non-MHC and MHC genes relevant to DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: Flucloxacillin DILI treated as a defined outcome in an iSAEC case cohort (51 cases vs 282 matched controls); epistasis analysis (Taxonomy 3) revealed significant non-chromosome-6 SNP epistasis interacting with MHC genes, with putative effects on leukocyte migration, lipid processing, apoptosis, natural killer cell cytotoxicity, and endoplasmic reticulum stress (e.g., DDR1, GJB1 involvement).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that DILI cases related to drugs such as flucloxacillin, which was well represented in the cohort (195 cases), were recorded as causal agents of DILI. These drugs showed smaller, non-significant increases in rs2476601 minor allele frequency compared with controls.
raw_record.extra_details: 195 cases in the cohort, identified as a causal agent of DILI and associated with an HLA risk allele; rs2476601 association not significant (OR 1.24, 95% CI 0.90–1.71, P = .18).

raw_record.support_text: In the RUCAM-based ranking of drugs causing DILI with verified causality, Flucloxacillin is listed at position 2 among the top-ranking drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: Ranked #2 in the RUCAM-based top-ranking of drugs causing DILI with verified causality, derived from 3,312 RUCAM-assessed DILI cases (Teschke, 2018d).

raw_record.support_text: Flucloxacillin, a widely prescribed antibiotic, is associated occasionally (in <1 in 10,000 patients prescribed the drug) with DILI. The DNA samples studied were from 51 patients of Northern European ethnic origin who had suffered moderate to severe DILI with a clear causal link to flucloxacillin, and direct HLA typing confirmed carriage of HLA-B*5701 as a strong risk factor for flucloxacillin-related DILI (odds ratio 80.6).
raw_record.extra_details: Moderate to severe DILI with a clear causal link to flucloxacillin in 51 patients of Northern European origin; DILI frequency <1 in 10,000 patients. GWAS: top SNP in HCP5 gene p = 8.7 × 10-33, linked to HLA-B*5701; HLA-B*5701 carriage OR 80.6 (95% CI 23-285), confirmed in a replication cohort of 16 cases. Only 1 in 500-1000 B*5701-positive patients prescribed flucloxacillin develop DILI, so genotyping has low positive predictive value.

raw_record.support_text: Patient 1, a 39-year-old woman, was prescribed flucloxacillin 500 mg four times a day for five days for a boil. She presented four weeks later with pruritus and jaundice (bilirubin 68 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 565 IU/L; normal 60-230). A liver biopsy was interpreted as cholestatic hepatitis, and intrahepatic cholestasis was recorded. Flucloxacillin was prescribed again with subsequent exacerbation of jaundice; no other apparent cause was present, and the attending clinician ultimately considered flucloxacillin liver toxicity the likely cause of the cholestatic jaundice, which resolved by November 1989.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis (liver biopsy) with pruritus, jaundice and elevated bilirubin/alkaline phosphatase following flucloxacillin 500 mg QID for 5 days for a boil; latent period about 4 weeks; rechallenge with flucloxacillin exacerbated the jaundice; jaundice resolved by November 1989; no alternative cause apparent; attending clinician assessed flucloxacillin as the likely cause.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a series of four cases of biopsy-proven cholestatic hepatitis following treatment with flucloxacillin, presenting 17 to 28 days after commencing the drug. Liver biopsies showed centrilobular canalicular cholestasis with portal and lobular inflammation and eosinophil infiltration, consistent with drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis. Flucloxacillin was attributed as the cause of the liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Cases were in elderly patients aged 62-81 years.
raw_record.extra_details: Four cases (1M, 3F) with severe delayed cholestatic hepatitis; jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, pale faeces appeared 17-28 days after commencing flucloxacillin and 7-14 days after cessation before presentation. Marked elevations of serum bilirubin, ALP, GGT and AST in all patients; extrahepatic biliary obstruction excluded by ERCP in three and ultrasound/CT in one; negative serology for hepatitis A/B, CMV, ANA, AMA. Biopsy showed centrilobular canalicular cholestasis, hepatocyte swelling, mild lobular inflammation, sinusoidal eosinophil infiltration, portal infiltrate of lymphocytes, macrophages, neutrophils and eosinophils; no portal oedema or bile duct proliferation. Symptoms resolved with bilirubin normalisation in 19-60 days in all patients; two patients had persistent ALP/GGT elevations 111 and 380 days after cessation. One patient had mild peripheral eosinophilia; none had rash or fever.

raw_record.support_text: Case 1: a 65-year-old man with maturity-onset diabetes and osteomyelitis developed marked jaundice after 6 weeks of flucloxacillin (Heracillin) 1500 mg/24 h orally. Biochemically there was cholestasis with markedly elevated serum bilirubin (peak 364 mmol/l, normal <22) and slightly elevated ALP (32 U) and ASAT (33 U). After flucloxacillin withdrawal bilirubin returned to normal over 8 weeks, and a biopsy showed moderate cholestasis; the diagnosis of drug-induced canalicular cholestasis was established. The abstract frames the two patients as developing reversible cholestatic jaundice during treatment with oxacillin derivatives.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Concurrent glibenclamide (Daonil) for diabetes continued unchanged during recovery; indication osteomyelitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Flucloxacillin 1500 mg/24 h perorally for 6 weeks for osteomyelitis of proximal phalanx of left big toe. Marked jaundice, hepatic tenderness. Serum bilirubin peaked at 364 mmol/l (normal <22) on day 7 and normalized over 8 weeks; ALP 32 U (normal <10), ASAT 33 U (normal <20). Biopsy two weeks after admission showed moderate cholestasis (canalicular cholestasis); ERCP and ultrasound normal; Coombs' direct test negative, no hepatitis-associated antigens, no eosinophilia or fever. Repeat biopsy at 3 months showed Kupffer cell proliferation, enhanced intracytoplasmic vacuolization with scattered hepatocyte necroses. Bilirubin normalized while glibenclamide was maintained, supporting flucloxacillin as the causal agent.

raw_record.support_text: The study objective is to estimate the risk of cholestatic hepatitis of uncertain origin in patients who had recently received erythromycin, a drug which is known to cause this disorder. It is a retrospective cohort study using data recorded on general practitioners' office computers, covering 366,064 people who received erythromycin across about 600 UK general practices.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective cohort study using automatically recorded data from general practitioners' office computers in ~600 UK practices; 366,064 people who received erythromycin. The paper frames erythromycin as a drug known to cause cholestatic hepatitis and aims to estimate the risk of cholestatic hepatitis of uncertain origin in recent recipients.

raw_record.support_text: Erythromycin is listed among the drugs responsible for drug-induced hepatitis, investigated in 2 human hepatitis cases using an ex-vivo drug antigen lymphocyte transformation test after a therapeutic 500 mg dose with blood collected 120 min after intake.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed in 'List of drugs responsible for the hepatitis' in the context of a study evaluating the ex-vivo drug antigen lymphocyte transformation test for diagnosing drug-induced hepatitis; 2 cases; dose 500 mg, blood collected 120 min after intake.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that jaundice usually occurs 10-12 days after starting erythromycin treatment (within 1-2 days if previously exposed to the drug), with liver function tests usually indicating cholestasis, accompanied by fever, rash, and pruritus, suggesting the jaundice is probably attributable to hypersensitivity cholestasis. The concluding statement in the case report asserts that erythromycin base must be added to the list of erythromycin derivatives that can cause rash and liver function disturbances.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of erythromycin base-associated hypersensitivity (cholestatic) hepatitis with jaundice, cholestasis on liver function tests, fever, rash, and pruritus; jaundice developed within 1-2 days because the patient had previously received the drug. Latency 10-12 days typical, shorter on rechallenge in prior recipients. Both allergic and toxic mechanisms may be involved in macrolide hepatotoxicity; reactive metabolites may cause minor liver lesions and slightly raised serum aminotransferase activity, and covalently modified plasma membrane proteins may trigger an immune response. In vitro rat liver plasma-membrane damage was shown for erythromycin estolate but not the base (supporting preclinical finding).

raw_record.support_text: Erythromycin, a macrolide antibiotic introduced in 1952, is reported to cause fatal fulminant hepatic failure in an elderly man after intravenous erythromycin lactobionate for a lower respiratory infection, and a combined cholestatic and hepatocellular injury in nine patients after initiation of erythromycin estolate or other erythromycin derivatives, with eight of nine developing jaundice within 3 weeks. The risk of cholestatic jaundice associated with erythromycin was reported in a retrospective cohort study.
raw_record.extra_details: Reports include fatal fulminant hepatic failure in an elderly man after IV erythromycin lactobionate; combined cholestatic and hepatocellular injury in 9 patients (8 jaundiced within 3 weeks) after erythromycin estolate or other erythromycin derivatives; risk of cholestatic jaundice reported in a retrospective cohort study.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents a patient with erythromycin-induced hepatitis whose initial radiologic studies showed nonspecific pseudotumoral liver infiltration (echogenic, poorly demarcated periportal lesions on ultrasound and hypoattenuated lesions on CT). Liver biopsy showed severe cholestasis with bile plugs, mild inflammatory infiltration, and some liver cell pleomorphism; ultrasound 10 weeks after treatment showed normal liver echogenicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of erythromycin-induced hepatitis presenting as pseudotumoral liver infiltration; US and contrast-enhanced CT showed poorly demarcated periportal/hypoattenuated lesions; biopsy showed severe cholestasis with bile plugs and mild inflammatory infiltration with liver-cell pleomorphism; imaging normalized 10 weeks after treatment. The authors note a lack of definitive proof that the radiologic abnormalities were due solely to erythromycin-induced hepatitis versus additional focal hepatic steatosis, and acknowledge the radiologic findings were nonspecific and could represent other nontumoral conditions.

raw_record.support_text: Erythromycin-associated DILI case reports were analyzed for liver-injury pattern, eosinophilia, hepatic necrosis, inflammatory reaction, and death/liver transplantation outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: 35 individual case reports; median age 45 y; 23 female/12 male; median treatment duration 1 week; HC 31%, Cs/mixed 69%; peripheral eosinophilia present in 34% (29/35 reported); hepatic eosinophilia present in 21% (14/35 reported); hepatic necrosis 20%; inflammatory reaction 67%; death or liver transplant 3%; liver biopsy reported in 15/35 cases.

raw_record.support_text: Ten of 80 patients receiving propionyl erythromycin ester lauryl sulfate developed evidence of hepatic injury, and 2 of these developed jaundice. Clinical features in 4 of 10 patients developing hepatic abnormality while receiving erythromycin were similar to those of viral hepatitis; 2 were initially diagnosed as viral hepatitis until the physicians accepted drug induction. A rise of SGPT to a high level of 2,060 in one patient after challenge led the authors to conclude the hepatic abnormality is hepatocellular rather than cholestatic. One liver biopsy showed periportal infiltration with lymphocytes, polymorphonuclear leukocytes, and many eosinophils with no bile stasis.
raw_record.extra_details: Administered as propionyl erythromycin ester lauryl sulfate (erythromycin estolate). Hepatic injury in 10/80 patients, 2 with jaundice; 4 of 10 resembled viral hepatitis; 1 presented like acute cholecystitis or pancreatitis. SGPT rose to 2,060 after challenge, supporting hepatocellular rather than cholestatic injury. One liver biopsy showed periportal lymphocytic infiltrate with polymorphonuclear leukocytes and many eosinophils, no bile stasis, in a non-jaundiced patient.

raw_record.support_text: Erythromycin is listed at position 9 in the RUCAM-based ranking of drugs causing DILI with verified causality (Table 10).
raw_record.extra_details: Ranked #9 in the RUCAM-based top-ranking of drugs causing DILI with verified causality (Teschke, 2018d).

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude erythromycin sensitivity is the likely cause of acute liver failure in this patient. They note that cholestatic jaundice due to erythromycin estolate is well known and that the patient had simple erythromycin BP, suggesting the erythromycin molecule itself, as well as the ester, is hepatotoxic.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-case report of acute liver failure with an unusually selective factor X deficiency (1% of normal), a less marked factor VII deficiency (24%), and a prolonged prothrombin time that increased despite 11 units of fresh frozen plasma and 8 units of factor IX concentrate (also containing factors II and X). The patient improved and at 1-month follow-up factor X activity was 136%, prothrombin time 31 s, AST 48 iu/litre, alkaline phosphatase 399 iu/litre. Liver biopsy was declined. Erythromycin sensitivity proposed as likely cause; the paper argues the erythromycin molecule itself, in addition to its esters, is hepatotoxic.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that for 10 RUCAM-based cases of iDILI (idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury) caused by erythromycin with an established HLA association, no suggestions of possible mechanistic steps leading to the liver injury were presented.
raw_record.extra_details: 10 RUCAM-based iDILI cases; causality assessed via RUCAM; established HLA association; no mechanistic steps proposed.

Liver function tests usually indicate cholestasis, with other symptoms including fever, rash, and pruritus, and the jaundice is considered probably attributable to 'hypersensitivity cholestasis'.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had previously received erythromycin, with jaundice developing within 1-2 days after re-exposure rather than the usual 10-12 days.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic jaundice with fever, rash, and pruritus; liver function tests indicated cholestasis; mechanism framed as hypersensitivity cholestasis. Both allergic and toxic mechanisms are suggested for macrolide hepatotoxicity, with the reactive metabolite possibly having mild hepatotoxic potential. An in vitro rat study (Dujoune and Salhab) showed erythromycin estolate, unlike the base, directly damaged rat liver cell plasma membranes (enzyme leakage, surface-scanning electron microscopy).

raw_record.support_text: A 10-year-old girl prescribed erythromycin ethylsuccinate for a respiratory illness developed jaundice, pruritus, abdominal pain, nausea, pale stools and dark urine after two doses. Investigations showed conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, elevated transaminases, alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase; viral hepatitis, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency and Wilson disease were excluded. Liver biopsy showed moderate panlobular parenchymatous degeneration with cholestasis and numerous intra- and intracellular bile plugs, consistent with a cholestatic jaundice associated with erythromycin. Clinical condition and liver function improved over 6-8 weeks after cessation of erythromycin, and she remained well at 1 year follow-up.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (10-year-old girl); erythromycin ethylsuccinate formulation; prior single exposure to erythromycin without problem; respiratory illness indication.
raw_record.extra_details: Symptoms began after two doses. Labs: total bilirubin 246 umol/L (conjugated 224 umol/L), ALT 278 IU/L, AST 173 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase rising to 1,209 IU/L, GGT 121 IU/L. Liver biopsy at week 4 showed panlobular parenchymatous degeneration with cholestasis and bile plugs, no periportal fibrosis; consistent with cholestatic jaundice. Recovery occurred over 6-8 weeks after drug cessation; well with normal LFTs at 1 year. Mechanism of erythromycin liver injury thought to be hypersensitivity or direct toxicity from a metabolite eliciting an immunologic response (author's discussion).
