raw_record.support_text: Case 3: a 53-year-old housewife received erythromycin (600 mg, 3 days) for a sore throat in October 1976. Hemorrhagic papules appeared on skin and oral mucosa 10 days later and jaundice 20 days later. After steroid therapy her course (except jaundice) improved. On admission abnormal data included serum total bilirubin 29.1 mg/dl (direct 24.3), alkaline phosphatase 1054 IU/l, and cholesterol 1062 mg/dl (continued in next paragraph). A diagnosis of drug-induced intrahepatic cholestasis was made, with mechanical obstruction of the extrahepatic biliary tree excluded at laparotomy; a wedge biopsy showed marked centrolobular bile stasis with feathery degeneration of hepatocytes and mild septal fibrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single 53-year-old female case; co-exposure to steroid therapy; competing mechanical obstruction excluded at laparotomy.
raw_record.extra_details: Erythromycin 600 mg for 3 days for sore throat; jaundice appeared 20 days after drug exposure. Lab values: serum total bilirubin 29.1 mg/dl (direct 24.3 mg/dl), alkaline phosphatase 1054 IU/l, cholesterol 1062 mg/dl. Biopsy showed marked centrolobular bile stasis with feathery degeneration of hepatocytes and mild septal fibrosis; many portal tracts devoid of interlobular bile ducts with acidophilic degeneration and occasional rupture. Elevation of alkaline phosphatase, cholesterol, and bilirubin remained unchanged for 41 months with slight fluctuation; patient alive. Case table labels the diagnosis 'chronic intrahepatic cholestasis** = probably drug-induced'.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that, in their 48-year-old female patient who presented with pruritus, jaundice, dark urine, hypocholia, nausea, vomiting and epigastric pain one week after taking 3 tablets of zolmitriptan for a severe migraine episode, the liver disease was very probably related to zolmitriptan use, based on the temporal relationship of symptoms to intake, resolution with conservative measures while avoiding re-exposure, and the exclusion of other causes of acute hepatitis (negative viral and autoimmune serology, normal abdominal ultrasound).
raw_record.extra_details: 48-year-old woman with no other risk factors for liver disease, no alcohol, drugs or other potentially hepatotoxic agents, no transfusions. Took 3 tablets of zolmitriptan one week before onset for severe migraine. Presentation: intense pruritus, jaundice, dark urine, hypocholia, nausea, vomiting, moderate epigastric pain. Elevated AST (355 U/l, normal <31), ALT (331 U/l, normal <31), alkaline phosphatase (530 U/l, normal <270), GGT (206 U/l, normal <32) and bilirubin (4.31, normal <1). Negative HCV/RNA, HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM, HAV IgM, EBV IgM, CMV, HEV IgM, HSV-1/2 IgM, Toxoplasma IgM; negative ANA, AMA, ASMA, p-ANCA and LKM-1. Normal albumin, prothrombin and abdominal ultrasound. Complete recovery with conservative measures; liver biopsy avoided. Paper notes the predominant presentation of drug-related liver disease is usually acute hepatitis or cholestatic liver disease and that the mechanism of acute toxic hepatitis is believed to be immunoallergic, tending to occur in immunologically susceptible individuals.

raw_record.support_text: The authors identified four individuals who, after consumption of Epistane (EPI, an orally administered 17α-alkylated testosterone derivative with a 2a-3a epithio ring), developed long-lasting cholestasis. In three patients the serum bile acid pool was increased 14- to 61-fold, mainly on account of primary conjugated bile acids (cholic acid conjugates). The paper concludes that EPI could cause cholestasis by inducing bile acid synthesis and favoring bile acid accumulation in hepatocytes, at least in part via androgen receptor activation, and anticipates that this explains the idiosyncratic nature of EPI-induced cholestasis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Four young males who took EPI orally in an intensive administration posology (body-builder misuse); onset was sudden and recovery of normal liver functions took many weeks after discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: EPI is 17α-methylated epitiostanol (C20H32OS, CAS 2363-58-8), a potent AR agonist. Patients developed severe cholestasis with jaundice and pruritus; some required MARS albumin dialysis to lower bilirubin levels. Pure (bland) cholestasis with prominent conjugated bilirubin rise and moderate/minimal ALT, AST, AP elevations, no hepatocellular necrosis. In vitro: EPI (0.01 µM) upregulated CYP7A1 (~65%) and CYP8B1 (~67%) and BA transporters (NTCP, OSTA, BSEP), downregulated FGF19; 40 µM activated LXR and PXR; 0.01 µM activated AR and induced bile acid synthesis/accumulation in cultured human hepatocytes. Human liver bank samples showed AR expression positively correlated with CYP8B1 in men. Context: AAS DILI rose from 1% (2007-2009) to 8% (2010-2013) of Spanish DILI Registry cases.

raw_record.support_text: When quetiapine was stopped and supportive management was started, the patient's laboratory profiles showed a persistently declining trend. The patient's improvement after stopping quetiapine strongly favored the drug being responsible for the hepatic injury. Because the injury persisted for weeks even after stopping the drug rather than resolving with drug washout, it points to the idiosyncratic nature of the injury, with the injury developing during dose escalation being coincidental rather than causal. Naranjo scale scoring gave a score of 8, categorized as a probable adverse drug reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case report. Naranjo ADR scale score 8 = probable ADR. Injury persisted for weeks after stopping quetiapine, improving only after drug cessation; dose escalation was considered coincidental rather than causal. Management followed American College of Gastroenterology guidelines, which note no definitive therapies are available for idiosyncratic DILI with or without acute liver failure. Quetiapine usually causes mild, transient, asymptomatic transaminase increases; recent case reports suggest idiosyncratic liver injury can be associated, mechanism unknown.

raw_record.support_text: According to the authors, to their knowledge there is only one documented case of subfulminant liver failure associated with quetiapine, and this case ultimately led to death.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as the only documented subfulminant liver failure case associated with quetiapine known to the authors; in the compiled table (El Hajj 2004) this case showed ALT 1245 units/L and total bilirubin 297 mg/dL and was fatal.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report that their patient developed an acute liver injury 3 days after starting quetiapine at a dose well within the therapeutic range, with no concurrent medications, and conclude the patient 'likely had a quetiapine-induced idiosyncratic reaction' given the very short duration of exposure before liver injury. Photomicrographs accompanying the report showed hepatocytic degeneration and necrosis, hepatocanalicular cholestasis, and portal and lobular lymphocytic infiltrate with lobular disarray.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver injury developed 3 days after starting quetiapine in the therapeutic dose range; latency very short. Histology showed hepatocytic degeneration and necrosis, hepatocanalicular cholestasis, and portal/lobular lymphocytic infiltrate. Authors note quetiapine is widely prescribed and physicians should be aware of potential serious hepatotoxicity.

Quetiapine (Seroquel; AstraZeneca) is an atypical antipsychotic generally well tolerated at 150-750 mg/day; acute liver injury is described as a rarely reported adverse effect. Other studies found methadone doses could be safely continued in patients with stable liver disease, and a cellular-level study found therapeutic doses unlikely to produce irreversible hepatocyte damage.

raw_record.support_text: A 44-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis started teriflunomide 14 mg orally once daily (plus vitamin D 60,000 IU daily) and after 54 days reported abdominal pain, loss of appetite, vomiting, and nausea, with worsening for a week. Laboratory results showed ALT 1384 U/L, AST 612 U/L, GGT 690 U/L, total bilirubin 1.20 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin 0.50 mg/dL. The case was considered probable hepatotoxicity associated with teriflunomide and treatment was suspended. The adverse reaction was notified to the Brazilian Pharmacovigilance Service, and the Naranjo causality score was 7, indicating the drug was probably associated with the reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Relapsing-remitting MS patient; teriflunomide 14 mg/day orally for <2 months (54 days) before symptoms; also daily vitamin D 60,000 IU (not implicated as cause). Symptoms: abdominal pain, loss of appetite, vomiting, nausea. Labs: ALT 1384 U/L, AST 612 U/L, GGT 690 U/L, total bilirubin 1.20 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.50 mg/dL. Treatment suspended; adverse drug reaction notified to Brazilian Pharmacovigilance; Naranjo causality score 7 (probable). Patient denied alcohol, other medications, herbal medicines; no prior liver disease. Background: transient ALT elevation up to 3x ULN expected in first 6 months of teriflunomide at frequencies 14.2%–15.8%, with discontinuation described in up to 3% of cases.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of probable teriflunomide-induced liver injury as assessed for causality using the updated RUCAM. The liver injury occurred approximately nine months after teriflunomide initiation and improved with discontinuation of the drug and treatment with cholestyramine.
raw_record.extra_details: 60-year-old woman with relapsing multiple sclerosis treated with teriflunomide 14 mg daily; onset ~9 months after initiation with initially normal liver tests. On presentation: AST 1,499 U/L, ALT 777 U/L, AP 478 U/L, total bilirubin 2.5 mg/dL, INR 1.20; jaundice, fatigue, anorexia, altered mental status. Causality assessed with updated RUCAM (probable score). Liver biopsy most consistent with drug-induced injury with a minor steatohepatitis component; treated with cholestyramine 4 g every 6 hours for accelerated elimination starting hospital day 7; liver tests improved and teriflunomide discontinued indefinitely. Competing causes (hepatitis/herpes serologies, autoimmune markers, iron overload, acetaminophen) largely excluded.

raw_record.support_text: Although disopyramide has fewer gastrointestinal side effects, cases of hepatotoxicity have been reported, as well as hepatic ischemia secondary to cardiac failure by passive congestion. Rarely, disopyramide can cause cholestatic jaundice that in most cases appears within the first week of taking the medication and generally resolves promptly on discontinuation. A case of severe hepatocellular toxicity with disseminated intravascular coagulation was reported, which improved after discontinuation of disopyramide.
raw_record.extra_details: Comparison of disopyramide-induced hepatotoxicity cases (Scheinman et al. two cases: hepatic necrosis with congestion on biopsy, elevated AST/ALT/LDH, improved on day six after discontinuation, recurrence of symptoms on rechallenge with the drug switched to procainamide; second case improved with diuresis, liver enzymes normalized, and recurred on rechallenge). Doody case: severe hepatocellular toxicity with disseminated intravascular coagulation (prolonged PT, elevated fibrin split products), liver enzymes and functions improved 14 days after discontinuation. Barkins et al. case: jaundice and abnormal liver enzymes after one week, prompt clinical resolution on discontinuation. Also noted hepatic ischemia secondary to cardiac failure/passive congestion (indirect mechanism) and negative inotropic effect worsening heart failure. Generally cholestatic jaundice appears within first week.

raw_record.support_text: A letter to the editor reports that cholestatic jaundice has been described in at least three patients on disopyramide, and the authors observed three additional patients with cholestasis probably related to disopyramide. The patients had no hepatosplenomegaly, fever, abdominal pain, or heart failure; tests for hepatitis B surface antigen, alpha-fetoprotein, and antimitochondrial antibodies were negative.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic jaundice; at least three prior reported patients plus three newly observed cases. Patients had no hepatosplenomegaly, fever, abdominal pain, or heart failure; tests for hepatitis B surface antigen, alpha-fetoprotein, and antimitochondrial antibodies were negative. Disopyramide (Norpace; G.D. Searle & Company) is an antiarrhythmic agent marketed in Europe since 1969.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report three new patients with cholestasis probably related to disopyramide (Norpace). The patients had no hepatosplenomegaly, fever, abdominal pain, or heart failure; tests for hepatitis B surface antigen, alpha-fetoprotein, and antimitochondrial antibodies were negative.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients: a 63-year-old man on digoxin, isosorbide dinitrate, and disopyramide 400 mg/d who became jaundiced 10 days after starting, with cholestasis lasting 4 months; a 60-year-old man on dipyridamole, K-strophanthin, and disopyramide 300 mg/d with jaundice 10 days later clearing after 7 months; and a 79-year-old woman on K-strophanthin, oxazepam, furosemide, and pentaerythritol tetranitrate who developed pruritus (without jaundice) 15 days after adding disopyramide 300 mg/d. Surgical exploration/IV cholangiography confirmed a normal biliary system in each. The authors attribute the cholestasis to disopyramide because no cholestatic reactions have been reported for the concurrent drugs, patients were on different drugs except disopyramide, there was a fixed 10-15 day interval between starting the drug and onset of cholestasis, and doses were within the normal therapeutic range.

raw_record.support_text: A 74-year-old man treated for paroxysmal ventricular tachycardia with intravenous disopyramide (2.0 mg/kg followed by 0.2 mg/kg/hour, then 150 mg po qid) developed abnormal liver function tests three days after initiation. Serum alanine aminotransferase peaked on the fourth day at 6,200 U/L (normal <35), alkaline phosphatase rose to 125 U/L (normal 25-100), bilirubin to 68 µmol/L (normal <20), and the prothrombin ratio was prolonged to 2.6. Complete reversal of the biochemical abnormalities over 14 days after disopyramide was ceased strongly suggested drug hepatotoxicity. Liver biopsy six days after cessation showed nonspecific inflammatory changes without intrahepatic cholestasis. Low cardiac output and congestive cardiac failure, other hepatotoxic agents, and hepatitis antigen/antibody were excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Administered intravenously (2.0 mg/kg then 0.2 mg/kg/hour) followed by oral disopyramide 150 mg qid for paroxysmal ventricular tachycardia. ALT peaked at 6,200 U/L (normal <35), ALP 125 U/L, bilirubin 68 µmol/L, prothrombin ratio 2.6. Abnormal liver tests appeared ~3 days after start, resolving fully over 14 days after drug cessation. Liver biopsy showed nonspecific inflammatory changes with no intrahepatic cholestasis (intrahepatic cholestasis noted as a rarely reported toxic effect of the drug). Low cardiac output and congestive heart failure, other hepatotoxic agents, and hepatitis antigen/antibody were reasonably excluded.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a new case of a male patient treated with cyproterone acetate (CPA) for advanced prostate cancer who developed acute liver failure (ALF) during treatment, with a fatal outcome. The authors note that CPA has been evidentially correlated with a wide spectrum of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) and is frequently related to ALF, that the first CPA-induced case of fulminant hepatitis with fatal outcome was described in 1989, and that 18 cases of ALF have been reported to date.
raw_record.extra_details: Steroidal synthetic progestagen and anti-androgen used in advanced prostate cancer. Injury manifested as fulminant (acute) hepatitis progressing to acute liver failure with encephalopathy in a patient without cirrhosis or preexisting liver disease, and resulted in death. First fatal case described in 1989; 18 cases of CPA-associated ALF reported to date. The presented new case involved a male patient; the letter does not specify causality scores, histology, laboratory values, or rechallenge.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that cyproterone acetate (CPA), an anti-androgenic drug for advanced prostate cancer, has been associated with drug-induced liver injury (DILI). The authors describe the phenotype and outcome of 22 patients with CPA-induced hepatotoxicity (the largest series reported to date) and observed a wide spectrum of acute liver injury associated with CPA therapeutic intake, comprising three cases of corticosteroid-responsive hepatitis, including a first-reported, well-documented case of associated autoimmune hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Anti-androgenic steroidal drug used for advanced prostate cancer, breast cancer, acne, hirsutism, precocious puberty, priapism and hypersexual disorder; described as a low-degree inducer of liver-related adverse reactions with a weaker association with hepatotoxicity than flutamide or bicalutamide. Largest series of CPA hepatotoxicity reported; wide spectrum of acute liver injury included three corticosteroid-responsive hepatitis cases, among them a first well-documented case of associated autoimmune hepatitis. Fulminant hepatitis cases are included in the CPA-induced liver injury spectrum.

raw_record.support_text: Cyproterone treatment was stopped and the patient's hepatic function progressively returned to normal. Use of the Naranjo probability scale indicated a highly probable relationship between acute hepatitis and cyproterone treatment in this patient, who had received oral CPA 300 mg/d for seven months for prostate adenocarcinoma.
raw_record.extra_details: 87-year-old man with prostate adenocarcinoma received oral CPA 300 mg/d for 7 months, presenting with jaundice, fatigue, arthralgias, myalgias, dark urine, white stools; no prior liver disease and no other medications or alcohol. Liver biopsy showed acute cholestatic hepatitis with focal hepatocellular necrosis, portal and lobular inflammation, and marked cholestasis with bile plugs; CT indicated mild steatosis. All viral hepatitis serologies, autoantibodies, alfa-fetoprotein and carcinoembryonic antigen were negative/within range. Liver function returned to normal within two weeks; patient recovered and remained healthy. Naranjo scale scored highly probable. The introduction also states CPA has been associated with 4 described cases of acute hepatitis, 10 cases of fatal fulminant hepatic failure, and 4 cases of hepatocellular carcinoma; acute hepatitis typically develops a few weeks to 2-3 months after starting CPA, while hepatocellular carcinoma develops from 6 months to 10 years later.

raw_record.support_text: A case series of 22 males (70 ± 8 years, range 54–83) with prostate cancer treated with cyproterone acetate (CPA) 150 ± 50 mg/day (range 50–200) who developed CPA-induced liver injury was collected from 1993 to 2013. Latency was 163 ± 97 days. Most patients were symptomatic showing hepatocellular injury (91%) and jaundice. Severity was mild in 1, moderate in 7, severe in 11 and fatal in 3 (14%); five developed ascites, four encephalopathy, and one had liver injury resembling autoimmune hepatitis. RUCAM was 'highly probable' in 19 (86%), 'probable' in 1, and 'possible' in 2. The authors conclude CPA-induced liver injury is severe, can be fatal, and may occasionally resemble autoimmune DILI.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly male prostate-cancer patients (70 ± 8 years; range 54–83); therapeutic daily dose 50–200 mg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: 22 cases. Latency 163 ± 97 days. Liver tests at onset: ALT 18 ± 13 x ULN, ALP 0.7 ± 0.7 x ULN, total serum bilirubin 14 ± 10 mg/dl. INR >1.5 in 14 (66%). Severity: mild 4%, moderate 32%, severe 50%, fatal 14%. Ascites in 5, encephalopathy in 4; 4 developed ALF features; 11 (50%) hospitalized. One case resembled autoimmune hepatitis; 3 required steroids (two with high ANA titres). Liver biopsy in 7 patients: two hepatocellular collapse, one submassive necrosis, two cholestatic hepatitis, one cirrhosis with iron overload, one autoimmune hepatitis. RUCAM highly probable 86%, probable 4%, possible 9%.

raw_record.support_text: A 66-year-old male patient with advanced prostate adenocarcinoma, treated with cyproterone acetate (CPA) 200 mg/day for advanced prostate cancer, developed severe drug-induced hepatotoxicity after about four months, presenting with marked fatigue, jaundice and dark urine. Laboratory values included total bilirubin 22.3 mg/dL, AST 1,487 IU/mL, ALT 2,044 IU/mL, AP 223 IU/mL, GGT 335 IU/mL, and prothrombin index 43% at a later point. Drug-induced hepatitis caused by CPA was suspected, other causes of liver injury were excluded, and the patient was diagnosed with toxic acute hepatitis according to the CIOMS scale with a score of 9. Liver biopsy showed extensive periportal necrosis, intense interface hepatitis, and evolution to active cirrhosis, improving after CPA withdrawal and corticosteroid treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly patient (66 years) with advanced prostate adenocarcinoma; treated with prolonged high-dose CPA (200 mg/day); prior treatment with bicalutamide and goserelin; comorbid corticosteroid-induced hyperglycemia/diabetes during management.
raw_record.extra_details: CPA, an oral anti-androgen, 200 mg/day; symptom onset after approximately 4 months of treatment. CIOMS/RUCAM causality score 9; rechallenge not performed for ethical reasons. Laboratory peaks: total bilirubin up to 29.1 mg/dL, AST 1359-1487 IU/mL, ALT 1655-2044 IU/mL, AP 223-242 IU/mL, GGT 195-335 IU/mL, PI 43%. Histology: extensive periportal necrosis, intense interface hepatitis with lymphocyte predominance, inflammatory septa, progressing to active cirrhosis; moderate steatosis on ultrasound; transient elastography fell from 72 to 19 kPa over two years. Managed with prednisone, budesonide, and ursodeoxycholic acid; patient recovered. The paper notes direct hepatotoxicity mediated by an idiosyncratic mechanism was hypothesized by some authors, and that adverse hepatic reactions may be more common in elderly patients with malignant disease on prolonged high doses.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports three patients who developed symptomatic hepatic dysfunction and states that the implication that oxacillin is the agent responsible is warranted. Two of the three had also received thiamylal sodium prior to onset, but barbiturates are not known to cause hepatitis, and none of the other received drugs are known hepatotoxins. All three received oxacillin intravenously, none had preexisting liver disease, blood transfusions, or hepatitis contact; the rapid reversibility of symptoms and abnormal liver function on discontinuation of oxacillin argues for drug-induced hepatitis rather than viral hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Three cases all received intravenous oxacillin; none had preexisting liver disease, blood transfusions, or known hepatitis contact. No patient was jaundiced; liver function abnormality was primarily a transaminasemia. Rapid reversibility of symptoms and liver function on oxacillin discontinuation (dechallenge) supported drug-induced hepatitis. Serologic hepatitis-associated antigen tests and liver biopsy were not performed. Authors attribute the pathogenesis to a drug-induced hypersensitivity reaction, supported by lack of dose-duration correlation and uncommon occurrence. Cited prior studies: Walker and Standiford noted SGOT elevation in 2 of 91 newborns/infants on intramuscular oxacillin 200 mg/kg/day (none of 13 at 400 mg/kg/day); Huang et al. noted transient SGOT elevation in 1 of 15 children with cystic fibrosis on oral oxacillin 50-100 mg/kg/day (total 162-840 g); an earlier study saw reversible transaminasemia in two of six patients on IM oxacillin 100 mg/kg/day.

raw_record.support_text: Using specified criteria, the authors identified eight cases of oxacillin-associated hepatitis among patients treated with oxacillin; 46 cases remained with normal liver functions during oxacillin therapy and were treated as the control group. Liver function abnormalities were characteristic of hepatocellular injury, with elevated serum transaminases and lactic dehydrogenases in all eight patients, alkaline phosphatase twice normal in only three, and normal bilirubin levels.
raw_record.extra_details: Total oxacillin dose before onset of hepatitis ranged from 16 to 300 g; symptoms (nausea/vomiting in four, heartburn in one) appeared 3 to 21 days after instituting oxacillin; three patients were asymptomatic; six patients were febrile, with a second temperature peak in five attributed to the hepatitis; one pruritic rash; hepatomegaly in four; hepatic tenderness in one. Resolution of abnormal liver functions occurred within 1 to 7 days (mean 4.6 days) in five patients, two were improving at discharge with normalization only 4 and 8 months later, and one was lost to follow-up. Eosinophilia observed in two patients. Route of exposure included intravenous and intramuscular administration.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of cholestatic hepatitis due to sodium oxacillin (Prostaphlin), documented by liver biopsy, and states that, as far as the authors know, no such case had previously been reported for this agent or other natural or semi-synthetic penicillins, whereas erythromycin estolate, triacetyloleandomycin, and chlorpromazine have caused this reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: 65-year-old white woman with cellulitis of the right leg; sodium oxacillin given orally at 2 gm/day, increased to 6 gm/day on admission, then 500 mg twice a day, total dose 76 gm. Pruritus (itching) developed around discharge and became marked; clinical icterus noted April 6. Elevated alkaline phosphatase (7.6 and 7.5 units), total bilirubin 2.15 and direct 1.92 mg/100 ml, sulfobromophthalein retention 25-28%, cholesterol 312 mg/100 ml; SGOT 76 King-Armstrong units. Liver biopsy May 1 showed mild bile pigment plugging in canaliculi and intracellular bile pigment without focal necrosis. Shelley's basophil degranulation test for hypersensitivity to oxacillin was negative. Cholecystogram showed no filling defects; patient received trimeprazine tartrate as antipruritic. Authors note the reaction is intrahepatic cholestasis due to allergic drug sensitivity.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that elevation of transaminase levels in their patient was directly attributable to oxacillin. Infectious, autoimmune, toxic, and Wilson's-disease causes of hepatitis were excluded, and hepatic dysfunction gradually resolved after discontinuance of oxacillin therapy; substitution with cefazolin produced no deterioration in liver enzyme profile or clinical symptoms.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of oxacillin-induced hepatitis in a patient treated at 200 mg/kg/day; hepatitis was diagnosed after 14 days of therapy, with initial ALT 1,452 U/mL, elevated AST, and prolonged prothrombin time that returned to normal; the patient was symptomatic (abdominal pain, fever) yet anicteric with no rash, lymphadenopathy, or joint involvement, and recovered after oxacillin was stopped. Literature cited: a series of 41 adults with oxacillin-induced hepatitis (AST/ALT 210/125 to 800/700 units), a 4-year-old girl (AST/ALT 1,110/1,359), and a heroin abuser (AST/ALT 1,380/1,164 on day 28); prior cases were mainly adults with underlying conditions such as drug abuse, endocarditis, and HIV infection. Elevated liver enzymes were reported from as early as 5 days to as late as 35 days after starting oxacillin, with serum alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin usually normal and higher daily doses suggested to increase hepatitis risk. Cholestatic hepatitis has also been reported with oxacillin in some patients. Mechanism uncertain (chemical vs immunologic); isoxazole ring degradation to 2-butanone and hydroxylamine postulated, with glutathione scavenging suggested protective; HIV-infected patients reportedly unusually sensitive to oxacillin chemical hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes eight cases of oxacillin-associated hepatitis and concludes the hepatitis was probably a hypersensitivity reaction, based on eosinophilia in two patients and pruritus in one, variable oxacillin dose before onset, recurrence of hepatitis upon rechallenge with oxacillin in one patient, and a statistically significant association with previous or subsequent penicillin allergy (three of eight versus none of 46, P<0.01). Withdrawal of oxacillin led to resolution of the liver function abnormalities, and the authors recommend liver function test evaluation in all patients receiving high-dose intravenous oxacillin.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose intravenous oxacillin; significant association with previous or subsequent penicillin allergy (3/8 vs 0/46). Several cases had concomitant drugs (methadone, acetaminophen, hydralazine, streptomycin, etc.) as potential co-exposures.
raw_record.extra_details: Eight-case case series. Presenting features included nausea, vomiting, hepatomegaly, hepatic tenderness, and abdominal distention; eosinophilia in two patients and pruritus in one. Hepatitis recurred on rechallenge with oxacillin in one patient; liver function abnormalities resolved on drug withdrawal. Prior reported oxacillin hepatitis cases: biopsy-proven cholestatic jaundice in a 65-y-old woman after 76 g oral oxacillin; hepatic injury in a 33-y-old woman after 270 g oral oxacillin; and three anicteric hepatitis cases after 9-12 days of high-dose intravenous oxacillin (Dismukes).

raw_record.support_text: In this patient series, abemaciclib was one of the two CDK4/6 inhibitors mainly involved in CDK4/6 inhibitor-induced liver injury (alongside ribociclib). The predominant liver-injury type was hepatocellular, with autoimmune features (positive anti-nuclear antibodies and/or elevated serum IgG) present in 32% of patients. Corticosteroids were given in 40% of patients and permitted resolution of liver injury that had not improved spontaneously. No patient developed fulminant hepatitis or died from the anti-CDK4/6-induced liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Paper argues CDK4/6 inhibitors should be included in the drug-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis (DI-ALH) category given autoimmune features (ANA and/or elevated IgG in 1/3 of patients), consistent histology, and corticosteroid response without relapse after discontinuation. Corticosteroids started about 1 month after hepatitis onset and were given in 40% of patients; some patients resumed a different CDK4/6 inhibitor after resolution without relapse. Management: discontinue at hepatitis grade 3 or 4. No fulminant hepatitis or death.

raw_record.support_text: A 65-year-old woman treated with ceftriaxone 2g q12 for S. pneumoniae bacteremia/pneumonia represented with lethargy and a mildly tender liver, and laboratory data showed a transaminitis (ALT 1129 IU/L, AST 1077 IU/L), elevated alkaline phosphatase 144 IU/L, and normal total bilirubin; viral and autoimmune hepatitis panels and CBC without eosinophilia argued against those causes and the presentation was described as drug-induced hepatitis. After ceftriaxone was discontinued (switched to vancomycin), transaminases and alkaline phosphatase began to fall within 48 hours and normalized two weeks later, and ceftriaxone was added to the allergy list. The case is titled 'Ceftriaxone-induced Acute Hepatitis: An Idiosyncratic Drug Reaction.'
raw_record.extra_details: Cephalosporin antibiotic given at 2g q12 for S. pneumoniae pneumonia/bacteremia with a planned one-month duration; injury presented about two weeks later with lethargy, fatigue, and mild liver tenderness; labs ALT 1129 IU/L, AST 1077 IU/L, ALP 144 IU/L, normal total bilirubin; CBC without eosinophilia; negative viral and autoimmune hepatitis panels; normal RUQ ultrasound; discontinued and switched to vancomycin; dechallenge showed transaminases/ALP falling within 48 hours and normalizing in two weeks; ceftriaxone added to the patient's allergy list. Lack of eosinophilia, lymphadenopathy, and typical drug rash argued against drug hypersensitivity and was considered more consistent with drug-induced hepatitis.

raw_record.extra_details: Metronidazole 250 mg b.i.d. per os added to vancomycin/netilmicin therapy for Bacteroides fragilis abscess; netilmicin stopped at the same time. Hepatotoxicity appeared 4 days after metronidazole initiation with drowsiness, vomiting, nausea, right-upper-quadrant pain and moderately enlarged liver; AST 1,450 IU/l (normal <27), ALT 650 IU/l (normal <20), no evidence of cholestasis. Pre-treatment values were unremarkable (AST 17, ALT 14). After metronidazole withdrawal enzymes decreased within 4 days and returned to normal in 15 days. Viral hepatitis A/B/delta and HIV serologies negative. Authors attribute toxicity partly to age and impaired renal function (hydroxy metabolite accumulation), since the parent drug half-life is not altered in renal impairment. Only 2 prior published cases of metronidazole-associated hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of curcumin-induced hepatocellular DILI in a 78-year old female admitted with jaundice after a one-month latency, with unremarkable evaluation for alternative etiologies. The Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) score of 6 for the supplement indicated a probable association. Peak AST and ALT were >20 times the upper limit of normal, a 48% decrease in AST/ALT occurred 7 days after discontinuation, and transaminitis resolved in 42 days; no re-challenge was performed. The authors conclude that curcumin supplements should be recognized as DILI triggers.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 78-year-old female patient; the culprit was an over-the-counter curcumin supplement taken once daily; long-standing co-medications (aspirin, citalopram, losartan, metformin, oxybutynin) taken for at least a year were not implicated.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM score of 6 indicated probable association (score >8 would indicate highly probable). Latency about one month. Jaundice with acholic stools for one week; no fever, abdominal pain, pruritus, or alcohol use. Peak AST and ALT >20x upper limit of normal. 48% decrease in AST/ALT at 7 days after supplement discontinuation; full resolution of transaminitis in 42 days. No re-challenge performed. Manifestation reported as Grade 3 DILI (severe hepatotoxicity) with complete recovery on discontinuation. Curcumin is a constituent of turmeric (Curcuma longa); supplement curcumin levels higher than the 3.14% curcuminoid content of turmeric powder.

raw_record.support_text: After a first course of sertraline therapy was associated with symptomatic hepatitis and an elevated serum ALT, the patient resumed sertraline for worsening depression; three weeks later her serum ALT rose significantly. Sertraline was discontinued again and her ALT fell to the normal range over 89 days, and was later shown to have dropped near normal within four weeks of the first discontinuation. Inadvertent rechallenge with sertraline was followed by a prompt rise in ALT, a rechallenge phenomenon the authors consider diagnostic of drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report (Persky and Reinus). Rechallenge (inadvertent) after resumption of sertraline produced a prompt rise in serum ALT, described as diagnostic of DILI. Liver biopsy during second admission showed lobular disarray with lymphocytic infiltrate, scattered neutrophils and eosinophils, spotty hepatocyte necrosis, and Councilman bodies, consistent with drug-induced or autoimmune hepatitis. Diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis was made initially and treated with oral prednisone 20 mg daily; ALT did not permanently normalize on corticosteroids, and hepatitis was later presumed sertraline-induced rather than autoimmune. Viral, autoimmune, and metabolic etiologies negative (anti-HAV, HBsAg, anti-HCV, ANA, ceruloplasmin, ferritin, CMV). Prior acetaminophen use was only at therapeutic doses with serum level <10 µg/ml at presentation. ALT normalized within 89 days after permanent sertraline discontinuation; depression subsequently treated with amitriptyline.

raw_record.support_text: The association of DILI with HLA-A*33:01/proxy SNP rs114577328 was specifically confirmed with sertraline, with a carrier frequency of 0.75 (3 of 4 sertraline-related DILI cases).
raw_record.extra_details: Confirmed HLA-A*33:01/rs114577328 association with sertraline-induced DILI; A*33:01 carrier frequency 0.75 (3/4 sertraline-related cases).

raw_record.support_text: Sertraline is listed among the causal DILI drugs known to have HLA alleles as the main genetic risk association, and the paper found enrichment of rs2476601 among European DILI cases due to such drugs. It is recorded as one of the drugs causally implicated in the DILI cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: Known to have HLA alleles as main genetic risk association for DILI; 6 cases in rs2476601 analysis, OR 1.17 (95% CI 0.15–9.27), P = .88.

raw_record.support_text: This case illustrates severe hepatotoxicity with clinical presentations attributed to sertraline treatment for depression, evidenced by marked elevations in aminotransferase levels (AST and ALT), bilirubin, ALP, and GGT, which gradually normalized within 90 days following the discontinuation of sertraline. Marked improvement in liver tests after sertraline was discontinued supported the diagnosis of sertraline-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report of sertraline treatment for depression. On admission (day 0) AST 236 U/L, ALT 553 U/L, ALP 153 U/L, GGT 117 U/L, total bilirubin 87 mmol/L, direct bilirubin 64 mmol/L; peak ALT 872 U/L on day 3. Acute liver injury with significant initial elevation of liver enzymes and bilirubin; gradual improvement by day 10 and progressive recovery to near-normal levels by day 90 after discontinuation. Dechallenge with marked improvement in liver function tests supported the diagnosis. Patient continued cognitive behavioral therapy thereafter; no antidepressants administered because the patient declined pharmacotherapy.

raw_record.support_text: The patient's adverse drug reaction was scored with the Naranjo algorithm, which categorizes reactions as Definite (score 9), Probable (5–8), Possible (1–4), or Doubtful (≤0). The patient's total Naranjo score was 7, corresponding to a probable adverse drug reaction, i.e., probable sertraline-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo causality score 7 (probable). Present case: 6 months of therapy, nausea, weakness, scleral jaundice and dark urine; maximal ALT 1,880 U/l, AST 810 U/l, total bilirubin 3.5 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 1.2 mg/dl. The paper also reviewed six earlier case reports of possible sertraline-induced hepatotoxicity, one of which (Kim et al., 1999) followed a suicidal overdose. Both transaminase and ALP–GGT increases suggested a mixed injury for the present and some prior cases. Presence of eosinophils in the liver biopsy suggested an immunologic mechanism, and an idiosyncratic reaction was also assumed.

raw_record.support_text: In the authors' patient, the temporal relationship between sertraline initiation and symptoms, along with biochemical and symptomatic improvement following drug discontinuation, strongly pointed toward sertraline-induced hepatotoxicity. The patient was also taking ranitidine and metoclopramide, but the paper judged their contribution theoretically possible yet unlikely to be of major clinical significance because ranitidine is only a minor substrate of cytochrome P450 2D6. The diagnosis of sertraline-induced hepatotoxicity requires exclusion of viral, autoimmune and hereditary causes.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient was concurrently on ranitidine and metoclopramide (co-exposure); contribution from these co-medications was considered theoretically possible but unlikely to be of major clinical significance. Diagnosis required exclusion of viral, autoimmune and hereditary liver conditions.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of sertraline-induced hepatotoxicity (acute liver injury). In a separate cited case (Persky and Reinus), inadvertent rechallenge with sertraline in a 23-year-old woman produced a prompt rise in ALT, suggestive of an anamnestic response; intentional rechallenge was not performed in the authors' patient due to medical risk. Theories of mechanism include immunologically mediated hepatitis supported by eosinophils on liver biopsy and the idiosyncratic reaction, and mitochondrial dysfunction with ATP depletion and inhibition of mitochondrial respiration. Sertraline inhibits cytochrome P450 2D6, which can raise levels of co-administered drugs. Sertraline-induced liver toxicity is considered rare.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a patient who developed jaundice and elevated liver enzymes after 17 months of acetohexamide therapy for diabetes, with symptoms appearing shortly after a substantial dose increase. Peripheral eosinophilia and fever accompanied the liver damage, suggesting a hypersensitivity reaction. The hepatitis resolved after acetohexamide was discontinued and insulin therapy began, with bilirubin and liver enzymes normalizing gradually and the patient remaining in good health one year later. The authors discuss that a metabolite of acetohexamide might have been the offending agent at the higher dose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Therapy for diabetes (insulin likely for diabetic control); patient was asymptomatic for 17 months and developed symptoms after a substantial increase in acetohexamide dosage; the authors speculate a metabolite of acetohexamide may have been the offending agent at the increased dose.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented as 'Acetohexamide-Induced Hepatitis'. Admission labs: total bilirubin 7.0 mg/dL (normal 0-1.0), alkaline phosphatase 567 U/L (0-110), SGOT 149 U/L (0-40), WBC 11.4 x10^3/µl, eosinophils 0.300 x10^3/µl; values peaked by day 2-6 then normalized by day 30 (bilirubin 0.8, alkaline phosphatase 183, SGOT 29, eosinophils normal). Peripheral eosinophilia and fever supported a hypersensitivity reaction. Recovery after discontinuation of acetohexamide and institution of insulin. The patient remained in good health 1 year after the jaundice episode. The authors note only two prior case reports of acetohexamide-induced liver disease: Goldstein and Rothenberg (jaundice 3 weeks after acetohexamide 500 mg daily plus chlorothiazide 500 mg daily, biopsy showing acute parenchymal disease and portal eosinophilia, resolution on discontinuation, but persistent hepatomegaly with macronodular cirrhosis on second biopsy and rechallenge with both drugs not inducing further damage), and Duncan et al. 1965 (patient on multiple medications including tolbutamide, phenytoin, phenobarbital, probenecid, colchicine, quinine, with past ethanol abuse, nonspecific biopsy changes). Balodimas et al. reported 20 cases of jaundice among an estimated 200,000 acetohexamide recipients up to 1965.

raw_record.support_text: Following post-marketing exposure, two cases of reversible hepatocellular liver injury were reported by different healthcare professionals, suggesting drug-related liver injury had occurred. In both patients, hepatic biochemical test abnormalities resolved when atomoxetine was stopped, and one case of hepatitis recurred following rechallenge with atomoxetine, supporting a causal relationship. These cases were deemed sufficient evidence of an increased risk of liver toxicity to warrant a 2004 label change for atomoxetine. Considering the now extensive exposure (>4 million patients after 4 years), these reactions are very rare and fit the pattern of an idiosyncratic drug reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Three cases of liver injury probably related to atomoxetine are known to Eli Lilly and Company; case 4 was reclassified as only possibly related because of a second hepatitis episode after atomoxetine was discontinued, while cases 2 and 3 were deemed probably related. Estimated global exposure was about 2.2 million patients when the initial cases arose, and >4 million patients after 4 years. Spontaneous adverse event reporting rate of liver injury, regardless of aetiology, was <0.01% (351 cases among 4,328,000 exposed patients); reporting rate was 23.7 per 100,000 person-years, within the range of background liver injury rates (0.7–164.9 per 100,000 person-years). A 2004 US package insert label change included a warning with a Dear healthcare professional letter. Preclinical testing in rats, mice and dogs showed no liver toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The discussion states that LEF (leflunomide) leads to drug-induced liver injury or even acute drug-induced hepatitis, probably by inhibiting the activity of the CYP2C9 enzyme. After LEF treatment, AST and ALT levels rose in all patients, with 14 cases showing increases twice the normal limit (including one chronic HBV patient with alcoholism diagnosed as fatty liver disease) and 5 cases with HBV-DNA increases related to hepatitis B activity. In the other groups, 9 cases with elevated liver enzymes and negative HBV-DNA returned to normal transaminase levels once LEF was discontinued. The paper concludes that LEF-induced liver injury is transient and reversible after dose reduction or discontinuation, that LEF should not be given if ALT exceeds three times the normal value (>120 U/L), and that cholestyramine or activated carbon treatment is recommended, with LEF safely resumable in most cases once ALT normalizes.
raw_record.extra_details: RA patients treated with LEF at 10 mg/d.; mechanism proposed as CYP2C9 enzyme inhibition; AST and ALT rose in all 115 treated patients; 14 cases reached twice the normal upper limit (one was a chronic HBV infection with alcoholism diagnosed as fatty liver disease); 5 cases had HBV-DNA increases linked to hepatitis B activity; 9 enzyme-elevated, HBV-DNA-negative cases returned to normal transaminases after LEF withdrawal; injury described as transient and recoverable after dose reduction or cessation; recommendation to stop if ALT >3x normal (>120 U/L) and to use cholestyramine or activated carbon; LEF can typically be resumed once ALT normalizes with enhanced liver monitoring.

raw_record.support_text: Two cases of hepatotoxicity occurred after high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone treatment of a demyelinating disease. The first patient developed a histologically documented acute hepatitis and recovered after 3 weeks; the second showed a mild augmentation of liver enzymes that normalized within a few days. The causal relationship between hepatotoxicity and methylprednisolone treatment was deemed probable in both cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1: 33-year-old man with first episode of demyelinating encephalopathy, 4-day high-dose IV methylprednisolone (total 2.5 g); 5 weeks later AST 349 U/L and ALT 1042 U/L; liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis with focal liver cell necrosis in acinar zones 2-3, monocyte/macrophage infiltration, Kupffer cell hyperplasia, acidophil bodies, and focal microvesicular steatosis; recovery within 20 days. raw_record.support_text: Methylprednisolone (a glucocorticoid) is discussed as a cause of human drug-induced liver injury, including acute liver failure, hepatic steatosis, hepatitis, and autoimmune hepatitis. Possible mechanisms are a direct mitochondrial effect with altered beta-oxidation leading to steatosis; immune suppression permitting viral hepatitis (one patient with lethal acute liver failure had high anti-cytomegalovirus IgM); and a rebound autoimmune response after sudden discontinuation (three of seven patients developed ALF after treatment completion, with liver-kidney microsomal antibodies or antinuclear antibodies). In the Marino series, acute hepatic failure occurred in 0.8% of 800 patients with a lethal outcome in 0.3%.
raw_record.extra_details: Glucocorticoid (methylprednisolone pulse) therapy. Three proposed mechanisms: direct mitochondrial damage/altered fatty-acid beta-oxidation causing steatosis (positive correlation between acute liver failure and dosage, onset during therapy, preexisting steatosis in five of seven patients by ultrasonography); immune suppression permitting viral-induced hepatitis (gammaglobulin high anti-CMV IgM in one patient with lethal ALF; ALT/AST ratio <1 in all described cases; HBV, CMV not observed in five of seven patients, HSV and HCV negative); rebound mechanism causing autoimmune hepatitis (ALF in three of seven patients 4.9 +/- 1.2 weeks after treatment completion, positive LKM antibodies with lymphocytic consolidation in one and ANA in another; none received maintenance steroid). Marino study: acute hepatic failure in 0.8% of 800 patients, lethal outcome 0.3%. Le Moli report: asymptomatic AST/ALT increase depends on total methylprednisolone dosage, associated with increased bilirubin or GGTP and reduced alkaline phosphatase, typically after first administration, not correlating with preexisting steatosis or diabetes.

raw_record.support_text: In a population of 97 patients with methylprednisolone (MP)-related liver injury, 73.2% of injuries were hepatocellular, 15.5% cholestatic, 9.3% mixed, and 2.1% not specified. Severity was grade 1 in 45.4%, grade 2 in 30.9%, grade 3 in 5.2%, and grade 4 in 1%, with grade unknown in 17.5%. The intravenous route accounted for the majority of cases (61 of 77 hepatocellular), while 17 cases used oral MP.
raw_record.extra_details: DILI registry/case-series of 97 patients (77 intravenous, 17 oral, route absent in 3). Clinical signs in 18 cases (23.3%): mainly asthenia (27.8%) and digestive disorders (38.9%); median injury duration 38 days (range 4-140 days) in 38 cases. Two patients died, but only one death was attributed to MP. Liver biopsy in 13 patients (16.9%) showed fibrosis (n=1), necrosis (n=1), lymphocytic infiltrate (n=2), inflammatory disorders (n=1); 2 cases histologically compatible with autoimmune hepatitis despite negative autoimmune serology, one with centrolobular damage and eosinophils. Non-drug causes excluded in 51 cases (66.2%). MP rechallenge data in 19 patients: re-introduced in 13, with new liver injury in 10 (76.9%), totaling 18 recurrences in 10 patients; all recurrences were hepatocellular (matching initial injury) with same grade except one case of severe liver deficiency (prothrombin rate 36%) after the second course; all recovered without specific treatment. Oral MP subset (n=17): 52.9% hepatocellular, 29.4% mixed, mostly grade 1-2 with one severe case (decreased prothrombin rate).; aliases: MP

raw_record.support_text: A 47-year-old woman developed weakness, fatigue, pruritus, and scleral icterus 10 days after completing a self-prescribed 7-day course of oral methylprednisolone; she was also taking topiramate. Admission liver tests were ALT 2478 U/L, AST 1600 U/L, total bilirubin 10 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 8 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 138 U/L, and GGT 242 U/L; no other causes of liver dysfunction were identified. The final diagnosis was mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic liver injury caused by methylprednisolone, with enzyme levels returning to normal within 45 days after drug discontinuation. An objective Naranjo-scale causality assessment indicated hepatotoxicity was probably related to methylprednisolone, making this the third published case of methylprednisolone-induced toxic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The study reports two patients with itraconazole (ITZ)-induced cholestatic liver injury who had markedly high serum ITZ concentrations. The paper then characterizes the mechanism using ITZ-treated rats and MDR3-expressing LLC-PK1 cells, showing that ITZ inhibited MDR3-mediated biliary phospholipid secretion, which the authors conclude is involved in ITZ-induced cholestasis.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients presented with itraconazole-induced cholestatic liver injury with markedly high serum ITZ concentrations; the specific clinical phenotype is cholestatic liver injury/cholestasis. Mechanistic work in ITZ-treated rats and MDR3 (ABCB4)-expressing LLC-PK1 cells showed drastically reduced biliary phospholipids (rather than bile acids) and significantly reduced MDR3-mediated efflux of [14C]phosphatidylcholine at clinically relevant ITZ concentrations, whereas BSEP-mediated [3H]taurocholate transport was not significantly affected. The authors conclude MDR3 inhibition is involved in ITZ-induced cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: A 46-year-old woman with onychomycosis treated with itraconazole 200 mg daily for 5 weeks developed jaundice, elevated transaminases (AST 2571, ALT 3789 IU/L), and progressive hepatic failure with ascites and coagulopathy. A liver biopsy showed cholestatic hepatitis with bile plugs, hepatocellular ballooning, and patchy necrosis, and the condition was judged consistent with acute cytotoxic and cholestatic injuries caused by drug-induced hepatotoxicity. Her hepatic failure was attributed to itraconazole and improved with corticosteroid treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Onychomycosis indication; itraconazole 200 mg daily for 5 weeks. Liver tests rose to AST 2571 IU/L and ALT 3789 IU/L at admission; later total bilirubin 12.8 mg/dL, albumin 2.3 g/dL, INR 2.77 with ascites and coagulopathy. Biopsy showed cholestatic hepatitis with canalicular bile plugs, pericentral zonal ballooning, and patchy hepatocyte necrosis. Negative viral hepatitis and autoimmune serology; patient developed erythema multiforme. Treated with intravenous methylprednisolone (40 mg q8h, tapered), then oral prednisolone; condition stabilized and liver chemistries returned to normal by ~2 weeks after discharge; discharged 36 days after admission.

raw_record.support_text: In a 72-year-old woman treated with itraconazole plus corticosteroids for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, the patient developed jaundice and significantly abnormal liver tests (AST=485 IU/L, ALT=182 IU/L, gamma-GT=933 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase=758 IU/L) after four months of antifungal treatment; the diagnosis of an acute liver failure due to a drug-induced hepatitis associated with the antifungal treatment was established and itraconazole was stopped immediately, with the authors explicitly attributing the hepatitis to itraconazole.

Drug-induced hepatitis with jaundice arising about four months after starting itraconazole for ABPA; laboratory values AST=485 IU/L, ALT=182 IU/L, gamma-GT=933 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase=758 IU/L indicate significant hepatic cytolysis and cholestasis; itraconazole was immediately stopped; the authors excluded intake of any other treatment associated with drug liver toxicity before establishing the diagnosis of acute liver failure due to drug-induced hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: A 61-year-old woman with no apparent risk factors for liver injury developed acute hepatitis one week after the final dose of a long-term course of pulse itraconazole therapy (200 mg orally twice daily, 1 wk on, 3 wk off, for 24 wk) for onychomycosis. Liver function tests showed alanine aminotransferase 3330 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 3250 U/L, and bilirubin 21 mg/dL. The patient underwent liver transplantation 17 days after admission; histology showed massive panlobular necrosis, and the patient died about 4 months later. The Naranjo probability scale graded the relationship of itraconazole therapy and the acute hepatitis as probable.
raw_record.extra_details: Pulse-dosed regimen of 200 mg orally twice daily, 1 week on, 3 weeks off, for 24 weeks for onychomycosis; liver enzyme monitoring not performed during treatment. Lab values: ALT 3330 U/L, AST 3250 U/L, bilirubin 21 mg/dL. Histology: massive panlobular necrosis; reduced liver volume and mild ascitic fluid accumulation. Liver transplantation performed 17 days after admission; the patient died about 4 months later after post-transplant complications and a rejection crisis. Naranjo probability scale rated causality as probable. Serologic evaluation ruled out infectious or other etiological causes.

raw_record.support_text: The clinical, biochemical, serological, and histological data of three patients with itraconazole-induced liver disease are described. All three developed a clinical-biochemical-histological picture of cholestatic hepatitis with damage to the interlobular bile ducts, and beginning ductopenia was found in two cases. Jaundice occurred in all patients and was not accompanied by clinical signs of an allergic reaction, suggesting itraconazole causes liver damage via metabolic rather than immunoallergic mechanisms. The authors suggest itraconazole be added to the list of drugs that can cause a drug-induced vanishing bile duct syndrome, and note azoles generally produce liver injury via a metabolic idiosyncratic reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients with itraconazole-induced cholestatic hepatitis with interlobular bile duct damage; beginning ductopenia in two cases, possibly evolving to chronic drug-induced bile duct pathology/vanishing bile duct syndrome. Jaundice occurred in all patients without immunologic hallmarks (no fever, rash, eosinophilia, or eosinophil-rich/granulomatous infiltrate), and injury occurred after a longer period of exposure, suggesting a metabolic rather than immunoallergic idiosyncratic mechanism. Histological data for itraconazole hepatotoxicity were previously lacking.

raw_record.extra_details: 39-year-old agricultural worker admitted with asthenia and jaundice; itraconazole 400 mg/day for 3 days for genital Candidiasis. Peak values: total bilirubin rose to 578 µg/dl, ALT 2426 rising to 1976 U/L, AST 1549 U/L, GGT 95 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 225 U/L. Liver biopsy showed distortion of lobular architecture, disruption of hepatocyte plates, diffuse lobular leukocyte/eosinophil infiltration, multiple foci of liver cell necrosis, moderate intracellular cholestasis, and enlarged portal tracts with loose collagenous fibrosis forming incomplete porto-portal bridges. Serologies for hepatitis A/B/C, leptospira, CMV, EBV, HSV and autoantibodies (ANA, ASMA, AMA) were negative. Treated with tapering prednisone 30 mg; liver function parameters normal 6 weeks later. CIOMS scale final score 7.

raw_record.support_text: A 35-year-old woman with Cushing's syndrome treated with mifepristone (escalated to 1,200 mg daily about a month prior) presented with abdominal pain, jaundice, and itching. Labs showed total bilirubin 20.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 18.6 mg/dL, ALT 27 U/L, AST 49 U/L, and ALP 258 U/L with normal PT/INR. Transjugular liver biopsy revealed diffuse canalicular and cytoplasmic bile stasis consistent with drug-induced cholestasis, and a diagnosis of mifepristone-associated DILI was made. Mifepristone was discontinued and her symptoms and liver tests gradually improved.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adult female patient with Cushing's syndrome receiving chronic high-dose mifepristone (escalating from 300 mg to a final 1,200 mg daily); concurrent stable levothyroxine therapy; no rechallenge performed.
raw_record.extra_details: 35-year-old woman; biopsy showed diffuse canalicular (long arrow) and cytoplasmic (short arrow) bile stasis, consistent with drug-induced cholestasis (intrahepatic cholestasis). Peak values: total bilirubin 20.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 18.6 mg/dL, ALT 27 U/L, AST 49 U/L, ALP 258 U/L; PT/INR normal. RUCAM score calculated as 7, making mifepristone a 'probable' cause; authors note that without rechallenge full RUCAM categories could not be assessed and the score may be under-calculated, possibly making mifepristone 'highly probable'/'highly likely'. Viral hepatitis serologies and autoimmune/metabolic workup negative. Following discontinuation biochemistry improved (T. Bili 1.7 mg/dL by one month); ursodeoxycholic acid was started; symptoms resolved. Authors state this is one of the first reported cases of mifepristone-associated DILI, citing one prior case report.

raw_record.support_text: A 63-year-old Caucasian female with Cushing disease, without prior liver disease, was started on mifepristone and semaglutide. Ninety days after initiating mifepristone she developed deep jaundice, severe pruritus, fatigue, and nausea; liver tests showed a mixed hepatocellular/cholestatic pattern, serologies were negative, and liver biopsy showed severe cholestasis without bile duct injury plus focal endothelialitis within a central venule. Symptoms resolved and liver tests normalized four months after stopping mifepristone. The Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method score indicated probable causality for mifepristone.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports the recent Phase III failure of the authors' clinical BACE1 inhibitor atabecestat due to drug-induced liver injury (DILI). This is cited as the reason compound 15 was deemed not to contribute to de-risking the liver toxicity observed with atabecestat, leading to discontinuation of further study of compound 15. The hepatic toxicity described for compound 15 (bile duct hyperplasia, ALP elevation, hepatocellular single-cell necrosis) was observed in dog repeated-dose toleration studies, and the paper notes it is unclear whether that dog toxicity translates to the clinical setting.
raw_record.extra_details: BACE1 (beta-secretase) inhibitor that failed a Phase III clinical trial due to DILI. Reported as context for discontinuing the related candidate compound 15; no specific biochemical pattern, phenotype, or severity is stated for the atabecestat DILI. Compound 15's own hepatic toxicity (bile duct hyperplasia, ALP elevation, hepatocellular single-cell necrosis) was seen in dog studies and its translation to humans is explicitly uncertain, so no human DILI claim is made for compound 15.

raw_record.support_text: The phase 2/3 atabecestat program was discontinued in May 2018 based on detection of elevated liver enzymes. Of 475 patients exposed to atabecestat, approximately 24% had ALT/AST of >1.5x ULN and 11% had ALT elevations >3x ULN, with time to onset of elevated liver enzymes of 32-344 days. The paper explicitly frames these as 'atabecestat-induced liver injury' reactions and concludes it is likely the DILI reactions experienced by these patients were mediated at least in part by the adaptive immune system with CD4+ responses being primary. Patient 6 showed persistent liver enzyme elevations one month after cessation and a liver biopsy indicating a zone 3-predominant necroinflammatory process with lymphocyte infiltration.
raw_record.extra_details: Indication: Alzheimer's disease. Doses 5, 10, 25, 50 mg. Program discontinued May 2018 due to elevated liver enzymes; 475 patients exposed, ~24% ALT/AST >1.5x ULN, 11% ALT >3x ULN; elevations heterogeneous and sometimes transient while on treatment. No skin rash and/or eosinophilia; no HLA association identified. Time to onset 32-344 days. Patient 6: persistent liver enzyme elevations one month after cessation; liver biopsy zone 3-predominant necroinflammatory process with lymphocyte infiltration. Mechanism: immune-mediated via HLA-DR-restricted CD4+ T-cell activation; a plasma Cmax of 0.7 µM at 25 mg qd is below the 10 µM needed to activate T-cells in vitro; T-cell stimulatory concentrations may be reached on liver accumulation (15-fold higher in humanized liver vs plasma in TK-NOG mice, DIAT ~12% of atabecestat in liver). PBMC diagnostic assays largely negative; patient 6 showed subtle increased granzyme B in response to DIAT.

raw_record.support_text: A case of fever, disseminated maculopapular skin rash and acute hepatitis appeared in a Negro four days after completion of a thirty-seven-day course of sulfamethoxypyridazine, a long-acting sulfonamide derivative. The clinical, laboratory and pathological features were attributed to drug-induced hypersensitivity hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a single patient. Hepatitis appeared four days after completion of a 37-day course of the long-acting sulfonamide. Presenting features included fever and disseminated maculopapular skin rash. Liver needle biopsy showed scattered, circumscribed areas of inflammation involving parenchyma, supporting stroma and vessel walls, with periportal foci of necrosis, loss of parenchymal cells, Kupffer cell proliferation and mononuclear infiltrate. Bone marrow damage was also noted to a lesser extent. Lesions resembled those of classic serum sickness; the pathogenetic role of circulating drug antibodies was not demonstrated and the hypersensitivity origin was considered quite probable. The authors note that sulfonamide-induced allergic syndromes may be protracted or life-threatening and recommend prompt drug withdrawal and supportive therapy, with corticosteroids possibly reducing severity.

raw_record.support_text: Four cases of sulphonamide hepatitis occurred within 11 months in one non-hepatic-specialty clinic, suggesting the illness is more common than thought. In all cases sulphamethoxypyridazine was one component and was confirmed to be the causal agent in the case tested; drugs containing this sulpha comprise only 29% of sulphonamides sold in Finland, which the authors take as evidence of its special hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Four cases reported in 11 months in one clinic; sulphamethoxypyridazine was a component in all and confirmed causal by challenge in the tested case; sulphonamides containing this drug comprise roughly 29% of total sulphonamide sales in Finland.

Sulphamethoxypyridazine was one component in all cases and was confirmed to be the causal agent in the case tested; the author states this sulphonamide seems to be specially hepatotoxic, noting that drugs containing it comprise only 29% of the total sulphonamides sold in Finland.

raw_record.support_text: A 32-year-old woman with a history of Basedow disease, who had taken benzylthiouracile and propranolol then stopped them, began bromazepam for anxiety on March 21st. On April 15th (25 days after bromazepam onset, 5 days after its withdrawal) she presented jaundice with dark urine and a cytolytic hepatitis with ALAT and ASAT above 20 times the upper normal range; viral serologies and hepatobiliary ultrasonography were normal, and the jaundice resolved with normal liver tests 29 days later. The case was notified to the Tunisian pharmacovigilance centre.
raw_record.extra_details: Begaud imputation intrinsic score 13 ('likely relationship') for bromazepam; benzylthiouracile and propranolol each scored 10 (responsibility excluded). raw_record.support_text: A 48-year-old HIV patient with anal carcinoma (and cirrhosis manifested by ascites) receiving oral budesonide 9 mg/day together with the CYP3A inhibitors ritonavir, clarithromycin, and fluconazole developed acute toxic hepatitis, with serum alanine aminotransferase flare up to 1,010 U/l and a liver biopsy showing ceroid macrophages and vesicular cytoplasmic inclusion bodies. Withdrawal of all medication lowered transaminases, while rechallenge with budesonide produced a significant increase in alanine aminotransferase. Budesonide trough levels were 8.0 and 7.8 ng/ml, far above reference levels, leading the authors to conclude that concurrent CYP3A inhibitors reduced budesonide phase I metabolism and caused hepatotoxicity, and that serious hepatotoxicity will occur if the budesonide dose is not reduced.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Required co-exposure to three CYP3A inhibitors (ritonavir, clarithromycin, fluconazole); patient with HIV infection, anal carcinoma, and cirrhosis with ascites.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral budesonide 9 mg/day; trough levels 8.0 and 7.8 ng/ml by LC/MS/MS on withdrawal day and one day prior, vs 0.5±0.3 ng/ml in noncirrhotics and 1.5±1.2 ng/ml in cirrhotics on the same dose. ALT flare up to 1,010 U/l; serology for viral and autoimmune hepatitis negative. Biopsy showed ceroid macrophages (sign of passed liver cell necrosis in resorption), no necroinflammatory activity, and vesicular cytoplasmic inclusion bodies in most hepatocytes. Withdrawal of all medication decreased transaminases; rechallenge with budesonide significantly increased ALT. Authors note hepatotoxicity of budesonide had never been reported before.

raw_record.support_text: This commentary reports on patients with dihydralazine hepatotoxicity who have circulating anti-liver-microsome (anti-LM) antibodies that react with a 53 kD protein identified as the drug-metabolizing enzyme P-450IA2. Anti-LM antibodies were present in the sera of five patients with dihydralazine-induced hepatitis and were not found in 28 other patients, including patients receiving dihydralazine without a toxic response, indicating the antibodies are specific for dihydralazine hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Five patients with dihydralazine-induced hepatitis; characteristic autoantibodies (anti-liver microsome/anti-LM) directed against the 53 kD P-450IA2 protein, absent in 28 controls including dihydralazine-treated patients without toxicity. Commentary notes only a small fraction of treated patients develop toxicity, attributed to interpatient differences in P-450/detoxifying enzyme activity. Mechanism discussion: reactive metabolite formed by P-450IA2 covalently binds and antigenically alters the P-450; antibody production may be incidental to hepatocyte lysis or may contribute to pathogenesis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors demonstrate that human autoantibodies found in dihydralazine-induced hepatitis are specifically directed against P-450IA2 (CYP1A2). All five available sera (NAL, WOL, DAC, MOU, and a dihydralazine patient without hepatic disease) behaved similarly, whereas control sera were not inhibitory. The authors propose that P-450IA2 may metabolize dihydralazine to a reactive metabolite capable of binding to the enzyme and acting as a hapten, and describe this as a drug-induced (autoimmune type) hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Dihydralazine is an antihypertensive drug. Study of autoantibodies from five patients (sera NAL, WOL, DAC, MOU) with dihydralazine-induced hepatitis, which specifically recognized and inhibited CYP1A2 (P-450IA2; anti-LKM2-like); control sera (preimmune, high-bilirubin patient) were non-inhibitory. Dihydralazine competitively inhibited 7-ethoxyresorufin O-deethylase in human liver microsomes at 200 µM, suggesting CYP1A2 may metabolize dihydralazine to a reactive metabolite that binds the enzyme as a hapten. Paper focuses on mechanism (autoantibody target), supporting the causal relationship of dihydralazine with human immune-mediated hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: In the Phase II proof-of-concept study (NCT02791191) of LY3202626 in patients with mild Alzheimer's disease, consistent with the Phase I study results, no evidence of hepatotoxicity was observed, no elevations of liver function tests meeting the definition of Hy's law occurred, and no statistical differences in any liver function test were seen between LY3202626-treated patients and placebo.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase 1 multiple-dose safety data likewise showed no meaningful alterations in liver enzymes that would suggest hepatic injury due to LY3202626 administration. In the Phase II interim analysis after approximately 140 patients randomized and observed for at least 24 weeks, no clinically meaningful separation in cognition or function was seen; the trial was terminated due to low statistical probability of detecting a significant effect on clinical outcomes, not safety concerns. Doses assessed included 3 mg and 12 mg QD (12 mg chosen as high dose).

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective evaluation of 52 patients with fulminant hepatic failure, 4 cases were attributed to idiosyncratic drug reactions, and the causes of drug-induced hepatitis were reported as sulfasalazine, atorvastatin, NH4Cl (ammonium chloride), and nefazodone. Each of these agents was thereby identified as the cause of drug-induced hepatitis leading to FHF in a human case.

raw_record.support_text: Two cases of early onset, nefazodone-induced acute liver failure are reported, presenting as early as 4 weeks after initiation of therapy. The paper also notes that nefazodone has well established potential hepatotoxic side effects, and symptoms of liver failure have previously been reported within 6 weeks of institution of therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Nefazodone (Serzone; Bristol-Myers Squibb) prescribed for reactive depression and work-related anxiety/depression. Patient 1 (61-yr-old woman) developed malaise, fatigue, jaundice 4 weeks after starting therapy, with raised liver enzymes/bilirubin and coagulopathy; over 48 h developed grade III encephalopathy and underwent successful liver transplantation; explanted liver showed submassive parenchymal necrosis without fatty changes or fibrosis. Patient 2 (46-yr-old man) developed fatigue and jaundice within 4 weeks of nefazodone, with coagulopathy and elevated liver enzymes/bilirubin; transjugular biopsy showed massive parenchymal necrosis in centrilobular areas extending to portal tracts; after discontinuation of nefazodone coagulopathy corrected and liver enzymes normalized over 3 months (dechallenge evidence). Hemochromatosis, Wilson's disease, and infectious or autoimmune hepatitis were excluded in both patients; both denied other drug ingestion. This is described as the shortest reported duration before onset of liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: Nefazodone is associated with rare hepatic adverse reactions including necrosis and failure, usually resulting in liver transplantation or death. The time course for development of liver failure following initiation of nefazodone therapy is variable, ranging from 49 days to 8 months. This case suggests that onset of hepatic failure may be chronologically related to dose escalation, and early subtle symptoms (fatigue, flu-like symptoms, nausea) could be overlooked, leading to further deterioration; early recognition of the failure and the likely causative agent may have been pivotal in avoiding transplant/death.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of hepatic failure, with hepatic necrosis also reported among nefazodone hepatic adverse reactions; failures usually result in liver transplantation or death. Latency of liver failure from initiation ranged from 49 days to 8 months, and onset may be chronologically related to dose escalation. Early subtle symptoms included fatigue, flu-like symptoms, and nausea.

raw_record.support_text: A 52-year-old patient with recurrent depressive disorder developed a fulminant increase in transaminases 6 weeks after first taking nefazodone, which did not normalize despite stopping the drug. The subsequent severe uncontrollable liver failure required orthotopic liver transplantation, and the patient died weeks later from transplant complications. The temporal relationship of the antidepressant intake, the histological finding consistent with drug-toxic liver damage, and the absence of other plausible diseases argue for nefazodone-mediated liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report another case of liver failure in close temporal relation to intake of the antidepressant nefazodone. Extensive internal medicine workup found no alternative explanation, excluding pre-existing liver disease, other toxic substances, alcohol/drug use, viral causes (hepatitis A/B/C, Epstein-Barr, cytomegalovirus), autoimmune liver failure, Wilson disease, and hemochromatosis. The liver biopsy histology (inflammatory portal infiltrates, periportal group necroses, cellular cholestasis) confirmed the hypothesis of drug-induced, probably nefazodone-mediated liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Concurrent comedication included doxepin, moclobemide, Moradorm, and dihydroergotamine; no reports of liver dysfunction exist for Moradorm or the dihydroergotamine product. Nefazodone had already been discontinued 8 days before admission to the internal hospital.
raw_record.extra_details: Nefazodone given at 300 mg for depression. At admission liver parameters: GOT 836 U/l, GPT 1947 U/l, gamma-GT 88 U/l, Quick 53%, PTT 37.8 s, LDH 466 U/l, bilirubin total 13.9 mg/dl, ferritin 10080 ng/ml. Liver biopsy showed marked cellular and canalicular cholestasis with inflammatory portal infiltrates and periportal-accentuated group necroses with collapse fibrosis. Patient developed hepatic encephalopathy 43 days after first clinical symptoms; liver transplantation was performed 10 days later. Patient died about 4 weeks post-transplant from an uncontrolled Aspergillus infection. MRI showed shrinking liver with ascites without portal hypertension or cirrhosis; ascites cytology unremarkable.

raw_record.support_text: A case of self-limited hepatitis with an influenza-like reaction to hydroxyurea therapy is presented. The association was strongly supported by recurrence on rechallenge with the drug. The patient presented with biochemical evidence of acute hepatocellular damage along with fever, malaise, drowsiness and delirium; symptoms and transaminase/bilirubin elevations settled within 36 hours of ceasing hydroxyurea, and a 1 g oral rechallenge on day seven re-triggered rigors, malaise, tachycardia (130 beats/minute), fever (40°C), drowsiness, delirium and mild re-elevation of hepatic enzymes within 5 hours, with liver function normal two weeks later.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single case report; low-dose hydroxyurea used for severe psoriasis in a patient for whom methotrexate was contraindicated.
raw_record.extra_details: Influenza-like reaction with fever, rigors/chills, malaise, drowsiness and delirium accompanying biochemical acute hepatocellular damage. Onset within 5 hours of ingestion and resolution within 36 hours of drug cessation; positive rechallenge with 1 g oral hydroxyurea on day seven re-triggered symptoms plus mild re-elevation of hepatic enzymes (resolved within 36 hours; liver function normal two weeks later). Self-limited hepatitis. The paper notes only one prior report of hepatic dysfunction caused by hydroxyurea, giving no details, and that Moschella reported an influenza-like reaction (fever, chills, malaise) in 6 of 60 psoriasis patients on hydroxyurea with no hepatic problems noted.
