raw_record.support_text: Oseltamivir is reported to cause liver function abnormality in humans, shown by elevated ALT and AST levels, with an occurrence rate of 0.1% (1 of 771 patients) in a clinical study. A documented case of oseltamivir-induced liver injury in a child resolved to normal liver function after prompt intervention. The paper frames these as oseltamivir-induced hepatotoxicity/liver toxicity and advises early detection and discontinuation given the unknown precise mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: Clinical study reported liver function abnormality (elevated ALT and AST) at 0.1% occurrence (1/771 patients); a documented oseltamivir-induced liver injury in a child recovered to normal liver function with prompt intervention. Hepatotoxic adverse events (liver disorders, hepatic cytolysis) could manifest from day 1 up to a year, with none beyond 5 days except mixed liver injury, which typically occurred over 2 weeks. Study observed DILI prevalence 4.19-fold higher in females than males. Precise mechanism remains unknown; putative CES1 gene variants (e.g., G143E/rs71647871) were associated with possible oseltamivir-induced hepatotoxicity, and cirrhosis decreases CES1 expression increasing risk of toxicity. Oseltamivir is a prodrug of oseltamivir carboxylic acid activated mainly by hepatic CES1.

raw_record.support_text: The authors identify olmesartan as the cause of an autoimmune-like chronic hepatitis. They cite the first report by Barge et al. (2017), a 61-year-old woman with anorexia, asthenia and weight loss of 10 kg without diarrhoea, abnormal liver tests and ANA-positive titres, with elastography and biopsy compatible with fibrosis and autoimmune hepatitis; after olmesartan withdrawal the clinical/analytical course improved, a second biopsy showed regression of fibrosis and resolution of interface hepatitis, and immunosuppressive drugs were not started. The paper's own case is also presented as olmesartan-induced liver injury: two months after olmesartan withdrawal, liver tests returned to normal (ALT 20, AST 25, GGTP 16, ALP 106 IU/L) and remained normal one year later while the patient stayed asymptomatic.
raw_record.extra_details: The paper's index case showed dechallenge: liver tests normalized two months after olmesartan withdrawal (ALT 20 IU/L, AST 25 IU/L, GGTP 16 IU/L, ALP 106 IU/L) and were still normal one year later. The mechanism of hepatic injury was suggested to be autoimmune/immune-mediated, analogous to the known olmesartan-associated sprue-like enteropathy. Reference case (Barge et al.): 61-year-old woman, ANA-positive, fibrosis and autoimmune hepatitis on elastography/biopsy, favorable evolution after withdrawal with regression of fibrosis and resolution of interface hepatitis, no immunosuppressive therapy needed. No rechallenge reported.

raw_record.support_text: In this cohort of hepatocarcinoma patients treated with Yttrium-90 (Y90) radioembolization, nine patients (7%) experienced radiation-induced liver disease (REILD), a recognized liver-injury complication of Y90. Current guidelines advise against Y90 use in patients with clinical liver decompensation or significantly abnormal liver function tests, particularly with total bilirubin >2 mg/dL or albumin <3.0 g/dL, to avoid the risk of REILD. Other reported toxicities included elevated liver enzymes (2.5–34%) and bilirubin levels (24–26%).

raw_record.extra_details: Radiation-induced liver disease (REILD) occurred in 9/128 (7%) patients. REILD was described as contributing to worsening synthetic liver function, worsening liver failure, encephalopathy, and ascites/fluid retention, alongside progression of HCC. The paper also states Y90 can cause worsening liver failure (paragraph 56) and cites increasing MELD and CP scores post-treatment reflecting liver decompensation/REILD (paragraph 58). One death one day after Y90 was attributed to procedural complications rather than REILD specifically. Alias: Y90.

raw_record.support_text: In the paper's 2 new patients, hepatic biopsy showed unicellular hepatocytic degeneration and cholestasis as well as multiple granulomas, a combination of cholestatic-hepatocellular injury and granulomas described as a reaction to phenylbutazone. Together with 9 published cases (total 11 patients on phenylbutazone or oxyphenbutazone), the injury is attributed to phenylbutazone; one reported patient (O'Brien) died shortly after onset of his phenylbutazone-associated illness and necropsy showed granulomas in multiple organs with polyarteritis nodosa and hypersensitivity angiitis ascribed to drug hypersensitivity.
raw_record.extra_details: Among 11 reported patients taking phenylbutazone or oxyphenbutazone, liver-function data were recorded for 10: 4 patients had total serum bilirubin 5.6-8.0 mg/100 ml, 2 below 2 mg/100 ml, 4 normal; serum alkaline phosphatase raised up to sixfold in all 5 specified cases; increased SGOT in 3 of 5 patients (181, 125, 182 Karmen units). Peripheral eosinophilia (6%, 6%, 11%) in 3 of 6 recorded patients. One patient (O'Brien) died; remaining patients recovered after drug withdrawal, with follow-up biopsies showing complete resolution at 4-6 months. Histology showed noncaseating granulomas (histiocytes/epithelioid cells, giant cells except in one case) with varying inflammatory cells. Mechanism presumed hypersensitivity: low incidence, short sensitization period up to 24 days, no dose correlation (1.8-70.0 g total), frequent fever, rash and eosinophilia, and recurrence after challenge. In the author's 2 cases the combination of cholestatic-hepatocellular injury with granulomas had not previously been reported for phenylbutazone.

raw_record.support_text: Among 72 patients with histologically proven or suspected liver disease, three had drug hepatitis diagnosed on conventional criteria, attributed to chlorpromazine, phenylbutazone, and aspirin (one case each).
raw_record.extra_details: Diagnosed as one case of drug hepatitis (1 of 3 drug-hepatitis cases) among a cohort of 72 patients with liver disease. Only diagnosis-level attribution is provided; no dose, histology, or outcome details reported.

raw_record.support_text: Phenylbutazone is described as a toxic agent recognised to cause toxic hepatitis with several fatalities and the formation of hepatic granulomas. In a series of 800 patients, 2 developed toxic hepatitis (incidence 0.25%); the first detailed report described 5 patients with jaundice 6 to 40 days after starting therapy, and there have subsequently been many reports of toxic hepatitis, including 8 fatalities. Hepatic granulomas were recorded in 11 patients, with fever, pruritus, jaundice, and occasionally eosinophilia.
raw_record.extra_details: Toxic hepatitis with several fatalities; incidence 0.25% (2/800); first report of 5 patients with jaundice appearing 6-40 days after start of therapy; 8 fatalities subsequently; hepatic granulomas in 11 patients accompanied by fever, pruritus, jaundice, occasionally eosinophilia.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of seven patients admitted with a systemic drug-induced reaction to phenylbutazone therapy (marked by febrile illness with salivary-gland swellings), two patients were clinically jaundiced and six had abnormal liver function tests. Laboratory findings in these phenylbutazone-treated patients included elevated bilirubin (up to 225 µmol/l in case 2), elevated AST (up to 150 Karmen units, normal 10-40), and elevated serum alkaline phosphatase (up to 64 King-Armstrong units, normal 5-15), reported as part of the drug-induced systemic illness.
raw_record.extra_details: Within a systemic drug-induced syndrome in 7 patients (fever, bilateral salivary gland swelling/sialadenitis, stomatitis, rash, pericarditis, pleurisy) attributed to first-time phenylbutazone prescribed for non-specific musculoskeletal pain/osteoarthritis, with onset 4-14 days after starting the drug. Liver features: 2 patients clinically jaundiced, 6 with abnormal liver function tests. Maximum values: bilirubin 225 µmol/l (case 2), AST 150 Karmen units (case 6, normal 10-40), SAP 64 King-Armstrong units (case 3, normal 5-15). Doses 300-600 mg (oral or rectal); fevers persisted 6-18 days after drug cessation. Sialadenitis is the paper's primary focus; liver injury is a secondary reported feature.

raw_record.support_text: Drug-induced liver injury from phenylbutazone has been described in at least 75 patients, less common than its myelotoxicity. Susceptibility increases with age and females are more commonly affected. About 65% of cases occurred within a month of starting therapy, while 10% developed after 12 months. Hepatotoxicity occurs in a generalized systemic illness (jaundice, abdominal complaints, rash, fever, arthralgia), and varying hepatic injury types include cholestasis, hepatocellular injury, mixed-hepatocellular injury, and granulomas; hepatocellular injury tends to occur with a generalized reaction whereas cholestasis tends to occur without systemic features.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Susceptibility increases with age and females are more commonly affected
raw_record.extra_details: DILI described in at least 75 patients; ~65% of cases within one month of therapy onset and 10% after 12 months; hepatotoxicity usually accompanied by systemic illness (jaundice, abdominal complaints, rash, fever, arthralgia), though a minority have liver disease without systemic illness; injury types include cholestasis, hepatocellular injury, mixed-hepatocellular injury, and granulomas; hepatocellular pattern associates with generalized reaction while cholestasis occurs without systemic features.

raw_record.support_text: Carbon tetrachloride is described as a directly cytotoxic drug, with evidence of liver involvement usually occurring within 48 hours of exposure. Abdominal pain, tender hepatomegaly and/or jaundice are usually the earliest signs, and liver function tests show changes suggesting hepatocellular damage that may closely mimic viral hepatitis; in the reported case the serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase level was elevated within 12 hours and rose to extremely high levels before falling. The hepatic injury is characterized histologically by centrilobular ballooning, fatty metamorphosis, necrosis, and leucocytic infiltration, referred to as carbon tetrachloride hepatitis, and if death from liver disease occurs it is within the first ten days after ingestion, usually from liver-cell failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Carbon tetrachloride poisoning by ingestion (supratherapeutic/overdose exposure) rather than ordinary therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Evidence of liver involvement usually within 48 hours; earliest signs were abdominal pain, tender hepatomegaly and/or jaundice. SGOT (glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase) elevated within 12 hours, rising to extremely high levels then falling rapidly, and such levels are rarely seen except in viral hepatitis and active chronic hepatitis. Hyperbilirubinaemia occurred within 12 hours and returned to normal in seven days; prothrombin depressed at first estimation and rapidly normalized; alkaline phosphatase usually within normal limits; bromsulphalein retention 13% at 45 minutes on day 7 (sensitive index of hepatic function). Histology showed typical carbon tetrachloride hepatitis: centrilobular (occasionally whole-lobule) ballooning, fatty metamorphosis, eventual necrosis with leucocytic infiltration, mild portal inflammation, lipofuscin staining of Kupffer cells; a second biopsy at 45 days showed minimal residual fatty metamorphosis, focal necrosis and prominent lipofuscin. If death from liver disease occurs it is within the first ten days after ingestion, usually from liver-cell failure with or without ascites and hepatic coma; survivors rarely have residual damage, though post-necrotic scarring reported in two cases. High transaminase levels also noted by Fry 1959, Dawborn 1961, New 1962; pathology descriptions per Moon 1950, Klatskin 1963.

raw_record.support_text: Carbon tetrachloride is described as a powerful hepatotoxin in humans and was was also historically used as a human and animal medicine to treat hookworm disease. Serum ALT and AST activities were commonly high in 12 patients with carbon tetrachloride intoxication, reaching values of roughly 10,000 U/L or above. Light microscopy in historical human cases showed often confluent centrilobular and midzonal liver cell necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Historical intoxication/poisoning setting (e.g., accidental ingestion of 50 mL in one patient for electron microscopy); carbon tetrachloride was also historically used as an anthelmintic medicine for hookworm disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Serum ALT and AST in 12 intoxicated patients reached values partly 10,000 U/L or above. Histology showed confluent centrilobular and midzonal liver cell necrosis; electron microscopy of an acutely intoxicated patient showed hepatocyte injured mitochondria with proliferation of dilated smooth endoplasmic reticulum. About 33% of total carbon tetrachloride is exhaled in breath after 1 h and only ~1% of incorporated CCl4 is responsible for liver injury; hepatic microsomal CYP2E1 converts CCl4 to toxic intermediates binding covalently to cellular macromolecules. Also used as an experimental toxic-fibrosis model in animals (serum ALT max mean 2910 ± 1320 U/L vs 30 ± 3 U/L controls; AST 5010 ± 2070 U/L vs 98 ± 20 U/L).

raw_record.support_text: In 1968 Hashimoto et al. described a 48-year-old schizophrenic woman who drank 500 ml of carbon tetrachloride. She became acutely ill, developed progressive toxicity with oliguria and coma, and died 2 days later. Autopsy examination of the liver revealed massive centrilobular and midzonal necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Ingestion of 500 ml carbon tetrachloride (supratherapeutic / self-poisoning).
raw_record.extra_details: Case reported by Hashimoto et al. 1968 in a 48-year-old schizophrenic woman; acute onset, oliguria, coma, death 2 days later. Autopsy showed massive centrilobular and midzonal hepatic necrosis. Carbon tetrachloride caused a large increase in neutral lipid fraction of total liver lipids, with conjugated diene configurations indicating extensive peroxidative degeneration of hepatic-cell structural lipids similar to that demonstrated in rats. Thioacetamide hepatotoxicity and postmortem autolysis studies in rats suggested the lipid peroxidation was not due to necrobiologic changes or autolysis.

raw_record.support_text: In the study cohort of 60 patients intoxicated by aliphatic halogenated hydrocarbons (AHH), 52 were intoxicated by a single AHH; of these, carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) injured 12 patients by intoxication. The paper's introduction attributes liver injury of AHH, including that caused by CCl4, to microsomal conversion to toxic intermediates via CYP2E1, framing these intoxicating chemicals as causes of human liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intoxication (supratherapeutic exposure) setting in a cohort of patients; intoxications occurred mostly by ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: CCl4 injured 12 of 60 AHH-intoxicated patients. Liver injury attributed to microsomal bioactivation to toxic intermediates through CYP2E1; cimetidine, introduced as therapy, reduced liver injury and lethality in the CCl4 animal model.

raw_record.support_text: Patient 17, a 48-year-old white male, ingested several hundred ml of carbon tetrachloride (CCl₄) in a suicide attempt, became somnolent on day 4 and stuporous on day 5, and developed acute hepatic failure/coma requiring whole-blood exchange transfusion, after which he recovered uneventfully. Serum bilirubin rose to a peak of 28 mg/100 ml even after coma cleared, and the elevation of BUN was attributed to CCl₄-induced renal damage. This is a human case of liver injury after overdose ingestion of carbon tetrachloride.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose via suicide attempt ingestion of several hundred ml; patient also developed CCl₄-induced renal damage as a co-occurring complication.
raw_record.extra_details: 48-year-old white male; somnolent on day 4 after ingestion, stuporous on day 5; exchanged with 3 liters of whole blood on day 6 and awoke 27 hours later; thereafter uneventful recovery. Prothrombin time 30 seconds (control) prior to exchange transfusion, 19 seconds immediately after, rose again to 26 seconds the next day, then fell progressively toward normal. Serum bilirubin continued to rise to a peak of 28 mg/100 ml after coma cleared, then plateaued and gradually fell. Elevated BUN attributed to CCl₄-induced renal damage; subsequent laboratory tests returned to normal.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case series of 11 patients poisoned with carbon tetrachloride via accidental ingestion or inhalation (e.g., drinking a mouthful of carbon tetrachloride instead of gin or beer, drinking a vermifuge of carbon tetrachloride plus paraffin, or inhaling vapors while varnishing). Multiple patients were jaundiced, and autopsies showed severe liver injury such as diffuse or pronounced centrilobular necrosis and pronounced fatty degeneration; several patients died (e.g., Patients II, VI, X, XI).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/supratherapeutic exposure via accidental ingestion or inhalation of carbon tetrachloride; several patients were chronic alcohol users or inebriated at exposure, and some co-ingested other solvents (trichloroethylene, denatured alcohol/methanol).
raw_record.extra_details: 11 patients poisoned with carbon tetrachloride; two died without medical treatment and nine were hospitalized. Presenting features included jaundice (icterus), oliguria/anuria, uraemia, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhoea. Autopsy findings in fatal cases included diffuse or pronounced centrilobular necrosis of the liver, fatty degeneration/pronounced fatty infiltration, and enlarged liver (e.g., 2280 g, 3100 g). Latency was short (ingestion/inhalation hours to a few days before admission). Route varied (ingestion, inhalation); patient IX was a medicolegal case presumed to have drunk carbon tetrachloride.

raw_record.support_text: A first-in-human phase I dose-escalation trial of ursolic acid liposomes (UAL) enrolled 63 subjects (4 patients with advanced solid tumors and 35 healthy adult volunteers for the toxicity study, plus 24 healthy volunteers for pharmacokinetics). Dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) was encountered at 74, 98, and 130 mg/m² and consisted of hepatotoxicity and diarrhea; the maximum tolerated dose was 98 mg/m².

raw_record.extra_details: Phase I MTD/DLT trial (registration ChiCTR-ONC-12002385). Doses evaluated: 11, 22, 37, 56, 74, 98, and 130 mg/m². Hepatotoxicity was a dose-limiting toxicity; MTD 98 mg/m². Other adverse events included grade 1 nausea, grade 2 abdominal distention, grade 1 microscopic hematuria, grade 2 elevated serum sodium, grade 1 vascular stimulation, and grade 1 skin rash. Linear pharmacokinetics for Cmax, AUC0-24h, and AUC0-inf.

raw_record.support_text: In the pediatric phase I study of clofarabine at The University of Texas M.D. Anderson Cancer Center, 25 patients (17 with ALL and 8 with AML) received clofarabine at 11.25 to 70 mg/m2/d intravenously for 5 days. Hyperbilirubinemia and skin rash were dose limiting at 70 mg/m2/d, and the maximum-tolerated dose was 52 mg/m2/d, establishing bilirubin elevation as a dose-limiting, drug-related hepatotoxic event in leukemia patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients with relapsed or refractory leukemia in a phase I dose-escalation study; hyperbilirubinemia was dose-limiting at the highest dose (70 mg/m2/d), with a maximum-tolerated dose of 52 mg/m2/d.
raw_record.extra_details: Clofarabine is a second-generation deoxyadenosine analog that inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and DNA polymerase; 25 patients (17 ALL, 8 AML); doses 11.25-70 mg/m2/d for 5 days; hyperbilirubinemia and skin rash both dose limiting at 70 mg/m2/d; MTD 52 mg/m2/d.

raw_record.support_text: In this pediatric phase 1 study of clofarabine (Cl-F-ara-A, infused intravenously over 1 hour daily for 5 days, dose levels 11.25-70 mg/m²/day), the dose-limiting toxicity was reversible hepatotoxicity and skin rash at 70 mg/m²/day for 5 days; the maximum tolerated dose was 52 mg/m²/day for 5 days. The paper additionally notes that a prior adult phase 1 trial defined the MTD at 40 mg/m² daily for 5 days with hepatotoxicity as the dose-limiting toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients younger than 21 years with relapsed or refractory leukemia, heavily pretreated, enrolled in a phase 1 dose-escalation study.
raw_record.extra_details: Clofarabine was given IV over 1 hour daily for 5 days at six dose levels from 11.25 to 70 mg/m²/day with 30% dose escalation (modified 3+3 design). Dose-limiting toxicity was reversible hepatotoxicity and skin rash at 70 mg/m²/day; MTD was 52 mg/m²/day for 5 days. At MTD, clofarabine triphosphate in leukemia blasts ranged 6-19 µM with complete sustained inhibition of DNA synthesis. Adult phase 1 trial defined MTD at 40 mg/m² daily for 5 days with hepatotoxicity as the DLT. Activity: 5 CR and 3 PR of 25 patients (32%).

raw_record.support_text: In a phase I study of intravenously administered clofarabine conducted at MD Anderson Cancer Center, the maximum tolerated dose for patients with hematologic and solid cancers was established at 40 mg/m²/day for 5 consecutive days, with hepatotoxicity identified as the dose-limiting toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase I study established maximum tolerated dose of 40 mg/m²/day for 5 consecutive days for patients with hematologic and solid cancers; hepatotoxicity was the dose-limiting toxicity at this dose.

raw_record.support_text: In a phase I clinical trial of 51 patients with indolent and acute hematologic malignancies and solid tumors who received clofarabine as a 1 h IV infusion daily for 5 days at escalating doses, a maximum tolerated level of 40 mg/m² was identified. At this level, severe but reversible hepatotoxicity was observed, thus defining the dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) of clofarabine.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity observed at the maximum tolerated dose of 40 mg/m²/day given as a 1 h IV infusion daily for 5 days in a phase I trial of 51 patients with indolent and acute hematologic malignancies and solid tumors; the toxicity was severe but reversible and defined the dose-limiting toxicity (DLT). Myelosuppression was the DLT at lower doses (2 and 4 mg/m²/day) in solid tumors and chronic lymphoid malignancies, respectively.

raw_record.support_text: A 47-year-old man died from fatal massive peripheral zonal hepatic necrosis after accidentally ingesting a solution of methyl ethyl ketone peroxide (MEKP) in dimethyl phthalate (about 10% active oxygen). His course included temporary cardiac arrest, abdominal burns, severe metabolic acidosis, rapid hepatic failure, rhabdomyolysis and respiratory insufficiency, ending in death 4 days later from hepatic coma with blood coagulation disorders. Microscopy showed massive periportal hepatic necrosis with atypical pseudoductular proliferation; the suggested mechanism involves lipid peroxidation by free oxygen radicals derived from MEKP.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Accidental ingestion while excessively inebriated, with co-exposure to alcohol during a fishing trip.
raw_record.extra_details: Ingested 50-100 ml of polymer-curing peroxide solution (MEKP in dimethyl phthalate) stored in a rum bottle; solution contains about 10% active oxygen. Course: cardiac arrest with successful resuscitation, metabolic acidosis (pH 6.86, base excess 28 mmol l-1), anuria, hepatic coma, fatal outcome 4 days later with blood coagulation disorders. Histology: massive periportal hepatic necrosis with atypical pseudoductular proliferation, probably bile-duct origin with atypia and mitoses. Suggested mechanism: lipid peroxidation by free oxygen radicals derived from MEKP. Report notes eight prior human cases of accidental or suicidal MEKP ingestion, with no prior reports of severe liver damage.

raw_record.support_text: A 57-year-old male unintentionally ingested a mouthful of methyl ethyl ketone peroxide (MEKP), a fiberglass fixing agent, while working on his boat. Approximately 12 hours post-ingestion his liver function tests worsened, with ALT rising to a peak of 761 U/L and AST to 576 U/L, and INR slightly elevated at 1.3. The paper states MEKP is highly toxic, causing corrosive effects in the gastrointestinal tract, hepatic necrosis, renal impairment and cardiovascular collapse, and concludes that despite a small ingestion it caused hepatotoxicity and gastrointestinal injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Unintentional (accidental) ingestion of a small amount (~mouthful) of liquid while working on a boat; treated with acetylcysteine infusion and supportive care.
raw_record.extra_details: Onset of worsening LFTs approximately 12 hours post-ingestion; ALT peaked 761 U/L, AST 576 U/L, INR peaked 1.3; ALT remained slightly elevated at 89 U/L on day 14 follow-up while AST was normal; patient clinically well at 14 days; MEKP confirmed in blood by headspace gas chromatography-mass spectrometry; presentation included profuse watery diarrhoea, diaphoresis, compensated metabolic acidosis with lactate 6.0 mmol/L, haemoconcentration (Hb 210 g/L); MEKP generally described as causing hepatic necrosis, renal impairment and cardiovascular collapse.

raw_record.support_text: In the lymphocyte stimulation test applied to the drugs used before the symptoms appeared (tegafur, kefral, OK-432, and cepharanthin), only tegafur gave a positive result (stimulation index, 173%). After hepatic function had fully recovered, a challenge test with 5-day continuous tegafur at 200 mg/day (one-quarter of the ordinary dose) reproduced anorexia, malaise, and moderate GOT/GPT elevation and was judged positive. Based on onset of acute liver injury after tegafur began, normalization after discontinuation, liver histology, LST, and challenge test, the authors diagnosed allergic liver injury induced by tegafur.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report (single patient on sustained tegafur). Laboratory values: total bilirubin 11.5 mg/dl (moderate jaundice), GOT 361 IU/l, GPT 722 IU/l, ALP 130 IU/l, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase 204 IU/l, serum iron 235 µg/dl, CRP negative; HBsAb(+), HBeAb(+), HBcAb(+), HBsAg(-). Histology: hepatocyte swelling with focal/spotty necrosis, mononuclear infiltration of Kupffer cells and lymphocytes, slight eosinophils, no cholestasis. LST stimulation index 173% (vs kefral 84%, OK-432 129%, cepharanthin 108%, 5-FU 100%). Positive challenge test at 200 mg/day for 5 days. Latency 14-21 days from start of drug; GOT peaked at 26 days, bilirubin at 30 days; eosinophilia; function normalized ~30 days after discontinuation and patient recovered. Tegafur is a 5-FU prodrug (1-(2-tetrahydrofuryl)-5-fluorouracil) used as anticancer/antimetabolite for alimentary carcinoma.

Patients developed hepatocellular and cholestatic types of injury. Diagnosis was based on temporal relationship between drug use and altered liver enzymes, subsequent improvement of liver enzymes upon discontinuation, and liver biopsy findings suggestive of drug-induced liver injury. raw_record.support_text: The paper describes the clinical course of seven patients who developed fulminant hepatic failure caused by ecarazine hydrochloride, an antihypertensive agent. Course details include massive hepatic cell necrosis (Case 1, fatal), zonal hepatic cell necrosis with a positive rechallenge and positivity for ANA (Case 2), a fatal case with jaundice, hemorrhage and renal failure (Case 3), and Case 4 with elevated ALT/AST to 1,090 IU/L and 1,205 IU/L after being prescribed ecarazine with warfarin and dilazep.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven patients developed fulminant hepatic failure attributed to ecarazine hydrochloride given as an antihypertensive agent. Case 1 (69-year-old man) died after hepatic encephalopathy and renal failure; necropsy showed massive hepatic cell necrosis. Case 2 demonstrated zonal hepatic cell necrosis on biopsy, ANA converted to positive (1:80), and rechallenge 2 weeks later produced fatigue with AST 1,305 IU/L, ALT 1,197 IU/L, total bilirubin 2.5 mg/dL that normalized after discontinuation; anti-HCV antibody and HCV RNA were negative. Case 3 (74-year-old man) died from exacerbated jaundice, hemorrhagic tendency and renal failure. Case 4 (postpartum woman) had ALT 1,090 IU/L and AST 1,205 IU/L with concurrent warfarin and dilazep co-medication. Cases treated with plasma filtration, plasma exchange and prednisolone.

raw_record.support_text: The editorial reports that todralazine, a hydralazine derivative used to treat hypertension, induces hepatic failure in humans: seven cases of todralazine-induced hepatic failure were previously reported, and a further case progressed to fulminant hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation 20 days after admission. Histology of the explant revealed submassive hepatocyte necrosis with little inflammation and little hepatocyte proliferation.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven cases of todralazine-induced hepatic failure previously reported; the new case had fulminant hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation 20 days after admission. Explant histology showed submassive hepatocyte necrosis with little inflammation and little hepatocyte proliferation. Todralazine is a hydralazine derivative used to treat hypertension. Murata et al. hypothesized reduced histone acetylation with subsequent failure of liver regeneration as mechanism; in a mouse model 4 months of todralazine feeding induced mild hepatitis with ALT rise (67 vs 27 control) and reduced acetylated H4, PCNA positivity, cyclin D1, and HAT activity; in vitro todralazine, isoniazid and hydralazine dose-dependently inhibited core histone acetylation.

raw_record.support_text: Benzbromarone is no longer commercially available in the USA and was withdrawn from the European market in 2003 due to the risk of severe hepatotoxicity. Case reports describe fulminant hepatitis associated with the use of standard doses of benzbromarone (100 mg/day) over short periods (three months). Only three such cases have been described since the early 1970s, and the paper notes it is debated whether banning benzbromarone was appropriate.
raw_record.extra_details: Withdrawn from the European market in 2003 and no longer commercially available in the USA due to risk of severe hepatotoxicity. Case reports of fulminant hepatitis at standard therapeutic dose of 100 mg/day over about three months. Only three cases described since the early 1970s; the paper notes it is debated whether banning benzbromarone was appropriate or done too hastily. In Brazil sales are permitted by ANVISA and benzbromarone is reported to have a safety profile identical to sulfinpyrazone. Benzbromarone is metabolized in the liver by cytochrome P450 and should be used with caution in patients with hepatobiliary diseases.

raw_record.support_text: A 62-year-old man who had been receiving benzbromarone 75 mg/day since the previous October to treat hyperuricemia was admitted with liver dysfunction (aspartate aminotransferase 1369 IU/ml). Benzbromarone was stopped, but jaundice progressed with grade 2 hepatic encephalopathy, total bilirubin 535 µmol/l, and prothrombin time 36.9%. After all other possible causes of hepatitis were excluded, the authors made a diagnosis of fulminant hepatic failure caused by benzbromarone. The patient died on the 62nd hospital day; autopsy showed a severely atrophic liver weighing 690 g with massive hepatic cell necrosis consistent with acute fulminant liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Benzbromarone (3,5-dibromo-4-hydroxyphenyl 2-ethylbenzofuran-3-yl ketone), a benzofuran derivative for hyperuricemia, given at 75 mg/day from October to March. Antinuclear antibody low-titer positive; tests for HAV to HGV negative; lymphocyte stimulation test for benzbromarone negative. The authors speculated an allergic or cytotoxic reaction to intermediate metabolites. Four similar fatal/suspected benzbromarone fulminant hepatic failure cases have recently presented in Japan (unpublished reports); one prior case showed hepatic injury 3 months after administration.

raw_record.support_text: Benzbromarone hepatotoxicity is reported in humans. A 1994 case report from the Netherlands described a woman who developed acute hepatitis attributed to benzbromarone, confirmed when she was rechallenged with the drug two years later. In the late 1990s and early 2000s in Japan, several cases of fulminant liver failure leading to death were attributed to benzbromarone, and the drug was eventually withdrawn from the market by Sanofi-Synthélabo in 2003 after reports of severe hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: A 1994 case report from the Netherlands of acute hepatitis in a woman was confirmed on rechallenge with the drug two years later; multiple cases of fulminant liver failure leading to death in Japan (late 1990s-early 2000s); drug withdrawn from market by Sanofi-Synthélabo in 2003 after reports of severe hepatotoxicity; still marketed in some European countries, not available in the US. Used as a uricosuric for gout at standard daily doses of 100 mg, with dose increases to 150-200 mg/day.

raw_record.support_text: Benzbromarone was reported to cause severe drug-induced liver injury in two patients treated for hyperuricaemia. A 58-y-old male treated for hyperuricaemia developed fever, jaundice and hepatic encephalopathy after 7 months of benzbromarone (unstated dose), with AST 736, ALT 1168, AP 792 and γGT 1102 IU/L; hepatic encephalopathy and increased PT ensued and liver biopsy at recovery showed fibrosis and bile-duct-like structures. A 53-y-old female took benzbromarone 100 mg/day with allopurinol for 2 months and developed fulminant hepatic failure (AST 3090, ALT 1140 U/L, PT 26.5 s); a positive lymphocyte stimulation test for benzbromarone was reported, she underwent living-related liver transplantation after failed haemodiafiltration/plasma exchange and died of sepsis 3 months later, with liver biopsy showing massive centrilobular necrosis consistent with fulminant hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients were treated for hyperuricaemia/gout; one case (female) co-administered allopurinol with benzbromarone, and benzbromarone was used for asymptomatic hyperuricaemia in three of the four patients in the paper's case series.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1 (58-y-old male): onset after 7 mo, unstated dose; mild fever, malaise, anorexia, dark urine, pruritus, jaundice; total bilirubin 135 mg/L, AST 736, ALT 1168, AP 792, γGT 1102 IU/L; HBsAb positive but other hepatitis virus markers negative; LST for benzbromarone negative; co-medications allopurinol, tocopherol, niacin, alprazolam, theophylline, azelastine, nilvadipine; condition deteriorated despite stopping benzbromarone, with hepatic encephalopathy and prolonged PT; treated with prednisolone 30 mg/day, plasma exchange and haemodiafiltration; recovery biopsy showed fibrosis, bile duct-like structure, lymphocyte aggregation, nuclear enlargement. Case 2 (53-y-old female): benzbromarone 100 mg/day plus allopurinol for 2 mo; diarrhoea, nausea, anorexia, fatigue, jaundice; albumin 2.5 g/dL, AST 3090, ALT 1140 U/L, LDH 945 U/L, AP 123 U/L, total bilirubin 233 mg/L, NH3 160.6 µg/dL, PT 26.5 s; HAV/HCV/EBV/CMV negative, autoantibodies negative; LST positive for benzbromarone; massive centrilobular necrosis on biopsy; death from sepsis 3 mo after transplant. Paper also estimated incidence of benzbromarone-induced hepatotoxicity in Europe at approximately 1 in 17,000 treated patients (based on ~5 fulminant hepatitis cases over 1995-2000 among ~84,000 treated patients), possibly higher in Japan.

raw_record.support_text: A 23-year-old female being treated for porphyria cutanea tarda was mistakenly given a single 1250 mg dose of chloroquine instead of the intended 125 mg. In contrast to typical chloroquine toxicity (mainly cardiac arrhythmias), she died 13 days after ingestion in a coma caused by irreversible, acute decompensation of the liver. Forensic autopsy and histological and toxicological investigations confirmed the findings, and the authors explain the severe hepatotoxic effect of chloroquine in this case from its pharmacological mechanism of action in p.c.t. The authors warn against exceeding the recommended p.c.t. dose of 125-250 mg twice weekly and consider clinically manifest p.c.t. a contraindication to chloroquine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Accidental overdose of 1250 mg instead of intended 125 mg; patient had porphyria cutanea tarda (chronic porphyria hepatica), which the authors consider a contraindication to chloroquine use.
raw_record.extra_details: Single oral dose of 1250 mg chloroquine (Resochin) instead of 125 mg; death occurred 13 days post-ingestion in a coma due to irreversible acute liver decompensation; confirmed by forensic autopsy and histological and toxicological investigations; the severe hepatotoxic effect is explained by chloroquine's pharmacological mechanism in p.c.t.; authors recommend p.c.t. dosing of 125-250 mg twice weekly and warn against exceeding it. Typical chloroquine overdose toxicity (cardiac arrhythmia) was not the course in this patient.

raw_record.support_text: In the described case, instead of the intended 125 mg chloroquine the 10-fold higher dose of 1250 mg was given, which almost inevitably had to lead to liver damage in the sense of a 'Flu' syndrome. The entire symptomatology of this 'Flu' syndrome, an expression of liver damage, occurred in the present case. No evidence for another cause of the neurological symptomatology was found, and the temporal course left no reasonable doubt of a causal relationship between the fatal liver damage and the chloroquine administration.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Porphyria cutanea tarda patient; 10-fold dosing error (1250 mg instead of 125 mg).
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal hepatotoxic 'Flu' syndrome; temporal course supports causality; transaminase (GOT/GPT) elevation occurred; peak urinary porphyrin excretion ca. 163 mg on day 3 after chloroquine, largely preserving the P.c.t. excretion pattern (uroporphyrin and heptacarboxyporphyrin markedly increased; delta-aminolaevulinic acid and porphobilinogen normal).

raw_record.support_text: A 23-year-old female patient with porphyria cutanea tarda died 13 days after taking 1250 mg chloroquine for P.c.t., ultimately from cerebral coma caused by an irreversible acute hepatic failure (akuter Leberzerfall), despite intensive therapy. Forensic autopsy, histology, and toxicology confirmed the clinical finding of chloroquine-induced hepatotoxicity. The paper explains the high hepatotoxic effect of chloroquine in this case and warns against exceeding the recommended dose of 2 x weekly 125-250 mg in the treatment of P.c.t.

raw_record.extra_details: Latency ~13 days from chloroquine intake to death; confirmed by forensic autopsy, histology and toxicology. Chloroquine also produced an expected mild (desired) liver damage ('flu syndrome') even at therapeutic doses in P.c.t., which the paper uses to explain the high hepatotoxicity. Cardiac arrhythmia was noted in usual chloroquine intoxication but was not the fatal mechanism here; fatal cardiac toxicity seen in other followed cases involved oral doses always above 10 g.

Systemic allergy with skin rash, fever, leucocytosis and eosinophilia; chloramphenicol-specific serum antibody 256:1 by passive hemagglutination; gamma-globulin 3.2 g/dl, Ig-G 1,730 mg/dl, Ig-A 54 mg/dl, Ig-M 1,260 mg/dl. Liver specimen showed centrolobular necrosis with inflammatory reactions. Positive parenteral challenge (intramuscular 1 g chloramphenicol) reproduced similar changes and consumed antibody (titer to 16:1) with Ig-M falling to 190 mg/dl (Fig. 3).

raw_record.support_text: Thiabendazole has produced several instances of cholestatic jaundice that may progress to a syndrome of chronic cholestasis resembling primary biliary cirrhosis (Rex et al. 1983).
raw_record.extra_details: Several instances of cholestatic jaundice that may progress to a chronic cholestasis syndrome resembling primary biliary cirrhosis (Rex et al. 1983).

raw_record.support_text: The paper attributes intrahepatic cholestasis to thiabendazole therapy. It reports the patient's course of cholestatic injury after thiabendazole (serum total bilirubin peaking at 40.5 mg/dl and alkaline phosphatase at 1385 IU/L, with bile plugs on liver biopsy) that resolved over months after drug cessation. The authors note six previously reported cases of intrahepatic cholestasis after thiabendazole plus additional unreported cases (including one cited by Zimmerman and two reported by Merck Sharp and Dohme), state that the syndrome should be considered in all patients manifesting jaundice shortly after thiabendazole ingestion, and emphasize that the complication is exceedingly rare given the large number of patients treated.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of intrahepatic cholestasis after thiabendazole. Liver biopsy showed bile in hepatocytes and Kupffer cells, bile plugs in centrilobular canaliculi, no bile duct injury or proliferation, patchy lipid vacuoles, and a modest lymphocytic/granulocytic infiltrate with prominent eosinophils; no cholangitis or fibrosis. Serum total bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase peaked at 40.5 mg/dl and 1385 IU/L 42 days after the first dose; serum albumin fell to 2.5 g/dl with moderate ankle edema, venous NH3 rose to 78 µg/dl with mental deterioration, serum creatinine rose to 3.5 mg/dl, and an episode of self-limiting upper GI bleeding required 3 U transfusion. Injury resolved with fluid therapy, protein restriction, and lactulose; bilirubin remained elevated 3 months and alkaline phosphatase 6 months after ingestion. Sonography and ERCP were normal. Six previously reported cases of intrahepatic cholestasis after thiabendazole plus additional unreported cases cited; complication deemed exceedingly rare given the large number of patients treated since 1967. Bayles reported abnormal liver tests in 5 of 14 patients treated with thiabendazole over months for chromomycosis.

raw_record.support_text: Eighteen cases of hepatic failure have been reported worldwide in patients receiving felbamate, and a panel of hepatologists that reviewed the information judged seven of those cases to have a likely association with felbamate. Assuming 130,000 to 170,000 persons were exposed worldwide, the risk of hepatic failure is 1 in 7200 to 9500 if all 18 reported cases are included, and approximately 1 per 18,500 to 25,000 exposures if only the seven likely cases are considered—similar to the valproate hepatic fatality rate. The mean time of onset of the felbamate-associated hepatic failure was 217 days (range 25 to 939 days), and 78% of affected patients were female.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported liver injury phenotype is hepatic failure (acute liver failure). 18 worldwide cases, of which a hepatologist panel judged 7 as likely felbamate-associated; estimated risk 1 in 7200-9500 (all 18) or 1 per 18,500-25,000 (7 likely); mean time of onset 217 days (range 25-939); 78% female predominance; risk said to be similar to valproate hepatic fatality. Context: felbamate use is now extremely limited; an FDA advisory committee in September 1994 recommended keeping it on the market, and the manufacturer urged discontinuation in most patients after aplastic anemia and hepatic failure reports.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that available clinical experience in the US in support of felbamate's approval (August 1993) as well as European trials provided no evidence of haematological or hepatotoxic activity, and that extensive preclinical data likewise provided no evidence of hepatotoxicity with either short-term or long-term administration.
raw_record.extra_details: Felbamate was introduced in the US in August 1993 for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and/or refractory partial onset seizures. The explicit negative conclusion is based on pre-approval US clinical experience and European trials, which provided no evidence of hepatotoxic activity.

raw_record.support_text: Felbamate therapy reportedly causes liver failure, with 18 cases of acute liver failure reported to date. Wallace Laboratories and the FDA recommended weekly monitoring of complete blood counts, reticulocyte counts, and liver function tests in patients receiving felbamate. This hepatotoxicity is presented as a serious, known side-effect risk of felbamate used for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome or medically refractory seizures.
raw_record.extra_details: 18 cases of acute liver failure reported; felbamate is largely banned for most epileptic conditions and approved only for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome or medically refractory seizures with no reasonable alternative. FDA and Wallace Laboratories recommended weekly monitoring of CBCs, reticulocyte counts, and LFTs. Aplastic anemia (31 reported cases, mostly adults, with concurrent medications) is also an associated side effect. The dosage is 20-35 mg/kg/day (maximum 90 mg/kg/day).

raw_record.support_text: Felbamate was initiated at 600 mg three times a day on June 27, 1994 and increased weekly by 900 mg/d to a total daily dose of 3,600 mg. The patient developed marked liver test abnormalities starting 24 days after felbamate initiation (AST up to 1,258 U/L, elevated direct bilirubin and protime), and autopsy showed massive to sub-massive hepatic necrosis. The authors attribute the injury to felbamate after excluding viral hepatitis (A, B, C, CMV, EBV, HSV) and deeming metoprolol, nifedipine, and phenytoin unlikely or non-fulminant causes. The patient died on August 4 due to multisystem organ failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of felbamate-induced fulminant hepatic failure. Latency 24 days after initiation; dose escalated weekly by 900 mg/d to 3,600 mg/d, later decreased to 1,800 mg/d due to GI irritation, then discontinued on hospital day 9. Peripheral eosinophilia 12.4% (abs 0.7 K/CUMM), elevated AST (601-1,258 U/L), GGT, direct bilirubin up to 18.7 mg/dL, protime rising to 22.4 sec; negative hepatitis A IgM, B, C, CMV, EBV, HSV serologies and cultures; ANA negative. Ultrasound showed enlarged liver. Autopsy: small liver (940 g), massive to sub-massive necrosis, lymphocytic portal infiltrate with few eosinophils, no fibrosis, no viral inclusions. Patient died August 4 from multisystem organ failure; liver transplant not considered. Metoprolol, nifedipine, and phenytoin considered and excluded as unlikely/alternative cause.

raw_record.support_text: A 65-year-old male with prostatism was started on Alfuzosin prolonged-release tablets at 10 mg perorally once daily. On the 9th day of therapy he developed loss of appetite, malaise, itching, dark urine, and jaundice; he had no history of aspirin, paracetamol, herbal medicine, or hepatic disease, and his liver tests were normal before treatment. Labs showed ALT 402 U/L, AST 175 U/L, ALP 235 U/L, γ-GT 327 U/L, total bilirubin 7.6 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin 5.8 mg/dL; ultrasonography, MRCP, and serology for viral and autoimmune/metabolic liver disease were negative or normal. His RUCAM score was 7 (probable adverse reaction to drug). Alfuzosin was discontinued and transaminases and bilirubin gradually normalized.
raw_record.extra_details: Alfuzosin is a quinazoline derivative and selective α1 blocker used for benign prostatic hyperplasia, metabolized in the liver with inactive metabolites excreted in feces; reported rare hepatotoxicity. Dose 10 mg prolonged-release tablets perorally once daily; symptoms (anorexia, malaise, pruritus, dark urine, jaundice) appeared at day 9 of therapy. Labs: AST 175 U/L, ALT 402 U/L, ALP 235 U/L, γ-GT 327 U/L, total bilirubin 7.6 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 5.8 mg/dL, leukocyte 5.8 K/μL. Normal ultrasonography, MRCP, and intrahepatic bile ducts; negative viral serology (HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM, anti-HCV, anti-HAV IgM, anti-HEV, HEV-RNA, HCV-RNA), autoimmune (ANA, AMA, ASMA, LKM-1, EMA, IgA) and metabolic (transferrin saturation, ferritin, alpha-1 antitrypsin, ceruloplasmin, urinary Cu2+, Kayser-Fleischer ring) workups. RUCAM score 7 = probable adverse drug reaction. Off-drug gradual normalization of transaminases and bilirubin.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of cholestatic hepatitis during treatment with moxonidine in an 83-year-old man treated with 0.2 mg moxonidine daily for moderate hypertension, and conclude there is convincing evidence of a causative role of moxonidine in this case. No other drug was given to this previously healthy patient, a liver biopsy showed features compatible with drug-induced inflammatory intrahepatic cholestasis, other diseases of the liver and bile ducts were excluded, and the patient recovered after stopping the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: 83-year-old man, previously healthy, no other prescribed or non-prescribed medication (single-agent attribution). Dose 0.2 mg moxonidine daily for hypertension; jaundice, itching, nausea and maculopapular rash developed 9 months after drug start. Liver tests rose to bilirubin 173 uM/L (peak 412 uM/L), ASAT >1000 U/L, ALAT 1560 U/L, with slight elevation of gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase and alkaline phosphatase; coagulation disorder, hypoalbuminaemia 17 g/L and generalized oedema led to hospital admission. Liver biopsy: severe localized intralobular and intraportal lymphoplasmocellular infiltrates with neutrophils and intracytoplasmatic intracanalicular cholestasis, mild small bile-duct proliferation, and focal pericellular fibrosis. Clinical phenotype is cholestatic hepatitis (drug-induced inflammatory intrahepatic cholestasis). Negative hepatitis B/C serology, negative ANA/AMA/ANCA, normal alpha-1-antitrypsin, caeruloplasmin and copper; no biliary dilatation or stones on ultrasound (2 cm hepatic cyst). Dechallenge with recovery: laboratory indices normal 8 weeks after stopping, patient well 1 year later. Postmarketing surveillance by the manufacturer reported no cholestatic hepatitis in more than 20,000 patients treated.

In BEACON there were fewer hepatobiliary serious adverse events in bardoxolone methyl-treated patients than placebo (4 vs 8 patients).

raw_record.support_text: In this patient, a case of drug-induced liver injury attributed to escitalopram, stopping escitalopram led to downtrending liver enzymes with eventual normalization of serum AST and ALT one week post-discharge. Other causes (gallstone disease, viral hepatitis, autoimmune liver disease) were excluded by CT scan and negative serology/testing. The case presented with fever and deranged liver enzymes, and was characterized as cholestatic liver injury with markedly elevated ALP and only slightly elevated ALT.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case: fever and deranged LFTs; on stopping escitalopram, enzymes normalized within one week post-discharge (AST 28->99->22, ALT 32->183->22, GGT 25->510->144, ALP 102->552->123, total bilirubin 17->24->7 over 4 June-24 July 2019). Negative workup for hepatitis A/B/C, autoimmune liver disease, and cholelithiasis. Patient had previously used fluoxetine (SSRI) without issues. Escitalopram is extensively metabolized by the liver via CYP3A4, CYP2C19, and to a lesser extent CYP2D6; hepatotoxicity may involve toxic intermediates. RUCAM scoring discussed as a diagnostic aid.

raw_record.support_text: A 68-year-old man was admitted with clinical jaundice with hepatitis, pruritus and dark urine; after an etiologic work-up for jaundice was negative, an adverse drug reaction with escitalopram was the sole possible explanation. Two days after escitalopram withdrawal pruritus resolved, clinical jaundice disappeared at ten days, and liver function tests normalized one month and three weeks after withdrawal. The authors state this is the first reported case where escitalopram was the only possible cause of cholestasis, with highly probable causality.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic and cytolysis liver injury; clinical jaundice, pruritus and dark urine; dechallenge with resolution of pruritus at 2 days, jaundice at 10 days, and normalized liver function tests at ~7 weeks after withdrawal. Etiologic study for hemolysis, viral hepatitis, cirrhosis, carcinoma, cholangitis, cholelithiasis and obstruction was negative. Reported as the first case of escitalopram as the only possible cause of cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a probable case of escitalopram-induced liver injury. A 56-year-old Chinese lady presented with fever and cholestatic liver injury two weeks after initiation of escitalopram for the treatment of psychotic depression. Investigations for stones, viral hepatitis and autoimmune liver disease were unyielding, and upon stopping escitalopram repeat liver function tests showed downtrending liver enzymes with eventual normalization of serum aminotransferase levels.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case: 56-year-old Chinese lady with psychotic depression; cholestatic liver injury with fever developed two weeks after escitalopram initiation; CT abdomen/pelvis and hepatitis A, B, C and autoimmune liver disease workup were unyielding; after drug cessation, AST and ALT downtrended and normalized by one week post-discharge. Probable causality per case report. Clinical phenotype: cholestatic liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a 49-year-old woman who developed severe toxic hepatitis 8 weeks after starting escitalopram 10 mg/day for depression, with initially cytolytic and then mixed biochemical pattern, two spontaneous cholestatic/jaundice reactivation flares despite drug withdrawal, and biopsy showing perivenular ballooned hepatocytes, microvacuolar steatosis, and eosinophilic necrosis consistent with hepatotoxicity. CIOMS causality assessment scored 7, corresponding to 'probable'. The authors state this is the first described case of toxic hepatitis due to escitalopram and caution that hepatotoxicity, even severe, should be considered during escitalopram treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 10 mg/day; symptoms present from 7 days before presentation, treatment started 8 weeks earlier; CIOMS causality score 7 ('probable'). Biopsy: perivenular balloonized hepatocytes, discrete microvacuolar steatosis, eosinophilic necrosis, moderate mixed inflammatory infiltrate (round cells and isolated eosinophils) in portal and lobular areas, no ductal injury or cholestasis. Biochemical pattern initially cytolytic then changed to mixed (max ALT 2,714 U/L, GGT 1,145 U/L, total bilirubin 6.3 mg/dl). Prolonged course with 2 spontaneous reactivation flares despite drug withdrawal; complete normalization at 20 weeks. Author reports this as the first described case of toxic hepatitis from escitalopram.

raw_record.support_text: A 49-year-old woman developed a severe toxic hepatitis 8 weeks after starting escitalopram 10 mg/day for depression, with jaundice, pruritus, elevated bilirubin and transaminases, and 2 spontaneous reactivation flares despite drug withdrawal; liver biopsy showed perivenular ballooned hepatocytes, microvacuolar steatosis and eosinophilic necrosis. The biochemical pattern was initially cytolytic and later mixed. The patient improved and normalized fully by week 20.
raw_record.extra_details: Escitalopram is the pure S enantiomer of citalopram, ~300x more selective for serotonin reuptake than noradrenaline, in the SSRI class. Dose 10 mg/day; symptoms began ~8 weeks after start. Labs: total bilirubin 6.1 mg/dl rising to 10.8 mg/dl and 6.3 mg/dl at flares; initial ALT 2,400 U/dl, AST 1,065 U/dl, GGT 224 U/dl, ALP 116 U/dl; later mixed pattern ALT 1,624-2,714 U/dl, GGT 703-1,145 U/dl. Biopsy: perivenular ballooned hepatocytes, microvacuolar steatosis, eosinophilic necrosis, moderate periportal round-cell/eosinophil infiltrate with lobular sparing, no bile duct lesion or cholestasis. CIOMS causality score 7 = 'probable'. Negative viral and autoimmune serology; no prior liver disease, alcohol, or herbal use. Dechallenge with subjective improvement but 2 icteric reactivation flares; full normalization at week 20. Reported as the first described case of escitalopram-induced toxic hepatitis, supporting that even severe hepatotoxicity can occur during escitalopram treatment. Underlying case: female, 49 years old.

raw_record.support_text: A 57-year-old patient died 24 hours after ingesting an abortifacient/laxative preparation containing 1,2-dichloroethane, from therapy-resistant cardiovascular failure. Along with the typical gastroenterocolitis and acute yellow liver dystrophy (acute liver failure), a severe hemorrhagic diathesis was observed. The complex coagulation disorder with thrombocytopenia and decreased activity of factors I, II, V, VII and XIII was interpreted as consumptive coagulopathy with secondary hyperfibrinolysis. Treatment recommendations, including immediate gastric lavage with paraffin oil and intensive liver protection, were given for acute liver failure from oral 1,2-dichloroethane poisoning.

raw_record.support_text: In the eight cases studied, the reaction began 23 to 37 days after the start of p-aminosalicylic acid therapy and was characterized by fever (101-105 F), rash, nausea, cervical lymphadenopathy, and, in two patients, hepatomegaly with tenderness and splenomegaly, one of whom had obvious jaundice with a bilirubin level of 4.6 mg per 100 cc. Laboratory studies showed abnormal liver function tests (elevated alkaline phosphatase, thymol turbidity, bilirubin, positive cephalin flocculation, and sulfobromophthalein retention), and the reaction subsided rapidly on drug discontinuation but recurred on readministration even at fractional doses. The authors conclude that the picture, which includes hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and abnormal liver function tests, strongly suggests hepatitis caused by p-aminosalicylic acid therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hypersensitivity/allergic reaction during therapeutic p-aminosalicylic acid therapy for tuberculosis; reaction clinically resembles infectious mononucleosis with hepatic involvement (hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, jaundice in one patient) in 8 reported cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Onset 23-37 days after start of therapy; fever 101-105 F; generalized erythematous macular (one urticarial) rash; eosinophilia 11-50%; atypical lymphocytes 1-21%; elevated alkaline phosphatase (13.7, 21.4, 52.6 units), thymol turbidity, bilirubin, 3-4+ cephalin flocculation, and sulfobromophthalein retention (15%, 20%); dechallenge produced resolution within hours/days to a month; rechallenge even in fractional doses caused exacerbation with reappearance of atypical lymphocytes, eosinophilia, and left shift. One cited reference describes lethal p-aminosalicylic acid intoxication (Muri).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that high-dose and long-term use of 6-thioguanine (6-TG) in children with ALL leads to chronic hepatotoxicity and portal hypertension, with hepatic sinusoidal obstruction/veno-occlusive disease as the key liver-injury picture. This was originally described in the MRCALL97 randomized controlled trial by Vora et al. (2006), in which 11% of children in the 6-TG group developed nonfatal HVOD. Clinical manifestations are described as mild hepatomegaly, hyperbilirubinemia, elevated transaminase, thrombocytopenia, and portal hypertension, and 6-TG-related HSOS during Baixiaoan treatment was associated with glutathione depletion and oxidative stress in hepatocytes.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemia during maintenance therapy; high-dose and long-term use; co-treatment context (e.g., Baixiaoan regimen, vincristine/methotrexate interactions).
raw_record.extra_details: 11% of children in the 6-TG arm of the MRCALL97 RCT (Vora et al., 2006) developed nonfatal hepatic veno-occlusive disease (HVOD). Main clinical manifestations: mild hepatomegaly, hyperbilirubinemia, elevated transaminase, thrombocytopenia, portal hypertension; >90% showed transient mild hepatomegaly, mild-to-moderate hyperbilirubinemia with elevated transaminase, and moderate-to-severe thrombocytopenia. One child with HVOD-like features died of adenovirus infection (autopsy-confirmed), needing differentiation from HSOS. Most reversible HVOD patients in the American CCG-1952 trial had only HSOS manifestations. 6-TG-related HSOS during Baixiaoan treatment associated with glutathione depletion and oxidative stress in hepatocytes; interactions with vincristine and methotrexate-induced homocysteine increases proposed to reduce anticoagulant protein levels. Imaging (Doppler ultrasound, multislice spiral CT with MPR and liver CTA) aids HSOS diagnosis.

raw_record.support_text: The study confirms that a significant proportion of children with ALL treated with 6-TG (6-thioguanine) as maintenance chemotherapy may develop chronic hepatotoxicity with portal hypertension, which can lead to variceal haemorrhage; the complication may present without antecedent veno-occlusive disease, and no children randomized to 6-MP maintenance were referred.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia) receiving 6-TG as maintenance chemotherapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic hepatotoxicity complicated by portal hypertension and oesophageal variceal haemorrhage; 10 children followed since hepatology assessment (5-46 months, median 30 months); one child had variceal bleeding 2 years after chronic hepatotoxicity was recognized and entered an endoscopic variceal banding programme; persistent splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia; 3 children had abnormal liver function tests at referral; variceal bleeding developed in 3 of the reported cases. On biopsy, 8 of 9 showed some sinusoidal dilatation, 1 had established nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH) and 4 had features compatible with early NRH; the injury is proposed to represent a spectrum of non-cirrhotic portal hypertension including NRH and hepatoportal sclerosis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state their data confirm warnings from previous 6-thioguanine (6-TG) studies that nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH) cannot be ruled out in patients with normal liver enzymes, and that NRH occurring in patients under 6-TG treatment may be underreported unless liver biopsy is performed.
raw_record.extra_details: A consistent reduction of portal pressure (HVPG) in all three patients with elevated portal pressure 1 year after discontinuation of 6-TG therapy supports a direct toxic effect of 6-TG. ASAT and ALAT were significantly higher in NRH patients but did not exceed twice the upper limit of normal; platelet counts were significantly lower; one female patient had cholestasis with AP and gamma-GT above twice the upper limit of normal, with high ANA (1:1,280) but no autoimmune hepatopathy features. Homocysteine, vitamin C, and folic acid were within normal limits.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective study of 38 patients referred for evaluation of elevated serum alanine aminotransferase and/or alkaline phosphatase levels without clinical signs of hepatic decompensation, the diagnostic work-up resulted in definite or plausible causes of elevated liver enzymes, with drug-induced liver injury due to thioguanine identified in 1 subject.
raw_record.extra_details: Thioguanine-attributed DILI identified as a definite or plausible cause of elevated liver enzymes in 1 of 38 patients (21 men, 17 women) referred for evaluation of elevated ALT and/or ALP; no clinical signs of liver cirrhosis; the cohort also included NAFLD (9), primary sclerosing cholangitis (8), hepatitis C (7), autoimmune hepatitis (7), primary biliary cirrhosis (2), alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency (1), and 3 cases with no diagnosis before liver biopsy.

raw_record.support_text: Endothelial cell injury secondary to azathioprine can cause nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH) and venoocclusive disease. While rare with azathioprine/6-MP, patients on thiopurines should be monitored not only for biochemical abnormalities in liver enzymes but also for signs of portal hypertension, including thrombocytopenia. For patients treated with 6-thioguanine, NRH is more commonly seen than with AZA/6-MP; in one series 17% of patients on 6-thioguanine had NRH, and 19 of 111 patients developed NRH confirmed by liver biopsy, including 3 of 19 with NRH despite normal liver enzymes and blood counts. A series of 14 patients followed for a minimum of 2 years with mean 6-TGN levels of 705 pmol/8x10^8 erythrocytes found no evidence of NRH.
raw_record.extra_details: NRH is more common with 6-thioguanine than with azathioprine/6-MP. 17% (19/111, biopsy-confirmed) developed NRH, 3 of whom had NRH despite normal liver enzymes and blood counts. Recommendation: use only in selected patients intolerant to other immunosuppressants, with close monitoring for hepatotoxicity and portal hypertension and metabolite-level testing. A series of 14 patients (mean 6-TGN 705 pmol/8x10^8 erythrocytes) showed no NRH.

The paper lists acute hepatitis as a side effect in the treatment cohort.

Case reports described elevated liver enzymes, splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia after 44 weeks of 6-TG that resolved after discontinuation, while two other cases failed to resolve after dose reduction or cessation.

Age was the only independent, albeit weak, risk factor for development of NRH.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that 6-TG-treated inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients are at significant risk for nodular hyperplasia, early fibrosis and, less often, venous outflow disease (Budd-Chiari). This is based on histologic study of 38 liver biopsies from patients treated with 6-thioguanine (6-TG), including 125 patients who received 6-TG for 1 to 3 years at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings restricted to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients treated with 6-thioguanine as an alternative to azathioprine/6-mercaptopurine; the majority of the 125 patients used 6-TG for 1 to 3 years.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of 38 liver biopsies from 37 patients. Reticulin staining showed nodular regeneration of varying degree in 20/37 patients (53%); only 4/20 were seen with hematoxylin and eosin. Minimal fibrosis was seen with trichrome in 13 biopsies (34%); sinusoidal collagen deposition was seen in 14/23 cases examined by electron microscopy (60%). The single biopsy with nodular hyperplasia obvious on hematoxylin and eosin also showed changes of venous outflow obstruction. Background states 6-TG-related hepatotoxicity, including liver biochemistry elevations, sinusoidal collagen deposition, and veno-occlusive disease, had been described with its use in neoplastic disease, and that 6-TG caused liver cell necrosis and jaundice generally with veno-occlusive disease (VOD), with VOD regarded as the most characteristic 6-TG lesion; VOD and Budd-Chiari syndrome have also been reported in patients taking thioguanine alone or with other drugs. Authors recommend periodic rebiopsy for patients without nodular hyperplasia or fibrosis who continue 6-TG.

raw_record.support_text: Thioguanine is associated with liver toxicity, especially nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH). The paper assessed whether liver histology alters during long-term maintenance thioguanine treatment in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients.

raw_record.extra_details: Sequential liver biopsies in 25 IBD patients (median 25 months, range 14-54 between first and second biopsy). Rates: perisinusoidal fibrosis 91%, sinusoidal dilatation 68%, nodularity 18% (unchanged between biopsies); phlebosclerosis trended from 36% first to 68% second biopsy (p=0.092). Nodularity resolved upon thioguanine withdrawal in 2 patients, and portal hypertension was observed in 2 patients with phlebosclerosis.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 22 thioguanine (TG)-treated inflammatory bowel disease patients with sequential liver biopsies, thioguanine was associated with histopathological liver changes including mild inflammation, steatosis, fibrosis and vascular irregularities that were mostly asymptomatic and non-progressive. Perisinusoidal fibrosis (91%), sinusoidal dilatation (68%) and nodularity (18%) were present in both first and sequential biopsies, with a trend for phlebosclerosis (36% first vs 68% second, p=.092); nodularity of any degree was present in six patients (27%). Three patients ceased thioguanine due to hepatotoxicity, and in two patients nodularity of the liver resolved upon thioguanine withdrawal, while two patients had portal hypertension in the presence of phlebosclerosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Inflammatory bowel disease patients (including Crohn's disease) treated with thioguanine; three of these patients had previously received thiopurines (mercaptopurine, azathioprine).
raw_record.extra_details: 22 IBD patients (predominantly Crohn's disease) with sequential liver biopsies. Histological findings included nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH; nodularity in 27% of patients at any grade, grade 1-2 with none reaching grade 3), phlebosclerosis, perisinusoidal fibrosis, sinusoidal dilatation, and perivenular fibrosis. Three female Crohn's disease patients ceased thioguanine due to hepatotoxicity (TG duration 18-25 months); dechallenge biopsies showed reduced phlebosclerosis, perisinusoidal fibrosis, and nodularity with improved liver tests in two patients. Four patients had preexisting splenomegaly/liver test abnormalities, and thrombocytopenia occurred in three patients. Liver test abnormalities at first and second biopsy in nine (26%) and five (20%) patients; mild steatosis and elevated gamma-glutamyl-transferase (43-92 U/L) noted. Two patients had portal hypertension in the presence of phlebosclerosis.

raw_record.support_text: 95 patients had acute hepatitis with features of veno-occlusive disease during the trial, and all instances were related to 6-thioguanine exposure: 82 had been assigned that drug, one was taking non-randomised 6-thioguanine, and 12 were patients assigned 6-mercaptopurine who developed veno-occlusive disease whilst taking 6-thioguanine during intensification. Diagnosis was centrally validated and required at least two of: tender hepatomegaly, ascites, hyperbilirubinaemia (>17 µmol/L), or persistent thrombocytopenia out of proportion to neutropenia for more than 4 weeks. In the 82 assigned 6-thioguanine, 85% of veno-occlusive disease episodes occurred during continuing treatment or interim maintenance. Most patients had transient tender hepatomegaly with mild to moderate hyperbilirubinaemia and raised aminotransferases; one patient died of biopsy-proven adenovirus infection.

raw_record.extra_details: 95 cases of acute hepatitis with veno-occlusive disease features; 82 patients assigned 6-thioguanine, 1 on non-randomised 6-thioguanine, 12 assigned 6-mercaptopurine who developed VOD while taking 6-thioguanine in intensification. Diagnosis required at least two of: tender hepatomegaly, ascites, hyperbilirubinaemia (>17 µmol/L), persistent thrombocytopenia out of proportion to neutropenia for >4 weeks. Among patients assigned 6-thioguanine, 85% of VOD episodes occurred during continuing treatment (75%) or interim maintenance (10%), 15% during intensification. >90% had transient tender hepatomegaly, mild-moderate hyperbilirubinaemia with raised aminotransferases, and moderate-severe thrombocytopenia. One patient died of biopsy-proven adenovirus infection after presenting with VOD features; two admitted to intensive care for pulmonary complications; ~20% needed platelet/RBC transfusions. All switched to 6-mercaptopurine after VOD. Liver tests normalised after mean 4 weeks (range 1-52). 24 patients (25% of affected) developed splenomegaly with persistent mild-moderate thrombocytopenia; a further 19 patients had splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia without antecedent acute VOD, all in 6-thioguanine recipients.

raw_record.support_text: 6-Thioguanine (6-TG), a prodrug immediately converted into 6-thioguanine nucleotide (6-TGN), was tested in 40 azathioprine-intolerant and 9 azathioprine-resistant Crohn's disease patients at 20 mg/d. Five of 40 patients (13%) did not tolerate 6-TG, including two with an increase in liver enzymes. In a separate small prospective study of 16 patients on 20-40 mg of 6-TG, one severe case of hepatotoxicity occurred after 44 weeks with recovery within 24 weeks after withdrawal of 6-TG. The authors note the considerable risk of hepatotoxicity, predominantly nodular regenerative hyperplasia, even in patients with normal liver function tests, and conclude that 6-TG should only be given in controlled study settings.

raw_record.support_text: Of the patients using thioguanine (TG), 14 (25%) had to discontinue therapy within 1 year, mostly due to adverse events or ineffectiveness. Out of 8 patients who had to discontinue TG due to hepatotoxicity, 5 were diagnosed with histologically proven nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH) of the liver in biopsies taken as part of a long-term TG safety study. Of these, 2 were asymptomatic, 2 had thrombocytopenia (platelet counts 46 and 67 x 10⁹/L after 15 and 28 months of TG), and 1 had symptoms of noncirrhotic portal hypertension (esophageal varices grade III-IV, splenomegaly) after 44 months. NRH patients had comparable 6-TGN concentrations as non-NRH patients (481 vs 415 pmol/8 x 10⁸ RBC, P = 0.80).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis); one patient with thrombocytopenia had low platelets before TG initiation.
raw_record.extra_details: 5 of 8 patients discontinuing TG for hepatotoxicity had histologically proven nodular regenerative hyperplasia; 2 asymptomatic, 2 with thrombocytopenia (platelets 46 and 67 x 10⁹/L after 15 and 28 months), 1 with noncirrhotic portal hypertension (esophageal varices grade III-IV, splenomegaly) after 44 months of TG. 6-TGN concentrations comparable between NRH and non-NRH patients (481 vs 415 pmol/8 x 10⁸ RBC, P = 0.80). Liver function test elevations in the total cohort were usually mild (<3.0 x ULN). NRH is a vascular lesion associated with liver injury; 2 TG-group deaths occurred during follow-up but were unlikely related to TG.

raw_record.support_text: In this study of patients with IBD, the authors confirmed the major relevance of 6-thioguanine (6-TG)-related drug-induced liver injury and the high risk for development of nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH). Unambiguous or most likely NRH was diagnosed on the basis of histological examination with silver-reticulin staining in 27.1% of the 59 patients with liver biopsy. 6-TG was used for a median of 18 months before liver biopsy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with inflammatory bowel disease receiving therapeutic 6-TG; NRH diagnosis required liver biopsy with silver-reticulin staining.
raw_record.extra_details: NRH prevalence in the survey was 27.1% of 59 biopsied patients, lower than the 61.5% and 54.1% reported by the Los Angeles working group. 6-TG was given for a median of 18 months before biopsy in this population (median initiation dose 40 mg/day) versus 8.5 months in Dubinsky et al.; doses up to 100 mg/day were used in a US study. Higher 6-TG dosage may relate to higher NRH rates. Patients with NRH were older (median 44 years vs 35, p=0.002) and more often female (68.8% vs 44.2%), with hepatotoxicity in 56.3% of NRH-positive versus 25.6% of non-NRH patients (p=0.03); hepatotoxicity had 56.3% sensitivity and 74.4% specificity for NRH. Pathogenesis may relate to high 6-thioguanine nucleotide levels, though other mechanisms are debated. Multivariate analysis identified age as a weak independent risk factor.

raw_record.support_text: Thioguanine, the active metabolite of azathioprine and mercaptopurine, is considered as an alternative agent in patients intolerant to those drugs. Although no controlled study is available, several series reported a high frequency of liver abnormalities with thioguanine, mostly nodular regenerative hyperplasia, an irreversible cause of portal hypertension. Because of this liver toxicity, thioguanine cannot currently be recommended for maintenance of Crohn's disease.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that hepatotoxicity is a known consequence of iron overdose and that iron poisoning leads to periportal hepatic injury by free radical generation and lipid peroxidation. Two pediatric patients with intentional (suicidal) ferrous sulfate overdose rapidly developed fulminant hepatic failure severe enough to require liver transplantation despite deferoxamine treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients (adolescents) with intentional suicidal ingestion of ferrous sulfate; overdose/supratherapeutic exposure context.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1: 17-year-old female ingested 10 pills ferrous sulfate (23 mg/kg elemental iron), serum iron 1000 µg/dL at 2h and 670 µg/dL at 4h; INR rose to 6.6 by 20h and >13; AST 2000 U/L, ALT 2424 U/L, total bilirubin 3.8 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL; developed Grade 1-2 then Grade 3 hepatic encephalopathy and lactic acidosis; treated with deferoxamine 15 mg/kg/hour for 24h, intravenous N-acetylcysteine, and CVVH; emergent living-donor left lobe liver transplant 4 days post-ingestion; explant histology showed diffuse parenchymal collapse, severe cholestasis and massive hepatic necrosis compatible with toxin-induced liver injury; recovered, well at 1 year. Toxicology negative for acetaminophen, acetylsalicylic acid, amphetamines, benzodiazepines, opiates, ethanol. Posited mechanism: free radical generation and lipid peroxidation.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports acute iron toxicity with hepatotoxicity. It states that hepatotoxicity caused by acute iron poisoning is associated with a high mortality rate, and describes a case of severe hepatic injury in an adult who overdosed on iron tablets with suicidal intent. Peak serum iron level (340 µg/dL) was lower than the reported hepatotoxic threshold (>1,700 µg/dL), yet rapid and significant elevations in aminotransferases (>4,000 U/L), total bilirubin (5 mg/dL), and prothrombin time (50 s) occurred within 48 hours; tests for acetaminophen, hepatatrophic viruses, and other causes of acute liver injury were negative, and the patient had a full recovery.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute iron overdose with suicidal intent: one-time ingestion of ~100 ferrous sulfate tablets (120 mg elemental iron/kg body weight) in an otherwise previously healthy 18-year-old woman; no other ingestion or co-medications except occasional ibuprofen.
raw_record.extra_details: Ingested as ferrous sulfate tablets. Peak serum iron 340 µg/dL, lower than the reported threshold associated with hepatotoxicity (>1,700 µg/dL); aminotransferases >4,000 U/L, total bilirubin 5 mg/dL, prothrombin time 50 s within 48 hours. Tests for acetaminophen, hepatatrophic viruses, and other causes of acute liver injury were negative. Treated promptly with deferoxamine followed by empiric N-acetylcysteine once liver injury was apparent. Paper notes iron is a known hepatotoxin and that acute iron-poisoning hepatotoxicity is associated with high mortality, and warns that unlike acetaminophen levels, iron levels do not offer reliable risk stratification for liver injury.
