raw_record.support_text: A 16-year-old female ingested 54 tablets of ferrous sulfate (358 mg/kg elemental iron) during an intentional overdose following a conflict. She presented with blood-tinged emesis, abdominal tenderness, serum iron >1000 µg/dL, and elevated liver enzymes. Her liver function worsened with massive transaminase elevations (AST 10378 U/L, ALT 9045 U/L), profound coagulopathy (INR >13), and stage 2 hepatic encephalopathy; she underwent emergent deceased donor liver transplantation on day 4, with explanted liver histology showing massive acute panlobular hepatic necrosis, centrilobular congestion/hemorrhage, and cholestasis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intentional overdose in an adolescent (16-year-old female) with depression; co-ingested omeprazole, diphenhydramine, and ibuprofen; treated with deferoxamine and IV N-acetylcysteine.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 358 mg/kg elemental iron; serum iron >1000 µg/dL initially falling to 404 µg/dL; initial AST 67/ALT 79 U/L and INR 1.1 rising to AST 10378/ALT 9045 U/L, INR >13, ammonia 137 µg/dL with stage 2 hepatic encephalopathy by day 3; transplant on day 4; explant showed massive acute panlobular hepatic necrosis with centrilobular congestion/hemorrhage and cholestasis; recovered with normal graft function at one year. Discussion notes hepatotoxicity is dose-related, with single-center study of 73 iron-intoxicated patients of whom 13 developed hepatotoxicity (AST/ALT >5x ULN), 9 severe, 5 died; serum iron >1000 µg/dL associated with clinically important hepatotoxicity while <700 µg/dL within 12 h unlikely hepatotoxic; coagulopathy can occur without hepatotoxicity via thrombin inhibition; fifth-stage GI strictures/fistulas not seen in these patients.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes the classic clinical course of iron poisoning, divided into five phases. The fourth phase, occurring 12-48 h post ingestion, is characterized by hepatotoxicity. The described case matched this classic description of iron poisoning, with liver injury shown by rising total bilirubin (to 253.1 µmol/L/14.8 mg/dL) and alanine aminotransferase (SGPT) rising to 2843 U/L by 48 h post ingestion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive overdose ingestion of an iron-containing product; the patient survived with recovery and treatment was given.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of iron poisoning in which hepatotoxicity marked the fourth phase (12-48 h post ingestion). Peak serum iron was 2992 µmol/L (16,706 µg/dL) at 5 h. Total bilirubin rose to 253.1 µmol/L (14.8 mg/dL) and SGPT/ALT to 2843 U/L by 48 h; LDH 2014 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 248 U/L. Treated with high-dose intermittent-infusion DFO (deferoxamine) mesylate chelation; the patient left hospital ~4 months after ingestion in good condition with good oral intake and was neurologically normal. Gastric outlet obstruction (phase-five complication) also developed and subsequently improved.

raw_record.support_text: Analysis of the characteristics of the cases of TR-induced jaundice led the authors to deduce that the mechanism for this idiosyncratic injury involves, at least in part, metabolic idiosyncrasy. Over 90% of 336 cases of TR-associated hepatic injury had been taking the drug for more than 30 days, some for as long as 6 months, when hepatic injury first became apparent (unpublished data). The prolonged and variable exposure before injury is considered more consistent with metabolic idiosyncrasy than with hypersensitivity, and a toxic metabolite of TR formed by the mixed function oxidase system is proposed as responsible for the injury.
raw_record.extra_details: TR (toremifene) is reported to cause idiosyncratic hepatic injury/jaundice in humans; 336 cases of TR-associated hepatic injury, over 90% had taken the drug for more than 30 days, some up to 6 months, before injury appeared. Mechanism attributed to metabolic idiosyncrasy via a toxic metabolite formed by the mixed function oxidase system (phenobarbital pretreatment enhanced the adverse effect in an in vitro isolated perfused rat liver model). Human injury reference derives from the authors' unpublished case data.

raw_record.support_text: In the report of doxapram effects in 2 infants with congenital central hypoventilation syndrome, the authors state that the other major complication associated with the maintenance doxapram infusion was hepatotoxicity. Liver size increased progressively during the infusion; at the time of abdominal surgery the liver was 6 cm below the right costal margin, yellow, and firm, and biopsy revealed severe fatty metamorphosis without necrosis or inflammation. Increased serum transaminase concentrations (SGOT 160 IU/L and SGPT 120 IU/L vs normal ranges 8-31 and 6-39 IU/L) provided additional evidence of hepatotoxicity, while serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase remained normal. Liver size and transaminase concentrations returned to normal within 10 days after stopping doxapram.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (infants) with congenital central hypoventilation syndrome; occurred during prolonged continuous maintenance doxapram infusion at 2 mg per kg body weight per hour, necessitating stopping the infusion after 5.2 days
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of 2 infants treated with doxapram. Hepatotoxicity occurred in Patient 2 during a 5.2-day maintenance infusion (loading dose 0.5 mg/kg/min for 14 min, then up to 7 mg/kg/h, stepped down to 2 mg/kg/h). Liver enlarged, yellow, firm; liver biopsy showed severe fatty metamorphosis without necrosis or inflammation; SGOT 160 IU/L and SGPT 120 IU/L vs normal 8-31 and 6-39 IU/L; bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase normal. Liver size and transaminases returned to normal within 10 days after discontinuation. Concurrent massive gastrointestinal hemorrhage required surgery the following day for a perforated duodenal ulcer, and hypoglycemia (25 mg/100 ml) occurred one day before the hemorrhage, confounding the clinical picture.

raw_record.support_text: In the present case, doxapram was prescribed for 24 h only and hepatic function quickly returned to normal after the infusion was stopped. In the absence of an obvious infective aetiology, the authors conclude that the hepatic necrosis was caused by the administration of doxapram.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single adult patient; infusion given for 24 h; competing infective aetiology excluded; absence of severe right ventricular failure and normal blood pressure throughout. Hepatic function returned quickly to normal after stopping the infusion.
raw_record.extra_details: Centrilobular liver necrosis without features of passive venous congestion (no sinusoidal congestion/haemosiderin-in-macrophages/fatty change in adjacent parenchyma). Mechanism of doxapram-induced hepatitis uncertain; doxapram is oxidized to principal metabolite AHR 5955 by the liver with a suggested enterohepatic pathway; whether that metabolite has pharmacological activity is unknown. Co-trimoxazole and other medications were continued during biochemical recovery, so they were not implicated in this case.

raw_record.support_text: A 59-year-old man had repeated admissions for fever, chills, abdominal pain, and marked transaminase elevations (AST 804 U/L, ALT 2116 U/L, total bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL) after tizanidine was newly added for chronic back pain; liver biopsy showed perivenular necrosis/hepatocyte dropout and macrosteatosis. Each time the patient resumed tizanidine at home he was readmitted with the same presentation, and after tizanidine was discontinued his LFTs returned to normal, symptoms resolved, and he remained asymptomatic over 6 months of follow-up. The authors present this as a case of tizanidine-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonist used for muscle spasticity, added for chronic back pain. Peak LFTs: AST 804 U/L, ALT 2116 U/L, total bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL with direct 1.6 mg/dL; undetectable acetaminophen levels. Liver biopsy: minimal fibrosis and inflammation with perivenular necrosis/hepatocyte dropout and macrosteatosis. Repeated dechallenge/rechallenge pattern (4 similar admissions when tizanidine was resumed); extended negative workup for viral, autoimmune, and infectious causes; symptoms resolved and LFTs returned to normal after discontinuation, with 6-month asymptomatic follow-up.

raw_record.support_text: Of three deaths associated with liver failure in patients treated with tizanidine, one case was thought probably related to tizanidine and the other two occurred in patients on other hepatotoxic agents. One additional case report described symptomatic jaundice associated with tizanidine that resolved after drug discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Three deaths associated with liver failure occurred in tizanidine-treated patients; one was considered probably related to tizanidine, while the other two were in patients on other hepatotoxic agents. A separate case report described symptomatic jaundice associated with tizanidine that resolved after drug discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that erlotinib administration with careful monitoring is a good alternative for patients who responded well to gefitinib treatment but whose gefitinib treatment had resulted in hepatotoxicity. This positions gefitinib as the agent that produced drug-induced hepatotoxicity in these patients. The retrospective study (7 patients, 2 male, 5 smokers) frames the observed liver injury as 'gefitinib-induced hepatotoxicity,' noting prior speculation that it may involve an allergic reaction and the clinical importance of CYP2D6 polymorphism.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective study of patients who responded well to gefitinib but developed hepatotoxicity and were switched to erlotinib as an alternative. 7 patients, 2 male, 5 smokers. Suggested mechanisms include an allergic reaction (Takeda et al. hypothesis), chemical structure/metabolic pathway differences, and clinical importance of CYP2D6 polymorphism (Kijima et al.). Gefitinib and erlotinib are metabolized by CYP3A4, CYP3A5, and CYP1A1; CYP2D6 contributes largely to gefitinib metabolism while CYP1A2 contributes to erlotinib. Study limited by retrospective design and small number of patients.

raw_record.support_text: Gefitinib is described as known to have adverse effects including hepatotoxicity, diarrhea, acneiform skin rash, and pneumonitis. In the retrospective cohort of 159 Chinese patients with advanced EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma, 17 (10.7%) were on reduced dose (250 mg alternate day) gefitinib, of whom 14 (82.4%) had the dose reduced because of hepatotoxicity and 3 (17.6%) because of cutaneous side effects, with toxicity assessed by CTCAE version 5.0.
raw_record.extra_details: 14 of 17 reduced-dose patients (82.4%) had gefitinib dose reduced because of hepatotoxicity; 3 (17.6%) because of cutaneous side effects. Involved 159 Chinese patients with advanced adenocarcinoma of lung with sensitizing EGFR mutations receiving first-line gefitinib. Toxicity assessed per NCI Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0. Reduced dose (250 mg alternate day) showed comparable progression-free survival to standard 250 mg daily (HR 1.121, 95% CI 0.655-1.917).

raw_record.support_text: A 64-year-old woman treated with gefitinib for NSCLC experienced coma, cellulitis, renal failure and hepatic failure (TTO 0 days) that required hospitalization; the causality assessment was 'Probable'.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 19 in the Sicilian SADR series; seriousness type hospitalization; ADRs included coma, cellulitis, renal failure and hepatic failure with TTO 0 days; outcome improved; causality 'Probable'.

raw_record.support_text: Several cases attribute liver injury to therapeutic Gefitinib in lung cancer patients. One report described a 61-year-old Japanese woman with lung adenocarcinoma on Gefitinib 250 mg once daily for 8 weeks who achieved complete remission but developed grade 2-3 liver dysfunction (liver metastasis and other liver disease excluded); after rechallenge she again developed grade 3 liver dysfunction and the regimen was changed to 250 mg every 5 days. Another report described a female EGFR-mutated lung adenocarcinoma patient who developed grade 4 liver dysfunction after 14 months of Gefitinib and recovered to grade 1 after stopping the drug with hepatoprotective therapy, then resumed Gefitinib. Two additional NSCLC patients with gefitinib-induced grade 2/3 liver dysfunction successfully switched to Erlotinib. Separately (para 18), 17 lung cancer patients who had taken Gefitinib and developed liver toxicity carrying CYP2D6*5 or *10 alleles could convert to Erlotinib (P=0.024), and after CYP3A4 inhibition, 7 patients carrying CYP2D6*5 or *10 again developed liver toxicity on Gefitinib rechallenge while 3 with normal alleles did not, implicating CYP2D6 functional deficiency as a contributor.
raw_record.extra_details: EGFR-mutated NSCLC/lung adenocarcinoma patients on 250 mg daily Gefitinib. Reported severities ranged from CTCAE-like grade 2 to grade 4 liver dysfunction; grade 4 case improved to grade 1 after drug cessation and hepatoprotective therapy, then resumed Gefitinib. Two patients switched to Erlotinib after gefitinib-induced grade 2/3 liver injury. CYP2D6*5/*10 (reduced/no activity) alleles and CYP3A4 inhibition were associated with Gefitinib liver toxicity in reported lung cancer patients (17-patient report, P=0.024); hepatotoxicity attributed to CYP2D6 functional deficiency when CYP3A4 was inhibited.

raw_record.support_text: In the conclusion, the paper states that the side effects of diarrhoea, skin rash, and hepatotoxicity induced by gefitinib were unrelated to plasma exposure to O-desmethyl gefitinib. This treats hepatotoxicity as a gefitinib-induced adverse effect, and the comparison found that hepatotoxicity (follow-up 1 year) was not associated with O-desmethyl gefitinib AUC0-24 or total gefitinib-plus-metabolite AUC in gefitinib-treated Japanese NSCLC patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Japanese patients with non-small-cell lung carcinoma receiving therapeutic gefitinib; hepatotoxicity follow-up period 1 year. Hepatotoxicity recorded in 20/36 patients and, per the analysis (P=0.962 for O-desmethyl gefitinib AUC0-24; P=0.519 for total AUC), was unrelated to O-desmethyl gefitinib exposure or total gefitinib-plus-metabolite AUC. The paper also cites Xin et al. [22] reporting that the trough plasma gefitinib concentration is not significantly associated with hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Two patients with non-small cell lung cancer developed grade 2/3 hepatotoxicity starting 4-6 weeks after initiation of gefitinib, with toxicity peaking between 10 and 20 weeks. Both were switched to erlotinib without further hepatotoxicity. One patient experienced recurrence of hepatotoxicity when gefitinib was briefly reintroduced (positive rechallenge). The authors conclude that patients with NSCLC receiving gefitinib should undergo routine monitoring of liver enzymes, and frame the events as gefitinib-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Two NSCLC patients on gefitinib (oral EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor) developed grade 2/3 hepatotoxicity with onset 4-6 weeks and peak 10-20 weeks after start. Both tolerated switching to erlotinib without further hepatotoxicity; one patient had recurrence of hepatotoxicity on gefitinib rechallenge (supporting causality), while the other achieved a durable near-complete response on erlotinib. Reported hepatotoxicity incidence 10-20% in phase II trials. No biochemical pattern (e.g., R ratio, hepatocellular vs cholestatic) or clinical phenotype beyond hepatotoxicity was specified.

raw_record.support_text: The study found hepatotoxicity was a common adverse event during long-term oral administration of gefitinib. Most patients showed an increase in aminotransferase (28.7%, mostly mild, 24.7%), followed by an increase in bilirubin (9.9%) and an increase in ALP (3.0%). The authors describe gefitinib-induced liver injury, with elevated aminotransferase being the most common laboratory evidence, and suggest gefitinib may also increase bilirubin by impairing hepatocytes.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral gefitinib for non-small-cell lung cancer (long-term administration); liver injury developed after 1-23 months (median 4 months), with median time to grade I, II, and III hepatotoxicity of 5, 3.5, and 2.5 months, indicating severe injury tends to present early. Grade III hepatotoxicity occurred in 4.0% of patients (four patients). Incidence was higher with >14 months of therapy (52.0% vs 27.5% for <14 months, P=0.012). Aminotransferase elevation 28.7%, bilirubin increase 9.9% (mostly simultaneous direct and indirect bilirubin increase), ALP increase 3.0%. Of 40 hepatotoxic patients, 32 (80%) recovered liver function, 8 (20%) had persistent grade 1 hepatotoxicity; 4 patients discontinued gefitinib due to hepatotoxicity (1 mild, 3 severe). Hepatoprotective drug combinations given for 1 week to 3 months.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of grade 3 (CTCAE v4.03) cytolytic hepatitis occurring in a patient treated with gefitinib, with recurrence of the hepatitis upon gefitinib reintroduction; switching to erlotinib did not lead to reappearance of hepatic toxicity. The case was notified to the Grenoble (France) pharmacovigilance center on 6 October 2011 and analyzed by the French imputability method. Transaminases rose on rechallenge (ASAT up to 6.7 N, ALAT up to 10.5 N), etiologic work-up (viral hepatitis B and C serologies, imaging) was negative, and no self-medication was reported.
raw_record.extra_details: 71-year-old man with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma (EGFR exon 21 mutation, KRAS wild-type) treated with gefitinib 250 mg/day first line; grade 3 (CTCAE v4.03) cytolytic hepatitis with transaminase elevation (peak ASAT 6.7 N, ALAT 10.5 N) starting ~9 weeks after initiation; recurrence upon reintroduction (rise within 4 days); switching to erlotinib caused no hepatic toxicity; negative hepatitis B/C serologies and imaging work-up; concurrent doxycycline prescribed for cutaneous toxicity prevention (not attributed as cause); causality analyzed by French imputability method; notified to Grenoble pharmacovigilance center.

raw_record.support_text: DILI-inducing antineoplastics were methotrexate, nedaplatin, cisplatin, carboplatin, pemetrexed, gefitinib and imatinib; antineoplastics accounted for 13 patients (3.07%).
raw_record.extra_details: Antineoplastic; antineoplastics accounted for 13 patients (3.07%) of DILI cases.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports multiple patients with gefitinib-induced liver injury: eight non-small-cell lung cancer patients switched to erlotinib after severe gefitinib-induced liver injury; two patients who developed grade 2-3 hepatotoxicity starting 4-6 weeks after gefitinib initiation, one of whom had recurrence on rechallenge; and several other patients who developed hepatotoxicity requiring gefitinib discontinuation. These cases constitute explicit human DILI attribution to gefitinib.
raw_record.extra_details: Tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for non-small cell lung cancer. Recurrence of hepatotoxicity occurred in one of two patients re-challenged with gefitinib and in one of eight patients switched to erlotinib; several patients tolerated erlotinib afterwards without hepatotoxicity. Gefitinib is discontinued more often than erlotinib because of hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Among 180 NSCLC patients treated with gefitinib, 87 (48%) developed at least grade 1 gefitinib-induced hepatotoxicity and 45 (25%) developed ≥2 grade hepatotoxicity; no statistical association was found between gefitinib-induced hepatotoxicity and clinical confounders.
raw_record.extra_details: Study in 180 EGFR-mutated (19 del, 21 L858R, other) NSCLC patients at Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center (2013-2018); hepatotoxicity graded per CTCAE (at least grade 1: 48%; ≥2 grade: 25%). Plasma concentrations of gefitinib and its four metabolites (M1, M2, G235, G236) were not associated with hepatotoxicity in the general subjects, so concentration monitoring could not predict gefitinib-induced hepatotoxicity. Among 194 SNPs, G>A rs4711998 (IL17/IL17A), C>T rs4795896 (CCL11), G>A rs4946935 (FOXO3) and G>A rs12722604 (IL2RA) were associated with gefitinib-induced hepatotoxicity; FOXO3 G>A rs4946935 was an independent risk factor by multivariate logistic regression and plasma AST/ALT was significantly correlated with gefitinib concentration in FOXO3 AA carriers. Metabolites were measured but not independently identified as injuring entities.

raw_record.support_text: In this study of gefitinib-treated patients, severe hepatotoxicity was defined as grade ≥ 3 or prolonged grade ≥ 2 adverse events per Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (version 4.0) that led to gefitinib cessation. Progression-free survival was compared between patients who switched from 250 mg daily to every-other-day dosing after severe hepatotoxicity and those on 250 mg daily who did not, with follow-up until March 31, 2018.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatotoxicity defined per CTCAE v4.0 as grade ≥ 3 or prolonged grade ≥ 2 that led to gefitinib cessation; standard dose 250 mg daily; patients with severe hepatotoxicity switched to every-other-day dosing; PFS (RECIST v1.1) compared between patients with and without severe hepatotoxicity; one patient with severe hepatotoxicity excluded from PFS analysis due to prior enrollment in another clinical trial.

raw_record.support_text: A total of 55 patients with NSCLC in whom gefitinib-induced hepatotoxicity had developed were enrolled. Median serum ALT was 236 IU/L (range 100-1119 IU/L), median time to onset after taking gefitinib was 41 days (range 7-228 days), and there were 25/28/2 grade 2/3/4 hepatotoxicity cases. Gefitinib rechallenge at reduced dose in 40 patients caused recurrence of hepatotoxicity in 19.
raw_record.extra_details: 55 adult NSCLC patients (11 men, 44 women; median age 73 y; 52 adenocarcinoma; EGFR mutations in 35). CTCAE v3.0 grade 2/3/4 hepatotoxicity counts 25/28/2; median ALT 236 IU/L; median onset latency 41 d (7-228 d). Rechallenge with reduced-dose gefitinib (alternate-day 250 mg) recurred in 19 of 40 patients. CYP2D6 *5/*10 allele analysis showed no significant enrichment (69.1% vs 62.6% in Japanese controls, P=.824).

raw_record.support_text: A 61-year-old Chinese female with EGFR-mutant (exon 19 deletion) stage IV NSCLC developed severe gefitinib-induced grade 4 hepatotoxicity after 14 months of gefitinib 250 mg/day, with ALT 1,130 U/l (grade 4) and AST 629 U/l (grade 3) by CTCAE v3.0. Because liver metastasis and other diseases were ruled out and no other medications were administered, the hepatic enzyme elevation was attributed to gefitinib. Liver function improved after gefitinib discontinuation (ALT falling to 98 and 69 U/l at 6 and 10 weeks), and a gefitinib rechallenge with hepatoprotective therapy maintained disease control with normal liver function for more than 6 months.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 250 mg/day (Iressa; AstraZeneca), injury appeared after 14 months of long-term administration. ALT 1,130 U/l (grade 4) and AST 629 U/l (grade 3), CTCAE v3.0. Liver metastasis and other diseases excluded; no co-medications. Dechallenge: ALT fell to 98 and 69 U/l at 6 and 10 weeks after discontinuation. Rechallenge at same dose with hepatoprotective therapy maintained normal liver function >6 months with disease control. Case of a 61-year-old non-smoking female NSCLC patient with EGFR exon 19 deletion, first-line therapy.

raw_record.support_text: In case 1, both gefitinib and erlotinib were administered and grade 3 hepatotoxicity occurred despite evident therapeutic effect; in cases 2 and 3, afatinib was directly chosen after gefitinib failed because of hepatotoxicity. The hepatotoxicity (grade 3) recorded for all three patients in the case table is attributed to gefitinib, which required switching treatment (afatinib was subsequently given without hepatotoxicity).
raw_record.extra_details: Three postoperative, EGFR mutation-positive NSCLC patients (Cases 1-3) developed grade 3 hepatotoxicity during gefitinib therapy that led to discontinuation/switching. The WJTOG3405 study reported severe transaminase elevation of grade ≥3 in 23.6% of gefitinib-treated Japanese patients. Gefitinib is metabolized in the liver by CYP enzymes such as CYP3A4 with >80% of dose found in feces; CYP2D6 gene polymorphisms are reported to be associated with gefitinib- and/or erlotinib-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In Chinese NSCLC patients receiving gefitinib, several NF-κB pathway SNPs were associated with gefitinib-induced hepatic toxicity: RELA rs11227247 (Fisher's exact test P=0.038, recessive model), NFKBIB rs2053071 (P=0.004, Fisher's; P=0.021 dominant model), and NFKBIA rs2233407 which was associated with severe hepatic toxicity (grade ≥2) (P=0.04, recessive model). Stepwise logistic regression confirmed RELA rs11227247 as a factor for gefitinib-induced hepatic toxicity (GG vs non-GG: OR=0.212, 95% CI 0.062–0.726, P=0.013). Gefitinib is thereby identified as the agent producing hepatic toxicity in these patients, with the studied SNPs framed as biomarkers predicting these adverse drug reactions.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings restricted to Chinese patients with non-small cell lung carcinoma receiving gefitinib as their anti-cancer therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic toxicity graded 0, 1, and 2+ (severe defined as grade ≥2). Associated genetic variants: RELA rs11227247 (hepatic toxicity, GG vs non-GG OR=0.212, 95% CI 0.062–0.726, P=0.013 on stepwise logistic regression; P=0.038 Fisher's exact, recessive), NFKBIB rs2053071 (P=0.004 Fisher's, P=0.021 dominant), NFKBIA rs2233407 (severe hepatic toxicity, P=0.04 recessive). Multiple other SNPs (ARFGEF3, DPT, IKBKB, IKBKE, NFKB1, NFKB2, NFKBIA, NR1H2, REL, SUMO4, TAB2, TAGAP, TNFAIP3) showed no significant association (NS). Gefitinib trough concentrations were available in 75 patients (median 231.15 ng/mL, range 47.8–773.6 ng/mL) with no significant genotype-dependent difference after FDR adjustment; the SNPs are presented as potential predictive biomarkers rather than the injuring entities.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports the first case of hepatic injury induced by Venoplant®, an extract of Aesculus hippocastanum (horse chestnut) with antiinflammatory activity. A 37-year-old man who received a 65 mg i.m. injection of Venoplant® developed jaundice and pruritus about 60 days later, with moderate elevation of total bilirubin, ALP, and γ-GTP, mild eosinophilia, and a positive lymphocyte stimulation test. Liver biopsy showed marked cholestasis with zonal necrosis in the centrilobular areas, features consistent with drug-induced hepatic injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single-case report; product (extract of Aesculus hippocastanum) administered by intramuscular injection; patient had a pathological left brachial bone fracture and giant cell tumor of bone.
raw_record.extra_details: 65 mg single i.m. injection several hours before admission. Liver function tests normal at admission; mild abnormality from Jan 12, 1984; jaundice and pruritus from Feb 14, 1984 (about 60 days after injection). Labs: total bilirubin 2.9 mg/dl, direct 1.1 mg/dl, SGOT 19 IU/l, SGPT 31 IU/l, ALP 649 IU/l (normal <280), γ-GTP 155 IU/l (normal <20), 8% eosinophils. CT and ERC excluded extrahepatic biliary obstruction. Liver biopsy: marked cholestasis with centrilobular zonal necrosis, little/no portal tract change. Lymphocyte stimulation test positive (index 290%) on exposure to Venoplant. Authors describe this as the first documented case of Venoplant-induced hepatic injury.

The rate of elevated alanine aminotransferase was not worse than control in both EXPLORE-Xa (betrixaban vs. warfarin: 1.8% vs. 0.3%) and EXPERT (betrixaban vs. enoxaparin: 2.0% vs. 5.3%, at discharge), and no case of elevated bilirubin was observed with betrixaban. These findings constitute an explicit negative conclusion regarding betrixaban as a human DILI cause.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report three cases of jaundice attributable to dextropropoxyphene use in patients who had not had liver disease, hepatitis exposure, or alcohol abuse. Case 1 involved Napsalgesic (dextropropoxyphene napsylate 50 mg with aspirin), with wedge liver biopsy showing intrahepatic cholestasis; Case 2 involved Depronal SA (dextropropoxyphene hydrochloride 150 mg) alone, with recurrence of jaundice on rechallenge after dechallenge; Case 3 involved Distalgesic (dextropropoxyphene hydrochloride 32.5 mg with paracetamol), with liver biopsy confirming intrahepatic cholestasis. All three patients recovered after stopping the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Three cases of jaundice attributed to dextropropoxyphene, which was a widely used analgesic with only two prior reported cases. Case 1: 54-year-old woman on Napsalgesic (dextropropoxyphene napsylate 50 mg + aspirin BP 500 mg), 4-8 tablets daily for backache, jaundice within a week; bilirubin 147 µmol/l, AST 43 U/l, ALP 230 U/l; biopsy showed intrahepatic cholestasis with portal triad excess of plasma cells, lymphocytes, and eosinophils; recovered. Case 2: 32-year-old woman on Depronal SA (dextropropoxyphene hydrochloride 150 mg), developed symptoms, resolved on dechallenge, and recurred on rechallenge with the single agent; bilirubin 88 µmol/l, AST 703 U/l, ALP 159 U/l; recovered. Case 3: 45-year-old woman on Distalgesic (dextropropoxyphene hydrochloride 32.5 mg + paracetamol 325 mg); bilirubin 170 µmol/l, AST 39 U/l, ALP 250 U/l; biopsy confirmed intrahepatic cholestasis; recovered. Hepatitis B surface antigen, smooth muscle, and antimitochondrial antibody tests negative. Case 2, with a single component, supports attribution to dextropropoxyphene despite combination products in cases 1 and 3.

raw_record.support_text: A study of 90 patients showed that dextropropoxyphene will cause hepatotoxicity; biopsies of these patients demonstrated that the drug can cause centrilobular cholestasis.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of 90 patients; hepatotoxicity attributed to dextropropoxyphene, with biopsies showing centrilobular cholestasis. Blood levels of the drug rise in chronic liver disease, intensifying its effects.

raw_record.support_text: Dextropropoxyphene was among the four drugs associated with the most instances of hepatic injury in a follow-up of 44 patients with drug-induced hepatotoxicity, in 4 of 44 patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Analgesic; 4 of 44 hepatotoxicity cases. Analgesic NSAIDs accounted for more than half of the cases in the cohort.

raw_record.support_text: A case report documents a cholestatic hepatitis attributed to propoxyphene (Darvon), an agent not previously reported as hepatotoxic, with recurrence of clinical and chemical abnormalities on rechallenge at a later date.
raw_record.extra_details: 39-year-old white male (JB) developed cholestatic hepatitis after taking propoxyphene with acetylsalicylic acid (Darvon Compound) as required for occipital headache. Recurrence of clinical and chemical abnormalities occurred on rechallenge. Findings included malaise, daily fever to 101.8 deg F, dark brown urine, tender liver edge 4 cm below costal margin, urinalysis positive for bile, total bilirubin 3.3 mg/100 ml, atypical lymphocytes.

raw_record.support_text: One case each of liver transplantation for suspected drug-induced liver injury was associated with apresoline, dextropropoxiphen and methotrexate with a probable causal relationship.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case among 17 transplant patients with a probable causal relationship; recorded as 'dextropropoxiphen'.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a series of patients with dextropropoxyphene-induced hepatotoxicity, noting that such reactions may represent an immune-mediated disorder. Rapid onset of symptoms following re-ingestion in two patients was interpreted as a hypersensitivity reaction upon rechallenge with dextropropoxyphene, matching prior reports in which rechallenged patients developed similar clinical, biochemical and histological abnormalities within days of re-exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Reports 9 patients plus 15 previously published cases; features included portal inflammatory infiltrate and an immune-mediated/hypersensitivity mechanism with rechallenge reactions developing within days of re-exposure. Symptoms and biochemical abnormalities could be confused with cholecystitis, possibly leading to under-reporting; the center detected a high incidence over 18 months suggesting the condition is more common than suspected. Marked interindividual variation in plasma levels after standard doses is noted.

raw_record.support_text: A 24-year-old male presented with abdominal pain, scleral icterus, pruritus, and jaundice after taking the health supplement RAD-140 for muscle growth for 5 weeks (up to 15 mg daily). He had a cholestatic pattern of liver injury with a peak total bilirubin of 38.5 mg/dL; liver biopsy supported a diagnosis of RAD-140-associated liver injury characterized by intracytoplasmic and canalicular cholestasis with minimal portal inflammation. Symptoms and liver injury resolved after cessation of the agent. The report concludes it was drug-induced liver injury caused by the SARM RAD-140.
raw_record.extra_details: RAD-140 (Testolone), a nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) taken as a consumer-available health supplement at up to 15 mg daily for 5 weeks for muscle growth. Previously healthy 24-year-old male. Only other medication was a fixed combination of acetaminophen 250 mg/aspirin 250 mg/caffeine 65 mg used 4 times daily as needed (no more than twice weekly) for headache; both agents were stopped 2 weeks before presentation. Peak total bilirubin 38.5 mg/dL; biopsy showed intracytoplasmic and canalicular cholestasis with minimal portal inflammation; ALT peaked at 313 IU/L (routine visit), INR up to 1.69. Jaundice, pruritus, and liver injury resolved after cessation (dechallenge with recovery). SARM not FDA-approved and banned by WADA.

Liver biopsy confirmed DILI with bland cholestasis, without evidence of autoimmune activity, and the patient's injury was attributed to RAD-140 based on the temporal relationship between drug initiation, symptom onset 4 weeks later, and serologic evidence of liver injury 4 weeks after symptom onset, with infectious and obstructive causes excluded.

Liver biopsy confirmed bland cholestasis without autoimmune activity; total bilirubin remained >20 mg/dL for over 1 month after cessation. Cholestasis refractory to cessation, treated with prednisone 40 mg daily with bilirubin normalization over ~2 months. Infectious hepatitides A/B/C and obstructive biliary causes excluded. raw_record.support_text: The paper documents for the first time a marked increase in malformed compacted mitochondria in the liver in a case of hepatic toxicity due to the antiretroviral drug Stavudine. The patient had hepatic toxicity manifesting as lactic acidosis, and the liver biopsy showed features of mitochondrial cytopathy except for the expected steatosis; liver function and lactic acidosis reversed when the drug was withdrawn (dechallenge).
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of antiretroviral (nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor) hepatic toxicity featuring lactic acidosis and mitochondrial cytopathy on liver biopsy. Electron microscopy showed mitochondrial proliferation with oncocytic changes, reduced and occasionally abnormal cristae, and dividing mitochondria with a median partition of two parallel inner membranes within a single outer membrane; steatosis was notably absent. Dechallenge: liver functions returned toward normal and lactic acidosis resolved upon drug withdrawal. Mechanism discussed as mitochondrial biogenesis/dysfunction with decreased electron transport, reduced ATP and NAD, and inhibition of fatty acid beta-oxidation.

raw_record.support_text: In the phenurone (antiepileptic drug) series, skin rashes developed in 4 patients, and in one case the dermatitis was accompanied by a hepatitis. Separately, the report asserts that phenurone goes beyond mesantoin or any other anticonvulsive/antiepileptic drug in the danger to which it exposes the liver.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis was reported in one patient whose dermatitis was accompanied by hepatitis; the drug was discontinued in patients with adverse effects. Skin rashes developed in 4 cases. Editorial assertion states phenurone presents a liver danger greater than mesantoin or other antiepileptic drugs, and also threatens the bone marrow in some instances.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that of the more widely used anticonvulsant drugs, phenacemide is the only one proved to have caused severe toxic effects on the normal liver, and that the clinician must continuously look for evidence of impending liver damage during therapy. It also cites earlier reports of nonfatal hepatitis: Lloyd-Smith described acute hepatitis with jaundice developing after 70 gm of phenacemide given for two months (serum bilirubin 4.4 mg/100 cc), with jaundice resolving one week after stopping the drug; Livingston and Kajdi noted nonfatal hepatitis in one of 104 patients; and Carter described two cases of acute hepatitis with recovery among 63 patients taking phenacemide.
raw_record.extra_details: Phenacemide therapy (anticonvulsant) caused fatal and nonfatal toxic liver injury. Eight fatalities were attributed to phenacemide therapy with pathological findings of acute yellow atrophy or massive necrosis of liver parenchyma (cases 4, 6, 8: acute yellow atrophy; case 7: massive necrosis; case 3: hepatorenal syndrome; case 5: acute severe parenchymal liver damage superimposed on mild portal cirrhosis). Deaths followed phenacemide doses of 42-669 gm over 25-210 days. Nonfatal hepatitis reports: jaundice after 70 gm over two months; 1/104 patients; 2 cases among 63 patients, all with recovery.

raw_record.support_text: A 30-year-old Latino male newly diagnosed with HIV started efavirenz-based HAART (tenofovir 300 mg, emtricitabine 200 mg, efavirenz 600 mg once daily). Eleven days after beginning therapy he developed a hypersensitivity reaction with rash and fever preceding severe drug-induced hepatitis, with peak liver enzymes of AST 3410 U/L and ALT 2132 U/L. Hepatitis resolved with HAART discontinuation. Rechallenge with tenofovir and emtricitabine one year later produced no adverse reactions. The Naranjo probability scale demonstrated a probable relationship between this adverse reaction and efavirenz, and the authors concluded efavirenz is the most probable cause of the rash and acute hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report: 30-year-old Latino male, newly diagnosed HIV, efavirenz 600 mg once daily with tenofovir 300 mg and emtricitabine 200 mg. Onset 11 days after starting therapy; hypersensitivity with erythematous maculopapular rash and fever preceding hepatitis; peak AST 3410 U/L and ALT 2132 U/L; resolved on discontinuation; rechallenge with tenofovir+emtricitabine one year later caused no adverse reaction. Naranjo score = probable. MEDLINE search (2004–Sept 2007) found 2 prior cases of rash preceding hepatitis with efavirenz, both in women. Mechanism speculated to involve efavirenz half-life/auto-induction and CYP2B6-mediated clearance (CYP2B6 responsible for ~90% of efavirenz clearance); higher efavirenz concentrations reported in black and Latino patients.

raw_record.support_text: Serious liver function elevation developed in 2 study subjects and resulted in unblinding of the study drug. One subject had hepatitis attributable to efavirenz and had been taking placebo (nutrition alone arm) for the study, so the efavirenz was the patient's anti-HIV therapy rather than the study drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case within a nutritional/oxandrolone/resistance-training trial for AIDS wasting; the affected subject was randomized to the nutrition-alone (placebo) arm, and the hepatitis was attributed to efavirenz taken as the patient's antiretroviral medication, described as 'serious liver function elevation' that led to unblinding.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case series of 81 patients with efavirenz DILI in a high HIV-prevalence setting with a massive increase of efavirenz-based first-line antiretroviral therapy. Three patterns of injury were observed, the most severe being submassive necrosis. A high baseline CD4+ count seemingly predicted risk for submassive necrosis, with female sex and younger age as additional factors, and the associated morbidity and mortality were noted as a serious concern. Clinicians were advised to manage suspected efavirenz DILI with rapid cessation of efavirenz.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 81 patients with efavirenz DILI in a high HIV-prevalence setting with massive expansion of efavirenz-based first-line ART in a developing-world program. Three patterns of injury observed; the most severe was submassive necrosis. High baseline CD4+ count predicted risk for submassive necrosis, with female sex and younger age as additional factors; associated morbidity and mortality noted as a serious concern. Authors recommend rapid cessation of efavirenz when DILI is suspected. Efavirenz is the prescribed antiretroviral, hepatotoxic in human therapeutic use.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the first biopsy-proven case of efavirenz-induced hepatitis. Hepatitis and hepatic laboratory abnormalities resolved after the entire antiretroviral regimen was stopped, and although dechallenge was not with efavirenz alone, the authors state that the causal role of efavirenz is obvious because zidovudine and lamivudine had been taken for 2 years without problems and efavirenz was the only new drug. They concluded that HCV infection played a limited role because HCV RNA remained negative throughout the course of hepatitis and no HCV-related abnormalities were found on liver biopsy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Concomitant HIV and HCV (serotype 1) infection; continued co-treatment with zidovudine and lamivudine; dechallenge involved stopping the entire antiretroviral regimen rather than efavirenz alone; initial supratherapeutic intake of 1200 mg/day for the first 3 days before settling at the prescribed 600 mg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: 45-year-old man with HIV infection; hepatitis and cutaneous rash developed within 4 weeks of switching indinavir to efavirenz (600 mg/day). Symptoms: nausea, right upper quadrant pain, rash, fever (38°C). Laboratory: ALT 718 IU/l (normal <38), AST 336 IU/l, GGT 1180 IU/l rising to 1611, ALP 684 IU/l rising to 928, eosinophilia (460 to 1110/mm3), bilirubin 18 µmol/l (no jaundice). Biopsy showed dense portal infiltrate of histiocytes, lymphocytes and eosinophilic polymorphonuclears with some apoptotic bodies; no interlobular bile duct damage and no microvesicular steatosis. Liver tests and eosinophilia returned to normal within 1 month after stopping antiretroviral treatment. Autoantibodies (antimitochondrial, anti-smooth muscle, anti-endoplasmic reticulum, anti-LKM, anti-nuclear) negative; HCV RNA negative throughout. No rechallenge attempted because of possible immuno-allergic mechanism. Efavirenz is a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (1,4-dihydro-2H-3,1-benzoxazin-2-one), extensively metabolized by P450 cytochromes to 8-hydroxylated metabolites then conjugated as glucuronides.

raw_record.support_text: In the direct hepatotoxicity section, NNRTIs such as nevirapine (NVP) and efavirenz (EFV) are reported to cause pathological features resembling direct hepatotoxicity (centrilobular and panlobular necrosis), with EFV-associated submassive necrosis linked to significant morbidity and mortality. A case identified by Elsharkawy and colleagues reported the first adult EFV-induced acute liver failure that required liver transplantation within 5 months after initiating therapy; this 43-year-old woman was a slow drug metabolizer, contributing to the severe presentation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: EFV used within combination antiretroviral regimens; index case was a slow drug metabolizer whose genotype contributed to severe presentation.
raw_record.extra_details: Direct hepatotoxicity producing acute hepatic necrosis with centrilobular/panlobular necrosis and submassive necrosis with an immune-allergic pattern (lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils); acute liver failure with encephalopathy and coagulopathy; liver transplantation required within 5 months in a 43-year-old woman; EFV-associated submassive necrosis on liver biopsy associated with significant morbidity and mortality. EFV was also the most common cause of skin rashes (incidence 10-17%) and CYP2B6 slow-metabolizer genotype was associated with increased risk of EFV adverse reaction.

raw_record.support_text: A case report describes an HIV-infected, drug-naïve female patient with a relatively low BMI, CYP2B6 516G>T (rs3745274) genotype and high efavirenz plasma concentration who was admitted 6 months after cART initiation (two NRTIs plus efavirenz) with drug-induced severe hepatotoxicity. Liver biopsy showed confluent parenchymal necrosis with mild-to-moderate portal tract inflammation and focal interface hepatitis; all other causes were excluded. The authors conclude that efavirenz has a potential harmful effect in patients with low BMI, specific genotyping, and interindividual pharmacokinetics affecting high plasma concentration.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Female, HIV-infected, drug-naïve patient on cART (two NRTIs plus efavirenz); relatively low BMI; CYP2B6 516G>T (rs3745274) genotype; high efavirenz plasma concentration; interindividual pharmacokinetics.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity arose 6 months after cART initiation. Aspiration liver biopsy showed confluent parenchymal necrosis with mild-to-moderate portal tract inflammation and focal interface hepatitis. All other possible causes of the liver injury were excluded. Efavirenz is an NNRTI used in first-line cART in resource-limited settings.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report 81 patients (50 retrospective and 31 prospective; median age 34 years) who met criteria for efavirenz DILI. Among those biopsied (n=73), three histological injury patterns were observed: a nonspecific hepatitis associated with grade 1–2 transaminase elevation (n=17), a mixed cholestatic-hepatitis with grades 2–3 elevation of ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase and mild/moderate jaundice (n=20), and submassive necrosis with grade 4 ALT/AST elevation, severe jaundice and coagulopathy (n=36). Skin involvement was not observed, in contrast to nevirapine DILI. No patients fulfilled clinical criteria for tuberculous immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients were HIV-infected adults receiving efavirenz-based antiretroviral therapy; in the prospective group 58% (n=18) were pregnant at ART initiation; 86% were Black, 73% female; 27% used or were currently using cotrimoxazole prophylaxis.
raw_record.extra_details: 81 patients total (50 retrospective, 31 prospective); median age 34 years; median CD4+ nadir 348 cells/µl (IQR 173–522); median duration on ART 20 weeks (IQR 12–24) at DILI onset. Liver-related mortality was 11% (n=9): 6% (n=3) retrospective and 19% (n=6) prospective; most deaths occurred within 1 week of presentation. Submassive necrosis was associated with an 'immuno-allergic' inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes, plasma cells, conspicuous eosinophils), higher transaminases (ALT 679 vs 101 vs 114 U/l, P<0.0001) and bilirubin (232 vs 86 vs 8 µmol/l, P=0.003) compared with mixed cholestatic-hepatitis and nonspecific hepatitis patterns, and higher INR (1.68 vs 1.18, P=0.0002). In multivariate analysis, submassive necrosis was independently associated with CD4+ >350 cells/µl (OR 9.4, 95% CI 2.5–35.8) and female gender (OR 9.0, 95% CI 1.4–59.8); age >30 years was protective. Median hospital stay 28 days (IQR 11–60); slow median biochemical resolution >6 months. Submassive necrosis patients were treated with low-dose prednisone (0.25 mg/kg/day); protease inhibitor-based ART successfully introduced after resolution.

raw_record.support_text: A 73-year-old woman began papaverine hydrochloride 80 mg four times daily for angina pectoris; the next day she developed tremulousness and fever, and the following day mild jaundice. She reported similar symptoms one year earlier during papaverine treatment. Papaverine was withdrawn after a total dose of 640 mg and the jaundice disappeared within a few days. Re-administration of papaverine reproduced the symptoms, and the drug was again withdrawn, with rapid general improvement.
raw_record.extra_details: Administered as papaverine hydrochloride 80 mg four times daily for angina pectoris in a 73-year-old woman (case 1); first episode after 640 mg total dose with tremulousness, fever (102.6°F/39.2°C) and mild jaundice, resolving within days after withdrawal; similar episode had occurred one year earlier during papaverine treatment; positive rechallenge reproduced the symptoms and rechallenge after a second withdrawal again confirmed the effect. Case 2: a 76-year-old woman on papaverine 80 mg four times daily developed dark urine after 32 days with elevated SGOT (AST), SGPT (ALT) and alkaline phosphatase; transaminases normalized within 14 days of withdrawal. Case 1 monitoring showed elevated serum bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, SGPT and SGOT. Both cases indicate hypoxia- or other-unrelated drug-related reversible liver injury; isolated jaundice and LFT elevations with recovery; no liver failure or death reported.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 157 drug-induced hepatitis (DIH) cases, the highest frequency of anti-N antibodies was observed in clometacin (8/29 cases) and papaverine (4/4)-induced hepatitis, with homogeneous nuclear fluorescence in anti-N positive cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Papaverine-induced hepatitis had anti-N antibodies in 4/4 cases, a high frequency; nuclear fluorescence was homogeneous. From a 157-case series of drug-induced hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Papaverine was among the drugs most often associated with autoimmune serologic reactions in the Homberg series of drug-induced hepatitis, with 4/5 cases showing serologic reactivity (antismooth muscle antibody, ASMA).
raw_record.extra_details: 4/5 cases associated with autoimmune serologic reactions, specifically antismooth muscle antibody (ASMA).

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that in their hospital they saw about 50 patients who received papaverine hydrochloride, 300 to 450 mg daily, and came across no patient with jaundice; liver-function tests (serum bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and transaminases) of 10 patients were within normal limits, providing no evidence of hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Authors' observational finding across about 50 patients receiving papaverine hydrochloride 300-450 mg daily: no cases of jaundice; liver function tests (serum bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, transaminases) in 10 tested patients were within normal limits.

raw_record.support_text: The editorial cites a convincing report in this issue of the Journal of hepatic disease induced by papaverine, coming as a surprise after more than a half-century of uneventful clinical use.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic injury after 3-5 weeks of exposure or previous exposure; associated fever and eosinophilic inflammatory infiltrates in the liver section; reproduction of hepatic injury on administration of a challenge dose (positive rechallenge); 20% hepatic injury among 15 patients receiving papaverine for one month or more; authors deduced hypersensitivity as mechanism, with editorial suggesting a possible mild intrinsic effect combined with hypersensitivity.

raw_record.support_text: In Case 3, a 63-year-old woman treated with papaverine 80 mg four times a day for basilar-artery insufficiency developed a marked increase in SGOT, SGPT, and alkaline phosphatase after 5 weeks of treatment, plus burning epigastric pain; symptoms resolved on withdrawal and recurred on rechallenge with papaverine. In Case 4, a 54-year-old woman treated with papaverine 80 mg four times a day developed rising SGOT and SGPT after 18-23 days, and rechallenge with papaverine produced anorexia and vomiting. The authors conclude in the discussion that an intimate connection between papaverine administration and hepatopathy was demonstrated in these cases despite no prior reports of papaverine hepatotoxicity; liver biopsy in Case 3 showed foci of necrotic liver cells with inflammatory infiltration including eosinophilic granulocytes and bile staining of liver cells.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 3: 80 mg q.i.d., latency 5 weeks, concurrent marked SGOT/SGPT and alkaline phosphatase elevation, burning epigastric pain, symptom recurrence on rechallenge and resolution within 24 h of withdrawal, normal cholecystography; biopsy showed preserved lobular structure, focal necrotic liver cells with pyknotic nuclei and karyorrhexis, focal granulocyte infiltration, Kupffer-cell hyperplasia, periportal inflammation with eosinophilic granulocytes, and centrilobular bile staining with rare minimal bile thrombi. Case 4: 80 mg q.i.d., SGOT/SGPT rose slightly at day 18 and were clearly pathologic at day 23; rechallenge with only half a day of papaverine caused anorexia and one episode of vomiting. Discussion notes no previous animal or human reports of papaverine hepatotoxicity; no previous liver disease or hemolytic tendency in either patient.

raw_record.support_text: In patients receiving flucytosine (150 mg/kg/day) with amphotericin B for cryptococcal meningitis, hepatitis occurred in 7 percent of patients but was clinically significant in only one case. Liver abnormalities were noted in 0 and 15 percent of patients in two previously cited series [1,9]. A toxicity table for flucytosine reported hepatic toxicity in 13 of 194 patients (7 percent), with elevated SGOT in 9 (5 percent), elevated alkaline phosphatase in 6 (3 percent), and elevated bilirubin in 1 (1 percent).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients were being treated for cryptococcal meningitis with flucytosine in combination with low-dose amphotericin B; some were renal transplant recipients.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity rates from the study table: hepatic toxicity in 13/194 patients (7%), elevated SGOT in 9 (5%), elevated alkaline phosphatase in 6 (3%), elevated bilirubin in 1 (1%). Dose was maximal-dose flucytosine at 150 mg/kg/day; therapy for four or six weeks. Hepatitis was clinically significant in only one case. Liver abnormalities were reported in 0% and 15% of patients in two referenced series [1,9]. Other flucytosine toxicities included bone marrow suppression (leukopenia, thrombocytopenia) and gastrointestinal effects.

raw_record.support_text: Three adolescents with a history of drug abuse developed acute hepatic injury after inhaling Carbona cleaning fluid, a commercial preparation containing trichloroethylene. Hepatic biopsies in two patients showed acute centrilobular necrosis, and both also showed mild centrilobular fibrosis, probably from previous injury from trichloroethylene exposure. The authors attribute the hepatic injury to inhalation of the trichloroethylene-containing solvent.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Inhalation ('sniffing') abuse in adolescents, not therapeutic use; subjects had a history of abusing other drugs (model airplane glues, amphetamines, heroin, cocaine, marijuana); Carbona cleaning fluid used contained 70% trichloroethylene and 30% petroleum distillates (Cases 1 and 2).
raw_record.extra_details: Three cases reported; two patients had acute hepatic and renal damage (renal tubular necrosis) and one had centrilobular hepatic necrosis; hepatic biopsies showed acute centrilobular necrosis and mild centrilobular fibrosis; icterus present; electrocardiographic and electroencephalographic abnormalities also noted.

In Cases 1 and 3, liver biopsy demonstrated centrilobular necrosis, a finding characteristic of chlorinated hydrocarbon hepatotoxicity, and fibrous tissue in the centrilobular zones suggested that repeated exposure may produce permanent hepatic alterations.

Abnormal hepatic tests or histology are otherwise reported only rarely in solvent sniffers.

raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report; injury described as mixed cholestatic and hepatocellular; patient gradually recovered after drug cessation (recovery/dechallenge outcome).

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN prospective study, 12 of 679 registrants had hepatotoxicity attributed to fluoroquinolones, including 1 case from gatifloxacin, along with 6 from ciprofloxacin, 4 from moxifloxacin, and 1 from levofloxacin. Median latency from start of fluoroquinolone therapy to symptoms was 4 days (range 1–39 days); 9 cases developed symptoms on medication; 7 had immunoallergic features; and cases were equally distributed among hepatocellular, cholestatic, and mixed injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 1 of the 12 DILIN fluoroquinolone hepatotoxicity cases was attributed to gatifloxacin. Cohort outcomes are reported in aggregate: median latency 4 days (1–39); 2 of 4 patients with hepatocellular injury and jaundice died, 1 of acute liver failure; 1 cholestatic patient developed vanishing bile duct syndrome requiring liver transplantation; 1 had persistently increased AP; mixed cases were mild without jaundice and all recovered; 7 cases had immunoallergic features, consistent with a hypersensitivity reaction.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe 2 patients who developed acute cholestatic liver injury and acute pancreatitis while being treated with gatifloxacin (Tequin, Bristol-Myers Squibb), representing case reports of gatifloxacin-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1: a 41-year-old woman treated orally at 400 mg/d for an upper respiratory tract infection (prior ciprofloxacin withdrawn for nausea/vomiting, not liver-related; no other medications). Presented 2 days after starting gatifloxacin with skin rash, dark urine, pale stools, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Laboratory findings: total bilirubin 87.2 µmol/L (5.1 mg/dL) with conjugated fraction 61.6 µmol/L (3.6 mg/dL), AST 139 U/L, ALT 145 U/L, albumin 30 g/L, alkaline phosphatase 8.03 µkat/L, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 8.62 µkat/L, amylase 1.38 µkat/L, lipase 6.5 µkat/L, prothrombin time 6.1 s. Viral and autoimmune hepatitis excluded; imaging showed no biliary obstruction. Liver biopsy showed portal edema and cholestasis with moderate macrovesicular steatosis. Abdominal pain resolved and prothrombin time normalized 2 weeks after gatifloxacin withdrawal; jaundice fully resolved after 1 year. Follow-up biopsy at 8 months showed increased portal fibrosis, early bridging fibrosis, and bile duct loss; persistent elevation of alkaline phosphatase and transaminases continued. Background note: less than 1% of exposed patients have increased bilirubin, aminotransferase, or amylase; 1 case of acute hepatitis previously reported.

raw_record.support_text: The authors attributed the patient's liver injury to levothyroxine because drug exposure preceded onset, underlying liver disease was excluded, cessation led to improvement in liver enzymes, and symptoms recurred rapidly upon rechallenge. A Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale total score of 8 supported a causal effect, and a Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method score of 11 indicated that an adverse drug reaction was highly probable. The improvement on drug cessation argued against transaminitis due to hypothyroidism itself.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report of levothyroxine-induced liver injury; Naranjo score 8 and RUCAM score 11 (highly probable). Disproportionate elevation of serum aminotransferases versus alkaline phosphatase, with elevated bilirubin and reduced albumin (albumin reduction attributed to negative acute-phase response). Liver enzymes normalized after drug cessation and recurred on rechallenge. No liver biopsy performed. DIAIH considered but argued against by negative autoimmune antibodies and no need for immunosuppression. One prior report (Kang et al.) observed DILI with levothyroxine tablet but not powder form, suggesting a possible causal role of additives, leaving the mechanism unclear. Treating hypothyroidism with triiodothyronine was effective without liver enzyme derangement.

raw_record.support_text: A 63-year-old woman with hypothyroidism was started on thyroxine (T4) 50µg/day. Twelve days after starting T4 she developed fever, skin rash, and liver injury that promptly resolved on T4 discontinuation. On rechallenge, liver injury with jaundice recurred, and a T4-added lymphocyte stimulation test (LST) was positive, leading to a diagnosis of allergic liver injury due to T4. She was subsequently compensated with T3 and had no recurrence of liver injury over about 14 months.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of drug-induced liver injury due to synthetic thyroid hormone (T4) in a 63-year-old woman with Hashimoto's thyroiditis. T4 dose 50µg/day; liver injury appeared 12 days after start, resolving on withdrawal; rechallenge reproduced liver injury with jaundice; positive T4-added lymphocyte stimulation test (LST). The paper discusses possible contributions of Hashimoto's disease, chronic cholecystitis, and whether this could represent a new paraneoplastic syndrome; coexisting findings included asymptomatic common bile duct stones, chronic cholecystitis, and early gastric cancer. T3 replacement was used for about 14 months without liver injury recurrence.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective study of 38 pediatric heart transplant recipients treated with atorvastatin (~0.2 mg/kg/day), there were no differences in serum alanine transaminase pre- versus post-atorvastatin therapy, indicating no drug-related liver injury. Reported complications were limited to muscle pain (n=2) and asymptomatic creatine kinase elevations (n=2), with rhabdomyolysis developing in 2 of these 4 patients; no patient had altered renal function.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric heart transplant recipients; atorvastatin used for post-transplant hyperlipidemia/lipid lowering.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective study of 38 patients; atorvastatin started 48.2 ± 54.4 months after transplantation at 0.2 ± 0.1 mg/kg/day. No change in alanine transaminase pre- vs post-therapy. Lipid changes: total cholesterol -20%, triglycerides -18%, LDL -26%, no significant HDL or VLDL change. Complications: muscle pain (n=2) and asymptomatic creatine kinase elevations (n=2); 2 of these 4 developed rhabdomyolysis (~5%); no renal function alterations. Author recommendation: baseline and routine creatine kinase screening in pediatric patients on HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors.
