raw_record.support_text: A 44-year-old Japanese woman treated with atorvastatin for 10 months was admitted with fatigue and altered liver function; serum alkaline phosphatase and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase were markedly elevated without jaundice. Based on a positive drug-induced lymphocyte-stimulation test, her liver disease was diagnosed as atorvastatin-induced hepatic injury. Anti-mitochondrial antibodies were also detected, but a liver biopsy did not show the characteristic features of primary biliary cholangitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Statin used as a lipid-lowering agent (Lipitor, an HMGCR inhibitor). Single case; diagnosis supported by a positive drug-induced lymphocyte-stimulation test. Elevated serum alkaline phosphatase and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase without jaundice; anti-mitochondrial antibodies were detected in serum, but liver biopsy showed no primary biliary cholangitis features (i.e., AMA positivity accompanied drug-induced hepatic injury, not PBC). Patient: 44-year-old Japanese woman, no significant medical history, BMI 24.2, no transfusion or alcohol history, allergies to cedar pollen and house dust.

raw_record.support_text: In this European prospective DILI registry, atorvastatin was among the most commonly implicated single causative agents in the 246 adjudicated DILI patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among the most commonly implicated single drugs in the European DILI registry.

raw_record.support_text: In this case report of a patient with concurrent DILI and rhabdomyolysis after a positive rechallenge with atorvastatin, a Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) score of 9 using the cholestatic/mixed liver injury subscale suggested atorvastatin as a highly probable cause of acute liver injury, and a Revised Electronic Causality Assessment Method (RECAM) score of 14 also provided evidence for atorvastatin as a highly probable cause of DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported case of concurrent DILI and rhabdomyolysis after positive rechallenge with atorvastatin. RUCAM (cholestatic/mixed liver injury subscale) scored 9: latency >90 d (+1), clinical course after withdrawal with >50% decrease in ALP within 180 d (+2), age >55 y (+1), no concomitant hepatotoxic drugs/herbs (0), all causes in group I and II ruled out (+2), reaction labeled in product characteristics (+2), doubling of ALP with other drugs initiated at the same time on readministration (+1). RECAM scored 14: onset >90 d while on drug (0), dechallenge with both ALP and total bilirubin declining <50% of peak within 1–30 days after discontinuation (+4), LiverTox category A (well-known cause of clinically apparent liver injury) (+3), competing diagnoses ruled out (0), re-exposure in same R-value category with ALP increase >2× baseline and latency <60 d plus liver biopsy with features of DILI (+7). US DILI Network prospective data: atorvastatin implicated in 8 of 22 (36.6%) statin-related DILI patients and was fifth highest drug associated with DILI among all drug categories in the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System database (1997–2019); overall incidence of statin-related DILI was 1.9%. Risk factors discussed include SLCO1B1 gene variants and CYP450 and HLA allele polymorphisms; coadministration of CYP450-metabolized drugs (certain antifungals, HIV protease inhibitors, fibrates, macrolide antibiotics) increases DILI risk.

raw_record.support_text: Case 4 describes a 72-year-old woman treated with atorvastatin for elevated blood lipids who, 11 months after starting the drug, was found to have very high elevations of liver enzymes with jaundice during cardiac follow-up. She was asymptomatic; liver ultrasound was unremarkable, auto-antibodies and viral serologies were negative, alcohol use was minimal, and she was also on metoprolol and aspirin. Atorvastatin was discontinued and liver enzymes normalized within three months and remained normal 2.5 years later. A liver biopsy showed preserved architecture with portal-tract inflammation (lymphocytes, occasional eosinophils and plasma cells), minimal lobular inflammation, no bile duct damage or cholestasis, minimal fatty degeneration, and portal-tract fibrosis of 2–3/6 on the Ishak scale. The paper's discussion states that the four cases of jaundice associated with statins had, per RUCAM causality assessment, probable or highly probable causality.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 4 of a 4-case series; 72-year-old woman, atorvastatin for hyperlipidemia, latency 11 months; jaundice with very high liver enzyme elevations; dechallenge led to normalization within 3 months, still normal at 2.5 years; RUCAM causality probabl or highly probable (aggregate of the series); biopsy: preserved architecture, lymphocytic portal infiltrate with occasional eosinophils and plasma cells, periportal inflammation, minimal lobular inflammation, no cholestasis or bile duct damage, minimal steatosis, portal fibrosis Ishak 2-3/6. The paper also cites Clarke and Mill reporting seven patients with suspected atorvastatin hepatotoxicity (three with jaundice, three biopsied). Liver_test: very high transaminase elevations with jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe their own published case of acute hepatitis in a 65-year-old woman while on atorvastatin, in which the drug was most likely to have triggered an autoimmune hepatitis. The patient was admitted with fatigue, jaundice and altered liver function tests after being treated with atorvastatin for 3 months for primary hypercholesterolaemia.
raw_record.extra_details: 65-year-old woman; treated with atorvastatin for 3 months for primary hypercholesterolaemia; presented with fatigue, jaundice and altered liver function tests; drug most likely triggered an autoimmune hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective Spanish DILI registry study of chronic liver diseases, 7 of 16 (63%) patients who underwent liver biopsy had liver cirrhosis. The paper identifies atorvastatin among the drugs responsible for the development of liver cirrhosis, with the presenting liver damage having a very variable initial clinical picture.
raw_record.extra_details: From a prospective Spanish DILI registry of chronic liver diseases; 7/16 (63%) biopsied patients had cirrhosis; drugs responsible were diverse and initial liver injury was clinically variable.

raw_record.support_text: In the Indian tertiary-care DILI cohort of 80 patients evaluated with RUCAM, atorvastatin was listed among the other drugs implicated as a cause of DILI at 2% of cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among slightly implicated drugs at 2% of 80 DILI cases (about 1-2 patients).

raw_record.support_text: In the US DILIN prospective study, statins were initially implicated in 61 of 1188 suspected DILI cases, but after formal adjudication only 22 (1.85%) were accepted as true statin-induced DILI; injury was mostly mild-moderate and self-limited, with 4 severe and 1 fatal case, and a predominantly hepatocellular pattern (n=12). Atorvastatin accounted for 8 of these 22 adjudicated cases. The paper attributes statin DILI to an idiosyncratic timing of onset with variable presentation and a likely class effect.
raw_record.extra_details: Adjudicated atorvastatin DILI cases: US DILIN n=8; Iceland study n=2 with estimated population risk of DILI of 27 per 100,000 (95% CI 4-98) persons treated with atorvastatin; Swedish study 1970-2004 n=8 (statin total) and 1988-2010 n=30 total atorvastatin with cholestatic-predominant phenotype; Spanish Registry n=16 (34%). Latency from exposure to clinically evident DILI ranged 34 days to >10 years. DILIN aggregate (all statins): 4 severe cases, 1 fatal, 15 (68%) jaundiced with total bilirubin ≥2.5 mg/dL, 4 (18%) with INR >1.5; hepatocellular (12) versus cholestatic (9).

raw_record.support_text: Two serious adverse events were considered to be treatment related by the study investigators: an increase in aspartate aminotransferase in 1 patient receiving atorvastatin 40 mg and hepatotoxicity in 1 patient receiving atorvastatin 80 mg. Five deaths occurred (sudden death, myocardial infarction, abdominal-pelvic tumor, cardiac arrest and septic shock), but none was considered related to study treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Atorvastatin 80 mg dose; hepatotoxicity reported as a serious adverse event considered treatment related by study investigators, occurring in 1 patient in a clinical trial comparing atorvastatin with rosuvastatin. The patient with atorvastatin 40 mg had an aspartate aminotransferase increase as a separate serious treatment-related event, but was not explicitly characterized as DILI/hepatotoxicity. Five deaths occurred overall (sudden death, myocardial infarction, abdominal-pelvic tumor, cardiac arrest, septic shock), none considered related to study treatment.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of 22 patients with statin-induced liver injury, 8 cases were attributed to atorvastatin (cases 1-8) at doses of 10-80 mg daily, with peak ALT up to 4560 U/L, mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic patterns, autoimmune features in some cases, DILIN causality scores of 1-3 and RUCAM scores of 5-12, all resolving, with worst severity scored 4+ (severe).
raw_record.extra_details: 8 cases (cases 1-8); doses 10-80 mg/day; time to onset 2.2-120 months; peak ALT 222-4560 U/L; peak bilirubin up to 30.2 mg/dL; patterns included hepatocellular, cholestatic, and hepatocellular with autoimmune features (HC-AI-P); severity up to 4+; all resolved; autoimmune cases treated with prednisone and azathioprine (case 7).

raw_record.support_text: Among 60 patients who experienced atorvastatin dose-related adverse drug reactions, the reported ADRs included transaminase (ALT, AST) elevation (n=9), transaminase elevation with CK elevation below four-fold the upper reference limit (n=4), and serious hepatic injury (n=7). Most ADRs were myotoxicity (61.7%) and were not serious (76.7%).
raw_record.extra_details: Serious hepatic injury occurred in 7 of 60 patients experiencing atorvastatin dose-related ADRs in a Croatian-ancestry case-control pharmacogenetic cohort; the ADR group was matched to 90 controls for age, gender, atorvastatin dose, and calcineurin inhibitor use (11 ADR patients and 14 controls took calcineurin inhibitors). Additional patients had isolated transaminase (ALT/AST) elevation (n=9) and transaminase elevation with CK elevation below four-fold upper reference limit (n=4).

raw_record.support_text: Atorvastatin was attributed to 16 DILI cases with hepatocellular (44%), cholestatic (25%) and mixed (31%) patterns. Seven cases (44%) met nR-based Hy's law criteria but had favourable outcomes without fatalities or liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: 16 of 843 registry DILI cases; Hep 44%/Chol 25%/Mix 31%; female 44%, lymphopenia 0%, eosinophilia 19%; 7 (44%) fulfilled nR-based Hy's law with no fatalities/liver transplantation; hepatocelluar subset had highest mean ALT and cholestatic subset high mean ALP.

raw_record.support_text: Among 16 chronic DILI patients with liver biopsy, seven had cirrhosis; the drugs related to liver cirrhosis in these cases included atorvastatin, reported as a single culprit agent.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic DILI case progressing to cirrhosis in a cohort comparing acute and chronic DILI; median follow-up 54 months in the chronic group.

raw_record.support_text: Atorvastatin is listed at position 3 in the RUCAM-based ranking of drugs causing DILI with verified causality (Table 10).
raw_record.extra_details: Ranked #3 in the RUCAM-based top-ranking of drugs causing DILI with verified causality (Teschke, 2018d).

raw_record.support_text: Among 73 cases included in the final causality-assessed analysis of statin-induced DILI, the vast majority were due to atorvastatin (n = 30) and simvastatin (n = 28). Other statin-associated liver injuries were due to fluvastatin (n = 11), pravastatin (n = 2) and rosuvastatin (n = 2). The biochemical types among the whole cohort were hepatocellular (59%), cholestatic (30%) and mixed (11%).
raw_record.extra_details: Largest contributor with 30/73 adjudicated DILI cases. Specific cases: F39 atorvastatin (10 mg) 120 days, causality possible, fatal outcome (death); F60 atorvastatin (40 mg) second treatment 30 days, highly probable, with positive rechallenge producing a similar liver-injury pattern ~1 month after re-exposure; F52 atorvastatin (10 mg) second treatment 30 days, highly probable, positive rechallenge. Causality grades across cohort: 52 possible, 14 probable, 7 highly probable. Median time to abnormal liver tests 3 months; ~35% jaundice at presentation; median ALT 10 x ULN. Rechallenge cases had negative viral (HAV/HBV/HCV/CMV/EBV) markers and no suspicion of alcoholic liver disease or hypotension.

raw_record.support_text: Among DILIN prospective study subjects with adequate MR cholangiography, four patients (7%) had sclerosing cholangitis-like changes. Case 3 implicated atorvastatin (50/F), with a 60-day latency; the patient was jaundiced and showed persistent abnormalities at 6 months. Analysis was restricted to patients with probable, highly likely or definite DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 3 of 4: 50-year-old female; latency 60 days; DILI onset to MRC 14 days; initial/peak ALT 630/630 U/L, ALP 783/982 U/L, bilirubin 14/17.8 mg/dL; initial R ratio 2; jaundiced; chronic DILI at 6 months per table. DILIN prospective study, 2004-14; causality adjudicated as probable/highly likely/definite.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective evaluation of 52 patients with fulminant hepatic failure, 4 cases were attributed to idiosyncratic drug reactions, and the causes of drug-induced hepatitis were reported as sulfasalazine, atorvastatin, NH4Cl (ammonium chloride), and nefazodone. Each of these agents was thereby identified as the cause of drug-induced hepatitis leading to FHF in a human case.
raw_record.extra_details: One of four idiosyncratic drug-induced hepatitis cases in a 52-patient FHF cohort; the drug-induced hepatitis progressed to fulminant hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: The Swedish DILI register reported a statin-related DILI episode in 1.2/100,000 users, with atorvastatin implicated in 30/73 (41%) cases, simvastatin in 28/73 (38%), and fluvastatin in 11/73 (15%), showing most commonly a cholestatic/mixed pattern, with 2 deaths due to acute liver failure and 1 liver transplantation. In the DILIN prospective study of 899 idiosyncratic DILI cases, atorvastatin was implicated in 1.0%, rosuvastatin in 0.8%, pravastatin in 0.4%, fluvastatin in 0.2%, and lovastatin in 0.2% of the definitive, highly likely, or probable total DILI cases, with atorvastatin and rosuvastatin showing a long latency period (>60 days).
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated in 30/73 (41%) of statin-DILI cases in the Swedish DILI register (statin DILI incidence 1.2/100,000 users); register statin DILI showed most commonly a cholestatic/mixed pattern, with 2 deaths from acute liver failure and 1 liver transplantation across the 73 cases (not attributable to a specific statin). In the DILIN prospective study, atorvastatin was implicated in 1.0% of adjudicated (definitive, highly likely, or probable) DILI cases and showed a long DILI latency profile (>60 days postexposure).

raw_record.support_text: Atorvastatin was implicated in two cases of drug-induced liver injury acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases; rash occurred with atorvastatin in one subject.

raw_record.support_text: A diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) precipitated by atorvastatin was made in patient B.J., who had prior elevated serum ALT and bilirubin, positive ANA and ASMA titers (1:160), and a liver biopsy showing chronic portal inflammation with plasma cells, piecemeal and bridging necrosis, and bridging fibrosis. Immunosuppression with prednisone and mycophenolate mofetil was started, after which serum liver tests fell and became normal within 7 months.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient B.J. became icteric (AST 1111 U/L, ALT 1550 U/L, total bilirubin 5.5 mg/dL, ALP 203 U/L in September 2004); liver biopsy showed marked chronic portal inflammation with plasma cells, piecemeal necrosis, moderate steatosis, bridging necrosis and bridging fibrosis (Ishak 3); ANA and ASMA positive at 1:160, anti-LKM-1 negative; treated with prednisone 40 mg/d and mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg BID beginning October 6 2004; liver tests normal within 7 months and remained normal; also consistent with class effect of statins unmasking AIH in genetically predisposed patients.

raw_record.support_text: Table lists atorvastatin as causing DILI in 2 patients (2% of 82), of whom 1 (50%) died. The narrative (p29) identifies atorvastatin as implicated in 2% of cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Atorvastatin implicated in 2/82 DILI cases (2%); 1 of 2 patients (50%) died

raw_record.support_text: Eight case reports in the table attribute liver injury to atorvastatin (available since it is the most commonly represented statin). Cases include a 67 M on atorvastatin 80 mg for 4 months (peak ALT 1,325 U/L, AST 1,612, bilirubin 132 µmol/L; jaundice, dark urine, decreased urine output), a 46 M on 10 mg for 6 months (peak ALT 1,632 U/L, ANA+, liver biopsy done), a 57 F on 40 mg for 3 months (peak ALT 3,195 U/L, ANA+ and ASMA+; rechallenge without recurrence), a 71 M on 80 mg for 1 month (peak ALT 1,385 U/L, ASMA+; simvastatin rechallenge without recurrence), a 63 M on 20 mg (peak ALT 1,049 U/L; rosuvastatin rechallenge), and two patients on 20 and 10 mg from Liu 2010 (ALT elevations; pravastatin rechallenge without recurrence). All show a predominantly aminotransferase (hepatocellular) pattern with clinical hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven reported cases at daily doses of 10-80 mg; latency from 10 hours to 6 months; presenting symptoms included generalized weakness, abdominal pain, jaundice, dark urine, fatigue, nausea, anorexia; peak ALT 124-3,195 U/L with bilirubin up to ~122.8 µmol/L and 13-9.2 mg/dL in some cases; ANA and ASMA positive in several cases suggesting autoimmune features; liver biopsy in one case (Kawasaki 46 M); rechallenge with alternative statins (simvastatin, rosuvastatin, pravastatin) in some cases showed no recurrence. Only 1 of 6 reviewed case patients was female.

raw_record.support_text: In a randomized 6-week trial in patients with hypercholesterolemia, clinically relevant increases in hepatic transaminases or creatine kinase, indicative of hepatotoxicity or myotoxicity, were not observed with atorvastatin. Isolated ALT >3 times the upper limit of normal elevations were seen in 1 patient each in the atorvastatin 20- and 80-mg groups, considered related to trial treatment except for the 20-mg patient (who had a myocardial infarction), but no persistent transaminase increases or clinically meaningful hepatotoxicity were observed.
raw_record.extra_details: Doses 10-80 mg over 6 weeks in hypercholesterolemia patients; isolated ALT >3x ULN in 20-mg (not considered treatment-related, prior MI) and 80-mg groups; no persistent transaminase or CK increases.

raw_record.support_text: Among 120 cases of symptomatic drug-induced eosinophilia, eosinophilic hepatitis was detected in 3 cases attributed to amoxicillin/clavulanate, atorvastatin, and simvastatin (one case each), within a hospital-based case series of drug-induced eosinophilia.
raw_record.extra_details: Eosinophilic hepatitis (drug-induced). One of 3 eosinophilic-hepatitis cases reported in a 42-month hospital case-series of drug-induced eosinophilia; causality assigned as an adverse drug reaction. Atorvastatin was also attributed to eosinophilic myopathy in 2 cases (non-hepatic, not part of this DILI record).

raw_record.support_text: The clinical course and laboratory data in the reported case were described as compatible with a diagnosis of severe acute cholestatic hepatitis, probably due to atorvastatin, in a 69-year-old man treated for hypercholesterolemia. Symptoms appeared about 1 week after reinitiating atorvastatin 10 mg/day following a 5-month period of treatment without adverse reactions; after the drug was discontinued and later taken again, the symptoms reappeared, which the authors considered a positive rechallenge. Viral hepatitis serologies and autoantibodies were negative, the patient denied alcohol, and liver tests plus eosinophil count normalized after discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of a 69-year-old man treated with atorvastatin 10 mg/day for hypercholesterolemia. Presenting symptoms were asthenia, nausea, pruritus and dark urine. Analytical changes during hepatitis: TB 2.6 mg/dl, AST 669, ALT 727, ALP 3767, GGTP 1359, eosinophil rise (1764). Positive rechallenge (symptoms reappeared after reinitiating therapy); symptoms first appeared ~6 days-1 week after reinitiation on Nov 17, 2000. Prior use of simvastatin, pravastatin, cholestyramine and gemfibrozil without attributed liver injury. Abdominal ultrasound showed mild steatosis. The paper notes atorvastatin has previously been associated with mild serum transaminase elevations and acute hepatitis; hepatitis also described with other HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors.

raw_record.support_text: Atorvastatin was attributed as the causative lipid-lowering agent in one DILI case, separate from the atorvastatin/ezetimibe combination case.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as the causative lipid-lowering agent in 1 of 22 DILI cases.

raw_record.support_text: A case report attributes the patient's drug-induced liver injury to atorvastatin. The patient had an initial R-value > 5, classifying the injury as hepatocellular, and a Roussel-Uclaf causality assessment method (RUCAM) score placing them in the 'highly probable' category for drug-related liver injury. The patient was diagnosed with autoimmune-like DILI, with weakly positive ANA and ASMA (1:640 titers, decreasing to 1:80 after discontinuation of atorvastatin). Liver tests rose to ALT 3756 U/L, AST 3172 U/L, and total bilirubin 90.1 micromol/L at diagnosis and returned to normal after stopping atorvastatin.
raw_record.extra_details: Used for dyslipidemia/high LDL management. RUCAM score rated 'highly probable'; initial R-value > 5 (hepatocellular). Autoimmune-like DILI with weakly positive ANAs and ASMA decreased from 1:640 to 1:80 after drug discontinuation. At diagnosis: ALT 3756 U/L, AST 3172 U/L, total bilirubin 90.1, direct bilirubin 60.3, ALP 397 U/L. Liver tests normalized by 30 days after stopping atorvastatin and remained normal on follow-up. No immunosuppressants needed. Cites Russo et al. reporting 6 of 12 statin hepatocellular-injury cases as autoimmune-like DILI.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a 74-year-old woman with hyperlipidemia who developed drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis (DIAIH) while taking atorvastatin, describing DIAIH as a poorly understood form of drug-induced liver injury with features mimicking idiopathic autoimmune hepatitis. Her first episode of elevated liver enzymes resolved about three months after atorvastatin was temporarily held, and a second, more severe episode with jaundice and markedly elevated total and direct bilirubin occurred after she had restarted atorvastatin for roughly 20 months.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 74-year-old female with hyperlipidemia (also iron deficiency anemia and peripheral arterial disease). First episode (2 years prior): AST 199 U/L, ALT 385 U/L, ALP 163 U/L, TBili WNL; ANA 1:640; resolved ~3 months after atorvastatin was held (dechallenge). After restart for ~20 months, second episode arose ~2 months before admission with AST 75/ALT95 then uptrending to AST 262, ALT 127, ALP 345, TBili 21.9, DBili 15.6 mg/dL, plus jaundice, lower extremity edema, polyclonal gammopathy, albumin 2.7 g/dL, and mild ascites; admitted for inpatient workup. Indicated as an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor statin. First episode diagnosis supported by negative workup (liver ultrasound, AMA, alpha-1 antitrypsin, ceruloplasmin, ferritin).

raw_record.support_text: A 72-year-old male developed acute-onset, long-lasting cholestasis after taking atorvastatin 20 mg/day for 40 days for mixed dyslipidaemia. He presented with asthenia, nausea, painless icterus, acholic stools and hyperchromic urine, with marked bilirubin elevation (total bilirubin 22 mg/dL; direct bilirubin 21 mg/dL) and alkaline phosphatase up to 4-fold normal. Liver histology showed cholestasis with cholangiolitis and interlobular bile duct damage. Liver tests normalized within 5 months after withdrawal (ALK phosphatase after 8 months). The Maria and Victorino clinical scale and Naranjo ADR Probability Scale rated atorvastatin as the probable cause of prolonged cholestasis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 72-year-old male with type 2 diabetes, mild hypertension, and chronic cerebral ischaemia; low daily alcohol intake reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Atorvastatin 20 mg/day for 40 days, onset of symptoms 40 days after commencement. Labs: AST 85 IU/mL (2.3x), ALT 81 IU/mL (2.2x), ALP 816 U/L (4.0x), GGT 455 U/L (7x), total bilirubin 22.44 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 21.15 mg/dL; INR 1.1. Histology showed cholangiolitis, lymphocytic infiltration of interlobular duct epithelium with cholangiocyte damage, ductular reaction, centrolobular bilirubinostasis with cholestatic rosettes and feathery degeneration. Non-liver causes (viral hepatitis A-E/G, CMV, EBV, autoimmune serology, biliary obstruction) excluded; no gallstones on ultrasound or MR-cholangiography. Transaminases/bilirubin normalized in 5 months (150 days), ALP after 8 months (237 days). Causality rated probable by Maria-Victorino clinical scale and Naranjo ADR Probability Scale.

raw_record.support_text: In the German Diabetes and Dialysis Study (4D Study), 1255 adult hemodialysis patients with type 2 diabetes and LDL cholesterol of 80–190 mg/dl were randomized to 20 mg of atorvastatin or placebo. After 3 years the primary composite cardiovascular endpoint was similar between groups, and the authors report that atorvastatin was very well tolerated, with no liver or muscular side effects and no premature withdrawal due to adverse events. This is an explicit statement that no liver injury was observed with atorvastatin in this trial population.

raw_record.extra_details: 4D Study: 1255 patients, 3 years follow-up; composite primary endpoint similar between atorvastatin (31.9%) and placebo (30.5%) (hazard ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.77–1.10; p=0.37); 42% LDL reduction at 4 months; authors explicitly report no liver side effects.

raw_record.support_text: A case series of seven patients (five female, one male, and one further female; ages 50-78 years) developed hepatotoxicity attributed to atorvastatin at therapeutic doses of 10-80 mg/day. Drug exposure to onset of the reaction ranged from 1 to 52 weeks. RUCAM causality scores ranged from 4 to 9. Liver histology showed cholestasis in two patients (cases 1 and 6) and hepatitis in one (case 5). Outcomes included death in one patient (case 5), persistently abnormal LFTs in one (case 4), and resolution in the remainder. Peak bilirubin reached up to 688 µmol/l and peak AST up to 1703 U/l.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: No non-default population or co-exposure restriction stated beyond general adult therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven cases reported as atorvastatin hepatotoxicity. Atorvastatin doses: 20, 10, 20, 10, 10, 80, 10 mg/day. Latency (weeks): 3, 4, 12, 5, 52, 1, 10. Duration of reaction (months): 10, 1, 3, >12, 1, 4, 2. RUCAM scores: 8, 8, 5, 8, 4, 9, 8. Case 1: 78-year-old male, jaundice with cholestatic biopsy showing non-specific cholestasis, distended bile canaliculi, feathery hepatocyte degeneration and a single focus of hepatocyte necrosis; peak bilirubin 184 µmol/l, ALP 1328 U/l, AST 175 U/l; resolved. Case 5: peak bilirubin 688 µmol/l, AST 1703 U/l, hepatitis histology; died. Case 4: persistently abnormal LFTs. Exclusion of other liver causes via normal ferritin, albumin, immunoglobulins, alpha-1 antitrypsin, prothrombin, viral serology, and negative liver autoantibodies; ultrasound excluded biliary obstruction. Competing co-medications present (e.g., atenolol, clopidogrel, lansoprazole, prednisolone in case 1) were not attributed as the cause.

raw_record.support_text: In case 2, a 16-year-old adolescent admitted to having taken methandrostenolone 10 mg three times daily for five days before symptom onset. Laboratory tests showed bilirubin 441 µmol/l, ALT 156 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 203 IU/l, and INR 1.1. Extended liver screening and abdominal ultrasound identified no other cause of the jaundice, so the diagnosis of methandrostenolone-induced cholestasis was made clinically. The bilirubin peaked at 635 µmol/l on day 7, and liver biopsy confirmed cholestatic liver disease with a weak inflammatory component. The patient was treated with cholestyramine, chlorphenamine, ursodeoxycholic acid, rifampicin, and naltrexone, with full liver recovery over four months.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 16-year-old adolescent; first anabolic-steroid use; bodybuilding-related abuse (supratherapeutic dosing of 10 mg three times daily for 5 days).
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of methandrostenolone (methandienone)-induced cholestasis in a drug-naïve adolescent. Laboratory values at admission: bilirubin 441 µmol/l (peak 635 µmol/l on day 7), ALT 156 IU/l, ALP 203 IU/l, INR 1.1. Presenting symptoms: severe pruritus, nausea, abdominal discomfort, jaundice for ~3 weeks. Liver biopsy showed cholestatic liver disease with mild lymphocytic and macrophage infiltrate (cholestatic hepatitis). Treated with cholestyramine, chlorphenamine, ursodeoxycholic acid, rifampicin, and naltrexone; prolonged 15-day hospitalization due to therapy-refractory pruritus; anxiety and low mood during hospitalization; complete liver function recovery over four months; no other cause of jaundice identified.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that hepatotoxicity is a well-known complication of non-steroidal anti-androgens and that fatal hepatotoxicity due to nilutamide has been described previously only twice. The reported fatal case in this paper is attributed to nilutamide therapy in a patient with metastatic prostate cancer; the only other medication taken was leuprolide, an LHRH analogue for which severe hepatotoxicity has not been noted. Nilutamide's manufacturer profile describes serum aminotransferase elevations in about 8% of patients, and the incidence of abnormal liver function tests was reported as 2-33% across various studies.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal DILI case report in a patient with metastatic prostate cancer treated with nilutamide for combined androgen blockade; the only co-medication was leuprolide (LHRH analogue), for which severe hepatotoxicity was not noted. Liver biopsy showed a mixed inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils, neutrophils) with cholestasis, ductular proliferation, interface injury, and spotty necrosis; lab values showed total bilirubin 30.2 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 17.7, AST 1540 U/l, ALT 977 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 138 U/l. Patient developed encephalopathy and acute-on-chronic liver failure, received plasmapheresis for 72 h without sustained improvement, developed pancytopenia, fungemia and bacteremia, was not a transplant candidate due to metastatic prostate cancer, and died 11 days after transfer. Manufacturer label reports aminotransferase elevation in ~8% of patients (vs 4% placebo); abnormal LFT incidence 2-33% in various studies; nilutamide is a nitroaromatic drug with potential nitroreductive bioactivation (oxidant stress) and mitochondrial complex I inhibition proposed as mechanisms.

raw_record.support_text: The onset of fulminant hepatic failure in these patients so soon after the start of hydroxychloroquine treatment, with histological changes compatible with a drug related cause, implicates hydroxychloroquine as the probable cause of the acute liver failure. The two cases had histology of acute massive necrosis without evidence of chronic liver disease, consistent with drug-related hepatotoxicity, although hydroxychloroquine itself had never previously been reported to cause fulminant hepatic failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients with systemic lupus erythematosus developed fulminant hepatic failure shortly after starting hydroxychloroquine treatment; histology showed acute massive necrosis with no evidence of chronic liver disease, entirely consistent with drug-related hepatotoxicity. These were noted to be the first reported cases of fulminant hepatic failure attributed to hydroxychloroquine, though other 4-aminoquinolones had been reported to cause it, suggesting all members of this drug group be considered potentially hepatotoxic.

raw_record.support_text: A 29-year-old woman with subacute lupus erythematosus was prescribed hydroxychloroquine (400 mg/day) and subsequently developed severe drug-induced liver injury. She was taking no other medications; three days after starting the drug she presented with nausea, fatigue, chills, malaise and dark urine with marked transaminitis (ALT 6380 and AST 4472 IU/L). The authors state that at the doses used to treat systemic lupus erythematosus and subacute cutaneous lupus, hydroxychloroquine carries a potentially life-threatening complication of hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report. Hydroxychloroquine dosed at 400 mg/day (dose used for SLE/subacute cutaneous lupus), prescribed to a 29-year-old woman for subacute lupus erythematosus; she was on no other medications. Onset of symptoms 3 days after initiation. Laboratory findings: ALT 6380 IU/L and AST 4472 IU/L (markedly elevated), dark urine with urine blood 150 µL but 0 RBC/HPF, leukopenia (2.4 K/µL), thrombocytopenia (84 K/µL), mild neutropenia and lymphopenia, normal eosinophil count; creatinine at baseline (0.5 mg/dL) and CK 28 IU/L. Described by authors as severe DILI and a potentially life-threatening complication of hepatotoxicity; hepatotoxicity described as dose-related context (lower doses are effective for PCT, higher SLE/SCLE doses carry hepatotoxicity risk). The case also identified concurrent porphyria cutanea tarda.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that a number of cases of liver injury from the sulfonylurea compound metahexamide have been observed, noting that among 1800 patients using metahexamide at least 10 cases of jaundice were reported, to which the author adds 3 more. A detailed case is given of a 56-year-old man with mild diabetes who developed mild definite jaundice on the 24th day of a 300 mg daily metahexamide trial, with chemical confirmation of obstructive icterus and a liver biopsy revealing central lobular necrosis with focal necrosis and mononuclear cell infiltration; the author states that jaundice due to central lobular necrosis will characterize this more serious toxic effect in patients receiving metahexamide. Table 1 also lists metahexamide as positive for liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: At least 10 cases of jaundice among 1800 metahexamide users reported, plus 3 additional cases observed by the author. Illustrative case: 56-year-old man with mild diabetes for 10 years, metahexamide 300 mg daily for about 3 weeks, mild definite jaundice on day 24, chemical confirmation of obstructive icterus, otherwise normal liver function studies, biopsy revealing central lobular necrosis with focal necrosis and mononuclear cell infiltration, resembling injury seen with sulfanilamide. Author characterizes jaundice due to central lobular necrosis as the more serious toxic effect of metahexamide.

raw_record.support_text: Savolitinib, a selective MET tyrosine kinase inhibitor conditionally approved in China in June 2021 for advanced NSCLC with MET 14 exon skipping mutation, lists nausea, vomiting, peripheral edema, pyrexia, and hepatotoxicity as its most common adverse reactions (ARs). raw_record.support_text: In patients diagnosed with acute hydrogen cyanamide (Dormex) intoxication at Tanta Poison Control Center, laboratory investigations associated with unfavorable outcomes included significant elevation of liver enzymes (SGOT, SGPT), serum bilirubin, and serum creatinine, and prolonged prothrombin time. The association between elevated liver transaminases, prolonged PT, and liver impairment was described, and the changes in pathological hepatic involvement were applied to Dormex-induced hepatotoxicity. Contributing hepatotoxicity mechanisms cited were cellular lysis with release of transaminases, impaired hepatic synthesis of coagulation factors, and prolonged PT.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute accidental/intentional poisoning (Dormex intoxication) cases presenting to a poison control center, with multiorgan/systemic involvement; hepatic impairment was part of overall poisoning severity and outcome assessment in 35 patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver enzyme elevation (SGOT up to 1575 U/L, SGPT up to 2480 U/L in the unfavorable-outcome subgroup), elevated total/direct/indirect bilirubin, and prolonged prothrombin time/INR were significantly associated with unfavorable outcomes; prolonged PT and impaired coagulation-factor synthesis linked to liver impairment. The obstruction of bile flow and acute drug-induced cholestasis were also suggested mechanisms (Zimmerman 1999). Dormex is a commercial form of hydrogen cyanamide used as a plant growth regulator.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of 30 patients with metformin-induced hepatotoxicity, metformin was discontinued in all patients. Four patients (13.3%) were rechallenged with metformin and two of them relapsed with hepatotoxicity. Liver function returned to normal in all 30 patients (100%) at a median time of 6 weeks (range 2–16), while two patients had persistently high ALP levels.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM causality assessment: probable 16/30 (53.3%), highly probable 13/30 (43.3%), possible 1/30 (3.3%). Injury pattern: hepatocellular 14 (46.7%), cholestatic 9 (30.0%), mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic 7 (23.3%). Severity: mild 5 (16.7%), moderate 18 (60.0%), severe 3 (10.0%), NA 4 (13.3%). All patients recovered; rechallenge relapsed in 2/4. Laboratory values (median, range): ALT 694.5 U/L (47–4701), AST 382.5 U/L (36–8091), TBIL 4.5 mg/dl (0.5–25.6), ALP 437 U/L (94–1001). Clinical features included jaundice (50%), fatigue, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain. Biopsy (13 patients) showed portal inflammation (61.5%), cholestatic hepatitis (38.5%), parenchymal inflammation (38.5%), bile duct inflammation with epithelial destruction (23.1%), fibrosis (15.4%). Maximum approved daily dose 2.5 g; hepatotoxicity seen in 20% of Asians in this analysis.

raw_record.support_text: Metformin, a biguanide, has been associated in two reports with acute cholestatic hepatitis and in one case with bland cholestasis. Symptoms of acute hepatitis developed 2–4 weeks after taking metformin, and full recovery was observed in all three cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Three cases total: two acute cholestatic hepatitis reports and one bland cholestasis. Onset of symptoms 2–4 weeks after initiation; full recovery in all cases.

raw_record.support_text: The case report's objective is to describe a patient with metformin-induced mixed cholestatic and hepatocellular injury who recovered after cessation of therapy and relapsed after rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: A 67-year-old woman hospitalized for jaundice with 1-week history of fatigue, weakness, abdominal bloating and jaundice, mild jaundice, slightly enlarged liver, no splenomegaly; began metformin 500 mg twice daily 6 weeks before admission for type 2 diabetes; concurrent acarbose, isosorbide mononitrate, salicylic acid, and diltiazem; no alcohol abuse, previous liver disease, blood transfusion, or toxin exposure. Positive causality evidence: recovery after cessation and relapse after rechallenge. Metformin hepatotoxicity has rarely been reported; other oral antidiabetic agents (acarbose, gliclazide, some thiazolidinediones mainly troglitazone) have been implicated in liver toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A 68-year-old man with newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus developed jaundice, pruritus, and liver enzyme abnormalities four weeks after starting metformin (initially 500 mg twice daily, later increased to 850 mg twice a day). An extensive work-up (hepatitis screen, ultrasonography, MRI, ERCP) was normal, and liver biopsy showed severe cholestasis and mild portal inflammation. After metformin was discontinued the liver enzymes normalized except for a persistently increased alkaline phosphatase, attributed to a prolonged cholestatic effect of metformin.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 68-year-old man with newly diagnosed diabetes. Metformin dosed 500 mg twice daily, later 850 mg twice a day; jaundice and pruritus appeared 4 weeks after initiation with liver enzyme abnormalities. Work-up including hepatitis screen, ultrasonography, MRI, and ERCP was normal. Liver biopsy revealed severe cholestasis and mild portal inflammation. Dechallenge: after discontinuing metformin, liver enzymes normalized except persistently increased alkaline phosphatase (AP), attributed to a prolonged cholestatic effect. Phenotype termed 'cholestatic hepatitis'. Authors conclude metformin can rarely be responsible for inducing liver damage.

raw_record.support_text: DILI-inducing antidiabetics were metformin, acarbose and glipizide; antidiabetics accounted for 6 patients (1.42%) of DILI cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Antidiabetic; antidiabetics accounted for 6 patients (1.42%) of DILI cases.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that metformin can induce hepatic injury (hepatocellular and/or cholestatic), and notes that metformin hepatotoxicity has rarely been reported, with possible mechanisms being direct, idiosyncratic, or a drug–drug interaction leading to acute hepatocellular and/or cholestatic jaundice.
raw_record.extra_details: Search of PubMed yielded six published metformin hepatotoxicity reports (Table 2): two cases of acute hepatitis, two cases of cholestasis, and two cases of mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic injury; the paper's own patient is the third reported case of mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic liver injury. In all cases signs and symptoms resolved and liver enzymes normalized after metformin discontinuation, except for a persistently increased alkaline phosphatase in one case attributed to a prolonged cholestatic effect. Liver biopsy was performed in three cases and rechallenge in one; no specific treatments were given. Bilirubin normalized after 2 months in the described case.

raw_record.support_text: Our patient developed acute cholestatic hepatitis 6 weeks after initiation of metformin therapy. Other causes of acute hepatitis were excluded, liver histologic characteristics were nonspecific, consistent with drug-induced hepatitis, and metformin withdrawal led to clinical recovery. A rechallenge with metformin 6 months later reproduced the same syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: Female patient with type 2 diabetes treated with metformin (and earlier gliclazide/metformin, withdrawn); acute cholestatic hepatitis appeared 6 weeks after rechallenge of metformin and resolved after discontinuation with normal LFTs at 4 months. Jaundice and elevated ALT (figure). Antinuclear antibodies present but autoimmune hepatitis not documented; liver histology nonspecific, consistent with drug-induced hepatitis. Authors note 3 prior reported cases of metformin hepatotoxicity (2 acute hepatitis, 1 bland cholestasis) and frame this as a well-documented idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity case. Disease may be misdiagnosed as acute viral or autoimmune hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: A 70-year-old white woman developed metformin-induced liver injury 5 weeks after starting metformin 500 mg twice daily for type 2 diabetes, and she was not on any other hepatotoxic agent. The case is reported to draw attention to this rare but important metformin side effect.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 70-year-old white woman with type 2 diabetes and hypothyroidism on only metformin 500 mg twice daily and levothyroxine, denying OTC medications, alcohol, or illicit drugs; injury developed 5 weeks after starting metformin, with no other hepatotoxic agent. Initial labs showed hepatocellular pattern: total bilirubin 2.2 mg/dL, ALT 1093 U/L, AST 1152 U/L, ALP 176 U/L, ALT/ALP ratio >5; normal INR and eosinophil counts. Metformin was discontinued with supportive care only; AST fell to 358 (day 2) and 71 (day 4), ALT to 747 (day 2) and 432 (day 4), bilirubin to 0.8 (day 3); labs normal 10 days after discharge. Viral hepatitis A/B/C, autoimmune and metabolic liver disease testing (iron, antimitochondrial/antinuclear/antismooth-muscle antibodies, ceruloplasmin, copper), abdominal ultrasound and MRCP were unremarkable. No rechallenge, causality instrument, or formal assessment reported.

raw_record.support_text: The diagnosis of drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis was established after reasonably excluding other possible etiologies. Among all the drugs the patient was receiving, metformin appears the most probably responsible agent, per the Nierenberg protocol: prior published cases of metformin-associated hepatotoxicity exist, latency from exposure onset to symptoms was a few weeks, the clinical picture improved to resolution after drug withdrawal, and other causes of hepatitis were excluded. No rechallenge was performed.

raw_record.extra_details: Metformin (dimetilbiguanida) 1700 mg/day. Presented with 2-3 weeks of dyspepsia/abdominal discomfort, then intense asthenia, anorexia, jaundice, coluria and generalized pruritus. Peak liver tests: total bilirubin 256 µmol/l, direct bilirubin 210 µmol/l, AST 1198 U/l, ALT 596 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 164 U/l, GGT 260 U/l. Injury resolved (analytical normal) within 3 months and remained normal at 9 months follow-up; no specific treatment given, insulin used to control diabetes. Viral, autoimmune, and tumor serologies, imaging (ultrasound, CT, cholangio-MRI) all negative. Liver biopsy not performed (patient refused). MEDLINE (1966-2004) search 'Metformin/adverse effects AND Hepatitis or Cholestasis' identified only 4 prior published cases; metformin hepatic toxicity described as extraordinarily rare. Comparison table of the 5 cases (Babich, Desilets, Nammour, Deutsch, present case) shows resolution in 4-12 weeks; one published case (Nammour) had rechallenge/concomitant pathology.

raw_record.support_text: After receiving metformin 500 mg/d for 3 weeks, a 73-year-old Japanese woman with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes presented with fatigue, jaundice, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, and abdominal pain and laboratory findings of severe hepatotoxicity (elevated AST, ALT, ALP, and total bilirubin). Immediate hospitalization and discontinuation of metformin led to improvement in liver function and resolution of symptoms within 3 weeks. The probability of an adverse drug reaction assessed with the Naranjo ADR probability scale was 4 (probable). The authors concluded metformin appeared to have caused mixed-type (hepatocellular and cholestatic) hepatic damage, and although rare, severe hepatotoxicity might be associated with metformin use.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly (73-year-old) Japanese woman with low body weight (33.5 kg) and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus.
raw_record.extra_details: Metformin 500 mg/day for 3 weeks before presentation. Symptoms included fatigue, jaundice, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, and abdominal pain. Laboratory findings: elevated aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, and total bilirubin. Naranjo ADR probability scale score 4 (probable). Liver function improved and symptoms resolved within 3 weeks after metformin discontinuation and hospitalization. Authors note hepatotoxicity is rare but may be associated with metformin. Metformin hydrochloride is widely used for type 2 diabetes mellitus; only 2 prior cases of possible metformin-induced acute hepatitis reported worldwide.

raw_record.support_text: In 22 high-risk uveal melanoma patients treated with adjuvant intra-arterial hepatic (i.a.h.) fotemustine, half of the patients experienced ≥ grade 3 hepatotoxicity, with one patient developing cholangitis 8 years later. The authors conclude that the treatment is feasible but that its toxicities are important.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-risk uveal melanoma patients receiving adjuvant intra-arterial hepatic (locoregional) administration of fotemustine.
raw_record.extra_details: 22 patients treated; planned 6-month duration starting with four weekly doses of 100 mg/m², then repeated every 3 weeks after a 5-week rest. Half (11) experienced ≥ grade 3 hepatotoxicity; one developed cholangitis 8 years later. Catheter-related complications occurred in 18%. Median follow-up 4.6 years for the fotemustine group vs 8.5 years for a 3:1 matched control group; median overall survival 9 years (95% CI 2.2-12.7) vs 7.4 years (95% CI 5.4-12.7; P=0.5). 5-year survival 75% vs 56%.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a patient who developed nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and fatigue 2 weeks after starting rosiglitazone therapy, and state that they believe the most likely cause of his symptoms and elevated liver enzyme levels was rosiglitazone-associated hepatotoxicity. Rosiglitazone was discontinued on admission, symptoms immediately improved, and liver enzyme levels returned to normal over ensuing weeks. Because the patient had no fever, rash, or eosinophilia, the authors concluded the liver injury caused by rosiglitazone seemed to be idiosyncratic rather than a classic immune mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: patient was an icteric, obese male with prior acetaminophen use (up to 4 g/d for 2 years, 3-4 tablets daily 3 months before admission) and prior brief exposures to troglitazone (discontinued after 1 week for nausea) and repaglinide (discontinued for nausea/dizziness); acetaminophen level on admission was 3.2 µg/mL (normal 10-30). Symptoms appeared ~2 weeks after starting rosiglitazone; rosiglitazone was discontinued on admission; symptoms resolved and liver enzymes returned to normal 7 weeks after discontinuation. No signs of hepatic failure at any time; aspartate aminotransferase fell rapidly while ALT remained elevated during 8 days of hospitalization. No fever, rash, or eosinophilia (peripheral eosinophil count 90 x 10^6/L). Abdominal CT consistent with fatty liver.

raw_record.support_text: In this randomized trial of rosiglitazone added to insulin in insulin-treated patients with type 2 diabetes, the paper reports that 'There was no evidence of hepatotoxicity in this trial.' The rosiglitazone-related adverse events observed were hypoglycemia, anemia, edema, arthralgia, weight gain, and hyperlipidemia, with no hepatic injury reported for rosiglitazone at therapeutic doses.
raw_record.extra_details: Trial of rosiglitazone (4 or 8 mg/day) added to insulin in inadequately controlled insulin-treated type 2 diabetes patients. Authors explicitly state no evidence of hepatotoxicity was observed in the trial.

raw_record.support_text: A 52-year-old man who had taken rosiglitazone 4 mg/day for 11 months for type 2 diabetes (plus insulin for 5 years and no other medication) developed hepatotoxicity during hospitalization, with ALT 488 U/L, AST 344 U/L, ALP 832 U/L, total bilirubin 4.61 mg/dL and direct bilirubin 3.63 mg/dL. Rosiglitazone was stopped after bilirubin rose further (total 14.67, direct 12.10 mg/dL), and other causes were excluded; the patient's newly diagnosed Hodgkin lymphoma was excluded by imaging and liver biopsy as a direct cause of the acute liver failure. Bilirubin continued rising to 49.29 mg/dL (direct >20 mg/dL) despite discontinuation, and the patient died 3 months after admission.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report in a 52-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and newly diagnosed Hodgkin lymphoma (excluded by imaging and liver biopsy as direct cause of liver failure; liver biopsy showed canalicular cholestasis with intact duct, no ductular proliferation, and no significant inflammation). Concurrent insulin for 5 years; rosiglitazone 4 mg/day for 11 months. Naranjo probability scale indicated rosiglitazone as the probable cause of acute liver failure. Other causes of hepatotoxicity excluded. Rosiglitazone withdrawn on hospital day 19; bilirubin continued to rise to 49.29 mg/dL (direct >20 mg/dL); patient died 3 months after admission. Paper concludes rosiglitazone may be associated with late-onset acute liver failure and physicians should monitor liver function. Troglitazone, the first thiazolidinedione, was withdrawn from the market for reported acute liver failure; rosiglitazone reported much safer with some cases of nonfatal early-onset hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 574 patients with Type 2 diabetes, low-dose rosiglitazone (2 or 4 mg/d) added to existing sulphonylurea therapy was reported safe and well-tolerated, with no significant hepatotoxicity or hypoglycaemia reported. Companion trials of rosiglitazone combined with metformin (26-week, n=348) and with insulin (26-week, n=319) reported that no patients had alanine aminotransferase > 3 times the upper limit of normal.
raw_record.extra_details: Negative conclusion based on combination-therapy trials in Type 2 diabetes: rosiglitazone 2-4 mg/d plus sulphonylurea (gliclazide/glibenclamide/glipizide), rosiglitazone 4 or 8 mg with metformin (2.5 g/d max), and rosiglitazone 2-4 mg/d with insulin. Trials reported no significant hepatotoxicity and no ALT > 3x ULN. Reported doses are mg/day; bd/t.i.d. wording in source tables.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report that rosiglitazone led to even more severe hepatotoxicity in their patient, manifested chiefly as a cholestatic hepatitis with nonsuppurative granulomatous cholangitis rather than hepatocellular injury, with serum aminotransferases within normal limits or only mildly elevated while alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin ranged from 3 to 20 times the upper limit of normal (peaks of 14.4 µkat/L alkaline phosphatase and 379 µM bilirubin). In paragraph 24, they state that severe and rapid worsening on inadvertent rechallenge with rosiglitazone provides additional strong evidence for rosiglitazone-induced liver injury, and that the overall course makes it unlikely the disease was due only to troglitazone.

raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis with nonsuppurative (destructive) granulomatous cholangitis on biopsy; hepatocellular pattern suggested in two prior cases (peaks ALT 1704 and 4800 IU/L) and lesser ALP elevations; type 4 delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction directed at biliary epithelium proposed; treated with prednisone, azathioprine, and ursodiol; marked improvement following cessation and severe worsening after inadvertent rechallenge at home after February 2000 admission.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states anastrozole has generally been considered to have a good liver safety profile in clinical trials and that anastrozole-associated hepatotoxicity was rare in the FAERS database, but cites several reported cases suggesting a probable correlation between anastrozole and liver damage: an 89-year-old woman with invasive lobular breast cancer developed acute mixed but primarily cholestatic hepatic damage after 2 months of anastrozole and recovered after drug withdrawal; a 58-year-old patient suffered similar cholestatic liver damage during anastrozole therapy; and a 70-year-old woman developed acute hepatitis with increased hepatic enzymes and positive serum antinuclear antibodies, with biopsy showing mild hepatic steatosis, moderate inflammation, and moderate to severe fibrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Generally considered good liver safety profile in clinical trials [51]; anastrozole-associated hepatotoxicity rare in FAERS database; reported cases: 89-year-old woman with invasive lobular breast cancer with acute mixed but primarily cholestatic hepatic damage after 2 months of anastrozole, mild conjunctival jaundice and transient hepatic enzyme elevation, prompt full recovery after drug withdrawal [52]; 58-year-old patient with similar cholestatic liver damage [53]; 70-year-old woman with acute hepatitis, increased hepatic enzymes and positive serum antinuclear antibodies, biopsy showing mild hepatic steatosis, moderate inflammation, and moderate to severe fibrosis [54].

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents a case of drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) attributed to anastrozole, supported by the temporal relationship of elevated liver function tests after initiation of anastrozole, elevated aminotransferases with normal or marginally elevated alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin, elevated ANA autoantibody titers, extrahepatic autoimmune manifestations, and a favorable response to immunosuppressive therapy. The authors state the presentation is characteristic of drug-induced AIH and that timing of onset, ANA positivity, the LFT pattern, improvement after anastrozole discontinuation, and response to immunosuppressive therapy point toward drug-induced AIH (paragraph 26). A liver biopsy was used to exclude other causes of liver disease, including anastrozole-related steatosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) attributed to anastrozole. Presentation included elevated LFTs following drug initiation, elevated aminotransferases with normal or marginally elevated alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin, elevated ANA titers, extrahepatic autoimmune manifestations, and favorable response to immunosuppressive therapy. Liver biopsy showed chronic hepatitis with increased plasma cells at the portal-lobular interface and rosetting; fibrosis may be associated depending on duration/severity. Biopsy was used to exclude anastrozole-related steatosis (which was suggested on CT but not present on biopsy). Differential highlighted the challenge of distinguishing idiopathic spontaneous AIH, drug-induced AIH, and other types of DILI.

The authors note that over the past 6 years more than 30,000 breast-cancer patients treated with third-generation aromatase inhibitors showed a good liver safety profile and no similar cases were found in the WHO database, indicating an uncommon, post-marketing-surveillance-detected drug-related event.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic biopsy showed extensive hepatocellular necrosis in zone 3 of the liver acinus, with cholestasis and middle macrovesicular steatosis also evident, and absence of inflammatory changes; injury was judged compatible with metabolically mediated hepatocellular liver injury. Anastrozole is extensively metabolised by N-dealkylation, hydroxylation, and glucuronidation; it (but not its metabolites) inhibits P450 1A2, 2C8/9, and 3A4. A later separate case of anastrozole-related hepatitis (without documented histology) was reported after submission. No similar cases were found in the WHO database; more than 30,000 aromatase-inhibitor-treated patients showed a good liver safety profile.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that arsenamide has a toxic effect upon the liver. In two cases treatment was followed by jaundice (three days and four weeks after the last injection), and one patient developed fatal necrosis of the liver after receiving only three injections. This liver injury occurred during therapeutic use of arsenamide (125 mg, 1.8-2.5 mg/kg daily IV, usually 10-12 doses) in patients with bancroftian filariasis.
raw_record.extra_details: Arsenamide (p-bis-(carboxymethyl-mercapto)-arsino-benzamide) used for bancroftian filariasis; dose 125 mg (1.8-2.5 mg/kg) daily by IV injection, usually 10-12 doses. Liver injury: jaundice in two cases (3 days and 4 weeks after last injection) and fatal hepatic necrosis in one patient after only three injections. Other minor toxic effects included vomiting, dizziness, headache, and weight loss. Competitive/alternative causes (infective hepatitis, malnutrition with tocopherol/cysteine deficiency) were considered and excluded: clean syringes/needles per injection and too-short incubation period ruled out viral hepatitis. Authors concluded use is not devoid of risk and, since filariasis is not fatal, arsenamide use is not justifiable for general treatment; advised keeping dose low (preferably below 0.6 mg/kg), hospital supervision, and protein dietary supplement to fortify the liver.

Laboratory values: AST 543 U/L, ALT 5 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 184 U/L, total bilirubin 2.3 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL. The abstract additionally notes jaundice, hemolysis (100%), cholestatic hepatitis (50%), and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (50%) among all eight flavonoid-induced oliguric acute renal failure patients.

raw_record.support_text: Some of the toxicity of lurbinectedin can be predicted from its mechanism of action. Many patients develop myelosuppression, and neutropenia or thrombocytopenia require the dose of lurbinectedin to be modified; the dose should also be modified if hepatotoxicity emerges. Hepatotoxicity was among the adverse effects seen in the phase II trial of lurbinectedin for small cell lung cancer.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity is described as a toxicity requiring dose modification of lurbinectedin. Related dose-limiting toxicities in the open-label phase II trial (105 patients with small cell lung cancer progressing after platinum-based chemotherapy) included myelosuppression, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. Lurbinectedin is metabolised by CYP3A4 (half-life 51 h); recommended to avoid strong/moderate CYP3A inhibitors such as azole antifungals, ciprofloxacin, erythromycin, phenytoin and phenobarbital. Given by intravenous infusion over an hour.

raw_record.support_text: The table describes 8 published cases of zafirlukast-induced acute liver injury, and the text notes published case reports of acute hepatocellular injury caused by zafirlukast (Accolate). Cases ranged from 2 to 18 months of drug exposure; interventions included steroids and orthotopic liver transplantation, and liver biopsy/explant findings included submassive hepatic necrosis, multilobular bridging necrosis, and eosinophilic infiltration.
raw_record.extra_details: 8 described cases (ages 36-68, mostly female): duration of drug exposure 4-18 months; time to normalization of enzymes after discontinuation from several weeks to 6 months; interventions included steroids and orthotopic liver transplantation (OLTx) in 2 cases with submassive hepatic necrosis; biopsy/explant findings included submassive hepatic necrosis with abundant eosinophils, multilobular bridging necrosis with parenchymal collapse, regeneration, and eosinophilic infiltration. Referred to as acute hepatocellular injury.

raw_record.support_text: All 9 published cases of zafirlukast-associated hepatotoxicity, when scored with the CIOMS instrument using available information, fell into the possible (3-6 points) or probable (6-8 points) categories except case 2, which scored highly probable (10 points) because of a positive response to an unintentional rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: 9 published cases; CIOMS causality scores: case 2 highly probable (10 points, positive rechallenge), others possible (3-6) or probable (6-8); hepatotoxicity rare, unpredictable, not obviously dose-dependent with estimated risk <1 in 50,000 exposed; associated with roughly <10 documented liver failure cases (about 10-fold fewer than troglitazone). Histologic features used in causality assessment include microvesicular steatosis, dense eosinophilic infiltrates, centrolobular zonal necrosis, and bile duct lesions.

raw_record.support_text: A 63-year-old woman developed acute hepatocellular injury. She had normal serum liver enzymes before starting zafirlukast (Accolate, AstraZeneca) 20 mg twice daily for asthma, and her symptoms began 8 weeks after starting the drug. Serology for hepatitis A/B/C, cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus and autoantibodies were negative and ultrasound was normal. A diagnosis of acute hepatocellular injury was suspected and zafirlukast was immediately discontinued, after which liver enzymes returned to near-normal by day 53 and normal by day 193.
raw_record.extra_details: 63-year-old Hispanic woman with asthma and prior cholecystectomy (July 1996, normal intraoperative cholangiography and liver biopsy); treated concurrently with inhaled salbutamol, formoterol and budesonide. Presenting symptoms: malaise, asthenia, anorexia, jaundice. On admission: total bilirubin 4.5 mg/dl, AST 980 IU/l, ALT 999 IU/l, GGT 258 IU/l, AP 323 IU/l (day 1), with scleral icterus and no ascites, flapping tremor or hepatosplenomegaly; normal prothrombin time, albumin, iron/copper metabolism and alpha-fetoprotein. Negative serology for hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV and anti-nuclear, anti-smooth muscle, anti-mitochondrial, anti-liver kidney microsomal antibodies; normal abdominal ultrasound. After zafirlukast discontinuation, liver tests improved progressively (day 53: total bilirubin 1.0, AST 39, ALT 30, GGT 45, AP 303) and were normal by day 193. Symptom onset 8 weeks after starting zafirlukast (20 mg twice daily).

raw_record.support_text: The scarcity of reports of zoxazolamine jaundice justifies the description of an additional case; the case patient revealed hepatocellular damage from the drug, similar to those reported by Hoffbauer, revealed by liver-function tests and the microscopic appearance of the liver specimen. The case report concerns a 40-year-old man with chronic gout on therapeutic zoxazolamine who developed mild jaundice and laboratory findings compatible with mild hepatocellular damage; zoxazolamine was discontinued after a diagnosis of acute hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Known drug (Flexin), muscle relaxant and uricosuric agent used for gout. Present case: 40-year-old male with chronic polyarticular gout, started on zoxazolamine 250 mg 4x/day in January 1960 (serum uric acid fell from 8.2 to 4.9 mg%), reduced to 250 mg twice daily then 250 mg/day; developed postprandial nausea, pyrosis, epigastric pain, mild jaundice, palpable slightly tender liver, and mild hepatocellular damage on liver-function tests; diagnosis of duodenal ulcer and acute hepatitis; drug discontinued. Earlier literature: two fatal cases of severe hepatocellular jaundice after zoxazolamine with red and yellow atrophy of the liver reported by Hoffbauer, though the pathologists were uncertain about the drug-liver damage relationship; a case by Jasper of jaundice about two weeks after 500 mg/day zoxazolamine for chronic gout, which recovered rapidly upon stopping and was attributed to cholestasis similar to chlorpromazine (elevated alkaline phosphatase, depressed serum cholesterol, positive cephalin flocculation, no pruritus, no liver biopsy).

raw_record.support_text: Through the cooperation of Frederick W. Hoffbauer, sections of 2 cases who developed fatal hepatic necrosis after the intake of zoxazolamine were studied, and both presented the same alterations as the cases of acute massive and submassive necrotic hepatitis following the administration of iproniazid.
raw_record.extra_details: Two fatal cases (sections provided by F. W. Hoffbauer, Minneapolis) presenting the same acute massive and submassive necrotic-hepatitis alterations as the iproniazid cases.

raw_record.support_text: Zoxazolamine was administered to 20 patients for its uricosuric action. Side effects were observed in two patients; one with probenecid skin sensitivity was also sensitive to zoxazolamine, and in another patient receiving the drug for control of hyperuricemia and recurring uric acid renal stones a rapidly fatal hepatitis developed after eight months of treatment with 250 mg daily. The authors note that three other cases of fatal hepatic necrosis after zoxazolamine and 32 instances of nonfatal hepatitis have been reported, attributing these liver injuries to zoxazolamine therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Primary case: patient receiving zoxazolamine (250 mg daily, 8 months) for hyperuricemia and recurring uric acid renal stones developed rapidly fatal hepatitis. Additionally, three other fatal hepatic necrosis cases and 32 nonfatal hepatitis instances reported after zoxazolamine. Drug (brand name Flexin) used as uricosuric in daily dosages up to 1000 mg (250-1000 mg maintenance) for gout and recurring renal stones. Other side effect noted: skin sensitivity to zoxazolamine in a patient also skin-sensitive to probenecid.

raw_record.support_text: Zoxazolamine is listed among the drugs involved in the viral-hepatitis-type (Group IV) drug-induced hepatic injury (61 cases), a lesion resembling viral hepatitis with spotty, zonal, and massive/submassive necrosis patterns.

raw_record.support_text: Tacrine, the first US-licensed acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (Cognex, Warner-Lambert), demonstrated clinical utility in studies, but hepatic toxicity of tacrine at therapeutic dose necessitated temporary cessation of the large-scale multicenter dementia drug trial. Ultimately it was this liver toxicity that made tacrine obsolete by the time donepezil was approved, despite promising Phase III trials and a US license granted in September 1993.
raw_record.extra_details: Tacrine (Cognex, Warner-Lambert) was the first US-licensed AChEI; hepatic toxicity at therapeutic dose led to temporary study cessation and eventually made the drug obsolete despite promising Phase III trials and a US license in September 1993.

raw_record.support_text: In the study of 69 patients, 37 suffered from tacrine-induced liver injury, following a rat-model finding that IL-6 polymorphism was a predisposing factor for tacrine-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: None of 69 patients, 37 developed tacrine-induced liver injury; discussed in the context of cytokine gene (IL-6) polymorphism as a potential DILI biomarker; initial supporting predisposition finding was from a rat model.

raw_record.support_text: This paper characterizes tacrine-induced liver injury in humans. Of 636 patients developing elevated transaminases during clinical trials, 5 had jaundice; all had ALT >3x ULN, 3 had significant alkaline phosphatase elevation, and 1 significant bilirubin elevation, and 3 patients recovered on drug discontinuation. A Hammel et al. case reported acute hepatitis in a 76-year-old woman after 20 days of tacrine 75 mg/d (jaundice and fever, markedly elevated bilirubin and ALT), with a liver biopsy showing marked centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis and mild inflammatory infiltration, and LFTs normal five days after discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: From NDA clinical-trial data: 636 patients developed elevated transaminases, 5 with jaundice (all ALT >3x ULN, 3 significant alkaline phosphatase elevation, 1 significant bilirubin elevation); 3 recovered on discontinuation. Manufacturer biopsy data for 7 patients with elevated transaminases showed hepatocellular necrosis in 6 and granulomatous hepatitis in 1; an Australian study of 4 patients with asymptomatic liver-enzyme increases found focal necrosis with slight fatty changes (1 with granulomatous hepatitis). Of 56 rechallenged patients in one study, 21.4% discontinued due to recurrence of elevated LFTs, with mean time to ALT elevation of 19 days (faster than initial onset). In the adverse-effects table (NDA trials), elevated transaminases occurred in 23.5% of 2706 tacrine-treated patients vs 1.5% of 342 placebo patients (difference 22.0%).; df: None

raw_record.support_text: In controlled clinical trials of tacrine for Alzheimer's disease (Cognex package insert, Parke-Davis 1993), increased ALT occurred as an adverse effect in 29% of tacrine-treated patients (n=634) versus 2% of placebo recipients (n=342), described as tacrine hepatotoxicity. The paper further reports that of 145 patients with serum ALT increases 3-10 times the upper limit of normal, 127 were successfully rechallenged and continued tacrine, but rechallenge is considered imprudent for patients with ALT increases 20 times or greater than normal or with signs of allergic response (rash, fever, eosinophilia), and tacrine should be stopped if jaundice occurs or serum ALT reaches three times the upper limit of normal.
raw_record.extra_details: Increased ALT in 29% of tacrine patients (n=634) vs 2% placebo (n=342) in controlled trials for Alzheimer's disease. Of 145 patients with ALT 3-10x ULN, 127 were successfully rechallenged (Watkins), showing a more rapid rise but lower peak ALT with eventual return to normal; rechallenge discouraged for ALT >=20x ULN or allergic signs (rash, fever, eosinophilia). Tacrine should be stopped if jaundice occurs or ALT >=3x ULN; monthly ALT monitoring advised due to possibility of late hepatotoxicity. Contraindicated in patients with jaundice related to tacrine treatment when total bilirubin >50 umol/L.

raw_record.support_text: In the Knapp et al. trial, tacrine titrated to the maximum tolerated dosage (80–160 mg/day) was compared with placebo in 653 patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease over 30 weeks, using the ADAS-noncog scale for behavioural symptoms. There were no statistically significant differences between treatment arms regarding behavioural symptoms, and the study had a very high withdrawal rate because of the hepatotoxic effects of the drug; of the 653 patients randomised, only 263 completed the study.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as a reason for high study withdrawal in 653 randomized patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease; tacrine dose titrated to maximum tolerated dosage (80–160 mg/day) over 30 weeks; only 263 of 653 patients completed the study.

raw_record.support_text: During therapeutic dose escalation, tacrine was administered at incremental dosages (40, 80, 120 and 160 mg/day) in four daily doses, up to the highest dose the patient could tolerate without side-effects. The side-effects that limited dose escalation explicitly included hepatotoxicity, as well as systemic cholinergic symptoms, indicating that therapeutic-dose tacrine caused hepatotoxicity in these Alzheimer's disease patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of tacrine treatment response in Alzheimer's disease patients (mean age approximately 77-78 years) stratified by ApoE epsilon-4 carrier status. Tacrine was titrated from 40 to 160 mg/day in four daily doses, with escalation limited by hepatotoxicity and systemic cholinergic symptoms; 76 patients were treated at 40 mg, 69 at 80 mg, 41 at 120 mg and 23 at 160 mg. The study's primary focus was the relation between ApoE phenotype and treatment response rather than characterization of the liver injury; no severity, biochemical pattern, or latency details for the hepatotoxicity were reported.

raw_record.support_text: Tacrine, the first cholinesterase inhibitor widely used for Alzheimer's disease, produced hepatotoxicity in clinical trials. The high study attrition rate in the pivotal 30-week trial of tacrine was attributed to hepatotoxicity and cholinergic side effects, and hepatotoxicity, along with frequent cholinergic side effects and a short half-life requiring qid dosing, limited the widespread use of tacrine.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity was reported as a cause of high trial attrition (with cholinergic side effects) in AD treatment trials, including a pivotal 30-week double-blind placebo-controlled multicenter trial; hepatotoxicity limited the drug's widespread use.

raw_record.support_text: Tacrine treatment in an eight week crossover trial for Alzheimer's disease was associated with raised liver enzyme activities: six patients dropped out because of high liver enzyme activities and two others had raised activities at the end of the study. The patient with the highest liver enzyme activities (a 76 year old woman) was admitted to an intensive care unit; liver biopsy showed extensive centrilobular necrosis without steatosis, consistent with acute cytolytic hepatitis. In all patients with hepatitis, liver enzyme values returned to normal three to four weeks after withdrawal of tacrine and remained normal six to 12 months later.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Alzheimer's disease patients; all patients also received oral lecithin during the trial (combined tacrine and lecithin treatment).
raw_record.extra_details: Crossover study of tacrine (maximum 125 mg daily) in 60 Alzheimer's disease patients; 8 of 60 had raised liver enzyme activities (tolerance section). One 76-year-old woman with highest liver enzyme activities required ICU admission; biopsy showed extensive centrilobular necrosis without steatosis. Dechallenge: liver enzyme values returned to normal 3-4 weeks after tacrine withdrawal and remained normal 6-12 months later. In the follow-up study, additional patients were withdrawn from tacrine treatment because of hepatitis. No steatosis on biopsy; plasma tacrine concentrations ranged 49-1140 mmol/l.

raw_record.support_text: In the 'Hepatotoxicity' analysis of this long-term tacrine treatment study, six patients stopped their treatment within the first 6 months due to marked elevation of liver enzymes; after a short break (<30 days) treatment was resumed without complications in 2 patients, while the other 4 dropped out. Five patients had minor increases in liver enzymes without discontinuation. One patient with moderately elevated liver enzymes at 16 months was investigated with ultrasonic X-ray and diagnosed with liver cirrhosis, was excluded, and switched to donepezil. Elevated liver enzyme levels were detected in 24% (n=12) of patients, but only 10% (n=5) had to terminate treatment because of hepatic side effects. Paragraph 68 notes the second most common cause of first-year dropout was liver side effects.

Elevated liver enzymes in 24% (n=12), treatment terminated due to hepatic side effects in 10% (n=5). Liver side effects were the second most common cause of first-year dropout. No significant correlation found between tacrine dose and outcome groups (RE vs UC) or 'time until NHP'.

raw_record.support_text: The most important factor limiting the tolerated dose of tacrine was liver toxicity. Raised liver enzyme concentrations have often been reported, with reported incidences ranging from 13% to 42%; in this trial 14 of 53 patients (26%) given tacrine during the dose-finding phase had liver enzyme concentrations three times the upper limit of normal. Although no permanent damage was reported and all subjects had normal concentrations within a month of withdrawing the drug, biopsies from patients with raised liver function test results showed damage ranging from focal inflammatory infiltration to extensive hepatocellular necrosis, and the authors consequently restricted doses to 100 mg daily.

raw_record.extra_details: Tacrine is a cholinesterase inhibitor used in the Alzheimer's disease trial. Raised liver enzyme concentration incidences of 13% to 42% have been reported in previous trials; 14/53 (26%) treated patients in the dose-finding phase had liver enzymes three times the upper limit of normal. Biopsies showed damage ranging from focal inflammatory infiltration to extensive hepatocellular necrosis. Doses were restricted to 100 mg daily because of this liver toxicity; mean best dose was 72.6 (SD 28.94) mg daily.
