raw_record.support_text: The hepatotoxic effects of tacrine occur in nearly half the patients treated with it. Although some patients have had increases in serum ALT as high as 20 times the upper limit of normal, no deaths have been associated with tacrine hepatotoxicity. Tacrine is described as a relatively pure hepatocellular toxin, with ALT increases usually without concomitant increases in alkaline phosphatase or bilirubin, and hepatotoxicity does not seem to be dose related.

Patients should be withdrawn at an ALT above 3x ULN and monitored for at least 18 weeks after initiating therapy and 6 weeks after dose increase.
raw_record.extra_details: 47% of permanently withdrawn patients were withdrawn due to pronounced ALT increases; 49% of controlled-trial patients had at least one increased ALT, 25% had ALT >3x ULN, and 2% had ALT >20x ULN; no deaths from tacrine hepatotoxicity; raised ALT was delayed with peak incidence at 6-8 weeks of exposure and 90% of increases by week 12; not dose related; age, weight, and concomitant drug/alcohol/nicotine use did not predict risk; ALT increases usually without alkaline phosphatase or bilirubin rises; jaundice indicates severe liver injury and mandates drug withdrawal and supportive therapy; some patients have malaise or nausea/vomiting, many are symptom-free; data from controlled clinical trials (n=634 tacrine, n=342 placebo) and Cognex package insert.

raw_record.support_text: The reported case had an R factor of 12, a hepatocellular pattern of liver injury, and a RUCAM score of 8, indicating a 'probable' association of the DILI with fosfomycin. A rechallenge was not performed for ethical reasons.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented case: acute liver injury with aminotransferases >1000 IU/L, R factor 12, RUCAM score 8 ('probable'). Fosfomycin is described as a rare cause of liver injury, presenting with mild aminotransferase elevations in 1%-2% of patients. Literature: Matsumori et al. reported a 30-year-old male with mixed-pattern injury three days after oral fosfomycin who developed features of liver failure (encephalopathy and coagulopathy) without need for liver transplantation, enzyme normalization four months after onset; Durupt et al. reported a 30-year-old female with cystic fibrosis who developed liver injury four days after parenteral fosfomycin with resolution one month after discontinuation and positive rechallenge twice (enzymes increased three days after administration, normalized within a week); Wang et al. reported a 50-year-old male with mixed liver injury three days after fosfomycin exposure resolving within a week; Ferreira et al. reported a 24-year-old female with hepatocellular injury one week after a single 3 g oral dose resolving three months after exposure. First-line management was discontinuation of the agent.

raw_record.support_text: In a French study in the Nièvre (1997-2000, population ~81,000 persons) reporting 34 well-characterized drug-induced hepatitis cases, 5 cases (15%) were related to lipid-lowering drugs, 2 of them with fenofibrate (and 3 with atorvastatin). The paper notes that serious clinical hepatic accidents occur much less frequently with statins (about 0.2/100,000 treated) than with fibrates (about 1/10,000).
raw_record.extra_details: Fenofibrate is cited as a fibrate for which the frequency of serious clinical hepatic accidents is estimated at 1/10,000, higher than for statins.

raw_record.support_text: Among 1229 patients with confirmed DILI, 7 cases (0.6%) were attributed to fenofibrate. Laboratory results at presentation showed hepatocellular, mixed and cholestatic injury, 6 cases presented with jaundice, and causality scores were highly likely in 5 and probable in 2. Outcomes included hospitalization in 4 patients, liver transplantation in 1, and chronic injury and death in another.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases were definite, very likely and probable DILI attributed to fenofibrate enrolled in the DILI Network study 2004-15; 7/1229 (0.6%) confirmed DILI cases. Median age 43 years (range 37-61). Latency 5-8 weeks in 4 patients and 18-56 weeks in the rest. No patient had routine monitoring. 6 presented with jaundice. 4 required hospitalization. 2 with delayed drug discontinuation had severe outcome: 1 liver transplantation, 1 chronic injury and death. Liver biopsy in 4 patients showed diverse injury patterns. HLA-A*33:01 present in 3 patients (43% vs 1% in control populations). Causality highly likely in 5 and probable in 2. Fenofibrate is a hypolipidemic with rare instances of hepatotoxicity and routine liver biochemistry monitoring recommended.

raw_record.support_text: The report presents a case of fenofibrate-induced severe jaundice in a 65-year-old Korean male with no prior history of liver disease, attributing the drug-induced liver injury to fenofibrate use for hyperlipidemia.
raw_record.extra_details: 65-year-old Korean male with hyperlipidemia and no prior liver disease; liver biopsy confirmed acute cholestatic hepatitis; liver enzymes and total bilirubin were elevated, detected incidentally on preoperative screening; abdominal ultrasound and CT showed no biliary obstruction; after steroid therapy for 3 wk the total bilirubin fell to 7.22 mg/dL.

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes a special case of acute severe hepatocellular injury 'highly likely induced by fenofibrate' after a short period of therapy in a patient without primary or secondary liver disease. Fenofibrate, a fibric acid derivative used to treat hypertriglyceridemia and dyslipidemia, is noted to cause DILI very rarely (only 0.6% of patients).
raw_record.extra_details: Acute severe DILI developed within only 4 days after initial fenofibrate treatment for hypertriglyceridemia; liver enzyme levels declined to normal within two weeks after discontinuation of fenofibrate. The rapidly-recovering sudden-onset presentation is described as different from those in the LiverTox database. Fenofibrate is a fibric acid derivative widely used for hypertriglyceridemia and dyslipidemia; DILI associated with fenofibrate occurs very rarely (0.6% of patients).

raw_record.support_text: In a 61-year-old man with no prior history, taking fenofibrate 160 mg per day led at day 15 to an acute hepatitis with cholestatic features; laboratory values returned to normal within 18 months. The paper concludes the causality is 'très vraisemblable' (very probable) based on suggestive chronological and semiological criteria with other etiologies reasonably excluded, and cites previous reports of fenofibrate hepatotoxicity including a similar published case of acute cholestatic hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: fenofibrate 160 mg/day; onset at day 15 of treatment; very high GGT contrasting with subnormal transaminases; initial generalized pruritus, dark urine, and unusual asthenia; no initial alkaline phosphatase (PA) dosage so a strictly cholestatic form could not be confirmed, but a cholestatic pattern was very suggestive; rapid biochemical recovery to normal within 18 months; benign clinical and biological course possibly aided by immediate drug discontinuation; no notable steatosis and non-evocative metabolic syndrome (deemed an improbable cause) since metabolic syndrome is the usual current indication for fenofibrate; extrinsic causality supported by known other forms of fenofibrate hepatotoxicity and one previously published similar case of acute cholestatic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Fenofibrate is listed among the causal DILI drugs known to have HLA alleles as the main genetic risk association, and the paper found enrichment of rs2476601 among European DILI cases due to such drugs. raw_record.extra_details: Known to have HLA alleles as main genetic risk association for DILI; 10 cases in rs2476601 analysis, OR 2.93 (95% CI 0.97–8.87), P = .06.

raw_record.support_text: A 74-year-old woman presented with jaundice and fatigue and was initially diagnosed as definite autoimmune hepatitis (AIH). After improving on budesonide, her ALT rose again to 421 IU/L and she was found to have been rechallenged with irbesartan, which had been discontinued before admission. A diagnosis of irbesartan-induced hepatitis was made; irbesartan was withdrawn and liver tests normalized within 6 weeks. The updated RUCAM causality score for irbesartan was 11, classified as highly probable. The case is framed as DILI with autoimmune features.
raw_record.extra_details: 74-year-old Caucasian woman with hypertension; presented with 2-week jaundice and fatigue; admission ALT 1011 U/L, bilirubin 3.6 mg/dL, IgG 31.1 g/L, ANA 1:5120; liver biopsy day 6 showed severe interface hepatitis consistent with severe AIH; simplified AIH score 7 (definite); irbesartan started 3 months earlier, discontinued 3 days before admission; after AIH diagnosis and initial budesonide response, irbesartan was recommenced and ALT rose to 421 IU/L within 2 weeks; drug withdrawn and liver tests normalized within 6 weeks; reported as DILI-AI (DILI with features of autoimmunity); rechallenge-associated relapse; RUCAM score 11 (highly probable); patient well with normal liver tests 3 years after presentation.

raw_record.extra_details: Biliary dilation from ketamine abuse first reported in 2007; a case of ketamine-induced cholangiopathy was reported in 2011. First case required ICU admission and a 10F plastic biliary stent, with 4 additional admissions on continued abuse; second case developed colicky epigastric pain 4-5 hours postingestion and was lost to follow-up; third case had gallbladder dyskinesia and coexisting bladder problems. Abnormal liver function tests were found in all 3 cases. Potential mechanism proposed as NMDA-receptor blockade in smooth muscle or through the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus.

raw_record.support_text: A 54-year-old ICU patient on prolonged ketamine infusions developed a persistent rise in alkaline phosphatase and GGT with normal bilirubin; MR cholangiopancreatography showed intrahepatic dilatation with a beaded appearance and a dilated common bile duct with distal narrowing, and liver biopsy showed biliary ductular reaction with lobular inflammation. The authors concluded the imaging and pathologic findings are consistent with a unique form of DILI: ketamine-induced sclerosing cholangitis (KISC).

raw_record.extra_details: Prolonged/repeated ketamine exposure: 15 days of IV ketamine infusions, then 5 days oral ketamine, and a later IV ketamine bolus upon re-intubation. Cholestatic-biased laboratory findings: Alk P peaked at 2,239 U/L with GGT 773 U/L (AST 1260, ALT 1729 U/L, bilirubin normal 0.4 mg/dL); after recovery, re-administration of IV ketamine produced an abrupt repeat rise (Alk P 1,720, GGT 538, AST 266, ALT 407 U/L) with normal bilirubin and normal INR, consistent with a dechallenge/rechallenge response. Serologic workup (ANA, AMA, ASMA, ANCA) unrevealing; HAV/HBV/HCV/HIV/EBV/HSV ruled out. MRCP showed intrahepatic beaded dilatation and dilated common bile duct with distal narrowing; biopsy showed biliary ductular reaction, lobular inflammation, and a small non-necrotizing lobular granuloma.

raw_record.support_text: Spisulosine (compound 21, ES-285), a deoxysphingosine-based marine mollusk natural product isolated from Spisula polynyma, was evaluated in Phase I clinical trials in patients with established solid tumors using various regimens (24 h IV infusion every three weeks, or 3 h IV infusion for five consecutive days every three weeks). Despite infrequent drug-induced grade 3 or 4 adverse effects and an encouraging pharmacokinetic profile, spisulosine's potential as an anticancer agent was impeded by dose-dependent hepatic and neurotoxicity, and further development was therefore terminated; the human trials were discontinued due to poor clinical outcomes, with the death of one patient attributed to drug-related central neurotoxicity rather than to the liver.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Phase I clinical trial dosing in patients with established solid tumors; development was terminated for poor outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: Also known as ES-285 and spisulosine 21. Dose-dependent hepatic toxicity was reported. Dose-limiting/grade 3-4 drug-induced adverse effects were infrequent. Regimens included 24 h intravenous infusion every 3 weeks and 3 h intravenous infusion for 5 consecutive days every 3 weeks. The single reported patient death was due to drug-related central neurotoxicity, not hepatic injury. In vitro data (not human DILI) showed anti-proliferative/cytotoxic activity against prostate (PC-3, LNCaP), breast, colon, HeLa, and other tumor cell lines.

raw_record.support_text: In this phase 1 trial of the investigational agent REM127 in patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease, adverse events in the hepatobiliary dysfunction system organ class were observed only in participants on active REM127 treatment and not in placebo recipients. One serious adverse event in the 350 mg dose group was considered related to study treatment and reported as toxic hepatitis. Drug-induced liver injury was reported in six participants leading to study discontinuation, and one case fulfilled Hy's Law criteria, led to hospitalization, and was reported as a suspected unexpected serious adverse reaction (SUSAR), prompting termination of the trial. Increased serum transaminases occurred in all 1400 mg (2/2) and 350 mg (2/2) participants and 1/5 in the 88 mg group versus none in placebo; increases typically started around the fourth week, peaked days to weeks after study discontinuation, and returned to normal in all participants over several weeks to months.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Investgational agent evaluated in a phase 1 clinical trial in patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease at daily oral doses of 88, 350, and 1400 mg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: AE terms reported included drug-induced liver injury, toxic hepatitis, hepatitis toxic, hepatic enzyme increased, alanine aminotransferase increased, blood lactate dehydrogenase increased, and transaminases increased. Six participants had hepatobiliary dysfunction leading to study discontinuation; trial was terminated early for safety. One case fulfilled Hy's Law, required hospitalization, and was reported as SUSAR. Transaminase elevations typically began around the fourth week (at last study-drug day or follow-up), peaked days to weeks after discontinuation, and resolved over several weeks to months; an associated decrease in total cholesterol was noted. No deaths or liver transplantations occurred. REM127 is a septin 6 (SEPT6) modulator; one participant received the co-medication quetiapine from Day 21 to Day 23.

raw_record.support_text: A 63-year-old woman died from acute liver failure while being treated with beclobrate, 100 mg/d, after 4 months of treatment she developed vomiting and jaundice. The drug was withdrawn, jaundice progressed, and she was hospitalized with acute liver failure. Her only medication during that time was beclobrate. She developed fulminant liver failure with irreversible hepatorenal syndrome and died 7 days later, 3 weeks after symptom onset. Autopsy showed acute liver dystrophy with extensive necrosis (liver weight 600 g).
raw_record.extra_details: 63-year-old woman with moderate hyperlipidemia previously treated with bezafibrate for 8 years, replaced by beclobrate 100 mg/d for persistently high cholesterol. Onset of vomiting and jaundice after 4 months; drug withdrawn. Fulminant liver failure with irreversible hepatorenal syndrome; died 7 days after hospitalization, 3 weeks after symptom onset. Autopsy: acute liver dystrophy with extensive necrosis, liver weight 600 g. Excluded causes: hepatitis A/B/C, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, rubeola, toxoplasmosis, antinuclear antibodies, leptospirosis, no infections, surgery, blood products, drug/alcohol abuse, or travel. Authors conclude beclobrate, the only drug administered in the months before acute liver failure, is implicated; note fibrate-type hypolipidemics occasionally raise liver enzymes and one hepatitis case with two fibrates has been reported, but acute liver failure had not been observed before.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the death of a 64-year-old man from acute hepatic failure attributable to beclobrate, a lipid-lowering agent. He had hypercholesterolaemia and also received chondroitin sulphate 500 mg thrice daily, with no history of self-medication or alcohol abuse. Six and a half months after starting beclobrate 100 mg daily he became anorexic and jaundiced; total bilirubin was 304 µmol/l (normal <17) with greatly raised transaminases. He was admitted 3 weeks later with a diagnosis of acute hepatitis and died 7 days later. Investigations showed no infectious (viral or toxoplasmosis) or obstructive cause.
raw_record.extra_details: Beclobrate is a lipid-lowering agent used at 100 mg daily for hypercholesterolaemia. Latency to jaundice/anorexia was 6.5 months after treatment start. Total bilirubin was 304 µmol/l (normal <17) with markedly raised transaminases; diagnosis of acute hepatitis at admission and death from acute hepatic failure 7 days after admission. Concomitant medication was chondroitin sulphate 500 mg thrice daily for osteoarthrosis of the hip; no self-medication or alcohol abuse; infectious (viral or toxoplasmosis) and obstructive causes excluded.

He had taken beclobrate 100 mg daily for 6½ months before becoming anorexic and jaundiced, with total bilirubin 304 µmol/l (normal <17) and very much raised transaminases; acute hepatitis was diagnosed and he died 7 days after admission. No infectious (viral or toxoplasmosis) or obstructive cause was found, and there was no history of self-medication or alcohol abuse; he also received chondroitin sulphate 500 mg thrice daily for osteoarthrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Concurrent treatment with chondroitin sulphate 500 mg thrice daily for osteoarthrosis of the hip; single case in a 64-year-old man.
raw_record.extra_details: Lipid-lowering agent (fibrate) for hypercholesterolaemia first diagnosed at age 56; onset of anorexia and jaundice 6½ months after starting beclobrate 100 mg daily; total bilirubin 304 µmol/l (normal <17) with markedly raised transaminases; admitted to hospital 3 weeks later with a diagnosis of acute hepatitis and died 7 days later; investigations excluded infectious (viral or toxoplasmosis) and obstructive causes; no history of self-medication or alcohol abuse.

This constitutes an explicit agent-specific negative conclusion about human DILI for indoximod.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase I dose-escalation study (N=48) of single-agent indoximod, an IDO pathway inhibitor. No MTD identified up to 2000 mg twice daily; recommended phase II dose 1200 mg twice daily. The authors explicitly note the absence of a significant hepatotoxicity signal when escalated to higher doses, in contrast to other IDO inhibitors; 3 cases of hypophysitis were the only drug-attributed DLT-related SAE.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a causal association between zolpidem treatment and liver damage in a single patient, supported by the time of onset of the reaction, a clinically significant decrease in serum alanine aminotransferase activity on dechallenge, exclusion of other causes of hepatitis, a normal biliary tract on ultrasound and radiological examination, and recurrence of the reaction with zolpidem readministration (rechallenge). The paper additionally notes that their pharmacovigilance service had not been informed of any other cases of hepatotoxicity associated with zolpidem given alone at a therapeutic dose.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report; causality suggested by temporal onset, clinically significant fall in serum alanine aminotransferase activity on discontinuation, exclusion of other hepatitis causes, normal biliary tract on ultrasound/radiological exam, and recurrence on zolpidem readministration (positive rechallenge). Pharmacovigilance service reported no other cases of hepatotoxicity with zolpidem alone at a therapeutic dose.

raw_record.support_text: A 51-year-old white man presented with jaundice, pruritus, fatigue, and anorexia of 2 weeks duration after completing a 10-day course of cephalexin (500 mg orally 3 times daily) started for a postoperative wound infection. Approximately 3 days after starting cephalexin he noted dark urine and pale stool, and within 24 hours of completing therapy developed fever, hives, pruritus, and jaundice. The report is framed as cephalexin-induced cholestatic hepatitis, documenting the temporal, clinical and biochemical course.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis with a mild panacinar hepatitis and eosinophils plus extensive cholestasis with canalicular bile plugs on liver biopsy. Laboratory values: total bilirubin 17.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 12.2 mg/dL, AST 40 U/L, ALT 87 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 272 U/L. No increased hepatic iron. Prior exposure included cefazolin 1 g preoperatively, single doses of meperidine and morphine, a wound bupivacaine pump, and a short course of hydrocodone/acetaminophen for postoperative pain, but the patient took no other medications at the start of cephalexin and had previously tolerated penicillin. Infectious hepatitis A, B, C serologies and autoimmune/antimitochondrial antibodies were negative; imaging (ultrasound, CT, ERCP) unremarkable. Onset of symptoms about 3 days into cephalexin with progression after completion.

raw_record.support_text: A 51-year-old white man developed jaundice, pruritus, fatigue, and anorexia after starting a 10-day course of cephalexin (500 mg orally 3 times daily) for a postoperative wound infection, about 3 days after starting therapy with dark urine and pale stool, followed within 24 hours of completing therapy by fever, hives, pruritus, and jaundice. Liver biopsy showed mild panacinar hepatitis with eosinophils and extensive cholestasis with canalicular bile plugs. A diagnosis of cephalosporin-induced cholestatic hepatitis was made; pruritus responded to ursodeoxycholic acid and symptoms resolved by 7 weeks postexposure, with biochemical abnormalities resolving 5 weeks later.

Within 24 hours of completing cephalexin he developed fever, hives, pruritus, and jaundice; the case is presented as cephalexin-induced cholestatic hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: First-generation oral cephalosporin; dose 500 mg orally 3 times daily for 10 days for a wound infection; onset ~3 days after starting. raw_record.support_text: A 61-year-old woman with breast cancer took cephalexin 500 mg twice daily orally for 10 days after tumor resection and a repeat course at the same dose for cellulitis. About one month later she developed fatigue and syncope, with a cholestatic pattern of liver enzyme elevation (total bilirubin 10.4 mg/dL, ALT 129 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 587 U/L, R-factor 0.7). After excluding viral and autoimmune etiologies and biliary obstruction, a biopsy showed cholestatic hepatitis with mild portal lymphocytic/eosinophilic infiltrate and marked bile-duct damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Cephalexin 500 mg twice daily orally for 10 days, repeated for cellulitis two weeks later; cholestatic pattern with R-factor 0.7, total bilirubin 10.4 mg/dL, ALT 129 U/L, ALP 587 U/L; cholestatic hepatitis on biopsy with marked bile duct damage and bile plugs in canaliculi; follow-up biopsy showed minimal ductular proliferation and resolution of bile duct damage/inflammation. Liver enzymes remained elevated, prompting budesonide initiation 142 days after onset.

The patient recovered after a successful liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: A 43-year-old female with no prior history of liver disease was transferred to the hepatology service with acute liver failure secondary to the use of Duract (bromfenac) taken for arthritis/club foot over approximately 5–6 months. After treatment with rFVIIa and laparoscopic liver biopsy, the biopsy revealed 60–80% necrosis, and the patient was referred for and successfully underwent liver transplantation.

Post-biopsy haematocrit fell from 34.3 to 28.5 and platelets from 129,000 to 119,000 with no identified bleeding source; no fibrinogen or PT values available. Liver biopsy showed 60–80% necrosis; patient successfully underwent liver transplantation.

A total of four patients receiving daily therapeutic doses of bromfenac developed acute liver failure leading to liver transplantation or death, and fatal fulminant hepatitis was considered associated with bromfenac use.

raw_record.support_text: In clinical use, bromfenac at recommended therapeutic doses of 25–100 mg/d for at least 90 days (labeled recommended duration >10 days) was associated with severe symptomatic hepatocellular disease with associated hypoprothrombinemia. There was no evidence of a hypersensitivity reaction. Extensive confluent parenchymal necrosis originating in central zones was associated with lymphocytic infiltrate with nodular regeneration in 2 subjects with more prolonged disease prior to transplantation. Histologic lesions included acute lobular hepatitis with bridging necrosis and fibrous expansion of portal tracts, and fulminant liver failure requiring liver transplant has been recorded after inadvertent rechallenge.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Therapeutic doses of 25–100 mg/d for at least 90 days, exceeding the labeled recommended duration of >10 days; delayed idiosyncratic onset.
raw_record.extra_details: During clinical trials bromfenac caused only reversible minor AST elevations. In clinical use it produced severe symptomatic hepatocellular disease with hypoprothrombinemia and no hypersensitivity reaction; extensive confluent parenchymal necrosis originating in central zones with lymphocytic infiltrate and nodular regeneration in 2 subjects with prolonged disease prior to transplant. Histology showed acute lobular hepatitis with bridging necrosis and fibrous expansion of portal tracts. Prognosis is usually good with resolution, but fulminant liver failure requiring liver transplant occurred after inadvertent rechallenge. Risk-benefit: continued use was not justified once delayed idiosyncratic severe hepatotoxicity was identified given the availability of alternatives.

raw_record.support_text: Bromfenac, a phenylacetic acid derivative introduced in the United States in 1997, was withdrawn from further clinical use in 1998 after reports of several cases of acute liver failure causing death or necessitating liver transplantation. Histology showed extensive, confluent parenchymal necrosis beginning in zone 3 (perivenular) with predominantly lymphocytic infiltration.

raw_record.support_text: Laboratory studies in the reported patient revealed obstructive jaundice with elevation of direct bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and cholesterol, and the liver biopsy findings were consistent with intrahepatic cholestasis. Jaundice confirmed liver disease and led to discontinuation of norethandrolone; a challenge dose was considered but not given because of the severity of the jaundice and its near-fatal outcome. An intradermal skin test of 2.5 mg norethandrolone in sesame oil produced no local reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of cholestatic jaundice during norethandrolone therapy. Initial symptom was generalized pruritus (attributed at the time to azotemia). Obstructive jaundice with elevated direct bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and cholesterol; liver biopsy showed intrahepatic cholestasis with bile stasis and minimal inflammation. Jaundice was severe and near-fatal; recovery followed drug discontinuation; rechallenge was not attempted. Norethandrolone is described as chemically closely related to methyltestosterone (absence of a 19-methyl group and an ethyl group on the 17 carbon).

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that Norethandrolone (17α-Äthyl-17-hydroxy-norandrostenon, brand 'Nilevar' Searle), a steroid with strong anabolic action, has a mild hepatotoxic effect that appears completely reversible. Nearly all treated subjects showed pathological retention in the Bromsulfalein (BSP) test, and a rise in glutamate-oxalate transaminase indicated cell lesion. At high dosage, cholestatic jaundice was not rare, and liver biopsies showed cholestasis and occasionally mild necrosis. These liver-function disturbances were reversible, but caution in therapeutic use was advised.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic jaundice (icterus) occurs not rarely at high dosage; histology showed cholestasis and occasional mild necrosis in liver biopsies. In a series of 54 severely underweight patients treated with 25 mg norethandrolone orally daily, all but 8 gained weight (average 6 kg in 24 weeks). Nearly all treated subjects showed pathological Bromsulfalein (BSP) retention, and glutamate-oxalate transaminase (GOT) rose. Liver function disturbances were described as reversible. Brand name 'Nilevar' (Searle); molecule is 17α-ethyl-17-hydroxy-norandrostenone (17α-Äthyl-17-hydroxy-norandrostenon) with androgen activity about 1/16 of testosterone.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that retention of bromsulphthalein and elevation of serum glutamic oxalacetic transaminase are the first signs of hepatic dysfunction in patients being treated with Norethandrolone, occurring in approximately 75% of patients within 2 to 3 weeks when the dose exceeds 25 mg daily. A smaller number progress to retention of bile with elevated serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase, with a histologic picture of cholestasis (bile pigment in hepatic and Kupffer cells, little or no inflammatory reaction), and these abnormalities were irreversible in the authors' cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose-related and largely predictable: BSP retention and SGOT elevation in approximately 75% of patients within 2-3 weeks when the dose exceeds 25 mg daily; a smaller proportion develop overt bile retention with elevated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase. Histology showed cholestasis with bile pigment in hepatic and Kupffer cells and little or no inflammatory reaction. Case 1 was treated with 30 mg Norethandrolone for 6 months, the drug being continued while the patient was jaundiced; the biochemical and histologic abnormalities were severe and, contrary to prior reports, irreversible. Neither the concurrent pemphigus nor Prednisolone was reported to cause this cholestatic picture, and no other drugs were taken.

raw_record.support_text: Among 647 metastatic breast cancer patients receiving docetaxel chemotherapy, 329 had abnormal liver function tests, of whom 67 were diagnosed with docetaxel-DILI (41 hepatocellular, 16 cholestatic, 10 mixed type), giving an overall docetaxel-DILI incidence of 10.35%.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Cohort restricted to metastatic breast cancer patients receiving docetaxel chemotherapy; patients with active HBV infection were excluded and chemotherapy was postponed until liver function normalized; all patients received prophylactic liver protectants.
raw_record.extra_details: Docetaxel-DILI was diagnosed by three independent experts using DILIN criteria; eligibility required ALT/AST >5x ULN, ALP >2x ULN, or ALT/AST 5x baseline or ALP 2x baseline on two consecutive draws, or bilirubin >2.5 mg/dL with any transaminase/ALP elevation. Overall incidence 10.35% (67/647); median time from initial exposure to DILI occurrence 14.01 days; most frequent clinical presentations were fever, jaundice, pruritus, and right upper abdominal pain, with jaundice and liver region pain more common in cholestatic type.

raw_record.support_text: In this study of 647 metastatic breast cancer patients, 67 of 647 (10.36%) were confirmed to have docetaxel-DILI. Patients receiving docetaxel plus vinorelbine and/or docetaxel plus capecitabine/gemcitabine combination chemotherapy were at increased risk of docetaxel-DILI, with a docetaxel-based combination regimen containing capecitabine/gemcitabine and/or vinorelbine showing a 2.66-fold increased risk. Multivariate logistic regression identified premenopausal status, past HBV infection, liver metastasis, and docetaxel combination as significant contributors to the occurrence of docetaxel-DILI.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Metastatic breast cancer patients under chemotherapy; occurrence increased with premenopausal status, past HBV infection, liver metastasis, and docetaxel-based combination chemotherapy (with capecitabine/gemcitabine and/or vinorelbine).
raw_record.extra_details: 67 of 647 patients (10.36%) confirmed to have docetaxel-DILI; incidence higher than early reported docetaxel-DILI rates. Combination regimen containing capecitabine/gemcitabine and/or vinorelbine gave 2.66-fold increased risk. Time to onset ranged 6.19-17.85 days. Cases classified as hepatocellular (n=41), cholestatic (n=16), and mixed (n=10) patterns; hepatocellular type had highest ALT/AST, cholestatic group highest bilirubin and ALP; jaundice and liver region pain most common in cholestatic group. Fever present in 31.34% of cases. Patients with more than three of the four risk factors had 36.61-fold (95% CI 10.18-131.62) increased risk; combined-risk AUC 0.7536. All patients received liver protectants concurrently.

Forty of these patients developed drug-induced liver injury (DILI) and were enrolled as cases, while 89 sex-, age-, and drug-matched patients without hepatotoxicity served as controls.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with metastatic breast cancer receiving docetaxel-based chemotherapy; case-control design restricted to this indication.
raw_record.extra_details: Of 129 docetaxel-treated metastatic breast cancer patients, 40 met DILI Network-based criteria and were compared with 89 matched controls without hepatotoxicity. DILI criteria included ALT/AST >5x ULN, ALP >2x ULN, or any enzyme elevation with total bilirubin >2.5 mg/dl, plus a causality assessment score >5 (categorized as probable or highly probable DILI). The study's main purpose was to assess IL10 and TNF single-nucleotide polymorphisms as susceptibility markers.

raw_record.support_text: Between 1/06 and 9/09, 6 of the 7 cases of DILI attributed to duloxetine in the DILIN Prospective Study were assessed as definite or very likely. Median patient age was 49 years, 6 (86%) were women, median latency from drug initiation to DILI onset was 50 days, 6 patients developed jaundice, and the median peak ALT in the 5 patients with acute hepatocellular injury was 1633 IU/L. Ascites developed in 1 patient and acute renal dysfunction in 2 others. All patients recovered without liver transplantation even though 3 had pre-existing chronic liver disease, and liver histology in 4 cases demonstrated varying patterns of liver injury.

Median latency to DILI onset was 50 days; 6 patients developed jaundice; median peak ALT in the 5 acute hepatocellular injury patients was 1633 IU/L; ascites in 1 patient and acute renal dysfunction in 2 patients (29%). All patients recovered without liver transplantation. Liver histology in 4 cases showed varying patterns of liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports the first case of hepatitis attributable to trifluoperazine, a recently introduced phenothiazine derivative. In a patient receiving the drug, clinical, laboratory, and biopsy findings of cholestatic hepatitis developed, identical to that seen with other phenothiazine compounds. The case details (48-year-old man, 1 mg twice daily) describe light stools, dark urine, right-upper-quadrant discomfort, and icterus.
raw_record.extra_details: Trifluoperazine given as Stelazine (Smith Kline and French Laboratories), 1 mg twice daily for 3 weeks before admission; cholestatic hepatitis with icterus, light stools, dark urine, and dull aching right-upper-quadrant pain. Reported as the first published case of hepatitis attributable to this drug; injury identical to that seen with other phenothiazine compounds. No prior medications had been taken for 9 months (competing causes excluded).

raw_record.support_text: This case report attributes the initial hepatic injury to trifluperazine use. On the Naranjo ADR probability scale the likelihood of an ADR due to trifluperazine in this case was probable (score 6), based on elevation of liver enzymes after initiation of trifluoperazine, deterioration of liver function under continued treatment, and a considerable decrease in enzymes after stopping the drug. Other causes of cholestatic jaundice were ruled out, and the authors recognized trifluperazine as a cause; they note only a few cases of cholestatic jaundice induced by trifluperazine have been reported since its introduction in 1958.
raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo ADR probability scale score 6 (probable). Liver enzymes rose after therapy initiation, deteriorated on continued treatment, and decreased substantially after drug discontinuation (dechallenge). Other causes of cholestatic jaundice ruled out. A prior 1968 case (Margulies et al.) reported jaundice in a 26-year-old woman with psychosis after 15 days of trifluoperazine. The drug has been marketed since 1958 with only a few reported DILI cases; small numbers of spontaneous reports are not necessarily a reliable risk indicator.

raw_record.support_text: Panadiplon, an experimental non-benzodiazepine anxiolytic, produced evidence of hepatic toxicity in phase I clinical trial volunteers, which was not predicted by rat, dog or monkey preclinical studies. Subsequent studies showed that a carboxylic acid metabolite of panadiplon caused redistribution of cellular coenzyme A stores and inhibition of β-oxidation, rendering hepatocytes sensitive to secondary stress (e.g., hypoxia), which subsequently produced apoptosis and hepatocellular necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Healthy volunteer subjects in a Phase I clinical trial of an investigational anxiolytic.
raw_record.extra_details: A carboxylic acid metabolite of panadiplon caused redistribution of cellular coenzyme A stores and inhibition of β-oxidation, rendering hepatocytes sensitive to secondary stress (e.g., hypoxia), producing apoptosis and hepatocellular necrosis. Hepatic toxicity was not predicted by rat, dog, or monkey preclinical studies. In vitro, co-treatment with pyruvate reduced the level of LDH leakage caused by panadiplon under hypoxic conditions (Bacon et al. 1996). This ximelagatran-related review is anchored to prior mechanistic data on panadiplon.

raw_record.support_text: A 32-year-old male with no prior hepatobiliary disease, taking 10 mg/day cetirizine for allergic rhinitis for 4 months, presented with asthenia, jaundice, pruritus, and hepatomegaly. Work-up showed elevated total bilirubin (28.7 mg/dl), GGT (12 U/l), and alkaline phosphatase (304 U/l) with normal transaminases; negative viral, autoimmune and metabolic serologies; and a liver biopsy demonstrating hepatocellular and canalicular cholestasis in zone 3 with scarce inflammation and no ductular damage. The authors considered cetirizine the probable cause of the cholestasis and suspended the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe intrahepatic cholestasis associated with cetirizine. Dose 10 mg/day for 4 months before admission; liver biopsy showed hepatocellular-canalicular cholestasis in zone 3 with scarce inflammation and no ductular damage. Bilirubin peaked at 38.7 mg/dl 15 days after discontinuation; treated with ursodeoxycholic acid 1200 mg/day with progressive improvement and normalization of bilirubin within 3 months. Symptoms comprised asthenia, jaundice, pruritus, and hepatomegaly.

raw_record.support_text: Cetirizine, a selective H1 receptor antagonist, was reported to cause true cholestasis in a 28-year-old man who had taken the drug for 2 years and developed progressive jaundice, anorexia, weight loss, acholic stools, and pruritus, with bilirubin up to 22.5 mg/dL. Liver biopsy showed prominent hepatocanalicular zone 3 cholestasis and mild hepatocellular damage. The mechanism is unclear but appears to involve an idiosyncratic reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: 28-year-old man, 2 years of cetirizine therapy; progressive jaundice, anorexia, weight loss, acholic stools, pruritus; bilirubin up to 22.5 mg/dL; biopsy showed hepatocanalicular zone 3 cholestasis with mild hepatocellular damage; symptoms improved over 8-10 weeks with slow resolution of laboratory abnormalities; true cholestasis not described before this report. Mild transient transaminase elevation occurs in <2% of patients.

raw_record.support_text: A 32-year-old man with no prior hepatobiliary disease presented with asthenia, icterus, pruritus and hepatomegaly after taking 10 mg/day of cetirizine for allergic rhinitis for 4 months. Laboratory tests showed total bilirubin 28.7 mg/dl and alkaline phosphatase 304 U/l with normal transaminases; a percutaneous liver biopsy demonstrated hepatocellular and canalicular cholestasis in zone 3 with scant inflammation and no ductular damage. The authors considered cetirizine the probable cause of the cholestasis and discontinued it.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of severe intrahepatic cholestasis (title). Dose 10 mg/day for 4 months for allergic rhinitis. Total bilirubin 28.7 mg/dl (direct 21 mg/dl), GGT 12 U/l, ALP 304 U/l, normal AST/ALT. Biopsy: hepatocellular and canalicular cholestasis in zone 3, scant inflammation, no ductular damage. Negative viral serologies (A, B, C, CMV, EBV) and negative autoantibodies (ANA, AMA, SMA, LKM); normal iron, ferritin, transferrin, copper, alpha-1-antitrypsin, urine copper; normal abdominal ultrasound and MR cholangiography. Cetirizine was suspended upon suspicion of probable causality.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of deliberate self-injection of T-61®, a veterinary euthanasia agent containing embutramide, mebezoniom and tetracaine dissolved in the organic solvent dimethylformamide (DMF), and states that delayed hepatotoxicity observed in nonfatal cases can be attributed to the solvent DMF or its metabolites. In the present case, the injection of about 0.12 to 0.16 mL/kg resulted in moderate hepatic impairment that peaked on day 14; the contribution of other factors such as sepsis, renal failure, parenteral feeding and drugs could not be excluded but was considered unlikely.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Deliberate self-injection (overdose) of the veterinary euthanasia agent T-61® in a non-therapeutic setting; competing factors (sepsis, renal failure, parenteral feeding, concurrent drugs) could not be excluded but were judged unlikely.
raw_record.extra_details: DMF-delayed hepatotoxicity is described as DMF-induced hepatotoxicity, also documented in the literature with liver function abnormalities and fulminant hepatic failure within 3-22 d following T-61® at DMF doses of 0.18-0.6 mL/kg. Present case dose 0.12-0.16 mL/kg produced moderate hepatic impairment peaking on day 14. Liver biopsy (electron microscopy) showed lipid-containing lysosomes and abundant vesicular endoplasmic reticulum. DMF is metabolized to N-hydroxymethyl-N-methylformamide (NMF), NMF and N-acetyl-S-(N-methyl-carbamoyl) cysteine identified in urine; significant NMF was found in hemodialysis and CAVH fluids. Authors question N-acetylcysteine since toxicity does not appear related to lysosomal destruction, lipoperoxidation or glutathione depletion. Acute renal failure also developed and recovered within three weeks.

raw_record.support_text: Among the recognized ADRs in this retrospective study of hospitalised patients, 'hepatitis probably caused by glibenclamide (laboratory control)' was one of the ADRs identified, detected via a laboratory investigation. The physician recognized this event but did not discontinue the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Recognized by the treating physician via a laboratory control. Retrospective study of 95 hospitalised patients; ADR probability evaluated with the adverse reactions probability scale (APS) according to Naranjo et al. The hepatitis was one of the 18 probable or definite ADRs detected by an abnormal laboratory test, and one of six ADRs recognized by physicians.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report an unusual case of liver disease in a patient treated with glibenclamide whose clinical and laboratory findings from a liver biopsy support the diagnosis of glibenclamide liver toxicity. Sulfonylureas are described as causing rare liver injury expressing as intrahepatic cholestasis or hepatitis, attributable to drug hypersensitivity or dosage.
raw_record.extra_details: A 64-year-old man with type II diabetes treated with glibenclamide 10 mg/day for 2 months developed muscle pain, fatigue, jaundice, dark urine, and mild pruritus. Laboratory values during hospitalization: total bilirubin up to 10.3 mg/dl, direct bilirubin up to 5.9 mg/dl, ALT (SGOT) up to 310 U/l, AST (SGPT) up to 265 U/l, GGT up to 590 U/l, and alkaline phosphatase (SAP) up to 147 U/l. Serology for hepatitis A/B/C, EBV, CMV, and autoantibodies (smooth muscle, mitochondrial, antinuclear) negative; ultrasound, ERCP, and CT normal. Liver biopsy 10 days after stopping glibenclamide showed necrosis of liver cells, mild intrahepatic cholestasis in central areas with several bile infarcts, portal infiltration by eosinophils and lymphocytes, and bile duct proliferation. Liver function improved after drug withdrawal, with complete clinical and laboratory recovery by 4 months. No rechallenge reported; no competing causes identified.

raw_record.support_text: A 61-year-old woman with a 4-year history of type II diabetes mellitus had her therapy changed from insulin to glyburide. Four weeks after beginning glyburide therapy, at a maximum dose of 10 mg twice daily, she developed jaundice, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, light stools, and dark urine. There was no history of previous liver disease or alcohol use, and liver tests just before glyburide therapy were normal. Hepatitis serologic studies were negative, glyburide was discontinued, and her clinical status and liver tests improved rapidly.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of suspected drug-induced liver injury attributed to glyburide in a 61-year-old woman with type II diabetes mellitus; onset 4 weeks after starting glyburide (maximum dose 10 mg twice daily), with jaundice, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, light stools, and dark urine. Normal liver tests prior to glyburide; negative hepatitis B surface antigen/antibody, core antibody, e antigen, and hepatitis A IgM serology; no history of previous liver disease, transfusion, injections, contact with jaundiced persons, or alcohol use. Glyburide was discontinued with blood glucose controlled by insulin, and clinical status and liver tests improved rapidly.

raw_record.support_text: A 41 year old previously healthy woman took fenbufen 900 mg/day for 10 days for a painful left knee and, four days after stopping, developed a generalized erythematous exfoliative rash, fever, rigors, lymphadenopathy, and jaundice. Investigations showed markedly elevated transaminases (aspartate aminotransferase 1015 IU/l), lactate dehydrogenase 2190 IU/l, and alkaline phosphatase 1233 IU/l, and a liver biopsy showed swollen liver cells with focal cholestasis and a picture of resolving hepatitis. She developed Coombs positive autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, improved on prednisolone 60 mg/day, and the liver function abnormalities completely resolved over follow-up.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of a systemic hypersensitivity reaction to fenbufen (NSAID). Dose 900 mg/day for 10 days; onset four days after stopping the drug. Jaundice with elevated ASAT 1015 IU/l, LDH 2190 IU/l, ALP 1233 IU/l, low albumin 30 g/l; eosinophilia (10.1 x 10^9/l), polyclonal immunoglobulin rise, Coombs positive autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and falling haemoglobin. Liver biopsy: swollen liver cells with focal cholestasis, portal polymorphs and bile ductule proliferation, consistent with resolving hepatitis. Rapid resolution of liver and haematological abnormalities on prednisolone 60 mg/day. Author attributes the hepatitis to drug-induced hypersensitivity; differential diagnosis of angioimmunoblastic lymphadenopathy was considered but drug-induced hypersensitivity was favoured. Fenbufen was the most commonly reported suspect drug on UK yellow cards in 1986-1987, with 80% of reports relating to mucocutaneous reactions; hepatitis with rash has been reported.

raw_record.support_text: A 41 year old previously healthy woman took fenbufen 900 mg/day for a painful left knee for 10 days and developed a generalised erythematous rash and became unwell with throat pain, fever, and rigors four days after stopping the drug. Liver tests were raised (aspartate aminotransferase 1015 IU/l, lactate dehydrogenase 2190 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 1233 IU/l) with eosinophilia and a grossly reactive bone marrow.
raw_record.extra_details: Fenbufen 900 mg/day for 10 days for left knee pain; hypersensitivity reaction with fever, rigors, rash, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia (10.1 x 10^9/l), Coombs positive autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, and deep jaundice. Liver biopsy showed swollen liver cells with focal cholestasis and a resolving hepatitis. Rapid resolution of jaundice and liver function with prednisolone 60 mg/day, complete recovery over a year. Fenbufen was the most commonly reported suspect drug on yellow cards in 1986-87, with reports of hepatitis with rash; the differential diagnosis was angioimmunoblastic lymphadenopathy.

raw_record.support_text: There were 11 cases of chlorpromazine jaundice (1.4%), 4 male (1.5%) and 7 female (1.3%), in a cohort of patients receiving chlorpromazine therapy. At onset the drug had been given for from sixteen to thirty-three days (mean twenty-two), and daily dosage and total quantity varied widely and were not significant. All patients took the chlorpromazine by mouth, though 5 had started with intramuscular injections for a few days. Jaundice lasted from one to twenty-six weeks, with a mean duration of two weeks when the 2 most severe cases (lasting thirteen and twenty-six weeks) were excluded, and one fatal case occurred.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence 1.4% (11 cases); 4 male, 7 female; no age group immune. Onset after 16-33 days (mean 22). Oral chlorpromazine (5 also started with intramuscular injections for a few days); jaundice duration 1-26 weeks, mean 2 weeks excluding 2 severe cases (13 and 26 weeks) and 1 fatal case. Presenting as icterus with occasional pyrexia, gastrointestinal disturbance, prodromal fever/malaise, morbilliform rash, or anorexia. During jaundice: pruritus common, mildly enlarged/tender liver, stools from normal to off-white, urine contained bile salts and pigments. Biochemical findings: plasma-alkaline phosphatase peak 15-70 King-Armstrong units per 100 ml (normal 2-12) and serum-bilirubin 3-23 mg; thymol turbidity, colloidal gold, Takata-Ara reactions and plasma-proteins normal in the 8 cases studied. The study noted coincidental infective hepatitis in patients not receiving chlorpromazine (clinically/biochemically indistinguishable) but incidence was significantly higher in the chlorpromazine population, with only 3 cases in the rest of the hospital population of over 2000 patients. Jaundice onset considered an absolute contra-indication to further chlorpromazine.
