raw_record.support_text: Jaundice following the use of one of the phenathiazine drugs, especially chlorpromazine, was observed in 10 patients. The injury was intrahepatic cholestasis, commonly showing bile plugs in the centrolobular areas, a scanty triad infiltrate often including eosinophils, and usually minimal liver cell necrosis, although in two patients necrosis involved much of the central third of the lobules. A 41-year-old woman had taken 75 mg of chlorpromazine daily for two weeks before the onset of jaundice.
raw_record.extra_details: 10 observed patients; 75 mg chlorpromazine daily for two weeks before jaundice onset in the described case; biopsy showed centrolobular bile plugs, scanty triad infiltrate with eosinophils, centrolobular hepatocyte enlargement with sharp borders, pigment-filled macrophages, minimal necrosis in most but central-third necrosis in two patients; two patients had moderate bile ductular proliferation with round cell infiltrate and mild connective tissue increase.

raw_record.support_text: Of more than 1,800 psychiatric patients at the Brockton Veterans Administration Hospital who received chlorpromazine daily for one month or longer, 19 developed icteric or anicteric hepatic dysfunction, all within a month of beginning drug therapy. During the investigative period these patients received no other drugs, remained adequately hydrated and nourished, and had no exposure to any hepatotoxic agent, supporting chlorpromazine as the cause of the hepatic dysfunction.
raw_record.extra_details: 19 of more than 1,800 psychiatric patients treated daily with chlorpromazine for at least one month developed icteric or anicteric hepatic dysfunction, all within one month of starting therapy. Oral chlorpromazine was given in divided doses of 75–1,200 mg/day (median 461 mg); dosages were maintained or increased during the investigative period. 50 of 68 patients had completely normal liver function tests prior to treatment (the 'Normal Liver Group'). No other drugs were given, no acute illness or fever occurred, and no exposure to other hepatotoxic agents was present; one patient had homologous serum hepatitis two years before.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 14 cases of chlorpromazine-induced jaundice (Chlorpromazin-Ikterus), detailing total chlorpromazine doses of 50-8200 mg, latency periods of 5-23 days, maximum serum bilirubin of 2.3-80 mg%, and jaundice lasting 2-68 weeks. Liver biopsies performed in 10 of the 14 cases showed bile thrombi in the intercellular bile canaliculi as the key histological criterion, consistent with chlorpromazine-induced cholestatic hepatitis; additional cases (O.L., L.U.) are described with elevated serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase after chlorpromazine administration.
raw_record.extra_details: Chlorpromazine-induced cholestatic jaundice with bile thrombi in intercellular bile canaliculi; 14 human cases, total doses 50-8200 mg, latency 5-23 days, max serum bilirubin 2.3-80 mg%, jaundice duration 2-68 weeks; liver biopsies in 10/14 cases; elevated alkaline phosphatase in some cases; deaths in cases 2 (circulatory death), 7 and 14 (abscessing pyelonephritis), and 13 (uremia) not directly attributed to liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: The paper's findings suggested the likelihood that chlorpromazine caused an increased viscosity of the bile, leading to stasis in the smaller bile passages. In Case 2, a 51-year-old man on chlorpromazine 25 mg three times daily for nervous tension developed grippe-like symptoms, nausea and vomiting, and icterus appearing on day 19, with obstructive-type icterus on laboratory testing and a liver biopsy showing marked intrahepatic bile stasis without extrahepatic mechanical obstruction.
raw_record.extra_details: Two case reports (Case 1 and Case 2). Histology showed marked bile stasis localized to central lobular zones, second pigment in central hepatocytes and Kupffer cells, and nonspecific lymphocytic portal infiltration; bile ducts and extrahepatic ducts were normal with no mechanical obstruction. Case 2 patient (51-year-old man with psoriasis of 30 years) took 25 mg TID, stopped on day 17, icterus appeared on day 19, presumed infectious hepatitis initially; exploratory laparotomy found no gross obstruction; jaundice and serum bilirubin improved after cortisone 25 mg TID. Liver was small, smooth, greenish and firm at laparotomy. Case 1 died with recurrent glioblastoma multiforme and bile nephrosis as other major anatomic findings.

raw_record.support_text: Chlorpromazine (Thorazine, Largactil) has been incriminated in the production of this syndrome of intrahepatic cholestasis; by June 1955, within two years of its introduction in France, at least 20 such cases had been reported from nine different medical localities in the United States literature alone. The uniformity of the clinical and histologic findings and the relatively large number of cases reported tend distinctly to incriminate chlorpromazine as the causative agent, and intrahepatic cholestasis is the only form of jaundice known to result from it.
raw_record.extra_details: At least 20 cases by June 1955 from nine US medical localities plus additional British-literature cases; aliases Thorazine, Largactil; intrahepatic obstructive jaundice possibly more frequent than published reports imply; intrahepatic cholestasis described as the only form of jaundice known to result from chlorpromazine.

raw_record.support_text: Kelsey and associates observed three types of pathologic liver conditions associated with chlorpromazine: a diffuse inflammatory change with biliary stasis producing obstructive jaundice with moderate alkaline phosphatase elevation, a type resembling acute hepatitis with parenchymal liver damage, and an uncommon early-cirrhosis type. Dreyfuss reported that the incidence of chlorpromazine jaundice was 4.4% in 362 patients given no extra fluids but dropped to 0.34% in 588 patients given about 2.3 L of additional fluids, supporting an inspissation-of-bile mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: Kelsey's three liver types: (1) diffuse inflammatory change with biliary stasis, obstructive jaundice with moderate alkaline phosphatase elevation and no abnormal parenchymal liver-function tests; (2) acute-hepatitis-like with elevated thymol turbidity and prothrombin deficiency; (3) uncommon early cirrhosis with marked azotemia and severe prolonged chronic liver disease. Dreyfuss fluid study: jaundice incidence 4.4% (362 patients, no extra fluids) vs 0.34% (588 patients, ~2.3 L extra fluids). Read/Harrison/Sherlock: 4 women developed obstructive jaundice after 1-4 weeks on 75 mg/day chlorpromazine, with very high serum cholesterol and xanthomas; clinical recovery in all, but serum cholesterol and phosphatase levels not normalized even 7-18 months later.

raw_record.support_text: In a large psychiatric hospital, nine patients with chlorpromazine jaundice (allergic cholangiolitis following administration of chlorpromazine) were studied in sufficient detail to warrant inclusion in the report; the authors state that liver cell damage is usual in this disease. They underwent intensive serial clinical, laboratory, and serial needle aspiration biopsy studies, documenting chlorpromazine-induced cholestatic liver injury with associated liver cell degeneration.
raw_record.extra_details: Nine psychiatric inpatients with chlorpromazine jaundice; 26 percutaneous needle aspiration biopsies. Histology showed liver cell damage typical of the disease: ballooning degeneration of liver cells, multinucleation, mitoses, unicellular and periportal focal necroses with Councilman-like bodies, and one fatal literature case (Rodin and Robertson) with diffuse non-inflammatory centrolobular necroses preserved supporting reticulum (feathery necrosis). Features of allergic cholangiolitis: jaundice, bile in urine, elevated serum bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase (Bodansky units) and cholesterol, eosinophilia; all nine present cases recovered, though some laboratory abnormalities persisted for months.

raw_record.support_text: In table 2, which lists patients who developed DILI, chlorpromazine (CPZ; doses 42.5-350 mg) was marked with an asterisk as the drug highly suggestive of DILI according to the RUCAM (score 10) in six patients (cases 1, 2, 3, 4, 13, 14), with co-administered but non-attributed drugs including diazepam, risperidone, lorazepam, haloperidol, valproate, and carbamazepine.
raw_record.extra_details: Six RUCAM-adjudicated cases (cases 1-4, 13, 14) with RUCAM score 10; doses 42.5-350 mg; patients were psychiatric inpatients; DILI described as moderate with mean maximal ALT 341-319 IU/l and AST 201-204 IU/l across the 19 DILI cases.

raw_record.support_text: Seventy-one patients with idiosyncratic drug-induced hepatitis were described and the causative drug for each patient was tabulated; diagnosis was considered definite or probable based on exclusion of other causes and temporal relationship.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases 8-12. Histology: drug-induced prolonged cholestasis (cases 8,10), acute mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic hepatitis (case 9), acute cholestatic hepatitis (case 11), none (case 12). Max bilirubin 7-750 µmol/l.

raw_record.support_text: Two patients developed obstructive jaundice during chlorpromazine therapy. For the first, jaundice appeared after 16 days of chlorpromazine at 100 mg/day and lasted 27 days, with fever and a flu-like onset followed by severe pruritus, mild eosinophilia, and a laboratory picture suggesting obstructive jaundice; recovery occurred with symptomatic management and drug withdrawal. The second received chlorpromazine 40 mg daily for 13 days and developed generalized pruritus, dark urine, light stools, and mild jaundice with obstructive liver-function findings and 21% blood eosinophils, recovering uneventfully 19 days after discontinuation. The authors state the jaundice in these cases is thought to be secondary to chlorpromazine therapy, and that jaundice from stone, other obstructive phenomena, or infectious hepatitis appears remote.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient 1: chlorpromazine 100 mg/day, jaundice after 16 days persisting 27 days, fever and flu-like onset, severe pruritus, mild eosinophilia, obstructive laboratory picture, active marginal ulcer and marked duodenal deformity; recovered after withdrawal and symptomatic management. Patient 2: chlorpromazine 40 mg daily for 13 days, generalized pruritus within a week, dark urine, light stools, mild jaundice at two weeks, obstructive liver-function tests, 21% eosinophils, duodenal spasm; icterus lasted about two weeks, uneventful recovery 19 days after stopping. Liver biopsy in the case reported by Zatuchni and Miller showed acute periportal inflammation, bile plugs in canaliculi, and numerous eosinophils, suggesting hypersensitivity as the principal mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that serious hepatic reactions may occur early in the course of chlorpromazine therapy, that reports of hepatitis have already appeared, and that the authors record their experience with three cases of hepatitis. In Case 1 a 65-year-old man on chlorpromazine HCl (Thorazine) 25 mg three times a day developed chills, fever, nausea, jaundice, pruritus, acholic stools, bile in urine, and a palpable soft liver, with elevated bilirubin and elevated alkaline phosphatase.
raw_record.extra_details: Thorazine, chlorpromazine HCl. Case 1: 25 mg three times a day starting January 3, 1955; symptoms including chills/fever/nausea began January 22 and jaundice was noted January 26. Laboratory findings included elevated bilirubin (1 min up to 6.6 mg/100 ml), alkaline phosphatase rising to 23-24 Bodansky units, acholic stools, bile in urine, pruritus, and a soft liver palpable two fingerbreadths below the costal margin. Patient was also given tetracycline and penicillin and treated with methionine, high vitamin B, and diphenhydramine. Paper reports three hepatitis cases attributed to chlorpromazine.

raw_record.support_text: The authors note that case reports of chlorpromazine jaundice (allergic cholangiolitis) have commonly failed to discover necrosis of liver cells in single biopsies, but that they studied 9 such patients by serial biopsies and found significant necrosis at some stage in each, with fairly large necroses occurring occasionally. They speculate that mild attacks of allergic cholangiolitis may be unaccompanied by liver cell necrosis, in which case serum transaminase levels would be expected to be unaffected.
raw_record.extra_details: Described as 'chlorpromazine jaundice (allergic cholangiolitis)'; studied in 9 patients by serial liver biopsies, all of whom showed significant hepatic necrosis at some stage, occasionally fairly large. In contrast to single-biopsy case reports that commonly fail to detect liver cell necrosis. Paper's primary purpose is validating serum glutamic-oxaloacetic/glutamic-pyruvic transaminase as an index of liver necrosis, not a DILI case report; mention of chlorpromazine is incidental.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of patients with drug-induced intra-hepatic cholestasis, most cases (34-51) had received chlorpromazine 50-300 mg daily; jaundice developed 4-42 days (mean 18 days) after starting treatment. Case 52 had taken perphenazine, a phenothiazine derivative, 24 mg daily for 56 days, and case 53 had received a third course of nitrofurantoin shortly before jaundice appeared.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed to intra-hepatic cholestasis; doses 50-300 mg daily; latent period 4-42 days (mean 18 days); cases 34-51. Jaundice lasted 14-140 days. Liver biopsy in 15 cases showed centrilobular biliary stasis with bile thrombi in distended canaliculi, without hepatocellular necrosis; portal infiltrates with monocytes, plasma cells and early eosinophils; most patients had eosinophilia.

raw_record.support_text: In the summary, of 21 observed patients with non-mechanical obstructive jaundice, 10 had drug jaundice (Arzneimittelikterus), attributed to Megaphen (chlorpromazine), Arsenobenzol (arsphenamine), Propycil (propylthiouracil) and methyltestosterone. The jaundice was characterized by intense prolonged icterus with pruritus, absence of urobilinogen in urine, elevated serum alkaline phosphatase and cholesterol, normal turbidity/flocculation tests, and frequently blood eosinophilia in drug jaundice, with histological features of cholestasis, periportal cell infiltration and tissue eosinophilia.
raw_record.extra_details: Called Megaphen in the paper. In observation #2, a patient received Megaphen again 61 days after a Megaphen jaundice without renewed reaction, and a liver biopsy at that time was normal (rechallenge without recurrence).

raw_record.support_text: Among 6 patients with obstructive jaundice studied with SGO-T measurements, one case was attributed to 'chlorpromazine jaundice' (others were common duct stricture, common duct stone, cholangiolitis, and pancreatic carcinoma). All obstructive-jaundice patients had elevated SGO-T, with the highest peak 210 and the lowest 104 units, and these peak levels never reached the heights seen in hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Chlorpromazine jaundice categorized among obstructive (cholestatic) jaundice patients; all 6 obstructive-jaundice patients had elevated SGO-T, peak values ranging from 104 to 210 units.

raw_record.support_text: The paper notes several dozen case reports of phenothiazine-induced jaundice persisting more than 6 months, many showing clinical and pathologic features similar to primary biliary cirrhosis (pruritus, persistently high alkaline phosphatases, hypercholesterolemia, xanthomas/xanthelasma, mild steatorrhea; liver biopsy with a paucity or absence of bile ducts, portal fibrosis, chronic portal inflammation, feathery degeneration, and cholestasis). These cases are attributed to chlorpromazine, a phenothiazine.
raw_record.extra_details: Several dozen case reports of phenothiazine (chlorpromazine)-induced jaundice persisting more than 6 months with primary-biliary-cirrhosis-like features. Nearly half of the chlorpromazine cases had persistently abnormal enzymes at follow-ups of 8-36 months; serial biopsies in 4 cases and the described patient showed progression of portal fibrosis despite drug withdrawal; cirrhosis developed in 2 patients, both with subsequent variceal hemorrhage. Weakly positive AMA titers (1:4) in 4/7 patients in one report; large doses associated with antinuclear antibodies and positive LE preps in some patients.

raw_record.support_text: Clinically and biochemically the jaundice during chlorpromazine treatment is of obstructive type, but the liver in the fatal case showed central necrosis and biliary stasis, severe lobular atrophy, relative preservation of portal areas, and absence of exudate, interpreted as 'subacute toxic hepatitis of blood-borne type'. Ante-mortem passive congestion of the liver contributed to a significant degree to the central necrosis. Of 11 affected patients, 9 ran an uneventful course to recovery, while one died after thirteen weeks' remittent illness.
raw_record.extra_details: Jaundice clinically and biochemically of obstructive type; direct serum-bilirubin invariably 2-2.5x indirect component. Fatal case additionally showed central necrosis, biliary stasis, severe lobular atrophy, absent exudate, described as 'subacute toxic hepatitis of blood-borne type'; ante-mortem passive congestion contributed significantly to the central necrosis. 9 of 11 cases recovered uneventfully; 1 chronic encephalitic recovered after stormy 26 weeks with residual raised alkaline phosphatase (45 King-Armstrong units) and impaired bromsulphalein clearance (83%); 1 chronic rheumatic heart-disease patient died after thirteen weeks' remittent illness (Boardman 1954).

raw_record.support_text: Seven livers came from patients with the clinical diagnosis of drug hepatitis attributed to the contraceptive pill (two cases), methyldopa (two), indomethacin (one), chlorpromazine (one), and isoniazid (one). The biopsy findings confirmed the drug hepatitis diagnosis and each patient was negative for HBsAg.
raw_record.extra_details: One of seven drug hepatitis cases in the series; clinical diagnosis of drug hepatitis confirmed by liver biopsy; patient negative for HBsAg.

raw_record.support_text: DILI-inducing antipsychotics included chlorpromazine, perphenazine, citalopram, flupenthixol, aripiprazole, clozapine and carbamazepin; antipsychotics accounted for 27 patients (6.37%) of DILI cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Antipsychotic; antipsychotics accounted for 27 patients (6.37%) of DILI cases.

raw_record.support_text: Eleven patients with jaundice due to chlorpromazine therapy were re-challenged with the drug (challenge test) at doses of 100-300 mg daily, comparable to the original therapeutic doses, from ten days to seventeen months after the initial jaundice episode. Clinical jaundice was reproduced in six patients, two developed fever and gastrointestinal symptoms with increased bromsulphathlein retention and serum alkaline phosphatase without clinical jaundice, one had fever and vomiting without hepatic tests, and two showed no reaction. Symptoms appeared within 12-24 hours and jaundice by 48 hours after the first challenge dose. Additional challenge episodes were generally milder, indicating reproducible drug-induced cholestatic jaundice attributable to chlorpromazine.
raw_record.extra_details: Phenotype is cholestatic (obstructive-type) jaundice; histology showed lobular distention with increased connective tissue, bile duct proliferation, cellular infiltration, large bile plugs and vacuolated hepatic cells in a patient receiving chlorpromazine 300 mg daily. Mechanistically framed as drug allergy: patch tests (3% aqueous, 48h) were uniformly negative in all groups; intradermal tests were variable/non-specific; challenge (re-administration) reproduced clinical jaundice in 6 of 11 previously jaundiced patients, prodromal symptoms with abnormal hepatic function tests in 2, prodromal symptoms alone in 1, and no change in 2. Recurrences occurred 10 days to 17 months after the initial attack, second episodes usually milder; some patients lost sensitivity within 3 weeks. One index patient died 34 days after jaundice onset while jaundice was subsiding and hepatic tests were improving (death not clearly attributed to liver failure). The agent's identity as cause of jaundice is asserted by the phrase 'jaundice due to chlorpromazine therapy'.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that in approximately 25 per cent of patients treated with chlorpromazine some evidence of hepatic dysfunction appears, usually detectable only as abnormal liver function tests (bromsulphalein retention and elevation of serum alkaline phosphatase and cholesterol), while jaundice appears in approximately 1 per cent and is usually of short duration. It notes that a rare fatality during the acute phase of jaundice has been observed, in about 10 per cent of patients chlorpromazine hepatitis lasts longer than three months, and prolonged jaundice over many months has been reported. The paper further presents a case (jaundice >300 days, xanthomatosis, hepatosplenomegaly) and a summary of five cases of chronic hepatic dysfunction with xanthomatosis attributed to chlorpromazine therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: About 25% of treated patients develop some hepatic dysfunction, usually asymptomatic, detectable only as abnormal liver-function tests (bromsulphalein retention, elevated serum alkaline phosphatase and cholesterol); ~1% develop jaundice, usually short; a rare fatality during the acute jaundice phase has been noted; ~10% have chlorpromazine hepatitis lasting >3 months. Chronic cases developed a xanthomatous liver disease with prolonged jaundice (197 days to 30 months), markedly elevated serum cholesterol (up to 2,500 mg/100 ml) and total lipids (up to 9,000 mg/100 ml), xanthomatosis, hepatosplenomegaly, portal hypertension, and biliary cirrhosis; the syndrome was termed 'hepatohypercholesterolemic cirrhosis' by Beattie et al. Elevated circulating coagulation factors (prothrombin, proconvertin, proaccelerin) were demonstrated; acetate-1-C14 studies suggested enhanced hepatic synthesis of cholesterol and phospholipid. Present case: jaundice >300 days, severe refractory pruritus, xanthomatosis, persistent hepatosplenomegaly.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 27 patients with intrahepatic cholestasis, the cholestasis was attributed to chlorpromazine in 13 patients. The main diagnostic criteria were a history of recent drug exposure preceding the episode of jaundice, gradual recovery on withdrawal of the drug, and rigorous exclusion of all other potential causes of jaundice; liver biopsy confirmed the diagnosis in 9 of the 27 intrahepatic cholestasis patients.
raw_record.extra_details: 13 of 27 intrahepatic cholestasis cases in the series attributed to chlorpromazine; diagnostic criteria included recent drug exposure preceding jaundice, gradual recovery on withdrawal, and exclusion of other jaundice causes; liver biopsy confirmed intrahepatic cholestasis in 9 of the 27 patients. Intrahepatic cholestasis and the contraceptive pill were the other ascribed causes within the same series.

raw_record.support_text: Chlorpromazine was among the four drugs associated with the most instances of hepatic injury in a follow-up of 44 patients with drug-induced hepatotoxicity, in 4 of 44 patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Psychotropic drug; 4 of 44 hepatotoxicity cases. Psychotropic drugs were among the most commonly cited causes after antibiotics and analgesic NSAIDs.

raw_record.support_text: Among nine patients selected for electrophoretic study of serum alkaline phosphatase isoenzymes, one patient's diagnosis was recorded as chlorpromazine-induced jaundice, explicitly attributing the patient's jaundice to chlorpromazine exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Mention occurs only as a clinical diagnosis in a list of nine patients whose sera were analyzed for alkaline phosphatase isoenzyme band L; no dose, latency, course, or other clinical detail is provided. The paper itself concerns alkaline phosphatase isoenzyme methodology, not the evaluation of chlorpromazine hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Among 73 patients with drug-induced hepatitis, mitochondrial antibody was found in 1 of the 15 patients with reactions to chlorpromazine; serum Australia antigen tests were negative in this case.
raw_record.extra_details: Drug-induced hepatitis diagnosed in a series of 73 patients; 15 reactions were attributed to chlorpromazine. Reported here for the association with serum mitochondrial antibody positivity.

raw_record.support_text: A 51-year-old female developed cholangiolitic (cholestatic) hepatitis / jaundice following chlorpromazine (Thorazine, Largactil); in a first episode (1955) she had fever, epigastric pain, anorexia, pruritus and dark urine after chlorpromazine 75 mg daily for ten days, symptoms subsiding on discontinuation; in a second episode (1960) she developed jaundice after only two doses (25 mg), with pruritus, dark urine, light-colored stools, icterus, a tender liver edge, mild eosinophilia, serum bilirubin rising to 3.3 mg/100 ml and alkaline phosphatase 33 King-Armstrong units, with normal SGOT; she made an uneventful recovery.
raw_record.extra_details: Clinical diagnosis of cholangiolitic (cholestatic) hepatitis consistent with findings and response to corticosteroid therapy; total serum bilirubin 3.3 mg/100 ml, alkaline phosphatase 33 King-Armstrong units, SGOT normal, cephalin flocculation and thymol turbidity negative, mild eosinophilia; serum electrophoretic pattern showed slight increase in alpha-2 globulin with normal gamma globulin despite presumed hypersensitivity; 51-year-old female.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that the risk of cholestatic hepatitis associated with chlorpromazine is well known, and this was the prevailing pattern among the exposed cases in their study, with an incidence rate similar to other studies. Chlorpromazine is also listed in a table of drugs with relative risk >5 for acute liver injury, with 3 exposed cases (2 cholestatic, 1 hepatocellular).
raw_record.extra_details: Antipsychotic. Rate of cholestatic hepatitis with relative risk >5; 3 exposed cases (2 cholestatic, 1 hepatocellular). Incidence rate similar to other studies.

raw_record.support_text: Zatuchni and Miller classified chlorpromazine jaundice with the drug hypersensitivity reactions characterized by cholestasis associated with intrahepatic biliary tract obstruction, a view that won general acceptance. Data collected by the Smith, Kline & French Laboratories show an overall incidence of overt jaundice of 1-2% in patients treated with the drug for at least one week; of about four million patients who received chlorpromazine, jaundice was recorded in 880 and there were thirteen deaths attributable to the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Classified as a drug hypersensitivity reaction with cholestasis and intrahepatic biliary tract obstruction, little or no hepatocellular damage (most closely related syndrome among cholestatic drugs). Incidence of overt jaundice 1-2% among patients treated at least one week; of ~4 million recipients, jaundice recorded in 880 and 13 deaths attributable to the drug. Werther & Korelitz case series: 22 patients at The Mount Sinai Hospital, average total oral dose 1,260 mg; prodromal symptoms (fever, epigastric/RUQ pain, chills, nausea, vomiting, myalgias, lassitude, maculopapular eruption) at a mean of 14 days lasting 4.5 days; eosinophilia usually present; jaundice after mean 18.6 days with pruritus, dark urine, light stools; highest bilirubin 14.8 mg%; elevated alkaline phosphatase (up to 36.4 King-Armstrong units) in 21/22, negative cephalin flocculation in all but 2, serum cholesterol >300 mg% (max 406 mg%) in 8/16; jaundice duration mean 30 days (range 7-122 days); uneventful recovery; liver biopsy in 6 cases showed characteristic cholestasis and periportal inflammatory infiltration (with eosinophils in 3 early samples) and centrolobular liver cell regeneration in 4.

raw_record.support_text: Among 171 patients with drug-induced liver injury and liver failure, chlorpromazine accounted for 0.6% of the 'other drugs' cases. Chlorpromazine was attributed as a causal drug in these DILI cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective cohort in Southwest China; chlorpromazine accounted for 0.6% of 171 DILI-associated liver-failure cases; DILI defined as any hepatotoxic drug within 6 months before onset.

raw_record.support_text: Among 72 patients with histologically proven or suspected liver disease, three had drug hepatitis diagnosed on conventional criteria, attributed to chlorpromazine, phenylbutazone, and aspirin (one case each).
raw_record.extra_details: Diagnosed as one case of drug hepatitis (1 of 3 drug-hepatitis cases) among a cohort of 72 patients with liver disease. Only diagnosis-level attribution is provided; no dose, histology, or outcome details reported.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 121 patients with various types of liver disease, Jirgl's serum flocculation reaction was strongly positive in patients with chlorpromazine jaundice (along with primary biliary cirrhosis and extrahepatic obstructive jaundice). The use of 'chlorpromazine jaundice' as a diagnostic category indicates recognized chlorpromazine-associated liver injury in humans.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported in the context of evaluating Jirgl's serum flocculation reaction; patients with chlorpromazine jaundice gave strongly positive reactions in a series of 121 liver-disease patients. The paper does not provide a formal causality assessment or biochemical pattern for the chlorpromazine-associated jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: In this study of 26 cases of drug-induced acute intrahepatic cholestasis (AIC), the causative drugs of four prolonged cases were identified as tiopronin, chlorpromazine and diclofenac. Two of these patients either died or underwent liver transplantation. The prolonged cases showed marked liver cell injury and cholestasis, with disappearance of interlobular bile ducts in the portal triads (vanishing bile ducts).
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as a causative drug of prolonged drug-induced acute intrahepatic cholestasis. Prolonged cases showed marked liver cell injury and cholestasis, vanishing interlobular bile ducts, and significantly higher maximal total bilirubin (35.2±13.8 mg/dL) with markedly longer bilirubin half-life (78.8±69.6 days) vs non-prolonged cases (16.8±8.1 mg/dL, 22.1±12.7 days). Canalicular MRP2 staining was weakened with pericanalicular vesicular redistribution. Two of the four prolonged patients died or underwent liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: In Group D (55 jaundiced patients with clearly hepatocellular cause), four cases of acute jaundice followed administration of known hepatotoxic drugs (chlorpromazine, two cases; para-aminosalicylic acid, two cases) and subsided on withdrawal of the suspected agent. The hepatocellular classification was established by histology in 28 of the 55 cases; the remainder (including these four drug cases) were judged by classical clinical and laboratory features, alongside infectious hepatitis and cirrhosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases of acute jaundice following administration of chlorpromazine (a 'known hepatotoxic drug' per the paper), listed among four hepatocellular jaundice cases; jaundice subsided on withdrawal of the suspected agent (dechallenge). Reported in the context of a serum adenosine deaminase activity study of jaundiced patients.

raw_record.support_text: In the UK general practice research database retrospective case-control study, the list of drugs causing DILI was topped by well-known 'hepatotoxic' compounds such as chlorpromazine, amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, flucloxacillin, macrolides and tetracyclines among others.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among well-known 'hepatotoxic' compounds in a population-based case-control study using the UK general practice research database (>5 million person-years, 1994-1999), which also flagged apparently innocent bystanders such as metoclopramide, chlorpheniramine and betahistine.

raw_record.support_text: Among 47 patients with parenchymal liver disease evaluated for the Jirgl flocculation test, the test was positive in 1 case of chlorpromazine-induced jaundice (included among the 14 false-positive reactions). The paper thus explicitly identifies a patient with jaundice attributed to chlorpromazine, though its purpose is validation of the Jirgl diagnostic test rather than analysis of the drug-induced injury.
raw_record.extra_details: One patient in the study series was diagnosed with chlorpromazine-induced jaundice; this case gave a positive (false-positive) Jirgl flocculation test (3+, bilirubin 14.0 mg%, alkaline phosphatase 26.8 Bodansky U.). In a cited series, 2 of 25 cases of intrahepatic obstructive jaundice were chlorpromazine-induced. The paper evaluates the Jirgl flocculation test and does not analyze the DILI relationship itself.

raw_record.support_text: The paper identifies chlorpromazine as a drug implicated in inducing liver injury, being the causative agent in 7 of 53 patients with drug-related liver disease. Chlorpromazine produced hepatocanalicular cholestasis in 6 and diffuse necrosis in 1.
raw_record.extra_details: Chlorpromazine was the causative agent in 7 of 53 patients; produced hepatocanalicular cholestasis in 6 and diffuse necrosis in 1.

raw_record.support_text: In 19 liver biopsy specimens from patients with chlorpromazine-induced jaundice, histologic findings included balloon degeneration (8 of 19), multinucleation of liver cells (18 of 19, 2 to 5 nuclei per cell), fatty change (5 of 19), and mitotic figures (5 of 19). Councilman-type necrosis and usual liver-cell necrosis each occurred in only 1 specimen, both from the same patient who had a recent history of severe alcoholism; the absence of Councilman necrosis is a major feature distinguishing chlorpromazine jaundice from viral hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Nineteen liver biopsy specimens among 20 patients with chlorpromazine jaundice were studied. Cholestatic features: capillary bile thrombi among liver-cell cords found in all 19 specimens (Fig. 2), bile duct proliferation of small hepatic ducts of slight degree in 3, and large bile 'lakes' or pigment accumulation in large ducts in none; absence of bile in large ducts/lakes is the major feature differentiating chlorpromazine-induced liver disease from obstructive jaundice of large bile duct origin. Inflammation in 10 of 19 (portal lymphocytes/histiocytes, polymorphonuclear leukocytes in 9, eosinophils in 3). Sinusoidal macrophages stuffed with pigment in 17 of 19. Balloon degeneration and hydropic change; the one necrosis patient had history of severe alcoholism. Treatment was as for cirrhosis (high-carbohydrate/high-protein diet, bed rest, B-complex vitamins); some received bile salts or antihistamines because the reaction was considered possibly allergic.

raw_record.support_text: Chlorpromazine is given as an example of a drug with very well documented hepatotoxicity with numerous case reports and case series and positive rechallenge, and in early DILI research it was commonly reported to be associated with hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Antipsychotic/phenothiazine; listed in Table 1 with more than 100 reported cases of drug-induced liver injury (LiverTox) and in GPRD as most strongly associated with DILI (crude incidence 1 per 739 users, risk >100 per 100,000 users).

raw_record.support_text: Mortality ranged from 0% with most of the drugs to 50% (2 out of 4 chlorpromazine-associated cases) in cholestatic/mixed liver injury with a probable or possible causal relationship.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic/mixed injury; 2 of 4 chlorpromazine-associated cases died (50% mortality), the highest among CS/mixed causes; also listed with 5 hepatocellular cases in cohort table.

raw_record.support_text: In biopsy specimens from two patients with Chlorpromazine-induced lesions, histological signs of biliary obstruction were seen, with bile thrombi mostly in the central lobular zone, accompanied by slight focal hepatocellular necrosis with slight leucocyte infiltration.
raw_record.extra_details: Biopsy showed biliary obstruction with bile thrombi (central lobular zone), slight focal hepatocellular necrosis and leucocyte infiltration; did not resemble virus hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Lemire and Mitchell observed three cases of chlorpromazine jaundice in elderly people; in two, transient eosinophilia of 7-17% was noted. Liver-function tests showed hyperbilirubinaemia, increased serum alkaline phosphatase, and normal thymol turbidity; two had liver biopsies and all three underwent surgery. raw_record.support_text: Jaundice from chlorpromazine usually runs a self-limited course briefer than that of viral hepatitis, and during the acute course liver biopsies usually show only minimal hepatocellular damage. The paper also notes that hepatitis may occur without clinical jaundice, manifesting as liver enlargement or tenderness, fever, abnormal liver function tests, or histologic evidence of 'allergic cholangiolitis,' all of which are considered chlorpromazine jaundice.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: The paper notes a definite hazard of permanent liver damage if patients are re-treated following an attack of jaundice or if treatment is continued without interruption.
raw_record.extra_details: Chlorpromazine jaundice is attributed to drug allergy; the paper concludes the probability that jaundice is due to drug allergy is high. Nine of eleven challenged patients demonstrated objective evidence of sensitivity for up to seventeen months after an attack. Other reports also reproduced jaundice upon challenge. Jaundice can be mild (serum bilirubin 2 mg/100 ml or less) and short (3-7 days) and may occur without clinical jaundice (liver enlargement/tenderness, fever, abnormal liver function tests, histologic 'allergic cholangiolitis'). Acute liver biopsies show minimal hepatocellular damage. After an estimated four million treated patients, 26 deaths in jaundiced patients were reported, with the drug thought responsible in 13; most fatal cases were complicated by agranulocytosis, heart failure, possible viral hepatitis, cirrhosis, or recent surgery, and one death with acute hepatic necrosis occurred in an 81-year-old. Jaundice runs a self-limited course briefer than viral hepatitis. Animal toxicity studies failed to reveal hepatic damage, but continued use in sensitized patients appears to lead to permanent toxic liver changes.

raw_record.support_text: A 70-year-old woman on dronedarone for atrial fibrillation (started 6 months before admission) presented with progressive fatigue and hyperbilirubinemia. Her total bilirubin peaked at 30.3 mg/dL, she developed coagulopathy refractory to therapy, and Doppler flow imaging showed reduced portal flow and beginning cirrhosis. The report contributed to the January 2011 US FDA Safety Announcement about rare but severe liver injury in dronedarone (Multaq) patients.

raw_record.support_text: Ximelagatran (Exanta), an anti-thrombin therapy, was investigated in 8,000–10,000 patients during clinical trials. An important percentage of treated patients exhibited considerably elevated levels of liver enzymes indicative of liver toxicity, and a few also developed jaundice; these effects were not seen in preclinical studies. The paper presents ximelagatran as a case study of drug-induced liver injury not predicted by animal models.
raw_record.extra_details: Alias: Exanta. Anti-thrombin therapy intended for patients with adverse reactions to warfarin or difficult to maintain on warfarin long-term. Liver effects not seen in preclinical studies. In complementary pharmacogenetics work, blood from 74 patients with raised liver enzymes and 169 with normal liver enzymes showed a replicated strong genetic association of elevated liver enzymes with MHC alleles DRB1*07 and DQA1*02, suggesting a possible immune pathogenesis (a genetic association, not itself an injuring agent).

raw_record.support_text: Ximelagatran, a first-generation thrombin inhibitor developed as an alternative to warfarin for anticoagulation, caused DILI in treated patients: up to 15% experienced elevations in serum ALT levels, which were severe and life threatening in some cases. An association between the HLA class II allele HLA-DRB1*07 and ALT elevations was observed in 74 ximelagatran-treated patients versus 130 ximelagatran-treated controls without DILI and was replicated. The paper frames this as an instance of human-specific and idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity not detected by conventional animal studies, attributed to immune dysregulation.
raw_record.extra_details: First-generation thrombin inhibitor used as an alternative to warfarin for anticoagulation. Up to 15% of treated patients experienced serum ALT elevations, severe and life-threatening in some cases. HLA-DRB1*07 association with ALT elevations observed in 74 treated patients vs 130 treated controls without DILI and replicated in an additional dataset. Neither preclinical nor clinical studies suggested an immune-mediated mechanism; guinea pig studies suggested possible skin sensitization and some manufacturing-exposed individuals developed skin rash. Ximelagatran and its metabolites selectively inhibited peptide binding to HLA-DRB1*0701, supporting immune dysregulation in pathogenesis. No suitable preclinical models; idiosyncratic human hepatotoxicity likely arises from complex genetic, non-genetic, and environmental interactions.

raw_record.support_text: Ximelagatran (36 mg bid) was as effective as warfarin in preventing stroke and systemic embolism in the SPORTIF III and V trials, but a higher proportion of treated patients had alanine aminotransferase levels three times the upper limit of normal with associated bilirubin elevation (6.1% vs 0.8% on warfarin). Three of these patients developed fatal hepatotoxicity, which led to FDA rejection and termination of drug development.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral prodrug of melagatran, direct thrombin inhibitor. SPORTIF III and V trials; ALT at least 3x ULN with associated bilirubin elevation in 6.1% of ximelagatran-treated patients versus 0.8% on warfarin; three patients developed fatal hepatotoxicity; FDA approval not granted due to liver toxicity and development terminated. Table 1 lists ximelagatran as not granted FDA approval due to liver toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In 2006, after reports of hepatotoxicity, the FDA halted clinical development of ximelagatran, an oral direct thrombin inhibitor intended for prevention or treatment of thromboembolic conditions, due to concerns about DILI. The paper uses this programme's extensive clinical trial data to describe the clinical signature of ximelagatran-associated liver injury and confirms that the DILI-CAT algorithm clearly identified a DILI signal for ximelagatran.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral direct thrombin inhibitor (Factor IIa inhibitor) designed for prevention or treatment of thromboembolic conditions; FDA halted clinical development in 2006 after reports of hepatotoxicity due to DILI concerns. DILI-CAT (data-driven algorithmic causality tool) identified a DILI signal for ximelagatran using clinical trial data. The intended setting was early drug development signal detection; ximelagatran is used as an example drug with a known potential hepatotoxicity phenotype.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective study of 74 cases and 130 controls, AstraZeneca identified HLA-DRB1*0701 as the major genetic risk factor associated with ximelagatran drug-induced liver injury (DILI), which led to the drug's withdrawal soon after its introduction on the market.
raw_record.extra_details: HLA-DRB1*0701 identified as the major genetic risk factor for ximelagatran DILI in a retrospective study (74 cases, 130 controls; OR 4, PPV 61%, NPV 73%); DILI led to market withdrawal shortly after introduction, highlighting the need for systematic DNA banking during drug development.

raw_record.support_text: From the US, a large cohort of DILI caused by ximelagatran that occurred in clinical trials was published by Lee et al., with RUCAM used to correctly assess suspected DILI cases in clinical trials.
raw_record.extra_details: Large cohort of DILI caused by ximelagatran in clinical trials (published by Lee et al., 2005), with suspected DILI cases assessed by RUCAM.

raw_record.support_text: In the EXTEND study, 11 patients treated with ximelagatran who had normal ALAT at the end of the 35-day treatment period showed an ALAT increase >2× ULN 3 weeks later. One otherwise healthy patient developed severe liver injury, from which he recovered fully; no causative explanation other than ximelagatran administration could be found despite rigorous investigation. This event led to termination of the EXTEND study, termination of all studies using ximelagatran, and withdrawal of ximelagatran from the market.
raw_record.extra_details: Injury arose in the EXTEND study of ximelagatran (oral thrombin inhibitor) for VTE prophylaxis; 11 of the ximelagatran-treated patients with normal ALAT at end of 35-day treatment showed ALAT increase >2× ULN 3 weeks later; one otherwise healthy patient developed severe liver injury and recovered fully. Liver injury also occurred after ximelagatran withdrawal, precluding ALAT-based monitoring. Study, all ximelagatran studies, and drug were terminated/withdrawn from the market.

raw_record.support_text: The thrombin inhibitor ximelagatran showed a strong hepatotoxicity signal in clinical trials: an incidence of ALT >3 x ULN in 7.9%, ALT >10 x ULN in 1.9%, and elevated ALT with bilirubin >2-fold in 0.5% of patients. Adjudication of the latter cases (meeting modified Hy's Law criteria) decreased their incidence to closer to 0.1%, but there were several cases of acute liver failure. The drug was not approved in the US and, as a result of its hepatotoxicity, was voluntarily withdrawn from the market in Europe after short-term use.
raw_record.extra_details: Clinical trial incidences: ALT >3 x ULN 7.9%, ALT >10 x ULN 1.9%, elevated ALT with bilirubin >2-fold 0.5%. Cases meeting modified Hy's Law criteria adjudicated down to ~0.1%. Several cases of acute liver failure. Not approved in the US; voluntarily withdrawn from the European market after short-term use due to hepatotoxicity. Thrombin inhibitor.

raw_record.support_text: The paper cites ximelagatran (Exanta), an oral thrombin inhibitor poised to replace coumadin, as a drug that suffered the fate of premarketing clinical trial discontinuation when several episodes of severe liver injury occurred during pre-approval trials.
raw_record.extra_details: Brand name Exanta; oral thrombin inhibitor intended to replace coumadin (warfarin). Several episodes of severe liver injury occurred during pre-approval (premarketing) trials, which halted the drug's development. Cited as an example that even a single case of severe DILI in a clinical trial can signal the end of the drug under study.

raw_record.support_text: One study examined DILI due to the oral anticoagulant ximelagatran. The drug showed no evidence of hepatotoxicity in preclinical testing, but elevated ALT levels (>3× ULN) were observed in ~8% of patients treated with the drug for >35 days. Although in most patients ALT levels returned to normal within 6 months whether or not treatment was continued, the drug was withdrawn from the market because of rare occurrences of severe hepatic injury. Plasma samples from a subset of patients treated in the SPORTIF clinical trial were analyzed.
raw_record.extra_details: Elevated ALT >3× ULN in ~8% of patients treated >35 days; ALT returned to normal in most patients within 6 months regardless of continued treatment; drug withdrawn from the market due to rare severe hepatic injury; no hepatotoxicity observed in preclinical testing; analysis of plasma from a subset of patients in the SPORTIF clinical trial.

raw_record.support_text: Ximelagatran, the first direct oral anticoagulant, had its FDA application withdrawn in 2006 after several cases of serious hepatotoxicity were detected in its clinical trials.
raw_record.extra_details: First direct oral anticoagulant; several cases of serious hepatotoxicity detected in clinical trials led to withdrawal of the FDA application in 2006.

raw_record.support_text: Ximelagatran, an oral direct thrombin inhibitor, was evaluated in the SPORTIF-III and SPORTIF-V trials in 7329 atrial-fibrillation patients versus warfarin; the efficacy results did not prove non-inferiority, there was a suspicion of slightly raised MI risk in venous-thromboembolism prevention trials, and evidence of liver toxicity, combined with these findings, prevented FDA registration in 2004. The developer then withdrew ximelagatran from the market (for the orthopaedic-surgery indication) and terminated further development, triggered by new patient safety data including an adverse-event report of serious liver injury in a clinical trial.
raw_record.extra_details: Serious liver injury reported as an adverse event in a clinical trial; liver toxicity evidence prevented first US registration application in 2004 and market withdrawal on 14 Feb 2006 for the orthopaedic-surgery indication. In the ESTEEM trial (1883 post-MI patients on aspirin, ximelagatran 24/36/48/60 mg bid; p:211), occurrence of transient elevation of liver enzymes was similar to other long-term studies with the compound. Liver injury was a concern in long-term oral use across AF (SPORTIF) and post-MI settings.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that ximelagatran, an oral thrombin inhibitor, was withdrawn from the market because of serious hepatotoxicity, and that genome-wide association studies of DNA from 74 patients with ALT levels greater than 3 times the upper limit of normal on ximelagatran and 130 treated individuals without hepatotoxicity found increased ALT associated with HLA alleles DRB1*07 (OR, 4.41) and DQA1*02 (OR, 4.41), validated in 10 cases and 16 controls.
raw_record.extra_details: Withdrawn from market due to serious hepatotoxicity; not metabolized by the liver. ALT-associated alleles DRB1*07 (OR 4.41, P=9.1×10^-6) and DQA1*02 (OR 4.41) in 74 cases vs 130 treated controls; corroborative immunologic studies supported relevance of DRB1*07.

raw_record.support_text: The commentary states that 'Ximelagatran was stopped because of hepatic injury during clinical trials,' indicating that the drug's development was halted due to drug-induced liver injury observed in clinical trial subjects.
raw_record.extra_details: Ximelagatran's development was stopped because of hepatic injury (drug-induced liver injury) encountered during clinical trials, which prevented marketing.

raw_record.support_text: In the search for novel anticoagulants, ximelagatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, caused unacceptable rates of liver toxicity compared with warfarin in the SPORTIF V trial.
raw_record.extra_details: Direct thrombin inhibitor; hepatic safety evaluated in the randomized SPORTIF V trial for anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation/stroke prevention; rates of liver toxicity were unacceptable and comparable to warfarin, prompting the pursuit of alternative agents.

raw_record.support_text: Ximelagatran, an oral direct thrombin inhibitor developed for prevention and treatment of thromboembolic conditions, had its pending FDA and EMA marketing applications withdrawn in February 2006 due to reports of abnormal liver tests and DILI during clinical trials. In trial data, 7.9% of treated patients had ALT >3x ULN versus 1.2% of the comparator group; combined ALT >3x ULN and total bilirubin >2x ULN occurred in 37 patients (0.5%), 11 of whom had no alternative cause, and one of these patients sustained severe liver damage with liver failure and eventually died.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral direct thrombin inhibitor for prevention/treatment of thromboembolic conditions; pending FDA and EMA applications withdrawn February 2006 due to abnormal liver tests and DILI in clinical trials; ALT>3x ULN in 7.9% vs 1.2% comparator; combined ALT>3x ULN plus TBL>2x ULN in 37 patients (0.5%), 11 with no alternative cause, one of whom had severe liver damage with liver failure and died; already approved in several European and South American countries at time of FDA withdrawal; animal studies and primary human hepatocyte cultures showed no hepatotoxic effects even at concentrations considerably above therapeutic plasma levels; cellular mechanism unknown.

raw_record.support_text: In a double-blind randomized trial in patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, 117 patients (6.0%) taking ximelagatran had serum ALT elevations >3 times ULN versus 15 (0.8%) taking warfarin (P<.001). Elevations typically occurred 2-6 months after starting treatment and returned toward baseline without clinical sequelae, either spontaneously (45 patients) or after treatment cessation (68 patients). Within 30 days of ALT elevation >3 times ULN, total bilirubin rose above 2 times ULN in 9 ximelagatran patients; one patient with ALT >3 times ULN had hepatic necrosis on liver biopsy and died, with autopsy showing resolving hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Randomized trial (n=1953 per arm) in high-risk nonvalvular atrial fibrillation patients; ximelagatran fixed dose, converted to melagatran (direct thrombin inhibitor). ALT >3xULN in 117 (6.0%) vs 15 (0.8%) warfarin, P<.001. Elevations 2-6 months after start; returned to baseline spontaneously (45) or after cessation (68). Total bilirubin >2xULN within 30 days in 9 ximelagatran patients (1 warfarin). One patient had hepatic necrosis on biopsy 20 days after stopping ximelagatran and died 145 days after randomization following corticosteroid; autopsy showed resolving hepatitis (nodular islands of regenerating hepatocytes without active inflammation) and hemorrhagic perforation of duodenal ulcer. Another patient with ALT 11xULN (bilirubin 1.6 mg/dL, 1.45xULN) developed fatal GI hemorrhage. ALT returned below ULN in all but 5 patients (1 death not attributed to DILI).

raw_record.support_text: In the absence of systemic disease findings and other diseases affecting the liver, and with no history of other drug usage, drug cessation was followed by complete resolution of the clinical and biochemical evidence of hepatotoxicity. The case was diagnosed as coumarin-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of coumarin-induced hepatitis; no history of other drug usage, excluding competing causes; ALT was 52 and liver enzymes normalized with complete resolution of symptoms two months after cessation. Coumarin (cis-o-coumarinic acid lactone, 1,2-benzopyrone), a natural product (tonka bean, lavender oil) now synthetically produced, has been used since the mid-1980s to reduce lymphedema and experimentally for metastatic renal cell carcinoma, prostatic cancer, and malignant melanoma. Reports of adverse effects in humans are rare and idiosyncratic, whereas coumarin is a well-recognized dose-dependent rat hepatotoxicant.

raw_record.support_text: In Australia, coumarin itself was authorized for the treatment of lymphedema in 1993, but in 1996 the Australian regulatory authorities suspended the drug due to the apparition of ten cases of hepatotoxicity with two fatalities. Coumarin is considered safe at a maximum 0.001% topical cosmetic level with a maximum estimated exposure below 0.02 mg/kg.
raw_record.extra_details: Coumarin was authorized in Australia for lymphedema treatment in 1993 and suspended in 1996 after ten reported cases of hepatotoxicity with two fatalities. Indication: lymphedema.

raw_record.support_text: Vanscheidt et al. treated 114 of 231 patients with lower-limb oedema secondary to chronic venous insufficiency with 90 mg coumarin and 540 mg troxerutin daily for 16 weeks in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, monitoring ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase and gamma-GT at baseline and weeks 4-16. No hepatotoxicity was reported; relative risk of elevations greater than 1.25 times the physiological range of GGT, ALT and AST was 4.9% in the active group vs 2.1% in placebo, and values returned to normal during or after treatment. A separate safety publication concluded coumarin treatment is safe and well-tolerated.

raw_record.extra_details: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in Germany, 231 patients total (114 active); liver function monitored at baseline and after 4, 6, 8, 12, 16 weeks; no hepatotoxicity reported; minor reactions in 25 cases (21.9%) active vs 14 (12.0%) placebo; elevations >1.25x physiological range of GGT/ALT/AST 4.9% active vs 2.1% placebo, resolving during or after treatment; separate publication concluded coumarin is safe and well-tolerated.

raw_record.support_text: In the placebo-controlled clinical trial of coumarin for lymphedema, hepatotoxicity occurred in six patients during the first 6-month treatment period; all six were unblinded after the hepatotoxicity and were taking the active drug coumarin (P=.03 comparing incidences on the two study arms). No relationship was found with age, prior surgery/radiotherapy, prior cellulitis, duration of lymphedema, time since previous surgery, or concomitant tamoxifen.

raw_record.extra_details: Six of 66 treated cases gave a 9% hepatotoxicity incidence, much higher than the previously cited <0.5–1%. NCI toxicity grades ranged 1–4. One patient (No. 42) developed clinical hepatitis with jaundice (SGOT 2315, total bilirubin 19.5, alkaline phosphatase 214; resolved by 10/96, SGOT 33 by 12/10/96). Other cases were mostly asymptomatic elevated transaminases (e.g., SGOT up to 946) that resolved after drug discontinuation; in patient No. 17 coumarin was not stopped and SGOT dropped from 151 to 35.

raw_record.support_text: In the reported case, a patient who received a sulfonamide developed a granulomatous hepatitis attributed to drug hypersensitivity (allergic cause considered certain for sulfonamide reactions). Needle biopsy of the liver showed characteristic lesions of focal necrosis and cholestasis with granulomas containing multinucleated giant cells, and a granulomatous reaction was also found in a scalene node biopsy. The sulfonamide given was sulfadimethoxine at a dose of 2 gm, and the patient recovered completely without specific therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose was 2 gm (contrasted with larger 8-340 gm total dosages of sulfonamides in documented allergic reactions). Liver biopsy showed focal necrosis, cholestasis, and granulomas containing multinucleated giant cells, consistent with sensitization to sulfonamides; granulomatous reaction also in scalene node biopsy. Patient recovered completely without steroids or specific therapy. Dosage noted as not critical in drug hypersensitivity.

raw_record.support_text: In a case report of acute diphenhydramine poisoning in a woman who ingested diphenhydramine (comprehensive toxicology detected diphenhydramine; acetaminophen, salicylate, and ethanol were not detected), she developed an anion gap metabolic acidosis, hepatorenal insufficiency, and pancreatitis, and died 11 hours after ED arrival. Autopsy showed pericentral necrosis and micro-vesicular steatosis of the liver; this liver injury was attributed to the diphenhydramine overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute diphenhydramine poisoning/overdose; patient also developed pancreatitis and hepatorenal insufficiency in the setting of shock and multiorgan failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient became unresponsive and was intubated; hyperkalemia (K 7.8) treated; anion gap metabolic acidosis; methemoglobin level of 20%, hemolysis, metamyelocytes and nucleated RBCs; autopsy revealed pericentral necrosis and micro-vesicular steatosis of the liver, green discoloration of lips/nails/brain/internal organs, mild intra-alveolar edema, and ascites; toxicology detected no drugs at autopsy and was negative for acetaminophen, salicylate, and ethanol. Patient died 11 hr after arrival.
